translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This opening formula teaches that every undertaking should begin by seeking God's help and acting under His authority, with awareness that He is the source of all mercy. By naming God's two attributes of mercy, Ar-Rahman (mercy that embraces all creation) and Ar-Rahim (mercy that is constant and especially directed to the believers), the verse frames the believer's actions, including reciting the Qur'an, within humility, dependence on God, and hope in His compassion, so that one's words and deeds begin with God's name and aim at His pleasure.

translation: All praise is due to God, Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse teaches that every form of praise and gratitude ultimately belongs to God alone, because He is the source of all perfection and blessing. By calling Him 'Lord of the worlds' (Rabb al-'Alamin), it affirms that He is not merely the Creator but also the Sustainer, Nurturer, and Master of everything that exists, including humans, jinn, angels, and every realm of creation. The believer is thus directed to begin from a posture of thankfulness and humility, recognizing that all favors, whether seen or unseen, come from God, and that no other being is worthy of worship or ultimate devotion.

translation: The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: These two names of God, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, affirm that mercy is the defining attribute through which God relates to creation. Ar-Rahman denotes an all-encompassing mercy that extends to every creature, believer and disbeliever alike, in sustenance, life, and guidance. Ar-Rahim denotes a mercy that is constant and specific, culminating in forgiveness and reward for those who turn to Him. Placed right after the opening invocation of God's name and before the declaration of His sovereignty over the Day of Judgment, the verse teaches that a person should approach God with hope and love as well as awe, so that reverence for His authority is balanced by trust in His compassion.

translation: Master of the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God alone holds absolute sovereignty over the Day of Recompense, when every soul will be held to account and no one else will have any power to intercede, command, or help except by His leave. It teaches the believer to live with constant awareness of accountability: since the final reckoning belongs wholly to God, hope and fear should be directed to Him, and a person should shape his conduct in this life in light of the justice that awaits in the next. Coming right after God's mercy, the verse balances compassion with justice, so that faith rests between hope in His mercy and reverence for His judgment.

translation: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Fatihah 1:5) is the pivot of the opening chapter, turning from praising God in the third person to addressing Him directly. By placing 'You' before the verb in both clauses, the Arabic grammar conveys exclusivity: worship is owed to God alone, and ultimate reliance is placed on Him alone. It joins two inseparable principles: sincere devotion, which is God's right over the servant, and dependence on divine aid, which is the servant's need. Worship is put first because a person is obliged to serve God before asking anything of Him, and seeking help follows because no one can fulfill worship without God's assistance. The plural 'we' shows that the believer prays as part of a community, standing alongside other worshippers in humility, free from both self-sufficiency and reliance on created things.

translation: Guide us to the straight path.
interpretation: This verse is a heartfelt prayer in which the believer, having praised God and affirmed that worship and help are for Him alone, asks for the most essential gift: guidance. The 'straight path' is the clear, balanced way of truth and righteousness, free from excess and deficiency, that leads to God's pleasure. The request for guidance is not only about being shown the way but also about being granted the success to follow it and remain steadfast on it. The plural 'us' shows that the believer seeks guidance as part of a community, and that even the rightly guided constantly depend on God to be kept on the path throughout life.

translation: The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray.
interpretation: This verse clarifies what the 'straight path' requested in the preceding verse actually is: the way of those whom God has blessed with guidance, as described elsewhere in the Qur'an (the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous). It defines the path both positively and negatively. The believer asks to follow the example of those who combined sound knowledge with sincere action, and to avoid two failure modes: that of those who knew the truth yet knowingly rejected or abandoned it out of arrogance or desire (those who incurred wrath), and that of those who sought to worship or act without proper knowledge and so wandered from the truth (the astray). Thus the verse teaches that true guidance requires both knowing what is right and acting upon it, and that a person must constantly seek God's help to stay balanced between neglecting knowledge and neglecting practice.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Mim.
interpretation: These disjointed letters, which open Surah Al-Baqarah and a number of other surahs, are best understood as a challenge and a reminder of the Qur'an's miraculous nature. The Qur'an is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs knew and used with great eloquence, yet they could not produce anything like it. By opening with letters pronounced individually, God draws the listener's attention to the revelation that follows and signals that the Book is made from ordinary building blocks of speech, while its inimitable style and message come from a divine source. Their exact meaning is ultimately known to God alone, and the believer receives them with humility, awe, and attentiveness to the guidance that follows.

translation: That is the Book, in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is a revelation whose divine origin and truth stand beyond reasonable doubt, so it is a firm and trustworthy source of knowledge. Its guidance is described as benefiting the muttaqin, those who are conscious of God and guard themselves against wrongdoing. This implies that benefiting from the Book requires an open, sincere heart and a readiness to be moved by its message. Doubt arises not from any flaw in the Book, but from the reader's own inner state, while those who approach it with reverence and humility find in it clear direction for belief and conduct.

translation: Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.
interpretation: The verse describes the foundation of true God-consciousness (taqwa) as a harmony of inner conviction and outward action. Belief in the unseen means trusting in realities beyond sensory perception, such as God, the angels, revelation, and the Hereafter, on the strength of sound reasoning and trust in divine guidance rather than on direct observation. This faith does not stay as a private idea: it is expressed in establishing prayer, which keeps the believer's relationship with God alive through consistent and sincere devotion, and in spending from what God has granted, which expresses gratitude and responsibility toward others. The phrase 'what We have provided' reminds the believer that wealth, health, knowledge, and ability are trusts from God, so giving is a sharing of His gifts rather than a loss. Together, faith, worship, and generosity show that guidance benefits those whose hearts are committed to God and whose lives serve both Him and His creation.

translation: And those who believe in what has been revealed to you [O Muhammad], and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain [in faith].
interpretation: The verse describes the righteous as those whose faith is comprehensive and free of sectarian bias: they accept the Qur'an and also the earlier scriptures sent through previous prophets, recognizing revelation as one continuous divine guidance from the same God. It also says their belief in the Hereafter is not mere assumption but firm, settled certainty (yaqin). This certainty shapes their conduct, since someone who is sure of accountability and the afterlife lives with responsibility, sincerity, and awareness of God. Such unity of faith in revelation and conviction in the Last Day is a mark of true guidance.

translation: Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the God-fearing described just before it, those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, spend from what God has provided, and are certain of the Hereafter. It teaches that their faith and deeds place them on a clear path of guidance that comes from God and is not merely their own achievement. The phrase 'upon guidance' conveys that they are firmly established on it, like a rider mounted on a steed, carried and directed by it. Because they hold to this divine guidance, they are the ones who attain true success (falah): they gain what they seek of God's pleasure and Paradise, and they are saved from what they fear of loss and punishment. The repetition of 'those' stresses their distinction, showing that guidance and success are linked, and that real prosperity lies in following God's guidance, not in worldly gain.

translation: Indeed, those who have disbelieved - it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.
interpretation: The verse speaks of those whose disbelief has hardened into stubborn, willful rejection after the truth became clear to them. Their refusal does not come from a lack of evidence or warning but from arrogance and persistent turning away, so they have closed themselves off to guidance. The Prophet's warning is therefore not wasted, since his duty is to convey the message, but it will not change hearts that have settled on rejection. The verse consoles the Prophet, relieving him of grief over those who refuse, and teaches that guidance ultimately lies with God, while the messenger's responsibility is only to deliver the message.

translation: Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering; and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes the spiritual consequence of persistent, stubborn rejection of truth. Having been shown clear signs and warnings and repeatedly turning away out of arrogance, such people gradually lose the capacity to receive guidance: their hearts no longer understand, their ears no longer truly listen, and their eyes no longer perceive the signs. The 'sealing' is a just recompense for their own choices, not an arbitrary act, since it follows their deliberate and habitual rejection. It teaches that continued neglect and disbelief harden the soul until it becomes closed to the truth, and that this state leads to a grievous punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: And among the people are those who say, 'We believe in God and in the Last Day,' but they are not believers.
interpretation: This verse, which opens the Qur'an's portrait of the hypocrites (munafiqun), teaches that faith is not established by words alone. These people profess belief in God and the Last Day to gain the social and political benefits of belonging to the Muslim community, yet their hearts do not hold the conviction their tongues declare. By stating that 'they are not believers,' the Qur'an judges faith by inner sincerity and by the harmony between heart, speech, and action. The verse also warns every reader to examine whether their own outward religiosity reflects genuine inner commitment, because God knows what lies within the hearts, whatever people claim.

translation: They seek to deceive God and those who believe, but they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse describes the hypocrites, who profess faith outwardly while concealing disbelief, imagining that this show protects their interests and fools God and the believers. In reality, God is fully aware of what is in their hearts, and the believers are guided by revelation, so the ruse deceives no one but themselves. By clinging to falsehood they forfeit guidance, corrupt their own hearts, and store up punishment for themselves, and their heedlessness is such that they do not even realize that the harm of their scheming falls back upon their own souls.

translation: In their hearts is a disease, and Allah has increased their disease; and for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.
interpretation: The 'disease' in the hearts of the hypocrites is spiritual sickness: doubt, hypocrisy, envy, and hostility toward the truth. Because they persisted in this inner corruption and insincerity, Allah increased them in it, as a consequence of their own choices. Rejecting guidance and clinging to falsehood hardens the heart further, just as a neglected illness worsens. The painful punishment awaiting them is the just recompense for their lying, since they claimed faith with their tongues while concealing disbelief in their hearts, and they also denied the truth of the revelation and the Messenger.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Do not spread corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."
interpretation: The verse exposes a self-deception typical of hypocrites: when they are warned against causing corruption, whether by undermining faith, sowing discord, allying with the enemies of the believers, or disobeying God, they do not admit their fault but recast it as righteousness. Their claim to be 'only reformers' shows that they have so inverted moral standards that they see their harmful conduct as beneficial, and they thereby close the door to repentance, since a person who believes he is already doing good will never correct himself. The following verse confirms this reading by declaring that they are indeed the corrupters, though they are unaware of it.

translation: Indeed, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive it.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Baqarah 2:12) answers the hypocrites who claimed they were only 'reformers'. God turns the claim back on them: the real spreaders of corruption are those who conceal disbelief behind a show of faith, who ally with the enemies of the believers, and who undermine the community from within. Corruption on earth begins with disobeying God and abandoning His guidance, so their sin damages both the moral order and society. The phrase 'but they do not perceive' shows that their self-deception has dulled their awareness. Persistent wrongdoing, justified by flattering names such as 'reform', can blind a person to his own harm, so that he regards evil as good and does not recognize the danger he poses to himself and others.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Believe as the people have believed,' they say, 'Shall we believe as the fools have believed?' Indeed, it is they who are the fools, but they do not know.
interpretation: The hypocrites are invited to adopt a sincere, wholehearted faith like that of the true believers, but they dismiss the believers as foolish, imagining that faith costs worldly security, status, and advantage. The verse turns the charge back on them: true foolishness is to trade lasting guidance and salvation for short-term worldly gain, and to sacrifice the hereafter for the sake of social convenience. Their deeper tragedy is that they lack awareness of their own condition, since self-deception has blinded them to the truth that they are the ones who have lost sound judgment.

translation: And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking."
interpretation: This verse exposes the duplicity of the hypocrites (munafiqun). Outwardly, when they meet the believers, they profess faith to protect their social standing and safety, but their hearts remain with the leaders of disbelief and opposition, whom the verse calls their 'devils', meaning the arch-deceivers among humans and jinn who incite them to evil. In private they reassure these allies of their loyalty and dismiss their declared faith as mere mockery. The point is that faith claimed with the tongue but denied by the heart is empty, and God knows the hidden reality behind every public pretense, so the hypocrites' mockery of the believers is in truth a deception that falls back upon themselves.

translation: God mocks them, and prolongs them in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: God repays the hypocrites' mockery of the believers in kind: their ridicule rebounds on them, not as a petty jest but as a just recompense. Since they persist in deceit and arrogance, God does not force them to change but lets them continue, extending their time and respite in their rebellion. This is a form of gradual abandonment: their false sense of security and worldly ease become a trap that deepens their blindness. They stumble about in confusion, unable to see the truth, because they chose to turn away from guidance. The verse teaches that being left to one's own persistent wrongdoing, without the grace of guidance, is itself a grave punishment.

translation: Those are the ones who have purchased error in exchange for guidance, so their trade has not profited them, and they were not guided.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of commerce to show the tragic folly of the hypocrites. They had access to guidance, the clear truth of faith, yet they gave it up and took misguidance in its place, as if making a bad bargain. A merchant's success is measured by profit and by preserving his capital; they lost both. They lost the guidance they had been offered, and they gained nothing real in return, since the worldly security, status, or advantage they sought through feigned belief is fleeting and ends in ruin. The statement 'they were not guided' stresses that they lacked the insight to make a sound choice, so their loss is complete: they forfeited the true capital of the soul, which is its receptiveness to God's guidance, and ended up with a worthless exchange.

translation: Their likeness is that of a person who kindled a fire; then when it lit up all around him, God took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.
interpretation: The verse likens the hypocrites to a man who kindles a fire and for a moment benefits from its light, just as the hypocrites outwardly profess faith and enjoy the protections and benefits of belonging to the Muslim community. Because their hearts never truly accepted belief, God removes the light they had borrowed, leaving them in layered darkness: the darkness of disbelief, of deceit, and of confusion. They cannot find guidance or see the way out. The point is that outward profession without sincere inner faith gives only a temporary illumination, and once it is taken away, the person is left in utter spiritual blindness and loss.

translation: Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will not return.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 2:18) describes the hypocrites who, after kindling a fire and losing their light, are left in darkness. Having heard the truth but not heeded it, spoken it but not sincerely, and seen the signs but not reflected on them, they are likened to people without functioning hearing, speech, and sight. The faculties they possess have become useless for guidance because they refuse to benefit from them. The consequence is that they cannot turn back from their error to faith and sincerity. Their persistent denial and hypocrisy have hardened their hearts, so they remain in misguidance and do not repent unless God wills it.

translation: Or [their example is] like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are depths of darkness, thunder and lightning; they put their fingers in their ears against the thunderclaps, in fear of death. But God encompasses the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse gives a second parable for the hypocrites, following the parable of the one who kindled a fire. The rainstorm stands for the revelation, which brings life to hearts just as rain brings life to the earth. For those whose hearts are diseased, though, it comes with darkness, thunder and lightning, which are the warnings, the threats, the trials and the demands of faith and obedience. They find these burdensome, so they plug their ears and shrink from hearing the truth, fearing it will cost them their worldly comfort, their security or their lives. Their fear is misplaced. Blocking their ears cannot save them from death, any more than hypocrisy can save them from God's judgment. God encompasses the disbelievers in His knowledge and power, so none of them can escape Him or outwit Him, and their schemes and evasions change nothing about their fate.

translation: The lightning almost snatches away their sight. Whenever it flashes for them, they walk in it, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. And had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is able to do all things.
interpretation: This verse continues the parable of the hypocrites in Surah al-Baqarah. The lightning stands for the brilliant, overwhelming truth of the Qur'an and its clear proofs, which dazzles the hypocrites and almost overpowers them because it exposes their falsehood. When the truth shines and they see worldly benefit in it, such as safety, a share of spoils or standing among the Muslims, they move along with the believers and outwardly follow. But when trials, hardship or a demand for sacrifice descend like darkness, they halt, hesitate and fall back, because faith never took root in their hearts. Their wavering shows that their guidance is conditional on convenience rather than conviction. The closing words remind them that they remain entirely within God's power: He could remove their hearing and sight altogether, so their temporary reprieve is mercy and a respite, not security. Since God has power over all things, no hypocrite can escape His judgment, and the right response is sincere, steadfast faith in both ease and hardship.

translation: O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous.
interpretation: The verse calls every human being, without exception, to devote worship to God alone, and it grounds that call in the fact that He is the Creator of all generations, past and present. Since every person and every community owes its existence to Him, no one else deserves worship. The purpose of worship is not to benefit God but to refine the worshipper: sincere devotion cultivates God-consciousness (taqwa), a constant awareness of Him that leads a person to guard against disobedience and harm and to live uprightly. Worship is therefore the means by which people attain moral and spiritual protection in this life and the next.

translation: [He] who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky rain and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to God while you know.
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to worship God alone in His evident favors: the earth is stable and habitable like a bed, the sky is a protective roof above, and rain revives the land to yield sustenance. Since every blessing that sustains human life comes from the one Creator and Provider, it is irrational and ungrateful to assign partners, whether idols, powers, or other causes, to share in devotion that belongs only to Him. The phrase 'while you know' stresses that people have the innate awareness and the evidence to recognize this, so associating others with God is a willful contradiction of what reason and the signs in creation already make clear.

translation: And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant [Muhammad], then produce a surah the like of it and call upon your witnesses and helpers other than God, if you are truthful.
interpretation: This verse sets out an open, rational challenge to those who doubt the divine origin of the Qur'an. If they truly believe it is merely human speech, then with all their eloquence and with whatever allies, experts, and idols they can summon besides God, they should be able to produce even a single chapter of comparable quality in its language, wisdom, guidance, and consistency. The challenge is itself the proof: because no one can meet it, the Qur'an's inimitability shows that it comes from God and that Muhammad, described here honorably as God's 'servant', is truly His messenger. The verse also teaches that sincere doubt should be answered with evidence rather than coercion, and that those who claim to be truthful must be willing to put their claim to the test.

translation: But if you do not do it—and you will never be able to do it—then beware of the Fire whose fuel is people and stones, prepared for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse follows the Qur'an's challenge to produce a chapter like it (2:23). Having issued the challenge, God declares that the opponents will fail, and the prediction 'you will never do it' stands as a miracle in itself, since it was confident and unqualified and history has borne it out. Failure to meet the challenge is proof that the Qur'an is divine revelation and not human speech. The logical consequence is that rejecting it is not a matter of honest doubt but of stubborn denial, so the hearers are urged to protect themselves from the Fire. The Fire is described as fueled by people and stones: the people are those who persisted in disbelief, and the stones are the idols or objects they worshipped in place of God, so that what they trusted for protection becomes part of their punishment. The phrase 'prepared for the disbelievers' indicates that the Fire already exists and is a certain reality, and it serves as a sober warning that calls people to reflect, believe, and submit before it is too late.

translation: And give glad tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom as sustenance, they will say, 'This is what we were provided with before,' for they will be given it in likeness. And they will have therein purified spouses, and they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse sets out the reward of the faithful, in contrast to the punishment of the disbelievers described just before it. Paradise is granted to those whose faith is joined with righteous action, since belief alone is not enough without deeds that prove it. The gardens with flowing rivers express abundance, beauty and tranquility. The fruits resemble what believers knew in this world in form and name, so they recognize them and feel at ease, yet they surpass worldly fruits in taste and excellence, so every encounter brings fresh delight rather than monotony. The 'purified spouses' are free of every physical and moral impurity, which means companionship in Paradise is complete and wholesome. The promise of eternal abiding completes the blessing, because no joy is perfect if it is feared to end. The verse thus encourages believers to persevere in faith and good works, trusting a reward that is lasting, perfect and certain.

translation: Indeed, God is not shy to strike an example of anything, even a gnat or something above it. As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, they say, 'What did God intend by this as an example?' By it He leaves many astray and by it He guides many; and He leaves astray by it only the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's parables are not diminished by the smallness of their subjects, since truth is not measured by the size or grandeur of the thing used to illustrate it. A gnat, or something even smaller or larger, can carry a profound lesson about God's power, wisdom, and the reality of human weakness. The same parable becomes a test that reveals hearts. The believers receive it with humility and recognize it as truth from their Lord, so it increases their guidance and faith. The disbelievers meet it with scorn and skepticism, asking what God could possibly intend by it, and their arrogance and stubbornness lead them further into error. Misguidance here is not arbitrary: God lets astray only the fasiqun, those who have already abandoned obedience and left the bounds of truth by their own choice, so their deviation is the consequence of their own conduct.

translation: Those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth - those are the losers.
interpretation: This verse describes the defining traits of the openly disobedient (al-fasiqun) mentioned in the preceding verse, and it shows that their real loss is spiritual. They violate the covenant God took from humanity: the primordial pledge to acknowledge Him alone, and the commitments made through revelation and the messengers. They also cut the bonds God ordered to be maintained, which include ties of kinship, the bond between believers, and the link between people and the prophets and their guidance. Breaking these sacred bonds leads to spreading corruption in society and on earth through injustice, discord, and the abandonment of God's law. The verse concludes that such people are the true losers. They squander the most valuable thing they have, their capacity for faith and righteous action, and so forfeit success in this world and the next, whatever worldly gains they may appear to have.

translation: How can you disbelieve in God, when you were lifeless and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life, and then to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke that appeals to human experience: disbelief makes no sense when your whole existence is a series of gifts and acts of power that you did not create and cannot control. You were nothing, without life, and God brought you into being. The same One who gave life from lifelessness holds your death and your resurrection, and your final return is to Him for reckoning. Since life, death, and revival all rest in His hands, a person has no rational ground for denying Him or ingratitude toward Him. The proper response to this reality is faith, gratitude, and accountability, because the one who originated you is able to return you and will call you to account.

translation: It is He who created for you all that is on the earth, then He turned to the heaven and fashioned it into seven heavens, and He has knowledge of all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the earth and its resources were created as a bounty for humankind, so that they may benefit from them, reflect on them, and give thanks to their Creator. The same God who made the earth and then ordered the heavens in perfect proportion is not limited in knowledge or power. His comprehensive knowledge shows that creation is purposeful and wise, not accidental, which makes denial of Him and of the resurrection unreasonable. Human beings should therefore see the world as a trust and a sign pointing to God, and respond with faith, gratitude, and responsible use of what has been given to them.

translation: And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am placing upon the earth a successor." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."
interpretation: The verse announces God's decision to appoint humankind, beginning with Adam, as stewards or vicegerents on earth, entrusted with inhabiting it, upholding justice, and carrying out God's commands. The angels' question is not an objection or arrogance but an expression of curiosity and a plea for understanding. They reasoned from the foreseen potential for corruption and bloodshed in a being given free will, and contrasted it with their own constant worship. God's reply, 'I know what you do not know,' affirms that His wisdom encompasses what they cannot see: that humanity, despite its capacity for wrongdoing, will also bring forth prophets, righteous people, knowledge, and a worship freely chosen rather than innately compelled. The lesson is that human beings hold a position of honor and responsibility, and that divine wisdom surpasses limited creaturely understanding, calling for trust in God's plan.

translation: And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, 'Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: The verse shows that God endowed humankind, in Adam, with the capacity for knowledge: the ability to learn, name, and comprehend things, and to hold concepts in the mind and express them in language. This gift is the basis of Adam's worthiness to be vicegerent (khalifa) on earth. When the angels had questioned the appointment of a being who might cause corruption, God did not argue with them. He demonstrated Adam's distinction through knowledge, which the angels, for all their devotion and glorification, had not been given in this form. The challenge 'if you are truthful' tests their claim that they were more fit for the role. It teaches that knowledge, not mere worship or outward piety alone, is a key qualification for stewardship, and that all knowledge ultimately comes from God as a gift, which calls for humility.

translation: They said, "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 2:32) records the angels' response when God showed them Adam's knowledge of the names and asked them to name things they did not know. They begin by declaring God's transcendence above any imperfection, including any suggestion that their earlier question about creating humankind implied a flaw in His plan. They then acknowledge the limits of their own knowledge, which is entirely a gift from God and not something they possess independently. By attributing to God both perfect knowledge and perfect wisdom, they affirm that His decisions, such as appointing a vicegerent on earth, rest on knowledge and purpose that creatures cannot fully grasp. The lesson is humility before divine knowledge: true understanding begins with recognizing that all knowledge comes from God, and that trust in His wisdom should accompany whatever we know and whatever we do not.

translation: He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names." And when he had informed them of their names, He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you used to conceal?"
interpretation: This verse shows that Adam's distinction lies in the knowledge God granted him, and that knowledge, not mere worship or status, is the basis of his role as vicegerent on earth. When Adam named what the angels could not, they saw that God's wisdom in creating humankind exceeded what they understood, and their earlier objection, 'Will You place therein one who will cause corruption?', was shown to rest on partial knowledge. God's reminder that He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth teaches humility before divine wisdom: creatures see only a part, while God sees the whole. His knowledge of 'what you reveal and what you used to conceal' means He knew both the angels' spoken question and what lay unspoken in their hearts, so human beings should purify their inner intentions as well as their outward words and deeds, since nothing is hidden from God.

translation: And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse shows that Iblis's fall came from pride, not ignorance. Told plainly to honor Adam, he refused out of arrogance, setting his own opinion and sense of superiority above God's command. The angels' obedience shows the right response to a divine order: submission even when the wisdom behind it is not fully grasped. The text says Iblis 'was among the disbelievers' because his refusal was a rejection of God's authority, not merely a lapse. This makes arrogance the root of disbelief and warns that pride toward God's command, or toward other people whom God has honored, can destroy a person's standing before Him.

translation: And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from it abundantly wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse shows that Adam and his wife were given a home of complete bounty and freedom, with only one limit set to test their obedience and to teach that human dignity and happiness depend on honoring divine boundaries. The prohibition was not a deprivation, since everything else was permitted without restraint, but a moral training in self-restraint and gratitude. The phrase 'do not approach' forbids even drawing near the tree, which teaches that avoiding the first steps toward temptation protects a person from falling into sin. Disobedience is called 'wrongdoing' because it is first an injustice against one's own soul, as it forfeits the blessing and peace one was granted, and then a failure to give the Creator His due of obedience.

translation: But Satan caused them to slip out of it, and removed them from the state in which they had been. And We said: 'Go down, some of you enemies to others. On the earth you will have a dwelling place and provision for a time.'
interpretation: The verse shows that Adam and Eve's removal from Paradise came about through Satan's deception, which led them to disobey, and that disobedience has consequences. Yet their descent to earth was not mere punishment; it was the start of humanity's appointed role. Earth is a temporary home with provision and means of livelihood, so human life is a limited stay and a test, not a final destination. The enmity set between Satan and humankind, and among people when desires and interests clash, means that life requires constant vigilance, self-discipline and reliance on God's guidance. Because the stay is only 'for a time', a person should not be attached to worldly comforts as though they were permanent, but should use them as a means of preparing for the return to God.

translation: Then Adam received from his Lord some words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, it is He who is the Accepter of repentance, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: After his slip in the Garden, Adam was not left in despair; God Himself taught him words of repentance and humility, which he received and voiced with a sincere heart, acknowledging his wrong and seeking forgiveness (as in 7:23, 'Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers'). God's acceptance of this repentance shows that the path back to Him is always open, that error does not make a person condemned forever, and that even the ability to repent is itself a mercy and guidance from God. The verse also implies that human beings do not inherit Adam's sin as a burden, but instead inherit his model of turning back to God. The closing names, al-Tawwab and al-Rahim, affirm that God repeatedly turns toward His servants in forgiveness, and that His mercy outweighs their faults.

translation: We said: 'Go down from it, all of you. Then if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.' (Qur'an 2:38)
interpretation: After Adam's slip and repentance, God makes clear that descending to earth is not the end of divine care but the start of human accountability and trial. Life on earth is a stage in which God does not leave humanity to wander blindly: He promises to send guidance through revelation and messengers. The verse sets out a simple principle of salvation. Those who accept and follow that guidance will be spared the fear of the future and the grief over what is past, in this world through inner security and trust in God, and above all on the Day of Judgment. Human beings are therefore not condemned by Adam's mistake. Each person's fate depends on whether they respond to God's guidance, which makes the path to peace open to all.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – they are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide eternally.
interpretation: The verse sets out the consequence of a deliberate rejection of truth. Disbelief here is not mere ignorance but active denial of God's clear signs, whether in revelation, in creation, or in the messengers sent to guide people. Because such people knowingly turn away from the guidance that was made plain to them, they become the 'companions of the Fire,' meaning that the Fire is their fitting and lasting abode. Their long-held stance of defiance in life is mirrored by the permanence of their state in the Hereafter. The verse works as a warning, balancing the promise made to the believers just before it. It urges the reader to take God's signs seriously and to respond to them with faith and humility rather than rejection.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant, and I will fulfill your covenant; and of Me alone be afraid.
interpretation: God addresses the Children of Israel, calling them to reflect gratefully on the many blessings He gave their forebears, such as deliverance from Pharaoh, revelation, and being favored among the peoples of their time. Gratitude is meant to be shown in obedience: they are to keep the covenant they made with God to worship Him alone, follow His commandments, and believe in the messengers He sends, including the final Prophet foretold in their scriptures. In return God promises to fulfill His side, which includes reward, protection, and mercy. The verse ends by directing their fear to God alone, not to their own leaders, tribal pressure, or worldly powers, so that fear of God, rather than fear of people, will govern their faith and conduct and keep them from concealing the truth or rejecting it out of worldly interest.

translation: And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you, and be not the first to disbelieve in it; and do not exchange My verses for a small price; and fear Me alone.
interpretation: God addresses the Children of Israel, calling them to accept the Qur'an because it confirms the essence of the revelation they already possess, namely tawhid, prophethood, and the promise of a coming messenger. Since they were the people of earlier scripture and knew its signs, their rejection would set a damaging precedent for others, so they are warned against being the first to disbelieve and the leaders of denial. They are also forbidden to trade away God's revelation, whether by hiding or distorting its guidance, for worldly gain such as status, wealth, or the favor of followers, since any such gain is trivial compared to the truth. The verse ends by directing them to fear God alone and not their people or worldly powers, because loyalty to truth requires putting reverence for God above social and material pressures.

translation: Do not mix truth with falsehood, and do not conceal the truth while you know it.
interpretation: The verse (2:42) warns against blurring the line between right and wrong, whether by dressing falsehood in the garb of truth through confusing arguments, selective quotation, and distortion, or by deliberately hiding the truth out of self-interest, fear, or pride. Its address to the People of the Book, who knew from their scriptures the truth about the Prophet and the message, extends to everyone who has knowledge. The phrase 'while you know' makes the sin worse: it is not ignorance but willful suppression. The moral lesson is that those who hold knowledge bear a duty to present the truth clearly and honestly, keeping it distinct from falsehood, because mixing the two misleads others and corrupts society's moral compass.

translation: And establish prayer, and give zakat, and bow down with those who bow down.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Children of Israel in Surah al-Baqarah (2:43), commands them to embrace the core practices of true faith: to perform prayer fully and properly, to purify their wealth and care for the needy through zakat, and to join the community of Muslims in congregational worship. The phrase 'bow with those who bow' singles out ruku' (bowing) as a mark of humility and submission, and calls them to leave arrogance behind, accept the final message, and pray together with the believers rather than apart from them. In this way, faith is shown to be lived through both devotion to God (prayer) and service to people (zakat), within the unity of a worshipping community.

translation: Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, even though you recite the Scripture? Then will you not reason?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who know the revealed Book yet fail to act on what they command others to do. Knowledge of scripture creates a greater responsibility to live by it, so a person who calls others to goodness while neglecting it in his own conduct contradicts himself and shows a failure of sound reasoning. The closing question, 'Will you not reason?', appeals to the conscience: true understanding of the Book must show itself in consistency between word and deed, and anyone who guides others must first discipline himself and begin reform with his own soul.

translation: And seek help through patience and prayer; and indeed, it is difficult except for the humbly submissive [to Allah].
interpretation: The verse teaches that believers facing hardship, temptation, or the demands of obedience should draw strength from two sources: steadfast patience (restraining oneself from disobedience, persevering in obedience, and enduring trials) and prayer, which links the servant to God, renews inner resolve, and brings tranquility. It then notes that prayer, with the discipline and self-restraint it requires, feels heavy and burdensome to the heedless, whose hearts are attached to worldly desires. Only the khashi'un, those whose hearts are humble before God, fearful of His reckoning and hopeful of His reward, find it light and a source of comfort, because their certainty of meeting their Lord makes obedience easy and sacrifice meaningful.

translation: Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that to Him they will return.
interpretation: The verse describes the people for whom humility in prayer and patience is light, not heavy. The word 'yazunnūna' here carries the sense of firm conviction rather than doubt: their certainty of standing before God and returning to Him shapes how they live. Because they expect to be held accountable, they approach worship with a humble heart, and they find strength to endure hardship and restrain their desires. In this way, faith in the Hereafter is the root of khushū' (reverent humility), since awareness that every deed will be answered for softens the heart, steadies the soul in obedience, and makes patience and prayer sources of help rather than burdens.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.
interpretation: God calls the Children of Israel to gratitude and faithfulness by reminding them of the blessings He gave them: deliverance from Pharaoh, prophets and scripture sent among them, sustenance in the wilderness, and a covenant. The 'preference over the worlds' refers to their distinction among the peoples of their own time through these gifts and the mission of guiding others. It is not a permanent, unconditional superiority. The favor brings responsibility, so remembering it means obeying God, keeping the covenant, and recognizing the truth when it comes, including the final message. Honor depends on obedience and not on lineage.

translation: And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse warns people to prepare for the Day of Judgment by living with God-consciousness now, because on that Day every worldly means of rescue will be useless. No person can bear another's burden or pay off another's account, not even close kin. Intercession will not be accepted as a claim or entitlement, and it will not help those who relied on false hopes, since it is permitted only by God's leave and only for those He approves. No ransom or payment will be taken, so wealth and status will be worthless. No ally or protector will be able to help them against God's judgment. The lesson is personal accountability: salvation depends on faith and righteous deeds done in this life, not on lineage, wealth, or misplaced reliance on others. The verse addressed the Children of Israel, who took pride in their ancestry and assumed they would be spared, but its message applies to everyone.

translation: And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.
interpretation: God reminds the Children of Israel that their deliverance from Pharaoh's oppression was a favor that demands gratitude and obedience. The word 'bala'' carries a double sense: both the suffering under Pharaoh and the rescue from it were tests from God, who tests His servants with hardship to see their patience and with relief to see their thankfulness. The lesson for believers is that trials come in both adversity and ease, and that salvation comes from God alone, so the proper response is to remain steadfast in hardship and grateful in deliverance, rather than to forget His grace and fall into disobedience.

translation: And when We parted the sea for you, and saved you, and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel that their deliverance from Pharaoh was an act of God's power and mercy, not of their own strength. By splitting the sea into passable paths, God turned the very obstacle that trapped them into the means of their escape, and turned it into the means of destruction for their oppressors. The phrase 'while you were looking on' stresses that they witnessed the event with their own eyes, which leaves no room for doubt. This makes their later ingratitude, such as worshipping the calf, all the more blameworthy. The lesson for believers is that God supports the oppressed who rely on Him, that tyranny eventually ends in ruin, and that those who witness God's signs owe Him gratitude and obedience.

translation: And [remember] when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [as a god] after he had gone, while you were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel how quickly they betrayed their covenant. While Moses was away on the mountain to receive revelation and guidance, they turned to worshipping a calf, the most basic form of shirk, even though they had just been delivered from Pharaoh by clear signs. They are called wrongdoers because worshipping anything besides God places devotion where it does not belong and wrongs the soul first of all. The verse teaches that faith demands steadfastness in the absence of the prophet or guide, and that gratitude for God's favors must not give way to impatience or to the pull of visible, tangible idols. It also stresses that wrongdoing is a deliberate choice made with knowledge, since they acted while fully aware of the truth they had been shown.

translation: Then We pardoned you after that, so that perhaps you would be grateful. (Qur'an 2:52)
interpretation: The verse points to God's mercy toward the Children of Israel after they worshipped the calf in Moses' absence. They had committed a grave wrong, yet God forgave them and gave them another chance. The pardon is not an end in itself: it is meant to lead to gratitude (shukr), which means acknowledging the favor and showing it through obedience, humility, and avoiding the wrong that needed forgiveness. The verse teaches that divine forgiveness is a gift that calls for a changed life, not a license to repeat the offense, and that a person who has been spared a deserved consequence should answer with thankfulness in both heart and conduct.

translation: And [remember] when We gave Moses the Scripture and the Criterion, so that you might be guided.
interpretation: God reminds the Children of Israel that He granted Moses the Torah together with the Furqan, the means of distinguishing truth from falsehood and right from wrong, so that they might find the straight path. The verse presents revelation not merely as a body of laws but as a source of moral discernment and guidance. It is a divine favor that carried responsibility: those who received it were expected to use this clarity to walk in right guidance, rather than to fall into error as they did with the golden calf mentioned in the preceding verses.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people: 'O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [as a god], so repent to your Creator and kill [one another/yourselves]; that is better for you in the sight of your Creator.' Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse shows that idolatry is a grave injustice a person commits against his own soul, and that sincere repentance may demand costly submission to God's command. The Israelites, having worshipped the calf, were told to carry out a severe act of atonement: those who had stayed faithful were to kill those who had worshipped the calf, or, in a view held by some, each person was to put his ego and sin to death through total self-surrender. By obeying, they proved the sincerity of their repentance, and God, who is ever-accepting of repentance and merciful, forgave them. The lesson is that true repentance requires obedience and sacrifice, that God's command is ultimately for the believer's good, and that His forgiveness is always available to those who turn back to Him.

translation: And [recall] when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah plainly," so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel of a grave act of arrogance: after witnessing clear signs, a group among them made their belief in Moses conditional on seeing God with their own eyes, which amounts to demanding that the unseen be subjected to sensory proof and putting God's messenger to the test. Their punishment, a thunderbolt that struck them as they watched, shows that faith in God rests on trust in revelation and the evidence of His signs, not on dictating terms to the Creator, and that insolence toward Him brings swift consequences. It also shows how limited human beings are, since they cannot bear what they presume to demand.

translation: Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might give thanks.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 2:56) refers to the Children of Israel, who asked to see God plainly and were struck by a thunderbolt, then revived by God's mercy. Their revival after death is a sign of God's power and grace, a second chance given to them. The purpose of that favor is gratitude: a person who recognizes that life itself, and any reprieve from destruction, is a gift should respond by thanking God through faith, obedience, and humility, instead of persisting in arrogance and demands as they did earlier. The verse also points to resurrection, since the God who can restore life after death once can do so again.

translation: And We shaded you with clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails, saying: 'Eat of the good things We have provided for you.' And they did not wrong Us, but it was themselves they were wronging.
interpretation: The verse recalls God's favors to the Children of Israel in the wilderness: shelter from the desert sun and food that came without toil. These blessings were meant to inspire gratitude and obedience, so the command to eat of the good things is an invitation to enjoy lawful provision with thankfulness. The closing clause teaches that human disobedience and ingratitude cannot harm God, who is free of all need and unaffected by what His creatures do. Sin and ingratitude rebound on the sinner, who loses God's favor and harms his own soul. Wrongdoing is therefore ultimately self-harm, and obedience is ultimately to one's own benefit.

translation: And when We said: Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating, and say 'Relief (forgiveness)', We will forgive you your sins, and We will increase the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse recalls God's favor to the Children of Israel after the wilderness: He granted them a town to settle in, with plentiful provision, on the condition that they show humility and seek forgiveness. Entering the gate bowing and saying 'hittah' (a plea for the lifting of sins) is meant to turn the moment of victory and comfort into one of gratitude and repentance rather than arrogance. God's reward is twofold: forgiveness of past wrongs for everyone who obeys, and further blessing, in this world and the next, for those who go beyond bare obedience to excellence (ihsan). The lesson is that blessings are best received with humility and with a heart turned to God, and that sincere repentance together with good conduct invites greater mercy and bounty.

translation: But those who did wrong substituted a word other than the one that had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the heaven because of their transgression.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Children of Israel, who were commanded to enter the town humbly, saying 'Hittah' (a plea for forgiveness), so that their sins would be pardoned. The wrongdoers among them mocked and distorted the command, changing the words and entering arrogantly, as reported in the traditions, dragging themselves on their backsides and mockingly saying something like 'a grain in a hair'. This shows that obedience to God lies not only in the outward act but in sincerely accepting His words as given, and that tampering with divine instruction out of defiance or mockery is a form of wrongdoing and open disobedience (fisq). Their punishment, a plague or scourge from the sky, was not arbitrary but a just consequence of their persistent transgression, serving as a warning that disregarding and altering God's commands invites His retribution.

translation: And [remember] when Moses asked for water for his people, so We said, "Strike the rock with your staff." Then there gushed forth from it twelve springs; every group of people knew its drinking place. "Eat and drink from the provision of God, and do not act wickedly upon the earth as corrupters."
interpretation: The verse shows that provision comes from God alone, and that He answers sincere supplication through His chosen messenger, even by means that defy ordinary expectation. The staff and the rock were only the outward occasion; the true cause was God's command and power. By assigning each tribe its own spring, God removed any cause for rivalry and quarrel, showing that His bounty was ordered, ample and just. The closing command teaches that gratitude for such blessings requires enjoying them lawfully and not spreading corruption, strife or ingratitude on earth. Receiving God's gifts places on a community the duty of moral responsibility and harmony.

translation: And [remember] when you said, 'O Moses, we cannot endure one kind of food; so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its green herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions.' He said, 'Would you exchange what is better for what is lesser? Go down to [any] settlement, for you will have what you have asked.' And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That was because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That was because they disobeyed and were transgressing.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Children of Israel for their ingratitude and discontent with the manna and quails, the pure, effortless provision God gave them in the wilderness. Longing for ordinary produce, they rejected a higher blessing for a lower one, and Moses reminds them that such produce is available in any town, so their demand reflects mere appetite and weariness with patient reliance on God. Their pattern of complaint, disobedience, rejecting God's signs, and killing prophets led to moral and social degradation, humiliation and poverty, and divine displeasure. The lesson is that persistent ingratitude and transgression, not mere circumstance, bring spiritual decline, while gratitude and obedience preserve God's favor and dignity.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever truly believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—they will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve. (Qur'an 2:62)
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation in God's sight depends on the reality of a person's faith and conduct, not on communal labels or claimed lineage. Every community that received guidance is judged by the same standard: sincere belief in God, conviction that there will be a Day of Judgment and accountability, and righteous action that proves the belief is real. Those who meet this standard are promised a reward from their Lord, which means safety from fear of the future and freedom from sorrow over what is past. The verse is a rebuke to any group that assumes its name or heritage guarantees divine favor, and it affirms that God's justice is universal and that the door to His reward is open to anyone who responds to the truth with faith and good works.

translation: And [remember] when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and remember what is in it, so that you may become mindful of God."
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel that their acceptance of the Torah was a binding covenant, made solemn by the towering mountain above them as a sign of God's might and the gravity of the commitment. The command to hold to the revelation 'with strength' means to receive it with earnest resolve and to act on it, not with mere lip service or half-hearted adherence. To 'remember what is in it' means to keep its teachings in mind, study them and apply them in practice, and the goal is taqwa: a God-consciousness that guards a person from disobedience. The lesson is that divine guidance is a trust that demands firm commitment and continual remembrance, and that its purpose is to shape a person's character and conduct.

translation: Then after that you turned away. And had it not been for the favor of God upon you and His mercy, you would surely have been among the losers.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Children of Israel, who took a solemn covenant and then broke it by turning away from their commitments after clear proofs and warnings. It teaches that their escape from ruin was not owed to their own deeds but to God's grace, which gave them repeated chances through forgiveness, prophets and reminders, and held back deserved punishment. The 'loss' refers to destruction in this world and the next. By extension, every believer is meant to see that being saved from the consequences of one's failings is due to divine mercy, which calls for gratitude, humility and renewed commitment rather than complacency.

translation: And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, 'Be apes, despised and humiliated.'
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel of a known episode from their own history, in which a community among them violated the sanctity of the Sabbath. They had been commanded to rest from worldly labor and fishing on that day, but they used cunning pretexts to get around the prohibition while keeping its outward form. Their punishment was a divine decree of degradation. Many commentators hold that they were physically transformed into apes, while others, following Mujahid, hold that their hearts and conduct were transformed and not their bodies. In either reading, the lesson is that evading God's commands through legalistic tricks is a serious form of disobedience that brings disgrace, and that knowledge of past nations' fates should lead people to honor divine limits sincerely and not just outwardly.

translation: So We made it an exemplary punishment for those who were present at the time and for those who came after it, and an admonition for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse refers to the people of the Sabbath-breakers among the Children of Israel, whom God transformed into apes as punishment for transgressing the limits He set. The punishment was made a deterrent and public lesson: those alive in that era saw the consequence of defying God's command through trickery, and later generations learned of it through revelation and tradition. It also serves as counsel for the God-fearing, who benefit from such warnings by guarding themselves against outward obedience that hides disobedience in spirit, and by taking God's limits seriously rather than seeking loopholes around them.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, God commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant."
interpretation: The verse shows how a prophet's divine command is met with suspicion and flippancy by a people reluctant to submit. Moses relays the order to slaughter a cow, which was connected to resolving a murder case among them, but they respond not with obedience but with accusation, reading a sincere command as a joke because it seemed unrelated to the problem at hand. Moses' reply is that mocking people with a message from God, or speaking about God without truth, is a form of ignorance (jahl) that he would never fall into, so he seeks God's protection from it. The lesson is that true knowledge lies in trusting and obeying God's commands even when their wisdom is not immediately clear, while ridicule and demands for rational justification before submission reflect ignorance, and that a messenger must be grave and truthful in conveying God's word.

translation: They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what she is." He said, "He says: She is a cow neither old nor young, but middle-aged between the two. So do what you are commanded."
interpretation: The verse shows how the Children of Israel kept putting questions to Moses about a command that was plain, and each question made the command narrower. The cow was first described only by age, in the middle between old and immature, and this was the first of several limits placed on them. The lesson is that people should obey divine commands promptly and not press for details out of reluctance or stubbornness, because needless questioning makes the duty harder. Moses ends with a direct call to obey: 'So do what you are commanded.' In this reading, true submission means acting on what is clear and not looking for ways to delay it.

translation: They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what her color is." He said, "He says: she is a yellow cow, bright in color, pleasing to those who look."
interpretation: The Children of Israel kept adding questions to a simple command to sacrifice a cow (Surah al-Baqarah 2:67), and each question brought a further restriction. Their demand to know the color shows a habit of over-questioning and seeking exemptions instead of obeying at once. God's answer, a bright, pure yellow that delights the eye, narrowed their options and made the command harder. The lesson is that needless hair-splitting over a clear command burdens the one who asks, while prompt, sincere obedience would have been easier and safer.

translation: They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what she is. Indeed, all cows look alike to us, and indeed we, if God wills, will be guided."
interpretation: After their first questions, the Children of Israel kept asking for more detail about the cow they were told to sacrifice, and this showed their hesitation and reluctance to obey at once. Had they sacrificed any cow when first commanded, they would have fulfilled the order. Their persistent questioning made the requirements stricter for them. Their phrase 'if God wills' shows they knew guidance comes only from God, and it is a lesson that every intention and plan should be tied to God's will. The verse also warns against needless questioning about a clear command, since this can turn ease into hardship, and it teaches that quick, sincere obedience is better than delay and evasion.

translation: He said: 'He says she is a cow not broken in to plow the earth or irrigate the field, sound and without blemish.' They said: 'Now you have brought the truth.' So they slaughtered her, though they almost did not.
interpretation: After repeated questioning about the cow, the Children of Israel were given ever more precise specifications that made their task harder, and only when the description was complete did they accept it as the truth. The verse shows how needless hair-splitting and stalling in the face of a clear divine command narrows one's options and makes obedience burdensome. Their slaughtering of the cow 'though they almost did not' points to their reluctance, whether from the cow's high price and rarity or from their inward hesitation and unwillingness to submit. The lesson is that one should respond to God's commands promptly and simply rather than seeking excuses, since ease lies in immediate obedience.

translation: And [remember] when you killed a soul and disputed over it, while God was bringing out what you were concealing.
interpretation: The verse refers to the story of the murdered man among the Children of Israel, whose killer was unknown. Each party shifted blame onto others and denied responsibility, but God declared that He would expose what they were hiding. He did so by commanding them to strike the corpse with part of the slaughtered cow, so that the dead man was revived by God's leave and named his killer. The lesson is that no crime can be concealed from God, who brings hidden truths to light, and that shifting blame cannot defeat His knowledge and justice. The episode also stands as a proof of His power to give life to the dead.

translation: So We said, "Strike him with a part of it." Thus does God bring the dead to life, and He shows you His signs so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse comes from the story of the cow of the Children of Israel, where a murdered man's killer was unknown. When they struck the corpse with a piece of the slaughtered cow, God revived him briefly so that he could name his killer. The verse teaches that the same God who brought this dead man back to life can resurrect all the dead on the Day of Judgment. Such signs are shown to appeal to human reason, so that people reflect on God's power, accept the reality of resurrection, and abandon stubbornness and disobedience.

translation: Then, after that, your hearts became hardened, so they are like stones or even harder in hardness. For indeed, among stones are some from which rivers burst forth, and indeed, among them are some that split open so water comes out from them, and indeed, among them are some that fall down for fear of God. And God is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Children of Israel after they witnessed clear signs, such as the revival of the slain man, and still did not soften. It criticizes spiritual hardness: their hearts, which should have yielded to such miracles, became like stones, indeed harder, because stones at least serve a purpose and respond to God's command by giving water, splitting, or falling in awe, while a hardened heart gives no benefit and does not respond to admonition or reverence. The lesson is that moral and spiritual insensitivity after receiving clear evidence is worse than lifeless nature's submission, and it is a warning to every believer to guard the heart against hardness through remembrance and obedience, since God is fully aware of every deed and will hold people accountable.

translation: Do you then hope that they will believe in you, when a party of them used to hear the word of God and then distort it after they had understood it, while they knew?
interpretation: God is consoling the Prophet and the believers by warning them not to place high hopes in the sincere faith of those among the Children of Israel who were hostile or insincere. Their history shows that the problem was not a lack of understanding or evidence but stubborn willfulness: some among them heard God's revelation, comprehended it fully, and still deliberately altered its meaning or wording to suit their desires, fully aware of what they were doing. Someone who knowingly corrupts the truth after grasping it is moved by pride and self-interest rather than ignorance, so expecting them to submit to a new message that challenges those interests is unrealistic. The verse teaches that guidance depends on a sincere heart and not merely on hearing or knowing the truth.

translation: And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when some of them are alone with others, they say, "Do you tell them what Allah has disclosed to you, so that they may argue against you with it before your Lord? Do you not understand?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy and self-defeating logic of some among the People of the Book. Outwardly they flatter the believers by claiming faith, but in private they rebuke one another for sharing knowledge from their scripture, such as the descriptions of the Prophet Muhammad, fearing it would become evidence against them on the Day of Judgment. The deeper point is that they imagine they can conceal truth from God, when God knows both what they hide and what they declare. Their fear of being argued against 'before your Lord' actually concedes that God is aware of the truth and will hold them to account. The rhetorical question 'Do you not understand?' shows how irrational it is to fear human argument while ignoring divine knowledge. The lesson is that concealing truth and showing two faces is foolish, and sincerity before God is the only sound course.

translation: Do they not know that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 2:77) rebukes those who knowingly distort the truth or hide it from others, supposing that their secret schemes and hidden intentions go unnoticed. It reminds them, and every reader, that nothing is hidden from God: inner thoughts and outward deeds are equally known to Him. Knowing this should lead a person to sincerity, honesty and accountability, since pretending piety in public while concealing deceit in private achieves nothing before an All-Knowing Lord.

translation: And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Scripture except through wishful fancies, and they do nothing but conjecture.
interpretation: The verse describes a group among the People of the Book who lacked direct knowledge of the Torah because they could not read it. Instead of understanding its actual teachings, they depended on what their leaders told them, on wishful hopes (such as the belief that they would be saved merely by their lineage or affiliation), and on baseless assumptions. Their religion rested on conjecture rather than certain knowledge. The lesson is that faith should be grounded in knowledge of revelation and sound understanding, not in blind imitation, empty wishes, or guesswork, and that those who follow their leaders without verifying the truth bear responsibility for their ignorance.

translation: So woe to those who write the scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from God," in order to exchange it for a small price. Woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.
interpretation: This verse condemns those religious figures among the People of the Book who deliberately fabricated or altered scripture by their own hand and falsely attributed it to God in order to gain worldly profit, such as wealth, status, and the favor of the masses. The verse pronounces a threefold warning of doom. The first is for the act of falsifying and ascribing lies to God. The second is for the written product itself, which misleads others and remains a lasting source of sin. The third is for the ill-gotten gain they obtained from it. The lesson is that distorting religious knowledge or claiming divine authority for personal opinion in exchange for worldly benefit is among the gravest of sins, because it corrupts guidance for others and makes the one who does it answerable for both his deed and its consequences.

translation: And they say, "The Fire will touch us only for a number of days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant from God—for God never breaks His covenant—or do you say about God what you do not know?"
interpretation: The verse rebukes the presumption that membership in a chosen community guarantees near-immunity from the consequences of one's deeds. Claims about one's fate in the Hereafter cannot rest on lineage, wishful thinking, or inherited self-confidence; they require a genuine assurance from God Himself. Since no such covenant was given, and God never breaks a promise He has made, the claim is exposed as baseless speculation attributed to God. The challenge teaches that knowledge of divine matters must come from revelation, not desire, and that attributing unfounded promises or leniency to God is itself a grave wrong. Salvation depends on faith and righteous action, not on group identity or false hope.

translation: Yes, whoever earns evil and is encompassed by his sin—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that punishment will touch a person only briefly, and it sets out a principle: eternal punishment belongs to the one whose sins so surround him that no good is left in him. 'Earning evil' means persisting in wrongdoing, and 'being encompassed by his sin' means that sin takes hold of his heart and life from every side, as when he dies in unrepentant disbelief and rebellion, leaving no room for faith or repentance. Such a person has shut himself off from guidance, so his dwelling is the Fire forever.
