The verse warns that small sins left unrepented can accumulate until they overwhelm a person, and it calls the believer to turn back to God quickly before sin becomes a barrier around the soul.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds - those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation is built on faith joined with action: belief alone is incomplete unless it is shown in righteous conduct, and good deeds have no standing without sincere faith. Those who combine the two are called 'companions of Paradise', a phrase that conveys closeness and belonging, as if Paradise is their rightful home and their lasting company. Their stay there is not temporary, since their reward is everlasting and is not followed by loss, fear, or end. In contrast to the fate of the people of the Fire mentioned alongside, the verse offers reassurance and motivation to the believer to persevere in faith and good works, trusting that God's promise of eternal reward is certain.

translation: And [remember] when We took the covenant from the Children of Israel: Worship none but God; and be good to parents, to relatives, to orphans, and to the needy; and speak to people good words; and establish prayer and give zakat. Then you turned away, except a few of you, and you were [habitually] turning aside.
interpretation: The verse recalls the binding covenant God took from the Children of Israel, which joins devotion to God alone with ethical and social duties: kindness to parents and kin, care for the vulnerable, gracious speech toward all people, and the acts of worship and charity (prayer and zakat). It shows that true monotheism is not only belief but a way of life in which worship of God and good conduct toward others are inseparable. The closing rebuke, that they turned away except for a few while remaining averse, points to their breaking of the covenant after accepting it. It is a reminder that a faithful remnant upholds the commitment while most abandon it out of heedlessness, and it warns every community entrusted with revelation against the same neglect.

translation: And [remember] when We took your covenant: you shall not shed your own blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes. Then you affirmed it, while you were witnesses.
interpretation: God reminds the Children of Israel that He took a binding covenant from them to preserve the sanctity of life and home within their community. The phrase 'your own blood' and 'yourselves' treats the community as a single body, so killing or expelling a fellow member is like doing it to oneself. They acknowledged this covenant and bore witness to it, so they cannot claim ignorance. The verse prepares for the following verses, which rebuke them for breaking it by fighting and expelling one another, and it warns that knowingly violating an accepted divine commitment brings greater blame.

translation: Yet here you are, killing one another and driving a group of your own people out of their homes, backing each other against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, although their expulsion was itself forbidden to you. Do you then believe in part of the Scripture and disbelieve in part? What is the reward for those among you who do that, except disgrace in the life of this world? And on the Day of Resurrection they will be sent back to the most severe punishment. And God is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Children of Israel in Medina for selective obedience to the Torah. They had covenanted not to shed one another's blood or expel one another from their homes. Yet, allied with rival Arab tribes (the Aws and Khazraj), they fought their own kin and drove them from their homes. When those same kinsmen were taken captive, they ransomed them, citing the Torah's command to free captives, while ignoring its prohibitions on killing and expulsion. The Qur'an condemns this as accepting the parts of revelation that suit one's interests and rejecting those that do not, which amounts to disbelief in the Scripture. The lesson is that faith requires submitting to God's commands as a whole, not following them according to desire, tribal loyalty or convenience. Those who do otherwise face humiliation in this world and the severest punishment in the next, and God is fully aware of their deeds.

translation: Those are the ones who have bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter; so the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse describes those who knowingly trade away eternal reward for fleeting worldly gain, as the preceding context speaks of people who conceal or reject God's guidance for the sake of worldly benefits. Such a trade is portrayed as a ruinous bargain: they give up what is lasting and receive what is temporary. Because they chose this deliberately, their consequence is final. Their punishment will neither be reduced in severity or duration, nor will anyone come to their aid, whether through intercession, a helper, or any worldly power or connection they once depended on. The lesson is that worldly advantage obtained at the expense of faith and truth is a net loss, and that accountability in the Hereafter rests entirely on one's own choices.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture and followed up after him with messengers. And We gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the Holy Spirit. Is it not that every time a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant, so a party you denied and a party you kill?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Children of Israel by pointing to a long history of divine favor met with resistance. God gave them guidance through the Torah and a continuous line of prophets, and strengthened Jesus with clear signs and the Holy Spirit (understood as Gabriel). Yet their response was governed by desire rather than truth: whenever a messenger brought a command that clashed with their whims, interests, or status, pride kept them from submitting. They rejected some prophets and went as far as killing others. The lesson is that rejection of revealed truth often comes not from lack of evidence but from arrogance and from following one's desires over God's guidance, and that a believer must measure his desires by revelation rather than measure revelation by his desires.

translation: And they said, "Our hearts are wrapped (covered)." Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 2:88) rejects the excuse of those who claimed their hearts were already sealed or filled with knowledge, and so had no need of the Prophet's message. They used this claim to avoid accepting the truth. The Qur'an answers that the barrier is not a natural defect in their hearts but the result of their own persistent rejection: Allah distanced them from His mercy as a consequence of their disbelief. Their hearts became hardened and closed because they chose to turn away from the truth. As a result, they believe only a little, since their faith is minimal, superficial, and does not bring true submission to God's revelation. The verse teaches that people are accountable for their disbelief, and that persistent rejection of guidance can progressively close the heart to it.

translation: And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what was with them—and before that they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved—but when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the stubbornness of those among the People of the Book who knew, from their own scriptures, the description of the Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an, and who used to threaten their pagan Arab neighbors that a promised prophet was about to appear and that they would triumph with him. When the Qur'an came and matched what they already possessed, and they recognized it as the truth, envy, tribal pride, and the wish to keep worldly status led them to reject it because the messenger was not from among them. Their disbelief was therefore not due to ignorance but to willful denial after clear knowledge, which is the gravest form of unbelief. For this reason the verse ends with God's curse, meaning expulsion from His mercy, upon those who knowingly reject the truth after it has been made clear to them.

translation: Wretched is that for which they have sold their souls: that they disbelieve in what God has revealed, out of envy that God should send down His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants. So they have incurred wrath upon wrath, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns the People of the Book who recognized the truth of the revelation but rejected it, not from honest doubt but from envy that prophethood was granted to someone outside their own community. They bartered away their souls, meaning their own salvation, for a worthless price: pride and jealousy. Their rejection is thus a self-inflicted loss, since God's favor is His to give to whomever He wills and no group holds a monopoly over it. The phrase 'wrath upon wrath' indicates layered divine anger: one for their earlier wrongdoing and breaking of covenants, and another for rejecting the final messenger after knowing his truth. Their punishment is described as humiliating, fitting the arrogance and envy that led them to deny, since the disgrace of the punishment answers the pride that drove their disbelief.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Believe in what God has sent down,' they say, 'We believe in what was sent down to us,' and they disbelieve in whatever comes after it, though it is the truth confirming what they already have. Say, 'Then why did you kill God's prophets before, if you were believers?'
interpretation: The verse exposes the selective and self-serving nature of the faith of those who claim to follow only their own revealed scripture. Their claim to believe 'in what was sent down to us' is not a principled adherence to revelation but an attachment to communal identity, since they reject the Qur'an even though it confirms the truth of their own scripture. Their sincerity is tested by their history: if they truly believed in what God revealed, they would not have killed the prophets who brought it. Their past murder of prophets shows that their rejection is not about loyalty to earlier revelation but about refusing to submit whenever God's truth conflicts with their desires. True belief means accepting all truth from God, whoever the messenger is, and not limiting it to what suits one's group or inclinations.

translation: And Moses certainly came to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf as a deity after he had gone, while you were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse reproaches the Children of Israel for their ingratitude and inconsistency. Despite having witnessed unmistakable signs through Moses, such as the staff, the parting of the sea, and the clear message of God's oneness, they turned to worshipping a calf as soon as he was absent for a short time. This shows that faith grounded only in witnessing miracles, without sincere inner commitment, is fragile. The phrase 'while you were wrongdoers' stresses that this was no honest error but a deliberate injustice: first against God, by associating partners with Him, and then against themselves, by bringing ruin upon their souls after knowledge had come to them. The lesson is that clear evidence demands steadfast loyalty to God's guidance whether or not the messenger is present.

translation: And (recall) when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you, (saying): 'Take what We have given you with firmness, and listen.' They said: 'We hear and we disobey.' And their hearts were made to drink in the calf because of their disbelief. Say: 'Wretched is that which your faith commands you, if you are believers.'
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel that their history is one of broken covenants: even after witnessing a overwhelming sign, Mount Sinai suspended over them to impress the gravity of the Torah's commands, they verbally affirmed hearing while in practice choosing disobedience. Their attachment to the golden calf is described as something that penetrated their hearts like water absorbed into the body, showing that idolatry had become deeply rooted in them as a consequence of their disbelief. God then challenges their claim of believing in what was revealed to them: a true faith could never prompt such conduct as rejecting the prophets, breaking the covenant, and worshipping the calf, so their claim of faith is exposed as hollow, and genuine belief is shown to require obedient action, not merely words.

translation: Say: If the home of the Hereafter with God is exclusively for you, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse challenges the claim of some among the People of the Book that Paradise belongs to them alone. If they were truly certain of their special standing with God and of a guaranteed reward, they would long to leave this world and meet Him, as someone sure of a better home eagerly desires to reach it. Their reluctance to wish for death, because of their attachment to worldly life and their awareness of their own misdeeds, exposes the emptiness of the claim. The lesson is that salvation depends on faith and righteous action rather than on lineage, group identity, or wishful assertion, and that true confidence in the afterlife is shown by sincere belief and good conduct, not by empty boasting.

translation: But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forth. And God is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse says that those who claimed the abode of the Hereafter was theirs alone, and who were challenged to prove their sincerity by wishing for death, will never actually wish for it. Their deeds, such as disbelief, rejecting truth, breaking covenants, and injustice, weigh on their consciences and make them dread meeting God and being held accountable. Their avoidance of death therefore shows that their claim was empty, and that they know in their hearts they are unprepared for the judgment ahead. The closing phrase reminds us that God knows exactly who the wrongdoers are, including what they conceal and what they publicly claim, so no false pretension can be hidden from Him and He will recompense each person with perfect justice.

translation: And you will surely find them the most greedy of people for life, even more than those who associate others with God. Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years, yet being granted long life will not remove him from the punishment. And God is All-Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse points to a deep attachment to worldly life among those who knew the truth yet rejected it and denied the hereafter. Because they are conscious, at some level, of the accountability awaiting them, they cling to this life more tightly than even the idolaters, who do not believe in resurrection. Their craving for a thousand years shows fear of facing the consequences of their deeds. The verse teaches that length of life is no protection from divine reckoning: what matters is the quality of one's deeds, not the number of one's years. Since God sees everything people do, no amount of time can hide or erase their record, and the only true security is faith and righteous action.

translation: Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel — it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by God's permission, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and glad tidings for the believers.
interpretation: This verse answers those among the People of the Book, who claimed that Gabriel was their enemy and so refused to believe in the Qur'an. The Prophet is told to respond that Gabriel is merely an instrument who delivers revelation not by his own will but by God's permission. Hostility toward him is therefore hostility toward God's command itself, and it makes no sense, because the message he brings agrees with the earlier scriptures and does not contradict them. The revelation is sent down upon the Prophet's heart, the seat of understanding and certainty, so it is firmly preserved and truly received. It serves as guidance and good news for the believers, while those who reject it out of hatred for its angelic carrier deprive themselves of that benefit. The verse teaches that one cannot accept some of God's messengers or means of revelation while rejecting others, and that rejecting the truth because of who conveys it is mere prejudice.

translation: Whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael, then indeed God is an enemy to the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith is indivisible: hostility toward any of God's chosen servants, whether angels or messengers, is in reality hostility toward God Himself, since they act only by His command. Gabriel and Michael are singled out after the general mention of angels to stress their high rank and to rebuke those who claimed to love some angels while hating others, as some of the Jews did regarding Gabriel. Such a person is not merely mistaken but a disbeliever, and God declares Himself the enemy of such people, meaning He opposes them and withholds His mercy and favor from them. The verse therefore calls believers to love and honor all whom God has honored, and warns that rejecting part of the divine message and its bearers amounts to rejecting God.

translation: And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verses of the Qur'an are plain and self-evident in their proofs, leaving no genuine room for doubt in a sincere seeker. Rejecting them is therefore not the result of any obscurity or lack of evidence, but of moral corruption: those who have willfully abandoned obedience to God and followed their desires, pride, and envy choose to deny what is clearly true. The verse teaches that disbelief after clear proof stems from the stubborn rebelliousness of the heart, not from an intellectual deficiency in the message.

translation: Is it not the case that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the habit of breaking agreements that was seen among many of the Children of Israel in their dealings with God and with the Prophet. It expresses astonishment that they would repeatedly make pledges, such as the covenant to follow the revealed guidance and to support the messenger, and then throw them aside as if they were of no weight. The phrase 'a group of them' shows that the breach came from some, while the closing statement 'most of them do not believe' shows that the real root of the faithlessness was a lack of sincere faith. A person who truly believes honors his promises, because he knows God is a witness over every covenant. Treating pledges lightly therefore reflects hollow belief, and fidelity to one's word is shown to be a mark of genuine faith.

translation: And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inconsistency of those who claimed to follow revelation. The Messenger came confirming the truth already in their Scripture, so accepting him should have been the natural consequence of their faith. Instead, a group of them cast aside God's Book, which includes rejecting the Scripture's own testimony to him. The image of throwing it 'behind their backs' means deliberate, contemptuous disregard, not mere forgetfulness. The phrase 'as if they did not know' shows that their rejection was not from ignorance, since they knew the truth well. They acted like people with no knowledge out of stubbornness, envy, and attachment to worldly interests. Knowledge without action and submission becomes a proof against its bearer.

translation: And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Yet the two angels never taught anyone until they said, 'We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.' So people learned from them that by which they cause separation between a man and his wife. But they could not harm anyone thereby except by God's permission. And they learned what harms them and does not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever buys it will have no share in the Hereafter. And evil indeed is that for which they sold themselves, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse describes how a faction among the People of the Book abandoned God's revealed scripture and followed the sorcery that devils spread, falsely attributing it to Solomon's kingdom in order to discredit him as a prophet. The Qur'an clears Solomon of unbelief and places the blame on the devils who taught magic. The episode of Harut and Marut shows that knowledge of magic was a test from God: the angels gave a clear warning that it was a trial and a path to disbelief, yet people still learned from them the kind of magic that destroys marriages. This shows how readily human beings choose harmful knowledge over guidance. The verse also affirms that nothing, including magic, has any effect apart from God's permission, so true power and harm lie in His will alone. Those who trade their eternal reward for such practices make a ruinous bargain, and their foolishness lies in knowing the consequence yet still choosing it.

translation: And if they had believed and been mindful of God, a reward from God would have been far better, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse says that the people who chose sorcery and gave up God's guidance traded something lasting for something worthless. Faith and God-consciousness lead to a reward from God that is better than any worldly gain, power, or trickery that can be had by turning away from Him. Their failure is one of knowledge and insight: if they truly understood the value of God's reward, they would have chosen belief and piety over the fleeting benefits of what they pursued. Real knowledge is therefore knowing what has lasting worth and acting on it, and a person who does not act on it is as though he does not know.

translation: O you who believe, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" (look upon us), and listen. And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.
interpretation: God teaches the believers to guard their speech and show respect toward the Prophet. The word "ra'ina" meant "pay attention to us," but it sounded like a Hebrew word of insult, and in Arabic it could suggest "our shepherd" or carry a sense of mockery. Some of the People of the Book used it with that double meaning to ridicule the Prophet. The believers are told to use the unambiguous "unzurna" (look upon us, give us time) and to listen attentively, so that no one can exploit their language and the Prophet's dignity is kept intact. The verse shows that words that can be misused for disrespect should be avoided, and that good manners and attentive listening to the Messenger are part of faith. Those who knowingly mock or disbelieve face a painful punishment.

translation: Neither those who disbelieve from among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord. But God singles out for His mercy whomever He wills, and God is the Possessor of immense bounty.
interpretation: The verse reveals that the envy of the disbelievers is the root of their hostility toward the believers: they resent that divine revelation and guidance came to the Muslim community and not to them, so they begrudge it and would like it taken away. God consoles the believers by affirming that His mercy, above all the gift of prophethood and the Qur'an, is not earned by lineage or claimed by any group as a right; it is a favor that He grants to whomever He wills according to His wisdom. Therefore the believers should not be troubled by the jealousy of others, but should be grateful for this great bounty and hold fast to it, since God's grace is vast and no one can block what He bestows.

translation: Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that God has power over all things?
interpretation: God, as the Lord of revelation, may lift or replace a ruling from an earlier revelation, or let it fade from memory, according to what suits the changing needs of people and the stage of their guidance. When He does, He gives a replacement that is better for them in benefit and ease or at least equal in value. Such change is not a sign of error or changing knowledge on God's part, but of His wisdom, mercy, and gradual education of humankind. Because His power extends over everything, He is able to bring about whichever ruling serves His purpose, and believers should accept His decree with trust rather than objection, as the earlier communities who disputed such changes did.

translation: Do you not know that to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? And you have besides God neither protector nor helper.
interpretation: The verse reminds the believer that absolute sovereignty over all creation rests with God alone, so He alone has the power to legislate, to abrogate, and to decree whatever He wills. Because all authority is His, no one else can truly protect a person from harm or give help against what He has decreed. The lesson is to place trust and reliance in God alone, to submit to His commands and rulings, including any changes in them, and to abandon dependence on created beings who can neither protect nor help without His permission.

translation: Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has certainly strayed from the right path.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against putting the Prophet through demanding, obstinate, or skeptical questioning, such as asking for miraculous proofs or needless details about matters God has left unspecified, as the Children of Israel did with Moses when they demanded to see God openly or asked endless questions about the cow. Such questioning grows out of doubt and stubbornness rather than a sincere wish to learn, and it can lead to hardship, rebellion, and loss of faith. The verse teaches that a believer's attitude toward the Messenger should be trust, obedience, and sincere inquiry, not challenge. It closes by stating that whoever trades faith for disbelief, by letting stubborn questioning erode their trust in revelation, has abandoned the straight path and wandered into clear misguidance.

translation: Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from their own selves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook until God brings about His command. Indeed, God is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse discloses the inner motive behind the efforts of many among the Jews and Christians to unsettle the believers' faith: it is not ignorance or honest doubt, since the truth had already become manifest to them, but envy rooted in their own souls, a resentment that God's favor of guidance and prophethood had come to others. In response, the believers are taught a posture of moral strength and restraint: to forgive and overlook their hostility and not to answer spite with spite, while the matter is left in God's hands until He decides it by His own command, whether through permission to fight, victory, or some other ruling He wills. The closing reminder that God has power over all things reassures the believers that their patience is not weakness, for the outcome rests with One who is fully capable of vindicating the truth and handling their adversaries in His own time.

translation: And establish prayer and give zakat. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with God. Indeed, God is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse links worship of God with service to people: prayer maintains the believer's relationship with the Creator, and zakat purifies wealth and cares for the needy. It then reassures believers that no good deed is ever lost or forgotten. Whatever they offer in this life, whether small or large, open or hidden, is preserved by God and will be found again, rewarded, in the Hereafter. Because God sees everything people do, believers should act sincerely, without needing recognition from others, and should stay mindful that they are accountable for their actions.

translation: And they say, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse rebuts the claim of the People of the Book that salvation belongs only to their own community. The Jews said only Jews would enter Paradise, and the Christians said only Christians would. The Qur'an calls this claim mere wishful thinking (amani), meaning a hope with no basis in revelation or reason. It then challenges them to bring clear evidence (burhan) if they are truthful. The verse teaches that entry into Paradise is not decided by group identity, lineage, or empty assertion. Claims about divine matters need proof, and the following verse says that those who submit themselves to God and do good will have their reward. Faith therefore has to rest on sincere submission and righteous deeds, not on sectarian pride.

translation: Yes indeed! Whoever submits his whole self to God while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation is not the monopoly of any community or label, as some claimed that only they would enter Paradise. It rests on two conditions: sincerity of devotion, meaning that a person directs his whole being and intention to God alone, and excellence in conduct, meaning that this inner submission is shown through righteous action in line with God's guidance. Whoever combines the two is assured of a reward that God Himself guarantees, along with freedom from fear of the future and from sorrow over the past.

translation: The Jews say, "The Christians have nothing to stand on," and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing to stand on," though they both recite the Scripture. Likewise did those who have no knowledge speak the like of their saying. So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.
interpretation: The verse exposes the sectarian arrogance of each community in denying all legitimacy to the other, even though both claim to follow divinely revealed scripture that should lead them to humility, justice, and recognition of the truth wherever it exists. Their mutual rejection is a sign of partisanship rather than knowledge, and the verse likens it to the speech of the ignorant, such as the pagan Arabs who dismissed everyone else's beliefs. Having scripture does not guarantee right guidance unless it is applied with sincerity and fairness. Since human disputes over religious claims cannot be settled by mutual condemnation, the final verdict belongs to God alone, who will judge with perfect knowledge and justice on the Day of Resurrection. The believer is therefore taught to avoid sweeping, bigoted denunciations of others and to leave ultimate judgment to God.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God from having His name mentioned in them and strives toward their ruin? It was not for such people to enter them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns, as among the gravest forms of wrongdoing, obstructing people from worshipping God in His houses of prayer and working to destroy them, whether physically by demolition or by preventing remembrance, prayer and devotion within them. Such people violate the sanctity of places set apart for God, so they do not deserve to enter them with authority or confidence. If they enter at all, it should be in awe and fear of God and of the believers who protect them. Their punishment is twofold: humiliation and defeat in this life, and a severe torment in the next. The verse is traditionally linked to those who barred believers from the Sacred Mosque or destroyed places of worship, but its principle is general: places of worship must be respected, and attacking them or hindering God's worship is a grave injustice.

translation: To God belong the East and the West. So wherever you turn, there is the Face of God. Indeed, God is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that no direction or place confines God, because all places belong to Him and His presence, knowledge, and mercy encompass everything. The specific direction of prayer is a command of worship and a means of unifying the believers, not a limitation on God Himself. So when a person sincerely turns to God, whether because of travel, difficulty, uncertainty about direction, or in remembrance of Him, they are never outside His reach, and their sincere intention is known to Him. It also frees believers from narrow attachment to particular places as if holiness belonged to the place itself, directing their hearts to God, whose vast generosity and knowledge include every sincere act of devotion.

translation: And they say, 'God has taken a son.' Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.
interpretation: The verse rejects the claim that God has a child by pointing to His perfection and self-sufficiency. Having offspring implies need, likeness, and a share in being, and these cannot belong to the Creator. Everything in the heavens and the earth is His creation and possession, and all of it submits to His will and decree. A being who owns and commands all creation, and to whom all things are subject, cannot have a son who shares His nature. The claim of sonship is therefore incompatible with God's absolute lordship, since whatever exists is a servant of God and not a part of Him.

translation: The Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute creative power and uniqueness: He brought the heavens and the earth into being without any prior model, matter, or helper, so nothing in creation can be His offspring or partner. His will is carried out instantly and without effort or need for means, as His command 'Be' is immediately followed by existence. This refutes the claim that God has a son, since One whose command brings all things into being has no need of progeny, and everything in creation is subject to His will.

translation: And those who do not know say: 'If only God would speak to us, or a sign would come to us.' Likewise those before them said the like of their saying; their hearts are alike. We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain.
interpretation: The verse describes the stubbornness of people who lack true knowledge: instead of reflecting on the many signs already present in revelation, creation, and the Prophet's message, they demand extraordinary, personal proofs, such as God addressing them directly, as though they deserved special treatment. Their demand is not a sincere search for truth but arrogance and obstinacy, a pattern repeated by earlier nations whose hearts were alike in their denial. God says the signs have already been made clear, but only those with firm certainty (yaqin), who are open to the truth and reflect sincerely, benefit from them, while those set on denial will never be satisfied by any further sign.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you (O Muhammad) with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blaze.
interpretation: God affirms the Prophet's mission: he was sent with the truth, which is the true religion and revelation, to give glad tidings of Paradise to those who believe and obey, and to warn of punishment those who disbelieve and disobey. His duty is only to convey the message clearly. He is not held responsible for those who reject it and end up among the people of Hellfire, since guidance in the heart is in God's hands and accountability rests on each person. This consoles the Prophet, relieving him of grief over the stubbornness of the disbelievers, and reminds him that his task is delivery of the message, not compelling belief.

translation: Never will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their creed. Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the (true) guidance. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against God no protector and no helper.
interpretation: The verse teaches that seeking the approval of those who oppose the truth is a futile pursuit, since their satisfaction is conditional upon abandoning one's own faith entirely. It directs the believer to anchor himself in divine guidance alone, because only God's guidance is true and every other path is mere human preference. The warning, though addressed to the Prophet, is a general lesson for his community: once a person has received clear knowledge of revelation, yielding to the whims of others for the sake of social acceptance or compromise forfeits God's protection and support, and nothing else can compensate for that loss. The believer should therefore remain steadfast in principle, be courteous without compromising belief, and measure success by God's pleasure rather than people's approval.

translation: Those to whom We have given the Scripture, who recite it as it ought to be recited, those believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith in revelation is shown not by merely possessing or reading the Scripture but by reciting it rightly: understanding it, reflecting on it, following its commands, and avoiding its prohibitions. Those among the People of the Book who engage with their revealed scripture sincerely and faithfully recognize the truth it contains, and this recognition leads them to believe in the message the Qur'an confirms. Whoever rejects the truth of revelation after it has been made clear has lost the most important thing, which is guidance and salvation, and so is truly the loser, whatever worldly gain he may hold.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.
interpretation: God calls the Children of Israel to gratitude and faithfulness by reminding them of the blessings He gave them: sending prophets and scripture among them, delivering them from Pharaoh, and granting them sovereignty and provision. Their 'preference over the worlds' refers to their distinction among the peoples of their own time, as the bearers of revelation. It was a responsibility and a trust, not an inherent or lasting superiority. The reminder implies that these favors obliged them to obey God, uphold the covenant, and accept the message He sent, and that failing to do so would forfeit the standing they had been given.

translation: And beware a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will any intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse warns that on the Day of Judgment each person stands alone before God, accountable for what they earned. No one can bear another's burden or take another's place, and no ransom can buy release. Intercession will not help anyone who has not earned God's permission and pleasure, and no ally or supporter can shield a person from the consequences of their deeds. Its message is that salvation depends on faith and righteous action, not on lineage, status, wealth, or reliance on others, so a person should prepare in this life through taqwa (God-consciousness), repentance, and good deeds, before the opportunity ends.

translation: And [remember] when his Lord tested Abraham with certain commands and he fulfilled them. He said, 'Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people.' Abraham said, 'And from my descendants?' He said, 'My covenant does not include the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that leadership in matters of faith is earned through trial, obedience, and complete submission to God, as Abraham was elevated to the status of imam only after he successfully fulfilled the commands with which he was tested. His natural concern for his offspring is not rebuked, but God's answer establishes that the divine covenant of spiritual leadership is not an inherited right of lineage or kinship. It is conditional upon justice and righteousness, so anyone who commits injustice, whether against God by disobedience and associating partners with Him or against other people, is excluded from it, regardless of descent from a noble prophet.

translation: And when We made the House (the Ka'bah) a place of return for the people and a place of safety, [We said]: 'Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer.' And We commanded Abraham and Ishmael: 'Purify My House for those who circle it, those who stay there in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate.'
interpretation: The verse presents the Ka'bah as a divinely established center of worship and security: people return to it again and again out of longing and devotion, and it is a sanctuary where fear is removed and sanctity is protected. Believers are directed to pray at the Station of Abraham, honoring the example of the Prophet who built the House in complete submission to God. The command to Abraham and Ishmael to purify the House means keeping it free of idolatry, impurity and anything that contradicts pure monotheism, so that it remains reserved for sincere worship. The three groups named, those who circumambulate, those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate, cover the main forms of worship performed there. The verse thus links the sanctity of the place with a covenant of pure devotion to God alone, and it establishes the Abrahamic roots of the Muslim rites.

translation: And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this a secure land and provide its people with fruits — whoever of them believes in God and the Last Day. He said: And whoever disbelieves, I will let him enjoy himself for a little while, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: Abraham prays for Mecca to be a place of safety and material sustenance, but initially limits the provision to believers, reflecting his awareness that the prophetic covenant of leadership excluded wrongdoers (as in the preceding verse). God's reply corrects this narrowing: His worldly provision is a general mercy given to all people, believer and disbeliever alike, as part of this-worldly testing, while the distinction between them lies in the hereafter. Worldly comfort is therefore no proof of God's approval; it is brief, and those who persist in disbelief will be driven to the Fire, an evil end. The verse teaches that security and sustenance are blessings to be met with faith and gratitude, not signs of immunity from accountability.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael [with him, saying], "Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing."
interpretation: The verse teaches that true worship is marked by sincerity and humility. Abraham and Ishmael were building the Ka'ba, one of the greatest acts of devotion, yet they did not rely on the deed or take pride in it. Even as they worked, they asked God to accept it, because an action has value only if God accepts it. Their appeal to God as the All-Hearing and All-Knowing shows their trust that He hears their prayer and knows their intentions. The believer should therefore do good deeds with a pure heart, fear that they might be rejected, and pray for acceptance rather than assume it.

translation: Our Lord, make us submissive to You, and from our descendants a community submissive to You. Show us our rites of worship, and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: This is the prayer of Abraham and Ishmael as they raised the foundations of the Kaaba. Though already devoted to God, they ask Him to keep them steadfast in full submission, showing that guidance and firmness in faith are gifts from God and not to be taken for granted. They extend their concern to future generations, seeking a lasting community of believers, which reflects the responsibility of prophets and parents to care for the faith of those who come after them. Their request to be shown the rites of pilgrimage shows that worship must be learned from God's guidance and not invented by human opinion. Their plea for repentance, even from such righteous servants, models humility: no one is free from shortcoming, and turning back to God is a constant part of the believer's life, grounded in the confidence that God is ever-returning with mercy to those who turn to Him.

translation: Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This is part of Abraham's and Ishmael's prayer while raising the foundations of the Kaaba. They ask God to raise up from their own descendants a prophet who shares their language and lineage, so that the guidance is accessible and familiar to them. The verse outlines the prophetic mission in stages: conveying revelation by reciting God's signs, which awakens hearts to faith; teaching the Book and the wisdom, meaning not just the text but its understanding, rulings and the sound application of its principles in life; and purification, meaning cleansing souls from polytheism, vice and moral corruption and nurturing them in sincerity and good character. The closing names, the Almighty and the All-Wise, express confidence that God is able to fulfill the request and will do so at the time and in the manner His wisdom decrees. Tradition understands the prayer as answered in the Prophet Muhammad, whose mission combined these three tasks of conveying, instructing and purifying.

translation: And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who has made a fool of himself? And indeed, We chose him in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse says that rejecting the pure monotheism of Abraham (submission to God alone, without partners) is not a matter of sound reasoning but of self-deception and folly. Someone who turns from the path of the man God chose, whose excellence is attested in this life and whose righteousness is assured in the next, harms himself most of all, because he abandons the way of truth and wisdom and the guidance that leads to salvation. True intelligence lies in following the clear, upright way of Abraham, which is the way of submission to God, and the one who forsakes it has in effect wronged and degraded his own soul.

translation: When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted myself to the Lord of all the worlds."
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 2:131) describes Abraham's immediate and wholehearted response to God's call. Islam here means total surrender of the heart, will, and conduct to God, not merely verbal assent. Abraham does not hesitate, ask for proof, or set conditions; once the command comes, he answers at once. His words, 'Lord of all the worlds,' show that his submission rests on recognizing God as the sole Creator and Sustainer of everything, so no other being deserves the same obedience or devotion. The verse presents Abraham as the model of pure monotheism and sincere obedience, and it implies that true faith consists of responding to God's call with prompt, complete, and conscious surrender.

translation: And Abraham instructed his sons to follow this way, and so did Jacob, saying: 'O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims (those who submit to Him).'
interpretation: The verse shows that faith in One God is the legacy the prophets cared about most, passing it to their children as their most precious inheritance. The command 'do not die except as Muslims' does not concern the moment of death alone. Since nobody knows when death will come, it means holding firmly to submission to God throughout life, so that one is found in that state whenever death arrives. The religion is described as 'chosen' by God, meaning it is a divine gift to be treasured and preserved, not a human invention. The verse also teaches that parents bear a responsibility to guide their families toward God and to make sound belief and righteous conduct the main concern of their upbringing.

translation: Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob, when he said to his sons, 'What will you worship after me?' They said, 'We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac, one God, and to Him we submit.'
interpretation: The verse rebuts the claim of the People of the Book that the prophets' legacy belongs to their own sects. By asking whether they were present at Jacob's deathbed, it reminds them that they were not, and that his final concern was not wealth or worldly affairs but the faith of his children. His question 'What will you worship after me?' shows that preserving pure monotheism was the central purpose of the prophetic line. His sons' answer, affirming one God and submission (islam) to Him, shows that the religion of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob was one: exclusive worship of God and surrender to His will. Faith therefore is not inherited by lineage or sectarian label, but is a conscious commitment that each generation must carry on, and true adherence to the prophets means following their tawhid and submission, not claiming their names.

translation: That was a nation which has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned, and you will not be asked about what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches individual moral responsibility: each person and community is judged only by its own deeds. Descent from righteous forebears such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob gives no spiritual credit, and the wrongdoing of earlier generations is not charged to their descendants. Claiming lineage or heritage is therefore no substitute for faith and righteous action, and people should focus on their own conduct and accountability before God rather than relying on ancestors' merits or arguing over their legacy.

translation: And they say, 'Be Jews or Christians, and you will be rightly guided.' Say, 'Rather, [we follow] the creed of Abraham, upright in faith, and he was not of those who associate others with God.'
interpretation: The verse rejects the claim of the People of the Book that guidance is confined to their own communal labels, each insisting that others must adopt its identity to be saved. The Qur'an redirects the believers to the pure monotheism of Abraham, who predated both Judaism and Christianity and was a hanif, one who turned away from falsehood and inclined wholly toward God. Guidance is thus found not in belonging to a sect or inherited label but in sincere, exclusive devotion to God alone, free from any form of shirk. Because Abraham is revered by Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike, he serves as the common, neutral standard by which all claims are measured, and the verse implies that whoever truly follows his path of pure submission is rightly guided.

translation: Say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.
interpretation: This verse establishes the universal, inclusive foundation of faith in Islam: belief in God is inseparable from belief in all the revelations and messengers He sent. The believer is taught to affirm the unity of the divine message across history, from Abraham and his descendants to Moses, Jesus, and all other prophets, because they all brought the same essential truth of worshipping one God. To make no distinction means not accepting some prophets while rejecting others, as people before had done, and not elevating any of them above their human status as servants and messengers. The closing phrase, 'and to Him we submit,' makes clear that true religion is not tribal or ethnic loyalty but willing submission to God alone, which is the shared religion of every prophet. The verse therefore calls Muslims to a faith that is confident in its own revelation while respectful and affirming of the earlier prophets' true missions.

translation: So if they believe in the like of what you have believed in, then they have been rightly guided; but if they turn away, they are only in schism. Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Baqarah 2:137) sets the standard of true guidance: it is found by sincerely believing in the same truth the Prophet and his Companions believe in, namely faith in Allah and in all His revelations and messengers without discrimination. If the People of the Book accept this, they are on the right path. If they refuse and turn away, their position is not one of principled difference but of stubborn opposition and division, since they have abandoned the common truth for the sake of hostility. The believers are then reassured that they need not fear the plots of those who oppose them, for Allah will protect them and give them victory over them. This reassurance rests on His attributes: He hears everything they say and knows their intentions and actions, so nothing of the believers' sincerity or of the opponents' scheming is hidden from Him.

translation: [Our religion is] the color of God, and who is better than God in coloring? And we are worshippers of Him.
interpretation: The verse presents faith in God as a defining 'dye' that permeates a believer's whole being, in contrast to outward rituals or markers of identity such as baptism, which some earlier communities used to signify belonging. God's 'color' is the pure natural disposition (fitra) and the monotheistic way of life that He has ordained, and it should saturate a person's beliefs, character, and actions just as dye saturates cloth and cannot be easily removed. No one can offer a better way of shaping the human soul and life than God, since He alone knows what suits and perfects His creatures. The closing declaration, 'we are worshippers of Him,' shows that this inner coloring is realized in sincere, exclusive devotion and obedience to God, so that a believer's identity is defined by servitude to Him alone rather than by lineage, group affiliation, or ritual form.

translation: Say: Do you dispute with us about God, while He is our Lord and your Lord? To us belong our deeds and to you your deeds, and we are sincere to Him.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to challenge the claim of the People of the Book that their religion and lineage give them a special standing with God. Since God is the Lord of all people, no group owns Him or has exclusive access to Him, so arguing over Him is pointless. What counts in His sight is not the label or community one belongs to but one's own deeds, for each is accountable only for what he does. The believers' distinction is therefore not ethnic or sectarian pride but ikhlas, devoting worship and obedience purely to God without associating anything with Him. The verse moves the dispute from claims of privilege to sincerity of faith and action.

translation: Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: Do you know better, or does God? And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has received from God? And God is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim of the People of the Book that the earlier prophets belonged to their later, named religious communities. Judaism and Christianity as distinct labels arose long after Abraham and his descendants, so those prophets were simply submissive monotheists, not members of a sectarian identity. By telling the Prophet to ask whether they or God know better, the verse shows that sectarian claims cannot override divine knowledge. It then condemns those who hide truth they know from their own scriptures, such as the testimony to Abraham's pure monotheism and the foretelling of the final Prophet, as the gravest kind of wrongdoing, because knowingly suppressing a witness entrusted by God is a betrayal of that trust. It closes with a warning that God sees all that people do, so no concealment or distortion escapes His accounting.

translation: That was a nation which has passed on. It will have what it earned, and you will have what you have earned, and you will not be asked about what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches individual moral responsibility. Descent from righteous ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, brings no merit and no blame to later generations. Each person is judged only by their own beliefs and actions. People should not rely on the status of their forebears for salvation, nor be held accountable for the deeds of those before them. Instead, they should focus on their own faith and conduct, because every soul is answerable for what it has earned.

translation: The foolish among the people will say, "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they used to face?" Say, "To God belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path."
interpretation: This verse anticipates the objections of those who would mock or doubt the change of the prayer direction from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca, and it prepares the believers with a ready answer. The reply is that no direction has an intrinsic sanctity independent of God: all directions, east and west, belong to Him, so He may designate any orientation for worship as He wills. The qiblah is therefore a matter of obedience to divine command, not of attachment to a place, and the change is a test of submission. Those who are guided understand that true righteousness lies in following God's instruction, and that such guidance is a gift from Him, granted to whom He wills, leading to the straight path, while the objectors, by clinging to form and habit over revelation, show their lack of insight.

translation: And thus We have made you a justly balanced community, so that you may be witnesses over humankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you. We did not appoint the direction of prayer that you formerly faced except to make evident who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels. It was indeed a hard thing, except for those whom God has guided. And God would never let your faith go to waste. Indeed, God is, to humankind, Most Kind and Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse presents the Muslim community as a moderate, balanced and just nation, standing between extremes of excess and neglect in belief, worship and conduct. Because of this, it is entrusted with bearing witness to humanity about the truth of God's guidance, just as the Prophet bears witness over the community by embodying and conveying that guidance. The change of the qibla from Jerusalem to the Kaaba is explained as a test of sincerity and obedience: it separated those who truly submit to the Messenger and follow divine command from those whose attachment was to habit, tribe or tradition and who therefore turned back. Such a change was heavy on the heart except for those whom God had guided and who trusted His wisdom. The verse ends with reassurance that the prayers offered earlier toward the former direction, and the faith behind them, are not lost, since God in His mercy and kindness never wastes the faith and deeds of believers.

translation: We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you [believers] may be, turn your faces toward it. Indeed, those who were given the Scripture well know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.
interpretation: This verse marks the change of the direction of prayer from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca. It shows God's care for the Prophet Muhammad, who longed in his heart and looked expectantly to the sky for this change, and God responds by granting what pleases him. The command is universal and lasting: wherever believers are, they must face the Sacred Mosque in prayer, which unifies the community in a single orientation. The verse also notes that the People of the Book recognize, from what their own scriptures teach about the coming prophet and the legacy of Abraham, that this change is true and from God, even if some of them deny it out of stubbornness or envy. The closing reminds that God is fully aware of their deeds, which is both a warning to those who conceal the truth and a reassurance to the believers.

translation: Even if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah. Nor are you a follower of their qiblah, nor do some of them follow the qiblah of others. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse, revealed after the change of the direction of prayer from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah, teaches that the People of the Book's rejection of the new qiblah is not due to a lack of proof but to stubbornness and envy, so no miracle or argument would satisfy them. Their refusal is rooted in partisanship, which is shown by the fact that they are even divided among themselves, as Jews and Christians each hold to their own direction. The Prophet is therefore told to stand firm on the truth revealed to him and not to seek their approval or compromise, since the guidance he has received is clear knowledge. The warning that following their whims after receiving that knowledge would make him a wrongdoer is a stern lesson, addressed to the Prophet and through him to every believer, that truth must never be traded for the desires of others or for social acceptance.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons, yet indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know.
interpretation: The People of the Book, especially their scholars, are so certain of the truth of Muhammad's prophethood and of the direction of prayer toward the Ka'bah, which their own scriptures describe, that their recognition is as sure as a father's recognition of his own child. Despite this certainty, some of them deliberately hide it out of envy, pride, or fear of losing status. The verse shows that rejection of truth often comes not from ignorance but from willful concealment, which makes the sin graver, since they knowingly suppress what they know to be right.

translation: The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the truth, especially the divine guidance that God has revealed and His command concerning matters such as the direction of prayer, comes only from God, the Lord who nurtures and guides the Prophet. Since its source is God, it needs no further proof and leaves no room for hesitation. The Prophet is told not to be among the doubters. This is a way of firmly strengthening the believers' certainty and warning every listener against wavering, and it is not an implication that the Prophet himself doubted. True knowledge of right and wrong is measured by revelation from God, not by the denials, disputes and misgivings of those who reject it.

translation: For every community there is a direction to which it turns; so race one another toward good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed, God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse tells believers not to let disputes over the direction of prayer, which differs among communities and religions, distract them from what matters. Each community has been given or has chosen its own orientation, but what truly distinguishes people is not the direction they face but how they compete in righteous deeds. The believers are therefore urged to spend their energy racing to do good rather than quarrelling over outward forms. The verse also reminds them that wherever they die or are scattered on earth, God will resurrect and gather them all on the Day of Judgment to account for their deeds. This is possible because God has power over all things. The reminder of accountability gives urgency to the command to hasten toward good.

translation: And from wherever you go out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; indeed, it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse affirms the command to face the Kaaba in prayer as a permanent, universal rule for the Prophet and the believers, whatever journey or place they find themselves in. The change of direction (qibla) is not a whim or a passing arrangement but a truth that comes from God, so the believers should accept it with certainty and without doubt. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of everything people do warns that He sees who obeys this command sincerely and who resists or objects to it, and it reassures the faithful that their obedience, along with the opposition of the doubters, is known and will be accounted for.

translation: And from wherever you go out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you all may be, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you, except those among them who have wronged; so do not fear them, but fear Me, that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse repeats and universalizes the command to face the Sacred Mosque in Mecca in prayer, wherever a believer is, so that the Muslim community has a single, unmistakable direction that sets it apart. Its distinct and settled identity removes any basis for the People of the Book or the Meccan polytheists to argue against it, for example by pointing to the Prophet's following their qibla or to a contradiction with Abraham's legacy. Those who are determined to be unjust will object regardless, out of stubbornness rather than any real proof, so believers should not fear their criticism and should hold only God in awe. Obeying this command is part of God's completing His favor on the community, giving it a clear religious identity and law, and it opens the way to guidance for those who submit to His commands.

translation: Just as We have sent among you a Messenger from yourselves, who recites to you Our verses, purifies you, teaches you the Book and the wisdom, and teaches you what you did not know.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 2:151) presents the sending of the Prophet Muhammad as a great divine favor that parallels the favor of the change of the qibla mentioned just before it, and it should move believers to remember God and thank Him (as the following verses command). The favor lies in four functions of the Messenger, who is from among them and so is known to them in lineage, honesty and character: he recites God's revelation to them, thereby grounding their faith in the word of God; he purifies them, cleansing their hearts and conduct from polytheism, vice and the corruption of pre-Islamic ways; he teaches them the Book and the wisdom, meaning both the text of the Qur'an and its meanings, rulings and the sound practice that puts it into effect; and he teaches them what they could not have known by themselves, such as the knowledge of God, the stories of earlier prophets, the unseen, and the way to salvation in this life and the next. The verse thus calls the community to gratitude by remembering the transformation from ignorance to guidance that came through the Messenger.

translation: So remember Me; I will remember you. And be grateful to Me, and do not be ungrateful to Me.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Baqarah 2:152) teaches that the believer's relationship with God is reciprocal. When people remember God through prayer, supplication, obedience, and mindfulness of His commands, God remembers them with mercy, guidance, forgiveness, and support, and this divine remembrance is a far greater honor than anything the servant offers. Gratitude is shown not only by words of thanks but also by using God's blessings in ways that please Him, whereas ingratitude means forgetting the Giver, neglecting His commands, or misusing His gifts. The verse calls the believer to a life of constant awareness of God, in which remembrance and thankfulness keep the heart connected to Him and secure His continued favor.

translation: O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, God is with the patient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that believers facing hardship, temptation, or the burdens of obedience should rely on two inner and outer supports: steadfast patience, which keeps the heart firm against distress and impulse, and prayer, which renews one's connection to God and brings strength, humility, and clarity. The closing assurance that God is with the patient means that His special companionship of support, guidance, and protection accompanies those who endure with trust in Him, so that patience is not passive resignation but an active reliance on God that transforms hardship into spiritual growth.

translation: And do not say about those who are killed in the cause of God, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse teaches that martyrs who give their lives for God's cause are not to be regarded as ended or lost. Death in God's path is not annihilation but a transition to a special, honored life with their Lord, a life of a different order from worldly existence, whose nature lies in the unseen and cannot be grasped by human senses. The believers are thus consoled for their losses and encouraged to be steadfast and sacrificial in faith, knowing that sacrifice for God is never wasted but is rewarded with a living, blessed state beyond human perception.

translation: And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and fruits; but give good tidings to the patient.
interpretation: This verse teaches that hardship is a built-in part of the believer's life in this world, not a sign of God's neglect or displeasure. Fear, scarcity, financial loss, bereavement, and failed harvests are trials through which God distinguishes sincere faith from mere profession and refines the character of the believer. The verse mentions the trials in advance so that they do not shock the believer when they come, and it pairs them with the promise of glad tidings for those who practice patience. Patience here is not passive resignation but steadfast trust in God, restraint from despair and complaint, and continued righteous action. The one who endures with this attitude turns loss into spiritual gain, earning God's reward, nearness, and mercy, as the following verses make clear.

translation: Those who, when a calamity befalls them, say: 'Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we shall return.'
interpretation: The verse describes the response of true patience (sabr) in hardship: the believer meets loss not with despair or complaint but by remembering the reality of existence. Saying 'We belong to God' acknowledges that everything one has, including life, health, wealth and loved ones, is a trust from God and not an absolute possession, so its being taken back is the Owner's right and wisdom. Saying 'To Him we shall return' reminds the believer that this world is temporary and that the final return is to God, who will compensate patience and loss with reward and mercy. The phrase thus turns affliction into a moment of submission, perspective and hope, anchoring the heart in trust in God rather than in what has been lost.

translation: It is those who will receive blessings from their Lord, and mercy; and it is those who are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse, which follows the description of the patient who say 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return' when afflicted by calamity, shows the reward for steadfastness. Their patience and submission to God's decree bring them His praise and forgiveness (the 'salawat'), His compassion (the 'rahma'), and the confirmation that they are truly guided: they found the right path by understanding that life, loss, and trial are all in God's hands, and by responding to hardship with trust in Him rather than despair or complaint.

translation: Indeed, Safa and Marwa are among the symbols of God. So whoever performs pilgrimage to the House (Hajj) or the lesser pilgrimage (Umrah), there is no blame upon him for walking between them. And whoever volunteers good on his own accord, then indeed God is Appreciative and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse removes a hesitation some early Muslims felt about walking between Safa and Marwa, since the pre-Islamic Arabs had placed idols near these hills and associated the rite with idolatry. By declaring the two hills to be among God's own sacred symbols, the verse reclaims the rite as an act of devotion to God, rooted in the memory of Hagar's search for water for her son Ishmael, and affirms that walking between them (sa'y) is a legitimate and integral part of Hajj and Umrah. The closing statement extends the lesson beyond this ritual: any good a person does freely and sincerely, beyond what is obligatory, is noticed and valued by God, who rewards generously ('Appreciative') and knows the intentions behind every deed ('All-Knowing'). Worship is thus judged by sincerity and devotion to God alone, not by the associations that people have attached to a place or practice.

translation: Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear to the people in the Scripture, those are cursed by God and cursed by those who curse.
interpretation: The verse warns that knowledge of truth is a trust, not a private possession. Those who hold revealed guidance, especially scholars of earlier scripture who knew the truth about the Prophet and the commandments, and by extension anyone entrusted with religious knowledge, must not hide it for worldly gain, fear, or partisanship. Since God has already made the truth plain in the Book, concealing it is a deliberate act of obstructing people from guidance, and so it carries one of the gravest penalties: being cast far from God's mercy. The phrase 'those who curse' indicates that this rejection is not only from God but is echoed by all creation, including angels, believers, and everything that suffers from the loss of truth. The lesson is that spreading truth and clear guidance is a moral duty, and withholding it out of self-interest harms both the concealer and the community.

translation: Except those who repent, make amends, and make clear [what they had concealed]; those I will forgive, for I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 2:160) follows the warning of God's curse on those who conceal the clear signs and guidance He revealed. It shows that the door of repentance stays open even for those guilty of this grave sin, but genuine repentance has three parts. First, they turn back to God and abandon the wrong. Second, they repair what they corrupted, in both their conduct and their relationship with God and people. Third, they publicly declare the truth they had hidden, because a sin of concealing knowledge is not undone by private regret alone; it requires undoing its effect on others. Whoever does this, God accepts and forgives, and He highlights His own names, 'the Ever-Relenting' (al-Tawwab) and 'the Most Merciful' (al-Rahim), to assure believers that His mercy exceeds any sin when a person sincerely returns to Him.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers — upon them is the curse of God, the angels, and all of mankind.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest consequence of unbelief is reached when a person persists in denying the truth until death, leaving no chance for repentance. Such a person places himself outside God's mercy, and this rejection is so complete that it is met with a universal condemnation: God's curse, meaning expulsion from His mercy, together with the angels' and people's rejection of this stance. Even the people's curse is understood as the natural verdict of sound conscience and reason against knowingly rejecting truth and persisting in falsehood. The verse also draws a firm line between those who turn back before death, whom the preceding verses show can be forgiven, and those who die unrepentant, for whom the door of mercy is closed once life ends. It is a warning to take advantage of the time given for repentance before it is too late.

translation: They will abide therein eternally; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be given respite.
interpretation: The verse stresses the finality of the fate of those who persist in disbelief and die rejecting the truth, having earned God's curse. Their punishment has three features: it is perpetual, with no end to their stay; it is undiminished, with no easing of its intensity; and it is without reprieve, with no further delay or chance to repent. This shows that the opportunity for repentance and change belongs only to this worldly life. Once death comes and accountability begins, the matter is sealed. The verse warns people to turn back to God and correct themselves while time and choice remain, and not to count on a later chance that will never be given.

translation: And your God is One God; there is no god but Him, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes pure monotheism (tawhid) as the foundation of faith: all worship, devotion, and obedience belong to God alone, with no partner or rival, so humanity's purpose and loyalty should be unified under a single Lord rather than divided among many powers.
