So the husband must give her a gift of consolation (mut'a), whose amount depends on his financial position, with the rich giving more generously and the poor giving what he can afford. It must be given in a fair, honorable and gracious way, without stinginess or reproach. The closing phrase 'a duty upon the doers of good' shows that this is a binding moral and legal obligation, and that treating a divorced woman with generosity and kindness is a mark of true righteousness (ihsan), preserving her dignity and softening the pain of separation.

translation: And if you divorce them before you have touched them, while you have already specified a dowry for them, then give half of what you specified, unless they waive it or the one in whose hand is the marriage contract waives it. And that you waive is nearer to piety. And do not forget graciousness between yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse sets a fair rule for a divorce that happens before consummation when a dowry has already been named: the husband owes half of it, which balances the wife's loss of marriage prospects and the husband's loss of the marriage. The verse then goes beyond strict legal rights and urges generosity. The wife may forgo her half, or her guardian, the one who holds the marriage contract, may waive it on her behalf. Alternatively the husband may give the full amount. Choosing to forgive and give more than is required is closer to God-consciousness (taqwa). The command not to forget 'graciousness between yourselves' teaches that even at the painful end of a marriage, believers should act with kindness and magnanimity rather than insisting on the bare minimum of their rights, knowing that God sees all they do.

translation: Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devout obedience.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to maintain all the obligatory prayers consistently, punctually, and with proper conditions, and singles out the 'middle prayer' for special emphasis, since a prayer that stands between others is easily neglected amid daily distractions. Many scholars, following reports from the Prophet, identify it as the afternoon prayer (Asr), the time when people are most absorbed in work and worldly affairs. The closing phrase teaches that prayer is not merely an outward ritual: one must stand before God in humble, devoted obedience, with a present heart and stillness, free from heedlessness and idle talk. Thus the verse unites preservation of the prayers' form and timing with the inner spirit of submission to God.

translation: But if you are in fear, then pray on foot or riding. And when you are secure, remember God [by performing the prayer fully] as He taught you what you did not know.
interpretation: This verse grants a concession in times of danger, such as war or imminent threat: the obligation of prayer is never dropped, but its form is eased. A believer who fears an enemy or other peril may pray while walking or mounted, facing any direction and with gestures in place of full bowing and prostration. Once safety returns, the believer must go back to the complete, regular form of prayer, which is what 'remembering God' means here. This return is framed as gratitude for divine guidance, since God taught the believers, through revelation, the right way to worship and live, which they could not have known by themselves. The verse shows that the faith balances devotion with realistic ease, and that the remembrance of God is to be maintained in every circumstance, with its perfected form restored in times of peace.

translation: And those of you who die and leave behind wives: a bequest for their wives, provision for a year without being driven out. But if they leave of their own accord, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves in a rightful manner. And God is Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: This verse sets out a moral and social safeguard for widows. A man nearing death is urged to make a bequest so that his widow is provided for with maintenance and lodging for up to a year, and she should not be forced out of her marital home during that time. The widow keeps her freedom, however: if she chooses to leave, for example to remarry after completing the prescribed waiting period, her guardians and the deceased's family bear no blame for any lawful and honorable choice she makes about her own life. Many interpreters hold that the one-year provision was later softened by the verses on inheritance and the four-month-and-ten-day waiting period, which turned the year into a recommended kindness rather than a binding obligation. Either way, the verse teaches compassion toward the bereaved, protection of women's dignity and security, and respect for their autonomy. It closes by reminding believers that God is Almighty, so His limits must be observed, and Wise, so His rulings serve the real interests of people.

translation: And for divorced women there shall be a provision according to what is fair — an obligation upon the righteous.
interpretation: The verse establishes that a divorced woman is not to be sent away empty-handed or with bitterness; she is owed a gift or provision (mata') that is fair and befitting the husband's means and her standing. By calling it an obligation upon the God-fearing, the Qur'an ties this kindness to taqwa: those who are conscious of God show themselves not merely by avoiding wrongdoing in ending a marriage, but by treating the woman with generosity, dignity, and compassion at the very moment when resentment is most likely to prevail. Divorce thus must be ended with honor, and a believer's piety is measured by fairness toward a former spouse.

translation: Thus does God make clear His signs to you, so that you may understand.
interpretation: This verse, which closes a passage of legal and moral guidance (as in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:242, after the rulings on divorce and the rights of women), teaches that God's commands are neither arbitrary nor obscure. He explains them clearly so that people may use reason to grasp their wisdom, and that understanding should lead them to live by them. Faith and obedience in the Qur'anic view are meant to rest on reflection and insight, not blind imitation, and the purpose of the clear signs is to cultivate a rational, conscious commitment to justice, mercy and righteous conduct in daily life.

translation: Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? Allah said to them, 'Die'; then He restored them to life. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty to the people, but most of the people do not give thanks.
interpretation: The verse recalls a community who fled their homes in great numbers out of fear of death, whether from plague or from battle, as many commentators explain. Their flight did not save them, for Allah decreed their death and then revived them. The lesson is that no precaution can outrun Allah's decree: life and death are wholly in His hand, and fear of death must never lead people to abandon duty, patience, or struggle in His cause. Their revival shows His power to resurrect and His mercy, since He gave them another chance to reflect and mend their ways. The closing statement notes that Allah's bounty to humankind is constant and abundant, yet most people neglect gratitude, forgetting that their very lives are a gift. This verse leads into the following call to fight in the way of Allah and to trust Him rather than fear death.

translation: And fight in the cause of God, and know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The command to fight is tied strictly to 'the cause of God', meaning a just and righteous purpose, not worldly gain, aggression, or personal ambition. The closing reminder that God hears and knows is both a warning and a comfort. It is a warning because He hears every word and knows every intention behind the fighting, so it must be sincere and within the limits He has set. It is a comfort because He hears the pleas of the believers and knows their sacrifices and hardships, so none of them is lost. The verse therefore joins outward action to inward accountability: struggle is legitimate only when it is done for God's sake, under His constant awareness.

translation: Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over? And God withholds and extends [provision], and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse invites believers to spend generously in God's cause, especially in supporting the needy and in defending the community, describing such giving as a 'loan' to God to show how certain and generous the reward is. A 'goodly loan' is wealth given sincerely, from lawful earnings, without reproach or expectation of worldly return. God multiplies it manifold, in this life and the next. The closing reminders answer the fear that giving will cause poverty: God alone narrows or expands provision, so hoarding cannot secure wealth and spending cannot ruin anyone. Since all will return to Him, what a person sends ahead is what will be found with Him, and what is held back is lost.

translation: Have you not considered the assembly of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Appoint for us a king, and we will fight in the way of God.' He said, 'Might it be that, if fighting were prescribed for you, you would not fight?' They said, 'And why should we not fight in the way of God, when we have been driven out of our homes and from our children?' But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that eager declarations of courage are easy to make in times of comfort or grievance, but true faith is proven only when the actual duty arrives. The Israelite leaders demanded a king and boasted of their readiness to fight because of the injustice of exile and separation from their families, yet when fighting was actually made obligatory, nearly all of them abandoned their pledge. The prophet's cautious question reveals a wise understanding of human weakness: sincerity is measured by action, not by words. Only a small, steadfast minority kept their promise, showing that commitment to God's cause is rare and that God knows those who wrong themselves by breaking their covenant and shirking duty after pledging to uphold it.

translation: And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, God has appointed Talut (Saul) as king over you." They said, "How can he have kingship over us while we are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been given an abundance of wealth?" He said, "Indeed, God has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature. And God gives His dominion to whom He wills. And God is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing."
interpretation: The verse teaches that legitimate leadership rests on divine selection and real merit, not on lineage, social standing, or wealth. The Israelites objected on worldly grounds: they saw themselves as nobler and Talut as poor. Their prophet answered that God chose him because he had the qualities leadership truly requires, namely knowledge and wisdom for sound judgment, and physical strength and stature for courage and command in battle. Sovereignty belongs to God alone, who grants it by His wisdom to whomever He wills, so people should submit to His decree rather than argue from pride or material criteria. God's vast generosity and complete knowledge mean He knows who is fit to rule and can provide for whomever He appoints.

translation: And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, in which is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."
interpretation: When the Israelites doubted Talut (Saul) as king because he lacked wealth and noble status, their prophet offered a clear, divinely sanctioned proof of his appointment: the return of the Ark of the Covenant, which they had lost. The Ark was a source of sakina, a settled calm and reassurance of heart that strengthened them, and it held relics left by the houses of Moses and Aaron, linking the new leadership to the legacy of earlier prophets. Its being borne by angels shows that God Himself was establishing Talut's authority, so that his kingship rested on divine choice rather than on worldly rank. The verse closes by saying that this sign is convincing only for those who truly believe, since faith is what lets a person accept God's decree and submit to the leadership He has appointed.

translation: And when Talut set out with the soldiers, he said, "Indeed, God will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who scoops up a handful with his hand." But they drank from it, except for a few of them. Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, "We have no power today against Jalut and his soldiers." But those who were certain that they would meet God said, "How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's permission! And God is with the patient."
interpretation: The verse shows that true strength in a community lies in discipline, obedience to rightful leadership, and firm faith rather than in numbers. The river is a test that separates those who can restrain their desires and follow commands, even in thirst and hardship, from those who give in to appetite. Most failed the test, and even among those who crossed, many felt daunted when they saw the enemy's might. Only those with certainty of meeting God, who kept the Hereafter in view, were steadfast, reminding the others that victory comes by God's permission and not by sheer numbers, and that God supports those who persevere with patience.

translation: And when they went forth to face Goliath and his soldiers, they said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people." (Qur'an 2:250)
interpretation: When the small believing band under Talut (Saul) confronted the overwhelming might of Goliath's army, they did not rely on their numbers or strength but turned to God in supplication. Their prayer has three stages: first they ask for patience, imagined as water poured out abundantly until it fills the heart, so that fear and anxiety are removed; then for steadfastness of foot, so that they do not flee or waver in battle; and only then for victory over the opposing disbelievers. The verse teaches that victory comes from God, and that inner endurance and firmness are the necessary preparation for outward success. Believers facing hardship should first seek strength of heart and constancy, and then ask God for help, trusting that He grants triumph to the few who are patient and sincere over the many who are arrogant.

translation: So they routed them by God's leave, and David killed Goliath, and God gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him of what He willed. And if God did not repel some people by means of others, the earth would surely be corrupted; but God is possessed of bounty over all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse shows that victory comes only through God's permission and support, after the believers' steadfastness and trust in Him, as with the small band of Talut's army defeating the tyrant Jalut's forces. David, a youth among the believers, became the instrument of that victory by slaying Goliath, and God then honored him with sovereignty and prophetic wisdom and taught him what He willed, such as the crafting of armor and the Psalms. The verse then states a universal divine law: God restrains the aggression of the wicked by empowering others to stand against them, so that no single tyrannical power goes unchecked and the earth is not overrun by corruption, oppression and chaos. That this balance exists is itself a grace from God to all creation, since the world's order is preserved not by human merit alone but by His bounty.

translation: These are the verses of God; We recite them to you in truth. And indeed, you [O Muhammad] are among the messengers.
interpretation: God affirms that the revelations, including the accounts of earlier peoples just narrated, are authentic and free from falsehood or human invention, delivered by God Himself through recitation to His Prophet. The accuracy of these unseen narratives, which Muhammad could not have known by ordinary means, serves as proof of the source of the revelation. On that basis God confirms the Prophet's status as a true messenger in the line of earlier prophets, which comforts him against the denial of his opponents and calls people to accept his message.

translation: Those messengers—We have favoured some of them over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke directly, and some He raised in rank. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear proofs and supported him with the Holy Spirit. Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them. But they disagreed: some believed and some disbelieved. And had God willed, they would not have fought one another, but God does what He wills.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the prophets, though united in their message, were granted different distinctions by God: Moses was addressed directly, Muhammad and others were raised in rank, and Jesus was given clear signs and strengthened by Gabriel. These distinctions are God's gifts, not human achievements. The verse then explains that the conflicts and bloodshed among later communities did not arise from any lack of guidance, since clear proofs had come to them, but from human choice, as people divided into believers and disbelievers. Because God has granted humans free will within His wider will, He permits this disagreement and strife as part of the trial of life. Nothing happens outside His knowledge and power, yet people remain responsible for the faith or disbelief they choose, so believers should hold fast to the guidance, honor all the messengers, and not be shaken by the existence of conflict in the world.

translation: O you who believe, spend from what We have provided for you before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession. And the disbelievers - they are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse urges believers to give charity and spend in God's cause now, while they still have the means and the opportunity, because the Day of Judgment will offer no chance to make up for neglected duties. On that Day, the things people rely on in this world to escape hardship will be of no use: one cannot buy one's way out (no trade), one cannot be rescued by the loyalty of a close friend, and one cannot count on intercession except by God's leave. Wealth is thus a trust to be turned into lasting reward through generosity before death or the Hour cuts off the chance. The closing statement says that those who reject faith and withhold what is due to God and to people wrong themselves most of all, by placing worship, wealth, and trust in the wrong things and forfeiting their only means of salvation.

translation: God—there is no deity but Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is there that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not weary Him. And He is the Most High, the Magnificent.
interpretation: This verse, Ayat al-Kursi, establishes absolute divine oneness and shows that God alone is worthy of worship because His attributes are perfect and complete. He is Ever-Living and the Sustainer on whom all existence continually depends, so He never suffers the weakness of fatigue, sleep, or neglect, and creation is never left without His care. Everything belongs to Him, so no being holds independent power. Even intercession, which people may hope for, is not a right of any creature but occurs only by His leave, which removes reliance on anyone besides Him. His knowledge is total, covering past and future and what is seen and unseen, while human knowledge is limited and given only as He wills, which calls for humility. The vastness of His Throne, embracing the heavens and earth, points to His immense dominion, yet maintaining it costs Him no effort. The verse closes by affirming His loftiness above all creation and His greatness, which should lead the believer to trust, reverence, and seek refuge in Him alone.

translation: There is no compulsion in religion. Right guidance has become distinct from error. So whoever disbelieves in Taghut and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which never breaks. And God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: Faith is a matter of the heart and free conviction, so it cannot be imposed by force; coerced belief has no value before God. Because the truth has been made clear through reason, revelation, and evident signs, every person is left with a free and accountable choice rather than an excuse. Whoever rejects every false object of worship and authority that draws people away from God, and sincerely commits to God alone, has anchored himself to a secure, unbreakable support that will not fail him in this life or the next. God hears what people profess and knows what is truly in their hearts, so He will judge the sincerity of each person's choice.

translation: God is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of the darkness into the light. But those who disbelieve, their patrons are the false deities (Taghut); they bring them out of the light into the darkness. Those are the companions of the Fire, and they will abide in it forever.
interpretation: The verse presents two opposing paths of guardianship that shape a person's spiritual destiny. God, as the guardian of believers, takes them out of the many darknesses of doubt, ignorance, desire, and error, using the plural 'darknesses', and leads them into the one light of truth, using the singular 'light', which shows that truth is unified while falsehood takes many forms. Those who reject faith give their allegiance to the Taghut, meaning anything that transgresses the bounds of God and is obeyed in place of Him, such as tyrants, false ideologies, or one's own base desires. These lead their followers away from whatever natural light of guidance they had and into deeper darkness. The result of choosing between these two guardianships is lasting: following misguidance leads to the Fire, while the believer's trust in God leads to light and salvation. The verse invites each person to examine whom they take as their guide and where that guidance is leading them.

translation: Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because God had given him kingship? When Abraham said, 'My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death,' he said, 'I give life and cause death.' Abraham said, 'Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.' Thereupon the disbeliever was confounded. And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse shows how worldly power can breed arrogance and blind a person to the truth, so that he disputes with the clear proof of God's lordship. The king twisted Abraham's argument by claiming to give life and death, probably by pardoning or executing a prisoner, and so confused real creation with the power to spare or kill. Abraham did not get stuck in that quibble. He moved to an argument that could not be answered: the cosmic order obeys God alone, and no one else can reverse it. The king was dumbfounded because the proof exposed the limits of human power. The closing statement teaches that clear evidence alone does not bring guidance to those who persist in wrongdoing, arrogance and stubbornness. Their injustice, in rejecting the truth they recognize and in claiming a status that belongs to God, bars them from God's guidance. The verse also affirms that sound reasoning and wisdom are legitimate ways to defend faith.

translation: Or like the one who passed by a town that had fallen into ruin, its roofs collapsed upon its walls. He said: 'How will God bring this back to life after its death?' So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up. He said: 'How long have you remained?' He said: 'I have remained a day or part of a day.' He said: 'Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and drink, which has not spoiled; and look at your donkey. And We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh.' When it became clear to him, he said: 'I know that God has power over all things.'
interpretation: The verse offers a concrete, lived demonstration of resurrection to answer the human tendency to doubt that life can return to what is dead. The man's question is not stubborn denial but a search for understanding, and God answers it by enacting the event within his own experience: he is made to die and be raised after a century, and his perception of time proves unreliable, since he thinks only a day has passed. The preserved food alongside the decayed donkey shows that God's command governs decay and preservation alike, so that He preserves what He wills and recomposes what He wills, assembling bones and clothing them with flesh. The man himself becomes a sign to others, and his final declaration shows that certainty comes when knowledge moves from abstract belief to witnessed reality: God's power is absolute and extends over everything, including the revival of dead lands, dead bodies, and dead communities.

translation: And [remember] when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Do you not believe?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] so that my heart may be at ease." He said, "Take four birds and incline them to yourself, then place on every hill a portion of them, then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise."
interpretation: Abraham's question is not born of doubt but of a desire to move from knowledge by certainty ('ilm al-yaqin) to direct witnessing ('ayn al-yaqin). God does not rebuke him; He affirms that faith and the longing for deeper reassurance can coexist. The lesson is that the believer may seek inner tranquility through a sign, and God graciously grants it. The birds, cut up, scattered across hills, and then returning alive at Abraham's call, show that resurrection is no difficulty for the One who gathers scattered parts. Abraham himself handles the birds first, so he knows them well and cannot mistake the miracle. The closing reminder that God is 'Aziz (Almighty, whose will cannot be thwarted) and Hakim (Wise, who acts with purpose) tells us that this power is exercised with wisdom: resurrection is both certainly possible and a purposeful part of the divine order.

translation: The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that sprouts seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. And God multiplies for whom He wills; and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity given sincerely for God's sake is never lost or diminished but is returned in vastly increased measure, just as a single seed, once planted in fertile soil, yields hundreds of grains. Spending in God's cause, whether on the poor, on the needy, or on works that serve the community and the faith, is therefore an investment whose reward is far greater than the amount given. The multiplication is not mechanical but depends on God's will and on the sincerity, purity of intention, and quality of the giver's act, and God, whose generosity is limitless and who knows every intention, rewards each person according to what He knows of their heart. The believer is thus encouraged to give freely and without fear of poverty, trusting in God's boundless provision.

translation: Those who spend their wealth in the cause of God and then do not follow up what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, theirs is their reward with their Lord; no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity is accepted and rewarded only when it is given with a pure intention and a clean heart, for God's sake alone. Reproaching the recipient with the favor done, or hurting him with words or deeds, cancels the spiritual value of the gift and wounds human dignity. Those who give without expecting gratitude or holding their generosity over others secure a reward that is guaranteed with God, along with freedom from fear of the future and grief over the past, because their giving was an act of sincere devotion and not a means of gaining status or power over others.

translation: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need and Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity is valued by the spirit in which it is given, not merely by the material act. A gentle, decent reply to a person in need, or overlooking their shortcomings and importunity, brings more spiritual good than a gift that is followed by reproach, reminders of one's generosity, or humiliation, because such harm cancels the gift's worth and wounds the recipient's dignity. Allah needs nothing from anyone's gifts, so He is not served by charity tainted with arrogance, and yet He is forbearing, not hastening to punish those who err, which calls believers to imitate His patience and gentleness toward the needy.

translation: O you who believe, do not nullify your charitable gifts with reminders of your generosity and with hurt, like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in God and the Last Day. His likeness is that of a smooth rock covered with a layer of soil: a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare and hard. Such people have no power over anything of what they earned. And God does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the worth of charity lies in the sincerity behind it, not in the amount given. Reproaching the recipient with one's favors or harming them with words or attitude cancels the spiritual reward, as though the gift had never been given. The one who gives only for show is compared to a smooth rock with a thin film of soil: from outside it appears fertile and promising, but the first heavy rain washes the soil away and reveals the barren stone beneath. In the same way, showy giving looks good on the surface, but on the Day of Judgment it is exposed as empty, since it was never grounded in faith in God and the Last Day, and the giver finds no reward from it. The verse calls believers to give purely for God's sake, with humility and kindness toward those they help, and to guard their good deeds from pride and hypocrisy.

translation: And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and to confirm their souls is like a garden on a hill: heavy rain falls on it and it yields its fruit twofold; and if no heavy rain falls on it, then a light drizzle. And God is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse contrasts with the wasted charity of those who show off, by illustrating the charity of the sincere. Their spending springs from a pure intention—seeking God's pleasure—and from a firm inner conviction, since giving trains the soul in steadfastness and frees it from miserliness. Such giving is likened to a garden on elevated, well-drained, fertile ground: it receives abundant rain and doubles its produce, and even if only light dew falls, it still thrives. The lesson is that sincere charity is never fruitless: a large gift brings great reward, and a small gift offered with the same sincerity also brings goodness and growth, because what matters is the intention and the heart behind it, not merely the quantity. The closing reminder that God sees all that people do assures the giver that no deed, great or small, escapes God's notice, and warns that He knows the true motives behind every act of giving.

translation: Would any of you wish to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, in which he has all kinds of fruits, and old age strikes him while he has weak offspring, and then a whirlwind containing fire strikes it and it is burned up? Thus does God make clear to you His signs, so that you may reflect.
interpretation: This verse gives a parable about deeds that are ruined by insincerity and by invalidating acts such as boasting about charity, causing hurt to the recipient, or showing off. It follows the verses on spending in God's cause. A person who does good works builds, as it were, a lush garden, and he will need its reward most on the Day of Judgment, just as an old man with weak children needs his garden most when he can no longer work or provide for himself. If his deeds are destroyed by a fiery whirlwind, which stands for sin, hypocrisy and ill-intention, he is left at the moment of greatest need with nothing, and has no time or strength to start again. The lesson is to guard one's good deeds, keep them sincere for God's sake, and reflect on how fleeting this life is and how urgent the need for lasting reward in the Hereafter.

translation: O you who believe, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth. And do not seek out the bad of it to spend, while you yourselves would not take it except by closing your eyes to its defects. And know that Allah is Free of need and Worthy of all praise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity must come from the best and purest of one's lawful wealth, whether earned through trade and work or produced from the land, and not from inferior, spoiled, or unwanted goods. A believer should test his giving by his own standard: if he would be reluctant to accept such a thing himself, except by overlooking its flaws out of need or embarrassment, then offering it to others as charity is a failure of sincerity and respect toward the poor and toward God. The closing reminder that God is Free of need and Praiseworthy clarifies that He does not need anyone's gifts; charity benefits the giver's soul and the recipient, and God is worthy of being given only what is good, so one should give with generosity and honor.

translation: Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to commit immorality, while God promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And God is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse, which comes in the context of encouraging charitable giving, exposes how Satan manipulates human fear. He instills the dread that spending in God's cause will lead to destitution, and this fear breeds stinginess and hoarding, which in turn opens the door to moral corruption and shameful conduct, since a heart enslaved to the fear of lack loses trust in God and drifts toward greed and disobedience. In contrast, God offers a promise rooted in certainty: forgiveness of sins for those who give, and bounty in the form of increased provision, blessing and reward in this life and the next. The believer is therefore asked to choose whose promise to trust, the whisper of fear or the pledge of the One who is vast in His generosity and knows perfectly the intentions of givers and what is best for them.

translation: He grants wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is granted wisdom has indeed been given much good. But none will remember except those of understanding.
interpretation: Wisdom is a divine gift, not merely a product of intelligence or learning. It is the ability to understand the truth, to place things where they belong, and to act rightly in speech and conduct, and God bestows it on whomever He wills according to His knowledge of their sincerity and readiness. Whoever receives it has received an immense good, because it guides every decision toward what benefits him in this life and the next. Yet only people of sound intellect, whose minds are not clouded by desire, arrogance, or heedlessness, truly reflect on God's signs and admonitions and benefit from them. The verse thus teaches us to seek wisdom humbly through sincere devotion, reflection, and prayer, and to recognize it as a blessing from God, not a source of pride.

translation: And whatever you spend of expenditure or vow of a vow, indeed God knows it. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.
interpretation: Every act of giving and every pledge made to God, whether done secretly or openly and whether sincere or for show, is fully known to Him, so nothing is lost with Him and each person will be repaid according to the intention behind it. The verse encourages sincerity and fulfilling one's vows. It also warns that those who wrong themselves and others, for instance by spending for show, spending in disobedience, breaking vows, or withholding what is due, will find no one to defend or rescue them from the consequences when God holds them to account.

translation: If you disclose your charitable acts, they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you, and He will expiate for you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the value of charity lies in the sincerity behind it, not in whether it is public or private. Giving openly is praiseworthy because it sets an example and encourages others to give, so long as the giver is free of show. Giving secretly is better because it protects the giver's sincerity and the dignity of the poor person, who is spared embarrassment. Charity given with a pure intention is also a means of spiritual cleansing, since God uses it to erase some of the giver's sins. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of everything people do tells believers that He knows their true motives, so they should give for His sake alone and not for people's praise.

translation: It is not upon you [O Prophet] to make them find guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills. Whatever good you spend is for your own souls, and you spend only seeking the Face of Allah. And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity is not to be conditioned on the recipient's faith or on whether they accept guidance. The believers (and the Prophet) are responsible only for conveying the message and doing good, while guidance itself lies solely in God's hands. Giving should therefore be extended even to needy non-Muslims without using aid as leverage for conversion. The verse also stresses that the true beneficiary of spending is the giver, whose soul is purified and rewarded, and that sincere giving is done purely for God's sake, not for show, praise, or worldly return. God promises complete and fair recompense, with no loss or injustice to the giver, which encourages generosity free from anxiety about scarcity or ingratitude.

translation: [Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted in the cause of God, unable to move about in the land [for trade]. The ignorant one would think them wealthy because of their restraint. You know them by their mark; they do not beg from people persistently. And whatever good you spend, indeed God is Knowing of it.
interpretation: The verse directs the believers' charity toward a especially deserving group: those whose circumstances, such as devotion to God's cause, striving, or being confined by duty, have kept them from earning a livelihood. Their dignity and self-restraint hide their need, so that outsiders mistake them for well-off. True generosity therefore requires attentiveness: the giver should seek out the needy who are silent and modest rather than only respond to those who ask loudly. Their need can be perceived through signs such as humble appearance and demeanor. The closing assurance that God knows whatever good is spent teaches that no act of giving, however quiet or small, goes unnoticed or unrewarded, and it encourages sincere giving for God's sake rather than for recognition.

translation: Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true generosity is not tied to a particular time or manner, but is a constant state of devotion to God. Those who give continually, whether hidden to protect sincerity or public to encourage others, are rewarded for the intention behind the giving. Their reward is secured with God Himself, so it cannot be lost or diminished. In the Hereafter they are freed from fear of what lies ahead and from grief over what they left behind, because what they gave away has become their lasting provision with God.

translation: Those who consume interest will not stand [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one stands who is being beaten by Satan into insanity. That is because they say, 'Trade is just like interest.' But Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden interest. So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists may keep what is past, and his affair rests with Allah. But whoever returns to it, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moral and spiritual gravity of usury (riba). Those who devour it will rise on the Day of Judgment disoriented and stumbling, like someone convulsed by Satan's touch, a visible sign of how their corrupted dealings unbalanced their souls and society. Their error lies in a flawed argument that equates lawful trade with interest, ignoring that trade involves real exchange, shared risk and mutual benefit, while riba extracts guaranteed gain from another's need, creating exploitation and injustice. The ruling rests on God's authority: He alone defines what is lawful and unlawful, and human analogies cannot override His command. Divine mercy is offered to those who heed the warning and stop: past gains are not held against them, and their final judgment is left to God. Persistence in the practice after the admonition, in defiance and justification, leads to the severe consequence of abiding in the Fire, showing that the gravity lies in obstinate rejection of God's guidance, not merely in a past lapse.

translation: God deprives usury of all blessing, and causes charity to grow in blessing. And God does not love any ungrateful sinner.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth gained through usury, though it appears to increase on the surface, is stripped of true blessing and lasting benefit by God. It may be destroyed, it may bring social ruin, or it may leave its owner without peace or good outcome. Charity, though it seems to reduce one's wealth, is multiplied by God in reward, blessing, and even in social well-being, because it nurtures compassion and solidarity among people. The verse ends with a warning: those who persist in exploiting others through usury, denying God's bounty and persisting in wrongdoing, are ungrateful and sinful, and they forfeit God's love.

translation: Indeed, those who believe, do righteous deeds, establish prayer, and give zakat will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true salvation rests on faith joined with action: belief in God that shows itself in righteous conduct, in worship through prayer (the bond between the servant and the Creator), and in giving zakat (the bond between the believer and society). Those who bring these together are promised a reward that is secured with their Lord, not dependent on worldly recognition, so it cannot be lost or wasted. The promise that they will have no fear and no grief means that on the Day of Judgment, and in the afterlife generally, they will be free from dread of what lies ahead and from sorrow over what they left behind. It also suggests a settled inner peace in this life for those who live by faith and righteous action.

translation: O you who believe! Fear God and give up what remains of usury (riba), if you are truly believers.
interpretation: The verse ties faith directly to economic conduct: genuine belief is shown by obeying God even when it costs money. After the earlier ruling against riba, some people still held outstanding interest claims from before the prohibition. The command to 'give up what remains' means believers must not collect these claims and must break completely with exploitative lending, in which wealth grows from another person's need and hardship rather than from real effort, shared risk, or goodwill. By opening with 'fear God' and closing with 'if you are believers,' the verse treats abandoning usury as a test of sincerity of faith and of God-consciousness, and it calls for a just economy where the strong do not profit from the weak.

translation: And if you do not, then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you shall have your capital sums; you shall neither wrong nor be wronged.
interpretation: This verse sets out the consequence of persisting in usury (riba) after being commanded to abandon it: it is a grave defiance of God's law, tantamount to waging war against God and His Messenger, and the community is entitled to confront such practice. Yet the door of repentance stays open. Whoever repents keeps the original principal of his loan, so he loses nothing of what he actually lent, while he forfeits only the unjust surplus. The closing phrase establishes the principle of economic justice behind the prohibition: the lender must not wrong the borrower by extracting exploitative gain, and the lender must not be wronged by losing his rightful capital. Fairness for both parties is the aim.

translation: And if the debtor is in hardship, then let there be a postponement until a time of ease. But that you remit it as charity is better for you, if only you knew.
interpretation: This verse sets out a merciful ethic for lending in Islam. A creditor whose debtor cannot repay because of real hardship must not press him, jail him, or burden him with extra charges, but must give him time until his circumstances improve. The verse then urges something higher than patience: forgiving part or all of the debt as charity (sadaqah). It is better for the creditor because it purifies his wealth and heart, earns great reward from God, and builds compassion and solidarity in society. The closing phrase, 'if only you knew', invites believers to recognize that what they give up for God's sake is not lost but is repaid by Him with far greater good, in this world and the next.

translation: And fear a Day in which you will be returned to God. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse is a solemn reminder that every human being will one day return to God for judgment, and so it calls believers to live with God-consciousness (taqwa) now, preparing for that Day through faith and righteous conduct. On that Day, justice will be perfect: each person will receive the full recompense of what they themselves earned, whether good or bad, with nothing added to their burden and nothing withheld from their reward. No one will bear the account of another, and no one will suffer injustice. Knowing this should lead a person to hold themselves accountable, avoid wrongdoing, and trust in God's absolute fairness.

translation: O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. Let a scribe write it between you with justice. The scribe must not refuse to write as God has taught him; so let him write, and let the debtor dictate, fearing God his Lord and not diminishing anything of it. If the debtor is feeble-minded, weak, or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate with justice. And call to witness two witnesses from among your men. If there are not two men, then one man and two women from those you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other can remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are called. Do not be averse to writing it down, whether small or large, along with its term. That is more equitable in God's sight, stronger as evidence, and more likely to prevent doubt among you, unless it is an immediate transaction that you conduct between yourselves, in which case there is no blame on you if you do not write it. Take witnesses when you trade with one another. Neither scribe nor witness should be harmed; if you do so, it is wickedness in you. Fear God, and God teaches you; and God has knowledge of all things.
interpretation: This verse establishes a framework for protecting financial rights and social trust: any deferred debt should be documented in writing by a just, impartial scribe, with the debtor himself dictating the terms as an acknowledgment of his obligation, or his guardian doing so if he is incapable. Witnesses add a second layer of verification, and the stated purpose of the rules is fairness, strong evidence, and the removal of doubt and future disputes. Exemptions for immediate, on-the-spot trade show the law's practicality, avoiding needless burden, while the ban on harming scribes and witnesses and the repeated call to God-consciousness show that these legal procedures are to be carried out with integrity and awareness of God, who is the source of such guidance.

translation: If you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, then pledges taken into possession (suffice). And if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted discharge his trust, and let him fear God, his Lord. And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it, his heart is indeed sinful. And God is All-Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse completes the rules of documenting debts in Surah al-Baqarah by addressing situations where writing is not possible, such as travel. In that case, a security pledge handed over to the creditor provides assurance in place of a written record. Where mutual trust exists and no pledge is taken, the debtor bears a moral and religious duty to repay faithfully, and the verse grounds that duty in God-consciousness: he must fear God, who is his Lord and who watches over his dealings. The verse then warns against concealing testimony, because justice in transactions depends on truthful witnesses. It describes the one who hides it as having a sinful heart, which locates the sin in the inner conscience and not merely in the act of silence. It closes by reminding believers that God knows everything they do, so that financial honesty rests on accountability to Him and not only on legal procedure.

translation: To God belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, God will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's dominion is total and extends to the inner life as well as to outward deeds. Because everything belongs to Him, nothing in the human heart, whether openly expressed or kept hidden, is outside His knowledge, and He will bring it into account. This is a call to sincerity and to guarding one's intentions, beliefs, and inner dispositions, not only one's visible actions. Yet the accounting is not automatic condemnation: forgiveness and punishment rest on His will, which is joined with wisdom, justice, and mercy, and which He exercises with perfect power. A believer should therefore live with awareness of God, purify the heart, and hope for His forgiveness while fearing His reckoning.

translation: The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. All of them believe in God, His angels, His Books, and His messengers, saying: 'We make no distinction between any of His messengers.' And they say: 'We hear and we obey. We seek Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.'
interpretation: The verse describes the ideal model of faith in Islam: it is complete, unified, and joined to action. The Prophet himself is first among the believers in holding firmly to the revelation, which shows that he does not merely convey the message but lives by it. The faith of the community is built on the same pillars: belief in God, the angels, the revealed scriptures, and all the messengers, without accepting some and rejecting others, because all of them came from one God with one essential message of tawhid. Real belief is not only a conviction of the heart but also submission in practice, expressed in 'we hear and we obey', in contrast with those who heard and said 'we disobey'. Even so, the believers remain humble and aware of their shortcomings, so they ask for God's forgiveness, and they keep in mind that every person will return to Him and be held to account. The verse thus joins sound belief, obedience, humility, and awareness of the Hereafter.

translation: God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. It will have what it has earned, and it will bear what it has earned. Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like the one You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with more than we have the strength to bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so grant us victory over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This closing verse of Surat al-Baqarah shows that divine law is grounded in mercy and fairness: God's obligations always fall within what a person can actually do, and each person is judged only by what they have deliberately earned, whether good or evil. Because of this, believers are taught to supplicate with confidence, asking God not to hold them to account for honest forgetfulness or error, not to impose on them the heavy, restrictive burdens that were placed on earlier communities as a consequence of their disobedience, and not to test them beyond their endurance. The prayer moves through three stages of divine compassion, pardon (erasing the consequence of sins), forgiveness (covering the sins), and mercy (granting favor going forward), and it ends by affirming God as the believers' sole Protector and asking for His help against those who reject the truth. The verse thus pairs personal responsibility with humble reliance on God, assuring the believer that religion is meant to be livable and that God's support is the final refuge.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Mim.
interpretation: These disconnected letters, which open Surah Al-Baqarah and several other surahs, are best understood as a challenge and a sign of the Qur'an's miraculous nature. The Qur'an is composed of the very letters the Arabs used in their speech, yet its eloquence and depth cannot be matched. By opening with letters pronounced individually, the verse draws the listener's attention to the revelation that follows, and it reminds them that human beings, despite mastering this alphabet, cannot produce anything like it. Their precise meaning is known fully only to God.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divinity belongs to God alone, because only He possesses perfect, self-subsisting life that is never preceded by non-existence nor followed by an end. Al-Hayy means His life is complete and needs nothing, and Al-Qayyum means He stands by Himself and upholds everything else, so that every creature depends on Him moment by moment for its being, provision, and order. Whatever depends on another for its existence or continuation cannot be worthy of worship; therefore, worship, trust, and ultimate hope are rightly directed only to the One who lives without need and sustains all that exists.

translation: He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is revealed by God with truth, free from falsehood, and that it stands in continuity with earlier revelation rather than breaking from it. Its confirmation of the Torah and the Gospel means it verifies their original divine source and their core message of God's oneness, worship of Him alone, and moral guidance, which the Qur'an presents as the same message brought by all prophets. The Qur'an thus acts as a criterion and a guardian over previous scriptures, confirming what is authentic in them and correcting later deviations. The verse invites the People of the Book to recognize the Qur'an as the continuation and culmination of the guidance they already follow.

translation: Before this, as guidance for mankind; and He has sent down the Criterion (the Furqan). Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Almighty, the Lord of retribution.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's revelation has always been a continuous chain of guidance: the earlier scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel, guided people in their times, and the Qur'an is the Furqan, the decisive standard that separates truth from falsehood and right from wrong. Since these signs are clear and the means of discernment have been given, rejecting them is not an excusable mistake but a deliberate turning away from clear evidence, and this is why it carries a severe punishment. The closing names, 'Azīz (Almighty) and Dhū Intiqām (Possessor of retribution), teach that no one can overpower God or escape His justice, and that His retribution is the just consequence for those who knowingly reject His guidance and the truth, not arbitrary vengeance.

translation: Indeed, nothing is hidden from God, whether on the earth or in the heaven.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute and all-encompassing knowledge: no deed, intention, secret, or hidden matter in the whole of creation, seen or unseen, escapes Him. The believer is meant to draw two lessons from this. First, a sense of constant mindfulness (taqwa), in which one acts with sincerity and integrity even when alone, since God is aware of both outward actions and inner thoughts. Second, a source of reassurance, because no injustice, hardship, or sincere effort goes unnoticed by Him, and so He will bring each person to account with perfect knowledge and justice.

translation: He is the One who shapes you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse points to God's absolute power and wisdom through something hidden from all human eyes and control: the forming of each human being in the darkness of the womb. Differences in appearance, sex, character, and destiny are not accidents but the outcome of His will. Since He alone fashions every person individually, with no partner or helper, He alone deserves worship. His being 'the Almighty' means that no one can resist or alter His decree, and His being 'the All-Wise' means that each creation is shaped with purpose and perfect measure. The verse thus refutes the claim that Jesus or anyone else born of a womb could be divine, for whoever is formed in a womb is a created being, shaped by God and dependent on Him.

translation: It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise in meaning, which are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous. As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow the ambiguous part of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But no one knows its true interpretation except God. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.' And none will remember except those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse teaches how to approach the Qur'an's different kinds of verses. Clear verses, which deal with core beliefs, laws and morals, are the anchor and reference point ("mother of the Book"). Ambiguous verses, which touch on matters beyond human perception or admit more than one reading, must be understood in light of the clear ones. People with crooked hearts do the opposite: they cherry-pick the ambiguous verses to stir up doubt and division or to support their own agendas, claiming a final word on matters only God fully knows. The deeply learned respond with humility and faith, returning the unclear to the clear and affirming that everything comes from the same Lord, so it cannot truly contradict itself. Only those who use their intellect sincerely take this lesson to heart, so sound understanding requires both knowledge and a humble, submissive heart.

translation: Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.
interpretation: This is a supplication of those firmly grounded in knowledge, who recognize that guidance is not secured by their own effort but remains entirely in God's hands. Hearts are fragile and can swerve toward doubt, ambiguity, or error even after being guided, so the believers ask God to keep them steadfast on the truth, just as they accepted the clear and the unclear verses alike with faith. They also ask for mercy from God's own presence, which is a gift beyond what they deserve or earn, and they conclude by appealing to His name al-Wahhab, the One who gives freely and generously without being compelled or compensated. The verse teaches humility, constant dependence on God for perseverance in faith, and the need to ask for steadfastness until death.

translation: Our Lord, You will surely gather mankind together on a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.
interpretation: This verse, the closing of a supplication made by those firmly grounded in knowledge (Qur'an 3:7-9), expresses that true understanding of revelation leads to certainty in the Hereafter. Having asked God to keep their hearts from deviating, they affirm their conviction in the Day of Gathering, when every soul will be brought to account and receive its due recompense. Their appeal rests on God's perfect faithfulness: since He never breaks His promise, the believer can trust in the reality of resurrection and judgment, and so lives with accountability, hope for mercy, and steadfastness in faith, asking God to keep them guided until that Day.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve - never will their wealth or their children avail them against God at all. And it is they who are the fuel of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly assets people most rely on for security and status, namely wealth and offspring, carry no weight on the Day of Judgment for someone who persistently rejects faith. Money cannot ransom a person, and children cannot intercede or shield them from God's judgment. Real protection comes only from faith and righteous deeds. Those who die in disbelief, having put their trust in transient things instead of God, will themselves become the fuel of the Fire, which stresses that the consequence is a result of their own choice and that nothing in this world can reverse it.

translation: Like the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes a consistent divine pattern: when nations persistently reject clear signs from God, they are not punished arbitrarily but as a direct consequence of their own sins. Pharaoh's people and earlier communities had power, wealth and status, yet these did not protect them once they denied the truth. The verse warns the disbelievers of the Prophet's time that they are no different, and that their fate will follow the same law unless they change. It also reassures believers that the apparent strength of those who oppose the truth is temporary, because God's justice is certain and His punishment is severe for those who persist in denial and wrongdoing.

translation: Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered together into Hell, and wretched is that resting place.
interpretation: The verse is a divine message the Prophet is commanded to deliver to the disbelievers, assuring the believers that the apparent strength of those who reject the truth is temporary. Their worldly power, numbers and wealth will not protect them: they will be defeated in this world, as happened to them at Badr, and in the next world they will be driven to Hell. Calling Hell a 'resting place' (mihad), a word normally meaning a comfortable bed or cradle, is a deliberate irony. The disbelievers sought ease and security in their rejection of faith, yet the only 'bed' awaiting them is a place of torment. The verse thus strengthens the faith and steadfastness of the believers and warns the disbelievers that final victory and a good end belong to truth, not to worldly might.

translation: There was already a sign for you in the two forces that met in battle: one force fighting in the cause of God, and the other disbelieving. The believers saw them, with their own eyes, as twice their number. God supports with His victory whom He wills. Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who have insight.
interpretation: The verse points to the Battle of Badr as a lasting proof that victory does not depend on numbers or material strength but on God's will and support. A small, poorly equipped group of believers, whose sincerity and reliance on God were firm, prevailed over a much larger force that rested on its own power and pride. Whether the believers saw their enemy as doubled or the disbelievers saw the believers as doubled, God shaped perception and events so that fear and steadfastness fell where He willed, showing that the outcome is in His hands. The verse then calls on people of insight to draw a lesson: to look beyond outward appearances, put their trust in God, stay firm in truth, and not be deceived by the apparent strength of falsehood.

translation: Beautified for people is the love of desires—of women, sons, heaped-up treasures of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and fertile land. That is the enjoyment of worldly life, but with God is the best destination.
interpretation: The verse teaches that attraction to worldly things is a natural part of human nature and a test, not something evil in itself. Spouses, children, wealth, status, livestock and land are lawful sources of comfort, but they are only temporary provisions (mata') of this life. The danger lies in letting them become the ultimate goal, so that the heart is bound to what fades and forgets the return to God. By contrasting them with 'the best destination' (husn al-ma'ab) with God, the verse calls the believer to keep worldly goods in their proper place: to enjoy them with gratitude and moderation, use them in obedience to God, and direct the heart's deepest longing toward the lasting reward of the Hereafter.

translation: Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who are mindful of God, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever, and purified spouses, and approval from God. And God is All-Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: After describing the attractions of worldly life such as women, children, wealth, horses, livestock and farmland, the verse redirects the believer's aspirations toward a far superior and lasting reward. The worldly pleasures are fleeting and often distract from God, whereas what awaits the God-conscious is eternal: gardens that never wither, companions free of all impurity and flaw, and above all God's pleasure (ridwan), which is the greatest of all rewards because it brings with it the assurance that God will never be displeased with them afterward. The qualification 'for those who are mindful of God' shows that this reward is reached through taqwa, meaning that one uses worldly blessings with restraint and gratitude rather than being enslaved by them. The closing statement that God sees His servants is both a reassurance and a warning: He knows who truly deserves this reward by their sincerity and conduct, and no deed or intention is hidden from Him.

translation: Those who say: Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse describes the righteous (the muttaqun) as people whose faith is joined with humility and dependence on God. They present their belief as the means (wasila) through which they ask for forgiveness, and they do not rely on their own deeds to claim salvation. Their prayer shows that true faith involves awareness of one's shortcomings and fear of accountability, so they ask God to erase their sins and shield them from Hell. The believer is thus someone who lives between hope in God's mercy and fear of His punishment, and who turns to Him in constant supplication.

translation: The patient, the truthful, the devoutly obedient, those who spend in the way of God, and those who seek forgiveness before dawn.
interpretation: This verse, which continues the description of the God-fearing (muttaqin) in Surah Al Imran 3:17, shows that true piety is built on a set of complementary inner and outer qualities. Patience gives steadfastness in obedience and in trials. Truthfulness makes the heart, tongue, and deeds consistent with each other. Devout obedience (qunut) is humble, constant submission to God. Spending is generosity that frees the believer from attachment to wealth and serves others. Seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours joins these with humility: even after worship and good works, the believer does not feel self-satisfied but stands in the quiet of the night, when sincerity is greatest and distraction is least, admitting shortcomings and hoping for God's mercy. The verse therefore describes a believer whose character is strong in public conduct and humble in private devotion.

translation: Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and so do the angels and those endowed with knowledge, upholding justice. There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents the oneness of God (tawhid) as a truth established by the strongest possible testimony: God's own witness through His signs and revelation, the angels' witness from their direct knowledge of Him, and the witness of people of knowledge, whose reflection on creation and revelation leads them to the same conclusion. Pairing these witnesses together elevates the rank of true knowledge, since knowledge is shown to lead to faith in One God. The phrase 'upholding justice' means that God's governance of the universe and of moral life is perfectly balanced and equitable. Monotheism is therefore not merely a theological claim but the foundation of a just order, because a single, just Lord requires that no created being be worshipped or obeyed against His law. The closing repetition, with the names 'the Almighty' and 'the All-Wise', affirms that His power is joined with wisdom, so His justice is never arbitrary or weak.

translation: Indeed, the religion in the sight of God is Islam (submission to Him). Those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy and rivalry between themselves. And whoever disbelieves in the signs of God, then indeed God is swift in taking account.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the only way acceptable to God is wholehearted submission to Him alone, the single message carried by all the prophets, and not any sectarian label or inherited identity. It explains that the divisions among the People of the Book did not arise from ignorance or from any lack of clarity in revelation. They arose after clear knowledge reached them, when envy, rivalry, and the desire for status and authority led them to distort, dispute, and split into factions. The closing warning is that anyone who rejects God's signs, whether by denying them or by twisting them to serve worldly motives, will not escape. God's reckoning is swift and precise, so no deviation is hidden or delayed beyond His knowledge, and one should therefore return to humble submission to the truth once it is clear.

translation: So if they dispute with you, say: 'I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me.' And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: 'Have you submitted?' If they submit, they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, your duty is only to convey the message. And God is All-Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: When people argue with the Prophet about the truth of his message, he is told not to be drawn into endless debate but to state plainly where he stands: he and his followers have wholly devoted their whole selves ('face', the center of one's being and orientation) to God alone. He then extends an open invitation to everyone, both the People of the Book and the unlettered Arabs, asking whether they too will submit. The verse sets out the limits of his role. Guidance belongs to those who submit, and if they refuse, his responsibility ends with clearly delivering the message, since he cannot compel faith. The closing reminder that God sees all His servants means He knows who is sincere and who is stubborn, and He alone will judge and recompense them. This consoles the Prophet and removes from him the burden of results.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God, and kill the prophets without right, and kill those among the people who command justice, give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 3:21) shows that rejecting God's revelation naturally leads to hostility toward those who convey it and uphold it. Disbelief here is not merely a private matter of belief but becomes active oppression: first denying the signs, then killing the prophets unjustly, then killing ordinary people who call others to fairness and justice (qist). The verse treats silencing truth-tellers and reformers as a grave crime that stands in the same line as killing prophets. The instruction to 'give them tidings' of a painful punishment is ironic. Good news is replaced with a warning, which makes their expected reward a severe and just recompense. The lesson is that arrogance toward the truth and violence against those who command justice bring divine punishment, and that believers should stand firm for justice even when it is costly.

translation: Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse describes the fate of those who reject God's signs and oppose His guidance (as in the preceding verse of Surah Al Imran, 3:22). Their good deeds are nullified because those deeds were not grounded in faith and sincerity toward God. In this world their efforts bring no lasting blessing, no true standing, and no real success, whatever outward gains they may appear to have. In the Hereafter their deeds carry no weight on the Scale and earn no reward. Having turned away from God, they will find no one to rescue them or intercede for them, since all power and help belong to God alone. The verse is a warning that deeds are valued by God according to the faith and sincerity behind them, not by their outward appearance.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They are invited to the Book of God so that it may judge between them, then a group of them turns away, averse.
interpretation: The verse (Q 3:23) rebukes the People of the Book, Jews in particular according to many commentators, for knowing that their scripture contains clear rulings yet refusing to submit to it when its judgment goes against their desires. They claim to follow the revelation, but when called to let God's Book settle their disputes, such as the matter of stoning for adultery or the truth of the Prophet's message, a party among them turns away willfully. The verse teaches that real faith means accepting divine judgment even when it is inconvenient. Professing belief while rejecting God's ruling out of stubbornness and desire is a sign of heedlessness and hypocrisy, and a warning to any community that claims to follow revelation.

translation: That is because they said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a limited number of days.' And what they used to invent has deceived them in their religion.
interpretation: The verse explains why some of the People of the Book turned away from God's judgment: they held a false belief that their punishment, if any, would be brief and light, as though belonging to a chosen community exempted them from accountability. This invented assurance became a self-made illusion that gave them false security, so they neglected repentance and righteous action. The lesson is that fabricating hopes about God's mercy without basis in revelation, and relying on lineage or religious identity instead of faith and deeds, is a delusion that corrupts religion and leads a person to ruin.

translation: So how will it be when We gather them together for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul is paid in full what it has earned, and they will not be wronged?
interpretation: The verse (Al Imran 3:25) warns those who rejected God's revelation and held false comforts, such as the belief that punishment would touch them only briefly. It asks them to imagine their condition on the Day of Judgment, a day whose coming is certain. On that day no one will be able to rely on lineage, claims of favor, or wishful thinking. Each person will receive the full and exact recompense for what they did in life, whether good or evil. God's judgment will be perfectly just, with no one burdened with another's guilt, deprived of any reward they earned, or punished beyond what they deserve. The rhetorical question 'how will it be' stirs fear and reflection, urging people to hold themselves accountable now and to correct their beliefs and conduct before the certain reckoning.

translation: Say: O Allah, Owner of all sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and take sovereignty away from whom You will; You honor whom You will and humble whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all power, rule, honor and status are ultimately possessed and granted by God alone, so human authority is only a temporary trust that He gives or removes according to His wisdom and justice. Rulers and nations should therefore not become arrogant in their might, and the weak and the oppressed should not despair, since rise and fall are in God's hand. Even what appears to be loss or humiliation falls within His wise purpose, because all good comes from Him and His power encompasses everything. The believer is thus called to turn to God in humility, seek honor and success from Him rather than from people or worldly power, and trust in His decree.
