translation: You cause the night to enter into the day, and You cause the day to enter into the night; You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living; and You provide for whom You will without measure.
interpretation: The verse points to God's absolute and continuous control over the cycles of creation. The alternation of night and day, with each gradually merging into the other as the seasons change, and the emergence of life from lifeless matter (seed from the dead earth, a believer from a disbelieving household) and of death from life, show that every change in the world is governed by one will. The same power that orders these cosmic and natural processes also distributes sustenance and sovereignty as He wills, not constrained by calculation or by anyone's merit or entitlement. The lesson for the believer is to look to God alone for provision, honor, and power, and not to depend on human strength or status, since One who governs time and life itself can give without limit.

translation: Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies in preference to the believers. Whoever does that has nothing to do with God, except when you guard yourselves against them out of real caution. God warns you to beware of Him, and to God is the final return.
interpretation: The verse sets out the principle that a believer's primary loyalty, support and intimate trust belong to the community of faith, not to those who oppose the faith. To prefer disbelievers as close allies over fellow believers, especially in ways that harm the believers or compromise religion, severs one's real connection with God. The exception for guarding oneself recognizes situations of fear or compulsion, where outward courtesy or caution is permitted to protect life and safety, without allowing inward betrayal of faith or the community. This does not forbid justice, kindness and fair dealing with peaceful non-Muslims, which are affirmed elsewhere in the Qur'an. It forbids alliances that undermine religion or the believers. The closing warning reminds believers that God Himself is to be feared more than any people, and since everyone will return to Him for reckoning, loyalties should be decided by accountability before Him and not by worldly gain or fear.

translation: Say: Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, God knows it. He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that nothing of a person's inner life escapes God, so faith and loyalty cannot be mere outward display. In context (the preceding verse warns believers against taking disbelievers as allies in place of believers), secret intentions, hidden sympathies and concealed motives are as fully known to God as open words and deeds. His knowledge reaches everything in the heavens and the earth, and His power over all things means He is able to hold people to account for what they hide. The purpose is to cultivate sincerity and God-consciousness: a believer should purify the heart and keep inner conviction consistent with outward conduct, since accountability extends to the unseen depths of the self, not only to visible actions.

translation: On the Day when every soul will find present before it whatever good it has done, and whatever evil it has done, it will wish that there were a great distance between itself and that evil. And God warns you of Himself; and God is Compassionate toward His servants.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment no deed is lost or forgotten: every act of goodness will be found present and will bring joy, while every evil act will stand before its doer as a source of regret, so that the person will long to be separated from it by a vast distance. The warning 'God cautions you of Himself' is itself an act of mercy, since God alerts people in advance to the reality of accountability so that they may correct themselves while there is still time. This is why the verse ends by stating that God is Compassionate toward His servants: His warning is not meant to crush them but to move them to repent, do good, and avoid evil, combining fear of His justice with hope in His mercy.

translation: Say, [O Muhammad], "If you love Allah, then follow me, [so] Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: This verse sets the test of genuine love for God: a claim of love is not proven by words or feelings alone but by following the Prophet Muhammad, who conveys God's guidance and models it in his conduct. Obedience to him is the practical expression of devotion to God. The reward is reciprocal and greater than what the believer offers: whoever follows the Prophet is loved by God, and that divine love brings forgiveness of sins. The closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, reassure believers that although they are imperfect, sincere effort to follow the Prophet's way leads them to God's pardon and mercy.

translation: Say: Obey God and the Messenger. But if they turn away, then indeed God does not love the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse (Q 3:32) makes love of God concrete: it is shown through obedience to Him and to His Messenger, not through claims or feelings alone. The Messenger is the practical model through whom God's guidance is understood and lived, so obeying him is part of obeying God. Turning away from this obedience after the truth has become clear is a form of rejection (kufr), and those who persist in it forfeit God's love. The statement does not mean God ceases to be just or merciful to them, but that they lose the special closeness and approval reserved for those who submit and follow the guidance.

translation: Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Imran above all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah's choosing of certain prophets and their righteous households is an act of divine selection based on His knowledge of their purity and devotion, not on mere lineage. By naming Adam, the first human and prophet; Noah, the father of the second beginning of humanity; and the families of Abraham and Imran, from whom came many prophets including Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Jesus, and Mary, the verse presents a continuous chain of guidance. Their being preferred 'above the worlds' means they were distinguished above the people of their own times through prophethood and moral excellence, so that humanity might follow this single path of submission to God. It also prepares the context of the surrounding passage, which shows that true honor lies in faithful obedience to Allah and that the message brought by Muhammad is the continuation of this blessed line rather than a departure from it.

translation: They were offspring, one from the other; and God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse (Al 'Imran 3:34) describes the chosen families mentioned just before it: Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of 'Imran. They are linked by lineage and, more importantly, by shared faith, sincerity and righteousness, each generation carrying forward the guidance of the one before. God's selection of them was therefore not arbitrary, because He hears their words and supplications and knows their inner sincerity and worthiness. The closing names, 'All-Hearing, All-Knowing', point to God's awareness of the prayer of the wife of 'Imran, who vowed her unborn child to His service, and to His knowledge of who truly deserves to be chosen.

translation: When the wife of Imran said, 'My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, devoted entirely to Your service, so accept it from me. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.'
interpretation: The verse shows a mother's sincere dedication of her unborn child to God. By vowing the child as 'muharraran', freed from worldly obligations and set apart for devotion and service at the sanctuary, she gives up her own claim on what she most dearly hopes for. Her plea 'accept it from me' shows humility and awareness that no act of devotion has worth unless God accepts it, and her closing appeal to God as the All-Hearing and All-Knowing shows trust that He hears her private prayer and knows her intention and what lies hidden in her womb. The lesson is that true worship rests on sincere intention, surrender of what one cherishes, and reliance on God's acceptance rather than on one's own deeds.

translation: So when she delivered her, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered a female" — and God knew best what she had delivered — "and the male is not like the female. And I have named her Mary, and I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from Satan, the accursed."
interpretation: The verse shows the humility and devotion of the mother of Mary (the wife of Imran). She had vowed her unborn child to the service of God, expecting a son, since only males customarily served in the temple. When a daughter was born she voiced her surprise and a touch of sorrow, but the parenthetical remark that God knows best what she bore shows that God's choice was wiser than her expectation: this girl would be greater than any son she had hoped for, becoming the mother of the Messiah Jesus. Her words 'the male is not like the female' acknowledge the difference between what she wished for and what God gave, while implying that this daughter was exceptional. By naming the child Mary and at once placing her and her descendants under God's protection from Satan, she teaches that a believer responds to unexpected outcomes with trust and prayer, and that the best protection for children is entrusting them to God from the moment of birth.

translation: So her Lord accepted her with a gracious acceptance and caused her to grow in a good, wholesome way, and entrusted her to the care of Zechariah. Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her. He said, 'O Mary, from where does this come to you?' She said, 'It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without measure.'
interpretation: The verse shows God's direct care for those who are devoted to Him. Mary, dedicated to God's service by her mother, was not left without support: God accepted her, nurtured her in purity and righteousness, and placed her under the guardianship of a righteous prophet. The provision found in her prayer chamber, which seemed to come from outside the ordinary means, is a sign of divine favor and honor, while her answer shows the depth of her faith and God-consciousness, since she attributed every blessing to God rather than to herself or to any worldly cause. The closing statement teaches that God's bounty is limitless and not bound by human calculation or expectation, so the believer should trust Him as the true Provider, and that He gives to whom He wills out of His wisdom and generosity, as Zechariah's own hope for a child in the following verses illustrates.

translation: There and then Zechariah called upon his Lord. He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication."
interpretation: When Zechariah saw how God provided Mary with sustenance out of season, with no apparent worldly means, his heart was stirred to hope that the One who could do this could also grant him a child despite his old age and his wife's barrenness. His prayer shows the proper etiquette of supplication: he turns to God as 'Rabb' (his Lord and Nurturer), asks for the child as a gift 'from Yourself' (min ladunka) rather than through ordinary causes, and asks specifically for 'good' offspring, meaning righteous descendants who will carry on faith and prophetic guidance, not merely an heir for worldly purposes. He concludes by affirming his certainty that God hears every prayer. The verse teaches that witnessing God's signs should increase our hope in His boundless power and move us to ask Him for what seems impossible.

translation: Then the angels called out to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: "Indeed, God gives you good tidings of Yahya (John), confirming a word from God, and noble, chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous."
interpretation: The verse shows that God answers the sincere supplication of a devoted servant at the very moment he is engaged in worship. Zechariah had asked for righteous offspring despite his old age, and the reply came while he was praying, which teaches that closeness to God in prayer is the setting in which hope is fulfilled. The qualities given to Yahya also define the ideal of prophetic leadership. He would affirm Jesus as 'a word from God', meaning that he would be the first to believe in the miraculous creation of Jesus by God's command 'Be'. He would be 'sayyid', a noble leader, honored for his knowledge, forbearance and piety. He would be 'hasur', one who restrains himself from worldly desires and devotes himself to God. And he would be a prophet among the righteous, so that his prophethood was joined with moral excellence. The verse therefore presents Yahya as a model of faith, self-discipline and righteous guidance, and presents his birth as a sign of God's power to give what seems impossible.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, how shall I have a son when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?' He said, 'Even so does God do what He wills.'
interpretation: Zechariah's question is not doubt in God's power but wonder and a request for reassurance, expressing how great the gift is given the natural impediments of his advanced age and his wife's barrenness. The angel's answer, 'Even so does God do what He wills,' teaches that God's will is not bound by natural causes or ordinary expectations. The same Power that created the natural order can suspend or transcend it, so the birth of John (Yahya) is a sign that nothing is beyond God's will, and believers should hold their hope in Him even when circumstances seem to make fulfillment impossible.

translation: He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days except by gesture. And remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the evening and in the early morning."
interpretation: Zechariah, stunned by the promise of a son in his old age, asks for a sign so that his heart may be reassured and he may know when the promise begins to take effect. The sign is a miracle: though his body is sound, he is unable to speak to people for three days, except by gestures. His tongue is held back from ordinary conversation but remains free for worship. This shows that the inability is not an illness but a divine act that marks the beginning of the miraculous conception. The command to remember God abundantly and glorify Him morning and evening teaches that in moments of silence from worldly talk, one should turn fully to God. The best response to a great blessing is increased remembrance and gratitude, and the period of withdrawal from people becomes a time of spiritual devotion in preparation for the blessing.

translation: And [remember] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds."
interpretation: This verse presents Mary's elevation as a divine act of grace, not a result of lineage or worldly status. Her being 'chosen' means God selected her for a unique mission: devotion, the miraculous birth of Jesus, and serving as a sign for all people. Her being 'purified' points to the cleansing of her heart and conduct from sin and from the slanders that would later be directed at her, so that she could bear that trust with integrity. The repetition of 'chosen' stresses two stages: first being accepted for worship and sanctuary service, then being distinguished above the women of her own time or of all ages for her exemplary faith, obedience, and patience. The verse teaches that true honor comes from God's acceptance and from purity of faith and character, and it prepares Mary for the trial ahead by assuring her that she is under God's care.

translation: O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow down with those who bow down.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to Mary after the angels declare her chosen and purified above the women of the worlds, teaches that divine favor calls for deeper gratitude and worship rather than pride. Being chosen does not exempt a person from devotion; it increases the duty of humble, constant obedience. The command moves from the inner state of qunut (sustained, humble submission of heart) to the outward acts of sujud and ruku', showing that true devotion joins inner humility with bodily worship. The phrase 'with those who bow down' stresses that worship is not only private but is also shared with the community of believers, so that even the most honored servant of God stands in the same rank of servitude as all others.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen, which We reveal to you, [O Muhammad]. You were not with them when they cast their pens [to determine] which of them would take charge of Mary, and you were not with them when they disputed.
interpretation: God affirms that the story of Mary's birth and upbringing, which Muhammad could not have witnessed, is knowledge that reached him only through revelation. He was not present when the priests and worshippers of the temple cast lots with their pens to decide who would be Mary's guardian, each wanting the honor of raising her, nor when they argued among themselves over it. Since he had no human source for these hidden events and was unlettered, his accurate account of them stands as evidence of the truth of his prophethood and of the Qur'an as divine revelation. It also shows how highly regarded Mary was, since people competed to care for her.

translation: When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God gives you good tidings of a Word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, honored in this world and the Hereafter, and among those brought near to God."
interpretation: This verse presents Jesus as a miraculous creation of God, not as a divine or semi-divine being. He is called a "Word from Him" because he came into being through God's creative command "Be," without a human father, and so he is a sign of God's power. His identity is stated plainly: he is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, which links him to his mother and affirms his human lineage. The phrase "honored in this world and the Hereafter" shows that his dignity is a gift from God. In this life he is honored through prophethood, miracles, and his mission to the Children of Israel. In the next life he is honored through his high rank and his place among those nearest to God. The announcement also honors Mary, who is chosen to receive a message of great good news. The verse thus gives Jesus a position of high honor while keeping him within the bounds of servanthood to God.

translation: He will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity, and he will be among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse, part of the glad tidings given to Mary about Jesus (Qur'an 3:46), presents his speaking as a sign of divine support and a mark of his prophetic mission. His speech as an infant, defending his mother's honor and declaring himself God's servant, was a miracle that testified to her innocence and to his own truthfulness. Mentioning his speech in maturity alongside it implies that the message he delivered as an infant was the same one he carried as an adult: calling people to worship God alone, with no change or deviation between the two stages of his life. Describing him as one of the righteous affirms that his character was consistently upright, so that his miraculous beginning was matched by a life of sincerity and obedience to God.

translation: She said, "My Lord, how will I have a child when no man has touched me?" He said, "Thus does Allah create what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."
interpretation: Mary's question is not doubt but amazement and a request to understand how the promised child would come about, since she knew that children ordinarily come through marriage. God's reply teaches that His power is not bound by the natural causes He has set in the world. Ordinary means such as a father are His habit, not a limit on Him, so the birth of Jesus without a father is as easy for Him as any other creation. Creation requires no effort or preparation from Him, only His will, expressed in the command 'Be.' The verse calls the believer to trust God's power and accept what seems impossible by human standards.

translation: And He will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel.
interpretation: This verse, part of the glad tidings given to Mary about Jesus (Qur'an 3:48), shows that God prepares Jesus for his mission through divine knowledge. 'The Book' refers to the skill of writing and the understanding of revealed scripture, while 'wisdom' is sound judgment and the ability to place knowledge and action in their right place. The Torah is mentioned because Jesus came confirming the law of Moses, and the Gospel because it was the revelation entrusted to him personally. The verse therefore teaches that prophethood is not self-made but a gift of God's instruction: Jesus' learning, insight and message all originate from God, which affirms his role as a true messenger who continued the line of earlier prophets rather than founding a separate, divinely independent authority.

translation: And [God will make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying]: 'I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: I create for you from clay the likeness of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by God's permission. And I heal the blind from birth and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by God's permission. And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.'
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus' miracles as proofs of his prophethood, not of divinity. Each act is explicitly tied to 'God's permission,' stressing that the power belongs to God alone and that Jesus is a servant and messenger through whom God manifests signs. The miracles address the people's circumstances: creation-like acts, healing and raising the dead, and knowledge of the unseen details of their private lives. They serve as evidence to verify his message, and the closing line makes clear that these signs benefit only those willing to believe, since faith depends on a receptive heart and not merely on witnessing wonders.

translation: And [I come] confirming what was before me of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you. And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear God and obey me.
interpretation: In this verse Jesus declares that his mission does not abolish the earlier revelation but affirms the Torah's divine origin and its core guidance. He was sent to lift certain burdens and restrictions imposed upon the Children of Israel, whether because of their disobedience or the rigidity of legalistic practice, so that the religion returns to ease and mercy. His authority rests not on his own claim but on clear signs (miracles) granted by God, which prove his prophethood. He then calls his people to the two pillars of faith: taqwa, a conscious reverence of God, and obedience to the messenger, whose obedience is in reality obedience to God, since he conveys only what God has commanded.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Jesus (peace be upon him) in Surah Maryam and Al Imran, makes clear that he himself is a servant of God and not divine. He affirms that the One who created and sustains him is the same Lord who sustains everyone else, so the only fitting response is to worship that Lord alone. Worship rooted in recognizing God's exclusive lordship is the single, balanced road without deviation, free of both excess and neglect, that leads a person to God and to salvation. Anyone who claims otherwise about Jesus departs from the very path he himself called people to.

translation: When Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said: 'Who will be my helpers in the cause of God?' The disciples said: 'We are the helpers of God. We believe in God, and bear witness that we are Muslims (submitters to God).'
interpretation: The verse shows that when Jesus perceived stubborn rejection among his people, he sought sincere supporters whose aid would be directed to God's cause, not to his own person. The disciples' response shows that true discipleship rests on faith and submission: they declare themselves helpers of God, affirm belief in Him, and call Jesus to witness that they are 'muslims', meaning those who surrender wholly to God. The message is that Islam, as submission to God alone, was the essence of the religion of all prophets, and that faith must be confirmed by active support for the truth when it is met with denial.

translation: Our Lord, we believe in what You have revealed and we follow the Messenger, so record us among those who bear witness.
interpretation: This is the supplication of the disciples of Jesus, who pair their inner faith in God's revelation with practical obedience to His messenger, showing that true belief is not complete without following the guidance brought by the prophet. Their request to be recorded among 'those who bear witness' is a plea to be counted with the community that testifies to the truth of God's oneness and the messengers' message, whether as witnesses to the truth in this life or as witnesses over humanity on the Day of Judgment. It teaches that a believer should combine faith, obedience, and humble prayer, relying on God to confirm and preserve him among the righteous witnesses rather than trusting in his own deeds.

translation: And they plotted, and God plotted; and God is the best of those who plot.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 3:54) speaks of the plotting of those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved in Jesus and sought to harm him. God's 'plotting' is not deceit or wrongdoing as humans understand it, but His subtle and just counter-plan that foils the schemes of the wrongdoers without their awareness. While they devised their plans against Jesus, God's superior design protected him by raising him to Himself and rendering their plot ineffective. The lesson is that no human scheming can overcome God's will and wisdom, and that He alone is the most effective in bringing about justice and defending His chosen servants.

translation: When God said: 'O Jesus, I will take you [in death or in full receipt] and raise you to Myself, and purify you from those who disbelieve, and I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ.'
interpretation: The verse is God's reassurance to Jesus after the plot of his enemies against him. God promises four things: that He will cause Jesus's earthly term to be completed so that no enemy can harm or kill him; that He will raise him to a place of honor in His presence; that He will cleanse him from the slander and company of those who rejected him; and that those who truly follow Jesus, by believing in him as God's servant and messenger, will remain uppermost over the deniers in proof and support until the Day of Resurrection. The verse ends by reminding all of the final return to God, where He alone will settle the disputes about Jesus and the truth of his message, so that human disagreement does not undermine the certainty of God's decisive judgment.

translation: As for those who disbelieved, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: This verse (Al Imran 3:56) declares that persistent, willful rejection of God's truth after the clear proofs have come carries real consequences. The 'severe punishment in the world' includes humiliation, defeat, fear, anxiety and the loss of inner peace and security that often accompany a life turned away from God, as well as the worldly ruin that can befall those who oppose truth through oppression. In the Hereafter the punishment is a fuller and more lasting reckoning. The phrase 'they will have no helpers' stresses that no power, ally, wealth, or intercessor can protect them from God's decree, so the verse is a warning that human support is worthless against divine justice, and it also reassures the believers, here the followers of Jesus, that God defends His truth and those faithful to it.

translation: As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. And God does not love the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse sets two outcomes side by side: sincere faith joined with righteous action earns full, undiminished recompense from God, who withholds nothing owed to the believers and gives generously beyond what they deserve. The closing statement that God does not love the wrongdoers shows that injustice, whether through disbelief, denying others their rights, or wronging oneself by disobedience, places a person outside God's love and favor. Faith is therefore not mere belief but must be proven through good deeds, and divine justice ensures that the righteous are rewarded and the unjust are not.

translation: This We recite to you, [O Muhammad], of the verses and the wise reminder.
interpretation: After recounting the story of Jesus' birth and the Christians' dispute about him (Surah Aal Imran 3:59 and preceding verses), God affirms that what the Prophet is being told is not human conjecture but revelation from Him. The narrative is part of God's clear signs, which prove the truth of the Prophet's message since he could only have known these matters through divine inspiration. The Qur'an is described as 'al-dhikr al-hakim', a reminder that is wise, meaning it is free of contradiction and error, firmly established, and full of wisdom that settles disputes. The verse thus calls people to rely on this revealed account, rather than on speculation, for the truth about Jesus and other matters of faith.

translation: Indeed, the likeness of Jesus in the sight of God is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, 'Be,' and he was.
interpretation: The verse answers the claim that Jesus must be divine because he was born without a human father. It points out that Adam had neither father nor mother, yet no one considers him divine. Both were brought into being by God's creative command 'Be', so an extraordinary birth shows God's power and does not make Jesus more than a human servant and messenger. God's ability to create is not limited by ordinary causes, and the miraculous origin of Jesus is no ground for worshipping him.

translation: The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 2:147) affirms that the truth is whatever comes from God, and not what is shaped by the claims of people, their desires, or the disputes among them. It is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, but its call extends to every believer: after the question of the direction of prayer (the change of qibla to the Ka'bah) and the rejection of that change by some of the People of the Book, who knew the truth yet concealed it, the believer is urged to hold firm. Certainty rests on revelation from the Lord who nurtures and guides, so doubt has no place in the heart. The believer should not let the denial of opponents or the confusion they spread shake their confidence in what God has revealed.

translation: Whoever disputes with you concerning him after the knowledge that has come to you, say: 'Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us earnestly invoke and place the curse of God upon those who lie.'
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Prophet Muhammad's debate with the Christian delegation of Najran over the nature of Jesus, shows that once clear knowledge has come through revelation, further argument is pointless, and the final recourse is a mutual invocation (mubahala) in which each side calls on God to curse the liar. By having each party bring their families and themselves, the verse shows the seriousness and sincerity of the challenge: only someone fully certain of the truth would stake his own life and the lives of his loved ones on it. The verse thus affirms that the truth about Jesus being a created servant and messenger of God, not divine, is so firmly established that the Prophet could confidently submit it to divine judgment, while the call itself invites opponents to reflect on whether they are truly sure of their own claims.

translation: Indeed, this is the true narrative. And there is no deity except Allah. And indeed, Allah is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: After recounting the story of Jesus, his miraculous birth, and the Christian claim to his divinity (Qur'an 3:59-60), the verse affirms that the Qur'anic account is the authentic, reliable history, free from the exaggerations and distortions that later arose about him. The conclusion drawn from this true account is that Jesus was a created human messenger, and that divinity belongs to God alone, who has no partner, son, or equal. The closing names, al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and al-Hakim (the Wise), reinforce the point: God's power is such that He creates as He wills, whether Adam without parents or Jesus without a father, and His wisdom is such that nothing He does is without purpose, so He needs no offspring or helper to share His rule.

translation: But if they turn away, then indeed God is All-Knowing of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse (Al Imran 3:63) closes the passage inviting the People of the Book to the pure worship of God alone. It teaches that the Prophet's duty is only to convey the message clearly. If people reject it after the proof has been presented, their refusal is not a matter of ignorance but of corruption (fasad), whether in belief, in ethics, or in the order of society. God knows their true motives, their hidden schemes and their actions, so nothing escapes Him. The verse is therefore both a consolation for the believers, who need not despair or force anyone to believe, and a quiet warning to the deniers that they will be held to account. Those who turn from truth out of stubbornness are classed as corrupters, and God will judge them with full knowledge.

translation: Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a common word between us and you: that we worship none but God, that we associate no partner with Him, and that none of us take others as lords besides God. And if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims (submitting to God).
interpretation: The verse is an invitation to dialogue grounded in the shared core of the Abrahamic faiths: pure devotion to the One God. It asks that no human being, whether priest, scholar, or ruler, be given the authority to make lawful or unlawful what God has not, or be obeyed as though divine. Real monotheism means freedom from all forms of human lordship and exclusive submission to God alone. The verse also sets out a respectful way of engaging others: first offer common ground, and if they refuse, do not argue or coerce, but simply affirm your own submission to God and let them be witnesses to it.

translation: O People of the Book, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not then use reason?
interpretation: The verse rebukes Jews and Christians who each claimed Abraham as belonging to their own religion. It points to a plain historical fact: the Torah was sent down after Abraham's time through Moses, and the Gospel after that through Jesus. Abraham therefore could not have been a follower of a Judaism or Christianity that took its defined form only through those later scriptures. The argument is one of simple reasoning and chronology, and the closing question 'Will you not use reason?' shows that the claim is irrational. The verse prepares for the next verses, which state that Abraham was a upright monotheist (hanif) and a Muslim, meaning one who submitted to God, and not a sectarian adherent of a later communal label. True kinship with Abraham comes from following his pure monotheism and submission to God, not from claiming his lineage or appropriating his name for a particular group.

translation: Here you are—those who argued about what you have some knowledge of; so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of? And God knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the People of the Book for their dispute over Abraham. They had argued about matters on which they had some knowledge, such as what was revealed to them in the Torah and the Gospel about their own religious affairs, and even that was questionable. But they then argued about Abraham, claiming he was a Jew or a Christian, when they had no knowledge of this, because the Torah and the Gospel were revealed only after his time. The verse teaches that debate must rest on knowledge and evidence, and that a person must not speak confidently about what he does not know. It also teaches that the truth about past prophets and unseen matters belongs to God alone, who knows the reality of Abraham's faith (that he was a upright monotheist, not a Jew or a Christian), and that people should defer to His revelation rather than to conjecture and partisanship.

translation: Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was upright, one who submitted to God (a Muslim), and he was never among the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Abraham's religion predates the formation of the Jewish and Christian communities, so neither can claim him exclusively as their own. He stood for pure monotheism: he turned away from every form of falsehood (hanif) and surrendered himself wholly to God (muslim, in the sense of one who submits), and he never associated partners with God. True kinship with Abraham is therefore measured by adherence to his pure, God-centered faith and submission, not by lineage or by belonging to a later sectarian label.

translation: Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe. And Allah is the Protector of the believers.
interpretation: Closeness to Abraham is determined not by lineage, claims of inheritance, or communal affiliation, but by adherence to his pure monotheism and submission to God. The ones with the truest claim to him are those who truly followed his path in his own time, the Prophet Muhammad who carries the same message of pure devotion to One God, and the believers who follow that Prophet. This answers the Jews and Christians who each claimed Abraham as their own, showing that spiritual kinship rests on faith and conduct. The closing phrase reassures the believers that God is their ally and guardian, supporting and aiding them as heirs to the faith of Abraham.

translation: A party of the People of the Book wish they could lead you astray, but they lead astray only themselves, and they do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse (Aal 'Imran 3:69) discloses the hidden desire of some Jews and Christians to turn the believers away from their guidance, whether by casting doubt, distorting the truth, or inviting them to abandon the faith. It tells the believers that this effort will ultimately rebound on those who make it. By striving to misguide others and rejecting the truth they know, they bear the burden of their own deviation and add to it the guilt of trying to mislead others, while the believers who hold firm to God's guidance are protected. Their tragedy is compounded by their heedlessness: they do not realize that they are the true losers, because their hearts are blinded by envy and stubbornness. The verse thus reassures the believers and warns that those who plot against truth harm only their own souls.

translation: O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the verses of God while you bear witness?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Jews and Christians for rejecting the clear signs of God, including the revelation brought by Prophet Muhammad, even though they know in their hearts that these signs are true. Their own scriptures describe the coming Prophet and affirm the unity and message of God, so their disbelief is not due to ignorance but to stubbornness, envy, and attachment to status or tradition. The words 'while you bear witness' show that denial after knowledge is a graver fault than denial from ignorance, and they call people of knowledge to honesty and accountability for what they know to be true.

translation: O People of the Scripture, why do you mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Jews and Christians for deliberately confusing people about the truth. They did this by blending genuine revelation with distortions, misleading interpretations and invented claims, so that the two could not be told apart. They also hid clear signs they knew to be true, especially the descriptions of the Prophet Muhammad in their own scriptures. The decisive phrase is 'while you know': their fault was not ignorance but willful concealment, which makes it a betrayal of the trust given to those who hold knowledge. The lesson is that anyone entrusted with knowledge must keep truth distinct from falsehood and must not suppress it for worldly interest, pride, or group loyalty.

translation: A group of the People of the Book said: 'Believe in what was sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, so that perhaps they will turn back.'
interpretation: The verse exposes a scheme by some Jewish scholars in Medina to undermine the early Muslim community by feigning conversion. They would pretend to accept Islam in the morning, then publicly renounce it in the evening, claiming they had examined the new religion and found it lacking. Because they were known as people of scripture and knowledge, their apparent disillusionment might make weaker believers doubt their faith and leave it. The verse shows that the Qur'an knows the hidden plots against the believers, and it reassures the community that such deception cannot extinguish the truth, since God discloses the schemes of those who plot against His religion.

translation: And do not believe except in one who follows your religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God—that anyone may be given the like of what you were given, or that they may argue with you before your Lord. Say: Indeed, grace is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse exposes the jealousy and communal exclusivism of a group among the People of the Book, who told one another to trust only those who followed their own religion and to conceal what God had revealed to them, fearing that Muslims would receive revelation like theirs or use their own scripture as proof against them on the Day of Judgment. God instructs the Prophet to answer that true guidance is only God's guidance, not a monopoly of any group or lineage. Prophethood and revelation are God's favor, wholly in His hand, and He gives them to whomever He wills according to His boundless generosity and perfect knowledge of who is fit to receive it. No people can restrict His grace, and envy cannot prevent His bounty from reaching those He chooses.

translation: He singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Baqarah 2:105, and similarly Al-Imran 3:74) teaches that divine mercy, including guidance, prophethood, and revelation, is a gift from God and not something earned by lineage, group affiliation, or the wishes of any people. Those who resent the believers receiving the Qur'an have no claim to dictate where God places His favor. God chooses recipients of His mercy according to His wisdom and knowledge of who is fit for it, and His generosity is so vast that no one's receiving it diminishes what He gives to others. The believer is therefore called to gratitude and humility rather than pride, and to recognize that any good they have is a bounty from God.

translation: Among the People of the Scripture is he who, if you entrust him with a heap of gold, will return it to you; and among them is he who, if you entrust him with a single dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him demanding it. That is because they say, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered people.' And they speak a lie about God while they know.
interpretation: The verse teaches fairness and honesty in judging others: the Qur'an does not condemn the People of the Scripture as a single block, but acknowledges that some are scrupulously trustworthy even with great wealth, while others betray trust over a trivial sum and return it only under constant pressure. The cause of such betrayal is a self-serving moral justification: those who say that no sin or accountability attaches to taking the property of the 'unlettered' (the Arabs or other outsiders to their community) are inventing a false religious ruling and attributing it to God. Their wrong is compounded because they know that God never permitted such injustice. The lesson is that trustworthiness is a universal obligation owed to all people regardless of faith or community, and that attributing one's greed or prejudice to divine law is a grave lie.

translation: Indeed, whoever fulfills his covenant and is mindful of God—surely God loves the righteous (those who are conscious of Him).
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that people can evade accountability or gain God's favor through lineage, claims of privilege, or trickery with oaths and trusts. It teaches that nearness to God is secured only by honoring one's commitments, whether to God (faith and obedience) or to people (promises, trusts, and agreements), and by taqwā, a constant God-consciousness that restrains a person from betrayal and wrongdoing. Those who combine faithfulness to their word with awareness of God are the ones He loves, so integrity in covenant-keeping is presented as a mark of true piety and a path to divine love.

translation: Indeed, those who exchange God's covenant and their oaths for a small price will have no share in the Hereafter, and God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them; and they will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns against betraying trust and swearing falsely for worldly gain. Those who break their covenant with God, or use oaths in His name to take what is not theirs, such as property, rights, or advantage, trade something sacred and lasting for something trivial and fleeting, however large the gain may appear in this world. The punishment fits the offense. They treated God's name and covenant as cheap, so they lose any portion of the Hereafter. They are denied God's address and His merciful regard, and He does not cleanse them of their sins. The severity shows how grave dishonesty in the name of God is: oaths and promises are sacred obligations, and exploiting them for material gain forfeits one's standing before God.

translation: And indeed, among them is a party who twist their tongues with the Scripture so that you may think it is from the Scripture, though it is not from the Scripture. And they say, 'It is from Allah,' though it is not from Allah. And they speak a lie about Allah while they know.
interpretation: The verse exposes a deliberate act of scriptural falsification by some among the People of the Book: they distort the recitation through tongue-twisting, altering intonation, wording, or meaning, so that listeners mistake their own additions and interpretations for divine revelation. The deeper point is that the sin is compounded by knowledge and intent. They do not err innocently; they knowingly attribute human words to God in order to lend false authority to their views, and so deceive others. The verse thereby warns that attributing anything to God without sound basis is a grave lie, and that believers must carefully verify what is claimed to be revealed and not be swayed by skilled recitation or the appearance of religious authority.

translation: It is not for any human being to whom God has given the Scripture, the judgment, and prophethood to then say to people, 'Be worshippers of me instead of God.' Rather, [he would say], 'Be devoted scholars of the Lord, because of what you have been teaching of the Scripture and because of what you have been studying.'
interpretation: The verse affirms the purity of prophethood and revelation: a prophet, having been entrusted with divine scripture, wisdom, and authority, could never call people to worship him, since his whole mission is to direct people to God alone. The true outcome of learning and teaching the Book is to become rabbānī, meaning people thoroughly devoted to God, who are shaped by knowledge and make their learning a means of obedience and closeness to Him. Knowledge of scripture is therefore not for status or for gaining followers, but for cultivating sincere servitude to God, and anyone who claims divinity or demands human worship for himself contradicts the very message he carries. This also refutes the claims of those who say that prophets such as Jesus asked to be worshipped.

translation: Nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have become Muslims (those who submit to God)?
interpretation: The verse says that no true prophet would ever call people to worship him or to treat angels or other prophets as divine lords besides God. Elevating any created being to the status of a lord, whether by worshipping it or by giving it the right to legislate what is lawful and forbidden, amounts to disbelief. Such a call would contradict the very message of submission to God that the prophets bring and that their followers have already accepted. So anyone who claims that Jesus or any other prophet asked to be worshipped is mistaken, because the prophets' mission was pure monotheism and they would not lead people from faith back into disbelief.

translation: And when God took the covenant of the prophets, saying: 'Whatever I give you of the Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall support him.' He said: 'Do you affirm and accept My binding commitment on that?' They said: 'We affirm.' He said: 'Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that all prophethood is a single, unified divine mission, and that every prophet was bound by a solemn covenant with God to believe in and aid any later messenger who came confirming the truth they had been given. Loyalty to one's own prophet therefore cannot be a reason to reject a subsequent one sent by the same God. Since the covenant was taken from the prophets themselves, their followers are even more strictly bound by it. This implies that followers of earlier scriptures are obliged to believe in the final messenger, Muhammad, who confirms what came before him. The scene of the prophets affirming the covenant, God calling them to bear witness, and God Himself witnessing with them underscores the gravity and binding force of this commitment.

translation: Then whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 3:82) comes after God recounts the covenant He took from the prophets to believe in and support the messenger who would confirm what they had been given. It teaches that once the truth has been made clear through a binding covenant and unmistakable proofs, turning away from it is no mere error or ignorance but fusūq, a deliberate exit from obedience to God. Those who knowingly abandon a commitment they have recognized as true place themselves outside the bounds of faithful submission. The verse stresses that responsibility rises with knowledge: the clearer the guidance and the firmer the pledge, the graver the fault of breaking it.

translation: Do they seek other than the religion of God, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who turn away from submission to God (Islam) and look for some other way of life. All creation already lives under God's command: the heavens, the earth and everything in them follow His laws and decree, and no being can escape His will. Believers submit willingly and by choice, while others submit unwillingly, since they cannot resist His decree over their birth, sustenance, sickness, death and the natural order. Because everything ends in return to Him, seeking any religion other than His is irrational and futile. The sensible course is to submit to Him freely and sincerely now, before the return when submission will be compelled and no choice remains.

translation: Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses, Jesus, and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith as accepting the unity of divine revelation. All prophets, whatever their era or people, brought the same essential message from the one God, so a believer honors every one of them and rejects the sectarian habit of accepting some messengers while denying others. Being a Muslim, in the sense of one who submits, means surrendering wholeheartedly to God and recognizing the continuity of His guidance from Abraham through Moses and Jesus to the final revelation, without favoritism or division among His messengers.

translation: And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.
interpretation: This verse (Al 'Imran 3:85) affirms that the only path accepted by God is islam in its fundamental sense: submission and devotion to God alone, the single message carried by all the prophets, from Noah and Abraham to Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad, peace be upon them. To seek any other way, whether by rejecting God's final revelation after it has become clear, by associating partners with Him, or by inventing a way of worship He has not sanctioned, is to build one's life on something God will not accept. Such deeds will not count for the person on the Day of Judgment, and he will have lost the very purpose for which he was created, which is true loss because nothing can compensate for it. The verse is a call to return to sincere submission to God, which is the way of salvation.

translation: How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and after they had witnessed that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs had come to them? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse expresses the improbability, and indeed the unfitness, of divine guidance for those who knowingly turned away from the truth. They had believed, borne witness to the Prophet's truthfulness, and seen clear evidence, yet they reverted to disbelief out of stubbornness, envy, or worldly interest rather than ignorance. Since their rejection came after certainty and with full knowledge, they have wronged themselves by placing falsehood where truth belongs. God's withholding of guidance from them is therefore a just consequence of their own deliberate choice, not an arbitrary act: guidance is not forced upon those who, having recognized the truth, willfully reject it, and so God leaves such wrongdoers to the path they have chosen.

translation: Those—their recompense is that upon them is the curse of God, the angels, and all people together.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 3:87) teaches that those who knowingly turn away from truth after having accepted it and witnessed clear proofs have forfeited the mercy that guides and protects. Their punishment is not arbitrary but a fitting consequence of their own choice: by rejecting what they recognized as true, they place themselves outside God's mercy. The curse is described as universal, from God, the angels, and humankind, indicating that the moral conscience of creation, both heavenly and earthly, stands against betrayal of truth after knowledge. It warns that persistent, deliberate wrongdoing alienates a person from all sources of goodness and leaves them estranged from the moral order of the cosmos.

translation: They will abide therein eternally; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be given respite.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who die in disbelief and are rejected by God's mercy: their punishment has no end and no relief. They will not experience even a moment of ease, nor will they be granted a delay or a second chance to repent or make amends, since the time for repentance and action belongs to this worldly life. It is a stern warning that the opportunity to turn back to God is now, while one is alive, and that after death accountability is final.

translation: Except for those who repent after that and reform themselves; for indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse opens the door of divine mercy even after grave wrongdoing. Coming after verses that set out serious penalties and condemnations, it makes an exception for those who do two things: sincerely turn back to God, and then demonstrate that repentance by correcting their conduct and making amends where they have wronged others. Repentance in the Qur'anic view is therefore not just a verbal regret but a real moral transformation joined to righteous action. When a person does this, God's forgiveness and mercy are promised, which shows that no sin places a person beyond God's pardon so long as they return to Him in sincerity before it is too late.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve after having believed and then increase in disbelief – their repentance will never be accepted, and it is they who are the ones astray.
interpretation: The verse describes people who abandon faith after knowing it and then persist and grow deeper in rejection, hardening their hearts. Their repentance is not accepted because it is not sincere: it is either uttered only when death or hardship is at hand, or it comes while they are still sliding further into denial and hostility to the truth. Sincere repentance requires abandoning the sin and turning wholeheartedly back to God, and these people have instead settled into misguidance. They are called 'the astray' because, having once had the guidance, they deliberately turned away from it and went further from the path than those who never knew it. The verse is a warning against persisting in disbelief and delaying repentance until the door of sincere return has closed.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers - never would the earth's fill of gold be accepted from any of them, even if they offered it as ransom. For those there will be a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the opportunity for salvation lies in this worldly life, and that once a person dies persisting in disbelief, nothing can reverse their fate. Wealth, which people rely on in this world to solve their problems and buy their way out of difficulty, becomes worthless on the Day of Judgment; even an earth-sized quantity of gold offered as ransom would not be accepted. Acceptance of deeds depends on faith and sincerity, not on material value. Nor will any intercessor or ally be able to rescue them from the punishment, since there is no helper against God's judgment. The verse is therefore a warning to repent and embrace faith before death, while repentance can still be accepted.

translation: You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love. And whatever you spend of anything, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.
interpretation: True righteousness is not achieved through outward acts or spending what is surplus or worthless, but through the sacrifice of what is dearest to the heart, such as cherished wealth and possessions. Giving what one loves shows that devotion to God outweighs attachment to the world and purifies the soul of miserliness. Yet every act of giving, whether large or small, openly or in secret, is fully known to God, so its reward is certain and no sincere gift is lost.

translation: All food was lawful for the Children of Israel, except what Israel (Jacob) made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse answers the claim of the Jews that Islamic dietary laws contradict earlier revelation, or that God's laws never change. It teaches that the original rule for foods is permissibility, and that the particular restrictions on the Children of Israel did not originate as eternal divine prohibitions. Jacob had forbidden certain food to himself, as a personal vow or abstention, and it was later reflected in their practice. The further restrictions in the Torah came afterward as a consequence of their transgression. By challenging them to bring the Torah and recite it, the Qur'an shows that the claim is unsupported by their own scripture, and that Muhammad's message agrees with the true religion of Abraham, in which lawful things are broad and prohibitions come only by God's command.

translation: Then whoever fabricates a lie about God after that, those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse (Q 3:94) warns that once clear proof has been presented, such as the Torah showing which foods were forbidden and why, persisting in attributing falsehood to God is a grave injustice. Inventing rulings or claims and ascribing them to God, after the truth has been made evident, puts a person among the wrongdoers (zalimun). The wrong lies in placing falsehood where truth belongs, and in abusing the authority of divine revelation to serve one's own claims. It shows that accountability grows with knowledge: someone who has received the evidence and still lies about God has no excuse.

translation: Say: Allah has spoken the truth. So follow the creed of Abraham, inclining away from falsehood toward the truth, and he was not among those who associate partners with Allah.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to declare that Allah's account, including His statement that the foods the Israelites prohibited to themselves were lawful before the Torah was revealed and that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, is true. It then calls people to follow the pure monotheistic path of Abraham, which rests on devotion to God alone and rejection of all idolatry. In this way, the verse shows that the authentic faith of the earlier prophets is the same as the message brought by Muhammad. The claims of the People of the Book to exclusive ownership of Abraham's legacy are therefore refuted, and anyone who sincerely worships God alone is a true follower of his way.

translation: Indeed, the first House established for mankind is the one at Bakkah (Mecca), blessed and a guidance for all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Kaaba is the oldest house of worship dedicated to the One God, built before any other sanctuary, including Jerusalem's temple, and thus it is the true and original focal point of monotheistic devotion. It is called blessed because of the spiritual and worldly good that flows from it: the reward of pilgrimage and prayer, security, and the gathering of believers from every nation. It is a guidance for all peoples because it unites them in worshipping one Lord, orients their prayer toward a single direction, and recalls the pure monotheism of Abraham. The verse thereby answers those who disputed the change of the qibla, showing that turning to the Kaaba restores the primordial center of worship rather than introducing something new.

translation: In it are clear signs: the Station of Abraham. Whoever enters it is secure. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by all people who are able to find a way to it. But whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is free of need of all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse presents the Sacred House in Mecca as a place whose sanctity is evident through unmistakable signs, such as the Station of Abraham, where he stood to build the Ka'bah, and through the security granted to all who enter it, which reflects God's protection of the sanctuary. Because of this sacred status, God makes pilgrimage a binding obligation on every person who has the physical and financial means to reach it, so the duty is conditioned on real ability and is not a burden beyond capacity. The closing warning explains that anyone who denies this obligation or rejects the faith harms only himself, since God has no need of any creature and His majesty is not diminished by anyone's disbelief, nor is it increased by anyone's worship.

translation: Say: O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God, while God is a Witness over what you do?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke addressed to the Jews and Christians who knew the truth from their own scriptures yet rejected the clear signs of God, including the Prophet's message and the Qur'an. The question 'why do you disbelieve?' is not a request for information but a reproach: no sound justification exists for denying signs that are plain to them. The verse ends by reminding them that God sees and witnesses everything they do, including their concealment of the truth and their obstinacy, so their disbelief is not hidden from Him and will be reckoned with. Their knowledge of the earlier revelation makes their rejection more blameworthy, since they are denying what they recognize.

translation: Say: O People of the Scripture, why do you turn away from the path of God those who have believed, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And God is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those among the People of the Book who obstructed believers from Islam by sowing doubt, stirring up discord, and distorting the straight path of God to make it seem flawed. Their offense is made graver by the fact that they are 'witnesses': their own scriptures contain signs that confirm the truth of the Prophet and his message, so they act against what they know and not out of ignorance. The closing warning reminds them that God sees all their schemes and will hold them to account, so their efforts to mislead others are neither hidden nor without consequence.

translation: O you who believe, if you obey a group of those who were given the Scripture, they will turn you back, after your belief, into disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse (Al Imran 3:100) warns the believers against yielding to the influence and counsel of those among the People of the Book who harbor hostility toward Islam and seek to sow doubt and discord. Such people do not wish well for the community's faith, and if the believers submit to their guidance, especially in matters of religion, they risk being led step by step away from their faith and back into disbelief. The verse stresses that faith is a precious gift needing vigilance, and that the believers should hold fast to the Qur'an and the Prophet rather than defer to those who aim to undermine their unity and conviction, as occurred when some tried to stir up old tribal enmity between the Aws and Khazraj.

translation: And how could you disbelieve while the verses of God are being recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds firmly to God has indeed been guided to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse expresses astonishment at the idea that the believers might revert to disbelief, since they have the two greatest safeguards against it: the continual recitation of God's revelation, which brings clear proof and guidance, and the living presence of the Prophet, who teaches, models, and corrects. It was revealed in the context of attempts by some of the People of the Book to sow discord between the Aws and Khazraj and pull them back into old enmities. With such guidance at hand, to fall into disbelief or division would be inexcusable. The verse then gives the remedy: whoever clings firmly to God, by trusting Him, obeying Him, and holding to His book and way, is already placed on the straight path and protected from going astray. Reliance on God, rather than on shifting loyalties or the schemes of others, is what secures a believer's faith and unity.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims [in submission to Him].
interpretation: The verse calls believers to a God-consciousness that is sincere and constant: to obey Allah without disobeying Him, to remember Him without forgetting Him, and to be grateful without ingratitude, striving to the best of one's ability. Since no one knows when death will come, the command not to die except in a state of submission means that a believer should live every day in steadfast surrender to Allah, so that whenever death arrives, it finds them firm in faith and obedience. In this way, the quality of one's final moment is shaped by the consistency of one's whole life.

translation: And hold firmly to the rope of God all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of God upon you: when you were enemies, He brought your hearts together, and by His favor you became brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does God make clear to you His verses, that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to unity grounded in a shared anchor: the 'rope of God', which is His covenant and revealed guidance, the Qur'an and the way it prescribes. Holding to it together is what protects the community from fragmentation, since division arises when people cling to tribal loyalties, desires, or rival authorities instead of the common divine reference. The Arabs before Islam were riven by long feuds, such as those between the Aws and Khazraj, and the verse reminds them that their reconciliation and brotherhood were not their own achievement but a gift of God who softened and joined their hearts. It also reminds them that they were heading toward ruin, 'the brink of a pit of Fire', through disbelief and strife, and that God rescued them through faith. The remembrance of this favor is meant to inspire gratitude and to deter a return to discord, and the closing note says God clarifies His signs so that people may stay rightly guided, which is only possible for a community that remains united upon His book.

translation: And let there be among you a community calling to goodness, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. It is they who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse makes it a duty for the Muslim community to have a body of people who are qualified and dedicated to guiding others toward what is good, which includes faith and righteous conduct. They are to command what is recognized as right by reason and revelation, and to prevent what is wrong and harmful. Doing this requires knowledge, wisdom, and gentleness, so that the call is made with understanding and not with ignorance or harshness. The task preserves the moral and spiritual health of society and protects it from corruption and division, which is why the verse follows its call to hold fast to God's rope and not be divided. Those who carry out this duty sincerely are called the successful, meaning that true success, in this world and the next, lies in both being righteous themselves and working to uphold righteousness in the community.

translation: And do not be like those who became divided and disputed after the clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Al Imran 3:105) warns the believers against repeating the mistake of earlier communities, especially the People of the Book, who split into factions and fell into disputes not out of ignorance but after clear evidence and guidance had reached them. Their division was driven by envy, stubbornness, and worldly interests rather than by a lack of knowledge. The verse teaches that unity upon the truth is a duty, and that disagreement which abandons clear revelation and fragments the community is a grave sin. The warning of a great punishment underscores the seriousness of knowingly turning clear guidance into a cause of sectarian strife, and it urges Muslims to hold fast together to the rope of God, as commanded in the preceding verses.

translation: On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said to them], 'Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to reject.'
interpretation: The verse describes how, on the Day of Judgment, the inner reality of people becomes visible on their faces. The whitening of faces is a sign of faith, honesty, and the joy and honor of God's approval, while the blackening is a sign of disbelief, shame, and grief. The rebuke addressed to the blackened faces, 'Did you disbelieve after your belief?', indicates that the primary reference is to those who had accepted faith, or had the clear means to recognize the truth, and then turned away through division, hypocrisy, or denial, as the preceding verses warn against splitting into factions after clear proofs have come. Their punishment is not arbitrary but a direct consequence of their own persistent rejection, as shown in 'for what you used to reject.' The verse thus warns believers to hold firmly to unity and sincere faith, since the final outcome is determined by one's lasting stance toward the truth.

translation: But as for those whose faces will be whitened, they will be in the mercy of God; therein they will abide forever.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Imran 3:107) describes the final state of the believers who remained faithful. Their radiant faces are an outward sign of inner faith, joy, and God's acceptance on the Day of Judgment. The verse says they are 'in God's mercy' rather than 'in Paradise' to teach that entry into and enjoyment of Paradise are ultimately gifts of divine mercy, not merely the wage for deeds. Their eternal stay there means this mercy is permanent and secure, with no fear of loss or ending. The verse thus encourages believers to hold fast to unity and obedience, trusting that God's mercy will envelop them.

translation: These are the verses of God; We recite them to you in truth. And God does not desire any injustice to the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelations, including the warnings and accounts of earlier nations' fates, are a true and reliable disclosure, not myth or speculation. It then clarifies that the punishments and consequences described are never acts of arbitrary wrong by God toward any of His creation; rather, they follow from people's own rejection, corruption, and injustice. God's judgment is perfectly just, and since He does not will injustice for any of the worlds, whatever suffering befalls wrongdoers is the result of their own choices, while the revelation itself is a mercy that warns them so they might return to the right path.

translation: To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to God all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty: everything in creation is His possession, so no being holds real ownership or independent authority. Because He is the origin and owner of all things, He is also their final destination. Every affair, whether the deeds of people, the outcomes of events, or the settling of disputes and injustices, ultimately returns to Him for judgment. This should lead the believer to humility, trust in God's justice, and accountability. Worldly power and outward success are temporary, and the final word belongs to God alone.

translation: You are the best nation brought forth for humankind: you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in God. Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse describes the Muslim community's excellence as conditional on a mission and not a matter of lineage or title. Its rank comes from being raised up for the benefit of all people, which it fulfills by guiding society toward goodness, resisting corruption, and grounding both in sincere faith in God. Enjoining right and forbidding wrong are the practical proof of that faith, and the community stays 'best' only while it keeps this role. The remark about the People of the Book shows that the door to this same honor remains open to them. Their belief would have been better for them in this world and the next. The verse is also fair to them, since it acknowledges that some are true believers while most have departed from obedience to God. Moral integrity, not group identity, is the standard of merit.

translation: They will never harm you except for some minor hurt. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you in flight; then they will not be helped.
interpretation: God reassures the believers that the People of the Book who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing pose no real threat to them. Their harm will be limited to trivial annoyances such as verbal abuse, taunts, and slander, which cannot damage the believers' faith or community. If they actually take up arms, they will be routed and flee, and no one will come to their aid. The verse conveys that those who hold firmly to truth and righteousness are granted divine protection, while their opponents, for all their scheming, are ultimately left weak and without support.

translation: Humiliation has been struck upon them wherever they are found, except for a rope from God and a rope from the people. They have drawn upon themselves wrath from God, and wretchedness has been struck upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress.
interpretation: The verse explains that the abasement and moral poverty that came to afflict those among the People of the Book being addressed was not an arbitrary or racial fate but a consequence of their own conduct. Their security and standing could only come through a covenant of protection from God (adherence to His guidance) or through treaties and protection from other people, since they had lost the inner strength that comes from faithfulness. The cause is stated clearly: persistent rejection of God's revelations, killing prophets unjustly, and habitual disobedience and overstepping of limits.
