The verse thus teaches a general moral law: when a community rejects truth, persecutes those who call to righteousness, and normalizes transgression, it forfeits dignity and inner stability, and becomes dependent on external support, while its condition is tied to its deeds rather than to its lineage.

translation: They are not all alike: among the People of the Book there is an upright community who recite the verses of God during the hours of the night, and they prostrate themselves.
interpretation: The verse teaches justice and fairness in judging others: the failings of some among the People of the Book must not be used to condemn them all. Those who remain steadfast on the truth, who stand in night prayer, reflect on God's revelation and bow in humble worship, are honored by God for their sincerity. Righteousness is measured by a person's own faith and devotion rather than by the group they belong to, so believers are called to be equitable, to recognize the good wherever it is found, and to be inspired by the example of those who devote the quiet hours of the night to God.

translation: They believe in God and the Last Day, and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and they hasten to do good deeds; and those are among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse describes the righteous among the People of the Book as a community whose faith leads to action. Belief in God and the Last Day is the foundation of accountability, and it shows itself outwardly in concern for society: they call others to what is good and discourage what is harmful, rather than keeping their faith private. They also compete eagerly in good works and do not delay or procrastinate. The verse teaches that true righteousness combines sound belief, social responsibility, and prompt, enthusiastic goodness, and that those who embody all three are counted by God among the righteous.

translation: And whatever good they do, they will never be denied its reward. And Allah is All-Knowing of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the description of the upright among the People of the Book who recite God's verses in the night, believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin good and forbid evil, and hasten to good deeds, assures that no act of goodness is ever lost or left unrecognized by God. The verb 'yakfurūhu' here means to have a blessing concealed or its due ungratefully denied, so God, who is the Most Appreciative, will never deny them the reward for their good, however small it may seem. The verse closes by tying reward to God's perfect knowledge of those who have taqwa: He knows their sincerity, their hidden intentions, and their struggles, so recompense is based on what is truly in the heart rather than on outward appearance or group identity. It therefore both consoles the righteous and encourages perseverance in goodness with God-consciousness.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve - neither their wealth nor their children will avail them against God at all. And it is they who are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly assets people lean on for security, such as money, family, and status, have no power to shield a person from God's judgment if he persists in rejecting faith. Wealth and offspring are among the greatest sources of pride and protection in this life, yet on the Day of Judgment they are worthless as ransom or intercession for the one who denied the truth. The only thing that benefits a person then is faith and righteous deeds. The verse therefore warns against placing ultimate trust in material means and reminds believers to prioritize their relationship with God over worldly attachments, because a disbeliever's persistence in denial, despite his possessions and children, leads to the Fire, where his stay is lasting.

translation: The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind carrying a bitter, freezing cold, which strikes the harvest of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. God did not wrong them; rather, they wrong themselves. (Qur'an 3:117)
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity and good deeds offered without true faith, or while persisting in disbelief and wrongdoing, are like a crop destroyed by a freezing wind just when its owners expect to reap it. Their spending may look fruitful and may bring worldly praise or reputation, but it brings no lasting reward in the Hereafter because it lacks the foundation of sincere belief and seeking God's pleasure. The ruin is not an injustice from God. It is the result of their own choices: by rejecting truth and corrupting their intentions they bring about the loss of their efforts, so they are the ones wronging themselves.

translation: O you who believe, do not take as intimate confidants those outside your own community; they will spare no effort to corrupt you. They wish for you to suffer and fall into hardship. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their hearts conceal is greater. We have made the signs clear to you, if you would use your reason.
interpretation: The verse instructs believers to be discerning about whom they entrust with their private affairs, counsel, and secrets. Those who harbor enmity toward the believing community and wish it harm, even if they sometimes let their hostility slip in speech, conceal far deeper animosity. Sensitive matters and the community's vulnerabilities should therefore not be placed in the hands of such people, since they would exploit them to cause ruin. This is not a command to be unjust or unkind to others, but a call for prudence in trust: allegiance and confidence should be given on the basis of demonstrated goodwill, and the believers are urged to use their reason to read the clear signs of a person's intentions.

translation: Here you are, loving them while they do not love you, and you believe in all of the Scripture. When they meet you they say, 'We believe,' but when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you in rage. Say: 'Die in your rage! Indeed, God knows well what is within the hearts.'
interpretation: The verse admonishes the believers for extending sincere affection to hypocrites and hostile People of the Book who do not reciprocate it. It contrasts the believers' open, sincere faith, which accepts all the revealed books including those the others claim to follow, with the duplicity of those who feign belief in public yet seethe with envy and resentment in private, so intense that they gnaw their fingertips in anger at the believers' unity and strength. The command 'Die in your rage' is not a wish for their death but a declaration that their hatred will not harm the believers or halt the progress of Islam; their fury will only consume them, and it will remain unfulfilled. The closing statement that God knows what lies within hearts reassures the believers that no hidden malice escapes Him, and warns the hypocrites that their concealed feelings are fully known and will be accounted for, so the believers should not rely on such people as close confidants.

translation: If a good thing touches you, it distresses them; but if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you in the least. Indeed, God encompasses whatever they do.
interpretation: The verse (Al 'Imran 3:120) exposes the deep-seated envy of those who bear hostility toward the believers: they are pained by the believers' success and gladdened by their hardship, so their enmity is not a passing mood but a settled disposition. Rather than advising the believers to retaliate or to despair, it prescribes two inner remedies, patience (sabr) and God-consciousness (taqwa). Patience keeps the believers steady under hardship and restrained from reacting rashly, while taqwa keeps them within God's limits and attentive to Him in every circumstance. With these two qualities, the plotting of their enemies loses its power to truly harm them, because the believers' safety rests on their relationship with God and not on the goodwill of others. The closing statement that God encompasses all that the enemies do gives reassurance: no plot is hidden from Him or beyond His control, so He can thwart it or turn it into something harmless, and the believers can therefore proceed with confidence and calm.

translation: And [remember, O Muhammad,] when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for battle. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse recalls the morning of the Battle of Uhud, when the Prophet left his household and personally arranged the Muslim ranks, assigning each group its place, including the archers on the hill. It teaches that sound leadership involves careful planning and organization, while placing trust in God. The closing attributes remind the believers that Allah heard everything said in the consultation and the debates over whether to fight inside Medina or outside it, and knew the intentions of every heart, including those who wavered and the hypocrites who withdrew. Thus the believers are to act diligently, yet remain conscious that God is aware of their words and inner states and that the outcome rests with Him.

translation: When two groups among you were about to lose heart, though God was their protector. And in God let the believers put their trust.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Battle of Uhud, when two clans of the believers, Banu Salimah and Banu Harithah, inclined toward faltering and withdrawing after Abdullah ibn Ubayy pulled back his followers. It teaches that such moments of weakness are natural human impulses, which did not become actual desertion because God, as their guardian, steadied their hearts and kept them firm. The closing command makes the lesson general: believers should not rely on their numbers, strength, or planning, but should entrust their affairs to God, whose support turns fear into steadfastness, while still taking the necessary means.

translation: And Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were weak. So fear Allah, that you might be grateful.
interpretation: God reminds the believers of the battle of Badr, where a small, poorly equipped band of Muslims, far fewer in number and in arms than the Meccan army, triumphed. The victory was not due to their strength but to God's support, which shows that success comes from Him alone. Recalling this favor is meant to strengthen their trust in Him in later trials such as Uhud, when they faced difficulty, and to teach that reliance on God and obedience to Him, rather than numbers or material means, bring help. The command to be mindful of God (taqwa) is therefore the fitting response to His past favors, and gratitude is expressed by obeying Him, remaining steadfast, and not attributing triumph to anything other than His will.

translation: When you said to the believers, "Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"
interpretation: This verse recalls the Battle of Badr, when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) reassured the believers, who were few in number and poorly equipped against a much larger Quraysh army. The rhetorical question 'Is it not sufficient for you?' is meant to strengthen their hearts and remind them that their true support comes from God, not from numbers or material strength. The promise of angels sent down from heaven shows divine care for the faithful and teaches that victory depends on trust in God, steadfastness, and obedience. The angels serve as a reassurance and glad tidings to calm hearts, while the real source of victory remains God alone.

translation: Yes! If you are patient and fear God, and the enemy comes upon you suddenly in this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked (for battle).
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Battle of Uhud (and recalling Badr), promises the believers more than the three thousand angels mentioned just before it, but makes the increase conditional on two qualities: steadfast patience (sabr) and God-consciousness (taqwa). Divine help is not automatic; it depends on the believers' endurance in the face of hardship and their obedience to God and His Messenger. The phrase 'from this very moment' means that if the enemy attacks swiftly and suddenly, God's support will arrive just as swiftly, with angels visibly marked to signify their mission. The lesson is that spiritual discipline and moral steadfastness are the means through which God's aid descends, and that victory ultimately comes from Him, serving to reassure and strengthen the hearts of the believers.

translation: And Allah made it not except as glad tidings for you and so that your hearts would be reassured by it. And victory is only from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the angelic reinforcements promised to the believers at Badr were not the cause of their victory but a sign of good news and a means of calming their anxious hearts. Real victory does not depend on numbers, weapons, or even unseen helpers, since these are merely instruments. It comes only from God, who has the power to grant it and the wisdom to give it to whom He wills. The believers are therefore taught to put their trust in God alone, using the means available to them while knowing that the outcome rests with Him.

translation: [And this was] so that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved or suppress them, so that they turn back disappointed.
interpretation: This verse (Al Imran 3:127) explains one of the wisdoms behind God's support of the believers at Badr: that victory was meant to weaken the disbelievers by destroying some of their leaders and fighters, or to humiliate and crush their pride and defiance, so they would retreat in failure, their hopes of overcoming the believers unfulfilled. The meaning is that God's aid to the believers carries a purpose, which is to break the strength and arrogance of falsehood, either through the loss of a portion of its forces or through the disgrace of defeat, leaving its adherents frustrated and despairing in their opposition.

translation: You have no part in the matter—whether He turns to them in mercy or punishes them—for indeed they are wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse (Aal 'Imran 3:128) teaches the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that the final decision about people's fate belongs to God alone. After the setback at Uhud, when he was wounded and grieved by the disbelievers who harmed him and his companions, he was told that his task is only to convey the message and to strive, not to determine who is guided or who is punished. Whether God accepts their repentance and forgives them, or punishes them, rests entirely with His knowledge and wisdom. If He punishes them, it is a just consequence of their own wrongdoing, since they have wronged themselves and others through disbelief and transgression. The verse thus affirms divine sovereignty, humbles even the greatest of prophets before God's authority, and urges patience and reliance on God rather than impatience for vengeance.

translation: To God belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty over all creation: since everything belongs to Him, no one can compel or hold Him to account over whom He forgives or punishes. Yet His will is not arbitrary or harsh, because the verse ends by stressing that forgiveness and mercy are His defining attributes. Believers should therefore hold fast to hope in His pardon while remaining mindful of His justice, and should turn to Him in repentance, trusting that His mercy prevails over His punishment.

translation: O you who believe, do not consume usury, doubled and multiplied, and fear God so that you may prosper.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers and forbids them from living off interest-based gain, which in the pre-Islamic practice meant that an unpaid debt would be doubled again and again until the debtor was crushed. The phrase 'doubled and multiplied' describes the oppressive, exploitative reality of usury that the community was accustomed to, and it exposes the injustice at its core: wealth grows at the expense of the needy. The command to be mindful of God ties the economic prohibition to faith, teaching that true success (falah) in this life and the next comes not from compounding wealth through exploitation, but from conscious reverence for God, which restrains greed and fosters fairness and compassion in financial dealings.

translation: And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 3:131) commands believers to protect themselves from Hell by obeying God and avoiding what leads to it, especially the sins mentioned just before it, such as consuming usury. By describing the Fire as prepared for the disbelievers, it warns that persistent disobedience and heedlessness of God's limits can draw a believer toward the conduct of those who reject Him. True faith must therefore be accompanied by reverent fear, accountability, and obedience, so that a person may be saved from a punishment meant for those who deny the truth.

translation: And obey Allah and the Messenger, that you may be shown mercy.
interpretation: This verse (Al 'Imran 3:132) teaches that mercy is the fruit of obedience. Obeying Allah means following His commands as revealed in the Qur'an, and obeying the Messenger means following his guidance and example, which explains and applies that revelation. The phrase 'that you may be shown mercy' indicates that those who submit to this twofold obedience become deserving of Allah's compassion, in this world through guidance, security and ease of heart, and in the Hereafter through forgiveness and entry into Paradise. Coming after warnings against consuming usury and against disobedience, it presents obedience as a protection from loss and a way to Allah's mercy, not as a burden.

translation: And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse urges believers to treat repentance and good works as urgent, not to be postponed, because life is short and the chance to act may end at any time. Forgiveness comes first, since a person must be cleansed of sins before entering Paradise. The image of a Garden as vast as the heavens and the earth conveys the immensity of God's reward and shows that it is far greater than any worldly gain, so it is worth competing for. It is reserved for the muttaqin, those who are mindful of God and guard themselves against disobedience, and the verses that follow describe them as people who give in ease and hardship, restrain their anger, pardon others, and quickly seek forgiveness after a lapse. Piety is thus shown as active devotion and moral effort, not only belief.

translation: Those who spend in times of ease and times of hardship, who restrain their anger, and who pardon people. And God loves those who do good.
interpretation: The verse describes the character of the God-fearing (al-muttaqin) as one of generosity and self-mastery that does not depend on circumstances. They give charity whether they are wealthy or in difficulty, which shows that their giving springs from devotion to God and not from comfort or convenience. They also swallow their anger when provoked, holding back from retaliation although they could act on it, and they go further by forgiving those who wronged them. The verse then ties these three qualities together under ihsan, doing good. Giving with one's wealth, mastering one's temper, and pardoning others are all ways of treating people beyond what strict justice requires, and God's love is promised to those who live this way. The lesson is that true spiritual strength lies in disciplining the self through generosity, restraint, and forgiveness, and not in asserting oneself over others.

translation: And those who, when they commit an immoral act or wrong themselves, remember God and seek forgiveness for their sins - and who forgives sins except God? - and who do not persist in what they have done while they know.
interpretation: The verse describes the mark of the God-fearing: they are not sinless, but when they slip, whether in a flagrant sin or in a wrong that harms only themselves, their consciousness of God awakens at once and drives them to repent. It teaches that forgiveness belongs to God alone, so a sinner should not despair or turn to anyone else for pardon. True repentance, however, requires more than words: it means abandoning the sin and refusing to keep committing it knowingly. The difference between the believer and the heedless is therefore not the absence of error but the readiness to return to God, acknowledge the wrong, and stop.

translation: Those—their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally. And excellent is the reward of those who work [righteousness].
interpretation: The verse shows that God's reward for the believers who repent and turn away from persistent wrongdoing combines two blessings: first, the removal of the burden of their past sins through forgiveness, and second, the granting of lasting joy in the gardens of Paradise. Forgiveness is mentioned before the gardens because a person must be cleansed of sin before enjoying the highest reward. By calling it 'the reward of those who work,' the verse teaches that Paradise is the due recompense for sincere effort and righteous deeds, offered by God's generosity, and that faith must be expressed in action. The phrase 'excellent is the reward' affirms that no worldly labor or sacrifice compares to what God gives in return, which encourages steadfastness and repentance.

translation: Many ways of life and divine practices have passed away before you; so travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied the truth.
interpretation: God reminds the believers, in the aftermath of the setback at Uhud, that He deals with nations according to consistent, established laws: falsehood may prevail for a time and the believers may be tested, but arrogance, injustice and denial of the truth ultimately lead to ruin, while patience and faith lead to a good outcome. By urging them to travel and look at the ruins and histories of earlier peoples such as 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Lot, the verse invites reflection and the drawing of lessons, so that the believers will not despair over temporary hardship or be deceived by the apparent success of the deniers, and will hold firm in the certainty that the final victory belongs to the truth and to those who are mindful of God.

translation: This is a clear declaration for all people, and a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of God.
interpretation: The verse (Q 3:138) teaches that the Qur'an, together with the lessons of past nations mentioned before it, is a plain explanation open to all humanity, clarifying truth from falsehood and the fate of those who deny versus those who believe. Yet its full benefit, in the form of guidance that leads to right action and admonition that softens the heart, is realized only by the God-conscious (muttaqin), because their awareness of God and readiness to heed make them receptive. Thus the message is universal in its availability but specific in its fruit: those who approach it with piety and humility are the ones who are actually guided and reminded by it.

translation: Do not lose heart and do not grieve, for you will be the superior ones, if you are believers.
interpretation: The verse was revealed after the setback at Uhud to console the Muslims. It teaches that real superiority comes from faith, not from momentary military outcomes or numbers. Believers are told not to give in to weakness or sorrow over losses, because trust in God and steadfast adherence to the faith bring ultimate success and dignity. Their elevation is conditional on keeping true faith, which includes obedience, patience, and reliance on God. Hardships are therefore trials to strengthen them and not reasons for despair.

translation: If a wound has touched you, a similar wound has already touched the other people. And these days of fortune and misfortune We rotate among people, so that God may know those who believe and may take witnesses from among you. And God does not love the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse consoles the believers after their setback at Uhud by teaching that victory and defeat are not signs of God's favor or abandonment but part of a divine rotation of fortunes that He sets among all peoples. The enemy suffered similar wounds at Badr, so hardship should neither break the believers' spirit nor shake their faith. These reversals serve as a test that separates sincere believers from the hesitant, making their faith evident through patience and steadfastness, and they honor some with martyrdom, which is the status of bearing witness to the truth with their lives. The closing statement, that God does not love the wrongdoers, assures believers that worldly success does not mean God approves of the oppressors. Their temporary triumphs are not endorsements, and justice will ultimately prevail.

translation: And so that God may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse (Al 'Imran 3:141) comes after the trials the believers faced at Uhud, and it explains one divine wisdom behind such hardship: the alternation of victory and setback is a means of refining the community. Hardship sifts true faith from weak or hypocritical claims, cleanses believers of sins and flaws, and strengthens their patience, sincerity, and reliance on God. Disbelief, in contrast, carries within it the seeds of its own undoing. Through their arrogance, transgression, and persistent opposition to truth, the disbelievers are gradually brought to ruin, so their apparent successes are only temporary. The verse thus teaches believers that setbacks are not signs of divine abandonment but part of a purposeful process that ends in the purification of the faithful and the downfall of falsehood.

translation: Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while God has not yet made evident those among you who strove hard, and made evident those who are steadfast?
interpretation: The verse teaches that entry into Paradise is not won by profession of faith alone but must be confirmed by trial. God's knowing here means that He makes known in actual events, so that what He knew beforehand becomes manifest in deeds. Real faith is shown when a believer strives in God's cause, whether by struggling against his own desires or by defending the faith, and when he stays patient under hardship, loss, and setback. The verse was revealed to console and sober the believers after the setback at Uhud: hardship is a sifting that separates the sincere from the merely hopeful, and Paradise is reached only through proven striving and patient endurance.

translation: You used to wish for death before you met it. Now you have seen it, while you were looking on.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat Al Imran (3:143), addresses the believers after the setback at Uhud. Some of them had longed for martyrdom and had wished to take part in a battle like Badr, which they had missed. Yet when the fighting came and death was right before their eyes, some faltered or fled. God reminds them that wishing for martyrdom is easy, but real faith is proved by steadfastness when the moment actually arrives. The verse is a gentle rebuke that teaches believers not to ask for trials lightly, to measure their sincerity by deeds rather than words, and to stay firm in patience and courage when tests do come.

translation: Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he were to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back on his heels will never harm God in the least, and God will reward the grateful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith must rest on devotion to God and His message, not on the continued presence of any human being, even the Prophet. It was revealed after the setback at Uhud, when a rumor spread that Muhammad had been killed and some believers lost heart. By reminding them that earlier messengers also died, it shows that prophethood is a mission and not an eternal state, and that the truth outlives its bearers. Abandoning the faith when its human leader is gone harms only the one who abandons it, since God is in no need of anyone's loyalty. Those who stay steadfast and show gratitude for the guidance they received will be rewarded.

translation: And it is not for any soul to die except by Allah's permission, at a decree appointed for a fixed term. And whoever desires the reward of this world, We give him of it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him of it. And We will reward the grateful.
interpretation: The verse, revealed after the setback at Uhud, teaches that the time of death is fixed by God and cannot be hastened by fighting or delayed by fleeing, so believers should not be gripped by fear or let rumors of the Prophet's death shake their commitment. It then shows that a person's outcome follows his intention and aim. Whoever fights or acts only for worldly gain receives what has been allotted of it, with no share in the next life. Whoever aims at God's reward in the Hereafter receives it, and God also grants him what has been decreed for him in this world. The ones who are truly rewarded are the grateful, those who recognize God's favor, stay firm in His religion, and hold to it in both ease and hardship.

translation: And how many a prophet has fought alongside many devoted God-fearing followers; they did not lose heart for what afflicted them in the cause of God, nor did they weaken, nor did they yield. And God loves the steadfast.
interpretation: The verse, revealed after the setback at Uhud, reminds believers that hardship in the path of God is a recurring pattern in the history of earlier communities and does not signal defeat or divine abandonment. The devoted followers of earlier prophets met wounds and losses with three kinds of resilience: inner resolve (they did not lose heart), strength of action (they did not weaken), and dignity before the enemy (they did not submit or humble themselves). Their steadfastness, rather than outward victory, is what earned God's love. The lesson is that faithfulness is measured by perseverance and loyalty to the cause even when a prophet's or leader's fate is uncertain, and that the believer's commitment must rest on God, not on any individual or on immediate results.

translation: And their only words were: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, make our feet firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people."
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 3:147) describes the steadfast devoted followers of earlier prophets who met hardship in battle without panic or boasting. Their only response was humble prayer. They began by seeking forgiveness, acknowledging that their own sins and transgressions could be the cause of hardship and a barrier to divine help. Only after this self-examination did they ask for firmness and victory. The lesson is that true steadfastness and success come from inner purification and dependence on God. Victory is requested as a gift from Him, not as something earned by one's own strength, and repentance should precede and accompany any struggle.

translation: So God gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter. And God loves those who do good.
interpretation: The verse concludes the account of the steadfast believers who, after suffering hardship and loss in battle, did not weaken or yield but turned to God in repentance and prayer for firmness and victory. God honored them with a reward in this world, namely help, victory over their enemies, and a good standing and honor among people, and He reserved for them the finest reward in the Hereafter, which is His pleasure and Paradise. The verse describes the Hereafter's reward as 'excellent' in contrast to the worldly reward, to show that the worldly gain is minor and temporary while the lasting, perfect recompense lies with God. The closing phrase explains the cause: God's love is for the muhsinin, those who excel in worship by being conscious of God as if they see Him, and who excel in conduct by being patient, sincere, and steadfast, so their good works are met with His love and ample reward.

translation: O you who believe, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will turn about as losers.
interpretation: God warns the believers that taking guidance or counsel from those who reject the faith, and yielding to their wishes, leads step by step to abandoning the truth. The phrase 'turn you back on your heels' pictures a reversal of direction: a person who had been moving forward in faith is made to retreat into disbelief or into compromise with it. The result is loss in both worlds, since the one who gives up guidance forfeits the purpose of his life and his reward in the hereafter. The verse, revealed in the aftermath of the setback at Uhud when hypocrites and opponents were sowing doubt among the Muslims, teaches that believers should rely on God as their protector and helper rather than on those who are hostile to their faith, because deferring to them in matters of religion brings only ruin.

translation: Rather, God is your Protector and Master, and He is the best of helpers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 3:150) comes after a warning against obeying the disbelievers, who would turn the believers back on their heels and leave them as losers. It teaches that true protection and guardianship belong to God alone, not to those who oppose faith. Believers should not seek security or support by yielding to the enemies of truth or compromising their religion out of fear, since only God's help is dependable. Whoever has God as their guardian needs no other, because no ally can match His help or avert His decree. The verse thus calls believers to place their trust in Him and remain steadfast, even in times of weakness, defeat, or hardship.

translation: We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, because they associated with God that for which He sent down no authority. Their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse, revealed after the setback at Uhud, reassures the believers that God Himself will undermine the confidence of those who deny Him. The fear that fills their hearts is a direct consequence of their shirk: they rest their trust on false deities and powers that have no proof or divine warrant behind them, so they have no real source of security. Those who ground their lives in falsehood are inwardly unstable and fearful, while those who rely on God find strength and calm. The verse also teaches that their fear in this world foreshadows their final fate: the Fire is their lasting home, and it is a terrible dwelling because shirk is the gravest injustice, putting created things in the place due to the Creator alone.

translation: And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until you lost courage and fell into dispute about the order and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love. Among you are some who desire this world, and among you are some who desire the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them to test you; and He has already pardoned you. And Allah is full of bounty to the believers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Battle of Uhud, where the Muslims were first victorious because Allah kept His promise of support, so long as they obeyed the Prophet. Their defeat did not come from a failure of Allah's promise but from their own conduct: the archers on the hill wavered, disagreed over whether to hold their post or go after the spoils, and disobeyed the Prophet's command once victory appeared certain. The verse shows that the believers were not all alike in motive, for some were drawn by worldly gain while others sought the Hereafter, and it makes clear that obedience and discipline are conditions of divine help. The reversal was a trial meant to purify intentions and expose weaknesses, and it taught the community a lesson. Yet Allah pardoned them and did not destroy them for their error, which shows His grace toward the believers even when they falter, and that trials and mistakes can become occasions for growth and repentance.

translation: When you were climbing up the mountain in flight, not turning to look at anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind. So God repaid you with distress upon distress, so that you would not grieve over what escaped you nor over what afflicted you. And God is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse recalls the moment at Uhud when, after the Muslim ranks broke, many fled up the mountain in panic, so overcome by fear that they did not even look back for their companions, while the Prophet stood firm calling them to return. Their punishment was a succession of griefs: the sorrow of defeat and loss, added to the grief of having disobeyed and abandoned the Messenger, and the distress of the rumor that he had been killed. The purpose of this layered hardship was educational: by experiencing such intense trials, their hearts were hardened and trained so that they would no longer be consumed with sorrow over lost spoils, victory, or wounds and deaths suffered, since they learned that obedience and steadfastness matter above worldly gain or loss. The closing statement reminds them that God knows their true inner states and deeds, so His response is perfectly just and wise, both in chastening them and in later forgiving them.

translation: Then, after the distress, He sent down upon you security: drowsiness overcoming a group of you, while another group, anxious only for themselves, entertained false thoughts about God, the thoughts of pre-Islamic ignorance. They said, 'Do we have any say in the matter?' Say: 'The matter belongs entirely to God.' They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you, saying, 'If we had had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here.' Say: 'Even if you had been in your homes, those for whom death was decreed would have come out to the places where they were to fall.' This is so that God may test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts. And God knows well what lies within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse describes the aftermath of the Battle of Uhud and shows how the same event separated people by the state of their hearts. For the sincere believers, God sent calm sleep after fear and grief, a sign of His care and of the peace that trust in Him brings. The hypocrites and the weak in faith stayed consumed by worry about their own safety. They blamed the loss on poor planning and doubted God's wisdom and promise, which is the 'thought of ignorance'. The verse's central lesson is that all outcomes, including life and death, are within God's decree, and no precaution or staying at home can change an appointed end. Hardship therefore serves as a trial that exposes what hearts conceal, purifies the believers of doubt and weakness, and confirms that God knows inner intentions fully, whatever people say outwardly.

translation: Indeed, those of you who turned back on the day the two armies met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip, because of some of what they had earned. But Allah has certainly pardoned them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the Muslims who fled or withdrew at the Battle of Uhud when the two armies met. Their flight was not simple cowardice that came from nowhere; Satan was able to make them stumble because of earlier wrongs they had committed, such as disobeying the Prophet's instructions and being drawn to worldly gain. Sins weaken a person's resolve and open the door for Satan's influence, just as good deeds strengthen one against it. Yet the verse ends with mercy: Allah pardoned them, showing that He is Forgiving of their error and Forbearing, not hastening to punish. The lesson is that believers should recognize how past sins can lead to later failures, quickly repent, and rely on Allah's pardon rather than despair.

translation: O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers when they traveled through the land or went out to fight: 'If they had stayed with us, they would not have died and would not have been killed' – so that Allah makes that a regret in their hearts. And Allah gives life and causes death, and Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against adopting the mindset of the hypocrites and disbelievers, who attribute death to travel or battle and claim that staying home would have saved their companions. Such thinking is rooted in denying divine decree, and it only deepens grief and regret in their hearts, because they see loss as a failure of human planning rather than as part of Allah's decree. Believers are taught instead that life and death are wholly in Allah's hands: no one dies before his appointed time, and no one is saved by staying behind. This conviction frees them from fear that would keep them from striving, jihad, and seeking sustenance, and it brings contentment with what Allah has decreed. The closing reminder that Allah sees all that people do calls believers to accountability, since their words, beliefs, and responses to loss are all observed and will be judged.

translation: And if you are killed in the cause of God or die, then forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they accumulate.
interpretation: The verse consoles believers who fear death while striving for God's sake, whether they are slain or die naturally. It teaches that the pardon and mercy God grants to those who set out in His path are worth more than all the wealth and worldly gains others hoard in life. Whoever holds this truth in mind will no longer see death in God's cause as a loss, but as a passage to something far more valuable than the fleeting possessions of this world, and so should not hold back from sincere striving out of fear of dying or love of worldly gain.

translation: And if you die or are killed, it is surely to God that you will be gathered.
interpretation: This verse (Al 'Imran 3:158) consoles believers and frees them from fear of death in God's cause. Whether a person dies a natural death or is killed in battle, the end is the same: everyone returns to God for reckoning and recompense. Since death is certain and the return to God is inescapable, clinging to life by avoiding struggle in His path is pointless, and what matters is to be found in obedience and sincerity when that meeting comes. It therefore turns the believer's attention from the manner or timing of death to readiness for the Hereafter, which gives courage and steadfastness.

translation: It was by Allah's mercy that you were gentle with them. Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. Then when you have made a decision, put your trust in Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who put their trust in Him.
interpretation: The verse teaches that gentleness is a mercy from Allah and the basis of effective leadership. It was revealed after the setback at Uhud, when some Muslims had disobeyed orders, and yet the Prophet was told to treat them with kindness rather than harshness. People are drawn to a leader who is forgiving and compassionate, and they scatter from one who is rough and hard-hearted. The verse lays out a sequence for dealing with people and decisions: first pardon their faults, then seek forgiveness for them, which shows care for their standing with Allah, and then consult them on affairs, which honors their opinions and builds a sense of shared responsibility. Once consultation has been done and a decision reached, the leader must not waver or be paralyzed by worry over outcomes, but should rely on Allah, since effort and consultation are the means while the result rests with Him. Allah's love for those who trust in Him shows that true reliance joins sincere effort with a heart that depends on Allah alone.

translation: If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And in Allah let the believers put their trust.
interpretation: The verse teaches that victory and defeat ultimately depend on divine will, not on numbers, weapons, or worldly means. Revealed in the context of the Battle of Uhud, it reminds the believers that their success comes from earning Allah's support through obedience, steadfastness, and sincerity, and that disobedience and reliance on themselves alone can lead to His withdrawing that support. Since no power can defeat those whom Allah supports, and none can aid those whom He abandons, the believer should anchor their hope and reliance in Allah alone. This reliance (tawakkul) is not passive: it means taking the available means while recognizing that the outcome rests with Him, which frees the heart from fear of people and from arrogance in success.

translation: It is not for any prophet to act dishonestly (to take from the spoils unlawfully). Whoever acts dishonestly will come on the Day of Resurrection bearing what he took dishonestly. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute integrity of the prophets, who could never betray a trust or secretly take from the war booty, a charge that had been whispered after the Battle of Uhud when some suspected the Prophet of keeping part of the spoils. It then lays down a universal principle: anyone who misappropriates what belongs to the community or to others, whether booty or any entrusted property, will not escape. On the Day of Resurrection the hidden theft will be exposed, with the person carrying the very thing he embezzled, publicly disgraced before all creation. Nothing is lost or overlooked, for every soul will be given the full and exact recompense of its deeds, with no injustice done to anyone. The lesson is that trustworthiness in handling shared and public resources is a sacred duty, and that divine justice ensures accountability for even secret wrongdoing.

translation: Is then one who follows the pleasure of God like one who has earned the wrath of God, and whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is that destination.
interpretation: The verse denies that the righteous and the wrongdoers can ever be equal. A person who orients his beliefs, choices, and conduct toward seeking God's approval, obeying revealed guidance even when it costs him worldly gain, travels a path leading to honor and mercy. A person who turns away from that guidance, or betrays trust for worldly profit, returns burdened with God's anger, and his final dwelling is Hell. The rhetorical question stresses that moral choices have real consequences. Every person is ultimately headed to one of two outcomes, determined by whether he lived seeking God's pleasure or defying it, so the believer should make God's approval the aim of every action.

translation: They are of [varying] ranks with Allah, and Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse (Q 3:163) teaches that people stand at different levels before God, each rank fixed by the sincerity and quality of their deeds, not by lineage, status, or outward claims. Those who follow God's pleasure are elevated in degrees, while those who incur His wrath fall to lower ones. Because God sees everything people do, including intentions hidden from others, His judgment is perfectly just and no action is overlooked or wrongly weighed. The verse is both an encouragement to strive for righteousness and a warning to stay mindful of one's conduct.

translation: Indeed, Allah conferred a great favor upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although before that they had been in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse (Aal Imran 3:164) presents the sending of the Prophet Muhammad as the greatest divine favor to the believers, and it shows that his mission has a threefold function: conveying revelation, purifying souls, and instructing in the Book and wisdom. That he came 'from among themselves' means he was of their own people, known to them in lineage, honesty, and character, so they could follow him as a living model and had no excuse to doubt his sincerity. Reciting the verses establishes the foundation of faith, purification (tazkiyah) cleanses hearts and conduct from idolatry, vice, and moral corruption, and teaching the Book and wisdom (the Prophet's Sunnah and the understanding of how to apply the law) turns the text into guidance for a way of life. The closing phrase reminds believers that without this guidance they were lost in clear misguidance, so gratitude and adherence to his teaching are the proper response to such a favor.

translation: Is it that when a calamity struck you, although you had inflicted twice as much, you said, 'How is this?' Say, 'It is from yourselves.' Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse addresses the believers after the defeat at Uhud, where they lost about seventy men, having inflicted double that number of losses on the polytheists at Badr. When they wondered in astonishment how this could happen to them while the Messenger was among them and they were fighting for God's cause, God directs the Prophet to answer that the cause lay within themselves. The archers disobeyed the Prophet's command to hold their position, and the fighters quarreled over the spoils. The lesson is that defeat and hardship are consequences of one's own failings, such as disobedience, disunity and worldly attachment, and not an injustice from God. Believers should therefore look inward to examine and correct themselves before blaming outside circumstances. The closing reminder that God has power over all things teaches that victory and loss alike are within His power and wisdom, and that He can grant success when the believers fulfill the conditions of steadfastness and obedience.

translation: And what befell you on the day the two armies met was by God's permission, so that He might make evident the believers.
interpretation: The setback the Muslims suffered at Uhud, when they met the army of the Quraysh, was neither chance nor a sign that God had abandoned them. It happened by His decree and knowledge, and it served a purpose: to distinguish the sincere believers, who stayed steadfast and patient under trial, from those whose faith was weak or hypocritical. Hardship is thus a means of testing and purifying the community, so that what is hidden in hearts becomes plain in action. Believers should therefore take such trials as a lesson and a refinement of their faith, not as grounds for despair.

translation: And that He might make evident those who were hypocrites. It was said to them, "Come, fight in the cause of God, or defend." They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." They were that day nearer to disbelief than to faith, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. And God knows best what they conceal.
interpretation: The hardships at Uhud served as a test that exposed the true state of people's hearts. Hypocrites, who professed faith outwardly, were revealed when they were called to fight or at least to defend their community, and they made a flimsy excuse that they did not expect real fighting. Their excuse was a lie and showed that their inner allegiance leaned toward disbelief more than faith at that moment, since faith is proven by commitment and sacrifice, not by empty words. The verse teaches that mere verbal claims are worthless when they contradict what is in the heart, and that God, who knows all hidden intentions, uses trials to separate the sincere from the insincere.

translation: Those who said of their brothers while they themselves stayed behind: 'If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.' Say: 'Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: The verse (Al 'Imran 3:168) refers to the hypocrites who stayed behind from the battle of Uhud and then blamed the believers who went out and were martyred, claiming that obeying them and staying home would have saved their lives. God instructs the Prophet to answer with a challenge that exposes the emptiness of this claim. Death is decreed with a fixed appointed time and is not averted by staying behind or by avoiding battle. If they truly believe that human planning can prevent death, they should use it to ward off their own death when it comes. Since they cannot, their claim is false, and the martyrs' fate was not caused by their decision to fight but by God's decree. The verse teaches reliance on God's decree, rebukes cowardice disguised as cleverness, and shows that cowardly excuses do not change the appointed hour.

translation: Do not think of those who have been killed in the cause of God as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision.
interpretation: The verse consoles the families of martyrs and encourages believers by teaching that death in God's cause is not an end or a loss. Those who sacrifice their lives for God and His truth enter a special, honored life in God's presence, which is beyond human perception. There they are sustained and shown God's favor. Their worldly deaths are therefore not a defeat, and their sacrifice earns lasting honor and reward. This should strengthen believers' courage and steadfastness and ease their grief.

translation: Rejoicing in what God has given them of His bounty, and they rejoice for those who have not yet joined them, who remain behind them, that there is no fear upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse describes the martyrs who fell in God's cause (as the preceding verse about those slain in God's way indicates). Their joy is not only for their own honor and the provision and favor God has granted them, but extends to their brethren still alive in the world, whom they await. They are glad because they know that those who follow them on the path of faith and sacrifice will also be spared the fear of the Hereafter and will not grieve over what they left behind. This shows the selflessness of the believers: even in their own bliss they care for those they left behind, and it consoles the living that steadfastness in faith leads to a state free from fear and sorrow.

translation: They rejoice in a favor from God and His bounty, and that God does not let the reward of the believers be lost.
interpretation: The verse (Al Imran 3:171) describes the martyrs who, in their state of life with their Lord, feel joy because of God's grace and generosity: their sacrifice has been accepted and they have been honored with a station beyond what they hoped for. Their joy is also an assurance to every believer that no good deed, whether struggle, patience, or sincerity, is wasted or forgotten with God. The reward is certain and is granted both as what is deserved and as added bounty, so faith that is expressed through steadfast action will always be fully and generously repaid.

translation: Those who responded to God and the Messenger after injury had afflicted them – for those who did good among them and were mindful of God, there is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse refers to the believers who, after being wounded at Uhud, answered the Prophet's call to pursue the enemy the next day despite their pain and exhaustion. It teaches that true faith is proved by obedience at the hardest moments, when the body is weak and fear is strong. The great reward is promised not merely to those who responded, but to those who joined that response with ihsan (excellence and sincerity in their deeds) and taqwa (God-consciousness and avoidance of disobedience). Obedience in hardship, when combined with sincerity and piety, elevates a believer's rank and brings immense reward from God.

translation: Those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them," but it increased them in faith, and they said, "Sufficient for us is Allah, and [He is] the best Disposer of affairs." (Qur'an 3:173)
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith is strengthened rather than shaken by intimidation and worldly threats. When the believers were warned that a large hostile force had assembled against them, they did not give in to fear or doubt. Instead, the warning drove them to rely more fully on God, and their trust was shown in the words 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' It shows that belief is not merely a claim but grows through trials, and that sincere reliance on God (tawakkul) means doing what one can while entrusting the outcome to Him, finding in Him security and sufficiency whatever the power of the opposing side.

translation: So they returned with favor from God and bounty, no harm having touched them, and they followed the pleasure of God. And God is the possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the believers who answered the Prophet's call to pursue the enemy after the battle of Uhud, even though they were wounded, and who put their trust in God when people tried to frighten them with the size of the enemy's forces. Because they relied on God and obeyed, God rewarded them: they came back safe, with no harm or fighting befalling them, and with the added gain of favor and bounty (such as security, the preservation of their strength, and the enemy's fear of them). Their true achievement, however, was that they sought God's pleasure, which is greater than any worldly gain. The verse teaches that whoever trusts in God and responds to His command with obedience will be protected and enriched by His grace, and that God's bounty far exceeds what people expect or deserve.

translation: It is only Satan who frightens you of his allies; so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.
interpretation: The verse says that the fear of the disbelievers' power, which some people felt after the battle of Uhud when they were warned that the enemy had gathered a great force against them, is a whisper of Satan. He uses it to weaken believers' resolve and to push them away from striving in God's cause. Believers should not let such intimidation rule their hearts, because the allies of Satan have no power except what God permits. Fear of God, which means reverence for Him and awareness of His authority, should be the only fear that governs their decisions. Such fear is a mark of true faith, and it frees the believer from fear of people. Whoever trusts God and fears Him alone will remain steadfast in the face of threats, because he knows that benefit and harm are in God's hands.

translation: And let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will never harm God at all. God intends that He assign them no share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who was deeply pained by the people who rushed toward disbelief and opposition, often after showing a hint of faith. God tells him not to grieve, for their rejection can never diminish God's might or harm His cause; the only ones harmed are the disbelievers themselves. Their eagerness for disbelief is met with a just consequence: God's decree that they will have no portion of reward or goodness in the Hereafter, because they chose to forfeit it by their own deeds, and a severe punishment awaits them. The lesson is that the believer's task is to convey the message with steadfastness and not be overwhelmed by sorrow over those who reject it, trusting that God's religion does not depend on anyone's acceptance and that divine justice will account for everyone.

translation: Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief in exchange for faith will never harm God in the least, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a bad bargain: a person who turns away from faith and takes up disbelief has traded something of infinite worth for something worthless. God is utterly self-sufficient, so no one's rejection can diminish His dominion or cause Him any loss. The only one harmed is the disbeliever, who forfeits guidance and brings upon himself a painful punishment. Belief benefits the believer, and disbelief damages only the one who chooses it.

translation: And let not those who disbelieve think that the respite We grant them is better for them. We only grant them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: God's delay in punishing the disbelievers is not a sign of His approval or of their success, and it is not a good for them. Their long life, wealth and worldly ease are a test and a gradual drawing-in (istidraj). Because they persist in rejecting the truth, the respite only lets them pile up more sins and so deepens their accountability. In the end they will face a punishment that humiliates them, which is a fitting answer to the arrogance with which they treated the truth. The verse also warns believers not to be deceived by the apparent prosperity of wrongdoers, and it warns every person not to take God's patience as a license to carry on in disobedience, but to use the time given to repent and correct himself.

translation: God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He separates the wicked from the good. Nor would God let you have access to the unseen, but God chooses from among His messengers whomever He wills. So believe in God and His messengers. If you believe and are mindful of God, you will have a great reward.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in connection with the aftermath of the Battle of Uhud, explains that hardships and trials are a divine means of sifting the sincere believers from the hypocrites, so that the community's ranks do not remain mixed and unclear. God does not expose the hidden contents of hearts to people directly through ordinary knowledge; knowledge of the unseen is given only to the messengers He selects, through revelation, so people should not demand to know who is truly sincere or hypocritical but should rely on God's guidance. The believers are therefore called to place true faith in God and in all His messengers and to practice God-consciousness, with the promise that steadfast faith and piety will be rewarded with a great recompense.

translation: Let not those who are miserly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. What they were miserly with will be placed as a collar around their necks on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse warns that withholding wealth, especially obligatory charity such as zakat and spending in God's cause, is not a means of security or gain but a source of harm. Wealth is a bounty from God, not something people truly own, so hoarding it out of greed reflects ingratitude and misplaced attachment. The image of the hoarded wealth becoming a collar around the miser's neck on the Day of Judgment shows that what they clung to will become their burden and punishment. The reminder that God inherits the heavens and the earth means everything people possess will return to Him when they die and pass away, so clinging to it is futile, whereas spending it for good brings lasting reward. Finally, God's full awareness of all deeds means that both hidden stinginess and sincere generosity are known and will be recompensed accordingly.

translation: Indeed, God has heard the saying of those who said, 'God is poor, while we are rich.' We will record what they said, and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, 'Taste the punishment of the Burning Fire.'
interpretation: This verse was revealed in response to some of the Jews of Medina who mocked the Qur'anic call to give a 'goodly loan' to God, saying that God must be poor if He asks for money while they are wealthy. The verse shows that God hears and knows every word, including scornful and blasphemous speech, and that nothing said is lost: it is recorded for reckoning. Their mockery is linked to an older pattern of wrongdoing, the killing of prophets unjustly, which suggests that this is not a one-off slip but the expression of a hardened attitude of arrogance toward divine guidance. The verse teaches that God is utterly self-sufficient and that it is people who are in need of Him. Charity is a means by which people benefit themselves and earn reward, and God's calling it a loan is an honor and encouragement to people, not a sign of need. Those who ridicule God's commands and reject His messengers will face just recompense in the Fire, where the punishment fits the offense.

translation: That is because of what your hands have sent forth, and because God is never unjust to His servants.
interpretation: The suffering of the punishment is the consequence of the deeds a person has committed in this life, not an arbitrary act. Attributing it to what 'your hands' sent ahead stresses that people are personally accountable for their own choices, which they have forwarded to the Hereafter as a record awaiting them. God's justice is absolute and intensive: He never wrongs anyone by adding to their punishment, withholding a reward they have earned, or punishing them for what they did not do. Hence the blame for the torment rests on the wrongdoers themselves and not on any injustice from their Lord.

translation: Those who said, 'Indeed, God has taken a covenant from us that we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering that fire consumes.' Say: 'Messengers have already come to you before me with clear proofs and with that which you speak of, so why did you kill them, if you are truthful?'
interpretation: The verse answers certain People of the Book who rejected the Prophet Muhammad by claiming that God had made them promise not to believe in a messenger unless he produced a sacrifice consumed by heavenly fire. The Qur'an exposes this as a pretext rather than a sincere condition. Earlier prophets had indeed brought clear signs, including the very miracle of the consuming fire that these people demanded, yet their forebears still killed them. If their real concern had been to see this proof, they would have believed those earlier messengers instead of murdering them. Their refusal therefore comes from stubbornness and arrogance, not from a lack of evidence, and the verse shows that demands for further miracles are often excuses used to avoid submitting to the truth.

translation: And if they deny you, then messengers before you were also denied, who came with clear proofs, with the scriptures, and with the illuminating Book.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by reminding him that rejection is the common fate of truthful messengers. Their being denied did not stem from any lack of evidence, since they brought clear miracles and signs, scriptures containing admonitions and wisdom, and a Book that illuminates the path of guidance. Denial therefore reflects the stubbornness and arrogance of the deniers, not a flaw in the message or the messenger. The Prophet should remain patient and steadfast, following the example of earlier prophets, and trust that truth will ultimately prevail while the deniers bear responsibility for their choice.

translation: Every soul will taste death. And you will only be given your full recompense on the Day of Resurrection. So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed attained success. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.
interpretation: The verse teaches that death is a certain end for every created being, so no one should be deceived into thinking worldly life is permanent. Complete and true justice is not fully realized in this world, since some wrongdoers prosper and some righteous people suffer; the full settlement of deeds is deferred to the Day of Resurrection, when each person receives what they earned. Real success is therefore not wealth, status, or comfort, but being spared the Fire and entering Paradise, a victory that is final and unsurpassable. By contrast, worldly life is described as a deceptive pleasure: it dazzles and tempts people into heedlessness, yet it is brief and fleeting like goods that serve a purpose for a moment and then vanish. The believer is thus urged to keep the afterlife as the ultimate goal, using this world as a means rather than an end, and finding patience and consolation in the face of hardship and loss.

translation: You will surely be tested in your wealth and in yourselves, and you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with God much abuse. But if you are patient and mindful of God, then indeed that is among the matters requiring firm resolve.
interpretation: The verse tells believers that hardship is a certain part of faith: they will be tried through loss of property and through harm to themselves, such as illness, fear, or hardship, and they will also endure verbal insults and slander from opponents of other faiths. The right response is not retaliation driven by anger but patience and God-consciousness, meaning steadfastness under provocation and restraint within the limits God has set. Such conduct is described as 'azm al-umur', the mark of strong character and resolve, because it takes real determination to remain firm in principle and composed in conduct when tested. In this way the verse prepares the community for adversity and presents patience as a deliberate, active strength rather than passive weakness.

translation: And [remember] when God took a covenant from those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they threw it behind their backs and exchanged it for a small price. And wretched is what they purchase.
interpretation: The verse says that knowledge of revelation is a trust, not a private possession. Those who are given the Scripture, meaning the scholars and keepers of divine guidance, are bound by a solemn covenant to teach it openly and honestly, even when the truth is inconvenient or threatens their status, income, or alliances. The people of earlier scriptures broke this covenant by discarding the Book's teachings, as if they had thrown them behind their backs, and by hiding or distorting its rulings and its news of the coming Prophet in return for worldly gain such as wealth, position, and popular approval. The worldly gain is called a 'small price' because even the greatest worldly profit is trivial next to the truth and the reward of the Hereafter. The closing words condemn this trade as an utterly losing bargain. The lesson applies to every community: those entrusted with religious knowledge must not suppress or sell the truth.

translation: Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done, and love to be praised for what they have not done, do not think they are in safety from the punishment; and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse (Al Imran 3:188) condemns people who take pride in their deeds and crave praise for good they never did, such as those who hid the truth yet wished to be commended as people of knowledge and sincerity. The interpretation is that outward show and false self-presentation are grave moral faults. Rejoicing in one's achievements is not the issue; the issue is claiming credit for what one has not done, or being pleased with deception, concealment of truth, and hypocrisy. God warns that such people should not imagine they will escape accountability, for their claim to virtue will not protect them from punishment. The verse teaches honesty, sincerity, and seeking God's approval rather than the praise of people.

translation: To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true and absolute sovereignty rests with God alone, since He created the heavens and the earth and sustains them. Whatever authority humans hold is only a temporary trust that He grants, and so it is subject to His will and accountability before Him. His power over all things means that nothing lies beyond His ability and nothing can frustrate His purposes. For the believer, this should inspire humility before God, trust in Him in times of hardship, and hope in His promises of help, forgiveness, and justice, because the One who owns all things and can do all things is the One to whom they turn.

translation: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of the night and the day, there are signs for people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse (Q 3:190) teaches that the order and design of the cosmos, such as the vastness of the heavens and earth and the precise, regular succession of night and day, are open signs pointing to a wise, powerful Creator. These signs are truly perceived only by 'ulu al-albab', those who use their reason and reflect deeply rather than looking superficially. So the verse summons believers to make contemplation of creation a path to recognizing God's oneness, power, and purpose, turning observation into faith and remembrance, as the following verses describe: those who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on creation.

translation: Those who remember God while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying]: 'Our Lord, You did not create all this in vain. Glory be to You! Protect us from the punishment of the Fire.'
interpretation: The verse describes people of true understanding whose awareness of God is constant and not limited to formal worship; whatever their physical state, their hearts and tongues stay attached to Him. Their remembrance (dhikr) is joined with reflection (tafakkur), so that contemplating the order, vastness, and precision of the cosmos leads them to see purpose and wisdom behind creation rather than randomness. From this recognition they conclude that existence has meaning and that humans are accountable, which moves them to glorify God and to pray for protection from the Fire. The verse teaches that faith is complete when devotion of the heart and the use of reason work together, with observation of creation leading to humility, gratitude, and fear of the consequences of heedlessness.

translation: Our Lord, whomever You admit into the Fire, You have indeed disgraced him; and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.
interpretation: This verse is part of the supplication of those who reflect on creation (Al Imran 3:191-194). It voices their awareness that entering Hell is not merely physical suffering but profound humiliation and disgrace before all creation, which is the worst loss of the Hereafter. It also stresses that on the Day of Judgment no one can rescue the wrongdoers, who persisted in injustice by associating partners with God or by wronging themselves and others, since no intercessor or ally can overturn God's judgment without His permission. By saying this, the believers show fear of God's punishment, seek refuge in Him, and affirm that salvation lies only in His mercy and in avoiding wrongdoing.

translation: Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, saying: 'Believe in your Lord,' so we believed. Our Lord, so forgive us our sins, and remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die in the company of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse is the supplication of the people of understanding (ulu al-albab) who reflect on God's creation. Their reflection leads them to answer the call of the Prophet, who summons people to faith, and they respond with immediate belief. Having believed, they do not rely on their faith alone but humbly ask God for forgiveness of major sins, the effacing of lesser misdeeds, and a good end, to die among the abrar, the righteous who are devoted to obedience. It teaches that true faith is a response to divine guidance coupled with humility, repentance, and a longing to end life in the company of the pious.

translation: Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not break Your promise.
interpretation: This verse is the supplication of the people of reflection and understanding, who, after contemplating creation and affirming faith, ask God to fulfill His promises of forgiveness, mercy, support in this world, and Paradise in the next. Their plea not to be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection shows that the believer's deepest fear is humiliation before God and all creation on that Day. They do not ask because they doubt God's promise, since they affirm that He never breaks His word, but because asking is itself an act of worship and humility. It reflects that the believer holds fast to hope grounded in God's truthfulness while remaining anxious about whether their own deeds and sincerity make them worthy of what was promised, so they seek it as a grace from God rather than a right they have earned.

translation: So their Lord responded to them: "I will not let the deed of any doer among you be lost, whether male or female; you are one from another. So those who emigrated, and were driven out of their homes, and were harmed in My cause, and fought and were killed, I will surely remove from them their misdeeds, and I will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God. And God has with Him the best reward."
interpretation: This verse (Q 3:195) shows God answering the prayers of the people of understanding mentioned in the preceding verses. It affirms divine justice: no effort made for God's sake is wasted, and spiritual worth is not determined by gender, since men and women are of one origin and stand equal in accountability and reward. The hardships it lists, such as emigration, expulsion, persecution, fighting and martyrdom, are sacrifices that earn forgiveness of sins and entry into Paradise. The reward is a gift from God Himself, who holds the finest recompense, so believers should look to Him rather than to worldly compensation.

translation: Let not the prosperous movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you.
interpretation: This verse (Al Imran 3:196) warns the believer not to be misled by the worldly success of those who reject faith, such as their trade, travel, wealth, and power. Such prosperity is not a sign of God's approval or of the truth of their way.
