It is only a fleeting, trivial enjoyment (as the next verse says, 'a little enjoyment'), after which their final abode is Hell. The believer should measure success by faith and righteousness and the lasting reward of the Hereafter, not by outward worldly gain, and so should stay steadfast and not envy or imitate the disbelievers.

translation: A brief enjoyment, then their abode is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 3:197) teaches that the worldly prosperity and freedom of movement enjoyed by those who reject faith is fleeting and of little worth when set against eternity. Because it ends with the Fire, it is not a sign of God's favor, and believers should not be deceived by it or envy it. The word 'resting place' (mihad) is used ironically: it normally means a comfortable bed, yet here it names Hell, which is the opposite of rest and so adds to the severity of the warning.

translation: But those who fear their Lord will have Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a hospitable welcome from God. And what is with God is better for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the brief, deceptive enjoyment of those who disbelieve with the lasting reward of the God-conscious. True success lies not in worldly prosperity, which is fleeting, but in taqwa, a living awareness of God that shapes one's conduct. Paradise is described as a 'nuzul', the honored welcome prepared for a guest, which shows that God receives the believers with generosity and dignity, and that their reward is a gift from Him and not merely a wage. The closing statement that what is with God is better for the righteous (al-abrar) reminds believers that even the greatest worldly comforts cannot compare with what God has stored for them. This should console those who endure hardship and keep them from envying the apparent ease of the wrongdoers.

translation: And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in God and in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before God. They do not exchange the verses of God for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, God is swift in account.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the People of the Book are not all alike: a sincere minority, whose faith is real rather than tribal, recognize the unity of divine revelation. Because they believe in the Torah or Gospel and also in the Qur'an, they accept the truth wherever it comes from, and their belief is shown by humility before God rather than pride or sectarian rivalry. They refuse to sell out the truth for worldly gain, such as status, wealth, or leadership, which others among them obtained by concealing or distorting scripture, including the descriptions of the Prophet. God promises that such people receive their full reward with Him, doubled in recognition of their faith in both revelations, and He is swift in reckoning, so no good deed is lost and justice is neither delayed nor neglected.

translation: O you who believe, be patient, outlast one another in patience, remain steadfast at your posts, and be mindful of God, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse sets out a graded path to lasting success for the believing community. First comes personal patience (isbiru): enduring hardship, steadfastly obeying God, and restraining oneself from disobedience. Next is 'sābiru', meaning to surpass the opponent in endurance, so the believers' perseverance must exceed that of those who oppose them, whether in conflict, trials, or the long struggle to uphold the truth. 'Rābiṭū' means to stay constantly prepared and vigilant, guarding the frontiers of the community, and by extension holding fast to one's duties and keeping the community united and ready. All of this is anchored in taqwā, consciousness of God, so that patience and vigilance are done for His sake and not for pride or worldly gain. The promise of falāḥ, success in this life and the next, comes to those who join inner endurance, outward readiness, and God-consciousness.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul, and created from it its mate, and spread from the two of them many men and women. And fear God, in whose name you demand your rights from one another, and (respect) the ties of the womb. Indeed, God is ever an Observer over you.
interpretation: The verse grounds all social ethics in the shared origin of humanity: because every human being descends from one soul, people are fundamentally one family and equal in dignity, so no one has grounds to oppress or look down on another, whether man or woman, strong or weak. Taqwa (God-consciousness) is therefore the foundation of just dealings. People invoke God's name when asking things of each other, which means they must honor that name by fulfilling their obligations, and they must preserve the bonds of kinship, since severing family ties violates both God's right and the rights of relatives. The closing reminder that God is constantly watching over them means that no wrong, public or hidden, escapes His knowledge, which should make a person accountable in conscience and treat others, especially the vulnerable such as orphans and women, as the passages that follow in the surah require.

translation: And give orphans their properties, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their properties along with your own properties. Indeed, that is ever a great sin.
interpretation: This verse establishes the guardian's duty of trust toward orphans: when they reach maturity and are capable of managing wealth, their property must be returned to them intact and in full. Guardians must not swap the orphan's valuable assets, such as healthy livestock or fine goods, for inferior ones of their own, nor secretly blend the orphan's wealth into their own and spend it as though it were theirs. The Qur'an calls such conduct a 'great sin' (hoban kabira) because it exploits the weakest members of society, who cannot defend themselves. It teaches that the measure of a community's justice is how it treats its most vulnerable, and that honesty in stewardship is a matter of accountability before God.

translation: And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans, then marry those women who seem good to you: two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then marry only one, or what your right hands possess. That is more likely to keep you from injustice.
interpretation: The verse was revealed to curb the exploitation of orphan girls under the guardianship of men, who would marry them for their wealth and deny them fair treatment and dowry. It tells guardians that if they fear they cannot be just to orphans, they should turn to other women in marriage instead. Marriage to more than one wife is permitted only within limits, up to four, and it depends on the ability to treat wives equitably. Because the condition of justice is strict, the verse points to monogamy as the safer course for anyone who doubts he can be just. The closing phrase, 'that is more likely to keep you from injustice,' shows that the aim of the rule is to prevent oppression and protect the vulnerable, especially orphans and women, within the family.

translation: And give the women their bridal gifts graciously. But if they willingly remit to you any part of it, then consume it with enjoyment and ease.
interpretation: The verse establishes the dower (mahr) as a right belonging to the wife herself, not to her guardians or her husband, and it is to be paid as a freely given, sincere gift rather than grudgingly or as a mere price. It protects women's financial independence: the husband may not claim any of it by pressure or pretense. Only if the wife, of her own good will and without coercion, chooses to give back some portion may he lawfully benefit from it, and then it is pure and wholesome for him. The emphasis on 'willingness of the soul' makes the wife's genuine consent the sole condition that renders the remitted amount lawful.

translation: And do not entrust to the weak-minded your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it, clothe them, and speak to them words of kindness and honor.
interpretation: Wealth is a trust that sustains the life and stability of the community, so it must not be handed over to those who lack the judgment to manage it and would squander it, whether through youth, foolishness, or poor discretion. Such people are not to be abandoned or humiliated, though. Their guardians remain responsible for spending on their food and clothing out of the wealth itself, and for treating them with gentle, respectful words that console them and encourage their growth in responsibility. The verse balances protecting property from waste with preserving the dignity and welfare of the one who is under guardianship.

translation: Test the orphans until they reach the age of marriage; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property. Do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up. Whoever is rich, let him abstain entirely; and whoever is poor, let him consume it in a fair and reasonable manner. And when you hand over their property to them, call witnesses in their presence. And Allah suffices as a Reckoner.
interpretation: This verse sets out the guardian's duty toward orphans' wealth as a trust, with a clear process and accountability. Guardians should train and observe orphans as they mature, assessing their ability to manage money, and release the property only once they reach adulthood and show sound judgment (rushd), not merely when they reach a certain age. Until then, guardians must not exploit the property by spending it extravagantly or by hurrying to use it up before the orphans come of age and can claim it. A wealthy guardian should refrain from taking anything for his own use, since his guardianship is a service to be given freely, while a poor guardian may take a modest, customary amount in fair compensation for his work, without excess. When the property is handed over, it should be done before witnesses, to prevent later disputes and protect both sides. The closing statement reminds guardians that even if people never find out about any wrongdoing, God is the ultimate Reckoner who knows every account, which makes the guardian's own conscience and fear of God the final safeguard of the orphans' rights.

translation: For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it be little or much — a obligatory, fixed share.
interpretation: This verse establishes inheritance as a legally binding right for both men and women, overturning the pre-Islamic Arabian custom in which women and children were often excluded and only adult male fighters inherited. By repeating the entitlement for each group and stressing that it applies to any estate, small or large, the verse closes the loophole of withholding small inheritances or denying heirs on the pretext of insignificance. Describing the share as 'mafrud' (obligatory, divinely decreed) means it is not a favor or a matter of discretion for relatives or guardians, but a right fixed by God that no one may waive on another's behalf or withhold. The detailed proportions are given in the verses that follow, but this verse lays down the principle of justice and the dignity of women as rightful owners of wealth.

translation: And when the relatives, the orphans, and the poor are present at the division of the inheritance, provide for them from it, and speak to them kind words.
interpretation: The verse teaches that an inheritance is an occasion for generosity and compassion, not only for the legal distribution of shares. When relatives who are not entitled to a fixed share, orphans, and needy people are present as the estate is divided, the heirs should give them something voluntarily from the wealth as a gift, so that they do not feel resentment or envy while watching others receive what they do not. The instruction to speak kindly adds that the giving should be accompanied by gentle, respectful words, without belittling them, reproaching them, or making them feel they are a burden. Together, the verse shows that Islam links wealth with social solidarity and good character: the heirs share part of their unexpected gain, and they treat the recipients with dignity, which preserves family ties and softens hearts.

translation: And let those fear (God) who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them be conscious of God and speak words that are right and just.
interpretation: The verse appeals to a person's natural parental concern: just as someone who is dying fears for the fate of his own helpless children and wishes they be treated with justice and kindness, he should feel the same fear about the orphans in his care and about the dying person's heirs when he is present at a bequest. Anyone who is in a position to advise, manage, or take charge of the property of the weak should put himself in the place of the vulnerable, fear God by not wronging them or consuming their wealth unjustly, and speak honest, fair, and upright words. This means giving sincere counsel in wills, avoiding deceit and harshness, and treating orphans with fairness and gentleness, as one would hope others would treat his own children after his death.

translation: Indeed, those who devour the wealth of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will be burned in a Blaze.
interpretation: The verse warns that taking an orphan's property through injustice is not a harmless gain but a grave sin whose consequence is certain punishment. The wealth that seems lawful and beneficial to the wrongdoer is described as fire in his belly, which means that what he takes will become the very cause of his torment in the Hereafter. Orphans are weak and have no one to protect their rights, so God Himself stands as their guardian and threatens severe punishment for anyone who exploits their helplessness. The message is that guardians and relatives must safeguard orphans' wealth with honesty and fairness, and that betrayal of this trust carries the gravest accountability.

translation: God instructs you concerning your children: the male receives the equivalent of the share of two females. If there are only daughters, two or more, they receive two-thirds of what the deceased leaves. If there is only one daughter, she receives half. For the parents of the deceased, each receives one-sixth of what he leaves, if he has a child. If he has no child and his parents are his heirs, then his mother receives one-third. If he has siblings, his mother receives one-sixth. All this is after any bequest he may have made or any debt is paid. You do not know which of your parents or children is nearer to you in benefit. This is an obligation from God. Indeed, God is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes a binding, divinely fixed system of inheritance that replaces pre-Islamic customs which often excluded women and children from inheriting. By setting out specific shares for children, daughters, and parents, and by requiring that debts and bequests be settled first, it ensures that wealth is distributed in a just and orderly way among close family members. The male's double share is understood in light of his financial responsibility to support family members, including maintaining wives, children and relatives, whereas a woman's wealth is her own and she bears no such obligation. The statement that people cannot know who among their parents and children will benefit them most warns against letting human judgment or favoritism decide the distribution; God, who is All-Knowing and Wise, has determined the portions with perfect knowledge of what is best, so they are to be accepted as a sacred obligation rather than altered by personal preference.

translation: And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is a fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they may have made or any debt. And for them (your wives) is a fourth of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you may have made or any debt. And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor offspring (kalala) but has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they share in a third, after any bequest made or any debt, without harm being caused. This is an ordinance from God, and God is All-Knowing, Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse sets out a just, divinely ordained system of inheritance that protects the rights of spouses and extended family, with shares that vary according to whether descendants exist, which reflects the differing financial responsibilities and needs of each case. It requires that debts and legitimate bequests be settled first, and it forbids using a will to harm the heirs (for example by bequeathing beyond the permitted third or contriving debts to deprive them). By stating that these shares are 'an ordinance from God', it teaches that the distribution of wealth after death is not left to human whim, bias or family disputes, but is a matter of fairness and obedience to God. The closing attributes, All-Knowing and Forbearing, remind believers that God knows the true wisdom behind these shares and the intentions of those who carry them out, and that He is patient with human shortcomings while still holding them to account.

translation: These are the limits set by God. Whoever obeys God and His Messenger, He will admit him into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. And that is the great triumph.
interpretation: Coming after the rulings on inheritance in Surah An-Nisa, this verse presents those rulings as boundaries set by God, not as human customs to be adjusted by preference or family interest. Staying within them, and following the guidance of God and His Messenger even when it costs one's own desires, is a form of obedience that God rewards with eternal Paradise. The verse teaches that real success is not the wealth or advantage gained by bending the rules, but the lasting salvation gained by submitting to God's justice, which is why it calls this reward the 'great triumph.'

translation: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, abiding therein eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse, which comes after the inheritance laws in Surat An-Nisa, warns that the boundaries God has set, such as the fair division of inheritance among rightful heirs, are not optional guidelines but binding limits. Rejecting God's ruling and the Prophet's guidance, or knowingly overstepping these limits out of disregard for divine justice, is a deliberate rebellion against the Lawgiver, and it brings a severe and lasting consequence. The 'humiliating punishment' reflects the fact that the transgressor sought to elevate his own desires, status or greed over God's command, so his punishment is one that strips him of dignity. The verse stresses that obedience to God and His Messenger is the foundation of a just social order and of salvation in the hereafter.

translation: And those of your women who commit immorality – bring against them four witnesses from among you. And if they testify, then confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.
interpretation: This verse laid down an early, interim ruling for dealing with proven sexual misconduct among women in the nascent Muslim community. It sets a very high evidentiary bar: four upright Muslim eyewitnesses are required, which protects women from false accusation and discourages public exposure of private wrongdoing. Only once guilt was established by this standard were they to be restrained in their homes, a measure of confinement and protection from further sin, lasting until death or until God provided a 'way' (sabīl), a further legislation. Most interpreters, following Ibn ʿAbbās, understood that this 'way' was later revealed in Sūrat al-Nūr (24:2) and in the Prophet's practice, which prescribed flogging for the unmarried and stoning for the married. The verse thus shows the gradual unfolding of Islamic law, and its emphasis on strict proof before punishment.

translation: And the two among you who commit it, punish them both. But if they repent and reform, then leave them alone. Indeed, God is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, following the preceding verse about the women who commit lewdness, addresses two persons who commit an indecent act (understood by many scholars as illicit relations or related lewdness) before a fixed legal punishment was prescribed. It instructs the community to impose a disciplinary measure of reproach and censure upon both offenders, without escalating to harsher treatment. The aim of the penalty is correction rather than vengeance: if they sincerely repent and amend their conduct, the community must cease rebuking and shaming them and let the matter rest, not bringing up their past. The verse closes by grounding this in God's own attributes: since God constantly accepts repentance and is merciful, believers should likewise treat the repentant with forgiveness and mercy, so that the door to reform stays open.

translation: Acceptance of repentance by God is only for those who do evil out of ignorance and then repent soon after; it is those to whom God turns in forgiveness. And God is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse explains that God has bound Himself, out of His mercy, to accept repentance from those who sin through ignorance, meaning a lapse of judgment, heedlessness, or being overpowered by desire rather than denying God or knowingly defying Him, and who then hasten to repent without persistent delay. Repentance is accepted when it is prompt and sincere, before the sinner grows hardened in wrongdoing or reaches the point of death. The closing names, 'All-Knowing' and 'All-Wise', teach that God knows the true state of each person's heart and the reasons behind their sins, and that His acceptance of repentance is placed with perfect wisdom on those who truly merit it.

translation: And repentance is not accepted from those who keep on doing evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed, I now repent," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers. For those We have prepared a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 4:18) teaches that repentance is accepted only while a person still has the opportunity to change, meaning that it must be sincere and made before the final moment of life. Someone who postpones turning back to God through a lifetime of wrongdoing, and then repents only when death is plainly before him, is not repenting from true remorse or free choice. He is acting out of helplessness, once the unseen has become visible and the chance to act has gone. The same applies to one who dies in disbelief, because his state is fixed at death. The verse is thus a warning against procrastination and a call to repent promptly, because God's mercy is vast but the time to benefit from it is limited by the approach of death. Putting off repentance while relying on a last-minute change of heart is a dangerous delusion, and the painful punishment prepared for such people shows how serious it is to waste the life God has given.

translation: O you who believe! It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will. And do not constrain them in order to take away part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. And if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing in which Allah has placed much good. (Qur'an 4:19)
interpretation: The verse abolishes the pre-Islamic custom whereby a deceased man's relatives treated his widow as part of the inheritance, either marrying her without her consent or preventing her from remarrying until she gave up her dower. More broadly, it establishes that a woman is a free person with rights, not property, and forbids harassing or confining a wife to extract her money, except where she is proven guilty of flagrant misconduct. It then lays down the standard of married life: treating wives with kindness and fairness in speech, spending, and companionship. Finally, it counsels patience when a husband feels aversion toward his wife, reminding him that human dislike is not a reliable judge, and that God may place great good in what one dislikes, such as righteous children, a change of heart, or spiritual reward for patience. Marriage is therefore to be governed by justice, compassion, and trust in God's wisdom rather than by coercion or personal whim.

translation: And if you wish to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a great amount of wealth, do not take back any of it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?
interpretation: The verse protects a wife's financial rights when a husband chooses to end a marriage and marry someone else. Whatever the husband gave her as dowry or gift, even if it was a qantar (a very large sum), becomes her rightful property, and he may not take any of it back or pressure her into returning it in order to free himself. Reclaiming it would be an unjust accusation (buhtan) against her, as though she had no right to it or had done something to deserve its loss, and a clear sin. The verse teaches that the marital bond is one of trust and fairness, and that a husband's freedom to divorce does not license him to deprive his wife of her due wealth.

translation: And how could you take it back, when you have been intimate with one another, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:21) forbids a husband from taking back the dowry or gifts he gave his wife when he divorces her. It stresses that the closeness of marital life and the binding covenant of marriage, which the wife enters under God's name and with the commitment to live together with kindness or part with kindness, create a profound bond of trust and mutual rights. To demand back what was given after this intimacy and pledge would be an act of injustice and betrayal, since the marriage contract is a sacred, weighty obligation, not a transaction that can be undone at the husband's whim with the wife's loss.

translation: And do not marry women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality and an abomination, and an evil way.
interpretation: God prohibits a man from marrying his father's former wives, whether the father divorced them or died, since doing so violates the respect and honor owed to a father and the sanctity of the family. This was a practice in pre-Islamic Arabia, where a son might inherit his father's widow as if she were property. The phrase 'except what has already passed' means that what was done in ignorance before the prohibition is forgiven and not held against them, though it must cease from now on. The verse then condemns the act with three descriptions: it is a fahishah (a grave indecency by nature and reason), maqt (something that arouses God's hatred and people's revulsion), and an evil path (leading to corruption of family bonds and dignity). The ruling also elevates the status of women, who are not to be passed down like inherited goods, and protects family relationships from disorder and enmity.

translation: Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters, your foster-mothers who nursed you, your foster-sisters through nursing, the mothers of your wives, your stepdaughters who are in your care born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage—but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame on you—and the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you combine two sisters in marriage, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes the categories of women whom a man may never marry, forming the core of Islamic marriage prohibitions, and these are grounded in three kinds of relationship: blood kinship (mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, nieces), nursing (a woman who nursed a child becomes like a mother and her daughters like sisters, so the sanctity of family extends to milk kinship), and marriage ties (mothers-in-law, stepdaughters if the marriage with their mother was consummated, and daughters-in-law of one's own sons). It also forbids having two sisters as wives at the same time, to protect family bonds from rivalry and severed ties. The exemption for 'what has already passed' means that unions made in pre-Islamic ignorance are not held against people, though they must end them going forward, and the closing reference to God's forgiveness and mercy reflects that the law is given as a protection of family honor and social harmony, with leniency for past mistakes.

translation: Also prohibited to you are married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is God's decree upon you. Lawful to you is everything beyond these, that you seek with your wealth in honorable marriage, not in fornication. So for the enjoyment you derive from them, give them their due dowries as an obligation. There is no blame on you for whatever you mutually agree upon after the obligation has been set. Indeed, God is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse completes the list of prohibited marriage partners by forbidding women who are already married, except captives of war whose previous marriages were dissolved by their captivity, according to the common classical reading. It then affirms that all women outside the prohibited categories are lawful, provided a man seeks them with his wealth, through the dowry, within a chaste and lawful marriage rather than illicit sex. The phrase about 'enjoyment' (istamta'tum) is understood as the conjugal intimacy of marriage, for which the husband owes the wife her dowry as a binding duty. The verse also allows the couple to agree afterward, by mutual consent, to adjust the dowry, such as the wife waiving part of it or the husband increasing it. The closing reminder of God's knowledge and wisdom indicates that these rules are set with full awareness of human needs and are designed to protect dignity, rights, and the moral order of family life.

translation: And whoever among you lacks the means to marry free, believing women, then [let him marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing young women. And God knows best your faith; you are one from another. So marry them with the permission of their guardians and give them their dowries in a fair manner, as chaste women, not fornicators, nor taking secret lovers. And when they are married, if they commit an indecency, then upon them is half the punishment that is upon free women. That is for those among you who fear hardship [falling into sin]. But that you be patient is better for you. And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse offers a legal concession for believing men who cannot afford the dowry and costs of marrying free believing women: they may marry believing slave women, but only with the consent of the women's owners and with a proper dowry paid to them, on condition that these women are chaste and not engaged in open or secret illicit relationships. The reminder that God knows best the faith of all and that 'you are one from another' stresses the spiritual equality of believers regardless of social status, so that a slave woman's worth lies in her faith, not her station. If such a married slave woman commits fornication, her penalty is half that of a free woman, reflecting mitigation due to her more vulnerable circumstances. The concession is meant only for one who truly fears falling into sin from prolonged celibacy; otherwise, patience and abstaining from such marriage is better, and God's forgiveness and mercy are reaffirmed as the ease behind these rulings.

translation: God wishes to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those who came before you, and to accept your repentance. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's legislation is an act of mercy and guidance, not a burden. By setting out lawful and forbidden things, as He did for the righteous communities before, God shows believers the path that earlier prophets and their faithful followers walked, so they can avoid the errors of those who strayed. His offer to accept repentance means that human failing is not the end: when people slip, the door to return remains open. The closing names, Knowing and Wise, affirm that these rulings flow from perfect knowledge of human nature and from wisdom in what serves human welfare, so trust in them is well placed.

translation: And Allah wishes to accept your repentance, but those who follow their desires wish that you deviate [into] a great deviation.
interpretation: The verse sets two competing invitations before the believers. God's will for them is mercy: to turn to them, forgive them, and guide them back to the straight path whenever they err. Those who are enslaved to their appetites want the opposite. They are not satisfied with going astray alone, so they try to pull others far away from God's limits, normalizing what He has forbidden, such as the unlawful relationships described in the preceding verses. The phrase 'a great deviation' warns that following desire is not a small slip but a steep slide away from truth, and that believers must choose God's path of repentance and restraint over the pull of those who profit from their downfall.

translation: Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for the human being was created weak.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 4:28) shows that divine legislation is rooted in mercy and in God's knowledge of human limits. The commands and permissions of the Law are not meant to crush people but to ease their lives. Because humans are created weak, with strong desires, fluctuating resolve, and vulnerability to error, God lightens their obligations. He offers concessions, such as lawful marriage to believing slave women for those who cannot afford free women, and He forgives their lapses when they turn back to Him. Human weakness is not a source of shame but a reason to rely on God, to seek His help in obedience, and to accept the ease He has built into religion.

translation: O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, but only through trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, God is ever Merciful to you.
interpretation: The verse lays down a foundation for a just economy: property is sacred, and it may legitimately change hands only through honest exchange that both sides freely accept. Anything gained by fraud, usury, theft, bribery, deception or coercion is 'falsehood' and is forbidden. The command not to 'kill yourselves' joins economic injustice to the destruction of the community. Because believers are one body, wronging or killing another is in effect harming oneself, and a society built on exploitation eventually destroys itself. The verse also forbids suicide and self-destructive conduct, including ruining oneself through greed and illicit gain. It ends by saying that God's prohibitions are a mercy to humankind, protecting lives, property and social trust.

translation: And whoever does that in transgression and injustice, We will soon cast him into the Fire. And that is always easy for God.
interpretation: The warning is aimed at anyone who commits the prohibited acts mentioned just before it, namely consuming others' wealth wrongfully and killing one another, and does so knowingly, out of hostility and wrongdoing rather than by mistake or necessity. Such a person will face punishment in Hell. The verse ends by stressing that carrying out this punishment is effortless for God. No one's power, status or ability to evade can prevent it, so no wrongdoer should presume he will escape. The aim is to deter people from violating the sanctity of life and property.

translation: If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your lesser misdeeds and admit you to a noble entrance.
interpretation: God shows His mercy by tying forgiveness to a person's effort at restraint. A believer who makes a sincere, sustained effort to stay away from the grave sins, such as associating partners with God, murder, usury, and wronging others, will find that God covers the minor slips and ordinary shortcomings that human weakness makes unavoidable, without needing to hold each one to account. Such a person is then promised a 'noble entrance', which is honored admission into Paradise, with dignity and without disgrace. The verse encourages people to aim first at guarding against the great wrongs, trusting in God's generosity for the rest. It is not permission to take small sins lightly, since persistent minor sins can become grave, and repentance is still required.

translation: And do not covet what Allah has favored some of you over others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches contentment with the distinct provisions, roles, and capacities that God has apportioned among people, and warns against the envy that corrodes community life. Rather than longing for what God has given to another, whether in wealth, status, or the different responsibilities assigned to men and women, each person is told that their own effort and standing are recorded and rewarded: every man and every woman receives a due share of what they earn. The remedy for the desire to have more is not resentment but turning to God in supplication, asking from His boundless bounty, since He knows perfectly who deserves what and why He distributes as He does. Thus the verse redirects ambition away from jealousy and toward personal striving, trust in divine wisdom, and prayer.

translation: And for everyone We have appointed heirs to what the parents and the nearest relatives leave behind. And as for those with whom your right hands have made a pledge, give them their share. Indeed, God is ever a Witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God has established a system of inheritance in which every person has rightful heirs, namely the parents and close kin, who receive from what the deceased leaves. It also addresses those bound to a person by solemn covenants, such as pacts of alliance or mutual support that were common in pre-Islamic Arabia. Such allies are to be given their due share, understood either as a bequest or a gift made in good faith, so that commitments are honored and not betrayed. The closing reminder that God witnesses everything means that no one can cheat heirs or allies or withhold what is owed without accountability, and it makes fairness and fidelity in dealing with wealth and promises a matter of conscience before God.

translation: Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because God has given some of them an advantage over others and because they spend from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in the husband's absence what God has guarded. As for those women from whom you fear defiance, admonish them, then forsake them in the beds, and then strike them lightly. But if they obey you, do not seek any way against them. Indeed, God is ever Most High and Great.
interpretation: The verse sets out a framework of family responsibility in which the husband carries the duty of guardianship and financial upkeep, and this obligation, not any inherent superiority, is the basis of his leadership in the household. The righteous wife is described as devout before God and faithful in protecting the marriage, her husband's honor and his property when he is absent, in a way God Himself has safeguarded. When serious discord or ill-will arises, the verse prescribes a graduated, restrained approach aimed at reconciliation rather than punishment: first counsel and advice, then temporary separation in the bed, and only as a last symbolic measure a light, non-harmful act (understood by many interpreters, following the Prophet's explanation, as something like a light touch with a toothbrush-like object that causes no injury or humiliation, and which many scholars discourage altogether). Once the wife returns to harmony, all further pressure or grievance must cease, and the closing reminder that God is Most High and Great warns husbands that any abuse of their authority will be answered by a Power far above them, so the authority is a trust, not a license for oppression.

translation: And if you fear a breach between the two of them, appoint an arbitrator from his family and an arbitrator from her family. If they both desire reconciliation, God will bring about agreement between them. Indeed, God is ever Knowing and Aware.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when a marriage is on the verge of collapse and the couple cannot settle their dispute alone, the matter should not be left to anger, pride, or hasty divorce, nor be imposed by force. Instead, the community, or the families, should intervene with fairness by appointing one wise, trusted mediator from each side, so that both spouses are represented and understood and neither feels wronged. The decisive condition is sincere intent: if the mediators and the couple truly desire reconciliation rather than victory, God grants them success and restores harmony between the spouses. The closing reminder that God is All-Knowing and All-Aware warns that He knows the hidden motives behind the dispute and the mediation, so everyone involved must be honest and seek the good of the couple and their family.

translation: Worship God and associate nothing with Him; and be good to parents, to relatives, to orphans, to the needy, to the neighbor who is near and the neighbor who is a stranger, to the companion at your side, to the wayfarer, and to those your right hands possess. Indeed, God does not love those who are arrogant and boastful.
interpretation: The verse binds devotion to God with ethical duty toward people, showing that true monotheism is not complete without social responsibility. Worship of God alone is the foundation, and it is immediately followed by a widening circle of obligations: first to parents, then to kin, then to the vulnerable (orphans and the poor), then to neighbors near and far, companions, travelers, and those under one's authority. Goodness (ihsan) means more than fulfilling minimal duties; it means generous, kind, and sincere treatment. The verse closes by naming arrogance and boastfulness as the inner disease that blocks all this, because a proud person looks down on others and withholds care from them. Thus God's love is for the humble who serve Him and treat others with kindness and dignity.

translation: Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon other people, and conceal what God has given them of His bounty. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns a pattern of miserliness that goes beyond personal greed: such people withhold their wealth from those entitled to it, encourage others to do the same, and hide the blessings God has granted them, whether wealth, knowledge, or status, out of ingratitude and to avoid their duties of charity and sharing. Concealing God's favor is treated as a form of denying it, which is why the Qur'an calls them 'disbelievers' (kafirun, those who cover over God's grace). Because their arrogance and hoarding degrade the needy and spread selfishness in society, their punishment is described as humiliating, a fitting response to their pride and contempt for others. The lesson is that gratitude to God is shown by openly acknowledging His blessings and spending from them generously.

translation: And [also] those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in God or in the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion, then what an evil companion he is.
interpretation: The verse condemns charity and spending that are driven by show and the desire for social praise rather than sincere faith. Such giving is empty because it is not grounded in belief in God and accountability on the Day of Judgment, so it earns no reward. The verse also teaches that people who live for display and reject sincere devotion have effectively let Satan become their constant companion, whispering to them, beautifying vanity and pride, and steering their choices. Having Satan as a close associate leads to a bad end, so the verse warns believers to purify their intentions, give for God's sake alone, and guard against the influence of Satan.

translation: And what harm would have come upon them if they had believed in God and the Last Day, and spent out of what God has provided for them? And God has always been All-Knowing of them.
interpretation: The verse (4:39) rebukes those who spend their wealth for show and who are stingy, not believing truly in God and the Last Day. It asks rhetorically what they would have lost by choosing faith and sincere charity: nothing harmful would have befallen them, and instead they would have gained lasting reward and God's pleasure. Their refusal comes from misplaced values, not from any real cost. The closing phrase reminds that God knows their hidden intentions, whether sincerity or pretense, so no motive in spending or withholding is concealed from Him, and each will be recompensed accordingly.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong anyone even by the weight of an atom; and if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's perfect justice and boundless generosity in the reckoning of deeds. On the Day of Judgment no one will be treated unjustly in even the tiniest measure: no sin will be increased beyond what it deserves and no good act will be overlooked or diminished. Yet while evil is requited only with its like, good is treated with grace. A single good deed is multiplied manifold, and beyond that multiplication God grants, out of His own bounty, a 'great reward' that exceeds what the deed would earn by strict measure. The believer is thus encouraged never to belittle a small act of goodness, since it is preserved, magnified and generously repaid by a Lord who is both perfectly just and abundantly merciful.

translation: So how will it be when We bring forth from every nation a witness, and bring you (O Muhammad) as a witness against these people?
interpretation: The verse warns of the terror of the Day of Judgment, when no one will be able to deny their deeds. Every prophet will testify before God about how his community responded to the message, and Prophet Muhammad will testify against his own people and those to whom he was sent, confirming that the message was delivered and the proof established. The rhetorical question 'how will it be?' conveys the severity of that moment, urging those who disbelieve or neglect God's rights and the rights of others to reflect now and correct themselves before they stand in front of witnesses whose testimony cannot be refuted.

translation: On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not be able to conceal from God any statement.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment the reality of each person's deeds will be so overwhelming and fully exposed that the deniers and those who defied the Messenger will long to be swallowed by the earth and become dust, like the animals, in order to escape the shame and punishment awaiting them. Any attempt to hide or deny what they did and said will be futile, because God knows everything, and their own tongues, hands, and limbs will testify against them. The verse teaches that no deception or concealment is possible before God, so a person should be sincere and obedient to the Messenger now, while there is still time to repent.

translation: O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor while in a state of major ritual impurity, except when passing through, until you have bathed. And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you has come from the toilet, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. Indeed, God is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse shows God's gradual and merciful approach to regulating believers' lives, and it ties prayer to awareness and purity. Prayer is a conscious conversation with God, so a believer must be fully present in mind, understanding the words they recite, which rules out intoxication, and in a state of physical cleanliness, which requires bathing after major impurity. The verse also stresses ease in religion: when water is unavailable or harmful because of illness or travel, dry ablution (tayammum) with clean earth is a valid substitute, so no hardship prevents a person from worshipping. The closing reminder that God is Pardoning and Forgiving shows that these concessions come from divine mercy, and that the aim is to keep the believer's connection with God constant, sincere, and attainable for everyone.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They purchase misguidance and wish that you, too, would lose the way.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:44) points to people among the People of the Book who had received knowledge of revelation but traded the guidance they knew for error, exchanging truth for worldly gain, status, or desire. Their misguidance is not passive: they want believers to go astray as well. The lesson is that possessing religious knowledge does not guarantee guidance, since knowledge corrupted by envy, self-interest, and love of leadership can become a tool of deception. Believers are therefore warned to be discerning, to hold fast to the clear path of revelation, and not to be swayed by those who seek to lead others away from it.

translation: And God knows best who your enemies are. And God suffices as a protector, and God suffices as a helper.
interpretation: The verse reassures the believers that God knows the true hostility hidden in the hearts of those who oppose them, including those who feign friendship while plotting against the faith, so the believers need not rely on their own guesswork or on alliances with such people. Since God alone is the sufficient guardian who looks after their affairs and the sufficient helper who grants victory, believers should place their trust in Him rather than fear their enemies or seek protection from them.

translation: Among those who are Jews are some who distort words from their proper places and say, 'We hear and we disobey,' and 'Hear, may you not be made to hear,' and 'Ra'ina,' twisting it with their tongues and slandering the religion. Had they said instead, 'We hear and we obey,' and 'Listen, and look upon us (unzurna),' it would have been better for them and more upright. But God has cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe only a few.
interpretation: The verse exposes the deceitful conduct of some among the Jews toward the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): they altered the meaning of divine words by changing their interpretation and context, and they mocked the Prophet with double-meaning phrases. They said 'we hear' aloud while inwardly adding 'and we disobey'; they said 'hear' as though honoring him while meaning 'may you not hear' as a curse; and they twisted 'ra'ina' (meaning 'give us your attention') with their tongues so that it sounded like a word of insult, thereby ridiculing the faith. The verse shows that sincere respect and obedience, expressed in the plain words 'we hear and we obey' and the courteous 'unzurna', would have been better and more upright. Their persistent stubborn rejection and insincerity distanced them from God's mercy, so only a small number of them truly believe.

translation: O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them backward, or curse them as We cursed the Sabbath-breakers. And the command of God is always carried out.
interpretation: This verse is a warning addressed to the People of the Book, especially the Jews of Medina, urging them to believe in the Qur'an because it confirms the truth of the earlier revelations they already possess, so rejecting it contradicts their own scripture. The threat of 'obliterating faces and turning them backward' is understood as a severe punishment: either a literal disfigurement, or a figurative image of spiritual ruin in which a people lose their sense of direction and guidance and are sent back toward misguidance and disgrace. The reference to the 'companions of the Sabbath', who were cursed for violating God's commandment through trickery, reminds them that earlier generations who defied divine law were punished. The closing phrase affirms that when God decrees a punishment, it is inevitable, so delay in its coming should not be mistaken for safety.

translation: Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills. And whoever associates partners with God has indeed invented a tremendous sin.
interpretation: The verse teaches that shirk, dying while ascribing partners to God, is the gravest wrong, because it denies the very basis of the relationship between creator and creature: God's oneness and exclusive right to be worshipped. Someone who persists in it until death, without repentance, closes the door to forgiveness for himself. Sins less than shirk, such as moral lapses and failings, remain within God's will and mercy: He may forgive them without punishment or hold the person to account, as His wisdom and justice decide. This keeps believers balanced between hope and fear: they should never despair of God's mercy for their sins, nor feel secure from His reckoning. The phrase 'invented a tremendous sin' shows that shirk is a fabrication against God, since it attributes to Him what has no truth, and it is therefore a lie of the greatest magnitude.

translation: Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, it is God who purifies whomever He wills, and they will not be wronged even by a thread's worth.
interpretation: The verse rebukes self-praise and the claim of moral or spiritual superiority, as made by those who deemed themselves pure and righteous because of their lineage, status, or religious affiliation. True purity is not established by one's own declaration but is a gift from God, who knows hearts and purifies whoever is sincere and deserving. Human worth is therefore measured by God's judgment alone, not by self-assessment. God's justice is complete: nobody will be wronged even by the tiniest amount (the fatil, the thread in a date stone's groove), so each person will receive exactly what their deeds merit. The believer should respond with humility, self-scrutiny, and reliance on God to purify the soul rather than boasting about their own goodness.

translation: See how they invent lies about God! And that alone is sufficient as a blatant sin.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:50) expresses astonishment and censure at those who falsely attribute to God things He never said or sanctioned, such as claiming personal purity and divine favor, or declaring lawful and unlawful what God did not. It teaches that attributing falsehood to God is among the gravest of wrongs, so grave that it needs no additional offense to condemn the one who does it. The 'clear sin' is plain to anyone with sound reason, because it combines arrogance, deception of others, and disrespect toward the Creator. The believer should therefore be careful to speak about religion only with knowledge and to avoid self-righteousness, since true purification belongs to God alone.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in jibt and taghut, and they say of the disbelievers, 'These are better guided in the way than those who believe.'
interpretation: The verse condemns a group among the People of the Book who, despite having received knowledge of revelation, let envy and worldly rivalry lead them into believing in false objects of devotion and submitting to falsehood and tyrannical powers. In order to oppose the Prophet and the believers, they flattered the idolaters of Makkah by declaring them more rightly guided than the Muslims. The lesson is that possessing religious knowledge does not guarantee guidance; when scholars abandon sincerity and justice, and let hostility and partisanship bend their judgment, they end up calling falsehood truth and preferring open polytheism to the truth, which exposes the depth of their moral and spiritual corruption.

translation: Those are the ones whom God has cursed; and whoever God curses, you will never find for him any helper.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:52) teaches that being cursed by God means being removed from His mercy and guidance, which is the consequence of persistent arrogance, rejecting the truth, and choosing falsehood over faith despite having received revelation. Those who bring this on themselves are cut off from divine support, so no ally, power, or intercessor can rescue them from the outcome of their own choices. True help and protection come only from God, and anyone who forfeits His mercy by rejecting the truth is left without any real defender.

translation: Or do they have a share in the dominion? Then they would not give people even the speck on a date-stone.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who envy others for the favor God has granted them, especially the People of the Book who begrudged the Prophet and the believers the gift of revelation. It asks whether they hold a share of God's sovereignty, and answers that if they did, their stinginess would be so extreme that they would not give others even the smallest trace of it, as small as the tiny groove on a date-stone. Their envy and miserliness thus expose how unfit they are to hold control over God's bounty. Sovereignty belongs to God alone, and He grants His favor and guidance to whom He wills, regardless of human jealousy.

translation: Or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty? But We gave the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those, particularly among the People of the Book, who begrudge the Prophet Muhammad and the believers the favor of prophethood and revelation. It reminds them that God's bounty is not new or unprecedented: He had already granted the descendants of Abraham, whom the Jews claim as their forefathers, the Book, wisdom, and a mighty dominion, as with David and Solomon. Since the Prophet Muhammad is also of Abraham's lineage, there is no justification for envy. God distributes His favor as He wills, and envy is a moral failing that blinds people to the continuity of divine guidance and leads them to reject truth out of resentment.

translation: Among them were some who believed in him, and among them were some who turned away from him. And Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.
interpretation: The verse refers to the descendants of Abraham's family, to whom God gave scripture, wisdom and a great kingdom, and it shows that receiving the same divine favor led to different responses. Some accepted the truth and the message that came to them, and so benefited from the blessing. Others rejected it and actively obstructed it, hindering both themselves and others from following it. For those who turn away in this way, God warns that Hell is enough as a punishment, a raging fire that needs nothing added to it. The point is that guidance is offered to all, each person is responsible for their own choice, and persistent rejection and obstruction of the truth brings a just and severe recompense.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our verses, We will drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are fully burned, We will replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, God is ever Mighty and Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the punishment of those who knowingly reject God's revelation is real, continuous, and just, not a brief or fading suffering. The renewal of the skins shows that the pain is felt in full and does not end through the body being consumed, because the skin is the organ of sensation and its constant replacement means the torment is never dulled. The purpose clause 'so that they may taste the punishment' stresses that the suffering is experienced fully as a consequence of their denial, rather than being arbitrary. The closing names, 'Mighty' and 'Wise', complete the meaning: God has the power to carry out this punishment and no one can resist or escape it, and He does so with wisdom, placing the recompense exactly where it is deserved, so it is neither excessive nor unjust. The verse thus serves as a serious warning to take God's signs seriously and not to reject them out of arrogance or neglect.

translation: But those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to deep, abundant shade.
interpretation: The verse sets the reward of the believers against the fate of the disbelievers mentioned just before it. Faith must be joined with righteous action, and together they lead to Paradise. The promise is described in terms of complete and lasting comfort. The flowing rivers and the eternal dwelling stand for abundance and security without end. The 'purified spouses' are companions free of every physical and moral flaw, which means that the believers' joy will be unmarred. The 'deep shade' is a lasting, protective comfort, and it is especially vivid to people who knew the harshness of desert heat. It suggests that Paradise offers protection and peace as well as pleasure. God's own words, 'We will admit them,' show that the entry into Paradise is an act of divine generosity and honor, granted to those whose faith was proven by their deeds.

translation: Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent indeed is the instruction God gives you. Indeed, God is ever Hearing and Seeing.
interpretation: This verse lays down the moral foundation of both personal and public life: integrity in what is entrusted and fairness in what is decided. 'Trusts' extend beyond returned deposits and borrowed goods to every responsibility one holds, including offices of authority, secrets, knowledge, and the duties owed to God, so that power and position are understood as a trust to be handed to those who deserve it and exercised for their benefit. The command to judge with justice then applies this principle to authority: whoever has power over others must rule without favoritism, kinship bias, or enmity, treating all parties as equal before the truth. God describes this as an excellent admonition because it brings order and trust to society and protects the weak from the strong. The closing reminder that God hears every word and sees every action means that no breach of trust or act of injustice is hidden, which makes accountability before Him the ultimate safeguard of honesty and justice.

translation: O you who believe, obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you believe in God and the Last Day. That is better and more excellent in outcome.
interpretation: The verse sets out the chain of legitimate authority in a believing community. Ultimate and independent obedience belongs to God, and obedience to the Messenger is the practical expression of it, since he conveys and explains God's revelation. Obedience to those in authority, such as rulers, scholars and leaders who administer the community's affairs, is conditional and derivative: it holds only so long as they stay within the bounds set by God and His Messenger, which is why the verb 'obey' is not repeated for them. When disagreements arise between people, or between people and their leaders, the final criterion is not personal opinion, tribal loyalty or political interest but the Qur'an and the Prophet's guidance. Returning disputes to this source is presented as a test of true faith in God and the Last Day, because a believer who expects to be held accountable submits to divine judgment. Doing so brings better results in this world, through justice and unity, and a better final outcome in the hereafter.

translation: Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, wishing to seek judgment in disputes from the Taghut, although they were commanded to reject it? And Satan wishes to lead them far astray.
interpretation: The verse exposes a contradiction between professed faith and actual conduct. Claiming belief in the Qur'an and earlier revelations is not enough if a person turns for judgment and arbitration to any authority that opposes God's law, which is what 'Taghut' signifies: anything that is obeyed or referred to in rebellion against God. True faith requires both affirming God's revelation and rejecting every false source of authority, so seeking rulings from such a source nullifies the claim to belief. The verse also warns that this behavior is not mere error but the work of Satan, who gradually draws people away from the truth until they end up in deep, hard-to-reverse misguidance.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you in aversion.
interpretation: The verse shows that hypocrisy is exposed when a person is asked to submit to divine revelation and to the Prophet's judgment. The hypocrites claim faith, but when invited to let the Qur'an and the Messenger settle their disputes, they do not merely hesitate; they turn away with intense, deliberate aversion. The emphatic word 'sudud' (a strong turning away) shows that their refusal comes from a heart that dislikes being governed by God's law and prefers other arbiters that suit its desires. Real faith is therefore measured by willing acceptance of God's guidance, especially when it conflicts with one's own interests, and not by outward profession.

translation: How, then, when a calamity befalls them because of what their own hands have sent forth, do they come to you swearing by God, 'We intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation'?
interpretation: The verse addresses the hypocrites who, having turned away from the Prophet's judgment and sought the rulings of false authorities (taghut), will one day be struck by a calamity that is the consequence of their own deeds. When that happens, they rush to the Prophet with oaths, claiming their intent was only to do good and to reconcile between parties. It exposes the hollowness of their excuses: their sudden need for the Prophet in times of hardship reveals that their rejection of his judgment was deliberate, and their pledges of good intention are an attempt to cover their hypocrisy. The lesson is that sincerity is shown by consistent submission to God's guidance in times of ease as well as hardship, and that calamities often stem from one's own wrongdoing, so false oaths cannot excuse what God knows to be in their hearts.

translation: Those are the ones whom God knows what is in their hearts; so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them about themselves a word that reaches deep into their souls.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:63) addresses the Prophet regarding the hypocrites. Since God knows what they conceal in their hearts, the Prophet need not punish them or expose them. Instead, he is to overlook their faults, counsel them with gentle warning, and speak to them in private, in words that are eloquent and penetrating, so as to awaken their consciences, remind them of God's reckoning, and call them back to sincere faith. It teaches that the best way to treat those with diseased hearts is with forbearance joined with wise, heartfelt advice, leaving their inner judgment to God.

translation: We did not send any messenger except that he should be obeyed by God's permission. And if, when they wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked God's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Ever-Accepting of repentance, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the purpose of prophethood is not merely to convey a message but to be followed as God's authorized representative, so obedience to the Messenger is in reality obedience to God, made possible and legitimate by His leave. It then opens the door of repentance to those who err, especially those who had shown disobedience or resentment toward the Prophet's judgment: the remedy for wronging oneself is to return sincerely to God, acknowledge the fault, seek forgiveness, and reconcile with the Messenger, whose intercession reflects his station. When this happens, God's response is certain: He accepts repentance and forgives out of His mercy. In this way the verse joins submission to divine guidance with hope in divine forgiveness.

translation: But no, by your Lord, they do not truly believe until they make you the judge in whatever disputes arise among them, and then find in themselves no discomfort about what you have decided, and submit completely.
interpretation: The verse makes true faith depend on more than verbal profession: it requires accepting the Prophet's judgment in every dispute, in both outward action and inward feeling. Believers must refer their disagreements to the Prophet's ruling, which in practice means the revelation and the Sunnah. They must also let go of any resentment, doubt, or tightness of heart toward that ruling, even when it goes against their own interests or inclinations. Finally, they must submit fully, in a surrender that is willing and sincere rather than reluctant or merely formal. Faith is thus shown to be a matter of obedience and contentment with God's law as conveyed by His Messenger.

translation: And if We had prescribed for them, 'Kill yourselves or leave your homes,' they would not have done it, except for a few of them. But if they had done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and a stronger affirmation of their faith.
interpretation: The verse points to the gap between professed submission and real obedience. Some people claim they would obey God in anything, yet when given even easy commands they hesitate. God, in His mercy, has not burdened believers with extreme trials such as self-sacrifice or exile, and He has made His commands within their capacity. If so few would have borne the harshest commands, then the ordinary duties they have actually been given should be carried out gladly and without objection. Acting on divine counsel brings real benefit: it is better for a person in this world and the next, and it strengthens faith, since each act of obedience makes the heart more steadfast, while hesitation and disobedience weaken conviction.

translation: And then We would surely have given them from Ourselves a great reward.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nisa 4:67) completes the thought of the preceding verses, which speak of those who hesitate to obey the Messenger and to do what they are exhorted to do. It says that had they truly done what they were admonished to do, obeying God and His Messenger with firm resolve, God would have granted them an immense reward directly from His own bounty, a reward whose greatness is beyond what deeds alone would earn. The phrase 'from Ourselves' (min ladunna) stresses that this recompense flows from God's special grace and generosity, not merely from the measure of human effort, and the word 'then' shows that this reward follows immediately and certainly upon sincere obedience. The lesson is that wholehearted submission brings divine favor far exceeding what people might expect, while hesitation and reluctance cause them to forfeit it.

translation: And We would surely have guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 4:68) completes the thought of the preceding verses, which speak of the great reward God would have granted to those who submit to the Messenger's command and do what they were admonished to do. Beyond the reward from Him, God would also have guided them to the straight path, which is the path of truth and uprightness leading to His good pleasure and to Paradise. The meaning is that obedience brings not only a future recompense but also continued divine guidance in this life: whoever acts upon the guidance he has received is granted further guidance, is kept steadfast in faith, and is led safely to the end of the journey. Guidance is therefore both a gift from God and a consequence of a person's sincere response to it.

translation: And whoever obeys God and the Messenger — those will be in the company of those upon whom God has bestowed favor: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.
interpretation: The verse promises that sincere obedience to God and His Messenger elevates a believer in the hereafter to the companionship of the best of humanity, in ranks of nearness to God. Being 'with' them does not mean equal in rank, but sharing the same abode of Paradise and enjoying their fellowship. It teaches that obedience is the path to honor, and that the ultimate reward includes not only Paradise but the joy of an excellent, righteous company, in contrast to the loneliness and regret of those who disobey. It also motivates believers to emulate the four categories: the prophets in receiving and conveying guidance, the truthful in their unwavering honesty and faith, the martyrs in sacrifice, and the righteous in good deeds.

translation: That is the bounty from God, and God suffices as All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse (4:70) follows the promise that those who obey God and the Messenger will be in the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. It teaches that such a lofty rank is not earned by deeds alone but is a gift of God's grace, which He gives to whom He wills. God also knows perfectly who is truly sincere and deserving, so no one needs another witness or judge: His knowledge of hearts and intentions is sufficient, and He will place each person in the position that fits their faith and sincerity.

translation: O you who believe, take your precautions, then go forth in detachments, or go forth all together.
interpretation: The verse instructs believers to be vigilant and well prepared against their enemies before engaging them, and not to march carelessly. Preparedness means gathering knowledge of the enemy's strength, readying arms and resources, and keeping a guard. Once ready, they are given flexibility in how to proceed: they may advance in small companies or squads, or mobilize in one united army, depending on what the circumstances and the military situation demand. This teaches that faith is joined with prudent planning, and that the choice of tactics should follow the needs of the moment rather than rigid habit.

translation: And indeed, among you is one who lags behind; then if a calamity strikes you, he says, 'Allah has certainly favored me in that I was not present with them.'
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:72) exposes the hypocrites within the Muslim community, who hold back from jihad and pose as part of the believers while their hearts are not with them. When the believers suffer a setback, such as defeat, loss, or hardship, the hypocrite takes it as a blessing from God that he stayed behind, seeing worldly safety as the only measure of benefit. This reveals a materialistic outlook that ignores the reward of steadfastness, sacrifice, and sharing in the community's trials. The verse teaches that true faith means standing with the believers in hardship as well as in ease, and that viewing a believer's affliction as a cause for self-congratulation reflects spiritual blindness and weak faith.

translation: And if a bounty from God reaches you, he will surely say, as though there had never been any affection between you and him, "Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I could have achieved a great success!"
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrite who lagged behind from jihad (Q 4:72-73). When the believers suffer a setback, he congratulates himself for staying home. When they are granted victory and spoils, he speaks as though he were a stranger to them, with no bond of faith or brotherhood, and his only regret is that he missed the material gain. His 'great success' is war booty, not God's pleasure or the reward of the hereafter. His fickle attitude shows that his concern is worldly profit, and that his religion is a matter of convenience and not sincere commitment to God and His community.

translation: So let those fight in the cause of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the cause of Allah and is killed or is victorious, We will bestow upon him a great reward.
interpretation: The verse calls on believers who value the eternal life of the Hereafter above the fleeting pleasures of this world to strive and fight for the sake of God, meaning in defense of the faith and the oppressed and for the sake of justice, not for worldly gain, glory, or conquest. Their 'selling' of this life signifies a conscious exchange, willingly giving up worldly attachments, comfort, and even life in return for God's pleasure and the afterlife. The promise that the fighter will receive a great reward whether he is killed (as a martyr) or is victorious shows that success in God's sight is not measured by outward outcomes but by sincerity and sacrifice. Either result brings reward, so the believer's heart is freed from fear of loss and is motivated by purpose rather than by the result.

translation: And what is the matter with you that you do not fight in the cause of God and for the oppressed among the men, women, and children who say, 'Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper'?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the believers for hesitating to fight and presents armed struggle as a moral duty tied to defending the helpless, not as a quest for conquest or gain.
