translation: So because of their breaking their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of God, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, 'Our hearts are covered,' — nay, God has sealed them because of their disbelief, so they believe only a little.
interpretation: The verse explains that the punishments and curses that befell the Children of Israel were consequences of their own conduct: violating the covenant, rejecting God's signs, killing prophets unjustly, and using the claim that their hearts were 'covered' (closed to guidance) as an excuse to avoid accepting the truth. God rejects this excuse, stating that their hearts were not naturally incapable of receiving guidance; rather, the seal on their hearts was a result of their persistent disbelief and stubbornness. Repeated rejection of truth hardens the heart until receptivity is lost, so only a small number of them, or only a little faith, remains. The lesson is that spiritual blindness is a consequence of one's own choices, and people are accountable for it rather than being entitled to blame an inherent incapacity.

translation: And for their disbelief, and for their saying against Mary a monstrous slander.
interpretation: God explains that part of what brought His rejection upon the Children of Israel was their persistent disbelief, together with the grave falsehood they uttered against Mary, the mother of Jesus, when they accused her of unchastity because she bore a child without a husband. The verse calls this charge a 'great slander' (buhtan azim) because it denies the purity and honor of a righteous woman whom God had chosen and purified, and because it rejects a clear sign of God's power in the miraculous birth of Jesus. Their accusation was not a matter of ignorance but a deliberate defamation born of stubborn disbelief, and so it is counted among the reasons for their censure.

translation: And for their saying, "We have killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of God." They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. And indeed, those who differ concerning him are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they certainly did not kill him.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim of some of the Children of Israel that they executed Jesus, and affirms his honored status as God's Messenger, which stands in contrast to their boast of having killed him. It teaches that God protected His messenger: the attempt to kill and crucify him did not succeed, and the matter was made unclear to those involved, so that someone or something was taken to be him. The people who argued over what happened, whether Jews, Christians, or others, built their claims on conjecture rather than certain knowledge, so their disagreement shows that their accounts are unreliable. The closing emphasis that they did not kill him with certainty settles the matter by divine revelation, which alone gives sure knowledge, and shows that God's messengers are ultimately under His protection and that He raises them in rank, as the following verse states.

translation: Rather, God raised him up to Himself. And God is ever Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God honored and protected Jesus (peace be upon him) by lifting him to Himself, so that the plot of his enemies did not succeed and they gained no power over him. It teaches that God's decree overrules the schemes of human beings: He is 'Aziz' (Almighty), so no one can overcome His will or thwart His protection of His messengers, and He is 'Hakim' (All-Wise), so His raising of Jesus was an act of wisdom, serving as a sign for humanity, vindicating His prophet, and exposing the falsehood of the claim that his enemies had killed or crucified him. The lesson for the believer is that true honor and safety lie with God, and that He rescues His servants in ways that people cannot anticipate.

translation: There is none among the People of the Book but will believe in him before his death; and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.
interpretation: The verse refers to Jesus, son of Mary. Before his death, after his return to earth near the end of time, every one of the People of the Book who is alive then will come to believe in him as a servant and messenger of God. They will recognize that he was neither killed and crucified nor divine, so the Jewish denial of him and the Christian exaggeration about him will both end. On the Day of Resurrection he will testify against them about what they said of him and how they responded to his message, confirming that he conveyed the call to worship God alone.

translation: So for wrongdoing on the part of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them certain good things which had been lawful to them, and for their hindering many people from the way of Allah.
interpretation: The verse explains that the dietary and other restrictions placed on the Jews were not arbitrary but a divine punishment for their moral failings. Their injustice, which includes breaking the covenant, rejecting signs, and killing prophets, together with their turning many people away from the path of God, led God to withdraw from them some wholesome things that had earlier been permitted. The prohibitions thus serve as a consequence of their conduct, showing that God's laws respond to human deeds and that obstructing others from guidance is a grave wrong that brings hardship.

translation: And for their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse explains that the Children of Israel were subjected to specific restrictions and hardships because of their wrongdoing. Two of these wrongs are named: practicing usury (riba) even though it was prohibited to them, and acquiring other people's property through illegitimate means such as bribery, fraud, and exploiting religious authority. Both acts show a deliberate disregard for divine commands and for justice in economic dealings, since they knew the prohibition and still violated it. The closing phrase restricts the threat of painful punishment to those among them who persist in disbelief, so the verdict is based on persistent rejection and wrongdoing rather than on ancestry. The lesson for every community is that exploiting others financially and defying clear divine prohibitions bring both worldly consequences and a grievous punishment in the hereafter.

translation: But those among them who are firmly grounded in knowledge, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you; and (especially) those who establish prayer, those who give zakat, and those who believe in God and the Last Day—to those We will give a great reward.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes the sincere, knowledgeable people among the People of the Book from those criticized in the preceding verses for wrongdoing and rejecting the truth. Real depth in knowledge leads a person to recognize the continuity of divine revelation and to accept the Qur'an as confirming earlier scriptures, rather than clinging to communal prejudice. Such people join the believers in faith in all revelation, and their faith is shown in practice through prayer, charity, and belief in God and the Last Day. The verse therefore teaches that God's great reward depends on sound knowledge, true faith, and righteous action, not on group identity, and that He fairly acknowledges the righteous among any community.

translation: We have sent revelation to you as We sent revelation to Noah and the prophets after him. We also sent revelation to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms.
interpretation: This verse answers those who demanded a miraculous book sent down all at once, or who denied Muhammad's prophethood, by showing that his revelation is not a novelty but part of a single, continuous divine tradition. God links Muhammad to the long chain of messengers, from Noah through Abraham's line to Jesus and the later prophets, establishing that the source, the message of divine oneness, and the method of revelation are the same for all of them. Naming prophets who came with scripture (David's Psalms) and those who came without a distinct book shows that revelation takes different forms, yet its essence is shared. Thus rejecting Muhammad while claiming to accept earlier prophets is inconsistent, since his call confirms theirs and stands in their lineage.

translation: And [We sent] messengers whose stories We have already related to you before, and messengers whose stories We have not related to you. And to Moses Allah spoke directly, with [real] speech.
interpretation: The verse affirms that revelation is not a novelty unique to Muhammad, peace be upon him: God sent a long line of messengers, only some of whom are named in the Qur'an, while others are known to God alone. This answers those who demanded a special proof or denied that God would send a human messenger, since prophethood has always been part of God's way with humanity. The mention of Moses being spoken to directly, emphasized by the verbal noun 'takliman', rules out any metaphorical reading and affirms that God truly speaks. It also shows that messengers differ in rank and mode of communication, yet all share one message and one source, so believers must accept all of them without distinction.

translation: Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that mankind would have no argument against God after the messengers. And God is ever Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: God sent the messengers to announce His reward to the believers and warn of His punishment to the disbelievers, so that no one could claim on the Day of Judgment that guidance never reached them or that they were unaware of what God required. By sending prophets, God completes His proof against humanity and leaves them without excuse: whoever is punished is punished after clear warning, and whoever is rewarded is rewarded after clear guidance. The closing description of God as Almighty and All-Wise affirms that He could have judged people without sending any messengers, but in His wisdom He chose to establish justice through clear communication, and that His decrees are always carried out with both power and perfect wisdom.

translation: But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness as well. And God suffices as a witness.
interpretation: When some of the People of the Book denied the Prophet's message or refused to acknowledge it, this verse offers him reassurance. Human denial does not weaken the truth of revelation, because the highest testimony is God's own. He affirms the Qur'an through its inimitable nature, its coherence, and the clear signs that accompany it. The phrase 'He sent it down with His knowledge' means the Qur'an carries God's perfect knowledge. It contains what He knows to be best for people: guidance, law, and truth about the unseen, and it is also sent down with full knowledge of the Prophet's worthiness to receive it. The angels' witness adds a further heavenly affirmation. The verse closes with 'God suffices as a witness', which tells the believer that no further proof is needed, and that the Prophet can rest secure in God's testimony whatever people say.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and hinder others from the path of God have strayed far, far away into error.
interpretation: The verse teaches that disbelief combined with obstructing others from God's path is the gravest form of misguidance. Such people are not only lost themselves but also work to keep others from guidance, so their error is compounded. The phrase 'far astray' suggests they have gone so far from truth that returning becomes very difficult, because they have rejected clear evidence knowingly and used their influence to turn people away from it. It is a warning that denying the truth is serious, and actively blocking others from it is a greater wrong.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved and committed wrong—Allah would never forgive them, nor guide them to any path.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 4:168) describes people who combine disbelief with injustice, whether by wronging themselves through rejecting the truth or by wronging others and obstructing God's way. If they persist in this state until death, God's forgiveness and guidance are closed to them. The closing is not arbitrary. It is the consequence of their own choice, since they turned away from the guidance offered to them and held on to their wrongdoing. Having rejected the path of truth, they are left with no path but the one that leads to the Fire, as the following verse says. The verse is a warning that persistent disbelief joined with oppression forfeits both pardon and direction, and an invitation to repent and believe while the door of mercy is still open.

translation: Except the path of Hell, in which they will abide forever. And that is, for God, easy.
interpretation: The verse declares that those who persist in wrongdoing and disbelief, having rejected guidance, are left with no road but the one that matches their chosen course, and it ends in Hell. God does not wrong them: He withholds guidance only from those who have by their own choice closed themselves to it, so their destination is the natural consequence of their deeds. The phrase 'And that is, for God, easy' reminds us that nothing hinders God's justice. No power can protect the wrongdoers or prevent the punishment, and no one's disbelief or rebellion can make Him unable to carry out what He has decreed. It is a warning to humans not to take God's patience for weakness, and to take seriously that their choices in this life lead to a lasting outcome.

translation: O mankind, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe, it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse addresses all of humanity, not one community, and shows that the Prophet's message is a universal call grounded in truth from the Creator. Belief is presented as being in people's own interest, since its benefit returns to them in guidance, peace, and salvation. God does not need their faith. Their disbelief diminishes nothing of His dominion, because everything in the heavens and the earth is already His. The closing names, Knowing and Wise, teach that God knows who is deserving of guidance and who turns away, and that He arranges His commands, His sending of messengers, and His judgments with perfect wisdom. So the invitation to believe is an act of mercy, not a need on His part.

translation: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion, and do not say about God anything but the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God and His word which He directed to Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say 'Three.' Desist; it is better for you. God is only one God. Glory be to Him that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse calls the Christians to moderation and to reject exaggeration in faith, in particular the elevation of Jesus to divinity or to being God's son. It affirms his honored status as a human messenger of God, created by God's command 'Be', which is what is meant by 'His word' cast to Mary, and a 'spirit from Him' because his life was breathed into him by God's will, not because he is part of God. The right response is pure monotheism: to believe in God and all His messengers, abandon the doctrine of the Trinity, and recognize that God is absolutely one, transcendent, and free of needing offspring, since everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him as Creator and Owner, and He alone is sufficient to manage all creation.

translation: The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of God, nor would the angels who are close to Him. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, He will gather them all to Himself.
interpretation: The verse refutes the Christian claim of the divinity of Jesus by pointing out that Jesus himself, and even the highest ranks of creation, the angels nearest to God, regard being servants of God as an honor and never as a humiliation. If the very figures some people exalt take pride in servitude to God, no one else has any grounds for arrogance toward worship. The closing warning tells those who scorn worship out of pride that they cannot escape accountability, since all will be brought back to God on the Day of Judgment, where each will be judged and the arrogant will face the consequences of their pride.

translation: As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and increase them out of His bounty. But as for those who disdained and were arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find for themselves besides God neither protector nor helper.
interpretation: The verse sets out the two destinies that follow from how people respond to God's worship. Faith joined with righteous action earns full, unwithheld recompense, and God's generosity then goes beyond what is strictly deserved, so the reward exceeds the deeds. Arrogance, meaning the refusal to submit to God and to serve Him as a servant should, brings a painful punishment. On that day the arrogant will have no ally to defend them and no helper to rescue them, because all power belongs to God alone. Pride before God is therefore self-defeating: those who thought themselves too great to be His servants end up completely without support, while those who humbly serve Him receive more than they earned.

translation: O mankind, there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light.
interpretation: God addresses all of humanity, not one community alone, to affirm that guidance has reached them with certainty and leaves no excuse for doubt. The 'proof' (burhan) is the decisive evidence, embodied in the Prophet Muhammad and the truth he brought, which appeals to reason and settles disputes about God's oneness and the true path. The 'manifest light' is the Qur'an, which illuminates the way as light dispels darkness: it clarifies right from wrong, removes confusion and ignorance, and guides those who hold to it toward God's mercy and a straight path. The verse thus calls people to accept the evidence and follow the revelation, since they have been given both the proof that convinces the mind and the light that guides the heart and conduct.

translation: As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and will guide them to Himself on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation rests on two linked foundations: sincere faith and firm reliance on God. Holding fast to Him means taking refuge in Him, clinging to His revelation, and trusting Him in all affairs. The reward is threefold. The first is mercy, which covers forgiveness and entry into Paradise. The second is bounty, meaning gifts beyond what deeds alone would deserve. The third is guidance, a straight path leading to God Himself. Guidance is therefore not only a starting point but a continuing gift. God steadies the believer in this world and brings him safely to nearness to Him in the next, so that both the journey and its destination come from His grace rather than from human effort alone.

translation: They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the one who dies leaving no parent or child (kalalah): if a man dies leaving no child but has a sister, she shall have half of what he leaves; and he would inherit from her if she had no child. If there are two sisters, they shall have two-thirds of what he leaves. And if the heirs are brothers and sisters, then the male receives the share of two females. God makes clear to you, lest you go astray. And God has knowledge of all things.
interpretation: This verse closes Surat al-Nisa' by settling the inheritance law for the kalalah, a person who dies with no surviving direct heirs (no children, and by the understanding of the Companions, no father either). In that case the estate passes to siblings: a lone sister takes half; two or more sisters share two-thirds; a brother inherits the whole estate of a childless sister; and mixed siblings divide the estate so that each male receives twice the share of a female. The verse shows that inheritance is a fixed, divinely apportioned right rather than a matter of custom or personal preference. Its statement that God explains 'lest you go astray' means that these detailed shares protect the community from error, injustice and family conflict, and that obedience to them reflects trust in God's all-encompassing knowledge of what is best for people.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who believe, fulfill your contracts. Lawful for you are the livestock animals, except what is recited to you, not treating hunting as permissible while you are in a state of ihram (pilgrim sanctity). Indeed, God decrees what He wills.
interpretation: The verse opens Surah al-Ma'idah by establishing that faith is shown through faithfulness to every binding commitment: the covenant with God to obey His commands, and the agreements people make with one another, such as trade contracts, marriage, treaties and oaths. After laying this foundation of integrity, it gives an example of how God's law also binds believers: He permits the meat of grazing livestock (camels, cattle, sheep, goats) as a blessing, while excluding what He specifies as forbidden, such as carrion and blood, and forbidding hunting during ihram. The verse thus teaches that lawful and unlawful are determined by God alone, not by human whim, and that submitting to His restrictions, even on what is normally permitted, is part of keeping one's covenant with Him. The closing phrase affirms that His rulings come from perfect wisdom and sovereign authority, so believers should accept them without objection.

translation: O you who believe, do not violate the rites of God, nor the sacred month, nor the sacrificial animals, nor the garlands marking them, nor those heading to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure. But when you have left the state of pilgrim sanctity, you may hunt. And let not the hatred of a people, because they once barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to commit aggression. Cooperate with one another in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and transgression. And fear God; indeed, God is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the sanctity of God's symbols and of the pilgrimage, and the safety of those traveling to it, must be honored even toward people with whom believers have a history of conflict. Past injustice or resentment never justifies retaliation that breaks God's limits or turns into aggression. It then lays down a lasting social principle: believers should join together in whatever is good and God-conscious and refuse to assist anything sinful or oppressive, whoever is involved, even friends or kin. Accountability is anchored in taqwa, awareness that God's punishment is severe for those who transgress His bounds.

translation: Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which a name other than God's has been invoked; and the animal strangled, or beaten to death, or killed by a fall, or gored to death, or what a wild beast has eaten, except what you are able to slaughter properly; and what is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek to divide by divining arrows. That is wickedness. Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favor upon you, and approved Islam as your religion. But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse sets out the boundaries of lawful and unlawful food as part of a complete moral and legal framework. Foods that are unclean, that result from unnecessary suffering or death by unslaughtered means, or that are tied to idolatrous practices (invoking other than God, sacrificing at altars, or divination by arrows) are forbidden, because the believer's eating should be purified from both physical harm and associating partners with God. The declaration that the religion is perfected and God's favor completed marks the community's attainment of a stable, self-sufficient guidance, so that the believers should no longer fear the disbelievers' power but hold God alone in reverence, and accept Islam as the way of submission to Him. The closing concession shows the law's mercy: necessity in real hunger lifts the prohibition, provided one does not intend transgression or take advantage of the exemption, and God forgives and shows mercy to those who act within these limits.

translation: They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "Lawful for you are all good and wholesome things, and what you have trained of hunting animals, training them as hounds, teaching them from what God has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention God's name over it. And be mindful of God. Indeed, God is swift in reckoning."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the default in Islamic law is permissibility: everything good, pure and wholesome is lawful, and prohibitions are the specific exceptions. As an example, it permits food obtained through trained hunting animals such as dogs or falcons, provided they are properly taught, hunt for their owner and do not eat the prey themselves, and the hunter mentions God's name over the game. The knowledge of training animals is presented as a gift from God, so using it should be coupled with gratitude and observance of His limits. The closing command to be mindful of God, with the reminder that He is swift in reckoning, teaches that even permitted enjoyment of food and sport carries accountability, so believers should stay within the bounds God has set and remain conscious that they will soon answer for their conduct.

translation: This day all good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And lawful for you are chaste women from among the believers and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their dowries, taking them in honest wedlock, not in fornication, nor taking them as secret lovers. And whoever denies the faith, his work has become void, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's religion is a mercy that permits all that is wholesome and pure, and it establishes a basis for decent social relations between Muslims and the People of the Book. Food that Jewish and Christian communities slaughter and prepare in accordance with their own scriptures is lawful for Muslims, and Muslim food is likewise lawful for them, which allows for shared hospitality and coexistence. Marriage to chaste believing women, and to chaste women from the People of the Book, is permitted on the condition that it is a real, honorable marriage: the husband pays the dowry as a right owed to the woman, and the union is conducted openly and with commitment, not as illicit sex or a hidden affair. The closing warning reminds believers that these permissions do not dilute faith: whoever rejects belief after having received it forfeits the reward of his deeds and is ruined in the Hereafter, so lawful relations with others must never become a reason to abandon one's own faith.

translation: O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves. But if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you has come from relieving himself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. God does not wish to place any hardship upon you, but He wishes to purify you and to complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse lays out the physical purification required for prayer as an act of worship and an expression of divine mercy. Wudu (washing the face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and washing the feet to the ankles) prepares the believer to stand before God, and a fuller bath is required after major impurity. When water is unavailable or harmful, because of illness, travel, or its absence, the law offers an easy alternative in tayammum with clean earth, so that the obligation of prayer is never blocked by hardship. The closing lines show the purpose behind these rulings: they are not meant to burden the believer but to cleanse body and soul, to complete God's favor through guidance and ease, and to cultivate gratitude.

translation: And remember Allah's favor upon you and His covenant by which He bound you when you said, 'We hear and we obey.' And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what lies within the hearts.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to treat their faith as a pledge they have already made, not as a loose preference. Their guidance and their place in the community of Islam are a gift from God, and by accepting it they entered a covenant, declaring 'we hear and we obey.' Remembering this gift and promise should move them to honor it in practice, especially in upholding justice and fulfilling obligations even when it is hard. The command to fear God, followed by the reminder that He knows what is in the hearts, teaches that obedience cannot be merely outward or verbal. God knows hidden intentions, doubts, and the gap between what a person says and what he truly feels, so sincerity must back up the oath. Awareness of God's inner knowledge is the real safeguard of faithfulness to the covenant.

translation: O you who believe, be steadfast for God, witnesses in justice; and let not the hatred of a people lead you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to piety. And fear God; indeed, God is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to make justice a matter of devotion to God rather than personal interest, loyalty, or emotion. Believers must uphold fairness consistently, testifying and judging truthfully even toward those they dislike or oppose, because animosity is never a legitimate reason to wrong anyone. Justice is described as closer to taqwa (God-consciousness), meaning that fairness in dealing with others is a measure and fruit of one's reverence for God. The closing reminder that God knows all that people do warns that hidden biases and unfair motives are not concealed from Him, so the believer's integrity must be maintained in private as well as in public.

translation: God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation rests on faith joined with action: belief alone is incomplete without good deeds, and deeds without belief lack their foundation. God, whose promise is always true, assures such people that He will erase their sins and shortcomings out of His mercy, and that He will also grant them a reward far exceeding what their limited efforts could earn. This shows that divine generosity goes beyond strict recompense, so believers should have hope, remain steadfast, and continue doing good, trusting in God's grace more than in their own merit.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse sets out the consequence of a twofold fault: inward rejection of faith (kufr) joined with outward denial of God's revelations and signs (takdhib). The phrase 'companions of the Jahim' (blazing fire) implies lasting association, so that those who persist in rejecting the truth, after clear signs have reached them, become inseparable from the fire, just as a companion is from his companion. It serves as a sober counterpart to the promise given to the believers, reminding the reader that belief and denial are not morally neutral, and that willful rejection of divine guidance after it has been made clear is a choice that carries real and enduring accountability.

translation: O you who believe, remember the favor of God upon you when a people intended to stretch out their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear God. And upon God let the believers rely.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to ground their gratitude in lived experience: God protected them from a real threat when enemies planned to attack and were restrained, so their safety was a gift and not the product of their own strength alone. Remembering this favor should lead to taqwa, a conscious fear of God that keeps them obedient and just, even toward those who wished them harm. It should also lead to tawakkul, trust in God. Believers should take the means available to them, but they should place their final reliance on God rather than on their own power, allies, or planning, since the One who defended them before can be relied on to defend them again.

translation: And Allah took a covenant from the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders. And Allah said, "I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers and support them, and lend Allah a good loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever among you disbelieves after that has truly strayed from the soundness of the path."
interpretation: The verse shows that divine favor and nearness are tied to a binding covenant: Allah's promise of being 'with' the Israelites, meaning His support, protection, and knowledge, depends on their fulfilling concrete obligations in worship (prayer), social duty (zakah and generous spending in His cause), and faith and loyalty toward His messengers. Appointing a leader from each tribe shows that keeping the covenant requires organized, accountable communal leadership. In return, they were promised forgiveness of sins and Paradise. Breaking the covenant after such clear terms is no small lapse but a deliberate departure from the straight path, so the responsibility for their misguidance is their own. The lesson reaches every community that receives a covenant from God: blessing follows faithfulness, and a person who knowingly abandons it forfeits the guidance that was offered.

translation: So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hardened. They distort words from their proper places, and they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. You will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them. So pardon them and overlook; indeed, Allah loves those who do good.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment is a consequence of moral choices: when the Children of Israel repeatedly violated their covenant with God, they were distanced from His mercy, and their hearts gradually lost the capacity to be moved by guidance. This hardness shows itself in concrete behavior, such as twisting the meaning of revealed texts to suit their desires and neglecting the share of the divine message that would have reformed them. Yet the verse is not an indictment of every individual, since it acknowledges a few exceptions, which upholds fairness in judging a community. It then directs the Prophet toward noble conduct: despite continual betrayal, he is to forgive and overlook, because patience and magnanimity are forms of ihsan, the excellence that God loves. The lesson is that one may recognize wrongdoing clearly and still respond with generosity and restraint, hoping that kindness may soften hearts or at least preserve the believer's own integrity.

translation: And from those who say, 'We are Christians,' We took their covenant; but they forgot a portion of that by which they were reminded, so We stirred up among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will soon inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse explains that the Christians, like the Children of Israel before them, accepted a covenant to believe in God's message and follow His messenger, yet they neglected and abandoned a significant part of what they were commanded, including the pure monotheism and the obligation to follow the final Messenger. As a consequence of breaking the covenant, God left them to their own divisions, so doctrinal disputes and sectarian hostility spread among their groups, and this animosity persists until the Day of Resurrection. The lesson is that abandoning divine guidance leads to fragmentation and mutual hatred, whereas unity comes through holding fast to the revealed covenant; and in the end, God will confront them with the truth of their deeds and hold them to account for them.

translation: O People of the Scripture, our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you much of what you used to hide of the Scripture, and overlooking much. There has come to you from God a light and a clear Book.
interpretation: God addresses the Jews and Christians, saying that Prophet Muhammad was sent to them as a witness against their concealment of revealed truths, such as the prophecies about him, the ruling of stoning for adultery, and the true teaching about the nature of Jesus. He exposes only what is needed to establish the truth and guide people, and he forgives and passes over many of their other concealments and faults out of mercy. The verse then describes what accompanies him: the light of guidance, which dispels the darkness of ignorance and misguidance, and the Qur'an, a clear Book that explains the truth plainly. The People of the Scripture therefore have no excuse for continuing in their denial, since the truth has been made manifest to them.

translation: By it God guides those who follow what pleases Him to the ways of peace, and brings them out from the darkness into the light by His leave, and guides them to a straight path.
interpretation: The 'it' refers to the Qur'an and the Messenger who brings it (Q 5:15). Guidance is not granted to everyone indiscriminately but to those who sincerely seek God's pleasure and strive to follow what He approves. For them the Qur'an opens the paths of safety and peace, meaning the ways of religion and conduct that bring inner security in this world and salvation from punishment in the next. It lifts them out of the darkness of unbelief, ignorance, doubt and desire into the light of faith and certain knowledge, yet this happens only by God's permission, so success is a gift from Him and not merely a human achievement. Finally, He keeps them firmly on the straight path, so guidance is not a single moment but a continuing journey in which God leads the believer from one stage of insight and righteousness to the next.

translation: Those who say, "God is the Messiah, son of Mary," have indeed disbelieved. Say: "Who could then prevent God in the least if He willed to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth?" To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them. He creates whatever He wills, and God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that Jesus is God by appealing to reason: anyone who can be destroyed, as Jesus, his mother, and all humanity can be if God so wills, is a created being who depends on God and has no power to resist His will, so he cannot be divine. Divinity requires absolute, independent power and sovereignty, which belong to God alone as owner of the heavens, the earth and everything between them. Jesus' miraculous birth does not make him divine, since God creates whatever He wills in whatever manner He wills, and His power is not limited by the ordinary course of creation.

translation: The Jews and the Christians say, "We are the children of God and His beloved ones." Say, "Then why does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are human beings among those He has created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. To God belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, and to Him is the final return."
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim of any community that it holds a privileged, unconditional status with God by virtue of lineage or religious label. The Qur'an answers with a logical argument: if they were truly God's children and beloved, He would not punish them for their sins, yet their own scriptures and history record that they were punished for wrongdoing. This shows that nearness to God is not inherited or claimed but depends on faith and righteous conduct. They are ordinary human beings, part of His creation, subject to His justice and mercy like everyone else. Forgiveness and punishment lie wholly in God's will, which is exercised with wisdom and justice, since He is the absolute Sovereign over everything and all will return to Him for judgment. The lesson is humility and personal accountability: no group can rely on its identity for salvation.

translation: O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you after a period of cessation of messengers, lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings or warner." But there has now come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: After a long gap in prophethood, during which divine guidance had faded and the earlier scriptures were distorted or neglected, God sent Muhammad to the Jews and Christians as a clear explainer of the truth. His coming removes any excuse they might offer on the Day of Judgment that no one had come to give them glad tidings of reward or warn them of punishment. The proof against them is therefore complete: the Messenger gives hope to the obedient and warning to the heedless, and the verse closes by affirming God's absolute power, since He can send a messenger when He wills, grant success to the message, and hold people to account for how they responded.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people: 'O my people, remember the favor of God upon you when He appointed among you prophets, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to anyone else among the nations.'
interpretation: Moses reminds the Children of Israel of God's blessings in order to awaken gratitude and stir them to obedience before urging them to enter the Holy Land. The prophets among them were a spiritual honor, and being made 'kings' means they were freed from the bondage of Pharaoh and became masters of themselves, with their own households, property, and authority. The favors God had given them, such as the manna and quails, the clouds that shaded them, the splitting of the sea, and the Torah, were unmatched among the peoples of their time. The reminder is meant to show that a people so favored should not shrink from fulfilling God's command, and that gratitude must be expressed through steadfast action, not mere recollection.

translation: O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has assigned for you, and do not turn back in flight, for then you will turn back as losers.
interpretation: Moses urges the Children of Israel to take courage and enter the sacred land that God had decreed for them, trusting His promise rather than their own fear of its inhabitants. To refuse, retreat, or lose heart in the face of the divinely promised task would not be a neutral choice but a real loss: they would forfeit the blessing, honor, and security God had prepared for them, and their disobedience and lack of reliance on God would leave them losers in both worldly and spiritual terms. The verse teaches that obedience to a divine command, together with trust in God's promise, is the path to success, while turning back out of cowardice leads to ruin.

translation: They said, "O Moses, indeed within it is a people of great strength, and indeed we will never enter it until they leave it. If they leave it, then we will enter."
interpretation: The verse exposes the fearful and faithless attitude of the Israelites when commanded to enter the Holy Land. Instead of trusting God's promise and acting on Moses' command, they let the apparent might of their enemies outweigh their reliance on God. Their condition, 'until they leave', shows a desire for victory without struggle or sacrifice: they wanted God to remove every obstacle for them while they stayed passive. The lesson is that divine help is tied to obedience, courage and effort, and that using the strength of others as an excuse to abandon a God-given duty is a sign of weak faith. Faith requires taking the necessary steps in trust, not waiting for hardships to disappear on their own.

translation: Said two men from among those who feared (God), upon whom God had bestowed favor: 'Enter upon them through the gate, for once you have entered it, you will surely be victorious. And upon God rely, if you are believers.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith joins reasoned action with total reliance on God. The two God-fearing men, Joshua and Caleb according to most commentators, did not counsel passive waiting for a miracle. They urged the Israelites to take the practical step of entering the gate and confronting the enemy, and they trusted that victory would follow once that step was taken. Their courage came from fear of God, which freed them from fear of people, and their confidence came from the favor God had given them in the form of insight and steadfastness. Tawakkul (reliance on God) is therefore not an excuse for inaction. It is the inner trust that accompanies effort, and the verse makes it a condition of belief: 'if you are believers.' Reliance on God is thus a measure of the sincerity of faith.

translation: They said: 'O Moses, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are staying right here.'
interpretation: This verse shows the refusal of the Children of Israel to obey Moses' command to enter the Holy Land after he urged them to trust God's promise of victory. Out of fear of its powerful inhabitants, cowardice, and a lack of trust in God, they put the whole burden of the struggle on Moses and his Lord, while they chose comfort and inaction. Their words, 'go, you and your Lord, and fight,' display disrespect toward God and His prophet, and they stand as a warning that faith requires obedience and action backed by reliance on God, not passive waiting while others strive. Their refusal was the cause of the punishment of wandering in the wilderness that followed.

translation: He (Moses) said: My Lord, I have control over none but myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: After the Children of Israel refused to enter the Holy Land and chose to sit back rather than fight, Moses recognized that he could answer only for himself and Aaron, since only they would obey him. He admits the limits of his authority and turns to God in his helplessness, asking Him to judge between the obedient few and the rebellious community. The verse shows that a prophet's duty is to convey and to lead by example, not to force hearts, and that when a community persistently disobeys, the righteous should disassociate from it and entrust the final decision to God.

translation: [Allah] said, "Then indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years, during which they will wander throughout the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."
interpretation: After the Children of Israel refused to follow Moses into the Holy Land out of fear and said they would never enter while its tyrannical inhabitants remained, Allah decreed that entry would be withheld from them for forty years. In this period they would wander aimlessly in the desert of Sinai, unable to settle or reach their goal, a fitting consequence for their cowardice and disobedience. The verse also consoles Moses, telling him not to feel sorrow over a people who persisted in transgression and rejected Allah's command, since the outcome was a just result of their own choices. It teaches that disobedience to divine guidance can delay or deprive a community of blessings it might have attained, and that a prophet's duty is to convey the message, not to grieve over those who deliberately turn away.

translation: And recite to them the true account of the two sons of Adam, when they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. The latter said, 'I will surely kill you.' The former said, 'Allah only accepts from those who are mindful of Him (the righteous).'
interpretation: The verse teaches that acceptance of deeds by God depends on the inner state of the doer, namely God-consciousness (taqwa), and not on the outward form or size of the act. The rejected brother's response exposes the root of many wrongs: instead of examining his own shortcomings and correcting himself, he turned his envy against the one whose offering was accepted and threatened to kill him. The righteous brother's calm reply places the cause of rejection where it truly lies, in the lack of sincerity and piety, not in any fault of his brother. The story thus warns against jealousy and resentment toward those whom God favors, and calls people to self-reflection and sincerity when their efforts seem unrewarded.

translation: If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I shall not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: These are the words of the righteous son of Adam (Abel) to his brother (Cain), who threatened to murder him out of envy after God accepted only one of their offerings. Abel declares that he will not initiate or return violence in kind to commit murder, and the reason he gives is his reverent fear of God, who is Lord of all creation and before whom every act will be accounted for. His restraint is not weakness or cowardice but a principled refusal to shed innocent blood out of fear of God. The verse teaches that true piety (taqwa) restrains a person from wrongdoing even when provoked, and that a believer should prefer to be wronged rather than become a wrongdoer by killing unjustly. It does not abolish legitimate self-defense in general; rather, it shows the moral height of a man who would not let hatred drive him to bloodshed, leaving justice to God.

translation: Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, so you will be among the companions of the Fire. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This is the speech of the righteous son of Adam to his brother who threatened to kill him (Q 5:29). He says that he will not raise his hand against his brother, out of fear of God, and so if the brother murders him, the murderer will carry the burden of killing him together with his own earlier sins, and the sum of these will bring him to Hell. The words 'I want' do not mean he desires his brother's damnation; they mean he accepts his own death rather than become a killer, knowing that the consequence of aggression falls upon the aggressor. Bearing 'my sin' is commonly understood as the wrongdoer taking on the wrong he has done to his victim, as the victim's rights over him are settled against his account. The closing phrase makes it a general principle: the Fire is the fitting and just recompense for those who commit injustice, above all unjust bloodshed.

translation: So his soul prompted him to kill his brother, and he killed him, and he became one of the losers.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 5:30) shows how murder begins in a person's inner self. Envy and anger, left unchecked, wear down the conscience until the soul makes the crime seem easy and even permissible. The word 'tawwaʿat' implies that his lower self made the act agreeable and compliant to him after he had hesitated. The final phrase 'he became one of the losers' says that he gained nothing from the act. He lost his brother, his own peace of mind, and his standing with God, and he faced the burden of the sin and its punishment in this world and the next. The lesson is to guard the heart against envy and to resist the whispers of the self before they harden into wrongdoing.

translation: Then God sent a raven scratching at the ground, to show him how to cover the corpse of his brother. He said, "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this raven and cover my brother's corpse?" And he became one of those who regret.
interpretation: This verse describes the aftermath of Cain's murder of Abel (Qabil and Habil). Having killed his brother, he did not know what to do with the body. God taught him through a humble creature, the raven, which dug into the earth, showing that burial is the dignified way to treat the dead. The lesson is that human beings learn from the natural world, and that a person who has committed a grave sin may be humbled even by the example of a bird. His cry of 'Woe to me!' expresses shame at his ignorance and helplessness, which was exposed after the crime. His regret ('he became one of those who regret') was the sorrow of one who sees the consequences of his deed and his own lowliness, not necessarily repentance seeking God's forgiveness. The verse warns that sin brings loss and remorse, and that pride and envy lead a person to ruin, leaving him lower than even the creatures he considers beneath him.

translation: For this reason We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all of mankind. And Our messengers certainly came to them with clear proofs; then indeed many of them, even after that, were transgressors in the land.
interpretation: The verse establishes the supreme sanctity of human life. Because of Cain's murder of his brother, as told just before, God ordained that unjust killing of a single person is a crime against humanity as a whole, since it violates the right to life that every human shares and erodes the security of all; likewise, preserving a single life, by rescuing someone or refraining from harm, is akin to preserving all humanity, because it upholds that same sacred right. Taking a life is lawful only as legal retribution for a killing or as punishment for spreading corruption and violence in the land, and only through due process. The closing statement warns that although clear signs and messengers came with this guidance, many still persisted in excess and transgression, showing that knowledge of the law does not prevent injustice unless it is accompanied by obedience and restraint.

translation: The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption on earth is only that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is a disgrace for them in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse sets out the severe penalty for hirabah, meaning armed rebellion and violent lawlessness that terrorizes society: highway robbery, killing, and spreading fear and insecurity in the land. Such crimes attack the order and safety that God's law protects, so they are treated as war against God and His Messenger. The punishments listed (execution, crucifixion, cutting off hands and feet on opposite sides, or banishment) are commonly understood as graded according to the gravity of the crime. Killing and robbing may call for the harshest penalties, robbery without killing for amputation, and intimidation alone for exile or imprisonment. The verse stresses that this deterrent protects the community, and that the worldly punishment is a disgrace which does not exhaust the guilt: a grave punishment in the Hereafter remains for those who do not repent. The following verses show that those who repent before being apprehended are spared these penalties.

translation: Except for those who repent before you gain power over them; so know that God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:34) follows the stated punishment for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and spread corruption in the land. It sets out an exception: if such offenders sincerely repent and give up their hostility before the authorities overpower or capture them, the specific penalties for hirabah (armed brigandage and spreading terror) no longer apply to them. The condition of repenting 'before you gain power over them' shows that repentance is credible when it is freely chosen and not forced by helplessness or capture. It also reflects God's mercy and the door of return that stays open even to grave offenders, while the closing reminder that God is Forgiving and Merciful encourages the wrongdoer to turn back and assures the community that justice in Islam aims at reform and the restoration of security as well as at punishment. Rights owed to other people, such as returning stolen property or compensating for harm, are not erased by repentance, since the verse removes the fixed punishment tied to the public offense but not the duties owed to individuals.

translation: O you who believe, fear God, seek the means of nearness to Him, and strive in His cause, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse lays out a path to true success in three connected steps. First, taqwa: living with constant awareness of God by avoiding what He forbids and doing what He commands. Second, seeking the wasila, which means drawing close to God through sincere acts of worship and obedience, such as prayer, charity, and good deeds done with sincerity, rather than relying on lineage, status, or intermediaries. Third, striving (jihad) in God's cause, which covers the struggle against one's own desires, the effort to uphold truth and justice, and defending the faith when necessary. Success (falah) in this world and the next comes from combining inner devotion, a living relationship with God, and committed action, so that faith is not merely belief but a disciplined, active way of life.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve—if they had everything that is on earth, and the like of it along with it, to offer as ransom from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them; and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse stresses that on the Day of Judgment worldly wealth, however vast and even doubled, has no value and cannot buy anyone's way out of God's punishment. Those who persist in rejecting faith and die in that state cannot rely on possessions, status or any compensation they once trusted in this life; only faith and righteous deeds done before death carry weight. The imagery of offering the whole earth twice over shows the absolute finality of divine justice and warns people to secure their salvation now, while repentance and good works are still accepted, because after death no ransom or bargaining is possible.

translation: They will wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it, and theirs will be a lasting punishment.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ma'idah 5:37) describes the final state of those who disbelieved and rejected the truth: even if they possessed everything on earth, and double it, to ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted. Their longing to escape the Fire shows the intensity of their suffering and the regret that comes too late, while the declaration that they will never leave it affirms that the divine judgment is final and that there is no ransom, intercession, or escape for them. The phrase 'a lasting punishment' means the torment is constant and unceasing, not temporary or interrupted. The lesson is that the opportunity to change course, repent, and believe exists only in this worldly life, so a person should act now, before the time comes when no wish or wealth can alter their fate.

translation: As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, a deterrent punishment from God. And God is Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:38) lays down a fixed legal penalty for theft, presenting it as just retribution for the wrongdoing the thief has committed and as a deterrent (nakāl) that protects society's property and security. The same ruling applies equally to men and women. The closing attributes, 'Almighty' and 'Wise', indicate that the punishment springs from God's authority and wisdom: it is meant to deter crime and preserve public order, not to be arbitrary cruelty. Classical jurists understood it as applying only when strict conditions are met, such as theft of a protected amount of property taken from secure custody, with no doubt, necessity, or coercion involved, and the surrounding verses offer repentance and reform (5:39), which reflects God's mercy alongside his justice.

translation: But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms himself, indeed Allah will accept his repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:39) follows the ruling on the thief and shows that divine justice is joined with mercy. Punishment in this world does not close the door to God's forgiveness. Repentance is sincere only when it is joined with reform: the wrongdoer must stop the wrong, make amends where possible, such as returning what was taken or restoring the rights of others, and then live righteously. When a person does this, God accepts the repentance and forgives, because forgiveness and mercy are among His essential attributes. The verse therefore offers hope to every sinner and encourages the repair of both one's relationship with God and one's relationships with others.

translation: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things Competent.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's sovereignty over the whole creation is absolute, and so His judgments are never arbitrary but are exercised with perfect wisdom and justice. Because every created being is His possession and under His authority, no one can compel Him or hold Him to account. Punishment and forgiveness are in His hands, and are decided by His knowledge of people's deeds, intentions, repentance and sincerity. The reminder that He has power over all things assures the believer that no sinner can escape His reckoning and that no repentant person is beyond His mercy. It therefore calls the reader to humility, to fear of His justice, and to hope in His forgiveness, and to trust that whatever He legislates or decrees is rightly ordained.

translation: O Messenger, let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you—among those who say 'We believe' with their mouths while their hearts have not believed, and among those who are Jews. They are avid listeners to falsehood, avid listeners for other people who have not come to you. They distort words from their proper places, saying, 'If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware.' And whoever Allah intends to put to trial, you can do nothing for him against Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not intend to purify. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and steadies him against distress over hypocrites and some Jewish groups who rush toward disbelief. Their faith is only verbal, while their hearts remain unconvinced. They eagerly listen to lies and act as spies or conduits for others who are too arrogant or hostile to come in person. They twist the meaning of revealed texts, taking them out of context to suit their desires. They are ready to accept a ruling only if it matches their wishes ("if you are given this, take it") and reject it if it does not ("if not, beware"). The verse shows that guidance is ultimately in God's hands: when someone persistently chooses falsehood and insincerity, God leaves them to their trial and does not purify their hearts, and the Prophet cannot change this for them. Their punishment is disgrace in this world, as their deceit is exposed and they are humiliated, and a great punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: They are avid listeners to falsehood, devourers of what is unlawful. So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them. If you turn away from them, they cannot harm you in the least. But if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
interpretation: The verse describes a moral condition: those who habitually lend their ears to lies and consume illicit gain, especially through bribery and corrupt dealings, have a heart that is not truly seeking truth, so their coming to the Prophet for judgment is often a search for convenience rather than for God's ruling. The Prophet is therefore given freedom: he may decline to adjudicate their disputes, and he need not fear their enmity, since God protects him and no harm can reach him except by God's will. Yet if he does choose to judge, he must do so with strict fairness, even toward people of bad character and even toward opponents, because justice is owed to every human being regardless of their faith or conduct. The closing statement that God loves the just makes equity an act of devotion and a mark of closeness to God, showing that a judge's integrity must never depend on how he feels about the litigants or on fear of the consequences.

translation: But how do they come to you for judgment while they have the Torah, in which is the ruling of God? Then they turn away after that. Those are not the believers.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ma'idah 5:43) exposes the insincerity of those who came to the Prophet seeking a ruling that suited their desires. They already possessed the Torah, which contained God's clear judgment on the matter, yet they ignored it, and then they also turned away from the Prophet's ruling when it did not match what they wanted. Seeking a judge only when his verdict is convenient, and abandoning revealed guidance when it is not, shows that their claim of faith is hollow. True belief means submitting to God's ruling willingly and wholeheartedly, not selectively following it according to personal interest, which is why God says of them, 'Those are not the believers.'

translation: Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light. By it the prophets who had submitted to God judged for those who were Jews, as did the rabbis and the scholars, according to what they were entrusted to preserve of God's Book, and they were witnesses over it. So do not fear people, but fear Me, and do not sell My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed - those are the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Torah was a genuine divine revelation that served as guidance and light for the Children of Israel, and that its authority was upheld by successive generations of prophets and learned leaders who were entrusted with preserving and applying it. It establishes that those entrusted with God's law carry a duty of faithful stewardship: they must apply it with justice, bearing witness to its truth, without being swayed by fear of people's disapproval or by worldly gain such as bribes or status. The closing warning means that rejecting or setting aside God's ruling, knowingly and out of preference for human desires or interests, amounts to a denial of God's authority over one's life. Judging by God's revelation is thus presented as an act of faith, while deliberately abandoning it in favor of other considerations is a form of ingratitude and disbelief toward the One who sent it.

translation: And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds equal retribution. But whoever forgoes it by way of charity, it will be an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse sets out the principle of proportional justice: punishment for harm must match the harm done, neither exceeding it nor falling short, so that the weak and the powerful stand equal before the law and society is protected from cycles of vengeance and excess. Yet it does not make retaliation a rigid obligation, because it urges mercy: the victim or the victim's family who willingly forgo their right out of charity have that generosity counted as an expiation that wipes away some of their own sins. The closing statement warns that abandoning God's revealed standard of justice, whether by favoring one's own judgment, favoring the powerful, or being harsher or more lenient than God commands, is itself an injustice, since it wrongs people and transgresses against the One who knows what is truly fair.

translation: And We sent following in their footsteps Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah; and We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, confirming what was before it of the Torah, and as guidance and instruction for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus not as the founder of a new religion but as a link in a single chain of divine revelation. He followed the earlier prophets who had judged by the Torah, and he came to affirm it rather than abolish it. The Gospel he received carried the same two gifts as the Torah: guidance, which shows the right path, and light, which removes doubt and confusion. Its repeated confirmation of the Torah shows continuity between the scriptures, with the same core message of tawhid and righteous conduct. The verse ends by saying that this revelation is guidance and admonition specifically for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), meaning that only those with a conscious reverence for God and an open heart actually benefit from revealed scripture.

translation: And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse commands the followers of Jesus to hold themselves accountable to the guidance God placed in the Gospel, including its confirmation of the Torah and its glad tidings of the final Messenger, rather than to their own desires or inherited customs. Judging by God's revelation is the standard of true faith, and abandoning it is not a mere error but a deliberate departure from obedience. The word 'fasiqun' describes those who step outside the bounds of God's authority after knowing it, much as a fruit bursts out of its husk. The verse thus teaches that every community is answerable to the revelation it was given, and that willful rejection of divine law, after the truth has been made clear, places a person among the transgressors.

translation: And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have appointed a law and a clear way. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one community, but He intends to test you in what He has given you; so race to good deeds. To Allah is your return all together, and He will inform you about that in which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse affirms the Qur'an as the final revelation that verifies the truth preserved in earlier scriptures and stands as a criterion over them, confirming what is authentic and correcting what has been altered or abrogated. The Prophet is therefore commanded to adjudicate by God's revealed law alone, without yielding to people's whims or social pressure. The verse then explains that diversity among religious communities, each with its own law and path, is part of God's wise design and a test of how people use what they have been given. Instead of wasting energy in sectarian disputes, believers should compete in righteous deeds, since all will return to God, who will resolve every disagreement with certain knowledge on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many among mankind are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true justice and authority come only from divine revelation, never from the shifting inclinations of people or from pressure by those who want to dilute the truth. Even the smallest compromise, being lured away from 'some' of what was revealed, is treated as a real danger, so firmness on the whole of the guidance is required, along with vigilance against subtle persuasion. When people reject the ruling of God, the believer should not be shaken or conclude that the message has failed, because their turning away is itself bound up with their accumulated sins, and God lets the consequences of those sins overtake them as a form of recompense. The closing reminder that many people are defiantly disobedient consoles the Prophet and later believers that the majority's rejection is no measure of truth, and that adherence to revelation must not depend on popular acceptance.

translation: Is it, then, the judgment of the Age of Ignorance that they seek? But who is better than God in judgment for a people who have firm faith?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 5:50) rebukes those who turn away from God's revealed law and prefer rules shaped by desire, tribal custom, or human whim, which it calls the 'judgment of jahiliyyah.' Jahiliyyah here is not only a historical era but a way of judging that is detached from divine guidance, and it can recur whenever people replace God's standard of justice with their own biases. The rhetorical question shows how irrational this choice is, since no judge can be wiser, more just, or more knowing than the Creator. The closing phrase 'for a people who have firm certainty' means that only those with real conviction recognize that God's rulings are the best, and they accept them with trust and submission.

translation: O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another. And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse warns believers against giving their ultimate loyalty, trust, and political or religious allegiance to those who oppose the community of faith and are aligned against it, so that the believers' identity, security, and principles are not compromised. The ruling concerns walāʾ, meaning binding alliance and solidarity at the expense of faith and the community, not ordinary kindness, justice, or fair dealing, which the Qur'an elsewhere commands toward peaceful non-Muslims (60:8). The statement that whoever takes them as allies is 'one of them' is a stern warning that siding fully with a group in its stance against the believers makes one share in its position and its consequences. It also teaches that those who wrongly place their allegiance against their own faith and community, and so wrong themselves, are left without divine guidance.

translation: So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening towards them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may strike us." But perhaps Allah will bring about the conquest or a decision from Him, and then they will become, over what they concealed within themselves, regretful.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites, whose hearts are sick with doubt and weak faith. They rush to ally themselves with the Jews and Christians, justifying this by claiming fear that a reversal of fortune, such as famine, defeat, or political upheaval, might befall them and that these allies could protect them. Their excuse reveals a lack of trust in God and a reliance on worldly calculations rather than on Him. The verse answers them by pointing to God's power: He may grant the believers victory, or bring about some decisive command from Himself, such as exposing the hypocrites or causing the downfall of their allies. When that happens, the hypocrites will be filled with regret over the doubt, ill intent, and hidden loyalties they harbored in secret, since their calculations proved false and their concealed motives were made manifest.

translation: And those who believe will say: 'Are these the ones who swore by God their most solemn oaths that they were indeed with you?' Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, or when God's support for the believers becomes clear in this world, the believers will look with astonishment at the hypocrites, who once swore emphatic oaths of loyalty and solidarity with the Muslims while secretly allying themselves with the enemies of the faith. Their pledges were only words, not backed by sincere faith, so their outward religious acts and oaths brought no benefit. Because their deeds lacked sincerity and were driven by hypocrisy and worldly calculation, God nullified them, leaving the hypocrites in complete loss, with neither worldly standing nor reward in the Hereafter. The verse teaches that claims of loyalty are worthless without sincere faith, and that God exposes falsehood in the end.

translation: O you who believe, whoever among you turns back from his religion, then Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble towards the believers, firm and honored against the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah and not fearing the blame of any critic. That is the favor of Allah, which He grants to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's religion does not depend on any particular person or group; if some believers abandon the faith, God will replace them with others who embody true devotion. These people are marked by mutual love with God, which shows in sincere obedience and worship. Toward fellow believers they are gentle, merciful and modest, while toward those who oppose the truth they are dignified and steadfast, refusing to be humiliated or compromised. They strive in God's path with their wealth, words and lives, and they are not swayed by social pressure, ridicule or criticism when they act on what is right.
