Such a character is not earned merely by effort but is a grace from God, who gives it to whomever He wills with perfect knowledge of who is fit for it. The verse is therefore both a warning against complacency and apostasy and an encouragement that God's cause will always be carried by sincere servants.

translation: Your protector and ally is only God, and His Messenger, and those who believe: those who establish prayer and give zakat while they bow down (or: in humble submission).
interpretation: The verse defines the circle of true loyalty and guardianship (walāyah) for the believers: their support, friendship, and allegiance belong first to God, then to His Messenger, and then to the community of believers who embody faith through practice. The believers are marked by establishing prayer, which is their bond with God, and by giving zakat, which is their bond with people. The phrase 'wa hum rāki'ūn' is best understood as describing their humble submission to God in all these acts, so that their worship and charity are done sincerely and with a obedient heart. The verse thus directs Muslims to place their trust and alliance within the God-centered believing community rather than with those who oppose or mock the faith, as the surrounding verses about not taking Jews and Christians as allies make clear.

translation: And whoever takes as allies God, His Messenger, and those who believe – then indeed, the party of God – they are the victorious.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true strength and ultimate success come from placing one's loyalty and trust in God, following His Messenger, and standing in solidarity with the community of believers, rather than seeking protection or alliance with those hostile to the faith. Those who align themselves with God's guidance and with the believers become part of 'the party of God,' a body defined not by worldly power or numbers but by sincere devotion and obedience. Such people are promised eventual triumph, because victory ultimately belongs to God and to those who side with Him. The triumph is not only military or political but also moral and spiritual: the steadfastness, unity, and integrity of the believers will prevail over falsehood in the end.

translation: O you who believe, do not take as allies those who take your religion as a mockery and a game, whether from among those who were given the Scripture before you or from among the disbelievers. And fear God, if you are truly believers.
interpretation: The verse sets a limit on close friendship and alliance: a believer's deepest loyalty must follow their faith. Those who ridicule the religion and treat its worship and beliefs as sport, whether People of the Book or open disbelievers, show contempt for what the believer holds most sacred. Taking them as intimate confidants or political allies would endanger the believer's dignity and faith, and would suggest approval of the mockery. This does not forbid justice, kindness, or ordinary dealings with peaceful non-Muslims, which other verses affirm. It forbids aligning oneself with those who scorn the faith. The closing call to fear God makes the point that sincere belief requires keeping one's loyalties in accord with God's guidance, so that avoiding such alliances is a test of true faith.

translation: And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game. That is because they are a people who do not use reason.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ma'idah 5:58) shows that mockery of the adhan and the prayer comes from a failure of understanding, not from any real flaw in the worship. Those who ridicule the call to prayer cannot grasp the meaning and weight of what they are mocking: the remembrance of God, the humbling of the self before its Creator, and the summons to success and salvation. Their scorn exposes a heart and mind closed to reflection. A person who truly reasons would recognize the dignity of calling people to worship the One God and would at least respect it. The believer is therefore taught to hold the prayer in high honor, not to be shaken by ridicule, and to see such mockery as evidence of the mockers' ignorance.

translation: Say: O People of the Book, do you resent us for anything other than that we believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down before, while most of you are defiantly disobedient?
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to challenge the People of the Book by exposing the irrationality of their hostility and mockery toward the believers. The only 'fault' they can find in Muslims is faith itself: belief in God and in all revelation, both the Qur'an and the earlier scriptures, without distinguishing between the messengers. Such a trait deserves praise, not resentment. The closing clause explains the real cause of their enmity: most of them are fasiqun, people who have departed from obedience to God and from their own scriptures. Their hostility is therefore rooted in their corruption and rebellion, not in any wrong committed by the believers. Since they themselves have strayed from the truth, they resent those who hold to it.

translation: Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and was angry with, and made some of them apes and swine, and who worshipped false deities (Taghut). Those are worse in position and further astray from the right path.
interpretation: The verse answers the People of the Book who mocked and disparaged the believers for their faith and prayer. The believers are told to turn the charge around: if there is anything truly deserving of censure and a bad outcome, it is the record of those who earned God's curse and anger by persistent disobedience, breaking His covenant, and transgressing His limits, to the point that some were transformed into apes and swine as a punishment, and who gave their devotion to Taghut, meaning whatever is obeyed or worshipped in rebellion against God. The point is that real shame and ruin lie not in sincere faith, which they ridiculed, but in rebelling against God and turning to false objects of worship. Those who do so occupy the worst standing in the sight of God and are the farthest from the straight and balanced path.

translation: And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," while they have entered with disbelief and have gone out with it. And God knows best what they were concealing.
interpretation: The verse describes the hypocrites among the People of the Book and others who came to the Prophet and the believers claiming faith, yet their hearts never changed. They arrived carrying disbelief and left carrying the same disbelief, untouched by the guidance they heard. Their profession of faith was only verbal and was meant to deceive or to spy on the Muslims. The closing phrase warns that deception cannot hide anything from God, who knows what lies in hearts, even if people are fooled by outward appearances. The believers are thus taught to be cautious and not to be misled by mere claims, and the hypocrites are warned that their concealed intentions are fully known and will be judged.

translation: And you see many of them hastening to sin and transgression and to their consuming of what is unlawful. Evil indeed is what they have been doing.
interpretation: The verse portrays moral corruption as a habit that has become second nature: these people do not stumble into wrongdoing occasionally but race toward it. The word 'hastening' shows eagerness and the absence of any inner restraint or shame. It names three connected vices: 'sin' (personal wrongdoing against God), 'transgression' (violating the rights of others), and 'consuming unlawful gain' (bribery, usury, and wealth taken through injustice). The final phrase, 'evil indeed is what they have been doing', is a strong judgment that such conduct is shameful in itself, whatever worldly profit it may bring. The verse is a warning that when people make unlawful earnings and injustice routine and normal, they bring ruin on themselves and on society, and it calls believers to guard against becoming like them.

translation: Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their sinful speech and their consumption of unlawful gain? Evil indeed is what they have been doing.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the religious leaders of the earlier communities, the rabbis and scholars, for staying silent while their people openly spoke sinful words and consumed illicit earnings such as bribes and usury. It teaches that failing to enjoin good and forbid evil, when one has the knowledge and standing to do so, is a grave wrong in itself. The Arabic word for 'doing' used for the leaders' silence (yasna'un, implying skilled, deliberate work) is a stronger term than the one used for the people's wrongdoing, which suggests that the leaders' neglect is judged as at least as blameworthy as the sins they ignored, because those with religious authority bear a special duty to speak out against corruption in their society.

translation: The Jews said, "God's hand is tied up." Their own hands are tied up, and they are cursed for what they said. Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. We have cast enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it. They strive throughout the land spreading corruption, and God does not love the corrupters.
interpretation: The phrase "God's hand is tied" is an idiom for miserliness or inability. Some Jews, in a period of hardship, spoke of God as withholding His bounty or being powerless to give, which is a grave insult to His majesty. The Qur'an turns the charge back on them: it is they who are tight-fisted and shackled, in character and in fortune, and they are cursed for such blasphemy. God's "two outstretched hands" express His boundless generosity and power; He gives and withholds according to His wisdom, not out of lack. The verse adds that the revelation to Muhammad, rather than guiding those who reject it out of envy and stubbornness, only deepens their rebellion and disbelief, since a heart that refuses truth grows harder when it is presented. As a consequence of their conduct, God has placed enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Judgment, and whenever they kindle war against believers, God frustrates their plans. Because their striving is aimed at corruption on earth, and God does not love those who spread it, their schemes are doomed to fail.

translation: If only the People of the Scripture had believed and been mindful of God, We would surely have erased their misdeeds and admitted them into the Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: This verse shows that God's door of mercy remains open even to those who previously fell into error, including the People of the Book who rejected the message of Muhammad. Faith (iman) together with God-consciousness (taqwa) brings two results: the forgiveness of past sins, as true belief wipes away earlier wrongdoing, and the reward of eternal Paradise. Their denial was not due to any lack of opportunity or any divine barrier, but their own choice, since sincere belief in the final message and righteous conduct would have brought them the same forgiveness and bliss granted to every believer.

translation: If only they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them—evil is what they do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine adherence to divine revelation, by living by its commands and not merely reciting it, brings God's abundant provision and blessing in both spiritual and worldly life. 'Eating from above and from beneath the feet' signifies plentiful sustenance from every direction, such as rain from the sky and produce from the earth. The People of the Book had this path open to them, and it included believing in the final revelation, which their own scriptures pointed to. The verse also makes a fair distinction: a just, moderate group among them followed the truth, while most chose corrupt conduct and so forfeited that blessing. Thus, prosperity and well-being are tied to obedience and justice, while neglecting revelation leads to loss.

translation: O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And God will protect you from the people. Indeed, God does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad to proclaim the whole of the revelation openly and without hesitation or fear of opposition, since withholding even part of it would amount to failing in the entire mission, because the message is a single indivisible trust. God reassures him that He Himself guarantees his protection from the harm and plots of people, so fear of them should never restrain him from delivering the truth. The closing statement reminds him that those who obstinately reject the truth will not be guided by God, so their hostility should not trouble him; his duty is only to convey, while guidance and outcome rest with God.

translation: Say: O People of the Book, you stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been sent down to you from your Lord. But what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that claiming religious affiliation is worthless without actually living by God's revelation. The People of the Book have no real standing, and no valid basis for their claims to salvation, unless they put into practice the guidance of their own scriptures, which includes accepting the Qur'an, since their books pointed to the final message and its Prophet. Being sincere to the Torah and Gospel therefore leads to believing in what was revealed to Muhammad. Yet for those whose hearts are governed by envy and stubbornness, hearing the truth only hardens them further, so each new revelation increases their rebellion and rejection, much as rain makes good soil flourish but makes weeds grow too. The Prophet is consoled and told not to grieve over them, for his duty is only to convey the message, while guidance and misguidance rest with God, and their rejection is their own responsibility.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians — whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds — there shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation with God does not depend on belonging to a particular community or on a label of religious identity, but on the reality of faith and action. Each group named, whether the believers, the Jews, the Sabeans or the Christians, is judged by the same standard: sincere belief in God, conviction that there will be a Day of Judgment and accountability, and the practice of righteous deeds. Whoever fulfills these conditions is promised security from fear of the hereafter and freedom from grief over what has passed. The verse therefore stresses personal responsibility and divine justice, and it warns against relying on communal pride or claims of exclusive privilege.

translation: We took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent messengers to them. Whenever a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, some they denied and some they killed.
interpretation: The verse shows that the Children of Israel's rejection of their prophets came from desire, not from any lack of proof. They had bound themselves by a covenant to obey God's guidance, and God kept sending messengers to remind them of it. But they accepted revelation only when it matched their wishes. When a prophet's message challenged their appetites, pride, or worldly interests, they either dismissed him as a liar or, when denial was not enough to silence him, killed him. The verse also teaches a wider lesson: when people let their whims decide what is true, they turn against the truth and those who carry it, and a covenant with God means nothing unless they submit to his guidance even when it is hard on them.

translation: They thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf. Then God turned to them in forgiveness; then many of them again became blind and deaf. And God is All-Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse describes how the Children of Israel, having received covenants and messengers, assumed that no harm or accountability would follow their breaking of the covenant, supposing that their status as a chosen people shielded them from punishment. This false security made them heedless: they stopped seeing the signs of God and stopped listening to the truth, a spiritual blindness and deafness rather than a physical one. When hardship came, God accepted their repentance and showed mercy, yet many relapsed into the same heedlessness once relief arrived. The lesson is that complacency about divine accountability dulls moral perception, and that God's mercy is no license to repeat wrongdoing. God observes every deed, so no one escapes with impunity, and returning to heedlessness after being forgiven is a graver failing.

translation: Those who say, 'God is the Messiah, son of Mary,' have certainly disbelieved. The Messiah himself said, 'Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord. Whoever associates partners with God, God has forbidden Paradise to him, and his refuge is the Fire. And there will be no helpers for the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: The verse holds that claiming divinity for Jesus contradicts the very message Jesus himself preached. He called his people to worship God alone and affirmed that God is his Lord just as He is theirs, which places him among God's servants and not as a partner in divinity. Associating partners with God (shirk) is portrayed as the gravest wrong, because it assigns to a creature what belongs only to the Creator. Its consequence is exclusion from Paradise and the Fire as a final abode. The closing phrase shows that on the Day of Judgment no person, saint, or intercessor can rescue those who persist in this wrongdoing, so deliverance depends on pure monotheism and not on reliance on others.

translation: They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, God is the third of three." And there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse rejects the Trinitarian doctrine that divinity is shared among three persons, affirming absolute divine oneness (tawhid) as the foundation of true faith. Associating partners or divisions with God is declared a denial of the truth, since God is singular, self-sufficient, and has no equal. Yet the verse ends with a call to repentance: those who persist in this belief face painful punishment, while implicitly those who desist and return to pure monotheism are offered the path to forgiveness and mercy.

translation: Will they not then turn in repentance to God and seek His forgiveness? And God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:74) comes after God condemns those who claimed that He is one of three, a grave act of disbelief. Even so, He does not close the door of return. The rhetorical question expresses both astonishment and invitation. It is astonishing that people would persist in a sin as great as associating partners with God when forgiveness is so easily available, and it is an invitation to repent. True repentance involves abandoning the false belief, regretting it, and turning back to the worship of God alone, together with asking His pardon. The closing names, Ghafur and Rahim, give the reason for hope: God's forgiveness is vast, and His mercy reaches even those who have committed the gravest wrongs, if they sincerely return to Him.

translation: The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. His mother was a truthful woman. Both of them used to eat food. Look how We make the signs clear to them, then look how they are deluded away from the truth.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that Jesus is divine by pointing to plain facts of his human nature. He was a messenger in a long line of messengers who came and passed away, so he was neither the first nor unique in his office. He and his mother needed food, and whoever needs to eat has bodily needs, is dependent, and is created, which is incompatible with being God, who needs nothing. Mary is honored as 'siddiqa', a woman of utmost truthfulness and faith, but not as divine or as a mother of God. The closing call to 'look' twice points to the clarity of the evidence and to the strange fact that people still turn away from it, so that the signs are plain and the fault lies in the heedless, distorted reasoning of those who reject them.

translation: Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which has no power to harm you or to benefit you? And Allah — He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse challenges the logic of worshipping anything other than God. Whatever is worshipped besides Him, whether an idol, a created being, or any imagined power, can neither bring harm nor grant benefit by its own will, so devotion to it is irrational and misplaced. Worship belongs only to the One who actually holds the power over benefit and harm. The closing description, that God is the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, reinforces this: unlike lifeless or powerless objects of worship, God hears every prayer and statement, including the false claims made about Him, and knows every intention and action, so He alone is worthy of being called upon and trusted, and He will hold people to account with perfect knowledge.

translation: Say: O People of the Book, do not exceed the bounds in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the whims of a people who went astray before, and led many astray, and strayed from the right path.
interpretation: The verse calls Jews and Christians to religious moderation and to hold to revealed truth rather than inherited desires. 'Excess' (ghuluw) means pushing reverence beyond its proper limits, as when Christians raised Jesus to divinity or when some people deified or denigrated prophets and scholars. Such excess is not the truth God revealed but a product of human passion. The 'people who went astray before' are earlier generations whose speculation and imitation of their leaders corrupted the faith, and who then misled many others. The verse warns that blindly following the desires and traditions of such predecessors, instead of weighing them against revelation, leads away from the 'even path' (sawa' al-sabil), which is the balanced way of pure monotheism, free from both exaggeration and neglect. It also stands as a general warning to every community against religious extremism and against taking its beliefs from inherited whims rather than divine guidance.

translation: Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and of Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the curse upon the disbelieving among the Children of Israel was not arbitrary or based on lineage, but was the consequence of their own conduct. Two prophets, David and Jesus, whose messages came centuries apart, each pronounced a curse, which shows that the rebellion persisted across generations and that the warning was repeated and consistent. Their disobedience of God's commands and their transgression of His limits, by violating the Sabbath, wronging others, and rejecting the guidance sent to them, brought about their removal from God's mercy. The lesson for every community is that closeness to God depends on obedience and on respecting the boundaries He set, not on belonging to a chosen people, and that persistent sin and aggression invite divine censure.

translation: They used not to forbid one another from the wrongdoing they committed. Evil indeed was what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns a community that lost its moral accountability: wrongdoing became normalized because no one restrained others from it. The sin is not only in committing evil but in the collective silence and complicity that let it spread. Enjoining good and forbidding evil is a shared duty that protects a society's moral life, and abandoning it is itself a grave offense, which is why God calls what they did 'evil indeed.' The verse warns that tolerating and failing to challenge known wrongs makes people partners in them.

translation: You see many of them taking those who disbelieve as allies. How wretched is what their souls have sent forward for them: that God has become angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 5:80) criticizes those among the People of the Book, especially the hypocrites and wrongdoers of the Children of Israel, who sided with the idolaters of Makkah against the Prophet and the believers out of worldly interest, tribal solidarity, or hostility to Islam. Their alliance is described as the worst provision they have put forward for their own afterlife, because it did not bring them safety or honor but earned them God's anger. That anger results in lasting punishment. The deeper meaning is that giving one's loyalty and support to falsehood against truth, in preference to faith and the community of believers, is a self-inflicted loss. What a person's soul prepares in this life, whether through allegiance, choices, or deeds, determines their condition in the next, and God's displeasure is the gravest consequence of all.

translation: And if they had believed in Allah and the Prophet and in what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:81) states that genuine faith in God, in the Prophet, and in the revelation sent to him is incompatible with befriending and allying with those who are hostile to the faith and who oppose it, as those described in the preceding verses did when they allied with disbelievers against the believers. Taking such people as close allies exposes a contradiction between a person's claim to belief and his conduct, so the verse implies that the alliance itself proves the weakness or absence of true faith. It then explains why such allegiance persists: many of them have left obedience to God and stepped outside the bounds of His commands, so their loyalties follow desire and worldly interest instead of the truth they claim to hold.

translation: You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate others with God; and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe to be those who say, 'We are Christians.' That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse describes the general attitude of particular groups toward the early Muslim community, not a ruling on whole peoples for all time. Hostility is linked to stubborn rejection and persecution of the believers, as shown by the Jewish tribes and the idolaters who opposed the Prophet. The warmer attitude of the Christians of that time is traced to moral and spiritual qualities: they had devoted scholars and ascetics who valued knowledge and devotion, and they were free of pride that blocks acceptance of truth. Humility and sincere devotion soften the heart and make people receptive to those who submit to God, while arrogance breeds enmity. The lesson is that closeness between communities is determined by character, humility, and sincerity, and that believers should judge by these qualities and not by labels alone.

translation: And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses."
interpretation: This verse describes the sincere response of people of true faith, traditionally understood as righteous Christians (such as the delegation that heard the Qur'an and wept), when they encounter revelation. Their tears are not mere sentiment but flow from recognition: their hearts know the truth because it harmonizes with what they already knew of God's guidance. Genuine knowledge of truth softens the heart and moves it to humility, which leads them to affirm faith and pray to be counted among 'the witnesses', meaning those who testify to the truth of God's message, belong to the community of Muhammad ﷺ who bear witness over mankind, and share in the reward of the faithful. The lesson is that true receptivity to truth shows in humility, emotion, and a longing to stand with the people of truth rather than in arrogance or rejection.

translation: And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth, while we aspire that our Lord admit us among the righteous people?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:84) voices the response of sincere Christians who recognized the truth upon hearing the Qur'an and wept. They present their faith as the only reasonable course: since the truth has plainly reached them, rejecting it would be irrational and would contradict their deepest hope, which is to be counted among the righteous in God's mercy. Their rhetorical question shows that belief is not a burden but a fitting response to clear evidence, and that sincere longing for God's acceptance naturally leads a person to embrace the truth once it is manifest, rather than cling to inherited habits or pride.

translation: So God rewarded them for what they said with Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. And that is the recompense of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:85) speaks of those among the Christians who heard the Qur'an, recognized the truth, wept, and said, 'Our Lord, we believe, so write us among the witnesses.' God's reward was granted not merely for the words they uttered, but for the sincere faith that their words expressed, a faith that moved their hearts to tears and to acceptance of the truth. The verse teaches that genuine belief, openly affirmed and joined with humility before the truth, is met with eternal bliss in Paradise. The closing phrase, 'that is the recompense of those who do good (muhsinin)', shows that excellence (ihsan) in faith, meaning sincerity and responding to the truth when it is clear, is what earns God's everlasting reward, and that this reward is open to anyone who responds in this way, whatever their prior community.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of the Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the punishment of Hell is not for mere ignorance but for a deliberate two-part rejection: inner disbelief (kufr) joined with outward denial of God's revealed signs, whether the verses of scripture or the signs in creation. Having been given clear evidence, such people knowingly turn away from it. The phrase 'companions of the Hellfire' (aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm) expresses that they become its permanent inhabitants, inseparable from it as a companion is from a friend. This is a fitting consequence of having rejected the guidance that would have led them to salvation, and it stands as a counterpart to the preceding promise to the believers, so that the reader sees the two destinies and is moved to choose faith.

translation: O you who believe, do not forbid the good things which God has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse teaches that believers must not impose on themselves prohibitions that God has not imposed, whether through excessive asceticism, vows of self-denial, or by declaring lawful pleasures such as good food, drink, and marriage to be forbidden. Only God holds the right to make things lawful or unlawful, and to forbid what He has permitted is to overstep the bounds He has set, just as indulging in what is forbidden is. The command not to transgress calls for a balanced path: enjoy the wholesome provisions God has made lawful with gratitude and moderation, avoid both extremes of harsh self-deprivation and reckless excess, and stay within the limits of God's law. Those who go beyond these limits forfeit God's love.

translation: And eat of what God has provided for you, lawful and good; and fear God, in whom you are believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith is expressed in everyday conduct, including what a person eats. Believers should enjoy the sustenance God has granted them, but only what is both lawful (halal), meaning acquired by permissible means and not forbidden in itself, and wholesome (tayyib), meaning pure and beneficial. It follows an earlier warning against forbidding for oneself the good things God has made lawful, so it rejects both extremes: reckless indulgence in what is forbidden and ascetic denial of what is permitted. The closing command to be mindful of God, in whom they believe, ties the matter to accountability: their profession of faith obliges them to keep within God's limits in earning and consuming, and to be grateful for His provision rather than treating it as a matter of mere appetite.

translation: God does not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He holds you accountable for oaths you have deliberately made. The expiation for breaking such an oath is to feed ten poor people with the average of what you feed your own families, or to clothe them, or to free a slave. Whoever cannot afford this must fast three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn. But keep your oaths. Thus God makes clear His revelations to you, so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse shows God's mercy and justice in the matter of oaths. Words that slip out of the tongue by habit, such as saying 'No, by God' or 'Yes, by God' without any intention of binding oneself, carry no penalty, because the heart did not commit to them. Responsibility arises only when a person consciously and deliberately swears to do or not do something and then breaks that oath. For this, God prescribes a practical expiation that benefits society: feeding or clothing ten needy people at a moderate standard, or freeing a slave, with fasting three days as an option for those who lack the means. This gives people a way to repair their lapse without hardship. The command to 'keep your oaths' warns believers not to treat swearing by God lightly, to avoid swearing needlessly, and to honor their commitments. The verse closes by teaching that such clear legal guidance is a blessing that calls for gratitude.

translation: O you who believe! Intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it, that you may be successful.
interpretation: God addresses the believers to warn that things which cloud the intellect, lead to greed and loss through chance, and tie the heart to false objects of worship or superstition are not harmless habits but spiritual and moral filth that Satan makes attractive. These practices destroy clear judgment, breed enmity and hatred between people, and distract from remembrance of God. The command to 'avoid' them is stronger than merely refraining, as it means keeping away from them and all that leads to them. True success, in this life and the next, depends on this protection of the mind, the community, and one's devotion to God alone.

translation: Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of God and from prayer. So will you not desist?
interpretation: The verse exposes the hidden purpose behind intoxicants and gambling: they are tools through which Satan undermines both community and faith. Intoxication clouds reason and loosens self-restraint, while gambling breeds greed, loss, and resentment, so quarrels, grudges, and broken bonds follow among people who once lived in harmony. At the same time, absorption in drink and chance-games consumes time and attention and dulls the heart, so a person drifts away from remembering God and from establishing prayer. The closing question, 'So will you not desist?', is a firm moral appeal rather than a request for information: having seen the social and spiritual harm, a rational believer should abandon these practices decisively and turn back to obedience.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear delivery of the message.
interpretation: The verse joins obedience to God with obedience to His Messenger, since the Messenger conveys God's commands and shows how to live by them, and it warns believers to guard against disobedience and its consequences. Responsibility is then made clear: the Messenger's duty is only to deliver the message plainly and unmistakably. He has already fulfilled it, so if people turn away, no blame falls on him. The fault and the accountability fall on those who heard the clear message and rejected it, and they will answer to God for their choice.

translation: There is no blame on those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten before, so long as they are mindful of God and believe and do righteous deeds, then remain mindful and believe, and then remain mindful and do good. And God loves those who do good.
interpretation: This verse was revealed after the prohibition of wine, when some Companions asked about those who had died while having drunk it before it was forbidden. It teaches that no sin attaches to what was permitted at the time, or was consumed before a prohibition came, provided a person was sincere in faith and righteous conduct. The threefold repetition of taqwa (God-consciousness) describes progressive stages of spiritual growth: first, fearing God by avoiding what is forbidden and believing in His commands; then, continuing in that faith and obedience steadily; and finally, reaching ihsan, excellence, by worshipping God as though seeing Him and doing good to others. The verse's lesson is that God's judgment rests on sincere faith, obedience once a command is known, and the pursuit of excellence, and that God loves those who reach this level of goodness.

translation: O you who believe, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach, so that Allah may make known who fears Him unseen. Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: While in the sacred state of pilgrimage (ihram), the believers are tested with game that comes so close that they could easily seize it by hand or spear. The real test of faith is obedience when no one is watching and temptation is easy. Fearing Allah 'in the unseen' means restraining oneself out of awareness of God's presence, not out of fear of people. Whoever breaks the prohibition after this clear warning and test has no excuse, and deserves a painful punishment. The verse teaches that divine commands are often tested through easy opportunities for disobedience, and that true piety is shown in private self-restraint.

translation: O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in a state of ihram. Whoever of you kills it intentionally, the compensation is an equivalent of what he killed from livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering brought to the Ka'bah; or an expiation by feeding poor people; or the equivalent of that in fasting, so that he may taste the consequence of his deed. God has pardoned what is past, but whoever returns to it, God will take retribution from him. God is Almighty, Owner of retribution.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the state of ihram during pilgrimage is a time of sanctity in which hunting wild land animals is forbidden, as a discipline of reverence and restraint. If a pilgrim deliberately violates this, he must make amends proportionate to the offense: the penalty is not arbitrary but is set by the judgment of two fair, knowledgeable Muslims who determine the livestock animal closest in kind or value to the game killed. He may then give that animal as an offering at the Sacred precinct for the poor, or instead pay the value in food for the needy, or fast a number of days equal to the meals that would have been fed. These options show God's mercy and flexibility, while the purpose, 'that he may taste the consequence of his deed,' shows that the penalty is meant to awaken conscience and accountability. God forgives past violations committed before the ruling or in ignorance, but one who knowingly repeats the offense after being informed faces divine retribution, because God is Mighty and just in requiring that His sacred limits be honored.

translation: Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for travelers; but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in a state of ihram. And fear God, to Whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: God removes hardship for those in a state of pilgrimage by permitting what the sea yields, whether caught fresh or taken as food and preserved, so that both residents and travelers have sustenance on the journey. At the same time, He forbids hunting land animals while one is in ihram, to instill reverence for the sanctity of the state of pilgrimage and the sacred precincts, and to train the believer in self-restraint and obedience. The verse closes by tying these rulings to taqwa: the believer should observe these limits out of awareness of God, knowing that every person will be gathered before Him and held accountable for whether they honored His boundaries.

translation: God has made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a means of support and stability for people, as well as the sacred month, the offering animals, and the garlands. That is so that you may know that God knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that God has full knowledge of all things.
interpretation: The verse says that God's ordinances around the Sacred House are a source of social stability and moral order, not merely ritual. The Kaaba, as a place of sanctuary, gathers people in security and gives them a shared center of worship and livelihood. The sacred month provides a recurring period of enforced peace in which travel, trade, and pilgrimage can proceed without fear of war. The offering animals and the garlands that mark them are signs that protect the pilgrims and the poor who benefit from the sacrifices. Together they form a system of safety, justice, and mercy that tribes who were often at war could rely on. The verse then draws a theological lesson: that such wise, protective legislation reflects the fact that God's knowledge encompasses everything in the heavens and the earth, including what people need for their welfare. The order of these rites is therefore evidence of divine knowledge and care, and it should lead believers to trust God's commands and to be mindful that nothing they do or conceal is hidden from Him.

translation: Know that God is severe in punishment, and that God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 5:98) joins warning and hope so that a believer lives between fear and hope. God's severe punishment is a deterrent that should keep a person from transgressing His limits and from complacency in sin, while His forgiveness and mercy are an invitation to repent and return. Neither attribute should be held alone: fear without hope leads to despair, and hope without fear leads to heedlessness. A sound faith balances both, motivating the believer to obey God, to turn back quickly after falling short, and to trust that sincere repentance will be met with mercy.

translation: The Messenger's duty is only to convey the message. And God knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: The verse draws a line of responsibility: the Messenger is accountable only for delivering the message clearly, not for forcing hearts to believe or for the choices people make afterward. Guidance and the reckoning belong to God. The verse also warns that outward compliance is not enough, because God knows both what people show and what they hide in their hearts. A person cannot rely on outward display or on concealing a hidden intention, since the inner state is as open to God as the outward act. The verse therefore calls for sincerity and an awareness that one will be answered for in public and in private alike.

translation: Say: The bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the bad impresses you. So fear God, O people of understanding, that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worth is measured by quality and moral purity, not by quantity or popularity. Whether in earnings, deeds, beliefs, or people, what is lawful and good has real value and brings lasting benefit and God's blessing, while what is unlawful and corrupt brings harm and loss in the end, however plentiful it is or however many people follow it. Believers should not be deceived by the large numbers of those who do wrong, nor by the appeal of ill-gotten gain. People of sound intellect should use their reason to tell good from bad, choose the good, and be mindful of God. Success in this life and the next comes from that God-consciousness, not from abundance.

translation: O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made plain to you. Allah has pardoned what is past; and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse teaches believers to practice restraint in religious inquiry and not to press the Prophet with needless or excessive questions about matters Allah has deliberately left unspecified. Such questions can backfire: an answer might impose a burden, a new obligation, or a hardship, or expose private matters that would embarrass or grieve the questioner. Where Allah has been silent, that silence is a mercy, and people should accept the scope of the religion as given rather than seek to complicate it. The remark that questions asked during revelation would be answered warns that the answer could become binding law, making the questioner responsible for a ruling that might otherwise never have existed. The closing words show Allah's forgiveness and forbearance: He has pardoned past excessive questioning and the things He left unaddressed, so believers should rest in His leniency, focus on what He has clearly commanded, and avoid needless hair-splitting.

translation: A people before you asked about such things, then they became disbelievers because of them.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 5:102) comes after the command not to ask the Prophet about matters that, if made plain, would only burden believers. It teaches that excessive, challenging questioning about religious matters is a danger. Earlier communities pressed their prophets with demands and questions about details of the law, and when answers came with obligations they found heavy, they neglected or rejected them and so fell into disbelief. The point is that faith should be met with trust and obedience, not with needless probing that seeks to evade or test the revelation. Believers should accept what God has made clear, leave silent what He has left unspecified as a mercy, and ask only what benefits them in religion and life.

translation: Allah has not instituted any such thing as a bahirah, a sa'ibah, a wasilah, or a ham; but those who disbelieve invent a lie against Allah, and most of them do not use reason.
interpretation: The verse refutes pre-Islamic Arab superstitions in which certain livestock were dedicated to idols and declared forbidden: a she-camel with its ear slit, one set free to roam, one linked to a particular birth pattern, and a stud camel exempted from work after fathering a number of offspring. God states that He never legislated these prohibitions. Declaring lawful things unlawful, and attributing that to God, is a fabrication against Him. The verse also faults the followers of such customs for not using reason: they follow ancestral tradition and invented religious authority blindly, instead of examining whether a ruling really comes from divine revelation. The lesson is that only God has the right to make things lawful or unlawful, and that no religious practice should be adopted without sound knowledge or evidence.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,' they say, 'Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon.' Even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?
interpretation: The verse condemns blind imitation of ancestral customs when these conflict with divine revelation. Tradition alone is not a valid criterion of truth. When people are invited to measure their beliefs and practices against revelation and the Prophet's guidance, they should reflect and examine them rather than cling to inherited habits out of attachment or pride. The rhetorical question at the end exposes the weakness of this argument: an ancestor's example has authority only if he had knowledge and right guidance. Following forebears who lacked both is no safeguard and leads to error. The verse therefore calls on believers to ground faith and conduct in knowledge, reason, and divine guidance rather than in unexamined cultural inheritance.

translation: O you who believe, you are responsible for yourselves. Those who have gone astray cannot harm you if you are rightly guided. To God is the return of you all, and He will then inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches personal responsibility for one's own faith and conduct. A believer's first duty is to keep himself upright in belief and action, and the misguidance of others cannot damage him so long as he holds to guidance. Guidance includes fulfilling one's obligations, among them calling others to good and forbidding wrong as far as one is able. So the verse is not a license to give up enjoining good or to withdraw from society. It consoles believers who grieve over those who reject the truth, and it reminds them that each person will be judged individually. Every soul returns to God, who will reveal the truth of all deeds and give each person what he earned, so no one will be questioned about another's choices.

translation: O you who believe, when death approaches one of you, let there be testimony among you at the time of making the bequest: two just men from among you, or two others from outside your community if you are travelling in the land and the affliction of death befalls you. Detain the two of them after the prayer, and if you doubt them, let them both swear by God: 'We will not sell this oath for any price, even if it concerns a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of God; for then we would surely be among the sinners.'
interpretation: This verse lays down a procedure for safeguarding a dying person's will, especially when he is on a journey far from his own community. He should have two upright witnesses to his bequest, ideally Muslims, but if none are available, two others from outside the community may serve. Because the witnesses are trusted with the property and final wishes of the deceased, they are to be held after the prayer, when people are most mindful of God and gathered together, and made to swear by God if there is any suspicion of dishonesty or concealment. Their oath affirms that they will not trade truth for worldly gain, will not favor even a relative, and will not hide what they witnessed, since false or hidden testimony is a grave sin. The verse thus underscores the sanctity of testimony as a trust owed to God, and shows that justice in inheritance and bequests must be protected by solemn accountability before Him.

translation: But if it is discovered that the two (witnesses) were guilty of a sin, then two others shall stand in their place from among those whose right was violated, the two nearest in claim, and they shall swear by God: 'Our testimony is truer than the testimony of those two, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse completes the ruling in Surat al-Ma'ida on bequests made while traveling, when no Muslim witnesses are present and two non-family witnesses are entrusted with the deceased's property. If it later becomes clear that these two trustees lied, concealed, or misappropriated part of the estate, the matter is not closed. Two of the heirs, the nearest and most entitled, take their place and swear by God that their testimony is more truthful than the trustees' and that they are not exceeding the limits of justice, since doing so would make them wrongdoers. The verse shows that Islamic law protects rights through a process of redress: false testimony or breach of trust can be challenged, and a binding oath before God is an instrument of justice. It also reminds believers that accountability to God underlies all testimony and trusts.

translation: That is more likely to make them give testimony in its true form, or fear that other oaths will be given after their oaths are rejected. And fear God and listen; and God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse gives the wisdom behind the legal procedure in the preceding verse on bequests witnessed during travel, where the witnesses swear an oath if doubt arises. Having witnesses take an oath after prayer, and knowing that the heirs may in turn swear to contradict them, makes people more likely to testify honestly and exactly as they saw things. They fear shame before God and exposure before people if their oaths are refuted by counter-oaths. The verse then commands taqwa (God-consciousness) and attentive obedience, because laws like this only work when people truly hold themselves accountable before God. It ends with a warning that those who persist in defiance, such as by giving false testimony or betraying a trust, put themselves outside God's guidance.

translation: On the Day when God gathers the messengers and says, 'What response were you given?' they will say, 'We have no knowledge; indeed, You alone are the Knower of the unseen.'
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection God will assemble the messengers and ask them how their peoples responded to their message, a question meant to expose and shame those who denied them. The messengers will disclaim knowledge, not because they were unaware of what people said to them outwardly, but out of humility and awe before God, and because they recognize that the true state of hearts, the sincerity or hypocrisy behind any response, and what their communities did after they departed, are known fully only to God. Their answer shows their complete deference to God's perfect knowledge, and it reminds believers that the ultimate judgment of faith and deeds belongs to the One who knows all hidden things, while human knowledge, even that of prophets, is limited to what is apparent.

translation: When God says: 'O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit so that you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel; and when you would create from clay the shape of a bird by My permission, then breathe into it and it would become a bird by My permission; and you would heal the blind from birth and the leper by My permission; and when you would bring forth the dead by My permission; and when I restrained the Children of Israel from harming you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those among them who disbelieved said: This is nothing but obvious magic.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment God will remind Jesus of the blessings He gave him and his mother, not because Jesus has forgotten them, but to affirm publicly that every miracle was a gift granted solely by God's permission and not a sign of Jesus's own divinity. By repeating 'by My permission' after each miracle (creating the bird, healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead), the verse refutes the claims of those who deified Jesus and shows he was a servant and messenger supported by God. It also shows that even the clearest proofs may be rejected by stubborn disbelievers, who dismissed them as magic, while God protected His prophet from their harm.

translation: And when I inspired the disciples: 'Believe in Me and in My Messenger.' They said: 'We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims (submitting to God).'
interpretation: The verse recalls one of God's favors upon Jesus, son of Mary: He placed in the hearts of his closest followers, the disciples, the inclination to believe in God and in His messenger. This shows that their faith was ultimately a gift and guidance from God, not merely the result of Jesus's own effort. Their reply, 'We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims,' shows that true faith combines inner conviction with outward submission to God's will. It also shows that the essence of the message of all prophets is the same: worship of the One God and surrender to Him, which is what 'Islam' means in its broad sense. The disciples call on Jesus to be a witness to their declaration, making their faith a public, binding commitment.

translation: When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, is your Lord able to send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?" He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."
interpretation: The disciples' question, phrased as whether God is 'able,' sounds like doubt about God's power, or at least a demand for a sign as a condition of reassurance. Jesus answers by calling them to taqwa, reverent awareness of God. A true believer does not test God or place conditions on faith, and should trust that God's power is complete and His wisdom perfect without needing miracles to confirm it. His reply also warns that requesting a miraculous sign brings heavy responsibility: once a sign is seen, denying it brings severe consequences, as the verses that follow make clear. The lesson is that faith rests on trust and obedience, not on demanding proofs, and that fear of God is the safeguard against presuming upon Him.

translation: They said: 'We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts be reassured, and that we know that you have indeed told us the truth, and that we be among those who bear witness to it.'
interpretation: The disciples of Jesus (peace be upon him) explain that their request for a table spread with food from heaven is not born of doubt or mere appetite, but of a desire for firmer faith. They name four aims: to eat from it as a blessing, to have their hearts settle into calm certainty, to gain direct knowledge that Jesus has been truthful in his message, and to serve as witnesses to the miracle for those who come after them. The verse shows that seeking a sign to deepen conviction and move from belief by report to certainty by observation is different from stubborn demand for proof, and that believers carry the responsibility of testifying to what they have seen of God's signs.

translation: Jesus, son of Mary, said: 'O God, our Lord, send down upon us a table spread with food from heaven, that it may be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers.'
interpretation: Jesus's prayer shows that a request for a blessing is rightly framed as an act of gratitude and worship, not as a demand for a spectacle. He asks for the table so that its day becomes a recurring festival of remembrance and thanks, shared by the first and last generations of believers, and a sign from God confirming the truth of His message. By closing with 'provide for us, for You are the best of providers,' he acknowledges that all sustenance, whether miraculous or ordinary, comes from God alone, and that the human role is to turn to Him in humility, seeking provision while recognizing His generosity.

translation: God said: "Indeed, I will send it down upon you. But whoever among you disbelieves afterward, then I will punish him with a punishment such as I have not inflicted upon anyone among all the worlds."
interpretation: This verse is God's answer to the prayer of Jesus, who asked for a table spread with food as a sign and a source of provision for his followers. God grants the request, but the miracle raises the level of accountability. Once people have seen such a clear and undeniable sign, they have no excuse left, so disbelief after it is a deliberate rejection of established truth and not ignorance or doubt. The severity of the warning follows from this principle: the greater the blessing and the clearer the proof, the heavier the responsibility. Those who witness the miracle and still deny God are therefore judged more strictly than any others.

translation: And when God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God'?" He said: "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within my self, and I do not know what is within Yours. Indeed, it is You who are the Knower of the unseen."
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment God will question Jesus before the assembled nations, not because He lacks knowledge, but to expose before witnesses the falsehood of those who deified Jesus and Mary, and to shame them with the testimony of the one they venerated. Jesus answers with humility and total submission. He begins by declaring God's transcendence above any partner, then disowns the claim by saying it would be wrong for him to assert anything with no right to it. He does not rest on a bare denial but hands the matter to God's perfect knowledge: if he had said such a thing, God would already know it. He acknowledges the vast difference between creature and Creator: God knows the innermost secrets of his soul, while he cannot comprehend anything of God's essence or hidden knowledge. He closes by affirming that God alone is the Knower of all unseen things. The lesson is that divinity belongs to God alone, that even the most honored prophets are servants who never call people to worship themselves, and that all hidden matters are known only to God.

translation: I said to them only what You commanded me: 'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are a Witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse records Jesus' answer when God questions him on the Day of Judgment about whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods. Jesus affirms that his message was pure monotheism, the same command given to all prophets: worship God alone, who is Lord of both him and his followers. This places Jesus firmly in the position of a servant and messenger, not a deity. He states that his responsibility was limited in time and scope: he observed and testified to their conduct only while he lived among them. After God took him, God alone was the true Watcher over their beliefs and deeds, so Jesus bears no responsibility for the deviations that arose later, such as the deification of himself. The closing phrase acknowledges that God's knowledge and witness encompass everything, which shows that all judgment belongs to God, who knows what was said, what was done, and what was hidden.

translation: If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed it is You who is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse (5:118) is the words of Jesus on the Day of Judgment when God questions him about what his followers claimed regarding him. Jesus does not plead for them or condemn them, but submits entirely to God's sovereign judgment. By saying 'they are Your servants,' he affirms that God has complete ownership and authority over His creatures, so any punishment would be just and not a wrong done to them. By saying 'You are the Almighty, the All-Wise,' he affirms that if God forgives, it is not out of weakness or error but from might and wisdom, since God forgives only in a way that accords with perfect wisdom. The verse thus models perfect etiquette before God: disavowal of his followers' false claims, humble acknowledgment of divine prerogative, and leaving the final decision to God's justice, power, and wisdom.

translation: God will say: This is the Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: This verse, from the end of Surat al-Ma'idah, answers the scene in which Jesus is questioned about what his people claimed. It teaches that on the Day of Judgment the only thing that rescues a person is truthfulness: sincerity in belief, speech, and action, and faithfulness to the covenant with God. Worldly status, lineage, and claims count for nothing then, while those who were honest with God and with themselves find their truthfulness has become their saving merit. Their reward is the Gardens, eternal and unending, and above it the greatest blessing of all, mutual contentment. God is pleased with them because of their obedience and sincerity, and they are pleased with Him because of what He has given them. This reciprocal pleasure is why the verse calls it the supreme success, a success greater than anything else that could be achieved.

translation: To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and all that is in them, and He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone is the true Owner and Sovereign of the entire creation, seen and unseen. Whatever people appear to possess, whether wealth, authority or knowledge, is only held in trust and can be taken away at His will. Since the Creator rules everything and nothing lies beyond His power, the believer should place complete trust in Him, depend on no one else for ultimate help, and hold firmly to worship of Him alone. The verse also invites humility before Him and confidence that He is able to fulfil His promises and to judge with perfect justice.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light; yet those who disbelieve hold others equal with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all praise belongs to God alone because He is the sole originator of everything, from the vast heavens and earth to the contrasting realities of darkness and light. His making of these opposites, with order and purpose in both, points to a single, all-powerful Creator who manages the universe. Against this clear evidence, the verse expresses wonder at the inconsistency of those who reject Him: after recognizing that He alone creates and sustains, they still set up rivals or equals to Him in worship and devotion. The argument is that gratitude and worship should be directed only to the One who gave existence, and that associating partners with Him is irrational as well as ungrateful.

translation: He is the One who created you from clay, then decreed a term; and a specified term is with Him. Yet you still doubt.
interpretation: The verse points to God's absolute authority over human existence: He originated humanity from clay through the creation of Adam, from whom all people descend, and He has fixed a limit for every life, the span that ends in death. Alongside it is another appointed term known only to Him, the time of resurrection and the Last Day, whose timing no creature can know. Since the One who made humans from lowly clay can plainly bring them back to life, it is irrational to doubt the resurrection and the accounting that follows. The verse rebukes those who, despite such clear evidence in their own origin and mortality, remain in doubt about the afterlife and their accountability before their Creator.

translation: And He is God in the heavens and in the earth; He knows your secret and your open speech, and He knows what you earn.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone is worshipped and obeyed as the true deity throughout all of creation, above and below, and that nothing escapes His knowledge. He knows what people conceal in their hearts and what they declare openly, and He knows all their deeds and what they gain from them, whether good or evil. This is a reminder of divine omniscience and accountability: since every private thought and public action is known to God and will be reckoned, a person should live with awareness of Him, be sincere in inner intention as well as outward conduct, and not imagine that any wrongdoing can remain hidden.

translation: And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: The verse describes a persistent habit of heedlessness among the deniers: whenever clear evidence reaches them, whether in the verses of revelation or in the signs of creation across the heavens, the earth, and their own selves, they do not pause to reflect or weigh it. Their refusal does not stem from a lack of proof but from an arrogant, stubborn disposition that turns away reflexively. The point is that guidance is withheld not because signs are scarce but because hearts are closed to them. Turning away is itself the cause of their remaining in error, and it warns the believer against becoming indifferent to God's signs and urges attentive reflection whenever they are encountered.

translation: They have indeed denied the truth when it came to them; but soon there will come to them the news of what they used to mock.
interpretation: The verse warns that rejecting the truth outright, without reflection, when it is plainly presented through the Prophet and the revelation, is a grave wrong. Those who ridiculed the message treated it as a joke, but the consequences of their mockery will inevitably become known to them. The 'news' (anba') refers to the reality and outcome of what they scorned: the warnings of punishment, the triumph of the truth, and the reckoning in this world and the next. What they dismissed as empty words will be shown to be real, and when it arrives, their mockery will turn into regret, since the truth does not depend on their acceptance to be established.

translation: Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent the sky upon them with abundant rain, and made rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins, and raised up after them other generations.
interpretation: The verse warns those who deny the message that worldly power, wealth and prosperity are no protection from God's judgment. Earlier peoples were stronger and better provided for than the Quraysh, with abundant rain, flowing rivers and firm authority, yet their sins brought about their ruin. This shows that blessings are a trial and a trust, not proof of God's approval. The cause of destruction is moral: persistent sin and rejection of the truth. God's power is complete, since He can remove one generation and bring up another with no loss to His dominion. Those who see the fate of earlier nations should therefore take heed, give thanks, and repent before the same law applies to them.

translation: And even if We had sent down to you a written scripture on parchment, and they had touched it with their own hands, those who disbelieved would surely have said, 'This is nothing but obvious magic.'
interpretation: The verse shows that the disbelievers' rejection comes from stubbornness and not from a lack of evidence. The Quraysh demanded a tangible miracle, such as a book sent down from heaven. God tells the Prophet that even if He granted this, and they verified it by touching it with their own hands so that deception of the senses was ruled out, they would still dismiss it as plain sorcery. A heart that has closed itself to the truth will explain away any sign, however clear. Guidance depends on a sincere willingness to accept the truth, not on the quantity or kind of miracles shown, and this consoles the Prophet that their refusal to believe is no failing in his message.

translation: And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" But if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided at once, and then they would be given no respite.
interpretation: The disbelievers demanded visible proof, an angel appearing with the Prophet, as a condition for believing. The verse answers that God's way is to test people through faith in the unseen. If an angel were sent openly, the proof would be so overwhelming that no room for choice would remain, and if they still rejected it after seeing it, God's decree of destruction would immediately fall upon them, with no further delay or chance to repent. So withholding such a sign is a mercy, since it preserves their time and opportunity to reflect, believe and amend themselves.

translation: And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have obscured for them what they are obscuring.
interpretation: The disbelievers demanded that an angel be sent down as the Messenger. God answers that even if He had granted their wish, the angel would have had to appear in human form, since people could not bear to see an angel in his true form or converse with him. They would then have raised the same doubt they raise now, saying 'this is only a man like us', so the confusion they bring on themselves would remain. The verse shows that sending a human messenger is a mercy and a wisdom, because he can be understood, imitated and approached. Their rejection comes from stubbornness, not from any lack of clear proof.

translation: And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encircled by the very thing they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by reminding him that ridicule of truth-bearers is an old pattern in human history, not a sign that his message is false. It also carries a warning: the punishment those mockers scoffed at, the warnings of divine reckoning they treated as a joke, eventually overtook and engulfed them. Mockery of the truth does not change reality, and what people deride as empty threats can become the very thing that destroys them. The believer is therefore urged to be patient and steadfast, trusting that God's promise will be fulfilled and that the outcome favors those who convey and follow the truth.

translation: Say: Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of those who denied.
interpretation: The verse calls people to reflect on history and not to rely on assumptions alone. By traveling and observing the ruins and remains of past nations that rejected the truth and their messengers, one sees that arrogance, injustice, and denial lead to ruin, while the warnings of the prophets prove true. The command to travel is not only physical but also an invitation to learn from experience and draw moral lessons, so that a person corrects their course before suffering the same fate.

translation: Say: 'To whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth?' Say: 'To God.' He has prescribed mercy upon Himself. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. Those who have lost their own souls, they do not believe.
interpretation: The verse leads the questioner from the evident fact of God's ownership of all creation to the conclusion that the One who owns everything is also the One who will hold people to account. The answer 'To God' is given by the Prophet himself because it is undeniable. God's self-prescribed mercy shows that His dominion is not tyrannical: He delays punishment, gives people time to repent, and grants them guidance, and His gathering of humanity on the Day of Resurrection is itself part of His justice and mercy, since wrongs will be set right and the righteous rewarded. Those who deny this have not merely made an intellectual error but have ruined themselves. They have squandered the capacity for faith and the salvation of their souls, so the loss is theirs alone, and their disbelief is the result of that self-inflicted ruin.

translation: To Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day; and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. (Qur'an 6:13)
interpretation: The verse asserts God's total sovereignty over everything that exists within the cycle of time. Whatever 'dwells' or settles in the night and the day, meaning every creature and every thing that exists, moves or rests, is His possession and under His dominion. Since all of creation belongs to Him, no one else deserves worship or devotion. The closing names, 'the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing,' remind the believer that nothing is hidden from Him: every word spoken and every hidden intention is heard and known. This should inspire both reassurance, because He hears the pleas of the oppressed and knows their situation, and accountability, because every deed and utterance is known to the One who owns all things.

translation: Say: 'Shall I take as a protector anyone other than God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who feeds and is not fed?' Say: 'I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit, and [I was told]: Never be among those who associate partners with God.'
interpretation: The verse establishes that all dependence and allegiance belong to God alone. The Prophet is told to ask a rhetorical question exposing the irrationality of seeking a protector besides the Creator of the cosmos, who sustains every creature while needing nothing himself. Everything created is needy, so only the Self-Sufficient One is fit to be turned to for guardianship, help and worship. The Prophet's role as the first to submit shows that a messenger must first embody the message himself, leading by example in total surrender to God. The prohibition against shirk shows that submission is complete only when it is free of any partnership, whether in worship, trust or ultimate loyalty.

translation: Say: Indeed, I fear, if I were to disobey my Lord, the punishment of a mighty Day.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to declare that his position as a messenger gives him no immunity from accountability. If even he, the one who conveys the revelation, would fear the punishment of the Day of Judgment should he disobey God, then everyone else has far greater reason to fear it. The verse removes any claim to privilege and teaches that obedience to God is a duty on all people alike, and that real faith is joined with awe of God's judgment.
