It also affirms that the Prophet's call to monotheism is sincere, since he does not exempt himself from the warning he delivers.

translation: Whoever is spared from it (the punishment) on that Day, God has indeed shown him mercy; and that is the clear triumph.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment, deliverance from punishment is not earned by a person's own power or deeds alone but is a sign of God's mercy. The one who is turned away from the torment has been enveloped in divine compassion. This rescue is described as the manifest success, because every worldly gain pales beside it. The true measure of success in life is therefore salvation in the hereafter, and the believer should live in awareness of that Day, seeking God's mercy through faith and righteous conduct.

translation: And if God touches you with harm, none can remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things Able.
interpretation: The verse teaches that benefit and harm are ultimately in God's hands alone. Hardship cannot be lifted by any created being, whether a person, an idol, or a worldly means, unless God wills it. Likewise, any good that reaches a person comes only through His power, which encompasses everything. Believers are therefore called to place their trust in God alone, to be patient and turn to Him in times of difficulty, to be grateful in times of ease, and not to fear or hope in anyone besides Him. Worldly means are only instruments that act by His permission.

translation: And He is the Supreme over His servants, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 6:18) affirms that God's dominion over creation is absolute: every created being is subject to His will and power, and none can escape or resist His decree. Yet His supremacy is not arbitrary force. It is joined with perfect wisdom (hikma), meaning He places everything in its proper place and acts with purpose, and with complete awareness (khibra) of the inner and outer realities of His servants, including their intentions, secrets, and needs. The lesson for the believer is both reverence and reassurance: one should submit to a Lord whose power is unmatched, while trusting that His commands and decrees are just, wise, and informed by full knowledge, so that nothing in one's life is overlooked or wasted.

translation: Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: God is Witness between me and you. And this Qur'an has been revealed to me so that I may warn you by it and whomever it reaches. Do you truly bear witness that there are other gods alongside God? Say: I do not bear witness. Say: He is only One God, and I am free of what you associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse sets out a challenge to those who deny the Prophet's message: the most authoritative testimony possible is God's own, and God testifies to the truth of Muhammad's mission through the Qur'an itself, whose inimitable revelation is the proof of its divine origin. Because the Qur'an is a warning that reaches everyone it is conveyed to, the responsibility to heed it extends beyond its first audience to all later generations. The rhetorical question to the polytheists exposes the weakness of their claim, since they have no real evidence for other gods and their testimony rests on nothing. The Prophet is told to reject that testimony firmly, to affirm pure monotheism (tawhid), and to publicly disassociate himself from all forms of shirk, showing that faith requires both affirming God's oneness and clearly renouncing idolatry.

translation: Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost their own souls—they do not believe.
interpretation: The People of the Book, especially their scholars, know with certainty that Muhammad is a true messenger and that the revelation he brings is true, because their own scriptures describe him and confirm his message. Their recognition is as firm and instinctive as a father's recognition of his own child, with no doubt or confusion. Their refusal to believe therefore is not due to lack of evidence but to stubbornness, envy, worldly interests, and pride. By knowingly rejecting the truth, they have destroyed their own souls and forfeited their share of guidance and salvation, so they remain in disbelief despite knowing the truth.

translation: And who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against God or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest form of injustice is to misrepresent God, whether by attributing to Him claims, partners, or rulings He never made, or by rejecting the clear signs He has sent. Such a person corrupts the very source of truth and guidance, so the wrong is not only against others but against the Creator and the moral order that rests on His revelation. The closing statement affirms that this path ends in failure: whatever worldly gains, status, or influence such wrongdoers may seem to enjoy, they will not attain true success, which is salvation and lasting well-being before God. The verse thus calls for honesty and humility toward divine truth, warning against both fabricating religion and arrogantly dismissing its evidence.

translation: And on the Day when We gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated partners with God: 'Where are your partners whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, all creatures will be gathered before God for judgment, and the idolaters will be confronted with a rebuking question. The question is not asked to seek information but to shame them and expose the emptiness of their false worship. The beings and idols they invoked, hoped in, and claimed would intercede for them or share in God's divinity will be absent and powerless to help. This shows that attachment to anything besides God is an illusion that collapses when the truth becomes manifest, and that only God has real authority and power on that Day.

translation: Then their only argument will be to say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were never polytheists."
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, when the idolaters are tested and confronted with the reality they denied, their only 'fitna' (excuse, defense, or the outcome of their trial) will be to swear falsely that they never associated partners with God. This shows how deeply their worldly attachment to falsehood had taken hold: faced with the truth, they have no real justification left, so they cling to denial and lies, even swearing by the very God they had associated others with. The verse teaches that shirk and worldly deception leave a person with no valid argument before God, and that the soul's habit of lying and evading responsibility will be exposed and fail on the Day when every deed is made plain.

translation: Look how they lied against themselves, and what they used to invent has abandoned them and gone astray from them.
interpretation: The verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the idolaters will deny their shirk and swear they were never polytheists. Their denial is a lie that only harms themselves, since it cannot deceive God and brings them no benefit. The false gods and intercessors they fabricated and relied on, hoping for help and mediation, vanish and fail them completely in their hour of need. Everything they built their lives upon turns out to be baseless, leaving them with nothing but the consequences of their own falsehood.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you; but We have placed coverings over their hearts so that they do not understand it, and heaviness in their ears. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it, until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, 'This is nothing but the tales of the ancients.'
interpretation: The verse describes people who are physically present when the Prophet recites the Qur'an but gain nothing from it, because their persistent stubbornness and rejection have closed their hearts and dulled their hearing to the truth. The 'coverings' and 'heaviness' are the consequence of their own arrogance and refusal, which God allows to harden into a spiritual barrier. They listen only to find fault, not to seek guidance, so even clear signs and miracles do not move them. Their arguments end in a dismissive slogan, calling revelation 'tales of the ancients', which shows that their denial arises from a closed heart and not from any lack of evidence. The lesson is that guidance requires a sincere, open heart, and that continued rejection of truth can make a person incapable of perceiving it.

translation: And they forbid others from it and keep away from it themselves; yet they destroy none but themselves, and they do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse (Al-An'am 6:26) describes the leaders and opponents of the Prophet's message who combine two faults: they dissuade people from following the Qur'an and the Messenger, and they themselves also distance themselves from him. Their obstruction does not harm the truth or the Prophet; the real damage falls upon themselves, since by rejecting guidance and misleading others they bring on their own ruin and bear the burden of those they misled. They are unaware of this, because their heedlessness and pride blind them to the consequences of their conduct, which will become evident only when they face the reckoning.

translation: If only you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire and say, 'Would that we could be returned, so that we would not deny the signs of our Lord and would be among the believers.'
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment when the deniers of truth, confronted with the reality of the Hereafter, are overwhelmed by regret. What they once rejected is now plainly visible, and they wish for a second chance to live differently. Their wish is not a sign of true repentance but a reaction to seeing the consequences: the next verses explain that what they used to conceal has become manifest, and that even if they were sent back they would return to what they had been forbidden. The lesson is that faith must be embraced now, while it is a free choice of the heart and reason, since once the unseen becomes seen, belief can no longer count as a test, and the time for action has passed.

translation: Rather, what they used to conceal before has become clear to them. And if they were sent back, they would return to that which they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.
interpretation: The wish of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment to be returned to the world and to believe is not born of sincere repentance. Rather, when the punishment is laid before them, the truth they used to hide in their hearts, the knowledge that the Messengers were truthful and the revelation was true, along with their hidden hypocrisy and sins, is exposed and they can no longer deny it. Their plea is only a response to the fear of the torment, not a real change of heart. God, who knows their inner nature, declares that if they were given a second chance they would revert to the same disbelief and disobedience they were forbidden from, because their stubbornness is rooted in their character. Their promise to believe is therefore a lie.

translation: And they said: There is nothing but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected.
interpretation: This verse (Al-An'am 6:29) exposes the worldview of those who deny the Hereafter: they confine existence to the material life they can see and reject accountability after death. The Qur'an presents this denial as the root of heedlessness, since if life ends with death, there is no final justice and no ultimate purpose behind moral restraint. Their claim is an assertion made without proof, set against the Qur'anic argument that the One who created humans the first time is able to bring them back, and that the world's apparent injustices point to a day when everyone is held to account.

translation: If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say, 'Is this not the truth?' They will say, 'Yes, by our Lord!' He will say, 'Then taste the punishment for having disbelieved.'
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when those who denied the resurrection are confronted with the reality they rejected. Their standing before God strips away every excuse. The question 'Is this not the truth?' is a rebuke: what they mocked and denied is now plainly before them. Their answer, 'Yes, by our Lord!', is an admission forced by certainty, and it comes too late to benefit them, since faith is only valuable when chosen in this life, while the unseen is still a matter of belief. Swearing by 'our Lord' shows that they knew His lordship all along, which makes their denial in life a stubborn choice rather than ignorance. The punishment is therefore a just consequence of their persistent disbelief, not an arbitrary act. The verse warns people to accept the truth of the Hereafter now, while acceptance can still be of use.

translation: Lost indeed are those who denied the meeting with God, until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they say: 'Alas for us, for what we neglected concerning it!' while they bear their burdens on their backs. Truly, evil is what they bear.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who deny accountability before God have ruined themselves, because their denial led them to waste their lives in heedlessness. Their loss is concealed from them during worldly life, and it becomes plain only when the Last Hour strikes without warning, when regret can no longer change anything. The image of sins carried on their backs shows that their misdeeds are not abstract but a real, crushing weight of responsibility that they will have to bear. The verse warns that belief in the meeting with God is the foundation for living responsibly, and that neglecting preparation for the Hereafter ends in bitter remorse.

translation: The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement; but the Home of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God. Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: The verse tells us that worldly life, when pursued as an end in itself, is fleeting and ultimately unserious, like a game that absorbs attention but leaves nothing lasting once it ends. Its pleasures, status, and possessions distract people from what truly matters. The Hereafter is the enduring reality, and it is better for those who live with God-consciousness (taqwa), since their conduct in this life is guided by accountability and sincerity. The closing question, 'Will you not use your reason?', calls the listener to reflect: a rational person weighs the temporary against the eternal and chooses to invest in lasting good rather than being consumed by transient diversion. This does not condemn life or its lawful enjoyments, but warns against giving the world priority over the Hereafter.

translation: We know indeed that what they say grieves you. It is not you they are calling a liar, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of God.
interpretation: God consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in his distress at the accusations and rejection of his people. The verse explains that the rejection is not truly directed at him personally, since they knew him to be truthful and trustworthy before his mission. Their denial is in reality a stubborn rejection of God's revelation, driven by arrogance and injustice. The Prophet should therefore not grieve, because the offense is against God and His signs, and God will deal with those who deny them. This also teaches every caller to truth that opposition to the message is not a verdict on their own worth, and that they should remain steady and patient.

translation: Messengers before you were indeed denied, yet they patiently endured being denied and harmed until Our help came to them. None can change the words of God. And there has already come to you some of the accounts of the messengers.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the face of his people's rejection and hostility. It teaches that opposition to truth is the universal experience of God's messengers, and that their path was one of steadfast patience through denial and injury until divine support arrived at the time God had decreed. The phrase 'none can change the words of God' affirms that God's promise of victory for His messengers and the ultimate triumph of truth is firm and unalterable, so believers should not despair or hasten the outcome. The closing reminder that the stories of earlier prophets have reached him offers him models of perseverance and assurance that the same divine pattern will unfold in his own case.

translation: And if their turning away is hard on you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky so that you may bring them a sign... But if God had willed, He would have gathered them all upon guidance. So do not be among the ignorant.
interpretation: God consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who was deeply grieved by his people's rejection of his message and longed for them to believe. The verse tells him that guidance is not in his power: even if he could dig into the earth or climb to the heavens to bring a miracle, it would not force faith upon those whose hearts are closed. Belief must come from free choice, and God, in His wisdom, did not will to compel all people to guidance, since He created humans with the freedom to accept or reject. The closing warning, 'do not be among the ignorant,' is a gentle reminder not to let excessive sorrow or eagerness lead him to ignore this divine wisdom and the way God has ordained matters. His duty is to convey the message with patience, while the outcome of guidance rests with God alone.

translation: Only those who hear will respond. As for the dead, God will resurrect them, then to Him they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse (Al-An'am 6:36) teaches that true response to the divine message comes only from those whose hearts are alive and who listen with real attentiveness and openness, not merely with their ears. The stubborn disbelievers who turn away are likened to the dead, because their hearts are unresponsive to guidance, so the Prophet should not grieve over their rejection or imagine that he can compel them to believe. Guidance is in God's hands. Just as He will raise the physically dead on the Day of Resurrection and bring all of them back to Him for judgment, He alone can bring spiritually dead hearts to life, and every soul will finally be accountable before Him for whether it heard and responded or refused.

translation: And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, God is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."
interpretation: The verse addresses the stubbornness of those who reject the Prophet: they demand a specific miracle of their own choosing, as though their belief depended on it, while ignoring the many signs already present in creation and in the Qur'an itself. The reply affirms that God's power to send any sign is beyond question, so their demand is not due to any lack on God's part. The real problem is their ignorance. Most of them fail to grasp the wisdom behind God's withholding of such signs: miracles demanded on request, once rejected, bring a decisive punishment, and faith is meant to rest on reflection and sincere seeking rather than on spectacle. Their insistence reveals a lack of understanding of God's wisdom and of the signs that are already clear to anyone who reflects.

translation: There is no creature crawling on the earth, nor any bird flying on its two wings, but they are communities like yourselves. We have neglected nothing in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse points to the animal kingdom as a sign of God's design and justice. Every species is a community like human communities: each has its own nature, order, instincts, and means of livelihood, all created, sustained, and guided by God. This should lead people to reflect on God's wisdom and to see that humans are not the only beings under His care and knowledge. The statement that nothing has been neglected in the Book means that God's knowledge and decree encompass every creature and every matter, nothing being left out of His record, and the guidance in the Qur'an is complete regarding what people need for their religion. Finally, all creatures will be gathered before their Lord, which affirms that divine justice will be fully established, even to the point of rights being restored among creatures, so that no one can imagine that their deeds or the deeds of others go unnoticed or unaccounted for.

translation: Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in layers of darkness. Whomever God wills, He lets go astray, and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse portrays those who persistently reject God's signs as people who have lost the faculties that guidance depends on. They do not truly listen to the truth, they do not speak it, and they stumble in the darkness of their ignorance, arrogance, and desires, so they cannot see the way. Their deafness and muteness are spiritual, not physical: they hear the message but do not take it in, and they cannot voice honest acknowledgment of it. The closing statement affirms that guidance and misguidance lie within God's power and wisdom. His willing is not arbitrary; it is tied to people's own dispositions and choices, so He leaves astray those who turn away from His signs and sets on the straight path those who are sincere and open to the truth. The believer is therefore reminded to depend on God for guidance and to be grateful for it, while recognizing that willful denial leads to deeper darkness.

translation: Say: 'Have you considered: if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon anyone other than God, if you are truthful?'
interpretation: The verse challenges the idolaters with a question drawn from their own instinct. When real catastrophe strikes, whether a worldly punishment or the overwhelming terror of the Last Hour, false deities are forgotten and people turn by nature to God alone as the only one with power to rescue. Since they themselves know in moments of extreme need that no partner can help them, their worship of others in times of ease is shown to be baseless and contradictory. The phrase 'if you are truthful' calls on them to prove their claim that their idols have any power, which they cannot do, so pure monotheism is the only consistent position.

translation: No, it is Him alone you call upon, and He removes that for which you called upon Him, if He wills, and you forget whatever partners you associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse points to the natural instinct of monotheism that appears in moments of extreme distress. When disaster strikes, even those who worship others besides God abandon their false deities and turn to God alone, because they know deep down that only He has the power to relieve hardship. Whether He answers and lifts the affliction is entirely subject to His will and wisdom, not to any claim on Him. The moment of crisis exposes the emptiness of idolatry, as people forget their supposed partners, showing that their shirk is a habit of ease and heedlessness rather than a conviction of the heart. It is meant to remind people that the God they call on in desperation is the one deserving of their devotion at all times.

translation: And We certainly sent messengers to nations before you, and We seized them with hardship and affliction that perhaps they might humble themselves.
interpretation: God shows that His way with earlier communities was not to punish them at once, but first to send messengers and then to test them with poverty, illness, loss, and distress. These trials were a form of mercy and a call to return, meant to soften hardened hearts and rouse people from heedlessness so that they would turn to God in humility and supplication. Hardship is therefore a means of awakening and correction, and the right response is repentance and submission rather than stubbornness. The verse also comforts the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, by showing that rejection by his people follows a familiar pattern in the history of the nations.

translation: If only, when Our affliction came upon them, they had humbled themselves! But their hearts hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse shows that hardship sent by God is meant to awaken people and bring them back to humility and repentance. The peoples before them were struck with misfortune as a warning, yet they did not turn to God in supplication. Their hearts had grown hard through persistent heedlessness, so the warning had no effect on them. Satan made it worse by dressing up their sins and neglect as good and justifiable, so they went on in them without remorse. The lesson is that a person should respond to trials with self-examination and turning to God, because hardness of heart combined with self-justification is a path to ruin.

translation: So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and behold, they were in utter despair.
interpretation: The verse shows God's way with nations who ignore warning. After hardship fails to rouse them and they abandon the reminder, God does not punish them at once. He gives them abundant wealth, ease and worldly success, which is a gradual drawing-in (istidraj). Their prosperity is not a sign of divine approval but a test and a deferral. They grow complacent and exult in their gains, forgetting the Giver, and then the punishment comes without warning, when they are least prepared. They are left mubsilun, stunned, hopeless and speechless, with no means of escape. The lesson is that worldly prosperity while persisting in heedlessness and sin is a danger, not a blessing. Believers should answer blessings with gratitude and obedience and heed reminders before they are overtaken by sudden ruin.

translation: So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wrongdoing, when persistent and unrepented, ends in complete destruction by divine justice: no trace or continuation of the oppressors remains. Such an end is not cause for gloating but for gratitude, because the removal of injustice is a mercy to creation and a vindication of truth. Praising God as 'Lord of the worlds' acknowledges that His sovereignty and care extend to all beings, and that His judgment upon the wrongdoers is part of His wise and just governance, securing relief for the believers and the wider world.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if God were to take away your hearing and your sight, and seal your hearts, which deity other than God could restore them to you? Look how We diversify the signs, yet still they turn away.
interpretation: The verse argues from human dependence: hearing, sight and understanding are not self-owned faculties but trusts granted moment by moment by God. If He withdrew them and sealed the heart so that no insight or guidance could enter, no false deity, idol, or created power could give them back. The only logical conclusion is that worship and devotion belong to God alone. The closing rebuke shows the paradox of stubbornness: although God presents His proofs in many forms, through nature, reason, warnings and revelation, the deniers still avert themselves. Their rejection stems from willful aversion rather than a lack of evidence.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of God comes upon you suddenly or openly, will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?
interpretation: The verse warns that divine punishment can arrive without notice (suddenly) or in plain view (openly), and that it falls justly on those who persist in wrongdoing, chiefly shirk and rejection of the truth, rather than on the righteous. Its point is that people should not take comfort in their delay or in their worldly security, since destruction is the consequence of their own injustice. They should turn to faith and right action before the punishment comes, while those who believe and do good have no cause to fear it.

translation: We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and as warners. So whoever believes and reforms themselves, there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The role of the prophets is clear and limited: they bring glad tidings of reward to those who respond, and warn of consequences for those who reject, but they are not sent to perform whatever miracles people demand or to compel anyone to believe. The verse then states the outcome of accepting their message: true faith must be joined with righteous action and moral reform, not mere profession. Those who combine the two are assured security in the Hereafter, free from fear of punishment and from sorrow over what they left behind or missed, because God has guaranteed their safety and their reward.

translation: But those who deny Our signs, the punishment will touch them because of their transgression.
interpretation: This verse (Al-An'am 6:49) establishes that punishment for those who reject God's revelations is not arbitrary but a direct consequence of their own conduct. The word 'yafsuqun' denotes going out from the bounds of obedience, so the denial of the signs is not merely an intellectual error but a willful departure from the limits set by God, persisting in defiance after the truth has become clear. The verb 'yamassuhum' (will touch them) suggests that the punishment will reach and afflict them inevitably, as though it seeks them out. The lesson is that moral and spiritual rebellion carries real consequences, while the messengers, as the preceding verse states, only bring glad tidings and warnings, leaving each person accountable for the response they choose.

translation: Say: I do not tell you that I possess the treasures of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me. Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal? Will you not then reflect?
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to state the true limits of his station so that people do not attribute divine or angelic powers to him or demand miracles as proof of his message. He does not control God's provision or sustenance, has no independent knowledge of the unseen beyond what God discloses, and is a human being, not an angel. His authority rests solely on following revelation, which makes him a conveyor of guidance and not a source of it. The closing question contrasts the blind and the seeing as a metaphor: the one who is spiritually blind, heedless of the signs of God and the truth of revelation, cannot be equal to the one who sees by the light of guidance. The verse ends by urging people to use reason and reflection to recognize this difference and to judge the message by its truth, not by extraordinary claims about the messenger.

translation: And warn by it those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having no protector or intercessor besides Him, so that they may become mindful of God.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to aim his warning with the Qur'an at those whose hearts are alive to the reality of the Day of Judgment, since they are the ones who will actually benefit from it. Those who fear being gathered before God are aware that on that Day no ally, relative, or intercessor can rescue a person apart from God's own permission. This awareness is meant to cultivate taqwa, a constant God-consciousness that shapes conduct: a person who knows that all support disappears on that Day will rely on faith and righteous deeds in this life rather than on worldly connections, status, or wishful hopes in anyone else's help.

translation: And do not drive away those who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. You are not accountable for anything of their reckoning, nor are they accountable for anything of yours, that you should drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that a person's standing before God rests on sincerity and devotion, not on wealth, rank, or social prestige. When the Prophet was pressed by the powerful elite of Quraysh to remove the poor, humble believers from his gatherings, he was commanded to keep them close, since their constant remembrance of God, done purely for His sake, gives them honor. Each person answers to God for his own deeds: the Prophet is not responsible for the inner state or the reckoning of these believers, and they are not responsible for his. Dismissing sincere worshippers to please the arrogant would therefore be an injustice, because it puts worldly status above faith and wrongs those whom God has honored. The lesson is that a community of faith must treat the sincere with dignity, avoid class-based discrimination, and leave judgment of hearts to God alone.

translation: And thus We have tried some of them by means of others, so that they say, 'Are these the ones whom God has favored from among us?' Is God not most knowing of those who are grateful?
interpretation: God tests people by means of one another: the wealthy and noble are tried by the presence of poor, humble believers beside the Prophet, and their pride makes them scorn those believers and ask mockingly how such people could have been favored with guidance over them. The verse answers that guidance is not a prize for rank or wealth. God knows the hearts of those who truly recognize His favor and respond with gratitude, and He grants them faith and guidance, so a person's worth is measured by thankfulness and sincerity rather than by status.

translation: When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has decreed mercy upon Himself: whoever among you does evil out of ignorance, then repents afterward and reforms himself, then indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: The verse teaches that believers are to be received with honor and the greeting of peace, and it assures them that God's mercy is a self-imposed commitment rather than something forced upon Him. Even sins committed in ignorance, meaning out of heedlessness, weakness, or the pull of desire without denying God, are forgiven when followed by sincere repentance and a real change in conduct. The door of forgiveness is thus open to every believer who turns back and amends his ways, and no one should despair of God's mercy because of past wrongdoing.

translation: And thus We explain the verses in detail, so that the way of the criminals may become clear.
interpretation: God makes His revelations clear and distinct so that the path of the wrongdoers is unmistakable to the believers. Truth and falsehood are set apart in such detail that no one can confuse the way of those who persist in denial and sin with the way of guidance. Knowing the path of the wrongdoers is itself a protection: once their conduct and their false arguments are exposed, the believer can avoid following them and stand firm on the clear path of God.

translation: Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah. Say: I will not follow your desires; for then I would have gone astray, and I would not be among the rightly guided.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to declare openly that his rejection of idolatry is not a personal preference but a binding divine prohibition, and that he will not compromise his faith to appease the polytheists. Their worship of other deities rests on whims and inherited desires rather than on revealed knowledge, so following them would mean abandoning the guidance he received from God. The verse teaches that true guidance lies only in submission to revelation, that yielding to the majority's desires in matters of belief leads to misguidance, and that a believer must remain steadfast in monotheism whatever the social pressure to conform.

translation: Say: Indeed, I stand upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it. I do not possess that which you seek to hasten. The decision belongs to none but God; He relates the truth, and He is the best of those who decide.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to declare that his position rests on certain, clear evidence from God, not on conjecture or desire, and that the disbelievers' rejection does not weaken that evidence. When they mockingly demand that the punishment be brought forward, he clarifies that he is only a messenger with no power over its timing, for the authority to judge, to delay or to hasten, belongs to God alone. God makes the truth known and decides between truth and falsehood with perfect justice and knowledge, so no judge is better than He. The verse teaches humility before divine authority, patience with God's timing, and confidence that He will vindicate the truth.

translation: Say: If what you are impatient for were in my hands, the matter between me and you would already have been decided. And God knows best who the wrongdoers are.
interpretation: The Prophet is told to make clear that he has no power over the punishment the disbelievers demand he hasten. Bringing it on, delaying it, and deciding between truth and falsehood belong to God alone, according to His wisdom and knowledge. If the decision were his, the dispute would have ended already and the wrongdoers would have been destroyed. The delay is therefore no sign that the Prophet is false or that the threat is empty. It is a mercy and a respite, and God, who knows exactly who deserves punishment and when, will bring about the judgment at the proper time.

translation: With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. He knows what is on the land and in the sea. No leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear record.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's knowledge is absolute, all-encompassing, and exclusive in its reach over the unseen. The 'keys of the unseen' signify that access to hidden realities, such as the future, the Hour, and what lies in wombs and hearts, belongs to God alone, so no human, prophet, or created being can claim independent knowledge of them. His knowledge extends from the vast expanses of land and sea to the smallest details: a single falling leaf, a seed buried in the dark soil, and everything fresh or withered. All of this is precisely preserved in a clear record, showing that nothing in creation is left to chance or escapes His awareness. The believer should therefore feel humility before God's knowledge, trust in His wise ordering of all affairs, and awareness that every deed is known and recorded, which encourages sincerity, accountability, and reliance on Him alone.

translation: It is He who takes your souls by night and knows what you have earned by day; then He raises you up again in it so that a term appointed [for your life] may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return, and then He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse points to sleep as a daily reminder of death and resurrection: God takes the souls in sleep as He will at death, and waking is a small rehearsal of being raised after death. Since He knows even what people do with their limbs by day, no deed is hidden from Him. Each person's lifespan is fixed and cannot be hastened or delayed, so every awakening is a gift of time that should be used well. Because all will finally return to Him and be told the truth of their deeds, a believer should live with constant awareness of accountability, renewing repentance and good conduct each day, since the night may be the last.

translation: He is the Supreme over His servants, and He sends over you guardian angels, until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take his soul, and they do not fail in their duty.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's dominion over His creatures is absolute: nothing escapes His power, and every human being is subject to His will. Out of His care and wisdom He appoints angels who watch over a person and record their deeds, so that no one is left unattended and no deed is lost. These guardians preserve a person for their appointed term, and when that term ends, the angels charged with taking souls carry out their task exactly as commanded, neither hastening death by a moment nor delaying it. The lesson is that life, protection, and death are all governed by God's precise decree, so a believer should live with awareness that their deeds are recorded, that their life lasts only as long as God has decreed, and that they will surely return to Him for accounting.

translation: Then they will be returned to God, their true Master. Truly, His is the judgment, and He is the swiftest of reckoners.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every soul, after death and resurrection, must go back to God, who is its only true Lord and Protector. The 'false' masters people depended on in this life, such as wealth, status, idols and their own desires, cannot help them then, and only God's guardianship is real and lasting. On that Day, authority and final judgment belong to Him alone; no one can appeal against or overturn His ruling. Describing Him as the swiftest of reckoners means He needs no time, effort or witnesses to account for everyone's deeds, since His knowledge encompasses everything. The believer is therefore called to live with awareness of accountability: to take God as their master now, to act justly, and to prepare for a reckoning that is certain, precise and swift.

translation: Say: Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land and the sea, when you call upon Him humbly and in secret: 'If He saves us from this, we will surely be among the grateful'?
interpretation: The verse argues from human experience against polytheism. In moments of extreme peril, such as a storm at sea or being lost in a desert at night, people drop their false gods and turn sincerely to God alone, pleading openly and privately and promising gratitude. This instinctive turning shows that the natural recognition of God's exclusive power over rescue lives in every heart. It therefore exposes the inconsistency of those who return to idolatry or ingratitude once the danger has passed. The verse calls people to carry into times of ease the same sincere reliance and thankfulness they show in hardship.

translation: Say: "God delivers you from it and from every distress, yet you still associate partners with Him."
interpretation: The verse (Al-An'am 6:64) rebukes the inconsistency of human beings. In moments of extreme peril, such as the darkness of land and sea, people call upon God alone with humility and promise gratitude, and it is God alone who rescues them from that danger and from every other hardship. Once they are safe, however, they revert to worshipping others besides Him, whether idols, created beings, or worldly means they trust in instead of Him. The point is that since God alone is the One who saves in times of need, He alone deserves worship at all times, and turning to partners after being saved is ingratitude and a contradiction of what their own hearts recognized in distress.

translation: Say: He is able to send upon you punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confuse you into factions and make some of you taste the violence of others. See how We explain the signs in various ways so that they may understand.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human security rests entirely on God's protection, and that divine punishment can arrive in more than one form. It may come from outside, as calamities from the sky or the earth, such as storms, floods or earthquakes. It may also come from within society, as division into hostile factions, with one group tasting the violence of another. The last of these is a warning that civil strife, sectarianism and mutual bloodshed are themselves a form of divine chastisement, often caused by people's own sins and by their turning away from God's guidance. The closing call to see how the signs are varied and repeated invites reflection: God presents His warnings in different ways so that people may understand, repent, and return to unity and obedience before the punishment falls.

translation: Your people have denied it (the Qur'an), though it is the truth. Say: 'I am not a guardian over you.'
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by showing that the truth of a message does not depend on how many people accept it, since even his own people rejected the Qur'an although it is the truth. It also sets out the limits of his role: he is a messenger who conveys and clarifies, not a warden who forces belief or controls people's choices. Guidance and the final reckoning belong to God alone, so the Prophet is not to be burdened with the result of their denial, and no one may be compelled in matters of faith.

translation: For every prophecy there is a appointed time and place of fulfillment, and you will soon come to know.
interpretation: Every report or warning that God has announced, including the warnings of punishment for those who deny the truth, has a fixed time at which it will come true and be established as reality. The deniers should not take delay as proof that the warning is false, since God's timing is wise and exact. When the appointed moment arrives, whether in this world through the triumph of truth over falsehood or in the Hereafter through reckoning, they will see with certainty that what the Messenger conveyed was real, and they will know the consequences of their denial.

translation: And when you see those who engage in vain discourse about Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different conversation. And if Satan should cause you to forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse sets out an ethic of protecting the sanctity of revelation: believers are not to lend their presence, and so their tacit approval, to gatherings where God's signs are mocked, denied, or distorted. Turning away is a principled withdrawal that ends once the talk changes, which shows that the objection is to the disrespect, not to people as such, and leaves room for dialogue. The second part acknowledges human frailty: if forgetfulness, which the verse attributes to Satan's influence, leads a person to stay in such company, he must leave as soon as he remembers and not persist out of embarrassment, social pressure, or habit. The lesson is that a person's company shapes his faith, and that staying silently among those who ridicule the sacred makes one complicit in their wrongdoing.

translation: Those who are mindful of God are not accountable for anything of their [the wrongdoers'] reckoning; but it is a reminder, so that they may be mindful of God.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 6:69) comforts the believers who sit among people who mock God's signs. Once they have avoided or left such gatherings, the righteous carry no burden for the mockers' wrongdoing, because every person answers only for his own deeds. Their duty is not to force others to believe, but to remind and advise them. If the mockers listen, the reminder may awaken God-consciousness in them, so they stop their mockery and become mindful of God. If they do not, the responsibility for their conduct rests with them alone.

translation: Leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement, and whom the life of this world has deceived. But remind with it (the Qur'an) lest a soul be given up to destruction for what it has earned; it will have no protector nor intercessor besides God, and even if it offered every possible ransom, it would not be accepted from it. Those are the ones given up to destruction for what they have earned. For them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to disengage from those who mock and trivialize religion, treating sacred matters as sport while being absorbed and misled by worldly life, and not to be distressed by their rejection or waste effort arguing with those who scoff. Yet his duty of reminding through the Qur'an continues, so that people are warned of the real danger: that a person may be handed over to ruin and be held captive by the consequences of their own deeds. On the Day of Judgment, no ally, helper, or intercessor can rescue them apart from God's permission, and no ransom, however vast, can buy their release. Ultimate responsibility is personal, because each soul is bound by what it has earned. Those who persisted in denial find that their own choices have become their chains, and they face boiling drink and painful torment as the just result of their disbelief.

translation: Say: Shall we call upon, besides God, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after God has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured away in the land, bewildered, while he has companions calling him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us'? Say: Indeed, God's guidance is the true guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse answers those who urge believers to return to idolatry by exposing its irrationality and danger. Worshipping anything besides God, which has no power to help or harm, is a regression, a turning back on one's heels after receiving guidance. The one who abandons guidance is likened to a traveler lured by devils into a wilderness, bewildered and lost, while his former companions on the right path call him back to safety. The lesson is that true guidance comes only from God, that deviation leads to confusion and ruin, and that real freedom and clarity lie in submitting wholly to the Lord of the worlds, not in following misleading voices or abandoning the truth under pressure.

translation: And [it has been commanded]: establish the prayer and be mindful of Him; and it is He to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse joins worship and moral awareness to the reality of the Last Day. Establishing prayer means maintaining a regular, sincere connection with God. Taqwa, or God-consciousness, means guarding oneself against what displeases Him. The verse grounds both in the certainty that every person will be gathered before God for judgment. Remembering that final gathering gives a person the motivation to pray and live uprightly, because he knows that he is accountable to God and that his ultimate return is to Him.

translation: It is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And on the day He says, 'Be,' it is. His word is the truth. His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown. Knower of the unseen and the seen; and He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation is purposeful and grounded in truth, not play or chance, so it points to a Creator whose will is effortless and absolute: when He commands, things come into being. Because His word is truth, His promises of resurrection and judgment are certain, and on the Day of the Trumpet all apparent human power and ownership will fall away, leaving sovereignty to Him alone. His knowledge of both the hidden and the manifest, joined with wisdom and complete awareness, means that no deed or intention escapes Him and that His judgment will be perfectly just. The believer is therefore called to live with accountability, trust in God's wisdom, and rejection of any partners in worship.

translation: And [remember] when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error."
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's first public stand for pure monotheism, and he begins with the person closest to him. By confronting his father with a question, he exposes the irrationality of worshipping carved objects that people make with their own hands, instead of issuing a bare command. His firm judgment that his father and his people are in clear error shows that loyalty to truth takes precedence over family ties and social custom. It also shows that calling people to God should combine respect in tone with clarity about the truth: he addresses Azar as 'my father', yet he does not soften the fact that idol worship is misguidance. The verse thus teaches that tawhid has to be affirmed openly and that tradition and lineage cannot justify error.

translation: And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who have firm certainty.
interpretation: God granted Abraham insight into the inner reality and sovereign order behind creation, so that he could see that everything in the heavens and the earth is subject to God's authority and power. This vision was not merely to inform him but to move his faith from inherited belief to certainty grounded in direct reflection and witness. It prepared him to challenge his people's worship of created things, since he came to see that what is created, changing, and dependent cannot be divine. The verse teaches that certainty (yaqin) is attained through contemplating creation as a sign of the Creator, and that God guides the sincere seeker to that level of conviction.

translation: So when the night covered him, he saw a star; he said, 'This is my Lord.' But when it set, he said, 'I do not love those that set.'
interpretation: This verse shows Abraham reasoning step by step toward the truth, using a gradual argument to expose the falseness of worshipping created things. By saying 'This is my Lord' he adopts his people's viewpoint for the sake of argument, and then he refutes it. The star appears, then vanishes, and anything that changes, disappears, and is absent cannot be God, who must be eternal, ever-present, and unchanging. His words 'I do not love those that set' teach that worship and love belong only to the One who is permanent and never fails, so that his people can see by their own reason that heavenly bodies are dependent creations and not deities.

translation: Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my Lord." But when it set, he said, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who go astray."
interpretation: In this verse Abraham continues his step-by-step reasoning with his people, who worshipped celestial bodies. By saying "This is my Lord" he speaks as a debater adopting his opponents' premise in order to test it, not as a sincere statement of belief. When the moon sets, he shows that anything that disappears and changes cannot be a lord, since a true God must be ever-present, unchanging, and in control of all things. His prayer, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among those who go astray," shows that guidance comes only from God and that human reasoning needs His help to reach the truth. It also gently warns his people that they are in error, preparing them for his final declaration of pure monotheism, in which he turns his face to the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

translation: Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, 'This is my Lord; this is greater.' But when it set, he said, 'O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate with God.'
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham's method of reasoned argument with his people, who worshipped celestial bodies. By provisionally voicing their own premise, 'this is my Lord, this is greater,' he led them step by step to see its flaw: whatever rises and sets is changing, dependent, and contingent, and so cannot be a lord or deserve worship. When the sun, the largest and brightest of the bodies they venerated, disappeared, its setting disproved its divinity. He then publicly disowned their idolatry, declaring himself free of all partners associated with God. This establishes that true divinity belongs only to the Creator who is eternal, unchanging, and not subject to any disappearance, and that tawhid rests on reflection upon creation rather than blind imitation.

translation: Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with God.
interpretation: The verse expresses Abraham's declaration of pure monotheism after he reasoned his way past the false objects of worship, the stars, moon, and sun. To 'turn the face' is to direct one's whole being, with sincerity and intention, to God alone. He grounds this devotion in God's being the Originator of the heavens and the earth, since only the Creator, not the created things that rise and set, deserves worship. Being 'hanif' means turning away from every form of falsehood and staying firmly upright on the natural disposition (fitrah) toward truth. The closing disavowal of shirk makes clear that true faith requires both affirming God's oneness and rejecting every partner ascribed to Him, so that sincere devotion is directed to God alone.

translation: And his people argued with him. He said: 'Do you argue with me about God, when He has guided me? I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then remember?'
interpretation: This verse describes Abraham's response when his people disputed with him over his monotheism. He rests his confidence on the guidance God has given him, which makes arguing for idols pointless. He declares that the false gods have no power to harm him, because benefit and harm come only from God's will. If anything befalls him, it happens because his Lord willed it, not because of those idols. He then grounds this trust in God's all-encompassing knowledge: nothing escapes the One who knows all things, so relying on Him is the only sound course. The closing question, 'Will you not then remember?', calls his people to reflect and return to the natural recognition of God's oneness. The verse teaches that true faith brings fearlessness toward created things, together with humble submission to God's will and knowledge.

translation: And how should I fear what you have associated with God, while you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down no authority to you? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?
interpretation: In this verse Abraham answers his people's attempt to frighten him with their false gods. He turns their threat back on them with a rational argument: it is illogical to fear powerless objects that have no proof or divine sanction behind them, while the people themselves feel no fear of committing the gravest wrong, which is to ascribe partners to the Creator without any evidence. Real security belongs to the one who worships God alone, relying on sound proof and revelation, and not to the one who follows baseless claims. The question 'which of the two parties has more right to security?' invites honest reflection, and the answer is clear: the monotheist is the one who should feel safe, while the polytheist should be the one who is afraid, since he stands on no clear proof and is exposed to God's displeasure.

translation: Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing—for them is security, and they are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 6:82) teaches that true security, in this world and the next, belongs to those whose faith is pure and uncorrupted. 'Wrongdoing' (zulm) here is understood, as the Prophet explained to his Companions when they were alarmed by the verse, as the greatest wrong, namely shirk (associating partners with God), as in Luqman's words, 'Indeed, shirk is a great wrong.' So those who affirm God's oneness sincerely and do not taint their faith with polytheism are promised safety from fear and punishment and are guided on the straight path. Lesser sins do not cancel this promise of security, though they may diminish its fullness, so believers should still strive to keep their faith free of every kind of injustice.

translation: And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Abraham's reasoning about the stars, moon and sun, which led him to affirm that only the Creator who does not set or change deserves worship, was not merely his own cleverness but guidance and proof granted by God. God gave him this clear argument to defeat his people's idolatry. Elevation in rank, whether in knowledge, certainty, or nearness to God, is a gift God bestows on whomever He wills according to His wisdom, and He gives it to those who sincerely seek the truth, as Abraham did. God does this with perfect wisdom, placing honor where it is deserved, and with full knowledge of who is fit to receive it.

translation: And We granted him Isaac and Jacob; each of them We guided. And Noah We guided before, and among his descendants were David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward those who do good.
interpretation: The verse shows that guidance is a divine gift that God bestows on the righteous across generations, and it is not limited to one lineage or person. Abraham's reward for his steadfast faith and his sincere devotion was a righteous family, with prophets descending from him. The closing phrase, 'Thus do We reward those who do good,' means that these prophets, who endured kingship, hardship, and persecution, were honored because of their excellence (ihsan) in worshipping God and obeying Him. It teaches that those who devote themselves sincerely to God will be given guidance, a good legacy, and a lasting reputation, and it affirms that the prophets all belong to one continuous path of monotheism.

translation: And Zachariah, and John, and Jesus, and Elias; every one of them was among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 6:85) continues the list of prophets whom God guided and rewarded, and it singles out a group distinguished by righteousness (salāḥ). Zachariah, John, Jesus and Elias were known for asceticism, purity and devotion to God. The phrase 'every one of them was among the righteous' teaches that righteousness is the shared mark of the prophets. They were chosen because of their upright character and sincere submission to God, not because of lineage or worldly status. It also presents them as models for believers, showing that guidance comes from God and leads to a life of integrity, humility and devotion, even though the prophets lived in different times and faced different circumstances.

translation: And Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot — and each of them We favored over the worlds.
interpretation: God affirms that these prophets, though they lived in different eras, lands, and circumstances, and though some were given kingdoms or great miracles while others faced rejection, exile, or trial, were each raised in rank above the people of their own times. Their excellence came from God's choice and from their steadfastness in faith, patience, and obedience, not from worldly power or numbers. The verse teaches that true honor lies in devotion to God and in carrying His message, and that the righteous form one noble lineage of guidance, so believers should honor all of them without distinction and take them as models.

translation: And from among their fathers, their descendants, and their brothers — We chose them and guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, coming after the mention of prophets such as Ibrahim, Ishaq, Yaqub, Nuh, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa, Ilyas, Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut, extends God's favor beyond those named to some of their forefathers, offspring and siblings. It teaches that divine selection and guidance are a grace God bestows on whom He wills, and that guidance is not confined to a single lineage or person but flows through families of righteousness. Being chosen (ijtiba') is God's act of drawing someone near for a mission, while guidance to the straight path is what keeps them upright on the way of pure monotheism. The verse thus affirms the unity of the prophetic message across generations: all of them share one path, which the Prophet Muhammad is then commanded to follow.

translation: That is the guidance of Allah by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. But if they had associated others with Him, then worthless for them would be whatever they used to do.
interpretation: Guidance is entirely a gift from God, not something earned by human power or lineage; He grants it to whomever He wills among His servants, according to His wisdom and to those who sincerely seek it. The verse then warns that even the noblest of people, such as the prophets mentioned just before it, would have lost the reward of all their righteous deeds had they committed shirk. This shows that sound belief in God's oneness is the foundation on which every good deed rests, and that without it no deed carries weight with God.

translation: Those are the ones to whom We gave the Scripture, the judgment, and prophethood. So if these people disbelieve in it, We have already entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet that God's guidance does not depend on any one people's acceptance. The earlier prophets, mentioned in the preceding verses, were given revelation, wisdom and prophethood, and if the Prophet's own contemporaries reject the message, God has appointed others who will uphold it faithfully. Many commentators identify these people as the Companions and the believers who supported the Prophet, or more broadly every community of true believers throughout history. The verse consoles the Prophet in the face of denial and shows that truth is preserved by God through sincere believers, so rejection by some cannot diminish it.

translation: Those are the ones whom God has guided, so follow their guidance. Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it. It is nothing but a reminder for all the worlds.
interpretation: After mentioning a line of prophets (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Noah, David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, Jesus, Elijah, Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, Lot), the verse directs the Prophet Muhammad, and through him every believer, to take these messengers as models. What is meant is the core of their guidance: pure monotheism, patience, gratitude, steadfastness in truth, and sincerity in calling people to God, rather than the particular laws that differed between them. The Prophet is also told to declare, as they did, that he asks no payment for conveying the message. His call is not for worldly gain but is purely a reminder for all humankind and jinn, not just a single people. Sincere preaching is therefore free of self-interest, and the Qur'an is a universal admonition meant to awaken people to the truth.

translation: They did not esteem God with the esteem due to Him when they said, 'God has not sent down anything to any human being.' Say: 'Who sent down the Book which Moses brought as a light and guidance for people? You make it into parchments, which you show while concealing much of it; and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your forefathers.' Say: 'God.' Then leave them to amuse themselves in their false discourse.
interpretation: The verse says that denying revelation is a failure to grasp God's true greatness, since a God who creates and guides humanity would not leave it without guidance. The argument is turned on those who deny it: they themselves accept the Torah of Moses as a divine light, so their claim that God sends nothing to humans contradicts their own belief. Their selective handling of that scripture, displaying the parts that suit them and hiding the rest (including what points to the Prophet), exposes their dishonesty. The Qur'an also reminds them that it taught them knowledge they and their ancestors lacked, which is a mark of God's favor. The Prophet is told to answer the question himself with 'God', because the answer is undeniable, and then to leave the stubborn deniers alone, since their debate is not a sincere search for truth but idle play in falsehood.

translation: And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming that which came before it, so that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Mecca) and those around it. Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are ones who guard their prayers.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a continuation and confirmation of earlier revealed scripture, and as a source of lasting goodness for those who follow it. Its message begins with Mecca, the 'Mother of Cities', as the spiritual and social center of Arabia, and from there extends outward to all surrounding peoples, and by implication to all humanity. The verse also says that real faith in the Qur'an follows from real awareness of accountability in the Hereafter: a person who expects to stand before God takes the warning seriously and accepts the Book. The sign of this sincere belief is steady, careful observance of prayer, which keeps a believer's awareness of God and the Last Day alive in daily life.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him, and one who says, 'I will send down the like of what God has sent down'? If you could only see the wrongdoers in the agonies of death, while the angels stretch out their hands, saying, 'Give up your souls! Today you will be repaid with the punishment of humiliation, for what you used to say about God other than the truth, and for being arrogant towards His signs.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest wrong is to misrepresent God, whether by fabricating falsehood in His name, falsely claiming divine inspiration, or mockingly claiming one can produce revelation equal to His. Such people deny the unique authority of God's word and corrupt religion for worldly ends. The verse then portrays their moment of death as a foretaste of accountability: angels harshly demand their souls, and the punishment is called one of humiliation because it answers their arrogance. Their sin was twofold: speaking untruth about God and refusing, out of pride, to submit to His signs. Thus falsehood about the divine and arrogance toward the truth are shown to bring disgrace, beginning at death and continuing beyond it.

translation: And you have come to Us individually, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind your backs what We bestowed upon you. And We do not see with you your intercessors, those whom you claimed were partners in your affairs. The bond between you has been severed, and what you used to claim has abandoned you.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment every person stands before God stripped of all worldly support: alone, with no wealth, status, family, or followers, just as they were at birth. The verse teaches that the things people rely on in this life, such as possessions and the false deities or intermediaries they believed would intercede for them, have no power or standing before God. All ties of dependence and allegiance built on falsehood are cut, and the idols and false hopes vanish, leaving each soul accountable for its own deeds. It is a reminder to place trust in God alone and to prepare for that individual reckoning rather than lean on worldly means or false patrons.

translation: Indeed, God is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings forth the living from the dead, and is the Bringer forth of the dead from the living. That is God; so how are you deluded away from the truth?
interpretation: The verse points to God's creative power in the everyday cycle of nature as proof of His oneness and lordship. The seed buried in the earth looks lifeless, yet God splits it open and a living plant emerges. Life comes from what seems dead, and living things in turn become dead matter. Only the One who controls the boundary between life and death can do this, and no idol, created being, or force of nature shares in it. The closing question, 'how are you turned away?', is a rebuke: after such clear signs, it is unreasonable to ascribe divinity to anything besides God or to deny Him, and people should reflect on the world around them and acknowledge Him alone.

translation: He is the Cleaver of the daybreak, and He has made the night for rest and stillness, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the ordaining of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy in the regular order of time: He splits the darkness with the dawn, turns the night into a time of calm and repose for His creatures, and sets the sun and moon on exact courses so that people can measure days, months, and years and organize their worship and affairs. This precise, unfailing system is not a matter of chance but the decree of One who is Almighty, so that nothing can disrupt it, and All-Knowing, so that it fits perfectly with the needs of His creation. Reflecting on it should lead a person to recognize God's lordship, give thanks, and turn to Him alone.

translation: And it is He who made for you the stars so that you may be guided by them through the darknesses of the land and the sea. We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse presents the stars as a deliberate gift of God's mercy and wisdom: they serve as natural guideposts for travelers lost in the darkness of deserts and open seas, so human beings can find their way. Beyond physical navigation, this points to a larger truth, that the One who arranged the heavens to guide bodies through darkness has also arranged signs in creation to guide hearts and minds toward Him and away from the darkness of ignorance and polytheism. The closing phrase says that these signs are made clear and distinct, but only those who use their knowledge and reflect on them truly benefit, so that understanding the creation leads to recognizing the Creator and being grateful to Him.

translation: And it is He who produced you from one soul, and there is for you a place of settlement and a place of storage. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and care in the origin and course of human life: all humanity descends from a single soul (Adam), showing the unity of mankind and that creation is wholly in God's hands. Each person then passes through stages, with a 'mustaqarr' (a place of settlement) and a 'mustawda'' (a place of temporary deposit). A common reading takes the settled state to be the child's fixed lodging in the mother's womb or, more broadly, the life in which a person stays until his appointed term, and the deposit to be the sperm in the father's loins or the grave and the interval before resurrection. The lesson is that human beings are not in control of their beginning, their stay, or their end; every stage is ordained and entrusted by God. The closing phrase says that such signs are made clear to those who truly reflect and grasp deeper meanings (yafqahun), so that they will recognize their Creator and Sustainer, and prepare for the final return to Him.

translation: And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth with it the growth of every kind of plant; from it We brought forth greenery, from which We produce grain in tightly packed layers. And from the palm tree, from its spathe, come clusters of dates hanging low and near; and gardens of grapes, and olives and pomegranates, similar to one another and yet dissimilar. Look at its fruit when it bears fruit and at its ripening. Indeed, in all that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse directs human attention to the ordinary cycle of rain, growth and harvest as evidence of God's unique lordship and providence. A single source of water gives rise to a great variety of plants, grains, dates, grapes, olives and pomegranates that resemble each other in some ways but differ in shape, taste and use. This diversity from one origin cannot be explained by blind chance; it points to a purposeful Creator who plans, sustains and provides. The command to 'look' at the fruit as it forms and ripens invites reflective observation that leads to gratitude and faith, and the verse notes that only those open to belief truly draw this lesson from nature's signs.

translation: Yet they have made the jinn partners with God, though He created them; and they falsely attribute to Him sons and daughters without any knowledge. Glory be to Him! He is far exalted above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the irrational nature of polytheism: those who associate the jinn with God in worship or obedience overlook that the jinn are themselves created beings, and a created thing cannot share in the divinity of its Creator. Likewise, ascribing children to God, whether sons as some Christians and Jews claimed or daughters as the Arab pagans claimed about the angels, is an invention made up with no knowledge or revelation behind it. Having children implies need, kinship, and likeness to creatures, all of which are impossible for the One who is self-sufficient and unique. The verse ends by affirming God's absolute transcendence, declaring Him free of every imperfection and far above whatever human claims and descriptions attribute to Him.

translation: He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a child when He has no consort, and when He created everything, and He has full knowledge of all things?
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that God has offspring by appealing to reason. Having a child implies a mate, a shared nature, and a need for continuation or support, all of which belong to created beings. God originated the heavens and the earth without any prior model or helper, so He is utterly unlike His creation. Since everything that exists is His creation, nothing can be a part of Him or equal to Him; whatever is claimed to be His child is in fact a created being and His servant. His all-encompassing knowledge shows that He needs no offspring, and that those who attribute a son to Him speak without knowledge. Divine perfection and self-sufficiency are therefore incompatible with begetting.

translation: That is God, your Lord; there is no god but Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him. And He is the Disposer of affairs over all things.
interpretation: The verse draws a logical link between God's creative power and the right to be worshipped: since God alone brought everything into existence, nothing else deserves devotion, so worship should be directed to Him exclusively. His role as 'wakil' means that He sustains, manages and governs all of creation, so a believer can entrust their affairs to Him with confidence and need not seek security or provision from any other source. Worship and trust in God thus go together, and both stem from recognizing Him as the sole Lord and Creator.
