interpretation: This verse (Al-A'raf 7:23) is the response of Adam and Eve after eating from the forbidden tree. It teaches that true repentance begins with honest self-accusation: instead of blaming others or making excuses, as Satan did, they admitted that the harm of disobedience fell upon their own souls. They also recognized that salvation does not come from their own merit but only from God's forgiveness and mercy, and that without them a person is truly ruined. The verse thus becomes a model supplication for every believer who errs: acknowledge the fault, feel humility and need before God, and seek His pardon, which restores the servant to His mercy.

translation: He said, 'Go down, some of you as enemies to others. On earth you will have a place of settlement and provision for a time.'
interpretation: After the slip in the Garden, God decrees that humankind's life will move from the place of ease to the earth, where hardship and testing are part of the human condition. Enmity among people, and between humans and Satan, arises from competing desires, envy and heedlessness, so life on earth involves struggle and the need for vigilance. Yet the verse also contains mercy: the earth is a fitting abode with sustenance and enjoyment, but only 'for a time', a limited term. This reminds people that the world is a temporary station, not their final home. They should use its provision with gratitude and moral responsibility, and prepare for the return to God when the appointed time ends.

translation: He said: "Therein you shall live, and therein you shall die, and from it you shall be brought forth."
interpretation: God addresses Adam, Eve, and Iblis, and by extension all their descendants, to say that the earth is the appointed setting for human existence. Life is lived on it, with its trials and its enmity between humans and Satan. Death returns people to it in the grave. The resurrection will bring them out of it for reckoning. The verse sets out the whole span of a person's journey, from life through death to being raised, as lying within God's will and control. It reminds people that their stay on earth is temporary and that they should prepare for the return to God.

translation: O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts, and as adornment; but the clothing of righteousness - that is best. That is from the signs of God, that perhaps they will remember.
interpretation: God reminds humanity that even material clothing is a blessing from Him, serving both a necessity (covering shame) and a beauty (adornment). Yet the verse elevates a deeper kind of covering: taqwa, God-consciousness, which is the true garment of the soul. Outer dress protects the body's dignity, while taqwa protects the heart and character from moral nakedness, such as shamelessness, pride, and sin. Thus real honor lies not in appearance or display but in inward piety expressed through modesty and good conduct. God presents these as signs so that people reflect, give thanks, and seek to clothe themselves spiritually as well as physically.

translation: O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise, stripping them of their garments to show them their private parts. Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you do not see them. Indeed, We have made the devils allies to those who do not believe.
interpretation: God warns all of humanity to learn from the story of Adam and Eve: Satan's strategy is gradual deception, leading people from obedience into disobedience until they are stripped of their protection, modesty, and honor, just as he caused the first couple to lose their garments of Paradise. The verse stresses that his danger is real because he and his helpers observe people from where they cannot be perceived, so people must remain constantly vigilant, hold fast to faith, righteousness, and modesty, and seek God's refuge. Satan's guardianship extends only to those who reject faith, since by turning away from God they open themselves to his influence, whereas believers who stay mindful of God are shielded from his power.

translation: And when they commit an indecency, they say, 'We found our fathers doing it, and God has commanded us to do it.' Say, 'Indeed, God does not command indecency. Do you say about God what you do not know?'
interpretation: The verse condemns using blind imitation of ancestors and false attribution to God as excuses for wrongdoing. Those who practiced shameful acts, such as the idolaters' circumambulating the Ka'bah naked, justified them by appealing to inherited custom and then claimed divine sanction to give them legitimacy. The Qur'an refutes this on the ground that God's nature and commands are inseparable from goodness and justice, so He never enjoins what is indecent and shameful. Whatever is truly from God cannot contradict that standard. The closing rhetorical question reproaches them for the grave sin of speaking about God without knowledge, and teaches that religious claims must rest on revealed, verifiable knowledge rather than on tradition, habit, or desire.

translation: Say: My Lord has commanded justice. And set your faces upright toward Him at every place of prostration, and call upon Him, devoting religion sincerely to Him. Just as He originated you, you will return.
interpretation: The verse answers those who justify their indecencies by claiming that God commanded them. God commands only justice and moderation, never immorality. Justice means giving everything its due, above all giving God His right to be worshipped alone, then giving people their rights. Believers are told to direct themselves wholly to God in every act of worship, in every place of prostration, with their hearts and bodies turned to Him and not to idols or intermediaries. They must make their prayer and devotion purely for Him, free of show and of associating partners with Him. The closing reminder, that as God brought them into being the first time they will be returned to Him for reckoning, points to the accountability that should motivate this sincere, upright worship. Just as His power created them from nothing, He is able to resurrect them, and they will be judged by how they lived.

translation: A group He guided, and a group became deserving of misguidance. Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of God, while thinking that they are rightly guided. (Qur'an 7:30)
interpretation: The verse teaches that humanity returns to God divided into two groups: those whom God guided because they sought and followed the truth, and those who earned misguidance through their own choices. Misguidance here is a consequence of their persistent turning away from God and aligning themselves with Satan's whispers, which they treated as guidance, not an arbitrary decree. The most sobering point is their self-deception: they believe they are on the right path. This warns that sincerity of belief alone is not proof of correctness, because a person can follow falsehood, desires, or corrupt customs and still feel certain. Believers are therefore urged to measure their beliefs and conduct against God's revelation, remain humble and self-critical, and ask God constantly for guidance, rather than relying on their own confidence or on what is popular.

translation: O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.
interpretation: The verse sets out a balanced way of life in which outward and inward conduct both honor God. 'Adornment' at every place of prayer means dressing decently and cleanly, covering oneself, and approaching worship with dignity and care, which answers the pre-Islamic practice of circumambulating the Ka'ba unclothed. The permission to eat and drink affirms that God's lawful provisions are to be enjoyed rather than rejected through ascetic extremes. The prohibition of excess then sets a limit: enjoyment must not become wastefulness, gluttony, extravagance, or the crossing of lawful bounds. The closing statement that God does not love the excessive makes moderation a matter of faith and character, not just a matter of health or economics. Worship and daily needs are both to be handled with modesty, gratitude, and restraint.

translation: Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision? Say: They are for those who believe in the life of this world, and exclusively theirs on the Day of Resurrection. Thus We make the signs distinct for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse rejects the notion that religious devotion requires renouncing lawful pleasures, such as clean clothing, adornment, and wholesome food. God created these blessings for human benefit, and no one has the authority to forbid what He has made lawful. Although unbelievers also enjoy them in this world, they are a shared bounty here, whereas on the Day of Resurrection they will be purely and exclusively for the believers, free of any accountability, regret, or deprivation. The believer therefore enjoys the good things with gratitude and moderation, while the one who denies God's favor will have no share in them in the Hereafter. God clarifies His rulings in this way for people who use knowledge and reflection to distinguish true religion from man-made austerity and prohibitions.

translation: Say: My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether open or hidden, sin, unjust oppression, associating with God that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about God what you do not know.
interpretation: The verse answers those who claimed to forbid lawful things by their own invention, by showing what God has truly prohibited. These prohibitions form a moral ladder from the outward to the inward and from wrongs against people to wrongs against God. Open and secret indecencies teach that God holds accountable both public conduct and private hidden acts. Sin and unjust aggression cover wrongdoing against oneself and against others. The last two are the gravest: worshipping others beside God with no proof, and attributing to God rulings or claims one has no knowledge of. The verse thus establishes that the right to declare things lawful or forbidden belongs to God alone, and that religion must rest on revealed knowledge and not on conjecture, custom, or desire.

translation: And for every nation there is a appointed term; so when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.
interpretation: God has fixed for every community a set span of existence, determined by His knowledge and wisdom and tied to the moral course the community follows. Its rise and fall are not left to chance or to the wishes of its people. When that appointed time arrives, whether it ends in destruction for persistent wrongdoing or in the natural close of its era, nothing can postpone it even for a moment, and nothing can hasten it. The verse warns the wrongdoers who mock and demand that punishment come quickly: their delay is not a sign of escape or of weakness on God's part, but a respite within a fixed decree, and they should use it to repent and reform before the term is complete.

translation: O children of Adam, if messengers from among you come to you, relating to you My verses, then whoever fears God and reforms himself, there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: God addresses all of humanity as the descendants of Adam and tells them that guidance will keep reaching them through messengers drawn from their own kind, who are able to convey the divine message in a way people understand. The verse sets out a single condition for security: taqwa, which is conscious awareness of God that leads to avoiding what He forbids, together with islah, the active moral and spiritual reform of one's conduct. Faith is therefore not enough as a mere claim. It must be joined to a lived change that repairs one's relationship with God, with others and with oneself. Those who respond in this way are promised freedom from fear of the future, meaning the Day of Judgment and its consequences, and freedom from grief over what they have left behind, so they are given lasting inner peace in this world and the next.

translation: But those who deny Our verses and arrogantly turn away from them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the deserved punishment is not for mere error or ignorance but for a deliberate rejection of God's clear signs joined with pride. Denial of the revelation, coupled with arrogance that refuses to submit to truth because it would mean lowering oneself before God or His messengers, hardens the heart and closes the path of repentance. Such a person's entire orientation in life is set against guidance, so the Qur'an calls them 'companions of the Fire', meaning that the Fire becomes their lasting abode and defining company, just as the righteous are companions of Paradise. Their eternal stay reflects the persistence of the disbelief and arrogance in which they chose to remain until death.

translation: So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God or denies His signs? Those will receive their portion of what is decreed for them, until, when Our messengers (the angels) come to take their souls, they say, 'Where are those you used to call upon besides God?' They say, 'They have abandoned us.' And they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest wrongdoing is to attribute falsehood to God, such as claiming partners or false rulings for Him, or to reject His revelations. Such people are not stripped of worldly provision immediately; they live out the share of life, sustenance, and respite appointed for them. But this worldly allowance does not signify divine approval. When it ends and death arrives, the angels confront them with the emptiness of what they relied on. The false deities and idols they invoked are nowhere to be found and cannot help, and the wrongdoers are forced to admit their own disbelief. Thus the verse warns that worldly ease for the deniers is temporary, and that the falsehoods they trusted will fail them at the moment of greatest need.

translation: He will say: 'Enter into the Fire among nations that passed away before you, of jinn and humans. Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister nation, until, when they have all gathered together in it, the last of them will say of the first of them: Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment from the Fire.' He will say: 'For each is double, but you do not know.'
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when God tells the disbelievers among the later generations to join the earlier disbelieving communities of jinn and humankind in Hell. Instead of finding solidarity there, each community curses the one that preceded it and set the example of misguidance, since followers blame their leaders and predecessors. The later generations ask God to double the punishment of those who led them astray. God's answer shows His perfect justice: every group receives a double punishment, the leaders for their own disbelief and for misleading others, and the followers for their own disbelief and for following falsehood and imitating it without reason. The people in Hell do not realize the extent of what each group deserves or suffers. The verse warns against blind imitation and shows that shifting blame onto others will not save anyone on the Day of Judgment, because each person is responsible for their choices.

translation: And the first of them will say to the last of them: 'You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn.'
interpretation: This verse is set on the Day of Judgment, when the misguided followers who blamed their leaders ask for the leaders' punishment to be doubled. The leaders (the first) answer the followers (the last) by rejecting the claim that they hold greater guilt. They say that the followers have no advantage over them, since both groups chose disbelief freely and neither was compelled. Leaders may have invited to error, but the followers accepted the invitation by their own will, so everyone bears responsibility for their own deeds. Blaming others, or following the crowd or authority blindly, is no excuse before God, and each person receives the punishment their own earnings deserve.

translation: Indeed, those who deny Our signs and arrogantly turn away from them — the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse says that arrogant rejection of God's revelation cuts a person off from divine acceptance and from salvation. Their deeds and souls are not raised to God, and they are barred from Paradise. The image of a camel passing through the eye of a needle expresses impossibility, since a camel cannot fit through a needle's eye. Their entry into Paradise is therefore as impossible as that. The root of this fate is not simple ignorance but willful denial joined with pride, which closes the heart to truth. The closing phrase 'thus We recompense the wrongdoers' shows that this is a just and consistent divine law: the punishment matches the crime of hardened, arrogant defiance.

translation: They will have a bed of Hell beneath them, and above them coverings of fire. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse portrays punishment that surrounds the disbelievers and wrongdoers completely, from below and from above, so that there is no escape or relief from any side. The bed and covering, which in this world stand for rest and protection, become instruments of torment, a reversal of comfort that fits those who turned away from God's signs and arrogantly wronged themselves and others. The closing phrase, 'Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers,' affirms that this is not arbitrary cruelty but just recompense, in which the penalty matches the wrong. It is a warning that persistent injustice, especially rejecting truth and denying God's right, ends in consequences that engulf a person entirely.

translation: But those who believe and do righteous deeds - We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity - those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse reassures believers that the path to Paradise is not out of reach. God asks of people only what they are able to do, so faith and righteous action are measured against each person's own ability and circumstances. The parenthetical statement that no soul is burdened beyond its capacity shows that religion is built on mercy and ease, not hardship. Those who sincerely strive within their means, even if their deeds are imperfect or few, are counted among the people of Paradise and are promised everlasting life in it. Eternal reward is thus a generous result of sincere belief and effort within one's ability, not of flawless or superhuman performance.

translation: And We shall remove whatever rancor is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this; and we would never have been guided had Allah not guided us. Certainly the messengers of our Lord came with the truth." And they will be called out to: "This is the Garden, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."
interpretation: The verse describes the inner and outer perfection of the people of Paradise. Before enjoying its comforts, their hearts are purified of all resentment and ill-feeling, so that their bliss is not marred by envy or enmity, and harmony reigns among them. Their response to this honor is gratitude and humility: they attribute their salvation not to their own merit but to God's guidance and grace, acknowledging that without His guidance they would have been lost, and affirming that the prophets truly spoke the truth. Yet the announcement that they have 'inherited' Paradise 'for what they used to do' shows that human striving matters: their deeds were the means and the sign of their sincerity, while the Garden itself remains a gift from God, who granted both the guidance and the ability to act righteously.

translation: And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire: 'We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?' They will say: 'Yes.' Then an announcer will announce among them: 'The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse shows that on the Day of Judgment, God's promises and warnings are fully vindicated, leaving no room for doubt. The people of Paradise speak not out of gloating but as a declaration of certainty that the divine promise of reward was true, and they ask the people of the Fire to confirm that the warning was equally true. The admission of the people of the Fire, 'Yes,' is a forced acknowledgment of the truth they denied in the worldly life, when denial could have benefited them. The public announcement that God's curse, meaning His exclusion from mercy, is upon the wrongdoers makes clear that the punishment is a just consequence of their own injustice, particularly turning away from God's path and rejecting His message. The lesson for the believer is to take God's promise seriously now, while there is still time to act, since the reality of the Hereafter will confirm everything the revelation declared.

translation: Those who hinder people from the path of God and seek to make it crooked, and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse describes the wrongdoers as people who do more than reject faith themselves: they actively bar others from God's way and try to distort it, either by casting doubt on its teachings or by twisting its guidance to suit their desires and interests. Their root problem is denial of the Hereafter. Because they do not expect to be held accountable, they feel free to corrupt the straight path and mislead others without fear of consequences. The verse suggests that disbelief in accountability fuels both moral crookedness and the effort to obstruct others from truth, and it warns that those who spread this distortion bear responsibility for the harm done to others as well as to themselves.

translation: And between the two groups is a partition; and upon the Heights are men who recognize each one by their mark. And they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, though they long to.
interpretation: The verse describes the Day of Judgment, when a barrier separates the people of Paradise from the people of Hellfire. On the elevated place called al-A'raf stand men whose good and bad deeds are evenly balanced, so they have been neither admitted to Paradise nor cast into Hell. From this height they can see both groups and recognize each by the signs on their faces: radiance and joy for the blessed, darkness and grief for the condemned. They greet the people of Paradise with 'Peace be upon you,' and the verse says they have not yet entered but still hope, in longing and expectation, for God's mercy to admit them. The passage shows the precision of divine justice, the reality of each person's accountability, and the hope that remains in God's mercy even for those whose fate is not yet decided.

translation: And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: This verse describes the people of the Heights (A'raf), who are neither in Paradise nor in Hell. When their gaze happens to fall upon the inhabitants of the Fire, they are struck with dread and turn to God in humble supplication, asking not to be counted among the wrongdoers and share their punishment. The lesson is that even those who are spared from Hell remain in awe of God's justice and in need of His mercy, and that a believer should always keep fear and hope together, taking refuge in God from the fate of the oppressors and never feeling secure in his own deeds.

translation: And the people of the Heights will call out to men they recognize by their marks, saying: "Of what use to you was your amassing of wealth and numbers, and your arrogance?"
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the people of al-A'raf, those whose good and bad deeds are balanced and who stand on the elevated place between Paradise and Hell, will recognize the leaders of disbelief by the marks of their faces, such as blackened faces. They will rebuke them by pointing out that the wealth, followers, and power they gathered in the world, and the pride that made them reject the truth and look down on the believers, have not saved them from punishment. The verse teaches that worldly resources and arrogance bring no benefit before God, and that pride against the truth leads to ruin.

translation: Are these the ones about whom you swore that God would never touch them with mercy? [To them it is said:] Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve.
interpretation: This verse is set in the dialogue between the people of the Heights (al-A'raf) and the arrogant disbelievers who are in the Fire. The arrogant leaders used to mock the poor and humble believers, swearing that God would never grant them mercy or any standing. On the Day of Judgment, the tables are turned: the very people the arrogant despised are now honored with entry into Paradise, in complete security and joy. The verse teaches that worldly status, wealth and pride are worthless before God, that true honor lies in faith and righteousness, and that no one may presume to determine who is or is not worthy of God's mercy, since mercy belongs to God alone and He grants it to whom He wills among the sincere.

translation: And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise: 'Pour upon us some water or some of what God has provided you.' They will say: 'Indeed, God has forbidden both to the disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse portrays the reversal of worldly fortunes on the Day of Judgment. Those in the Fire, suffering unbearable thirst and hunger, humbly beg the people of Paradise, whom they may once have scorned, for even a little water or sustenance. The reply is that God has forbidden these blessings to those who rejected faith. This shows that the comforts of the Hereafter are a reward for belief and righteous conduct and are not available to those who denied God's message and mocked it, and that, once the opportunity for repentance in this life has passed, no plea or intercession can change a person's destiny. It is a warning to value faith and gratitude for God's provision now, before the time for action ends.

translation: Those who took their religion as amusement and play, and whom the life of this world deceived. So today We will forget them, just as they forgot the meeting of this their Day, and just as they used to deny Our signs.
interpretation: The verse describes people who treated faith as a trivial pastime, engaging in it casually or mockingly, or setting aside what God had made lawful and obligatory for idle diversion, while worldly comfort and success lulled them into complacency. Because they lived as though they would never be called to account, they neglected preparing for the Day of Judgment. God's 'forgetting' them does not mean that He lacks knowledge, since nothing escapes Him, but that He leaves them without mercy, relief, or care, treating them as they treated the meeting with Him. Their punishment mirrors their conduct: as they disregarded the Day and denied the signs that pointed to it, they are now disregarded. The verse warns that religion should be taken seriously and that worldly illusions must not displace remembrance of accountability.

translation: And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed on the basis of knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: God declares that the Qur'an is no random or hastily composed scripture; it is a Book whose teachings, rulings, promises, warnings, and accounts are made distinct and clear, and this clarity springs from God's perfect, all-encompassing knowledge, so it contains no ignorance, error, or contradiction. Its purpose is practical: it guides toward truth and right conduct, and it is a mercy that brings well-being in this life and the next. Yet this benefit is realized only by those who believe, since they open their hearts to it and act on it, whereas those who reject it, though it was brought to them with full clarity, are left without excuse and gain nothing from its guidance.

translation: Are they waiting for anything but its final fulfillment? On the Day its fulfillment comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: 'The messengers of our Lord did come with the truth. Are there any intercessors to intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we may act differently from what we used to do?' They have indeed lost themselves, and what they used to invent has abandoned them.
interpretation: The verse says that those who reject the Qur'an are in effect only waiting for its warnings to come true, meaning the promised reckoning, resurrection, and punishment. When that Day arrives, the reality of what the Qur'an foretold becomes plain, and those who neglected it and ignored its guidance in worldly life will admit that the messengers told the truth. Their admission comes too late. They will look for intercessors or a second chance on earth to do righteous deeds, but the time for action has passed, because this world is the place of testing and the hereafter is the place of recompense. Their loss is total: they have ruined their own souls by wasting them in disbelief, and the false gods, false hopes, and fabricated claims they relied on will vanish and be of no help to them.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne. He covers the day with the night, which pursues it rapidly; and the sun, the moon and the stars are subjected by His command. Indeed, His is the creation and the command. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse grounds the Lord's exclusive right to worship in His exclusive power to create and govern. The One who brought the heavens and earth into being in measured stages, who sustains the ceaseless alternation of night and day, and who keeps the sun, moon and stars obedient to His command is the only One worthy of devotion and supplication. Everything in the cosmos functions as a subservient instrument with no independent authority, so nothing in it can rightly be taken as a partner to God. By stating that both 'creation' (khalq) and 'command' (amr) belong to Him, the verse teaches that He alone brings things into existence and He alone legislates and directs their course, in the natural order and in religious law. The fitting human response is submission, gratitude and reverence, and the closing praise, 'Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds', affirms His abounding greatness, goodness and lordship over all that exists.

translation: Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse teaches the proper manner of prayer: supplication should come from real humility and inner need, and be made quietly and sincerely, free from showing off and from a loud, theatrical display. Quiet prayer reflects certainty that God hears everything, even whispers, and it protects the heart from pride and the wish for people's praise. The warning against transgression ('al-mu'tadin') covers overstepping the proper bounds in supplication, such as shouting, asking for what is sinful or impossible, or presuming on God. It also covers going beyond limits more broadly. Prayer is thus a relationship of humble, sincere servanthood, not an act of entitlement or public performance.

translation: And do not spread corruption upon the earth after it has been set in order, and call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of God is near to those who do good.
interpretation: The verse commands people not to ruin the earth, whether through idolatry, injustice, bloodshed, or the destruction of what is good in it, after God has set it right by sending prophets, revealing guidance, and establishing natural and moral order. It then directs believers to pray to God with a balanced heart: fearing His punishment and the consequences of their shortcomings, while hoping for His mercy and acceptance. Finally, it assures them that God's mercy is close to the muhsinin, those who do good and excel in worship and conduct. In other words, such people, who avoid corruption and worship sincerely, are the ones most deserving of God's nearness and compassion.

translation: It is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they have carried heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, send down water upon it, and bring forth with it every kind of fruit. Likewise We shall bring forth the dead, so that you may remember.
interpretation: The verse points to the natural cycle of rain and revival as a sign of God's power and mercy. The winds that herald rain and move the heavy clouds to barren land show that life-giving provision is directed by God's will and not by chance. Just as He revives lifeless earth and brings forth all kinds of fruit from it, He is able to raise the dead on the Day of Resurrection. The visible, repeated renewal of the earth is meant as a reminder, so that people reflect and do not deny the resurrection, recognizing that the One who brings life to dead land can bring life to the dead.

translation: And the good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord, but that which is bad produces nothing except with difficulty. Thus do We diversify the signs for a people who are grateful.
interpretation: The verse is a parable that follows the image of rain in the preceding verses. The same revelation, like the same rain, falls on different hearts and yields different results. A receptive, pure heart takes in the guidance and bears abundant fruit in faith, good character, and righteous deeds, all by God's enabling permission. A heart corrupted by arrogance, stubbornness, or love of falsehood gains little from the same guidance. What it produces is meager, tainted, and given grudgingly. The difference lies in the condition of the receiver, not in any deficiency in the message. God diversifies His signs with examples like this for the grateful, those who recognize the blessing of guidance, appreciate it, and put it to use, so that they may examine their own hearts and cultivate them to receive the truth.

translation: We sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous Day."
interpretation: The verse presents the core message shared by all prophets: pure monotheism is the foundation of faith, and everything else follows from it. Noah's address, "O my people," shows he spoke out of kinship and sincere concern, not hostility. His warning is the caring alarm of someone who foresees real danger, not a threat made out of spite. The "tremendous Day" points to accountability, whether the coming flood in this world or the Day of Judgment, and it makes clear that rejecting God's oneness carries grave consequences. The call to worship God alone is thus joined to a moral urgency: people are answerable for how they respond to revelation.

translation: The chiefs of his people said: "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:60, in the account of Noah) shows the typical reaction of the arrogant elite to a prophet's call to monotheism. The leaders, whose status and wealth rested on the existing social and religious order, could not bring themselves to examine his message on its merits. They answered with accusation, calling him astray, and judged him by their own customs and standards. The Qur'an presents this as a recurring pattern: those with power and privilege are often the first to reject reform, and they treat the truth as error because it threatens their position. The verse also consoles the Prophet Muhammad and later believers that being slandered and dismissed by the dominant majority does not mean one is wrong. The one who is truly in manifest error is the one who rejects clear guidance out of pride.

translation: He said: "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This is the Prophet Nuh's (Noah's) calm reply when his people accused him of being clearly astray (verse 7:60). He does not answer insult with insult but gently addresses them as 'my people', showing his care for them. He denies the charge of misguidance and explains the true source of his message: it is not his own invention or confusion but a revelation from God, the Lord of all the worlds. The verse teaches that a true caller to God responds to slander with gentleness and clarity, and that the authority of the message lies in its divine origin rather than in the status of the messenger. Describing God as Lord of all the worlds also reminds the people that the One who sent him is their own Sustainer too, so he has the right to guide them.

translation: I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I give you sincere advice, and I know from God what you do not know.
interpretation: In this verse, Prophet Noah (Nuh) describes the three marks of a true messenger when answering his people who accused him of being astray: he faithfully delivers the revelation without altering or withholding anything, he wishes good for his people and offers advice free of any self-interest, and he has knowledge granted by God, namely the truth about God's power, His reckoning, and His punishment, which his people lacked because of their heedlessness. The verse teaches that a prophet's authority rests not on personal opinion but on trustworthy transmission of divine knowledge, and that sincere counsel and honest delivery of the message are the basis of any call to God.

translation: Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among yourselves, to warn you, that you may be mindful of God, and so that you may receive mercy?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who found it strange that revelation should come through a human being like themselves. It argues that this is the wisest and most merciful way to guide people: a messenger from their own community speaks their language, shares their condition, and sets a practical example they can follow, which an angel or a being of another kind could not do. The warning he brings is meant to awaken people to the consequences of their conduct. That awareness leads to God-consciousness (taqwa), and God-consciousness opens the way to His mercy. So the messenger's humanity is no ground for rejecting him. It is part of God's kindness and of the purpose of guidance.

translation: But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 7:64) shows that rejecting a prophet after clear warning leads to a just end, while faith and obedience bring deliverance. Nuh's people did not lack evidence; they refused to accept it. Calling them 'a blind people' means their blindness was of the heart and insight, not of the eyes. They saw the signs of God in creation and in the message of His messenger but would not perceive their meaning, so they were deaf to guidance out of stubbornness and arrogance. The ark was a mercy for the believers, and the flood was a consequence for those who hardened themselves against the truth. The lesson is that spiritual blindness is a self-inflicted condition that leads to ruin, and that salvation lies with those who heed God's signs and stay with His messenger.

translation: And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, 'O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then be mindful of Him?'
interpretation: The verse shows that every prophet was sent from within his own people, as 'their brother,' so the message came from someone whose honesty and lineage they already knew, which removes any excuse for rejecting him as a stranger. Hud's call opens with the same essential message given to all prophets: pure monotheism, worship of God alone, as the basis of a sound life and society. His closing question, 'Will you not then be mindful?', is a gentle rebuke that appeals to reason and conscience. It suggests that fear of God and awareness of His power, which should be natural to people who have been given strength and blessings, is the logical response to recognizing that nothing else deserves worship.

translation: The chiefs of his people who disbelieved said: "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed, we think you are among the liars." (Qur'an 7:66, concerning the people of Hud)
interpretation: The verse shows how the arrogant elites, comfortable in their power and status, respond to a prophetic call to truth: instead of weighing the message, they attack the messenger's character. By calling Hud foolish and a liar, they label as irrational anyone who departs from the established order and ancestral custom. Their accusation reveals that their rejection stems from pride and the fear of losing their position rather than from evidence. The verse also consoles believers who face ridicule and slander for calling to monotheism, showing that such insults are the age-old response of those who refuse to submit, and it invites them to answer with patience and gentleness, as Hud does in the following verse when he replies, 'O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.'

translation: He said: 'O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse records the Prophet Hud's calm reply (Qur'an 7:67) after his people accused him of foolishness for calling them away from idol worship. He does not answer insult with insult, but gently denies the charge and addresses them as 'my people' to show his concern for them. He bases his claim not on personal wisdom or ambition but on his role as a messenger sent by God, the Lord of all the worlds. The lesson is that those who call to truth should respond to slander with composure and kindness, and should make clear that their message comes from divine authority rather than from themselves. Calling God 'Lord of the worlds' also implies that He is the Lord of everyone, including those who reject the message, so His guidance is for all.

translation: I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am to you a trustworthy adviser.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Hud to his people (Qur'an 7:68), presents the two qualities that make a messenger credible: faithfulness in delivering what God has revealed, without addition, omission, or distortion, and sincere, selfless concern for the good of those addressed. The word 'amin' (trustworthy) indicates that his advice is not driven by personal gain, pride, or hidden motives, and that his people had known him as reliable. The lesson is that true guidance joins truthfulness to the source with sincerity toward the audience, so that those who call others to God must be both honest conveyors of the message and caring, trustworthy counselors.

translation: Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among yourselves, to warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you in stature. So remember the favors of God, that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse is the prophet Hud's reply to his people, 'Ad, who found it strange that revelation would come through a mortal like themselves. Hud tells them there is nothing odd in it: God's guidance naturally reaches people through one of their own, who speaks their language, understands their situation, and can serve as a living example. Their astonishment reflects pride, not reason. He then reminds them of their blessings: God let them inherit the earth after Noah's people were destroyed, which should warn them that nations who deny the truth can be replaced, and He gave them exceptional physical strength and stature. These gifts are meant to prompt gratitude and humility, not arrogance. Remembering God's favors means acknowledging their Giver, obeying Him, and heeding His messenger. The verse teaches that true success (falah) comes from gratitude and obedience, while forgetting God's blessings and rejecting His warning leads to ruin.

translation: They said: "Have you come to us so that we worship God alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."
interpretation: The people of 'Ad answer the Prophet Hud's call to pure monotheism with stubborn attachment to ancestral custom. They treat inherited tradition as a binding authority above revelation and reason, and regard giving up their forefathers' idols as unthinkable. Their demand that Hud bring the promised punishment shows mockery and arrogance: they do not take the warning seriously and think it empty. The verse shows how blind imitation of ancestors and contempt for warnings harden hearts against the truth and invite divine judgment.

translation: He said: "Defilement and wrath from your Lord have already fallen upon you. Do you dispute with me about names that you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority? So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."
interpretation: This verse records the Prophet Hud's reply to his people, the 'Ad, when they rejected his call to worship God alone and clung to the worship of their ancestral idols. He tells them that by persisting in disbelief they have already earned God's displeasure: 'rijs' is the spiritual filth and hardening of the heart that comes with shirk, and 'ghadab' is the divine anger that follows it. He then exposes the emptiness of their idols: they are merely names that the people and their forefathers invented, with no reality of divinity behind them and no revelation or proof from God to justify them. Worship grounded only in inherited custom and human invention carries no authority. Hud ends by telling them to wait for God's judgment, while he too waits, confident in God's promise. The verse teaches that true religion requires divine authority and evidence, not tradition or whim, and that clinging to falsehood after the truth has been made clear brings God's punishment, while the believer waits with trust in God's decree.

translation: So We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the roots of those who denied Our signs; and they were not believers.
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:72, about Prophet Hud and the people of 'Ad) shows that deliverance comes only through God's mercy, not through the strength or planning of the believers. Hud and his followers were rescued because God willed it out of grace. Their opponents, who rejected clear signs out of arrogance, were utterly uprooted, so that no trace of their line remained. The phrase 'they were not believers' explains the cause: their destruction was the consequence of persistent denial and their refusal to accept guidance after the truth had been made clear. The lesson is that faith and obedience lead to God's protection, while stubborn rejection of His signs ends in ruin.

translation: And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord. This is the she-camel of God, a sign for you. So leave her to graze in God's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you."
interpretation: The verse shows that every prophet brings the same core message of pure monotheism, and that this call is backed by clear evidence, not mere claims. The she-camel was a tangible sign from God that tested Thamud's sincerity: by calling her "God's she-camel" and the land "God's earth," the verse reminds people that all provision and ownership belong to God and that they are only stewards. Leaving her to graze freely meant respecting God's sign and the rights He has set, while harming her would be an act of defiance against God Himself. Hence the warning that rejecting a clear sign and violating its sanctity brings a painful punishment, showing that arrogance after receiving clear proof leads to ruin.

translation: And remember when He made you successors after the 'Aad and settled you in the land: you build palaces on its plains and carve homes out of the mountains. So remember the favours of Allah, and do not commit evil in the land, spreading corruption.
interpretation: Prophet Salih reminds the people of Thamud that their power, security and skill were gifts from God, who gave them the earth after the destroyed people of 'Aad. Their ability to build lavish palaces in the lowlands and carve dwellings from the mountains was a blessing and not a sign of self-sufficiency. The proper response is gratitude, which means remembering the Giver, acknowledging His favours, and using them responsibly. Ingratitude, arrogance and corruption, such as oppression, idolatry and wrongdoing, would repeat the fate of 'Aad. The verse teaches that worldly strength and prosperity are a trust and a test, and that remembering past nations' fate should restrain people from spreading corruption.

translation: The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said to those who were considered weak, to those among them who believed: "Do you know that Salih has been sent by his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with." (Qur'an 7:75)
interpretation: The verse shows the contrast between the arrogant elite of Thamud and the believers they looked down upon. The elite's question is mocking and rhetorical: they pose it as though the prophethood of Salih were doubtful, hoping to shake the faith of the believers through ridicule and social pressure. The believers answer calmly and with certainty, affirming not only Salih himself but the message he brought. Their reply shows that true faith is not measured by wealth, rank, or status, and that those whom society counts as weak are often the most receptive to truth, because arrogance blocks the hearts of the powerful from accepting guidance. It also teaches that believers should respond to scorn with firm, dignified confidence in what God has revealed rather than with defensiveness.

translation: Those who were arrogant said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed."
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 7:76) shows that arrogance is a barrier to accepting truth. The elite of Thamud, intoxicated by their power and status, did not reject Prophet Salih's message because of any lack of evidence, as the miracle of the she-camel was clear before them. They rejected it because accepting it would mean submitting to God and standing level with the people they looked down upon. Their wording, 'in that which you have believed', is a way of scorning the believers and avoiding any acknowledgment of Salih's prophethood. It teaches that pride in worldly rank leads people to deny clear truth and to mock those who follow it, and that such denial is often a refusal of humility rather than an honest intellectual doubt.

translation: So they hamstrung the she-camel and rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said, 'O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are truly one of the messengers.'
interpretation: The verse shows how persistent denial hardens into open defiance. The people of Thamud first rejected Salih's warning, then killed the camel, which was a sign sent by God and carried a clear command: let her graze and drink on her day, and do not harm her. By killing her they did more than commit an act of cruelty. They openly defied God's order and showed contempt for the proof that had been given to them. Their challenge to Salih, 'bring us what you threaten us with', reveals a false confidence: they treated God's patience as weakness and divine warnings as empty words. The verse teaches that arrogance and mockery of revealed warnings, together with a refusal to heed clear signs, bring on deserved punishment. It also warns that God's delay in punishing is a respite and not a sign of approval, and that a challenge to a messenger is a challenge to the One who sent him.

translation: Then the earthquake seized them, and by morning they were lying prostrate, lifeless, in their homes.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment comes suddenly and decisively to those who persistently reject the truth and defy God's messengers. The people, confident in their strength and in their homes, were destroyed in a single moment, and the very places in which they felt secure became their graves. This teaches that worldly power, comfort and status give no protection from God's decree once His warning has been scorned, and it calls the listener to heed the message of the prophets, show humility, and learn from the fate of earlier nations before it is too late.

translation: So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you, but you do not like advisors."
interpretation: After the people of Salih were seized by the earthquake and left lifeless in their homes, he turned away from them, speaking to them in grief and as a final reproach. He affirms that he fulfilled his duty completely by delivering God's message and sincerely wishing them good, so no blame rests on him. The real cause of their ruin was their own nature: arrogance and attachment to desire made them dislike anyone who honestly warned them, so they rejected sincere counsel until it was too late. The verse teaches that a sincere advisor's responsibility ends with conveying the truth, and that rejecting good advice because it is unwelcome leads to destruction.

translation: And [We sent] Lot, when he said to his people: "Do you commit such an immorality as none among the nations has committed before you?"
interpretation: The verse presents Lot's rebuke of his people for a deviant sexual practice that they themselves invented, since no community before them had done it. The prophet's question is one of reproach, not of seeking information. It stresses that the act is a grave moral transgression against natural disposition (fitra), and that the greater guilt lies in originating a new form of corruption and establishing it as a social norm. The verse teaches that moral decline is a deliberate departure from the innate order God set for human beings, and that prophets are sent to call communities back from such departures, even when those communities have grown accustomed to them.

translation: Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a transgressing people.
interpretation: The verse is the prophet Lot's rebuke of his people for abandoning the natural, lawful relationship that God ordained between men and women and turning to lust-driven acts with men. The Qur'an calls this 'musrifun' (transgressors), meaning they exceeded the bounds of fitrah (innate human nature) and divine limits. Their wrongdoing was not a matter of a single act but a pattern of excess in which appetite overruled both reason and revelation. The verse teaches that human desire must be channeled within the boundaries God has set, and that crossing them corrupts both the individual and society.

translation: And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."
interpretation: When Prophet Lot called his people away from their indecent acts, they offered no argument or rebuttal, because they had none. They simply resorted to threatening to banish him and his family. Their reason for expelling them was that these people 'keep themselves pure,' meaning they avoid the filth of the people's sexual immorality. This is said in mockery and scorn, but it unintentionally reveals the truth: purity had become a crime in their society, and wrongdoers cannot tolerate the presence of those who refuse to share their corruption. The verse teaches that when falsehood loses in reason, it turns to force and exclusion, and that the righteous may be resented simply for being clean when those around them are not.

translation: So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who stayed behind.
interpretation: The verse shows that salvation depends on a person's own faith and deeds, not on kinship or closeness to a prophet. Lot's wife lived in his household and was married to a messenger, yet she sided with the wrongdoing of her people and did not share her husband's belief, so she was left behind to be destroyed with them. Divine rescue is granted to the righteous who obey God, while ties of blood or marriage give no protection to those who reject Him or secretly support evildoers.

translation: And We rained upon them a rain [of stones]. So see how was the end of the criminals.
interpretation: The verse refers to the destruction of the people of Lot, upon whom God sent a rain of baked clay stones as punishment for their persistent immorality and their rejection of their prophet. The rain is described in its terrible, unusual form, unlike the life-giving rain that brings mercy, to show how God can turn what is normally a blessing into a means of ruin for those who transgress. The command to 'see how was the end' invites every listener to reflect on history and take a lesson: those who persist in wrongdoing, corrupt the natural order, and spurn the warnings of God's messengers will not escape His justice, and their end is ruin and disgrace, while the message of the prophets remains a warning to later generations.

translation: And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord. So give full measure and weight, do not deprive people of their due, and do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set right. That is better for you, if you are believers."
interpretation: Shu'ayb's message joins faith to ethics: worshipping God alone is inseparable from honesty and justice in everyday dealings. Fair weights and measures, and not cheating people of what is theirs, are treated as acts of devotion, not merely social courtesies. Corruption in the land after God has set it right, through revealed guidance and the moral order the prophets established, includes economic injustice and fraud that erode trust and harm society. Shu'ayb says that living righteously in trade and public life is better for the people, in this world and the next, and is a mark of true belief.

translation: And do not sit on every path threatening, and barring from the way of God those who believe in Him, and seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He multiplied you. And see how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: This is part of Prophet Shu'ayb's admonition to the people of Madyan. He forbids them from lying in wait along roads and public routes to intimidate people, to obstruct those wishing to follow the path of God and join the believers, and to distort that path by casting doubt and slandering it so that it appears crooked. The ban on such conduct is joined to a call to gratitude: they should remember that God increased their numbers from a small group, so their growth is a blessing that demands righteousness rather than oppression. He then warns them to reflect on the fate of earlier corrupters, who were destroyed, implying that obstructing faith and spreading injustice brings ruin, while the blessings of numbers and strength give no immunity from God's justice.

translation: And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent, and a group who have not believed, then be patient until God judges between us, and He is the best of judges.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Shu'ayb to his people of Madyan, teaches that when a community divides over the truth of the message, believers and deniers alike should neither resort to violence nor despair, but wait patiently for God's decisive judgment. Patience here is active steadfastness: the believers hold firm to their faith and the deniers are warned that the matter will not remain unresolved. God's judgment will be perfectly just, vindicating the truthful and exposing the false, because no judge is more knowing, more fair, or more able to enforce the verdict than He.

translation: The chiefs of his people, who were arrogant, said: "We will surely drive you out of our town, O Shu'ayb, you and those who believe with you, unless you return to our faith." He said: "Even if we are unwilling?"
interpretation: The verse shows the typical response of entrenched, arrogant power to a message of truth: when the elite cannot refute the argument, they resort to threats and coercion, offering the believers only exile or the abandonment of their faith. Shu'ayb's reply, a rhetorical question, exposes the injustice and absurdity of forcing belief, since faith is a matter of conviction of the heart and cannot be imposed on someone who despises the falsehood being demanded of him. It teaches that true religion cannot be coerced, and that believers should remain steadfast under pressure, refusing to trade their convictions for security or belonging.

translation: We would have invented a lie against God if we returned to your creed after God has saved us from it. It is not for us to return to it unless God, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In God we have put our trust. Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of those who judge.
interpretation: This verse records the reply of Shu'ayb and his followers when the arrogant leaders of Madyan threatened to expel them or force them back into the old religion of idolatry and corrupt dealings. They say that going back to disbelief after God has rescued them from it would amount to slandering God, as though the falsehood they left had been true and their faith false. Yet their firmness is joined with humility: they do not rely on their own strength, and they acknowledge that nothing happens apart from God's will, so they place their steadfastness under His will and ask Him to keep them firm. They affirm that His knowledge covers everything, including their hearts, their future, and the real state of their people, and so they entrust their affairs to Him. Their closing prayer asks God to decide between the believers and the rejecters with truth, openly vindicating the right and exposing the wrong. The lesson is that a believer should hold fast to faith under pressure, never attribute his steadfastness to himself, depend on God alone, and leave the final judgment to the best of judges.

translation: The chiefs of his people who disbelieved said, "If you follow Shu'ayb, then surely you will be losers."
interpretation: The verse shows how the elite of Madyan tried to protect their power and wealth by frightening ordinary people away from the Prophet Shu'ayb's message. Because he called for honest measures and weights and for justice in trade, the leaders saw his teaching as a threat to their unfair gains. They therefore described obedience to him as 'loss,' meaning loss of profit, status and advantage. The Qur'an presents this as a pattern of the people of falsehood: they measure gain and loss only by worldly benefit, while true loss lies in rejecting guidance and the ruin that follows it. The warning they used against others became their own fate, for the destruction came upon them and they were the real losers.

translation: Then the earthquake seized them, and morning found them lying prostrate, lifeless, in their homes.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment comes suddenly and decisively to peoples who persistently reject God's message and its messengers after clear warning has been given. Their strength, their settled homes, and their sense of security offered no protection. The image of them lying motionless in their own dwellings stresses how complete and abrupt their end was: the places in which they felt safest became their graves. For the reader, it is a warning against arrogance and obstinate denial of truth, and a reminder that worldly power and stability depend wholly on God's will.

translation: Those who denied Shu'ayb became as though they had never prospered in their dwellings. Those who denied Shu'ayb were the ones who were the losers.
interpretation: The verse shows that worldly power and comfort mean nothing once God's judgment arrives. The people of Madyan had mocked Shu'ayb and threatened him and his followers with expulsion, believing they were secure and that they were the winners. Yet when the punishment seized them, they were wiped out so completely that no trace of their prosperity or presence remained, as though they had never lived there. The repetition of 'those who denied Shu'ayb' reverses their boast. They had said that those who followed Shu'ayb would be the losers, but in the end the deniers were the real losers, because they lost both this world and the next. True success lies in faith and obedience to God's messengers, not in wealth, numbers or status.

translation: So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you sincerely. So how could I grieve over a disbelieving people?"
interpretation: After the punishment struck the people of Shu'ayb (in the context of Surah al-A'raf, the people of Madyan), the Prophet turned away from their ruins, addressing them as a way of reproach and an expression of his own acquittal rather than as hope of a reply. His words teach that a messenger's duty is fully discharged through clear delivery and sincere counsel, and that the outcome rests with God. Natural human sorrow at the destruction of one's people is checked by the awareness that they were given every chance and knowingly rejected the truth; thus grief is not warranted for those who persisted in disbelief after full warning. The believer is thereby consoled: once he has done his part with sincerity, he is free of responsibility and should not be consumed by sorrow over those who chose their own ruin.

translation: And We did not send a prophet to any town except that We afflicted its people with hardship and adversity, so that they might humble themselves and turn to Allah in supplication.
interpretation: This verse shows a divine pattern: when a prophet came to a community, God often tested its people with poverty, hunger, sickness, and loss. The hardships were not meant as mere punishment but as a merciful means of awakening. Hardship breaks arrogance and heedlessness, and a heart softened by suffering is more ready to hear the prophetic message, acknowledge its dependence on God, and turn to Him in humility and supplication. The verse teaches that trials can be an invitation to return to God, and that the real failure lies in not letting them soften the heart.

translation: Then We replaced the bad condition with good, until they flourished and multiplied and said, 'Hardship and ease also touched our forefathers.' So We seized them suddenly, while they were unaware.
interpretation: After testing a people with hardship to awaken them, God gives them prosperity in place of it, yet instead of recognizing the favor and turning to Him in gratitude, they treat both good and bad times as ordinary cycles of fate that befell their ancestors as well. This reading strips events of any moral meaning and fosters heedlessness: they see neither a warning in adversity nor a blessing in ease. Their complacency is then met with a sudden punishment, showing that ease can itself be a trial and that persistent neglect of divine signs invites a catastrophe that arrives with no warning.

translation: If only the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened up for them blessings from heaven and earth. But they denied the truth, so We seized them for what they used to earn.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith joined with God-consciousness is the root of true prosperity and security, while rejecting the message brings ruin. Belief (iman) and piety (taqwa) are not obstacles to well-being; they are the means by which God opens the doors of abundance, such as rain from the sky and fertility, provision and stability from the earth. The blessings are also not only material; they include peace, contentment and lasting benefit that grow in what one has. The earlier communities were destroyed not by arbitrary punishment but as the consequence of their own deeds: their denial of the messengers and the injustice and corruption that followed from it. So the verse calls every society to recognize that its moral and spiritual condition is tied to its fortunes, and that turning back to faith and righteousness is the path to goodness, while persistent denial leads to the seizing that people bring upon themselves.

translation: Do the people of the towns then feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke of heedlessness. God's punishment can strike at the moment people are least prepared and least expecting it, in the stillness of night when they are asleep, so they have no chance to flee or defend themselves. Having recounted how earlier communities were destroyed after they rejected the messengers, the Qur'an asks the people of the present towns whether they imagine they are exempt from the same fate. The question is meant to shake false security, which is born of worldly comfort and forgetfulness of God, and to move people to repentance, faith, and righteous action before the punishment comes suddenly and cannot be averted.

translation: Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are playing?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke to heedless people who, because of their comfort and distraction with worldly amusements, imagine that God's punishment cannot reach them. It teaches that divine punishment can strike suddenly, at the very time people feel safest and are most absorbed in frivolity, with no warning that they can prepare for. The mention of the forenoon, a time of daylight, activity, and ease, stresses that nothing guarantees safety except faith and obedience. True security comes from piety, awareness of accountability, and humility before God, while false security leads to negligence of His commands and to destruction.

translation: Do they then feel secure from the plan of God? None feels secure from the plan of God except the people who are losers.
interpretation: The verse warns against complacent false security in the face of God's hidden, just response to wrongdoing. God's 'plan' (makr) refers to His unseen way of dealing with those who persist in sin and heedlessness, whereby He may give them respite and blessings while they drift toward their own ruin, then seize them when they least expect it. A true believer lives between fear and hope, never assuming that outward comfort means divine approval or that they are immune from accountability. Only those who have squandered their spiritual capital, the 'losers,' can feel entirely safe from God's reckoning, because their arrogance and neglect have blinded them to the consequences of their deeds.

translation: Is it not clear to those who inherit the land after its former people that, if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins, and seal up their hearts so that they do not hear?
interpretation: The verse addresses those who succeed earlier generations in the land and warns them that the destruction of previous peoples is a lesson, not a mere historical fact. The same God who punished the earlier nations for their sins can punish their successors, so their possession of the land is no proof of divine favor or security. It also describes a spiritual consequence: persistent sin and heedlessness harden the heart until it is sealed, and a person loses the ability to listen to guidance and benefit from admonition. The point is that learning from the fate of past peoples is a mercy, and ignoring it leads to the worse punishment of a heart closed to truth.

translation: Those are the towns whose accounts We relate to you. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they would not believe in what they had denied before. Thus does God seal the hearts of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent rejection of the truth hardens the heart until it can no longer accept guidance. The earlier peoples, such as those of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb, were not lacking evidence: their messengers brought clear signs. Yet because they had first denied the truth out of stubbornness and habit, that denial became fixed in them, and even clear proofs could not move them to faith. The 'sealing' by God is a just consequence of their own choices, not an arbitrary act. When a person repeatedly turns away from the truth, God lets the heart become closed to it. The stories are told to the Prophet to console him and to warn his hearers to heed the signs before their hearts harden in the same way.

translation: And We did not find in most of them any covenant; rather, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 7:102) describes earlier nations who were warned by their messengers yet persisted in denial. It explains that most of them had no loyalty to any pledge, whether the natural covenant of recognizing God's lordship that is rooted in human nature, or the commitments they made to their prophets and to one another. Because they broke their word and turned away from the truth after clear proofs came to them, they were not merely mistaken but had stepped outside the bounds of obedience to God. The lesson is that faithfulness to one's covenant with God and with people is a mark of true faith, while breaking it leads to moral corruption and ultimately to ruin.

translation: Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wronged them (by rejecting them). So see how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: After the earlier messengers and their destroyed peoples, God sent Moses with clear miracles to Pharaoh and his ruling elite. Though the signs were manifest proofs of truth, they treated them unjustly by denying them out of arrogance and obstinacy, even though their hearts were convinced of their truth. The verse invites the listener to reflect on the outcome of those who spread corruption through disbelief, oppression, and rejection of divine guidance: they were destroyed by drowning in the sea. It is both a warning to those who persist in arrogance and denial and a consolation to believers that falsehood and tyranny, however powerful, end in ruin while truth prevails.

translation: And Moses said: "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: Moses opens his address to Pharaoh by declaring the source of his authority, not himself or his people, but the Lord of all the worlds. By describing God as Lord of all creation, he implicitly challenges Pharaoh's claim to supreme lordship, since a ruler of one land is only a created being under the sovereignty of the One who sustains every realm. The statement is calm and direct, showing that a prophet's mission rests on delivering a divine message, not on personal ambition, and that true authority belongs to God alone. It also frames the confrontation correctly from the start: the dispute is not political rivalry but a summons to acknowledge God's universal lordship and to submit to His command.

translation: It is only right that I say nothing about God except the truth. I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord, so let the Children of Israel go with me.
interpretation: Moses tells Pharaoh and his court that his role as a messenger binds him to absolute truthfulness about God: he cannot attribute to God any claim, command, or message that is not true. Because he speaks only the truth, his demand is not a personal or political ambition but a divine command, backed by clear signs (the staff and the shining hand) that prove his mission. On that basis, he asks for the oppressed Children of Israel to be freed from bondage and allowed to leave with him, showing that true prophethood joins integrity in conveying God's word with a call for justice and the liberation of the oppressed.

translation: He said, 'If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you are among the truthful.'
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's reply to Moses (Qur'an 7:106) after Moses declared himself a messenger from the Lord of the worlds and asked that the Children of Israel be let go with him. Pharaoh does not engage with the message itself. He shifts the discussion to a demand for proof and challenges Moses to show a miracle, which presents him as a ruler who wants evidence while he actually expects Moses to fail. The verse shows how arrogant power responds to a call to truth: by putting the burden of proof on the messenger and doubting his sincerity ('if you are among the truthful'). It also sets up the miracles that follow, the staff turning into a serpent and the shining hand, which God gives as clear signs to establish His messenger's truthfulness and to leave the deniers without excuse.

translation: So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clear, manifest serpent.
interpretation: This verse presents the miracle given to Moses (peace be upon him) as a clear, undeniable sign of God's power and of the truth of his prophethood before Pharaoh. The staff, an ordinary object, became a real, visible serpent, not a trick or illusion, and this shows that God can change created things at will and that He supports His messengers with signs that human power and sorcery cannot imitate. The word 'mubin' (manifest) stresses that the sign was evident and left no room for doubt, so that rejecting it could come only from arrogance and stubbornness, not from lack of proof.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the beholders.
interpretation: This verse describes the second sign given to Moses (peace be upon him) to show Pharaoh and his court. His hand, ordinarily of a brownish complexion, became radiantly white when drawn out from his garment, not from leprosy or disease, but as a luminous miracle that was plain to everyone who watched. The phrase 'for the beholders' stresses that the sign was public, visible and undeniable, leaving no room for claiming it was an illusion or private delusion.
