It served as divine proof of the authenticity of Moses's prophethood and of God's power to alter created things as He wills, so that those who saw it would have no excuse to reject the message.

translation: The chiefs among Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a knowledgeable sorcerer."
interpretation: When Moses showed the signs of his prophethood, the ruling elite did not engage with the truth of the message. Instead they dismissed it by labeling him a skilled magician, a charge meant to protect their own authority and to keep the common people from believing him. By describing him as 'knowledgeable' in sorcery, they conceded that what he did was extraordinary, yet attributed it to trickery and learned craft rather than to divine power. The verse shows a recurring pattern in the history of prophets: those who hold power and status often meet clear evidence with slander and with fear of losing their influence, and they steer public opinion by discrediting the messenger rather than examining the message.

translation: He wants to drive you out of your land by his magic, so what do you advise?
interpretation: This verse is the speech of Pharaoh's chiefs, as reported in Surat al-A'raf (7:110) and Surat ash-Shu'ara (26:35), about Moses. After seeing the signs Moses brought, they could not refute them, so they accused him of being a sorcerer. They then claimed his real aim was political: to expel the Egyptians from their own land and take power. The accusation turns a message of faith into a supposed threat to the people's homeland and interests, which is a common way for entrenched elites to rouse fear and resistance against a prophet. Pharaoh then asks his council 'what do you advise?', which shows that despite his claim to be a lord, he needed counsel, and that the ruling circle was deciding how to oppose the truth by plotting and gathering sorcerers instead of reflecting on the signs.

translation: They said: "Put him and his brother off for a while, and send summoners into the cities to gather [the magicians]."
interpretation: After Moses showed his signs, Pharaoh's chiefs advised against acting hastily or violently against him and Aaron, and urged a delay while they gathered the best magicians from across the land to confront him. The verse shows how tyrannical power answers a clear sign with political maneuvering and the mobilization of human skill, not with reflection on the truth. It also shows their confidence that Moses' miracle was only sorcery that other sorcery could defeat, and that numbers and expertise could extinguish a divine message. The very plan they devised to discredit Moses became the setting in which God's truth was made manifest, since the magicians' defeat later exposed the difference between trickery and a true miracle.

translation: They will bring to you every skilled, knowledgeable magician.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:37) records the counsel of Pharaoh's courtiers after Moses showed his signs. Rather than weigh the message, they proposed to meet it with Egypt's most expert sorcerers, assuming that what Moses did was only magic and could be matched or surpassed by greater skill. The word 'alim' (knowledgeable) shows they wanted the most masterful practitioners available. The verse thus shows how a tyrannical establishment responds to divine truth: it gathers worldly expertise and spectacle to discredit the prophet. In the Qur'an's account this backfires, since the magicians' recognition that Moses's miracle was beyond sorcery becomes the proof of its divine origin, and they believe.

translation: And the magicians came to Pharaoh. They said, "Will we indeed have a reward if we are the victors?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the worldly motive of those who stand against truth: the magicians, hired to confront Moses, think first of payment and status rather than of right or wrong. Their question to Pharaoh shows that falsehood relies on material incentives and the favor of rulers. It sets up the contrast with their later transformation, when they encounter the clear sign of God and abandon reward and fear of Pharaoh to submit in faith, showing that sincere recognition of truth can overcome even entrenched worldly interests.

translation: He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:42, Surat al-Shu'ara') records Pharaoh's reply to the magicians after they asked whether they would receive a reward if they defeated Moses. He promises them both material reward and elevated status as members of his inner circle. The verse shows how tyrants lure people with worldly favor, wealth, and proximity to power in order to secure their loyalty against the truth. The irony is that these same magicians, once the truth became clear to them, chose faith over Pharaoh's promised rewards and were brought near to God instead, which shows that real nearness lies with God and not with worldly rulers.

translation: They said, "O Moses, either you throw (your staff) first, or we will be the ones to throw."
interpretation: The sorcerers of Pharaoh offer Moses the choice of who goes first, and this shows how confident they were in their craft. They saw the encounter as a contest of skill between equals, not as a confrontation with divine truth. Their polite courtesy hides a certainty that their tricks would prevail. The verse also prepares for the lesson that falsehood, however impressive in appearance, has no real standing against a sign from God. Moses did not need to seize the initiative. His trust in God let him allow them to begin, so that their illusions would be shown in full and then overturned, which made the truth plainer to everyone watching.

translation: He said, "You throw first." Then when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people, struck terror into them, and produced a mighty sorcery.
interpretation: Moses' permitting the magicians to go first shows his confidence in God's truth and sets up a decisive public contest. The magicians' feats were illusions that worked on perception, not real transformations: they 'bewitched the eyes' of the onlookers, who saw ropes and staffs as moving serpents. The fear they caused and the description of 'mighty sorcery' show how convincing falsehood can appear at first, which makes the truth more evident when it overcomes it. The verse teaches that the power of deception is real in its effect on people, yet it is only an appearance, and it cannot stand against a miracle that comes from God.

translation: And We inspired Moses: 'Throw down your staff,' and behold, it swallowed up all that they were falsely fabricating.
interpretation: This verse shows that Moses acted by divine revelation, not by his own cunning or skill. When he cast down his staff, God turned it into a real, living power that devoured the magicians' ropes and rods, which were only illusions and deceptions. The lesson is that falsehood, however impressive it appears, has no real substance and is overwhelmed when truth is supported by God's command. The miracle exposed the emptiness of the sorcerers' tricks and prepared the way for the truth to become manifest.

translation: So the truth was established, and what they had been doing was proven false and came to nothing.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:118) describes the moment Moses' signs overcame Pharaoh's magicians. When the staff swallowed their illusions, the truth of God's miracle showed itself as real and firmly established, while the sorcerers' tricks were exposed as empty deception with no lasting reality. The lesson is that falsehood may appear impressive for a while, but it cannot stand against truth once truth is manifest. Divine truth prevails over human trickery, and the sorcerers' own defeat led them to recognize it and submit in faith.

translation: So they were defeated right there, and they turned back humiliated.
interpretation: This verse (Al-A'raf 7:119) describes what happened to Pharaoh's magicians and his court after Moses threw down his staff and it swallowed up their illusions. The falsehood they had staged was exposed in front of the people they had gathered to witness it, so they lost the contest on the spot. The humiliation was complete: they came out of it disgraced, and their pride and power were broken. The lesson is that falsehood, however elaborate its display, cannot stand against clear truth supported by God. When truth confronts falsehood openly, falsehood is vanquished, and those who rely on arrogance and trickery end in disgrace.

translation: And the magicians were cast down in prostration.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:120, also echoed in 26:46) describes the moment the magicians of Pharaoh, after seeing Moses' staff swallow what they had fabricated, recognized that what he brought was not sorcery but a sign from God. The passive wording 'were cast down' conveys that the truth overwhelmed them so completely that they fell in submission almost involuntarily, as if the clarity of the miracle compelled their bodies to bow. Those who were most expert in deception were the best able to tell illusion from genuine divine power, and their sincere recognition turned them from opponents of the prophet into believers, showing that real knowledge, when met with honesty, leads to faith and humility before God.

translation: They said: 'We believe in the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse records the immediate declaration of faith by Pharaoh's sorcerers after they witnessed that Moses's miracle was real and not magic. Having been the most skilled in their craft, they recognized better than anyone that what they saw exceeded human trickery and could only come from God. Their words show that true faith begins with acknowledging God's lordship over all creation, not merely over one people or one ruler, which directly rejects Pharaoh's claim to divinity. The verse teaches that sincere recognition of truth can overturn status, fear, and worldly interest, and that guidance may come suddenly to those who approach evidence with honesty.

translation: The Lord of Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:48, also 7:122) records the declaration of faith by Pharaoh's magicians after they witnessed Moses' miracle and fell prostrate. By naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron, they affirm that the Lord they now believe in is the one true God, the Lord of all the worlds, who sent His messengers, and not Pharaoh, whom the people had been made to treat as lord. The statement shows that sincere recognition of truth can transform a person in an instant, even those who had been aligned with falsehood, and that true lordship belongs only to God, whose power is confirmed through His prophets.

translation: Pharaoh said: "You have believed in him before I gave you permission! This is surely a plot you have plotted in the city to drive its people out of it. But soon you will know!"
interpretation: Pharaoh, seeing the magicians turn to faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron, cannot admit that the truth has defeated him, so he recasts their conversion as a political conspiracy. By saying they believed 'before I gave you permission,' he shows that he sees himself as the master of people's consciences and claims an authority that belongs to God alone. By accusing them of scheming with Moses to expel the Egyptians from their land, he stirs up fear among his people and gives himself a pretext for the harsh punishment he is about to announce. His threat 'soon you will know' is the typical language of a tyrant who resorts to intimidation when he has no argument left. The verse shows how oppressive rulers distort the truth, brand sincere believers as traitors, and use fear of losing power and homeland to hold back people from following the truth.

translation: I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all.
interpretation: These are Pharaoh's words to his magicians after they believed in the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Faced with the loss of his authority, he turns to brutal threats and public punishment, since he cannot refute their faith with argument. Cutting off a hand and a foot from opposite sides was meant to cripple them and make them an example, and crucifixion was meant to humiliate them before the people and frighten others from following Moses. The verse shows how tyranny answers truth with force once its claims are exposed. It also shows that the magicians' faith, which stayed firm despite this threat, was stronger than the power of the ruler.

translation: They said: Indeed, to our Lord we will surely return.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Az-Zukhruf (43:14), is part of the supplication taught to travelers when they mount their rides. It means that a believer, even while enjoying the ease of the means God has subjected to him, should remember that every journey ends in the final journey back to God. The verse ties gratitude for blessings to humility and awareness of accountability: worldly travel is temporary, and the true destination is the return to the Lord, so one should prepare for it with faith and righteous conduct.

translation: You take revenge on us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims (in submission to You).
interpretation: This is the reply of Pharaoh's magicians after they believed in Moses and Pharaoh threatened them with mutilation and crucifixion. They point out that the only 'offense' for which he punishes them is their faith in God's clear signs, which exposes the injustice of tyranny: truth is treated as a crime. Having recognized the truth, they do not bargain or retreat, but turn to God and ask Him to flood them with steadfastness, as though patience were water poured out over them, so that they will not waver under torture. They also ask to die in a state of submission to God, showing that the believer's greatest concern is to keep faith to the very end rather than to escape worldly suffering.

translation: The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?" He said, "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are dominant over them."
interpretation: The verse shows how entrenched power uses fear and the language of public order to defend injustice. Pharaoh's nobles, whose privileges depend on his rule, call Moses' message of monotheism and liberation 'corruption in the land,' casting the truth-bearers as a threat to society and to the established religion and political order. Pharaoh answers by renewing the old policy of killing newborn boys and sparing girls, a way to break the Israelites' strength and keep them subjugated. His boast that 'we are dominant over them' reveals arrogance and reliance on worldly power, forgetting that God's will can overturn it. The verse warns that tyrants brand reformers as troublemakers and answer truth with oppression, and it prepares for the believers' steadfastness and God's eventual victory, which the following verses go on to describe.

translation: Moses said to his people: "Seek help in God and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He causes whom He wills of His servants to inherit it, and the best outcome is for the righteous."
interpretation: When Pharaoh threatened the Children of Israel with oppression, Moses directed them to the two sources of strength in hardship: reliance on God, and steadfast patience rather than despair or hasty rebellion. The verse teaches that worldly power is not permanent and not owned by tyrants, since sovereignty over the earth belongs to God alone, who grants it to whomever He wills according to His wisdom and justice. The final victory and good end are not promised to the strong or numerous but to those who are God-fearing, who keep their duty to Him and remain upright. The believer therefore endures trials with hope, knowing that oppression is temporary and that taqwa and patience are what ultimately lead to deliverance and succession on earth.

translation: They said, 'We were harmed before you came to us and after you have come to us.' He said, 'Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then He will observe how you act.'
interpretation: The verse shows the Children of Israel complaining to Moses that their suffering under Pharaoh did not end with his mission, and Moses answers by turning their attention from grievance to hope and responsibility. He tells them that relief is possible through God's will, since the tyrant may be destroyed and they may inherit authority in the land. But he stresses that this is not only a privilege: succession in the land is a trial. God will see whether they act with justice, gratitude, and obedience or with corruption and ingratitude. The lesson is that patience in hardship should be joined to trust in God, and that worldly power is a test of conduct rather than proof of divine favor.

translation: And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, that perhaps they would remember.
interpretation: God describes how He afflicted Pharaoh's people with years of famine and a decrease in crops as a merciful warning rather than a final punishment. Hardship is meant to soften stubborn hearts, break their arrogance, and remind them of their dependence on their Lord, so that they might turn from denial and heed Moses' message. The verse teaches that calamities can serve as divine reminders that call people to reflection and repentance before harsher consequences come.

translation: But when good came to them, they said, 'This is our due.' And if an evil befell them, they attributed it to evil omens from Moses and those with him. Indeed, their omen is only with Allah, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance and inconsistency of Pharaoh's people. When they enjoyed prosperity, fertile land and ease, they credited themselves, treating it as something they deserved by right rather than a bounty from God. When drought, scarcity or hardship struck, they blamed Moses and his followers, claiming they were the cause of the bad luck. The Qur'an corrects this superstition: the fortune and misfortune that befall people are decreed by God and are tied to His wisdom, as trials or consequences of their own disbelief and wrongdoing, not to any prophet or believer. Their 'omen' (ṭā'ir) — the true cause of their ill fortune and the record of their deeds — lies with God. Most of them fail to understand this because they are heedless and blind to the real causes behind events, so they ascribe blessings to themselves and calamities to the righteous.

translation: And they said, 'Whatever sign you bring us with which to bewitch us, we are not going to believe in you.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:132) shows the stubborn arrogance of Pharaoh's people after Moses presented clear signs. Their refusal had nothing to do with a lack of evidence. They had already decided not to believe, so they dismissed every miracle as sorcery. It teaches that when a heart is closed by pride and obstinacy, no proof, however clear or great, will bring it to faith. Rejecting the truth in advance makes a person blind to signs and leaves them deserving of the consequences that followed.

translation: So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood as distinct signs, but they behaved arrogantly and were a criminal people.
interpretation: This verse shows that God's punishment of Pharaoh's people came gradually, in a series of clear and separate signs, each meant to awaken them and give them the chance to repent. Each affliction was distinct, so they could not explain it away as coincidence, and the interval between one and the next was a mercy that gave time to reflect. Yet instead of humbling themselves and heeding Moses, they met the signs with arrogance. Their pride hardened them into habitual wrongdoing, so they became 'a criminal people.' The lesson is that persistent refusal to accept truth after clear evidence is not a failure of proof but a failure of humility, and that God warns before He punishes.

translation: And when the plague fell upon them, they said, "O Moses, invoke your Lord for us by the covenant He has made with you. If you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe in you and will surely send the Children of Israel with you."
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:134) shows how Pharaoh's people turned to God only under duress. When punishment struck them, they recognized Moses's special standing with his Lord and begged him to pray on their behalf, appealing to the covenant God had granted him, namely that his prayers are answered. They promised belief and the release of the Israelites, but these promises were bargains made out of fear and not sincere conviction. The next verses confirm this, since once the affliction was lifted they broke their word. The lesson is that faith born only of hardship, and quickly abandoned in ease, is not true faith, and that stubborn arrogance can persist even after clear signs and direct experience of God's power.

translation: But when We removed from them the affliction for a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their pledge.
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:135) shows the pattern of Pharaoh's people: when a punishment struck them, they promised Moses to believe and to release the Children of Israel if the affliction were lifted. God lifted it, but only for a set period they were bound to reach, which is their appointed doom. As soon as the relief came, they went back on their word. Their pledges were driven by fear of hardship, not by sincere faith. A delay in punishment is a respite and a test, not a sign of safety or divine approval, and those who break their covenant after being granted mercy store up a more severe reckoning when their appointed time arrives.

translation: So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.
interpretation: This verse (Al-A'raf 7:136) shows that divine punishment is the consequence of a moral and spiritual failure, not an arbitrary act. The people of Pharaoh were destroyed because they rejected God's clear signs, and because they were heedless of them, meaning they saw the signs yet never reflected on them or took lessons from them. Heedlessness is presented as the root of denial: when a people repeatedly ignores warnings and clear evidence, they eventually bring upon themselves a just recompense. Their drowning in the sea mirrors their arrogance and tyranny, as the very power and means they relied on became the instrument of their downfall, while the believers were saved.

translation: And We made the people who had been oppressed and considered weak inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed. And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people used to make, and what they used to construct.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's promise comes true for those who endure hardship with patience. The Children of Israel were oppressed under Pharaoh, yet their steadfastness brought them honor and inheritance of the blessed land, while the great works and structures of the arrogant tyrants were wiped out. It teaches that worldly power and grand construction offer no protection against divine decree, and that lasting victory belongs to the patient believers who trust in God's promise, however long relief takes to arrive.

translation: And We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to the worship of idols they had. They said, 'O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods.' He said, 'Indeed, you are a people who act ignorantly.'
interpretation: The verse shows how quickly the heart can slip back into old habits and imitation of surrounding cultures, even after witnessing a great miracle like the parting of the sea. The Israelites had just been saved from Pharaoh by God's direct intervention, yet at the sight of people clinging to tangible idols, they longed for something visible and familiar to worship. Moses' reply, 'you are a people who are ignorant,' identifies the root of their request as ignorance of God's nature, not mere error of conduct: God is One, transcendent, and cannot be represented by any made object. It teaches that true faith requires real knowledge of God's oneness, and that exposure to the religious practices of others, along with a desire to fit in, can lead people to ask for what contradicts the very guidance they have been given, so one must guard against such imitation by firm understanding of monotheism.

translation: Indeed, those people—what they are engaged in is bound to be destroyed, and what they used to do is worthless.
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:139) is Moses's warning to the Children of Israel after they asked him for a god like the idols they saw a people worshipping. He tells them that idol worship and the way of life built on it are doomed to ruin and have no real value. Any religion or practice that rests on worshipping something other than God has no lasting foundation, and its followers' efforts come to nothing. Only devotion to the One God endures and carries true worth.

translation: He said: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while it is He who has favoured you over all the peoples?"
interpretation: Moses rebukes his people after they asked him for an idol to worship, like the idolaters they had passed by. His argument is that it makes no sense to seek any deity besides the One God, who alone created them, delivered them from Pharaoh, and raised them above the other nations of their time. Gratitude for such favour demands exclusive worship of Him, so turning to an idol would be both irrational and ungrateful. The verse teaches that divine blessings place a duty of tawhid on the one who receives them, and that honour and distinction come from God, not from created things.

translation: And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted upon you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a great trial from your Lord.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Children of Israel that their deliverance from Pharaoh's tyranny was a favor from God, which calls for gratitude and loyalty to Him. The word 'bala'' (trial) carries two senses, and the verse can be read as holding both: the suffering under Pharaoh was a great test of their patience and faith, and the rescue was a great test of their thankfulness. In this reading, hardship and ease alike are trials from God. The right response to the first is steadfast patience, and to the second, gratitude and obedience. Recalling the oppression and the salvation is meant to keep believers humble, mindful that every condition in life is a test, and that deliverance comes from God alone, not from human strength.

translation: And We appointed for Moses thirty nights, and We completed them with ten more, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron, 'Take my place among my people, act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.'
interpretation: The verse shows that drawing near to God comes through a prepared, deliberate period of devotion and discipline, and that the extension from thirty to forty nights was a divine test and completion, not a delay. It also shows the responsibility of leadership: before going away for a sacred encounter, Moses did not leave his community without guidance. He delegated Aaron as his deputy and gave him a short charter for leading: stand in for me, work to reform and keep the people united on righteousness, and refuse to follow or accommodate those who spread corruption. Spiritual elevation is therefore tied to responsibility toward others, and good leadership means continuing to work for reform and avoiding the path of the corrupt, even when the leader is absent.

translation: And when Moses came at the time We appointed, and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You." He said, "You will never see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me." But when his Lord manifested His glory to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. Then when he recovered, he said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers."
interpretation: The verse teaches the limits of human capacity before the majesty of God in this worldly life. Moses, honored with direct speech from God, longed to behold his Lord, and God's reply "You will never see Me" shows that the frail human being in this world cannot bear the vision of divine glory. God did not rebuke him harshly but gave a demonstration: if a solid mountain crumbles when only a trace of His manifestation touches it, a human being could not endure the full reality. Moses' collapse and his response of glorifying God, repenting for asking something beyond what was fitting, and affirming his faith show the proper attitude of a servant: humility, awareness of God's transcendence, and readiness to return to God when one oversteps. Longing for God is noble, but it must remain within the bounds God has set, and the ultimate vision is a promise reserved for the hereafter.

translation: He said: 'O Moses, I have chosen you above the people for My messages and for My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the grateful.'
interpretation: God singles Moses out for two distinctions: being entrusted with His revealed messages, and being addressed by Him directly, a privilege that set him apart from the people of his time. Because of this honor, he is told to receive the revelation and the guidance given to him with firmness and resolve, and not to be disheartened by the weight of the task. He is also to show gratitude, which means acknowledging the favor in his heart, praising God with his tongue, and acting on what he was given. The verse teaches that divine favor is a trust requiring thankfulness and obedience, not a source of pride.

translation: And We wrote for him on the tablets an admonition concerning all things and a detailed explanation of everything, [saying]: 'Take hold of them with firmness, and command your people to adopt the best of them. I will show you the home of the defiantly disobedient.'
interpretation: After Moses received the Tablets, God gave him a complete moral and legal guide: it contained counsel to soften hearts and clear detail to settle rulings. Guidance is only valuable when it is applied, so Moses is told to hold it with resolve and not with half-hearted compliance. His people are told to follow the best of what it contains, meaning that within the divine law one should aim for the most excellent course, such as choosing forgiveness over retaliation, patience over revenge, and the most virtuous deed when several permissible options exist. The closing warning, 'I will show you the home of the defiantly disobedient,' reminds them that those who abandon God's law end in ruin, and that the fate of earlier transgressors, visible in their ruined dwellings and in the final outcome awaiting them, is a lesson that should push the believers toward firm obedience.

translation: I will turn away from My signs those who behave arrogantly in the earth without right; and even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it; and if they see the path of guidance, they will not take it as a path; but if they see the path of error, they will take it as a path. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.
interpretation: The verse describes a spiritual consequence of arrogance: those who haughtily refuse the truth and deny God's signs are gradually deprived of the ability to understand and benefit from them. Their pride hardens their hearts, so that even clear proofs do not convince them, and they shun the way of righteousness while eagerly following the way of misguidance. This is not an arbitrary act of compulsion but a just recompense for their own prior choice to reject the signs and to be heedless of them. Persistent denial and negligence lead God to leave them to their chosen course, so that their perception is darkened and their error becomes their path.

translation: Those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, their deeds have come to nothing. Are they rewarded for anything other than what they used to do?
interpretation: Deeds done without faith in God's revelations and without accountability before Him have no weight on the Day of Judgment. Whatever good such people did was done without seeking God's pleasure or expecting a meeting with Him, so it earns no reward in the next life. The closing question stresses God's justice: He does not wrong them but repays each person according to what he did, so their losses are the natural result of their own choices and denial.

translation: And the people of Moses, after he had gone, took for themselves from their ornaments a calf, a body that had a lowing sound. Did they not see that it neither spoke to them nor guided them to any way? They took it for worship, and they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the irrationality of idolatry. The Israelites fashioned a god from their own jewelry, so the object of worship was literally the work of human hands and was made from the very things they owned. Its lowing was only a hollow sound that gave the illusion of life, and was neither speech nor guidance. The Qur'an argues that anything worthy of worship must be able to communicate and guide, since guidance is the greatest need of human beings, and a lifeless idol can do neither. By worshipping it they placed worship where it does not belong, which is the essence of wrongdoing (zulm). The verse also warns that people are quick to fall into misguidance once divine guidance is no longer immediately present among them, and that clinging to what is attractive and tangible instead of using reason and reflection leads to ruin.

translation: And when they were seized with remorse and saw that they had gone astray, they said: 'If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.'
interpretation: The verse describes the moment the Children of Israel, after worshipping the golden calf in Moses' absence, awoke to the gravity of their error. The idiom 'saqata fi aydihim' conveys the bitter regret and shock of someone who realizes too late what he has done, as if the matter has fallen into his hands and he can do nothing about it. Their recognition of having gone astray led them to turn humbly to God, acknowledging that salvation lies only in His mercy and forgiveness, not in their own deeds. The lesson is that true repentance begins with honest recognition of one's sin, followed by remorse and complete dependence on God, and that without divine mercy a person is destined for ruin.

translation: And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "How evil is what you did in my place after I left! Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" And he cast down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself. Aaron said: "Son of my mother, the people deemed me weak and were about to kill me, so do not let the enemies gloat over me, and do not place me among the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse shows how strongly Moses felt about the worship of the calf, which he regarded as a grave betrayal of monotheism. His anger was not personal but zeal for God's right to be worshipped alone. Casting down the tablets and seizing Aaron expressed an overwhelming, spontaneous reaction to a catastrophic sin, not contempt for revelation or his brother. Aaron's reply, addressing Moses tenderly as 'son of my mother', shows his gentleness and his innocence. He had tried to restrain the people but was overpowered and threatened, so he feared that harsh treatment from Moses would give the enemies cause to rejoice and would wrongly count him among the wrongdoers. The lesson is that zeal for faith must be tempered by justice and by hearing the facts, and that a leader who has genuinely tried to prevent wrong, yet lacks the power to stop it, is not blameworthy. Once the matter was clarified, Moses turned to seeking forgiveness for himself and his brother.

translation: He said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy."
interpretation: After Moses confronts Aaron over the people's lapse into calf-worship and finds him innocent of intentional wrongdoing, he turns from anger to prayer. By asking forgiveness for himself, he acknowledges that even a prophet may fall short, perhaps in the vehemence of his reaction or in the burdens of leadership. By including his brother, he restores their bond and shows the right way to settle a dispute among the righteous: reconciliation, then a shared appeal to God. Asking to be admitted into God's mercy shows that salvation depends on divine grace rather than on one's own deeds, and describing God as the Most Merciful of the merciful expresses complete reliance on Him, whose compassion exceeds all human compassion.

translation: Indeed, those who took the calf [for worship] will be afflicted by wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. And thus do We recompense those who invent falsehood.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:152) tells us that turning to anything besides God for worship, as the Children of Israel did with the golden calf after Moses left them, is not a trivial error but a grave betrayal that carries consequences. Divine anger and public disgrace are the due result of ascribing divinity to a created thing and fabricating falsehood about God. The closing statement widens the lesson beyond that one episode: it is a standing divine principle that anyone who invents lies against God, by innovating in religion, making up false deities, or attributing to Him what He has not said, will meet the same fate of estrangement from His favor and abasement. The verse also implies that true honor lies in sincere devotion to God alone, while idolatry and religious fabrication lead to lasting disgrace.

translation: But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed - indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:153) shows that no sin is too great to be forgiven if a person sincerely turns back to God. It was revealed in the context of the Children of Israel who worshipped the calf and were then offered pardon. Repentance (tawbah) means abandoning the wrong, regretting it, and resolving not to return to it, and it must be joined with renewed faith (iman), which includes sound belief and a return to obedience. When someone does this, God's forgiveness and mercy await them, and the past is wiped away. The verse invites despairing sinners to hope and encourages them to return to God rather than persist in wrongdoing.

translation: And when the anger subsided in Moses, he took up the tablets; and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord.
interpretation: After Moses' anger over the people's worship of the calf cooled, he returned to the tablets he had cast down and took them up again, showing that his anger was for God's sake and that he held the revelation in high regard. The verse teaches that the divine law written on them is a source of guidance, showing the right path, and of mercy, bringing ease and well-being in this life and the next. Yet its benefit is reserved for those whose hearts hold reverent fear of God (rahbah), because awe of God makes a person receptive to the revelation and leads them to act upon it, whereas the heedless do not benefit from it.

translation: And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. Then, when the earthquake seized them, he said: "My Lord, had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me as well. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done? It is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of those who forgive."
interpretation: The verse shows the ideal posture of a leader and intercessor before God in a moment of crisis. Moses, having brought representatives of his people to the appointed meeting, responds to their sudden punishment not with blame but with humility and pleading. He acknowledges God's absolute power and will, includes himself in the plea ('destroy them and me'), and expresses the hope that the whole community will not be punished for the folly of a few. By calling the event a 'trial' (fitnah) through which God tests people, leading some astray and guiding others according to His wisdom, he affirms that all outcomes are in God's hands and that guidance depends on God's grace. He then takes refuge in God as the sole Protector (Wali) and asks for forgiveness and mercy, recognizing that God is the best of forgivers. The lesson is that true servants of God respond to calamity with tawhid, repentance, humility, and reliance on divine mercy rather than self-justification.

translation: And decree for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter; indeed we have turned back to You. He said: My punishment I inflict upon whom I will, but My mercy encompasses all things. So I will decree it for those who are mindful of God, give zakat, and those who believe in Our signs.
interpretation: The verse records Moses' prayer on behalf of his people after the incident of the calf, asking for well-being in both worlds, and God's reply. God makes clear that His punishment is just and falls only on those who deserve it by His wisdom, while His mercy is so vast that it touches every creature in this life. Yet the special, lasting mercy of the Hereafter is written for those who show its marks: God-consciousness that restrains them from wrongdoing, purification of their wealth and selves through zakat, and sincere faith in God's signs, accepting and following them. Divine mercy is thus limitless in its scope, but receiving its fullest form is bound to piety, charity, and belief.

translation: Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel; he commands them to what is right and forbids them from what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the bad things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light that was sent down with him — it is they who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse describes the people who deserve God's special mercy: those who follow Muhammad, whose coming and character were foretold in the earlier scriptures. His mission is a comprehensive moral and legal reform. It upholds what reason and sound human nature recognize as good, forbids what they recognize as corrupt, and lifts the heavy restrictions and rigid burdens that had weighed on earlier communities, such as excessive ritual strictness. Success is not achieved by claiming to believe alone. It requires four things: faith in him, respect for him, active support of his mission, and following the Qur'an, the light revealed with him as guidance. Those who combine all four are the truly successful, both in this world and in the next.

translation: Say, O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all, to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in God and His words, and follow him that you may be guided.
interpretation: This verse affirms the universality of Muhammad's prophethood: unlike earlier prophets who were sent to specific peoples, he addresses all of humanity, whatever their nation or religion. The authority behind his message is grounded in God's absolute sovereignty over creation, His sole divinity, and His power over life and death, which means that accepting the message is a matter of submitting to the One who owns everything and to whom all return. The call to faith combines belief in God with belief in His Messenger, and it describes the Prophet as 'unlettered' (ummi) and as one who himself believes in God and His words, showing that he is not a claimant to divinity but a servant who embodies the faith he teaches, and that his message is a divine revelation rather than the product of human learning. Following him in practice, not merely believing in him, is presented as the path to true guidance, so that guidance is attained through both sincere faith and obedient emulation of the Prophet.

translation: And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it they act justly.
interpretation: This verse affirms that even within the Children of Israel, despite their many failings described in the surrounding verses, there was a righteous group who remained faithful to divine revelation. They were not only guided themselves but guided others to the truth, and they applied that truth in their judgments and dealings with fairness. The verse teaches that true righteousness joins knowledge of the truth with its practice in justice, and that the Qur'an judges communities fairly, acknowledging the good among them rather than condemning them wholesale.

translation: We divided them into twelve tribes, as distinct communities. And We inspired Moses, when his people asked him for water: 'Strike the rock with your staff.' Then twelve springs gushed forth from it, and every group knew its drinking place. We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails: 'Eat of the good things We have provided for you.' They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse recalls God's care for the Children of Israel: He organized them into twelve tribal communities and gave each its own spring, which prevented quarrels over water. He also provided shade, food, and water in the harsh desert, so all their needs were met by divine mercy, and Moses' staff was only the means for a miracle that came from God. Despite these favors, their later disobedience, ingratitude, and rebellion did not harm God, who is free of all need. The harm of sin falls only on the sinner, who deprives his own soul of God's blessing and guidance.

translation: And [remember] when it was said to them: 'Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say "Relieve us of our burden," and enter the gate prostrating, and We will forgive you your sins. We will increase the doers of good [in reward].'
interpretation: The verse shows that God's favor toward the Children of Israel came paired with simple acts of gratitude and humility. They were given the blessing of a settled home and lawful provision, and in return they were asked to show submission in word and deed: to ask forgiveness with the words 'hittah' and to enter the gate bowed down, which crushes arrogance and acknowledges dependence on God. In this way, forgiveness is presented as easily within reach for anyone who combines sincere repentance with humble obedience. The closing promise, that God will give even more to those who do good, teaches that the door of divine mercy stays open beyond mere pardon: repentance cleanses the past, while excellence in conduct earns further reward and elevation. The surrounding context shows the tragedy of those who altered the words and ignored the command, which illustrates that blessings are lost not through God's stinginess but through human arrogance and mockery of His instructions.

translation: But those who did wrong among them substituted a word other than the one that had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the heaven because of their transgression.
interpretation: The verse recounts how the wrongdoers among the Children of Israel were commanded to enter the town in humility, saying a word of seeking forgiveness (hittah), but they altered both the words and the spirit of the command, mocking it and treating divine instruction as something to be bent to their own whims. Their changing of the word was not a mere slip of speech but an outward sign of inward arrogance and disobedience. God's punishment, described as a plague or scourge from the sky, came as just recompense for their persistent wrongdoing, teaching that distorting God's commands, whether in word or in meaning, is itself a grave injustice, and that obedience requires sincerity and humility, not merely outward compliance.

translation: And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath: when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them. Thus did We test them because of their defiant disobedience.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet to remind the Jews of his time of the history of a coastal community among their predecessors, whose story they know and which exposes their ancestors' pattern of evasion. That community was forbidden to fish on the Sabbath, and God tested them by making the fish appear in abundance on the very day fishing was prohibited, while they vanished on ordinary days. The trial was a consequence of their habitual wrongdoing: because they were inclined to disobey, God exposed the weakness of their obedience by placing temptation directly in front of them. Some of them used legal trickery to circumvent the command, showing that outward observance without sincere submission is no real obedience, and that persistent sinfulness invites ever-greater tests.

translation: And when a community among them said, 'Why do you preach to a people whom God is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?' They said, 'As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they may become God-fearing.'
interpretation: The verse, from the account of the Sabbath-breakers among the People of the Sabbath, shows that enjoining good and forbidding evil remains a duty even when people seem unlikely to change. The reformers gave two reasons for continuing to admonish: first, to discharge their responsibility before God so that they could say they had not neglected the obligation; second, out of hope that the wrongdoers might still heed the warning and turn to God-consciousness. The group that asked 'Why do you preach?' had despaired of the sinners and saw advice as pointless, but the reply teaches that a believer's duty is to convey the message and hope for guidance, leaving the outcome to God, and that despair of people's reform is not a valid excuse for silence.

translation: So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong with a severe punishment because they were defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse explains that divine reminders, if persistently ignored and abandoned, lead to a point where God's protection is withdrawn from the heedless. At that moment, salvation is granted not to those who merely kept personal piety, but to those who actively forbade wrongdoing and upheld moral responsibility in their community. Those who persisted in transgression and open defiance of God's command were struck by a harsh punishment, which was the just consequence of their continual rebellion rather than an arbitrary act. The lesson is that forgetting divine guidance is the root of communal decline, that enjoining good and forbidding evil is a means of deliverance, and that sin practiced openly and persistently brings about ruin.

translation: So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, 'Be apes, despised and rejected.'
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 7:166) describes the fate of a community that knowingly and arrogantly broke God's prohibition, namely violating the Sabbath. Their punishment came only after they had been warned and had defiantly persisted, so it was a consequence of deliberate rebellion rather than of simple error. Many commentators, such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, take the transformation literally, as a divine decree that turned them into apes as a humiliating sign. Others, such as Mujahid, read it figuratively, as a transformation of their hearts and character into baseness and lack of understanding. On either reading, the lesson is that persistent, arrogant disobedience of God's clear commands, after warning, brings abasement and loss of honor, and that God's decree takes effect the moment He wills it: 'Be', and it is.

translation: And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them the worst torment. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:167) speaks of God's decree concerning the Children of Israel after they transgressed and broke their covenant: as a consequence of persistent disobedience, God ordained that nations and rulers would repeatedly rise over them and subject them to humiliation and hardship throughout history. The point is that divine law holds communities accountable for their moral and spiritual conduct, and that rejecting God's guidance brings consequences in this world as well as the next. The verse ends by balancing warning and hope: God's punishment comes swiftly to those who persist in wrongdoing, yet His forgiveness and mercy remain open to anyone who repents and returns to Him, so the door of repentance is never closed.

translation: And We divided them throughout the earth into communities; among them were the righteous, and among them were others less than that. And We tested them with good things and bad things, that perhaps they might return.
interpretation: The verse describes God's dealings with the Children of Israel after their disobedience: He scattered them across the earth in separate groups, so they no longer lived as one united nation. Their scattering was not a sign that all of them were corrupt, since some remained upright and others fell short of that standard. God then tested them with both ease and hardship, with blessings such as prosperity and health, and with trials such as want and affliction. The purpose was to turn them back to obedience and repentance. The lesson is that the rise and fall of a people's fortunes are a means of moral testing and a summons to return to God, and that every community contains a mix of the righteous and the lesser, so judgment must not be passed on all of them alike.

translation: Then there succeeded them a generation who inherited the Scripture; they take the goods of this lower world and say, 'It will be forgiven us.' And if similar goods came to them again, they would take them. Was not the covenant of the Scripture taken from them that they would not say about God anything but the truth, and they have studied what is in it? And the home of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God. Will you not then reason?
interpretation: The verse describes a decline in religious integrity after the righteous predecessors: later generations inherited the divine Book but treated knowledge as a means to worldly gain, accepting bribes and material benefits to distort rulings or conceal the truth. They excused their sin with false hope, presuming forgiveness while persisting in the same wrongdoing whenever the opportunity returned, which shows they had no real repentance. God rebukes this by reminding them that they had pledged to speak only the truth about Him and had studied the Book, so they were without excuse, since their offense was committed knowingly. The verse concludes that the Hereafter is better for the God-conscious, and calls on people to use their reason and prefer lasting reward over fleeting worldly profit. Knowledge of scripture is thus a trust demanding sincerity and action, and relying on mercy while deliberately repeating sin is self-deception.

translation: And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer – indeed, We do not let the reward of the reformers go to waste.
interpretation: This verse (Al-A'raf 7:170) teaches that real adherence to divine scripture is not a matter of claiming it or reciting it, but of living by its guidance and upholding its commands, with prayer as the clearest sign of that devotion. Prayer keeps a person in constant connection with God and shapes their conduct. Those who hold firmly to the Book and maintain prayer become people who set right themselves and their communities, and God assures them that their efforts toward righteousness and reform will never be lost or wasted, in contrast to those who inherited the Book but neglected it for worldly gain.

translation: And [remember] when We raised the mountain above them as if it were a canopy, and they thought it was going to fall upon them: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and remember what is in it, so that you may become mindful of God."
interpretation: The verse recalls a moment when God made the Children of Israel feel the awesome weight of His covenant, as the mountain loomed over them like an overhanging cloud ready to fall. The scene was meant to impress upon them that revelation is not to be treated casually or accepted halfheartedly. They were commanded to take the Torah with resolve and earnestness, not with laziness or selective compliance, and to keep its teachings continually in mind by studying, reflecting on, and acting upon them. The ultimate aim is taqwa, God-consciousness: the Book is received properly only when it shapes one's conduct and keeps one aware of accountability before God. The lesson reaches beyond that community, warning all believers that faith requires firm commitment and constant remembrance of divine guidance, not mere acknowledgement.

translation: And [remember] when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them bear witness over themselves, [saying]: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes, we bear witness.' [This was] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: 'Indeed, we were unaware of this.'
interpretation: The verse points to the natural, innate disposition (fitra) with which God created every human being: an inborn recognition of His lordship and oneness. The 'taking' of offspring from the loins of Adam's children and the testimony 'Yes, we bear witness' is understood as God implanting in human nature, and in the signs of creation, an inherent awareness that He alone is Lord. Because this knowledge is rooted in each soul, and reinforced by revelation and the signs in the universe, no one can excuse themselves on the Day of Judgment by claiming ignorance of God's oneness or saying they were heedless of it. Responsibility for faith therefore rests on every person, since the evidence is within their own selves.

translation: Or lest you say: 'It was only our forefathers who associated others with God before us, and we were but descendants after them. Will You then destroy us for what the falsifiers did?'
interpretation: This verse completes the argument of the covenant in the previous verse, in which God took from the descendants of Adam an acknowledgment of His lordship, rooted in the natural disposition (fitra) He placed in every human being. Its meaning is that no one will be able, on the Day of Resurrection, to excuse their own shirk by blaming their ancestors or claiming they merely followed tradition. Since the knowledge of God's oneness is innate in every soul and is reinforced by the signs in creation and the message of the prophets, each person is personally accountable for turning away from it. Blind imitation of forefathers is therefore not a valid defense, and the responsibility for deviation rests on the one who chooses it, not on those who came before.

translation: And thus We explain the verses in detail, so that perhaps they may return.
interpretation: God makes clear His signs and proofs distinctly, just as He has detailed the covenant and the truths in the preceding passage, so that people may recognize the truth without confusion. The purpose of this clear explanation is not merely to inform but to prompt a change of heart: that those who have strayed through denial, heedlessness, or sin may turn back (yarji'un) to God, to faith, and to obedience. The word 'perhaps' (la'allahum) reflects that the return remains a matter of human choice, since God provides the guidance and the clarity, while each person is responsible for responding to it by repenting and returning to the straight path.

translation: And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan followed him up, and he became one of the deviators.
interpretation: The verse warns that receiving knowledge and divine guidance is no safeguard in itself; it must be held to with sincerity and action. A person who was given clear understanding of God's revelations, yet abandoned them by following his desires and neglecting their demands, shed them as one sheds a skin. By leaving the protection of guidance he lost his spiritual safeguard, so Satan caught up with him and made him his follower, and he ended among those who are lost in error. The lesson is that knowledge without humility, gratitude and obedience can become a cause of one's downfall, and that a person must constantly cling to God's guidance and seek refuge in Him from falling away after having known the truth.

translation: Had We willed, We would have raised him by means of them, but he clung to the earth and followed his own desire. So his likeness is that of the dog: if you drive it away it pants, and if you leave it alone it pants. That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So narrate the narrative, that perhaps they will reflect.
interpretation: The verse describes a person who was given knowledge of God's revelation yet did not rise by it, because he inclined toward worldly gain and followed his whims. Raising a person in rank is not achieved by knowledge alone but by acting on it with sincerity, and God's will to elevate him was tied to his own choice, which he forfeited. His state is compared to a panting dog, whose restless, insatiable craving continues whether it is pressed or left alone. Likewise, a person enslaved to desire stays greedy and unsatisfied, and neither admonition nor neglect changes him, since the problem lies in his heart and not in a lack of guidance. The same likeness applies to those who deny God's signs, for the clear signs bring no benefit to a heart ruled by appetite. The closing command to recount such stories calls on people to reflect on them, take warning, and guard themselves against the same fall.

translation: Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and it was themselves they used to wrong. (Qur'an 7:177)
interpretation: The verse says that those who reject God's signs, after the truth has become clear to them, end in a wretched condition, and the example set for them is a bad one, like that of someone who is given knowledge and strips himself of it. Their denial does not harm God or His message at all. Its whole harm falls on their own souls. By turning away from guidance they deprive themselves of mercy, clarity and salvation, and they bring ruin on themselves. The lesson is that wrongdoing in matters of faith is ultimately self-inflicted injustice, and that anyone who denies revelation out of arrogance or desire is really wronging himself.

translation: Whoever God guides is truly the guided one, and whoever He leaves to go astray, those are the losers.
interpretation: True guidance is a gift that originates with God, so no one can claim to have attained the right path through their own self-sufficiency. Those whom God guides are the ones who arrive at truth and lasting success, because He grants them insight, receptivity of heart, and steadfastness. Those who persistently turn away from the signs of God, closing their hearts to truth out of arrogance or heedlessness, are left to their own misguidance, and they bear the real loss: they squander their souls, their purpose, and their eternal destiny, which is a loss no worldly gain can compensate for. The verse calls the believer to humble dependence on God, to seek guidance sincerely, and to fear the consequence of rejecting it.

translation: And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. They are like livestock; rather, they are even more astray. Those are the heedless.
interpretation: The verse says that people who end up in Hell are not lacking the faculties of understanding; they have hearts, eyes and ears, but they refuse to use them for their real purpose, which is to reflect on God's signs, see the truth in creation and hear the guidance of revelation. Because they keep these faculties from their proper function, they are like cattle, who follow appetite and instinct without reflecting on truth. They are even worse than cattle, because animals never had the capacity for moral reasoning and cannot be blamed, while humans were given it and wasted it. The phrase 'created for Hell' describes the outcome known to God's knowledge, brought about by their own willful heedlessness and not by compulsion. Their basic fault is ghaflah, a deliberate neglect of God and the Hereafter that dulls the heart until the truth no longer affects it.

translation: And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so invoke Him by them. And leave those who deviate concerning His names; they will be recompensed for what they used to do.
interpretation: God's names express perfect attributes such as mercy, knowledge, power, and justice, and no name or quality of His is lacking in beauty or perfection. Believers are therefore told to call upon Him through these names, choosing the name that suits their need, as when asking for forgiveness by 'the Forgiving' or for provision by 'the Provider,' and to know and live by their meanings. The verse also warns against 'ilhad,' deviating from the truth about these names, whether by denying them, giving Him names He has not given Himself, likening Him to creation, or ascribing His names to false deities, as the idolaters did when deriving names for their idols from His. Believers are told to leave such people and not be drawn into their distortions, and the verse closes by assuring them that God will repay such deviators in full for what they did.

translation: And among those whom We have created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.
interpretation: The verse affirms that in every age God has preserved a group of people who stay true to the truth, calling others to it and establishing justice by it in their own judgments and dealings. The truth is thus both the source of their guidance and the standard of their fairness. It shows that guidance is not only knowing the truth but also acting upon it with justice, and that the world is never left entirely without sincere, upright people who uphold the truth, even when most people go astray. Many commentators understand this as a reference to the righteous among the believers, who carry the message and live by it.

translation: And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them on step by step to destruction from where they do not know.
interpretation: This verse (Al-A'raf 7:182) means that God does not punish deniers abruptly. Instead, He lets them continue in their wrongdoing while granting them health, wealth, and ease. Each blessing deepens their false sense of security and heedlessness, so they sink further into sin and arrogance and mistake God's delay for approval. They do not realize that this gradual increase in comfort is itself drawing them toward their downfall, until the punishment seizes them suddenly at a moment they never anticipated. It is a warning that worldly prosperity is not proof of God's favor, and that persistent rejection of the truth, combined with being left to one's own devices, leads to ruin.

translation: And I grant them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:183) teaches that God's delay in punishing those who deny His signs is not a sign of His approval or their safety. He gives them time and allows them to continue in their heedlessness and wealth, and this very leniency draws them step by step toward their ruin without their awareness. His 'plan' is 'matin', meaning strong and unbreakable, so no cunning or power can resist or escape it. The verse is a warning to the arrogant and a reassurance to the believers that justice will certainly be fulfilled in its appointed time.

translation: Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion. He is only a clear warner.
interpretation: The verse calls the disbelievers to honest reflection on the character and life of the Prophet Muhammad, who has lived among them and is known to them as a companion. Their accusation that he is possessed or mad collapses once they consider the wisdom of his words, the consistency of his conduct, and the clarity of his message. He makes no claim to power or hidden knowledge; his role is only to warn plainly of the consequences of rejecting God, so the charge of madness is a way of avoiding the truth and not a reasoned judgment.

translation: Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and into everything God has created, and considered that perhaps their appointed term has already drawn near? In what statement after this, then, will they believe?
interpretation: The verse calls on those who deny the Prophet's message to reflect on the signs of God's sovereignty in the cosmos and in every created thing, since these point to a single Creator and to the truth of the revelation. It also warns that death may come suddenly, because each person's lifespan is unknown and may be nearly over, so there is no room for delay in believing. If the clear evidence in creation and the Qur'an's warning fail to move them, no other speech could convince them, and that leaves them with no excuse. The closing question is a rebuke: the Qur'an is the most truthful discourse, so whoever rejects it will not be guided by anything else.

translation: Whomever God lets go astray, there is no guide for him; and He leaves them wandering blindly in their transgression.
interpretation: Guidance ultimately lies in God's hands, and He lets go astray those who, after the truth has reached them, persistently turn away from it and choose arrogance and heedlessness. Once a person has closed his heart to the signs and warnings, God leaves him to the consequence of his own choice, so no created being can bring him to the truth. Such people keep stumbling in confusion and hesitation, unable to see clearly because they refused the light when it came to them. The verse teaches humility and dependence on God for guidance, and it warns that persistent rebellion hardens the heart and deepens misguidance.

translation: They ask you about the Hour: when will it come to anchor? Say: Knowledge of it is only with my Lord; none can reveal its time except Him. It weighs heavily upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come to you except suddenly. They ask you as if you were well informed about it. Say: Knowledge of it is only with God, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the exact timing of the Last Hour is a matter of the unseen that God has reserved for Himself alone. Even the Prophet, the most knowledgeable of people about God's revelation, was not given this knowledge, and he is instructed to say so plainly. The questioners, who ask out of curiosity or mockery, are redirected from the question of when it will happen to the reality that it will certainly happen, suddenly and with immense weight over all creation, so that the heavens and the earth themselves feel its gravity. The point is that people should not occupy themselves with fixing a date they can never know, but should be prepared at every moment through faith and righteous action. Most people fail to grasp this, either denying the unseen or presuming to know what belongs only to God.

translation: Say: I have no power to bring benefit or to ward off harm from myself, except what God wills. Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no harm would have touched me. I am nothing but a warner and a bearer of good news to a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse affirms the limits of the Prophet's human nature and the absolute sovereignty of God. Muhammad, like every other created being, cannot bring about benefit or avert harm on his own except by God's permission, and knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone. If he had known the unseen, he would have prepared for every opportunity and avoided every misfortune, but since he does not, he experiences both ease and hardship like other people. The verse thus guards against attributing divine powers to prophets or saints and ties true reliance to God alone. His role is defined by his message: to warn of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing and to give glad tidings of reward, benefiting those who open their hearts in faith.

translation: It is He who created you from a single soul, and made from it its mate so that he might find rest and comfort in her. Then when he covered her, she bore a light burden and went about with it. But when she grew heavy, they both called upon Allah, their Lord: "If You grant us a sound, righteous child, we will surely be among the grateful."
interpretation: The verse reminds humanity of its common origin and of the divine wisdom in marriage: God made the spouse of the same kind so that tranquility and affection would exist between the two. It then describes the stages of pregnancy, in which the early burden is light and barely noticed, but becomes heavy as the child grows, which is when anxiety about the child's health and wellbeing arises. At that moment the parents turn to God in sincere supplication, promising gratitude if He grants them a sound, healthy child. The verse thus sets up a lesson about human nature: people remember God and pledge thankfulness in times of need and anxiety, and the following verses rebuke those who, once their prayer is answered, forget their promise and attribute God's gift to others. True gratitude means keeping faith with God and worshipping Him alone, both in hardship and in blessing.

translation: But when He gave them a sound, righteous child, they ascribed partners to Him in what He had given them. Exalted is God above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse rebukes ingratitude after a prayer is answered. In the preceding verses, a couple in need of a child pray to God, promising to be grateful if He gives them a sound child. When God grants it, they forget their promise and attribute the blessing, or part of it, to something other than Him. They may credit created causes, or name the child in a way that implies servitude to someone besides God, or they may attribute the gift to idols, fortune, or the stars. The verse teaches that every blessing, including children, comes from God alone, and that gratitude means devoting oneself to Him exclusively and keeping one's promises to Him. It ends by declaring that God is far above any partner or share ascribed to Him, since He needs no associate in giving or sustaining anything.

translation: Do they associate with Allah those who cannot create anything, while they themselves are created?
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:191) offers a rational rebuke of polytheism. Whoever deserves worship must have the power to create, sustain, and control, since worship is due only to the one who originates everything. The idols and false deities people worship create nothing, and they are themselves made, whether they are carved by human hands or are created beings such as angels, prophets, or spirits. Something that is made and dependent cannot be a partner to the Creator, who depends on nothing. Worshipping such beings reverses the proper order of things, because the created is elevated to the rank of the Creator. The verse therefore calls people to reflect and to direct their worship to Allah alone.

translation: And they are unable to give them any help, nor can they help themselves.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:192) exposes the powerlessness of the idols that people worship besides God. Beings that cannot aid those who worship them, and cannot even defend themselves from harm or destruction, have no claim to be worshipped. True divinity requires the power to help, protect, and sustain, and only God possesses it. The verse is a rational argument that calls people to leave dependence on false deities and turn to the One who is truly capable.

translation: And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:193) addresses the idolaters and exposes the helplessness of the false deities they worship besides God. Those idols are lifeless and have no hearing, understanding, or will, so they cannot respond to a call to guidance or follow anyone who invites them to the right path. Whether the worshippers speak to them or stay silent makes no difference, because they cannot benefit, answer, or guide. The point is to show the folly of worshipping what cannot even respond, and to turn people toward God alone, who hears, answers, and guides.

translation: Indeed, those whom you invoke besides God are servants like yourselves. So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse challenges idol-worship by exposing the false basis of it: whatever is worshipped besides God is itself created and dependent, just as its worshippers are, so it cannot hold the powers of a lord. If these beings truly had the power to hear and answer prayer, they would answer when called. Their silence and inability prove that they are powerless, and that only God, the Creator who hears and responds, deserves worship and supplication.

translation: Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they grasp? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear? Say: Call upon your partners (whom you associate with God), then plot against me, and give me no respite.
interpretation: The verse is a rational refutation of idol-worship. The idols the polytheists worship are inferior even to their own worshippers, since they lack the basic faculties of movement, action, sight and hearing that humans have. A thing that cannot walk, seize, see or hear cannot help, guide or protect anyone, so it cannot deserve worship.
