The Prophet is then commanded to challenge the polytheists openly: let them summon their idols and all join in scheming against him without delay. This shows his complete trust in God, who alone is his protector, and exposes the powerlessness of the false gods, who can neither harm him nor defend their followers.

translation: Indeed, my protector is Allah, who has sent down the Book, and He is the one who takes care of the righteous.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to declare, in response to the idolaters who threatened him and urged him to turn back to their gods, that his reliance is on Allah alone. The One who revealed the Qur'an as guidance and proof is the One who supports and defends him, and He does not abandon those who are righteous. Allah's guardianship is therefore a promise of help and protection for believers who obey Him, so they need not fear the power of those who worship others besides Him. The verse also ties divine protection to the Book: those who hold fast to the revelation and live righteously are under Allah's care.

translation: And those whom you invoke besides Him are unable to help you, nor can they even help themselves.
interpretation: The verse exposes the futility of idolatry through a simple argument from impotence: whatever is worshipped alongside God, whether idols, false deities, or created powers, has no real capacity to benefit or protect. If these objects of devotion cannot even defend themselves from harm, such as being broken, abandoned, or destroyed, they can hardly give aid to their devotees. It therefore calls the listener to turn away from misplaced dependence on created things and to rely on God alone, the only source of true help and power.

translation: And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear; and you see them looking at you, yet they do not see.
interpretation: The verse describes those who have shut themselves off from truth: their hearing and sight are intact physically, but because their hearts are closed by stubbornness and attachment to falsehood, they gain no benefit from the call to guidance. They may face the Prophet and appear to look at him, yet they perceive neither the truth of his message nor the signs of his sincerity and prophethood. The point is that real hearing and seeing mean understanding and accepting guidance, so those who refuse to reflect are likened to the deaf and blind, and are as useless in their response as idols which have eyes painted on them but cannot truly see.

translation: Hold to forgiveness, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:199) lays out a threefold code of conduct for the Prophet and for believers. First, to be lenient and accept people as they are, overlooking their faults and taking what they can easily offer rather than demanding perfection from them. Second, to call others to what is known to be good and right, so that gentleness never turns into passive acceptance of wrongdoing. Third, when one meets people who are foolish, obstinate or abusive, to withdraw from them with dignity and not answer ignorance with ignorance. Together these form a balanced approach to social life: patience and mercy in dealing with people, firmness in upholding goodness, and restraint and self-respect in the face of hostility, which protects one's heart and keeps the call to truth gentle and effective.

translation: And if an evil suggestion from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when anger, temptation, or a whisper pushes a person away from patience, forgiveness, or righteous conduct, the remedy is to turn immediately to God for protection rather than rely on one's own strength. This is especially relevant after the preceding command to repel evil with what is better: Satan will try to provoke a harsh reaction or stir up resentment, so the believer must consciously take refuge in God. The closing names, the Hearing and the Knowing, reassure the believer that God hears the plea for refuge and knows the inner struggle, and thus is able to guard the heart against Satan's incitement.

translation: Indeed, those who are God-fearing, when a touch of temptation from Satan afflicts them, remember [God], and at once they see clearly.
interpretation: Even the righteous are not immune from Satan's whispers, such as a sudden surge of anger, desire, or a passing evil thought. What distinguishes them is that they do not persist in it. Their God-consciousness makes them recall God's commands, His watchfulness, and the consequences of sin, and this remembrance acts like a light that lifts the veil of delusion. Their spiritual insight returns, they recognize the deception for what it is, and they turn back to obedience and repentance, whereas those who lack taqwa are drawn deeper into error.

translation: And their brothers [the devils' followers] they draw on further into error, and then they do not stop short.
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:202) says that those who do not fear God have companions among the devils, and these devils keep pulling them deeper into misguidance without ever relenting. Unlike the God-fearing, who remember God and regain their sight when a touch of Satan afflicts them (verse 201), the heedless are bound to the devils like brothers. The devils feed their delusions, make wrongdoing appear attractive, and push them from one sin to a greater one without tiring or easing off. The lesson is that remembering God (dhikr) and taqwa are the protection that breaks the cycle. Without them a person is steadily led further into error, since the devils never cease while the person never turns back.

translation: And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, 'Why have you not chosen one?' Say: 'I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This is a set of clear insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe.'
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:203) answers those who mock the Prophet and demand miracles on their own terms, as though he could produce signs at will or invent them. The Prophet is told to state his role plainly: he is not the author of revelation but its follower, and he receives only what God sends, when God sends it. The Qur'an itself is then presented as the greatest sign. It is basa'ir, evidence that opens the inner eye to truth, as well as guidance and mercy. Yet only those who are open to faith benefit from it. Their belief makes them receptive, while those who demand more proof remain blind to the proof already before them. The point is that real guidance does not depend on spectacular wonders. It lies in humbly accepting divine revelation and following it.

translation: And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an deserves a particular reverence: when it is recited, believers should give it their full attention, with hearts and ears open and tongues stilled. Such attentive silence is the condition for the Qur'an to do its work on a person, since guidance enters a heart that is receptive, not distracted or talking. The verse links this respectful listening to the hope of God's mercy, meaning that mercy is gained by humbly receiving His word, letting it reshape one's understanding and conduct, and not by merely hearing its sounds. Many scholars have applied the command especially to the congregational prayer and the Friday sermon, but its spirit extends to any occasion when God's words are being recited.

translation: And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness in speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the most sincere remembrance of God is inward and humble: it springs from a heart that is submissive, aware of God's majesty, and fearful of falling short, and it is expressed in a gentle voice rather than a loud or showy one. This quiet devotion protects against ostentation and keeps the worshipper's attention truly on God. It is to be kept up at the start and the end of each day, so that remembrance frames all of one's time. The closing warning against being 'among the heedless' shows that neglect of God is the real spiritual danger. Constant, sincere, quiet remembrance keeps a person aware of God, whereas heedlessness gradually hardens the heart and leads it away from Him.

translation: Indeed, those who are near your Lord do not disdain to worship Him; they glorify Him, and before Him they prostrate.
interpretation: The verse points to the angels, those nearest to God, who for all their closeness and honor never grow proud or consider themselves above worship. Their nearness leads to deeper humility rather than arrogance. Worship is thus the natural state of every being that truly knows God, and pride in the face of God is a deviation from the way of the closest creatures. The verse invites human beings to follow their example by constantly glorifying God and prostrating to Him, and it is why a prostration of recitation is made at this verse, so that the reader joins the angels in humility and submission.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. They ask you about the spoils of war. Say: The spoils belong to God and the Messenger. So fear God, set right what is between you, and obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers.
interpretation: This verse was revealed after the Battle of Badr, when the Muslims disagreed over how to distribute the war gains. By declaring that the spoils belong to God and His Messenger, the verse removes the matter from personal claims and competition, and places its distribution under divine authority, administered justly by the Prophet. The verse then draws the moral lesson: disputes over worldly gain must not damage the unity of the community, so believers are commanded to be mindful of God, to reconcile and mend relations among themselves, and to obey God and His Messenger. Obedience and harmony are presented as proof of true faith, showing that faith is demonstrated by putting God's judgment and communal peace above material benefit.

translation: The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith by inner states that show up in a believer's heart and conduct. Faith is not a claim made by the tongue. It is a living reality that responds to God. The trembling of the heart at His mention is reverent awe, a mindfulness of His greatness, His nearness, and His accountability, and it keeps a person from heedlessness and disobedience. Hearing the Qur'an increases faith, which shows that faith is not fixed. It grows with reflection, understanding, and action on revelation, and it can weaken with neglect. Reliance on God, which completes the verse, means that after doing one's part, a believer entrusts the outcome to the Lord, free from dependence on creation and from despair. Together, awe, growth through revelation, and trust form a balanced inner life and the mark of sincere believers.

translation: Those who establish prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them.
interpretation: This verse describes the believers who combine devotion to God with care for His creation. To establish prayer means to perform it fully and consistently, with humility and presence of heart, so that it shapes one's conduct and keeps a person connected to God. Spending from what God has provided shows that wealth and ability are trusts from Him rather than personal possessions, and that gratitude is expressed by sharing them through obligatory charity, voluntary giving, and support for family and those in need. Pairing prayer with spending shows that true faith is both vertical, in worship of God, and horizontal, in service to others, and neither is complete without the other.

translation: Those are the believers in truth. They will have high ranks with their Lord, forgiveness, and an honorable provision.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:4) comes after describing the qualities of true believers: hearts that tremble at the mention of God, faith that increases when His verses are recited, reliance on Him alone, steadfast prayer, and spending from what He has provided. The verse teaches that genuine faith is not a mere claim on the tongue but a reality proven by inward states and outward deeds, and that those who embody these qualities earn the title of believers 'in truth.' Their reward is threefold: elevated ranks in God's presence, which vary according to the degree of their faith and works; forgiveness that erases their shortcomings; and a generous provision, which signifies God's lasting and noble bounty in the Hereafter, free from deficiency or reproach. The message is that faith has levels, and that true faith is rewarded with both honor and mercy.

translation: Just as your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth, while indeed a party of the believers were averse to it.
interpretation: The verse draws a comparison with the preceding discussion of the spoils of Badr, about which the believers disagreed. Just as some believers disliked leaving Medina to confront the Quraysh caravan and ended up facing the army at Badr, yet God's decree brought about victory and good for them, so too their reluctance over how the spoils were divided should be set aside in submission to God and His Messenger. What people dislike may contain great good, and the right course is to trust God's command and the Prophet's guidance, since God's choice for the believers is better than their own preferences. The Prophet's going out was by God's command and in accordance with truth, and the outcome vindicated it.

translation: They dispute with you about the truth after it has become clear, as though they were being driven to death while they looked on.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anfal 8:6) describes a group of believers who, before the Battle of Badr, were reluctant to march out to meet the Meccan army, even though the Prophet's command was divinely guided and its rightness was plain to them. Their fear of facing a much larger and better-equipped force made the prospect of battle feel like walking open-eyed to certain death. The point is that hesitation born of fear and worldly calculation can persist even after the truth is manifest, yet God's decree turned out to be the means of their victory and the vindication of the truth. The verse teaches that true faith means trusting God's command and His messenger over one's own estimate of risk, because what the heart dreads as ruin may be the very path God has chosen for deliverance.

translation: And [remember] when God promised you that one of the two groups would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours, but God willed to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse recalls the lead-up to the Battle of Badr. God had promised the believers either the Meccan trade caravan or the Quraysh army, and many of them hoped for the lightly defended caravan, which promised easy gain and no fighting. God's purpose was larger than their preference. By bringing them into confrontation with the armed Quraysh force, He meant to vindicate the truth by fulfilling His decree and promise, and to break the power of the leaders of disbelief, cutting them off at the root. The lesson is that God's wisdom and plan for the triumph of truth surpass human desires for comfort and quick gain, and that believers should trust His choice even when it leads through hardship and trial.

translation: So that He may establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even if the wrongdoers dislike it.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:8) explains the divine purpose behind the events of Badr: God arranged the outcome so that the truth of Islam would be proven and made firm, and the falsehood of idolatry would be shown to be void. The victory of a small, ill-equipped believing force over a much larger army was not a matter of chance but a manifestation of God's will and a demonstration that truth ultimately prevails through His support, however much those who persist in wrongdoing may resent and resist it. The lesson is that God's purposes are accomplished regardless of the opposition of the criminals, and that believers should place their trust in Him rather than in numbers or material means.

translation: (Remember) when you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one after another."
interpretation: This verse recalls the eve of the Battle of Badr, when the outnumbered Muslims, aware of their weakness, cried out to God for rescue. Their sincere supplication was met with an immediate response: God promised to support them with angels arriving in successive ranks. The verse teaches that victory does not come from numbers or material strength but from God, and that earnest turning to Him in times of distress is answered. The angels served as reassurance and strengthening of the believers' hearts, so that they would stand firm, while the true source of help remained God alone.

translation: Allah made it only as glad tidings and so that your hearts may be reassured by it. And victory is only from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The reinforcement of angels sent to the believers at Badr was not a replacement for Allah's power, but a mercy: it gave the believers good news of support and calmed their anxious hearts in the face of a much larger enemy. The verse then reminds them that the cause of victory is never the angels, their own numbers, or their weapons, but Allah alone. He is Almighty, so no force can prevent what He decrees, and All-Wise, so He grants or withholds victory according to perfect wisdom. The believers should therefore rely on Allah rather than on the means, while still striving and using those means.

translation: When He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sent down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby, to remove from you the defilement of Satan, to strengthen your hearts, and to make your feet firm thereby.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:11) recalls God's favors to the believers at Badr, when they were few, anxious, and thirsty. The sleep that overcame them was a divine mercy that calmed their fear and renewed their strength, showing that real security comes from God and not from numbers or equipment. The rain served several purposes: it allowed ritual and physical purification, and it removed the whispering of Satan, who had stirred up despair and doubt by suggesting that God's help would not come while they were weak, thirsty, and impure. It also bound their hearts with certainty and patience, and it firmed the sand beneath their feet so they could stand and fight. The lesson is that God supports the sincere through both inner means (tranquility and steadfast hearts) and outer means (water and solid ground), and that trust in Him dispels Satan's fear-mongering.

translation: When your Lord inspired the angels: 'I am with you, so make firm those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve; so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip.'
interpretation: This verse recalls God's direct support of the believers at the Battle of Badr. God assures the angels of His presence with them and tasks them with strengthening the believers' hearts and resolve, so that victory is understood to come from divine aid and not from numbers or equipment alone. At the same time, He casts fear into the hearts of the disbelievers, which undermines their morale and ability to fight before the blows even land. The command to strike above the necks and at every fingertip is understood as an instruction to fight decisively and thoroughly against the enemy forces, targeting their heads and their means of wielding weapons, so that their aggression is fully disabled. The lesson is that faith, steadfastness, and reliance on God bring inner firmness for the believers, while opposing God's truth brings fear and defeat.

translation: That is because they opposed God and His Messenger; and whoever opposes God and His Messenger — indeed, God is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse explains the reason behind the disgrace and defeat that befell the disbelievers: it was not chance or mere political circumstance, but the direct consequence of their deliberate hostility and separation from God and His Messenger, taking a side opposed to divine guidance. The word 'shaqqu' implies placing oneself in a separate camp, as if cleaving away from the community of truth and standing against it. The verse then lays down a general principle beyond that particular event: anyone who takes the same stance of opposition and defiance will face God's severe retribution, which may come in this world through humiliation and loss, and in the next through a harsher punishment. It is both an explanation of past events and a warning that obedience to God and His Messenger is the path of safety.

translation: That is for you, so taste it! And indeed, for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Anfal (8:14), addresses the disbelievers after the defeat they suffered at Badr, and it carries a tone of rebuke. Their worldly humiliation is described as a foretaste of a greater and lasting punishment. The command to 'taste it' presents the suffering as something they must experience firsthand, a consequence of their denial and hostility to the truth and not an arbitrary harm. The verse teaches that divine justice has two stages: disbelief and opposition to God's message can bring a disgrace in this world, but that is only a small portion of the real reckoning, which is the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. It warns people to take heed from earlier consequences before the final one arrives.

translation: O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing in battle, do not turn your backs to them in flight.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:15) lays down a rule of steadfastness for believers in a lawful, defensive battle: when an organized hostile army marches in force against them, they must not flee and abandon their comrades and their position. Fleeing in the face of the enemy weakens the community's morale and endangers everyone, so the command calls for courage and discipline grounded in trust in God. The following verse allows only for tactical maneuvering or regrouping with other fighters, which is not true flight. The verse thus treats desertion in the face of an advancing enemy as a grave wrong, while connecting firmness to faith.

translation: And whoever turns his back to them on such a day—unless maneuvering for battle or joining another company—has certainly incurred wrath from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:16) makes fleeing from the battlefield a grave sin when believers face an enemy in a legitimate, defensive fight, because desertion endangers the whole community and shows a lack of trust in Allah. It allows only two exceptions: a tactical withdrawal meant to regroup and return to the fight, and retreating to join another body of believers for support. Both serve the goal of fighting, not escape. The severe warning of divine wrath and Hell shows the seriousness of steadfastness and discipline in defending the community, while the allowed exceptions show Islam's realism and respect for sound strategy over reckless self-destruction.

translation: It was not you who killed them, but God who killed them. And you [Muhammad] did not throw when you threw, but God threw. And [He did this] so that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him. Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse, revealed regarding the Battle of Badr, teaches that human action achieves its results only through God's enabling power and will. The believers' victory over a much larger force was not the product of their own strength, numbers, or skill, but of divine support, and the Prophet's throwing of a handful of dust, though a real human act, reached its effect only because God made it do so. This does not erase human responsibility; rather it directs the believers away from pride and self-reliance toward humility and gratitude, so that success is credited to God. The 'good trial' is that God gave the believers victory and spoils, which both honored them and tested their thankfulness and steadfastness. The closing names, All-Hearing and All-Knowing, affirm that God heard their pleas for help and knew their sincerity and needs, so His aid came with perfect wisdom.

translation: That is for you; and know that Allah will weaken the scheming of the disbelievers.
interpretation: After announcing the believers' victory at Badr and the punishment awaiting the disbelievers, the verse affirms that the outcome was by Allah's decree and not by the believers' own strength. Beyond this event, it states a lasting principle: however carefully the disbelievers plan and plot against the truth, Allah undermines and nullifies their scheming, so their plans fail and cannot overcome those who rely on Him. This should give the believers confidence and steadfastness, and it warns the disbelievers that their power and cunning will not save them.

translation: If you sought a decision, the decision has indeed come to you. And if you desist, it is better for you. But if you return, We will return, and your host will not avail you at all, even if it be numerous. And indeed, God is with the believers.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:19) addresses the Quraysh disbelievers, who before Badr had prayed that God grant victory to whichever party was in the right. God tells them the decision has now come: the Muslims' victory at Badr and their own defeat showed where the truth lay. He then offers them a way out: if they stop fighting the Prophet and persecuting the believers, that is better for them in this world and the next. If they return to hostility, God will return to defeating them, and their large numbers and equipment will not protect them, because victory comes from God rather than from numerical strength. The verse ends by stating that God is with the believers, supporting and defending those who have faith, and that this divine support is the true cause of their success.

translation: O you who believe, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to make obedience to God and His Messenger a practical commitment, not just a claim of faith. Turning away after hearing the message is especially blameworthy because it is not a result of ignorance but of willful neglect. Hearing here means understanding and accepting the guidance, so whoever hears the truth and then ignores it has failed the very purpose of listening. True faith is shown by acting on what one has heard.

translation: And be not like those who said, 'We have heard,' while they do not listen.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anfal 8:21) warns believers against claiming obedience verbally without true inner receptiveness and practical response. Real hearing in the Qur'anic sense is not merely the perception of sounds or words but attentive understanding that leads to acceptance and action. Those who say 'we hear' while their hearts remain unmoved and their conduct unchanged are hypocrites or heedless people, and the believers are urged to make their words match their deeds, responding to God and His Messenger with sincere submission.

translation: Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not use reason.
interpretation: God calls those who refuse to hear the truth, refuse to speak it, and refuse to reflect on it worse than animals, because animals follow their natural instincts and fulfill the purpose they were created for, whereas these people were given hearing, speech, and intellect and yet choose to waste them. Their deafness and dumbness are not physical defects but a moral and spiritual failure: they close their ears to the guidance of the Qur'an and the Prophet, do not voice or acknowledge the truth, and do not apply their intellect to what is plainly in front of them. Because they have the ability to understand and still reject, they fall below the level of beasts and are held more blameworthy before God.

translation: Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear; but even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away, averse.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anfal 8:23) explains that the hearing meant here is the hearing of understanding and acceptance, not merely of the ears. Those who heard the message and rejected it had no sincere openness to truth in their hearts, so God did not grant them the inner receptivity that makes guidance take root. Even if He had made them grasp the message in its full clarity, their stubbornness and arrogance would have led them to turn away knowingly. Thus their deafness to guidance is not due to a lack of proof but to the corruption of their own intentions; God's withholding of such hearing is a just response to what He knows of their inner state, and the verse warns believers not to be like them by hearing without responding.

translation: O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true life, spiritual and moral as well as worldly, lies in answering the call of God and His Messenger at once, without delay or hesitation. The revealed guidance revives the heart, gives purpose, and brings honor in this world and the next. The believer is warned not to postpone obedience, because the heart is not under one's own control: God can turn it, and He can come between a person and his intentions, so the chance to do good may be lost, or a heart that keeps refusing may be left to harden. This should lead to humility, constant prayer for steadfastness, and quick action when truth is made clear. The verse ends by reminding that everyone will be gathered before God and held to account, so the response to His call now decides one's condition then.

translation: And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong, and know that God is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns the believing community that wrongdoing, when left unchecked, brings consequences that reach everyone, not only those who commit it. A society that sees injustice, corruption or disobedience and stays silent, or fails to enjoin good and forbid evil, shares in the resulting calamity, because the harm spreads through the whole community. The believers are therefore called to take collective responsibility: to guard themselves against sin, to correct wrongdoing where they can, and to avoid complacency. The closing reminder that God is severe in punishment underlines the seriousness of this duty and the need for vigilance and accountability.

translation: And remember when you were few, regarded as weak in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away, but He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, so that you might be grateful.
interpretation: The verse calls the early Muslim community to recall its former vulnerability in Mecca, when it was small, oppressed and in constant fear of being seized by stronger tribes, and to see its present security as the result of God's care and not of its own strength. The shelter in Medina, the support that brought victory such as at Badr, and the lawful sustenance that followed were all God's gifts. The remembrance is meant to produce gratitude, which means humility, obedience to God and Messenger, and not taking security or power for granted. Believers who recall how God lifted them from weakness should trust Him in later trials and show thanks by faithful action.

translation: O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith carries a duty of faithfulness, and that betraying God and His Messenger is bound up with betraying the trusts people hold. Betraying God and the Messenger means neglecting obligations, violating what has been made lawful and unlawful, or undermining the community's interests through disloyalty. Betraying one's trusts means abusing responsibilities, property, secrets, and positions of authority that others have entrusted to you. The phrase 'while you know' stresses that this betrayal is not an innocent mistake but a conscious act, which makes it more blameworthy. In this reading, honesty in dealings with people is part of one's loyalty to God, so a believer's integrity must show in both worship and everyday social responsibility.

translation: And know that your wealth and your children are but a trial, and that with God is a great reward.
interpretation: Wealth and children, though natural blessings and objects of deep attachment, are a test of one's faithfulness. They can draw a person away from obedience to God, honesty in trust, and fulfillment of duty, as the verse's context of betraying trusts out of concern for family and property shows. The believer is therefore urged not to let love of possessions or offspring outweigh loyalty to God, since what God holds in store for those who pass this test is far greater and more lasting than anything these worldly attachments can provide.

translation: O you who believe, if you fear God, He will grant you a criterion to distinguish right from wrong, will absolve you of your misdeeds, and will forgive you. And God is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:29) teaches that God-consciousness (taqwa) is the source of inner clarity and spiritual reward. A believer who remains mindful of God and avoids what displeases Him is granted a furqan: a God-given discernment, insight and moral light that lets him tell truth from falsehood and guidance from error in confusing situations, and, as many commentators add, a way out of difficulty and a decisive support from God. Alongside this clarity comes purification, for God erases the believer's lesser sins and forgives the rest, removing their consequences. The closing phrase reminds us that these gifts are not wages earned by the believer's deeds alone but come from God's immense generosity, which exceeds what anyone could deserve.

translation: And [remember, O Muhammad] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you, or kill you, or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of those who plot.
interpretation: The verse recalls the Quraysh's council at Dar al-Nadwa in Mecca, where the leaders debated how to stop the Prophet: imprisoning him, banishing him, or killing him. Their scheming was met by God's greater, unseen planning, which protected the Prophet, led him to emigrate safely to Medina, and turned their plots back on them. Calling God 'the best of planners' means His design always prevails and is just, since it is aimed at defending truth and defeating falsehood, unlike the deceit and injustice in human conspiracies. The lesson for believers is that no hostile scheme can overcome God's will, so they should trust Him and stay steadfast even when enemies seem to hold the upper hand.

translation: And when Our verses are recited to them, they say: 'We have already heard; if we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the tales of the ancients.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance and insincerity of those who reject revelation. Rather than reflecting on the message, they dismiss it with a boastful claim that they could easily produce something similar, though they never did so despite the Qur'an's repeated challenge to bring a comparable text. Their label of 'tales of the ancients' is a way of belittling the Qur'an as mere old folklore, which spares them from facing its moral and spiritual demands. The verse shows that rejection often stems from pride and unwillingness to submit rather than from a lack of evidence, and that empty claims of ability, unaccompanied by action, are no refutation of the truth.

translation: And [remember] when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment."
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anfal 8:32) exposes the arrogant stubbornness of the disbelieving Quraysh. Their challenge was not an honest search for truth but a mocking dare, voiced in the belief that no punishment would ever come. Instead of saying 'guide us to it if it is true,' which would have been the sincere response, they asked for destruction, showing that their rejection came from pride and tribal obstinacy rather than lack of evidence. The lesson is that a heart hardened against the truth would rather invite calamity than submit, and that Allah's delay in punishing such people is mercy and a respite, not proof that the message is false. The following verse makes this clear: Allah would not punish them while the Prophet was among them and while they sought forgiveness.

translation: But Allah would not punish them while you, [O Muhammad], are among them, and Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness.
interpretation: The verse explains why divine punishment was withheld from the Quraysh despite their opposition. Two things protected them: the presence of the Prophet among them, since God's mercy toward a community encompasses the one sent to guide it, and their seeking of forgiveness, which acts as a shield against destruction. Once the Prophet had left and they no longer sought forgiveness, they had no such protection. The verse also teaches that repentance and istighfar are lasting safeguards against collective calamity, so that as long as people turn back to God and ask His pardon, He delays His punishment and gives them the chance to mend their ways.

translation: And why should Allah not punish them, when they bar people from the Sacred Mosque, though they are not its rightful guardians? Its rightful guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse explains that the Quraysh's claim to custodianship of the Sacred Mosque gave them no immunity from divine punishment. Guardianship of a sacred place is a matter of moral and spiritual qualification, not lineage or control. Those who obstruct worshippers, as they did by expelling the Prophet and the believers and preventing them from performing pilgrimage, forfeit any right to it. Only people with taqwa, those who revere God and uphold the purpose for which the House was built, are its true guardians. Most of the disbelievers do not realize this because they confuse worldly authority and inherited status with true entitlement before God.

translation: Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse condemns the idolaters of Quraysh, who claimed to be the custodians of the Sacred House yet turned their worship there into empty noise: they circled the Kaaba whistling and clapping, mocking true worship and perhaps drowning out the Prophet's recitation. What they called prayer had no humility, remembrance of God, or sincerity, so it could not give them any claim to guardianship of the sanctuary or protect them from God's punishment. The command to taste the punishment is a rebuke showing that their suffering is the just consequence of their persistent denial of the truth, not of mere ritual failure. Outward rites without reverence and faith carry no weight with God.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to hinder people from the path of God. They will spend it, then it will become a source of regret for them, and then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered into Hell.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth used to obstruct the truth is ultimately futile and self-destructive. The disbelievers pour out their money to oppose God's path, believing it will secure victory for their cause, but the outcome is the reverse: the money is lost, the failure of their effort leaves them with bitter regret, and their opposition is finally defeated, because God's guidance cannot be halted by human resources. Their loss is not confined to this world, since their regret in this life is only a prelude to being driven into Hell in the next. The lesson is that the worth of spending depends on its purpose: wealth spent to support truth brings reward, while wealth spent to suppress it brings loss in both worlds.

translation: So that God may separate the wicked from the good, and place the wicked one upon another, heap them all together, and cast them into Hell. Those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse says that worldly life mixes believers with disbelievers and lawful gain with unlawful gain, and that the Day of Judgment is the time of final sorting. On that day God will remove the corrupt, meaning corrupt people, deeds, and wealth spent to hinder others from God's path, from the pure. He will pile the corrupt together like a heap, with each one adding to the weight of another's ruin, and throw them into Hell. Their loss is total because they spent their wealth and effort on falsehood and gained only punishment. The lesson is that no corruption is lost in the crowd or hidden by outward success, and that only purity of faith and purity of deeds will count as true gain.

translation: Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them; but if they return to their ways, then the precedent of the earlier peoples has already come to pass.
interpretation: The verse offers disbelievers an open door to repentance: if they abandon unbelief and their hostility to the truth, God will wipe out their past wrongs, so that no earlier sin bars them from a fresh start. This shows the breadth of divine mercy, which erases the record of those who sincerely turn back. At the same time it carries a warning. If they go back to opposing the truth and fighting the believers, they should recall God's established way with earlier nations who persisted in denial and were destroyed or defeated. Divine justice follows a constant pattern, so the choice rests with them: accept forgiveness through desisting, or face the same fate as those before them.

translation: And fight them until there is no more persecution (fitnah) and the religion, all of it, is for Allah. But if they desist, then indeed Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse permits fighting against those who aggressively persecute believers, but only for a limited purpose: to end oppression and coercion in matters of faith so that worship and obedience can be freely and sincerely directed to God alone. It is not a license for endless war or for forcing belief. The aim is a situation in which no one is tormented or prevented from following their conscience. Once the aggressors stop their persecution, hostilities must also stop, and the believers must not go on attacking them. God knows the real intentions and deeds of everyone, so He will judge those who desist and those who persist, and no one's sincerity or hypocrisy escapes Him.

translation: And if they turn away, then know that Allah is your Protector and Master. What an excellent Protector, and what an excellent Helper!
interpretation: The verse tells the believers not to be shaken or discouraged when their opponents refuse the truth or break away from peace and obedience. The believers' security does not rest on the enemy's goodwill, on their own numbers, or on their strength, but on Allah, who is their Guardian and Patron. Whoever has Allah as their Protector cannot truly be abandoned or defeated, because He is the best of all protectors and the best of all helpers. This calls the believers to place their trust in Him and to go on acting with steadfastness and justice, confident that His support is enough, whatever others choose.

translation: And know that whatever you obtain as spoils of war, one-fifth of it belongs to God, the Messenger, the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, if you truly believe in God and in what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of Criterion, the day the two armies met. And God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse sets out how war booty is to be divided: it is not the property of the fighters alone, and the believers must give up one-fifth of it for a collective, divinely ordained purpose. That share is spent on the cause of God and the Messenger, the Prophet's relatives, and the vulnerable members of society: orphans, the poor, and travelers in need. This turns the spoils of battle from a source of greed and dispute, which had arisen among the Muslims after Badr, into a means of social solidarity and justice. Accepting this ruling is made a test of sincere faith, 'if you truly believe in God and what We revealed,' meaning that real belief shows in submitting to God's commands about wealth even when it costs one something. The reminder of the Day of Criterion, the Battle of Badr, teaches that the victory came from God's aid and not from the fighters' own strength, so the gains belong to God first and should be handled according to His command. The closing statement that God has power over all things reassures believers that He can bring about such victories again and that He will compensate those who obey Him.

translation: When you were on the nearer side of the valley, and they were on the farther side, and the caravan was below you. Had you made an appointment to meet, you would surely have differed over the appointment. But it was so that God might accomplish a matter that was already ordained, so that whoever perished might perish after clear evidence, and whoever lived might live after clear evidence. And indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse recalls the circumstances of the Battle of Badr and shows that the meeting of the believers and the Quraysh army was not a matter of human planning but of divine arrangement. The Muslims were camped on the near side of the valley closest to Medina, the Quraysh on the far side, and Abu Sufyan's caravan was on lower ground near the coast. Had the two sides set a time and place, disagreement, hesitation and the believers' fear of their enemy's superior numbers would have made them fail to keep it. God brought the two forces together unexpectedly so that His decree would be fulfilled: the victory of truth over falsehood at Badr. This was a clear, manifest sign, so that anyone who persisted in disbelief and was destroyed would perish after the proof had been made plain to him, and anyone who embraced faith and lived spiritually would do so with certainty and clear evidence. The closing statement that God is All-Hearing and All-Knowing reminds that He hears what people say and knows their intentions and circumstances, and that He orders events with perfect knowledge and wisdom.

translation: When God showed them to you in your dream as few; and had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost courage and disputed with one another about the matter. But God saved you. Indeed, He knows well what is within the hearts.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's mercy toward the believers before the Battle of Badr. God showed the Prophet the enemy as a small force in his dream, and he relayed this to his companions, which strengthened their morale and resolve. Had he seen them as numerous, fear would have weakened the believers, and disagreement would have arisen over whether to fight or withdraw. God's gentle management of events, which unfolded without the believers' awareness, spared them from discord and cowardice, and the closing phrase reminds that He knows the inner states of hearts, including their fears and hopes, and shapes events in accordance with that knowledge.

translation: And [remember] when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you appear few in their eyes, so that God might accomplish a matter that was already ordained. And to God all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Battle of Badr, where God shaped how each army perceived the other. The believers saw the idolaters as few, which strengthened their courage to engage, and the idolaters saw the believers as few, which made them underestimate them and fight rather than avoid battle. This convergence was no accident. It was a divine arrangement that brought the two sides to a decisive clash, so that God's already-decreed purpose, the vindication of truth and the defeat of disbelief, would be fulfilled. The closing phrase, 'to God all matters return,' teaches that outcomes are not determined by numbers, strength, or human planning. Causes and events all end with God's will and judgment, so believers should place their trust in Him rather than in their own resources.

translation: O you who believe, when you meet a company [of the enemy in battle], stand firm and remember God often, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that success in the hardest moments, such as facing an enemy in battle, depends on two things: steadfastness and constant remembrance of God. Firmness is the outward discipline of holding one's ground without panic or retreat, while remembering God is the inward support that keeps the heart tranquil, strengthens trust in His help, and purifies intention so that the fight is for His sake and not for pride or gain. Believers are told to remember God 'often' even in the most intense moments, which shows that remembrance is never to be abandoned, and that real success (falah) in this world and the next comes from joining courage with a heart attached to God.

translation: And obey God and His Messenger, and do not quarrel with one another, lest you lose heart and your strength depart; and be patient. Indeed, God is with the patient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a community's strength depends on unity under shared guidance. Obedience to God and the Messenger gives believers a single standard to return to, so personal opinions, rivalries and ambitions do not split them. Once they quarrel, they lose courage and cohesion, and the 'wind' that carries their power, meaning their momentum, authority and the awe they command in others, fades away. The way to avoid this is patience: restraining the self, holding firm in hardship, and putting up with disagreement for the sake of the common cause. The promise that God is with the patient assures believers that steadfastness and discipline are met with God's support and help, and that their weakness comes from division, not from lack of numbers.

translation: And do not be like those who came out from their homes in arrogance and to be seen by people, and who hinder others from the path of God. And God encompasses all that they do.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Battle of Badr, warns believers against adopting the character of the Quraysh who marched out with pride, display, and ostentation, seeking praise and prestige rather than truth. The believers are told that their striving must be sincere and purely for God's sake, free from vanity and showing off, and that they must not act as obstacles to others on God's path. The closing phrase reminds them that God knows and encompasses everything people do, including their hidden motives, so no intention or deed escapes Him and every action will be weighed accordingly. The lesson is that sincerity (ikhlas) and humility are the foundation of any act of struggle or worship, while arrogance and hypocrisy lead to failure and divine reckoning.

translation: And [remember] when Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and indeed I am your protector." But when the two armies came within sight of each other, he turned back on his heels and said, "Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I see what you do not see; indeed, I fear God. And God is severe in punishment."
interpretation: The verse shows how Satan deceives people: he beautifies their wrongdoing, fills them with false confidence and promises of protection, then abandons them when the consequences become real. Referring to the Quraysh before Badr, it says they marched out in arrogance, trusting in their numbers and in Satan's whispered assurance of safety. When the two forces met and the angelic support for the believers became apparent to him, Satan fled, disowning his followers and claiming a fear of God. The lesson is that Satan's promises are empty and his allegiance is only a snare; those who follow him are left alone at the moment of crisis, while reliance on God and awareness of His severe retribution is the only true protection.

translation: When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, 'These people (the believers) have been deluded by their religion.' But whoever puts his trust in God, then surely God is Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: At Badr, the hypocrites of Medina and those with weak faith looked at the small, poorly equipped band of Muslims marching to face a far larger Qurayshi army and judged it reckless, concluding that the believers' religion had deceived them into courting destruction. The verse rebukes this purely material calculation. The believers' confidence rested on reliance (tawakkul) on God, not on numbers or equipment, and whoever relies on God will not be abandoned, because God is 'Aziz (Almighty), whom no force can overcome and who gives victory to the weak against the strong, and Hakim (All-Wise), who orders events with perfect wisdom. What looked like delusion to the doubters was in fact well-founded trust in the One who controls all outcomes, and the result at Badr vindicated it.

translation: If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs, and saying: 'Taste the punishment of the Burning Fire.'
interpretation: The verse describes the moment of death for those who persisted in disbelief and opposition to the truth: it is not a gentle release but the start of their accountability. The angels who take their souls strike them on the face, which they turned away from guidance, and on the back, which they turned toward truth, so the blows mirror their stance in life. The words 'taste the punishment of the Burning Fire' tell them that the suffering begun at death is a foretaste of the greater punishment of the Hereafter, and that it is the just consequence of their own choices. The address to the Prophet ('If only you could see') underscores how terrible the scene is, as a warning to hearers to reflect before that moment arrives.

translation: That is because of what your hands have sent forth, and because God is never unjust to His servants.
interpretation: The punishment the wrongdoers face is not arbitrary but is the direct consequence of their own deeds and choices, which are here described as what their 'hands' have sent ahead of them to the Hereafter. God's justice is perfect: He does not wrong anyone by adding to their burden or denying them their due. The verse teaches that every person is accountable for what they themselves have earned, and that any suffering they meet in the Hereafter is the fair outcome of their own conduct rather than any injustice from their Lord.

translation: Like the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they disbelieved in the signs of God, so God seized them for their sins. Indeed, God is Strong and severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse points to a consistent divine pattern: when nations persistently reject clear signs and revelation, their wrongdoing brings about their downfall. The disbelievers of Quraysh, who were defeated at Badr, are warned that their fate follows the same path as Pharaoh's people and earlier denying communities. Their power, status and numbers could not protect them, because God's strength is absolute and His punishment is just, being a direct consequence of their own sins rather than arbitrary harshness. The lesson is to take heed of history, accept the truth when it comes, and recognize that worldly might is no defense against God's decree.

translation: That is because God would never change a favor which He has bestowed upon a people until they change what is within themselves, and because God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 8:53) states a divine principle: God does not withdraw blessings such as security, prosperity, or power from a community as an arbitrary act, but only after that community alters its inner state, through ingratitude, corruption, injustice, and turning away from the guidance and the moral conduct for which the blessing was given. The punishment of Pharaoh's people and others like them came about because they first changed themselves, so the loss of their favor was the result of their own choices and not an injustice from God. The closing words, that God is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, affirm that He hears what people say and knows their intentions and hidden states, so He judges with perfect knowledge and justice. The verse thus places responsibility for a community's fortunes on its own moral and spiritual condition and calls people to gratitude and self-reform in order to keep God's favors.

translation: Like the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins, and We drowned the people of Pharaoh, and all of them were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment follows a consistent pattern rather than being arbitrary. The disbelievers of Quraysh, who rejected the Prophet and the signs brought to them, are warned that they are following the same path as earlier nations such as Pharaoh's people. Those nations were not destroyed because of mere power or chance, but because they denied God's clear signs and persisted in sin and injustice. The destruction of Pharaoh's people by drowning, despite their might and worldly power, shows that no strength can protect a people who reject truth and oppress others. The closing phrase, 'and all of them were wrongdoers,' makes clear that they wronged themselves through disbelief and wronged others through oppression, so the punishment was just, a consequence of their own conduct rather than an injustice from God. The lesson is that nations and individuals should take heed from history, repent, and accept guidance before the same fate overtakes them.

translation: Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are those who disbelieve, for they will not believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human worth before God is measured by the use of the faculties of reason, hearing, and conscience He has given, not by outward form or status. Animals follow their nature and fulfil the purpose for which they were created, but those who knowingly reject the truth, after clear signs have come to them, and who persist in that rejection with hardened hearts, have wasted the very capacities that set them above animals. This is why they are called the worst of creatures. The phrase 'for they will not believe' points to a settled stubbornness, not a passing doubt: they have closed their hearts so firmly that no evidence or warning moves them. The verse is therefore a warning that accountability grows with awareness, and that the one who is given the ability to understand yet deliberately turns away falls lower than those who never had that gift.

translation: Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they have no fear of God.
interpretation: The verse describes a group, understood by most commentators to be certain Jewish tribes of Medina, who repeatedly made treaties with the Prophet and then violated them whenever it suited them, as in the conflict with Quraysh at the Battle of the Trench. Their breach was not an occasional lapse but a habitual pattern, and it came from lacking taqwa, meaning no awareness of God and no concern for the consequences of betraying a solemn pledge. The verse teaches that keeping covenants is bound up with God-consciousness, and that people who regularly betray agreements show they do not truly fear God. Such people are rightly treated as untrustworthy and dangerous to the community, so the believers must deal with them firmly and not rely on their promises.

translation: So if you overcome them in war, then disperse by [making an example of] them those who are behind them, so that perhaps they will remember.
interpretation: The verse speaks of those who repeatedly break their treaties and covenants (as described in the preceding verses, Al-Anfal 8:55-58). When the believers gain the upper hand over such treaty-breakers in battle, they are to respond with a decisive and deterring response, so that other hostile parties watching from behind, who might be planning similar betrayal or aggression, are scattered and frightened away from it. The aim is deterrence, not vengeance: a firm stance against perfidy in wartime should lead others to reflect, take heed, and refrain from treachery and attacks on the Muslim community, thereby reducing further bloodshed and securing peace. This is bound to the context of war against active covenant-breakers and is not a general license for cruelty, since Islamic teachings elsewhere restrict conduct in war to justice and proportion.

translation: And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back their treaty to them on equal terms. Indeed, God does not love the treacherous.
interpretation: This verse sets an ethical rule for ending treaties. If there are real signs that a party to a covenant is preparing to betray it, the believers may not attack by surprise or act as though the pact still stands while secretly treating it as void. They must openly announce the termination, so that both sides know the treaty is over and stand on equal footing. Even when the other party is suspected of treachery, Muslims must stay honest, transparent and just, because God dislikes betrayal in every form. Suspicion alone does not license deceit, and war must not begin by breaking faith.

translation: And let not those who disbelieve think that they have outstripped [Allah's reach]; indeed, they cannot cause [Him] to fail.
interpretation: The verse assures believers and warns the disbelievers that no one can escape Allah's power or judgment. Those who reject the truth may imagine that, because they are not punished immediately, or because they have won a temporary advantage, they have gotten away with it or outrun the consequences of their deeds. The verse corrects that illusion. Everyone is within Allah's knowledge and dominion, and nothing can frustrate His will. Any respite is a delay that tests people and gives them time to repent, not an escape. The believers can therefore trust in Allah's justice, while the disbelievers should recognize that their schemes and strength cannot defeat His decree.

translation: And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of tethered horses, by which you may strike fear into the enemy of God and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know, but God knows them. And whatever you spend in the cause of God will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse commands the believers to maintain real, continuous readiness, using whatever means of strength their era makes available, from the cavalry of the Prophet's time to any later equivalent in arms, training, and resources. The purpose of this preparation is deterrence: to make aggressors fear attacking the community, so that war is prevented rather than sought. The 'others whom you do not know' are hidden or potential adversaries, such as secret enemies, hypocrites, or future threats, whom only God knows, so the community must stay vigilant and not rely only on visible dangers. The verse ends by urging generous spending for this just cause, promising that no sacrifice will be lost or undervalued, since God will repay it fully, whether in this life or in the next.

translation: And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [as well] and rely upon God. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that peace is the preferred course whenever the opposing side sincerely leans toward it. After the earlier instructions about readiness and fighting in Surah al-Anfal, the Prophet is told not to prolong conflict out of pride or suspicion, but to accept a genuine offer of peace. The command to rely on God addresses the natural fear that the enemy may be deceiving or planning betrayal. The believer acts on the apparent sincerity of the offer, takes reasonable precautions, and leaves the hidden intentions to God. The closing names, the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, assure the believers that God hears the proposals and knows the true motives behind them, so He will protect those who choose peace in good faith and hold accountable those who use it to deceive.

translation: And if they intend to deceive you, then indeed Allah is sufficient for you. He is the One who supported you with His help and with the believers.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:62) reassures the Prophet that if enemies feign peace as a ruse to deceive him, he need not fear or refuse the offer of peace, because Allah is his sufficient protector and will expose their schemes. His confidence rests on past experience: Allah already strengthened him with direct divine aid, such as at Badr, and with the believers whose hearts He united in loyalty. The meaning is that a believer should act in good faith and accept sincere offers of peace while relying on Allah rather than on suspicion or on material strength alone, since the One who granted victory before can protect against betrayal now.

translation: And He brought their hearts together. If you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have brought their hearts together, but God brought them together. Indeed, He is Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that real unity among people is a gift from God and cannot be bought or forced by wealth or worldly means. The Arabs of Medina, especially the Aws and Khazraj, had long been divided by blood feuds and pride. Faith in God and love for the sake of the truth softened their hearts and made them brothers, something no amount of money or effort by the Prophet could have achieved alone. This unity came from God's might, since He controls hearts and turns them as He wills, and from His wisdom, since He joined them through the message of Islam at the right time and by the right means. The lesson is that lasting harmony among believers is founded on sincere faith and reliance on God, and that the believers should be grateful for it and preserve it.

translation: O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and for those of the believers who follow you.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:64) assures the Prophet Muhammad that he needs no support beyond God, who suffices him as protector, helper, and sustainer, and that this same divine sufficiency extends to the believers who follow him. It teaches that true reliance (tawakkul) rests on God alone, even while believers take practical means such as preparation and unity. The victory and security of the community come not from numbers or material strength but from God's support, so a small group of sincere followers, bound to the Prophet in faith and obedience, can face a far larger enemy with confidence and steadfastness.

translation: O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a hundred, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to rouse and encourage the believers for battle, assuring them that faith and steadfastness multiply their strength: each steadfast believer can prevail over ten disbelievers. The reason given is that the disbelievers fight without true understanding. They do not grasp the purpose of life or the truth, and they have no hope of divine reward or help from God, so they lack the inner conviction and resolve that sustain the believers. Victory therefore depends not on numbers alone but on patience, certainty of faith, and reliance on God.

translation: Now Allah has lightened the burden for you, knowing that there is weakness in you. So if there are among you a hundred who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.
interpretation: This verse reflects divine mercy and realism in legislating hardship. Earlier (8:65), the believers were told that one steadfast fighter could overcome ten of the enemy, a standard demanding great strength of faith and resolve. Here God eases the obligation, acknowledging human frailty, so that the expected ratio becomes one to two: a steadfast group should hold firm against double its number. The ease is not a lowering of the importance of patience but an adjustment to the believers' actual capacity, and victory remains conditional on sabr (steadfastness) and on God's permission, not on numbers or material strength alone. The closing phrase, 'Allah is with the steadfast,' assures that God's support, guidance, and help accompany those who endure with perseverance, making steadfastness the true source of strength.

translation: It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has fought and prevailed in the land. You desire the fleeting goods of this world, while Allah desires the Hereafter. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse was revealed after the Battle of Badr, when some Muslims favored taking ransom for the prisoners of war. It teaches that a prophet and his community should not take captives for the sake of ransom or material gain until the enemy's power has been broken and the believers' position is firmly established. Sparing prisoners for the sake of money reflects a preference for worldly gain, whereas Allah wants His followers to aim at the higher goal of the Hereafter, which includes strengthening the truth and weakening the forces of aggression. The closing reminder that Allah is Almighty and All-Wise affirms that His rulings come from perfect wisdom and power, and that victory comes from Him, not from wealth.

translation: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:68) addresses the Muslims after the Battle of Badr, when they accepted ransom for the prisoners of war rather than executing them. It conveys that God had previously decreed, in His prior knowledge and ruling, that He would not punish a people for an act of ijtihad done in good faith before a prohibition was revealed, and that He had made war booty lawful for this community. Because of this prior decree and His mercy, the believers were spared a severe punishment. The lesson is that decisions taken in a time of war should be guided by the objective of establishing the truth and strengthening the religion rather than by worldly gain, and that God's mercy and forgiveness extend to His servants when they err without ill intent.

translation: So eat of what you have taken as war booty, lawful and good, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: After the Battle of Badr, the Muslims had disagreed about the captives and the spoils, and they were rebuked for wanting worldly gain. This verse then removes their anxiety by declaring that the booty, once rightly distributed under God's ruling, is lawful and wholesome for them to enjoy. The command to eat is a permission to benefit from it without guilt, but it is joined with a command of taqwa: they must keep within God's limits, not let the pursuit of spoils corrupt their intentions in fighting, and not take any share unjustly. The verse ends by reminding believers that God forgives their earlier lapses, such as their eagerness for ransom and worldly gain, and shows mercy by making what was once forbidden to earlier nations lawful for them.

translation: O Prophet, say to those captives who are in your hands: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what has been taken from you, and He will forgive you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, revealed after Badr, addresses the prisoners who had been made to pay ransom and who feared they had lost everything. It tells them that their real worth lies in the sincerity of their hearts and not in their wealth or status. If they turn to faith and sincerity, God will compensate them with something better than the ransom they paid, whether in this world through provision and honor, or in the next through reward, and He will forgive their past disbelief and hostility. The verse shows God's mercy even toward former enemies, and it teaches that the door of repentance and renewal stays open to everyone, and that God judges by what is in the heart.

translation: But if they intend to betray you, they have already betrayed God before, and He gave you mastery over them. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the captives of Badr, reassures the Prophet that if those prisoners, while professing goodwill or repentance, secretly plan deceit against him, he need not fear it. Their treachery is nothing new: by rejecting the covenant of faith that God placed in human nature and by persisting in disbelief and hostility, they had already betrayed God, and He allowed the believers to defeat and capture them at Badr. The same God who gave victory over them before can do so again, so the Prophet should deal with them with clemency and trust in God rather than suspicion. His knowledge of what hearts conceal and His wisdom in ordering events mean that deceit cannot ultimately succeed against those who rely on Him.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and emigrated and striven with their wealth and their lives in the cause of God, and those who gave shelter and aid—they are allies of one another. But those who believed and did not emigrate—you have no obligation of alliance toward them at all until they emigrate. And if they seek your help in the matter of religion, then you must give help, except against a people between whom and you there is a treaty. And God is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse sets out the bonds of solidarity in the early Muslim community of Medina. The Emigrants (Muhajirun), who gave up home and property for their faith, and the Helpers (Ansar), who sheltered and supported them, formed one bonded community with mutual protection, support, and responsibility. Believers who stayed in Mecca and did not emigrate were still brothers in faith, but they were not part of this political and social covenant, so the full obligations of mutual protection did not apply to them until they joined the community. Even so, faith keeps a claim of brotherhood: if such believers are oppressed for their religion and ask for help, Muslims must support them. That duty is limited by honoring treaties, so the community may not break a binding agreement with another people, even to help fellow believers. The verse shows that religious solidarity and the keeping of covenants must be held together, and it closes by reminding believers that God sees their conduct and will hold them to account for honoring both.

translation: And those who disbelieve are allies of one another. If you do not do this, there will be turmoil (fitnah) in the land and great corruption.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the disbelievers stand together in mutual support and solidarity against the believers, so the believers must likewise maintain real solidarity with one another: supporting, protecting, and inheriting from each other according to the bonds of faith, and holding firm to the covenant of mutual allegiance mentioned in the preceding verses. If the believers neglect this and let their ties dissolve or be set aside for other loyalties, their community will be weakened and divided. The result would be fitnah, meaning persecution, confusion, and the loss of the believers' security and ability to practice their faith openly, together with widespread corruption in society as falsehood and oppression gain the upper hand over truth and justice. The verse thus presents the unity and mutual allegiance of the believers as a safeguard for religion and for social order.

translation: Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the cause of God, and those who gave refuge and help—it is they who are the true believers. For them is forgiveness and a generous provision.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anfal 8:74) teaches that true faith is proven by action and sacrifice rather than by profession alone. The Emigrants (Muhajirun) showed it by leaving home and wealth and striving for God's religion, and the Helpers (Ansar) by sheltering and supporting them at cost to themselves. God calls them the true believers because their inner conviction was confirmed by costly deeds, and He rewards them with forgiveness for their sins and a noble, generous provision, which includes lawful sustenance in this world and abundant, honorable bounty in the Hereafter.

translation: And those who believed afterward and emigrated and strove with you – they are of you. But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another in the decree of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This closing verse of Surat al-Anfal widens the community of believers beyond the first generation. Those who accepted faith later, migrated, and struggled alongside the early Muslims are counted as full members of the community, sharing its rights, honor, and responsibilities, because belonging is based on faith and sacrifice, not on being first. It then clarifies that, while the pact of brotherhood and mutual support between Emigrants and Helpers had given them inheritance rights over one another during the early period, this was a temporary measure. Now blood relatives take precedence in inheritance, in accordance with God's ordained law in His Book. The verse ends by affirming that God knows all things, so His rulings reflect perfect wisdom and suit every circumstance, and His legislation is to be trusted and followed.

translation: A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those of the polytheists with whom you made a treaty.
