interpretation: This opening verse of Surat At-Tawbah announces that Allah and His Messenger formally end the covenants with those polytheists who had violated their agreements, chiefly the Quraysh and their allies who broke the terms of Hudaybiyyah. Its address to the believers ('you made a treaty') shows that the Muslim community, as the treaty party, is being informed of the public termination of those pacts. The declaration is not an arbitrary act of aggression but a response to betrayal, and it gives the covenant-breakers a clear, public notice and a fixed period (set out in the following verses) so that the break is conducted openly and justly, not by treachery. The verse thus teaches that treaty obligations are serious, that breaking them has consequences, and that ending them must be done with clear announcement.

translation: So travel freely throughout the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape God, and that God will disgrace the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tawbah 9:2) grants the idolaters who had broken their treaties with the Muslims a fixed period of safe passage, four months, to move about without fear of attack, so that they may reflect, decide, and either embrace faith or make arrangements for their future. It is a declaration of fair warning rather than sudden aggression: the grace period removes any excuse for them. The reminder that they cannot frustrate God means that no one, whatever their strength, plans, or flight, can place themselves beyond God's power or decree; and the promise that God will disgrace the disbelievers teaches that persistent denial and treachery against truth end in humiliation and defeat, while justice is ultimately upheld by God.

translation: And a proclamation from God and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage: that God is free of obligation toward the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape God. And give glad tidings of a painful punishment to those who disbelieve.
interpretation: This verse is a public declaration made at the gathering of the greatest pilgrimage, announcing the formal end of the treaties and protections that had been extended to the idolaters who persisted in hostility and broke their pacts. The release from obligation is directed at those who rejected faith and violated their agreements, and it is made openly so that no one can claim ignorance. Yet the door of mercy remains open: repentance, meaning abandoning idolatry and turning to God, is better for them in this world and the next. Persisting in defiance will not let anyone out-maneuver or evade God's power, and the warning of painful punishment is the consequence awaiting those who remain in disbelief and stubborn opposition.

translation: Except those of the polytheists with whom you made a treaty, and who have not diminished you in anything nor supported anyone against you; so fulfil their treaty to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous (those who are mindful of Him).
interpretation: This verse sets a moral exception within the declaration of release from obligations toward the polytheists in Surah At-Tawbah. Treaty-partners who have proven faithful, neither breaking any term of the agreement nor aiding an enemy against the Muslims, must be treated with full justice: their covenant is to be honored completely until its agreed expiry. It teaches that Islam's ethic of keeping promises does not depend on shared belief but on the other party's own fidelity, and that fulfilling agreements is a mark of taqwa, God-consciousness, which God loves. Hostility is therefore directed only at those who betray, not at peaceful, trustworthy covenant-holders.

translation: But when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and seize them, and besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then let them go on their way. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse is best understood in its historical context: the Muslim community of Arabia was in a state of war with specific Meccan polytheist tribes who had broken their treaties and persecuted and fought the believers. After the grace period of the four sacred months, during which fighting was forbidden, the verse authorizes military action against those hostile, treaty-breaking combatants. The surrounding verses support this reading: those who kept their treaties are exempted (9:4), and anyone seeking asylum must be granted safety and escorted to a place of security (9:6). The command to 'let them go on their way' upon repentance shows that the aim was to end hostility and bring about security and the community's integration, not to destroy people for their beliefs, and the verse closes by stressing God's forgiveness and mercy, which leaves the door open to reconciliation once the aggression has ceased.

translation: And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of God; then escort him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.
interpretation: Even in the midst of a state of war with those who fought the believers, Islam commands that an individual who seeks safe passage in order to learn about the message must be granted security. He is to be given the opportunity to hear the Qur'an and understand the call without pressure or coercion, and when he has heard it, he must not be harmed but must be conveyed safely to a place where he feels secure, whether he accepts the faith or not. The reason given, 'because they are a people who do not know,' shows that much of their opposition stems from ignorance of the truth, so the believers are obliged to remove that ignorance through clear exposition and good conduct rather than force. The verse thus establishes the principle that faith is based on knowledge and free conviction, and that protecting a seeker's life and giving him a hearing is a duty of the Muslim community.

translation: How can the polytheists have a covenant with God and with His Messenger, except those with whom you made a treaty at the Sacred Mosque? So long as they remain true to you, remain true to them. Indeed, God loves the righteous.
interpretation: The verse asks how a covenant could stand with polytheists who have openly shown hostility and been ready to break every pledge whenever they gained the upper hand, so that no binding agreement with God and His Messenger can be expected to endure with them. It then excepts those who made a treaty with the Muslims at the Sacred Mosque, meaning the tribes who honored the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and did not betray it. The Muslims are commanded to deal with these tribes on the basis of reciprocity: as long as they keep faith and observe the terms, the believers must keep faith with them and fulfill the agreement to its term. The closing phrase, 'God loves the righteous', shows that fidelity to covenants is a part of piety (taqwa). Even in the context of war and the dissolution of treaties, Muslims must distinguish between the treacherous and the faithful, and must not treat the innocent as guilty.

translation: How [can there be a treaty with them]? If they were to gain the upper hand over you, they would not observe toward you any tie of kinship or any covenant. They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: God explains why the idolaters who persistently broke their agreements deserve no further trust: their record shows that when they have power they respect neither blood ties nor pledges. Their friendly words and promises are only a show to deceive the believers, while their hearts hold hostility and a determination to betray. Because most of them have abandoned honesty and loyalty to their word, a covenant with them would offer no real security, and the believers are therefore right to be cautious and to expect treachery from them until they prove sincere.

translation: They have sold the signs of God for a small price, and so they have turned people away from His path. Truly, evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who trade away divine guidance for worldly gain such as wealth, status, or the convenience of keeping their desires. By preferring these trivial benefits, they abandon or distort God's revelation, and their example and their concealment or misuse of the truth lead others away from the straight path. Their wrong is double: they lose guidance themselves and become obstacles to others. God calls their conduct evil because no worldly return, however large it may seem, can equal the worth of His signs.

translation: They do not observe toward a believer any tie of kinship or covenant of protection. And it is they who are the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse describes the polytheists who broke their treaties: their hostility is so deep that they respect no claim of kinship or binding pledge when dealing with believers. Because they violate every moral and legal bond that would normally restrain a person, and attack those who have done them no wrong, they are the true aggressors. The Qur'an thus places the blame for the conflict on their treachery and shows that the believers' stance toward them is a response to repeated betrayal of oaths, not aggression on the believers' part.

translation: But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then they are your brothers in religion. And We explain the verses in detail for a people who know.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 9:11) shows that sincere repentance changes the standing of those who were hostile to the believers. Once former aggressors abandon their enmity and show their change of heart through concrete acts, namely establishing prayer, which restores their bond with God, and giving zakah, which restores their bond with the community, they are no longer treated as enemies. They enter the fellowship of faith with the same rights and dignity as other believers, and the believers must accept them as true brothers and sisters without holding their past against them. The closing phrase, 'We explain the verses in detail for a people who know,' adds that God makes His rulings clear, and only those who reflect and have knowledge grasp the wisdom of this mercy: faith is a path open to anyone who returns sincerely, and its brotherhood rests on shared belief and practice rather than on lineage or past conflicts.

translation: But if they break their oaths after their covenant and defame your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for indeed, they have no binding oaths, so that they may desist.
interpretation: The verse sets conditions for fighting the polytheists who had made treaties with the Muslims. Fighting is permitted only if they violate their sworn agreements and attack Islam with slander and mockery. The 'leaders of disbelief' are those who instigate and lead the hostility and treachery, and by being confronted, their followers are deterred. Their oaths are described as worthless because they have shown they do not honor them. The aim of the fighting is not vengeance or conquest but to make them stop their aggression and treaty-breaking, so that they desist and peace and security are restored.

translation: Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths and resolved to expel the Messenger, and they were the ones who began hostilities against you the first time? Do you fear them? But Allah has more right that you should fear Him, if you are believers.
interpretation: The verse urges the believers to overcome hesitation and fear in confronting those who betrayed their treaties, plotted to drive the Prophet out of Mecca, and initiated aggression against the Muslims. It makes clear that the fighting is justified by the enemy's treachery and aggression, not by mere hostility. The deeper lesson is that fear of people must never outweigh reverence for God: true faith means that awe of God takes priority over dread of any human power, so a believer should stand firm in defending truth and justice when duty requires it, trusting God rather than fearing the enemy.

translation: Fight them; God will punish them at your hands, disgrace them, give you victory over them, and heal the hearts of a believing people.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 9:14) encourages the believers to fight the aggressors who broke their treaties and drove out the Messenger and persecuted the Muslims, promising that God's help comes through human effort. God makes the believers His instruments: their action brings just retribution on those who wronged them, humiliates the oppressors, and grants victory. It also promises emotional and spiritual relief, as the long-suffering believers, who endured persecution, betrayal, and loss, will have their hearts healed and their grievances answered. The verse links faith, righteous striving, and divine support, teaching that victory is ultimately from God yet realized through the believers' steadfast action against oppression.

translation: And He will remove the rage from their hearts. And God turns in mercy to whom He wills. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:15) follows the command to fight those who broke their treaties and aggressed against the believers. It teaches that the real healing for the believers' wounded hearts comes from God: He lifts the anger and pain that years of persecution and betrayal left behind, and gives them relief through vindication. It also shows that God's mercy stays open even to former enemies. Some of them may repent and embrace faith, and God accepts that repentance, because He alone knows what lies in hearts and who is sincere. His decisions about who is punished and who is forgiven are never arbitrary. They rest on perfect knowledge and wisdom, so believers should not take vengeance into their own hands, but trust God's judgment and welcome the repentance of those whom He guides.

translation: Or did you think that you would be left alone, while Allah has not yet made evident those among you who strove hard, and who did not take, besides Allah and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate confidant? And Allah is fully Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse teaches that faith is not established by a mere claim; it is proven through testing. Allah knows everything beforehand, so "has not yet known" means that He has not yet made manifest in reality, before people and in deeds, who is truly sincere. The sincere are those who strive in His cause with their wealth, selves, and efforts, and who keep their deepest loyalty and trust for Allah, His Messenger, and the believers alone. They do not take as a 'walijah', a close confidant or secret ally, those who oppose the faith and whose loyalties lie with its enemies. The verse stresses that outward profession is not enough: true commitment is shown by striving and by undivided allegiance, and since Allah is fully aware of all deeds and intentions, no hidden hypocrisy or divided loyalty can escape Him.

translation: It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of God while bearing witness against themselves of disbelief. Those—their deeds have become void, and in the Fire they will abide forever.
interpretation: The verse means that those who associate partners with God have no rightful claim to tend or serve God's houses of worship, since the upkeep of a mosque is an act of devotion that presupposes faith in God alone. Their own words and practices testify to their disbelief, for example, when they worship idols and still claim to honor the sanctuary. This contradiction nullifies any merit in their service, such as building, repairing, or providing for pilgrims. Deeds are valued by God only when rooted in sincere faith, so without it their good works are rendered void and carry no weight in the Hereafter, and their persistence in disbelief leads to eternal punishment in the Fire.

translation: Only those who believe in God and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakat, and fear none but God may maintain God's mosques. It is hoped that such people will be among the rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:18) teaches that true stewardship of places of worship belongs to those whose inner faith is confirmed by outward practice. Belief in God and the Last Day gives accountability and sincerity. Establishing prayer ties a person to God, and giving zakat ties them to society. Fearing only God frees them from fear of people, so they will not compromise the truth to please others or avoid harm. Maintaining a mosque therefore means more than building or decorating it. It means filling it with worship, remembrance, learning, and service to the community. Because the idolaters of Mecca took pride in tending the Sacred Mosque while lacking true faith, the verse shows that their upkeep earned no merit with God. The phrase 'it is hoped' (asa) signals that even those who have all these qualities should not feel certain of salvation. Guidance is a gift from God, and the believer remains between hope and humility.

translation: Do you consider giving drink to the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque to be equal to the one who believes in God and the Last Day and strives in the cause of God? They are not equal in the sight of God. And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward acts of service, however honorable, cannot be put on the same level as genuine faith joined with sacrifice for God's cause. The Quraysh took pride in serving the pilgrims and tending the Sacred Mosque while they held to polytheism, and they thought this entitled them to a rank equal to or higher than that of the believers who had migrated and struggled. God makes clear that worth before Him rests first on sound belief in Him and the Last Day, followed by committed action for His sake. Good deeds that are not grounded in true faith do not raise a person's standing, and those who cling to idolatry and take pride in worldly or ceremonial privileges are wrongdoers who have put things in the wrong place. God withholds His guidance from such people because of their persistence in injustice and arrogance.

translation: Those who have believed, emigrated, and striven in the cause of God with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with God. And it is they who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true standing before God is measured by faith joined with costly action, not by outward service or lineage. In context, it answers those who thought that giving water to pilgrims or maintaining the Sacred Mosque equaled the merit of believers who left their homes and sacrificed property and life for God's cause. Faith comes first, then hijra, the sacrifice of home and security for the sake of religion, then jihad, the striving with wealth and self. Together these raise a person to the highest ranks with God, and such people are the ones who truly attain success, both in salvation and in God's pleasure, because they gave up what they loved most in order to obey Him.

translation: Their Lord gives them glad tidings of mercy from Him, and of His good pleasure, and of Gardens wherein they will have lasting bliss.
interpretation: The verse (At-Tawbah 9:21) shows that God Himself announces the reward to the believers who have faith, migrate, and strive in His cause, and that He does so in an ascending order of blessings. First comes His mercy, which covers their sins and shortcomings. Then comes His pleasure, the greatest reward, since it is the lasting assurance that He is satisfied with them and will never be angry with them afterward. Finally come the Gardens, whose bliss does not fade, end, or diminish. The sequence teaches that the true success of the believer lies first in winning God's mercy and approval, and that the pleasures of Paradise follow as a consequence. It also contrasts the permanent rewards of the hereafter with the fleeting gains of this world, and encourages steadfastness in sacrifice for the sake of God.

translation: They will abide therein forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse tells us that the blessing of Paradise is unending: those who enter it will never be removed from it or see its joys fade. The final clause, 'with Allah is a great reward,' tells believers that whatever they give up in this life, whether wealth, comfort, or worldly attachments, is small compared with what Allah holds in store for them. The reward is described as 'great' because it comes from Allah, whose generosity has no limit, and because it lasts forever. This should lift the believer's aspirations beyond fleeting worldly gains and strengthen their patience and sincerity in obeying Allah, in the confidence that He will not let any good deed go to waste.

translation: O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith. And whoever among you takes them as allies, it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that loyalty to God and faith takes precedence over ties of blood and family. The prohibition is not against kindness or dutiful treatment of relatives, which the Qur'an elsewhere enjoins even toward disbelieving parents in worldly matters. It concerns wilāyah, meaning intimate alliance, support, and putting trust in those who actively choose disbelief over belief, particularly when that alliance would harm the believing community or compromise one's religion. Whoever places such allegiance above their commitment to God wrongs themselves by misplacing their loyalty, and wrongs their faith and community, which is why they are called wrongdoers (ẓālimūn). The verse teaches believers to order their loves and loyalties so that devotion to God stands above every natural attachment.

translation: Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your extended family, wealth you have acquired, commerce whose decline you fear, and dwellings with which you are pleased are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His decree. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse sets the standard for true faith: love for Allah, His Messenger, and sacrifice in His cause must take precedence over every worldly attachment. Family bonds, property, business, and comfortable homes are not forbidden in themselves, and loving them is natural. The warning applies when attachment to them outweighs obedience to Allah and leads a person to abandon duty, such as the hijrah or jihad in the context of its revelation, out of fear of losing them. Such a person has put worldly ties above his commitment to Allah, and the verse threatens him with Allah's decree, a punishment or loss of divine favor. The closing words say that those who knowingly place worldly interests above Allah's commands step outside obedience, and Allah withholds guidance from those who persist in that defiance. Faith is therefore proved by what a person chooses when his duty to Allah conflicts with his worldly interests.

translation: Indeed, God has given you victory in many battlefields, and on the day of Hunayn, when your great numbers impressed you, but they availed you nothing, and the earth, despite its vastness, became narrow for you, and then you turned back, retreating.
interpretation: The verse teaches that victory comes from God alone and not from numbers, strength, or material means. At Hunayn some Muslims were pleased with their large army and felt self-reliant, so God let them experience a moment of crisis and confusion in which their numbers were useless and they fled. The lesson is to guard against pride and over-reliance on resources, and to place trust in God while still making the necessary effort. Ease and support follow humility and dependence on Him, as the next verses show when God sent down His tranquility upon the Messenger and the believers.

translation: Then God sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down forces you did not see, and punished those who disbelieved. And that is the recompense of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the aftermath of the Battle of Hunayn, when the Muslims, after being overconfident in their numbers, were initially routed and panicked. God then restored calm and steadfastness to the Prophet and the faithful, which turned their fear into resolve, and aided them with unseen angelic forces, so that the tide turned and the disbelieving enemy was defeated, captured and humbled. The lesson is that victory comes not from numbers or material strength but from God's support and the inner peace He grants to those who trust Him; and that defeat and punishment in this world are the fitting consequence for those who persist in denying the truth and fighting against it.

translation: Then after that God turns in mercy to whom He wills. And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the door of repentance remains open even after defeat, hardship, and the consequences of wrongdoing. After God has dealt with people through trials, whether in the aftermath of the battle of Hunayn, where some of those who had opposed the Muslims later embraced Islam, or in any situation of human failing, He grants repentance and guidance to whomever He wills, according to His wisdom and the sincerity of their hearts. The closing names, Ghafur (Forgiving) and Rahim (Merciful), show that His acceptance of repentance flows from His nature: He erases sins and treats the repentant with compassion, so no one should despair of His mercy or consider themselves beyond forgiveness.

translation: O you who believe, the polytheists are indeed impure, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs. And if you fear poverty, Allah will soon enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in Surah At-Tawbah, sets out the rule that after the year 9 AH idolaters are no longer permitted to enter or perform rites at the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, which is to be kept for the worship of the One God alone. Their 'impurity' is understood chiefly as a spiritual and moral uncleanliness arising from shirk, not physical filth, and the ruling protects the sanctity of the sanctuary. The Muslims worried that barring the polytheists would end the pilgrim trade and fairs on which Mecca's economy depended, so God reassures them that fear of poverty must not override obedience. He promises to provide for them from His bounty according to His will and wisdom, teaching that faith-based decisions should not be compromised by material anxiety, and that sustenance ultimately comes from God, who knows what is best and orders all things wisely.

translation: Fight those among the People of the Scripture who do not believe in God or in the Last Day, who do not forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not follow the religion of truth, until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled.
interpretation: Revealed in the context of the early Muslim community's conflict with hostile powers on its borders (the Byzantine campaign leading to Tabuk), the verse addresses armed confrontation with those who actively opposed the nascent Muslim polity, and not a general license to attack all non-Muslims. Its purpose is to end military resistance and establish political order: once the opposing party submits to the authority of the state and pays the jizya, a tax in lieu of military service that guarantees protection and the right to keep their faith, the fighting must stop. The phrases about not believing and not forbidding what God has forbidden describe the grounds of their hostility and their rejection of the truth, while 'humbled' (sāghirūn) is best understood as accepting the legal and political order of the state, ending the war and living under its protection with their lives, property and worship secured.

translation: The Jews said, 'Ezra is the son of God,' and the Christians said, 'The Messiah is the son of God.' That is their saying with their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May God destroy them! How deluded they are!
interpretation: The verse rebukes the attribution of offspring to God as a baseless claim, one that has no support in revelation or reason and is merely uttered by the tongue. It says these beliefs are not new but echo the older myths of pagan peoples who likewise gave God sons or divine offspring, so the People of the Book are portrayed as unknowingly copying idolatrous ideas. The phrase 'May God destroy them' is an expression of strong censure, not a literal prayer, conveying how grave it is to compromise God's absolute oneness and transcendence. The closing question, 'How deluded they are!', expresses astonishment that people could be turned away from the clear truth of divine unity toward such an obvious falsehood.

translation: They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God, and also the Messiah, son of Mary, though they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no god but Him. Glory be to Him above whatever they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse criticizes the giving of absolute religious authority to human beings. When the Jews and Christians accepted the scholars' and monks' rulings on what is lawful and forbidden, even where these contradicted God's revelation, they in effect gave them the status of lords, since the right to legislate belongs to God alone. The Christians went further and raised the Messiah to divinity, although he was only a servant and messenger. The verse affirms that the original command to every community was pure monotheism: worship and obedience belong to the One God alone. Any submission that places human authority on a level with divine command, or any claim of divinity for a creature, is shirk, from which God is utterly exalted.

translation: They wish to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God refuses anything except to perfect His light, even though the disbelievers dislike it.
interpretation: The verse likens the efforts of those who reject the truth—their slander, mockery, and false claims against the message of Islam—to someone trying to blow out a great light with a puff of breath. Just as a mouth's breath cannot put out the sun or a blazing lamp, mere words and propaganda cannot defeat divine guidance. God's will is that His light, namely the revelation, the Prophet's message, and the religion of truth, will be brought to completion and prevail, regardless of the opposition and resentment of those who disbelieve. The lesson is reassurance for the believers: the ultimate success of God's guidance is certain, and human opposition, however loud, is futile against it.

translation: It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists detest it.
interpretation: God declares that the mission of Muhammad was not a human project dependent on worldly power, but a divine commission that carries its own proof of success. The 'guidance' is the knowledge and clarity that lead people to God, while the 'religion of truth' is the way of life, rooted in submission to the One God, that is consistent with reality and justice. The promise that it will 'prevail over all religion' means that its arguments, its moral soundness and its ultimate authority will rise above every other creed and system, whether by clear proof, by lasting dominance, or by the gradual spread of its truth, however much those who associate partners with God resent and resist it. The verse thus reassures believers that opposition cannot extinguish God's light, and that the final outcome belongs to the truth he sent.

translation: O you who believe! Indeed, many of the rabbis and monks devour the wealth of people unjustly and turn people away from the path of Allah. And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the cause of Allah — give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns the believers against corruption among religious leaders who exploit their spiritual authority for material gain, taking people's money through false pretenses, bribes, or unlawful fees, and who obstruct others from the truth in order to protect their own wealth and status. It then extends the warning to anyone who accumulates wealth and withholds it from its rightful obligations, such as zakat, charity, and spending for the common good and the cause of God. The point is that wealth is a trust to be circulated for justice and benefit, and hoarding it while neglecting these duties, or acquiring it through religious deceit, brings a painful punishment. The danger lies in the love of wealth overriding obedience to God and responsibility toward society.

translation: On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, their sides, and their backs will be branded with it: 'This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard.'
interpretation: This verse, which follows the warning against those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in God's way (Q 9:34), shows that the wealth a person hoards and withholds from its rightful obligations, such as zakat and charity, becomes the very instrument of their punishment. The wealth they thought would secure them is turned into burning metal that brands the front, sides, and back of the body, which suggests that the miser turned away from the needy on every side. The closing words, 'this is what you hoarded for yourselves', reveal the bitter irony that what they stored up for their own benefit has become their torment. The verse teaches that wealth is a trust to be used justly and generously, and that clinging to it in defiance of God's command ruins the owner in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of these, four are sacred. That is the correct religion, so do not wrong yourselves during them. And fight against the polytheists all together as they fight against you all together. And know that Allah is with the righteous.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the division of time into twelve months is a divine ordinance fixed at creation, not a human convention to be manipulated, as the pre-Islamic Arabs did by postponing sacred months to suit their wars. Four of these months are sacred, set aside as times of peace and heightened reverence, and honoring this divine order is part of the upright religion. Wronging oneself in them means committing sin or violating their sanctity, since sin is graver in sacred times. The command to fight the polytheists collectively, just as they fight the believers collectively, calls for unity and a united front in defensive reciprocity against an enemy who wages war on the community as a whole. It closes by reminding believers that divine support is granted to those who maintain taqwa, observing God's limits even in conflict and not transgressing them.

translation: Indeed, the postponing [of sacred months] is an increase in disbelief by which those who disbelieve are led astray. They make it lawful one year and unlawful another year, to match the number [of months] that Allah has made sacred, thereby making lawful what Allah has made unlawful. The evil of their deeds has been made attractive to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse condemns the pre-Islamic Arab practice of nasi', in which the sacred months (during which fighting was forbidden) were shifted around according to tribal interests, such as when they wished to wage war in a sacred month. They would declare a sacred month permissible one year and compensate by declaring another month sacred, so that they kept the count of four sacred months while violating the actual times Allah had set. The Qur'an calls this an increase in disbelief because it is not a mere calendar adjustment but an act of altering Allah's law in line with human desires, treating what He forbade as lawful and what He ordained as negotiable. Its deeper lesson is that when people tamper with divine limits through clever technicalities, preserving the outward form while emptying it of meaning, their moral sense becomes corrupted so that their bad deeds look good to them, and persistence in such willful distortion and rejection deprives them of Allah's guidance.

translation: O you who believe, what is the matter with you that when it is said to you, 'March forth in the cause of God,' you cling heavily to the earth? Are you content with the life of this world in place of the Hereafter? Yet the enjoyment of the life of this world, compared with the Hereafter, is but little.
interpretation: This verse rebukes believers who hesitate and make excuses when summoned to strive in God's cause, as happened with the expedition to Tabuk, which came in harsh summer heat and at harvest time. Their sluggishness is portrayed as being weighed down toward the earth, meaning attachment to comfort, ease, and worldly interests. The verse asks whether they truly prefer the fleeting pleasures of this life over eternal reward, and it answers that worldly enjoyment is trivial next to the Hereafter. The lesson is that faith demands sacrifice and a sense of priorities: when duty to God calls, a believer should rise above attachment to worldly comfort, because the lasting reward of the next life far outweighs any temporary gain or ease.

translation: If you do not march forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people, and you cannot harm Him in the least. And Allah has power over all things.
interpretation: This verse warns the believers that holding back from striving in God's cause when they are called to it carries grave consequences: a painful punishment, whether in this world through humiliation and defeat or in the next. It also teaches that God's religion does not depend on any particular people. If the believers abandon their duty, God can raise another community that will carry the message faithfully and replace them. Their neglect does not diminish God in any way, for He is self-sufficient and all-powerful; the benefit of obedience and the harm of disobedience return only to the people themselves. The verse ends by reminding them that God's power is absolute, so neither the punishment nor the replacement is beyond Him.

translation: If you do not aid him, Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved drove him out, as one of two, when they were both in the cave, when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.' Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with soldiers you did not see, and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, while the word of Allah is the highest. And Allah is Mighty and Wise.
interpretation: The verse reminds the believers who were reluctant to march out for the campaign of Tabuk that God's cause does not depend on their help. Even when the Prophet Muhammad was alone, expelled from Mecca and hiding in the cave of Thawr with Abu Bakr while their pursuers were close by, God protected and strengthened him. His reassurance to his anxious companion, 'Do not grieve; God is with us,' shows that true trust in God brings inner peace (sakina) and that divine support, sometimes through unseen forces, outweighs worldly weakness or small numbers. The verse teaches that the believers' duty to strive is a privilege and a test for their own sake, because God's victory is certain: falsehood is brought low and His word prevails by His might and wisdom.

translation: March forth, whether light or heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of God. That is better for you, if only you knew.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to answer the summons to defend the faith and community without waiting for ideal conditions. 'Light and heavy' covers every circumstance: young or old, healthy or weak, wealthy or poor, eager or reluctant, equipped or lacking. Struggle is to be undertaken with both possessions and persons, so sacrifice must be total rather than partial. The verse says this commitment is truly 'better for you', because its worth surpasses worldly comfort, and its reward is honor, spiritual growth and God's pleasure in this life and the next. The phrase 'if you only knew' suggests that those who grasp the real value of what lasts will see that holding back out of ease or attachment to property is a loss, and that acting out of faith is a gain.

translation: Had it been a gain close at hand and a journey of moderate length, they would have followed you; but the distance was too far for them. And they will swear by God, "If we had been able, we would have gone out with you." They destroy themselves, and God knows that they are surely liars.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. Their motive was worldly self-interest, not inability: they would have joined the Prophet if the reward were easy spoils and the trip short and comfortable, but the hardship, distance and sacrifice revealed what was in their hearts. Their false oaths of excuse, sworn in God's name, only add to their guilt, because lying and invoking God's name to cover cowardice and lack of sincerity bring about their own ruin in this world and the next. God knows the hidden truth behind their excuses, so no pretext can deceive Him, and genuine faith is shown by willingness to sacrifice when it is costly, not only when it is profitable.

translation: May God pardon you [O Prophet]; why did you grant them permission [to stay behind] before it became clear to you who were truthful and before you knew who were the liars?
interpretation: The verse (Surah At-Tawbah 9:43) gently corrects the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for permitting some hypocrites to stay behind from the expedition to Tabuk before their sincerity was tested. It opens with pardon, showing God's tenderness toward His Messenger, and then points out that it would have been better to withhold permission until the genuine believers, who would have come out in any case, were distinguished from those who merely offered false excuses. The lesson is that outward excuses should be weighed against real conduct and that the truth of people's faith is revealed through trials, so that leaders should not hasten to judgments or concessions that allow the insincere to hide behind pretexts.

translation: Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask you for exemption from striving with their wealth and their lives. And Allah is All-Knowing of the righteous.
interpretation: The verse sets out a test of true faith: believers who are certain of God and the Day of Judgment do not look for excuses to stay behind when the call to struggle in God's cause comes. Their belief in meeting God makes them eager to give their wealth and their lives, so they volunteer readily without seeking permission to be excused. Seeking exemption without genuine need therefore signals weak faith or doubt, as the following verses make clear. The closing phrase, 'And Allah is All-Knowing of the righteous,' assures the sincere that God knows their intentions and will reward them, and it implies that God also knows those who only pretend, so outward claims cannot hide inner reality.

translation: Only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day ask you for exemption, and their hearts are in doubt, so in their doubt they waver.
interpretation: This verse (al-Tawbah 9:45) teaches that seeking to be excused from striving in God's cause, when there is no real excuse, is a sign of weak or absent faith rather than of sincere belief. A true believer who trusts God and expects the Day of Judgment is eager to sacrifice for the sake of God and does not look for ways to stay behind. Those who request exemption do so because doubt has settled in their hearts. Since they have no firm certainty to anchor them, they hesitate and go back and forth, unable to commit to either course. Their wavering reveals their inner state: lack of conviction makes a person indecisive and unwilling to bear hardship, while certainty brings resolve and readiness to act.

translation: And had they truly intended to march out, they would have made some preparation for it. But Allah disliked their setting out, so He held them back, and it was said, 'Stay behind with those who stay behind.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the insincerity of the hypocrites who offered excuses to avoid the expedition to Tabuk. Their failure to make any preparation, such as gathering provisions, mounts and weapons, proves that they never genuinely intended to go. Allah, knowing that their presence would bring no benefit and would only spread discord and corruption among the believers (as the following verses explain), willed that they not join the army and caused them to be discouraged and left behind. The words 'it was said, Stay with those who stay behind' are a divine decree of rejection, placing them among the women, children, sick and others who remain at home, and a rebuke that their staying was a result of their own hearts' lack of sincerity. It teaches that true intention is shown through action and preparation, and that Allah's wisdom may keep away from righteous work those whose hearts are not sound.

translation: Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you except confusion, and they would have hurried about in your midst seeking to sow discord among you, and among you are those who would listen to them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse explains the divine wisdom in the hypocrites' staying behind from the expedition to Tabuk. God had caused them to remain behind as a mercy to the believers, because their presence in the army would have brought only harm: weakness, corruption, and disorder in the ranks. They would have rushed about among the believers spreading rumors, slander, and doubt, sowing mistrust and division to turn them against one another and undermine their unity and resolve. The verse also warns that some among the believers were prone to listen to such whisperings, either because they were naive and easily swayed or because they carried information back to the hypocrites, so the danger of the hypocrites' influence was real. It ends by reminding that God fully knows the wrongdoers, their hidden intentions and their schemes, so the believers need not fear them, and God will expose and deal with them as He wills.

translation: They had already sought to cause discord before, and they turned matters upside down for you, until the truth came and the command of God prevailed, while they were averse.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:48) addresses the Prophet about the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. It reminds him that their scheming is nothing new: from the early days of his mission, as at Uhud and before, they plotted to split the believers, spread doubt, and undermine his leadership by twisting affairs and devising stratagems against him. Despite all this, God's truth triumphed and His religion became manifest, against the hypocrites' wishes. The lesson is that sedition by those whose hearts are not sincere cannot defeat God's decree, so the believers should not grieve over the hypocrites' absence, since their absence spared the community further corruption, and God's cause succeeds regardless of the opposition.

translation: And among them is he who says, 'Grant me exemption and do not put me to trial.' Surely into trial they have already fallen. And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse refers to hypocrites at the time of the expedition to Tabuk, when some, such as al-Jadd ibn Qays according to the commonly reported account, asked the Prophet's permission to stay behind, pretending that they feared being tempted by the women of the Romans or that they feared falling into sin. They presented their excuse as piety, but God exposes it: the real fitnah, meaning sin, hypocrisy and the abandonment of the Prophet and of jihad, is exactly what they have already fallen into by shirking their duty and preferring comfort and self-preservation over obedience. Their attempt to avoid a supposed trial is itself a deeper failure. The verse ends with a warning that Hell surrounds the disbelievers, so there is no escape for them, neither through clever excuses in this world nor in the Hereafter.

translation: If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if a calamity strikes you, they say, 'We took our precaution beforehand,' and they turn away rejoicing.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:50) exposes the inner state of the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. Their hearts are so filled with envy and hostility toward the Prophet and the believers that any success, victory, or blessing granted to the Muslims grieves them, while any hardship or setback that afflicts the Muslims delights them. When misfortune strikes, they boast of their cunning in having avoided the danger by staying behind, and walk away gloating. Their reaction shows that their loyalty lies not with the community of faith but with their own selfish interests, and that their attitude toward the believers' fortunes reveals the sickness in their hearts. The verse also consoles the Prophet and the believers: the hypocrites' joy at their misfortune is shortsighted, as the next verse teaches that nothing befalls them except what God has decreed, and in Him alone should the believers place their trust.

translation: Say: "Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has decreed for us; He is our Protector. And upon Allah let the believers rely."
interpretation: The verse teaches that every event in a believer's life, whether pleasant or painful, happens within God's knowledge and decree, so nothing occurs by blind chance or by the power of enemies alone. Since God is the believer's Mawla, the Guardian and Master who cares for those devoted to Him, the believer can face hardship with calm and contentment instead of fear or despair. Trust in God (tawakkul) does not mean abandoning effort; it means doing what one can and then entrusting the outcome to God, confident that what He decrees is ultimately good. This trust is the distinguishing mark of true faith.

translation: Say: Are you awaiting for us anything but one of the two best outcomes? And we are awaiting for you that God will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or at our hands. So wait; indeed, we are waiting with you.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to answer the hypocrites who hoped for the believers' misfortune. For the believers, every outcome is good: either victory and spoils, or martyrdom with God's pleasure and reward. The hypocrites, by contrast, can expect only loss, either a divine punishment sent directly from God or defeat at the believers' hands. The believers' confidence rests on trust in God's promise, so whatever happens they are the winners, while those who bet against the truth are the ones set to lose. The closing challenge to 'wait' is a calm declaration that the outcome will expose who was right.

translation: Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly, it will never be accepted from you. Indeed, you have been a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse (Surah At-Tawbah 9:53) responds to hypocrites who offered to give money as a way to excuse themselves from joining the struggle or to appear righteous. God tells them that their charity, whether given freely or under compulsion, will not be accepted, because acceptance of deeds depends on faith and sincerity of the heart, not on the outward act of giving. Since their spending is not rooted in true belief and is tainted by hypocrisy and disobedience (fisq, meaning they have departed from obedience to God), the deed is void of value before Him. The lesson is that worship and good works are valued by God only when they come from genuine faith and sincere intention, and that outward generosity cannot make up for inner rejection and insincerity.

translation: And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in God and in His Messenger, and they do not come to prayer except while lazy, and they do not spend except while unwilling.
interpretation: Acceptance of deeds by God depends on the sincerity and faith that lie behind them, not on their outward form or size. The hypocrites gave money and joined in prayer, yet because their hearts rejected God and His Messenger, their acts were empty of worth. Their laziness in prayer and reluctance in giving reveal that they did these things only to avoid blame or to keep up appearances among the believers, not out of love for God or hope for His reward. The verse teaches that outward acts of worship without true belief and willing devotion carry no weight with God, and that real worship requires a heart that is eager to pray and glad to give for His sake.

translation: So let not their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through these things in the life of this world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse warns the believer not to be dazzled by the worldly prosperity of hypocrites and disbelievers, because what looks like a blessing is in reality a trial and a source of torment for them. Their wealth and children bring anxiety, attachment to the world, the burden of obligations they resent, and distraction from faith. Because these things hold their hearts, they persist in disbelief until death takes them in that state. Worldly abundance is therefore no sign of divine favor, and true success is measured by faith and obedience rather than material possessions.

translation: They swear by God that they are truly of you, yet they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 9:56) exposes the hypocrites among the people of Medina. They took false oaths to convince the believers that they shared their faith and were part of their community. Their oaths were not driven by sincere conviction but by fear: they dreaded the consequences of showing their true disbelief, whether exposure, loss of social standing and security, or punishment at the hands of the Muslim community. The lesson is that claims and oaths do not make someone a true believer. Real belonging to the community of faith rests on sincere inner conviction and conduct, not on outward profession shaped by fear or self-protection. God knows what lies in hearts, and the pretense of those who fear people more than they fear God will ultimately be revealed.

translation: If they could find a refuge, or caves, or any place to enter, they would turn to it, rushing headlong in flight.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' deep aversion to the Muslim community and to the obligations of faith, such as jihad and sincere commitment. They stay among the believers only out of fear and self-interest, not conviction. Their inner state is so unstable that if they found any hiding place, whether a fortress, a cave, or a tunnel, they would bolt toward it at once, like a headstrong horse that cannot be restrained. This shows that their outward association with the believers is forced and fragile, and that their hearts are set on escaping the responsibilities and risks that true belief brings.

translation: And among them are some who criticize you concerning the distribution of charities; if they are given from it, they are satisfied, but if they are not given from it, at once they become angry.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy of those whose objections to the Prophet's handling of zakat were never about justice or principle, but about self-interest. Their approval or anger rose and fell with their own share. Their faith was shallow and tied to worldly gain, so they judged the Prophet's fairness by what they personally received, not by the rules God had set for dividing charity. The verse warns that real faith means accepting God's and His Messenger's judgment with contentment, whether or not it favors one personally.

translation: If only they had been content with what God and His Messenger gave them, and said, 'God is sufficient for us; God will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger; indeed, to God we turn in hope.'
interpretation: The verse describes the attitude that would have been better for those who criticized the Prophet's distribution of charity and war gains. It teaches contentment with what God has apportioned through His Messenger, and it lays out a sequence of faith: accept the share given, declare that God alone is sufficient, trust that He will grant more from His bounty, and direct all hope and desire to Him rather than to the distributor or to worldly gain. Resentment and greed are replaced by gratitude, reliance on God (tawakkul), and the understanding that provision ultimately comes from God, with the Messenger as the means of its delivery.

translation: Alms are only for the poor and the needy, for those employed to collect them, for those whose hearts are to be reconciled, for freeing captives and slaves, for those burdened with debt, for the cause of God, and for the wayfarer. This is an obligation from God, and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse sets out the eight categories of legitimate recipients of zakat, which makes the distribution of obligatory charity a matter of divine law and not of personal preference or political favor. By restricting the word 'only' to these categories, God ensures that zakat serves its purpose of relieving real need and strengthening the community: it supports the destitute (the poor and the needy), pays those who administer the system fairly, wins over and secures the loyalty of hearts that may be inclined toward the faith or the community, helps free people from bondage, relieves those crushed by debt, supports efforts in God's path, and assists travelers stranded away from their means. The closing phrases, 'an obligation from God' and 'All-Knowing, All-Wise', teach that this allocation is not a human invention but a binding duty grounded in God's perfect knowledge of human needs and wisdom in balancing social welfare, so believers should accept and implement it with sincerity and justice.

translation: And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ear." Say, "An ear of goodness for you; he believes in God and trusts the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe." And those who harm the Messenger of God will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The hypocrites mocked the Prophet by calling him 'all ear', meaning he gullibly listens to whatever anyone tells him, so they could speak ill of him and then excuse themselves by swearing falsely when confronted. The Qur'an turns the insult into a mark of virtue: his listening is good for them, because he is not naive but gracious. He hears people out and accepts their outward words, concealing their faults rather than exposing them, while his belief rests on God's revelation and he gives credence to the sincere believers. His forbearance is a mercy to the believers, and a restraint on his dealing with the hypocrites, whom he leaves to God. Yet this gentleness must not be mistaken for weakness or license, for harming God's Messenger by words or deeds is a grave offense that carries a painful punishment.

translation: They swear by God to you [believers] in order to please you, but God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:62) exposes the hypocrites who make oaths before the believers to excuse themselves and win people's approval, while neglecting what truly matters. If their faith were sincere, their first concern would be to please God and His Messenger through honest obedience and true loyalty, not to seek the favor of people through false oaths. Pleasing God and His Messenger is one and the same pursuit, since obeying the Messenger is obeying God. The verse teaches that genuine faith is measured by seeking God's approval above human approval, and that oaths and outward displays cannot replace sincerity of heart.

translation: Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever? That is the great disgrace.
interpretation: The verse (Surah At-Tawbah 9:63) rebukes the hypocrites who swore false oaths and drew back from obedience. To 'oppose' (yuhaadid) literally means to place oneself on the other side of a boundary from God and His Messenger, that is, to stand in deliberate enmity and defiance of the limits and commands God has set. The verse says such a stance is not a trivial matter: its consequence is eternal punishment in Hell, which the Qur'an calls the 'great disgrace' (al-khizy al-'azim). The disgrace is more than physical suffering; it is the humiliation and exposure of those who hid disbelief behind outward claims of faith. The question 'Do they not know?' implies that this truth is plain and should have deterred them, so their persistence in hostility is willful heedlessness rather than ignorance.

translation: The hypocrites fear that a surah may be revealed about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: "Keep mocking; indeed, Allah will bring out what you fear."
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:64) shows that the hypocrites lived in constant anxiety, because their outward words and their hidden disbelief were at odds, and they knew that revelation could expose their secrets at any moment. Their mockery of the faith and the believers was a cover for this fear. The command "Say: keep mocking" is a form of warning and rebuke rather than permission, as it means their ridicule will not protect them. God assures that He will surely disclose what they conceal, so no hidden hypocrisy can remain permanently hidden from Him. The lesson is that inner sincerity matters, that God knows the contents of hearts, and that mocking sacred things leads to exposure and accountability.

translation: And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing idly and playing." Say, "Was it Allah, and His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 9:65) addresses the hypocrites who, during the expedition to Tabuk, mocked the Prophet and the believers. When their mockery was exposed, they excused themselves as mere casual banter and play. The Qur'an rejects this excuse: ridiculing Allah, His revelation, or His Messenger is not trivial joking but a grave offense that touches the very foundation of faith. Matters of religion are not a subject for jest, and claiming to have been 'only playing' does not remove the guilt of mockery. The following verse makes this clear by saying, 'Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief,' showing that scorn for the sacred can contradict genuine faith, and that one must hold the sacred in reverence in both earnest speech and humor.

translation: Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after you had believed. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group, because they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse was addressed to hypocrites who mocked God, His verses, and His Messenger during the expedition to Tabuk, then came to offer excuses by claiming they were only joking and chatting. God tells them their excuses are void, because mocking the sacred is not a harmless jest but an act of disbelief that exposes the faith they professed as hollow. It also shows that belief can be nullified by words and attitudes of ridicule toward religion. The second part says that God's pardon is not for everyone: He may forgive those who sincerely repent and turn away from the mockery, while punishing those who persist in it and in their hypocrisy, since they were habitual wrongdoers whose conduct showed that they were not truly believers. Punishment is thus tied to their own persistent guilt and not to arbitrary judgment.

translation: The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another: they enjoin what is wrong, forbid what is right, and withhold their hands. They have forgotten God, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse portrays hypocrisy as a shared moral character rather than a matter of gender: hypocrites resemble one another in inner corruption and in how they behave, and they reinforce one another. Their conduct inverts the believers' mission of enjoining good and forbidding evil, since they promote vice and discourage virtue. Their closed fists signal stinginess and refusal to spend in God's cause or help those in need. Their 'forgetting' God means neglecting His commands and living without accountability. God's 'forgetting' them is a just response: He withdraws His guidance, mercy, and grace from them and leaves them to their own devices. The closing statement says that hypocrisy ends in fisq, a deep and habitual rebellion that takes a person outside obedience to God.

translation: God has promised the hypocrites, men and women, and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. God has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.
interpretation: The verse says that hypocrisy is not a minor fault but is as grave as open disbelief, because the hypocrite outwardly professes faith while inwardly rejecting it, which is a deceit that damages both his own soul and the community. God therefore puts hypocrites and disbelievers under one fate: Hell, where they stay. The phrase 'It is sufficient for them' means that no further punishment is needed, since the fire is a full and fitting recompense for their crimes. Being cursed by God means being cast out of His mercy, which adds a spiritual loss to the physical suffering. The 'lasting punishment' shows that the torment does not end. The warning is meant to make believers sincere, so that their inner faith matches their outward words and deeds.

translation: Like those before you: they were stronger than you in power and greater in wealth and children. They enjoyed their share, and you have enjoyed your share as those before you enjoyed theirs, and you indulged in idle talk as they indulged. Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse warns the hypocrites by pointing to earlier nations who had more strength, wealth and offspring than they did, yet were destroyed. Those nations spent their portion of worldly life on pleasures and falsehood, mocking the prophets and plunging into vain and misleading talk, and they gained nothing lasting. The hypocrites follow the same path: they consume their worldly share of enjoyment and join in futile, mocking discourse against the truth. The result is the same, because deeds not grounded in sincere faith and obedience to God bring no benefit, no blessing or reward in this life and none in the next, so such people are the true losers. The lesson is that worldly power and wealth do not protect anyone from God's judgment, and that turning one's share of life into mere indulgence and mockery of faith ends in total loss.

translation: Has the news not reached them of those before them: the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. So it was not God who wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse warns the hypocrites and deniers that history offers clear lessons: earlier nations that rejected their prophets and the clear signs they brought were destroyed, each in a way that fit its wrongdoing. Their destruction was not an act of injustice by God, who sent warnings and gave them every chance to believe. It was the consequence of their own choices, since by persisting in disbelief and corruption they harmed themselves and brought about their own ruin. Those who ignore these accounts risk the same end, and the verse invites reflection and repentance before it is too late.

translation: The believing men and believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, establish prayer, give zakat, and obey God and His Messenger. Those—God will have mercy on them. Indeed, God is Almighty and Wise.
interpretation: The verse describes the believing community as one built on mutual solidarity, in contrast to the hypocrites, who are described in the preceding verses as bound together in wrongdoing. Believers, men and women alike, stand as protectors, supporters and friends to one another, and this bond finds expression in shared moral responsibility: they call society toward goodness and warn against evil. Their faith is also shown in worship, through prayer, and in care for others, through zakat, and it culminates in obedience to God and His Messenger. God promises that mercy will reach those who combine these qualities, a promise that is certain because He is Almighty and cannot fail to fulfil it, and Wise, since He gives mercy to those who deserve it. Mercy is thus tied to a combination of communal solidarity, moral activism, worship and obedience, not to belief in the heart alone.

translation: God has promised the believing men and the believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual Eden. But the good pleasure of God is greater still. That is the supreme triumph.
interpretation: The verse sets out a hierarchy of reward for the faithful. The gardens, rivers, and fine dwellings are real blessings, but they are surpassed by God's pleasure (ridwan) with them. Material delights are a means and a sign of divine favor, not the final goal. Being accepted by God and having His contentment is the highest bliss, and it makes the believers' success the greatest of all. The verse also names believing women alongside men, which shows both are equally promised the same reward according to their faith and deeds. It contrasts with the preceding verses on the hypocrites, who are threatened with Hellfire, and it directs the believer to seek God's approval above worldly or even heavenly enjoyment.

translation: O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be firm and severe with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to exert every effort in resisting those who reject the truth and those who feign faith while working against it, each by the means suited to their case: armed struggle against the openly hostile disbelievers when they wage war, and argument, exposure, and firm application of the law against the hypocrites, who were in the community and so could not be fought as open enemies. 'Be firm with them' means refusing to yield or compromise on the truth, and not being deceived by their flattery or excuses; it does not license cruelty, since the Prophet's character is elsewhere described as mercy. The closing warning that Hell is their refuge reminds believers that the ultimate judgment belongs to God, and that firmness in this world is rooted in the seriousness of the consequences of persisting in disbelief and hypocrisy.

translation: They swear by God that they said nothing, yet they certainly uttered the word of disbelief and disbelieved after their submission to Islam, and they plotted what they could not attain. They resented nothing except that God and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty. If they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, God will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have on earth neither protector nor helper.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites who deny their hostile words with false oaths, though their statements amounted to open disbelief and showed they had abandoned the faith they outwardly professed. It notes they even schemed against the Prophet, but failed. Their grievance was absurd: their only 'complaint' was that God and His Messenger had brought them prosperity, so their hostility was born of ingratitude rather than any real wrong done to them. Even so, the door of mercy stays open: sincere repentance would be better for them, while persisting in turning away would bring painful punishment in this life, through disgrace, insecurity and loss, and in the next, with no one on earth able to protect or help them. The lesson is that ingratitude and hypocrisy lead to ruin, while repentance is always available.

translation: And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and surely be among the righteous."
interpretation: The verse (Surah At-Tawbah 9:75) exposes the hypocrisy of those who make solemn promises to God when they are in need, vowing generosity and righteousness if only they are given wealth. Their vow shows that they know where provision comes from, yet their sincerity is untested until blessing arrives. The verse warns that faith must not be conditional on prosperity: a person who pledges good deeds in return for future favors, and does not honor the pledge once enriched, reveals a heart divided between professed devotion and attachment to worldly gain. True righteousness is to give thanks and give charity in every circumstance, and a covenant made with God is a binding trust that must be fulfilled.

translation: But when He gave them of His bounty, they were miserly with it, and turned away, being averse.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:76) describes the hypocrites who had sworn to God that if He gave them of His bounty they would give charity and be among the righteous. When God granted them wealth, they broke their promise: they withheld it out of greed and turned their backs on their obligations to God, indifferent to the covenant they had made. Its meaning is that blessings are a test, and that fine words in times of need mean nothing if they are not matched by gratitude and generosity once ease arrives. Miserliness and turning away from one's pledge to God is a mark of hypocrisy, and the verse warns that those who bargain with God yet fail to honor their word will be held to account, as the following verse says it leads to hypocrisy settled in their hearts.

translation: So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they will meet Him, because they broke their promise to God which they had made to Him, and because they used to lie.
interpretation: The verse (At-Tawbah 9:77) describes the consequence of those who vowed to God that they would give charity and be righteous if He gave them from His bounty, and then, once enriched, withheld it and turned away. Their breaking of the covenant and their habitual lying were not left without consequence: God punished the sin with a deeper sin. Hypocrisy was lodged in their hearts and stayed with them, so that they were denied the grace of sincere repentance until they die and meet God for reckoning. The meaning is that wrongdoing can bring about a spiritual condition that perpetuates itself. Betraying a pledge to God and lying corrupt the heart, so that duplicity becomes its settled state, and the person is left to the results of his own choices. It is a warning that trifling with promises made to God, and treating truthfulness lightly, can lead to losing sincerity of faith altogether.

translation: Do they not know that God knows their secrets and their private counsels, and that God is the Knower of all that is unseen?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 9:78) rebukes the hypocrites who broke their covenant with God and concealed disbelief behind outward professions of faith. It reminds them that hiding their intentions and whispering in private gains them nothing, because God's knowledge encompasses both what is concealed in the heart (sirr) and what is spoken in secret conversation (najwā). Since God is 'Allām al-ghuyūb, the One whose knowledge of the unseen is complete and perfect, no deception can succeed before Him, and every hidden act will be accounted for. The verse calls the believer to sincerity and constant awareness of God, so that inner reality matches outward conduct.

translation: Those who criticize the believers who give willingly in charity, and those who find nothing to give except their own effort, and ridicule them — God will ridicule them, and they will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns the hypocrites who mocked believers whatever they gave. When wealthy Muslims donated generously, the hypocrites accused them of showing off, and when poor Muslims gave the little they could afford, the hypocrites scoffed that God had no need of such a trifle. The verse teaches that charity is judged by sincerity and by what the giver is able to give, not by its size, and that belittling the good deeds of believers is a grave sin. The phrase 'God will ridicule them' means that God will repay their mockery with a fitting recompense: He will expose their hypocrisy and humiliate them, in this world and the next, and they will suffer a painful punishment. Mockery of sincere worshippers is thus shown to be self-destructive for the mocker.

translation: Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, God will never forgive them. That is because they disbelieved in God and His Messenger. And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that forgiveness depends on sincere faith and repentance, not on the status of the one who intercedes. The hypocrites persisted in rejecting God and His Messenger while outwardly claiming belief, so even the Prophet's repeated prayers for them would not benefit them. 'Seventy' is an idiom for a great many times, not a literal limit. Their exclusion from forgiveness is not arbitrary but a consequence of their own stubborn disbelief and open defiance (fisq), which closes them to guidance. Intercession cannot replace a person's own faith and turning back to God.

translation: Those who were left behind rejoiced at their staying behind the Messenger of God, and they disliked striving with their wealth and their lives in the cause of God, and they said, 'Do not march out in the heat.' Say: 'The fire of Hell is far hotter,' if only they could understand.
interpretation: The verse exposes the shallow reasoning of the hypocrites who skipped the expedition to Tabuk. They chose short-term bodily comfort, avoiding the summer heat, over obedience to God and His Messenger, and they even discouraged others from going.
