translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, 'These are the ones who lied against their Lord.' Behold, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that attributing falsehood to God, whether by claiming He has partners, by inventing laws and claims in His name, or by denying what He revealed, is the gravest form of injustice, since it corrupts the very source of truth and guidance. On the Day of Judgment, such people will be brought before their Lord with no chance to hide, and those who bear witness (the angels, the prophets, and the righteous) will publicly testify against them. This public exposure is itself part of their punishment, a disgrace matched to the public nature of their lies. The closing declaration that God's curse is upon the wrongdoers means they are removed from His mercy, which is the fitting outcome for those who wronged both the truth and themselves by distorting it.

translation: Those who hinder people from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, while they are disbelievers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse describes the wrongdoers as people whose harm is twofold: they actively obstruct others from following God's path, and they try to distort it by twisting its teachings, casting doubt upon it, or presenting it as flawed so that it fits their desires and interests. What drives this behavior is their denial of the Hereafter. Because they do not believe they will be held accountable before God, they feel no restraint in misleading others and corrupting religion. Disbelief in the Last Day is thus the root of moral recklessness, and the verse warns that to turn people away from guidance and to distort it is a grave wrong that incurs God's rejection.

translation: Those were not able to escape [God's reach] on earth, nor did they have any protectors besides God. The punishment will be doubled for them. They were unable to hear, and they did not see.
interpretation: The verse (Hud 11:20) says that those who invented lies about God and barred people from His path can never outrun His power or defeat His plan, whether in this world or the next, and that no ally or patron can shield them from His judgment. Their punishment is doubled because they were guilty twice over: they went astray themselves and they led others astray. Their inability to hear and see does not mean they lacked physical faculties. It means they did not use their hearing and sight to accept the truth and reflect on the signs of God, so they were as good as deaf and blind to guidance. Since they closed their ears and eyes to the truth, they bear responsibility for their loss.

translation: Those are the ones who have lost their own souls, and what they used to fabricate has abandoned them and gone astray from them.
interpretation: The verse declares that those who invented falsehood about God and set up partners beside Him have ruined themselves in the deepest sense: they staked their own souls on illusions and forfeited their eternal wellbeing. On the Day of Judgment the false gods, intercessors, and claims they relied upon will prove empty and vanish, offering no help or defense. Their loss is therefore twofold, the loss of their own selves and the failure of everything they trusted in place of God, showing that falsehood cannot ultimately sustain anyone when the truth is revealed.

translation: Without doubt, it is they who in the Hereafter will be the greatest losers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 11:22) tells us that those who invented lies about God and barred people from His path will lose everything on the Day of Judgment. The word 'akhsarun' (the greatest losers) means that their loss is not just one among many but the most complete. They traded eternal reward for fleeting worldly gains, so they will find that their deeds have earned them nothing, their false gods will abandon them, and the effort they spent hindering others from God's path will turn into a burden on them. The verse teaches that true success and failure are measured by one's final standing before God, not by worldly status or apparent advantage.

translation: Indeed, those who believe, do righteous deeds, and humble themselves before their Lord — they are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse teaches that entry into Paradise rests on three connected foundations: sound faith, righteous action, and inward humility before God (ikhbat). Faith is not complete as a mere claim; it must be shown through good deeds, and those deeds must be accompanied by a tranquil, submissive heart that turns to God in reverence and dependence, free from arrogance or self-reliance. Those who combine these qualities are described as the 'companions' of Paradise, which suggests that they are its true and rightful inhabitants, and their eternal stay there is God's lasting reward for a life in which belief, conduct, and humility were united.

translation: The likeness of the two groups is as the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are the two equal in likeness? Will you not then take heed?
interpretation: God compares the disbelievers and the believers to two kinds of people. The disbelievers are like someone who is blind to the signs of God in creation and deaf to the call of revelation, so they cannot perceive guidance or benefit from admonition. The believers are like someone who sees clearly and hears attentively, who reflects on the signs, listens to the truth and follows it. Just as no one with sound reason would consider the blind and deaf equal to the one who sees and hears, the one who rejects the truth cannot be equal to the one who accepts it, either in understanding, conduct or final destiny. The closing question urges people to reflect and remember, so that they recognize the plain difference between guidance and misguidance and choose the path of faith.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people, [saying]: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner."
interpretation: The verse establishes that prophethood is a mercy and a duty of guidance: Noah was sent not with a hidden or ambiguous message but as an open, unmistakable warner, calling his people from idolatry to the worship of God alone before the consequences of their disbelief overtook them. By describing himself as a 'clear warner' (nadhir mubin), Noah signals that he was a messenger whose warning was plain and honest, leaving his people with no excuse. It also situates the Qur'an's account of Noah within the universal pattern that God never punishes a people without first sending a clear warning, which consoles and strengthens the Prophet Muhammad by showing that earlier messengers faced the same task.

translation: That you worship none but God. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful Day.
interpretation: This verse sums up the core message of the prophets, here voiced by Noah to his people: worship belongs to God alone, and any devotion given to idols, created beings, or other powers is a grave wrong. Noah's warning comes from care, not hostility. He fears for them because rejecting the truth has consequences, and the Day of Judgment will bring a painful reckoning for those who persist in associating partners with God. The verse links sincere monotheism with moral accountability: how a person answers the call to worship God alone shapes their ultimate fate, and a true messenger warns out of compassion for his people.

translation: The chiefs of his people who disbelieved said: 'We see you only as a human being like ourselves, and we see that none have followed you except those who are the lowest among us, without deep thought. We do not see in you any superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars.'
interpretation: The verse shows the typical arrogance of the elite when confronted with a prophetic message. Noah's opponents judged truth by social status and outward appearance rather than by evidence. They rejected the idea that a messenger could be human, and they despised the poor and weak who responded first, treating wealth and rank as signs of worth and divine favor. Their objection that the believers followed 'without thought' ignored that sincere hearts readily recognize truth, while pride and vested interests blind those with power. The verse teaches that the value of a message is not measured by the status of its followers, and that prejudice, class pride, and refusal to reflect lead people to dismiss the truth by accusing its bearers of lying.

translation: He said: O my people, have you considered, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has granted me mercy from Himself, but it has been made obscure to you, shall we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it?
interpretation: Noah answers his people's charge that he is merely a man like them. He argues that his message rests on clear proof from God and that his prophethood is a mercy from Him. Their hearts are blind to that proof because of their arrogance and stubbornness, so they cannot see it. Noah says he has no power to force faith on them, because faith must come from free conviction and willing acceptance, not coercion. His duty is only to convey the message clearly, and guidance is in God's hands. The verse thus affirms that religion cannot be imposed by force and that rejecting the truth despite its clarity is the people's own responsibility.

translation: And O my people, I do not ask you for any wealth in return for it. My reward is only from God. And I will not drive away those who have believed; indeed, they will meet their Lord. But I see that you are a people who are ignorant.
interpretation: Noah (peace be upon him) tells his people that his call is free of worldly motive: he demands no payment for conveying the message, since his reward rests with God alone, which shows his sincerity. When the arrogant elite demand that he dismiss the poor and humble believers who follow him, he refuses, because those believers have a standing with God: they will meet their Lord, who will hold to account anyone who wrongs them, and who values faith rather than social rank or wealth. He then rebukes his people for ignorance, because they judge people by status and riches rather than by faith and righteousness, and fail to grasp the reality of prophethood and the true criteria of honor before God.

translation: And O my people, who would help me against God if I were to drive them away? Will you not then reflect?
interpretation: Noah, answering the elite who demanded that he expel his poor and humble followers, explains that these believers hold a standing of sincere faith with God, and that mistreating or rejecting them would be an injustice for which he would have no protector on the Day of Judgment. A person's worth in God's sight is determined by faith and righteousness, not by wealth, rank or social status, and a messenger cannot trade away the dignity of the believers to win the approval of the powerful. His closing question, 'Will you not reflect?', calls his people to recognize this moral truth and to abandon their arrogant standards of judging people.

translation: I do not say to you that I possess the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel; and I do not say about those whom your eyes look down upon that God will never grant them any good. God knows best what is within their souls. Indeed, if I did so, I would surely be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: In this verse Noah answers his people's objections by affirming the limits of his role as a messenger: he is a human servant of God, not a possessor of divine wealth, not a knower of the hidden, and not an angel, so his authority rests solely on revelation and not on extraordinary powers or status. He also refuses to join the elites in despising the poor and humble believers who followed him, or to pass judgment that God will withhold goodness from them, because only God knows the true state of hearts and the worth of a person lies in sincerity and faith, not in worldly rank. To condemn them without knowledge would be an injustice, so he places himself among the wrongdoers if he were to do so. The lesson is humility in those who call to God, and the prohibition of scorning believers or judging their inner state and ultimate fate.

translation: They said: "O Noah, you have disputed with us and have prolonged your dispute with us; so bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."
interpretation: The verse shows how people who are stubborn in disbelief respond when they have no answer to clear arguments. Noah's people do not refute his reasoning; they complain that he has argued with them too much and then mock him by demanding the punishment he has warned of. Their challenge is not a sincere search for truth but an expression of arrogance and a refusal to reflect. They treat divine warning as a mere threat and make the timing of God's judgment a test of the prophet's honesty, forgetting that such matters belong to God alone. The verse teaches that persistent rejection can harden hearts until people prefer to gamble with their own destruction rather than accept a message they dislike.

translation: He said: "Only Allah will bring it upon you, if He wills, and you cannot escape."
interpretation: This verse is Noah's reply to his people when they challenged him to hasten the punishment he had warned them of. He tells them that the timing of divine punishment is not his to command, nor theirs to demand; it rests solely with God, who sends it according to His will and wisdom. The Prophet is only a warner, and the hour of judgment is determined by God alone. Once God decrees it, no one can frustrate His plan or flee from it, since all creation is within His power. The verse teaches humility before God's authority, the folly of mocking warnings, and the certainty that human defiance cannot nullify God's decree.

translation: And my advice will not benefit you, even if I wished to advise you, if God intends to let you go astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This is the speech of Noah to his people after they stubbornly rejected his warnings. He tells them that advice only helps those whose hearts are open to guidance; when a people persist in arrogance and denial, God's decree lets them remain in the misguidance they have chosen, and no amount of sincere counsel can change that. Their going astray is not outside God's authority, since He is their Lord who governs all affairs, and the verse ends with a reminder that they will return to Him for reckoning. Noah's words thus combine a statement of the limits of the preacher's power, which lies only in conveying the message, with a warning that accountability to God is certain.

translation: Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "If I have invented it, then upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of the crimes you commit."
interpretation: This verse (Hud 11:35) answers the disbelievers' accusation that the Prophet fabricated the revelation and falsely attributed it to God. Instead of arguing at length, the Prophet is told to respond with a principle of personal accountability: if the charge were true, the guilt and its consequences would fall on him alone, and no one else would be burdened by it. Yet he is entirely free of responsibility for the wrongdoing of those who deny the message and accuse him falsely, since each person answers for his own deeds. The response shows the Prophet's confidence in his truthfulness, since no one would risk such a grave sin knowing he alone must bear it. It also warns the deniers that their rejection and slander are their own crime, for which they will answer before God, while the Prophet's duty is only to convey the message.

translation: And it was revealed to Noah: "No one of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not grieve over what they used to do."
interpretation: This verse marks a turning point in Noah's mission. After centuries of calling his people, God tells him that the door of faith has closed for the rest of them: their stubborn rejection has become settled, and no new believers will join the few who already follow him. The instruction not to grieve is a consolation and a release from emotional burden. A prophet's duty is to convey the message, not to force guidance, and he is not responsible for their persistence in disbelief or for their mockery and harm. Noah is to set aside his sorrow and prepare for God's decisive judgment, which the following verses describe as the building of the Ark. The verse teaches that when the truth has been fully conveyed and rejected, the believer should rely on God's wisdom and timing rather than despair over the refusal of others.

translation: And construct the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they will be drowned.
interpretation: God commands Noah to build the ark under His watchful protection and precise guidance, so that the work is neither left to human guesswork nor exposed to the interference of his opponents. The phrase 'under Our eyes' conveys divine care and oversight, while 'Our inspiration' means that the design and method come by revelation. Noah is also told not to plead for the wrongdoers among his people, because after long years of calling them and their persistent rejection, God's judgment has been decreed and is final. The verse shows that divine mercy is bound up with justice: the believers are saved by obedience to God's instruction, while those who persist in injustice and denial meet their appointed destruction, and even a prophet's intercession cannot alter a ruling that has been established.

translation: And he was building the ark, and every time a company of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him. He said, 'If you ridicule us, then we will ridicule you just as you ridicule.'
interpretation: The verse shows the steadfastness of Prophet Noah (peace be upon him) in carrying out God's command despite the mockery of the disbelieving elite, who saw no sense in building a ship far from any sea. His reply is not mere retaliation but a confident warning: their scorn rests on ignorance of what is coming, and the day will arrive when the flood exposes who was truly foolish. The believer's response to derision, then, is to continue the work of obedience with certainty in God's promise, leaving the final judgment to the outcome that God brings about, when the mockers become the ones deserving of ridicule for their heedlessness.

translation: So you will soon know who it is that a punishment will come to that will disgrace him, and upon whom an everlasting punishment will descend.
interpretation: The verse is the warning Noah gave his people when they mocked him as he built the ark. It tells them that the outcome will settle who was right: those who ridiculed him will themselves be struck by a punishment that humiliates them in this world, the flood, and by a lasting punishment in the Hereafter that never ends. The mockery of the believers is therefore short-lived, because events will soon show who is on the side of truth and who is on the side of falsehood. The verse also teaches believers to stay patient and confident in God's promise, since the final disgrace belongs to those who persist in denial and arrogance.

translation: Until, when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said: 'Load into it two of every kind, a pair, and your family—except those against whom the word has already gone forth—and those who believe.' But none believed with him except a few.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine judgment arrives at its appointed moment, and that the gushing of the oven, the sign of the flood's onset, marks the point where respite ends and the command is carried out. Noah is told to preserve life by taking a pair of every kind, which shows God's mercy and order even amid punishment. The exclusion of family members against whom the word had been decreed teaches that salvation depends on faith and righteous response to God, not on kinship or lineage. The closing note that only a few believed despite Noah's long preaching shows that truth is not measured by the number of its followers, and that the believers are few but are the ones saved.

translation: And he said, "Embark upon it; in the name of Allah be its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: Noah calls his believers to board the ark while placing every stage of the voyage under God's name and authority. Its sailing and its coming to rest are not governed by the skill of the builder or the strength of the vessel, but by God alone, so safety is sought through reliance on Him rather than on the means. Ending with God's forgiveness and mercy shows that the believers' deliverance from the flood is not a reward earned by their own merit, but a grace from a Lord who forgives their shortcomings and has compassion on them, in contrast to the wrongdoers who are drowned.

translation: And it sailed with them through waves like mountains, and Noah called out to his son, who was standing apart: "O my son, board with us, and do not be with the disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse portrays the overwhelming scale of the flood, with waves towering like mountains, while the ark, by God's power and protection, carries the believers safely through. In the midst of this terror, Noah's call to his son shows a father's mercy and the duty to convey guidance until the last moment. The son stood 'apart', not only physically but in belief, having separated himself from his father's faith. Noah's plea, 'do not be with the disbelievers', shows that salvation depends on faith and following God's message, not on family ties, and that the door of repentance stays open until the moment judgment arrives.

translation: He said: "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." Noah said: "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for those on whom He has mercy." And the waves came between them, and he was among those drowned.
interpretation: The verse shows that salvation depends on God's mercy and on following His guidance, not on worldly means, lineage, or human reckoning. Noah's son relied on a mountain, a created thing that seemed safe, and he trusted his own judgment over his father's warning. Noah answered that when God's decree comes, nothing in creation can shield anyone from it, and only those whom God has shown mercy will be safe. Even the closest family tie, that of father and son, could not save someone who rejected faith. The sudden rising of the waves between them shows how swiftly God's decree is carried out and how final the separation is when the chance to repent is gone.

translation: And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold [your rain]." And the water subsided, the matter was decided, and the ark came to rest on Mount Judi. And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse shows that all of creation obeys God's command absolutely. The earth and sky are addressed as if they hear and obey, and the flood begins and ends only by His will. The phrase 'the matter was decided' means God's decree was fulfilled: the believers were saved and the deniers were destroyed, so the outcome was never left to chance or to human power. The ark's resting on Judi marks the safety given to Noah and his followers after their trial. The closing curse, 'Away with the wrongdoing people,' teaches that persistent injustice and rejection of God's message lead to ruin and exclusion from His mercy, and that this ruin is a just consequence, not an arbitrary punishment.

translation: And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family; and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."
interpretation: Noah's appeal is not a defiance of God but a distressed father's plea rooted in the divine promise to save his family (11:40). As the flood engulfed his son, Noah, trusting that God's promise is true, asked how the son could be among the drowned. The verse shows a prophet's human love and anxiety, while he still affirms God's perfect justice by calling Him the most just of judges and leaves the matter to His wisdom. The following verses clarify that kinship in God's sight rests on faith and righteous deeds, not blood alone, and that Noah should not ask about what he has no knowledge of.

translation: He said: O Noah, he is not of your family; indeed, his conduct was unrighteous. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant.
interpretation: God corrects Noah's plea for his disobedient son by teaching that kinship in the sight of God is defined by faith and righteous action rather than by blood. The son, by rejecting the message and persisting in unrighteous conduct, severed the bond of true family belonging and so was not included in the promise to save Noah's family. Noah is gently warned not to petition for what he does not fully understand, since God's wisdom and justice encompass hidden realities beyond human perception. The verse teaches humility in supplication: even a prophet must submit to divine knowledge, and love for one's relatives must not override acceptance of God's judgment. The admonition 'lest you be among the ignorant' is a loving elevation of Noah's rank, urging him to remain with those who know and trust God's wisdom.

translation: He said, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers."
interpretation: Noah, upon being rebuked for pleading for his son who had drowned, responds with humility and immediate repentance. The verse teaches that a servant should not make requests of God in matters whose wisdom and outcome he cannot know, since God's judgment is based on perfect knowledge and justice, and familial love or emotion must not override submission to His decree. Even a prophet recognizes his complete dependence on God's forgiveness and mercy for salvation, understanding that without them no one, however exalted, can avoid loss. True devotion therefore combines trust in God's wisdom, swift return to Him after a slip, and awareness that one's success rests on His grace rather than one's own merit.

translation: It was said: "O Noah, disembark in peace from Us and with blessings upon you and upon nations (descending) from those with you. But there will be other nations whom We shall grant enjoyment for a time, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."
interpretation: After the flood, God commands Noah to leave the ark secure under His protection, with lasting blessings on him and on the believing communities that will arise from his companions. The verse also shows that Noah's descendants will divide into two paths: the believers, who receive peace and blessing, and others who are given worldly enjoyment for a set time. Their comfort is no sign of God's approval, because if they persist in disbelief and wrongdoing, a painful punishment from God will reach them. Worldly provision is therefore a test and a respite, not proof of salvation, while true security and blessing come from faith and obedience.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen, which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed, the best outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: After recounting the story of Noah and his people, God tells the Prophet Muhammad that this detailed account could only have reached him through revelation, since neither he nor his unlettered community had any prior knowledge of it. This serves as proof of the truth of his prophethood. The verse then draws a lesson from the story: just as Noah endured long years of rejection and hostility and was finally vindicated while his deniers perished, the Prophet should remain steadfast against the harm of his opponents, because the ultimate triumph and good end belong to those who are mindful of God and fear Him, not to those who deny and oppose.

translation: And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are not but inventors [of falsehood]."
interpretation: Hud, like every prophet before and after him, began his call with the foundation of all revelation: pure monotheism. By calling him 'their brother,' the verse shows that God sends messengers from among their own people, who are known to them in lineage, character, and language, so that they have no excuse for rejecting the message on the grounds that it came from a stranger. His charge that they were 'inventors' means that their worship of idols and their claims that these idols had any power to benefit, harm, or intercede were baseless fabrications with no knowledge or revealed authority behind them. Worship belongs to God alone because He is the Creator and Sustainer, and associating partners with Him is not a legitimate difference of opinion but a lie against God.

translation: O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from He who created me. Then will you not reason?
interpretation: This is the speech of a prophet (Hud, in Surah Hud 11:51) to his people, affirming the sincerity of his message. He asks for no wage, wealth, or status for conveying it, so no worldly motive can be suspected behind his call. His only recompense is with God, who brought him into being and who alone can truly reward him. Invoking God as his Creator also reminds the people that the One who made them is the One to be worshipped. The closing question, 'Will you not reason?', urges them to see that a man who gains nothing materially, yet endures their hostility, must be truthful, and that his message deserves to be weighed with intellect instead of being rejected out of stubbornness.

translation: "And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will send the sky upon you with abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength, and do not turn away as criminals."
interpretation: In this verse the Prophet Hud tells the people of 'Ad that repentance is the key to both spiritual and worldly well-being. Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) means asking God to pardon past sins, while turning back (tawba) means abandoning sin and returning to obedience. When a community does both, God opens His blessings to it: abundant rain, which brings fertile land, prosperity and security, and added strength on top of the strength they already have, which can include population, wealth, and power. This shows that faith and righteousness are not opposed to material progress but can be a cause of it, and that the hardships of a people are often tied to their moral state. Hud's closing warning, not to turn away as criminals, is a call not to persist in arrogance and rejection of the truth, since that is the path of wrongdoers who bring ruin on themselves.

translation: They said: 'O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we are not going to abandon our gods on your say-so, and we are not believers in you.'
interpretation: The people of 'Ad answer their prophet with stubborn denial rather than reasoned argument. They claim Hud brought no clear evidence, though his message was plain and consistent with sound reason and the earlier revelation. What they call a lack of proof is really an unwillingness to accept it, because they are attached to the customs and idols of their forefathers. Their refusal to abandon their gods 'on his say-so' shows that they put inherited tradition above truth. The verse teaches that rejection of the prophets often comes from pride, habit and fear of losing status, not from a real absence of evidence. It also shows that when a people has already decided not to believe, no sign will move them, and they close the door to guidance themselves.

translation: We only say that some of our gods have afflicted you with evil. He said: Indeed, I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves, that I am free of what you associate with Him.
interpretation: The people of Hud, unable to refute his arguments, attribute his preaching to madness inflicted by their idols for his having insulted them. Hud answers with calm confidence, publicly declaring his complete disavowal of their idols. By calling God as witness, and challenging them to witness as well, he shows that he fears neither their gods nor their threats, since these idols have no power to harm or benefit. His firm stand demonstrates the strength of a prophet who relies wholly on God and shows that true tawhid frees a person from fear of anything besides God.

translation: ...besides Him. So plot against me, all of you together, then give me no respite.
interpretation: This is the challenge of the Prophet Hud (peace be upon him) to his people, who had accused him of being struck by the evil of their gods. He declares his total reliance on God and his freedom from their false deities, and he dares them to unite their strength and schemes against him without delay. His confidence shows that harm and benefit are in God's hands alone, that idols have no power, and that whoever trusts in God fully need not fear any creature, however many they are or however much they plot.

translation: Indeed, I have placed my trust in God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds it by its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.
interpretation: Hud declares to his people that his reliance rests wholly on God, who is Lord of both the believer and the denier, so no threat from them can harm him without God's leave. To say God holds every creature 'by the forelock' is an image of complete mastery: nothing moves, prospers or suffers except within His power and will, and no one can escape His authority. The closing words, 'my Lord is on a straight path,' mean that God's dominion is exercised with justice and wisdom; He does not wrong anyone, and He leads truth to triumph and holds each to account. Trust in God is therefore reasonable and safe, because the One who controls all things is perfectly just.

translation: But if you turn away, then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will make another people succeed you, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.
interpretation: This is the reply of the Prophet Hud to his people of 'Ad, and it teaches that a messenger's duty ends with delivering the message clearly; guidance itself is not in his hands. If they reject it, the loss is theirs alone. God does not depend on any people, so He can replace them with a community who will obey Him, and their disbelief cannot diminish His dominion in the slightest. His being 'Guardian over all things' means He preserves and sustains all creation and keeps account of every deed. It also assures the believers that He protects His messengers from the schemes of their enemies, so the messenger can rely on Him, free from fear of his people's threats.

translation: And when Our decree came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse shows that deliverance from divine punishment comes through God's mercy rather than through the believers' own deeds or strength. When God's command for the destruction of the disbelieving people of 'Ad was carried out, Hud and his companions were set apart and spared. Their faith made them deserving of that mercy, yet the rescue itself is attributed to God's grace. The phrase 'a severe punishment' stresses how grave the fate was from which they were saved, and it reminds the reader that God keeps His promise to protect those who believe and remain steadfast, even when they are few and surrounded by a hostile majority.

translation: And such were 'Ād: they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.
interpretation: The verse points to the ruins and the story of 'Ād as a lasting lesson, and it shows that their destruction came from three connected failings: rejecting God's clear signs, disobeying the messengers sent to them (rejecting one messenger is in effect rejecting all, since they bring the same message), and submitting to the orders of arrogant, stubborn leaders instead of the guidance of God. It warns that blind obedience to oppressive and defiant authority, especially when it contradicts revelation, is itself a form of rebellion against God and leads a people to ruin. True accountability lies in following truth rather than power.

translation: And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Indeed, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting God and His messengers brings not only destruction but a lasting disgrace: the people of 'Ad are remembered with condemnation in history, and their rejection will bring them further rejection and ruin on the Day of Judgment. By denying the message of Hud, they in effect denied their Lord, and so their name became a byword for arrogance and ruin. Their fate serves as a warning that worldly power and strength cannot protect those who persist in disbelief, and that the consequences of defiance follow a people in both this life and the next.

translation: And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. He brought you into being from the earth and settled you in it, so seek His forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."
interpretation: Salih's message follows the same call as every prophet: pure monotheism, grounded in gratitude. Thamud's very origin from the earth and their being made its inhabitants, with its resources and the ability to build and prosper, are blessings that come only from God, so worship belongs to Him alone. Having received this trust, they are called to repent: first to seek forgiveness for the shirk and wrongdoing they have already committed, then to return to God sincerely in obedience. The verse closes with reassurance that no intermediary is needed, since God is close to those who turn to Him and answers their prayers and repentance, so there is no excuse for delay.

translation: They said: 'O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in grave doubt, suspicious, about that to which you call us.'
interpretation: The verse (Hud 11:62) shows how Salih's people reject his message by appealing to ancestral tradition rather than evidence. They admit that they once respected him and expected him to become a leader and a source of benefit, which shows they knew his good character. Once he called them to worship God alone, they treated him as a disappointment. Their claim of 'disquieting doubt' is not an honest search for truth but a defensive excuse. They hold on to inherited customs, treat the worship of their forefathers as proof of its correctness, and view any challenge to those customs as a betrayal of the community. The verse warns that blind imitation and social pride can stop people from accepting clear guidance, even from someone whose honesty they have long known.

translation: He said: 'O my people, consider: if I stand upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has granted me mercy from Himself, who would help me against God if I were to disobey Him? Then you would add nothing for me except loss.'
interpretation: This is the prophet Salih's reply to his people, who urged him to abandon his message and return to their ways. He argues that his prophethood rests on certain knowledge and on divine mercy, so he cannot trade the truth for their approval. If he disobeyed God by hiding or compromising the message to please them, no one could shield him from God's punishment, since all protection and help come from God alone. Following their advice would therefore not benefit him at all. It would only ruin him, and their counsel to abandon the truth would only increase his loss. The verse teaches that a person who has clear insight from God must remain steadfast in obedience and not be swayed by social pressure, because disobedience to God leaves no refuge and no helper.

translation: And O my people, this is the she-camel of God, a sign for you. So leave her to graze on God's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest an imminent punishment seize you.
interpretation: Prophet Salih tells the people of Thamud that the she-camel, brought forth miraculously in answer to their demand for a sign, is a test of their obedience and a proof of his prophethood. Calling her 'the she-camel of God' marks her as sacred and under divine protection, and the phrase 'God's earth' reminds them that the land and its pasture belong to God, not to them, so they have no right to deny her sustenance. The command to leave her alone and not harm her is a moral trial: respecting a clear sign from God brings safety, while defying it by hurting her would invite swift, unavoidable punishment. The verse teaches that rejecting or violating God's clear signs after they have been shown leads to destruction, and that stewardship of what God has made obliges us to refrain from wrongdoing.

translation: But they hamstrung her, so he said: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise that will not be proven false."
interpretation: The verse shows that when the people of Thamud killed the she-camel, which was God's clear sign to them, they crossed the line from doubt into open defiance. Prophet Salih's response is not a new warning but the announcement of a short, final period of respite before punishment. The three days are an act of divine patience, giving them one last chance to repent, and also a test of whether they would heed the sign. Their enjoyment in their homes during this time is bitterly ironic, since they were living out the last of their lives with no security. The phrase 'a promise that will not be proven false' stresses that God's threat is as certain as His promise: once a people persist in rejecting the signs after clear proof, the sentence is fixed, and the delay is mercy, not a sign that the warning was empty.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Almighty.
interpretation: Salvation of the believers comes only through God's mercy, not through their numbers or their own power. Even their faith and good deeds are a means that God's grace makes effective. The rescue was twofold: protection from the physical destruction that struck the people of Thamud, and protection from the humiliation and disgrace of that day, which exposed the arrogance of the deniers. The closing names, the Strong and the Almighty, affirm that God's decree cannot be resisted, so those who rely on Him are safe while those who oppose Him, however powerful they appear, will be overcome.

translation: And the Cry seized those who had done wrong, and by morning they lay lifeless, prostrate in their homes.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment comes suddenly and decisively upon peoples who persist in injustice, chiefly by rejecting God's message and oppressing others. The word 'zulm' means wrongdoing in its widest sense, from disbelief to transgression against people. Their end was a single blast that left them motionless in the very homes where they had felt secure, a sign that worldly strength, status and dwellings give no protection from God's decree. The verse is a warning to later generations to heed the messengers and to reform before the appointed time arrives, since the fate of earlier wrongdoers is an enduring lesson and not just a story.

translation: As if they had never prospered there. Indeed, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Away with Thamud!
interpretation: The verse portrays how complete and sudden the destruction of Thamud was: after the mighty blast struck them, no trace of their former prosperity, comfort, and strength remained, as though they had never lived in their homes. Their ruin was not arbitrary but the direct consequence of their ingratitude and their rejection of their Lord and His messenger Salih. The closing curse, 'Away with Thamud,' declares that they were removed from God's mercy, and serves as a warning that worldly power and abundance offer no protection to those who persist in denying the truth.

translation: And certainly Our messengers came to Abraham with glad tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace." And he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf.
interpretation: The verse shows the noble character of Abraham in honoring guests. When the angelic messengers greeted him with peace, he returned the greeting, and the words of his reply, "Peace" in the nominative form, are understood to convey a firmer and more lasting salutation than theirs. Without delay, and before even asking who they were, he hurried to serve them the best of what he had, a roasted calf. This teaches that generosity and hospitality are marks of the righteous, that a greeting should be answered in kind or better, and that a host should be prompt and ungrudging in welcoming guests, even strangers, while the divine tidings of a son were being brought to him in the midst of this noble conduct.

translation: But when he saw that their hands did not reach toward the food, he found them strange and felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot."
interpretation: Abraham had offered his guests a roasted calf, and in the custom of hospitality, refusing food signaled possible ill intent, so their untouched hands made him uneasy and afraid. The verse shows that the visitors were not ordinary men but angels, who have no need of food. Once they sensed his fear, they calmed him at once by revealing their mission: they came not to harm him but to carry out God's decree against the wrongdoing people of Lot. This teaches that even a prophet experiences natural human fear, that reassurance comes from God through His messengers, and that God's punishment is directed at those who persist in transgression, not at the righteous.

translation: And his wife was standing by, and she laughed; then We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, of Jacob.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's promise of offspring comes by His power and not by ordinary expectation. Sarah, an elderly woman who had long been childless, laughed in joyful astonishment when the angels who visited Abraham announced the destruction of Lot's people. Her laughter was a reaction of relief and wonder at the good news, and God then confirmed that she would bear Isaac and that Isaac in turn would have a son, Jacob. This shows that God's mercy reaches the righteous in unexpected ways and times, rewarding Abraham's household with a lasting line of prophets, and that nothing is beyond His decree, whatever the apparent limits of age or circumstance.

translation: She said: 'Woe to me! Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman, and this husband of mine is an old man? Indeed, this is a truly astonishing thing!'
interpretation: Sarah's exclamation upon hearing the angels' glad tidings of Isaac is not a denial of God's power but a spontaneous expression of human amazement at something that defies the ordinary course of nature. Her words 'Woe to me' are an idiom of surprise, not distress. The verse shows that even the righteous respond with wonder when God's decree overrides natural causes, and the angels' reply that follows (asking whether she wonders at God's command) reminds believers that God's will is not bound by biological limits, and that His mercy and blessings extend to the household of Abraham.

translation: They said: 'Do you wonder at the decree of God? The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious.'
interpretation: The angels rebuke Sarah's astonishment at the news of a child in her old age, reminding her that God's command is not bound by natural limits, since what He decrees comes to pass however improbable it seems. They also console her by stating that God's mercy and abundant blessings have long rested on Abraham's household, so being singled out for such favor is in keeping with the household's established standing. The closing words, 'Praiseworthy and Glorious,' ground the promise in God's character: He is worthy of praise for His acts and generous gifts, and exalted in majesty and power, so nothing He wills is beyond Him. The believer should respond to divine promises with gratitude and trust rather than doubt.

translation: So when the fear left Abraham and the good news had reached him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: After Abraham's fear of his unrecognized guests subsided and he was reassured by the glad tidings of a son, Isaac, his compassion turned to the people of Lot. His 'pleading' with God was not defiance but an expression of his gentle, forbearing, and merciful nature, as the following verse describes him as forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning to God. He hoped that the doomed people might be spared or given time to repent, and that Lot, who lived among them, would be protected. The verse shows that a believer's joy in personal blessings does not make him indifferent to the fate of others, and that it is permissible to supplicate and intercede with God out of mercy, while the divine decree, based on the people's persistent wrongdoing, remains with God's wisdom and justice.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and constantly turning back to God.
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham as a model of balanced spiritual character. His forbearance (hilm) means he restrained his anger and met provocation with patience and gentleness, even when his people rejected him. His being 'awwah' shows a heart so sensitive and humble before God that it sighs in awe, supplication, and compassion for others. And 'munib' shows that his gentleness was grounded in a habit of returning to God in every situation, repenting and relying on Him. In context, it explains why Abraham pleaded for Lot's people: his mercy and clemency moved him to intercede, yet he accepted God's decree when it came. True strength of faith is thus gentle patience joined to a God-conscious heart.

translation: O Abraham, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will come to them a punishment that cannot be repelled.
interpretation: The angels address Abraham after he began pleading on behalf of Lot's people, urging him to stop interceding for them. Their fate has already been decreed by God's final and binding judgment, which no prayer or mediation can change. The verse shows that, although Abraham's compassion and forbearance were praiseworthy, once persistent wrongdoing has reached its limit, God's justice is carried out and the punishment becomes inevitable and irreversible.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them and felt powerless to protect them, and he said, "This is a trying day."
interpretation: When the angels arrived in the form of handsome young men, Lot did not know they were messengers of God. He knew his people's depraved habits and feared they would assault his guests and shame him, while he lacked the strength or support to defend them. His grief and anxiety made him call it an 'oppressive, severe day', one of intense hardship. The verse shows that even a prophet experienced real human distress and helplessness before the decree of God, and that relief came only through divine intervention, as the unfolding of the story makes clear.

translation: And his people came rushing towards him, and before that they used to commit evil deeds. He said, 'O my people, here are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear God and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single right-minded man?'
interpretation: Lot's plea shows a prophet's moral courage when his guests were threatened by a community hardened in sin through long habit. His words, 'here are my daughters,' are best understood as pointing to the lawful path of marriage (the women of the community, as a prophet is like a father to his people), not as a literal offer to hand over his daughters. He contrasts the purity of what God has made lawful with the corruption of their lust. He appeals first to their fear of God, then to their sense of honor and hospitality, since dishonoring a guest is a disgrace to the host. His final question, 'Is there not among you a single right-minded man?', is a lament that moral sense had vanished from the whole town, so that no one remained to restrain the crowd or defend what is right. The verse teaches that persistent sin dulls conscience and shame, and that a believer must defend the sanctity of those under his protection by appealing to faith and reason.

translation: They said, "You already know that we have no claim to your daughters, and you surely know what we want."
interpretation: This is the reply of Lot's people when he appealed to them to take his daughters in lawful marriage instead of committing indecency against his guests. They openly reject his offer, saying they have no right or desire in women, since their appetites have turned away from what is natural. By saying 'you know what we want,' they admit that their aim is the shameful act itself and show that they are stubborn in their corruption. Their words reveal a people whose desires have overruled reason and natural disposition, so that appeals to decency, honor, and lawful alternatives no longer move them, and this prepares the way for their destruction.

translation: He said: "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support!"
interpretation: This is Prophet Lot's anguished cry (Surah Hud 11:80) when his people pressed him to hand over his guests. He wishes he had the physical strength or a powerful clan to defend those under his protection. It voices his human helplessness in the face of widespread corruption and his sense of being alone and without worldly support. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that God has mercy on Lot, for he was in truth taking refuge in a strong support, namely God Himself. The verse shows that even a prophet may feel the weakness of human means, while the real and unfailing support is always with God. Immediately after, the angels reveal who they are and that Lot is secure.

translation: They said: "O Lot, we are the messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So travel with your family during a portion of the night, and let none of you turn around—except your wife; indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"
interpretation: After Lot's anguish at being unable to protect his guests from his corrupt people, the angels reveal their true identity and reassure him that God's power shields him, so the mob cannot harm him. They instruct him to leave with his believing family in the dark of night and not to look back, a sign of complete and urgent submission to God's command and detachment from the doomed town. His wife, who sided with the wrongdoers in heart, is excluded from deliverance and will share their punishment, showing that salvation depends on faith and not on family ties. The promise of destruction at dawn, with the rhetorical question 'Is not the morning near?', comforts Lot and underscores that God's judgment is certain, precisely timed, and close at hand.

translation: So when Our command came, We turned it upside down, and rained upon it stones of baked clay, layered one upon another.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment arrives at its appointed time, after the people of Lot had persisted in their immorality and rejected the warnings of their prophet. The overturning of the towns, so that their highest parts became their lowest, is a fitting recompense: those who inverted the natural order and the moral order were themselves turned upside down. The stones of hardened clay, falling in continuous succession, show that the punishment was complete and left no escape. The verse is a lasting warning that God's patience with wrongdoers is not unlimited, and that when the decree comes it cannot be averted by their numbers, their strength or their settled habits.

translation: Marked [for punishment] with your Lord; and it is not far from the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The stones that rained upon the people of Lot were marked by God, each one designated for its target, which shows that divine punishment is precise and just and never random. The closing phrase is a warning to every wrongdoer in every age: the fate that struck Lot's people is not remote or bound to the past, and similar punishment can reach any who persist in oppression and transgression, since God's justice can overtake them at any moment.

translation: And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb. He said: O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day.
interpretation: Shu'ayb's call joins the right of God to the rights of people: faith in One God and honesty in trade belong together. A people who acknowledge no authority above themselves feel free to cheat others in measure and weight, so correcting worship comes first and correcting economic conduct follows from it. His reminder that he sees them in prosperity points out that their wealth is a blessing from God, which calls for gratitude and fairness, not for exploiting it through fraud. Their ease is no proof that their conduct is right, and it may be a test. His warning of a Day that encompasses them means that no one escapes accountability: neither hidden cheating nor outward success can protect against a reckoning that surrounds every person. The verse teaches that social justice and integrity in dealings are part of true monotheism and not separate from it.

translation: And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice, and do not deprive people of their due, and do not commit evil in the land as corrupters.
interpretation: The Prophet Shu'ayb urges his people to move beyond merely avoiding cheating and to actively uphold fairness in every transaction, giving each person exactly what they are owed. He teaches that dishonesty in trade is not a small private wrong but a form of corruption that damages trust and social order, so integrity in everyday dealings is part of faith and a safeguard for the whole community's well-being.

translation: What remains with God (His lawful provision) is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The Prophet Shu'ayb tells his people, who were cheating in weights and measures, that the modest, lawful gain God leaves after honest dealing is better than wealth gained through fraud, because it carries blessing and God's approval, and the benefit of that is realized only by those who truly believe. He then makes clear that his role is only to convey the message and advise them. He is not their watcher who can force them to obey or protect them from the consequences of their choices, so each person is responsible for their own conduct before God.

translation: They said: "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we cease doing with our wealth whatever we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly-guided!"
interpretation: The people of Madyan answer Shu'ayb's call to monotheism and honest dealing with mockery and defiance. They treat his prayer as the source of what they see as absurd demands, and they cannot grasp how worship could dictate economic ethics. Their words show that they see religion as a private ritual with no authority over public life, trade, or property, and that they cling to ancestral custom as proof of truth. They also claim absolute ownership of their wealth, so that they may deal in it however they like, including by cheating in weights and measures. Their closing words, 'You are the forbearing, the rightly-guided,' are sarcasm. They mean that a man known for mildness and good sense should not say such things. The verse thus shows how people who are attached to inherited ways and unrestrained gain mock those who call them to God and to justice, and how they deny that faith has any claim on their economic conduct.

translation: He said: "O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has provided me from Himself with a good provision? I do not wish to contradict you by doing what I forbid you from. I only want reform as much as I am able. My success is only through God. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn."
interpretation: In this verse the Prophet Shu'ayb answers his people's accusations by grounding his call in integrity and consistency between word and deed. He points out that his message rests on clear proof from God and that God has blessed him with lawful, good provision, so he has no need to seek gain from them or compromise the truth. He assures them that he will not secretly practice what he forbids, which would be hypocrisy, since a sincere reformer must live by what he preaches. His only goal is to set right their beliefs and dealings, within his capacity, while recognizing that results and success depend entirely on God's grace and not on his own effort. He therefore places his trust in God alone and repeatedly turns back to Him in repentance and devotion, which models for every caller to truth the combination of sincerity, personal example, effort, humility, and reliance on God.

translation: And O my people, let not my dissension cause you to be struck by the like of what struck the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: Prophet Shu'ayb warns his people that their stubborn opposition and hostility toward him, merely because he calls them to truth, should not drive them to persist in denial, since persisting leads to the same divine punishment that destroyed earlier nations: the flood for Noah's people, the wind for 'Ad, and the earthquake or cry for Thamud. He adds that the fate of Lot's people is recent in time and close in place, so they have a clear and near warning and no excuse for ignoring it. The verse teaches that history's lessons are meant to be heeded, and that obstinate enmity toward a sincere reformer brings ruin, while repentance and acceptance of the message bring safety.

translation: And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Most Loving.
interpretation: The verse, from Prophet Shu'ayb's address to his people (Hud 11:90), teaches that repentance has two parts: first asking God to erase past wrongdoing, then turning back to Him by changing one's conduct and returning to obedience. The order matters. Seeking forgiveness clears the burden of past sins, while repentance is the commitment to a new direction. The closing names, Rahim (Merciful) and Wadud (Most Loving), show that God does more than tolerate returning sinners. He welcomes them with affection, which removes despair and invites even those who have wronged deeply to come back, trusting that His response will be mercy and love rather than rejection.

translation: They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you as weak among us. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, for you are not mighty over us."
interpretation: The verse shows how a people who reject the truth respond when they have no argument against it. Shu'ayb's community claim not to grasp his message, which is really a refusal to listen and a dismissal of his words. They measure him by worldly standards of power, numbers and status, so they call him weak because he lacks a mighty following. They admit that only respect for his clan, not respect for his message or for God, restrains them from stoning him. This reflects the arrogance of those who judge truth by the strength of its bearer and not by its content. It also shows that the prophet's protection came from God, who used tribal loyalty as the means to keep him safe, even as the people ignored the divine authority behind his call.

translation: He said: "O my people, is my clan more honored by you than God, while you have cast Him behind your backs? Indeed, my Lord encompasses whatever you do."
interpretation: Shu'ayb rebukes his people for their misplaced fear. They spared him from harm only out of respect for his family and tribal standing, not out of reverence for God or for his message as a prophet. He points out the absurdity of fearing a small clan while disregarding the Creator who sent him. To 'cast God behind one's back' means to ignore His commands and treat Him as something of no consequence. He ends with a warning: God fully encompasses everything they do, in knowledge and power. Their deeds are not hidden, and they will be held to account, so tribal protection cannot shield them from His judgment.

translation: "And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and who is a liar. So watch and wait; indeed, I am watching with you." (Qur'an 11:93, the words of Prophet Shu'ayb to his people)
interpretation: In this verse Shu'ayb, having exhausted his arguments and warnings, ends his appeal by calmly withdrawing the argument and leaving the matter to God's judgment. His invitation to 'act according to your position' is not approval of their conduct but a firm challenge: each side will continue on its chosen path, and time will show whose path is true. He does not claim to decide the outcome himself; rather, he entrusts it to the unfolding of events, when the disgracing punishment will fall on the wrongdoers and the liar will be exposed. The closing call to 'watch and wait' reflects the confidence of a prophet who trusts God's promise, and it conveys that truth is ultimately vindicated by God's decree, not by the power or numbers of those who deny it.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us; and the Blast seized those who had done wrong, and by morning they lay lifeless, fallen prostrate in their homes.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment arrives only at its appointed time, and that when it does, salvation for the believers is not earned by their deeds alone but is granted as God's mercy. Shu'ayb and his followers were rescued before the judgment fell, while the wrongdoers of Madyan, who persisted in injustice such as cheating in weights and measures and rejecting their prophet, were destroyed suddenly by a single mighty cry. Their being found motionless in their own dwellings stresses how complete and abrupt their end was: the security and worldly possessions they relied on offered no protection. The lesson is that injustice and denial of the truth lead to ruin, while faith in God brings deliverance through His mercy.

translation: As if they had never prospered there. Behold! Away with Madyan, just as Thamud was taken away.
interpretation: The verse says that the people of Madyan, who rejected the Prophet Shu'ayb, were wiped out so completely that no trace of their former prosperity remained, as though they had never lived or thrived in their homes. Their fate resembled that of Thamud, who were also destroyed by a mighty blast for denying their prophet. The lesson is that worldly comfort, wealth and numbers give no protection against God's judgment once a people persist in injustice, cheating in trade, and rejection of the truth. The curse 'away with Madyan' expresses that they deserved their ruin and removal from God's mercy, and it warns later generations to heed the message of the prophets before it is too late.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: God affirms that Moses was not sent as a mere claimant but was backed by divine proofs: miraculous signs such as the staff and the shining hand, together with unmistakable, evident authority that left no excuse for denial. The verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad and the believers that the pattern of the messengers is consistent: each came with clear evidence from God, and the rejection that Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun showed (as the following verses relate) arose from arrogance and stubbornness, not from any lack of proof. Thus the truth of a prophet's mission is established by God-given evidence, and the one who rejects it after such clarity bears the responsibility.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse points out that Moses was sent with clear signs to Pharaoh and his ruling elite, yet they chose blind obedience to a tyrant over following divine guidance. Pharaoh's command is described as lacking 'rushd', meaning sound judgment and righteousness, because it led its followers to misguidance in this world and to destruction in the next. The lesson is that people are accountable for whom they obey: following a ruler whose orders contradict truth and justice is a grave error, and the worldly power or status of a leader does not make his decisions wise or good.

translation: He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them down into the Fire; and wretched is the place to which they are led.
interpretation: The verse (Hud 11:98) speaks of Pharaoh, who led his people in this world by misguiding them and urging them to reject Moses, so he will lead them on the Day of Resurrection to Hellfire as he led them in worldly error. Leadership in falsehood brings shared ruin: followers who obeyed a tyrant against the truth will join him in punishment. The Fire is called a wretched watering place because a place of arrival should bring relief and quenching, but this one brings only torment, so it is the worst destination anyone could be brought to.

translation: And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection as well. Wretched is the gift that is given.
interpretation: The verse says that the people of 'Ad, Pharaoh and the other nations who rejected God's messengers and followed tyrants did not merely perish. A curse of rejection and ill repute pursued them. In this life, they are remembered with condemnation, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be cursed before all creation. The phrase 'wretched is the gift given' calls this curse a gift in bitter irony: the only thing they are given in return for their arrogance and disbelief is a curse stacked upon a curse, first in this world and then in the Hereafter. It is a warning that the worldly power and honor of the wrongdoers is fleeting, while the consequences of their denial endure.

translation: That is from the accounts of the towns which We relate to you (Muhammad); some of them are still standing, and some are like a field that has been reaped.
interpretation: After recounting the fates of earlier peoples such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Abraham's and Lot's folk, Shu'ayb's people and Pharaoh's, God tells the Prophet that these stories are true reports of unseen history revealed to him as a warning and consolation. The phrase 'some standing and some reaped' describes the traces left by destroyed communities: some towns still have visible ruins, walls or remains that testify to their past, while others were utterly uprooted and erased, like a harvested field leaving no trace. The lesson is that the might and settled civilization of a people give no protection from God's punishment when they reject His messengers, and that the visible ruins and the vanished traces alike should move people to reflect and heed the warning.

translation: We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. So their gods, whom they invoked besides God, availed them nothing when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing for them but ruin.
interpretation: The destruction of earlier nations was not an act of injustice by God but the natural consequence of their own choices: by rejecting the messengers and worshipping false deities, they harmed their own souls. The idols they trusted could not shield them when God's decree arrived, and devotion to them only hastened their loss. The verse teaches that shirk and wrongdoing are self-inflicted harm, that God's judgment is always just, and that nothing besides God can protect a person from the consequences of their deeds.

translation: And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed, His seizing is painful and severe.
interpretation: The verse sets out a lasting divine principle: God's punishment of wrongdoing communities is not arbitrary or exceptional to the ancient peoples whose stories were just told, but follows a consistent pattern. When a town persists in injustice, namely idolatry, oppression, and rejection of the messengers, it brings destruction on itself, and God's seizing of it is both painful and severe. The verse works as a warning to the Prophet's contemporaries and to every later generation that wealth, power, and delay of punishment give no immunity. The lapse of time before punishment comes is a respite, not a pardon, and the only protection is to turn back from wrongdoing in faith and repentance.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed.
interpretation: The destruction of earlier wrongdoing nations, as recounted in the preceding verses, is a lesson for those whose hearts are alive with fear of God's punishment in the Hereafter. Seeing how God seized the nations that denied their messengers in this world, such a person reasons that the promised Day of Judgment is certain and the punishment there is greater and more enduring. The verse then describes that Day: all of humanity, from first to last, will be gathered together for it, with no one left behind, and it will be a Day witnessed by all, including angels, prophets, and creatures, when every deed is laid bare before everyone. The aim is to awaken awe and to move the believer toward obedience and repentance before that inescapable gathering.

translation: And We do not delay it except for a counted term.
interpretation: This verse (Hud 11:104) refers to the Day of Judgment. Its coming is not delayed out of neglect or inability, but because God has fixed for it an exact, numbered appointment within His knowledge. Nothing about it is random or open-ended: the time of the world is measured and limited, and when the appointed term is complete it will arrive neither earlier nor later. The apparent delay should therefore not make people doubt the promise or grow heedless, since every passing day brings them closer to a fixed reckoning.

translation: On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the blessed.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the awe of God's authority will be so complete that no one can plead, argue, or intercede unless God allows it. All worldly power and eloquence will vanish, and human beings will stand in complete submission before Him. On that Day people will be divided into two groups according to the faith and deeds they carried with them in life: those who are wretched through their rejection and wrongdoing, and those who are blessed through their belief and righteousness. The verse is a reminder to prepare for that Day now, while the opportunity to choose and act still remains.

translation: As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, where they will have sighing and wailing (groaning and gasping).
interpretation: The verse describes the state of those who sealed their own misery through disbelief and persistent wrongdoing. Their punishment is not only fire but also the visible and audible signs of intense suffering: 'zafir' is the forceful exhaling of breath in anguish and 'shahiq' is the choking, drawn-in gasp that follows. Together they depict people overwhelmed by pain, who cannot hold themselves together and whose very breathing is a cry of torment. The verse thus teaches that the consequence of rejecting guidance is real, total and inescapable misery, and it calls the listener to reflect on his choices now so that he may be among the blessed on that Day rather than among the wretched.

translation: Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.
interpretation: The verse stresses that the fate of the people it describes rests wholly on God's absolute will, not on any independent power. The phrase 'as long as the heavens and the earth endure' uses an expression familiar to the Arabs to convey long duration, while the exception 'except what your Lord wills' reminds the reader that no one has a claim against God and that nothing limits His authority. The exception does not mean that the abode will end. It affirms that the duration is granted and sustained by God's will alone, and that He is free to do whatever He intends. The closing words, 'Your Lord is the Doer of what He intends,' reassure believers that His decree is carried out without hindrance, and they warn against presuming to know God's judgment apart from what He has revealed.

translation: But those who are blessed will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift never to be cut off.
interpretation: The verse describes the final reward of the blessed: eternal life in Paradise. The phrase 'as long as the heavens and the earth endure' uses a familiar Arabic expression for perpetuity, so it signals endlessness and not a time limit. The exception 'except what your Lord wills' affirms that God's will is absolute and that the believers' bliss depends wholly on His grace and not on any independent right or power of their own. The verse closes by removing any fear that the exception means an end to their reward, since it is a gift that is never cut off. Paradise is therefore an unending bounty from God, given by His mercy, and its permanence is secured by His promise.

translation: So be not in doubt about what these people worship. They worship only as their forefathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will give them their full share, undiminished.
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that the idolatry of his people is baseless and should cause him no uncertainty about its falsehood or its fate.
