Their worship is not founded on proof or revelation but on blind imitation of their ancestors, inheriting a custom without reflection. Just as earlier nations that followed the same path were requited for it, God will give these people their full due, whether of worldly provision or of the consequences of their deeds, with nothing reduced or withheld. The verse therefore affirms divine justice: no wrong will be done to them in their recompense, and their persistence in inherited error will meet its deserved outcome.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but differences arose concerning it. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, judgment would have been decided between them. And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt about it.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that the rejection and disputes he faces over the Qur'an are nothing new: even the Torah given to Moses was accepted by some and denied or distorted by others, so disagreement over revealed truth does not prove the message false. The 'word that preceded from your Lord' is God's prior decree to grant humanity respite and postpone final judgment until an appointed term, which is why the deniers are not destroyed at once and the dispute is not settled immediately in this world. Their stance is not firm conviction but troubling uncertainty: they are in doubt that unsettles them, without real certainty in their denial. Final judgment between the believers and the disputers is therefore deferred to the Day of Resurrection.

translation: And indeed, every one of them, your Lord will surely pay them in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Aware of what they do.
interpretation: The verse affirms divine justice and perfect knowledge: every community and individual, whether believing or disbelieving, will receive full recompense for what they did, with nothing lost, added unjustly, or overlooked. God's reckoning is not based on guesswork or outward appearance, because He is fully aware of every action and intention. This offers reassurance to the righteous who endure patiently and a warning to wrongdoers who think their deeds go unnoticed, urging all to act with accountability and steadfastness, as the final outcome rests on God's exact knowledge.

translation: So remain upright, as you have been commanded, and those who have repented along with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse commands steadfastness on the straight path of faith and obedience, in the manner God prescribed and not according to personal inclination, whether through excess or negligence. This duty is shared by the Prophet and the believers who turned back to God with him, which makes uprightness a collective discipline as well as a personal one. The warning against transgression (tughyan) means going beyond the limits God has set, in religious practice, in conduct toward others, or in arrogance after success. The closing reminder that God sees everything people do grounds this steadfastness in constant awareness of God, so that moderation, accountability, and sincerity hold even when no one else is watching.

translation: And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you, and you have no protectors besides God; then you would not be helped.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against leaning on, trusting, or being complicit with wrongdoers, whether through approving their injustice, flattering them, or relying on them in ways that strengthen their oppression. Such inclination, even without committing the wrong oneself, makes one share in its consequence. The one who supports injustice puts himself in danger of punishment, and at that point no ally or helper can save him, since God is the only true protector. The verse therefore calls for a moral independence: Muslims should keep their loyalty and dependence on God alone, and distance themselves from oppression and those who practice it, while still being just and fair in dealing with people.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: God commands the believer to anchor daily life in regular prayer: at the day's two ends (dawn and the afternoon or sunset prayers) and in the early hours of the night (the evening prayer). These prayers frame the whole day with remembrance of God. The verse then offers reassurance: sincere good deeds, with prayer foremost among them, wipe out the minor sins a person commits, as light dispels darkness, so a lapse need not lead to despair, provided one turns back to God and sets right what was wrong. The verse closes by saying that this teaching is a reminder and counsel for those who are mindful of God and heed admonition, helping them stay steadfast and return quickly to Him after they slip.

translation: And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of those who do good to be lost.
interpretation: The verse (Hud 11:115) calls the believer to steadfastness in obedience, in avoiding sin, and in enduring hardship and the harm of opponents. Patience is tied to ihsan, doing good with sincerity and excellence, as if one is in the presence of God. The assurance that God never wastes the reward of the muhsinin means that no good deed, however small or unseen, and no hardship borne for God's sake is forgotten or lost. Its full recompense is preserved with Him, whether it is given in this world or in the next. The believer is therefore invited to keep trust in God's justice and generosity when results are slow to appear, and to see patience as an investment that is certain to be repaid.

translation: Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of virtue and discernment who forbade corruption in the earth, except for a few of those whom We saved from among them? But those who did wrong pursued the luxury and comforts they were given, and they were criminals.
interpretation: The verse (Hud 11:116) teaches that a society's survival depends on the presence of a reforming, morally upright group that actively opposes corruption and injustice. Earlier nations were destroyed not merely because of unbelief but because few among them stood up to forbid wrongdoing; only a small number of such reformers existed, and they were the ones God saved. The majority of the wrongdoers, instead, devoted themselves to the pursuit of luxury, wealth, and indulgence, letting pleasure blind them to truth and justice, and so they became habitual criminals. The verse is thus both a warning and a call to the community to maintain people of conscience who enjoin good and forbid evil, for when comfort-seeking and silence prevail over reform, collective ruin follows.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers.
interpretation: God's destruction of communities is never an act of injustice on His part. He does not wipe out a society merely for the existence of shirk or errors of belief when its people still act with integrity, justice, and mutual reform in their dealings. Punishment in this world comes upon nations when corruption, oppression, and wrongdoing become widespread and people cease to enjoin good and prevent evil. A society that keeps reforming itself, even if flawed, is spared, while one that sinks into injustice and refuses correction invites its own ruin. The verse thus teaches that the survival of communities depends on the presence of righteous reform among them.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community; but they continue to differ.
interpretation: God has the power to make all people a single community of one faith and one path, but He created humans with free will and the capacity to choose. Diversity of belief, opinion and way of life is therefore part of the divine wisdom and the test of this worldly life, not a failing in God's power. The Prophet should not grieve or force people to believe, since differences among people will persist as a natural consequence of the freedom they have been given, and each will be held accountable for the choices made with it.

translation: Except those upon whom your Lord has bestowed mercy; and for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with the jinn and mankind all together.'
interpretation: People will always differ in belief and path, and only those whom God has granted mercy are guided to the truth and united upon it. God created humankind with free will and the capacity to choose, so that some would follow His mercy and others would turn away, which is the wisdom behind their creation and their differences. His decree that Hell will be filled with jinn and humans reflects His perfect foreknowledge of those who would knowingly choose disbelief and wrongdoing, not compulsion on His part. It is a reminder that mercy is attained through sincere submission to God, and that accountability is just and certain.

translation: And all that We relate to you of the accounts of the messengers is that by which We make your heart firm. And in this there has come to you the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: God explains that the purpose of telling the stories of earlier prophets is to strengthen the Prophet Muhammad's resolve. By learning how previous messengers faced rejection, hardship and mockery yet remained steadfast and were finally granted victory, he finds reassurance that his own struggle follows a established divine pattern and that God's help will come to those who persevere. Beyond consoling him, these accounts, and the surah that contains them, convey the truth about God's ways in dealing with nations. They offer believers a warning against the errors that destroyed earlier peoples and a reminder that spurs them toward faith, patience and righteous action.

translation: And say to those who do not believe: 'Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 11:121) instructs the Prophet to answer the stubborn rejecters with calm confidence rather than argument or coercion. The phrase 'act according to your ability and position' is not an approval of their path but a firm, almost challenging dismissal: they are free to pursue their opposition and their way of life with all the power and status they have, while the believers will keep on in their faith and righteous work. The deeper meaning is that each side's deeds will bear fruit and be judged, so the matter is left to God, who will reveal whose course was right. It teaches the believer to remain steadfast, to put trust in God over human outcomes, and to refrain from despair or compromise when facing hostility, since the final verdict belongs to God alone.

translation: And wait; indeed, we are waiting. (Qur'an 11:122)
interpretation: This verse closes the account of the Prophets' struggles in Surah Hud by turning to those who persist in disbelief after the message has been delivered. The believers are told to say, in effect, that the matter is now in God's hands. The disbelievers may wait for whatever they imagine will befall the believers, while the believers wait with confidence for God's promise: that truth will prevail, that justice will be done, and that every deed will meet its consequence. It teaches that after clearly conveying the message and doing one's duty, a believer should not despair or retaliate in anger. Instead, the believer should show patient trust in God's timing. Both groups wait, but their expectations differ, since the believers wait for God's promised help and the deniers wait only for the outcome of their own denial.

translation: To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him all affairs are returned. So worship Him and put your trust in Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse closes Surat Hud by grounding the believer's conduct in God's absolute knowledge and authority. Because only God knows what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and because every matter, whether apparent causes or final outcomes, ultimately returns to Him for judgment, the only sound response is to devote oneself to worshipping Him alone and to rely on Him fully. Worship and trust go together: worship means obeying Him and striving sincerely, while trust means entrusting the results to Him after doing one's part, especially when facing opposition and denial as the Prophet and earlier prophets did. The final assurance that He is never heedless of what people do is both a comfort to the patient believer, whose efforts and hardships are not lost, and a warning to the wrongdoer, whose deeds are all recorded and will be accounted for.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: The disconnected letters 'Alif Lam Ra' are best understood as a challenge and a marker of the Qur'an's miraculous character: the Book is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs knew and used, yet it is beyond what they could produce. The verse then affirms that the Qur'an's verses are 'clear' (mubin), meaning that they make plain what is true and false, lawful and unlawful, and guidance and misguidance. The clarity is that of a Book which illuminates the path for those who reflect on it with sincerity, leaving no excuse for those who turn away.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you might understand.
interpretation: God explains that He revealed the Qur'an in clear Arabic, the language of its first audience, so that its message could not be dismissed as obscure or foreign. The purpose of this clarity is to engage human reason: the Qur'an is not meant to be received blindly but to be pondered, so that people grasp its signs, reflect on its guidance, and recognize its truth. Revelation in a comprehensible language places responsibility on the listeners to use their intellect and respond with faith and right action.

translation: We relate to you, [O Muhammad], the best of narratives through what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although you were, before it, among the unaware.
interpretation: God affirms that the Qur'an's storytelling, exemplified by the story of Joseph, surpasses every other account in its truthfulness, eloquence, and moral depth, because its narratives are not mere entertainment but carry guidance, wisdom, and lessons about patience, trust in God, and the ultimate triumph of the righteous. The verse also underscores the Qur'an's divine origin: Muhammad had no prior knowledge of these accounts, being unaware of them before revelation, so the precise and beautiful telling of such stories can only be explained as inspiration from God rather than human authorship or learning.

translation: When Joseph said to his father, 'O my father, indeed I have seen eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.'
interpretation: The dream is a divine foreshadowing of Joseph's future elevation. The eleven stars stand for his eleven brothers, and the sun and moon for his father and mother (or mother's stand-in, his aunt). Their prostration is not worship but a gesture of honor and submission, which was later fulfilled when his family came to Egypt and bowed before him as a ruler. It marks the beginning of his prophetic destiny, and the dream is a true vision, one of the early forms of revelation granted to prophets, that promised him honor and authority after hardship.

translation: He said, 'O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a plot. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.'
interpretation: Jacob, recognizing that Joseph's dream of the eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him signified a future elevation of rank, warns his young son to keep it secret. He knows that the brothers, already feeling that their father favors Joseph, would be moved by envy to scheme against him. By adding that Satan is mankind's open enemy, Jacob explains that such envy and the harmful plotting it breeds are whispered by Satan, who sows discord among family members. The verse teaches prudence: blessings and glad tidings should not be disclosed to those who may envy them, and one should guard against the paths through which Satan stirs up hostility.

translation: And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of narratives [dreams] and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: In this verse Jacob comforts Joseph after hearing his dream of the eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. He tells his son that the honor shown in the dream is a sign of divine selection: just as God gave Joseph this vision, He will elect him for prophethood and favor, give him insight into the hidden meanings of dreams and events, and perfect His blessings on him and Jacob's family, in the same way He perfected them on Abraham and Isaac through prophethood and a righteous lineage. The closing words, 'Your Lord is Knowing and Wise,' teach that God knows precisely whom to choose and carries out His plans with wisdom, even when the path to them, as Joseph's coming trials will show, involves hardship. Joseph's elevation is thus not by chance or personal merit alone but by God's knowledge and wise design.

translation: Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers there are signs for those who inquire.
interpretation: The story of Joseph and his brothers is not mere narrative but a source of lasting lessons for anyone who sincerely seeks understanding. It shows that God's wisdom and decree prevail over human scheming: the brothers' envy, which sought to destroy Joseph, became the means of his elevation. It teaches that patience, steadfast faith, and moral integrity in the face of betrayal, slavery, temptation, and imprisonment lead to honor, and that forgiveness and mercy are nobler than revenge. Those who ask and reflect with an earnest heart will discover in it guidance about trust in God, the consequences of jealousy and wrongdoing, and the certainty that God's plan unfolds in ways people cannot foresee.

translation: When they said, "Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are, although we are a group of strong men. Indeed, our father is in manifest error."
interpretation: This verse reveals the root of the brothers' jealousy: they measured their father's love by outward strength and usefulness, reasoning that a numerous, capable group deserved more affection than two young boys. Their accusation that Jacob was in 'manifest error' refers not to a lapse in faith but to what they saw as an unjust and mistaken judgment in showing preference. The verse shows how envy distorts perception, leading people to blame even a righteous and wise parent, and how it can be the first step toward justifying wrongdoing, as the plot against Joseph that follows demonstrates.

translation: Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face (attention) will be free for you alone, and after that you can be a righteous people.
interpretation: The verse reveals how jealousy can lead people to rationalize grave wrongdoing. Joseph's brothers, envious of their father's special love for Joseph, believe that removing him will turn Jacob's undivided attention toward them. They also plan to ease their consciences by promising themselves they will repent afterward and become righteous. The verse warns against sinning with the intention of repenting later, and shows how envy and a desire for favor can distort moral judgment, turning family ties into enmity and making a crime seem like a reasonable solution.

translation: One speaker among them said: 'Do not kill Joseph, but cast him into the bottom of the well; some travelers will pick him up, if you are going to do something.'
interpretation: The verse shows one of Joseph's brothers (traditionally Reuben, the eldest, or according to some, Judah) trying to avert the worst crime. Unable to talk the group out of their hostility, he proposes a lesser course: instead of shedding Joseph's blood, throw him into the hidden depths of a well where passing caravans would find and take him away. His real aim was to save Joseph's life, since a well on a travelers' route made rescue likely. It illustrates how, in a group bent on wrongdoing, a person with some conscience may seek to limit the harm, and how God's hidden plan works through even the brothers' scheming, preparing the path by which Joseph would be taken to Egypt and raised to his destined station.

translation: They said: 'O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, when indeed we are sincere well-wishers to him?'
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:11) shows the brothers opening their scheme with a show of wounded innocence. Their question implies that their father's evident reluctance to send Joseph with them is unjust, and they stress their sincerity (nush) to disarm his fears. The deeper meaning is that outward protestations of goodwill can mask hidden envy and malice. The brothers' very need to insist on their trustworthiness reveals a guilty conscience, and their pretended concern for Joseph is a cover for the plot they have already agreed upon. The verse also hints at Jacob's wise caution: he had sensed the jealousy in their hearts, which is why he had never entrusted Joseph to them before.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow that he may enjoy himself and play, and indeed we will be his guardians. (Qur'an 12:12)
interpretation: The brothers of Yusuf speak to their father Ya'qub with calculated persuasion, hiding their envy behind a show of affection and concern. They present the outing as harmless recreation, so that the request seems like a kindness to the boy, and they stress their guardianship to answer the fear they know their father has. The verse shows how jealousy can disguise itself in gentle, reassuring language, and how a plot against an innocent person may be wrapped in a promise of protection. It also shows Ya'qub's position, since the brothers feel compelled to reassure him about Yusuf's safety, which reflects his love for his son and his awareness of the brothers' resentment.

translation: He said, "Indeed, it saddens me that you should take him away, and I fear that the wolf may devour him while you are heedless of him."
interpretation: Jacob's words show a father's tender love and prophetic caution. His grief at being parted from Yusuf, even briefly, shows his deep attachment, while his fear of the wolf is a prudent concern, not a lack of trust in God. The verse teaches that trusting God does not rule out taking precautions against foreseeable harm, and that a guardian's negligence, 'while you are heedless', is the usual way harm comes to those entrusted to us. It also shows that Jacob sensed the brothers' lack of sincere care. Unwittingly, he supplied them with the excuse they would later use, a reminder of how a hurtful lie can be built from our own spoken fears.

translation: They said: 'If the wolf were to devour him while we are a strong group, then surely we would be losers.'
interpretation: The brothers of Yusuf answer their father Jacob's fear that a wolf might eat Yusuf if they were careless. They argue that, being a strong band of many men, it would be shameful and a mark of utter worthlessness to let that happen. Their words stress that a group able to protect one boy but failing to do so would deserve to be called losers, so they use this self-assurance to calm Jacob's worry and win his consent to take Yusuf with them. The verse also shows how their confident, persuasive speech hid their real intentions, and how people can use reassuring appeals to honor and strength to disguise a plot.

translation: So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, We inspired him: 'You will surely inform them of this deed of theirs while they do not perceive.'
interpretation: The verse shows God's care for Joseph at the moment of his greatest helplessness. As his brothers carry out their plan, God sends him a revelation that comforts him and promises that the situation will be reversed. Years later he will confront them with what they did, and they will not recognize him as the brother they threw into the well. The well is therefore not the end of Joseph's story but the beginning of his path toward honor and authority. The brothers' scheming cannot override God's decree, and what looks like a catastrophe to people is part of a wise divine plan that the plotters themselves cannot see.

translation: And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Yusuf (Joseph), shows the brothers returning at nightfall to deceive Yaqub (Jacob) about Yusuf's fate. They chose the cover of darkness and staged tears so that their grief would look genuine and shield their lie. The verse shows how outward displays of emotion, such as weeping, are not proof of truthfulness, and how a guilty conscience can fabricate a show of sorrow to hide a wrong. Their false tears contrast with Yaqub's real grief and his patient trust in God, which the story goes on to show.

translation: They said: "O our father, we went off racing one another and left Joseph with our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you would not believe us, even if we were truthful."
interpretation: The brothers' words reveal a guilty conscience behind a rehearsed lie. After throwing Joseph into the well, they came back at night weeping and offered an excuse built on Jacob's own earlier fear that a wolf might eat him. They claimed they had been racing (in archery or running) and had left Joseph to guard their things. Then they added, 'You would not believe us even if we were truthful.' This was a defensive move: they knew their story was weak, so they tried in advance to blame their father's suspicion and make his doubt look unreasonable. The verse shows how deceit tends to give itself away, since people who lie often protest too much and try to shift blame onto the one they have wronged. It also shows Jacob's patient insight, because he was not misled by their tears or by the story, and answered with 'beautiful patience' and reliance on God.

translation: And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said, "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is most fitting; and it is God whose help is sought against what you describe."
interpretation: Jacob (Yaqub) recognized that the blood on Joseph's shirt was staged, since the shirt was not torn as it would have been had a wolf devoured him. He therefore refused to accept his sons' story and told them that their own selves had made an evil deed seem attractive to them. Rather than despair, rage, or complain, he chose a patience free of grievance and lament, a patience that entrusts the matter to God. He affirmed that only God can give help and strength against the lie his sons were describing, and that God alone would reveal the truth and bring relief in His time.

translation: And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, "Good news! Here is a boy!" And they hid him away as merchandise, while God was Knowing of what they did.
interpretation: The verse shows how God's hidden plan unfolds through ordinary events: a passing caravan's water-drawer, seeking only water, finds Yusuf in the well, and the brothers' crime becomes the first step toward his rise. The finders concealed the truth of how they found him and treated a human being as a commodity to be sold, hoping for profit. Yet the closing phrase, 'God was Knowing of what they did,' reminds the reader that nothing escapes God's knowledge: He knew the brothers' envy, the caravan's greed, and Yusuf's innocence, and He was steering all of these toward a purpose none of the actors perceived. It consoles the believer that apparent abandonment and exploitation are still under divine oversight, and that wrongdoers' schemes are used within God's wider wisdom.

translation: And they sold him for a paltry price, a few counted dirhams, and they were of those who held him in little regard.
interpretation: The verse shows how little worth Joseph's brothers, or the caravan that found him, placed on a human life that God was preparing for greatness. The price was 'paltry' (bakhs) both in being low and in being unjust, since a free person was sold as a slave. The silver was paid in a small number of coins that could be counted out rather than weighed, which marks the transaction as insignificant. Those who sold him were indifferent (zāhidīn) to him, so they made no effort to bargain for a higher price or to learn his worth. The lesson is that people's judgment of value can be blind and that worldly valuations do not match God's. The one they discarded cheaply was a noble prophet whom God would raise to honor and authority, so human contempt cannot cancel what God has decreed for His servant.

translation: And the one from Egypt who bought him said to his wife, 'Make his stay honourable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.' And thus We established Joseph in the land, so that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And God is predominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: The verse shows how God's plan unfolds through what seem to be ordinary or even harsh circumstances. Joseph, sold as a slave, is bought by a high official who instructs his wife to treat him with honour, which reveals how God placed favour and respect in the heart of the one who purchased him. This was no accident but the first step in God's establishing Joseph in the land, preparing him for authority and for knowledge of the interpretation of dreams and events, meaning insight into the deeper realities and outcomes behind occurrences. The closing statements teach that God's will cannot be thwarted by human schemes, such as the brothers' plot to get rid of Joseph, and that most people fail to perceive the wisdom behind events, judging only by outward appearances of hardship while God is steadily bringing about a greater outcome.

translation: And when he reached his full maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse, about Prophet Musa (Moses) in Surah Al-Qasas, teaches that God grants wisdom and sound understanding to those who reach spiritual and intellectual maturity through righteous living. 'Hukm' is the capacity for right judgment and discernment, and 'ilm' is true, beneficial knowledge. These were not merely the product of age or upbringing but a divine gift, bestowed on Musa after years of being protected and raised under God's care. The closing phrase makes this a universal principle: those who consistently strive to do good (muhsinin), in worship and in conduct toward others, will be rewarded by God with insight, guidance, and honor, just as Musa was before his mission.

translation: And she in whose house he was sought to seduce him from himself, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you!" He said, "I seek refuge in God. Indeed, he is my master, who has made my stay agreeable. Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed."
interpretation: The verse shows how faith and moral integrity hold firm under intense temptation. Yusuf is placed in the most favorable circumstances for sin: he is alone, the doors are locked, the invitation is explicit, and the woman holds power over him. Yet his first response is to turn to God, seeking refuge in Him rather than relying on his own strength. He then gives reasons for refusing: betraying the master who honored him and gave him a good home would be ingratitude and a breach of trust, and, deeper still, God is his true Lord who has favored him, so disobeying Him would be wrongdoing. His closing statement, that wrongdoers never truly succeed, teaches that gains won through sin and betrayal are illusory and end in loss. Chastity is thus grounded in God-consciousness, gratitude, and loyalty, not merely in the absence of opportunity.

translation: And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was] that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen, sincere servants.
interpretation: The verse (Yusuf 12:24) shows Yusuf's protection from sin. The woman's resolve to seduce him was firm and deliberate, whereas any inclination in Yusuf was only the natural, fleeting human instinct that never became intent or action. It was checked at once by the 'proof of his Lord', meaning the clear certainty and God-given awareness of God's prohibition and of his duty of faithfulness and gratitude to his master and to God. This is why he is described as one of the 'mukhlasin', those whom God has purified and chosen for Himself. Their sincerity earns divine protection, so that evil and indecency are turned away from them. The lesson is that purity is attained through the servant's sincere devotion together with God's safeguarding, and that a believer facing temptation should hold fast to the awareness of God's proof, which averts wrongdoing.

translation: And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended evil toward your wife, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"
interpretation: The verse shows how quickly a guilty person turns to accusation in order to cover up their own wrongdoing. Yusuf ran for the door to flee from sin, and the wife chased him, so that the tearing of his shirt from behind became evidence of his innocence: it showed he was fleeing and she was pursuing. When her husband unexpectedly appeared, she did not wait to be questioned. She seized the initiative, shifted the blame onto Yusuf, and spoke of 'your wife' to stir the husband's sense of honor. She also framed the punishment in a lenient-sounding way, imprisonment or a painful punishment, so as to appear fair while pressing for him to be punished. The lesson is that God protects His sincere servants and uncovers the truth through clear signs, even when falsehood is voiced with confidence and power, and that fleeing from temptation is the response of the God-fearing.

translation: He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me." And a witness from her household testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars."
interpretation: Joseph, when accused by the wife of the 'Aziz, defends himself by naming the true instigator rather than keeping silent. The verse then shows how the matter is settled through reasoned evidence instead of competing claims: a relative of the woman proposes a physical test. If the shirt was torn at the front, it would suggest that Joseph advanced on her and she resisted, so she would be truthful. The test is framed this way to prepare for its converse in the next verse, where a tear from behind proves her guilt and his innocence. The lesson is that God vindicates the truthful through clear signs, even by the testimony of someone from the accuser's own side, and that justice should rest on evidence and sound inference rather than on status or accusation.

translation: But if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Yusuf (Joseph) in Surah Yusuf (12:27), gives the second half of the evidence offered by a witness from Zulaykha's household to settle the dispute. If Yusuf's shirt was torn from the back, that would show he was fleeing from her and she was pulling him back, so her accusation was false and he was honest. The verse teaches that truth can be established through reasoned, circumstantial evidence, and that God vindicates the innocent. It also shows Yusuf's chastity and integrity, since his flight from temptation left a physical sign that exposed the falsehood.

translation: So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed, it is from your plot, O women. Surely your plot is mighty."
interpretation: The torn back of the shirt served as decisive evidence that Yusuf had been fleeing and was pursued, not the aggressor, which exonerated him and exposed the falsehood of the accusation. The ruler's words, directed at the woman and women of his household in general, acknowledge that deceptive scheming of this kind can be subtle, far-reaching and hard to detect, since it hides guilt behind a convincing accusation. The verse shows how truth can be revealed through clear, tangible signs, and that Yusuf's innocence and steadfast chastity were vindicated by evidence rather than by mere claims.

translation: Joseph, turn away from this; and you, woman, ask forgiveness for your sin. Indeed, you have been among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The speaker, the husband of the woman (the 'Aziz), having seen the evidence of Joseph's innocence, urges calm and discretion rather than vengeance. He asks Joseph to disregard the incident and not spread the matter, while directing his wife to seek forgiveness for her attempted seduction and false accusation. The verse shows that the fault was clearly hers, that wrongdoing calls for repentance, and that Joseph's integrity was publicly established even though the husband's response was mild and aimed at preserving the household's reputation.

translation: And women in the city said: 'The wife of the 'Azīz is trying to seduce her young servant away from himself; he has deeply infatuated her with love. Indeed, we see her in manifest error.'
interpretation: This verse shows how gossip spread through the elite circles of Egyptian society after the incident between Yusuf and the wife of the chief minister. The women of the city condemn her not merely for desiring Yusuf but for lowering herself, a woman of high rank, by pursuing her own household servant. The phrase 'shaghafahā ḥubbā' means that love had penetrated the innermost part of her heart, as the shaghaf is the heart's inner covering, suggesting an all-consuming passion. Their calling it 'manifest error' reflects social censure that is quick to judge others' moral lapses while being blind to its own weaknesses, a point the Qur'an then exposes when the women themselves are captivated by Yusuf's beauty. The lesson is that people readily criticize what they have not been tested by, and that gossip and judgment often arise from ignorance of the full circumstances.

translation: So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet with cushioned seats, and gave each one of them a knife, and said to Joseph, 'Come out before them.' And when they saw him, they were awestruck by him and cut their hands, and said, 'Perfect is God! This is not a human being; this is none other than a noble angel.'
interpretation: The verse shows how the wife of the governor answered the women's gossip about her not with argument but with a demonstration. By staging a banquet and handing each woman a knife, she placed them in the very situation that would expose them to the same overwhelming attraction they had condemned. Joseph's extraordinary beauty, together with the purity and dignity radiating from him, struck them so deeply that they lost awareness of themselves and wounded their own hands without feeling it. Their exclamation 'Perfect is God!' shows that the sight of such beauty moved them to glorify the Creator, and their words 'this is none other than a noble angel' show that they perceived in him a quality beyond ordinary human appearance, a loftiness of character as well as form. The episode thus serves to excuse her in their eyes, to reveal the weakness of those who judge others without having been tested, and to underline the greatness of Joseph's restraint, since he withstood a trial that left even onlookers overwhelmed.

translation: She said: "That is the one about whom you blamed me. I did indeed seek to seduce him, but he preserved himself. And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned and will surely be among the humiliated."
interpretation: The wife of the Egyptian nobleman, having displayed Yusuf before the gossiping women of the city who had censured her, no longer hides her passion. Once they were struck by his beauty, she openly admits her attempt and his steadfast refusal, which exposes her own weakness and his moral strength. Her words show that desire, when unchecked by faith, becomes arrogance and threat: she uses her status to coerce him with prison and disgrace. The verse underlines Yusuf's chastity as a deliberate act of self-restraint rooted in fear of God, even when facing temptation backed by power, and shows that the one who guards himself is honored by his integrity, while the one who abuses authority to pursue sin ends up humbled.

translation: He said, "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me. And unless You turn away their plot from me, I might incline toward them and become one of the ignorant."
interpretation: Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) shows that choosing hardship while remaining obedient to God is better than yielding to temptation and sinning. Even though he is righteous, he does not rely on his own strength; he acknowledges human weakness and asks God for protection, knowing that only divine help can keep a person from falling. By calling yielding to desire 'ignorance,' the verse teaches that sin is a lapse of true wisdom, since knowledge of God's commands should restrain a person from acting on impulse. It shows that purity depends on both sincere resolve and constant reliance on God.

translation: So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plot. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse (Yusuf 12:34) shows that God answers the sincere plea of a servant who seeks refuge in Him from temptation and acknowledges his own weakness. Yusuf had prayed that unless God turned away the women's scheming, he might incline toward them. His protection came not from his own strength alone but from relying on God, who heard his supplication and knew his sincerity and his need. The closing names, the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, teach that God hears every prayer, spoken or unspoken, and knows the hidden struggles of the heart. Salvation from moral trials therefore comes through turning to God for help, and He guards those who seek His protection.

translation: Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should surely imprison him for a time.
interpretation: Although the evidence of Joseph's innocence was plain to the household of the Aziz, namely the torn shirt at the back and the testimony of a witness from her family, the ruling elite put their own reputation and the wishes of the Aziz's wife ahead of justice. Rather than act on the truth, they decided to imprison the innocent Joseph for a period, so that the scandal would die down and the talk in the city would be silenced. The verse shows how power and social image can override clear proof, and how the righteous are sometimes made to bear the penalty for others' wrongdoing. Yet this imprisonment became part of God's plan, leading Joseph to his later rise in Egypt.

translation: And two young men entered the prison with him. One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." The other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, from which the birds are eating. Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you to be of the doers of good."
interpretation: The two young men, who were royal servants imprisoned alongside Yusuf (peace be upon him), came to him with their dreams because his conduct in prison had made him stand out as a man of goodness, sincerity, kindness and knowledge. Their description of him as one of the muhsinin shows that his character was visible to others, and that people trust and seek out those whose good conduct is evident. It also shows how Allah was preparing Yusuf for his role: prison became the setting in which his gift of dream interpretation would be revealed, leading eventually to his deliverance and rise. The verse teaches that righteousness earns people's confidence even in hardship, and that Allah can turn a place of trial into a means of opening the door to relief.

translation: He said: No food that you are provided with will come to you except that I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the way of a people who do not believe in God, and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: Joseph, in prison with two fellow inmates who ask him to interpret their dreams, first establishes his credibility by pointing to a God-given knowledge. He claims no skill of his own, saying his ability to foretell what is coming comes from what his Lord taught him. He ties that knowledge to his faith: he is able to do this because he abandoned the creed of people who deny God and the Afterlife, and he stayed true to monotheism. Before giving the interpretation, he uses the opening to call the two men to faith. This shows that a believer can use opportunities and trust to invite others to God, and that real knowledge and guidance are gifts that come from steadfastness in belief and from rejecting falsehood.

translation: And I have followed the creed of my forefathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with God. That is from the bounty of God upon us and upon mankind, but most people do not give thanks.
interpretation: In this verse (Yusuf 12:38), Joseph explains that his guidance rests on the pure monotheism inherited from his prophetic forefathers, and that being kept free from shirk was never his own achievement but a grace from God. Tawhid is a favor granted to the prophets so they could convey it to others, and it is a blessing for all people, since it frees them from servitude to created things and directs them to the Creator alone. Yet most people fail to be grateful: they ignore this blessing, turn to false deities, or credit guidance to themselves. Joseph thus presents his message to his two prison companions as a gift to be thankfully embraced, and he teaches that gratitude for faith is itself part of faith.

translation: O my two companions of the prison, are many scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?
interpretation: Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), while in prison, uses a rational question to call his fellow prisoners to pure monotheism. He contrasts the many divided, powerless objects of worship, each with limited authority and often in conflict with one another, with the one God, who is unique in His divinity and who subdues all things by His power. The verse teaches that only a single, all-powerful Lord deserves worship, since multiple deities would imply weakness, disagreement, and no real ability to benefit or harm, and that sound reason itself points to tawhid.

translation: You worship besides Him nothing but names which you have named, you and your forefathers, for which God has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs to none but God. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: Joseph, speaking to his two prison companions, argues that the idols the people worship have no reality or power of their own. They are empty labels that people invented and inherited from their ancestors, with no divine proof or revelation behind them. Since real authority, sovereignty and the right to legislate belong to God alone, only He deserves worship, and He has commanded that no one else be worshipped. Joseph calls this pure monotheism the straight, lasting religion, and he regrets that most people stay in ignorance because they follow inherited custom instead of seeking knowledge and evidence.

translation: O my two companions of the prison, as for one of you, he will pour wine for his master to drink; and as for the other, he will be crucified, and the birds will eat from his head. The matter about which you both inquire has been decreed.
interpretation: Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), having first called his two fellow prisoners to the worship of God alone, now gives the meaning of their dreams. He speaks plainly and without softening the fate of the second man, because the interpretation of a dream is a true disclosure of what God has already ordained, not a guess or a personal opinion. His closing words, 'the matter has been decreed', stress that the outcome is settled in God's knowledge and will, and that what he says is no mere conjecture. The verse also shows that a believer, even in hardship and imprisonment, conveys truth with certainty and honesty, uses his God-given knowledge to guide others, and reminds them that all events unfold by divine decree.

translation: And he said to the one of them whom he thought would be saved, 'Mention me in the presence of your lord.' But Satan made him forget to mention it to his lord, so [Joseph] remained in prison for several years.
interpretation: Joseph, after interpreting the dreams of his two fellow prisoners, asked the one he knew would be freed to remind the king of his unjust imprisonment. Seeking help through lawful worldly means is not a lack of trust in God, yet for a prophet of Joseph's rank, placing hope in a human intercessor was a lapse in complete reliance on God alone. Satan caused the freed man to forget, and so Joseph's imprisonment was lengthened by several years (between three and nine). The verse teaches that ultimate relief comes only from God, and that a believer's hope should rest on Him before any created means. It also shows that delay is a form of divine training, and that God's timing for Joseph's deliverance and elevation was better than any human arrangement.

translation: And the king said: "Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry. O chiefs, explain to me my vision, if you are able to interpret visions."
interpretation: The king's dream was a divinely directed sign that set in motion Joseph's release and rise to authority. The fat cows and green ears stand for years of abundance, while the lean cows that devour them and the dry ears stand for years of famine that consume what the good years produced. The king's appeal to his counsellors shows how limited worldly knowledge is: the court's learned men could not read the vision, and only Joseph, who had been taught by God, could give its true meaning and the practical plan to save the land. The verse thus shows that God uses a ruler's own troubled dream to bring out the hidden worth of His patient servant.

translation: They said: "A confused jumble of dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."
interpretation: The king's courtiers, unable to explain his vision of the seven fat cows devoured by seven lean ones and the seven green and dry ears of grain, dismiss it as mere jumbled nightmares that carry no meaning, and then plead ignorance of dream interpretation as a further excuse. Their reply exposes the limits of worldly knowledge and status: those closest to power could not decode a divinely sent vision. This prepares the way for Joseph, whose God-given knowledge of interpretation sets him apart and leads to his release from prison and his elevation, showing that true insight comes from God and not from rank or position.

translation: And the one of the two who had been saved, and who remembered after a period of time, said: "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."
interpretation: This is Qur'an 12:45, in the story of Yusuf. The former cupbearer of the king, who had been released from prison, recalls Yusuf's earlier ability to interpret dreams only when the king's court fails to explain the king's dream. His remembering after a long time shows how human forgetfulness and God's timing work together: Yusuf's release and rise were delayed until the moment God had decreed. The cupbearer asks to be sent to Yusuf, which indicates that true knowledge is often found in those who are overlooked or wronged, and that relief comes at the appointed time, not when people expect it. It teaches patience and trust in God's plan even when people forget one's kindness.

translation: "Joseph, O man of truth, explain to us about seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, so that I may return to the people and they may know."
interpretation: This is the plea of the released prisoner who remembered Joseph after the king's dream. He addresses Joseph as 'al-siddiq', one known for truthfulness, which shows that Joseph's honesty and integrity had made a deep impression on him even in prison. He does not fall back on his earlier neglect but goes straight to the one person he trusts to give a reliable interpretation. His wish to 'return to the people so that they may know' shows that the dream was a matter of public concern, and that the knowledge Joseph has is meant to benefit the whole community. The verse teaches that God gives some people knowledge and truthfulness so that others may turn to them in times of need, and that true knowledge is meant to be shared for the common good.

translation: He said: You shall sow for seven consecutive years as usual; and whatever you harvest, leave it in its ears, except for a little of what you will eat.
interpretation: In this verse, Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) answers the king's dream by laying out a practical plan for the years of plenty. The seven fat cows and seven full ears stand for seven years of abundance, so the people must keep up their farming with steady effort and not slacken because of the coming famine. He tells them to leave the harvested grain in its ears and not thresh it, because grain kept in its husk stays safe from weevils and spoilage and lasts much longer in storage. They should take out only the small amount needed for their food. The verse teaches foresight, discipline and moderation: prepare in times of ease for times of hardship, avoid wasteful consumption, and manage resources carefully, relying on God's guidance while taking practical measures.

translation: Then after that will come seven hard years which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you preserve.
interpretation: The verse is part of Prophet Yusuf's interpretation of the king's dream. The seven lean cows and dry ears of grain signify seven years of severe famine that follow the seven years of abundance. The years are described as 'hard' (shidad) because of their severity, and they are said to 'eat' what was stored, meaning that the people will exhaust their reserves of grain during the famine. Only a small portion, kept back as seed or protected through careful storage, will remain. The verse carries a practical lesson in foresight and planning: the wise course is to save in times of plenty, ration consumption, and preserve provisions for hard times.

translation: Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given abundant rain and relief, and in which they will press (grapes, olives, and oils).
interpretation: This verse completes Joseph's interpretation of the king's dream. After the seven years of drought and hardship, a year of deliverance will come: the rains will return, the land will become fertile again, and people will be relieved from distress. The phrase 'they will press' signifies abundance, since people will once more have enough fruit, grain, and produce that they can press grapes for wine or juice, olives for oil, and sesame or other crops. The verse shows that hardship is not permanent, that relief follows difficulty by God's mercy, and that Joseph, through divinely granted knowledge, foresaw even what the king's dream did not explicitly mention, namely the year of plenty after the years of famine.

translation: And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."
interpretation: Joseph refuses to leave prison merely on the king's summons, because release without a public clearing of his name would leave a stain on his honor and let people suspect he had been jailed justly. By asking the king to investigate the case of the women who cut their hands, he insists that his innocence be established first, so that he comes out vindicated and with dignity, and so that his later service to the king rests on trust. He names the women rather than the wife of the minister out of tact and courtesy toward the man who had sheltered him, and he leaves the wife's role to be revealed by the inquiry itself. His closing words, 'Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot,' show his reliance on God, who knows the truth of what happened, and they signal that the matter will be exposed whether or not people admit it. The verse teaches patience, concern for one's reputation when truth is at stake, and wisdom in seeking justice before accepting favor.

translation: He (the king) said: 'What was your affair when you solicited Joseph against his will?' They said: 'God forbid! We know no evil against him.' The wife of the 'Aziz said: 'Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him, and he is indeed among the truthful.'
interpretation: The verse shows how truth eventually prevails when it is investigated openly and fairly. The king's inquiry leads the women to bear witness to Joseph's innocence, and the wife of the 'Aziz, once the matter can no longer be concealed, confesses her own guilt and affirms his honesty. Her words 'now the truth has become manifest' reflect that falsehood, however long it endures, cannot stand against clear evidence and a conscience compelled to admit it. The verse also vindicates Joseph's chastity and integrity: his steadfastness in the face of temptation and his patience in prison are rewarded with public exoneration, teaching that God protects the righteous and brings their vindication in His own time.

translation: That is so he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that God does not guide the plot of the treacherous.
interpretation: Yusuf (peace be upon him) explains why he insisted on having his case investigated before leaving prison: so that the governor, his master, would know that he had never betrayed his trust behind his back by being unfaithful with his wife, even when he was absent and no one could see him. His fidelity was the same in private as in public. He adds the general principle that God does not allow the scheming of traitors to succeed or reach its goal; deceit may seem effective for a time, but God exposes it and it ends in failure, just as the women's plot was exposed and the truth came out. Yusuf thereby attributes his vindication to God rather than to himself, showing that honesty and trustworthiness are guided and protected by God, while treachery is left without His support.

translation: And I do not declare myself innocent. Indeed, the soul is ever inclined to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:53) shows humility even after Yusuf's innocence has been proven. He does not credit his own purity to himself or claim to be free of the human tendency toward wrongdoing. The human self, left to its own desires, pulls toward evil, and only God's mercy protects a person and keeps them upright. Any moral strength or avoidance of sin is therefore a gift from God and not a personal achievement. The verse ends with hope: God forgives those who falter and shows mercy to those who turn to Him, so a believer should neither be arrogant about their virtue nor despair over their weakness.

translation: And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will make him exclusively mine." Then when he had spoken to him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established with us and trusted."
interpretation: After Yusuf's innocence was publicly proven, the king no longer saw him as a prisoner but as a man of rare wisdom, and he wanted him as a close confidant. Once the king heard Yusuf speak and judged his knowledge, character and composure for himself, he granted him a secure position of authority and trust. The verse shows that truthfulness and patience under hardship are eventually rewarded by God, who raises the righteous through lawful means. It also shows that trust and standing come from proven competence and integrity, and that these qualities become evident when a person is given the chance to speak and act.

translation: He said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian."
interpretation: In this verse Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) asks the king of Egypt to place him in charge of the country's treasuries and food stores, not out of greed for power but because he saw that he was uniquely qualified to protect the people from the coming famine. He grounds his request in two qualifications that define fitness for public office: 'hafiz' (trustworthy, a protector who will not squander or misuse what is entrusted to him) and 'alim' (knowledgeable, skilled in managing and distributing resources wisely). The verse teaches that authority should be sought only when one has integrity and competence, and that it is legitimate to seek a position of responsibility when the aim is to serve the public good and prevent harm, not for personal gain.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy on whom We will, and We do not let the reward of those who do good be lost.
interpretation: Just as God delivered Joseph from the well and from prison, He raised him to authority in Egypt, giving him such security and freedom of movement that he could dwell wherever he chose. This honor was not the product of his schemes or of human power, but a gift of God's mercy, which He gives to whomever He wills according to His wisdom. The verse also teaches that God never wastes the reward of the muhsinin, those who act with excellence in worship and conduct. Joseph's patience, chastity, trustworthiness, and good conduct toward both his brothers and his fellow prisoners were rewarded in this world with honor and power, and what God has stored up for him in the Hereafter is even greater.

translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are ever mindful of God.
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:57) teaches that whatever worldly honor, provision, or authority a believer may receive, as Joseph did when God established him in the land, is small compared with the reward God has prepared in the next life. That reward is reserved for those who combine sincere faith with ongoing God-consciousness, meaning that they guard themselves against disobedience and keep their conduct upright in times of both hardship and ease. Worldly success is therefore not the final measure of a person's standing, and the believer should keep their hope fixed on the lasting reward of the Hereafter.

translation: And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him; he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.
interpretation: The verse shows how time and circumstance change people and perceptions. Joseph recognized his brothers because they had changed little and he had never stopped thinking of them, while they could not imagine that the boy they had thrown into the well was now the powerful, dignified ruler of Egypt. Their expectations blinded them: they pictured him as a slave or dead, not as a minister in royal splendor. It also points to God's hidden planning, in which the very brothers who sought to destroy Joseph stand before him, unaware, as the fulfillment of his childhood dream draws near, and Joseph holds knowledge and power that lets him act with wisdom and restraint rather than revenge.

translation: And when he had furnished them with their supplies, he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?"
interpretation: Joseph, still unrecognized by his brothers, uses his generosity and fair dealing as a gentle argument to persuade them to return with Benjamin. By pointing to the full measure he had given and his good hospitality, he builds their trust and makes the request seem reasonable, while quietly testing their honesty about the brother they had described and moving toward reuniting his family. The verse shows how kindness and proven good conduct earn trust and make people receptive to a request, and how wisdom can guide events patiently toward a hidden purpose.

translation: But if you do not bring him to me, then there will be no measure of grain for you from me, and you shall not come near me.
interpretation: Joseph, as the minister in charge of Egypt's grain, sets a condition to test his brothers' honesty and to bring about the reunion with his full brother Benjamin. He ties their continued access to provisions to bringing Benjamin as proof of their claim that they are an honest family with another brother. The threat is double: no more grain would be sold to them, and they would be barred from entering his presence or the land. Its purpose is to compel them to return with Benjamin, which shows both Joseph's wisdom and his kindness, because he makes the matter a test of their truthfulness while quietly working toward gathering his family.

translation: They said: "We will try to persuade his father to let him go with us, and we will surely do it."
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:61) shows the brothers answering Joseph's demand that they bring their other brother, Benjamin, to him. The word 'nurāwid' implies coaxing and gentle, persistent effort, which reflects their awareness that Jacob would be reluctant to part with Benjamin after what had happened to Joseph. Their added assurance, 'we will surely do it,' expresses firm resolve to meet the condition so that they could secure more grain. The verse thus shows how need and the threat of being denied provisions pushed them to take responsibility for the matter. It also quietly points to the weight of their past betrayal, since their promise would have to overcome their father's lingering distrust of them.

translation: And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise (payment) back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, that perhaps they will come back."
interpretation: Joseph secretly had the price his brothers paid for the grain returned to their packs. This was an act of generosity and shrewd wisdom. When they opened their bags at home and found their goods restored, they would recognize that he had not taken payment, and they would see his honesty and kindness as a reason to return to Egypt, and to bring Benjamin with them as he had asked. The returned payment would also remove any worry that they could not afford to come back, since they would have the means to buy more grain, and it would stir their sense of obligation to a man who had treated them so honorably.

translation: So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, the measure [of grain] has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may obtain our measure, and indeed we will be his guardians." (Qur'an 12:63)
interpretation: After returning from Egypt, Joseph's brothers report that the Egyptian ruler had warned that no more grain would be given to them unless they brought their youngest brother, Benjamin. They present this as a practical necessity for the family's survival and offer a pledge of protection over him. Their emphatic assurance ("we will surely be his guardians") is meant to overcome Jacob's fear, which was rooted in their earlier betrayal of Joseph. The verse shows how need pushes people to seek trust, and it also sets up Jacob's wary response, since promises of guardianship from those who once failed in that duty carry little weight with him.

translation: He said: "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted you with his brother before? But God is the best Guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."
interpretation: Jacob, remembering how his sons had failed him with Joseph, expresses his deep reluctance to trust their promises about Benjamin, since their earlier pledge to protect Joseph ended in loss. Yet, compelled by the famine and the need for food, he lets go of reliance on human guarantees and places the matter in God's hands. His words show that true safekeeping belongs to God alone, and that a believer, after taking the necessary means, entrusts the outcome to God's protection and mercy, hopeful that the One who is most merciful will not add grief to grief.

translation: And when they opened their baggage, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said, "O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise returned to us. So we will bring provisions for our family, and we will protect our brother, and we will obtain an extra camel-load; that is an easy measure."
interpretation: After returning from Egypt, Joseph's brothers discovered that the payment they had made for the grain had been secretly placed back in their bags. They present this to Jacob as proof of the Egyptian ruler's generosity and good faith, and as a reason to let Benjamin go with them on the next journey. Their argument is that they need nothing more to be convinced of the ruler's goodness, that the returned goods give them means to buy more food for their family, that they will guard Benjamin, and that his presence will earn them an additional camel-load of grain, which is easy for the ruler to give. The verse shows how they appeal to both practical need and assurances of safety to overcome their father's reluctance, while Jacob's earlier distrust, rooted in what happened with Joseph, remains the unspoken background of the exchange.

translation: He (Jacob) said: "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are overwhelmed." Then, when they gave him their solemn pledge, he said: "God is Guardian over what we say."
interpretation: Jacob, anxious after losing Joseph and then Benjamin's brother being detained in his mind as a risk, does not rely on his sons' word alone but demands a binding oath sworn by God, making the promise a matter of religious accountability. He allows only one exception, that they are completely overpowered by circumstances beyond their control. Once they swear, he entrusts the outcome to God, stating that God is the witness and guardian over their covenant. The verse teaches that a believer takes reasonable precautions and secures agreements with sincere commitments, yet ultimately places trust in God (tawakkul), recognizing that He alone guards and oversees all that is said and promised.

translation: And he said: O my sons, do not enter by one gate, but enter by different gates; and I cannot avail you anything against God. Judgment belongs to none but God. In Him I have put my trust, and in Him let all those who trust put their trust.
interpretation: Jacob (Yaqub) advises his sons to take a sensible precaution when entering Egypt, perhaps to avoid drawing attention or the evil eye, since they were a group of handsome brothers from one household. Yet he immediately places this precaution in its proper perspective: taking practical means is a duty, but it has no power of its own. He cannot shield them from anything God has decreed, for all command and final decision belong to God alone. The verse teaches the balance between tawakkul (reliance on God) and taking worldly means: a believer should act prudently and do what is within human ability, while the heart relies on God for the outcome, and true trust is placed in Him alone.

translation: And when they entered from where their father had instructed them, it would not have availed them against God at all, except for a need in the soul of Jacob which he satisfied. And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches the balance between taking worldly precautions and relying on God's decree. Jacob told his sons to enter Egypt by different gates out of concern for the evil eye and to avoid drawing attention as a group of eleven brothers. This was a natural, sincere measure that eased his heart, but he made clear that it could not repel anything God had willed: precautions are means, not the source of protection, and the outcome rests with God alone. Jacob's knowledge was divinely taught: he combined action with true reliance on God (tawakkul), neither neglecting the means nor attributing power to them. Most people do not grasp this subtle balance, and tend either to rely wholly on their own schemes or to abandon all effort under the pretext of trusting God.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother close to himself; he said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."
interpretation: This verse shows Joseph's tenderness and discretion in revealing his identity privately to Benjamin, his full brother, when the brothers came to Egypt. By drawing Benjamin near and telling him 'I am your brother,' Joseph comforts him after years of separation and of hardship caused by the older brothers' envy and mistreatment. The command 'do not grieve over what they used to do' means Benjamin should let go of sorrow over the past harms and wrongs inflicted on them both, because God has reunited them and turned their affliction into ease. It teaches that God relieves the distressed in His own time, and that a believer who has been wronged should respond with compassion and reassurance rather than bitterness.

translation: So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he put the drinking cup into his brother's saddlebag. Then a caller cried out: 'O caravan, you are surely thieves!'
interpretation: Yusuf, wishing to keep his brother Binyamin with him without cheating him or imposing on him by force, arranged a means by which the brother could be retained under a legal procedure known to the brothers themselves. By placing the royal drinking cup in Binyamin's load, he set up a situation in which the brothers' own law (the penalty for theft being the enslavement of the thief) would apply, as the following verses show. The call of the herald, 'you are surely thieves,' was an announcement made on the basis of the apparent fact that the king's cup was missing, not a definite accusation against the particular people who were innocent of it. It shows that this was a divinely guided plan, which God later describes as a stratagem He taught Yusuf, so that he could take his brother in a way that would not have been possible under the king's own law.

translation: They said, as they turned towards them: "What is it that you are missing?"
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:71) shows the brothers of Yusuf reacting calmly when the herald accuses them of theft. They turn to face the accusers and ask what is missing, rather than responding with anger or panic. Their question reflects their confidence in their own innocence and their wish to have the matter stated clearly before any judgment is made. It teaches that a person wrongly accused should face the charge openly, ask for the specifics, and let the facts be established, since fair judgment depends on knowing exactly what is alleged. It also quietly sets up the following verses, in which the claim is spelled out (the missing royal drinking cup) and the brothers confidently stake their word on their innocence, which leads to the unfolding of Allah's plan for Yusuf and Binyamin.

translation: They said: "We are missing the king's drinking cup. Whoever brings it will have a camel's load (of grain), and I guarantee it."
interpretation: The verse shows the herald's public announcement during the Yusuf story, where a reward is offered to anyone who recovers the missing royal measuring cup, and a binding pledge is made to honor it. The phrase 'I am responsible for it' (za'im) establishes the legal principle of kafala, or guarantee: a person may formally take on responsibility for a promised obligation, and the one who publicly proclaims a reward is bound to fulfill it. It also reveals how the search was framed as a matter of public order and royal property, setting up the ensuing test of Yusuf's brothers, whose claim of innocence would be judged by their own stated standards.

translation: They said, "By God, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were never thieves."
interpretation: The brothers of Joseph, accused of stealing the king's drinking cup, swear by God and appeal to what the Egyptians had already seen of their conduct: they had come only to buy food, had behaved honestly and peacefully, and had even returned the goods found in their saddlebags on their first visit. They argue that their known character is itself proof of their innocence, since people who are upright in their dealings do not commit theft, and theft would be a form of corruption in the land. The verse shows how a person's established record of integrity serves as a witness in their defense, and how a sincere oath by God is invoked when someone is falsely accused, though in the story the accusation is part of a divinely guided plan that leads to Joseph keeping his brother Benjamin with him.

translation: They said, "Then what shall be the penalty for it, if you are liars?"
interpretation: This verse, from Surat Yusuf (12:74), comes after Joseph's brothers are accused of stealing the king's drinking cup. Joseph's men ask the brothers to name the punishment for the thief if their claim of innocence proves false. The question draws the brothers into judging themselves by their own law. Because they confidently declare that the one in whose bag the cup is found should be taken as a slave, as was the practice in the family of Jacob, the matter is settled according to their own judgment and not by Egyptian law. This shows God's subtle planning for Joseph, who keeps his brother Benjamin with him without wronging anyone or resorting to the king's law. It also teaches that a person who confidently asserts his own innocence may bind himself to the very verdict that is later applied to him.

translation: They said, "The penalty for it is that the one in whose baggage it is found shall himself be the penalty for it. Thus do we penalize the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The brothers of Joseph, confident of their innocence, invoke the law they knew from the household of Jacob: a thief becomes the property of the one he wronged. By stating the ruling themselves, they bind themselves to it and unknowingly give Joseph the legal means to keep his brother Benjamin, without recourse to the Egyptian king's law.
