The verse shows how people readily pronounce harsh judgment on wrongdoing when they assume it does not touch them, and how God arranges events so that the very words people speak become the means by which His plan is carried out. The phrase 'Thus do we penalize the wrongdoers' presents theft as zulm, a wrong against another's rights, whose just recompense is the loss of one's freedom to the injured party.

translation: So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he extracted it from his brother's bag. Thus We planned for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law unless God willed. We raise in degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is One who is more knowing.
interpretation: The verse shows that Joseph's apparent stratagem was in truth divinely arranged. By searching the other brothers' bags first, he removed any suspicion of a plot and made the discovery in Benjamin's bag look natural. Under the king's law, a thief would be punished with a fine or a flogging, and so Joseph could not have kept his brother by that system. God willed a different outcome: the brothers themselves invoked their own law, under which a thief is taken into servitude, and this let Joseph keep Benjamin without breaking the king's law. God raises in rank those He wills through knowledge, wisdom and patience, as He raised Joseph. Yet no human knowledge is final, since above every knower there is One who knows more, and ultimate knowledge belongs to God alone.

translation: They said, "If he steals, then a brother of his had already stolen before." But Joseph kept it secret within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, "You are worse in position, and God knows best what you describe."
interpretation: The brothers, caught in an awkward situation when the royal cup was found in Benjamin's bag, tried to distance themselves from the accusation by slandering Benjamin and Joseph, insinuating that theft ran in the family. Joseph, who was standing before them in authority, bore this false charge with restraint and dignity. He swallowed the insult silently and did not reveal his identity or rebut them openly, showing patience and self-mastery in the face of slander. His inward reply, 'You are worse in position,' means that in the sight of God, their moral standing was lower, since they had wronged their brother by casting him into the well and lying to their father, while the accusation they made was false. He entrusts judgment to God, who alone knows the truth of what they allege. The verse teaches that a person of true character may suppress an answer to a slander, leaving the vindication to God, who knows the reality behind people's words.

translation: They said, 'O Exalted One (al-'Azīz), indeed he has a father who is an old man of great age, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you to be of those who do good.'
interpretation: After Joseph's cup was found in Benjamin's bag and the king's law allowed him to be kept as a servant, the brothers turned to pleading. They appealed to Joseph's compassion by pointing to their aged father, whose grief for Joseph had already been great and who would not bear losing another son. They offered to be held in Benjamin's place, and they based their appeal on Joseph's evident character, since he had treated them generously and honorably. Their plea shows that they wanted to keep the oath they had given their father to bring Benjamin back, and it shows a change in them from the time they had wronged Joseph, because they now cared for their father and for their brother. It also teaches that an appeal to a person's known goodness and kindness is a fitting way to ask for mercy.

translation: He said, "God forbid that we should seize anyone except the one in whose possession we found our property; indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."
interpretation: Joseph's reply to his brothers, who pleaded that he take one of them in place of Benjamin, affirms a principle of strict justice: punishment may fall only on the person actually found responsible, and it is unjust to seize an innocent person in place of the guilty one, even when offered willingly. By invoking God's protection against such an act, he treats substituting one person for another as a serious moral wrong. The wording is also careful: he says 'the one in whose possession we found our property' rather than 'the thief', which fits the divinely guided plan by which Benjamin was kept without Joseph telling a falsehood. The verse shows that justice must be upheld in practice, and that guilt and punishment cannot be transferred from one person to another.

translation: So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately. The eldest of them said: 'Do you not know that your father took from you a solemn pledge in God's name, and before that you were negligent regarding Joseph? So I will never leave this land until my father permits me, or God decides for me, and He is the best of judges.'
interpretation: After Benjamin was held in Egypt and the brothers lost hope of persuading the Egyptian ruler to release him, they withdrew to consult in private. The eldest brother reproached them with two failures: they had sworn a solemn oath before God to their father to bring Benjamin back, and they had already wronged their father and failed Joseph. Feeling the weight of broken trust and shame, he resolved to stay in Egypt rather than face Jacob without Benjamin, until his father released him from his duty or God opened a way for him through a decree, whether by freeing Benjamin or otherwise. His closing words, 'He is the best of judges', express reliance on God's justice, since human efforts had failed. The verse teaches the gravity of oaths made in God's name, the burden of past wrongdoing on the conscience, and that one should turn to God's judgment when means are exhausted.

translation: Return to your father and say: 'O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we testify only to what we know, and we could not be guardians of the unseen.'
interpretation: In Surah Yusuf (12:81), the eldest brother instructs the others to tell Jacob what happened in Egypt, after Benjamin was held because the king's cup was found in his saddlebag. They distance themselves from blame by saying they bear witness only to what they saw: the cup was found in his baggage, so by the ruling they themselves had accepted, he was detained. They also say they could not have known the hidden reality, or guarded against what lay beyond their sight, when they pledged to bring him back. The verse shows people defending their trustworthiness by pointing to the limits of human knowledge, and it prepares for Jacob's reaction. He does not accept their account at face value and responds with patient endurance, trusting that God will return his sons to him.

translation: And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan with which we came back. And indeed, we are truthful.
interpretation: This is the brothers' appeal to Jacob, who doubted their account of Benjamin's alleged theft in Egypt. They offer to let him verify their statement through independent witnesses. 'Ask the town' is a figure of speech (majaz) meaning ask its people, who knew what had happened, and 'the caravan' means the travelers who journeyed with them and could attest to the events. By pointing to public, corroborating testimony instead of only their own word, they try to show that they are honest and that they had no part in Benjamin's detention, and that they reported only what they saw and knew. The verse shows that a claim should be supported by verifiable evidence, especially when the speaker's credibility has already been damaged by past deceit.

translation: He said: "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed, it is He who is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."
interpretation: Jacob (peace be upon him), on hearing that Benjamin was accused of theft and detained in Egypt, does not accept the sons' account and tells them their own selves have again made an evil course seem fair to them, as they did in the matter of Joseph. Yet he does not respond with despair or complaint; he commits himself to 'beautiful patience', patience without grumbling or protest to people. His hope rests in God that He will return Joseph, Benjamin, and the eldest brother who stayed behind. He grounds this hope in two divine attributes: God's all-encompassing knowledge, which knows where his sons are and the hidden reality of events, and His wisdom, which orders trials and their outcomes for a purpose, even when the believer cannot yet see it. The verse teaches that faith in times of grief combines patient endurance, hopeful trust in God, and recognition that His decree is knowing and wise.

translation: And he turned away from them and said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!" And his eyes turned white from sorrow, and he was suppressing his grief.
interpretation: After his sons brought news that Benjamin had been detained in Egypt, Jacob withdrew from them to be alone with his sorrow. The new loss reopened the old wound of losing Joseph, so his grief centered on Joseph rather than only on Benjamin, which shows that his love and longing had not faded with time. His eyes whitened from constant weeping, meaning that his sight dimmed or was lost through long sorrow. Yet he was 'kazim', one who restrains his grief: he did not complain to people or voice bitterness against God or his sons, but held his pain within and turned to God in patience, as he had said, 'beautiful patience'. The verse teaches that deep sorrow and tears are not contrary to patience, so long as the heart is not given over to despair or complaint against God's decree.

translation: They said, 'By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become gravely ill or become among the perished.'
interpretation: Jacob's sons, seeing his unrelenting grief over Joseph after the loss of Benjamin as well, rebuke him out of concern and frustration. Their oath shows how persistent his sorrow had become: they feared that constant remembrance and weeping would waste away his body and bring him to death. The verse shows the human tendency to see grief as self-destructive, while Jacob's sorrow was in fact bound up with deep love and hope in God, as his reply in the following verses makes clear, where he says he complains of his sorrow only to God and knows from God what they do not know.

translation: He said: I only complain of my anguish and my sorrow to God, and I know from God what you do not know.
interpretation: Jacob, grieving over the loss of Joseph and Benjamin, teaches that true recourse in affliction is to turn to God alone rather than to people. Complaining to God is not a lapse in patience but an expression of dependence on Him, whereas complaining to creatures out of despair is what undermines patience. His words 'I know from God what you do not know' show a heart anchored in faith: he trusts that God's wisdom and decree hold a good outcome, that Joseph is alive, and that relief will come, so his sorrow is held within hope and certainty in God's plan.

translation: O my sons, go and inquire about Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of relief from God. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from God except the disbelieving people.
interpretation: Jacob, though overwhelmed by grief, models active hope grounded in faith: he tells his sons to take practical steps and search for Joseph and Benjamin rather than sit in resignation, while trusting that God's mercy and deliverance can come from where one least expects it. Despair of God's relief is presented as incompatible with true belief, because it implies doubting God's power, mercy and wisdom; the believer keeps striving and hoping however long and severe the trial, whereas those who deny God's power fall into hopelessness.

translation: So when they entered upon him, they said, "O 'Aziz, hardship has touched us and our family, and we have brought only a meager amount of goods, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards those who are charitable."
interpretation: This verse shows the brothers of Yusuf, in their third journey to Egypt, standing before him in humility and need, without knowing who he was. Famine had weakened their household, and their goods were so poor and of such low value that they were almost ashamed to offer them. So they appealed to the generosity of the ruler rather than to the worth of their payment, asking him to give them full measure as an act of charity. Their closing words, that Allah rewards the charitable, show that they appealed to his conscience and his faith, reminding him that kindness is repaid by God. The verse teaches that hardship brings people to humility, that one should ask with courtesy and acknowledge one's weakness, and that the reward for giving is with Allah. It also sets the scene for Yusuf's emotional moment of disclosure, as the ones who once wronged him now stand in need of his mercy.

translation: He said: "Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?"
interpretation: Joseph speaks this after his brothers come to him in need and do not recognize him. He does not open with revenge. He reminds them of their wrong with a question that stirs their conscience, so they will face it and repent. By attributing their deed to ignorance (jahl), he offers them an excuse, meaning they acted out of rashness, envy and a lack of foresight rather than settled malice. This shows his gentleness and nobility. A person of true faith, once he has power, can recall a wrong in order to guide the wrongdoer to repentance and prepare the ground for forgiveness, as the following verses and his words 'No blame will be upon you today' confirm.

translation: They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. God has certainly been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever is mindful of God and is patient, then surely God does not let the reward of those who do good be lost."
interpretation: Joseph answers his brothers' astonished question by crediting his reunion with his brother and his rise from the well and prison to God's grace rather than to his own cleverness. He then states the principle behind his story: lasting honor comes from taqwa, which means being conscious of God and avoiding sin even when tempted, as he was with the wife of the governor, together with patience in hardship, as he showed in the well, in slavery, and in prison. Those who combine these two qualities are muhsinin, people who do good, and God never lets their reward go to waste, whether in this world or the next. He gives this as a lesson to the brothers, and he does so without boasting or reproach, pointing them toward repentance and trust in God's justice.

translation: They said, "By God, God has indeed preferred you over us, and we were truly sinners."
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:91) shows the brothers' full admission before Joseph after they recognize him. Their oath by God and their acknowledgment that God had favored him with knowledge, prophethood, and authority show that the envy that drove their old plot has given way to humility. By calling themselves 'sinners' (khati'in, those who willfully err), they take responsibility for their wrongdoing instead of excusing it. The verse teaches that God's favor cannot be overturned by human scheming, and that real repentance begins with openly recognizing God's choice and one's own fault. This prepares for Joseph's forgiveness in the next verse.

translation: He said: "No blame will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful."
interpretation: This is Prophet Yusuf's response to his brothers after they confessed their wrong against him. Though he held power over them, he did not reproach or shame them; he lifted all censure at once and chose pardon over vengeance. By turning to a prayer that God forgive them, he shows that true nobility lies in forgiving when one is able to retaliate, and that the believer places the matter of final forgiveness with God, whose mercy surpasses every other mercy. The verse teaches that sincere repentance should be met with generosity, that forgiveness heals broken family bonds, and that the righteous do not exploit their position to humiliate those who have wronged them.

translation: Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. Then bring me all your family.
interpretation: Joseph, having revealed himself to his brothers, gives them his shirt as a means by which God will restore his father Jacob's sight, which had been lost through grief. The shirt carries Jacob's own cherished bond with his son. Its being laid on his face is a sign of God's power to turn sorrow into joy once the long-awaited news of Joseph reaches him. Joseph also asks that the whole family come to Egypt, so that the family, divided by jealousy and loss, is reunited and finds security and honor under his care. The verse shows that relief comes by God's leave through ordinary means, and that Joseph answers his brothers' wrongdoing with forgiveness and generosity, not vengeance.

translation: And when the caravan departed, their father said, 'Indeed, I find the scent of Joseph, if you would not think me weak-minded.'
interpretation: Jacob's perception of Joseph's scent, long before the caravan carrying the shirt reached him, shows how God can grant His prophets insight and consolation beyond ordinary means, as a sign that relief was near. His hope never wavered through years of grief, because his trust rested in God's promise rather than in outward circumstances. His caution, 'if you would not think me weak-minded', shows that those who perceive a truth others cannot often meet disbelief and mockery. The verse teaches that when a believer's patience is complete, God can open the way to relief from where no one expects it.

translation: They said, "By God, you are indeed still in your old error."
interpretation: This verse (Surah Yusuf 12:95) records the response of Jacob's family members when he said he could sense the scent of Joseph. They believed Joseph long dead and thought Jacob's hope of finding him again was an illusion. By 'your old error' they meant his long-standing, to them irrational, attachment to and expectation of Joseph's return, not misguidance in religion. The verse shows how people who judge by outward circumstances fail to understand the certainty of a prophet whose hope rests on trust in God and knowledge from Him that they do not share. It also illustrates how harshly close relatives can misjudge a person of deep faith and patience.

translation: Then when the bearer of good news arrived, he cast the shirt over his face, and he regained his sight. He said: 'Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know?'
interpretation: The verse shows the fulfilment of Prophet Jacob's long-held trust in God. When Joseph's shirt was laid over his face, his sight returned as a sign of divine mercy, confirming what he had always believed: that Joseph was alive and that relief would come. His words remind his sons that a believer's certainty rests on knowledge and hope received from God, which others cannot perceive from outward circumstances alone. The lesson is that patient endurance and unwavering reliance on God, even through prolonged hardship and the doubts of those around, end in vindication and joy, and that God's power can restore what seems lost by means that seem humanly impossible.

translation: They said: 'O our father, ask forgiveness for our sins; indeed, we have been sinners.' (Qur'an 12:97)
interpretation: After Yusuf's brothers have seen the consequences of their wrongdoing and the truth of Yusuf's station, they come to their father Yaqub with sincere admission of guilt. They do not make excuses or shift blame; they confess plainly that they were in error and ask him to intercede for them. The verse teaches that repentance begins with honest acknowledgment of one's sin, and that seeking the prayers of a righteous person is a legitimate means of seeking forgiveness, while the ultimate forgiveness remains with God. Yaqub's reply, that he will ask forgiveness for them from his Lord, shows the gentleness and mercy with which a repentant person should be received.

translation: He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you; indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful." (Qur'an 12:98)
interpretation: Jacob does not rush to grant forgiveness on his sons' behalf but defers the request for God's pardon to a later, more fitting time, commonly understood as the pre-dawn hours or a blessed night of prayer, when supplications are most likely to be answered. His promise shows that true forgiveness of wrongdoing ultimately rests with God, not with people, and that the aggrieved parent can only intercede. By closing with God's names 'the Forgiving, the Merciful', he turns his sons' hearts toward hope in divine mercy and reassures them that sincere repentance will be received, however grave the sin.

translation: Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said, "Enter Egypt, God willing, in security."
interpretation: Joseph's welcome of his parents shows the tenderness and honor owed to them: he draws them close to himself before the rest of the family settles. By saying "God willing" he attributes the safety and peace they will find to God's will rather than to his own power as a ruler, even though he holds authority in Egypt. The verse presents a believer in high position who stays humble, ties his promises to God, and sees the reunion of the family after long separation as a blessing from God, bringing security after years of hardship.

translation: And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. He said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision of long ago. My Lord has made it come true. He was truly good to me when He took me out of prison and brought you from the desert, after Satan had stirred up discord between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is subtle in what He wills. Indeed, it is He who is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."
interpretation: This verse shows the fulfillment of Yusuf's childhood dream, in which eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowed to him, and it teaches that God's plan unfolds in ways hidden from people, often through hardship, until its wisdom becomes clear. Yusuf does not boast of his rank or dwell on his brothers' wrongdoing. He attributes everything to God's favor, mentioning his release from prison and the family's reunion, and he places the blame for the old enmity on Satan's incitement rather than on his brothers, which preserves family harmony and models forgiveness and noble character. His closing statement that God is 'subtle in what He wills' (latif) means that God brings about His decrees through gentle, unseen, finely arranged means, and that He acts with perfect knowledge and wisdom. The believer should therefore trust God's timing and be patient through trials, since what looks like loss or injustice may be the path to the outcome God has prepared.

translation: My Lord, You have given me [something] of sovereignty and taught me something of the interpretation of events. Creator of the heavens and the earth, You are my protector in this world and in the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim [in submission to You] and join me with the righteous.
interpretation: This is Prophet Joseph's prayer after God reunited him with his family and raised him to authority in Egypt. At the height of worldly success, he does not credit himself but acknowledges that his power and his knowledge of interpreting dreams are gifts from God, and he describes them as only 'some' of what God holds, which shows humility. He affirms God as his sole protector in both this life and the next, and then asks for what matters most: to remain in submission to God until death and to be counted among the righteous. The verse teaches that worldly rank and blessings are not the goal, that gratitude should lead to dependence on God, and that a believer's greatest concern is a good end and the company of the righteous in the Hereafter.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. You were not with them when they agreed upon their plan while they were plotting.
interpretation: After recounting the story of Joseph and his brothers, God tells the Prophet Muhammad that this narrative could only have reached him through revelation, since he was not present when Joseph's brothers resolved to cast Joseph into the well and schemed against him. The verse affirms the authenticity of his prophethood: an unlettered man living among people with no access to this history could not have known such precise, hidden details unless God informed him. It also reminds the listener that the story's lessons, of envy, patience, and God's hidden planning that overturns the schemes of plotters, come from a trustworthy divine source.

translation: And most of the people, however eagerly you desire it, are not believers.
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:103) consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Belief is a matter of divine guidance and the free response of the heart, not something a messenger can force through his own eagerness, however earnest and compassionate his efforts. His duty is to convey the message clearly, while guidance rests with God alone. The verse also teaches that the majority are not a measure of truth, so a believer should not be discouraged by how few accept the message or take large numbers as proof of being right.

translation: And you do not ask them for any wage for it. It is only a reminder for all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:104) affirms the sincerity of the Prophet's mission. He asks no payment from people for conveying the Qur'an, so no one can accuse him of seeking worldly gain, and the people have no excuse of burden or cost for rejecting it. The Qur'an is not a message for one tribe or era but a universal reminder, addressed to humankind and jinn in every age, awakening them to the truth of God, their purpose, and their accountability. Its worth lies in its guidance, which is offered freely to all.

translation: And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth that they pass by, while they turn away from it.
interpretation: The verse points to the heedlessness of people who are surrounded by countless signs of God's existence, power, wisdom and mercy in the cosmos, such as the sun and moon, the alternation of night and day, the rain that revives dead land, the mountains, and the human self. They walk past these signs every day without reflecting on them or drawing the obvious conclusion that there is a Creator who deserves worship alone. The problem lies not in a lack of evidence but in a lack of attention. Their turning away is an act of the heart, a willful neglect that keeps them from faith. The verse thus calls the reader to contemplate creation and to treat the whole universe as a book of signs pointing to God.

translation: And most of them do not believe in God except while associating others with Him.
interpretation: This verse (Yusuf 12:106) points out that many people profess belief in God as Creator and Provider, yet their faith is compromised by shirk, whether the overt kind of worshipping idols, intermediaries, or saints, or the hidden kind of trusting in causes, wealth, or people as though they had independent power to benefit or harm, or performing deeds to be seen by others. True faith therefore requires pure monotheism: acknowledging God's lordship is not enough unless it is joined with devoting worship, trust, hope, and fear to Him alone.

translation: Do they then feel secure that an overwhelming calamity from God's punishment will not come upon them, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who reject the message for their false sense of security. Divine punishment and the end of the world are not announced on a timetable, and a person's heedlessness neither delays them nor protects him from them. A believer should not take his well-being for granted or postpone repentance and righteous action, because the moment of reckoning can come with no warning, when it is too late to prepare. Real wisdom is to live in constant readiness and humility before God.

translation: Say: This is my way; I invite to God upon clear insight, I and those who follow me. Glory be to God, and I am not of the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse defines the Prophet's mission and that of his true followers: calling people to God is not blind sentiment or partisan zeal, but must rest on certain knowledge and clear evidence (basira), with an understanding of what is being called to, the proof for it, and the wisdom of how to convey it. Whoever follows the Prophet is bound to carry on this same path of conscious, informed invitation to the worship of God alone. The exclamation of God's glory affirms His transcendence above any partner or deficiency, and the declaration of disassociation from the polytheists shows that the call is rooted in pure monotheism, free from any trace of shirk, whether open or hidden. Thus the true follower is known by both knowledge-based calling and uncompromising devotion to God alone.

translation: We did not send before you any but men, from the people of the towns, to whom We revealed. Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? And the home of the Hereafter is surely better for those who are mindful of God. Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: The verse answers the objection that a mere human being cannot be a messenger. God's way has always been to choose men from among settled communities, who share their people's language and way of life, so that they can be followed as examples and understood. Their message was therefore not an innovation. The verse then invites the deniers to learn from history: let them travel the earth and see the ruins of earlier nations who rejected their messengers, and so recognize that arrogance and disbelief end in destruction. It then reminds believers that worldly success and failure are not the measure of truth, because the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who guard themselves against God's displeasure through faith and righteousness. It closes with a rebuke, 'Will you not use your reason?', calling people to reflect on these lessons and not to cling to worldly appearances.

translation: Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them, and We saved whom We willed. And Our might is not turned back from the criminal people.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's help to His messengers often comes only after the severest trial, when hardship has lasted so long that human hope is nearly exhausted and the messengers fear that their people's denial may stand unanswered. The 'thought' of being denied is a passing human feeling of anxiety under prolonged pressure, not doubt in God's promise, and it does not diminish their faith. When the moment God has appointed arrives, deliverance comes suddenly, rescuing the believers He wills while His punishment strikes the wrongdoers without anyone being able to avert it. The lesson is patience and trust in God's timing: delay in victory does not mean its absence, and the end belongs to the righteous, while persistent wrongdoing meets a sure and unstoppable reckoning.

translation: In their stories there is certainly a lesson for people of understanding. It is not a fabricated narrative, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of everything, and a guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: This closing verse of Surat Yusuf teaches that the accounts of the prophets, especially the story of Yusuf and his brothers, are not entertainment or invented tales but carry lessons that people of sound reason can learn from: patience in hardship, the downfall of envy and plotting, God's power to turn trials into honor, and the reward of piety. The Qur'an is described as authentic revelation that confirms the earlier scriptures' true teachings, explains in detail all that people need in matters of faith and practice, and serves as guidance and mercy. Yet only those who believe benefit from this guidance, because they approach it with receptive hearts, reflect on it, and act upon it.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Meem, Ra. These are the verses of the Book. And what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe.
interpretation: The disjointed letters at the start of the surah point to the miraculous nature of the Qur'an: it is composed of the very letters the Arabs use in their speech, yet they cannot produce anything like it. The verse affirms that the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad is absolute truth from God, free of doubt, falsehood or human invention. That most people still do not believe shows that rejection does not come from any lack of evidence or clarity in the message. It comes from arrogance, stubbornness, heedlessness and attachment to inherited ways. The believer is therefore urged to hold firmly to the truth and not be shaken by the fact that the majority reject it, since truth is measured by its source and not by how many accept it.

translation: It is God who raised the heavens without any pillars that you can see, then established Himself above the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for an appointed term. He regulates the affair and details the signs, so that you may be certain of meeting your Lord.
interpretation: The verse argues from the order of the visible cosmos to the reality of a single, all-governing Creator and then to the certainty of the afterlife. The heavens stand without any support that human eyes can perceive, and the sun and moon move by fixed laws toward an appointed end, which shows that the universe is neither self-existing nor aimless but is sustained and directed by God's power and wisdom. His ongoing management of every affair and His clear explanation of the signs, both in creation and in revelation, are presented as proof that the One who creates, orders, and sustains with such precision is able to resurrect people and hold them to account. The purpose is to turn reflection on nature into firm conviction that every person will meet their Lord, which should shape how one lives.

translation: And it is He who spread the earth and placed therein firmly set mountains and rivers; and from all fruits He made therein two mates (pairs). He covers the night with the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse points to God's creative power and wise design as evidence of His oneness and of the truth of resurrection. The earth is laid out wide and made habitable; mountains steady it and rivers carry water that gives life; and every kind of fruit is created in pairs, which shows a deliberate order of growth and reproduction, not chance. The alternation of night and day, with one veiling the other, further shows a precisely regulated system that serves human rest and livelihood. Such order cannot come from anything but a single, all-knowing, all-powerful Creator, so those who truly reflect should recognize His sovereignty, be grateful to Him alone, and not doubt that He can raise the dead.

translation: And on the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees—clustered together from a single root and others not clustered—watered with one water; yet We make some of them better than others in produce. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who use reason.
interpretation: The verse points to the Creator's power and wisdom through the diversity found in nature. Plots of land lie side by side, drink the same water, and often share the same soil, yet they yield different fruits, tastes, colors, and qualities. Such variation cannot be explained by the physical causes alone, because the causes are identical while the results differ. It shows that a deliberate Will directs creation, choosing and distinguishing as He wills. This is evidence that the One who can bring forth such varied produce from a single source is able to resurrect the dead and to guide or leave astray whom He wills, and that those who reflect with reason will recognize His oneness and authority.

translation: And if you are to wonder, then wondrous is their saying: "When we have become dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; those have shackles around their necks; and those are the companions of the Fire, in it they will abide forever.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet that if anything deserves astonishment, it is the disbelievers' denial of resurrection. They have seen God's power in the heavens, the earth, and the first creation, yet they doubt that the One who created them from nothing can recreate them after they turn to dust. Their denial is not merely an intellectual error but a rejection of their Lord's power and promise. The verse then describes their fate: the shackles around their necks symbolize their bondage to arrogance, stubbornness, and misguided attachments in this life, and the humiliating restraint they will face in the next. Their permanent residence in the Fire is the just consequence of rejecting the truth of resurrection and accountability.

translation: They ask you to hasten the evil before the good, although exemplary punishments have already come to pass before them. And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The disbelievers mockingly challenge the Prophet to bring down God's punishment upon them immediately, instead of asking for mercy and well-being, showing their heedlessness and disbelief in the warning. They ignore the fate of earlier nations who denied their messengers and became examples and lessons. The verse explains that the delay of punishment is not neglect or weakness but a result of God's forbearance and mercy: He forgives people, giving them time to repent despite their wrongdoing. Yet this respite must not breed false security, for God is also severe in retribution against those who persist in denial. The verse thus balances hope in God's pardon with fear of His justice, calling people to repent before the opportunity ends.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.
interpretation: The disbelievers demand a miraculous sign beyond the revelation they have already been given, treating the Prophet's message as insufficient proof. The verse answers that the Prophet's task is not to produce miracles on demand but to warn people of the consequences of their choices, while guidance itself comes from God. Every community has been given someone to guide it to the truth, whether a prophet or a righteous guide who calls to God. So the Prophet's role is a continuation of a familiar pattern of divine guidance, and the demand for signs is merely an excuse to avoid accepting the clear message already before them.

translation: God knows what every female bears, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is in due measure.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's comprehensive and precise knowledge, using pregnancy as an example of a hidden matter no one else can see. He knows whether the embryo is male or female, healthy or not, single or multiple, and what its life will be. He also knows what the wombs reduce, through miscarriage, a shortened term or lesser development, and what they add, through a longer term or greater number and growth. Nothing in creation is random or without purpose. Every being, event, and provision is set according to a measure and wisdom that God has ordained, so that nothing exceeds or falls short of what He has decreed. This should lead people to trust His wisdom and to recognize that all knowledge of the unseen and all power over creation belong to Him alone.

translation: He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Grand, the Exalted. (Qur'an 13:9)
interpretation: God's knowledge encompasses everything, both what is hidden from creatures, such as what wombs carry, what hearts conceal, and what lies in the future, and what is plainly observable. Because His knowledge has no limits and nothing escapes it, He is truly great (al-Kabīr) and high above all His creation (al-Muta'āl), exalted beyond any likeness to created beings or any limitation of their understanding. The verse calls the believer to constant awareness that God sees both secret and open deeds, and to humble devotion to a Lord whose greatness and transcendence are absolute.

translation: It is all the same among you, whether one conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he hides himself by night or goes out boldly by day.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 13:10) teaches that God's knowledge is all-encompassing and does not differ between what is secret and what is public. A whisper made in private is as known to Him as a loud declaration, and a person hidden under the cover of night is as visible to Him as one walking openly in the daylight. Darkness, concealment and distance offer no escape from His awareness. The verse therefore calls people to constant God-consciousness, to sincerity in word and deed, and to accountability in private as much as in public, since nothing a person says or does is ever outside God's knowledge.

translation: For each person there are successive angels before him and behind him, who guard him by God's command. Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves. And when God intends harm for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector besides Him.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's care and His laws operate together with human moral responsibility. Each person is surrounded by angels appointed to watch over him within the limits God decrees, which shows that no one is left unattended and that every protection comes only by God's permission. Yet God does not withdraw blessings, security, or honor from a community, nor replace them with hardship, until the people themselves alter their inner state through ingratitude, injustice, and corruption. The same principle holds in the other direction: when people reform their hearts and conduct, God changes their circumstances for the better. Once God has decreed a punishment because of a people's own choices, nothing can avert it, and no guardian or helper apart from Him can shield them. The lesson is that people should take responsibility for their inner and moral condition and turn to God alone for protection.

translation: It is He who shows you the lightning, causing fear and hope, and who brings into being the heavy clouds.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy through the lightning and the clouds. Lightning is a sign that stirs two opposite feelings at once. People fear it because it may bring destructive thunderbolts, or because it may bring a storm that ruins travelers and crops. They also hope for it because it announces rain, which revives the dead land and brings sustenance. The clouds heavy with water are raised and formed by God's command, drawing moisture up and carrying it until He sends it down where He wills. The lesson is that the believer should live between fear and hope, and should see that benefit and harm both come from God alone. Natural phenomena are not independent forces but signs that call people to turn to the Creator, who controls them, in awe and in trust.

translation: The thunder glorifies His praise, and so do the angels out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whomever He wills, while they dispute about God, and He is severe in might and in the power of His plan.
interpretation: The verse shows that all of creation, from natural forces like thunder to the angels, submits to God in glorification and reverence, so that even the most terrifying phenomena are signs of His majesty and not independent powers. Against this universal submission, it points to the irony of human beings who argue and doubt about God, even though the very forces that frighten them proclaim His praise. The thunderbolt that strikes whom He wills is a reminder that His power is absolute and that no one can escape it or outmaneuver His plan. Disputing about Him is therefore folly, and the fitting response to these signs is humility, awe, and sincere turning to Him.

translation: To Him belongs the call of truth. Those whom they invoke besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches out his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it never reaches it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.
interpretation: The verse teaches that only God, the Living and All-Hearing, is worthy of being called upon, and that sincere prayer belongs to Him alone. Those who direct their pleas to idols, created beings, or any power besides Him are like a thirsty man who reaches out his open palms to water from afar, hoping it will rise to his mouth: the water is lifeless, cannot hear him, and cannot move, so his effort is futile and his thirst remains. In the same way, false deities have no power to hear, respond, or benefit, so the prayers of those who reject God's oneness are wasted, misdirected, and lost, because they are addressed to something that cannot answer them.

translation: And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and so do their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all creation is subject to God's sovereignty and submits to His will and laws. Believers prostrate willingly, out of love and obedience, while others submit unwillingly because they cannot escape His decree: they are born, fall ill, age, and die as He ordains. Even the shadows, which stretch and shrink with the sun's movement in the morning and evening, show a constant, involuntary submission to their Creator. The verse invites people to recognize that everything around them already submits to God, so they should choose to submit to Him willingly, as the rest of creation does.

translation: Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah. Say: Have you then taken protectors besides Him who possess no benefit or harm even for themselves? Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal? Or have they assigned to Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them? Say: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Irresistible.
interpretation: The verse is a sequence of arguments that the Prophet is told to put to the polytheists, showing that worshipping anything besides God is irrational. The polytheists themselves admit that God is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, so it is inconsistent to take as protectors beings that cannot even help or harm themselves, let alone others. Those who see God's oneness and those who reject it are no more alike than the blind and the seeing, or darkness and light: tawhid is clear guidance and insight, while shirk is ignorance and confusion. The verse then challenges the claim of partnership: if their idols had created something like God's creation, so that it was unclear who created what, they might have grounds to share worship. But nothing besides God creates anything, since He alone is the Creator of all things, the One, the Irresistible who has dominion over everything. Therefore He alone is worthy of worship.

translation: He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire, seeking ornaments or tools, there is foam like it. Thus God sets forth truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it vanishes as worthless scum; but what benefits people remains in the earth. Thus God sets forth parables.
interpretation: The verse offers a parable of truth and falsehood. Revelation is like rain from heaven, and hearts are like valleys, each receiving and holding it according to its own capacity. When the flood runs, foam rises on top, just as foam rises on molten metal in the furnace. Falsehood may look swollen, loud and dominant for a while, yet it is hollow and light, and it is cast aside and disappears. Truth, like pure water that nourishes the land or refined metal that is useful, is beneficial and so it endures and settles in the earth and in people's lives. The lesson is that falsehood's apparent triumph is temporary and deceptive, while truth, even if quieter, is what lasts and benefits, so the believer should not be dismayed by the clamor of falsehood but should hold to what is of real benefit.

translation: For those who responded to their Lord is the best reward. But those who did not respond to Him—if they had everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom. Those will have the evil reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.
interpretation: The verse sets two destinies side by side according to how people answer God's call. Those who heed their Lord by believing and obeying receive 'al-husna', the finest outcome: Paradise and God's pleasure. Those who refuse find that in the Hereafter, worldly wealth, the very thing many lived for, has no value. Even if they owned all the earth twice over, they would give it gladly to escape the punishment, yet no ransom will be accepted. The 'evil reckoning' means a strict and unforgiving accounting in which their deeds are weighed against them and nothing saves them. Their final home is Hell, a resting place only in name, since it offers no rest. The lesson is that responding to God's guidance in this life is the only thing that secures safety in the next, and that worldly possessions cannot buy salvation once the chance to respond has passed.

translation: Is he who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only those of understanding take heed.
interpretation: The verse contrasts two kinds of people: the one whose inner sight is open, who recognizes the Qur'an as truth from God and so lives by it, and the one who is spiritually blind, who sees the same signs yet does not perceive their meaning. The two cannot be equal, because knowledge of the truth shapes belief, conduct and destiny, while blindness to it leads to heedlessness and loss. The verse ends by noting that only people of sound intellect, those who use their reason and hearts rather than following desire or stubbornness, truly reflect, take admonition, and benefit from the revelation.

translation: Those who fulfill the covenant of God and do not break the pledge.
interpretation: The verse describes the people of sound intellect (ulu al-albab) by their integrity in keeping faith. The covenant of God is the primordial and ongoing bond between the Creator and humankind: to acknowledge His oneness, worship Him alone, and obey His guidance, together with the commitments that follow from it, such as honoring trusts, keeping promises to others, and upholding the rights that God has made binding. Fulfilling it means remaining loyal to it in both inner conviction and outward conduct, while not breaking the pledge means never betraying these obligations after affirming them. The verse teaches that true understanding is shown not merely in knowing the truth but in steadfast faithfulness to one's commitments toward God and, through Him, toward people.

translation: And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord, and dread the evil of the reckoning.
interpretation: The verse describes people of sound intellect who honor every bond God has ordered to be kept: ties of kinship first, but also the rights of neighbors, fellow believers, the weak, and the community at large, along with the bond between themselves and God through faith and obedience. Their upholding of these bonds springs from inner reverence for their Lord and a sober awareness that every deed will be weighed on the Day of Judgment. This fear is not paralysis but a moral vigilance that makes them careful about the rights of others, since they know a harsh reckoning awaits anyone who neglects them. In this way, social responsibility and God-consciousness are shown to be inseparable.

translation: And those who are patient, seeking the face of their Lord, and establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them secretly and openly, and repel evil with good—those will have the best outcome of the Home.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the final, lasting success of the Hereafter belongs to those whose conduct is rooted in sincerity toward God and expressed in disciplined worship and generous, kind character. Their patience is not mere endurance but is done for God's pleasure alone, free from showing off or seeking worldly recognition. Prayer keeps their relationship with the Creator alive, while spending from their provision, whether privately to protect sincerity or publicly to encourage others, purifies wealth and meets the needs of the community. Their repelling of wrong with goodness shows moral strength: they answer harm with forgiveness, kindness, and restraint, turning enmity into the possibility of friendship rather than feeding cycles of retaliation. Because such people align inner intention, devotion, charity, and ethical conduct, God promises them the good end of the abode, Paradise, as the true and enduring home in contrast to the transient life of this world.

translation: Gardens of Eden, which they will enter, together with the righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their offspring. And the angels will enter upon them from every gate.
interpretation: The verse shows that the reward of the faithful in the Hereafter is complete only when it is shared with those they love. Entry into the eternal gardens is by God's grace, and He reunites the believers with their righteous parents, spouses, and children. Their family bonds, which were rooted in faith and good deeds, endure beyond death, so their joy is made perfect by their loved ones' company. The angels come to them through every gate to greet them with honor and peace, which shows the high station of the people of Paradise and the welcome God gives to those who were patient and obedient.

translation: "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode!"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 13:24) describes the angels greeting the people of Paradise as they enter it. It teaches that patience (sabr) is the key to lasting reward: the believers endured hardship, obeyed God's commands, and refrained from disobedience, and their steadfastness in this fleeting life is what earns them the peace of the next. The angels' greeting acknowledges that every trial borne for God's sake was not wasted, and the phrase 'how excellent is the final abode' affirms that Paradise is the true and enduring home whose joy far outweighs the temporary struggles of worldly life.

translation: And those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and spread corruption in the land—for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 13:25) contrasts with the people of understanding described just before it, who fulfil God's covenant. It names three connected offenses that destroy both faith and society: violating the binding pledge a person has made with God (the natural disposition to acknowledge God's oneness, the covenant taken from humankind, and the commitments of faith), cutting the ties God ordered to be maintained (above all kinship, and by extension the bonds of faith, rights of neighbors, and the community), and as a result spreading corruption on earth through injustice, discord and oppression. The verse teaches that betrayal of one's relationship with God naturally leads to the breakdown of human relationships and then to wider social harm. Those who do this are cut off from God's mercy, which is the meaning of 'the curse', and their final dwelling will be a bad one, the opposite of the 'excellent final abode' promised to the faithful. Their punishment fits their deed: as they severed what should be joined, they are severed from mercy.

translation: God extends provision to whom He wills and straitens it. And they rejoice in the life of this world, whereas the life of this world, compared with the Hereafter, is nothing but brief enjoyment.
interpretation: Wealth and scarcity are not signs of God's favor or displeasure; they are distributions that follow His wisdom and serve as tests of gratitude and patience. Those who turn away from faith mistake abundance in this world for true success and become absorbed in it, forgetting that worldly life is fleeting and trivial when set against the lasting life to come. The verse calls the believer to hold worldly gains lightly, to avoid arrogant delight in them, and to place real value on what endures in the Hereafter.

translation: Those who disbelieve say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, God lets go astray whom He wills, and guides to Himself those who turn to Him in repentance." (Qur'an 13:27)
interpretation: The disbelievers' demand for yet another miracle is not a sincere search for truth but a pretext, since signs have already been shown and the Qur'an itself is a sign. The verse teaches that guidance does not come from the abundance of miracles but from the state of the heart. God leaves astray those who persist in stubbornness and arrogance, withdrawing His guidance from them as a consequence of their own choice. He guides to Himself those who turn back to Him in humility and repentance, who sincerely seek Him and are ready to accept the truth. Faith thus depends on openness and a return to God, not on the demand for ever more proofs.

translation: Those who believe, and whose hearts find peace and reassurance in the remembrance of God. Truly, it is in the remembrance of God that hearts find peace.
interpretation: The verse teaches that real inner tranquility does not come from wealth, status, or worldly signs and certainties, but from turning the heart toward God. Hearts are restless by nature, pulled by fear, loss, and desire, and they settle only when anchored to their Creator. Remembrance (dhikr) here is more than repeating words with the tongue: it is a lived awareness of God's presence, mercy, power, and promise, expressed in prayer, reflection on His signs, recitation of the Qur'an, and obedience. When a believer recalls that everything is in God's hands and that He is near and merciful, anxiety gives way to trust and contentment. The closing emphasis, 'Truly, it is in the remembrance of God that hearts find peace,' presents this as a universal rule: no other source can fully satisfy the human heart.

translation: Those who believe and do righteous deeds - blessedness is theirs, and a beautiful place of final return.
interpretation: The verse promises that true faith, when joined with good action, brings lasting happiness in this life and the next. 'Tuba' signifies a state of goodness, joy, and divine favor, often understood also as a tree in Paradise, while 'husn ma'ab' means that their ultimate return to God is a fair and honorable one. It teaches that belief alone is incomplete without deeds that give it evidence, and that the person who aligns heart and conduct with God's guidance will find contentment and security at the end of their journey, which is the true measure of success.

translation: Thus have We sent you among a community before which other communities have passed away, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my repentance and return.
interpretation: God affirms that the Prophet Muhammad's mission follows a well-established divine pattern: just as earlier prophets were sent to nations that came and went, he has been sent to his own people with the task of conveying revelation, not of compelling belief. The verse consoles him that rejection is nothing new, since his people deny even God's attribute of mercy (ar-Rahman), showing how deep their obstinacy is. The Prophet is instructed to answer their denial with a firm declaration of pure monotheism: the One they reject is his Lord, there is no deity besides Him, he relies on Him alone for support and outcome, and to Him he will return in repentance and submission. The lesson is that a believer meets hostility and disbelief not with despair but with steadfast faith, trust in God, and conveying the message faithfully.

translation: Even if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were moved, or the earth were cut apart, or the dead were made to speak, (it would not make them believe); rather, all authority belongs to God. Have those who believe not yet realized that, had God willed, He would have guided all people? And those who disbelieve will continue to be struck by disaster because of what they have done, or it will settle near their homes, until God's promise comes. Indeed, God does not break His promise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith does not depend on the magnitude of miracles but on God's will and the openness of the heart. The disbelievers demanded extraordinary signs, yet even a Qur'an that moved mountains, split the earth, or made the dead speak would not compel those whose hearts are closed, because guidance is ultimately in God's hands. The believers are therefore told to stop despairing over the stubbornness of the deniers and to stop wishing for miracles to convert them: God could have guided all humanity by compulsion, but He willed to leave people free to choose, so that belief would be sincere and accountable. Meanwhile, persistent rejection and wrongdoing bring their own consequences, whether calamities that strike the disbelievers directly or that fall near their dwellings as a warning, until God's promise of final victory for truth and judgment against falsehood is fulfilled, and that promise is certain because God never fails in His word.

translation: Messengers before you were indeed mocked, so I granted respite to those who disbelieved, then I seized them. So how was My punishment?
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that ridicule of messengers is an old pattern, not unique to him. God's delay in punishing the mockers is not neglect or approval but a deliberate extension of time, giving them the chance to repent while their wrongdoing grows. When that respite ends, His seizure comes with certainty. The closing rhetorical question invites the listener to recall the fate of earlier nations and see how terrible and just the punishment was, so that the believers may be patient and the deniers take warning instead of being deceived by their present ease.

translation: Is He who stands over every soul for what it has earned (like those who worship nothing)? Yet they have set up partners with God. Say: 'Name them! Or are you informing Him of something on earth that He does not know, or is it merely an outward form of words?' Rather, their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they have been barred from the path. And whoever God lets go astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse opens with a rhetorical question contrasting God, who is ever-watchful over every soul, knows all it does, and will requite it, with the powerless idols that neither see, know, nor control anything. It is absurd to equate them. The Prophet is told to challenge the polytheists to name or identify these partners and show what qualities or authority they have. If they claim the partners exist with real attributes, they would be informing God of something He does not know, which is impossible since He knows everything on earth. If they cannot, then the partners are nothing but empty words and names with no reality behind them. The cause of their error is that their deceptive reasoning and plotting against the truth have been made appealing to them, so they are turned away from the path of guidance. This follows God's way of leaving astray those who persistently choose falsehood, and when He leaves someone astray, no one else can guide him.

translation: For them is a punishment in the life of this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe; and they have no protector against God.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who disbelieve and turn away from God's guidance will not escape the consequences of their choice. In this world they may face humiliation, defeat, affliction, or distress as a just recompense and a warning, but that worldly suffering is limited and temporary. The torment of the Hereafter is far heavier and more enduring, because it is the final and complete reckoning. In that reckoning no power, ally, wealth, or intercessor can shield them, since protection comes only from God, and He will not grant it to those who persisted in rejecting Him. The verse is therefore both a warning and a reminder that true safety lies only in turning to God.

translation: The description of the Garden promised to the righteous: beneath it rivers flow; its provisions are everlasting, and its shade as well. That is the final outcome for those who were mindful of God, while the final outcome for the disbelievers is the Fire.
interpretation: The verse offers a glimpse of the unseen reward of Paradise through imagery that human minds can grasp: flowing rivers, endless provision, and constant shade. Unlike worldly pleasures, which fade, spoil, or depend on seasons, the Garden's blessings neither run out nor diminish. The word 'muttaqin' shows that this reward belongs to those who live with God-consciousness, guarding themselves against disobedience and keeping their duty to Him in private and public life. The closing contrast between the outcome of the righteous and that of the deniers makes plain that every path ends in a destination: the way of taqwa leads to lasting peace and delight, while rejection of truth ends in the Fire. The verse therefore calls the reader to weigh fleeting worldly gains against eternal consequences and to choose the path whose end is Paradise.

translation: Those to whom We have given the Book rejoice in what has been revealed to you; yet among the factions there are those who deny part of it. Say: 'I have only been commanded to worship God and not to associate anything with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return.'
interpretation: The verse distinguishes between the sincere People of the Book, who recognize the truth of the Qur'an because it confirms the core of their own scriptures and so rejoice at its revelation, and the partisan groups who reject parts of it out of tribal or sectarian interest, since it contradicts their innovations or threatens their standing. The Prophet is told to answer such rejection by stating plainly the essence of his mission: pure monotheism, worshipping God alone without partners, which is the common ground of all revealed religions. His call is directed only to God, and the final return of every person, including his opponents, is to Him, so the matter is ultimately settled by God and not by human disputes.

translation: And thus We have sent it down as a judgment in Arabic. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against God neither any protecting ally nor any defender.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an is God's final, clear authority, revealed in the Arabic tongue so that its people could understand it and be bound by its rulings, and through them it becomes a standard by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. It then warns, in the person of the Prophet as the most upright of men, that once clear knowledge has come from revelation, nothing may replace it: yielding to the whims of those who reject it, whether by compromising its rulings or by adopting their ways, would remove a person from God's protection. The warning is general and applies to every believer, since no worldly ally or power can shield anyone from God's displeasure if they abandon revealed guidance to please people's desires.

translation: We sent messengers before you and made for them wives and offspring. It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by God's permission. For every term there is a decree.
interpretation: The verse answers those who objected that Muhammad was an ordinary man who married and had children, and who demanded miraculous signs on request. God says that earlier messengers were also human beings with families, so prophethood does not require being an angel or living apart from ordinary human life. Messengers have no power to produce miracles by their own will; signs come only when God permits and wills them, so the messenger is a servant who delivers the message, not the controller of events. The closing phrase, 'for every term there is a decree,' means that every era, community, and matter has a fixed time and a written ordainment with God. Each revelation, law, sign, and punishment comes at its appointed moment according to His wisdom, and neither the demands of the deniers nor the messenger's wishes can hasten or delay it.

translation: God erases whatever He wills and confirms whatever He wills, and with Him is the Mother of the Book.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has complete authority over what He decrees in creation and in revelation: He may abrogate, remove, or alter what He wills, and He may establish and keep what He wills, according to His wisdom and the needs of each age and people. This changing of rulings, signs, and circumstances does not imply any change in God's knowledge, because the 'Mother of the Book' (the Preserved Tablet, His original and timeless knowledge) remains with Him, containing everything unchanged. So what appears to people as change, such as earlier laws giving way to later ones or events unfolding differently from expectations, is all within His perfect, eternal knowledge and plan, and no messenger or community can bring a sign or ruling except by His leave.

translation: And whether We show you part of what We promise them, or We cause you to die [before that], your duty is only to convey the message, and upon Us is the reckoning.
interpretation: The Prophet's task is limited to delivering the message clearly; he is not responsible for whether people accept it or for when the punishment or consequences promised to the deniers arrive. Whether God lets him witness some of the promised outcome in his lifetime or takes his soul first, the result does not change his duty or diminish the truth of the promise. The final accounting and judgment belong to God alone, who will settle matters with perfect justice at the time He wills. The verse consoles the Prophet and teaches every caller to the truth to do their part sincerely and leave the outcomes to God.

translation: Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders? And Allah judges; there is none to repeal His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: God reminds the deniers that they can observe His decree at work in the world: He steadily diminishes the lands of the disbelievers from their edges, as Islam spreads and their territory, power, and influence shrink while the believers' grow. This visible, gradual change is a sign that the outcome belongs to God alone, since He rules and no one can overturn or delay His ruling. Therefore the deniers should not be deceived by their present strength or by the delay of punishment, because the reckoning of God is swift and His promise will come to pass.

translation: Those before them also plotted, but all planning belongs to God. He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will soon know for whom the ultimate abode is.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and the believers by showing that the plots of the deniers are nothing new, since earlier nations schemed against their messengers too. Yet no scheme succeeds except by God's permission, because real and effective planning belongs to Him alone. He knows exactly what each person earns of deeds and intentions, so nothing the plotters hide escapes Him, and He repays each soul accordingly. The disbelievers will therefore come to know, when truth is made manifest, that the good final outcome in the Hereafter, and ultimately in this world too, belongs to those who were faithful and patient, not to those who schemed against God's guidance.

translation: Those who disbelieve say, 'You are not a messenger.' Say, 'Sufficient is God as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Scripture.'
interpretation: The verse teaches the Prophet to answer the deniers' rejection of his prophethood not with argument over their claims but by appealing to the highest testimony. God's witness is enough, because He knows the truth of the message and confirms it through the Qur'an's inimitability and the signs He has shown. Alongside that, the testimony of those who truly know the earlier scriptures, such as the sincere scholars among the People of the Book who recognize in their own books the description and glad tidings of this Prophet, further supports his claim. The truth of his mission therefore does not depend on the acceptance of those who deny it, but rests on divine testimony and on the corroboration of knowledge found in previous revelation.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. This is a Book which We have revealed to you, so that you may bring people out of the depths of darkness into the light, by the leave of their Lord, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as divine guidance whose purpose is the moral and spiritual transformation of humanity. 'Darkness' stands for ignorance, disbelief, idolatry, and moral confusion, while 'light' stands for faith, knowledge, and clarity of purpose. The Prophet's role is to convey and teach the Book, but the actual guidance occurs only 'by the leave of their Lord,' so the success of guidance rests with God's will and not with the messenger's power. The destination, the path of the Almighty (al-'Aziz) and the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid), indicates that this path is one of strength and worthiness of praise: following it leads a person to the One who is mighty and who deserves all gratitude, and it is a path that is secure, honorable, and good in its outcomes.

translation: Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse grounds true sovereignty in Allah alone: since everything in the heavens and the earth is His creation and possession, no one can claim independent authority or lordship besides Him. Those who reject this truth and the guidance sent through His Messenger are denying the very reality that sustains them, and so they stand in grave peril. The 'woe' is a solemn warning that persisting in disbelief, after the evidence of Allah's ownership and power is plain, leads to a severe punishment, while the implied counterpart is that those who acknowledge Him and submit to Him find safety and mercy.

translation: Those who prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter, and hinder others from the path of God, and seek to make it crooked—those are in profound error.
interpretation: The verse identifies the root of deep misguidance as a corrupted order of priorities: when a person loves worldly gain, status and pleasure more than the eternal life to come, he is drawn to protect those interests even at the expense of truth. That attachment leads him first to turn away from God's path himself, then to obstruct others from it by pressure, ridicule or persuasion, and finally to try to bend the straight path so that it suits his desires, by distorting its teachings or finding fault with it. Such a person has gone so far from guidance that his error is described as 'far-reaching,' meaning that returning to the truth becomes increasingly difficult the longer he persists in preferring the world, misleading others and twisting revelation to justify his course.

translation: We have not sent any messenger except with the language of his people, so that he may make things clear to them. Then Allah lets go astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: God's method in sending revelation is rooted in mercy and clarity: each prophet addresses his people in their own tongue, so that no one can claim the message was unintelligible or out of reach. The prophet's task is to convey and clarify, not to compel belief. Once the message is made plain, people diverge. Guidance and misguidance come through God's will, but that will is exercised with wisdom and justice. Those who sincerely seek the truth and accept it are guided, while those who stubbornly turn away are left to their own error. Since God is Almighty, no one can thwart His decree, and since He is All-Wise, His guiding and letting go astray are never arbitrary but follow what people have earned and what is fitting.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs, saying: 'Bring your people out from darkness into light, and remind them of the Days of God.' Indeed, in that are signs for everyone who is steadfastly patient and deeply grateful.
interpretation: The verse presents the mission of every prophet as liberation: guiding people out of the darkness of ignorance, disbelief, oppression, and heedlessness into the light of faith, knowledge, and justice. Moses is commanded to do this by reminding his people of the 'Days of God', the historic moments when God showed His power, such as saving them from Pharaoh, parting the sea, and destroying earlier nations that denied their messengers. Remembering these events revives awareness that God controls all outcomes, that hardship is temporary, and that blessings come from Him. The closing statement says that only those who are patient in trials and grateful in times of ease truly benefit from such reminders, since these two qualities together form the believer's balanced response to life: steadfastness when tested and thankfulness when favored.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people: Remember Allah's favor upon you when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtered your sons and spared your women. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.
