He sees that the promise runs against ordinary expectation, since he is old and his wife is barren, and he asks how such news can be real. The repeated question, 'then of what do you give glad tidings?', asks for confirmation and invites the angels to explain how a thing so far outside natural causes can come about. The verse shows that a believer can feel human wonder at God's promise while still trusting that nothing is beyond His will. It also prepares for the angels' answer in the next verse, which affirms that the tidings are true and tells him not to despair.

translation: They said: "We have given you glad tidings in truth, so do not be among those who despair."
interpretation: The angels, having announced to Abraham the coming of a son, urge him not to lose hope in God's mercy. Their words teach that God's promises are true and that His power is not limited by ordinary expectations such as old age or the apparent impossibility of the matter. A believer should therefore respond to God's good news with trust and gratitude, since despair implies doubt about His ability and generosity, and despairing of His mercy is incompatible with faith.

translation: He said: "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those who are astray?"
interpretation: This is the reply of Prophet Abraham (peace be upon him) to the angels when they brought him the news of a son in his old age. He was not doubting God's power or despairing of His mercy; rather, he was expressing wonder at the blessing. The verse teaches that despair of God's mercy is a sign of misguidance, since a person who truly knows his Lord knows that His mercy is vast and His power is unlimited, and that nothing is too difficult for Him, however impossible it may seem by ordinary means. A believer should therefore always keep hope in God, even when circumstances appear hopeless.

translation: He said, "Then what is your mission, O messengers?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 51:31) records Abraham's reaction after the angelic guests, who had first appeared to him as strangers, brought him the glad tidings of a son. Once his fear had settled and he understood they were no ordinary visitors, he asked about the weightier matter that had brought them. The word 'khatb' denotes a grave and significant affair, so his question implies that he sensed they had been sent on a momentous divine task beyond the good news they had delivered. The answer that follows, the destruction of the people of Lot, shows that the angels' mission combined mercy for the righteous with justice against the wrongdoers. It also reflects Abraham's wisdom and attentiveness: he was not preoccupied with his own joy but sought to understand the larger purpose of God's command, and his concern for the fate of others, which is also evident in his pleading on behalf of Lot's people elsewhere in the Qur'an.

translation: They said: 'Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals.'
interpretation: The angels, answering Abraham's question about their mission (Qur'an 51:31-32; 15:57-58), reveal that God has sent them against the people of Lot, whose persistent wrongdoing and immorality made them 'mujrimin', those who sever themselves from God's guidance and commit grave crimes. The verse shows that divine punishment is not arbitrary: it follows a people's stubborn rejection of truth and their persistence in corruption after they have been warned. The angels act only as agents carrying out God's command.

translation: Except the family of Lot; indeed, We will save them all.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:59) makes clear that God's punishment of the sinful people of Lot is not indiscriminate: those who believed and followed Lot's call are set apart and granted deliverance. The word 'all' stresses the completeness of their rescue, showing that God's protection of the righteous is total and that no believer is overlooked when judgment falls. It teaches that salvation depends on faith and obedience rather than on circumstances, and that divine justice always distinguishes between the wrongdoers and the faithful.

translation: Except his wife; We decreed that she would be among those who stay behind.
interpretation: The verse shows that salvation depends on faith and righteous conduct, not on family ties or closeness to a prophet. Lot's wife lived in his household but secretly sided with his people, so she shared their fate and was left behind to be destroyed with them. Divine decree here does not mean she was forced into disbelief. God's knowledge and decree encompass what she freely chose, and her destruction followed from that choice. The verse warns believers not to rely on lineage or association with the righteous in place of their own faith.

translation: So when the messengers came to the household of Lot,
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Hijr 15:61) marks the turning point in the story of Lot. The angels, who had earlier visited Abraham with glad tidings, now arrive in the form of men at Lot's home, bringing God's decree against his people. Their arrival shows that divine judgment comes at its appointed time after ample warning, and that the believing household is the one granted protection and deliverance. The verse also prepares for Lot's reaction, his unease at the strangers' presence given the depravity of his people, and highlights that God's messengers arrive both as mercy for the righteous and as a means of punishment for the transgressors.

translation: He said, "Indeed, you are people unknown to me."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:62, and similarly 51:25) records Lot's reaction when the messenger angels came to him in the form of unfamiliar young men. His words show his unease and caution: he did not recognize them, and he feared for their safety and his own because of the depravity of his townspeople, who were known to assault male strangers. The phrase is therefore not mere rudeness to guests but an expression of anxious wariness. It reveals the human side of a prophet, who felt worry and responsibility toward those under his protection before the angels disclosed their true identity and mission, which was to bring relief to him and punishment to his people.

translation: They said: "Rather, we have come to you with that about which they were in doubt."
interpretation: This verse is understood as the angels' reassurance to Lot (Lūṭ) when they came to him in the form of men and his people were pressing him. Lot feared that the strangers were people he could not protect his guests from. The angels told him they were not harmful strangers, but messengers who brought the very punishment that his people had doubted and mocked when he warned them of it. They had disbelieved in God's threatened judgment and kept disputing it, so the angels explain that the matter is now no longer a subject of doubt: the promised punishment has arrived. The verse thus teaches that God's warnings, however long they seem delayed or are denied by the heedless, come true at their appointed time, and that God relieves His faithful servants from distress by bringing the truth that the wrongdoers had questioned.

translation: And we have come to you with the truth, and indeed we are truthful.
interpretation: In this verse (Surah Al-Hijr, 15:64), the angels sent to Lot (Lut) reassure him in his fear and distress. They affirm that what they bring is the certain, decreed truth, namely the punishment that will befall his corrupt people, which the townspeople had doubted and mocked. Their added claim, 'and indeed we are truthful,' stresses that there is no deception or uncertainty in their message: God's promise of deliverance for Lot and the believers and of destruction for the wrongdoers is real and will be fulfilled. The verse teaches that divine decrees, however much they are denied or delayed, are true and will come to pass, and that the righteous can take comfort in God's assured justice.

translation: So travel by night with your family during a portion of the night, and follow behind them, and let none of you look back, and proceed to where you are commanded.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Hijr 15:65) is the angels' instruction to Lot to leave the doomed town secretly in the dark, just before the punishment arrives. His position at the rear shows his role as protector and shepherd of his family: he drives them forward, makes sure none lags behind, and sees that all are safe. The prohibition on looking back means they must not hesitate or linger out of attachment to the place or curiosity about the punishment, since this would expose them to danger and show a lingering heart for a people destined for destruction. Complete, unhesitating obedience and reliance on God are required for salvation. The destination is left unspecified ('where you are commanded') to teach that the believer should follow divine guidance step by step, trusting that God directs him to safety.

translation: And We decreed to him that matter: that the last remnant of these people would be cut off by morning.
interpretation: The verse shows that God informed Lot of a firm, settled judgment against his people, who persisted in immorality and rejected his warnings. 'Cut off' to the last remnant means the destruction would be total, leaving no survivor among the wrongdoers, and 'by morning' means it would arrive at a fixed time, at daybreak. Lot's family was to be saved beforehand, so the verse teaches that God's judgment on persistent transgression is certain and complete, that it comes at its appointed hour, and that He rescues the believers before it falls.

translation: And the people of the city came rejoicing at the good news.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Hijr 15:67) describes the townspeople of Sodom coming to the house of Lot, delighted because they had heard that handsome young guests were with him, and they hoped to satisfy their depraved desires. Their joy was the joy of sinners, a happiness rooted in transgression and heedlessness. It shows how far moral corruption had blinded them, so that they celebrated what would bring about their own destruction, and it sets the scene for Lot's plea that they fear God and not disgrace him before his guests. The verse thus teaches that rejoicing in sin is a sign of a hardened heart and that it often immediately precedes divine punishment.

translation: He said: "Indeed, these are my guests, so do not disgrace me."
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Hijr 15:68) shows Prophet Lot's appeal to his people when they pressed upon the angelic visitors who had come to him in the form of men. In his society the honor of a guest was bound to the honor of the host, so any harm or indecency done to the guests would be a disgrace to Lot himself. By appealing to their sense of decency and to the sanctity of hospitality, he is asking them to spare him public shame. The verse teaches that protecting a guest is a moral duty, and that a righteous person, even when outnumbered and powerless among a corrupt people, still upholds honor and tries to dissuade wrongdoing by reminding others of basic human values before the decree of God comes.

translation: And fear God, and do not disgrace me.
interpretation: The phrase is spoken by a prophet to his people (as with Lot, who says it concerning his guests in Surah Hud 11:78: 'So fear God and do not disgrace me in front of my guests'). It is a call to God-consciousness as the basis of right conduct. Lot appeals first to his people's awareness of God and only then to their sense of honor and decency, so that they will refrain from violating the sanctity of guests under his protection. The point is that fear of God is the true safeguard of moral limits, and that harming the vulnerable under one's protection brings shame on the whole community, not only on the one who protects them.

translation: They said: 'Did we not forbid you from [entertaining] the people of the worlds?'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:70) records the reply of the people of Lot when he tried to protect his guests. They reproach him for having ignored their earlier prohibition against offering hospitality or protection to strangers. The phrase shows how deeply corrupt they were: instead of reflecting on their own immoral conduct, they sought to restrict anyone who sheltered travelers, because that stood in the way of their wrongdoing. The verse indicates that when a society normalizes sin, it turns against those who uphold decency and hospitality and tries to silence them, treating the defense of the vulnerable as an offense.

translation: He said, "These are my daughters, if you are to do (something)."
interpretation: Prophet Lot, facing a mob of men who came lusting after his guests, appeals to them to turn from their immoral desire toward the lawful path of marriage. By pointing to 'my daughters,' he means the women of his community, who as a prophet he regarded as his own daughters in a spiritual and paternal sense, and whom they could lawfully marry. His words are not an offer to hand over his own children, but an effort to redirect them from a shameful act to what is natural and permitted, and to shield his guests from disgrace. The phrase 'if you are to do' expresses his hope that they might act rightly, and shows the depth of his distress and the lengths to which he went to persuade them before their punishment came.

translation: By your life, [O Muhammad], they were, in their intoxication, wandering blindly.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of the story of Lot's people (Surah al-Hijr 15:72). God swears by the life of the Prophet, an honor to him, to describe the state of Lot's people: they were so overtaken by their desires and heedlessness that, like drunkards, they lost sound judgment. Lot's warnings and advice could not reach them, and they kept stumbling in confusion and misguidance, unaware that destruction was approaching. The lesson is that persistent indulgence in lust and sin intoxicates the heart and blinds it to truth, so that a person cannot perceive the warning signs until punishment seizes them.

translation: So the Cry seized them at sunrise.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:73) describes the end of the people of Lot after they persisted in their immorality and rejected the warnings of their prophet. The mighty Cry, a divine punishment that struck at the break of dawn, shows that God's judgment arrives suddenly and decisively, when the wrongdoers are heedless and secure in their sins. The mention of sunrise, a time of new beginnings and hope, contrasts with the finality of their destruction and teaches that no moment of the day, and no worldly comfort, can shield a people from God's decree once they have exhausted His respite. It stands as a warning to every generation that arrogance and moral corruption lead to ruin, and that the signs of earlier nations should prompt reflection and repentance.

translation: So We turned the town upside down, making its highest part its lowest, and We rained down upon them stones of baked clay.
interpretation: The verse describes the manner in which God destroyed the people of Lot after they persisted in their transgression and rejected the warnings of His messenger. The overturning of the town, with its top made its bottom, is a fitting retribution: a people who inverted the natural order of human desire and morality had their own dwellings inverted. The shower of stones of sijjīl, hard clay baked as if by fire and marked for their targets, shows that the punishment was precise, decisive and from God alone, not a natural coincidence. The lesson is that persistent immorality and defiance of divine guidance bring ruin, that God's judgment fits the nature of the crime, and that the fate of earlier nations is a warning for those who come after.

translation: Indeed, in that are signs for those who carefully observe and discern.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Hijr, 15:75), which comes after the account of the people of Lot and their destruction, teaches that the fate of those people holds lasting lessons, but only people of perceptive insight benefit from them. The 'mutawassimin' are those who look beyond outward appearances and read the underlying meanings of events, as a physiognomist reads marks and traits. The verse means that God's signs are placed throughout history and creation for all to see, yet only those who reflect with discernment, sincerity and an open heart recognize that wrongdoing leads to ruin, and that God's justice and power operate in the world. Seeing the signs is therefore a matter of attentive, thoughtful perception rather than mere sight.

translation: And indeed, it (the town of the people of Lot, or the Wood-dwellers' land) lies on a road that still exists.
interpretation: The verse points to the ruins of the destroyed town of Lot's people, which lie along a well-known, enduring highway used by travelers, likely the trade route between the Hijaz and Syria. Their remains are therefore not hidden in some remote place but are plainly visible to passersby, so the Arabs of the Prophet's time passed by them regularly. The verse is a call to reflect: the evidence of God's punishment on those who denied the messengers and persisted in wrongdoing is still standing, and those with sound faith and insight should take a lesson from it and avoid the same fate.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the signs of God in creation and in His dealings with humankind are open to everyone, but only those with faith are moved to reflect on them and draw guidance from them. Belief opens the heart to see these signs as evidence of God's power, wisdom, and mercy, while those without faith pass by them unmoved. Faith is therefore more than inherited doctrine: it is a lens that turns ordinary observation into reflection, gratitude, and deeper certainty.

translation: And indeed, the Companions of the Thicket (Al-Aykah) were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the people of Al-Aykah, the community to whom the Prophet Shu'ayb was sent, brought destruction on themselves through their own injustice. Their wrongdoing consisted of disbelief in God, rejection of His messenger, and cheating others in trade by giving short measure and weight. God's punishment of them was therefore just rather than arbitrary, and it stands as a warning that societies that persist in corruption and in denying the truth after clear guidance will meet the same fate as earlier nations.

translation: So We took retribution from them; and indeed, both [cities] lie on an open, clear highway.
interpretation: The verse refers to the punishment of the people of Lot (the dwellers of Sodom) and the people of the Wood (Aykah, the people of Shu'ayb). After they rejected their prophets and persisted in wrongdoing, God destroyed them. The ruins of both communities remain along a well-known, plainly visible route that travelers pass, so that the evidence of their fate stands as a clear and lasting lesson. The point is that those who deny the messengers and transgress God's limits face a just recompense, and people of reflection should take warning from these visible remains rather than repeat the same errors.

translation: And certainly the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:80) refers to the people of Thamud, who lived in al-Hijr, a rocky land between the Hijaz and Syria. They rejected their prophet Salih, and because the message of all prophets is one, rejecting one messenger is in effect rejecting all the messengers. The verse stresses that denial of the truth is not merely a rejection of an individual but of the entire chain of divine guidance. It also serves as a warning to the Prophet Muhammad's opponents that stubborn disbelief, despite clear signs such as the she-camel and their strong rock-hewn dwellings, leads to destruction, and as consolation to the Prophet that earlier messengers faced the same rejection.

translation: And We gave them Our signs, yet they remained turning away from them.
interpretation: This verse, which speaks of the people of Thamud (the people of al-Hijr) in Surah al-Hijr, shows that God's guidance came to them clearly: the she-camel and the signs in creation and revelation were put before them as plain evidence. The fault lay not in any lack of proof but in their willful heedlessness. They saw the signs and did not reflect on them, did not draw the lesson, and did not submit to what the signs pointed to. Turning away is thus a choice of the heart and a mark of arrogance, and it is what brings about the downfall that follows. The verse warns that a person can be given every sign and still be misguided if they refuse to attend to it, so the responsibility for rejection rests on the one who turns away.

translation: And they used to carve out houses from the mountains, feeling secure.
interpretation: The verse describes the people of Thamud (Al-Hijr 15:82), who were highly skilled and powerful enough to hew dwellings out of solid rock. They believed these strongholds made them safe from calamity, from enemies, and even from God's punishment. The deeper lesson is that material strength, technical skill, and fortified homes give no true protection when God's decree comes. Their false sense of security led them to heedlessness and to rejecting the message of their prophet Salih. The punishment then struck them despite their mountain fortresses, which shows that real security lies in faith and obedience to God, not in worldly means.

translation: So the Blast seized them at early morning.
interpretation: The verse describes the sudden divine punishment that struck the people of Salih (or, in context of Surah al-Hijr, the dwellers of al-Hijr) at dawn. Though they had carved secure homes out of the mountains and trusted in their strength and possessions, none of it protected them when God's decree came. The mention of the morning shows that the punishment arrived suddenly, at a time when people felt safe and were just beginning their day. The lesson is that worldly power, wealth and fortified dwellings cannot avert God's judgment once it is decreed, and that persistent rejection of the messengers leads to ruin that comes without warning.

translation: So what they used to earn did not avail them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly gains such as wealth, power, status, and the fruits of their labor gave the disbelieving nations no protection when God's punishment came upon them. What people accumulate and rely on in place of faith and righteous action cannot shield them from God's decree, so true security lies in obedience to God and not in material strength.

translation: We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that is between them except with truth. And the Hour is surely coming, so overlook (their faults) with gracious forgiveness.
interpretation: The verse grounds the command to forgive in the purposefulness of creation. Because the universe was made with truth, meaning and justice rather than in vain, wrongdoing will not go unaccounted for, and the Day of Judgment will certainly come to set all things right. Since final justice is guaranteed and belongs to God, the believer need not hasten to avenge himself or answer harm with harm. He is called to 'a beautiful pardon': to forgive the hostility and mockery of opponents without bitterness, reproach or resentment, entrusting their reckoning to God and responding with patience and dignity.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is the All-Creator, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:86) reassures the Prophet Muhammad by affirming that God, who continually creates and is perfectly aware of every detail of His creation, knows exactly the state of those who reject him and will judge between them with full knowledge and justice. Because the Creator is also the All-Knowing, nothing is outside His wisdom or control, so the believer can bear opposition with patience and forgiveness, trusting that the One who fashioned all things also knows how to bring matters to their rightful end.

translation: And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated verses and the Great Qur'an.
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet Muhammad of the immense favor bestowed upon him, so that he is not distracted by the worldly enjoyments granted to the disbelievers. The 'seven oft-repeated' are most commonly understood as Surat al-Fatiha, whose seven verses are recited repeatedly in every unit of prayer. Joined with the 'Great Qur'an', it signals that the guidance and spiritual wealth he has received far surpass any material possession, and that true richness lies in revelation and in knowing and worshipping God. Hence he should not envy others' worldly provisions nor grieve over their denial, but remain content and steadfast in his mission.

translation: Do not stretch your eyes toward what We have given certain categories of them to enjoy, and do not grieve over them, and lower your wing [be gentle] to the believers.
interpretation: God directs the Prophet away from envying the worldly wealth, status, and comforts granted to some of the disbelievers, since such things are a passing enjoyment and a trial, while he has been given the far greater gift of the Qur'an and guidance. He is also told not to be consumed by sorrow over their refusal to believe, because his duty is only to convey the message and guidance rests with God. Instead, he should turn his care and humility toward the believers, treating them with gentleness, mercy, and kindness, as a bird lowers its wing to shelter its young.

translation: And say: Indeed, I am the clear warner.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet Muhammad to declare openly that his role is to warn people plainly of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, as earlier messengers warned their peoples. His task is not to compel belief or to control outcomes but to deliver an unmistakable message. The word 'clear' means the warning is direct and free of ambiguity, leaving those who reject it without excuse. Responsibility for the response then rests with each listener, while the reckoning rests with God.

translation: Just as We sent down [punishment] upon the dividers (al-muqtasimin).
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hijr 15:90) links back to the warning in the previous verse, 'I am the clear warner.' God says that the Prophet's warning is of the same kind as the punishment that befell earlier groups who divided and partitioned God's revelation, accepting parts of it and rejecting others according to their desires. The meaning is that whoever splits up the divine message and treats its truth selectively invites the same fate that came upon those who did so before, so the Quraysh and others should take heed and not oppose the Prophet by dividing the Book or by fragmenting into factions around it.

translation: Those who have broken the Qur'an into parts (accepting some and rejecting others).
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 15:91) condemns those who treat revelation selectively, taking what suits their desires, traditions, or interests and discarding what challenges them. The word 'idin' (parts or fragments) conveys the idea of cutting something into pieces. Faith requires submitting to the Qur'an as a unified whole, so picking and choosing among its teachings, or ridiculing and denying parts of it, is a form of disbelief. It is not true acceptance, and those who do so are warned of accountability for their conduct.

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely question them all.
interpretation: This verse is a solemn oath by God, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, affirming that on the Day of Judgment every person will be held to account, with no one exempt. The questioning is not for God to gain knowledge, since He already knows everything, but to establish proof and justice, so that each person faces what they believed, said, and did. Coming after the mention of those who divided the Scripture into parts, accepting some and rejecting others, it warns that selective faith and manipulation of revelation will not go unexamined. It also reassures the Prophet and the believers that the mockery and rejection they endure are recorded, and that final judgment rests with God alone.

translation: ...about what they used to do.
interpretation: This phrase, which closes a number of verses in the Qur'an (such as 'And they will surely be questioned about what they used to do'), stresses that every person is held accountable for their own deeds. On the Day of Judgment nothing will be overlooked or hidden, because God knows all that people did. Each soul will face the consequences of its own choices, so the believer is urged to act with sincerity and awareness that every action is recorded and will be answered for.

translation: So proclaim openly what you have been commanded, and turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hijr 15:94) commands the Prophet Muhammad to stop concealing the message and to declare it publicly and decisively, as the root meaning of 'fasda'' is to split or cleave something clearly, so the truth is to be made unmistakably plain. The instruction to 'turn away from the polytheists' does not mean abandoning them or ceasing to invite them, but not being deterred by their mockery, hostility, and rejection, and not giving weight to their opposition. It consoles and strengthens the Prophet: he is to carry out his duty with confidence and without fear of people, trusting that God will suffice him against those who ridicule him, as the following verses promise.

translation: Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:95) is God's reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad that he need not fear or be distressed by those who ridicule his message. God Himself takes charge of defending him and dealing with his scoffers, so the Prophet can proclaim the truth openly, as commanded in the preceding verses, without worry about their mockery or harm. The deeper lesson is that whoever stands firm in conveying God's message with sincerity will find God's protection sufficient, and that the mockery of opponents ultimately cannot undermine the truth or those entrusted with it.

translation: Those who set up another god alongside God—soon they will know.
interpretation: The verse warns those who associate partners with God that their false beliefs will be exposed. The phrase 'soon they will know' conveys a certain and approaching reckoning: whether through the clear signs of truth in this life or, at the latest, in the Hereafter, they will come to see that divinity belongs to God alone, that the gods they invented had no power to benefit or protect them, and that associating others with Him was the gravest error whose consequences they will be unable to escape.

translation: We certainly know that your chest tightens at what they say.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:97) consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, by assuring him that God is fully aware of the distress and grief he feels when the disbelievers mock, deny, and insult him and the message he brings. God's knowledge of his inner pain is itself a mercy and a reassurance that his suffering is neither unseen nor unvalued. The verse prepares the way for the remedy given in the following verses: to glorify his Lord with praise, to be among those who prostrate, and to worship God until certainty (death) comes. The lesson is that when people's hostility weighs on the heart, relief is found in turning to God through remembrance, prayer, and steadfast devotion rather than in dwelling on the words of opponents.

translation: So glorify the praises of your Lord and be among those who prostrate themselves.
interpretation: When the Prophet is pained by the ridicule and hostility of those who reject him, the remedy is not retaliation or despair but turning to God. Glorifying God while praising Him affirms that He is free of every defect and worthy of all praise, which steadies the heart against what opponents say. Joining this with prostration points to humble closeness to God: the believer finds relief and strength by submitting in worship, and prostration is the moment of greatest nearness. The verse teaches that constant remembrance and prayer are the believer's shelter and source of patience when facing hardship and mockery.

translation: And worship your Lord until certainty (death) comes to you.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hijr 15:99) commands the Prophet, and every believer after him, to make worship a lifelong duty that does not end at any stage of life. 'Certainty' (al-yaqin) is understood by the majority of commentators as death, because it is the one reality that no one can doubt once it arrives. Worship is therefore not tied to a season, a level of spiritual attainment, or a moment of ease. It must continue steadily until the last breath. The verse comes after the Prophet is told to glorify his Lord with praise and to prostrate, as a remedy for the distress caused by the mockers' ridicule. It teaches that the believer's strength against hostility and hardship lies in constant devotion and perseverance, and that no one is ever released from the duty of servitude to God while alive.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The command of God is coming, so do not seek to hasten it. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse addresses the disbelievers who mockingly challenged the Prophet to bring down the punishment he warned of. It declares that God's decree, whether the judgment on the deniers in this world or the Final Hour, is so certain that it is spoken of as having already arrived, since nothing can prevent it. Impatience is therefore pointless and foolish: its timing belongs to God's wisdom alone, not to human demand or ridicule. The verse closes by affirming God's absolute transcendence above any partner or equal, because polytheism is the root of their false confidence. Those who worship others beside Him have no protector who could avert His command, so the proper response is humility, repentance, and pure monotheism rather than defiance.

translation: He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills among His servants, saying: 'Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me.' (Qur'an 16:2)
interpretation: God sends the angels bearing revelation, which is the 'Spirit' because it gives life to hearts just as the soul gives life to bodies. He sends it by His own command to the prophets He chooses, and not because of anyone's merit, rank or demand. The content of this revelation is the core message of all the prophets: warn people that no one deserves worship except God alone, and call them to take Him as their only protector by fearing Him and obeying Him. The verse shows that prophethood is a divine selection and not something earned, and that the first duty of the messenger is to establish pure monotheism and to awaken God-consciousness (taqwa) in people.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth; exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.
interpretation: The creation of the heavens and the earth is not a game or an accident but is grounded in purpose, wisdom, and justice, which points to a Creator with a deliberate design and to accountability for human beings. Since God alone brought this vast order into being, nothing and no one else can share in His divinity or deserve worship alongside Him. The idols and partners people invent are powerless to create anything, so associating them with God is both false and unreasonable, and He is far above and free of such claims.

translation: He created man from a sperm-drop, and behold, he is an open adversary.
interpretation: The verse points to the contrast between humankind's humble origin and its arrogant conduct. God made man from a mere drop of fluid, which shows both His power and man's dependence on Him. Yet once man is formed and given reason and speech, he turns to open disputation. He argues against his Creator, denies resurrection, and contests the message of the prophets, forgetting that he was created from something so lowly. The verse calls man to humility and gratitude, and to reflect on his beginnings so that he will not rebel against the One who brought him into being.

translation: And the livestock He created for you; in them is warmth and [other] benefits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: After pointing to the creation of the human being, the verse turns to the animals as a sign of God's care for humankind. Their wool, hair, and hides provide warmth and clothing against the cold. They also bring many other benefits, such as milk, transport, and labor, and their meat is food. The verse invites people to see these everyday provisions as deliberate gifts from a Creator who made nature serve human needs, and so to respond with gratitude and with worship of Him alone.

translation: And you have in them beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you take them out to pasture in the morning.
interpretation: The verse points to the aesthetic and dignified dimension of the blessings God has placed in livestock, beyond their usefulness as food, clothing and transport. The sight of herds returning at dusk, full and content, and leaving at dawn to graze, gives their owners honor, standing and a sense of joy and prosperity in the eyes of people. The Qur'an thus affirms that appreciating beauty in God's creation is legitimate and part of His favor, and that such appreciation should lead one to gratitude and awareness of the Provider, not to pride or heedless enjoyment.

translation: And they carry your heavy loads to a land which you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Compassionate and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse points to the livestock (cattle and camels) mentioned just before it as a sign of God's mercy. Without these animals, people could not transport their heavy goods over long distances to far-off lands except through exhausting personal effort. By subjecting animals to human service, God lifted the burden of travel and trade from people and made life easier for them. The closing statement draws the lesson that such provisions are not accidental but flow from God's kindness and mercy toward His servants, which should lead them to gratitude and recognition of His care.

translation: And [He created] horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment; and He creates what you do not know.
interpretation: The verse points to God's favor in creating animals that serve both practical needs and human delight: they carry people and their burdens, and they also give beauty and dignity. It then widens the lesson by saying God continues to create things beyond human knowledge at the time of revelation. This is read as an allusion to future means of transport and other blessings that people had not yet known, so believers should recognize that God's provision is ongoing and greater than what they can perceive, and should respond with gratitude and humility rather than pride in their own knowledge.

translation: And upon God rests the direction of the right path, while some paths deviate. And had He willed, He would have guided you all.
interpretation: God has taken it upon Himself to make the straight path clear through reason, revelation, and the messengers, so that whoever seeks the way to Him can find it. Alongside it lie crooked paths of misguidance and error, which people may choose by their own inclination. Guidance is thus a matter of both clear direction from God and a person's choice to follow it. God could have compelled all of humanity to be guided, but His wisdom was to grant them free will and put them to the test, so that those who choose truth are distinguished from those who turn away.

translation: It is He who sends down water from the sky; from it you have drink, and from it come the plants and trees on which you pasture your animals.
interpretation: The verse points to rain as a sign of God's providence and a proof of His oneness. A single source of water sustains human beings, who drink it, and also makes vegetation grow, which feeds their livestock and so their livelihood. Since everything essential for life depends on this gift, which no idol or created being produces, gratitude and worship belong to God alone. The ordinary, repeated event of rain should lead people to reflect on the Creator behind it.

translation: With it He causes to grow for you crops, olives, date palms, grapes, and from all kinds of fruits. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse points to the water sent down from the sky as the means by which God brings forth the staples and delights of human life, from grain and olives to dates, grapes and every kind of fruit. The same water, falling on the same earth, yields plants that differ in taste, form and benefit. This shows that the growth is not the work of blind nature but of a Creator who is wise, willing and generous. Those who think carefully about this order will recognize God's power, knowledge and mercy, and will be moved to gratitude and to worship Him alone, since the One who revives the dead earth and provides for His creatures deserves to be acknowledged as their only Lord.

translation: And He has subjected to you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; and the stars are subjected by His command. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who use reason.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the regular cycles and motions of the heavens are not accidents or independent forces but ordered creations placed in the service of human life: night brings rest, day brings livelihood, the sun and moon give light, warmth, and the measuring of time, and the stars give guidance. Because they all move precisely under God's command, their order points to a single, wise Creator who deserves gratitude and worship alone. The verse ends by saying that only those who reflect and use their intellect will read these natural phenomena as signs, so understanding creation becomes a path to faith, and failure to see the signs is a failure to use reason.

translation: And whatever He has multiplied for you in the earth of varying colors. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who remember.
interpretation: God draws attention to the rich diversity of created things on earth, such as animals, plants, minerals and fruits, which differ in color, kind and benefit yet all serve human needs. This variety, coming from one source and one earth, points to a single wise Creator who plans and provides with purpose, not by chance. Only those who reflect and take heed grasp the sign, so they respond with gratitude and worship of Him alone, rather than passing over these blessings heedlessly.

translation: And it is He who subjected the sea so that you may eat from it tender fresh meat, and extract from it ornaments which you wear. And you see the ships plowing through it, so that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: The verse presents the sea as a deliberate gift from God, made serviceable to humankind though it is vast, powerful, and unruly by nature. Its provisions are food (fresh seafood), adornment (pearls and coral), and a highway for trade and travel by ships that cut through its waves. The verse treats these benefits as signs of divine care and not as natural coincidence. The stated purpose is gratitude: people should recognize the Giver behind the gifts, seek their livelihood lawfully through His bounty, and respond with thankfulness and worship rather than heedlessness.

translation: And He placed firmly set mountains on the earth so that it would not shake with you, and rivers and pathways, so that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse points to God's deliberate design of the earth as a stable and livable home. The mountains act like anchors that steady the earth's crust and keep it from convulsing beneath human feet. The rivers supply water and life, and the natural paths, such as valleys and passes between mountains, make travel possible. The purpose clause 'so that you may be guided' works on two levels. Physically, people can find their way from place to place. Spiritually, they are meant to reflect on the order and provision around them and be guided to the Creator who arranged it, so that they recognize His power and mercy and respond with gratitude and worship.

translation: And landmarks; and by the star they are guided.
interpretation: God points to His favors in creation: besides mountains and paths, He has set natural landmarks on the earth, such as mountains, hills, and valleys, by which travelers recognize their routes, and He has placed stars in the sky by which people find their direction at night on land and sea. The verse teaches that guidance in the physical journey is a gift from the Creator, and that this should awaken gratitude and recognition of His wisdom and care. Just as He provides signs for finding one's way in travel, He has also provided signs of revelation and reason for finding the way to Him.

translation: Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then take heed?
interpretation: This verse (An-Nahl 16:17) is a rhetorical question that exposes the irrationality of worshipping false deities alongside God. Only God brings things into being, sustains them, and bestows the blessings just mentioned in the surrounding verses, such as the heavens, earth, livestock, sea, and stars. The idols and beings people invoke create nothing; they are themselves created. It is therefore unreasonable to equate the Creator with the created or to give them a share in the worship that is due to the Creator alone. The closing phrase, 'Will you not then take heed?', urges people to reflect and recall what their own nature and reason already affirm, namely that the One who originates and sustains all things alone deserves devotion, and that their reasoning should lead them back to pure monotheism.

translation: And if you were to count the blessings of God, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse points to how vast God's favors are: they are so many, so continuous, and so woven into every breath, sense, and circumstance of life that no one can fully count them, let alone repay them with adequate thanks. Human beings inevitably fall short in gratitude and in fulfilling their duties toward the Giver. The closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, give hope: God does not hold people to a standard of perfect thanks, but pardons their negligence and keeps showering mercy on them. The believer is thus led to humility and constant gratitude, and to repentance for the shortcomings that remain.

translation: And God knows what you conceal and what you make public.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's all-encompassing knowledge: there is no gap between what a person hides in the heart or does in private and what they say or do openly, since both are equally known to Him. This should instill in the believer a constant awareness of God (muraqaba), leading to sincerity in intention and consistency between inner conviction and outward conduct, while also warning against hypocrisy and the false hope that wrongdoing can be hidden from Him.

translation: And those whom they invoke besides God create nothing, while they themselves are created.
interpretation: The verse offers a rational argument against idolatry: whoever is worthy of worship must be able to create and sustain, yet the idols, saints, or any beings people call upon besides God have no power to bring even the smallest thing into existence. They are themselves creatures, made and dependent, so they cannot be partners in divinity. Only the Creator, who is self-sufficient and needs no maker, deserves devotion, supplication, and trust, and turning to dependent beings for help is both illogical and a failure to recognize the true source of all power.

translation: They are dead, not living; and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.
interpretation: The verse describes the false deities that people worship besides God, which are lifeless and incapable of benefiting or harming anyone. The verse stresses their utter powerlessness: they have no life, and they do not even know when they themselves, or their worshippers, will be raised for judgment. Whatever lacks life and knowledge of the Hour cannot be a god, so worship belongs to God alone, who is the Living and the All-Knowing. The verse calls on people to abandon the worship of helpless things and turn to the One who gives life, resurrects, and holds knowledge of the Final Day.

translation: Your God is One God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are in denial, and they are arrogant.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine oneness is the foundation of faith and then diagnoses why some people reject it. Disbelief in the Hereafter is not mainly an intellectual failure but a moral and spiritual one. Those who deny that they will be held accountable remove the check on their conduct, so their hearts come to reject truth as a matter of habit, and arrogance keeps them from submitting to One God who has authority over them. Belief in the Hereafter thus nurtures humility and responsibility, while denying it fosters hardened hearts and pride that refuse to accept the message of tawhid.

translation: Without doubt, God knows what they conceal and what they make public. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse warns that nothing a person hides in the heart or displays openly escapes God's knowledge. Arrogance, which is the refusal to submit to truth and the looking down on others, often lies behind denial of the divine message, so people may conceal pride or hostility while outwardly appearing humble or doubtful. God's complete knowledge of both inner and outer states means that such pride will be accounted for. His not loving the arrogant means He withholds His approval and mercy from them and will hold them to account, so the verse calls people to humility and to honest submission to God in both private and public life.

translation: And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients." (Qur'an 16:24)
interpretation: The verse exposes the stance of those who reject faith when they are asked sincerely about the revelation. They do not answer with what was actually revealed. They dismiss it as 'tales of the ancients', old stories with no divine authority. This is a way of avoiding the truth while appearing to engage with it. Their denial comes from arrogance and an unwillingness to submit to God's guidance, not from any real evidence. It also shows that a heart closed to the Hereafter will belittle even the clearest guidance. The verses that follow warn that such people will carry the full weight of their own sins, and the sins of those they misled.

translation: Let them bear their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Truly, evil is what they bear.
interpretation: The verse explains the consequence of leading others astray, as in the preceding verse where disbelievers dismissed the revelation as 'tales of the ancients.' Those who reject the truth must carry the full weight of their own sins, with nothing lessened. Those who actively misguide others out of ignorance and without evidence also take on a share of the sins of their followers, because they were the cause of that error. This does not reduce the followers' own responsibility, since the verse says 'some of' their burdens. It teaches that influence carries moral accountability: whoever spreads falsehood, or calls others to misguidance, shares in the guilt of those who follow. The closing warning, 'evil is what they bear,' stresses how terrible this load will be on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Those before them also plotted, but God struck their building at its foundations, so the roof fell upon them from above them, and the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 16:26) offers a parable of how God overturns the schemes of those who plot against His message and His messengers. Their plots are likened to a building that they erect for their own security and power. God undermines it at its very foundations, so the structure they relied on for protection becomes the instrument of their destruction, collapsing upon them. The lesson is that the wrongdoers' cunning contains the seeds of its own ruin, and that divine punishment can arrive through unexpected channels and from the very place they thought secure. No amount of planning can shield them from God's decree, so the Prophet's opponents should take warning from earlier nations whose deceit rebounded upon them.

translation: Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, 'Where are My partners concerning whom you used to oppose and contend?' Those who were given knowledge will say, 'Indeed, disgrace this Day and evil are upon the disbelievers.'
interpretation: The verse shows that the disgrace of the deniers is not confined to this world: on the Day of Judgment God will publicly shame them by asking them to produce the false deities they set up beside Him and for whose sake they quarreled with the believers and the prophets. The question is rhetorical, exposing the emptiness of their idols, who cannot answer or help. Then the people of true knowledge, the scholars and believers who understood and upheld the truth, speak out and affirm that the disgrace and punishment fall squarely upon the disbelievers. This is both a vindication of the people of knowledge, whose standing is raised in front of all creation, and a reminder that real knowledge leads to tawhid and to confidence in God's justice, while persistent opposition to the truth ends in humiliation.

translation: Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, then they offer submission, saying: 'We were not doing any evil.' Yes indeed! Surely God is All-Knowing of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse shows that death exposes the reality that worldly denial can no longer conceal. People who persisted in disbelief and wrongdoing, and so wronged their own souls, meet the angels at death and suddenly abandon their defiance. They plead innocence out of fear and an attempt to escape consequences, as they once lied and rationalized their conduct in life. The angels, or God's response through them, reject the claim with 'Yes indeed!', because God's knowledge encompasses every deed, intention, and hidden thing. The lesson is that self-deception and excuses carry no weight before divine knowledge, so a person should honestly confront and correct their conduct while there is still time, rather than discovering the truth only at the moment of death.

translation: So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein forever. Wretched indeed is the abode of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that arrogance, the refusal to submit to truth and to acknowledge God's signs and messengers out of self-regard, is the root cause of damnation. Those who considered themselves too great to bow to revelation are told to enter Hell's gates, each group by its own gate according to its deeds, with no hope of leaving. By calling Hell the 'abode of the arrogant' rather than simply of disbelievers, the verse shows that their punishment mirrors their sin: those who exalted themselves in the world are brought low in the lasting humiliation of the Hereafter.

translation: And it was said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They said, "Goodness." For those who do good in this world there is good, and the home of the Hereafter is better. And excellent indeed is the home of the righteous.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the answer of the God-fearing with that of the deniers, who dismissed revelation as 'tales of the ancients' (verse 24). When asked about the revelation, the righteous give a straightforward, truthful reply: it is goodness, a guidance and mercy that leads to the best in both worlds. The verse teaches that doing good (ihsan) is rewarded even in this life, through a good life, God's help, a good name, and inner peace, yet this worldly reward is only a foretaste, since the abode of the Hereafter is far better and lasting. Piety (taqwa) is thus the qualification for that blessed home, and the verse invites the believer to see revelation as a source of good and to strive for excellence in deeds, with the eternal reward as the ultimate goal.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, beneath which rivers flow; they will have therein whatever they wish. Thus does Allah reward the righteous.
interpretation: The verse shows that the reward of the God-fearing is a complete and lasting fulfillment: the Gardens of Eden are an abode of permanence, not a passing enjoyment, and in them every desire is granted without effort or deprivation. The closing phrase 'Thus does Allah reward the righteous' ties this blessing to taqwa, meaning that conscious awareness of God, expressed in obedience and avoidance of wrongdoing in this life, is what earns this reward. It is not arbitrary, but a fitting recompense from a generous Lord for those who restrained themselves for His sake, so that what they gave up in the world is replaced by unending satisfaction in the next.

translation: Those whom the angels cause to die while they are in a state of goodness and purity, saying: 'Peace be upon you. Enter Paradise for what you used to do.'
interpretation: The verse describes the death of the righteous, whose souls the angels take gently while they are pure in belief, intention and deed, free from polytheism and wrongdoing. Instead of the terror that meets the wrongdoers at death, the angels greet them with peace and give them the glad tidings of Paradise. This shows that entry into Paradise is a reward tied to a life of faith and good works, though it is attained by God's mercy and grace. The believer's moment of death is therefore the beginning of honor and security, and it is the result of a life lived in purity and obedience to God.

translation: Are they waiting for anything but that the angels come to them, or that the command of your Lord comes? Likewise did those before them. And Allah did not wrong them, but they used to wrong themselves.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 16:33) shows that those who persist in denying the truth, despite clear signs, are in effect waiting for the moment when the matter is taken out of their hands: the angels arriving to take their souls or to carry out punishment, or God's decree of judgment descending upon them. Delay is not an exemption, since earlier nations behaved the same way, persisted in rejection and arrogance, and were destroyed once the decree came. The closing clause teaches divine justice: the punishment is not an injustice from God, because He sent messengers, gave warnings and gave people the chance to repent. By choosing disbelief and sin they brought the consequences on themselves, so their ruin is the result of their own wrongdoing and not of any unfairness from their Lord.

translation: So the evil consequences of what they did struck them, and that which they used to mock encompassed them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wrongdoing carries its own recompense: the harm the disbelievers brought upon themselves through their deeds returned to them as punishment. The very warning of God's judgment that they ridiculed and dismissed as an empty threat became a reality that surrounded them on every side, leaving no escape. Scorn for divine warnings does not cancel them; it only leaves a person unprepared when they come to pass.

translation: And those who associated others with God said, "If God had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without His sanction." Thus did those before them act. So is anything incumbent upon the messengers except clear delivery of the message?
interpretation: The polytheists use God's will as an excuse for their idolatry and their invented prohibitions, claiming that since God has not prevented them, He must approve of their practices. The verse rejects this argument as a false pretext, one that earlier nations also used to justify their disbelief. It confuses God's permissive will, by which He allows humans the freedom to choose and be tested, with His approval and command. God's allowing something to happen does not mean He is pleased with it. He has sent messengers with clear guidance to distinguish truth from falsehood, so people are accountable for their choices. The messengers' duty is only to convey the message plainly, not to force belief, so the responsibility for rejecting it rests entirely on those who reject it.

translation: And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid Taghut." Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom misguidance was justified. So travel through the earth and see how was the end of the deniers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that God's call has been the same in every age and community: pure devotion to God alone and rejection of every false power that draws people away from Him, whether idols, tyrants, or the whims that people obey in place of God. Guidance is not forced; after the message is delivered, people divide according to their own response. Those who sincerely seek the truth are granted God's guidance, while those who persistently turn away and reject it have misguidance confirmed upon them as a just consequence of their stubborn choice. Thus no one can claim that a warning never reached them, and the blame for going astray rests with the one who rejects. The closing command invites reflection on history: by observing the ruins and fate of earlier peoples who denied their messengers, one learns that denial of the truth leads to destruction, which serves as a warning and a lesson for the present.

translation: If you are eager for their guidance, [know that] indeed Allah does not guide those whom He leaves to go astray, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whose deep longing to see his people believe could weigh heavily on him. His duty is only to convey the message clearly; guidance itself lies solely with God. Those who persistently reject the truth and choose error after clear proofs have come to them are left in the misguidance they chose, and God does not guide them by compelling their hearts. On the Day of Judgment, no one will be able to help them or protect them from the consequences. The verse teaches that a preacher should strive sincerely but not grieve excessively over those who refuse, since results are in God's hands.

translation: And they swear by God their strongest oaths that God will not resurrect those who die. Yes indeed! It is a promise binding upon Him in truth, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: The verse answers those who deny the resurrection and back their denial with solemn oaths, as if emphasis could make a falsehood true. God refutes them with the emphatic 'Yes indeed!', affirming that resurrection is a true promise He has bound Himself to fulfil. Since God is truthful and all-powerful, bringing the dead back to life is neither impossible nor a breach of His promise. The deniers persist in error because most people lack true knowledge: they judge by the limits of their own experience and ignore God's power and wisdom, which require a day of reckoning where justice is established and the truth about their disputes is made clear.

translation: That He may make clear to them that wherein they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.
interpretation: The verse explains the wisdom behind the resurrection (see 16:38-39): on the Day of Judgment God will remove all doubt about the matters on which people disputed in this world, above all the truth of resurrection, monotheism, and the message of the prophets. On that day the truth will no longer be a matter of opinion but will stand plainly revealed. The deniers, who swore their strongest oaths that God would not raise the dead, will then realize with certainty that their claims were false and that they were lying, when their denial is exposed by what they witness with their own eyes. The verse thus affirms that divine justice requires a day when disagreement is settled conclusively and falsehood is exposed.

translation: Our only word to a thing, when We intend it, is that We say to it, 'Be,' and it is.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute and unhindered power: creation requires no effort, tools, time, or assistance from anyone. God's will alone brings things into existence, so nothing He decides can be delayed or prevented. This is a reminder against doubting His ability to originate life, to resurrect the dead, or to bring about any matter, and it frees Him from any comparison with created beings who must labor and plan to accomplish what they intend.

translation: And those who emigrated for the sake of God after they had been wronged, We will surely settle them in this world in a good place; but the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse promises the believers who left their homes and endured persecution for God's sake that they will not lose by their sacrifice. God will give them a good standing in this life, such as security, honorable dwelling, provision, and respect in the place they migrated to, as happened with the early Muslims who settled in Abyssinia and Medina and later rose to dignity and leadership. Yet this worldly reward is small beside the reward God keeps for them in the Hereafter, which is far greater. The closing phrase 'if only they knew' points to those who stayed behind or doubted, and says that if they understood how great the Hereafter's reward is, they would not hold back from sacrifice and would be eager to follow the emigrants.

translation: Those who are patient and in their Lord place their trust.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 16:42) describes the quality of the believers who migrated and endured persecution for God's sake: their steadfastness is joined with reliance on God. Patience means holding firm to faith and obedience through hardship, harm, and loss, without abandoning their principles. Tawakkul means that, having done what is within their power, they entrust the outcome entirely to God, knowing that He alone controls results. The pairing shows that true resilience is not mere stoic endurance but endurance rooted in conscious dependence on God, which is why such people are promised a good reward in this world and an even greater one in the Hereafter.

translation: And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know.
interpretation: God answers those who denied that a human being could be a messenger. Every prophet before Muhammad was a man chosen from among humankind and inspired by revelation, so his being human is no argument against his prophethood. The disbelievers are told to ask the people of the Reminder, meaning the scholars of the earlier scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel, who know the history of past prophets, if they doubt this. Those scholars will confirm that God sent only men as messengers. The verse also lays down a wider principle: whoever lacks knowledge should refer to those who have it.

translation: [We sent them] with clear proofs and scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder (the Qur'an) so that you may make clear to people what has been sent down to them, and that perhaps they may reflect.
interpretation: This verse teaches that revelation is not meant to be left as a text recited without understanding, and that the Prophet's role includes explaining it through word and example. The Qur'an provides the message, while the Prophet clarifies its meanings, applies its rulings, and shows how its guidance is lived out in practice. This is why his explanation, the Sunnah, is seen as inseparable from the Book. The closing phrase, 'that perhaps they may reflect,' shows that the purpose of the explanation is to awaken thought. People are meant to ponder God's signs, learn from earlier nations who rejected their messengers, and be moved from heedlessness to conscious faith and action.

translation: Do those who plotted evil deeds feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them up, or that the punishment will not come upon them from where they do not perceive?
interpretation: The verse warns that those who scheme against the truth and against believers should not be lulled into false security by their present ease or power. God's punishment does not depend on visible causes or expected channels: it can come through the very ground beneath their feet or from a direction they never suspected. Their plotting is thus self-defeating, since the One they ignore controls every means of seizing them. The verse calls for humility, reflection and repentance, and reminds us that delay in punishment is a respite rather than a pardon.

translation: Or that He may seize them while they are going about in their daily affairs, for they cannot frustrate Him.
interpretation: The verse warns the deniers that God's punishment does not need a special moment or warning. It can overtake them while they are busy traveling, trading, and pursuing their worldly goals, when they feel most secure and capable. Their movement, wealth, and planning give them no escape and no power to defeat God's will. The lesson is that a person should never be heedless or complacent about God's reckoning, because human strength and strategy cannot outpace or prevent His decree, and one should therefore turn to Him in humility and repentance before the seizure comes unexpectedly.

translation: Or that He may seize them gradually, in a state of dread and diminishing. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse (An-Nahl 16:47) shows that God's punishment does not always come as a sudden catastrophe. He may instead take people by degrees, through the steady loss of life, wealth, security, and blessings, so that they feel fear and decline and have time to reflect and turn back before final ruin. Even this gradual seizing is an act of mercy, because it works as a warning and a chance to repent, and God's gentleness in giving respite and calling people back is part of His being Kind and Merciful. Those who ignore evil and arrogantly plot against truth should therefore not take delay or slow decline lightly, and should use it to return to God.

translation: Do they not see everything that God has created, whose shadows incline to the right and to the left, prostrating themselves to God in humility?
interpretation: The verse points to the shadows of created things as evidence of God's sovereignty. As the sun moves through the day, the shadows of mountains, trees, buildings and other objects lengthen and shorten and shift from one side to the other. They do this according to laws God set and cannot escape, so the shadows are described as prostrating, which means they are submitting to His command. The things that cast them are likewise under His control, subject to His decree and unable to resist it. The verse reproaches those who see this constant, orderly submission in the world around them yet refuse to submit to God themselves, although they too are His creatures and no different in their dependence. Reflecting on it should lead a person to humble worship of God alone.

translation: And to God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of moving creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all creation, from the smallest creature on earth to the angels in the heavens, is subject to God's will and acknowledges His sovereignty by submission and prostration, each in a manner fitting its nature. Creatures do this by obeying the natural laws God set for them, and the angels do it through willing worship. The angels, though exalted and close to God, never regard themselves as above worship. This points to the fault of human arrogance: if the angels, with all their honor, do not disdain submission to God, then humans have even less reason to refuse it. The verse invites people to join the harmony of creation by willingly bowing in humility to their Lord.

translation: They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.
interpretation: The verse describes the angels, who combine reverent awe of God with complete obedience. Their fear is not the terror of a slave before a tyrant, but a deep consciousness of God's majesty and absolute sovereignty over them, expressed in the phrase 'from above them,' which signals His supremacy and power. This awareness shows itself in action: they never hesitate or deviate, but carry out every command given to them. True reverence for God is therefore proven by obedience, and the angels serve as a model of how awe of the Almighty should lead to submission and humility in deed, not just feeling. The prostration mark at the end of the verse invites the reader to join them in humbling themselves before God.

translation: And Allah has said: "Do not take two gods. He is only one God, so fear Me alone."
interpretation: The verse commands absolute monotheism: divinity cannot be divided or shared, because the One who created and sustains everything is the only one deserving worship. Since there is no partner who can benefit or harm independently, the proper reverence, awe, and fear of consequences belong to God alone. To fear Him alone frees a person from servility to created things, whether people, powers, or imagined deities, and directs obedience, hope, and accountability toward the single Lord.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is obedience due constantly and forever. Then is it other than God that you fear?
interpretation: The verse argues from God's absolute ownership and sovereignty to the exclusivity of worship. Since everything in creation belongs to Him, and since submission to Him is the permanent, unending way of life (din wasib: obedience that is constant and necessarily owed), it makes no sense to direct reverence, fear, or awe toward anything besides Him. Created beings and powers hold no independent authority, benefit, or harm, so the rhetorical question exposes the irrationality of shirk: how can one who understands that all belongs to God still fear or obey someone other than Him? The believer is called to make God-consciousness (taqwa) wholly God-centered.

translation: And whatever blessing you have is from God. Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out for help.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every favor a person enjoys, whether health, wealth, security or provision, originates from God alone, even if it appears to come through created means. It points to a contradiction in human nature: in hardship, when all supports fail, people instinctively turn to God and plead with Him in earnest, which shows that the recognition of His sole lordship is natural to the human heart. This should lead to gratitude and exclusive worship in times of ease as well, rather than remembering God only in distress and forgetting Him or associating partners with Him once relief comes.

translation: Then, when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate partners with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse exposes the fickleness of human nature: in moments of hardship, such as a storm at sea or severe illness, people turn sincerely to God alone and recognize that only He can rescue them. Yet as soon as He lifts the affliction, some of them quickly revert to ascribing partners to Him, whether by crediting their deliverance to idols, luck, their own skill, or other created things. The verse teaches that the sincere monotheism felt in distress should not be abandoned in times of ease, and that gratitude for relief means remaining devoted to God alone.

translation: So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, then; soon you will know.
interpretation: The verse describes how people, when relieved of hardship, turn to ingratitude and deny the favors God granted them, and it is not a real invitation to indulge. The command 'Enjoy yourselves' is a rhetorical threat: they may enjoy their brief worldly pleasure, but it is fleeting and will end. The phrase 'soon you will know' warns them that they will realize the consequences of their ingratitude and denial, in this life or at the final reckoning, when the truth they ignored becomes undeniable.

translation: And they assign a share of what We have provided them to what they do not know. By God, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.
interpretation: The verse condemns the idolaters for setting aside part of their crops, livestock, and wealth, which God alone provided, for idols and false deities that they know nothing about, since those objects have no power to benefit or harm and no real knowledge or authority behind them. Their devotion rests on baseless superstition rather than on any revelation or evidence. God then swears by Himself that on the Day of Judgment they will be held to account for the lies they invented about Him and for the false worship they built upon those inventions. The lesson is that gratitude and devotion belong to the true Provider alone, and that attributing divine rights or powers to anything else is a fabrication for which every person will answer.

translation: And they attribute daughters to God—glory be to Him—while for themselves they would have what they desire.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 16:57) rebukes the pre-Islamic Arabs who claimed that the angels were God's daughters. It exposes the contradiction in their reasoning. They were ashamed of having daughters themselves and preferred sons, yet they ascribed to God the very offspring they regarded as undesirable. This is both a rejection of the idea that God has any offspring, which is why God is glorified above such a claim, and a condemnation of the unjust, double standard in their attitude toward females. The verse teaches that God is transcendent beyond any need for children, and that people should not assign to the Divine what they themselves find demeaning.

translation: And when one of them is given news of a female child, his face remains darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.
interpretation: The verse exposes the irrational and unjust attitude of pre-Islamic Arab society toward daughters. A man who would attribute daughters to God, and yet regard their birth as a calamity for himself, shows a deep contradiction in his values. His darkened face and silent, choking sorrow reveal that this disdain was rooted in social pride, fear of shame and poverty, and not in any true judgment.
