Humbly offered, even modest, sincere effort is valued by God in a way that human beings often fail to value one another.

translation: To each of these and those We extend from the bounty of your Lord, and the bounty of your Lord is never restricted.
interpretation: God's provision in this worldly life is general and extends to everyone, believer and disbeliever, those who seek the immediate world and those who seek the Hereafter alike. Sustenance, health, and means are not signs of divine approval, since God's giving in this life is not withheld from anyone because of their disbelief or sin. The distinction between people lies in the Hereafter, where the verses that follow show ranks and degrees differing greatly. The verse thus teaches that worldly abundance is not a measure of nearness to God, and it calls on people to direct their striving toward the lasting reward rather than the transient one.

translation: Look how We have favoured some of them over others; and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favouring.
interpretation: The verse points to the visible inequality of provision, rank, and status in this world, which God distributes by His wisdom, and uses it to turn the believer's attention to the Hereafter. If worldly differences in wealth, health, and standing seem significant, the differences in the next life are far greater, since ranks there are determined by faith and righteous deeds rather than by worldly fortune. So a person should not be consumed by competing for transient worldly advantages, but should strive for the lasting degrees of Paradise, where the gap between people is vastly larger and eternal.

translation: Do not set up with God another deity, lest you sit down blameworthy and forsaken.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Isra 17:22) establishes pure monotheism as the foundation of all right conduct. Whoever associates anything with God, whether idols, desires, power, or wealth, places his trust and hope in what cannot truly benefit or protect him. The outcome is a double loss: he is blameworthy, condemned by his own conscience, by reason, and by God, because he has abandoned the truth and turned to falsehood; and he is forsaken, left without help, because the things he relied on have no power to aid him when he needs it most. The word 'sit' suggests helplessness and abandonment, as one who is left behind, unable to rise or act. True dignity and support come only from devoting worship and reliance to God alone.

translation: Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. If one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them even 'uff' (a word of annoyance), and do not scold them, but speak to them with a generous and noble word.
interpretation: The verse places kindness to parents directly after the command to worship God alone, showing that honoring them is among the greatest duties after the duty owed to God. It singles out old age because parents then become weak and dependent, and a child's patience is most tested. Even the smallest sign of irritation, such as a sigh or a sharp tone, is forbidden, and harshness in speech is prohibited. Beyond merely avoiding harm, the believer is required to respond with gracious, respectful, and dignified speech. True gratitude to parents is therefore shown through gentle character and humility, especially when they are most vulnerable.

translation: And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 17:24) teaches that kindness to parents must come from the heart and not be mere outward duty. The image of lowering the wing is drawn from a bird that spreads and lowers its wing over its young to shelter and protect them. In the same way, a grown child should treat aging parents with gentleness, modesty, and patience, never with arrogance or harshness, and should do so out of genuine compassion for their weakness. The prayer for mercy shows that the child's own efforts can never fully repay what parents have given. A person therefore turns to God to give them what they cannot, His mercy, in return for the care and sacrifice they gave in childhood. The prayer also keeps the child humble by reminding them of their own earlier helplessness, and it keeps the bond of gratitude alive even after the parents have died.

translation: Your Lord knows best what is within your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who repeatedly turn back to Him in repentance.
interpretation: This verse follows the command to treat parents with kindness and humility, and it teaches that God knows the true intentions hidden in the heart, not merely outward actions. If a person falls short in dealing with their parents or others by a slip of the tongue or a moment of frustration, but their heart is sincerely righteous and they intend good, God does not hold them to account harshly. For those who err and then return to Him again and again in repentance, He is abundantly forgiving. Thus the verse pairs sincerity of intention with the continual practice of turning back to God, offering hope that sincere repentance wipes away lapses.

translation: And give the relative his due, and the needy, and the traveler, and do not squander your wealth wastefully.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth is a trust carrying obligations, and that the first claim on generosity belongs to those bound to us by kinship, followed by the poor and the stranded wayfarer. These are called 'rights' (haqq), not favors, which means that giving to them is a duty owed rather than a charity that places the giver above the receiver. The command is then balanced by a prohibition on tabdhir, which is spending in the wrong places, in sinful ways, or beyond need without benefit. Real generosity is therefore disciplined: it directs resources to those who deserve them and avoids both stinginess and reckless waste, so that wealth serves justice and compassion instead of vanity or extravagance.

translation: Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.
interpretation: Squandering wealth, whether by spending it on sinful ends or by extravagance beyond need and right measure, is a kind of ingratitude toward God, who gave the wealth as a trust. Those who waste are called 'brothers of the devils' because they imitate Satan's character: he was given honor and ability yet used them in disobedience and rejected the favors of his Lord. In the same way, the wasteful misuse God's blessings and deny their due rights, such as those of relatives, the poor and the traveler, which the preceding verses command. True gratitude means spending with moderation and justice, and using blessings in obedience to the Giver.

translation: And if you must turn away from them [those in need] while seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle, easy word.
interpretation: This verse teaches etiquette in giving and refusing. When the Prophet (and by extension every believer) has nothing to give to relatives, the poor, or travelers who ask for help, and so must turn away from them while hoping for God's provision to arrive, he should not send them away harshly or with contempt. Instead, he should answer kindly, with a soft promise or a good supplication, such as 'May God provide for you' or 'When God gives us, we will give you.' The inability to give does not excuse harshness, since gentle words preserve the dignity of the needy, soothe their hearts, and are themselves a form of charity. The verse also links the believer's conduct to his own hope for God's mercy: one who hopes for mercy from his Lord should show mercy in speech to others, even when he has no material means to help.

translation: And do not let your hand be tied to your neck [in stinginess], nor extend it completely [in extravagance], lest you sit blamed and regretful.
interpretation: The verse commands moderation in spending. Tying the hand to the neck is a figure for miserliness, which withholds what is due to family, the poor and good causes, while stretching the hand out fully stands for wasteful excess that leaves nothing in reserve. A person who falls into either extreme meets consequences: the miser is blamed and shunned by others, and the spendthrift is left empty-handed, regretful, and exhausted, like a traveler whose mount has collapsed beneath him. The believer's wealth is a trust from God, to be spent with balance, generosity and foresight, taking a middle path between hoarding and squandering.

translation: Indeed, your Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, concerning His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.
interpretation: Wealth and scarcity are not signs of a person's worth or of God's favor or displeasure, but outcomes of a wisdom that rests on perfect knowledge of the inner and outer states of every servant. God knows what each person can bear and what will benefit or corrupt them, so He gives abundance to some as a test of gratitude and generosity, and restricts others as a test of patience and trust. Since the verse comes in the context of warnings against miserliness, extravagance, and killing children out of fear of poverty, it teaches that provision is in God's hands, so a believer should neither hoard out of fear nor squander out of pride, but strive lawfully and rely on the One who knows and sees what is best for them.

translation: And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, killing them is ever a great sin.
interpretation: The verse forbids killing children out of anxiety about economic hardship, a practice known in pre-Islamic Arabia. It grounds the prohibition in trust in God as the true Provider: sustenance does not come from parents' own power, so God who provides for the parents provides for their offspring as well. Fear of scarcity can never justify taking an innocent life, and doing so is a grave wrong against the child and against the sanctity of life. By extension, the verse teaches that material worries must never override moral duty, and that believers are to rely on God while striving honestly for their livelihood.

translation: And do not come near unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Isra 17:32) forbids not only the act of zina but everything that leads toward it, since the phrase 'do not come near' extends the prohibition to its causes and pathways, such as unchecked gazing, private mixing between unrelated men and women, and temptations that weaken self-restraint. The Qur'an describes zina as a 'fahisha', an extreme indecency that violates the dignity of the individual, breaks trust, confuses lineage, and wounds families, and as an 'evil path' because it leads to ruin in both worldly relations and the hereafter. The message is that protecting society and the soul requires guarding against the first steps toward sin and channeling desire into the lawful bond of marriage.

translation: And do not kill the soul which Allah has made sacred except by right. And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority, but let him not exceed limits in killing; indeed, he is ever supported.
interpretation: The verse establishes the sanctity of human life: no one may be killed except through a lawful, just cause such as a judicial verdict. When someone is wrongfully killed, his closest kin receive a legal right to seek justice, whether by demanding retribution, accepting blood money, or granting pardon. Yet this right is bounded by justice: the heir must not take revenge beyond the culprit, such as by killing several people for one death, killing an innocent relative of the murderer, or mutilating the body, as was customary in pre-Islamic blood feuds. The closing phrase means the heir is aided by divine support and the legal system, so he has no need to exceed limits, since the law itself secures his right and curbs the cycle of vengeance.

translation: And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best, until he reaches maturity. And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be asked about.
interpretation: God commands guardians to treat an orphan's wealth as a sacred trust: they may not touch it except to protect, invest, and increase it for the orphan's benefit, and they must hand it over once he reaches full maturity and sound judgment. The verse then widens the principle to every pledge, whether made with God or with people, since keeping one's word is a moral duty and each person will be questioned about the promises he made. Guardianship of the orphan is itself a covenant, so honesty with the vulnerable is tied to fidelity in all agreements.

translation: And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an accurate, even balance. That is better and more excellent in outcome.
interpretation: The verse teaches that honesty in trade and dealings is a moral duty, not only a commercial rule. Giving full measure and weighing with a true balance protects the rights of others, builds trust within society, and prevents the injustice that breeds enmity and corruption. God says such fairness is 'better' because it is right in His sight and brings blessing, and 'more excellent in outcome' (ta'wil) because in the end it leads to social harmony, lasting prosperity in this world, and reward in the Hereafter, whereas cheating may bring a brief gain but ends in loss and accountability.

translation: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart—about all those one will be questioned.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of intellectual and moral accountability: a believer must not speak, judge, accuse, or act on conjecture, rumor, or assumption, but only on verified knowledge. The faculties of hearing, sight and the heart (understanding and intention) are trusts from God, and each will bear witness and be questioned about how it was used. Thus one should be careful about what one listens to, what one looks at, and what one believes or concludes, because carelessly spreading unverified claims or passing judgment without proof is a wrong for which a person will answer before God.

translation: And do not walk upon the earth exultantly arrogant. Indeed, you will never tear the earth apart, nor will you reach the mountains in height.
interpretation: The verse teaches humility and warns against pride in one's manner of living and bearing. A person's arrogant strut is irrational given how limited he is: he cannot split the ground beneath his feet by stamping on it, nor can he rival the mountains in stature however much he stretches himself. Since human strength and stature are so small compared with the creation around him, there is no basis for boasting. The proper attitude is modest, grateful, and sober conduct, with awareness of one's dependence on God.

translation: All of that — its evil aspect — is detested in the sight of your Lord.
interpretation: This verse concludes a series of commands and prohibitions in Surah Al-Isra (17:23-38), which include worshipping God alone, honoring parents, giving relatives their due, avoiding extravagance and miserliness, not killing children, not approaching adultery, not taking life unjustly, not consuming orphans' property, keeping covenants, giving fair measure, not following what one has no knowledge of, and not walking on the earth arrogantly. The verse teaches that the prohibited acts among these, the evil ones, are hateful to God, not merely harmful or socially discouraged. Their wrongness rests on divine disapproval, so a believer should avoid them out of awareness of God's displeasure and not just fear of worldly consequences. The wording also implies that the good commands in the passage are loved by God, while the evil deeds, which violate human dignity, justice, and sincere devotion, are abhorrent to Him.

translation: That is part of the wisdom which your Lord has revealed to you. And do not set up another god alongside God, lest you be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and rejected.
interpretation: The moral and social commands given in the preceding verses, such as honoring parents, being just, being generous without extravagance, keeping covenants, and avoiding killing and adultery, are not arbitrary rules but wisdom revealed by God, in harmony with sound reason and human good. The passage that began with a command to worship God alone ends by returning to that foundation: ethical conduct is rooted in tawhid, and without it the rest collapses. Associating anything with God leads to ruin in the Hereafter, where the polytheist is condemned by his own conscience and others (blameworthy) and is driven away from God's mercy in disgrace (rejected). Though addressed to the Prophet, the warning applies to every believer, showing how serious shirk is.

translation: Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself females from among the angels? Indeed, you utter a grave statement.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Arabs who claimed that the angels were daughters of God. It points out the contradiction in their reasoning: they themselves despised having daughters and preferred sons for themselves, yet they ascribed to God the very offspring they held in low regard. Beyond this inconsistency, the verse makes clear that attributing offspring to God at all is a monstrous falsehood, since God is above needing children or having any partner. The angels are honoured servants of God, not His progeny, and to describe them otherwise is to speak a momentous lie that denies God's absolute oneness and transcendence.

translation: And We have certainly diversified [the arguments, parables and warnings] in this Qur'an that they may take heed, but it increases them in nothing except aversion.
interpretation: God has presented the truth in this Qur'an in many forms, through reasoning, parables, stories, promises and warnings, so that people might reflect and remember what their own nature already recognizes about their Creator and their accountability. Yet the verse shows that the same guidance affects hearts differently: those who are arrogant or stubborn in denial respond to every fresh explanation not with openness but with deeper revulsion and flight from the truth. The fault therefore lies not in the clarity or insufficiency of the message, but in the diseased receptivity of those who reject it, for whom increased clarity only hardens their aversion.

translation: Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they claim, then they would surely have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.
interpretation: The verse offers a rational proof of God's oneness. If the idols or deities that the polytheists worship were real gods sharing in divinity, they would be rivals of the Lord of the Throne and would try to overcome Him and take His sovereignty, as rival kings contend for supremacy. Since the universe runs in perfect order without conflict, with no sign of competing wills, it follows that there is only one God, who alone holds absolute authority over all creation. Some commentators add a complementary meaning: even if those beings existed, they would themselves be seeking nearness to the Lord of the Throne through worship and obedience, so they could not be worthy of worship themselves. Either way, the verse refutes the claim of partners with God.

translation: Glorified is He and exalted far above what they say, with a great exaltation.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Isra 17:43) affirms God's absolute transcendence above every false claim made about Him by the polytheists, such as that He has partners, associates, or offspring, or that other deities share in His divinity. The emphatic phrase 'exalted with a great exaltation' stresses that His majesty is not merely higher than these claims but utterly beyond any comparison with them. The lesson is that true worship must be directed to God alone, and that He should be described only in ways that befit His perfection, free of any deficiency or likeness to creation.

translation: The seven heavens and the earth and all who are in them glorify Him. There is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the whole of creation is in a constant state of worship, each part declaring God's perfection and praise in its own mode, whether by speech, by its very existence and order, or by a form of glorification that human beings lack the capacity to perceive. The pointed reminder that people do not grasp this glorification is a rebuke to those who ascribe partners to God or neglect Him: when everything around them is devoted to Him, their heedlessness is the exception. The closing names, Forbearing and Forgiving, show God's mercy toward humanity: despite their negligence and failure to join creation's praise, He does not hasten to punish them, but gives them time and opens the door to repentance and forgiveness.

translation: And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.
interpretation: When the Prophet recites the Qur'an, God places a veil over the hearts and perceptions of those who deny the Hereafter, so that they cannot grasp its guidance or benefit from its light. Their denial of accountability closes their minds to the message, and it is as if an invisible, unseen partition stands between them and the truth. The barrier is 'concealed' because it is not a physical obstruction but a spiritual blindness that they have brought upon themselves through their disbelief and arrogance, and it also shields the Prophet from their harm as he recites.

translation: And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion.
interpretation: The verse describes the spiritual state of those who persistently reject the message: because they stubbornly refuse to listen with sincerity, God leaves them with a kind of veil over their hearts and heaviness in their ears, so that the truth does not penetrate their understanding. This is a consequence of their own arrogance and obstinacy, not a compulsion without cause. Their inner closure shows itself outwardly when the Qur'an calls to the pure worship of God alone, without partners or intermediaries. Because that call overturns their cherished beliefs and customs, they recoil and walk away in disgust, revealing that their rejection stems from attachment to polytheism and pride rather than from any lack of clarity in the message.

translation: We know best how they listen when they listen to you, and when they confer privately, when the wrongdoers say: 'You follow none but a man bewitched.'
interpretation: God tells the Prophet that He knows the real intent behind the listening of the disbelieving leaders of Quraysh. They came to hear the Qur'an not to seek guidance but to find grounds for mockery and accusation, and in their secret counsels they plotted how to turn people away from him. Their charge that he was 'a man bewitched' was a slander meant to discredit his message by suggesting his words came from madness or sorcery rather than revelation. The verse comforts the Prophet by assuring him that nothing of their scheming is hidden from God, and it teaches that outward attendance at the truth is worthless when the heart is closed and hostile.

translation: See how they coin comparisons for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Furqan 25:9) addresses the Prophet about the disbelievers who described him with contradictory labels, such as 'bewitched,' 'poet,' and 'madman,' and who demanded that he be accompanied by an angel or given a treasure. Because these comparisons were made out of stubbornness rather than a search for truth, they lost their way. They invented slanders that contradict one another, so they cannot settle on any consistent argument against the message, and they cannot reach the path of guidance. Falsehood has no stable ground, and whoever rejects the truth out of arrogance ends up wandering in confusion.

translation: And they said, "When we have become bones and fragmented remains, shall we truly be raised up as a new creation?"
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 17:49) records the disbelievers' denial of bodily resurrection, which they dismissed as impossible because they saw it as contradicting the natural order. They assumed that once the body had decayed into bones and dust, it could not be remade. The Qur'anic response in the following verses points out that God, who created them in the first place from nothing, is able to re-create them in any form, even one as hard as stone or iron. Their doubt comes from judging God's power by the limits of human experience and capability, when the resurrection is simply another act of the Creator who originated creation to begin with.

translation: Say: 'Be stones or iron,'
interpretation: The verse challenges those who denied resurrection and doubted that God could raise them after their bodies had turned to bones and dust. They are told that even if they were to become the hardest and most lifeless of materials, such as stone or iron, they would still not escape God's power. The one who created them the first time can restore them to life, no matter what state they are in. Their disbelief rests on the assumption that decay or hardness puts them beyond God's reach, and the verse refutes this by showing that no substance, however resistant, can place a person outside God's power to resurrect and call them to account.

translation: Or some creation that is greater in your minds [to be revived]. Then they will say, 'Who will restore us?' Say, 'The One who originated you the first time.' Then they will shake their heads at you and say, 'When will that be?' Say, 'Perhaps it is near.' (Qur'an 17:51)
interpretation: The verse continues the answer to those who denied resurrection by saying that once they are dead and turned to bones and dust they cannot be raised again. God tells them to imagine becoming anything at all, even the hardest and most unlikely substance, or any creation they consider too great to be brought back to life, and it still would not escape His power. When they ask who will bring them back, the reply is that the One who created them from nothing the first time is able to recreate them, since repeating a creation is no harder than originating it. Their shaking of heads is a gesture of mockery and disbelief, and their question 'When will it be?' is asked in scorn rather than a sincere search for knowledge. The Prophet is told to answer that it may be near. This means the Hour is certain to come, so no one should treat it as far off, because everything that is coming is close, and people should prepare for it rather than mock it.

translation: On the Day when He calls you, and you respond with His praise, and you think that you remained in the world only a little while.
interpretation: The verse describes the resurrection, when God summons all people from their graves with a single call that none can refuse. They will rise obeying Him and acknowledging His praise, since even those who denied Him will recognize that He alone is worthy of praise and that His promise was true. On seeing the vastness of the Hereafter, they will feel that their time in the worldly life, and in the intermediate life of the grave, was very brief, like a short moment. The lesson is that worldly life is fleeting and should not deceive a person into denying the resurrection or neglecting preparation for the Day when everyone must answer God's call.

translation: And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan induces dissension among them. Indeed, Satan is ever a clear enemy to mankind.
interpretation: The verse teaches that believers must govern their speech, choosing the kindest and most truthful words, especially in disagreements with one another and with those who differ from them. Harsh, provocative or careless language is a gateway through which Satan sows discord, turning disagreement into hostility and breaking apart bonds of brotherhood. Since Satan is an open enemy of humanity, he exploits the tongue to stir up enmity, so gentle and righteous speech becomes both an act of worship and a protection against his whispering. By restraining the tongue and responding with what is best, a believer preserves unity, softens hearts, and denies Satan his opportunity.

translation: Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy on you, or if He wills, He will punish you. And We have not sent you, O Muhammad, as a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that final judgment about people's fate belongs to God alone, because He has perfect knowledge of their hearts, intentions, and deeds, while humans see only outward appearances. Believers should therefore avoid declaring with certainty who is destined for mercy or punishment, and should not harshly judge or look down on others, including the disbelievers who taunt them. God's mercy and punishment both operate through His will, which is always joined with wisdom and justice. The Prophet's role is to convey the message and warn, not to compel anyone to believe or to control their destinies; he is not their guarantor or overseer, so guidance and accountability rest with God.

translation: And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth. And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others, and to David We gave the Psalms.
interpretation: God's perfect knowledge of every being in the heavens and the earth means that He alone knows each one's true rank, worth, and capacity, so He alone is the One who assigns distinction. The preference of some prophets over others is therefore not arbitrary or open to human objection, including the objection of the Quraysh who doubted that Muhammad, an orphan and a man of modest means, could be chosen. It rests on God's knowledge and wisdom. The mention of David, who was given the Zabur, illustrates this: he was a king and also a prophet, yet his distinction came from the revelation God gave him and not from worldly power. The verse also hints that Muhammad's own standing, foretold in the Psalms as in other scriptures, is likewise a matter of divine choice and not of human estimation.

translation: Say: Call upon those whom you claim to be gods besides Him; they have no power to remove harm from you, nor to change it.
interpretation: The verse challenges those who worship others besides God by inviting them to test the claim: let them call upon the saints, angels, prophets, or idols they have appointed as intercessors and see whether these can lift a calamity or even shift it from one state to another. They cannot, because all power to relieve distress rests with God alone. Hence supplication and reliance are due to Him only, and the deities taken in His place are shown to be helpless, which exposes the emptiness of associating partners with Him.

translation: Those whom they invoke themselves seek access to their Lord, striving as to which of them may be nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared.
interpretation: The verse refutes those who call upon created beings such as angels, prophets, or righteous people, instead of God. The ones they call upon are themselves servants who seek nearness to God through obedience and good deeds, competing to be closest to Him. They live between hope for His mercy and fear of His punishment, which is the posture of true servitude. Since those being invoked are themselves in need of God, they cannot help or relieve anyone. Worship and supplication belong to God alone, and a sound faith keeps hope and fear in balance, because God's punishment is truly to be dreaded and guarded against.

translation: There is no town but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment. That has been written in the Book, inscribed.
interpretation: This verse expresses a divine law governing human societies: every community is subject to a decreed end. Towns are destroyed or afflicted when corruption, injustice, and rejection of God's guidance spread among them, and their fate follows the moral causes God has set in the world. Nothing is random or outside God's knowledge, since it is all recorded in the Preserved Tablet. The verse therefore warns people not to be deceived by worldly strength, prosperity, or long survival, and urges them to turn to faith and righteousness before such a decree overtakes them.

translation: And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the earlier peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a clear sign, yet they wronged themselves by it. And We do not send the signs except to warn and instill fear.
interpretation: God explains why He does not respond to the Meccans' demands for miracles of their own choosing: earlier nations were given exactly such miraculous signs and still denied them, and the consequence was destruction, as the example of Thamud shows. They were given a plain, visible miracle in the she-camel, yet they rejected it and slaughtered her, and so wronged themselves and brought ruin upon themselves. The point is that miracles demanded as proof do not produce faith in hardened hearts, and denying them after they appear brings swift punishment. God, in His mercy, withholds such signs from this community so that it is not wiped out, since the purpose of signs is to awaken awe and make people fear God's punishment so they turn back to Him, not to satisfy the curiosity or stubbornness of those who refuse to believe.

translation: And [remember] when We said to you, 'Indeed, your Lord encompasses the people.' And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people, and [likewise] the accursed tree in the Qur'an. And We warn them, but it increases them in nothing but great transgression.
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet that His knowledge and power fully surround all people, so no plot of the disbelievers can thwart His message or escape His reckoning. The night journey and ascension, and the mention of the tree of Zaqqum in Hell, were meant as tests that separate sincere believers from deniers. Believers affirmed them with faith, while the stubborn mocked them and asked how a tree could grow in Hellfire. Divine warnings do not soften hardened hearts. Instead they provoke further arrogance and rebellion in those who have chosen to reject the truth, which exposes their true state and makes the proof against them complete.

translation: And [remember] when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate yourselves to Adam,' so they prostrated, except Iblis. He said, 'Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?'
interpretation: The verse shows that Iblis's fall came from arrogance and from judging by outward origin instead of obeying God's command. The angels obeyed at once, but Iblis refused because he thought the substance he was made from was better than Adam's clay. In this reading, the prostration was an act of obedience to God and an acknowledgment of the honor He gave Adam, not worship of Adam. Iblis's question reveals the root of disobedience: putting one's own reasoning, pride, and sense of superiority above divine instruction. The lesson is that true faith means submitting to God's command even when pride or logic makes it seem unwelcome, and that arrogance and racial or material superiority can blind a person to truth.

translation: He said: "Do you see this one whom You have honored above me? If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely bring his descendants under my control, except for a few."
interpretation: In this verse Iblis, after refusing to prostrate to Adam, protests against God's elevation of Adam over him and, out of envy and pride, vows to take revenge on Adam's offspring. The verb 'la-ahtanikanna' draws on the image of putting a bridle or rein on an animal's jaw, so it means that he will lead people by their jaws, steering them wherever he wishes through temptation, desire, and heedlessness. His request for a reprieve until the Day of Resurrection shows that his hostility is directed at humanity, and his exception of 'a few' shows that he knows some people will withstand him. They are the sincere servants of God, whom God protects through faith, remembrance, and reliance on Him. The verse warns human beings that Satan is their declared enemy, and that anyone who follows their whims instead of guidance can be led astray by him.

translation: He said: "Go away! Whoever of them follows you, then indeed Hell will be your recompense, an ample recompense."
interpretation: After Iblis asks for respite and vows to lead Adam's descendants astray, God allows him to try, but warns that this permission is no excuse for anyone. Human beings keep their free will, and anyone who chooses to follow Satan's whispering over God's guidance takes responsibility for that choice. Iblis and his followers will share the same fate, and God's justice will give them a full, complete, and unstinting recompense in Hell. Satan has the power to tempt but not to compel, so each person is accountable for whether they obey him.

translation: And incite whomever you can among them with your voice, and assault them with your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them. But Satan promises them nothing except delusion.
interpretation: The verse is God's permission, as a test and not an approval, for Iblis to try every means of misleading human beings, and it is a warning to humans about how he operates. His 'voice' stands for every call to disobedience, such as music, falsehood, and whispered suggestions. His 'cavalry and infantry' stand for all his helpers among jinn and humans who rally to his cause. 'Sharing in wealth and children' means that he influences how wealth is earned and spent, through usury, theft, and extravagance, and how children are raised or named, through unlawful procreation and being drawn away from God. The promises he makes are of long life, worldly success, and escape from accountability. The verse closes by exposing these promises as pure delusion, since they bring only loss in the Hereafter. The believer is therefore urged to rely on God, who protects His servants from Satan's power, as the following verse says.

translation: Indeed, over My servants you have no authority. And sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to Iblis (Satan) in Surah al-Isra (17:65), declares that he has no power to compel or overpower God's sincere servants. His influence is limited to whispering and tempting, and it takes hold only of those who choose to follow him. Those who turn to God in faith and reliance are protected, because God Himself is their guardian and trustee, who suffices them in managing their affairs and defending them against Satan's schemes. Believers therefore need not fear Satan's plots; they need only place their trust in God, who is enough as their protector.

translation: Your Lord is the One who drives the ships for you through the sea, so that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed, He is ever Merciful to you.
interpretation: The verse points to the ease of sea travel and trade as a sign of God's mercy. The ability of ships to float and move on the water, and of people to use them to seek livelihood, profit, and provision in distant lands, is not a result of human power alone. It comes from God's design of nature and His care for His creatures. His mercy shows in how He subjects the sea to human benefit, so the believer should respond with gratitude and with devotion to Him alone, not to anything else, in ease and in hardship.

translation: And when harm touches you at sea, those whom you invoke vanish from you, except Him alone. But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away. And ever is man ungrateful.
interpretation: In moments of extreme peril, such as a storm at sea when all worldly means of rescue fail, the human heart instinctively returns to its natural disposition (fitra) and calls on God alone, because every false object of devotion becomes useless and is forgotten. This shows that the recognition of God's exclusive power is innate to people. Yet once they are saved and reach safety, they turn away from Him, go back to associating partners with Him or to heedlessness, and forget the favor. The verse ends by describing the human tendency toward ingratitude: people remember God in hardship but neglect Him in ease, so they are rebuked for acknowledging His oneness only when they are desperate.

translation: Do you then feel secure that He will not cause a side of the land to swallow you up, or send upon you a storm of stones, and then you will find for yourselves no protector?
interpretation: The verse warns that God's power is not confined to the sea. Those who, when in danger at sea, call on God alone and then turn away once they are safely on land should not assume that land is a refuge. The One who could drown them can just as easily make the solid ground sink beneath them or hurl stones at them from the sky. Safety comes only by God's will and mercy, not from the place one stands. When His decree comes, no guardian, helper, or intermediary can defend them. The verse calls people to gratitude, sincere devotion to God at all times, and humility about their own security.

translation: Or do you feel secure that He will not send you back into the sea another time, and send upon you a violent, shattering storm of wind, and drown you because of your ingratitude, and then you will find no one to take up your cause against Us in this matter?
interpretation: The verse warns people who call on God alone when danger strikes at sea, then forget Him and turn away once they reach safety on land. It tells them that their safety was never guaranteed by their own power. The One who rescued them at sea can bring them back to the same peril, and this time He can send a destructive gale that drowns them as a consequence of their ingratitude and denial. No protector, intercessor, or avenger could demand justice from God for them or pursue Him over what He has done. The verse calls people to gratitude and humility, and to remember that their security always depends on God's mercy, not on their own strength or on false deities.

translation: We have certainly honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea, and provided for them of the good things, and preferred them over many of those We created with a marked preference.
interpretation: The verse affirms the inherent dignity God has bestowed on human beings as a whole, regardless of their belief or status. This honor shows in their upright form, their faculties of reason, speech and moral choice, and in the means God has provided them: the ability to travel and settle across land and sea, and the wholesome sustenance of the earth. Their being favored over many other creatures is not a license for arrogance but a trust, and it calls for gratitude to God and for treating others with the respect that this God-given dignity demands.

translation: On the Day when We will summon every people with their leader, whoever is given his record in his right hand, those will read their record, and they will not be wronged even a thread's worth.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment each community will be called and gathered under the leader or guide it followed in life, whether a prophet and his scripture or a leader of misguidance, so that every person is bound to the path they chose to follow. Those who are given their record of deeds in the right hand are the people of salvation. They will read it joyfully and clearly, since their record contains their good deeds, and they will be rewarded in full with perfect justice. Not even the smallest amount, like the thin thread in a date stone, will be taken from their reward. The verse teaches that every person is accountable for the guidance they followed, and that God's judgment is absolutely just.

translation: And whoever is blind in this world will be blind in the Hereafter, and even further astray from the path.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 17:72) speaks of spiritual blindness: one who in this life shuts his heart to the signs of God, to the truth, and to guidance, and so fails to see the evidence of his Lord's power and mercy, will find himself in the Hereafter deprived of any guidance or means of finding the way to salvation. The blindness of the heart in this world is the root cause of the loss that follows. Because he refused to use the sight and insight he was given when the opportunity to repent and change was available, his state in the next life is even worse, being utterly lost with no path left to correct his course. The Hereafter is thus the manifestation and consequence of the inner condition one cultivated in this world.

translation: And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you, so that you would invent about Us something other than it; and then they would have taken you as a close friend.
interpretation: This verse shows how strong the pressure was on the Prophet Muhammad from the Quraysh, who tried to lure him away from the revelation by proposing compromises, such as asking him to substitute or modify parts of the Qur'an to suit their wishes. God reveals that had he yielded and attributed to Him words He had not spoken, the disbelievers would have embraced him as a close friend, because worldly favor and alliance with the powerful are the rewards for compromising the truth. The verse teaches that faithfulness to God's message must never be traded for worldly approval or friendship. The Prophet's steadfastness in the face of such temptation shows the integrity of the revelation and the fact that he conveyed it exactly as it was sent, without alteration.

translation: And had We not made you stand firm, you would have almost inclined to them a little.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Isra 17:74) shows that the Prophet's steadfastness against the pressure of the disbelievers came from God's support and not from himself. The Quraysh tried to tempt him into compromising the message, so the verse says that without God's confirmation, even the Prophet, the most protected of people, might have leaned slightly toward them. Yet the wording is careful: 'almost' and 'a little' mean that he did not actually incline to them at all, and that God's protection kept him from it. The lesson is that firmness in faith is a gift from God, that believers should never rely on their own strength, and that they should always ask God to keep their hearts steady, because even a slight compromise on truth can open the door to larger deviation.

translation: In that case, We would have made you taste a double portion in life and a double portion in death, and then you would find no helper against Us.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Isra 17:75) shows how seriously God holds those closest to Him to account. Had the Prophet, peace be upon him, come even slightly close to inclining toward the demands of the disbelievers, which the preceding verses mention, he would have been punished doubly, in this life and at death. The reason is that greater honor, knowledge and nearness to God bring greater responsibility, so a lapse by someone of high standing is judged more severely than the same lapse by an ordinary person. The verse ends by stressing that no one could defend him against God's judgment. This affirms that divine justice does not depend on rank, and that the Prophet's steadfastness came from God's protection and not from any claim to immunity.

translation: And they were about to provoke you to leave the land so as to expel you from it; and then they would not have stayed after you, except for a little while.
interpretation: The verse refers to the pressure the disbelievers of Makkah put on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), scheming to unsettle him and drive him out of his homeland. God warns that had they expelled their Messenger, it would have brought divine punishment upon them, in accordance with His established way (sunnah) with earlier nations who expelled or rejected their messengers: they would have survived only briefly after him before being destroyed. The verse thus consoles the Prophet, assures him that God is in control of events, and warns his opponents that expelling a prophet leads to their own ruin.

translation: [This is Our] established way with the messengers We sent before you, and you will not find any change in Our way.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's way in dealing with nations is constant and does not change. Whenever a people drove out or sought to destroy their messenger, God's consequence followed: the wrongdoers were destroyed and the messenger and the believers were saved. The Prophet Muhammad is reassured that the hostility of Quraysh to him, including their attempt to expel him from Mecca, would meet the same fate as earlier peoples who persecuted their prophets. God's laws of cause and consequence are firm and reliable, and are not altered by anyone's wishes, power or delay, so believers can trust that truth will prevail and injustice will bring its own downfall.

translation: Establish prayer from the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of the dawn. Indeed, the recitation of the dawn is ever witnessed.
interpretation: The verse sets out the rhythm of the daily prayers, tying worship to the movement of the sun so that a believer's whole day is framed by remembrance of God. The 'decline of the sun' marks the beginning of the midday and afternoon prayers, and the 'darkness of the night' marks the sunset and night prayers. The dawn prayer is singled out with a long recitation of the Qur'an, and it is described as 'witnessed' because the angels of the night and the angels of the day gather and attend it together. This gives the dawn prayer special honor and encourages believers to rise for it, since it is the prayer most burdensome to the sleepy and therefore most rewarded. The verse teaches that prayer is not an occasional act but a discipline that anchors time itself around devotion to God.

translation: And during part of the night, pray with it (the Qur'an) as an additional prayer for you; it may be that your Lord will raise you to a station of praise.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet to rise in the latter part of the night for voluntary prayer and recitation of the Qur'an, an act of devotion beyond the obligatory prayers that was specially prescribed for him. The night vigil builds spiritual strength and closeness to God, and its reward is a promised 'praiseworthy station' (maqam mahmud). Most commentators understand this as the great intercession on the Day of Resurrection, when all creation will praise him for interceding on their behalf. The verse teaches that sustained, sincere devotion in private hours of the night is the path to the highest honor with God.

translation: And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter by a sound entrance and to exit by a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority."
interpretation: This verse is a prayer taught to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and through him to every believer, asking God that every beginning and every ending in life be rooted in truth, sincerity, and righteousness. The 'entrance of truth' and 'exit of truth' mean that whatever one enters into, whether a task, a place, or a stage of life, one does so with honesty and in obedience to God, and that one leaves it in the same way, with integrity and with God's approval. Many commentators relate it to the Hijrah, entering Medina and departing Mecca, but its meaning is general. The final request, for a 'supporting authority from Yourself,' is a plea for divine help, clear proof, and strength, so that truth may prevail over falsehood and the believer need not rely on any power other than God.

translation: And say: "Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish."
interpretation: The verse declares that truth, embodied in the revelation and in the monotheism the Prophet brought, has decisively arrived and that falsehood, such as idolatry and every corrupt belief or practice, has been dispelled. Falsehood has no lasting foundation. Its nature is to fade and perish when confronted with truth, however powerful or widespread it may appear for a time. The believer is therefore called to speak with confidence and to trust that truth will ultimately prevail, because falsehood lacks real substance and endurance.

translation: And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers in nothing except loss.
interpretation: The Qur'an works as a cure for the believers' spiritual ailments, such as doubt, hypocrisy, arrogance and heedlessness, and often for bodily ailments too through reciting it with faith. It is a mercy because it guides them to righteousness and brings them closer to God. The effect of the Qur'an depends on the state of the heart receiving it. Those who wrong themselves through disbelief, stubbornness and injustice reject its guidance, so every time its truth is presented to them their denial hardens and their accountability grows. For them it deepens loss, not because the Qur'an is defective, but because they turn away from the healing it offers.

translation: And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself; but when evil touches him, he is despairing.
interpretation: The verse describes a weakness in human nature when it is not guided by faith. In times of ease and blessing, a person becomes heedless and arrogant: he forgets God, turns away from gratitude and obedience, and draws aside as though he has no need of his Lord. When hardship strikes, he loses hope and falls into despair, as if no relief could come, because his trust was in his own means and not in God. The believer is meant to be the opposite: grateful and mindful in prosperity, patient and hopeful in adversity, remaining connected to God in both states.

translation: Say: 'Everyone acts according to his own manner (disposition), but your Lord knows best who is more rightly guided in path.'
interpretation: The verse (Al-Isra 17:84) teaches that each person's deeds flow from his inner nature, character, and intention, so a person's actions reveal what he truly is: the believer acts from faith and sincerity, the disbeliever from his misguidance. The Prophet is told to leave people to their own course and not be distressed by their opposition, because the final judgment of who is truly better guided belongs to God alone, who knows hearts and hidden motives and will requite each according to what he has done.

translation: They ask you about the soul. Say: 'The soul is from the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that the true essence of the soul (al-rūḥ) belongs to the unseen realm that God has kept to Himself; it exists and operates by His command ('Be'), not by any process humans can fully grasp. The Prophet is instructed to answer not with a detailed definition but by redirecting the questioners to God's sovereignty over creation, and to remind them of the limits of human knowledge. However much people learn through reason and science, it remains small compared with God's knowledge, so humility is called for, and there is no need to press into matters whose reality God has not revealed. Belief in the soul's existence and its Divine origin is required, while knowledge of its precise nature is left to God.

translation: And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you; then you would find for yourself no advocate against Us regarding it.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Prophet, and through him every believer, that the Qur'an and the knowledge of revelation are a pure favor from God, not something held by human right or power. God could withdraw it from hearts and from written pages, and no one could defend, restore, or intercede for it against His will. The proper response is humility and gratitude: to hold fast to the revelation, act upon it, and recognize that its preservation depends entirely on God's mercy, as the following verse says, 'except for a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, His favor upon you has been great.'

translation: Except for a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, His favor upon you has been great.
interpretation: The verse (17:87) follows the warning that God could take away the revelation He gave the Prophet, and says it has been preserved only by God's mercy. The Qur'an remains in the Prophet's heart and in the world not through any human power or merit, but as a pure gift from his Lord. The statement that His favor upon him has been great points to the immense blessing of prophethood and revelation, and teaches that all guidance depends on God's mercy, so it should be met with gratitude and humility.

translation: Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to each other assistants and supporters.
interpretation: This verse issues a challenge that establishes the Qur'an's inimitability (i'jaz) and its divine origin. Even if the two rational creations, humans and jinn, pooled all their eloquence, knowledge, and skill and supported one another, they could never produce a book equal to it in its eloquence, its legislation, its unseen knowledge, its guidance, and its coherence. The point is that a text of this kind cannot be the speech of a human being, including the Prophet Muhammad, but must be revelation from God. The challenge remains open for all times as a lasting proof of the Prophet's truthfulness and of the Qur'an's authority.

translation: And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused anything except disbelief.
interpretation: God has presented the truth in the Qur'an in many forms and styles, using parables, stories, reasoning, warnings and glad tidings, so that every type of mind and heart can grasp it and no excuse remains for anyone. Despite this clarity and variety, most people reject it out of stubbornness, arrogance and attachment to their desires, not because of any lack of evidence. The verse shows that disbelief stems from the human will to refuse rather than from insufficient guidance, and it consoles the Prophet that the rejection of the majority does not diminish the truth of the message.

translation: And they said, "We will never believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth." (Qur'an 17:90)
interpretation: The verse shows the stubbornness of the Meccan disbelievers, who tied their faith to miracles of their own choosing instead of reflecting on the clear signs already before them, above all the Qur'an itself. Their demand was not a sincere search for truth but a way of evading it and testing the Prophet. It teaches that guidance does not depend on the number of miracles shown but on a heart open to the truth. The Messenger is only a human servant who conveys the message, and it is God alone who grants signs, according to His wisdom.

translation: Or you have a garden of date palms and grapevines, and you cause rivers to gush forth abundantly within it.
interpretation: This verse is part of the demands made by the disbelieving Quraysh leaders, who told the Prophet Muhammad that they would not believe in him until he produced extraordinary signs. They asked him, as proof of his prophethood, to possess a lush garden of palms and vines with rivers flowing through it. Their demand shows that they judged truth by worldly wealth and material display rather than by revelation, guidance, and moral character. The Qur'an presents this as an example of their stubbornness and misplaced priorities: a messenger's authenticity lies in the message he brings from God, not in owning gardens or performing miracles on demand. The Prophet is instructed in the following verses to answer that he is only a human messenger and that the miracles are in God's hands alone.

translation: Or cause the heaven to fall upon us in pieces, as you have claimed, or bring Allah and the angels before us face to face.
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh, in their obstinacy, demand impossible and mocking signs from the Prophet. They are not seeking guidance but challenging him, as they dare him to bring down divine punishment (the sky collapsing in fragments) or to make God and the angels appear in front of them as guarantors or witnesses. The verse shows that their rejection was rooted in stubbornness rather than lack of evidence, since the Qur'an itself was a sufficient miracle. It also teaches that signs are in God's hands alone, and the Messenger is only a human conveyer of the message, as the following verses affirm, so he cannot produce such wonders at the whim of those who refuse to believe.

translation: Or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the heaven; and we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down upon us a book that we may read. Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human being, a messenger?
interpretation: This verse records the last of the demands the disbelieving Quraysh made of the Prophet Muhammad as conditions for believing: that he possess a house of gold, and that he ascend to heaven and return with a physical book they could read. These demands show that their refusal was stubbornness rather than a sincere search for truth, since even the miracle of ascension would not satisfy them without further proof. The Prophet is told to answer with a declaration of God's glory, 'Subhana Rabbi', which rejects the idea that a human being can command miracles or that God can be dictated to. He then affirms his true station: he is only a human messenger who conveys what God reveals. Miracles come only by God's will and timing, not at the whim of the people being addressed, and the messenger's role is limited to delivering the message, not to producing wonders on demand.

translation: And nothing prevented people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has God sent a human being as a messenger?"
interpretation: The verse (Al-Isra 17:94) explains that the real obstacle to faith for many was not a lack of evidence but arrogance and a mistaken expectation. They considered it unfitting that God's messenger should be an ordinary mortal like themselves, eating, drinking, and walking in the markets, and they imagined that only an angel or a being of a different nature could carry divine revelation. This objection is a pretext that masks their unwillingness to submit to a guide who shares their human condition and whom they cannot claim to be superior to. The Qur'an answers in the following verse that if the earth were inhabited by angels walking in peace, God would have sent an angel as messenger, since a messenger must be of the same kind as those he teaches, so that he can be an example they can understand, imitate, and live up to. Thus prophethood being human is a mercy and a proof of wisdom, not a ground for denial.

translation: Say: If there were on the earth angels walking about in peace and security, We would have sent down to them from the heavens an angel as a messenger.
interpretation: God answers the objection of those who disbelieved because the messenger was a human being like themselves. A messenger must be able to relate to those he is sent to, to speak their language, to live among them, and to be an example they can follow and learn from. Since the earth is inhabited by humans, the fitting messenger is a human from among them. Had its inhabitants been angels, settled and at ease, an angel would have been the appropriate messenger to them. So the verse shows that the Prophet's humanity is not an argument against his message but a sign of divine wisdom and mercy, because guidance is only effective when the guide shares the nature, needs, and experience of those being guided.

translation: Say: Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. Indeed, He is ever All-Aware and All-Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to rest his case with God when the disbelievers reject his message and demand further proofs. God's testimony is enough because He knows the hidden and the apparent in every human being: He knows the sincerity of the Messenger in conveying the truth, and He knows the stubbornness, envy, or arrogance behind the denial of those who reject it. Since nothing is concealed from Him, He will judge between the two parties with perfect justice. The verse thus consoles the believer who is denied, warns the deniers that their inner motives are fully known, and teaches that ultimate vindication comes from God's knowledge and judgment rather than from winning human arguments.

translation: Whomever God guides is the truly guided one; and whomever He leaves to stray, you will never find for them protectors besides Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb, and deaf. Their abode is Hell; every time it subsides, We increase for them its blaze.
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is ultimately in God's hands: only those whom He guides, because they sincerely seek the truth, attain real and lasting guidance, while those who persistently reject it are left to the consequences of their own choice and have no ally who can save them from God's judgment. Their punishment mirrors their worldly state: they ignored the truth, refused to speak it, and refused to hear it, so on the Day of Resurrection they are raised unable to see, speak or hear, humiliated and helpless. Hell, whose flames are renewed whenever they begin to die down, shows that the penalty for arrogant denial is just, intense and continual, and it serves as a warning to turn to God while there is still time.

translation: That is their recompense, because they disbelieved in Our signs and said, "When we have become bones and crumbled dust, shall we really be raised up as a new creation?"
interpretation: The punishment of Hell just described is a fitting, just consequence of two things: their rejection of God's signs, and their arrogant denial of resurrection. They considered it impossible that bodies reduced to bones and dust could be re-created. The verse implies that this denial rests on a failure to reflect on God's power: the One who created them and the heavens and earth from nothing can surely bring them back to life. Their punishment is therefore not arbitrary but a just recompense for deliberately disbelieving the clear signs and dismissing accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them? He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt, yet the wrongdoers refuse everything except disbelief.
interpretation: The verse answers those who denied resurrection by asking how bodies could be raised after turning to bones and dust. It argues from what they can plainly observe: the One who brought into being the vast heavens and earth, which are far greater than humans, can surely recreate human beings. Resurrection is therefore not beyond His power, and the appointed term, the Day of Judgment, is certain and will arrive at its fixed time. Their denial is not due to a lack of evidence or reason, but to stubborn wrongdoing. The wrongdoers reject clear signs out of arrogance and persistence in injustice, so they cling to disbelief despite the evidence in creation.

translation: Say: If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy, you would surely withhold them for fear of spending. And man has ever been miserly.
interpretation: The verse points to a deep flaw in human nature: stinginess and the fear of loss. Even if people owned the limitless stores of God's mercy, which can never run out, they would still hold them back out of a fear of poverty, so that nothing reached others. God by contrast gives without limit and is never diminished by giving. This answers those who demanded that the Prophet produce miracles or provisions on their terms, or who begrudged that God chose a human messenger to receive His mercy and revelation. It also teaches that mercy, provision and guidance belong to God alone and are distributed by His wisdom, and it urges believers to overcome greed and be generous, trusting in God's boundless bounty.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel about when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him: 'Indeed, O Moses, I think you are bewitched.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that clear evidence is not enough to guide a heart that has closed itself to the truth. God sent Moses with unmistakable miracles (such as the staff, the white hand, the flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood, drought and scarcity of crops), yet Pharaoh met them with dismissal and an insult, claiming Moses was under a spell. Rejecters often explain away what they cannot refute by casting doubt on the messenger's sanity instead of examining his message. The command to ask the Children of Israel points to a well-known, widely witnessed history, offering consolation to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and a warning to the Quraysh: their demand for further miracles is futile, since stubborn arrogance, not a lack of proof, is what prevents belief.

translation: He (Moses) said: "You know well that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs; and indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed to destruction." (Qur'an 17:102)
interpretation: Moses answers Pharaoh's accusation that he was bewitched by telling him that the signs he witnessed were not magic or trickery but clear insights sent by God alone. Pharaoh knew in his heart that they were true, yet his arrogance and stubborn denial made him reject them. Because he knowingly resisted clear evidence, Moses warns that he is headed for ruin. The verse teaches that the greatest barrier to faith is often not a lack of evidence but pride and willful refusal to submit to a truth one recognizes, and that such refusal leads to destruction.

translation: So he (Pharaoh) wanted to drive them out of the land, but We drowned him and all those with him.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Isra 17:103) shows that the arrogant plans of tyrants against the believers rebound upon the tyrants themselves. Pharaoh sought to uproot Moses and the Children of Israel and expel them from Egypt, or to scare them off the land, yet God's decree turned his scheme against him. The very expulsion and destruction he intended for the believers became his own fate, as he and his entire army perished in the sea. It teaches that worldly power offers no protection against God's will, and that God ultimately grants safety and inheritance of the land to those who were oppressed, as the following verse says, 'And We said after him to the Children of Israel: Dwell in the land.'

translation: And after him (Pharaoh's destruction) We said to the Children of Israel: 'Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you all together as a mixed crowd.'
interpretation: After God destroyed Pharaoh and his army, He granted the Children of Israel security and settlement in the land from which Pharaoh had sought to expel them. This shows that the earth belongs to God, who gives its inheritance to whom He wills, and that the oppressor's plan to drive out the believers ends in his own ruin. The verse then reminds that this settlement is only temporary: when the promised Day of Resurrection arrives, God will gather everyone, the righteous and the wicked, intermingled in one assembly (lafīfan) for reckoning. No one escapes this gathering, so worldly power and residence on earth should not cause heedlessness of the final judgment.

translation: And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended. And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a bearer of good tidings and a warner.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is wholly free from falsehood in its origin, its transmission and its content. It was sent down with truth, meaning it contains true beliefs, just laws and accurate reports. It also descended with truth, meaning it was preserved on its way from God through the angel Gabriel to the Prophet without any alteration, addition or interference. Since the revelation is true, the Prophet's role is limited and clear: he is not a compeller or one who answers for people's choices. He conveys glad tidings of reward to those who believe and do good, and warns of punishment those who reject and do wrong. The responsibility of accepting or refusing the message then rests with each person.

translation: And [it is] a Qur'an which We have separated [into parts] so that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period, and We have sent it down progressively in stages.
interpretation: God explains the wisdom behind the gradual revelation of the Qur'an over about twenty-three years rather than all at once. Revealing it in portions, in response to events and questions, allowed the Prophet to recite it to people slowly and clearly, giving them time to understand, reflect upon, memorize, and act on each part. This gradual approach strengthened the hearts of the believers, made the guidance easier to absorb and apply step by step, and shows divine mercy and wisdom in teaching people according to their capacity.

translation: Say: Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down upon their chins in prostration.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to declare that God's truth does not depend on anyone's acceptance: the Qur'an's authority and value stand whether the disbelieving Quraysh believe in it or reject it. Their disbelief diminishes nothing of its truth, and the only loss is theirs. As a contrast, the verse points to the people of earlier knowledge, such as sincere scholars among the People of the Book who know the true scriptures and recognize the Qur'an as consistent with the revelation they hold. When they hear it recited, they are overcome with awe and humility and fall to the ground on their faces in prostration. The verse teaches that real knowledge leads to humility and submission before God, and that those who truly know recognize the truth and respond with reverence, while the arrogant remain unmoved.

translation: And they say: Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord was bound to be fulfilled.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Isra 17:108) describes the response of the people of earlier knowledge who recognize the truth of the Qur'an when it is recited to them. Hearing it, they fall in prostration and affirm God's perfection, declaring that He is far above failing to keep His word. Their exclamation shows that the Qur'an confirms what their own scriptures foretold about the coming of a final revelation and messenger, so they acknowledge with humility and gratitude that God's promise has come true. The verse teaches that genuine knowledge leads to humble submission and that sincere believers greet the fulfillment of divine promises with glorification of God, not arrogance.

translation: And they fall down upon their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility.
interpretation: The verse describes the response of those who were given knowledge before the Qur'an came when it is recited to them. Recognizing the truth of the revelation, they prostrate with their faces to the ground, moved to tears. Their weeping is not a momentary emotion but a sign of a heart that is truly alive; hearing God's words does not leave them unchanged but deepens their humility and submission before Him each time they are recited. True knowledge, therefore, is shown by reverence, tears of awe, and growing humility, not by pride or argument.

translation: Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. By whichever name you call upon Him, to Him belong the most beautiful names. And do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent in it, but seek between that a way.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God is one Lord with many beautiful names, so a believer may call on Him by any of them, such as Allah or al-Rahman, without imagining that different names mean different gods. This answers those who objected to the name al-Rahman and shows that every name points to the same perfect, unique Being. The second part teaches moderation in worship: prayer should be neither so loud that it invites mockery and disturbance, nor so silent that the worshipper's heart and those who wish to learn are left unengaged. The believer should take the balanced middle course, with a voice and manner that suit humility, sincerity, and the circumstances, which reflects the balance Islam asks for in all acts of devotion.

translation: And say: All praise is due to God, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in the dominion, and has no protecting ally out of weakness. And magnify Him with a great magnification.
interpretation: The verse closes Surah al-Isra by directing the believer to praise God for His perfect self-sufficiency and to affirm three negations about Him. He has no offspring, because having a child implies need and likeness to creation. He has no partner in His rule, because sovereignty is His alone. He needs no protector or helper, because He is never subject to humiliation or weakness, so any ally would be superfluous. Having established that God is complete and independent, the verse commands the believer to glorify Him in the fullest way, in both heart and speech, by declaring Him greater than any description, any rival, or any need. Faith is thus shown to be pure monotheism joined with gratitude and reverent exaltation.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to God, who has revealed the Book to His servant and has not placed any crookedness in it.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the right response to revelation is gratitude, because the Qur'an is a mercy and a guide for humanity. The Qur'an is free of any crookedness: it contains no contradiction, falsehood, or deviation in its wording, its rulings, or its message. Because it is straight and balanced, whoever follows it is led along a path that is upright and free of confusion, and that path ends in success. The reference to Muhammad as 'His servant' honors him by describing him as a devoted servant of God and the faithful bearer of a message that he did not author.

translation: [He has made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him, and to give good news to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a goodly reward.
