interpretation: The verse describes the Qur'an as upright and free of any crookedness, contradiction, or deviation, which is why it can serve as a sound and balanced guide. Its purpose is twofold: to warn those who reject or disobey of a severe punishment that comes directly from God, and to bring glad tidings to those whose faith is proven by righteous action. Faith alone is not enough; it must be accompanied by good deeds. The reward promised to such believers is 'goodly', meaning it is a beautiful and lasting recompense, namely Paradise. Revelation thus works through both fear and hope, so that people are moved to avoid wrongdoing and strive for righteousness.

translation: They will remain in it forever.
interpretation: This phrase, found in Surah Al-Kahf (18:3), describes the believers who do righteous deeds and receive a good reward from God. It means that the reward promised to them, Paradise, is not temporary or subject to ending: they will dwell in it eternally, never leaving it and never fearing its loss. The emphasis on permanence completes the picture of the reward, since a blessing that could end would carry anxiety, whereas God's gift to the faithful is secure, lasting and free of diminishment, which gives believers reason to persevere in faith and good works in this fleeting world.

translation: And to warn those who say, "God has taken a son."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 18:4) extends the purpose of the revelation beyond warning in general to a specific warning against attributing offspring to God. The Qur'an was sent to caution those who claim God has a son, whether the pre-Islamic Arabs who called the angels daughters of God, or Christians and others who ascribe sonship to Him. Such a claim compromises divine oneness and transcendence, since God is free of need, dependence, and likeness to creation. The verse singles out this belief because it is one of the gravest forms of associating partners with God, and it warns that a claim made without knowledge brings serious consequences in the Hereafter, as the following verses make clear.

translation: They have no knowledge of it, nor did their forefathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak nothing but falsehood.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Kahf 18:5) rejects the claim that God has taken a child, as made by those who attributed offspring to Him. It says the claim rests on no knowledge, neither theirs nor their ancestors', only on inherited imitation and conjecture. It calls the statement monstrous in its gravity, because it compromises God's oneness and transcendence and ascribes to Him what is unworthy of Him. Their words are pure fabrication with no basis in revelation or reason, so a belief about God's nature must rest on sure knowledge and not on tradition, assumption, or the habits of one's forebears.

translation: Perhaps you would consume yourself with grief over their footsteps, in sorrow, if they do not believe in this message.
interpretation: God consoles the Prophet Muhammad, who was deeply pained by his people's rejection of the Qur'an. The verse reminds him that his duty is only to convey the message clearly, not to force faith or to guarantee its acceptance. Guidance lies in God's hands, so he should not destroy himself with sorrow over those who turn away. This teaches that a caller to truth should combine sincere concern for people with trust in God and acceptance of the limits of his responsibility.

translation: Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it, so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.
interpretation: The beauty and bounty of the world, such as its wealth, greenery, pleasures, and people, are not ends in themselves but a test set by God. They are temporary adornments meant to reveal the sincerity and quality of human conduct. The believer is therefore called not to be dazzled or enslaved by worldly allure, but to use it responsibly and strive for the best of deeds, meaning those done sincerely for God and in accordance with His guidance, knowing that all of it will eventually pass away.

translation: And indeed, We will make all that is upon it (the earth) into barren dust.
interpretation: This verse reminds that the adornments of the worldly life, its buildings, gardens, wealth and all that people take pride in, are temporary. God will one day reduce everything on earth to bare, lifeless, dusty ground, with no vegetation or trace of its former splendor. The purpose is to loosen the believer's attachment to the transient world and to direct the heart toward the Hereafter, so that one does not grieve excessively over the disbelief of others or be deceived by the glitter of this life, since everything will return to God and be judged by deeds rather than worldly show.

translation: Or do you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were something wondrous among Our signs?
interpretation: The verse gently corrects any sense that the story of the youths who took refuge in the cave is the most astonishing of God's signs. Their sleeping for centuries and being awakened is indeed remarkable, but it is small compared with God's creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, and the origin of life and death. The One who made all these great wonders can easily preserve a few believers for generations and then raise them up. The verse therefore directs the reader to see the cave story as one sign among many, which affirms God's power, including His power to resurrect the dead, and which shows that He protects those who flee with their faith. It also teaches that true wonder should be directed to the whole of creation and not to a single extraordinary event.

translation: When the youths took refuge in the cave, they said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and prepare for us right guidance in our affair.
interpretation: The verse shows the youths turning to God alone when they had nothing else to rely on. They had left their people and their faith was under threat, so they fled to the cave, and the only provision they asked for was divine mercy and right direction. They asked for mercy 'from Yourself', meaning a special grace that comes directly from God, one that protects, sustains, and shelters them when worldly means are cut off. They also asked God to set their affair on the path of rectitude, so that the outcome of their flight would be guidance and success and not loss or confusion. The lesson is that when believers must withdraw to preserve their faith, they should combine the practical step of seeking refuge with sincere supplication, trusting that God will turn their hardship into mercy and their uncertainty into right guidance.

translation: So We cast a veil over their ears in the cave for a number of years.
interpretation: The verse describes how God caused the youths of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) to fall into a deep, uninterrupted sleep. Striking the ears is a figure of speech: since hearing is the last sense to leave a sleeper, and noise is what usually wakes one, blocking the ears means no sound could rouse them. This shows that their long sleep was a deliberate act of divine protection, sparing them from their persecutors and preserving them in the cave for years that were precisely counted and known to God. It stands as a sign of God's power over sleep, time, and life, and points to His ability to resurrect the dead.

translation: Then We raised them up so that We might know which of the two groups was better able to calculate the length of time they had remained.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Kahf 18:12) teaches that God's awakening of the People of the Cave after their long sleep served to make manifest, in the realm of human knowledge, what was already known to Him. The phrase 'so that We might know' does not imply that God gains new knowledge; it means that the reality becomes evident and established to people through events. The two groups, whether the disputing believers and disbelievers of their era or the youths themselves, who differed on how long they had slept, are shown to be limited in their estimates. Only God knows the true duration. The awakening was thus a sign of His power to resurrect the dead and a lesson that human reckoning is fallible and that certain knowledge belongs to God alone.

translation: We narrate to you their account in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.
interpretation: God introduces the story of the People of the Cave by affirming that His telling of it is true and free of the myths and embellishments found in other accounts. The verse stresses that these were young men, who are often the most inclined to follow the pull of their surroundings, yet they chose faith in their Lord against the prevailing idolatry of their society. Because they took the first step of sincere belief, God rewarded them with more guidance: He strengthened their hearts, gave them steadfastness, and made their path clear. The lesson is that divine guidance grows in whoever sincerely turns to God, and that faith, even when held by a few vulnerable youths, is supported by God's help.

translation: And We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said: 'Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will never call upon any deity besides Him. If we did, we would have certainly spoken an outrageous transgression.'
interpretation: This verse describes how God gave the youths of the Cave steadfastness and fearless resolve at the moment they faced their people and the tyrannical ruler. Their hearts were 'bound', meaning fortified with patience, certainty and courage, so they openly declared their faith in the one Lord who created and sustains the entire universe, rejecting every false god. They recognized that worshipping anything besides God would be a grave deviation from truth and justice, 'shatat', an excess beyond all limits. The verse teaches that when a believer stands firm for tawhid despite pressure, God supports him with inner strength and tranquility, and that true faith is shown through a clear, public affirmation of God's oneness grounded in reasoning that the Creator of the heavens and earth alone deserves worship.

translation: These our people have taken gods besides Him. If only they would bring a clear authority concerning them! Who, then, is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God?
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the youths of the Cave (Surat al-Kahf, 18:15), who stood firm in their faith and distanced themselves from their people's idolatry. They point out that their people's worship of other deities rests on no evidence: no revealed scripture, no rational proof, no clear authority. A claim about the divine, such as that others share in God's divinity and are worthy of worship, is a serious assertion that requires sound proof. Since the idolaters can produce none, their practice is mere fabrication and inherited custom. The rhetorical question at the end shows that attributing partners to God is the gravest wrongdoing, because it is a falsehood invented about the Creator Himself, and no one is more unjust than the one who commits it. The verse teaches that beliefs about God must be grounded in clear proof and not in social pressure or ancestral tradition.

translation: And when you have withdrawn from them and from what they worship besides God, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread over you some of His mercy and will prepare for you ease and comfort in your affair.
interpretation: This verse records the counsel the young believers gave one another after resolving to separate from their idolatrous people in faith and worship. It teaches that when a person cannot preserve his faith among those who reject it, and has broken with falsehood both inwardly and outwardly, he may physically withdraw to safety while placing full trust in God. The promise that God will 'spread His mercy' and 'prepare ease' shows that whoever sacrifices comfort, home, and social ties for the sake of his religion will find God's care exceeding anything he gave up. The cave, an apparently harsh and constricted place, becomes by God's providence a place of shelter, protection, and relief, which shows that true safety lies in reliance on God and not in worldly means.

translation: And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, turning away from them to the left, while they were in a wide space within it. That was among the signs of God. Whoever God guides is the rightly guided, and whoever He leads astray, you will never find for him a guiding protector.
interpretation: The verse shows God's care for the youths of the cave. He arranged the sun's path so that its rays never fell directly on them, protecting their bodies from harm and decay during their long sleep, while they lay in a spacious part of the cave with fresh air. This was not a natural coincidence but a sign of divine power and mercy toward those who took refuge in faith. The closing statement draws the lesson: guidance comes only from God, so whoever He guides through such signs is truly guided, while those who persist in rejecting truth are left to their misguidance and will find no one to lead them to the right path.

translation: And you would think them awake, while they were asleep. And We turned them over to the right and to the left, while their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold. Had you looked upon them, you would surely have turned away from them in flight, and would surely have been filled with awe of them.
interpretation: The verse describes God's preservation of the People of the Cave as a sign of His power over sleep, time, and the bodies of His servants. Their eyes and bodies looked alert, so they seemed awake, yet they were in a deep, miraculous sleep. God Himself turned them from side to side so the earth would not consume their bodies, which shows that their survival through the years was entirely His care and not their own doing. The dog lying at the entrance, still and watchful, adds to the picture of a guarded, sealed place. The awe that would have seized any onlooker was a protective covering from God: it kept people away so that no one would disturb or harm them until the appointed time of their waking. The lesson is that God protects those who flee with their faith to Him, and that He can preserve whom He wills by means beyond human expectation.

translation: And thus We raised them up that they might question one another. One of them said, 'How long have you remained?' They said, 'We have remained a day or part of a day.' They said, 'Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city, and let him see which of its foods is purest, and bring you provision from it. And let him be gracious and courteous, and let him not make anyone aware of you.'
interpretation: Just as God had caused the youths of the cave to sleep for centuries as a sign of His power, He raised them from that sleep, an act that shows resurrection is as easy for Him as sleep and waking. Their waking was meant to lead them to question one another and so to discover the extraordinary length of time that had passed, which would in turn make them a sign for the people of their era. Their answer, 'a day or part of a day,' reflects how the sleeper loses all sense of time. Yet they showed wisdom and humility by referring true knowledge of the duration to God ('Your Lord knows best'), and then turned to practical matters: sending one of them with their old coin to buy wholesome, lawful food. This teaches reliance on God together with taking sensible precautions, seeking pure and good provision, and acting with tact and discretion to avoid exposing themselves to persecution by a society that had been hostile to their faith.

translation: For if they come to know of your whereabouts, they will stone you to death or force you back into their religion, and then you will never succeed.
interpretation: The youths of the Cave, as they sent one of their number to the city, warned him to be discreet, because the townspeople were idolaters who persecuted believers. If their enemies gained the upper hand over them, they would either kill them by the cruel punishment of stoning or compel them by coercion to abandon monotheism and return to the ancestral creed of idolatry. The verse teaches that the worst loss is not physical death but the loss of faith, since reverting to disbelief after guidance means eternal failure and ruin in this world and the next. Success (falāḥ) is thus tied to steadfastness in belief, and it is better to guard one's faith with caution and prudence than to expose it to danger.

translation: And thus We made them [the People of the Cave] discovered, so that people would know that the promise of God is true and that there is no doubt about the Hour, when they were disputing among themselves about their affair. Some said, "Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them." Those who prevailed in their matter said, "We will surely build over them a place of worship."
interpretation: The verse teaches that God caused the sleepers' discovery as a tangible sign of resurrection: just as God preserved them asleep for centuries and then raised them up, He is able to raise all the dead on the Day of Judgment, so His promise is true and the Hour is certain. The discovery ended the people's dispute over resurrection, since the youths' awakening after so long showed it to be possible. The later quarrel over what to do with them shows how people, instead of reflecting on the lesson, turn to erecting monuments and shrines. The believers' statement, 'their Lord knows best about them,' models humility before God's knowledge, while the powerful faction's decision to build a place of worship over them hints at a misguided veneration of the righteous through their graves, which the Qur'an records without approving, directing attention to the lesson of God's power rather than to the physical remains.

translation: They will say, "Three, the fourth of them was their dog," and they will say, "Five, the sixth of them was their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say, "Seven, and the eighth of them was their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few." So do not argue about them except with outward argument, and do not seek a ruling about them from any of them.
interpretation: The verse teaches a principle of religious and intellectual discipline: the exact number of the People of the Cave is not part of the knowledge that benefits guidance, so people's conjectures about it are speculation. The Qur'an characterizes the first two claims as 'guessing at the unseen' (rajman bil-ghayb), while the third is stated without that criticism, hinting that it is probably closest to the truth, yet the final verdict is left to God, who alone knows their count, with only a few granted knowledge of it. The Prophet is therefore told not to engage in prolonged debate on this detail, only to offer a plain, clear answer based on what God has revealed, and not to consult those who speculate, since they have no sound knowledge. The lesson is to focus on the lesson of the story (faith, steadfastness, and God's power to resurrect) rather than on unprofitable details of the unseen.

translation: And never say of anything, 'I will surely do that tomorrow,'
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Kahf 18:23) teaches the believer humility and awareness that all power and knowledge belong to God. A person cannot guarantee any future action because the future lies wholly in God's will, and one's plans may be altered by circumstances beyond one's control. The verse is completed in the next one with the instruction to add 'if God wills' (in sha' Allah), which acknowledges human dependence on God, protects against false promises and arrogance, and keeps the heart attached to God in all intentions and plans. It was revealed in the context of the Prophet's promise to answer the questions of the Quraysh the next day without saying 'if God wills', and the revelation was delayed as a lesson.

translation: Except "if God wills." And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right conduct than this."
interpretation: The verse teaches that human plans are always subject to God's will, so a believer should never speak with certainty about the future without attaching the condition of God's will (saying 'in sha' Allah'). If one forgets to say it, he should say it as soon as he remembers, which restores awareness of his dependence on God. It also teaches humility and hope: the believer asks that God guide him to something better and more rightly directed than his present situation or knowledge, showing that guidance is always open to growth and that success depends on God alone.

translation: And they remained in their cave for three hundred years, and they added nine.
interpretation: The verse tells how long the People of the Cave slept: 300 solar years, which equals about 309 lunar years, so the phrase 'and they added nine' accounts for the difference between the two calendars. The verse shows that God's power extends over time itself, since He preserved the youths and then raised them up. It also teaches that people cannot perceive the true length of events on their own, and that precise knowledge of such matters belongs to God. The following verse says so directly: 'Say, God knows best how long they stayed.' The lesson is to rely on divine revelation rather than conjecture about unseen matters, and to take the story as evidence of resurrection after death.

translation: Say: God knows best how long they remained. His alone is the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and how well He hears! They have no protector besides Him, and He associates no one in His rule.
interpretation: The verse closes the story of the People of the Cave by settling the dispute over how long they slept: the question is referred back to God, because knowledge of such hidden matters belongs to Him alone, so people should not speculate or argue without knowledge. The reason is given in God's possession of the unseen and His perfect perception, since nothing in the heavens or earth escapes His sight or hearing. The verse then draws a lesson in divine sovereignty: creatures have no guardian or helper apart from God, and He shares His authority, whether in creation, command, or legislation, with no partner. Believers are therefore called to humility about what they cannot know, to rely on God alone, and to accept His judgment without ascribing any share of it to others.

translation: And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord. There is no changer of His words, and you will never find besides Him any refuge.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to hold firmly to the Qur'an by reciting it, conveying it, and living by it, whatever pressure he faces from those who ask him to alter or dilute the message. God's words, whether His promises, warnings, or rulings, are final and no one has the power to change or override them. Because His decrees stand, anyone who turns away from His revelation has nowhere else to turn: no other protector or shelter exists apart from Him. The verse thus calls for steadfastness in the revelation and reliance on God alone.

translation: And restrain yourself patiently along with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desire, and whose affair has become excess and neglect.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet, and every believer after him, to bind himself to the company of sincere, humble worshippers who devote themselves to God day and night seeking only His pleasure, regardless of their poverty or low social standing. Such people are the true measure of worth, and their companionship is a source of spiritual benefit. The believer must not turn his gaze from them toward the wealthy and powerful out of attraction to worldly glitter or status. The verse also warns against obeying or taking guidance from those whose hearts are heedless of God because they have chosen to follow their whims; their lives are marked by extravagance, loss of direction, and squandered priorities. Thus, true standing is determined by remembrance of God and sincerity, not by wealth or rank, and one's companions shape one's faith.

translation: And say: 'The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.' Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a fire whose enclosure surrounds them. And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.
interpretation: The verse declares that the truth has come from God in its final and unmistakable form, so the Prophet is told not to bargain over it or dilute it to please the powerful and wealthy who disdained the poor believers. Human beings are free to choose faith or disbelief, and this freedom is the ground of moral accountability. The words 'let him believe... let him disbelieve' are not permission but a stern warning: because the truth is clear, the choice is real and its consequences are real. Those who wrong themselves by rejecting it will be completely hemmed in by a fire, like a tent whose walls leave no escape. Their plea for relief will be answered with a mockery of mercy, water like molten metal that burns the face, showing that what they sought as comfort becomes added torment. The verse thus teaches that truth is not subject to human preference or social status, while each person remains responsible for the path they choose.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - indeed, We will not allow to be lost the reward of any who did well in deed.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Kahf 18:30) gives assurance that faith must be joined with righteous action, and that God guarantees that no sincere, well-performed deed will go unrewarded. 'Ihsan' in action means doing it sincerely for God's sake and in the best manner, in line with His guidance. Divine justice and generosity ensure that those who strive in faith and excellence will receive their full recompense, so the believer need not fear that effort made for God's sake will be wasted, even if people overlook it or the world does not reward it.

translation: For those there will be Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and will wear green garments of fine silk and heavy brocade, reclining therein on adorned couches. How excellent is the reward, and how good a resting place!
interpretation: The verse describes the lasting honor God grants to the believers who did righteous deeds, in contrast to the punishment of the wrongdoers mentioned just before it. The 'Gardens of Eden' are gardens of permanent residence, and the flowing rivers signify abundance and perpetual freshness. Gold bracelets and green silk garments express dignity, royalty and comfort, since in the ancient world these were marks of kings and the honored. Reclining on couches shows complete rest, security and freedom from toil and anxiety. The closing praise, 'How excellent is the reward and how good a resting place,' teaches that what believers receive is a full recompense for their patience and faith in this world, and a place of lasting peace, which should encourage steadfastness in obedience despite worldly hardship.

translation: And present to them an example of two men: to one of them We gave two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and We placed between them cropland.
interpretation: The verse opens the parable of the two men, which God gives to show the believers and the arrogant wealthy how fleeting worldly abundance is and how dangerous it is to be deceived by it. The first man is blessed with a perfectly ordered, fruitful estate: grapevines as the core, date palms as a protective border, and fields of grain in between, so that it provides food, wealth, and beauty in every form. The detail stresses that all this bounty is God's gift ('We made for him'), not the man's own achievement. The lesson is that blessings are a trial of gratitude and humility. Whoever attributes them to himself and forgets the Giver, as the story goes on to show, risks losing them and being brought to account.

translation: Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fail in it at all; and We caused a river to gush forth in the midst of them.
interpretation: The verse portrays the completeness of God's bounty to the man given the two gardens in the parable of Surat al-Kahf: each garden yielded its full harvest without any shortfall or blight, and a river flowing between them guaranteed constant irrigation and lasting fertility. The detail is meant to show how perfect and secure his worldly provision was, so that his later pride and forgetfulness of God, and his false belief that it would never perish, appear all the more blameworthy. It teaches that abundance is a gift from God, not something owed to the owner's own power, and that it can vanish at His command.

translation: And he had abundant fruit (wealth), so he said to his companion while conversing with him: 'I am greater than you in wealth and stronger in numbers (of followers and kin).'
interpretation: This verse, from the parable of the two garden owners in Surat al-Kahf, shows how worldly prosperity can breed arrogance and blind a person to his dependence on God. The owner of the gardens measures worth only by material possessions and social backing, boasting over his believing companion instead of thanking the One who gave him those blessings. His words reveal a heart attached to the temporary things of this life, forgetting that wealth and family are bestowed by God and can be taken away at any moment. The lesson is that true honor lies in faith and righteousness, not in riches or numbers, and that pride in blessings is the first step toward ingratitude and ruin.

translation: And he entered his garden while being unjust to himself, saying: 'I do not think that this will ever perish.'
interpretation: The verse (Al-Kahf 18:35) shows how wealth and success can blind a person to his dependence on God. The owner of the garden is called 'unjust to himself' because his arrogance and heedlessness lead him to treat the transient blessings of this world as permanent and self-secured. By claiming that his garden will never perish, he forgets that all provision is a loan from God that can be taken away at any moment, and he implicitly denies the reality of the Hereafter and God's power over all things. His own soul is wronged because pride and ingratitude cut him off from humility, thankfulness, and preparation for the afterlife, setting him on the path to ruin, as the following verses of the story show.

translation: "And I do not think the Hour will ever come. But even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find something better than this garden as a destination."
interpretation: This is the boast of the arrogant owner of the two gardens in Surat al-Kahf (18:36). Intoxicated by his wealth, he denies the Day of Judgment, then hedges: even if it were real, he assumes his worldly prosperity proves that God favors him and will give him an even better reward in the next life. The verse exposes a false sense of entitlement. It treats worldly success as a sign of divine approval and as a claim on the Hereafter, when in fact faith and righteous deeds, not wealth, determine a person's standing with God. Arrogance and heedlessness lead people to deny accountability or to presume on God's mercy without earning it.

translation: His companion said to him, while conversing with him: 'Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then fashioned you into a man?'
interpretation: The believing man reminds his proud neighbor, who is deluded by his wealth and gardens, that denying God is irrational and ungrateful. The man's own origin is humble, from dust and then a drop of fluid, and it was God alone who shaped him step by step into a complete human being. Whatever wealth or status he now enjoys is therefore a gift from his Creator and not something he earned himself. A being who owes his very existence to God has no ground for arrogance, and denying the Creator, His power to resurrect, and his own dependence on Him is a grave ingratitude.

translation: But as for me, He is God, my Lord, and I associate no one with my Lord.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the two garden owners in Surah al-Kahf (18:38), is the believing man's firm reply to his arrogant companion, who denied the Hereafter and boasted of his wealth. Against that denial the believer affirms pure monotheism: God alone is his Lord, and he gives no partner to Him in worship, in trust, or in the attribution of blessings. The deeper lesson is that faith means tracing every blessing, whether wealth, status, or a flourishing garden, back to God rather than to oneself, and that clinging to worldly possessions as if they were permanent is a hidden form of shirk. The believer's confidence rests in his Lord, not in what he owns.

translation: If only, when you entered your garden, you had said: 'What Allah wills! There is no power except with Allah.' Though you see me less than you in wealth and children,
interpretation: The believing man advises his boastful companion that the proper response to blessings is to attribute them to God rather than to one's own strength or cleverness. Saying 'Mā shā' Allāh, lā quwwata illā billāh' upon seeing one's prosperity acknowledges that every blessing exists only by God's will and that all ability comes from Him. It protects the heart from pride and self-reliance, and it guards against the loss of the blessing. The man's pride in his wealth and offspring, and his contempt for the poorer believer, was the very attitude he should have avoided; true worth lies in faith and gratitude, not in material abundance.

translation: Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and will send upon it a calamity from the heavens, so that it becomes a barren, slippery ground.
interpretation: The believing man in the parable of the two gardens answers his boastful companion with trust in God rather than in wealth. He shows that blessings come from God alone and can be taken away by Him. He expresses hope that God may reward his faith with something better than the garden, whether in this world or the next. He also warns that arrogance and ingratitude can bring sudden ruin, since a single decree from the sky can turn a lush, fruitful orchard into bare, slippery earth where nothing grows and no foot can stand firm. The verse teaches that worldly possessions are fragile and that the believer should rely on God and not be deceived by temporary prosperity.

translation: Or its water will become sunken deep into the earth, so that you will never be able to find it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Kahf 18:41) is part of the believer's warning to the proud owner of the two gardens. He tells him that the very source of his prosperity, the water that sustains his orchards, is not in his control. God could cause it to sink deep underground beyond reach, and no human effort or skill could retrieve it. The lesson is that worldly wealth depends entirely on God's grace and can vanish in an instant, so a person should not be arrogant about possessions or trust in them, but should be grateful and humble and recognize that all provision comes from God alone.

translation: And his fruits were encompassed by ruin, and he began to wring his hands over what he had spent on it, while it lay fallen upon its trellises, and he said, 'Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord.'
interpretation: The verse shows the moment a person's illusion of self-sufficiency collapses. The owner of the garden had trusted his wealth and assumed it would last forever, forgetting that God gave it and can take it away. When the garden is destroyed, he wrings his hands in grief and regret over everything he invested, and only then does he see that he had effectively made his wealth and his own power partners with God, trusting them instead of the One who controls all things. His wish that he had not associated anyone with his Lord is a late repentance. It teaches that worldly possessions are fragile and temporary, that reliance belongs to God alone, and that a person should recognize this and acknowledge God's sovereignty while blessings remain, not wait until loss makes the lesson plain.

translation: And he had no group to help him other than God, nor was he able to defend himself.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the owner of the two gardens in Surat al-Kahf (18:43), teaches that when God's decree of destruction comes upon a person who has been arrogant about wealth and status, nothing in creation can avert it. The wealth, children, and followers he boasted of could not protect him, and he himself had no power to save his property or himself. True support and victory belong only to God, so a person should rely on Him rather than on worldly means, and should be humble and grateful instead of proud of what he possesses.

translation: There, protection and authority belong to God, the Truth. He is best in rewarding and best in outcome.
interpretation: When worldly power, wealth and human allies prove unable to save anyone from loss, as in the parable of the two gardens, it becomes clear that true guardianship and sovereignty belong to God alone. Whoever relies on Him and obeys Him finds that He gives the best reward for faith and good deeds, and that the end of the path He guides to is better than any outcome that comes from trusting in something other than Him. The verse teaches that dependence on God is the only reliable foundation, in this life and the next.

translation: And present to them the parable of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingle with it, then it becomes dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is ever Able to do all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly life is fleeting and constantly changing. Like rain that revives the earth, the plants grow green and flourish, and then they wither, crumble into chaff, and are blown away by the wind, so too worldly life with its youth, strength, wealth, status and pleasures begins with freshness and beauty but swiftly ends in decay and disappearance. A person should therefore not be deceived by the world or set their heart on it as a final goal, nor measure worth by wealth and prestige, as the disbelieving elite did when they looked down on the poor believers. Instead, one should invest in what endures, namely righteous deeds, which the following verses call the lasting good. The closing statement that Allah has power over all things reminds us that the same Power that brings forth growth and life and then ends it also governs human fortunes, raising and bringing down, giving and taking away, and will bring all to account.

translation: Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. But the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.
interpretation: Wealth and offspring give worldly life its beauty and its appeal, but they are temporary, and people often place their hopes and pride in them. The verse redirects the believer toward what lasts: righteous deeds such as prayer, remembrance of God, charity, and good character. These carry a greater reward from God and are a surer foundation for hope, because their benefit continues into the Hereafter when wealth and children can no longer help. The believer should enjoy worldly blessings without being deceived by them, and should invest primarily in deeds that endure.

translation: And on the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare, and We gather them all together, leaving none of them behind.
interpretation: The verse portrays the upheaval of the Day of Resurrection: the mountains, symbols of firmness and permanence in this world, are uprooted and moved, and the earth is flattened and stripped of buildings, trees and anything that concealed it, so that nothing hides on it. On that open, exposed plain all human beings from every era are gathered for reckoning, and not one is omitted or forgotten. The meaning is a reminder that worldly power, status and apparent stability are transient, that no one can escape or hide from God's judgment, and that people should therefore prepare for the meeting with their Lord instead of being deceived by the fleeting adornments of this life, as the surrounding verses of Surat al-Kahf emphasize.

translation: And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: 'You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would never appoint for you a meeting.'
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection all people will be brought before God in ordered ranks, stripped of the worldly possessions, status, and followers they relied on, as bare and helpless as when they were first created. They will be told that the return they denied has come true: in their arrogance they had insisted that no appointed time of reckoning would ever arrive, and so they lived heedlessly. The verse reminds the listener that every person will stand alone before God, and that only what he sent ahead of faith and deeds will matter, not wealth or power.

translation: And the Book will be placed, and you will see the guilty fearful of what is in it, and they will say, 'Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out nothing, small or great, but has enumerated it?' And they will find what they did present before them. And your Lord wrongs no one.
interpretation: This verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when every person's record of deeds is laid open and the wrongdoers are overcome with dread as they see their entire lives documented with perfect precision, including even the smallest acts they had dismissed as insignificant. Their cry of woe expresses the shock of realizing that nothing was forgotten or overlooked, and that no excuse or denial can stand against such complete evidence. The statement that they find their deeds 'present' means that their own actions confront them as an undeniable reality, so the reckoning is based on what they themselves did rather than on any outside accusation. The closing affirmation that God wrongs no one underscores His perfect justice: no one is punished for what they did not do, no good is lost, and no punishment exceeds what is deserved. The verse thus calls the believer to self-accountability now, taking seriously both minor and major deeds before the record is opened.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, and he departed from the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse reminds humanity that Iblis's enmity is rooted in an act of arrogant disobedience, not in any lack of knowledge or ability to obey. Because he was of the jinn, made from fire, and not an angel, he had free will and chose to defy God's command, which shows that his rebellion was a deliberate moral choice. The verse then draws a practical lesson: since Iblis and his progeny have been openly hostile to Adam's descendants since that moment, it is irrational and unjust to make them protectors or guides, whether by following their whispers, obeying their temptations, or devoting oneself to what they promote, in place of God, who created, honored, and sustains humankind. Choosing the enemy as a patron over the Creator is a terrible bargain, and those who do so wrong themselves by trading guidance and mercy for deception and ruin.

translation: I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of their own selves, and I would never take those who lead others astray as helpers.
interpretation: God declares that Iblis and his offspring, whom some people take as protectors instead of Him, had no share in creation and were not consulted in it. They were not present when the heavens and earth were made, nor even at the creation of themselves, so they have no knowledge of the unseen and no authority over it. God has no need of helpers, and least of all would He rely on those who lead people into misguidance. The verse therefore refutes the idea that any being besides God deserves obedience or worship, since only the Creator who acts alone has the right to be followed.

translation: And [mention] the Day He will say, "Call upon My 'partners' whom you claimed," and they will call them, but they will not respond to them; and We will place between them a place of destruction.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, God will expose the emptiness of polytheism by challenging those who worshipped others besides Him to summon the false deities they imagined to be His partners, whether idols, angels, jinn, or human beings. Those objects of worship will be unable to answer or help, which proves they never had any power to benefit or protect. God will then set between the worshippers and the worshipped a barrier of ruin (mawbiq), commonly understood as a valley or abyss of Hell, so that they are separated and no bond or intercession remains between them. The verse teaches that reliance on anything other than God is futile and that every false attachment will be severed at the moment when it is needed most.

translation: And the criminals will see the Fire and will realize that they are about to fall into it, and they will find no way to escape from it.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, those who persisted in disbelief and wrongdoing will see Hell before being cast into it, and their certainty that they will fall into it will precede the actual entry, so they suffer fear and anguish in advance. The verse stresses that there will be no refuge, escape, or turning away from the consequences of their deeds. Whatever worldly means, allies, or excuses they once relied on will be useless, and this warns people to take heed and correct their course while there is still time in this life.

translation: And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for mankind every kind of example, but man has ever been, more than anything, argumentative.
interpretation: God explains that the Qur'an presents its guidance in many forms, using varied parables, arguments, stories, and warnings so that every type of mind and heart can grasp the truth. Despite this clarity, human beings are inclined to dispute and quarrel, not because evidence is lacking but because of pride, stubbornness, and the desire to defend their own positions. The verse teaches that rejection of the truth usually stems from obstinacy rather than any lack of proof, and it calls people to humility and sincere openness to the guidance rather than contentious disputation.

translation: And what prevented people from believing when the guidance came to them, and from seeking forgiveness of their Lord, except that the way of the earlier peoples should befall them, or that the punishment should come upon them face to face?
interpretation: The verse points out that nothing real obstructs people from faith and repentance once clear guidance has reached them; no lack of evidence or excuse stands in their way. Their refusal comes from stubbornness and arrogance, so they behave as though they are waiting for the fate that overtook earlier nations who denied their messengers, namely destruction according to God's established practice, or for the punishment to appear openly before their eyes. In other words, those who persist in rejecting the truth, despite guidance and the open door of seeking forgiveness, are in effect inviting the same consequences that befell past deniers. The verse is a warning and a call to respond to guidance and repent before it is too late, since divine punishment, once it comes, leaves no room for belief to benefit them.

translation: We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and as warners. But those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood in order to refute the truth thereby, and they take My signs and the warnings given to them as a mockery.
interpretation: The verse defines the messengers' role as limited to conveying God's message: they promise reward to the believers and warn of consequences to the rejecters. They are not sent to force belief or to produce miracles on demand. Because the message is clear, those who reject it cannot answer it with sound arguments, so they resort to false arguments, twisting words, raising baseless objections, and demanding impossible signs, hoping to shake the truth and make it look weak. Their deeper problem is attitude: they treat God's revelations and warnings as something to ridicule rather than reflect on. This mockery shows arrogance and a refusal to take the matter seriously, and it makes them liable to the very punishment they were warned about. The verse also reassures believers that falsehood, however loudly argued, cannot overcome the truth, and that the Prophet's task is only to deliver the message and leave the outcome to God.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have forwarded? Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if you invite them to guidance, they will never be guided then, ever.
interpretation: The verse says that the worst wrongdoing is to be given clear reminders from God and deliberately reject them while ignoring the consequences of one's own deeds. The 'coverings' and 'deafness' are the result of persistent, willful turning away: when a person repeatedly refuses the truth out of arrogance and heedlessness, God lets that refusal harden into a settled spiritual condition in which the heart can no longer grasp the message and the ears no longer receive it. This is a just consequence of their own choice, not coercion. Their inability to be guided is therefore the outcome of their own rejection, and it consoles the Prophet that his inability to convert such people is not a failure of his invitation, since guidance requires an openness that they have closed off themselves.

translation: And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy. If He were to hold them to account for what they have earned, He would have hastened the punishment for them. But they have an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge besides Him.
interpretation: The verse points to God's forbearance as an expression of His mercy: the delay of punishment for wrongdoers is not a sign of weakness, neglect, or approval of their disbelief, but a window of grace in which they may repent and be forgiven. Divine justice is certain, though, because every sinner has a fixed appointment, whose time God has decreed, and when it arrives there will be no escape, no shelter, and no one to turn to except Him. The believer should therefore neither be deceived by apparent impunity nor despair at the success of wrongdoers, but should hasten to repentance while the respite lasts.

translation: And those towns—We destroyed their people when they wronged, and We appointed a set time for their destruction.
interpretation: God's destruction of earlier communities was neither arbitrary nor hasty: it came only after they persisted in wrongdoing, namely disbelief, rejecting the messengers, and oppression. Even then, He fixed a determined time for their ruin and did not bring it until that time arrived. The verse warns the Quraysh and every later people that delay in punishment is not a sign of impunity. It is a respite and a warning, and persistent injustice leads to a ruin that comes at its appointed hour and cannot be avoided.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his young servant, "I will not cease traveling until I reach the junction of the two seas, even if I must go on for a long period of years."
interpretation: The verse shows the determination and perseverance required in the pursuit of knowledge. Moses, though a great prophet, sets out on a demanding journey to learn from a servant of God who possesses knowledge he does not, and he binds himself to persist without turning back until he reaches the appointed place, however long it takes. It teaches humility before knowledge, the willingness to travel and endure hardship to seek it, and the importance of firm resolve, expressed in his vow, in fulfilling a noble purpose.

translation: But when they reached the junction between the two seas, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, slipping away freely.
interpretation: The verse describes Moses and his young companion reaching the appointed meeting point with the servant of God (al-Khidr), the place where the sign was to appear. The fish they carried as provisions came back to life and slid away into the sea, leaving a trail like a tunnel. Their forgetting was not mere negligence but part of divine arrangement: the very sign that marked the destination slipped past them unnoticed, so that the journey would extend and its lessons be deepened. It teaches that God's decree unfolds through ordinary lapses, that seekers of knowledge must remain attentive to signs, and that human forgetfulness and effort operate within a wisdom that guides one to what is intended.

translation: So when they had passed beyond that place, he said to his servant, 'Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours.'
interpretation: This verse shows that Moses (peace be upon him) felt no weariness while he was traveling toward the place where he was to meet al-Khidr, but the fatigue and hunger only came after he had passed the appointed meeting point at the junction of the two seas. The tiredness he suddenly felt was a subtle sign that he had overshot the destination God had specified, which prompted the servant's recollection of the forgotten fish. It teaches that when a person goes beyond the path or limit God has set, he feels the hardship and strain, whereas while he is on the course ordained for him, God eases the effort. It also shows the humanity of a prophet, who experiences hunger and weariness and seeks food, and the legitimacy of taking the means of sustenance on a journey while seeking knowledge.

translation: He said, "Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed, I forgot the fish—and none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a amazing manner."
interpretation: The servant of Moses (Yusha' ibn Nun) confesses that he failed to tell Moses about the fish when they rested by the rock, which was the very sign marking the place where they were to meet the knowledgeable servant of God. He attributes his forgetfulness to Satan's distraction, teaching that Satan can cause people to neglect what matters most, even in the midst of a sacred journey, and that one should be honest in acknowledging one's lapses. The living fish leaping into the sea and making its path like a tunnel was a miraculous sign of God's power, showing that the journey's goal had been reached and that divine signs may occur quietly while a person's attention is elsewhere. The verse also reminds the reader that missing the signs of guidance often results from heedlessness, and that one must retrace one's steps to recover what was lost.

translation: He said: "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.
interpretation: Moses recognizes that the loss of the fish at the rock was the sign he had been promised, marking the place where he would meet the servant of God endowed with special knowledge. His statement "that is what we were seeking" shows that what looked like a mishap, forgetting the fish, was part of the divine plan guiding him to his goal. By retracing their steps carefully, the two travelers teach that the seeker of knowledge must be attentive to the signs of God, turn back from a wrong course when he realizes it, and pursue his aim with patience and persistence.

translation: Then they found one of Our servants, to whom We had granted mercy from Us and whom We had taught knowledge from Our own presence.
interpretation: The verse indicates that true knowledge and mercy are gifts that come from God, not just from human effort or study. The servant is described as 'one of Our servants', which honors him through his servitude to God and shows that real standing lies in devotion. His mercy and his 'knowledge from Our presence' (ladunnī knowledge) point to a special, direct divine instruction that goes beyond ordinary learning and reveals hidden wisdom behind events. It teaches humility: even a great prophet like Moses must seek out and learn from someone God has granted a different kind of understanding, and that human knowledge, however vast, remains limited before God's knowledge.

translation: Moses said to him: 'May I follow you on the condition that you teach me something of the right guidance you have been taught?'
interpretation: In this verse (Surah al-Kahf 18:66) Moses, despite being a mighty prophet and bearer of revelation, approaches the servant of God (traditionally identified as al-Khidr) with humility and courtesy, asking permission before following him and framing his request as a petition for learning rather than a demand. The verse teaches that seeking knowledge requires modesty, that no one, however elevated, has comprehended all knowledge, and that a student should honor the teacher and ask leave to accompany him. The word 'rushd' (right guidance) shows that the knowledge Moses seeks is not mere information but wisdom that leads to sound judgment and right action, and that God distributes different portions of knowledge to different servants.

translation: He said: Indeed, you will never be able to have patience with me.
interpretation: In this verse from Surat al-Kahf (18:67), the righteous servant of God, known in tradition as al-Khidr, tells Moses that he will not be able to bear accompanying him. The reason is that al-Khidr acts on knowledge given to him directly by God, and his actions will appear wrong or senseless on the surface because their hidden wisdom is concealed from Moses. Moses judges by outward appearances and the law he knows, so he will not be able to hold back from objecting to what he cannot understand. The verse teaches that patience depends on understanding, and that human beings, even prophets, have limited knowledge, so they should be humble before divine wisdom and recognize that events which seem harmful or unjust may carry hidden purposes known only to God.

translation: And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?
interpretation: In Surat al-Kahf (18:68), al-Khidr tells Moses why he will not be able to remain patient in his company. Patience depends on understanding. When a person sees events whose wisdom and purpose are hidden from him, he finds it hard to accept them calmly, especially when they appear outwardly wrong or harmful. The verse teaches that human knowledge is limited and that many events which seem unjust or senseless have hidden wisdom known only to God and those He teaches. The believer should therefore show humility and trust in divine wisdom, and should not judge by appearances alone. It also shows the need for patience and good manners in seeking knowledge, because a student who rushes to object before the whole picture is revealed will not benefit from his teacher.

translation: He (Moses) said: "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Kahf shows the proper manner of a seeker of knowledge toward a teacher. Moses, though a great prophet, humbly asks to accompany al-Khidr and promises patience and obedience. He ties his promise to God's will with "if God wills," acknowledging that he cannot guarantee his own steadfastness without divine help, which teaches that a believer should attribute every future resolve to God's will. The verse also shows that learning requires humility, patience, and submission to the guide, even when the teacher's actions seem puzzling at first. The story later shows how hard it is to keep this patience when judging only by outward appearances, which reminds us that human knowledge is limited and God's wisdom often lies beyond what we can see.

translation: He said: 'If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.'
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Kahf (18:70) shows that learning from a teacher requires patience, trust and good manners. Al-Khidr sets the condition that Moses must not question his actions until he chooses to explain them, because the wisdom behind events is not always visible at first. The lesson is that a student should not judge by appearances or rush to object before the full picture is revealed, and that some knowledge is only understood in time. It also reflects the limits of human perspective, since God's decrees often hold hidden wisdom that unfolds later.

translation: So they set out, until when they had embarked on the ship, he made a hole in it. Moses said, 'Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing.'
interpretation: In the journey of Moses with the servant of God (traditionally identified as al-Khidr), Moses judges only by outward appearances and the apparent rule of justice. Seeing an act that seemed to endanger innocent lives, and being unable to see its hidden wisdom, he protests out of his sense of duty to forbid wrong. The verse teaches that human knowledge is limited, that what appears to be harm may conceal a deeper good known only to God (the ship was damaged so it would not be seized by a tyrant king), and that patience and trust in divine wisdom are required when one cannot comprehend the reasons behind events. It also shows that even a prophet must be humble before knowledge granted by God to others.

translation: He said, 'Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me?'
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Kahf 18:75) is the second time al-Khidr reminds Musa of his warning. It shows that Musa's patience was bound to fail, because he judged by outward appearances while al-Khidr acted on knowledge of hidden wisdom given by God. The reminder is a gentle reproach. It teaches that a person limited to apparent knowledge cannot bear what he cannot fully comprehend, and that true patience requires trusting divine wisdom even when events seem wrong or unjust. It also teaches that a student must show humility and restraint before a teacher, and that human understanding is limited, so we should hold back hasty judgment until the full picture is revealed.

translation: He said: "Do not hold me to account for what I forgot, and do not burden me with hardship in my affair."
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Kahf 18:73) records Moses's reply to al-Khidr after he broke his promise not to question the Servant's actions. Moses does not deny the lapse. He admits it was forgetfulness and asks for leniency, which shows that sincere human error deserves forgiveness and that those who teach should be patient with learners. His plea 'do not burden me with hardship in my affair' asks al-Khidr not to make the path of learning and companionship too difficult. It teaches that seeking knowledge requires humility, an acknowledgment of one's weakness, and a willingness to ask for mercy, and that those who guide should be gentle and make things easy rather than hard.

translation: So they set out, until when they met a boy, he killed him. Moses said, "Have you killed an innocent soul who had killed no one? You have certainly done a deplorable thing."
interpretation: This verse (Al-Kahf 18:74) describes the second event in Moses' journey with the knowledgeable servant of God, traditionally identified as al-Khidr. Moses judges by the outward appearance of events and the clear rules of the law he knows: killing a young person who has apparently done no wrong is a grave offense. His protest shows that he cannot hold back from objecting to what looks like injustice, even after he promised to be patient. The deeper lesson, revealed later in the story, is that divine wisdom can work through events whose hidden purposes are unknown to humans, so that what appears to be evil may bring a greater good, such as protecting the boy's believing parents from being driven into rebellion and disbelief. The verse teaches humility about the limits of human knowledge, and the need for trust in God's wisdom when we cannot see the full picture.

translation: He said, "Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me?"
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Kahf 18:75) shows the servant of God, traditionally identified as al-Khidr, reminding Moses that he had warned him in advance. Moses had broken his promise of silence by questioning an act he did not understand. The reminder shows that true patience depends on more than outward endurance. It requires trust in knowledge and wisdom that lie beyond what one can see. Moses judged only by the apparent wrong, while Khidr acted on a hidden knowledge granted by God. The verse teaches humility in learning, and caution about judging events by their surface. It also teaches that human understanding is limited, so one must be patient with what one cannot yet comprehend and trust that divine wisdom lies behind events that seem troubling.

translation: He said: If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion; you will have reached from me an excuse.
interpretation: After forgetting his promise a second time, when he questioned the killing of the youth, Moses sets a final limit on himself and accepts the consequence in advance. He tells his companion that if he objects once more, the companion is entitled to part ways with him and would be fully excused for doing so, since Moses will already have been given repeated warnings and chances. The verse shows Moses' fairness and humility: he admits his own lapse, does not defend it, and holds himself to account. It also teaches that patience in seeking knowledge has limits, and that a teacher who has been tested repeatedly is justified in ending the companionship once a fair opportunity has been given.

translation: So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to host them. Then they found in it a wall about to collapse, and he set it upright. Moses said, 'If you had wished, you could have taken payment for it.'
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Moses and the servant of God (traditionally identified as al-Khidr) in Surah al-Kahf, shows how outward appearances can conceal hidden wisdom. The townspeople's stinginess toward hungry travelers would naturally call for rebuke, yet the servant repairs their wall without asking for anything in return. This puzzles Moses, who judges only by what is visible and by ordinary notions of fairness, so he suggests they should at least have taken a wage. The servant's act of goodness, done for a reason Moses cannot yet see, teaches that divine wisdom often goes beyond immediate human judgment. It also teaches that a righteous person does good for God's sake, not for reward or in response to how others behave, and that patience and trust are needed when the reasons for events are not yet disclosed. The explanation comes later in the story: the wall protected a treasure belonging to two orphans, so what looked like pointless generosity toward ungracious people was really mercy toward the vulnerable.

translation: He said, "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you were unable to be patient."
interpretation: Al-Khidr announces that the companionship has reached its end, because Moses broke his promise of patience three times. Parting is not an act of spite but the fair outcome of a condition that was set and not kept. Before they separate, Khidr gives Moses the explanation of his three actions, which seemed wrong on the surface. This shows that events which look like harm or injustice can contain hidden wisdom and mercy, known fully only to God and to those He teaches. The verse teaches that hasty judgment based on outward appearances is a failing, and that patience and trust in God's wisdom lead to understanding.

translation: As for the ship, it belonged to poor people who worked at sea, and I wished to damage it, because behind them was a king who was seizing every ship by force.
interpretation: Al-Khidr explains that an act that looks harmful on the surface can hold a hidden mercy. Damaging the ship was a deliberate, limited loss that protected the poor owners from a far greater one, the total confiscation of their only means of livelihood by a tyrant. A flawed ship would be passed over by the king's men, so the owners kept it and could go on earning their living. The verse teaches that human judgment sees only what is apparent, while divine wisdom sees the consequences that lie ahead. A believer should therefore trust God's decree even when events seem unjust or painful, and accept that a smaller hardship may be the means of averting a larger one. It also shows that Al-Khidr acted on God's command and knowledge, not on his own whim, which is why Moses could not see the reason at first.

translation: As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with transgression and disbelief.
interpretation: This verse, from the account of Moses and the righteous servant (al-Khidr) in Surah al-Kahf (18:80), teaches that what appears to be harsh or unjust may in truth be a mercy rooted in divine knowledge of the unseen. The boy's future rebellion would have overwhelmed his faithful parents, perhaps pressing them through love for him into sin or a loss of faith. God's decree of his death spared them that trial and, as the next verse indicates, was to be replaced with a more righteous and compassionate child. The lesson is that believers should trust God's wisdom and accept His decrees with patience, since they cannot see the full consequences of events, and that God protects the faith of His believing servants even through what seems to them a painful loss.

translation: So we wished that their Lord would give them in exchange one better than him in purity and closer in mercy (filial affection).
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Moses and al-Khidr (Surah al-Kahf 18:81), explains the wisdom behind the killing of the boy: God knew he would grow up to be rebellious and ungrateful and would burden his devout parents with transgression and disbelief. By removing him, God would replace him with a child who is more upright in character and purity, and more dutiful and compassionate toward his parents. The verse teaches that what appears to be a harsh loss may conceal divine wisdom and a greater good, and that believers should trust God's knowledge of the unseen consequences of events, since God's decree for His righteous servants is always to their ultimate benefit.

translation: As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father was a righteous man. So your Lord willed that they reach their maturity and bring forth their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.
interpretation: Al-Khidr explains that his rebuilding of the wall, which Moses had questioned, was in fact an act of divine mercy and not a random or pointless favor. The wall guarded a buried treasure that belonged to two orphans, and had it collapsed, the treasure would have been exposed and lost before they were old enough to protect it. God preserved their inheritance in honor of their father's righteousness, showing that a person's piety can benefit their descendants after death. Al-Khidr stresses that he acted only by God's command and not by his own will, and that apparent oddities in events often conceal wise purposes unseen at the time. The lesson is that believers should be patient and trust God's wisdom when events seem unjust or puzzling, since hidden benefits may be revealed later.

translation: And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: "I will recite to you an account of him."
interpretation: The verse shows that the Prophet answers questions through revelation and not through his own knowledge or opinion. When the people, probably prompted by the People of the Book, test him about a famous ruler of the past, God instructs him to promise only what He will recite to him: 'an account' (dhikr). The word dhikr signals that the story is told for reminder and moral lesson, not for historical detail such as dates or genealogy. The account that follows presents a righteous king whose power was given by God and used for justice and for helping the weak. It teaches that worldly authority is a trust from God and that the right response to power is gratitude, humility and service. The phrase 'I will recite to you' also stresses that the knowledge comes from God, so the account is reliable and is limited to what serves guidance.

translation: Indeed, We established him upon the earth and gave him the means to everything.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Kahf 18:84) speaks of Dhul-Qarnayn and shows that his power was a gift from God rather than something he achieved by himself. God gave him authority and stability on earth, and also granted him the means, such as knowledge, resources, strength and a route to accomplish what he set out to do. The verse teaches that worldly success depends on divine enabling together with the use of causes, and that those entrusted with power should use it with justice and gratitude, as Dhul-Qarnayn did in the verses that follow.

translation: So he followed a way.
interpretation: This verse describes Dhul-Qarnayn, who, having been granted authority on earth and the means to achieve all things, did not rely on power alone but deliberately chose and pursued a path. The lesson is that God's gifts of ability and resources must be matched by purposeful effort: a person should take the practical means (planning, knowledge, and action) while trusting in God, and use them in a journey of righteousness and service rather than idle reliance or arrogance.

translation: Until, when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of murky water, and he found near it a people. We said, 'O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you treat them with kindness.'
interpretation: The verse describes Dhul-Qarnayn's journey to the farthest west, where, from his vantage point, the sun appeared to sink into a dark, muddy sea or spring; this is an account of what he saw, not a statement about the sun's actual physical setting. The central lesson is that God places a powerful ruler before a people with a real moral choice: to exercise power through punishment or through kindness. The choice is given to him as a test of justice, showing that authority is a trust, and that even over people who may be disbelievers, the ruler is called to weigh his options before God and lean toward goodness and fairness, with punishment reserved for those who persist in wrongdoing.

translation: He said: 'As for him who does wrong, we shall punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment.'
interpretation: Dhul-Qarnayn lays out a just policy for governing the people he found: those who persist in wrongdoing, whether through disbelief or oppression, will face punishment in this world at his hands, and this is only a limited, worldly chastisement. The greater and more serious reckoning waits for them after death, when they are returned to God, whose knowledge of their deeds is complete and whose punishment is far more severe, an unprecedented and dreadful torment. The verse shows that a righteous ruler holds authority in the knowledge that he is himself accountable to God, and that worldly justice is only a pale shadow of the ultimate divine justice.

translation: But as for him who believes and does righteous deeds, for him is the best reward, and we shall speak to him of our command with ease.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Dhul-Qarnayn (Surat al-Kahf, 18:88), states the principle by which he would deal with his subjects. Whoever combines sound faith with righteous action will receive the finest recompense from God, namely Paradise and His good pleasure. In worldly life, such a person will also be treated with kindness and consideration: the ruler will assign him tasks that are easy rather than burdensome, and speak gently to him. The verse teaches that faith joined with good deeds is the basis of both lasting reward in the hereafter and honor and ease in dealings with others. It also shows the ideal of just governance, which rewards righteousness with generosity and gentleness instead of harshness.

translation: Then he followed a way.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Kahf 18:89) describes Dhul-Qarnayn after he had reached the west and then the east, when he set out on yet another journey by taking the means and paths that God had granted him. The interpretation is that a believer who has been given power and resources does not stop at past achievements. He keeps using the lawful means available to him, such as knowledge, planning, and effort, to pursue worthwhile goals and serve justice, while relying on God for success. The verse shows that God's gift of authority is joined to purposeful action and that progress comes by following the right means step by step.

translation: Until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had made no shelter from it.
interpretation: The verse describes Dhul-Qarnayn's second journey, to the farthest east. The people he found there lived in a primitive, exposed condition, with no buildings, clothing, or natural cover such as mountains or trees to shield them from the sun's intense heat. The phrase 'We had made no shelter from it' points to the extreme harshness of their environment and their simple, undeveloped way of life. It also shows the vast reach of Dhul-Qarnayn's power and travels, which took him from the setting of the sun to its rising, and it illustrates the diversity of peoples and conditions in God's creation, over which God granted him authority and for whom he was to act justly.

translation: Thus it was; and We had encompassed with Our knowledge all that he had with him.
