interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Kahf 18:91) comes at the end of the account of Dhul-Qarnayn's journey to the rising place of the sun, where he found a people with no shelter from it. It means that God's knowledge fully encompassed Dhul-Qarnayn, his power, his armies, his resources and his intentions, as well as everything that happened during his travels. Nothing about him or his conquests was hidden from God. His authority and success were therefore not his own doing but were granted, watched over and known by God in every detail, which reminds the reader that even the mightiest ruler remains wholly within God's knowledge and control.

translation: Then he followed a way.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Kahf 18:89) describes Dhul-Qarnayn after he had reached the west and then the east: he again chose a path and pursued means, travelling by the resources and abilities God had granted him. The word 'sabab' signifies a means, cause, or route, so the verse teaches that real success comes from deliberately taking up the proper means and exerting effort, while trusting that God is the One who grants those means and the outcome. Dhul-Qarnayn's journeys were not aimless conquest but purposeful, guided action, a model of combining planning and perseverance with reliance on God.

translation: Until, when he reached a place between the two mountain barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech.
interpretation: The verse shows Dhul-Qarnayn arriving at a remote mountain pass, where he met a people who were so isolated from other nations, in language and in contact with the wider world, that they could barely grasp what was said to them. Their near-incomprehension points to their cultural and linguistic remoteness, and it sets up their plea for protection from Yajuj and Majuj. It also shows that a just ruler reaches out to the weak and distant, using whatever means of communication he has to meet their needs, and that the power God gave him was to be used in serving people who could not help themselves.

translation: They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are spreading corruption in the land. So may we assign to you a tribute, on condition that you build a barrier between us and them?"
interpretation: The verse shows a people who were weak and oppressed turning to a capable, righteous ruler for protection from a destructive force. Their description of Gog and Magog as 'spreading corruption in the land' shows that the threat was not only military but also moral and social: constant harm, disorder and injustice that they could not stop themselves. Their offer of payment shows that they understood the value of his help and were willing to bear a share of the cost, while they still looked to him for the expertise and power that they lacked. The verse teaches that rulers and those with ability and resources are responsible for defending the vulnerable and for stopping corruption. It also teaches that seeking help from the capable in order to prevent harm is legitimate, and that a community should cooperate with its leaders in doing so.

translation: He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better, so assist me with strength; I will build a barrier between you and them."
interpretation: Dhul-Qarnayn answers the people who offered him payment to build a barrier against Gog and Magog by declining the money. He credits God's gift of authority and resources as better than any tribute they could give. He asks them instead to contribute labor and effort, since divine favor does not remove the need for human work. The verse presents the ideal of a righteous ruler: grateful and humble, free of greed, and relying on God while still organizing people to cooperate on a public good. The 'radm', a barrier more solid and layered than an ordinary wall, shows his intent to give a thorough, lasting protection.

translation: Bring me sheets of iron. Then, when he had leveled up the gap between the two mountain sides, he said: 'Blow!' Then, when he had made it fiery red, he said: 'Bring me molten copper to pour over it.'
interpretation: The verse shows how Dhul-Qarnayn built the barrier against Gog and Magog by combining the people's labor with sound engineering, not by miracle alone. The iron blocks were stacked until they filled the gap between the two mountains. Bellows were then used to heat the iron until it glowed like fire, and molten copper was poured over it so that the iron and copper fused into one hard, durable mass that was difficult to climb or breach. The lesson is that believers should use the means available to them, such as knowledge, skill, materials and cooperation, to protect the vulnerable, while still attributing the success to God's grace, as Dhul-Qarnayn does in the following verses.

translation: So they were not able to scale it, nor were they able to dig through it.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Dhul-Qarnayn (Surat al-Kahf, 18:97), describes the barrier he built from iron and molten copper to hold back Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj). It shows that the wall was perfectly constructed: it was too high and smooth to climb over, and too thick and hard to tunnel through. The lesson is that when a believing ruler uses his power, knowledge and resources sincerely to protect the weak, God grants his work strength and success, so that even the most corrupting forces cannot overcome it unless God permits. It also points to the limits of human ability, since the wall is effective only by God's will and lasts until the time He decrees.

translation: He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord; but when the promise of my Lord comes, He will turn it into dust. And the promise of my Lord is ever true."
interpretation: After building the barrier against Gog and Magog, Dhul-Qarnayn does not credit his own power or skill. He attributes the achievement to God's mercy toward the people, which shows humility and gratitude in a powerful ruler. He also reminds them that the barrier, however strong, is only a created thing that lasts as long as God wills. When the appointed time comes, which is the end of the world's order, God will level it to dust. The lesson is that worldly strength and works are temporary and depend on God, while His promise is certain and will be fulfilled.

translation: And on that Day We shall leave them surging over one another; and the Trumpet will be blown, and We shall gather them all together.
interpretation: The verse describes the state of humanity at the end of time. The surging of people like waves, in confusion and turmoil, one group pressing upon another, conveys the chaos and helplessness of the Day when worldly order collapses, and it is commonly linked to the release of Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj) mentioned in the preceding verses. Then the Trumpet is blown for the final resurrection, and God gathers all creatures, from the first to the last, in one place for judgment. The disorder of that moment gives way to complete divine control: no one can escape or remain scattered, for every soul is brought before its Lord. The verse is a reminder that human power and numbers mean nothing before God's command, and it calls the listener to prepare for accountability.

translation: And on that Day We will present Hell, in full view, to the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 18:100) describes the Day when the disbelievers will be brought face to face with Hell, no longer able to deny or ignore it. 'Presenting' it implies a vivid, unavoidable exposure: what they mocked and rejected in the world is laid out before them as a certain reality, so that the sight itself becomes the first part of their punishment. The context (the verses before and after) speaks of those whose eyes were veiled from remembrance of God and who could not bear to hear His message; on that Day their veil is lifted and they see plainly the consequence of their heedlessness. The verse thus warns that willful blindness to truth in this life ends in a clear and terrifying sight of it in the next.

translation: Those whose eyes were within a covering, heedless of My remembrance, and who were unable to hear.
interpretation: The verse describes the disbelievers who were spiritually blind and deaf in worldly life. Their eyes were veiled from seeing the signs of God in creation and in revelation, so they did not reflect on them and arrive at remembrance of their Lord. Their inability to hear is not physical deafness but a refusal and incapacity to listen to the Qur'an and the Messenger's call, caused by arrogance and persistent heedlessness. Because they closed their hearts to guidance, they became unable to benefit from it, and so their disbelief is presented as the consequence of their own willful neglect, for which they are held accountable.

translation: Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants as protectors instead of Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the disbelievers for imagining that worshipping or seeking protection from created beings, such as angels, prophets, or righteous people, who are only servants of God, can benefit or shield them against God. Those servants themselves disown such devotion and cannot grant help or protection apart from Him. The verse declares that this assumption is false, and that those who persist in disbelief and in taking others as patrons besides God will find Hell prepared as their place of arrival, like a hospitality offering for a guest, which carries an ironic tone of rebuke that their only welcome will be Hell.

translation: Say, "Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in respect of their deeds?" (Qur'an 18:103)
interpretation: The verse opens with a question to draw the listener's attention to a surprising truth: real loss is not only material failure but the waste of one's efforts in matters that count before God. The 'greatest losers' are those who labor hard, yet their work yields nothing in the end because it lacks sincerity toward God and is not grounded in true faith and right guidance. The next verses explain that these are people whose striving in worldly life was misguided while they believed they were doing good. The verse therefore warns the believer to examine his intentions and the soundness of his beliefs and actions, since effort alone, without faith and correct direction, is no guarantee of success in the Hereafter.

translation: Those whose efforts in the worldly life have been lost while they think that they are doing good work.
interpretation: The verse describes people whose striving in this life was misdirected, so it earns them nothing in the next. Their deeds are not grounded in true faith or in the guidance revealed by God, so those deeds are void on the Day of Judgment even though the doers are sincerely convinced of their own righteousness. The warning is that sincerity and a good opinion of oneself are not enough. Deeds are accepted only when they rest on correct belief and conform to God's guidance, and so a person should keep examining his beliefs and actions against revelation and should not be deceived by self-satisfaction.

translation: Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in the meeting with Him, so their deeds have come to nothing; and on the Day of Resurrection We will assign them no weight.
interpretation: The verse teaches that deeds are valued by God according to the faith and sincerity behind them. Those who reject God's signs and deny that they will stand before Him for judgment have severed the foundation that gives actions worth. Even if their works looked impressive in worldly terms, such as charity, labor, or achievement, these were done without belief in accountability and without seeking God's approval, so they are nullified. On the Day of Judgment, the scales will not give them any weight, because their good deeds are void and nothing remains to outweigh their disbelief. Their worldly standing counts for nothing before God, since real worth lies in faith and righteous action, not in outward show or status.

translation: That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Kahf (18:106), explains that the punishment awaiting the deniers is not arbitrary but a just consequence of their own choices. Two wrongs are named: rejecting faith, and treating God's revelations and His prophets as objects of ridicule. Mockery is a graver form of disbelief than mere denial, because it shows contempt for truth and for those who convey it, and it closes the heart to reflection and guidance. Hell is therefore presented as the fitting and proportionate outcome of arrogance and scorn, a reminder that the way one treats divine guidance in this life determines one's fate in the next.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise (Al-Firdaws) as a welcome (lodging).
interpretation: God promises that true faith joined with righteous action leads to the highest reward. The word 'nuzul' denotes the hospitality prepared for an honored guest, which suggests that Paradise is only the first welcome, and that God's generosity beyond it is greater still. Faith alone is not enough, and deeds without faith are not enough. The believer's inner conviction must be confirmed by outward good conduct, and those who live this way are received by God as honored guests in the best and most elevated part of Paradise.

translation: Abiding therein forever, they will not desire any change from it.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 18:108) describes the people who believed and did righteous deeds and who are given the Gardens of Al-Firdaws as their abode. It means that Paradise will so perfectly fulfill every longing of its inhabitants that their hearts will never be restless or seek a different place or state. In this world, people constantly tire of their circumstances and look for something better, even when they have what they once wished for. In Paradise, complete contentment replaces that restlessness: the joy of it never fades and nothing better can be imagined, so no one will wish to move elsewhere or change their condition. The verse teaches that true and lasting satisfaction of the soul is found only in God's reward, and it encourages the believer to strive for that abode rather than the passing and ever-changing pleasures of this life.

translation: Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as additional supply.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's knowledge, wisdom, and decrees are boundless, while all created things, even an ocean of ink and another like it added to it, are finite. Human beings can record only a tiny fraction of what God knows and commands, so they should approach divine knowledge with humility, recognize the limits of their own understanding, and acknowledge God's greatness and perfection.

translation: Say: I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed that your God is One God. So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord.
interpretation: The verse sets out the Prophet's true status: he is a mortal messenger, not divine and not possessed of hidden powers. His distinction lies only in receiving revelation, and its core message is pure monotheism. Anyone who longs for the meeting with God in the Hereafter must meet two conditions for their deeds to be accepted: the deeds must be righteous, meaning sincere and in line with God's guidance, and they must be done purely for God, with no shirk, whether open idolatry or the hidden shirk of showing off (riya'). Hope for the encounter with God is therefore proven by sound action and sincere devotion to Him alone, not by claims or by reverence for any human being.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.
interpretation: These five disconnected letters that open Surah Maryam are best understood as a challenge and a reminder about the Qur'an's miraculous nature. The revelation is composed of the very same Arabic letters the Arabs used in their eloquent speech, yet they could not produce anything like it, which shows that its source is divine rather than human. Their placement at the start of the surah also draws the listener's attention and prepares the heart to receive the narrative of God's mercy that follows, namely the stories of Zakariyya, Yahya, Maryam and Isa, and the other prophets. Ultimately, the true meaning of the letters is known only to God, and our proper response is to believe in them and reflect on the message they introduce.

translation: This is a mention of your Lord's mercy to His servant Zachariah.
interpretation: The verse opens Surat Maryam by introducing the story of Zachariah as a lesson in divine mercy. It teaches that God answers the sincere, humble supplication of His servants, even when worldly circumstances such as old age and a barren wife make the request seem impossible. Zachariah's quiet prayer for an heir was met with God's mercy through the gift of John, so the story invites believers to remember that God's mercy is not limited by natural causes and to turn to Him with hope and trust in every need.

translation: When he called upon his Lord with a secret, hidden call.
interpretation: This verse (Surat Maryam 19:3) describes how the Prophet Zakariyya called upon God in a low, private voice. The hiddenness of the prayer signals sincerity and humility: he was an old man, and his plea for an heir was a vulnerable one, so he kept it between himself and God, away from show or public notice. God hears even the quietest whisper of the heart and does not need loud speech, and a servant's closest, most intimate supplications are often those made in secret. Such a prayer is more likely to be free of ostentation and filled with complete reliance on God.

translation: He said: My Lord, indeed my bones have grown feeble, and my head is aflame with white hair, and never, my Lord, have I been unblessed in my supplication to You.
interpretation: Zakariyya opens his prayer by confessing his utter weakness and dependence on God, using the images of brittle bones, which are the body's support, and a head blazing with white hair, which spreads like fire through fuel. Together they show that old age has overtaken him completely and that no worldly means remain for him to hope for offspring. He then reminds himself of God's past generosity: each time he called on God he was answered, so he never felt disappointed. This teaches that the best way to pray is to admit one's helplessness, recall God's earlier favors, and approach Him with confident hope, trusting that He who has always responded can grant even what seems impossible.

translation: And indeed, I fear the heirs after me, and my wife has been barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir.
interpretation: In this verse, the prophet Zakariyya (Zechariah) confides in his Lord out of deep concern for the future of the message and the community. He does not fear for his wealth as such; rather, he fears that those who come after him among his kin may lack righteousness and may mishandle the religious trust and guidance he carries, so he asks for a righteous successor who will carry on the prophetic legacy. He acknowledges his means are exhausted: his wife is barren and he is advanced in age, so any child could come only by God's direct gift ('from Yourself'). The verse teaches that a believer should bring even seemingly impossible needs to God with humility and sincerity, relying on His power rather than natural causes, and that the highest desire for offspring is that they be devoted heirs to faith and guidance.

translation: Who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Jacob; and make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You].
interpretation: This is part of Zechariah's prayer (Maryam 19:6) asking for a son. The inheritance he seeks is primarily spiritual rather than material: succession to prophethood, knowledge, and the guardianship of the religious legacy of the House of Jacob, since prophets do not leave wealth as their concern. Zechariah, being old and fearing that those after him would neglect the faith, wants a successor who will carry on the message. His final plea, 'make him pleasing', asks that the child be granted righteousness, good character, and God's own approval, so that he be beloved to both his Lord and to people, ensuring that the inheritance is entrusted to someone worthy of it.

translation: O Zachariah, indeed We give you good news of a boy whose name is John. We have not assigned to any before him the same name.
interpretation: God answers Zachariah's prayer for an heir by announcing the birth directly, and He names the child Himself, which is a mark of honor. The uniqueness of the name Yahya, which no one had borne before, signals the child's special distinction and status. Many commentators also connect the name to life (hayat): the child would be born to an aged father and a barren mother, and his life and mission would be a sign of God's power to give life where it seems impossible. The verse teaches that God's gifts may exceed what a person asks for, and that He grants them in ways that surpass ordinary expectation.

translation: He said, "My Lord, how shall I have a son when my wife has been barren, and I have reached extreme old age?"
interpretation: Zakariyya's question is not doubt in God's power but an expression of wonder and humble gratitude at a blessing that defies natural means. He lays out the two apparent obstacles, his wife's lifelong barrenness and his own frailty from advanced age, and in doing so shows how completely the promised child depends on divine will rather than ordinary causes. The verse teaches that a believer may voice amazement and seek reassurance without lacking faith, and it prepares for God's reply that what is easy for Him needs no means, just as He created Zakariyya himself when he was nothing.

translation: He said, "Thus it will be. Your Lord says: 'It is easy for Me, for I created you before, when you were nothing.'"
interpretation: This verse is God's reply to Zechariah's astonishment at being promised a son despite his old age and his wife's barrenness. God answers by pointing to something Zechariah already knows: He brought him into existence from complete nothingness. Whoever can originate a human being from non-existence can easily bring a child from an old man and a barren wife. The verse teaches that nothing is beyond God's power, that causes such as age and barrenness do not limit Him, and that a believer should answer doubt or amazement by remembering his own creation, which is the clearest proof that renewing or granting life is easy for God.

translation: He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though sound in body."
interpretation: Zechariah, having been given the glad tidings of a son in his old age, asks God for a sign to mark the moment the promise begins to be fulfilled, seeking reassurance and a heart at rest rather than expressing doubt. God makes the sign a temporary inability to speak to people for three nights, even though he is healthy and has no illness or defect. This shows that the cause was not natural but a miracle from God, who suspends ordinary causes at His will. The silence also directs Zechariah to devote himself to remembrance, glorification, and gratitude to God, for he is still able to praise Him while being unable to converse with others. It teaches that God's favors may come with moments of withdrawal from worldly talk so that the believer's heart is turned wholly to Him.

translation: So he came out to his people from the prayer chamber and signaled to them to glorify God morning and evening.
interpretation: After Zechariah was given the sign that he would be unable to speak to people for three nights, despite being physically sound, he left the place of worship and communicated with his people by gesture rather than speech. He told them to keep glorifying God at the beginning and end of the day. The verse shows that the sign was not a cause for withdrawal or despair but a time of gratitude. Zechariah responded to the glad tidings of a son by turning his community toward remembrance and worship, and he did so even when speech was withheld from him. It also shows that a prophet's first concern upon receiving a blessing is to call others to thank and exalt the Giver, and that regular devotion at the day's two ends is a fitting response to divine favor.

translation: O John, take hold of the Scripture with strength. And We gave him wisdom (judgment) while still a child.
interpretation: God commands Yahya (John) to hold fast to the Book, the Torah and its teachings, with firm resolve, earnestness and diligence, not with weakness or negligence, which means learning it properly, acting upon it, and conveying it to others with steadfastness. The verse then notes that God endowed him from childhood with sound judgment, understanding and prophetic wisdom, which shows that divine favor is not restricted by age: God grants insight and the ability to bear a great responsibility to whom He wills, and He prepared Yahya from an early age for the mission he was to carry out.

translation: And [We gave him] tenderness from Us, and purity; and he was God-fearing.
interpretation: The verse describes the gifts God bestowed on Yahya (John) as a child: a deep compassion and mercy placed in his heart by God's own grace, an inner purity of soul free from sin and corruption, and a steady God-consciousness (taqwa) that guided his conduct. It teaches that the noblest qualities of character, such as mercy toward others, moral cleanliness, and reverent awareness of God, are bestowed by divine favor and are the foundation of true prophethood and righteousness.

translation: And dutiful toward his parents, and he was not arrogant or disobedient.
interpretation: This verse, describing Yahya (John) son of Zachariah, presents dutifulness to parents as a mark of true piety, placing it alongside devotion to God. Kindness to one's parents is shown as an expression of humility and gratitude, the very opposite of tyranny and rebellion. His freedom from arrogance and disobedience shows that a person granted wisdom and prophethood early in life remains lowly before God and gentle toward people, beginning with those closest to him. The verse teaches that real nobility of character is measured by humility, obedience to God, and compassion within the family, rather than by power or status.

translation: Peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised up alive.
interpretation: This verse, spoken of the Prophet Yahya (John) in Surah Maryam, shows that God granted him safety and security at the three most fearful thresholds of human existence: entering the world at birth, facing the unknown at death, and standing before God at the resurrection. It means that Yahya, because of his piety, purity, and obedience, was protected by God's peace from Satan's harm, from distress, and from terror at every stage, so that he moves from one state to the next in divine security and honor.

translation: And mention in the Book (the story of) Mary, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.
interpretation: The verse presents Mary's withdrawal as an act of devotion and purity: by leaving her family's company for a secluded place to the east, she turned away from worldly distraction to devote herself wholly to God. This retreat prepares the ground for the extraordinary event that follows, showing that God's choice of her was bound up with her sincerity, modesty and worship. The mention of the 'east' is often read as pointing to the place of sunrise and light, a fitting symbol of the spiritual illumination about to come to her, so the verse teaches that solitude in God's remembrance can be the setting for receiving divine favor and guidance.

translation: And she placed a screen to shield herself from them; then We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her in the form of a well-proportioned man.
interpretation: Maryam withdrew from her people to a secluded place and drew a veil between herself and them, devoting herself to worship in privacy and modesty. In that seclusion, God sent the angel Jibril, here called 'Our Spirit' to honor him as the bearer of divine revelation and life-giving command. He did not appear in his angelic form, which would have overwhelmed her, but took the shape of a perfectly formed human being so she could receive and bear his message calmly. This prepares the scene for the announcement of Jesus' miraculous birth, showing that the event was brought about by God's direct command through His angel, to a chaste woman who had sought seclusion for devotion.

translation: She said: 'Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing.'
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:18) shows Maryam's reaction of fear and modesty when a figure appeared before her in the form of a man while she was in seclusion. Her first response was not panic or reliance on her own strength but turning to God, invoking His name 'al-Rahman' (the Most Merciful) to evoke His mercy and protection. Her phrase 'if you are God-fearing' appeals to the stranger's conscience: if he has any piety, he will be restrained by awareness of God and will not harm her. The verse teaches that a believer, when facing a threat to her chastity or safety, should seek refuge in God first and appeal to the moral restraint of taqwa in others, and it highlights Maryam's purity, vigilance and deep God-consciousness before she knew that the visitor was the angel Jibril sent by her Lord.

translation: He said, 'I am only a messenger from your Lord, [sent] to grant you a pure boy.'
interpretation: The angel, appearing to Mary in the form of a man, answers her fear and her appeal for refuge in God by clarifying that he is no threat but an envoy of her Lord. The gift of a son is not the doing of the angel nor the result of any human cause; he is only the agent carrying out God's command. The phrase 'pure boy' (ghulaman zakiyyan) indicates that the child will be free from sin and faults, upright and blessed, which affirms Mary's own chastity and shows that the birth is a divine favor and sign, not a source of shame. The angel's words thereby reassure her and prepare her for the miraculous conception of Jesus.

translation: She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me, and I have never been unchaste?"
interpretation: Maryam's question (Surah Maryam 19:20) is not doubt in God's power but a sincere request to understand how a child could come to her. She grounds her astonishment in her known purity: she is unmarried and has never been unchaste. The verse affirms her chastity and shows that the birth of Jesus would lie outside the ordinary course of nature, which prepares for the angel's reply that this is easy for God, who creates by His command and makes the event a sign for humankind and a mercy from Him.

translation: He said, 'Thus it is; your Lord says: It is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter already decreed.'
interpretation: This verse is the angel's answer to Mary's astonishment at the news of a son when no man had touched her. It teaches that God's power is not bound by ordinary causes, since creating a child without a father is simple for the One who created all things from nothing. Jesus' miraculous birth is meant to be a sign for humanity of God's power and a mercy from Him, as Jesus would guide people to truth and bring them closer to God. The closing words, 'a matter decreed,' reassure Mary that this was settled in God's divine will and knowledge, so she should accept it with trust and not fear or doubt.

translation: So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Maryam (19:22) shows Mary's isolation and distress as the miracle of Jesus's conception unfolds. Her retreat to a distant place is not mere physical flight but an expression of her fear of how her people would receive an unmarried woman bearing a child. It shows that those chosen for great divine tasks are often tested first through solitude and hardship, and that she endured it in trust and submission to God, who would soon provide her with comfort, sustenance, and vindication.

translation: Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, 'Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been something forgotten and out of sight.'
interpretation: Maryam's cry is not a rejection of God's decree or a loss of faith, but the natural expression of a pure and modest woman overwhelmed by fear of public shame. She was alone, in physical agony, and knew that people would accuse her of immorality when they saw a child with no father. Her wish to have been 'forgotten and lost from memory' shows how heavy the trial was for her and how much she valued her honor. The verse teaches that even the most righteous servants may feel acute distress under severe trials, and that such human weakness does not conflict with patience or trust in God. God's relief then follows immediately, as He comforts her with the stream and the dates and with the child's own speech, showing that hardship is accompanied by divine care.

translation: Then he called out to her from beneath her: 'Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream.'
interpretation: In the loneliness and anguish of labor, Maryam is consoled by a voice from below her, understood as the infant Jesus or, in another reading, the angel Gabriel. The voice tells her not to despair, because God, who foresaw her distress, has already provided for her: a flowing stream for water and refreshment. The verse teaches that God's care reaches the believer in the moment of greatest vulnerability, and that relief comes with trust in Him. It also shows that provision is wrapped in reassurance, as God comforts the heart before addressing the body's needs.

translation: And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh, ripe dates.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to Maryam (Mary) during her labor pains after giving birth to Jesus, teaches that reliance on God does not cancel taking means. Although God could have provided food without any effort from her, He commanded her to shake the trunk of the tree, an act that would have been difficult for a woman in her weakened state. This shows that divine provision is joined with human effort, however small, and that trust in God (tawakkul) means striving with whatever ability one has while trusting that the result comes from Him. The fresh dates also served as nourishment and comfort for a woman who had just given birth, a sign of God's care for her in her isolation and distress.

translation: So eat and drink and be comforted. And if you see any human being, say: 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human.'
interpretation: God addresses Mary after the birth of Jesus, relieving her anxiety and shame by telling her to take comfort in the provision He has given her, the fresh dates and the stream, and to let her heart be at peace. Her silence is a means of divine protection: instead of arguing with accusers over her miraculous pregnancy, she is to commit herself to a vow of silence for the Most Merciful and leave her defense to Him. The child himself will speak on her behalf and prove her innocence. The verse teaches that when a believer is faced with slander that cannot be answered by ordinary means, the right course is to trust in God, avoid futile disputes, and let Him bring forth the vindication.

translation: Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said: 'O Mary, you have indeed done an unprecedented, monstrous thing.'
interpretation: After Mary withdrew and gave birth, she returned openly to her community carrying the infant Jesus, trusting in God's command and protection rather than hiding the child. Her people, seeing a child with no known father, judged by outward appearances and reacted with shock and accusation, calling it a 'fariyy', an outrageous, unheard-of deed. The verse shows the severe social trial that faced Mary, a woman known for chastity and descended from a pious family, and sets the stage for the miracle that follows: God vindicates her not through her own defense but through the speech of the infant, teaching that those who submit to God's decree and endure patiently will be vindicated by Him in ways beyond human expectation.

translation: O sister of Aaron, your father was not an evil man, nor was your mother unchaste.
interpretation: This is the reproach Mary's people directed at her when she came to them carrying the infant Jesus. They appeal to her righteous family lineage to heighten the gravity of what they believed to be a transgression. Calling her 'sister of Aaron' ties her to the pious, priestly descent of the house of Imran, or to a devout man of her time who bore Aaron's name, as the Prophet explained to the people of Najran. The point of their words is that she came from a family known for purity and integrity, so a child born outside marriage seemed to them utterly out of character and shameful. Their accusation sets the stage for the miracle that follows, in which Mary does not answer them herself but points to the infant, and the child Jesus speaks in the cradle to vindicate her innocence and declare his own prophethood.

translation: So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?"
interpretation: When Maryam was confronted by her people over the birth of her child, she did not answer them in words, in keeping with the vow of silence she had been commanded to observe. By pointing to the infant she placed the matter in God's hands and let the miracle itself serve as her defense. The people's astonished and scornful question shows that, by ordinary standards, it seemed absurd to expect an answer from a newborn. That disbelief sets the stage for the miracle that follows, in which Jesus speaks and declares himself a servant of God. The verse teaches that those who trust God and keep to His command can find their vindication come from where human reason expects none, and that God's power is not limited by the usual course of nature.

translation: He said: Indeed, I am a servant of God. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.
interpretation: In his first words, spoken as an infant in the cradle, Jesus (peace be upon him) declares his identity by affirming his servitude to God before anything else. By putting 'servant of God' first, he refutes the claims that he is divine or God's son, and he also answers the slander against his mother Mary by showing that his birth was part of God's design and that he was chosen for prophethood. The Scripture and prophethood are presented as gifts from God, not as qualities that belong to him by right, so his status as a prophet depends wholly on God's grace and choice.

translation: And He has made me blessed wherever I may be, and has enjoined upon me prayer and charity for as long as I live.
interpretation: In this verse, the infant Jesus (peace be upon him) speaks of his God-given station: his blessedness is not tied to a particular place or time but accompanies him everywhere, in that he is a source of goodness, guidance, and benefit to others wherever he goes. Alongside this blessing comes a lifelong duty: prayer, which binds a person to his Lord, and zakat, which binds him to his fellow human beings. The verse teaches that true blessedness is realized through devotion to God and service to others, and that these obligations are not temporary but continue for the whole of one's life, so that a prophet's greatness lies in steadfast obedience and humble servitude rather than in any claim to divinity.

translation: And [He has made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a tyrant, wretched.
interpretation: In this verse, Jesus (peace be upon him), speaking as an infant in the cradle, affirms that kindness and obedience to his mother are part of his God-given character. This shows that honoring parents, especially the mother, is an act of worship closely tied to faith. By denying that he was made 'jabbar shaqi' (an arrogant, oppressive and wretched person), he shows that pride and tyranny lead to misery, since the arrogant refuse to submit to God and treat others unjustly. Humility, gentleness and dutifulness are the marks of true servants of God, and they bring felicity, while arrogance is the path to wretchedness.

translation: And peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.
interpretation: These are the words of the infant Jesus (Isa) in Surah Maryam, spoken from the cradle. They affirm that God's safety and peace surround him at the three most vulnerable thresholds of human existence: entering the world, leaving it, and rising for judgment. By stating that he is a servant under God's protection and that his birth, death and resurrection all unfold by God's decree, the verse affirms his humanity and servanthood. It refutes the slander against his mother Mary and the claim that he is divine, since one who needs God's peace and is subject to death and resurrection is a created being. It also teaches that true security at every stage of life, and especially at the moments of greatest fear, comes only from God's grace.

translation: That is Jesus, son of Mary — a statement of the truth, about which they are in doubt.
interpretation: After recounting the story of Mary and the miraculous birth of Jesus in Surah Maryam, God affirms the authentic account of who Jesus is: a human being, born of Mary, and a servant and messenger of God, not a son of God nor a deity. This account is called the 'word of truth' because it is free from both the exaggeration of those who raised him to divinity and the denial of those who slandered his mother and rejected his miraculous birth. The verse points out that the people of earlier communities, Jews and Christians alike, dispute and doubt this matter, so the Qur'an comes as the decisive, correct statement that settles their disagreement and calls them back to the truth.

translation: It is not for God to take a son; glory be to Him! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is.
interpretation: The verse denies that God could have offspring, because begetting belongs to created beings who are limited, dependent, and in need of continuity through progeny. God is absolutely self-sufficient and perfect, so He has no need of a son. His power is shown in how He creates: no process, helper, or means is required, only His command 'Be.' Since He can bring anything into existence by His word alone, even the miraculous birth of Jesus, the claim that He needs a son is baseless, and Jesus is shown to be a creature of God's will rather than a partner in divinity.

translation: Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: Jesus (peace be upon him) is presented as declaring that he is a servant of God and not divine: God alone is the Lord of both him and his people, so worship belongs to Him alone. The verse teaches that pure monotheism, which means acknowledging God's lordship and devoting worship exclusively to Him, is the straight path that leads to salvation. Every deviation, such as attributing divinity or a share in God's lordship to any creature, strays from that path.

translation: But the factions differed among themselves; so woe to those who disbelieved from the witnessing of a great Day.
interpretation: The various groups who came after Jesus (peace be upon him) split into sects and quarrelled over his true nature: some denied him, some exaggerated his status to divinity, and some made him the son of God, though he himself called people to worship God alone. Their disputes were driven by rivalry, not by knowledge, and the verse warns that those who reject the truth will face severe ruin when they stand before God on the Day of Judgment. On that momentous Day every claim will be exposed, the truth will be made plain, and the deniers will have no refuge from the consequences of their disbelief.

translation: How well they will hear and how well they will see on the Day they come to Us! But today the wrongdoers are in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse points to a stark reversal: those who in this world turned a deaf ear to the truth and shut their eyes to the signs of God will, on the Day of Resurrection, hear and see with perfect clarity, when the realities they denied are laid bare before them. But that clarity comes too late to help them, since the time for acting on it has passed. The wrongdoers, by contrast, live today in plain misguidance, heedless of the warnings that were given. It is a call to use hearing and sight now, by listening to revelation and reflecting on the signs of God, before the Day arrives when perception will be complete but repentance will no longer be accepted.

translation: And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided, while they are [now] in heedlessness and they do not believe.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to warn people of the Day of Regret, so called because everyone will feel deep sorrow when the final judgment is passed and no further chance remains. The wrongdoers will regret their disbelief and neglect, and even the righteous may wish they had done more good. The phrase 'the matter is decided' means that destinies are sealed once and for all: the people of Paradise go to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire, and no repentance or return to worldly life is possible. The verse stresses that this regret is the fruit of present heedlessness and disbelief. Those who are absorbed in worldly distractions and refuse to believe now will be struck by sorrow when it is too late to change, so the warning urges people to wake up and prepare while there is still time.

translation: Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth and whoever is on it, and to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ownership held by human beings is only temporary and entrusted. When all creatures die and every possession passes away, God alone remains as the true heir and sovereign of the earth and all who live on it. Everyone will return to Him for reckoning, so a person should not be deceived by wealth, power, or worldly standing, but should live with accountability, humility, and preparation for meeting their Lord.

translation: And mention in the Book [the story of] Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth, a prophet.
interpretation: The verse holds up Abraham as a model of the 'siddiq', one whose words, beliefs and deeds are wholly consistent with truth. Being truthful in speech, sincere in faith, and faithful in action is presented as the foundation of his prophethood. Prophecy here rests on a character of utter honesty with God and with people, and he is mentioned so that believers may emulate his steadfast sincerity, especially when he stood for monotheism against the pressure of his own people and family.

translation: When he said to his father: O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, nor avails you in anything?
interpretation: Abraham addresses his father with gentleness and respect, using the affectionate 'O my father', yet poses a pointed rational challenge: worship is only fitting for a being that possesses the attributes of perfection, and idols lack hearing, sight, and any power to benefit or protect. The verse teaches that false worship is exposed as absurd by simple reasoning, and that calling people to monotheism is best begun with courteous speech and questions that awaken the conscience, appealing to the intellect rather than to confrontation. An object that cannot perceive the worshipper's plea, see his need, or repel harm from him cannot rightly be the object of devotion; only God, who hears, sees, and sustains, deserves worship.

translation: O my father, there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me and I will guide you to an even and straight path.
interpretation: Abraham addresses his idolatrous father with courtesy and humility. He does not claim superiority for himself but attributes his understanding to knowledge granted to him by God, which his father has not received. The verse teaches that the truth is judged by revelation and sound knowledge rather than by age, status, or family ties, and that a younger person may rightly call an elder to the truth. It also models gentle, respectful da'wah: the call is framed as an invitation to be guided together on a straight path, with kind address ('O my father') and no harshness or accusation.

translation: O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has ever been disobedient to the Most Merciful.
interpretation: Abraham's gentle plea to his father shows that idol worship is in reality obedience to Satan, since Satan is the one who makes false worship appealing and calls people to it. By stressing that Satan is disobedient to the Most Merciful, Abraham warns that following a rebel against God's mercy leads to sharing in his rebellion and his fate. He contrasts Satan's defiance with God's mercy, to show his father that turning away from the One who is merciful toward His creation in favor of His enemy is both ungrateful and ruinous.

translation: O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Gracious (the Most Merciful) will touch you, so that you become a companion (ally) of Satan.
interpretation: In this verse from Surah Maryam (19:45), Abraham addresses his idolatrous father with gentleness and compassion, using the affectionate 'O my father'. His concern is not about worldly harm but about a divine punishment that would befall his father if he persisted in worshipping idols. The verse teaches that persisting in disbelief is, in effect, taking Satan as a guardian and ally, and that the consequence of such allegiance is to share Satan's fate of punishment. Abraham's mention of God as 'the Most Gracious' shows that even the punishment comes from the One whose mercy is vast, and that it is warning and not hatred that motivates him: he fears for his father out of care, modelling a way of calling to the truth that combines sincere advice, courtesy toward parents, and clear warning about the consequences of misguidance.

translation: He said: 'Do you reject my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you. So leave me for a long while.'
interpretation: The verse shows how a father clings to inherited tradition and answers a gentle call to monotheism with threats instead of reasoning. Abraham's father does not engage with his arguments. He treats the rejection of the idols as a personal affront and responds with intimidation, which is the typical reaction of those who cannot defend their beliefs rationally. His command to Abraham to leave him 'for a long while' (or safely, unharmed) expresses the severing of family ties over a difference in faith. It teaches that the call to truth may cost a person even the closeness of his own family, and that the prophet's patience in the face of harshness is an example for every believer who meets hostility from loved ones.

translation: He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you; indeed, He has always been gracious to me."
interpretation: Ibrahim answers his father's threats and rejection with gentleness and dignity rather than retaliation. His greeting of 'salam' is a parting of peace, not an endorsement of his father's disbelief; it shows that a believer meets hostility with good manners and refuses to argue harshly even while separating from falsehood. His promise to seek forgiveness for his father expresses hope that God might guide him, and it rests on Ibrahim's own experience of God's kindness (hafiyy): since God has been so gracious to him, he trusts that God's mercy is vast enough to ask on behalf of others. Later, when it became clear that his father was an enemy of God, Ibrahim disassociated from him, so this promise reflects his earlier hope for his father's guidance.

translation: And I will withdraw from you and from what you invoke besides God, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be unfortunate in calling upon my Lord.
interpretation: Abraham, having been rejected by his father and his people, announces a principled separation from their idolatry, both physically and spiritually. He does not rely on them or their false gods but turns wholly to God in supplication. His 'perhaps' is not doubt about God's generosity but humility and good manners before Him: he does not presume that his prayer is owed an answer, yet he hopes that, unlike the idolaters whose prayers to idols bring them only loss and disappointment, his prayer to the One Lord will never leave him wretched or unanswered. The verse teaches that leaving falsehood for the sake of God is rewarded with His closeness, and that sincere prayer addressed to Him alone is never in vain.

translation: So when he had withdrawn from them and from what they worshipped besides God, We granted him Isaac and Jacob, and each of them We made a prophet.
interpretation: When Abraham left his people and their idolatry for the sake of God, accepting exile from home and family, God compensated him with something better than what he gave up. In place of the family and homeland he abandoned, God gave him righteous offspring: a son, Isaac, and a grandson, Jacob. God also raised both of them to prophethood, so his lineage became a continuing line of guidance. The verse teaches that whoever forsakes something for God's sake is repaid with a better and more blessed substitute, and that sincerity and sacrifice in the cause of truth bring both worldly and spiritual honor.

translation: And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy, and We granted them a tongue of truth, exalted.
interpretation: After Abraham, Isaac and Jacob turned away from their people and what they worshipped besides God, God rewarded them with His mercy, which includes prophethood, righteous offspring, provision and guidance. The phrase 'a tongue of truth, exalted' means that God gave them a lasting, honorable reputation: succeeding generations, across different faiths and communities, speak of them with praise, love and respect. Their good name was made to endure, truthful and lofty, as a worldly reward for their sincerity, alongside the greater reward awaiting them in the Hereafter.

translation: And mention in the Book Moses. Indeed, he was chosen (sincere), and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet Muhammad to recall Moses in the Qur'an as a model of devotion. He is described as 'mukhlas', one whose worship and purpose were purified for God alone, and whom God Himself selected and purified for His service. His sincerity was the foundation of his mission, which came in two ranks: as a prophet (nabi) who receives revelation and conveys news from God, and as a messenger (rasul) who is sent with a law and a message to a people, namely Pharaoh and the Children of Israel. The verse teaches that true sincerity before God precedes and underlies the high stations of prophecy and messengership, and that those who carry God's message must be pure in intention.

translation: And We called him from the right side of the Mount, and We brought him near in intimate converse.
interpretation: The verse describes Moses' moment of divine election: God summoned him from the side of Mount Sinai that lay to his right as he journeyed, and drew him into a special nearness in which God spoke with him directly, as one confides in a close companion. The call is not merely an audible sound but a sign of honor, showing that closeness to God is a gift He bestows on His chosen servants, and that revelation begins with God's initiative in addressing the human being and raising him to a rank of intimate communion, which prepared Moses for the prophetic mission he was about to undertake.

translation: And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:53) presents Aaron's prophethood as a pure gift of divine mercy, granted in answer to Moses' plea for a helper from his own family to share the burden of delivering the message to Pharaoh. It shows that prophethood is not earned by lineage or effort but bestowed by God's grace, and that God supports those who rely on Him by giving them companions and aid suited to their mission. It also honors the bond of brotherhood when it is devoted to a righteous purpose, since Aaron's role as a supporter of Moses became a means of mercy for both of them and for their people.

translation: And mention in the Book Ishmael. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: The verse holds up Ishmael as a model of integrity, naming faithfulness to one's word as his defining trait among the qualities of prophethood. The Qur'an singles out truthfulness in keeping promises because it is the foundation of trust between a servant and God and between people. Ishmael's reliability, shown in his patience and submission when he was tested, is presented as the moral character that qualified him for the office of messenger and prophet. The lesson for believers is that fulfilling commitments is a mark of true faith and a necessary quality for anyone who would carry a divine message.

translation: And he used to enjoin upon his family prayer and zakah, and he was, in the sight of his Lord, one with whom He was pleased.
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:55), speaking of Prophet Ismail, shows that true devotion begins at home: a believer's first responsibility in calling to righteousness is toward those closest to him. By commanding his family to uphold prayer, which binds a person to God, and zakah, which binds a person to society, he joined worship of the Creator with compassion for creation. His being 'pleasing to his Lord' indicates that God's acceptance is earned through sincere obedience and through guiding others by example, so that private faith becomes a lived, shared practice within one's household.

translation: And mention in the Book [the story of] Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth, a prophet.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet Muhammad, and through him every believer, to recall Idris as a model worth remembering. The key description is 'siddiq', meaning one whose speech, belief, and actions are consistently truthful and sincere, so that his inner conviction is confirmed by how he lives. It is joined with 'nabiyy', which shows that his integrity was the foundation of his prophethood: those who convey God's message must first embody honesty and faithfulness. The lesson is that closeness to God and elevated rank come through steadfast truthfulness in word, belief, and deed, and that such people deserve to be remembered and emulated.

translation: And We raised him to a high station.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:57) refers to the Prophet Idris, mentioned in the preceding verses as truthful and a prophet. The 'high station' is God's honoring of him with exalted rank, nobility, and nearness to Him because of his truthfulness, patience, and devotion. The elevation is understood chiefly as a spiritual rank, a lofty standing in God's sight and among the righteous, showing that true honor comes from sincerity and obedience to God rather than from worldly status.

translation: Those are the ones whom God favored among the prophets, from the offspring of Adam, and of those We carried with Noah, and from the offspring of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping.
interpretation: The verse sums up the line of prophets mentioned in Surah Maryam (Zechariah, John, Jesus, Abraham, Moses, Ishmael, Idris) and shows that their honor came from God's grace and choice, not from lineage alone. It describes the shared mark of those chosen: hearts so aware of God's majesty and mercy that His revelation moved them to humble prostration and tears. True nearness to God is shown through humility, gratitude and reverent fear when His words are recited, and believers are meant to follow this example of outward submission joined with inner emotion. The mention of the name 'the Most Merciful' suggests that their weeping came from love and awe of God's mercy, not only from fear.

translation: Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires; so they will soon meet with perdition.
interpretation: After the righteous prophets and their followers came generations who lost the spiritual and moral core of their faith. Neglecting prayer, whether by abandoning it or by delaying and emptying it of devotion, cut them off from remembrance of God and from accountability. Once that tie to God was loosened, their desires became their guide and their pursuit of pleasure unchecked. The verse shows that religious decline begins when worship is neglected and appetites take its place. 'Ghayy' means ruin, error, and the evil outcome of a misguided path, so the verse warns that such a people will meet the consequence of that deviation, namely loss and punishment, unless they repent, as the following verses allow.

translation: Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; such will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged in the least.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:60) shows that God's mercy remains open even to those who have fallen into neglect and sin, such as the generations that followed the prophets, neglected prayer, and pursued their desires. The door to salvation is open through three linked conditions: sincere repentance, which means turning back to God and leaving the sin; faith, which means correct belief and trust in Him; and righteous action, which proves that the repentance and faith are genuine. Whoever fulfills these will enter Paradise, and God will not diminish their reward in any way. Their earlier sins are forgiven by repentance, and their good deeds are fully counted without any loss or injustice, a sign of God's perfect justice and generosity.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever certain to be fulfilled.
interpretation: The verse tells us that Paradise is not a vague hope but a divine promise given by the Most Merciful, whose mercy is the very reason it is offered. The believers accept this promise on faith, without having seen it, and that unseen trust is what distinguishes them. God's pledge is bound to come true, so those who remain steadfast in repentance, faith, and righteous deeds can be fully confident that they will reach their everlasting home, and that no promise of God can fail or be delayed beyond His wisdom.

translation: They will not hear therein any idle talk, only 'Peace.' And therein they will have their provision morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse describes the condition of the people of Paradise (Maryam 19:62). Their blessed state is marked by a pure environment free of vain, harmful, or worthless speech, which stands for the removal of every source of annoyance and spiritual distress that burdens people in this world. The only speech they hear is salam: greetings of peace from the angels and from one another, along with the assurance of safety and the pleasure of their Lord. Their sustenance is ever-present and without lack, given to them 'morning and evening,' an expression of constant, uninterrupted abundance in a way people can understand. Paradise has no literal day and night as this world does, so the phrase conveys continual provision and honor. The verse teaches that true felicity is both material and moral, combining wholesome provision with a peaceful, clean-hearted society, and it encourages believers to guard their tongues and cultivate peaceful speech now if they hope for that company in the Hereafter.

translation: That is the Garden which We will give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Paradise is not gained by lineage, status, or wishful thinking, but is granted as a lasting inheritance to those whose lives were marked by taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that restrains a person from wrongdoing and moves them toward obedience. The word 'inherit' suggests that, just as an inheritance passes securely and by right to its heirs, Paradise is reserved by God's generous promise for the righteous, and it is ultimately a gift from Him rather than something earned by deeds alone. The phrase 'Our servants' honors the pious by linking them to God in devoted servanthood, showing that true nobility lies in humble piety.

translation: We [angels] do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And never is your Lord forgetful.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Gabriel and the angels (traditionally in answer to the Prophet's wish for Gabriel to visit more often), teaches that the angels have no independent will: they come and go only by God's permission and timing. The delay in revelation was therefore not neglect, since God's knowledge and dominion encompass everything past, future and present, and nothing slips His memory. Divine timing is wise and purposeful, so the believer should be patient and trust that God never forgets or abandons His servants.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any equal to Him?
interpretation: The verse grounds the command to worship in God's absolute lordship: since He alone created, owns, and sustains everything from the heavens to the earth and all between, He alone deserves devotion. The command to be steadfast in worship implies that worship is a continuing struggle, requiring patience against hardship, distraction, and the mockery of opponents, and it calls for constancy rather than occasional devotion. The closing rhetorical question, 'Do you know of any equal to Him?', challenges the listener to find anyone sharing His name, attributes, or right to be worshipped. The expected answer is none, so the verse affirms God's uniqueness and the folly of associating partners with Him.

translation: And man says, "When I am dead, will I truly be brought forth alive?" (Qur'an 19:66)
interpretation: The verse portrays the denial of resurrection by the human being who, judging by the limits of his own experience, finds it inconceivable that life could return after death and decay. His question is one of disbelief and mockery, not a sincere search for knowledge. The verses that follow answer it by reminding him that he was created from nothing before, and that the One who brought him into existence the first time is able to bring him back. Thus the verse exposes how forgetfulness of one's own origin leads to doubt about the Hereafter, and it invites reflection on the original creation as proof of the possibility of the second.

translation: Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:67) answers those who deny resurrection by appealing to their own origin. Since God brought human beings into existence from absolute nothingness, re-creating them after death is far easier and well within His power. Humans should reflect on their first creation, recognize their dependence on their Creator, and so accept the reality of the afterlife and be accountable for their deeds.

translation: By your Lord, We will surely gather them together with the devils, then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees.
interpretation: God swears by His lordship over the Prophet to affirm that resurrection and reckoning are certain, and that those who denied them will not rise as isolated individuals but will be assembled alongside the very devils who led them astray, showing that their end is tied to the companions they followed. They will then be made to stand around Hell kneeling in fear and helplessness, unable to stand because of the terror of what they see. Their kneeling is a humiliating public disgrace that strips away the arrogance they showed in the world, and it reveals that no power or status will protect them from the judgment about to be carried out.

translation: Then We will surely draw out from every sect those of them who were most insolent in their defiance against the Most Merciful.
interpretation: After resurrecting and gathering the disbelievers around Hell, God will separate each faction according to its sin and single out first the ringleaders, the ones most stubborn and rebellious against Him, who led others astray. They will be brought forward and dealt with first, since their guilt is greatest and their punishment will be proportionate to their arrogance and the misguidance they caused. This shows that divine justice discriminates between degrees of wrongdoing, and that those who lead others into disbelief bear a heavier burden than their followers.

translation: Then We surely know best those who are most deserving of being burned in it.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:70) affirms that God's knowledge is perfect and exact in assigning each person's fate. After describing the gathering of the deniers around Hell, it declares that God knows precisely who among them is most deserving of entering and burning in the Fire, since people differ in their degree of rebellion and arrogance against the Most Merciful. Punishment is therefore not arbitrary or uniform but proportioned to each person's deeds and the extent of their defiance, which shows divine justice and warns that no one's guilt is hidden or overlooked.

translation: There is not one of you but will come to it (the Fire). This is a decree from your Lord that must be fulfilled.
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:71) affirms that every human being will arrive at the Fire, an event God has irrevocably decreed. A widely held reading takes 'coming to it' to mean passing over the Sirat, the bridge stretched above Hell. The righteous cross safely and are saved by their faith and deeds, while the wrongdoers fall into it. The verse is a reminder to be mindful of the Hereafter, to live with God-consciousness, and to understand that deliverance comes only through God's mercy and the piety He enables, as the next verse states: 'Then We will save those who were righteous and leave the wrongdoers in it, on their knees.'

translation: Then We will rescue those who were mindful of God, and We will leave the wrongdoers in it (Hell), kneeling on their knees.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:72) follows the declaration that every person will come to Hell. It means that on the Day of Judgment all people will pass over or approach it, but God will then deliver the God-fearing from its torment, because of their piety and obedience, and bring them safely to Paradise. The wrongdoers, who persisted in disbelief and injustice, will be left there collapsed on their knees, helpless and terrified, unable to stand or escape. The verse teaches that salvation on that Day depends on taqwa, and that wrongdoing leads to humiliation and abandonment in the Hereafter, while God's justice and mercy distinguish the righteous from the unjust.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe: 'Which of the two groups is better in standing and finer as a company?' (Qur'an 19:73)
interpretation: When the disbelievers hear the clear revelations, they do not answer them with evidence. They turn to worldly status and argue that their wealth, comfortable homes, and large social gatherings prove they are favored and right, while the believers are mostly poor and have little standing. The verse shows the flawed reasoning of those who treat material prosperity and social prestige as a measure of truth or of closeness to God. The verses that follow answer this by reminding them how many earlier generations, who were richer in goods and appearance, were destroyed for rejecting the truth. Real worth is therefore found in faith and righteous deeds, not in worldly rank.

translation: And how many a generation have We destroyed before them, who were better in possessions and outward appearance.
interpretation: God warns those who boast of their wealth and status, as the disbelievers of Quraysh did, that worldly splendor offers no protection from His judgment. Many earlier nations possessed finer furnishings, greater riches, and more impressive appearance and standing than they do, yet when they rejected the truth and persisted in arrogance, God destroyed them. Material prosperity and a fine outward show are therefore not proof of God's favor or of being on the right path. The verse calls people to take heed from the fate of past nations and to measure worth by faith and righteous deeds rather than by luxury and display.

translation: Say: Whoever is in error, let the Most Gracious extend [life and respite] to him for a while, until, when they see what they were promised, either the punishment or the Hour, they will know who is worse in position and weaker in forces.
interpretation: The verse answers those who boasted of their wealth, status, and numbers as proof they were right. God tells the Prophet to say that being granted ease and a long respite is not a sign of divine approval but a test and a gradual drawing-out of the misguided, who are left to continue in their error. Their worldly comfort is only a delay, not a safeguard. When the promised reckoning arrives, whether as punishment in this life or the Hour itself, the illusion of strength will vanish, and it will become clear that the true losers in rank and the truly weak in support are those who relied on worldly power and rejected guidance, while the believers, though seemingly lowly, hold the better station.

translation: And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance. And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in outcome.
interpretation: Guidance is not a fixed state but grows: whoever accepts the truth and acts upon it, God rewards with further insight, steadfastness and ease in doing good, so that each step of obedience opens the way to the next. In contrast to the fleeting wealth, status and pride of the worldly-minded, the lasting good deeds, such as prayer, remembrance of God, charity and righteousness, are what truly profit a person. They are better in reward from God and better in their final return, because their fruit remains in the Hereafter when worldly possessions have vanished and those who relied on them are left with loss.

translation: Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, 'I will surely be given wealth and children'?
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:77) condemns the arrogance of a person who denies God's revelations yet presumes that worldly prosperity is his guaranteed due, as though wealth and offspring were proof of divine favor and a sign that he stands well with God. It teaches that material blessings are not a measure of one's standing before God, and that confidently claiming them while rejecting His signs is baseless presumption. The verse is traditionally linked to al-'As ibn Wa'il, who denied the resurrection and mocked Khabbab by saying that on the Day of Judgment he would be given wealth and children and then settle his debts. The rhetorical question 'Have you seen?' expresses astonishment at such audacity, and the following verses respond by asking whether he has access to the unseen or has made a covenant with God, thereby showing his claim to be empty and his punishment certain.

translation: Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant from the Most Merciful?
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:78) rebukes the disbeliever who boasted that he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter. God challenges the basis of such a claim by asking whether he has gained knowledge of the unseen, which belongs to God alone, or whether he has received a binding promise from God. Since he has neither, his confidence is baseless arrogance. The verse teaches that no one may presume a favorable outcome in the next life without revealed knowledge or a divine assurance, and that salvation rests on faith and righteous deeds, not on worldly prosperity or wishful thinking.

translation: Nay! We shall record what he says, and We shall extend for him the punishment, extending it greatly.
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:79) rejects the claim of the disbeliever who boasted that he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter, as he had been in this world. God's 'Nay' shows that his assumption is false and that worldly bounty is not proof of divine favor. His arrogant words are not lost: they are written in his record and will be held against him on the Day of Judgment. His punishment will not merely be applied but lengthened and multiplied, with no relief, as just recompense for his denial and for falsely claiming a promise from God that he never received.

translation: And We shall inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:80) answers the disbeliever who boasted that he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter. God says that all he claims to own and the status he boasts of will be taken from him at death and pass to God, the true inheritor of everything. He will stand before his Lord stripped of wealth, children, followers and power, with nothing but his own deeds. The verse teaches that worldly possessions and status give no security before God, and that only faith and righteous action count on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And they have taken gods besides Allah, so that they may be a source of honor and strength for them.
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:81) exposes the motive behind idolatry: people turn to false deities, whether idols, powerful figures, or other created things, seeking dignity, protection, and intercession. It teaches that true honor and power belong to God alone, and that whoever seeks glory through anything besides Him will find only weakness and disgrace. The false gods they rely on will not give them the might they hope for, as the next verse says, but will deny their worship and become adversaries against them on the Day of Judgment.

translation: No! They (the false gods) will soon deny their worship of them, and will become adversaries against them.
interpretation: The verse refutes the hope of those who took gods besides God, expecting them to be a source of honor and intercession. On the Day of Judgment, the very objects of their worship will disown the worshippers, rejecting their devotion and testifying against them.
