What they relied upon for strength and support becomes a cause of their disgrace and punishment. This shows that worship directed to anything other than God is not only futile but ultimately turns against the one who practices it.

translation: Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, urging them on and inciting them intensely?
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:83) shows that disbelief is not only a human choice but also a state in which God lets satanic forces hold sway over those who persist in rejecting guidance. The word 'ta'uzzuhum azzan' conveys a boiling, agitating pressure: the devils stir up the disbelievers' passions and doubts and push them continually toward sin, denial and opposition to the truth. It warns that whoever turns away from the remembrance of God leaves himself open to being driven by these forces, so he should take refuge in God and hold to faith to avoid their incitement.

translation: So do not be hasty against them; We are only counting out for them a (precise) number.
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:84) consoles the Prophet and instructs him not to hurry for the punishment of the deniers who persist in their wrongdoing. Their respite is not neglect: God keeps an exact account of their days, breaths, and deeds, and every moment is numbered until the appointed term arrives, at which point their reckoning will come at precisely the time God has decreed. The believer is therefore called to patience and trust in God's wisdom and timing, knowing that the wrongdoers' apparent ease is only a measured delay leading to a certain end.

translation: On the Day We gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as an honored delegation,
interpretation: The verse (Maryam 19:85) describes the honor given to the God-fearing on the Day of Resurrection. The word 'wafd' refers to a delegation that comes to a king as honored guests, welcomed and received with esteem, not driven or dragged. The righteous, who guarded themselves against disobedience in this world, are brought in dignity, often understood as riding in comfort, to the Most Merciful. The mention of the divine name 'al-Rahman' stresses that their reception is an act of God's mercy and generosity, and it stands in deliberate contrast with the disbelievers who are driven to Hell like thirsty herds in the next verse. The meaning is that taqwa in this life results in security, honor, and nearness to God in the next.

translation: And We will drive the criminals to Hell like thirsty herds driven to water.
interpretation: The verse depicts the humiliating fate of those who persisted in wrongdoing and rejected faith. The word 'wird' evokes thirsty animals herded to a watering place, but here the destination is not water that quenches; it is Hell. The righteous are gathered to the Most Merciful in honor and ease (as in the preceding verse), whereas the criminals are driven by force, in thirst, shame and helplessness, without choice or intercession. It teaches that the manner in which people are brought before God on the Day of Judgment reflects the course they chose in this life: those who ran after their desires and defied God's guidance are led, like beasts, to the end they earned.

translation: They will not have the power of intercession, except for those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment no one can intercede for another by his own right or status; intercession is possible only by God's permission. The only ones who are entitled to benefit from it, or to be granted it, are those who made a covenant with God in this life. That covenant is faith in God alone, sincere testimony that there is no god but Him, and adherence to His commands through righteous deeds. Salvation is therefore bound to a person's own commitment and belief, not to false reliance on idols, lineage, or imagined intercessors, and the verse warns the disbelievers who adopted false gods hoping for their intercession that such hope is groundless.

translation: And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."
interpretation: The verse condemns the claim, made by some Jews, Christians, and polytheistic Arabs who called the angels daughters of God, that God has begotten offspring. Taking a child implies need, limitation, and likeness to creation, whereas God is absolutely self-sufficient, unique, and beyond any partner or kinship. The use of the divine name 'al-Rahman' (the Most Merciful) heightens the offense: the One whose mercy encompasses all creation is in need of nothing, so ascribing a son to Him distorts the very nature of His lordship and mercy. The verse thus affirms strict divine oneness (tawhid) and rejects any attribution of offspring to God, a claim the following verses describe as so grave that the heavens would almost burst apart because of it.

translation: You have indeed brought forth something monstrous.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:89) comes as a condemnation of those who claim that the Most Merciful has taken a son. The word 'idd' denotes something so grave and terrible that it shakes the foundations of creation; the following verses say the heavens almost burst, the earth splits, and the mountains collapse in ruin at the claim. The verse teaches that attributing offspring or partners to God is not a trivial error of belief but an enormous wrong against divine oneness and majesty, and it calls the hearer to recognize the gravity of shirk and to hold fast to pure monotheism.

translation: The heavens are almost rent asunder by it, and the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruins.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:90) conveys the immense gravity of attributing a son to God (the preceding verse speaks of those who say the Most Merciful has taken a son). The verse personifies creation as reacting in horror: the heavens, earth, and mountains, which are among the most massive and stable features of the cosmos, nearly disintegrate at such a claim. The meaning is that shirk is not a trivial error of belief but an enormous affront to the truth of divine oneness and majesty, one that the whole of creation, which naturally glorifies and submits to God, recognizes as intolerable. It is a warning to humans to appreciate the seriousness of this sin and a reminder that creation bears witness to tawhid.

translation: That they attribute a son to the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:91) gives the reason for the cosmic outrage described in the preceding verse: the heavens nearly burst apart, the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin because people ascribe offspring to God. The claim is treated as a grave affront to divine oneness and majesty, not a minor error in belief. Using the name 'al-Rahman' (the Most Merciful) sharpens the point. The One whose mercy encompasses all creation has no need of a child, since offspring imply need, dependence, lineage and likeness to created beings, and God is exalted above all of these. The verse shows that creation itself recognizes God's absolute unity and transcendence, and that associating a son with Him is a violation so grave that it unsettles the order of the universe.

translation: And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a child.
interpretation: This verse (Maryam 19:92) declares that having offspring is utterly incompatible with God's nature. Taking a child implies need, limitation, and likeness to creation, whereas God is absolutely self-sufficient, eternal, and unique, with nothing resembling Him. The use of the name 'al-Rahman' stresses that God's mercy and perfection flow from His complete independence, not from any need for an heir or helper. The verse therefore refutes the claim that God has a son, affirming that such a claim diminishes the majesty of the Creator, who is far above it, and that every being in the heavens and earth comes before Him only as a servant.

translation: There is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he will come to the Most Merciful as a servant.
interpretation: This verse, following the claims that God has taken a son, teaches that every being, whether angel, human, or jinn, stands before God in the same relationship of servitude. No creature, however exalted, shares in divinity or stands in a relation of kinship to God. On the Day of Resurrection each will come alone, submissive, and fully dependent on God's mercy. The use of the name 'the Most Merciful' shows that God's sovereignty over all is exercised with mercy, and that creaturely status is not a humiliation but the true and honored place of every being before its Lord.

translation: He has indeed enumerated them and counted them precisely, one by one.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Maryam 19:94) affirms that God's knowledge encompasses every created being without exception. No one is overlooked or forgotten, and each person's existence, deeds, and fate are known and recorded exactly. It follows the declaration that everyone in the heavens and earth will come to the Most Merciful as a servant, so it stresses that on the Day of Judgment each individual will be held to account by One whose knowledge is complete and who neither errs nor neglects anyone. Those who attribute a child to God, and all others, are therefore fully accounted for before Him.

translation: And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment every person will stand before God stripped of all worldly support: no wealth, children, status, followers, or intercessors can accompany or shield them. Each soul will answer individually for its own deeds and intentions, so the verse reminds believers that salvation depends on personal faith and conduct, and that the ties and possessions people rely on in this life will not avail them there.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection.
interpretation: God promises that sincere faith joined with righteous action earns a gift of love: He will place love for the believers in the hearts of others and make them beloved to Him, to His angels, and to people, even among those who do not share their beliefs. This honor is not gained through worldly power, wealth, or self-promotion, but is bestowed by God's mercy (the name 'al-Rahman' is used here for that reason), as a reward in this life that anticipates the greater reward in the next. It also reassures the believers who were opposed and belittled in their early days: the esteem that opponents deny them is granted by God in the hearts of people.

translation: We have only made this Qur'an easy in your own tongue, [O Prophet], so that you may give glad tidings with it to the righteous and warn with it a people who are stubbornly contentious.
interpretation: God explains that the Qur'an was made easy by being revealed in clear Arabic, the Prophet's own language, so that its message could be understood without obstruction. Its purpose is twofold: to bring good news of God's pleasure and reward to those who are conscious of Him and guard themselves against wrongdoing, and to warn those who are obstinate in opposing the truth and who argue against it out of stubbornness rather than sincere inquiry. The ease of the message leaves no excuse for rejecting it, and shows that people's response depends on the state of their hearts, so that the same clear revelation becomes guidance for the God-fearing and a proof against the obstinate.

translation: And how many a generation have We destroyed before them! Do you perceive of them a single one, or hear from them even a whisper?
interpretation: The verse reminds the deniers of the message that earlier nations, many of them stronger and wealthier, were wiped out when they rejected God's guidance, and nothing remains of them: no person is seen and no faint sound is heard. It teaches that worldly power and numbers give no lasting protection, that God's judgment is certain, and that the only lasting outcome is one's standing with God. People should therefore take warning from the fate of past peoples instead of being deceived by present comfort or arrogance.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta-Ha.
interpretation: Ta-Ha belongs to the 'disjointed letters' (al-muqatta'at) that open a number of surahs, and their precise meaning is known only to God. One widely held interpretation is that these letters are a challenge and a reminder of the Qur'an's miraculous nature: the revelation is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs knew and used, yet they could not produce anything like it. The letters thus draw the listener's attention at the outset, signal that what follows is a divine address, and prepare the heart to receive the message of the surah, which comforts the Prophet Muhammad and affirms that the Qur'an was sent down not to cause hardship but as a reminder and mercy.

translation: We have not sent down the Qur'an to you, [O Muhammad], that you be distressed (Qur'an 20:2).
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet that the Qur'an was not revealed to burden him with hardship or anguish, whether through the grief he felt over his people's disbelief or through the exhausting effort of long night prayers. Rather, it is a mercy, guidance, and reminder for those who hold God in awe. His duty is to convey the message with ease, while guidance itself rests with God. The religion is thus one of ease and balance, not of unbearable strain.

translation: But only as a reminder for those who fear [Allah].
interpretation: The verse clarifies the purpose of the revelation: the Qur'an was not sent to burden or distress the Prophet (peace be upon him), as the preceding verse indicates, but to serve as a reminder and admonition. Its benefit is realized by those whose hearts are moved by awe of God, since fear of Him opens a person to receive guidance and to heed warnings. Those who are heedless or arrogant gain nothing from it, while those who fear God are awakened by it to faith and righteous action. Thus the Qur'an is a source of mercy and guidance, not hardship.

translation: A revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:4) grounds the authority of the Qur'an in the majesty of its source. The One who sent it down is the Creator of the earth and the lofty heavens, so this is no human composition or passing sentiment. It is a message from the Lord whose power spans the whole of creation. The verse implies that the same Lord who set the vast cosmos in order has sent this guidance to order human life, and that it is meant as a reminder and mercy, not a burden. Its weight and trustworthiness come from the greatness of the One who revealed it, which calls for humility, attentiveness, and obedience.

translation: The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty and majesty over all creation. His 'rising' over the Throne (the greatest of created things) signifies that He has complete dominion and governs every affair of the cosmos, while being utterly unlike His creation. Its mention alongside the name 'the Most Merciful' teaches that His rule is grounded in mercy, so the order of the universe and the guidance sent to humankind flow from His compassion. The mode of this rising is beyond human grasp and is affirmed in a manner befitting His transcendence, without likening Him to creatures or denying what He has said of Himself.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:6) affirms God's absolute and all-encompassing sovereignty over every level of creation: the heavens above, the earth, the space between them, and even what lies hidden beneath the damp earth, which is beyond human sight and reach. By naming the highest and the deepest realms, it shows that nothing in existence lies outside God's ownership, authority, and knowledge. The implication is that God alone deserves worship and trust, since He possesses and governs all things, and that nothing, however concealed, can escape His control. This also consoles the believer, who relies on the One whose dominion has no limits, and it establishes that the Qur'an being revealed comes from the Lord of all creation.

translation: And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is even more hidden.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:7) teaches that God's knowledge is absolute and does not depend on whether a person speaks loudly or quietly. Raising one's voice in prayer or supplication is unnecessary for God to hear, because He knows what is secret in the heart and even what is more concealed than that, such as thoughts and intentions a person has not yet become aware of or has not voiced. The believer should therefore approach God with sincerity and humility, conscious that nothing in the inner self is hidden from Him, and that prayer is a matter of the heart's honesty rather than of volume.

translation: Allah — there is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.
interpretation: The verse affirms that worship is due to God alone, because only He possesses every attribute of perfection. His names are 'most beautiful' because each one expresses complete, flawless qualities such as mercy, knowledge, power, justice and wisdom, with no deficiency or limit. Since these attributes belong to Him alone, no created being can share in divinity. The believer is therefore invited to know God through His names, to call upon Him by them in prayer, and to reflect their qualities in character, each in a manner fitting for a human servant, while recognizing that God's perfection is unmatched.

translation: Has the story of Moses reached you?
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:9) opens the account of Moses with a rhetorical question that is not a request for information but a way of arousing attention and preparing the Prophet Muhammad, and every listener, for a significant lesson. By recalling Moses, who was called to prophethood amid hardship, fear, and uncertainty, the verse offers consolation to the Prophet in the face of rejection by his people. It reminds him that God's chosen messengers have always been tested, then supported and given victory, so he should be patient and steadfast in conveying the message.

translation: When he saw a fire, he said to his family, "Stay here; I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance."
interpretation: The verse shows Moses (peace be upon him) in a moment of ordinary human need: lost and cold on a journey, he looks for warmth and directions. He seeks only a worldly benefit, yet God leads him through that humble search to the greatest guidance, which is prophethood and direct address from his Lord. The lesson is that when a person sets out in earnest to meet a need, and keeps his heart open to guidance, God may bring about something far greater than what he sought. His care for his family, by telling them to wait while he goes ahead, also shows responsible leadership and concern for those in his charge.

translation: So when he came to it, he was called: 'O Moses!'
interpretation: When Moses reached the fire he had seen from afar, expecting to find guidance or a burning brand for his family, what met him was no ordinary flame but a divine call addressed to him by name. The verse marks the turning point from a human errand to a prophetic encounter: the one who set out for warmth and direction was personally singled out by God and summoned into His presence. Being called by name signals intimacy and election, preparing Moses to receive revelation and the mission to confront Pharaoh. It also shows that God's guidance often comes in unexpected ways, meeting a person in the midst of seeking something ordinary and turning that moment into the beginning of a great responsibility.

translation: Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals; indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
interpretation: This verse is the divine address to Moses at the burning bush, and its command to take off his sandals teaches that encountering God calls for humility, reverence, and putting aside worldly attachments. The valley is sacred because of God's presence and revelation, not because of any inherent power in the place, and removing the sandals expresses readiness to receive the divine message with a humble heart and a body free from the dust and pride of the world. Declaring 'I am your Lord' first establishes that the command comes from the highest authority and prepares Moses for prophethood, which begins with submission to God alone.

translation: And I have chosen you, so listen to what is being revealed.
interpretation: God addresses Moses at the burning bush (Ta-Ha 20:13), telling him that his prophethood is a divine selection and not something he earned or sought. Since he has been singled out for this mission, the fitting response is complete, attentive listening and readiness to obey. The verse teaches that receiving revelation is a trust that calls for humility and focused attention, and that the one chosen by God must first become a listener before becoming a messenger. What follows in the next verse, the declaration of God's oneness and the command to worship and establish prayer, is the core of the message he is told to hear.

translation: Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.
interpretation: This verse, spoken to Moses at the burning bush (Ta-Ha 20:14), joins belief with practice: worship is owed to God alone because He alone is God, and prayer is the central act through which a person turns to Him. The phrase 'for My remembrance' means prayer exists to keep the heart conscious of God and to prevent heedlessness. Prayer is thus not a ritual performed for its own sake but a means of constantly renewing awareness of the Creator, so that faith is sustained in daily life.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is coming — I almost conceal it — so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Day of Judgment is certain, yet God keeps its exact time hidden, so much so that it is as though He would conceal it even from Himself, a figure of speech stressing the utmost secrecy. The concealment has a purpose: because no one knows when the Hour will come, people must remain constantly mindful, strive in righteousness, and never put off repentance and good deeds. The Hour will arrive so that perfect justice is done, and each person is repaid according to his or her own striving, whether good or evil, with nothing lost and no one wronged. Belief in the Hour thus becomes a motive for moral responsibility in this life.

translation: So let not he who does not believe in it (the Hour) and follows his own desire turn you away from it, lest you perish.
interpretation: The verse is a warning, addressed first to Moses and to every believer after him, to hold firmly to belief in the Hour and the Day of Reckoning. Those who deny the Hour do so because of no proof, only because they follow their own whims and desires, which free them from the moral accountability that belief would impose. Their disbelief is rooted in passion rather than reason. Believers must therefore not be swayed by such people, whether through argument, mockery, or social pressure, because yielding to them leads to ruin (tarda), meaning destruction in this world and the next. Steadfast faith in accountability is what guards a person against being drawn down by the desires of others.

translation: And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?
interpretation: God opens His address to Moses with a question about something utterly familiar, his staff. The question is not meant to gain information, since God knows what Moses holds. It draws Moses to acknowledge the object as an ordinary piece of wood, so that when it becomes a moving serpent he understands the miracle as God's direct power over creation and not a trick or a property of the staff. It also puts Moses at ease in the divine presence, since the question invites conversation, and it prepares him for the mission to Pharaoh, where he must trust that God can turn the ordinary into a sign of His might.

translation: He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it."
interpretation: Moses answers God's question about what is in his right hand with more than the simple answer required, and this shows the warmth of a servant who is glad to speak with his Lord. He lists the staff's everyday uses: it supports him as he walks, and he knocks leaves down from trees to feed his flock. He then adds that it serves other needs as well. The verse sets up what follows. The ordinary tool of a shepherd is about to become a sign of divine power when God commands him to throw it down and it turns into a serpent. The lesson is that the familiar means a person relies on are entirely under God's command. God can turn the simplest thing into a miracle, and a human being should recognize his own dependence and humility before God.

translation: He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:19) records God's command to Moses to cast down his staff, which he had just described as something he leans on, uses to beat down leaves for his flock, and finds other uses for. The command asks him to let go of the thing he relied on most, so that he would see for himself that God's power transforms it. When the staff became a moving serpent, Moses learned that what appears ordinary becomes a sign by God's will, and that true reliance belongs to God alone, not to any means. It also prepared him for his mission to Pharaoh, where he would depend on divine support rather than on material tools.

translation: So he threw it down, and behold, it was a snake, moving swiftly.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:20) shows God's power to change the nature of things at His command, and it is a sign given to Moses to strengthen his heart before he faces Pharaoh. The staff he leaned on and used for his daily needs became a living, moving serpent by God's will, which teaches that what seems ordinary and lifeless in human hands can become a vehicle of divine power when God wills. It also teaches that true support lies not in the means a person relies on but in God who controls them, so that Moses would trust God's help rather than material resources when he confronted Pharaoh's might.

translation: He said: "Take hold of it and do not fear; We shall return it to its former state."
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:21) records God's reassurance to Moses after his staff turned into a serpent. Moses fled in fear at the sight, so God commanded him to grasp it without dread, promising that it would revert to being an ordinary staff. The meaning is that whatever miracle or awe-inspiring sign God brings about is entirely under His control and cannot harm His chosen servant. Moses was being trained in trust: fear gives way to security once one obeys God's command, and the miracle was a sign of divine support to strengthen him for facing Pharaoh.

translation: And draw your hand close to your side; it will come out white, without any blemish, as another sign.
interpretation: After the sign of the staff turning into a serpent, God gives Moses a second miracle to confirm his prophethood before Pharaoh. By tucking his hand under his arm and withdrawing it, it would shine with a radiant whiteness, not from leprosy or any disease ("without blemish"), but as a divine sign. The command also carries reassurance: Moses is told to hold his arm close to his side, which calms fear, so that the miracles become a source of strength and certainty rather than terror. The verse teaches that God supports His messengers with clear, multiple proofs that attest to the truth of their message and strengthen their hearts for the mission ahead.

translation: So that We may show you of Our greatest signs.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Taha 20:23) follows God's miracles given to Moses, the staff turning into a serpent and the hand shining white when drawn from his side. The interpretation is that these were not mere wonders for display but a divine training and reassurance for Moses before he confronted Pharaoh. By witnessing signs of God's power firsthand, Moses would gain certainty and courage to carry out the mission, knowing that the One who sent him controls all things and can overcome the might of the tyrant. The phrase 'greatest signs' indicates that these miracles were among the most powerful proofs of God's authority, meant to strengthen the messenger's heart and to serve as evidence of the truth of his prophethood to others.

translation: Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed all bounds.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to Moses (peace be upon him), is a divine commission to confront tyranny directly. Pharaoh's 'transgression' (tughyan) is not merely personal wrongdoing but the overstepping of the limits proper to a created being: claiming absolute power and even divinity, oppressing the Children of Israel, and denying accountability to God. The command teaches that those who receive guidance bear the responsibility of calling even the most arrogant and powerful oppressors back to God, and that the reason for approaching them is their injustice and rebellion. It also shows that God sends a warner to the worst of sinners, offering them a chance to repent, as the following verses indicate with the instruction to speak to him gently.

translation: He said, "My Lord, expand for me my chest [grant me confidence and openness of heart]."
interpretation: This is Moses' prayer as he is commissioned to confront Pharaoh (Qur'an 20:25). By asking God to expand his chest, he seeks inner serenity, courage, patience, and clarity, so that fear, anxiety, and the weight of the mission do not hinder him. The verse teaches that before undertaking any great or difficult responsibility, one should first turn to God for strength of heart and calm of spirit, recognizing that outward success depends on inward readiness granted by Him.

translation: And ease for me my task.
interpretation: This is the prayer of Moses (peace be upon him) in Surah Ta-Ha (20:26), made after asking God to expand his chest. He knows that the mission of confronting Pharaoh and conveying the message cannot be accomplished by his own strength. He therefore asks God to remove obstacles and make the way easy. The verse teaches that success in any difficult undertaking, especially one done for God's sake, depends on divine facilitation. A believer should combine effort with humble supplication, seeking God's help to make hard tasks easy.

translation: And loosen the knot from my tongue.
interpretation: This is Moses' supplication in Surah Ta-Ha (20:27), made as he was commissioned to confront Pharaoh. Aware of an impediment in his speech, he asks God to remove whatever hindered his eloquence so that his message could be delivered clearly and be understood. The verse teaches that even a prophet does not rely on his own ability but seeks God's help for the task entrusted to him, and that a person should acknowledge his limitations before God and pray for the means to fulfil his duty. It also shows that effective communication of truth is a gift from God, and that sincere supplication is a proper preparation for any great responsibility.

translation: So that they may understand my speech.
interpretation: This is part of the supplication of Moses (peace be upon him) in Surat Ta-Ha (20:28), when he asked God to loosen the knot from his tongue. He did not ask for eloquence for its own sake but so that Pharaoh and his people would grasp his message clearly. The verse teaches that those who convey God's message should seek to make it clear and comprehensible, and that effective communication of the truth is a means by which hearts can be opened to guidance, while the success of that guidance ultimately remains with God.

translation: And appoint for me a minister from my family.
interpretation: This is part of the supplication of Moses (peace be upon him) in Surah Ta-Ha (20:29), made as he was commissioned to confront Pharaoh. Conscious of the weight of the prophetic mission and of his own limitations, including the impediment in his speech, he asks God to give him a helper who will share the burden of conveying the message. He asks for the helper to come from his own family because kin are the most trustworthy, the most likely to be sincere and supportive, and the most reliable in times of hardship. The verse shows that seeking help in a righteous cause is not a sign of weakness but an acknowledgment that strength comes from God, who provides the means. It also teaches that a person should rely on God while seeking out faithful companions for a great task. God answered by granting Aaron, his brother, as his partner in the mission.

translation: Aaron, my brother.
interpretation: In this verse (Qur'an 20:30), Moses asks God to appoint his brother Aaron as a minister and helper in the mission of confronting Pharaoh. Moses recognizes his own limitations, especially in eloquence, and understands that the weighty task of prophetic guidance is best carried out with a trusted, capable partner. The request shows that seeking support from righteous, reliable companions is not a sign of weakness but a wise and humble means of fulfilling a divine duty, and that such help is rightly sought through prayer to God, who grants it by His will.

translation: Strengthen my back with him.
interpretation: This is Moses' prayer in Surah Ta-Ha (20:31), asking God to strengthen him through his brother Aaron. The word 'azr' means strength or the back, which bears burdens, so Moses is asking that Aaron be made a source of support and firmness in carrying the heavy mission of confronting Pharaoh. The verse teaches that even a prophet seeks help from God through trustworthy companions, and that shared effort in a righteous cause is a divine gift that bolsters resolve and steadfastness.

translation: And let him share in my task.
interpretation: This is Moses' supplication in Surah Ta-Ha (20:32), asking God to make his brother Aaron a partner in the mission of delivering the message to Pharaoh. Moses recognizes that prophetic work is heavy and that support strengthens it, since Aaron was more eloquent and could help him convey the truth. The verse teaches that seeking help from righteous companions in the service of God is not a sign of weakness but a means of strengthening faith and effort, and that such assistance should be sought through prayer to God, who alone grants success.

translation: So that we may glorify You much.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 20:33) is part of Moses' supplication when he asks God to strengthen him with his brother Aaron as a partner in his mission. It shows that the purpose of seeking help and support is not worldly success but increased worship: with a companion in faith, one can persevere in glorifying God (tasbih) more frequently and sincerely. It teaches that righteous companionship and mutual support in the work of calling to God multiply remembrance and devotion, and that the believer's goals in any task should be to draw nearer to God and magnify Him.

translation: And that we may remember You much.
interpretation: This phrase is from Surah Ta-Ha (20:34), in the prayer of Moses when he asks God to make his brother Aaron a partner in his mission, so that together they may glorify God often and remember Him much. The verse shows that remembrance of God (dhikr) is strengthened by companionship and mutual support in righteousness. Those who carry a divine message are helped by a like-minded partner who keeps them mindful of God, so that constant devotion, in heart and tongue, sustains them through the hardship of the task.

translation: Indeed, You have always been Ever-Watchful over us.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:35) is part of Moses' supplication, said after he asked God to ease his task and to strengthen him with his brother Aaron so that they might glorify and remember God often. Moses grounds his requests in the fact that God knows his true condition. He knows Moses' weakness, his need for support, and the sincerity of his intention to serve the divine mission. Moses is asking for help not because God lacks knowledge of what is best, but because he acknowledges that God sees everything about them: their strengths, their limitations, and what will benefit the task of calling Pharaoh to the truth. The verse teaches that a servant should make supplication while humbly recognizing that God's all-seeing awareness encompasses his every need, and that God's past care is a reason to trust Him with the future.

translation: He said: 'You have been granted your request, O Moses.'
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:36) is God's answer to the supplications Moses made when he was commissioned to confront Pharaoh: that his heart be expanded, his task eased, the knot in his tongue untied so people would understand him, and his brother Aaron appointed as his helper. By saying 'You have been granted your request,' God shows that sincere prayer made in the course of a divine mission is answered, and that He supplies those He charges with a task with the means to carry it out. The address 'O Moses' is a mark of honor and reassurance, calming his fear and strengthening his resolve. The verse also teaches that a person should pair reliance on God with asking for specific help, and that God's response may come promptly and completely to those who submit to His command.

translation: And indeed, We bestowed Our favor upon you another time before.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:37) is addressed to Moses, reminding him that God's care for him did not begin with his prophetic mission. Before entrusting him with the message, God had already shown him favor at earlier moments in his life, which the following verses go on to recount: his rescue as an infant from Pharaoh's decree, his being cast into the river, and his being raised under God's watchful eye in Pharaoh's own household. The reminder is meant to reassure Moses as he is sent to confront Pharaoh, since the One who protected him when he was helpless and without power will surely support him now. It also teaches that divine favor comes before any merit, and that past kindnesses from God are grounds for trust and confidence in what lies ahead.

translation: When We inspired to your mother what was inspired,
interpretation: God reminds Moses (peace be upon him) of an early favor He granted him: when he was an infant under threat from Pharaoh's decree to kill the Israelite boys, God put into his mother's heart, by inspiration (wahy ilhām, not prophetic revelation), the guidance she needed to save him. The vague phrasing 'what was inspired' stresses the gravity and wonder of the matter, which was beyond ordinary human reckoning: to nurse him, and then, when she feared for him, to place him in a chest and cast it into the river, trusting that God would protect him and return him to her. The lesson is that God's care for those He chooses begins long before they are aware of it, and that He can bring safety out of what appears to be danger, so that Moses should have confidence in God's support as he faces Pharaoh.

translation: Place him in the chest, and cast it into the river; then let the river throw it onto the bank, and there an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him. And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you may be brought up under My eye.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's plan works through the very means that seem most dangerous. Moses' mother is told to put her infant in the river, which is the thing she would naturally fear most, and the river itself is made to obey God's command and deliver him to the bank. The enemy who would kill him, Pharaoh, becomes the one who shelters and raises him, so the tyrant's own household serves God's purpose of preparing the deliverer who will confront him. The words 'I cast upon you love from Me' mean that God put into hearts, beginning with Pharaoh's household, an instinctive affection for Moses, which protected him where force and strategy could not. 'Brought up under My eye' means that his upbringing was watched over and directed by God's care and guardianship at every stage. The lesson is that when a believer entrusts a matter to God and obeys, the outcome is secured by His power, even where all outward circumstances point to destruction.

translation: When your sister walked along and said, 'Shall I direct you to someone who will take care of him?' So We returned you to your mother so that her eye would be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a person, but We saved you from distress and tried you with severe trials. Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan. Then you came at the decreed time, O Moses.
interpretation: In this verse God reminds Moses of the successive favors He bestowed on him, showing that his whole life was carefully guided by divine providence. When Moses was an infant in Pharaoh's household and refused to nurse from the wet nurses, his sister's suggestion led him back to his own mother, which consoled her and ended her grief. Later, after he accidentally killed an Egyptian and feared for his life, God rescued him from anxiety and danger, and tested him through hardship and flight, which refined and prepared him. His years in Madyan were a period of preparation, and when he returned he came exactly at the time God had ordained for his prophethood, not by chance or by his own planning. The lesson is that God arranges events through hidden means and in due time, so Moses, who was being sent to confront Pharaoh, should trust that the One who protected him throughout his life will support him in his mission.

translation: And I have chosen you for Myself.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:41) is addressed by God to Moses after recalling the favors He bestowed on him. It means that God prepared, trained, and raised Moses under His own care and supervision, so that he would be a purified instrument of God's will and a messenger conveying His message. Moses was shaped by every event of his life, from the river to Pharaoh's palace to Midian, to serve God's purpose rather than his own or anyone else's. The verse stresses that prophethood is a divine selection and gift, not something earned by personal merit, and that the messenger's role is wholly devoted to God, who made him ready for the mission of confronting Pharaoh.

translation: Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me.
interpretation: God commissions Moses and Aaron for their mission to Pharaoh, equipping them with the miracles He has given them as proof of their truthfulness. The command not to grow weak or negligent in His remembrance teaches that remembrance of God is the true source of strength for anyone facing a tyrant. Constant awareness of God, through invocation, reliance upon Him, and obedience, sustains the messengers through hardship and keeps them steadfast. The message is that the mission's success depends not on worldly power but on a living connection with God, so that neither fear of Pharaoh nor the length and difficulty of the task should cause them to falter in it.

translation: Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed all bounds.
interpretation: This verse records God's command to Moses and Aaron to carry His message to Pharaoh, giving the reason for the mission: Pharaoh had exceeded the limits of servitude to God through tyranny, arrogance, and claiming lordship over others. The verse teaches that tyranny and oppression are to be confronted with the call to truth, and that even the most arrogant ruler is owed a direct summons to repentance. The mission is sent to him precisely because his transgression harms himself and his people, and God offers him the chance to return before judgment, as the following verses show by instructing the two prophets to speak to him gently.

translation: And speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he may be reminded or fear [God].
interpretation: God instructs Moses and Aaron, as they set out to confront Pharaoh, the most arrogant tyrant of their age, to approach him with courteous, soft words rather than harshness. The lesson is that the call to truth is most effective when delivered with gentleness and respect, since a kind tone can soften hearts and open the way to reflection. The phrase 'perhaps he may be reminded or fear' shows that the duty of the messenger is to convey the message in the best manner, while the outcome remains with God. If even Pharaoh was to be addressed gently, then all the more should believers speak gently when inviting others to the truth, always hoping for their remembrance and awe of their Lord.

translation: They said: "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten to harm us or that he will transgress."
interpretation: This is the plea of Moses and Aaron when God commands them to go to Pharaoh (Surah Taha 20:45). It shows their human fear of Pharaoh's tyranny, either that he would act rashly and punish them before they could deliver their message, or that he would exceed all bounds in arrogance and oppression against them. Their honest admission of fear, voiced to God rather than concealed, demonstrates that the prophets were not free of natural human anxiety, yet their response was to turn to their Lord and seek His reassurance. It teaches that fear of an oppressor is best brought before God, who then answers it with His promise of protection, as the next verse does: 'Fear not; indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see.'

translation: He said: "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see."
interpretation: God answers the fear of Moses and Aaron as they are sent to confront Pharaoh, a tyrant who threatened them. His assurance that He is with them is a promise of support, protection and watchful care, not just awareness. Because He hears every word Pharaoh speaks and sees every action taken against them, nothing can happen to them without His knowledge, and He will not let Pharaoh harm them or defeat their mission. Anyone who carries out a divinely appointed duty can therefore face even the most powerful opposition with calm trust, since fear loses its hold when one is certain that God is near and attentive.

translation: So go to him and say: 'We are two messengers of your Lord, so send the Children of Israel with us and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace be upon those who follow the guidance.'
interpretation: In this verse God instructs Moses and Aaron on how to deliver their message to Pharaoh. Their mission has two aims: to affirm that they speak on behalf of the Lord of Pharaoh himself, and to demand the liberation of the Children of Israel from bondage and oppression. The call is presented with a clear proof, a sign from God, so that it rests on evidence and not on mere claim. The closing words, 'peace be upon those who follow the guidance,' are not a greeting alone but a promise: safety and well-being in this life and the next belong to those who accept the truth, which implies a gentle warning that those who reject it forfeit that peace. Thus the verse shows the prophetic method of combining a firm demand for justice with an invitation to guidance.

translation: It has certainly been revealed to us that the punishment will fall upon whoever denies and turns away.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ta-Ha (20:48), is part of what Moses and Aaron were told to say to Pharaoh. It teaches that divine punishment is not arbitrary but follows from a conscious choice: rejecting the truth in the heart and tongue (denial), and then refusing to act on it or obey (turning away). The message is a warning that is also a mercy, since it sets out clearly beforehand what leads to ruin. It implies that safety lies in accepting the message and following its guidance, and that those who hear the call and still persist in rejection bear responsibility for the consequences.

translation: He (Pharaoh) said: "Who then is the Lord of you two, O Moses?"
interpretation: Pharaoh's question is addressed to both Moses and Aaron, but he singles out Moses by name because Moses was the main speaker and the leader of the mission. The question reflects Pharaoh's arrogance and his refusal to acknowledge any authority above himself. By asking "who is your Lord?" he treats the claim of a lord other than himself as strange and unfamiliar, since he had presented himself to his people as their supreme lord. The verse shows how tyranny and pride lead a person to feign ignorance of the Creator, and it sets up Moses's reply, which points to God through His creation and guidance (the following verse: 'Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form and then guided it').

translation: He said: Our Lord is the One who gave everything its created form and nature, then guided it.
interpretation: Moses answers Pharaoh's question about who his Lord is by pointing to a Lord known through His works rather than through titles. God gave every creature the particular constitution and form suited to its role, then guided it to fulfil that role. Each being is led to what it needs, such as the infant to the breast, the bee to its hive, and the human being to livelihood and to truth. Such precise design and purposeful guidance cannot come from a mortal claiming lordship. They point to one Creator who both creates and directs, and so Pharaoh's claim to divinity is refuted.

translation: He (Moses) said: "Then what is the state of the earlier generations?"
interpretation: This is Moses's reply to Pharaoh, who asked him about the earlier generations after Moses had presented the message of the Lord who created and guided all things (Surah Ta-Ha 20:51). Pharaoh was trying to divert the discussion and cast doubt on the message by pointing to his ancestors, who had not followed it. Moses's answer in the next verse (20:52) shows that he did not try to speculate about their fate: knowledge of them is with his Lord in a record, and his Lord neither errs nor forgets. The lesson is that the fate of past generations is a matter of God's perfect, all-encompassing knowledge and justice, and that appealing to the practices of ancestors is no valid argument against the truth. Each person must respond to the guidance brought to them and not be distracted by questions that lead away from it.

translation: He said, 'The knowledge of them is with my Lord in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets.'
interpretation: Moses answers Pharaoh's question about the fate of past generations by returning all knowledge to God. Nothing about those nations, their deeds, and their outcomes is lost, because it is all preserved in a Record with God. The verse also denies any deficiency in God's knowledge. He does not err, meaning He never misses or mistakes anything, and He does not forget, meaning nothing once known slips from Him. So every generation will be fully and justly accounted for, and Moses does not speculate about what only God knows.

translation: He who made the earth a cradle for you, and threaded paths for you through it, and sent down water from the sky, and by it We have brought forth pairs of diverse plants.
interpretation: The verse points to God's lordship and care for humankind as the proof that He alone deserves worship. The earth is made stable and gentle like a cradle so that people can live on it. Paths, whether valleys, mountain passes or routes between lands, are opened so that people can travel, trade and find their needs. Rain falls from the sky and revives dead land, bringing forth many kinds of plants in pairs, differing in taste, color, shape and benefit, some as food for people and some as fodder for animals. The sequence of these blessings is meant to move the reflective person from enjoying the gifts to recognizing the Giver, so that gratitude and exclusive devotion to God follow, and so that the order and variety in creation are seen as signs of a single wise and powerful Creator who has no partner.

translation: Eat and pasture your livestock. Indeed, in that are signs for those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse presents the provision of food and grazing land as evidence of God's care and power, not merely as a favor to be consumed heedlessly. Rain, plants, and animals form a connected system that humans did not create, and people of sound intellect (ulu al-nuha, those whose minds restrain them from folly) will reason from this order to recognize a wise Creator who sustains life. Such reflection should lead to gratitude, humility, and acknowledgment of God's oneness and of the resurrection, since the One who revives dead land can also revive the dead.

translation: From it (the earth) We created you, and into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you forth another time.
interpretation: The verse reminds human beings of their humble origin and certain destiny, set out in three stages: creation from the earth's clay, return to it in death and burial, and resurrection from it on the Day of Judgment. The same earth that nourished and sustained life is also the place of its end and its renewal. This should lead a person to humility and to the recognition that the One who originated them from dust is fully able to raise them again, so that they must prepare for accountability before God rather than be arrogant or heedless, as Pharaoh was when Moses reminded him of these signs.

translation: And We certainly showed him (Pharaoh) all of Our signs, but he denied and refused.
interpretation: The verse (Ta-Ha 20:56) tells that Pharaoh was not rejected for lack of proof: God showed him through Moses the full range of clear signs, such as the staff turning into a serpent, the shining hand, and the plagues. His rejection was therefore an act of stubborn arrogance and not of ignorance. 'He denied' means he called the signs and the message false in his heart and speech, and 'he refused' means he would not submit, obey, or let the Children of Israel go. The lesson is that guidance fails to benefit a person whose pride and attachment to power close him to the truth even after the evidence is completely clear, and that this leaves him fully accountable for his rejection.

translation: He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Moses?"
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:57) records Pharaoh's accusation against Moses, in which he recasts a message of divine truth as a political and sorcery-based threat. By calling Moses' signs 'magic', Pharaoh tries to discredit the miracles in the eyes of his people, and by claiming that Moses wants to expel them from their land, he stirs up fear for their homeland, security and status. The verse shows a common tactic of tyrants who face a call to truth: they slander the messenger, claim his real motive is worldly power, and play on the public's attachment to land and interests so that people reject the message without considering its evidence.

translation: "Then we will surely bring you magic like it, so set an appointment between us and you, which neither we nor you will fail to keep, at a place equally convenient [to both]."
interpretation: In this verse (Ta-Ha 20:58), Pharaoh responds to Moses' signs by dismissing them as mere sorcery and challenging Moses to a public contest. His demand for a fixed, binding appointment in a neutral place shows that he wanted to settle the matter before the people and use his own authority and magicians to discredit Moses. Yet the setting of a public meeting served God's plan: it gave the truth a visible stage, so that when Moses' staff overcame the magicians' tricks, the difference between divine miracle and human illusion would be clear to everyone, and the falsehood Pharaoh relied on would be exposed through the very challenge he proposed.

translation: He (Moses) said: "Your appointment is the day of the festival, and let the people be assembled when the sun has risen high (in the forenoon)."
interpretation: Moses chooses a time and setting that would make the contest with Pharaoh's magicians open and undeniable. The day of the festival was one when the whole population gathered, and the forenoon offered full daylight, so nothing could be hidden or disguised. By asking that the people be assembled publicly, Moses shows his confidence in the truth of his message. He wanted the clash between truth and falsehood to take place before everyone, so that the sign of God would be seen clearly and no one could later claim it was trickery or done in secret.

translation: Then Pharaoh turned away, gathered his scheming (his magicians and his plots), and then came.
interpretation: After witnessing the sign of Moses, Pharaoh did not take heed but turned his back on faith and devoted himself to opposing the truth. He mustered all his means of deception, namely his sorcerers, his stratagems, and his forces, to confront Moses, and then he came out to the appointed gathering to challenge him. The verse shows that arrogance leads a person to answer clear evidence with intensified plotting rather than reflection, and that falsehood relies on organized schemes while truth relies on God's support.

translation: Moses said to them: "Woe to you! Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment. And whoever invents a lie has certainly failed."
interpretation: Moses warns Pharaoh's magicians that denying the truth of his message, or attributing falsehood to God by calling His signs sorcery or claiming partners with Him, is a grave crime. The word 'woe' is an urgent and compassionate admonition, not merely a curse. He cautions that such fabrication invites God's total uprooting and annihilation of them through a punishment that leaves no trace, as befell earlier peoples who rejected their messengers. He closes with a general principle: whoever fabricates lies about God is bound to be disappointed and lose, because falsehood cannot endure against divine truth, and his efforts will end in ruin in this world and the next.

translation: So they disputed among themselves about their affair, and they kept their private counsel secret.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ta-Ha (20:62), describes Pharaoh's magicians after Moses warned them not to invent lies against God. Moses' words shook their confidence, and they fell into disagreement about how to respond to him. Some wavered, sensing that his message carried the weight of truth, while others held to confronting him. Their hushed consultation shows inner doubt: those who seek to oppose a clear truth cannot be united or certain, and the whispered deliberation reveals the unease of people who feel the force of the message even as they prepare to resist it. It also shows how truth, spoken plainly, can unsettle even its opponents and split their ranks.

translation: They said: "These two are indeed two magicians who want to drive you out of your land by their magic and to do away with your exemplary way of life."
interpretation: The verse shows how Pharaoh's circle, hearing Moses and Aaron, responded to their message with political fear and slander rather than reasoned argument. By calling the two prophets 'magicians,' they discredited the divine signs as mere trickery. They also stirred up the people's attachment to their homeland and inherited way of life, claiming the two intended to expel them and destroy their 'most excellent' tradition. This is the common tactic of entrenched power: it paints a call to truth as a threat to security, land, and social order, so as to rally the masses against reform and shield its own authority and interests.

translation: So gather your plan, then come in a line. And whoever overcomes today has indeed succeeded.
interpretation: These are the words of Pharaoh's magicians to one another as they prepare to face Moses. They urge themselves to settle on a single, unified plan, to use all their arts and tricks together, and to present themselves in an orderly, united rank so as to awe Moses and the onlookers. They believe that victory belongs to whichever side prevails that day, so they treat the contest as decisive. The verse shows how falsehood relies on coordination, display, and worldly pride, and it contrasts this with the truth Moses brings, which will soon expose their confidence as misplaced.

translation: They said, "O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw."
interpretation: The magicians' words show their confidence and their wish to treat the contest as a fair, courteous match. By offering Moses the choice of who throws first, they imply that they are sure of victory whatever the order. Moses's reply, "Throw," lets their tricks be exposed before the truth overturns them. This shows that falsehood relies on display and bravado, while truth, with God's support, can wait calmly and prevail. The verse also prepares the reader for the miracle that follows, in which Moses's staff swallows their illusions and the magicians recognize the truth and believe.

translation: He said, "Rather, you throw first." Then behold, their ropes and their staffs appeared to him, by their magic, as though they were moving swiftly.
interpretation: Moses, peace be upon him, lets the magicians act first, which shows his confidence in God's support and allows the truth to be revealed after their falsehood is fully displayed. The ropes and staffs did not truly change; the magicians' sleight of hand worked on the senses and imagination, so they only seemed to be live, darting serpents. This shows that sorcery is illusion, not a real transformation of creation, and that even a prophet experienced the natural human reaction of fear and awe at the sight, which prepares for God's reassurance to him in the next verses and for the clear contrast between trickery and a true miracle.

translation: And Moses sensed fear within himself.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:67) describes Moses' human reaction after the sorcerers cast down their ropes and staffs and they appeared to him to move like serpents. His fear was not cowardice or doubt in God's promise, but a natural instinctive reaction of a human being facing a dazzling illusion, and also concern that the people might be misled by the magicians' display and doubt the truth he brought. The verse shows that even prophets experience natural human emotions, while their trust in God remains firm. This fear was soon answered by divine reassurance in the following verses: 'Fear not, for you are the superior one,' directing him to throw down what was in his right hand.

translation: We said, 'Do not fear; indeed, it is you who are the superior one.' (Qur'an 20:68)
interpretation: When Moses saw the magicians' ropes and staffs seeming to move like snakes, a momentary fear came over him. God spoke to reassure him, affirming that he would prevail because he stood on truth and had divine support, while the magicians relied on illusion and trickery. The verse teaches that those who uphold the truth with God's backing need not fear the apparent power of falsehood. Fear is a natural human reaction, but God's promise of victory outweighs it. Worldly displays of power are fleeting and cannot withstand the truth that God supports.

translation: And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have crafted. What they have crafted is only the trickery of a magician, and the magician does not succeed, wherever he may come from.
interpretation: God commands Moses to cast down his staff, which will devour the ropes and staffs that Pharaoh's magicians have made to appear as moving serpents. The verse reassures Moses that his fear is unfounded, because the magicians' feats are only illusion and artifice, a product of human skill and deception, whereas his sign is a real miracle from God. It sets out a principle that falsehood, however dazzling or well staged, cannot ultimately prevail over truth supported by divine power. Sorcery rests on trickery and has no real reality or lasting success, wherever and by whatever means the magician operates, and so the staff's victory exposes the magicians' work as empty and prepares them to recognize the truth of Moses' message.

translation: So the magicians were cast down in prostration; they said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."
interpretation: The verse shows the overwhelming power of truth when it is manifest. The magicians, who were the greatest experts in their craft, recognized that what Moses brought was not sorcery but a genuine sign from God, because only they could tell the difference between illusion and a true miracle. Their sudden prostration, described as being 'cast down' as if moved by a force beyond their own will, shows that faith came upon them through divine guidance and the clarity of what they witnessed, not through gradual persuasion. By declaring belief in the 'Lord of Aaron and Moses' rather than in Pharaoh, they publicly rejected Pharaoh's claim to lordship, and chose submission to the one true God over worldly power, status, and reward. It teaches that sincere knowledge leads to humility before God, and that a person's expertise may become the very means by which they recognize the truth.

translation: He said: "Did you believe in him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more enduring."
interpretation: Pharaoh, shaken by the magicians' sudden submission to Moses' God, responds with tyranny rather than reason. He treats faith as something that requires the ruler's permission, exposing his claim to absolute authority over people's hearts and consciences. Unable to refute the clear sign they witnessed, he slanders Moses by alleging a conspiracy, calling him the magicians' master, in order to discredit the miracle and preserve his image before the people. He then threatens brutal, humiliating punishments: mutilation on opposite sides and public crucifixion on palm trunks, so as to terrorize others from following the truth. His boast that he will show 'which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting' reveals the arrogance of worldly power that relies on force, and ironically sets up the contrast the magicians answer next: the lasting reward and punishment lie with God, not with any tyrant.

translation: They said: "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us and over Him who created us. So decree whatever you are going to decree; you can only decree concerning this worldly life."
interpretation: This verse records the answer of Pharaoh's magicians after they recognized the truth of Moses' miracle and believed. Their faith was grounded in certain knowledge, so they refused to trade the clear signs and their Creator for the favor or fear of a tyrant. They declared that Pharaoh's power is limited: whatever punishment he imposes, whether threats, torture or execution, can touch only their brief earthly life, while the Hereafter and the final judgment belong to God alone. The verse teaches that real faith gives a person courage against oppression, because the believer weighs worldly loss against eternal reward and counts the worldly loss as small.

translation: Indeed, we have believed in our Lord so that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which you compelled us. And Allah is better and more enduring.
interpretation: The magicians, having seen the truth of Moses' sign, declare that their faith is a sincere turning to God in hope of His pardon. They do not seek safety from Pharaoh's threats but seek forgiveness for their past wrongs, including the sorcery they practiced under his coercion. By saying that God is better and more lasting, they set the eternal reward and mercy of the Lord against Pharaoh's fleeting worldly power, rewards and punishments. True faith rests on valuing what endures with God above what a tyrant can give or take away, which gives the believer steadfastness in the face of persecution.

translation: Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a wrongdoer, for him is Hell; he will neither die in it nor live.
interpretation: The verse warns that anyone who meets God having persisted in grave sin and disbelief, without repentance, will face a punishment that never ends. The phrase 'neither die nor live' means that death, which would end suffering, never comes, and the life he has is not a true life of ease, comfort, or fulfillment. It is a mere continuation of existence in torment. The verse stresses that accountability is certain, and that the criminal's fate is a just consequence of the choices made in this world.

translation: But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds, for such are the highest ranks.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true standing with God rests on faith joined with action: belief alone is incomplete without righteous works, and works are not accepted without faith. Those who meet God on the Day of Judgment in this state are raised to the loftiest degrees of Paradise, so that rank in the Hereafter is set by the sincerity of one's faith and the quality of one's deeds, not by worldly status. It also contrasts with the preceding verse about the criminal who comes to his Lord and finds Hell. The two verses together show that each person's final destination is decided by the state in which they meet God.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide eternally. And that is the reward of whoever purifies himself.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Paradise is not a random gift but the fitting recompense for tazkiyah, the inner and outer purification of the self. Purification means cleansing the heart of disbelief, arrogance, and sin, and nurturing it with faith, sincerity, and righteous deeds. Those who strive to refine their souls in this world are rewarded with an everlasting home of lasting peace and abundance, symbolized by flowing rivers and gardens of eternal dwelling. The closing phrase links the moral quality of a person's character to their ultimate destiny, showing that spiritual cleanliness is the path to eternal felicity.

translation: And We certainly inspired to Moses: 'Travel by night with My servants and strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken nor being afraid.'
interpretation: This verse shows God's care for the believers He saves when they are most vulnerable. Moses is commanded to leave Egypt by night with the Israelites, and when the sea blocks their way, God makes the means of rescue out of the very obstacle. The sea becomes a dry road through a miracle that comes by divine command and not by human power. The assurance 'fear not being overtaken, nor be afraid' addresses both outward danger from Pharaoh's pursuing army and the inner fear that comes with it. The lesson is that when a person obeys God's command and trusts in Him, God removes both the danger and the fear, and opens a path where none seemed possible.

translation: So Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers, and the sea covered them—covered them completely with what covered them.
interpretation: The verse shows that Pharaoh's arrogance and pursuit of the believers led directly to his destruction. The repeated phrase 'what covered them' (ma ghashiyahum) deliberately leaves the scale of the calamity unspoken, conveying that the overwhelming waters were so terrible and total that words cannot describe them. The very sea that opened as a path of salvation for Moses and the Children of Israel became the means of punishment for those who oppressed them. It reminds us that worldly power and armies cannot protect anyone against God's decree, and that God's help for the oppressed arrives in ways that overturn the plans of tyrants.

translation: And Pharaoh led his people astray, and he did not guide them.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Ta-Ha (20:79) shows that Pharaoh's leadership was a source of ruin, not guidance. He misled his people by presenting falsehood as truth, claiming divinity and rejecting Moses' message, and he led them to follow him to destruction in the sea. The added phrase 'and he did not guide' refutes his earlier claim, 'I only show you what I see and I guide you only to the path of right conduct' (40:29). The verse teaches that a leader who calls people away from God's guidance only brings them to loss, and that those who blindly follow such a ruler share in the consequences of their choice.

translation: O Children of Israel, We delivered you from your enemy, and We made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and We sent down upon you manna and quails.
interpretation: In this verse (Ta-Ha 20:80) God reminds the Israelites of the series of favors He gave them so that they would be grateful and obedient instead of turning to idolatry or disobedience. First came deliverance from Pharaoh's tyranny, which was a favor of safety and freedom. Then came the appointment at the right side of Mount Sinai, where Moses received guidance and revelation, a favor of religious and moral direction. Finally came the provision of manna and quails in the wilderness, which was a favor of sustenance requiring no labor. Together these blessings cover protection, guidance, and livelihood, and they imply that those who receive such abundant grace owe God thankfulness and steadfast obedience, and should not stray after the calf or transgress the limits He set.

translation: Eat of the good things We have provided for you, and do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and he upon whom My wrath descends has certainly fallen.
interpretation: God permits people to enjoy the wholesome provisions He has granted, but warns that enjoyment must stay within the limits He has set. Transgression here means ingratitude, wastefulness, taking what is unlawful, or forgetting the Provider by using His gifts to rebel against Him. Such abuse of blessings invites divine anger, and whoever earns it is ruined, like one who falls from a height into destruction, losing both his worldly standing and his hope in the Hereafter. The verse teaches that gratitude and moderation preserve blessings, while arrogance and excess bring about downfall.

translation: And indeed, I am Ever-Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided.
interpretation: God's forgiveness is vast but is tied to a complete path: sincere repentance from sin, true faith in the heart, righteous action that proves the faith, and then steadfastness upon guidance until the end. Forgiveness is not granted for empty claims or a momentary change; it is for those who turn back to God and keep to the straight path. The verse, addressed after the warning about the Children of Israel's worship of the calf, shows that no sin, even the gravest, closes the door of mercy to one who returns and persists in guidance.

translation: "And what made you hasten away from your people, O Moses?"
interpretation: In Surah Ta-Ha (20:83), God asks Moses why he came ahead of his people to the appointed meeting at Mount Tur. The question is not a request for information, since God knows the reason. It gently draws Moses' attention to the fact that he left his community behind in his eagerness for the encounter. Moses' reply in the next verse, that they are close behind him and that he hurried to please his Lord, shows that eagerness to meet God is praiseworthy, but a leader must still balance it with responsibility toward those entrusted to him. This is underscored by the news that follows: in his absence, his people were tested and led astray by the Sameri into worshipping the calf.

translation: He said: They are close behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased.
interpretation: Moses explains to God why he arrived at the appointed meeting place ahead of his people: his haste was not carelessness or abandonment of them but eagerness to please his Lord. The verse teaches that hurrying toward obedience and seeking God's approval is the highest motive for action, and that the believer's foremost aim is to earn divine pleasure. It also shows the humility of a prophet who, even while giving his reason, addresses God directly as 'my Lord' and places God's satisfaction above everything else, though his haste still left his people behind and exposed them to trial.

translation: He said: "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."
interpretation: God informs Moses, who has gone up the mountain to receive the revelation, that his people have been put through a trial in his absence. Their faith was tested, and many failed it. The trial was real, but the responsibility for the misguidance lies with the Samiri, who fashioned the golden calf and presented it to them as a god. The verse shows that God's testing does not remove human accountability. The people were tested, yet they chose to follow a deceiver instead of holding fast to the covenant and to the guidance of Moses and Aaron. It also warns that a community's faith can be fragile and quickly lost when its prophet is absent, if it is not firmly grounded in understanding and conviction.

translation: So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Then did the period of the covenant seem too long for you, or did you want wrath from your Lord to descend upon you, so you broke your promise to me?"
interpretation: After receiving the revelation on the mountain, Moses came back and found his people worshipping the calf. His anger was at their betrayal and his grief was over their misguidance. He rebukes them with questions that expose their lack of excuse. God had promised them guidance, the Torah, and honor if they remained faithful, and that promise was true and beautiful. Moses asks whether the time had been so long that they forgot it, which they could not plausibly claim since only a short time had passed. If not, then their act amounted to deliberately inviting God's wrath, since idolatry brings divine anger. The verse teaches that breaking a covenant with God is not a matter of forgetfulness or delay but a willful choice with serious consequences. It also shows that a righteous leader responds to deviation with righteous anger tempered by sorrow, and that he appeals to his people's conscience and to God's past favors in order to bring them back to the truth.

translation: They said: 'We did not break our promise to you of our own accord, but we were made to carry burdens of the people's ornaments, so we threw them [into the fire], and thus did the Samiri cast [his].'
interpretation: The Israelites, questioned by Moses after he returned and found them worshipping the calf, offer an excuse that shifts the blame from themselves.
