They claim they did not willingly betray their covenant to remain faithful, but that they felt burdened by the jewelry of the Egyptians that they had carried out with them. It was a weight of sin and a source of trouble for them, so they threw it into the fire at the Samiri's instruction, and he cast his share in the same way, producing the calf. The verse shows how people justify wrongdoing by pointing to circumstances or to a persuasive leader, while overlooking their own responsibility and their weak commitment to the covenant. Their claim that they acted without 'their own will' is exposed as a weak plea, since they had the freedom to refuse and chose to follow temptation.

translation: Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing sound, and they said, 'This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot.'
interpretation: The verse shows how easily people who lack firm faith are swayed by outward, tangible forms. The Samiri fashioned a lifeless golden image whose hollow lowing made it look impressive, and the Israelites took the sound for a sign of divinity. They then claimed that Moses had forgotten or strayed from his own god, when in fact it was they who forgot. The lesson is that worship belongs only to the unseen, living, all-hearing God, and that anything unable to speak, guide, harm or benefit cannot be a deity. Spectacle and sound do not prove truth, and following whims or a deceptive leader in place of revealed guidance leads to idolatry.

translation: Do they not see that it (the calf) could not return a word to them, and possessed no power to harm or benefit them?
interpretation: The verse (Taha 20:89) rebukes the Children of Israel for worshipping the golden calf and exposes the irrationality of idolatry. A true deity must at least be able to respond to its worshippers by speech or guidance, and must hold power over benefit and harm. The calf was a lifeless, mute object that could neither answer a call nor bring good or avert evil, so devoting worship to it defies reason and observation. The lesson is that worship belongs only to God, who hears, responds, and controls all benefit and harm. Anything that lacks these attributes, whether an idol or any created thing, is unworthy of devotion.

translation: And Aaron had already said to them before this, 'O my people, you are only being tested by it. Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command.'
interpretation: The verse shows that Aaron did not take part in the calf worship but warned the Israelites from the start. He told them the golden calf was only a trial of their faith, a test that exposed whether they would stay firm in monotheism or be led astray by a lifeless, powerless idol. He directed them back to the true Lord, whose Mercy (al-Rahman) is the source of all provision and guidance, which the calf could never give. He then called them to follow him as the prophet and deputy Moses had left in charge, and to obey his command to abandon the calf. The verse affirms that Aaron fulfilled his duty of clear admonition, and that the people's error came from their own stubborn choice, not from any lack of guidance.

translation: They said: 'We will not cease to be devoted to it (the calf) until Moses returns to us.'
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:91) shows how the Children of Israel answered Aaron when he warned them that the calf was only a trial and that their true Lord is the Most Merciful. Instead of heeding the warning, they insisted on staying in devoted worship of the calf and made their obedience conditional on Moses' return, as though the final judgment on right and wrong belonged to him alone rather than to the clear truth already brought to them. It shows how a heart attached to a visible, tangible object can stubbornly persist in falsehood even after being given clear guidance, and how people may postpone submitting to the truth by waiting for a figure of authority instead of acting on what they already know. It also shows the difficulty of Aaron's position, since his sincere admonition was met with obstinacy and the pull of the crowd.

translation: He (Moses) said: "O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,
interpretation: Moses, returning from the mountain to find his people worshipping the calf, turns to his brother and deputy Aaron and questions him. The question is not a request for information but a reproach: when Aaron saw the community fall into clear error, why did he not act decisively to stop it, and why did he not follow Moses and report to him or take a firm stand? The verse shows that leaders entrusted with guarding the community's faith are accountable for responding to deviation and cannot remain passive when the core of belief, the worship of God alone, is at stake. Moses' zeal for tawhid is so strong that even his own brother, a prophet, is called to account.

translation: "What prevented you from following me? Did you then disobey my command?" (Qur'an 20:93)
interpretation: Moses addresses his brother Aaron after returning to find the Israelites worshipping the golden calf. His words are a reproach: Aaron was left as his deputy to maintain the people's faith and uphold the command to reform and keep to monotheism. Moses asks why Aaron did not stand firm against the idolatry, resist it, and separate himself from those who strayed, following Moses' example of uncompromising steadfastness. The verse shows that those entrusted with leadership and guidance are accountable for acting on the trust given to them, and that obedience to a divinely guided leader includes actively opposing clear wrongdoing, not just refraining from it personally. Aaron's answer, that he feared causing division among the people, shows the tension between preserving unity and confronting error, which the verse brings into focus.

translation: He said: 'O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or by my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You caused division among the Children of Israel, and you did not heed my word."'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 20:94) records Aaron's reply to Moses after Moses returned and found the people worshipping the calf. Aaron appeals to Moses with the tender phrase 'son of my mother' to soften his brother's anger, and he explains that he did not use force against the worshippers because he feared it would split the community into warring factions. He judged that preserving the unity of the Children of Israel, while waiting for Moses to return and give authoritative judgment, was the lesser harm compared with a violent rupture. The verse shows that even in grave error, a leader may weigh the danger of communal strife and act with restraint and patience, and that Aaron's conduct was an honest judgment made out of concern for the community, not complicity in their sin.

translation: [Moses] said, "And what is your case, O Samiri?" (Qur'an 20:95)
interpretation: After Moses returned from his meeting with God and found his people worshipping the golden calf, he first confronted Aaron, then turned to the Samiri, the one who had fashioned it. By asking "what is your affair?", Moses does not seek information so much as demand that the man account for his motive and answer for his deed. The verse shows that a leader of a community must hold the instigator of corruption responsible and make him explain himself, and that those who lead people into false worship cannot hide behind the crowd. It also shows the method of just inquiry: the accused is questioned and given the chance to speak before judgment is passed, and the Samiri's reply, that he had seen what they had not seen and was swayed by his own soul, exposes how personal whim and self-deception can lie behind the invention of falsehood.

translation: He said: 'I perceived what they did not perceive, so I took a handful from the trace of the Messenger and threw it in; and thus my soul suggested to me.'
interpretation: Al-Samiri answers Moses' questioning about the golden calf by claiming he saw something the Israelites could not see: according to the common interpretation, he saw Gabriel riding a horse, and he took a handful of dust from beneath the hoofprint of the Messenger's mount, which carried life-giving power. He cast it onto the molded calf, and it lowed. He admits that he did this because his own soul embellished the act and made it appealing to him, so it was not a command from God but a self-driven deception, and his excuse exposes his responsibility for leading the people into idolatry.

translation: He said: 'Then go! Indeed, for you in this life is to say, "Do not touch me." And indeed, you have an appointment you will never fail to meet. And look at your god to which you remained devoted: we will surely burn it, then scatter its ashes in the sea, scattering them widely.'
interpretation: Moses pronounces judgment on the Samiri, who led the Israelites into making the golden calf. His punishment is social isolation: he will live as an outcast, shunned by people and warning them away from himself, a fitting penalty for one who corrupted the community's unity and faith. Beyond this worldly exile, a promised reckoning awaits him in the Hereafter that he cannot escape. Moses then turns to the calf, the object of the people's devotion, and vows to burn it and scatter its remains into the sea. This publicly exposes its powerlessness: a true god could not be destroyed and dispersed so easily. The scene affirms that worship belongs to God alone, and that false idols deserve no reverence.

translation: Your God is only Allah, other than Whom there is no god. He encompasses all things in knowledge.
interpretation: The verse closes the account of the calf episode in Surah Ta-Ha by returning to the heart of the message: worship belongs to God alone, not to any fabricated idol, since an idol like the golden calf can neither speak nor benefit nor harm. The reason given for this exclusive right to worship is God's all-embracing knowledge. Because He knows everything, whether seen or hidden, past or future, open deeds or secret intentions, He alone is fit to be worshipped, trusted, and obeyed. A true deity must know the needs and states of those who worship it, and only God does. The verse therefore calls the believer to rest in tawhid, to be mindful that nothing escapes God's awareness, and to take comfort that He knows their struggles and sincerity.

translation: Thus We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed. And We have certainly given you from Us a Reminder (the Qur'an).
interpretation: God tells the Prophet Muhammad that, just as He narrated the story of Moses and Pharaoh in the preceding verses, He recounts to him true reports of earlier nations so that they strengthen his heart, serve as lessons for his community, and prove his prophethood, since he could only know such accounts through revelation. The 'Reminder' from God's own presence is the Qur'an, a divine gift that awakens hearts, guides to truth, and preserves the lessons of past peoples. It is a great honor and blessing, and it places a responsibility on those who receive it to heed it, so that whoever turns away from it will bear the consequences, as the following verses warn.

translation: Whoever turns away from it will surely bear a heavy burden on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse (Ta-Ha 20:100) refers to the Qur'an, the reminder that God sent to the Prophet. Whoever turns away from it by neglecting it, denying it, or refusing to act upon its guidance is not merely missing out on a benefit. He is accumulating a weighty burden of sin, which he will carry as his own responsibility on the Day of Judgment. The image of a load shows that rejecting revelation is an active moral failing with real consequences. Guidance was made clear and accessible, so no excuse remains for those who knowingly turn away, and each person answers personally for the choice.

translation: They will abide in it (bearing the burden of their sin), and evil it will be for them as a load on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse follows the warning that whoever turns away from the Qur'an, the reminder, will carry a heavy burden (wizr) on the Day of Resurrection. It means that the consequence of rejecting divine guidance is not a passing penalty but a lasting state: the sin is imagined as a physical weight that clings to the person and cannot be shed, and they remain under it forever. The word 'load' shows that what they chose to carry in this world, by turning from truth in favor of heedlessness, becomes an unbearable weight in the hereafter. The lesson is that turning away from revelation is a choice that burdens the soul, and a person should therefore take up the guidance now, so as not to carry the heavy load of its rejection later.

translation: The Day when the Trumpet is blown; and We shall gather the guilty on that Day blue-eyed (or, with eyes dulled and faces darkened).
interpretation: The verse (Ta-Ha 20:102) describes the Day of Resurrection, when the angel sounds the Trumpet and all creation is raised for judgment. The wrongdoers who rejected faith will be assembled in a state of visible disgrace: 'zurqan' signifies their eyes turning a livid bluish-grey, a sign of terror, thirst, and blindness of heart made manifest. Just as they were spiritually blind to God's signs in this world, their outward appearance on that Day will reveal their inner ruin and humiliation, in contrast to the believers who are gathered in security. The verse warns that the hidden state of the soul becomes openly displayed when the final reckoning begins.

translation: They will murmur to one another: 'You stayed in the world only ten days.'
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:103) depicts the guilty on the Day of Resurrection, when the terror of that day and the sight of its reality make them lower their voices and whisper among themselves. They judge their stay in the world, or in the grave, to have been only about ten days, which shows how short and fleeting worldly life appears once the eternal Hereafter is before them. The lesson is that the pleasures people trade their faith and obedience for are fleeting, so one should not be deceived by the length of worldly life and should prepare for the Day of Judgment.

translation: We know best what they will say, when the most upright of them in conduct says, 'You remained only a day.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, when the disbelievers are gathered and asked how long they lingered in the world or in the grave, they will be so overwhelmed by the terror of that Day that they will drastically underestimate it. God tells that He knows precisely what they say among themselves in whispers. Even the one among them regarded as the wisest and most sound in judgment will say that they stayed only a single day, which shows that even their best opinion is mistaken and confused. The verse teaches that worldly life, however long it seemed, is brief and fleeting when measured against the reality of the Hereafter, and that those who chased it as their main concern were deceived about its true worth.

translation: And they ask you about the mountains, so say: My Lord will scatter them as dust, blasting them utterly.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the mountains, which people regard as the most solid and enduring features of the earth, will not endure on the Day of Resurrection. God will uproot them and reduce them to scattered dust, which shows that all earthly power and permanence is subject to His command alone. The earth will be leveled into a bare, flat plain on which nothing hides or obstructs, and this prepares people to stand before God for judgment with nothing left to shelter behind. The instruction to 'say' shows the Prophet should answer with certainty about the unseen from revelation, and it directs the believer to place trust in the Creator rather than in the apparent stability of the created world.

translation: Then He will leave it a level, barren plain.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:106) completes the answer to the question about what becomes of the mountains on the Day of Judgment. After the previous verse says that the Lord will scatter them into dust, this verse says that the ground where they stood will be left as a smooth, empty plain, with no hill, hollow, or vegetation. The interpretation is that on the Day of Resurrection the familiar features of the earth, which people relied on for shelter, strength, and worldly security, will be erased. Humanity will stand on an utterly flat expanse where nothing can offer concealment or refuge, so that every person faces God alone and is reminded that only God's power endures when the world's apparent permanence is removed.

translation: You will see in it no crookedness and no unevenness.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:107) describes the earth on the Day of Judgment, after the mountains have been scattered and ground into dust and the earth has been left as a smooth, level plain. The meaning is that it will be perfectly flat and even, with no valley, hollow, hill, or elevation anywhere. Nothing will obstruct the sight of those gathered, and no one will be hidden from the call of the summoner. It conveys the totality of God's power to remake creation, and the openness and exposure of all people before Him on that Day, when every person will stand in plain view for reckoning and nothing will be concealed.

translation: On that Day they will follow the Caller, in whom there is no crookedness; and voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a faint murmur.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, after the mountains are leveled and the earth is made a flat plain, people will be summoned and will rush straight toward the call of the summoner (the angel calling them to the gathering place), with no ability to swerve, evade, or turn aside, and the call itself is true and direct, with no deviation. Their pride and arrogance will vanish, and in awe of God's majesty all voices will fall silent, so that only the faintest whisper, such as the soft sound of footsteps or hushed murmuring, can be heard. The verse teaches that the worldly clamor, defiance, and denial will end in complete submission to God, so a person should humble themselves before Him now, before that Day compels it.

translation: On that Day, no intercession will be of benefit except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose word He is pleased with.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when all creatures will be humbled before God and people will follow the summoner without deviation, no one will have the power to intercede on his own authority or by status, lineage, or worldly rank. Intercession is entirely God's to grant. It benefits only when two conditions are met: the intercessor must have received God's explicit permission to speak, and the person interceded for must be one whose faith and statement God is pleased with, namely the declaration of tawhid and sincere belief. The verse refutes the notion that false deities, idols, or any created being can compel God or act as independent mediators. It teaches that all authority and mercy rest with God alone, so a person should depend on sincere faith and righteous deeds and not on the hope of an unconditional intercession.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them, while they do not encompass Him in knowledge.
interpretation: God's knowledge is total and unbounded: He knows everything that is past and future, hidden and apparent, in the lives of His creatures, whereas their knowledge is limited and partial. Human beings, angels, and all created beings cannot fully grasp His essence, attributes, or wisdom. The verse teaches humility before the Creator and affirms that no intercessor or created being can claim knowledge or authority independent of Him, so the only fitting response is submission and trust in His wisdom.

translation: And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence; and he who bore wrongdoing will have failed utterly.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection all pride and worldly status fall away, and every person stands submissive before God, whose life is perfect and who sustains everything. The verse teaches that wrongdoing, whether polytheism, injustice toward others, or transgression against oneself, is a burden carried into the Hereafter, and those who carry it will be ruined, because nothing can lighten it except the mercy of God, sincere repentance, and the setting right of wrongs before that Day.

translation: And whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer will fear neither injustice nor deprivation.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:112) teaches that faith is the condition for the acceptance of good deeds, and that God's reckoning is perfectly just. A believer who does righteous works need not worry that he will be wronged by having his reward cancelled or by being burdened with sins he did not commit (zulm), nor that his reward will be reduced or any of his good deeds neglected (hadm). The two words together express complete assurance: God neither adds to a person's punishment unjustly nor diminishes the recompense he has earned, so the believer can act with confidence and hope in God's fairness and generosity.

translation: And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have diversified in it the warnings, that perhaps they may be mindful of God, or that it may cause them to remember.
interpretation: God explains that the Qur'an was revealed in clear Arabic so that its first audience could understand it directly, and that it repeats its warnings in many forms, through stories of earlier nations, parables, and descriptions of the Hereafter, so that no excuse remains. The aim is twofold: that people come to fear God and so avoid disobedience and wrongdoing (taqwa), or, if they have not yet reached that level, that the Qur'an at least awakens in them remembrance and reflection, a lasting reminder that stirs the conscience and leads them back to the right path. Thus the repeated warnings are a mercy, meant to move hearts gradually, whether to full God-consciousness or at least to heedfulness.

translation: Exalted is God, the True King. And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say: 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.'
interpretation: The verse exalts God's absolute sovereignty and truth, then teaches the Prophet, and every seeker of knowledge after him, proper manners in receiving divine revelation: not to rush to recite or to seek its meaning before God has finished revealing it and made it clear, since understanding comes in God's time and by His measure. Instead of impatience, the believer should turn to God in humble supplication, asking Him to increase knowledge. This shows that knowledge is a gift from God, that patience and deliberate learning are required in acquiring it, and that no one ever reaches a point where he no longer needs more of it.

translation: And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot; and We found in him no firm resolve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human beings are prone to forgetfulness and weakness of resolve, and that this is the root of sin rather than deliberate defiance. God had given Adam a clear command (not to approach the tree) and warned him about Satan's enmity, yet Adam lapsed because he did not hold fast to the commitment with steadfast determination. The lesson is that remembering God's guidance is not enough without firm will to act on it, so believers must continually renew their remembrance, guard against Satan's whispers, and strengthen their resolve, while also seeing that Adam's fault was a human lapse followed by repentance and God's forgiveness, not an inherited stain.

translation: And [remember] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate yourselves to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis, who refused.
interpretation: The verse shows that true obedience to God means submitting to His command even when the reason is not fully grasped or when it wounds one's pride. The angels' prostration was not worship of Adam but an act of obedience to God and an acknowledgment of the honor He gave humanity. Iblis's failure was not ignorance of God or disbelief in His existence, but arrogant refusal: he set his own judgment and sense of superiority above the divine command. The verse warns that pride and rebellion against God's order, rather than lack of knowledge, are the root of spiritual downfall, and that the one who refuses to submit stands apart from those who obey, no matter how high his former rank.

translation: Then We said: O Adam, indeed this one is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not drive you both out of the Garden, lest you be wretched.
interpretation: God gives Adam a clear warning about the true nature of Iblis, whose hostility is not accidental but deliberate and rooted in his refusal to prostrate. By naming him an enemy, God teaches that the danger of Satan lies in his seeming to be an adviser while working to strip a person of blessing. The verse also links the loss of the Garden to 'shaqā' (wretchedness): the ease, security and provision of Paradise are tied to obedience, and leaving it through heedlessness brings toil and hardship. Addressing Adam alone with the warning 'lest you be wretched' points to his responsibility as the head of the household to labor, which is the lot of his earthly life. The lesson for people is to recognize the enemy early, hold to God's command, and understand that true well-being lies in obedience, while yielding to temptation leads to hardship and distress.

translation: Indeed, it is [assured] for you that you will not be hungry therein, nor will you be unclothed.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:118) shows God's complete provision for Adam in Paradise: his basic needs of food and clothing were guaranteed without toil. By naming hunger and nakedness first, it highlights that the real loss of disobeying God's command was falling from a state of effortless sufficiency into a life of labor and need. The lesson is that obedience keeps a person secure in God's care, while heeding Satan's temptation brings hardship, and that gratitude and trust in God's provision are better than chasing what He has forbidden.

translation: And indeed, you will not be thirsty therein, nor will you be exposed to the sun's heat.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:119) continues God's promise to Adam about life in Paradise, completing a picture of full provision: in the previous verse he is assured he will not hunger or be unclothed, and here he is assured he will neither thirst nor suffer the scorching sun. Together the four assurances cover food, clothing, drink, and shelter, the basic needs of human life. The point is that Paradise offered Adam complete comfort and security without toil or deprivation, so that he should not be tempted by Satan's whisper of an 'eternal tree.' Leaving that safe state through disobedience would bring hardship, labor, and want, as the verses that follow suggest. The lesson is that obedience to God keeps a person within His sufficient provision, while heeding Satan's promises leads to loss.

translation: But Satan whispered to him; he said, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the Tree of Eternity and to a kingdom that does not decay?"
interpretation: The verse shows how Satan tempts by exploiting humanity's deepest longings: the desire to live forever and to hold power that never fades. He does not command Adam to disobey openly. He whispers, presenting forbidden action as a helpful guide offering a better good. His promise is false, since the tree brings loss, not immortality, and the lesson is that evil often comes disguised as advice toward fulfillment. Attachment to lasting life and dominion, pursued outside God's limits, makes a person vulnerable to deception, and true security lies in obeying God's commands and heeding His warnings rather than the seductive whispers of those who wish us harm.

translation: So they both ate from it, and their nakedness became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray.
interpretation: The verse shows the immediate consequence of yielding to Satan's whisper: when Adam and his wife ate from the forbidden tree, the protective covering of divine grace was lifted and they became aware of their vulnerability and shame, which they tried to remedy by stitching garden leaves over themselves. Disobeying a clear command, even through forgetfulness and weakness rather than arrogance, causes a loss of ease and innocence. The Qur'an describes Adam's act as 'disobedience' and 'going astray' to teach that a lapse from God's guidance brings real harm, yet the surrounding verses show that sincere repentance leads to God's forgiveness and renewed guidance. Human beings are fallible, but the path back to God always remains open through turning to Him.

translation: Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:122) describes what followed Adam's slip in eating from the forbidden tree. It shows that God's mercy outweighs human error. Adam's lapse did not end his relationship with his Lord. After he turned back in remorse, God drew him close and chose him for prophethood and honor. God then accepted his repentance and guided him to the straight path, so that he could live on earth in obedience. The lesson is that sin followed by sincere repentance does not leave a person permanently disgraced. Repentance can raise a person to a higher station than before, and true guidance is a gift from God that comes to those who return to Him.

translation: He said: "Go down from it, all of you, some of you enemies to others. Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery."
interpretation: After Adam and Eve's slip, God's decree sends humankind to earth, where they will face struggle and rivalry, as the descendants of Adam and the forces of temptation oppose one another. Yet this descent is not abandonment. God promises that guidance will reach them through revelation and the messengers. The verse teaches that guidance is the only safeguard against the hardships of earthly life. Whoever follows it is protected from error in belief and conduct, and from the inner wretchedness and ultimate ruin that come from turning away. True security and contentment, in this world and the next, depend on following God's guidance, not on worldly circumstances.

translation: And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a depressed, constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.
interpretation: Whoever turns away from the guidance and the Qur'an that God has sent finds that worldly life, even with wealth or ease, brings an inner constriction: anxiety, dissatisfaction, and a heart that lacks certainty and peace, because it is cut off from its Source of tranquility. This hardship may also extend into the grave. On the Day of Resurrection he will be raised spiritually and literally blind, a fitting recompense: since he was blind to God's signs and guidance in this life, he will be deprived of sight in the next, unable to find his way, as the following verses indicate, when he is told that he forgot the signs just as he is now forgotten.

translation: He will say: "My Lord, why have You raised me up blind, when I used to see?"
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:125) depicts the person who turned away from God's remembrance and is resurrected blind on the Day of Judgment. He protests that he had sight in worldly life. The answer in the next verse makes the meaning clear: just as he forgot and ignored God's signs when they came to him, he is now forgotten. The blindness of the Hereafter is a fitting recompense for spiritual blindness in this life. Having eyes was no benefit, since he did not use his sight to perceive and heed the guidance, so his punishment mirrors his neglect: whoever refused to see the truth when able is deprived of vision when he most needs it.

translation: He (Allah) will say: "Thus it was: Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; and in the same way you are forgotten this Day."
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:126) answers the person who will be raised blind on the Day of Resurrection and asks why he was raised so, when he used to see in the world. God replies that the cause lies in the person's own conduct: God's clear signs and revelations reached him, yet he neglected them, turned away from them, and did not act on them, as one forgets something and leaves it behind. Therefore, as a just recompense of the same kind, he is forgotten on that Day, meaning he is abandoned and left in the punishment and deprived of God's mercy and care. The verse teaches that the consequence of heedlessness toward divine guidance is being treated in the Hereafter according to how one treated that guidance in this life.

translation: And thus We recompense the one who transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is surely more severe and more lasting.
interpretation: This verse (Ta-Ha 20:127) teaches that divine justice is consistent: whoever exceeds the bounds of God by indulging in disobedience and arrogance, and rejects the revelations of his Lord, is repaid in kind, as exemplified by the narrowed, spiritually blind life and heedless forgetting described in the preceding verses. Yet whatever hardship or deprivation such a person experiences in this world is minor compared to what awaits. The punishment of the Hereafter is harsher in its intensity and endures without end, whereas worldly suffering is limited and passes. The verse thus warns that rejecting God's guidance is not a harmless choice, and it urges people to look beyond the fleeting life of this world and to prepare for the lasting consequences of faith or denial.

translation: Is it not a guidance for them how many generations We destroyed before them, in whose dwellings they walk? Indeed, in that are signs for those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny the truth for ignoring the lessons of history. The ruins of earlier nations, such as Ad, Thamud, and others, lie in places the Arabs pass through on their journeys, and they stand as visible proof that arrogance, rejecting the messengers, and persisting in wrongdoing lead to ruin. Seeing the empty homes of those who once had power and wealth should lead a reflective person to see that the same fate can befall them if they follow the same path. Only people of sound intellect (ulu al-nuha), who use their reason to restrain themselves from error, will draw this warning from these signs and respond with faith and obedience.

translation: And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, and a term already appointed, the punishment would have been inevitable (binding).
interpretation: God, in His wisdom and mercy, has already decreed that He will not hasten the destruction of those who deny the truth, and has fixed for them an appointed term. Were it not for this prior decree and set time, the punishment would have fallen upon the deniers immediately and inescapably, as it did for earlier nations. Their delay is therefore not a sign of divine approval or weakness, but a respite granted by God's will, which gives them the chance to repent and gives the Prophet reason for patience while awaiting the fixed moment of reckoning.

translation: So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praises of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting; and during periods of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be satisfied.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet against the mockery and denial of his opponents by prescribing patience joined with regular worship as the remedy. Rather than answering insults with anger, he is told to anchor his heart in remembrance and praise of God throughout the day: before sunrise (dawn prayer), before sunset (afternoon prayer), in the hours of the night (evening and night prayers), and at the day's edges (including the noon and again the morning and evening periods). Constant devotion strengthens the believer's endurance and detaches him from the opinions of people. The closing phrase, 'that you may be satisfied,' indicates that this inner contentment, and God's pleasure and reward which bring it, is the fruit of patience and steadfast worship. The lesson is that spiritual peace comes from persistent remembrance of God, not from vindication by one's critics.

translation: And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to various groups of them, the splendor of worldly life, so that We may test them through it. But the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet, and through him every believer, not to look with longing or envy at the wealth, status and pleasures that God has granted some of the deniers. These are only the fleeting glitter of this life, given as a trial to show how people handle blessings, whether with gratitude and obedience or with arrogance and heedlessness. What God has stored for the believer, namely guidance, contentment, lawful sustenance in this world and the eternal reward in the Hereafter, is far better in quality and lasts forever, while worldly luxury fades. The believer should therefore keep their heart fixed on God's lasting gifts and not be dazzled by transient ones.

translation: And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the best outcome is for righteousness.
interpretation: The verse tells the believer to make prayer the center of the household, beginning with those closest to him, and to persevere in it patiently, since constancy in worship takes effort and discipline. Worship is not a means by which God gains anything, nor a burden that costs the worshipper his livelihood. God does not ask His servants to provide for Him, for He is the One who provides for them. So the worry of earning a living should not distract anyone from prayer or lead him to neglect it. The verse ends by saying that the final and lasting success, in this world and the next, belongs to those who have taqwa, meaning God-consciousness and obedience, and not to those who merely gain wealth or worldly status.

translation: And they said, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh demanded a miracle of their own choosing as a condition for believing, which reveals stubbornness rather than a sincere search for truth. The verse answers that the Qur'an is itself the greatest and clearest sign: it confirms the core message found in earlier scriptures about the oneness of God, accountability, and righteousness, and it came through an unlettered Prophet who had never studied those books. This agreement with the earlier revelations is evidence of its divine origin. Anyone seeking guidance already has sufficient proof, so the demand for further signs is merely an excuse to avoid submission.

translation: And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it (the Messenger's coming), they would have said: 'Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we might have followed Your revelations before we were humiliated and disgraced?'
interpretation: God's justice requires that no people be punished without clear proof having reached them. By sending Muhammad with a clear Book, God removes every excuse from the disbelievers of Quraysh. Had He destroyed them before the Messenger and the revelation came, they would have pleaded that no guidance had reached them, and that they would have believed and followed the signs had they been sent a messenger, so as to avoid the abasement and shame of punishment. Now that the Messenger has come, that plea is void, and whoever still rejects the message has only himself to blame for the consequences.

translation: Say: Everyone is waiting, so wait. You will soon know who are the companions of the even path, and who is rightly guided.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to answer those who disbelieve and await his downfall by telling them that every party is watching for the outcome, so let them keep waiting. The final outcome will make plain, beyond argument, who followed the straight and balanced path of truth and who was truly guided. Judgment is left to events and to God, not to claims: when the reality of the Hereafter and the consequences of each side's choices are revealed, the disbelievers will realize that guidance belonged to the believers, and the verse is both a consolation to the believers and a warning to the deniers.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The reckoning of mankind has drawn near to them, yet they are heedless, turning away.
interpretation: The verse is a warning that the Day of Judgment, when every person will be held to account for their deeds, is nearer than people imagine, since every life is short and its end is always close, and the Last Hour is not far in the measure of God's knowledge. Despite this, most people are absorbed in worldly pleasures, ambitions and distractions, and they turn away from the message of revelation and from reflecting on their final destiny. The verse calls the listener to wake from heedlessness, to take stock of their own actions before they are called to account, and to prepare through faith and righteous conduct rather than postponing repentance and reform.

translation: No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord except that they listen to it while they play.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anbiya 21:2) rebukes the heedless among the people. Whenever a new revelation or admonition from God reaches them, they do not receive it with sincere attention or let it change them. They hear it only with their ears while their hearts are absorbed in amusement and worldly distraction, treating a solemn warning as a pastime. It shows that the problem is not a lack of guidance but a negligent heart that has become so preoccupied with play and heedlessness that it cannot take the message seriously, which makes it ever more vulnerable to the approaching reckoning mentioned in the preceding verse.

translation: Their hearts are distracted. And those who did wrong conceal their private talk: "Is this man anything but a human being like yourselves? Will you then submit to magic while you see?" (Qur'an 21:3)
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner state of the deniers: their hearts are so absorbed in heedlessness and worldly amusement that the warning of the approaching reckoning, mentioned in the previous verse, cannot sink in. Rather than reflecting on the message, they hold secret conspiratorial meetings to discredit it. Their argument is that a prophet cannot be an ordinary human being, so they dismiss the Prophet as just a mortal like themselves and label the Qur'an 'magic' to scare people away from it. The irony is that their secret whispering is known to God, and their objection is hollow, since a human messenger who lives among his people is exactly what makes the guidance relatable and accessible. The root of their rejection is therefore not a lack of evidence but a distracted, unwilling heart that seeks excuses to avoid accountability.

translation: He said, "My Lord knows every word spoken in the heavens and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: The Prophet's reply to those who whispered secret schemes and mocked his message is that nothing said in secret or in the open escapes God. Since God's knowledge covers all speech everywhere in creation, the plotting of the disbelievers is already known to Him, and He hears what they say and knows what they conceal. This is both a warning to the opponents that they will be held to account for what they say and do, and a reassurance to the believers that God is aware of their situation and will deal justly with it.

translation: Nay, they said: 'These are jumbled dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign just as the earlier messengers were sent with.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the incoherence and insincerity of the Prophet's opponents: rather than reflecting on the Qur'an's message, they hurl shifting accusations, first calling it confused dreams, then a fabrication, then poetry. Their swift retreat from one charge to the next, each introduced with 'nay', shows that they hold no stable, reasoned position, and that their objection is stubbornness rather than a genuine search for truth. Their demand for a miracle like those given to earlier prophets is a pretext, since the Qur'an itself is the clear sign addressed to them, and those who refuse to see it would not be convinced by any other sign either.

translation: Not a single town before them, which We destroyed, believed; so will they believe?
interpretation: The verse addresses the Quraysh and other deniers who demanded miraculous signs as a condition for faith. God reminds them that earlier communities were given the very signs they demanded, yet they did not believe, and so they were destroyed. The rhetorical question 'will they then believe?' implies that these people are no more likely to believe than those before them, since their obstinacy comes from their stubborn hearts and not from a lack of evidence. Thus, demanding miracles is not a sincere search for truth, and God, in His mercy, withholds such signs from them so as not to hasten their destruction.

translation: And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the message (remembrance) if you do not know.
interpretation: God answers those who denied that a human could be a messenger: prophethood has always been given to human men, chosen and inspired by God, never to angels, so Muhammad is no novelty. The disbelievers are told to settle their doubt by consulting the scholars of earlier scriptures, the People of the Book, who know the histories of the previous prophets and can confirm that those messengers were mortal men. The verse also establishes the principle that one who lacks knowledge should turn to those who truly possess it and rely on their testimony.

translation: And We did not make them (the messengers) bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.
interpretation: The verse answers those who objected that a messenger should not be an ordinary human being who eats and walks in the markets. God explains that all the prophets sent before Muhammad were mortal humans with real bodily needs: they ate, they hungered, and they died. Their humanity was no flaw in their mission and did not contradict it. It was part of God's wisdom, so that people could follow them as examples and relate to them. Prophethood therefore rests on revelation and divine support, not on angelic or superhuman nature or on immortality. The verse also implies that no human being, the Prophet included, lives forever, so people should attach themselves to the message and to God, the Ever-Living, rather than to the messenger's person.

translation: Then We fulfilled the promise to them, so We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors (those who exceed all bounds).
interpretation: God affirms that His promises to His messengers are always truthful and come to pass. After the messengers endured denial and hostility from their peoples, God's promise of support came true: He rescued them along with the believers whom He willed to save, and He wiped out those who went to extremes in disbelief, injustice, and sin. The verse teaches that the outcome of the struggle between truth and falsehood is ultimately determined by God, that salvation is a result of His will and mercy, and that persistent transgression against His bounds leads to ruin, however long respite may last.

translation: We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Then will you not use reason?
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anbiya 21:10) tells that the Qur'an is the source of the people's honor, renown and standing: 'dhikrukum' is read as 'your eminence and high repute', since in following its guidance they attain dignity in this world and salvation in the next. Having been given such a Book, it is irrational to turn away from it. The closing question rebukes those who neglect it and calls them to reflect on how its teachings bring them lasting honor and well-being.

translation: And how many a town that was unjust did We shatter, and We raised up after it another people.
interpretation: The verse warns that God's destruction of earlier communities was not arbitrary but a consequence of their persistent wrongdoing, namely their injustice, their denial of the truth, and their rejection of the messengers. The word 'qasamna' (We shattered) evokes a total, crushing break that leaves no remnant of their power, showing that no civilization, however strong, is protected from divine judgment once injustice becomes entrenched. The closing clause, 'and We raised up after it another people,' shows that the world does not depend on any one nation: God replaces those who fall with others, who in turn are tested by how they act. The verse thus serves as a warning to the Prophet's audience to learn from history and to avoid the oppression and arrogance that bring about a people's ruin.

translation: Then, when they felt Our might, behold, they began to flee from it, running.
interpretation: When the wrongdoing people saw the first signs of God's punishment approaching after they had rejected their prophets, their arrogance gave way to panic and they tried to run from the town in a hurry. This shows that denial and complacency vanish once the reality of divine judgment is perceived. The flight is futile, because no one can escape a decree of God, and the verse that follows mocks them, telling them to return to their luxuries and homes, since the time for repentance has passed.

translation: Do not flee, but return to the luxury you were given in abundance and to your homes, so that you may be questioned.
interpretation: This verse is spoken, by way of mockery and rebuke, to the wrongdoing people who tried to run away when the punishment of God struck their town. They are told to go back to the comforts and dwellings that made them arrogant and heedless, as if they could still enjoy them. The command is ironic, because there is no escape from divine judgment once it arrives. The phrase 'so that you may be questioned' means they will be held to account for their ingratitude and wrongdoing, or, as some read it, that people may come to ask them about their wealth and status as they once did. The lesson is that worldly luxury offers no protection from God's decree, and that those who are corrupted by ease and reject His warnings will ultimately face a reckoning they cannot flee.

translation: They said: "Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:14, with similar wording in 68:31) depicts the moment when a people who had been arrogant and heedless see God's punishment descend on them. Their denial collapses, and they confess their wrongdoing. The cry "Woe to us!" shows the sudden clarity that comes with seeing the consequences of their actions. The confession comes too late to save them, because it is forced by the punishment and not offered freely through faith and repentance. The lesson is that a person should acknowledge his own injustice, whether in disbelief, in oppression of others, or in neglecting God's guidance, while there is still time to repent, because after the punishment arrives such admissions bring no benefit.

translation: And that cry of theirs did not cease until We made them like a harvested field, extinguished (lifeless like a dead fire).
interpretation: After the people of the wrongdoing town realized the punishment was upon them, they kept repeating the lament 'Woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers' (verse 14), but this confession came too late to save them. Their admission of guilt was not repentance accepted in time, since it came only when the punishment was already unavoidable. God's justice then cut them down completely, like crops reaped to the ground, and left them lifeless and still like a fire that has gone out. The verse teaches that arrogance and persistence in wrongdoing end in total destruction, and that one should repent and heed God's warnings while there is still time, rather than acknowledge the truth only when punishment has arrived.

translation: And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation is purposeful and not the product of idle amusement or caprice. The ordered heavens, the earth and everything between them point to a wise Creator who made them with truth and for a purpose. Human life therefore carries moral meaning and accountability: there will be a return to God, with justice for wrongdoing and reward for righteousness. A person who understands this should live seriously and responsibly, not heedlessly or aimlessly.

translation: Had We wished to take a diversion (amusement), We would have taken it from what is with Us, if We were to do so at all.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God did not create the heavens and earth in play or idle sport, but with wisdom, purpose, and truth, so that people will be held accountable. It rejects the idea that creation is meaningless, and it says that even if God had willed some amusement, which is far above His majesty, He would have taken it from His own presence, not from creation or from created beings. The phrase 'if We were to do so' negates the possibility altogether, showing that such a thing is not befitting of God. The lesson is that existence has a serious moral purpose, and that the truth ultimately overcomes falsehood.

translation: Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, falsehood vanishes. And woe to you for what you attribute (to God).
interpretation: The verse shows that truth is an active force that overcomes falsehood by God's decree. Like a blow that strikes the head of something and destroys it, truth breaks falsehood at its core and leaves it with no standing. Falsehood may seem strong for a time, but it cannot last once truth confronts it. The closing warning is directed at those who slander God with false claims, such as ascribing to Him a consort, a son, or partners, or treating creation as mere play. Their invented descriptions will bring them ruin, because what they assert has no basis and will be crushed, while they themselves will face the consequences of their words.

translation: To Him belong all those in the heavens and the earth. And those who are with Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they grow weary.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone holds absolute ownership and sovereignty over all creation, so no being has any independent claim against Him. It then points to the angels, those nearest to Him, as the model of right servitude: despite their closeness and high rank, they never see themselves above worship, and they never tire of it. If the most exalted creatures remain humble and tireless in devotion, then human beings, who are far more dependent and needy, have even less excuse for arrogance or neglect. Worship is therefore presented as the natural and fitting response to God's lordship, not a burden, and pride and fatigue in worship are signs of heedlessness rather than of any real independence.

translation: They glorify Him night and day, never slackening.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 21:20) describes the angels near God. Their glorification is constant and is not interrupted by tiredness, boredom or heedlessness. For them worship is as natural as breathing, so it takes no effort and does not wear them out. The point is that God is entirely self-sufficient and needs no worship from anyone, and that those who are closest to Him are the ones most devoted to remembering Him. Human beings, who tire easily and grow heedless, are meant to take from this an example of steadfastness and sincerity in devotion, and to strive toward that consistency as far as their nature allows.

translation: Or have they taken gods from the earth who can resurrect the dead?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical challenge to the polytheists. The gods they worship are made from earthly materials such as stone, wood and metal, and they have no power over life, death or resurrection. Only the One who creates and gives life can bring the dead back to life. Anything that cannot do this has no claim to divinity, so worshipping it is irrational and the argument for tawhid (God's oneness) stands.

translation: Had there been within the heavens and the earth gods other than God, both would have fallen into ruin. So glory be to God, Lord of the Throne, far above what they attribute to Him.
interpretation: The verse offers a rational proof of divine oneness (tawhid) from the order of creation. The heavens and the earth run in harmony, with consistent laws and no disorder. If several gods with independent wills ruled them, their purposes would sooner or later conflict, as rival rulers do, and the cosmos would descend into chaos and collapse. Since it remains orderly and unified, it must have one Sovereign, whose will and power alone govern it. The verse therefore concludes by declaring God exalted above the false claims of those who ascribe partners, offspring, or limitations to Him. He is Lord of the Throne, the seat of ultimate authority over all creation.

translation: He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:23) affirms God's absolute sovereignty and perfect wisdom. Because His knowledge is complete and His actions are always grounded in justice and wisdom, no one has the standing to demand an account from Him or to object to His decrees. Created beings, by contrast, have limited knowledge and are morally responsible, so they will be held to account for their beliefs and deeds. The verse teaches humility and submission before God's will, and reminds people that accountability applies to them, not to their Creator.

translation: Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me. Rather, most of them do not know the truth, so they are turning away.
interpretation: The verse challenges the claim of polytheism by demanding evidence that no one can supply. Belief in gods besides God has no support in reason or revelation: the Qur'an, which is the reminder for the Prophet's community, and the earlier scriptures sent to previous prophets all teach the same message of God's oneness. The polytheists have no proof from either source. Their persistence in worshipping others besides God comes from ignorance of the truth, not from any evidence, and because they do not know or seek the truth, they turn away from it and refuse to heed the reminder.

translation: And We sent no messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the core message of all prophets throughout history has been one and the same: pure monotheism (tawhid). Every messenger, whatever his people, era, or particular law, was commissioned first and foremost to call humanity to worship God alone and to reject the worship of anything besides Him. This shows that the Prophet Muhammad was not bringing a novel or strange doctrine but continuing the unbroken chain of divine guidance, and that differences among the prophets' legal codes were secondary to this foundational truth. The command 'so worship Me' links belief to practice: acknowledging God's oneness is not merely an intellectual proposition but requires exclusive devotion, obedience, and submission in all of life.

translation: And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.
interpretation: The verse rejects the claim, made by some who worshipped angels or ascribed divine offspring to God, that God has a child. God is exalted above any need for offspring, since having a son implies need, likeness to creation, and limitation, all of which are impossible for the Creator. Those whom people wrongly call His children, such as the angels, are in truth His honored servants. Their nobility and nearness come from obedience and servitude, not from any kinship with God, so their high rank is itself proof of their being created and devoted slaves, not partners in divinity.

translation: They do not precede Him in speech, and they act only by His command.
interpretation: The verse describes the angels, who are honored servants of God. They never speak ahead of God or say anything He has not permitted, and they do not act on their own initiative. Their words and deeds follow His command, which shows their perfect obedience and humility. Even the most exalted created beings depend on God's will, so no one can claim a share in His divinity or intercede with Him except by His leave.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for one with whom He is pleased, and they, from fear of Him, are apprehensive.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the angels, whom some people wrongly imagined to be God's children or independent intercessors. It teaches that God's knowledge encompasses everything about them, their past and future, their open and hidden affairs, so they have no power or knowledge apart from Him. Intercession is not a right they hold; it is only a permission God grants, and only for those whose faith and conduct He approves. Even these honored beings, nearest to God, live in reverent awe and trembling fear of Him. The lesson is that no created being, however exalted, shares in divine authority, so worship and hope must be directed to God alone, while intercession remains wholly dependent on His will and pleasure.

translation: And whoever among them says, 'Indeed, I am a god besides Him,' that one We would recompense with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divinity belongs to God alone, and that no created being, not even the honored angels referred to in the preceding verses, may claim a share in it. Even beings who are noble and close to God would face Hell if they claimed godhood, so the claim is the gravest wrong, because it places a creature in the position of the Creator. The closing phrase, 'Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers,' makes the principle universal. Wrongdoing at its root is putting something in the wrong place, and the greatest wrong is to give to a creature what is due only to God. The reward and punishment is therefore just and consistent for every person, whatever their rank or status.

translation: Do those who disbelieve not see that the heavens and the earth were joined together as one piece, and then We split them apart? And We made from water every living thing. Will they not then believe?
interpretation: The verse invites the deniers to reflect on observable signs of God's creative power and wisdom. The heavens and earth were originally a closed, unified mass that God opened up and separated. On one common reading, the sky was 'split' to release rain and the earth was 'split' to let plants grow, so that the ordered world and the provision of life are shown to be deliberate acts of a single Creator. Water, which is the source of all living things, is the clearest sign of this design, since nothing living survives without it. The closing question ('Will they not then believe?') is a rebuke. Such evident, ongoing signs of creation, order and sustenance point to One Lord who alone deserves worship, so continued disbelief after reflecting on them is unreasonable and ungrateful.

translation: And We placed in the earth firm mountains, lest it shake with them, and We made therein broad passes as roads, so that they may be guided.
interpretation: The verse points to God's care in preparing the earth for human life. The mountains act like stabilizing anchors that keep the earth steady, so people can live on it without being thrown into turmoil. The gaps and passes between the mountains are open routes that make travel, trade, and movement between regions possible. The phrase 'so that they may be guided' carries two meanings: physical guidance, in that people find their way from place to place, and spiritual guidance, in that reflecting on such deliberate design should lead them to recognize the Creator's wisdom and mercy and turn to Him in gratitude and faith.

translation: And We made the sky a protected ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs.
interpretation: The verse points to the sky as a sign of God's power and care: it stands above humanity like a roof that is kept safe from collapse and shielded from forces that would harm life on earth, and it is also guarded in the sense that it is preserved by God's decree and shielded from the devils' eavesdropping. Its order, stability, and the signs within it, such as the sun, moon, stars, and the regular succession of day and night, should lead the reflective person to recognize a Creator who is wise, powerful, and deserving of worship alone. Yet people remain heedless, treating these everyday wonders as ordinary and turning away from the lessons they carry. The verse therefore rebukes the neglect of reflection and shows that the failure to believe lies not in a lack of evidence but in the heart's refusal to attend to it.

translation: It is He who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; each floats along in an orbit.
interpretation: The verse points to the creation of the alternating night and day and of the sun and moon as signs of God's power, wisdom, and order. Each celestial body moves along its own appointed course, like something gliding smoothly, without colliding with or overtaking the others. This regularity is not accidental but shows a single Creator who designed and sustains the cosmos, and it invites human beings to reflect, to recognize their dependence on this ordered system, and to respond with gratitude and worship of God alone.

translation: We did not grant eternal life to any human being before you. So if you die, would they live forever?
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Anbiya (21:34) answers those who awaited the Prophet's death and gloated over it. It reminds them that death is a universal decree of God, which no prophet or other human being has escaped, since immortality belongs to God alone. The Prophet's death would therefore not prove him false or give his opponents any lasting advantage, because they too will die and be brought to account. The rhetorical question exposes the folly of rejoicing over another's mortality while ignoring one's own, and it calls people to prepare for the Hereafter instead of being absorbed in worldly life.

translation: Every soul will taste death. We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse teaches that death is a universal certainty that no one escapes, so life is a temporary stage rather than a final destination. Within this stage, God tests people through both hardship and ease. Hardship tests patience and trust in God, while ease and blessings test gratitude, humility, and responsible use of what one has been given. Since everyone will be returned to God for reckoning, a person should treat every circumstance as an opportunity to prove faith and righteous conduct, neither despairing in adversity nor becoming arrogant in prosperity.

translation: And when those who disbelieve see you, they take you only as an object of ridicule, saying: 'Is this the one who speaks of your gods?' While they themselves are disbelievers in the mention of the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anbiya 21:36) shows the irrational hypocrisy of the Meccan idolaters. They mocked the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) because he criticized their idols and denied them any divinity, treating this as a grave offense, yet they themselves rejected the remembrance of God, the Most Merciful, and refused to acknowledge His oneness and His revelation. The real object of reproach was therefore their own disbelief, not the Prophet's message. They were angered by the denunciation of false deities made of stone, while they showed no concern about denying the Creator who is the source of all mercy and the only one worthy of worship. The verse also consoles the Prophet and later believers, teaching that mockery is the usual response of those who reject truth, and that it reflects their own misguidance rather than any fault in the one who calls to God.

translation: Man was created of haste. I will show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten them.
interpretation: The verse points to impatience as a deep-rooted trait of human nature: people want results immediately and often demand that God's warnings or promised judgment come at once, as the disbelievers did when they mocked the Prophet and challenged him to bring on the punishment. God answers that His signs, whether His power in creation, the vindication of His messenger, or the fulfillment of His promise and warning, will certainly appear, but in His own time and wisdom, not at human urging. The believer is therefore called to restrain this natural haste with patience, trust in God's timing, and reflection, rather than hurrying toward what is promised or mocking what is warned of.

translation: And they say: "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The deniers of the message mock the Prophet and the believers by demanding a fixed date for the Resurrection and the punishment they have been warned about. Their question is not a sincere search for truth but a taunt, built on the assumption that if the promise is not fulfilled right now, it must be false. The verse exposes how disbelief hides behind challenges and delay, mistaking God's patience and the concealment of the Hour's timing for proof that the warning is empty. The knowledge of when it will come belongs to God alone, and the messenger's task is only to warn clearly, so the right response is to prepare for it rather than to demand its timing.

translation: If only those who disbelieved knew of the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces, nor from their backs, and they will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse warns that the deniers' arrogance and defiance stem from ignorance of what awaits them. On the Day of Judgment the Fire will surround them completely, striking their faces, which they once held up in pride, and their backs, so that no direction offers escape. They will have no power to defend themselves and no ally to rescue them. Had they truly known this reality, they would not have mocked the warnings or hastened to demand the punishment, but would have turned in faith and obedience to God while there was still time.

translation: Rather, it will come upon them suddenly and stun them, so they will be unable to repel it, nor will they be given respite.
interpretation: The verse warns that the promised punishment, or the Hour, will not arrive with advance notice that would let the disbelievers prepare or negotiate. It will overtake them abruptly, leaving them bewildered and speechless. Their wealth, power, and arguments will be of no use in averting it, and no extension of time will be granted for repentance. The lesson is that the opportunity to repent and change course exists only in the present life, so a person should not delay turning to God in the false hope of having more time later.

translation: And messengers before you were indeed mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encircled by the very thing they used to mock.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by reminding him that ridicule of God's messengers is an old pattern, not something unique to him. It also warns the mockers that the punishment they scoffed at, whether in this world or the next, will overtake them and surround them with no escape. Mockery of the truth does not stop it, and it ends in the ruin of the mockers. This calls the believer to patience and confidence in God's promise, and calls the arrogant to take heed before the reality they deride comes upon them.

translation: Say: Who can protect you by night and by day from the Most Merciful? Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to challenge those who mock the warnings of punishment by asking who, other than God, guards them through every hour of the night and day. Their safety, health and survival are sustained only by the mercy of God, the Most Merciful, and no false god or power can shield them from His decree if He wills harm. The question exposes their heedlessness. They do not lack signs or reminders, but they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord and ignore the One who preserves them. The use of the name 'the Most Merciful' underlines that their continued safety is a mercy they take for granted, and it makes their ingratitude and denial all the more blameworthy.

translation: Or do they have gods who can defend them besides Us? They are unable to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied against Us by any protection from Us.
interpretation: The verse challenges the idolaters' reliance on false deities, using a rhetorical question to expose how baseless it is. If they think their gods can shield them from God's punishment, those gods cannot even help themselves, so they cannot help their worshippers. Nor do those gods or the people who worship them have any protection, support, or companionship from God, since His help is only for those who submit to Him. The only true protector is God, and whatever is worshipped besides Him is helpless, so nothing can save a person from God's decree except God Himself.

translation: Nay, We let these people and their forefathers enjoy life until the lifespan grew long for them. Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders? Is it then they who will be the victors?
interpretation: The verse tells the disbelievers that their long enjoyment of worldly comforts was not a sign of God's approval or of their security; it was a respite that made them heedless and arrogant. They should look at what happens around them: God steadily diminishes the lands of the disbelievers from their edges, as Islam spreads and its territory expands while the power of the idolaters shrinks. Seeing the gradual erosion of their dominion, they should recognize that God's decree is at work and that their end is approaching. The closing rhetorical question, 'Is it then they who will be the victors?', rebukes their confidence: those whose power is receding cannot be the winners, but the believers, whom God supports, will prevail.

translation: Say: 'I only warn you by revelation.' But the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned.
interpretation: The Prophet's task is limited to conveying warnings that come from God through revelation, not from his own opinion or power. The failure of some people to respond is not due to any shortcoming in the message or the messenger, but to their own spiritual deafness: they have shut their hearts and ears to the truth out of arrogance and heedlessness. Just as the physically deaf cannot benefit from a call however loud or clear, those who refuse to listen with a receptive heart gain nothing from warnings, so guidance only benefits those who are willing to hear.

translation: And if even a whiff of the punishment of your Lord were to touch them, they would surely say, 'Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: The verse shows how fragile the denial of those who reject the truth is. Although they are heedless and arrogant now, even the faintest touch of God's punishment, no more than a breath or a hint of it, would be enough to break their pride and make them admit their guilt. Their confession would come out of fear, not out of true repentance, and so it would be too late to help them. The verse thus warns that admitting wrongdoing is best done now, by choice, through faith and obedience, before they are forced to admit it under punishment. It also suggests that if a mere trace of the punishment is enough to overwhelm them, they cannot imagine what the full punishment would be like.

translation: And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And if there be the weight of a mustard seed [of deeds], We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as Reckoners.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's perfect and absolute justice on the Day of Judgment. The 'scales of justice' signify an exact and fair accounting of every person's deeds, so that no one will be treated unjustly, whether by having good deeds overlooked or by being burdened with wrongs they did not commit. Even the tiniest deed, as small as a mustard seed, will be brought forth and weighed. The closing phrase, 'sufficient are We as Reckoners,' teaches that God needs no helper or witness to account for His creation, since His knowledge encompasses everything. The verse thus urges believers to be mindful of even small acts of good and evil, and to live with constant awareness of accountability before God, finding both hope that no good is wasted and caution that no wrong is hidden.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a illumination, and a reminder for the righteous.
interpretation: God reminds that revelation did not begin with Muhammad: He gave Moses and Aaron the Torah, which served as a criterion (al-Furqan) separating truth from falsehood and lawful from unlawful, as a light that dispels the darkness of ignorance and confusion, and as a reminder that awakens hearts to their duties and to God. Yet its benefit is for the muttaqin, those who are conscious of God and fear Him, for only they receive guidance from it and act upon it, whereas the heedless remain unmoved by even the clearest light.

translation: Those who fear their Lord in the unseen, and who are apprehensive of the Hour.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 21:49) describes the righteous as people whose reverence for God does not depend on seeing Him or on being observed by others. Their awe is real in private as in public, grounded in faith in what lies beyond perception. Their anxious concern about the Day of Judgment is not despair but a living awareness of accountability, which restrains them from wrongdoing and spurs them to good deeds. True guidance, then, benefits those whose hearts are moved by unseen realities, and the Qur'an's warning and remembrance is a light and a reminder specifically for people of this sort.

translation: And this [Qur'an] is a blessed reminder which We have sent down. Will you then deny it?
