interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a source of lasting good: it is a reminder that brings guidance, benefit, and growth in knowledge and faith to those who follow it, and it is a mercy from God just as earlier scriptures such as the Torah were. Because God has sent it down, and because its blessings are evident in its teachings and in its effect on hearts and societies, the closing rhetorical question rebukes those who reject it. Denying a revelation of such clear goodness is unreasonable, and the verse implies that rejecting it is a matter of stubbornness rather than a lack of evidence.

translation: And We had already granted Abraham his sound judgment before this, and We were well aware of him.
interpretation: God makes clear that Abraham's guidance and right-mindedness were not accidental or learned from his idolatrous surroundings but were a gift from God bestowed early in his life, before Moses and Aaron or before the confrontation with his people. Because God knew Abraham's inner nature, his sincerity, and his fitness for prophethood, He gave him the discernment to see the falsehood of idol-worship and to recognize the One true Lord. The verse thus presents Abraham as a model of one whom God guides because He knows the purity of his heart, and it prepares the ground for the account of his argument with his father and his people.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, "What are these statues to which you are devoted?"
interpretation: Abraham's question is not a request for information but a pointed challenge that exposes the emptiness of idol worship. By calling them 'statues' (tamāthīl), made and shaped by human hands, rather than by the names of gods his people gave them, he strips them of any sacred status. The phrase 'to which you are devoted' (ʿākifūn) highlights how people can give their time, loyalty and devotion to lifeless objects with no power to benefit or harm. He begins with his own father and community, showing that sincere calling to monotheism starts with those closest to us and uses reason to move hearts to question inherited customs that have no basis in truth.

translation: They said: 'We found our fathers worshipping them.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:53) records the answer of Abraham's people when he asked them what the idols they devoted themselves to really were. They offered no argument from reason or revelation to defend their worship. They fell back on inherited custom and ancestral precedent. The verse criticizes blind imitation (taqlid): a practice is not made true or right because earlier generations followed it. Beliefs have to be tested against evidence and sound judgment, and tradition alone is no proof. This is why Abraham answered that they and their forefathers were in manifest error.

translation: He said: "Indeed, you and your fathers have been in manifest error."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:54) records the reply of Prophet Abraham (peace be upon him) to his people after they defended idol worship by saying they found their forefathers worshipping the idols. Abraham answers that blind imitation of ancestors gives no legitimacy to falsehood. Tradition and majority practice are not criteria of truth, and both the generation that inherited the false practice and the one that began it are equally in clear misguidance. Truth is established by evidence and revelation, not by lineage or custom. By saying 'you and your fathers,' Abraham shows that error does not become right through repetition across generations, and he calls on people to rationally and independently examine what they worship.

translation: They said: "Have you come to us with the truth, or are you one of those who jest?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:55) records the reaction of Ibrahim's people after he challenged their worship of idols and told them that they and their forefathers were in manifest error. They were so accustomed to the inherited practice of idol worship that they could not take his claim seriously. Their question shows that they were unsettled and unable to refute him with proof, so they fell back on doubting whether he was in earnest. By asking whether he was truly stating the truth or merely playing, they treated their ancestral custom as the default that needed no defense, while the call to monotheism seemed to them either a startling claim or a frivolous joke. It illustrates how entrenched tradition can blind people to clear evidence, so that a sincere call to the truth is dismissed as trifling rather than weighed on its merits.

translation: He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them, and I am a witness to that."
interpretation: Abraham answers his people, who had asked whether he was speaking in earnest or jesting, by rejecting the idols they called 'the truth' and declaring that the only true object of worship is the one who originated the heavens and the earth. The proof is in creation itself: idols are themselves made things, while only the Creator who brought everything into being deserves devotion. By adding 'and I am among those who bear witness to this,' he does more than state a belief. He takes responsibility for the truth as a witness who testifies to it openly and stands by it, even against the weight of his community's inherited customs.

translation: And by God, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned and gone away.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Anbiya 21:57) records Abraham's quiet vow, after his people had rejected his argument against idol worship. He swears by God, the One he worships, that he will act against their idols once they leave for their festival. The oath shows his firm resolve to prove that these objects are powerless. He intends to break them, so that their inability to defend themselves exposes the falsehood of worshipping them and leads his people to reflect. The word 'kayd' (plot) here means a wise, hidden strategy, not wrongdoing. It is a lawful plan to demonstrate the truth, because the people would not listen to reason alone. The verse teaches that a believer should be determined in opposing falsehood, rely on God, and use wisdom and strategy to make clear the weakness of false gods.

translation: So he broke them into pieces, except for the largest of them, so that they might return to it.
interpretation: Abraham's act of smashing the idols while sparing the biggest one was a deliberate argument aimed at his people's reason. By leaving the chief idol intact, he set up a situation in which they would have to turn back to it and question it. When it could not answer or explain what had happened, its helplessness would expose the absurdity of worshipping objects that can neither speak, defend themselves, nor harm or benefit anyone. The verse shows that true guidance comes by awakening people's reflection and making falsehood refute itself, leading them to recognize that worship belongs to God alone.

translation: They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is surely among the wrongdoers." (Qur'an 21:59)
interpretation: After Abraham broke the idols into pieces, his people came upon the scene and, instead of questioning the helplessness of their gods, which could not defend themselves, they sought to punish the one who had done it. By calling him a wrongdoer (zālim), they reversed the true meaning of justice: the real wrong lay in worshipping powerless stones instead of God, yet they branded the one who exposed the falsehood as the offender. The verse shows how people attached to inherited beliefs and customs respond to a challenge to them with accusation and hostility rather than reflection, and how a misplaced devotion can blind them to the clear evidence in front of them.

translation: They said: 'We heard a youth mention them (the idols); he is called Abraham.'
interpretation: When the people of Abraham found their idols shattered, they did not know who had done it, so they began to search for the culprit. Those who had heard Abraham speak against the idols recalled that a young man, known by the name Abraham, had spoken of them with disparagement and denied their divinity. The verse shows that they inferred his guilt from his earlier words rather than from any proof, and it reveals how Abraham's open call to monotheism had already marked him out among his people. The word 'youth' (fatā) signals that he stood against established tradition and the authority of elders, as a young man firm in conviction, and it prepares the scene in which he will confront them publicly and use their own questions to expose the helplessness of their idols.

translation: They said, "Then bring him before the eyes of the people, so that they may bear witness."
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:61) shows the leaders of Abraham's people, after discovering that their idols had been smashed, choosing to put the suspect forward publicly rather than deal with him in secret. They wanted a public trial and public testimony, so that people would witness what he said and did, and so that his confession or his words could be used as evidence to justify punishing him. The phrase 'before the eyes of the people' suggests that they wanted to turn the matter into a public spectacle that would deter others and shore up their authority and their idol-worship. Yet God turned this plan to Abraham's advantage: the public setting gave him the platform to expose the helplessness of the idols, since they could not speak, defend themselves, or even identify who had harmed them. The verse thus teaches that falsehood often seeks the support of crowds and spectacle, while truth can use the very same stage to make its case clearly.

translation: They said, "Was it you who did this to our gods, O Abraham?"
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:62) records the idolaters' confrontation of Abraham after he smashed their idols, leaving only the largest one intact. Their question is rhetorical and investigative: they suspect him because he had earlier spoken against their idols, and they call them 'our gods' to show their attachment to inherited custom rather than reason. The interpretation is that Abraham's act was meant to expose the powerlessness of idols, and the question sets up the scene in which the people are drawn into admitting that their gods cannot speak, defend themselves, or harm anyone. This reveals the irrationality of worshipping what cannot act, and establishes the argument for tawhid, the worship of God alone.

translation: He said: "Rather, this—the biggest of them—did it. So ask them, if they are able to speak."
interpretation: Abraham uses a rhetorical, argumentative device rather than a literal lie. By attributing the smashing of the idols to the largest idol, he places his people in a logical trap: if the idols could speak, they could testify about who did it, and if they cannot speak, they plainly cannot hear, act, help, or harm, and so are unworthy of worship. His statement is meant to awaken their reason and expose the absurdity of worshipping lifeless stones, forcing them to admit the idols' powerlessness by their own mouths, which is what the following verses show them doing as they recognize their wrongdoing.

translation: So they turned back to themselves and said, 'Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:64) shows a moment of conscience in the people of Ibrahim after he challenged their idol worship. When they reflected inwardly, they recognized that the real wrong lay not in questioning the idols, who could not defend themselves, but in their own worship of lifeless objects that could neither speak nor protect. It teaches that sincere self-reflection can briefly awaken the fitrah (innate sense of truth), exposing the irrationality of false beliefs, even though the people did not follow this recognition with submission to the truth, as the next verse shows them relapsing into stubbornness.

translation: Then they were turned upside down onto their heads, saying: 'You surely know that these do not speak.'
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 21:65) describes the moment after Abraham smashed the idols and his people questioned him. Their reasoning was overturned, as though their heads were flipped, and they were forced to admit the truth against their own position. Their admission that the idols cannot speak became an unwitting proof of the idols' powerlessness and of the folly of worshipping them. Those who cannot speak, defend themselves, or benefit or harm anyone cannot be divine. The verse shows how falsehood, when confronted with clear reasoning, collapses under its own contradictions, and how a person's conscience may recognize the truth even while stubbornness prevents submission to it.

translation: He said: 'Do you then worship, besides God, that which cannot benefit you in the least, nor harm you?'
interpretation: This is Abraham's rebuke to his people (Surat al-Anbiya', 21:66). He appeals to their reason to expose the folly of idolatry. Worship belongs only to One who has power to give benefit and to avert harm, and the idols they carved with their own hands have neither power, so devoting oneself to them is irrational. The verse teaches that true worship must be directed solely to God, the sole Possessor of benefit and harm, and that blind imitation of ancestors cannot justify worshipping what is helpless.

translation: Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God! Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:67) is Abraham's exclamation of disgust at his people's idol worship, after the idols proved unable to defend themselves or answer a single question. Its meaning is that worshipping what can neither benefit nor harm, speak, or act is irrational and unworthy of human intellect. 'Uff' expresses utter contempt for both the worshippers and their false gods. The closing question, 'Will you not use your reason?', shows that true monotheism rests on sound reasoning: any thinking person who honestly reflects on the helplessness of idols should abandon them and turn to God alone, the Creator and Sustainer who alone deserves worship.

translation: They said: "Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act."
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Anbiya 21:68) shows how a community that cannot refute a clear argument turns to force. After Ibrahim (Abraham) broke their idols and exposed their helplessness by showing that the idols could not speak or defend themselves, his people had no rational reply. They chose the harshest punishment, burning him, and called it 'supporting your gods.' The irony is that those who claim to have gods worthy of worship must themselves defend those gods, which shows the gods' weakness. The verse also shows the tyrant's usual response to truth: when evidence fails, violence is used to protect false beliefs and the existing order. It further shows that Ibrahim's stand for tawhid (God's oneness) came at great personal risk, and that God's power is far greater than human schemes, as the following verse shows when He makes the fire cool and safe for Ibrahim.

translation: We said, 'O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:69) shows that God's command governs all natural forces, and that nothing, not even fire's power to burn, acts independently of His will. When Abraham's people cast him into the fire for destroying their idols, God did not simply extinguish it but commanded it to become coolness and safety, so that the very instrument meant to destroy him became a source of peace. The qualifier 'safety' is read as the sign that the coolness was made harmless, so Abraham was neither burned nor harmed by cold. The lesson is that those who place complete trust in God and stand firm for the truth are protected by Him, however overwhelming the danger, and that the plots of wrongdoers are powerless against His decree.

translation: They intended a plot against him, but We made them the greatest losers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:70) refers to the people of Abraham who, after he broke their idols, sought to destroy him by casting him into a fire. God shows that human scheming against His chosen servant cannot prevail against divine will: He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham, so their plot collapsed and they were left utterly defeated. Their loss was twofold, since they failed in their purpose and also saw clear proof of the truth they rejected, which left them without excuse. The lesson is that those who plot against God's messengers and the truth will end up bearing the loss they meant to inflict on others, while those who trust in God are protected.

translation: And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (al-Anbiya 21:71) describes God's rescue of Abraham and his nephew Lot from the persecution of their idolatrous people in Iraq, and their migration to the Holy Land of Greater Syria, including Palestine. The land is called blessed because of its fertility and its many prophets sent there, and because it became a source of guidance and spiritual benefit for all peoples. The deeper meaning is that when a believer leaves their home and endures hardship for the sake of God, God does not abandon them but brings them to a place of safety and blessing, and makes their sacrifice a source of lasting good for others beyond themselves.

translation: And We granted him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and each of them We made righteous.
interpretation: After Abraham left his people and endured trials for the sake of God, God rewarded him beyond what he asked. He had prayed for a righteous child, and God gave him Isaac, then added Jacob, a grandson, as a surplus bounty (nafilah). The verse shows that sacrifice for God is repaid with blessings that exceed expectations, including a righteous lineage. It also teaches that righteousness is a divine gift: God Himself made Abraham's descendants righteous, so guidance and virtue come by His grace and are not merely inherited or self-achieved. Abraham's family became a continuing line of prophethood and goodness.

translation: And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We inspired them to do good deeds, to establish prayer, and to give zakah; and they were worshippers of Us.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:73) describes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as chosen to be models of righteous leadership. Their authority was not worldly power but guidance by God's command, meaning they called people to the truth according to divine revelation and not personal opinion. God inspired them to do good, to pray and to give charity, which shows that true guidance combines devotion to God (prayer) with service to people (zakah and good deeds). The verse ends by stressing that they themselves lived by this message and were sincere worshippers, so their leadership rested on example as well as teaching. Those who guide others must first be devoted servants of God in their own conduct.

translation: And to Lot We gave judgment and knowledge, and We saved him from the town that used to commit abominations. Indeed, they were an evil people, defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse shows that God honors His prophets with wisdom and sound knowledge, and that this gift equips them to remain upright amid a corrupt society. Lot's deliverance from the town, whose people openly practiced foul deeds such as sexual perversion, highway robbery, and public indecency, shows that God rescues the righteous when corruption reaches its peak and judgment is due. The description of the townspeople as an evil and defiantly disobedient people explains why they were punished: their wrongdoing was a persistent habit and a rejection of divine guidance, not a passing lapse. The lesson is that faith and knowledge bring salvation, while persistent immorality and defiance of God's messengers bring destruction.

translation: And We admitted him into Our mercy; indeed, he was among the righteous.
interpretation: God's mercy is presented as a spiritual haven granted to those whose character and conduct are upright. The verse, which speaks of a prophet (in context, Ismail, Idris and Dhul-Kifl in Surat al-Anbiya, or Ishaq and Lut in similar passages), shows that entry into divine mercy is not merely a reward for outward deeds but a gift that God bestows on those who have been made and have remained righteous. Being 'among the righteous' is the stated reason for this honor, which teaches that patience, sincerity and steadfast obedience draw a person into God's protection, favor and nearness, both in this world and in the next.

translation: And [remember] Noah, when he called out before [Ibrahim and the others], so We answered him and saved him and his family from the great distress.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God responds to sincere supplication made in times of hardship. Noah, after long years of calling his people with little result, turned to his Lord in prayer, and God rescued him and his household from the great calamity of the people's persecution and the flood that destroyed the deniers. It shows that deliverance comes from God alone, that the believer's recourse in distress is prayer and trust in Him, and that faithfulness through prolonged trials ends in salvation for the righteous and ruin for the wrongdoers.

translation: And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were an evil people, so We drowned them all together.
interpretation: The verse describes God's vindication of Noah (Nuh) after centuries of calling his people to the truth. Their punishment was not arbitrary: it followed their persistent denial of clear signs and their entrenched wickedness, which made them a corrupting force. The flood that drowned them all shows that when a community rejects divine guidance after the evidence has been made plain, divine help comes to the believing messenger and justice overtakes the deniers. It is both a consolation to the faithful, who are assured that God's support will come, and a warning to those who reject God's signs, that moral corruption and arrogance bring about their own destruction.

translation: And [remember] David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of some people strayed into it at night and pastured there; and We were witnesses to their judgment.
interpretation: The verse points to how God grants judgment and understanding in varying degrees even among His chosen prophets, while He oversees every ruling. Two prophets gave different verdicts in the same case, which concerned a field ruined by another people's sheep. David, according to the common explanation, judged that the sheep be given to the owner of the field as compensation for the damage. Solomon proposed a more equitable solution: the field's owner would temporarily keep the sheep and benefit from their milk and wool, while the sheep's owner would restore the field to its former state. Once it was restored, each party would take back his property. The lesson is that God's all-encompassing knowledge and witnessing mean no judgment escapes Him, that legal reasoning (ijtihad) can legitimately yield differing conclusions, and that true justice aims at restoring balance and repairing harm rather than merely punishing. God gave Solomon the superior understanding of the case, yet both were praised for their judgment and knowledge, as the following verse indicates.

translation: And We made Solomon understand it; and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains to glorify Our praises along with David, and the birds as well. And it was We who were doing it.
interpretation: The verse refers to the case brought before David and Solomon, in which Solomon was granted the better understanding of the just ruling, without that implying any fault in David. God affirms that both prophets were given sound judgment and knowledge, so Solomon's insight is a special favor from God rather than a disparagement of his father. Among the gifts to David was that the mountains and birds joined him in glorifying God, echoing his praise, which shows that all creation is attuned to the worship of its Creator and that the prophets' abilities and miracles come from God's power alone. The closing phrase, 'and We were doers,' stresses that these wonders were not beyond God's ability, and that He does what He wills with His servants as signs of His power and favor.

translation: And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your own violence. So will you be grateful?
interpretation: God singles out David's gift of forging armor as a practical mercy to humanity: a skill taught by divine inspiration that shields people from the harm of war and the blows of one another in battle. The verse presents human craftsmanship and technology as God's favor, not as a merely human achievement. The closing question, 'So will you be grateful?', is a gentle rebuke and invitation. Gratitude is not only speech but also using such skills and blessings for protection, justice, and good, and acknowledging their true Giver instead of crediting oneself alone.

translation: And to Solomon We subjected the raging wind, running by his command toward the land which We had blessed. And We are, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse shows that God honored Solomon with a power beyond ordinary human ability: the strong wind, which normally no one can direct, was made to move at his word and carry him to the blessed land, understood as the land of Syria and Palestine. The wind's obedience was not Solomon's own strength but a gift and sign from God, who governs the forces of nature and lends them to whom He wills. The closing phrase, 'And We are of all things Knowing,' teaches that God's granting of such dominion was grounded in perfect knowledge and wisdom. He knew Solomon's gratitude and righteousness, and so entrusted him with this power without it corrupting him, and He knows what is fitting for every person and every matter.

translation: And among the devils were those who dived for him and did other work besides that; and We were guarding over them.
interpretation: God subjected to Solomon, as a sign of the vast dominion He granted him, a class of the jinn and devils who would dive into the seas to retrieve pearls and treasures, and who also carried out other labors such as building, crafting and construction. Their obedience was not due to their own inclination, since their nature inclines toward corruption, but because God Himself restrained them and kept them under watch, so that they could not flee, disobey, spoil what they made, or harm Solomon and his people. The verse shows that all power, even over unruly beings, belongs to God, who gives and restrains by His will.

translation: And [remember] Job, when he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."
interpretation: The verse presents Job's prayer as a model of supplication rooted in patience and humility. He does not complain against God or make a direct demand; he states his affliction honestly and then appeals to God's mercy by invoking His attribute as the Most Merciful. This teaches that the believer may acknowledge hardship and weakness before God without violating patience, because true patience is not the denial of pain but the refusal to despair or protest against God's decree. By leaving the form of relief to God's wisdom and resting his plea on divine mercy, Job shows that the best way to ask is through submission, trust, and recognition that God's compassion exceeds every other mercy, so relief comes from Him alone.

translation: So We responded to him and removed the affliction that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.
interpretation: This verse, from the account of the Prophet Ayyub (Job), shows that sincere supplication joined with patience is answered by God. After Ayyub endured prolonged illness and loss without complaint against God, turning to Him alone, God lifted his harm and restored his family and doubled their number, which was not a reward earned by his own right but a mercy from God. The account stands as a reminder to those who worship that trials are not a sign of God's abandonment, that patience and steadfast devotion lead to relief, and that God's generosity exceeds what a servant loses in His path.

translation: And [remember] Ishmael, Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; all were among the steadfast.
interpretation: God singles out these three prophets for the shared quality of patience (sabr), presenting steadfastness as the defining trait that united them despite their different eras and trials. Ishmael bore the trial of being offered in sacrifice and of settling in a barren valley, Idris persevered in obedience and the pursuit of truth, and Dhul-Kifl kept faith with the responsibilities and covenant he had taken on. Their patience, meaning endurance of hardship, constancy in obedience, and restraint from disobedience, is what qualified them for God's mercy and for being counted among the righteous, as the following verse affirms. The verse thus teaches believers that patience is a path to nearness to God and a model to emulate in times of trial.

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 21:86) speaks of Ishmael, Idris and Dhul-Kifl, who are mentioned just before it. It teaches that God's mercy is the ultimate reward for patient and steadfast servants, and that entering it is a divine favor granted because of their righteousness. Their patience under trials was not merely endured but crowned with God's acceptance and care, and it shows that righteousness (salah), which means being sound in faith, character and deeds, is the very quality that qualifies a person for that mercy. Being 'among the righteous' is the highest station, and God's mercy encompasses those who attain it both in this world and the next.

translation: And [remember] the Man of the Fish (Dhul-Nun, the Prophet Yunus), when he went off in anger and thought that We would not constrain him. Then he called out within the darknesses: 'There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.' (Qur'an 21:87)
interpretation: The verse teaches that even a prophet can err and that the way back to God is through humble repentance. Yunus left his people in frustration at their stubborn rejection before receiving God's permission, and his thinking that God would not 'constrain' him (from the root qadara, meaning to restrict or decree hardship, not a doubt in God's power) reflects his assumption that his departure would carry no consequence. Swallowed by the fish, he was enveloped in layered darknesses: the night, the depths of the sea, and the belly of the fish. In that helplessness he turned to God with a formula that joins three elements: affirming God's absolute oneness ('there is no god but You'), declaring God free from any fault ('glory be to You'), and owning his own fault ('I was among the wrongdoers'). The lesson is that sincere tawhid, glorification of God, and honest confession of one's own wrongdoing, rather than blaming circumstances, are the keys to relief from the most hopeless of situations, as the following verse confirms by stating that God answered him and saved him.

translation: So We responded to him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anbiya 21:88) refers to Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who called upon God from the darkness of the whale's belly, the sea, and the night, declaring God's oneness and confessing his own wrongdoing. God's answer shows that sincere repentance and turning to Him alone in the depths of distress bring relief, even when all worldly means are cut off. The closing phrase makes this a standing divine principle rather than a single event: whenever believers, like Yunus, turn to God with faith, humility, and acknowledgment of their faults, God rescues them from their anguish.

translation: And [remember] Zechariah, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone [without an heir], and You are the best of inheritors."
interpretation: Zechariah's prayer shows that a believer may openly ask God for what he most needs while acknowledging that God alone is the ultimate source of all provision. His plea not to be left 'alone' is more than a wish for a child. He wants a righteous successor who will carry on the prophetic mission and guidance after him, so that the message is not lost. By ending with 'You are the best of inheritors,' he expresses complete submission and contentment with God's decree. He recognizes that everything returns to God, who inherits the heavens and the earth. Even if his request were not granted, God's care would still be enough for him. The verse teaches humility, sincerity, and trust in supplication, and it shows that God answers such prayer, as the following verses say He did by granting Zechariah John.

translation: So We responded to him and gave him John, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear, and they were humbly submissive to Us.
interpretation: The verse shows that God answers the sincere prayer of Zechariah, who asked humbly for an heir, by granting him John despite old age and his wife's barrenness, which God remedied. It then explains the qualities that made them worthy of this favor: eagerness to do good without delay, a balanced devotion that joins hope in God's mercy with fear of His punishment, and deep humility before Him. The lesson is that a response to prayer is closely tied to a life of righteous action, sincere supplication, and reverent humility, and that God's power is not limited by apparent impossibilities.

translation: And [mention] the one who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her [garment] of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse presents Mary as a model of purity and devotion whose chastity was preserved, and it shows that God's power is not bound by ordinary causes. Jesus' birth without a father, through the breath of God's spirit, was a miraculous sign for all people of every age. It teaches that God creates as He wills, and that sincere faith and moral integrity can be raised by God to a place of honor and become a lasting lesson for humanity.

translation: Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:92) comes after the mention of the prophets and affirms that all of them, despite differences in time and place, brought the same message of pure monotheism, so the believers across history form one single community bound by faith in One Lord rather than by lineage, land, or language. Since God alone is their Lord, the logical consequence is that worship must be directed to Him alone, and unity of belief should draw people together. Division into sects and factions that turn religion into rival camps contradicts this foundational call to one community under one God.

translation: But they cut up their affair among themselves into factions; all of them will return to Us.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anbiya 21:93) laments how people, who were originally one community united upon the worship of the One God as taught by all the prophets, tore their religion into sects and rival parties, each claiming a share of the truth. Their division was not part of the divine design but their own doing. Yet the verse ends with a sober reminder that this fragmentation is not final: every faction, without exception, will return to God, who will judge between them and reveal the truth they disputed. The meaning is both a rebuke of sectarianism and a call to unity upon the original message of monotheism, with the awareness that accountability before God awaits everyone.

translation: So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort, and indeed, We are recording it for him.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:94) states the principle that good deeds are accepted and rewarded only when they are joined with faith. Anyone who does righteous works as a sincere believer will find that God does not let his striving go unappreciated or be wasted, since the word 'kufran' here means the denial or disregard of a favor, and God negates it completely. The phrase 'We are recording it for him' assures the believer that every deed, however small, is preserved with God, so that nothing is forgotten or lost and it will be brought forward for full recompense on the Day of Judgment. The verse thus encourages perseverance in goodness and gives the believer confidence that his efforts are noticed and valued by God.

translation: And it is forbidden for a town that We have destroyed that they should return.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Anbiya 21:95) is understood to mean that those who were destroyed for their persistent disbelief and wrongdoing have no chance to return to this world to repent or make amends. Their opportunity for repentance ended with their death, and the deeds they carried out in life are what they will be held to account for. It is a warning to the living to turn back to God and correct themselves while time and choice remain, since after destruction or death there is no second chance to come back and reform.

translation: Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, and they swarm down from every elevation.
interpretation: The verse points to a sign of the approach of the Last Hour. The barrier that now restrains Gog and Magog will be opened, and they will pour out in overwhelming multitudes, rushing swiftly from every height and direction like a flood, so that no place is safe from them. Their release shows that the world's order is nearing its end and that the promise of resurrection and judgment is close at hand. It is a warning to people to heed the truth and prepare for the Day of Account before the sudden onset of these events leaves them no time to repent.

translation: And the true promise has drawn near; then lo, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be fixedly staring: "Woe to us! We were indeed heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers."
interpretation: When the Day of Resurrection approaches and its promised reality becomes unmistakable, the disbelievers will be struck with terror, their eyes frozen in a fixed stare of horror. In that moment they cry out in anguish, admitting they had lived heedless of this day, as if distracted by worldly life. Then they correct themselves and acknowledge that their heedlessness was no excuse: it was their own wrongdoing, since the warnings had reached them and they rejected them. The verse shows that the reality of the Hereafter will strip away every pretext, and that heedlessness toward God's warning is itself a form of injustice to oneself and to the truth.

translation: Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell; to it you will come.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:98) warns the idolaters of Quraysh that the idols they venerate in place of God will not intercede for them or save them. Both the worshippers and their false objects of worship will be cast into Hellfire as its fuel, an image that shows the complete powerlessness of these idols and the folly of devotion to anything other than God. The phrase 'you will come to it' stresses that this destination is certain and inescapable for those who persist in associating partners with God. The idols, being lifeless stones, are thrown in not as punishment for them but to heighten the disgrace and anguish of their worshippers, who will see that what they trusted is useless. Those who were truly righteous, such as Jesus, Ezra, and the angels, who were wrongly worshipped by others, are excluded, as the following verses make clear, because they never approved of such worship.

translation: If these had truly been gods, they would not have entered it (Hellfire); and all of them will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the declaration that the disbelievers and what they worship besides God are fuel for Hell (Qur'an 21:98), offers a decisive argument against idolatry. A true deity must be able to protect itself and its worshippers from harm, so if the idols, which are false objects of worship, end up in the Fire alongside those who venerated them, that proves they have no divinity and no power to benefit or save. The worshippers and the worshipped are thus united in the same fate, and their permanence in it ('all are abiding therein') underscores the finality of the consequence. The verse's lesson is that only God, who is beyond all need and weakness, deserves worship, and that clinging to anything else as a divine intercessor is futile.

translation: They will have therein groaning, and they therein will not hear.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Anbiya 21:100) describes the state of the idolaters in Hellfire. Their torment is so intense that they let out heaving, anguished sighs and groans, like the gasping of one in unbearable pain. Alongside this, they will be unable to hear anything comforting or meaningful, whether speech, guidance, or any plea that might bring relief. The deafness is a fitting consequence of having refused to listen to the truth and the warnings of the messengers in the world. Thus they are left in isolation, with nothing but their own cries, and cut off from all mercy, as a just recompense for their rejection.

translation: Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already been decreed from Us — they will be kept far away from it (Hellfire).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:101) draws a contrast with the idolaters and what they worship, who are fuel for Hell in the preceding verses. It says that those who were granted God's prior promise of the 'husna' (the best, meaning Paradise and divine mercy) through faith, sincere obedience, and God's foreknowledge and favor are removed far from Hell. They will not enter it, nor feel its heat or hear its faintest sound, as the following verses add. The meaning is that salvation is first of all a gift from God's mercy and decree, which shows itself in a person's faith and righteous deeds. Those worshipped besides God who were themselves righteous, such as the prophets, angels, and pious people, are not included among the damned, because they were never pleased with being worshipped and God had already promised them the best outcome.

translation: They will not hear even its faintest sound, and they will abide eternally in what their souls desire.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the righteous who have been kept far away from Hellfire. They are so securely removed from it that not even its faint hissing or rustling reaches their ears, so no fear or anxiety disturbs their bliss. In Paradise, every wish of their souls is fulfilled, and this fulfillment is not temporary, for they dwell there forever. The verse thus joins two complete blessings: safety from every source of pain and fear, and the attainment of every pleasure and desire, along with the assurance that it will never end.

translation: The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them, saying: 'This is your Day, which you were promised.'
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when the terror of the Hour overwhelms all creation, those who were righteous and had been spared from the Fire will be kept free from fear and sorrow. This reassurance is a mark of God's honor toward them. The angels will meet them with welcome and glad tidings, reminding them that the Day they once heard about and strove for, through faith and good deeds in spite of denial and hardship in the world, has arrived, and that the promise of God is true and now fulfilled for them.

translation: On the Day when We will roll up the heaven like a scroll rolled up for writings. As We began the first creation, We will repeat it. It is a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We are ever doers.
interpretation: This verse describes the end of the present cosmos on the Day of Judgment, when God will fold up the vast heavens with ease, as a scribe rolls up a parchment when the writing is finished. This shows that the immense order of the universe is entirely subject to God's power and will end when He decides. The verse then answers doubts about resurrection: the One who brought creation into being from nothing can surely bring it back, and people will return just as they were first created, bare and dependent. God calls this a binding promise upon Himself, so it is certain and cannot fail, and He affirms that He is always capable of carrying out what He has decreed. The verse is meant to strengthen belief in the Hereafter and to remind people to prepare for accountability.

translation: And We have already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God's decree, recorded in earlier scripture (the Psalms of David) and confirmed after the 'Reminder' (the Torah or the preserved divine knowledge), is that the ultimate inheritance and stewardship of the earth belongs to those who combine faith with righteous conduct. It is a consoling promise to the believers: worldly power may temporarily rest with the arrogant and wrongdoers, but it is not lasting, and the final outcome, whether in this world through just leadership or fully in the next through the promised land of Paradise, is for the sincere, upright servants of God. Dominion is thus tied not to lineage or sheer force, but to righteousness.

translation: Indeed, in this [Qur'an] is a message sufficient for a people who worship.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an, with its warnings, promises, and guidance, contains all that a sincere servant of God needs in order to reach Him and attain felicity in this world and the next. Those who devote themselves to worshipping God, obeying Him, and submitting to His will are the ones who truly benefit from it, because they receive its guidance with open hearts and act upon it. It is a sufficient provision and a clear path for them, so they need no other source of guidance to arrive at the pleasure of God and the inheritance of the righteous.

translation: And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to all the worlds.
interpretation: The mission of the Prophet Muhammad is an expression of God's compassion toward all of creation, not only toward one people or generation. Through the guidance he brought, humanity is given knowledge of its Creator, a moral path that gives life order and purpose, and the hope of salvation. His message calls for justice, kindness, and restraint even in conflict, so that its benefit reaches believers through guidance, and reaches others through the mercy, protection, and ethical standards it establishes. In this way the verse presents prophethood itself as a gift of divine mercy to the whole of existence.

translation: Say: 'It is only revealed to me that your God is One God. So will you submit to Him?'
interpretation: The verse defines the core of the Prophet's mission: he is a human messenger who conveys only what is revealed to him, and the heart of that revelation is pure monotheism (tawhid). By ending with a question, 'Will you then submit?', it moves from stating a doctrine to calling for a response. Recognizing that God is One logically requires submitting to Him alone, with sincere worship and obedience, and no partners or intermediaries. The verse treats faith as a conscious choice that each person must answer for himself or herself.

translation: But if they turn away, then say: 'I have announced to you all alike [and equally]; and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far.'
interpretation: After the Prophet has conveyed the message and the evidence has been made clear, those who still turn away are left without excuse. He is told to declare openly that he has informed everyone equally, hiding nothing from anyone and favoring no group, so that no party can claim it was deceived or kept uninformed. The second part teaches that the exact timing of the promised reckoning and punishment is knowledge belonging to God alone. The Messenger's duty is to warn and make the message plain, not to fix the hour. The verse therefore joins fair, universal proclamation with humility before God's unseen knowledge.

translation: Indeed, He knows what is said openly, and He knows what you conceal.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's knowledge is complete and all-encompassing, so nothing escapes Him, whether spoken aloud or hidden in the heart. It follows the warning in Surat al-Anbiya' about people turning away from the truth, and reminds them that they cannot hide their real intentions, their secret plotting, or the doubts and denial they conceal behind their outward words. Because God knows both the open and the hidden, people will be held accountable for their inner state as well as their public conduct. The believer is therefore called to sincerity and God-consciousness in private as much as in public.

translation: And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and an enjoyment for a time.
interpretation: The Prophet is told to admit that he does not know the unseen: he cannot say whether the delay of the promised punishment or judgment is a test for the disbelievers, or only a brief period of worldly enjoyment before their term ends. The delay is not a sign of divine approval or of a false warning. It may be a trial that exposes how they act when given respite, and a short-lived comfort that ends at a time known only to God. People should not be deceived by their present ease, but should use the time to repent and turn to God before it runs out.

translation: He said, "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against what you describe."
interpretation: This closing verse of Surat al-Anbiya' shows the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) entrusting the final outcome of his struggle with the deniers to God. He asks God to decide between truth and falsehood with perfect justice, so that the truth is made manifest and falsehood is defeated. He affirms that God is al-Rahman, whose mercy encompasses His creation, even as He judges, and that He alone is the one whose aid is sought against the lies, mockery, and false claims the disbelievers make about the message and the believers. The believer's proper response to slander and hostility is thus not despair or retaliation by his own power, but patient reliance on God, who will vindicate the truth in His time.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the quaking of the Hour is a tremendous thing.
interpretation: The verse calls all of humanity, not only believers, to live with God-consciousness (taqwa) by keeping their duty to their Creator, and it grounds this call in the terrifying reality of the Last Hour. The 'quaking' signifies the cataclysmic upheaval that will shake the earth and every settled certainty at the end of time, an event so immense that no worldly power or security can withstand it. By describing it as 'a tremendous thing' without detailing it, the verse leaves the imagination to grasp its overwhelming gravity, so that the fear of that day becomes a motive to reform one's belief and conduct now, before the time to act is over.

translation: On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursing infant, and every pregnant woman will deliver her burden, and you will see the people intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated; but the punishment of God is severe.
interpretation: The verse describes the terror of the Hour as so overwhelming that it overturns the strongest human instincts: a mother's care for her suckling child and the natural protection of a pregnancy. People appear dazed and staggering like drunkards, yet they are not drunk with wine. Their bewilderment comes from the dread of God's severe punishment and the awesome reality of standing before Him. The point is a warning, urging people to fear God and prepare for that Day through faith and righteous action while there is still time, since on that Day attachments and worldly concerns give way to the sole concern of one's own fate.

translation: And among the people is he who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.
interpretation: The verse describes a type of person who argues about God, His power, His revelation, and especially the resurrection, without any sound knowledge or evidence, relying only on conjecture and desire. Such disputation is not honest inquiry but a surrender of the intellect to misguidance: by rejecting revealed truth, he becomes a follower of every defiant devil, whether among jinn or human beings, who beautifies falsehood for him. The verse warns that speaking about God without knowledge leads one to submit to evil influences, and that real knowledge is the necessary basis for any discussion of matters of faith.

translation: It has been decreed concerning him that whoever takes him as a friend, he will surely mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 22:4) speaks of the one who argues about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil (shaytan). It declares it a fixed decree that whoever befriends and obeys the devil will be led astray by him. The devil does not merely fail to guide; he steers his follower down a path whose end is the Blaze of Hell. Its meaning is a warning that submitting to the whisperings of evil, and to those who call to falsehood without knowledge, leads inevitably to ruin, so a person should anchor their beliefs in revealed guidance rather than speculation or blind following.

translation: O people, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then consider that We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, partly formed and partly unformed, in order to make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whatever We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then so that you may reach your full strength. And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most feeble age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it water, it quivers, swells, and grows from every beautiful kind of plant.
interpretation: God answers doubts about the Resurrection by pointing to what people can observe: their own stages of creation and the revival of dead land. Humans begin as lifeless dust and pass through carefully ordered stages in the womb, then infancy, maturity, and either death or senile decline. Each stage shows a power that originates and transforms life at will. Whoever can bring a living, thinking person out of dust and a drop of fluid, and can make the lifeless earth stir and flourish with rain, can surely raise the dead. Resurrection is therefore not an improbable event but a continuation of the same creative power already evident in human life and in nature, and the reminder of frailty in old age also shows that human knowledge and strength are gifts that depend entirely on God.

translation: That is because God is the Truth, and because He gives life to the dead, and because He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the order and wonder of creation, seen in the earth reviving after lifeless dryness and in the human being's growth from dust, sperm-drop, and clinging clot, are signs that point to God as the one true, ever-real Being whose existence and promise are certain. Since He brings life out of lifelessness in this world, resurrection after death is neither impossible nor far-fetched, but is an expression of His absolute power. The verse thus grounds belief in the Hereafter in the reality of God Himself: whoever acknowledges that He is the Truth and that nothing lies beyond His ability must accept that He will raise the dead and hold them to account, and should live in a way that reflects this certainty.

translation: And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will resurrect those who are in the graves.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the end of the world and the Day of Judgment are certain realities, not matters of speculation, and that God's power over creation extends to restoring the dead to life. Having just pointed to signs of His power in nature, such as the earth revived after lifeless dryness, the Qur'an presents resurrection as a logical consequence of God's truth and ability: the One who originates life can renew it. The implication is moral as well as metaphysical, because belief in a certain Hour and a certain resurrection means every person is accountable, so one should live with awareness that deeds will be weighed and justice will finally be established.

translation: And among the people is he who disputes about God without knowledge, or guidance, or an enlightening Book.
interpretation: The verse condemns argumentation about God's existence, attributes, or power that is not grounded in any legitimate source of knowledge. It names three possible foundations for sound discourse: knowledge (clear reasoning and sure understanding), guidance (the direction given through prophets and divinely inspired insight), and a luminous Scripture (revelation). One who disputes about God while having none of these is arguing from conjecture, ego, or desire. The lesson is that speaking about matters of faith and the unseen requires humility and evidence, and that stubborn, baseless disputation leads people astray and tempts them to lead others astray as well.

translation: Turning aside in arrogance to lead others astray from the path of God. For him in this world is disgrace, and on the Day of Resurrection We will make him taste the torment of the burning fire.
interpretation: The verse completes the description of the one who disputes about God without knowledge (22:8). He turns away with pride, twisting his neck and showing disdain toward the truth, and his arrogance is not merely personal: he uses his argument to mislead others from God's path. His punishment matches his offense. In this world he faces disgrace, such as defeat, humiliation, and the exposure of his falsehood, as happened to the leaders of disbelief at Badr. In the Hereafter he will be made to taste the torment of the blazing fire, which shows that those who obstruct others from guidance bear responsibility for their own sin and for the harm they cause.

translation: That is because of what your hands have sent forth, and because God is never unjust to His servants.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the punishment people face in the Hereafter is the direct result of their own deeds, which are referred to as 'what your hands have sent forth' because the hands are the usual means by which people act. Responsibility therefore lies with the human being, not with God. God's justice is absolute and extreme: He does not wrong anyone by adding to their burden, taking away their reward, or punishing them without cause. The recompense is exactly proportionate to what was earned, so no one will be able to object that they were treated unfairly.

translation: And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge: if good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial afflicts him, he turns over on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the clear loss.
interpretation: The verse describes a person whose faith is conditional and unstable, like someone standing on the very edge of a precipice, ready to fall at any shock. He worships God only as long as it brings him comfort, health, wealth, or security, and he feels reassured by his religion in times of ease. But when a hardship or test comes, he reverts to disbelief or doubt, blaming his faith or abandoning it. Such a person loses in both realms: in this world he gains neither the comfort he sought nor the patience and spiritual peace that sincere believers find in adversity, and in the Hereafter he forfeits reward because his devotion was never genuine submission to God but a transaction for worldly gain. The verse teaches that true faith means steadfast, unconditional servitude to God in both prosperity and trial, trusting His wisdom whatever befalls.

translation: He invokes, besides God, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-gone straying.
interpretation: The verse portrays the folly of turning in prayer and hope to anything other than God, whether idols, people, or imagined powers. Such objects have no power to bring benefit or ward off harm, so the person who relies on them has abandoned the only Source of real help. The Qur'an calls this a 'far-gone straying' because the person has wandered so far from truth and sound reason that returning becomes difficult. The lesson is that dependence and worship belong to God alone, and that attaching one's hopes to what is powerless is both a spiritual and an intellectual error.

translation: He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Evil indeed is such a protector, and evil indeed is such a companion.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Hajj 22:13) condemns the idol-worshipper who, instead of calling on God, invokes false deities that cannot help him. Such objects of worship bring only harm: they lead their devotees into misguidance and the punishment of the Hereafter, and any benefit imagined from them is remote and illusory. The verse therefore calls them an evil patron (mawla), who gives no protection, and an evil associate (ashir), who gives no true companionship. It urges the believer to place trust and devotion in God alone, since everything besides Him ends in loss.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into Gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation rests on faith joined with righteous action, and that the reward for it is entirely a matter of God's grace and sovereign will, not something creatures can claim as a right or compel. The closing phrase 'Allah does what He wills' reassures believers that His promise of Paradise is certain, since nothing can hinder His decree, and it also reminds them that the outcome of every soul, including the fate of those who disbelieve, is governed by His wisdom and power alone. Believers are thus invited to trust His promise and persevere in good works, hoping in His mercy rather than relying on their own deeds.

translation: Whoever thinks that Allah will never support him (the Prophet) in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope up to the sky, then cut it off, and let him see whether his scheme will remove that which enrages him.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who resent the Prophet's success and wish that God's help would be cut off from him. They are told that God's support is certain, and that if their rage cannot accept it, they should exhaust every possible means: let them tie a rope to the ceiling or to the sky and hang themselves, cutting off their own breath, and see whether this desperate act would remove the cause of their anger. The point is that no scheme, however extreme, can stop God's decree of victory for His messenger and the faithful. Their fury changes nothing, and the only outcome of their rage is their own harm, so they should submit to the truth rather than consume themselves in resentment.

translation: And thus We have sent it down as clear verses, and indeed Allah guides whom He wills.
interpretation: The Qur'an has been revealed in plain, unambiguous verses that leave no excuse for confusion about truth, since its proofs and rulings are clear to anyone who reflects. Yet clarity of the message does not by itself bring about faith, because guidance in the sense of inner acceptance and being granted success lies with Allah alone. He grants it to those who sincerely seek it and are open to the truth, while those who stubbornly turn away are left to their own course. The believer should therefore value the clear revelation, and also ask Allah continually for guidance and steadfastness.

translation: Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate partners with God — indeed, God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, God is Witness over all things.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Hajj, 22:17) lists the major religious communities and affirms that their disputes over truth, and their competing claims to salvation, will not be settled by argument in this world but by God's own final judgment on the Day of Resurrection. God does not need to rely on hearsay or claims, because He is a witness to everything: every belief held, every deed done, and every intention hidden. The ultimate decision on who was right belongs to Him alone, and it will be just and exact. The verse therefore reassures the believers that their faith will be vindicated and warns the others that no deed or conviction escapes God's knowledge, calling everyone to sincerity and accountability rather than to pride in their affiliation.

translation: Do you not see that to God prostrate those in the heavens and those on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals, and many of the people? Yet for many the punishment has become due. And whoever God humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed, God does what He wills.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all creation is subject to God's sovereign will and submits to Him by its very nature: the heavenly bodies, mountains, trees and animals follow the laws He set for them, in a constant state of obedience and glorification. Human beings alone are given the freedom to choose between willing prostration and rebellion. Many believers prostrate by choice and so join the harmony of the universe, while many others refuse and thereby earn the punishment that is justly due to them. Honor and disgrace are in God's hands alone: whoever He abases through their own arrogance and disbelief cannot be raised by anyone, because no one has power to grant honor against His decree. His will is absolute and wise, so no one should seek dignity through disobedience, but through humble submission to the One whom all creation already obeys.

translation: These are two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads.
interpretation: The verse portrays the age-old conflict between the people of faith and the people of disbelief, who stand opposed to one another over God: the believers affirm His oneness and submit to His guidance, while the disbelievers deny Him and resist His message. The verse then states what the deniers will face on the Day of Judgment. Fire will encompass them as closely as tailored clothing fits the body, so that there is no escape from it, and scalding water poured over their heads will torment them from above and penetrate within. The point is that rejecting God's truth carries a just and total recompense, in contrast to the honor promised to the believers in the verses that follow.

translation: By it (the boiling water poured over their heads) is melted what is within their bellies, as well as their skins.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Hajj, 22:20) describes the severity of the punishment of the disbelievers in Hell: the scalding water poured over their heads penetrates their bodies, dissolving both their innards and their outer skin. It shows that the torment is total, reaching inside and outside alike, so that no part of a person is spared. It serves as a stern warning, urging people to heed God's message and avoid the disbelief and wrongdoing that lead to such a fate.

translation: And for them are hooked iron rods (maces).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Hajj (22:21), describes part of the punishment awaiting the disbelievers in Hell. The 'maqami'' are iron rods or hooked maces used to strike and restrain, and the verse shows that the torment is not only the fire and boiling water mentioned in the surrounding verses but also physical humiliation and subjugation. Iron, the symbol of worldly strength and tyranny, becomes the instrument of their disgrace, so those who were arrogant and who oppressed others, or who rejected truth with stubborn pride, are met with a force that overpowers them completely. When they try to escape the anguish, they are driven back with these rods, making clear that there is no flight from divine justice and that the punishment fits the severity of their defiance.

translation: Whenever they want to come out of it, out of anguish, they are returned into it, and (it is said): "Taste the punishment of the burning Fire." (Qur'an 22:22)
interpretation: The verse portrays the hopelessness of the punishment awaiting those who persisted in denial and opposition to God's truth: every attempt at escape from the Fire, driven by the suffocating distress within it, is met with being forced back, so that there is neither relief nor exit. The command to 'taste' the punishment suggests that the suffering is not abstract but felt fully and personally, and the repeated return shows that the sentence is just and inescapable, a consequence of their own choices rather than an arbitrary act. The verse serves as a warning to reflect on one's beliefs and conduct while there is still time to repent and turn to God's mercy.

translation: Indeed, God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into Gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation and ultimate honor are tied to faith joined with action: belief alone is incomplete without righteous deeds, and the two together are what earn God's promise. The imagery of gold, pearls, and silk, which were symbols of the highest dignity and luxury in the world, shows that the believers who may have been humble or oppressed in this life are elevated in the next to a status of true nobility. Their reward is complete and perfectly fitting, a lasting honor from God that far surpasses worldly honor, and it encourages the believer to remain steadfast and patient, knowing that what is given up for God's sake is repaid with something better and everlasting.

translation: And they were guided to the best of speech, and they were guided to the path of the Most Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse describes the people of Paradise, who are rewarded for their faith. God granted them success in this world and the next to utter pure, good words, such as the declaration of God's oneness, His praise, glorification, and remembrance, and in Paradise their speech will be wholesome and free of idle talk or sin. They were also guided to the path of God, the One who is worthy of all praise in His essence, names, and actions, which is the straight path of Islam leading to His pleasure. The verse shows that right speech and right path are both gifts of divine guidance, and that those who were guided to good words and to God's path in life are the ones who reach the abode of peace in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and obstruct people from the way of God and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made for all people alike, the resident in it and the visitor, and whoever intends to commit deviation in it through wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Sacred Mosque and its sanctuary in Mecca are a open, shared sanctuary of God, not the private property of any tribe or authority. Those who bar believers from worship there, as the Quraysh did, and those who violate its sanctity through any deliberate wrongdoing or impiety, commit a grave offense because the place's holiness magnifies the gravity of sin committed in it. The warning of a painful punishment, attached even to the mere intention of wrongdoing in this place, shows that the sanctuary demands a special level of reverence, justice, and restraint from all who dwell in or visit it.

translation: And [remember] when We assigned to Abraham the site of the House, saying: 'Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it, those who stand in prayer, and those who bow and prostrate.'
interpretation: The verse shows that the Kaaba was founded on pure monotheism. God directed Abraham to its location and made his first charge the rejection of all partners with God, so that the House would be built on sincere devotion. Only then did He command physical purification of the sanctuary. Cleansing it of idols, impurity, and disorder is bound up with inner purity of faith. The House exists to serve worshippers engaged in the acts of worship named here: circumambulation (tawaf), standing in prayer (qiyam), bowing (ruku'), and prostration (sujud). Its purpose is therefore to be a clean, peaceful place of worship of the One God, and those entrusted with it must keep it free from shirk and defilement so that all who come to worship are welcome.

translation: And proclaim to the people the Hajj (pilgrimage); they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every distant mountain highway.
interpretation: After Abraham finished rebuilding the Kaaba, God commanded him to call humanity to pilgrimage. Though his voice could not physically reach everyone, the verse teaches that when a call is made in obedience to God, God carries it to the hearts of people across all places and ages. The verse shows that the pilgrimage is a universal summons: people come with devotion, whether on foot or on worn-out mounts, from the farthest and most difficult routes, accepting hardship and sacrifice. This reflects the sincerity and longing of believers, and shows that the Kaaba is the spiritual center that unites people of every land in worship of the One God.

translation: That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days over what He has provided for them of livestock animals. So eat from them and feed the miserable and the poor.
interpretation: The pilgrimage brings people real benefits, both spiritual, like forgiveness, worship and unity among Muslims, and worldly, like trade and meeting one another. It also asks believers to remember God by pronouncing His name when they sacrifice cattle, camels, sheep or goats during the appointed days (the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, with the days of sacrifice after Eid). This makes the slaughter an act of worship and gratitude to the Provider rather than a mere custom. The believer is told to eat from the sacrificial meat and to give generously to the needy who are in hardship, so that the rite becomes a means of sharing, compassion and social solidarity, and no one is left hungry on the days of celebration.

translation: Then let them complete their rites of cleansing, fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.
interpretation: After the pilgrim has offered the sacrifice, this verse marks the transition out of the state of ihram. 'Tafath' refers to the dishevelment and untidiness that come with ihram, so completing it means shaving or trimming the hair, cutting the nails, and bathing and cleaning oneself. This signals that the major restrictions are lifted and the pilgrim returns to a state of cleanliness. Fulfilling vows means that whatever a person pledged to God, whether sacrifices, charity or other acts of worship, must be honored, which shows that a promise made to God is a binding trust. The final command, to circle the Ancient House (the Kaaba, called 'ancient' because it is the first house established for the worship of God), refers to the Tawaf al-Ifadah, the obligatory circumambulation that completes the essential rites of Hajj. The verse thus presents Hajj as a sequence of spiritual purification, loyalty to one's word before God, and a return to the center of monotheistic worship.

translation: That is so. And whoever honors the sacred ordinances of God, it is better for him with his Lord. And the grazing livestock have been made lawful to you, except what is recited to you. So avoid the abomination of idols, and avoid false speech.
interpretation: The verse teaches that reverence for what God has declared sacred, whether rites, places, times, or limits He has set, is not merely outward ceremony but an act that brings real benefit to the believer in the sight of his Lord. Honoring these things is a sign of a living heart and of taqwa, and its reward is with God. The mention of livestock being lawful, except what the Qur'an specifies as forbidden, shows that God's law is generous: the prohibitions are few and defined, so people should not invent additional prohibitions, as the pagans did with certain animals, nor permit what He has forbidden. The command to avoid the filth of idols links purity to belief: idolatry is a spiritual contamination that must be shunned entirely, just as one avoids physical impurity. It is joined with avoiding false speech because lying, perjury, and attributing falsehood to God are the verbal counterpart of idolatry; both substitute fabrication for truth. Thus the verse calls the believer to purity of worship and honesty of tongue, and to submission to God as the only source of what is lawful and forbidden.

translation: Be upright devotees of God, not associating anything with Him. Whoever associates partners with God is as though he had fallen from the sky, so the birds snatch him away, or the wind sweeps him off to a far-off, remote place.
interpretation: The verse portrays tawhid (pure monotheism) as the only secure ground for the human soul. Whoever holds to God alone stands on firm footing, with his heart, purpose, and hope anchored. The one who commits shirk loses that anchor and is like someone who has dropped from the height of the sky, the place of safety and elevation, into utter ruin. The birds that tear at him stand for the desires, devils, and false masters that seize and shred a person's faith, while the wind that hurls him into a deep, distant place stands for the whims and misguidance that carry him into perdition with no way back. The image teaches that departing from the one God means falling from honor and stability into dispersal, helplessness, and destruction.

translation: That is so. And whoever honors the sacred rites of God, indeed it is from the piety of the hearts.
interpretation: True reverence for God's rites, such as the rituals of pilgrimage and the sacrificial animals, is not merely outward ritual observance but an expression of an inner state. Honoring these symbols of devotion with sincerity, care, and respect springs from taqwa, the God-consciousness that dwells in the heart.
