Their shelter on a tranquil, elevated, well-watered land signifies God's protection of those who submit to Him. After the hardship of Mary's childbirth and the hostility of her people, God gave them safety, stability and sustenance. The verse teaches that divine care follows the believers' trials, and that God provides refuge and provision to His chosen servants in the places and ways He decrees.

translation: O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I am All-Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: God links lawful, wholesome sustenance with righteous action, teaching that purity of what one consumes supports purity of deed and that both are part of devotion. Even the messengers, the best of humankind, are commanded to eat what is good and to act righteously, so no one is exempt and no one should renounce the lawful pleasures of life as a form of piety. The closing reminder that God knows all that they do shows that sound conduct is observed and weighed by God, so a person should be sincere in earning, enjoying, and acting, and be grateful for His provision.

translation: And indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so be mindful of Me.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all the prophets, whom the preceding verses mention, called humanity to one faith: devotion to the one God. Their followers form a single spiritual community bound by tawhid, no matter how their laws and circumstances differed. Since God alone is the Lord of all, the proper response is taqwa, a conscious reverence and fear of displeasing Him, which should hold the believers together in unity. Dividing into sects and factions around that shared foundation is a departure from the purpose of the prophetic message, as the following verse indicates when it says people broke their affair into factions.

translation: But they tore their affair (religion) apart among themselves into factions; each party rejoicing in what it has.
interpretation: The verse describes how the followers of earlier prophets, who were meant to be one community upon one faith in the One God, broke their unified religion into sects and rival groups, each treating its own portion of the teaching as the whole truth. Instead of seeking truth, every faction became complacent and self-satisfied, taking pride in its own doctrines, leaders and customs and regarding itself as the one on guidance. The interpretation is a warning that division in religion is born of arrogance and partisanship rather than of true knowledge, and that being pleased with one's own group is no proof of being right. The believer is called back to the original unity of the message and to measuring every group's beliefs against revelation rather than against group loyalty.

translation: So leave them in their confusion [and heedlessness] for a time.
interpretation: God instructs the Prophet Muhammad not to be distressed by the disbelievers' stubborn denial or to hurry for their punishment. They are submerged in ignorance, arrogance and heedlessness, like a person overwhelmed by deep water, and they will not be guided by argument now. The command to leave them until a appointed time carries both consolation for the Prophet and a veiled warning to them: their respite is temporary, and when the time God has set arrives, whether through defeat and death in this world or the reckoning in the next, the reality they ignored will become clear and they will face the consequences of their choices.

translation: Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mu'minun 23:55) rebukes those who are absorbed in their heedlessness and take worldly abundance as proof of divine favor. The verse questions the assumption that wealth and children are signs that God approves of them or is honoring them. In truth, such provision may be a gradual drawing-in (istidraj) and a test, which God extends to them while they persist in error, so that they are given time to either repent or increase in transgression. The following verse completes the thought: God is not hastening good things to them; rather, they do not perceive. The lesson is that true favor is measured by faith and righteous deeds, not by material prosperity.

translation: Are We hastening for them in good things? Rather, they do not perceive.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:56) rebukes the false assumption that worldly wealth, children, and ease are signs of God's approval. The disbelievers imagine that their prosperity is a reward for their way of life, but it is in fact a respite and a test, a gradual drawing-out that may lead them deeper into heedlessness and ultimately to a reckoning. They lack the awareness to see this. True good is not measured by material abundance but by faith and righteous deeds, and a person may be given worldly bounty while moving further from God's mercy.

translation: Indeed, those who are, out of awe of their Lord, apprehensive.
interpretation: This verse opens the description of the true believers (Surah Al-Mu'minun 23:57) by naming their inner state: a reverent awe of God that is mixed with caution and concern. Their khashyah (fear born of knowing God's majesty) is not paralyzing dread but a living awareness that keeps the heart alert. Because they know God's greatness and justice, they are anxious that their deeds may be insufficient or flawed, so they never grow complacent or boastful about their faith. This inner watchfulness is the root from which the other qualities that follow in the passage grow: belief in God's signs, avoiding idolatry, and giving charity while their hearts tremble that they will return to their Lord. True faith, then, is a balance of hope and humble apprehension, which moves a person to constant sincerity and striving.

translation: And those who believe in the signs of their Lord.
interpretation: This verse, from the description of the true believers in Surat al-Mu'minun (23:58), shows that real faith is not limited to a verbal declaration but means accepting everything God has revealed and established as evidence of His truth. The 'signs' (ayat) include the verses of the Qur'an and also the signs in creation and in the events of life. A believer who reflects on them, trusts them, and lets them shape belief and conduct has a faith that is active and conscious. Such belief in God's signs gives rise to humility before Him, obedience to His guidance, and protection from arrogance and heedlessness.

translation: And those who do not associate any partners with their Lord.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:59) describes a quality of the true believers: their devotion to God is pure and undivided. They do not commit shirk in any form, whether by worshipping others besides God, or by the subtler forms of associating partners with Him, such as performing good deeds for show, relying on created things as though they hold independent power to benefit or harm, or placing worldly desires above obedience to God. Their faith is sincere, so that their worship, trust, love, and fear are directed to God alone. The verse teaches that real success and security come only to those whose monotheism is complete, and that true belief is not merely affirming God's existence but keeping the heart and actions free from any rival to Him.

translation: And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they will return to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Mu'minun 23:60) describes true believers who perform acts of worship and charity, yet their hearts tremble with awe and anxiety that their deeds may not be accepted or may fall short of what God deserves. This fear arises from their certainty that they will return to God and stand before Him for reckoning. As narrated in the well-known report of 'A'isha, the Prophet explained that it refers not to those who sin and fear, but to those who pray, fast, and give charity while fearing that these will not be accepted. The verse thus teaches that real faith joins diligent good action with humility, absence of self-satisfaction, and constant awareness of accountability, so that the believer neither grows arrogant over his good deeds nor despairs, but keeps striving with a heart both hopeful and reverent.

translation: It is those who hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:61) describes the believers whose devotion is not passive or merely dutiful: they race toward acts of goodness with eagerness and urgency, and in doing so they come first. It teaches that true faith, marked by reverent fear of God, belief in His signs, avoidance of shirk, and giving charity while their hearts tremble over returning to their Lord, naturally produces energetic, competitive striving in righteousness. Such people do not postpone good or wait for an opportunity to be forced upon them; they seize it promptly, and because of this sincere zeal, they are described as being ahead of others in attaining God's reward.

translation: We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity, and with Us is a record that speaks the truth, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: God's justice is perfectly balanced with His mercy: people are held accountable only for what lies within their ability, so obligations are scaled to each person's strength and circumstances. Every deed is preserved in a record that testifies truthfully, leaving no room for denial, exaggeration, or omission. Because of this exact accounting, no one will suffer injustice on the Day of Judgment, with no good deed lost and no one punished for what they did not do. The verse reassures believers that sincere effort within their means is enough, and it warns the heedless that nothing will be concealed.

translation: Nay, their hearts are in heedlessness of this (Qur'an), and they have deeds besides that which they are doing.
interpretation: God describes the disbelievers' hearts as submerged, as if overwhelmed by deep waters, in heedlessness of the Qur'an and of the reckoning it announces, so its warnings never reach them. Beyond that heedlessness they have evil deeds, such as disbelief and sin, which they keep committing, and their persistence in these deeds is what keeps them from awareness. The verse indicates that their rejection stems from hearts clouded by negligence and by habitual wrongdoing, not from any lack of clear proof.

translation: Until, when We seize those of them who live in luxury with the punishment, behold, they cry out loudly for help.
interpretation: The verse shows how sudden and sobering divine punishment is for the affluent elites who were heedless and arrogant. While they enjoyed wealth and power, they ignored warnings and rejected the truth. When God's punishment finally seizes them, their pride collapses, and they groan and plead for rescue. But the time for repentance has passed, and the cry that would have been useful as sincere turning to God during their lives of ease is useless once the punishment has arrived. The verse warns that luxury can numb people to accountability, and that those who do not turn to God willingly will be forced to call out to Him in helplessness.

translation: Do not cry out for help today. Surely you will not be helped against Us.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the wrongdoers who lived in luxury and defiance of God's revelation, at the moment the punishment seizes them. When they begin to scream and plead for rescue, they are told that pleading is now pointless. The time for repentance was in this world, when the verses were recited to them and they turned away in arrogance. Once God's judgment has come, no ally, power, or intercession can shield them from it, because the only one who could save them is the one whose decree is being carried out. The verse teaches that humility and turning to God must come while there is still opportunity, since sincere cries for help after the decree has been executed bring no relief.

translation: My verses used to be recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels.
interpretation: This verse, Qur'an 23:66, rebukes those who rejected the message when it was clearly conveyed to them. The image of turning back on one's heels depicts an active retreat from the truth, as if a person facing the guidance deliberately steps backward away from it. The people addressed, the arrogant and heedless among the disbelievers, did not lack evidence or clarity, since the verses were recited to them plainly. Their failure lay in stubborn pride and unwillingness to accept. The verse teaches that guilt rests on one who knowingly turns away after the truth has reached him, and that hearing revelation brings a duty to respond with acceptance and obedience, not aversion.

translation: Behaving arrogantly towards it (the Sanctuary or the Qur'an), spending the night in idle talk, speaking ill and abandoning (the truth).
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, when God's signs were recited to them, turned back on their heels out of pride. Their arrogance was tied to the Book or to the Sacred House, in which they took false pride as its custodians while disregarding its message. At night they would gather to tell tales and talk idly, and in these gatherings they would speak ill of the Prophet and the Qur'an, and dismiss the truth with contempt. The verse shows that arrogance blocks one from accepting guidance, and that wasting time in vain talk and slander leads to rejecting divine revelation.

translation: Have they not then pondered over the Word (the Qur'an)? Or has there come to them something that did not come to their forefathers of old?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who reject the Prophet's message, pointing out that their denial is not grounded in careful reflection. Had they truly contemplated the Qur'an, its clarity, its coherence, and the truthfulness of the one who brought it would have led them to faith. It also challenges their excuse of clinging to ancestral ways: the coming of revelation is not unprecedented, since earlier peoples, including the descendants of Abraham and Ishmael in the Arabian tradition, had received warners and messengers before. Their rejection therefore stems from stubbornness and heedlessness rather than from real lack of evidence or novelty, and the verse calls them to sincere reflection (tadabbur) as the path to recognizing the truth.

translation: Or did they not recognize their Messenger, so that they are denying him?
interpretation: This verse (23:69) is a rhetorical question that rebukes the disbelievers of Quraysh for rejecting Muhammad. They had known him from childhood, knew his lineage, his truthfulness, and his trustworthiness, and had even called him 'al-Amin'. So they cannot plausibly claim ignorance of who he is or of his character as grounds for denial. Their rejection stems not from any lack of knowledge about the man but from stubbornness, arrogance, and dislike of the truth he brought. The verse shows that denial of a prophet is a matter of the heart's obstinacy rather than a lack of evidence.

translation: Or do they say, 'There is madness in him'? Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.
interpretation: The verse exposes the real reason behind the disbelievers' accusation that the Prophet is possessed. They do not truly believe he is insane, since they knew him as the most reasoned and trustworthy man among them. They use the charge as an excuse to dismiss a message that challenges their habits, pride, and worldly interests. The problem lies not in any defect in the messenger or the message, which is the truth, but in the hearts of those who dislike the truth because it conflicts with their desires. Rejection often comes from aversion and not from lack of evidence.

translation: Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and all those in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their Reminder, yet they are turning away from their Reminder.
interpretation: The verse teaches that reality and revelation are founded on truth and divine wisdom, not on human whims. The cosmos stays in order because it is governed by one perfect, all-knowing will; if the truth bent to the conflicting, ignorant, self-serving desires of people, the universe would fall into chaos, since desires differ and clash and no one has complete knowledge. The disbelievers' demand that revelation conform to their tastes is therefore baseless. God has given them a Reminder, which can mean the Qur'an that conveys their honor, their message, and their path to guidance, and the real tragedy is that they turn away from the very thing that would elevate them and set their lives right. The fault lies not in the lack of guidance but in their refusal to heed it.

translation: Or do you ask them for a payment? But the recompense of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse points out that the Prophet asks nothing from his people in return for his message, so they have no worldly excuse for turning away from him. Those who reject a messenger often claim that he wants wealth or status, but he seeks no payment from them. His reward comes from God, which is better and more lasting than anything people could give, because God is the best of those who provide. The verse consoles the Prophet and also exposes the weakness of the disbelievers' excuses: a sincere, disinterested caller to the truth deserves to be heard, not rejected.

translation: And indeed, you [O Muhammad] are calling them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:73) affirms the Prophet's mission and its integrity: what he invites people to is not a personal agenda or a path of confusion, but the clear, balanced way of worshipping God alone and living by His guidance, free from crookedness or excess. It underscores that the Prophet seeks no worldly reward and that his call is self-evidently true, so that those who turn away do so out of stubbornness, not because of any flaw in the message. The 'straight path' (sirat mustaqim) denotes the way of tawhid and righteous conduct that leads directly to God's pleasure and salvation.

translation: And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the Path.
interpretation: Denying the Hereafter removes accountability from a person's outlook, so he has no inner reason to hold to the straight path of truth and righteousness. The verse says such people turn away from the way of guidance, which is the balanced path of faith and good conduct that leads to God. Without the expectation of being judged, desires and worldly gain become the measure of right and wrong, and a person drifts further from the upright course. Belief in the Hereafter is therefore the anchor that keeps one on the straight path.

translation: And if We had shown them mercy and removed the harm that afflicted them, they would have persisted in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: The verse exposes the stubbornness of the arrogant disbelievers: their turning to God in hardship is not a sign of true change of heart. Even if God lifted their affliction out of mercy, they would not become grateful or repent; they would go back to their rebellion and heedless confusion. Their resistance to faith is rooted in the hardness of their hearts, not in a lack of signs or relief, so hardship is not what keeps them from guidance, and ease would not bring them to it.

translation: And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves to their Lord, nor do they plead (to Him).
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 23:76) shows how stubborn hearts can remain unmoved even by hardship. God afflicted these people with trials and punishment so that suffering might soften them and bring them back to humility and supplication. Instead they stayed arrogant and kept turning away. The lesson is that hardship is meant to wake a person to dependence on God, and that the real danger is a heart so hardened that neither blessing nor calamity brings it to repentance. A person should respond to affliction with humility and prayer, and not with greater defiance.

translation: Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment, behold, they are therein in utter despair.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Mu'minun 23:77) describes how people who persist in arrogance and heedlessness, despite repeated warnings and trials, are suddenly overtaken by a punishment they did not expect once their chances have run out. The 'gate of severe punishment' signifies an abrupt and overwhelming calamity, whether in this world or at death and the Hereafter, that opens when they least anticipate it. At that moment, all their pride and false hopes collapse, and they fall into mubilsun, a state of stunned silence, despair, and hopelessness, with no argument, escape, or hope of mercy left. The lesson is that God's delay in punishing is a respite, not approval, and one should heed admonition and return to Him before the door of repentance closes.

translation: And it is He who produced for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little do you give thanks.
interpretation: God reminds humankind that their faculties of perception and understanding—hearing, sight, and the heart (the seat of intellect and reflection)—are not self-made but gifts from Him, and they are the very means by which a person receives guidance, observes the signs in creation, and reasons toward the truth. Hearing is mentioned first because it receives revelation and instruction, then sight for contemplating the signs of God in the universe, then the heart for reflecting and drawing conclusions. The closing rebuke, 'little do you give thanks,' means that most people fail to use these faculties for their true purpose: gratitude is shown not merely by words but by employing hearing, sight, and understanding to recognize the Creator, acknowledge His oneness, and obey Him. Neglecting this is a form of ingratitude.

translation: And He it is who multiplied you throughout the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse points to two truths: the same God who spread humankind across the earth, in different nations, tongues and lands, is the One before whom all will finally be assembled. Humanity's dispersal in this world is therefore not a sign of separation or aimlessness. It is a stage in a journey with one origin and one destination. The reminder that all will be gathered to Him calls people to accountability, to gratitude for the blessing of life and increase, and to the awareness that the diversity and scattering of this life will end in a single reckoning before their Creator.

translation: And it is He who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day. Then will you not use reason?
interpretation: The verse points to God's absolute authority over the cycles of existence: life and death, and the regular succession of night and day. Just as the ordered alternation of night and day is beyond human control and shows precise design, so the giving and taking of life belongs to God alone. Anyone who reflects on these constant, observable signs should conclude that the One who governs them is the sole Creator and Sustainer, worthy of worship, and that He is able to resurrect the dead just as He renews day after night. The closing question, 'Will you not reason?', rebukes heedlessness and calls people to use their intellect to recognize God's oneness, power, and the reality of accountability.

translation: Rather, they said the like of what the earlier peoples said.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:81) describes the disbelievers of Makkah as repeating the same denial of resurrection voiced by past nations who rejected their prophets. Their rejection does not come from reason or evidence. It is blind imitation of earlier unbelief, a habit of hardened hearts across generations. The next verses show what they said: that after they have died and become dust and bones, they could not be raised again. The verse implies that their disbelief is a stubborn inherited pattern, and that they ignore the signs of God's power in creation, which make bringing the dead back to life no harder than creating them in the first place.

translation: They say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we really be raised up again?"
interpretation: The verse voices the disbelievers' denial of bodily resurrection, which they reject as impossible. They see death and decay, with the body reduced to dust and bones, as the final end, and they assume that something so thoroughly dissolved cannot be restored. The Qur'an cites this doubt in order to refute it. The God who created humans from nothing in the first place is fully able to recreate them, and judging His power by the limits of human experience is an error. The verse also shows that this denial is rooted in a narrow, material view of reality, one that ignores accountability in the Hereafter, and so leaves people careless of how they live.

translation: "We have been promised this, we and our forefathers, before. This is nothing but the tales of the ancients." (Qur'an 23:83 / 27:68)
interpretation: The verse records the disbelievers' scornful response to the message of resurrection and the Day of Judgement. Having heard that they will be raised after turning to dust, they dismiss it as an old, empty claim, noting that the same warning was given to their ancestors yet never came to pass, and so they conclude it is merely inherited folklore, not revealed truth. Their reasoning confuses the delay of a promise with its falsehood. The Qur'an presents this as a sign of heedlessness and arrogance: they judge a matter of the unseen by the limits of their own experience and refuse to reflect on the signs of God's power in creation, which show that the One who originated them the first time is able to bring them back again.

translation: Say: 'To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?'
interpretation: God commands the Prophet to put a question to the polytheists that exposes the weakness of their own position. They acknowledge that the earth and all its inhabitants have a Creator and Owner, so ownership and sovereignty over creation belong to God alone. It follows that worship, which is owed only to the one who creates, owns and sustains, must be directed to Him alone and not to idols or partners. The phrase 'if you should know' challenges them to use their reason and knowledge. Anyone who truly reflects will accept that the One who owns the earth and everything in it is the only One deserving devotion, and that He is able to resurrect the dead, which they denied.

translation: They will say, "[They belong] to God." Say, "Then will you not remember?"
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 23:85) follows the question put to the disbelievers about who owns the earth and all that is in it. Since they themselves admit that the earth and its inhabitants belong to God, the Prophet is told to press them with the question "Will you not remember?" Their own acknowledgment of God's sole ownership and creation should lead them to see the logical conclusion: only the Creator and Owner deserves worship, and nothing can be set up beside Him. The call to remember appeals to the natural, innate awareness of God (fitrah) that they already hold, and rebukes their heedlessness in affirming His lordship while neglecting to devote worship to Him alone. It also implies that the resurrection should not seem far-fetched to them, since the One who created and owns everything can certainly bring it back to life.

translation: Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:86) is a challenge to the polytheists of Mecca, asking them to reflect on who truly holds sovereignty over the whole of creation. The question points to the vastness of the seven heavens and the Mighty Throne, which is the greatest of created things and a symbol of God's absolute authority. The next verse records that they would answer 'To God', so the question draws out an admission from their own beliefs. Since they accept that God alone is the Creator and Lord of all that is vast and beyond human reach, it follows that they have no rational basis for worshipping anything else beside Him, and it should lead them to fear Him and to accept His oneness and His power to resurrect.

translation: They will say, "[They belong] to God." Say, "Then will you not fear Him?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:87) follows the question of who is Lord of the seven heavens and the mighty Throne. The idolaters of Mecca could not deny that God alone is the Creator and Sovereign of the cosmos, so they admit it. The Qur'an then uses their own admission against them: if God alone is Lord of everything, it is inconsistent to associate partners with Him, to deny the resurrection He has power to bring about, or to ignore His commands. The rhetorical question 'Will you not fear Him?' calls them to move from affirming God's lordship to practicing God-consciousness (taqwa) and exclusive worship, showing that true belief must lead to reverence and obedience, not merely acknowledgment of facts.

translation: Say: "In whose hand is the dominion over all things, and who protects while against Him there is no protection, if you should know?"
interpretation: The verse challenges those who acknowledge God as Creator to follow that acknowledgment to its conclusion: if absolute sovereignty over everything belongs to Him alone, then He alone can grant refuge and no one can shield anyone from Him. A person who is wronged or fearful can therefore seek safety only in God, and no power, whether idol, ruler, or created being, can protect anyone from His decree. Since the rejecters admit His lordship, the verse argues that this logically demands worshipping Him alone and fearing His judgment, which includes the resurrection they deny. The phrase 'if you know' rebukes their inconsistency, implying that real knowledge would lead to submission to God.

translation: They will say, "It is God's." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:89) comes after the questions asking who holds the dominion over all things and who protects while none can protect against Him. Even the polytheists admit that sovereignty and protection belong to God alone. The Prophet is told to ask them how, having admitted this, they are bewitched, deceived or turned away from the truth, so that they still worship others besides God or deny the resurrection. The verse shows that their denial is not due to a lack of evidence, since their own admission already implies God's unique right to be worshipped and His power to resurrect. It is due to a spell of delusion, desire and blind tradition that blocks sound reasoning from reaching its natural conclusion.

translation: Nay, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.
interpretation: The verse answers the pagans' claim that God has offspring or that the message is false. God affirms that the Qur'an and the call to monotheism are truth, and that the real falsehood lies with those who deny it. Their rejection comes not from lack of evidence but from stubborn lying, since they ascribe partners and children to God without any proof. The truth stands on its own clarity, and the deniers' charge against it reveals only their own dishonesty.

translation: God has not taken any son, nor is there any god along with Him. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Glory be to God above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse refutes both the claim that God has offspring and the claim that He has partners, using a rational argument from the order of creation. If there were several gods, each would be a sovereign with his own will and would claim exclusive control over his own creation, so the universe would split into rival domains. Their wills would inevitably conflict, and one would try to dominate another, since a deity who can be overpowered is not truly divine. Yet the cosmos is coherent, harmonious and governed by consistent laws, which shows that it comes from a single Creator whose will is unrivaled. Having a son would imply need, limitation and likeness to created beings, all of which are alien to God's perfection. The verse ends by declaring God transcendent above all that people falsely ascribe to Him.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.
interpretation: God's knowledge is total, encompassing both what is hidden from creatures and what is manifest to them, and this complete knowledge is itself the proof of His uniqueness. Idols, saints, or any other partners cannot know the unseen or witness all things, so they cannot share in divinity or deserve worship. Whoever alone possesses perfect, all-embracing knowledge alone deserves devotion, and He is therefore far above and beyond the false claims of those who ascribe partners to Him.

translation: Say: "My Lord, if You should show me what they are promised,"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:93) teaches the Prophet a supplication to be made in the face of the disbelievers' denial of the warned punishment. The conditional "if You should show me" acknowledges that the timing of divine punishment is known only to God, and that it may or may not occur within the Prophet's lifetime. By addressing God as "My Lord" and asking in humility, the Prophet is guided to seek protection from being counted among those afflicted when judgment falls upon the wrongdoers. The verse reflects that even the righteous must fear God's punishment and rely on Him for safety, since collective trials can strike a whole community, and it teaches the believer to respond to the mockery of opponents with prayer and dependence on God rather than with haste or challenge.

translation: My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:94) is a supplication the Prophet is taught to make when reminded of the punishment that God promises the disbelievers. It expresses humility and total dependence on God for protection, even for one who is righteous. By asking not to be counted among the wrongdoers, the believer acknowledges that safety from divine punishment comes only through God's mercy and guidance, and that one must always seek refuge from sharing in the fate or company of those who commit injustice and associate partners with God. It teaches that a believer should never feel secure from God's reckoning, and should keep a constant awareness of avoiding wrongdoing, both in action and in association.

translation: And indeed, We are able to show you what We have promised them.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:95) assures the Prophet Muhammad that God has full power to let him witness the punishment He has threatened against the disbelievers who denied the message. The disbelievers mocked the warnings of a coming reckoning, taking God's delay as proof that the threat was empty. The verse answers that the delay is not a sign of weakness or of a broken promise. God can bring about the promised punishment in the Prophet's own lifetime if He wills, and if He postpones it, He does so by His wisdom and patience. Either way, the threat is certain to come, and the disbelievers should not be deceived by the respite they have been given.

translation: Repel evil with that which is better. We are most knowing of what they describe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a believer should answer wrongdoing, insult, and hostility not in kind but with a better response, such as forbearance, forgiveness, kindness, and patience, because this approach softens hearts and often turns enemies into friends. It also means that when the disbelievers slander the Prophet or ascribe falsehood to God, he need not take vengeance or be troubled, for God fully knows what they allege and will deal with it justly. Entrusting judgment to God frees the believer to keep a gentle, dignified character.

translation: And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils."
interpretation: The verse teaches the believer to turn to God alone for protection against the constant whispering and provocation of evil forces, which push a person toward anger, error, and sin. The word 'hamazat' implies a forceful prodding, like goading an animal, showing that temptation is not just a gentle suggestion but an active pressure that a person cannot resist by their own strength. By addressing God as 'Lord' and asking for refuge, the believer admits their weakness and dependence on divine protection, recognizing that sincere reliance on God is the true safeguard of the heart against corrupting influences.

translation: And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they come near me.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:98) is part of a prayer the Prophet is taught to make against the whisperings of the devils. Here the believer asks God for protection from the very presence of the devils, not only from their incitements. Their presence at any moment, whether in prayer, recitation, anger, heedlessness, or the hour of death, can distract the heart, stir up evil, and lead a person astray. The believer recognizes that he cannot guard himself by his own strength, so he turns to his Lord for protection. The verse teaches complete dependence on God and the need to seek His shelter at every moment.

translation: Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: 'My Lord, send me back,'
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 23:99) shows the moment when the heedless person's illusions fall away. As long as life lasts, the one who denies the truth or neglects the afterlife postpones repentance and clings to worldly distractions. But when the angels of death arrive and the unseen becomes plain, he realizes his mistake and begs God for another chance to live. The plea is not a sincere, lasting turning back but a cry of regret at the point where the opportunity for action has ended. The lesson is that repentance and righteous deeds must be pursued now, while there is still time, because after death there is only the barrier (barzakh) until the Resurrection and no return to amend one's record.

translation: "That I might do righteousness in that which I left behind." No! It is only a word that he says; and behind them is a barrier (barzakh) until the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This verse answers the dying disbeliever who, on seeing the reality of death, begs to be sent back to the world so he may do good in the life and wealth he neglected. God rejects the plea with a firm "No!" and shows that his request is merely words spoken out of terror and regret, not a sincere resolve, for if he were returned he would go back to his old ways. The barzakh, the barrier between death and resurrection, stands before the departed souls: it blocks any return to the worldly life, and they remain in it until the Day of Resurrection. So the time for action is only this life, and after death repentance and good deeds can no longer be taken up.

translation: Then when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no ties of kinship between them on that Day, nor will they ask one another.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mu'minun 23:101) describes the terror of the Day of Resurrection. When the Trumpet sounds, worldly bonds of lineage, which people relied on for protection, pride, and support, will no longer benefit anyone, because every person will be consumed with their own fate and their own account before God. They will not ask about one another's well-being as they did in life, since the overwhelming dread of the moment preoccupies each soul. Only faith and righteous deeds will count, not ancestry or family connections. The verse thus calls people to put their trust in good deeds and not in lineage or worldly relationships.

translation: Then those whose scales are heavy [with good deeds] — it is they who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment, deeds will be weighed with perfect justice, and true success is not measured by worldly wealth, status, or power, but by the weight of one's righteous deeds, grounded in faith and sincerity. Those whose good deeds outweigh their wrongdoing will attain salvation from the Fire and entry into Paradise, which is the ultimate triumph. It is a call to give each day's actions lasting value, since only what is done for God carries weight in the final reckoning.

translation: And those whose scales are light - those are the ones who have lost their own selves; in Hell they will abide eternally.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a person's true capital is his own soul, and that the Day of Judgment is a reckoning in which only sincere faith and righteous deeds carry weight. Someone whose good deeds are too few, or are emptied of faith and sincerity, has nothing of value to set against his wrongdoing, so his scale is light. His loss is therefore not merely of wealth or status but of his very self, because he squandered the one thing he was given to secure his salvation and traded it for fleeting worldly pleasures. His eternal stay in Hell is the consequence of that ruin, since the disbelief or corruption that left him without any weighty deeds is what bars him from mercy. The verse is a warning to treat life as a trust and to fill one's scale with deeds that God accepts.

translation: The Fire will scorch their faces, and therein they will be grimacing, with lips drawn back in anguish.
interpretation: The verse depicts the humiliating and total nature of the punishment of the disbelievers. The face is the seat of dignity and honor, so the Fire striking it shows that their pride in this world is stripped away and replaced with disgrace. The word 'kalihun' pictures faces twisted and distorted, with lips shrunk back from the teeth, showing that their suffering is not only physical but visibly deforming, an outward sign of the inner regret and ruin they earned by rejecting God's signs. It warns that those who mocked the believers and denied the truth will find their arrogance reversed in the Hereafter.

translation: Were My verses not recited to you, and you used to deny them?
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, as they are brought before God. It reminds them that they have no excuse, because God's revelation had reached them clearly and repeatedly. The problem was not a lack of guidance or knowledge, but a willful rejection of the truth after it was made plain. Their punishment is therefore just: they were warned and given proof, yet they chose denial out of arrogance or attachment to worldly desires. The question is rhetorical, intended to make them admit their guilt and to show that God's judgment rests on a fully established argument against them.

translation: They will say: "Our Lord, our misfortune overcame us, and we were a people astray."
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mu'minun 23:106) shows the people of Hell admitting their fault on the Day of Judgment. By "our misfortune overcame us" they mean that the wretchedness they brought upon themselves, through persistent heedlessness, following desires, and rejecting the messengers, gained mastery over them until it led them to ruin. They do not deny their error but confess that they had been truly astray. Their words carry both acknowledgment of guilt and a plea for mercy, yet the confession comes too late, because the time for action was the worldly life. The lesson is that a person should examine his inclinations and choices now, since habitual sin and neglect of guidance can harden into a wretchedness that overpowers him, and that sincere repentance is valuable only while the opportunity remains.

translation: Our Lord, bring us out of it; and if we ever return [to disbelief and wrongdoing], then we will indeed be wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:107) is the plea of the people of Hellfire, who ask God to release them after they have realized the truth of what they denied in the world. They promise that if given another chance they will not repeat their disbelief, and they admit that returning to it would make them truly deserving of punishment. The verse teaches that the realization of truth comes too late once the Hereafter begins, and that the time for sincere repentance and righteous action is this worldly life. Their appeal is met by God's rebuke and their being told to remain in the Fire and not speak to Him, showing that regret in the Hereafter does not avert the consequences of choices made in life.

translation: He will say: "Begone into it (the Fire), and do not speak to Me."
interpretation: This is God's final answer to the people of Hell after they plead to be taken out and given another chance (Qur'an 23:107). The command 'ikhsa'u' is one of rebuke and banishment, the way one drives away a despised dog, which shows the disgrace of those who denied the truth. The prohibition 'and do not speak to Me' cuts off any further appeal, and it shows that their time for repentance and for having their pleas heard ended with this life. They had mocked the believers who prayed for mercy, so they are now denied any hearing. The verse teaches that the chance to turn back to God exists only in this world, and that after death the matter is settled by God's justice.

translation: Indeed, there was a group among My servants who would say: 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, for You are the best of those who show mercy.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:109) recalls the humble supplication of the believers in the world, whom the disbelievers used to mock and ridicule. God reminds the wrongdoers in the Fire that those they scorned were sincere servants who combined faith with humility, asking for forgiveness and mercy and acknowledging that God is the best of the merciful. The meaning is that true faith is shown through reliance on God's mercy rather than on one's own deeds, and that mocking the righteous for their devotion leads to bitter regret, since the very people who were ridiculed were those who attained God's mercy and success.

translation: But you took them for ridicule, until they made you forget My remembrance, while you used to laugh at them.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:110) is addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgement, rebuking them for mocking the believers who prayed to God for mercy and forgiveness. Their constant scorn of the righteous became such an absorbing preoccupation that it distracted them from remembering God, so the believers are said to have 'made them forget' His remembrance, though in truth the cause was their own heedlessness and arrogance. The verse teaches that mockery of the pious is a grave sin that hardens the heart and leads to neglect of God, and that the very people ridiculed in this world are those honored and rewarded in the next, as the following verse declares that God rewards them for their patience.

translation: Indeed, today I have rewarded them for their patience: it is they who are the triumphant.
interpretation: This verse is God's declaration on the Day of Judgment to those who endured the mockery and scorn of the disbelievers in this world. It teaches that patience (sabr) in faith, in obedience, and in the face of hardship and ridicule is never wasted, and that its true recompense is given in full on the Day of Judgment. Those who were laughed at and belittled for their belief are shown to be the real winners, because success is measured by God's final judgment and the eternal reward, not by worldly status or the passing laughter of those who rejected the truth.

translation: He (Allah) will say: 'How many years did you remain on the earth?' (Qur'an 23:112)
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, Allah asks the disbelievers how long they stayed in the worldly life, not because He lacks knowledge, but to make them realize how brief and fleeting earthly life was compared with the endless life of the Hereafter. The question exposes the folly of those who exchanged eternal reward for transient pleasures, and it leads them to admit that their time in the world seemed only a day or part of a day, so that they recognize how little the dunya was worth and how great their loss is.

translation: They will say: 'We stayed a day or part of a day; so ask those who keep count.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 23:113) describes the disoriented answer of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment when asked how long they remained on earth. Measured against the endlessness of the Hereafter and the weight of the reckoning they now face, their whole worldly life seems to have been a fleeting moment, so brief that they cannot even be sure of its length and defer to those who keep an exact count. The lesson is that worldly life, however long or full of pleasure it appears, is very short in comparison with eternity, so a wise person should not let it distract from preparing for the life to come.

translation: He will say: "You stayed only a little while, if only you had known."
interpretation: This verse (23:114) is God's reply to the people in Hell who, when asked how long they stayed on earth, could only say a day or part of a day. God tells them that their whole worldly life, however long it felt, was brief compared with the eternity of the Hereafter. The words "if only you had known" mean that had they understood how short this life is and how lasting the next one is, they would not have exchanged the permanent for the fleeting. They would not have given priority to worldly pleasures, disbelief, and heedlessness over faith and righteous deeds. The verse urges people to judge life by its end and to prepare for the Hereafter while there is still time.

translation: Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?
interpretation: God rebukes those who live heedlessly, as though human existence had no purpose and no final reckoning. The verse (Qur'an 23:115) argues that creation is the work of a wise Creator, so it cannot be aimless play. Human beings are created with reason, freedom and moral responsibility, and this implies accountability. Life is therefore a trial in which people are called to worship God, act justly and do good, and all will return to Him to be recompensed for their deeds. The question is rhetorical and works as a warning: denying the Return empties life of meaning, while remembering it gives life direction and moral seriousness.

translation: Exalted is God, the True King! There is no god but Him, the Lord of the Noble Throne.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone is supreme in sovereignty and that His kingship is real and everlasting, unlike the borrowed, temporary authority of human rulers. Because He alone is the true King and Lord of the Throne, which is the greatest of created things and a sign of His absolute dominion, no other being deserves worship, obedience, or ultimate devotion. Coming after the discussion of creation, resurrection, and accountability in Surah al-Mu'minun, it reminds the believer that the Day of Judgment is overseen by a just and sovereign Lord, so the sound response is to turn away from false gods and place complete trust and submission in Him alone.

translation: And whoever invokes, besides God, another deity for which he has no proof, his reckoning is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worshipping anything alongside God is a claim made with no rational or revealed evidence, so it is baseless and cannot be defended. The one who does so will not escape accountability: his judgment is not left to human opinion or to the false gods he trusts, but rests solely with his Lord, who knows his deeds and will repay them with perfect justice. The closing statement gives the final measure of success and failure: those who deny God's oneness and the truth of His signs will not attain true salvation, however prosperous or powerful they may appear in this world, because lasting success lies in faith and in answering to God with sincere monotheism.

translation: And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of those who show mercy."
interpretation: The verse ends Surat al-Mu'minun with a model prayer for the believer. It teaches that, whatever one's worship and good deeds, a person always needs God's forgiveness for shortcomings and His mercy for salvation. Forgiveness (maghfira) removes the burden of sins and their consequences, while mercy (rahma) brings God's care, guidance, and reward. Asking in this order, and then affirming that God is the best of the merciful, reflects humility and complete dependence on Him. Human compassion is limited and flawed, but God's mercy is perfect and all-encompassing, so the believer should always turn to Him in hope and never despair.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. This is a surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and We have sent down in it clear verses, so that you may remember.
interpretation: The verse opens Surah An-Nur by stressing the authority and seriousness of what follows. By calling the surah something God has both sent down and made binding, it signals that the rulings in it, such as those on chastity, modesty, family life, and social conduct, are obligations and not optional counsel. Its verses are described as clear, so that no one can claim ignorance or confusion about them. The aim is remembrance: that people will be mindful of God and of the moral nature they were created with, and will let these commands shape their conduct and protect the dignity and purity of the community.

translation: The fornicatress and the fornicator: flog each one of them with a hundred lashes. And let not pity for them take hold of you in the matter of God's religion, if you believe in God and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat an-Nur, establishes a fixed punishment (hadd) for unmarried men and women who commit unlawful sexual intercourse: one hundred lashes, applied equally to both sexes. It warns that compassion must not override a ruling of God, and it ties firm and impartial enforcement to genuine faith in God and the Day of Judgment, because those who believe in the Last Day submit to divine justice even when mercy tempts them to relax it. The command that a group of believers witness the punishment shows that its purpose is public deterrence and the protection of society's moral order and family lineage, not private vengeance or humiliation; seeing the penalty carried out openly warns the community and reinforces the seriousness of the offense.

translation: The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress does not marry except a fornicator or an idolater, and that has been made unlawful for the believers.
interpretation: The verse warns that marriage is a bond of moral and spiritual compatibility. Someone who persists in fornication, unrepentant and shameless, is drawn only to partners of similar character, or to those who do not hold to God's limits at all, such as idolaters. Believers are forbidden to marry such persistent and unrepentant sinners, since this would mean accepting immorality, endangering their own faith and family honor, and weakening the standards of chastity that the community upholds. The prohibition applies to those who persist in the sin and have not repented. Sincere repentance restores a person's eligibility for marriage, as other teachings of the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate.

translation: And those who accuse chaste women [of adultery] and then do not bring four witnesses, flog them with eighty lashes and do not accept any testimony from them ever after. And it is they who are the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 24:4) sets a strict standard of proof to protect the honor and reputation of chaste people, particularly women, from slander. Accusing someone of illicit sexual relations is so grave that it cannot rest on rumor or suspicion; it requires four credible eyewitnesses to the act itself. Anyone who levels the charge without that proof is deemed a slanderer, and the verse prescribes three consequences: a public punishment of eighty lashes, which deters careless talk and vindicates the falsely accused; permanent rejection of the slanderer's testimony, since someone who has damaged another's honor with an unproven charge has lost public trust; and the label of 'fasiq' (transgressor), a moral judgment on one who has violated the bounds of truthfulness and justice. The verse thus safeguards social cohesion and individual dignity by making false accusation costly, so that the community is not filled with scandal and baseless charges.

translation: Except for those who repent after that and make amends; for indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse opens the door of divine mercy even after grave wrongdoing. Repentance is not accepted as mere words: it requires turning away from the sin sincerely and then reforming one's conduct, which includes putting right the harm done to others and living righteously thereafter. When a person does this, God, whose forgiveness and mercy are boundless, pardons them, showing that no one is beyond redemption so long as they return to Him with genuine remorse and corrective action.

translation: And those who accuse their wives of adultery, and have no witnesses except themselves, then the testimony of one of them shall be four testimonies, swearing by God, that he is indeed among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse establishes the legal procedure known as li'an for a husband who accuses his wife of adultery but lacks the four witnesses normally required to prove such a charge. Instead of leaving him to face the penalty for false accusation, the law allows him to give four solemn oaths by God that he is telling the truth, which is the first stage of the process. The wife may then respond with her own oaths, as the following verses describe. The ruling shows God's mercy and wisdom in handling the delicate, private matter of marital infidelity: it protects the husband, who cannot produce witnesses to what happened in private, and it also safeguards the wife's honor by requiring a grave, God-invoking oath instead of accepting a bare accusation. In this way the community's moral order is preserved, and the final judgment on the truth is left to God.

translation: And the fifth [oath] is that the curse of God be upon him if he is among the liars.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nur 24:7) completes the procedure of li'an, the oath of mutual imprecation between spouses when a husband accuses his wife of adultery without having four witnesses. After the husband swears four times by God that he is truthful, the fifth oath calls down God's curse upon himself if he is lying. It shows that Islam treats an accusation of adultery with great gravity and demands the highest level of moral accountability. The man stakes his standing before God on the claim, so that no one may slander a spouse lightly. The procedure also protects the honor of the family and the community, and it leaves final judgment to God, who knows the truth hidden from human witnesses.

translation: And it shall avert the punishment from her if she testifies four times by God that he is indeed among the liars.
interpretation: This verse completes the ruling of li'an (mutual imprecation) between spouses, which applies when a husband accuses his wife of adultery and has no witnesses. After the husband swears four oaths and invokes God's curse on himself if he lies, the wife is given a way to defend herself. By swearing four oaths by God that her husband is lying, she escapes the legal punishment for adultery. This shows God's justice and mercy: the accusation alone does not condemn her, and she has a right to answer it. Both parties are placed under the weight of an oath before God, who knows the truth, and the matter is left to His judgment in the Hereafter while the worldly penalty is lifted from her.

translation: And the fifth [oath] is that the wrath of God be upon her if he [her husband] is among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse completes the procedure of li'an (mutual imprecation) between spouses when a husband accuses his wife of adultery without having four witnesses. After the husband swears four times by God that he is truthful and invokes God's curse on himself in a fifth oath if he lies, the wife may avert the legal punishment by swearing four times that he is lying. Here, the fifth oath is hers: she calls down God's wrath upon herself if her husband is telling the truth. The verse shows Islam's concern for protecting both the honor of the accused and the integrity of the family, by placing the final judgment in God's hands when human proof is lacking. It also stresses the gravity of oaths, since each party stakes their standing before God on the claim, and it removes the worldly penalty while leaving the ultimate truth to divine reckoning.

translation: And were it not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy, and that God is Ever-Relenting and Wise, [He would have exposed you and punished you].
interpretation: The verse is a deliberately unfinished sentence, and the omitted consequence is meant to be filled in by the listener's own sense of dread. It points to how much believers owe to God's grace. Ordinary people fall short in many ways, especially in how they speak of one another, how they accuse and how they swear oaths. If God dealt with each failing the moment it occurred, no one would be spared. People are spared because God's mercy covers them and because He is Tawwab: He keeps the door of repentance open and accepts those who turn back to Him. He is also Hakim: His wisdom shows in the laws He sets, in the way He delays punishment, and in the way He guides people toward repentance and reform. The verse tells the believer to be grateful, to hurry to repent, and to treat others with the same forbearance that God shows toward them.

translation: Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group among you. Do not think it bad for you; rather, it is good for you. Every person among them will have what he earned of the sin, and as for the one among them who took upon himself the greater part of it, for him is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse was revealed about the slander against Aisha, the wife of the Prophet, which a small group in the Muslim community spread. God consoles the Prophet, Aisha, her family and the believers, telling them that the ordeal is not ultimately harmful but beneficial: it brought her innocence to light through divine declaration, raised her rank, gave the believers and her family reward for their patience, exposed the hypocrites, and taught the community lessons about guarding speech, thinking well of fellow believers and verifying rumors. The verse also affirms individual accountability: each participant bears sin in proportion to his role, and the chief instigator, traditionally understood as Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites, who initiated and propagated the lie, faces a grievous punishment.

translation: Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of their own people, and say, 'This is a clear falsehood'?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the community for how it reacted to the slander against Aisha (the affair of the Ifk). When a believer hears an accusation against a fellow believer, the right response is to presume innocence and think well of them, not to pass the rumor along. The phrase 'of themselves' (bi-anfusihim) shows that the believers are like one body, so slandering one member is slandering oneself. Those who heard the charge should have rejected it at once as a plain lie, because accusing someone of immorality without proof is itself a grave wrong. The verse sets a standard: assume the best of fellow Muslims, do not spread unverified claims, and refuse to accept serious accusations without evidence.

translation: Why did they not bring four witnesses to it? But since they have not brought the witnesses, then it is they, in the sight of God, who are the liars.
interpretation: This verse (Surat an-Nur, 24:13) addresses those who spread the slander against Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and lays down a strict standard of proof for any accusation of illicit sexual conduct: four eyewitnesses. Anyone who levels such a charge without that proof is, in God's judgment, a liar, whatever he may personally believe or claim to have heard. The verse protects the honor of innocent people and the cohesion of the community by forbidding rumor, conjecture and hearsay from serving as grounds for accusation. The ruling stands regardless of whether the accusation might happen to be true. Without legal proof, the accuser is condemned as a liar and bears the guilt of slander.

translation: Were it not for God's grace upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, a great punishment would have touched you for what you plunged into.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 24:14) was revealed about the slander against Aisha, when some believers took part in spreading the rumor. It teaches that those who were caught up in it escaped immediate and severe punishment only because of God's gracious forbearance. His mercy in this world gave them time to repent and be forgiven, and His mercy in the Hereafter spares those who turn back to Him from the punishment they deserved. The verse warns that careless talk and spreading unverified accusations are grave sins, and that being spared is a call to sincere repentance and greater care with one's words.

translation: When you received it with your tongues and spoke with your mouths that of which you had no knowledge, and you thought it insignificant, while with God it was tremendous.
interpretation: The verse, from the passage on the slander against Aisha (the 'Ifk' incident), warns that spreading unverified rumors is a grave moral wrong, even when it seems trivial. Passing on a report by word of mouth without knowledge or verification makes one a partner in the harm done. People often underestimate the gravity of casual speech, treating gossip as harmless, yet God weighs it by its real consequences: destroyed reputations, broken trust, and social discord. The verse teaches that believers must be accountable for every word they repeat, verify claims before sharing them, and understand that something small in human eyes can be immense in God's sight.

translation: And why, when you heard it, did you not say: 'It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You (O God)! This is a tremendous slander.'
interpretation: The verse rebukes the believers for their passive reception of the slander against 'A'isha (the affair of the false accusation, ifk). Upon hearing such a rumor, a believer's immediate reaction should have been to reject it outright, recognizing that speaking of such a thing is unbefitting of a community built on faith and decency, and that repeating it is itself a wrong. Saying 'Subhanaka' expresses astonishment and declares God far above allowing such a thing to be true of the Prophet's household, and calling it a 'great calumny' teaches that unfounded accusations against the chaste must be denied at once rather than entertained, passed on, or investigated as if they were plausible.

translation: God admonishes you never to repeat the like of this, if you are believers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 24:17), revealed in the context of the slander against Aisha (the affair of the Ifk), teaches that true faith must restrain believers from spreading unverified accusations against chaste people. God's admonition is presented as a lasting moral warning: a believer who truly fears God and values the honor and dignity of the community will never again lend his tongue or ear to rumor and slander. The phrase 'if you are believers' makes avoidance of such conduct a mark of sincere faith, so that repeating it would contradict one's claim to belief.

translation: And Allah makes clear to you the verses; and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: God's clarification of His revelations and rulings is an act of mercy and guidance: He does not leave people in confusion about what is lawful, what is forbidden, and how to live righteously. The closing attributes explain why this guidance can be trusted. Because He is All-Knowing, His rulings rest on perfect knowledge of human nature, needs, and hidden consequences; because He is All-Wise, each command is placed where it brings real benefit and justice. The believer is thus invited to accept divine guidance with confidence and reflect on it, trusting that it is both fully informed and perfectly purposeful, even where the wisdom is not immediately apparent.

translation: Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: The verse (An-Nur 24:19) teaches that the offence is not limited to committing a shameful act or openly slandering; even inwardly desiring that scandal and accusations of indecency circulate about believers is blameworthy, and this desire becomes more serious when it turns into spreading rumors. Whoever takes pleasure in the exposure and defamation of believers, particularly by circulating unverified charges against chaste people as happened in the slander against Aisha, deserves a painful punishment in this world, such as the legal penalty for slander and social disgrace, and in the Hereafter, because such behavior erodes the moral fabric and mutual trust of the community. The closing phrase 'Allah knows, while you do not know' reminds believers that God knows the realities of hearts, intentions and hidden truths, and the real consequences of such talk, whereas people see only appearances and conjecture, so they must refrain from repeating what they cannot verify and leave judgment to Him and to lawful procedure.

translation: And were it not for the favor of God upon you and His mercy, and that God is Compassionate and Merciful, (you would have been ruined).
interpretation: The verse points out that the believers' safety from disgrace and punishment, especially after the affair of the slander (al-ifk) in Surah an-Nur, is due entirely to God's grace and mercy rather than to their own merit. God is not hasty to punish; He gives respite, guides people to repentance, and legislates rulings that purify them. The verse teaches humility and gratitude: those who have been spared a calamity, or granted guidance and forgiveness, should recognize that it is God's compassion that preserved them, and so they should refrain from arrogance and from spreading or taking part in wrongdoing.

translation: O you who believe, do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Whoever follows the footsteps of Satan, then indeed he commands immorality and wrongdoing. And were it not for the favor of God upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been purified, but God purifies whom He wills. And God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse warns believers that evil is entered by gradual steps, so one should avoid even the first small paths Satan lays out, since each step leads to the next until a person is committed to open indecency and what reason and revelation reject. It then reminds them that no one can claim moral or spiritual purity through their own strength: any freedom from sin and any growth in righteousness is a gift of God's grace and mercy, which guides people to repentance and good conduct. Purification therefore rests with God, who gives it to those He knows to be sincere in seeking it, and He hears their words and knows their intentions. This should lead the believer to humility instead of self-righteousness, to dependence on God, and to caution toward the subtle beginnings of temptation.

translation: And let not those among you who possess grace and abundance swear off giving to their relatives, the needy, and those who emigrated in the cause of God. Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not love for God to forgive you? And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in connection with Abu Bakr's vow to cut off support from his relative Mistah after Mistah took part in spreading the slander against Aisha, teaches that wealthy and capable believers should not let personal grievance, even a serious wrong done to them, stop them from doing good to those in need, especially kin and fellow believers who sacrificed for the faith. It calls for pardon and forbearance, and links human forgiveness to divine forgiveness: the one who hopes for God's mercy for his own faults should show mercy to those who wronged him. Charity is thus not to be withheld as a punishment, and a believer's moral stature is shown in rising above resentment.

translation: Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unaware, believing women [of immorality] are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse (Surah An-Nur 24:23) treats false accusation of adultery against innocent believing women as one of the gravest offenses, because it destroys a woman's honor and reputation and tears at the moral fabric of the community. The women are described as 'unaware' because they are pure of heart and would never think of such a deed, which makes the slander even more cruel. The 'curse' means those who slander are expelled from God's mercy: in this world they lose their dignity and credibility, becoming subject to legal punishment and rejection of their testimony, and in the Hereafter they face a severe torment unless they repent. Thus the verse establishes the sanctity of people's honor and warns that careless speech about the innocent carries a heavy, lasting accountability before God.

translation: On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will bear witness against them regarding what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse (Surat an-Nur 24:24) teaches that on the Day of Judgment, human beings will have no room for denial or excuse, because the very limbs they used in this life to speak slander, to commit wrongdoing, and to walk toward sin will be made to testify against them. The tongue that accused chaste believers falsely, the hands that acted unjustly, and the feet that carried them to disobedience will speak by God's leave, revealing the truth of their deeds. This is a reminder that every action is recorded and accountable, that nothing can be concealed from God, and that a person should therefore guard his speech and conduct now, treating his own body as a trust that will one day be a witness for or against him.

translation: On that Day, God will pay them in full their rightful due, and they will know that God is the Manifest Truth.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nur 24:25) speaks of the Day of Judgment, when God will give those who slandered chaste believers their full and just recompense, with nothing wronged or withheld. Here 'dīn' means the reckoning or requital, and it is called 'true' because it is exact and just. On that Day, all doubt will fall away, and even those who denied or were heedless will recognize with certainty that God is the clear, self-evident Truth. His promises, His warnings, and His justice are fully real, and the falsehood people clung to in this world, such as slander and deceit, will be exposed as baseless.

translation: Evil women are for evil men, and evil men are for evil women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. Those [the good] are innocent of what the slanderers say. For them is forgiveness and a generous provision.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah An-Nur, comes after the slander against Aisha, may God be pleased with her, and states a principle of moral affinity: people are generally drawn to and matched with those who resemble them in character, so the pure are joined with the pure and the corrupt with the corrupt. Since the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was the best and purest of creation, it is inconceivable that his wife would be unchaste, and the same holds for the righteous companions such as Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal who was falsely linked to her. The verse therefore declares the innocence of the pure from the lies of the slanderers and promises them God's forgiveness and an honorable provision, both in this world and the next, as vindication and reward for enduring the slander with patience.

translation: O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses until you have asked permission and greeted their inhabitants with peace. That is better for you, perhaps you will be mindful.
interpretation: The verse establishes the etiquette of respecting the privacy and sanctity of the home. A believer must not walk into another person's house unannounced; he must first seek the occupants' consent (istisan, making one's presence known so that the people feel at ease) and then offer the greeting of peace. This protects people's dignity, their private affairs and their sense of security, and it prevents suspicion, embarrassment and discord in the community. By joining permission with salam, the verse ties social conduct to goodwill and mutual trust, and God says this practice is better for the believers because it nurtures consideration and mindfulness in their dealings with one another.

translation: And if you find no one in them, do not enter until permission has been given to you. And if it is said to you, 'Go back,' then go back; it is purer for you. And God is All-Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that a house is a protected private domain, and that the right to enter belongs to its owner alone. Even when a house appears empty, a visitor may not enter without authorization, since an absent owner's right to privacy does not lapse and entry without consent is a violation of that trust. If the owner declines the visitor and asks them to leave, the visitor should depart without resentment or insistence, because the owner may have good reasons that need not be explained. Accepting refusal gracefully is described as 'purer' (azka) for the visitor: it cleanses the heart of pride, wounded ego and intrusive curiosity, and it preserves mutual respect and social harmony. The closing reminder that God knows what people do warns that adherence to these etiquettes is judged by God, who sees intentions and hidden conduct even when no one else is watching.

translation: There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is some benefit for you. And God knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: After laying down the rules of seeking permission before entering people's homes, the verse gives an exemption for non-residential buildings such as inns, shops, rest houses, storerooms, and public facilities, where one may enter without asking leave because they are set up for common use and benefit.
