The closing phrase reminds believers that this allowance is not a license to abuse it: God knows the true intentions behind a person's entry, whether it is for a legitimate need or for prying, mischief, or wrongdoing. Thus the exemption is bound to sincere purpose and accountability before God, who knows both the outward act and the hidden motive.

translation: Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, God is fully aware of what they do.
interpretation: The verse establishes lowering the gaze as the first safeguard of chastity, because the eyes are the gateway to desire, and whoever restrains his sight finds it easier to guard his private parts and keep away from sin. The command does not forbid looking altogether but calls for self-restraint and modesty in public life, so that a believer does not let his eyes dwell on what is unlawful. Its purpose is the purification of the soul ("purer for them"): inner purity, a clean heart and a more upright society are reached by controlling the senses before desire grows into action. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of what they do adds an inner sense of accountability, since the glance and the hidden intention are known to God even when no one else sees them, so obedience should come from God-consciousness and not merely from fear of people.

translation: And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not to display their adornment except what ordinarily appears of it. Let them draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, those their right hands possess, male attendants having no sexual desire, or children who are not yet aware of women's private matters. And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment. And turn to God in repentance all together, O believers, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse sets out a code of modesty for believing women that parallels the command given to men in the preceding verse. It begins with inward and outward discipline, which means restraining the eyes and guarding chastity. It then regulates public presentation. Adornment that is naturally visible, such as outer clothing or the face and hands according to many scholars, is permitted, while other adornment is reserved for the private circle of husbands and close relatives (mahrams), women, and those who pose no sexual threat, such as dependents without desire and young children. The instruction to draw the khimar over the chest establishes a concrete standard of covering. The prohibition on stamping the feet extends modesty to subtle behavior that draws attention to hidden adornment, so that the intent behind an action matters as well as its form. The closing call to repentance acknowledges that everyone falls short in this area, and it presents success (falah) as depending on sincere, collective return to God and on maintaining a community of purity, dignity, and mutual respect.

translation: And marry off the unmarried among you, and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants. If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty. And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse places on the community, especially guardians and those with means, a collective responsibility to help unmarried men and women, including widowed and divorced people, as well as righteous slaves, to enter lawful marriage. Marriage is promoted as a way to protect chastity and strengthen society. Poverty should not be treated as a barrier, because God promises to provide for those who seek the lawful path of marriage and who wish to remain chaste. Their provision comes through God's bounty, which can take the form of sustenance, blessing, or the shared effort of a married household. The closing names, 'All-Encompassing' and 'All-Knowing', remind believers that God's generosity is limitless and that He knows the real circumstances and needs of each person, so they can trust His promise and not fear financial hardship.

translation: Let those who cannot find the means to marry keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those of your slaves who seek a contract of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your young women to prostitution, if they desire chastity, in order to seek the goods of worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse sets out a program of moral and social protection for the vulnerable. Those who cannot afford marriage are told to practice restraint and patience, trusting that God will open means for them, rather than seek illicit outlets. The verse then moves to freeing slaves: when a slave asks for a contract to buy his or her freedom, the owner should agree if the slave is trustworthy and capable of earning, and should help by giving part of the wealth God has granted, reminding owners that their property is a trust from God rather than something wholly their own. Finally, it forbids forcing female slaves or dependent women into prostitution for profit, especially when they wish to remain chaste. Such exploitation is condemned as greed for the fleeting gains of this world. God's forgiveness and mercy are extended to the women who were coerced, since the responsibility and sin lie with those who compelled them, and they are not blamed for what was forced upon them.

translation: We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and an example from those who passed on before you, and an admonition for the righteous.
interpretation: God reminds the believers that the guidance He revealed is not vague or hidden but plainly explains what is lawful and unlawful, in particular the rulings on chastity, modesty and social conduct that precede this verse in Surat an-Nur. He adds that the Qur'an preserves the fate of earlier nations as a lesson: those who disobeyed God's limits were brought to ruin, and those who obeyed were honored, so people should draw lessons from their history rather than repeat their mistakes. The verse also describes the Qur'an as an admonition that actually benefits the God-fearing, because only those who are mindful of God have hearts open enough to take heed and turn the verses into action.

translation: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp; the lamp is within a glass; the glass is as if it were a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow forth even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah presents parables for the people, and Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse says that Allah is the source and sustainer of all guidance and reality, the One by whom the heavens and earth are illumined and made intelligible. The parable of the niche, lamp, and glass depicts how divine guidance is manifested in the believer's heart. The heart is like the niche, faith and guidance are the lamp, and the pure heart is like a clear glass that lets the light shine in full brilliance. The blessed olive tree, neither eastern nor western, signifies a guidance that is balanced, pure, and free from extremes or partisan distortion. Its oil, almost luminous before touching fire, points to a natural disposition (fitra) so receptive to truth that it nearly recognizes it before revelation arrives. When revelation does come, it is 'light upon light': divine revelation meeting an already receptive, sound nature, so that guidance is doubled and magnified. Yet this light is not earned by a person's own power. Allah guides to it whom He wills, according to His knowledge and wisdom. The parables are given so that people can grasp abstract spiritual realities through familiar images, and Allah knows fully who is fit to receive them.

translation: In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is remembered, He is glorified therein in the mornings and the evenings.
interpretation: The verse points to the mosques, the houses of worship that Allah has commanded to be honored, built, and kept pure, and in which His name is constantly invoked. Their being 'raised' means both physical construction and elevation in dignity, by keeping them clean and free of idle talk and sin. They are the places where the light of faith, described in the preceding verses, is most visibly found. Believers glorify Allah in them at the start and close of the day, and this shows that regular prayer and remembrance, especially in community, are the way hearts stay connected to Him and are sustained in the light of guidance.

translation: Men whom neither commerce nor trading distracts from the remembrance of God, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat; they fear a Day on which hearts and eyes will be turned about.
interpretation: The verse describes the true believers who frequent the houses of worship mentioned in the preceding verse. Their devotion is not abandoned for worldly gain: they work, trade, and earn a living, yet these pursuits never take priority over their obligations to God. They pause their business at the time of prayer, remain mindful of God throughout their day, and give charity from their wealth. What anchors this steadfastness is their awareness of accountability: they fear the Day of Judgment, when hearts will flutter between hope and dread and eyes will turn in terror, unsure of their fate. The lesson is that earning a livelihood is lawful and even praiseworthy, but faith is perfected when one's worldly dealings are kept subordinate to remembrance of God and fear of the Hereafter.

translation: That Allah may reward them according to the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty. And Allah provides for whom He wills without account.
interpretation: The verse explains the outcome for the believers who remain devoted in the houses of worship and fear the Day of Judgment: God will repay them according to the best of their deeds, not merely the average, overlooking their shortcomings and multiplying the reward. Beyond what their deeds strictly merit, He adds gifts purely out of His grace, showing that salvation and reward are ultimately from His generosity and not from human entitlement. The closing statement, that He gives without reckoning, means that His giving is not limited by measure or calculation; He is never constrained by what He gives, nor does anyone's reward diminish His treasures, so believers should hope for His limitless generosity in this world and the next.

translation: As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty man supposes to be water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and he finds God there with him, who pays him his account in full. And God is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse likens the good deeds of those who reject faith to a mirage: from afar they look like something that will bring relief and reward, and the person pins all his hope on them, just as a parched traveler runs toward shimmering 'water'. But when he arrives at the moment of death and judgment, he finds that his deeds, lacking faith and sincerity toward God, carry no weight and yield no benefit. His expectation collapses into disappointment, deepening his anguish. What he does find is God, before whom he stands, and God gives him exact and full recompense for what he actually earned, with no injustice. The closing statement that God is swift in reckoning warns that this reckoning is never far off and that no deed escapes His precise accounting, so a person should not be deceived by the apparent worth of deeds that are not founded on belief in God.

translation: Or [their deeds are] like darkness within a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is another wave, above which are clouds: darknesses, some of them above others. When one stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it. And he to whom Allah has not granted light, for him there is no light.
interpretation: This verse completes the parable of the previous verse, which likened the believer's heart to a light upon light. Here the state of the disbelievers is depicted as layers of darkness: the darkness of the deep sea, the darkness of wave upon wave, and the darkness of clouds that hide even the stars. These layers stand for the stacked darknesses within the unbeliever: ignorance, misguidance, doubt, and persistent denial, each compounding the other until the heart is so enveloped that it cannot perceive even what is closest to it, like one's own hand. Such a person cannot find his way to truth by himself. The closing statement teaches that guidance is wholly a gift from God: whoever God does not illuminate with the light of faith and revelation has no other source of light, for no worldly knowledge or intellect can replace divine guidance.

translation: Do you not see that it is God whom all those in the heavens and the earth glorify, and the birds with wings spread out in flight? Each one indeed knows its own prayer and its own glorification, and God is All-Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection on the universal worship pervading creation: every being, whether rational or not, acknowledges its Creator in the manner suited to its nature. The birds suspended in the air with outstretched wings are singled out as a visible sign of divine power and care, since nothing but God's laws and sustaining will hold them aloft. Each creature has been given an innate awareness of its own particular way of devotion, so none is without guidance, and nothing in creation is heedless of God. This implies that humans, who are endowed with choice and reason, should not be the exception by turning away from remembrance of God. The closing statement that God knows what they do assures the believer that no act of worship, however hidden, goes unnoticed, and warns that no deed of any creature escapes His knowledge.

translation: To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to God is the final return.
interpretation: The verse teaches that absolute sovereignty over all creation belongs to God alone, so no created being truly owns or rules independently of Him. Because everything originates in His dominion, everything also returns to Him, and every soul will stand before Him for judgment. This should instill humility in those who hold worldly power or wealth, since what they possess is only held in trust, and it should give believers reassurance that justice will ultimately be established. It also calls people to live with accountability, remembering that their final destination is not this world but God Himself.

translation: Do you not see that God drives the clouds gently, then joins them together, then makes them into layers piled up, and you see the rain come forth from within them? And He sends down from the sky mountains [of clouds] in which there is hail, and He strikes with it whomever He wills and turns it away from whomever He wills. The flash of its lightning almost takes away the sight.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection on the stages of cloud formation and rain as signs of God's deliberate power and wisdom, not of blind natural chance. Each stage is guided by Him: clouds are moved gently, gathered, stacked into dense masses, and then release rain and hail. That the same cloud may bring blessing or harm to one place and spare another shows that its course follows His will and not an automatic process. The dazzling lightning that almost blinds the eyes adds to the awe, reminding the believer of God's majesty and prompting gratitude, humility, and recognition that He alone governs the forces of nature.

translation: God alternates the night and the day. Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who have insight.
interpretation: The constant alternation of night and day, with their changing lengths, light and darkness, warmth and cold, is not a product of chance but of God's precise control and wisdom. This turning of time is a sign to those with perceptive hearts and minds that all things are subject to His power, that no condition is permanent, and that just as darkness gives way to light, hardship gives way to ease and the fortunes of nations rise and fall by His decree. Those with true insight reflect on this and draw lessons of humility, gratitude, and reliance on the One who governs the cosmos.

translation: And God has created every moving creature from water. Among them are those that walk on their bellies, among them those that walk on two legs, and among them those that walk on four. God creates whatever He wills. Indeed, God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse points to God's creative power and wisdom: all living creatures share one origin in water, which is the basis of life, yet they differ greatly in form and way of moving. The variety of crawling, two-legged and four-legged creatures, all coming from one source, shows that diversity is not the work of chance or of the material itself. It results from the will of the Creator, who shapes each kind as He wishes. The closing words, 'God has power over all things,' remind the reader that the One who can make such different beings from a single substance can do anything. This should lead people to reflect on the signs in creation, recognize God's oneness and might, and submit to Him in gratitude and worship.

translation: We have certainly sent down clear verses, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has made His revelation plain and open to understanding, so no one can claim the truth was hidden from them. Yet recognizing the clarity of the signs is not enough on its own, because accepting them and walking the straight path depends on God's guidance. That guidance is granted to those whose hearts are sincere and receptive to the truth, so a person should combine reflection on the verses with humble reliance on God to be led to the right way.

translation: They say, 'We believe in God and in the Messenger, and we obey.' Then a party of them turns away after that, and those are not the believers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the gap between verbal profession and real faith. Some people declare belief in God and His Messenger and promise obedience, but when obedience costs them something, particularly when they are called to accept the Messenger's judgment against their own interests, a group of them turns away. Faith in the Qur'anic sense is therefore not a mere statement of the tongue. It is confirmed by submission and action. Those whose conduct contradicts their claim, and who accept God's ruling only when it suits them, are denied the label of true believers, because real belief shows itself in willing obedience.

translation: And when they are called to God and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who claim faith yet accept divine judgment only when it serves their interests. When the Qur'an and the Prophet's ruling are offered as the arbiter of their disputes, a group among them turns away, because they fear the verdict will go against their desires. True faith means submitting to God's law willingly in every case, whether it benefits or harms oneself. Selective obedience, accepting the revealed rule when convenient and rejecting it when not, shows that a person is following their own whims rather than God, and is a mark of weak or false belief.

translation: But if the right is on their side, they come to him (the Messenger) in willing submission.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 24:49) exposes the hypocrites' insincerity in accepting judgment. When they are confident that a ruling will favor them, they hurry to the Messenger and accept his arbitration with full submission. This shows that their obedience is driven by self-interest and not by true faith. Their willingness to submit depends on whether the verdict suits their desires, and so they treat God's law as a tool to serve their whims, not as a binding authority. True faith requires accepting God's and His Messenger's judgment whether it benefits or harms one's own position.

translation: Is there a disease in their hearts? Or do they doubt? Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them in judgment? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses why some who claim faith turn away when called to the judgment of God and His Messenger. It offers three possible causes: hypocrisy or moral sickness of the heart, doubt about the Prophet's truthfulness, or a fear that God and His Messenger will be unjust. The third is absurd, since divine judgment is perfectly just, and the question is rhetorical, exposing the flaw in their own character. The real injustice lies within them: they refuse the right when it goes against their interests and accept judgment only when it favors them. Genuine faith means submitting to God's ruling with trust in His justice, even when it is contrary to one's desires.

translation: The only statement of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, is that they say, 'We hear and we obey.' And those are the successful.
interpretation: True faith is shown in practice, not in claims. A believer who is invited to submit a dispute to the judgment of God and His Messenger, meaning the revealed law, responds at once with willing acceptance and obedience, without hesitation, evasion, or conditions based on personal advantage. This contrasts with the hypocrites in the preceding verses, who turn away when the ruling goes against their interests. The verse says that those who submit sincerely to divine judgment, even when it is against their own desires, are the ones who will achieve real success in this world and the next.

translation: Whoever obeys God and His Messenger, and fears God and is mindful of Him, it is those who are the triumphant.
interpretation: True success in the Qur'anic view is not measured by worldly gain but by a threefold inner and outer discipline: outward obedience to God and the Prophet, inward reverence that makes one fear displeasing God, and ongoing God-consciousness (taqwa) that guards one's conduct. The verse teaches that obedience alone is incomplete without heartfelt awe and vigilant piety, and that those who combine these will attain the ultimate victory: salvation from punishment and the attainment of God's pleasure and Paradise. The emphatic phrasing 'it is those, they are the triumphant' limits true triumph to such people, implying that those who lack these qualities, whatever they may possess of worldly success, have not truly won.

translation: They swear by God their strongest oaths that if you were to command them, they would surely march out. Say: Do not swear; obedience is known. Indeed, God is Fully Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse addresses the hypocrites, who made emphatic oaths that they would go out to fight or do whatever the Prophet commanded, in order to cover over their doubtful sincerity. The reply, 'Do not swear; obedience is known,' means that real obedience is recognized by deeds and consistent conduct, not by loud oaths. A person whose obedience is genuine has no need to swear, because it shows in action, while excessive swearing often betrays an inner lack of conviction. God then warns that He is fully aware of what they do, so their oaths cannot deceive Him, and the outward show of loyalty is worthless if the heart and deeds do not match it.

translation: Say: Obey God and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon him is only what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with. And if you obey him, you will be guided. And the Messenger is responsible only for clear delivery of the message.
interpretation: The verse establishes that responsibility is individual and divided: the Prophet's duty is limited to conveying God's message plainly, while the duty of those who receive it is to respond with obedience. Obeying God is inseparable from obeying His Messenger, because the Messenger is the means by which God's guidance is made known and applied. If people reject the message, the Prophet is not blamed, since he has fulfilled his trust, and they alone bear the consequences of their refusal. Guidance is not forced; it is attained only by following the Messenger. The verse thus comforts the Prophet and warns the people that excuses vanish once the message has been clearly delivered.

translation: God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land, as He made those before them successors; that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them; and that He will surely replace their fear with security, so that they worship Me, associating nothing with Me. But whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse links worldly empowerment and security to sincere faith and righteous action. God's promise of succession, the firm establishment of the religion He approves, and the replacement of fear with safety is not given for its own sake but for a purpose: pure monotheistic worship free of any partners. The promise, as fulfilled for earlier righteous communities, is conditional on the believers' continued faith and good deeds, so stability and authority are a trust and a divine favor, not an entitlement. Whoever, after receiving such blessings, turns to ingratitude and rejects faith, steps outside obedience to God and becomes among the fasiqun, those who have departed from His command.

translation: And establish prayer and give zakah and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy.
interpretation: The verse links divine mercy to three practical commitments: worship that connects a person to God (prayer), generosity that connects a person to society (zakah), and following the Prophet, which means taking revelation as a lived pattern of conduct. Mercy here is a consequence of faith expressed in action, not a reward for belief alone. Prayer keeps the heart conscious of God, zakah purifies wealth and relieves the needy, and obedience to the Messenger gives both a trustworthy path for carrying out God's commands. Together they shape a balanced, disciplined, compassionate life, and the phrase 'that you may receive mercy' shows that these duties are paths to God's compassion in this world and the next, not burdens.

translation: Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape [God's reach] on earth. Their refuge is the Fire, and what an evil destination.
interpretation: The verse reassures believers and warns deniers that unbelievers, however powerful or successful they appear in this world, can never frustrate God's will or place themselves beyond His power, whether by flight, strength, or scheming. Worldly strength or delay of punishment is no sign of safety or divine approval. Their final abode is the Fire, an evil end, because accountability is certain and no one can outrun the decree of God.

translation: O you who believe, let those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not yet reached puberty ask your permission at three times: before the dawn prayer, when you put off your garments at midday, and after the night prayer. These are three times of privacy for you. Beyond these times there is no blame on you or on them, as they go about attending you, some of you with others. Thus God makes clear the verses to you, and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse sets a rule of household etiquette that protects privacy. Servants and children who are not yet mature are usually free to move in and out of the family's private quarters. At three times of day, though, adults are most likely to be undressed or in relaxed attire: on rising before dawn, during the midday rest, and after retiring at night. At those times even they must ask permission before entering, so that no one is embarrassed or exposed. Outside those times the need for permission is lifted, because constant close contact in daily life would make it a hardship. The verse shows that Islamic law balances modesty and dignity with ease, and that God's rulings take real human circumstances into account. It ends by affirming that God explains His signs with knowledge and wisdom.

translation: And when the children among you reach puberty, let them also ask permission [before entering], as those before them used to ask permission. Thus does God make clear to you His verses; and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse extends a rule of domestic privacy to young people who come of age. Earlier in the passage, children who had not reached puberty and servants were required to seek permission only at three times of undress: before dawn prayer, at midday rest, and after night prayer. Once a child reaches puberty, he or she becomes a full moral agent and must seek permission at all times before entering the private quarters of others, just as adults do, including adult relatives. The verse teaches that rights and responsibilities change with maturity, and that modesty, dignity and respect for the home's privacy are lasting values of a believing community. The closing phrases remind believers that these rulings come from God's knowledge of human nature and from His wisdom in regulating family life, so they should be accepted and followed sincerely.

translation: And as for women past childbearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame on them if they put off their outer garments, provided they do not display their adornment. But to refrain from that is better for them. And God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse grants an allowance to elderly women who are past the age of marriage and no longer attract men's desire. They may lay aside their outer covering, such as the cloak or veil worn over their regular clothes, in the presence of non-mahram men, without this being sinful. The concession is limited: it does not permit nakedness or the display of adornment and allure, since they must not be 'tabarruj' (flaunting beauty). The verse adds that continuing to dress modestly and keep the outer garment is better and more virtuous, showing that the law aims at preserving dignity and chastity rather than imposing hardship, and that the spirit of modesty is encouraged even where relaxation is allowed. The closing reminder that God hears all speech and knows all intentions warns that these allowances should be used with sincerity and not as a pretext for immodesty.

translation: There is no blame on the blind, nor on the lame, nor on the sick, nor on yourselves, if you eat from your own houses, or the houses of your fathers, or your mothers, or your brothers, or your sisters, or your paternal uncles, or your paternal aunts, or your maternal uncles, or your maternal aunts, or from houses whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame on you whether you eat together or separately. But when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from God, blessed and good. Thus God makes clear the verses to you, that you may understand.
interpretation: This verse removes undue hardship and sets out the etiquette of shared social life in the community. The disabled and sick were not to be seen as sinning when they ate with others or at others' homes, and no one should feel guilty about eating from the homes of close relatives, from property entrusted to them, or from a trusted friend's house, since mutual familiarity and generosity make the host's consent presumed. The principle is that close bonds of kinship and friendship allow informal sharing of food without the formality of explicit permission, so long as there is no abuse or harm. The verse also permits eating together or separately, discouraging scruples that would hinder fellowship. When entering any home, one should greet the people there with 'Peace be upon you', described as a blessed and good greeting from God, because it sanctifies the encounter, spreads affection and security, and reminds believers that their social conduct is part of their devotion. The closing line says that such clear guidance is meant to cultivate reason and sound judgment in everyday dealings.

translation: The believers are only those who believe in God and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not depart until they have asked his leave. Indeed, those who ask your leave are the ones who truly believe in God and His Messenger. So when they ask your leave for some of their affairs, grant leave to whom you will among them, and ask God's forgiveness for them. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith is shown in discipline, loyalty, and respect for legitimate leadership, especially when the community is gathered for a shared, important matter such as consultation, public affairs, or defense. A believer does not walk away from the collective responsibility on a whim, but seeks permission, which shows that he values the common good above personal convenience. At the same time, the verse shows mercy and balance: the Prophet, as leader, may permit those with genuine needs to leave, using his judgment, and he is told to pray for their forgiveness, since even a legitimate absence may involve some shortcoming in putting personal concerns ahead of the community's. Seeking leave is thus a sign of sincerity, and God's forgiveness and mercy cover the believers' human limitations.

translation: Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of one another. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, concealing themselves behind others. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment afflict them.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to treat the Messenger's summons and commands with special reverence and obedience, unlike casual calls between ordinary people. When he calls them to a gathering or a duty, such as the defense of the community, they must not treat it lightly, nor leave quietly without permission by hiding behind one another. Allah knows such hidden evasion. Anyone who deviates from the Prophet's command is warned that disobedience brings consequences: a fitnah, meaning a trial, hardship, or misguidance in this world, such as hardened hearts and being led astray, or a painful punishment in the hereafter. Obedience to the Messenger is thus bound up with obedience to Allah, and disregarding his authority is spiritually dangerous.

translation: Indeed, to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He knows well what state you are in, and on the Day when they are returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did. And God is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse closes Surat an-Nur by affirming God's absolute ownership and encompassing knowledge. Because everything in creation belongs to Him, no one can escape His authority, and nothing about a person's inner convictions, sincerity, hypocrisy, or outward conduct is hidden from Him. This knowledge is not abstract: it leads to accountability, for on the Day of Return each person will be told the true nature of their deeds, with nothing forgotten or misjudged. The meaning is a call to constant God-consciousness: since He knows your state now and will confront you with your record later, you should keep obedience to Him and His Messenger, as the surah's commands emphasize, in private as well as in public.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God is the source of abundant and everlasting goodness, and that His greatest act of grace is revealing the Qur'an, called the Criterion (al-Furqan) because it separates truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, and right from wrong. By calling the Prophet Muhammad His 'servant,' it honors him through his complete devotion to God and stresses that he is a human recipient of revelation, not a divine being. The purpose of the revelation is universal: the message is not limited to one people, place, or era, but is a warning for all humanity and jinn, calling them to believe in God alone and to prepare for accountability, so that no one can claim ignorance of the path of truth.

translation: He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, who has not taken a son, who has no partner in sovereignty, and who created everything and determined it with precise measure.
interpretation: The verse describes the One who deserves worship by pointing to attributes that no created being shares. Sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, so nothing else can be a rightful object of devotion. He is free of any need for offspring, since taking a son would imply lack, dependence, or a share in His divinity. He has no partner in His rule, so no power alongside Him can decide matters or intercede without His leave. Everything that exists was brought into being by Him and set by His decree, with its proper nature, measure, purpose, and term. The universe is therefore ordered and purposeful, not the product of chance or of rival deities, and the right response is to affirm His oneness and trust His wise ordering of all things.

translation: Yet they have taken besides Him gods who create nothing while they themselves are created, who possess neither harm nor benefit for themselves, and who have no power over death, nor life, nor resurrection.
interpretation: The verse refutes polytheism by showing that whatever is worshipped besides God lacks every attribute of divinity. A true deity must be a creator, yet these objects are themselves created. A true deity must be able to help or harm, yet they cannot even secure benefit or ward off harm for themselves, so they cannot do so for their worshippers. A true deity must control life, death, and the raising of the dead, yet they hold no power over any of these. Since only God has these powers, only He deserves worship, and turning to anything else is irrational as well as wrong.

translation: And those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a falsehood that he has invented, and other people have helped him with it." But they have certainly come with an injustice and a lie.
interpretation: The verse shows how the disbelievers of Makkah tried to discredit the Qur'an by accusing the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of fabricating it with help from others, such as foreign scribes. God answers that this accusation is itself a great wrong and a falsehood. It is unjust because it attributes forgery to the most truthful man among them, who was known to them as al-Amin, and because it denies a revelation whose eloquence and wisdom they could not match. It is a lie because a book of such unmatched language and guidance cannot be the product of a few ordinary helpers. The verse teaches that rejecting the truth often leads people to invent baseless slanders, and that such slanders rebound on those who utter them as injustice and falsehood.

translation: And they say: "Tales of the ancients which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."
interpretation: This verse records the disbelievers' slanderous explanation for the Qur'an: that Muhammad (peace be upon him) merely copied old legends from earlier peoples, having others write or recite them to him throughout the day. The accusation is self-contradictory, since the Prophet was unlettered and could not have written or read such texts, and his people knew his life intimately and had seen no such teacher or study. It shows the weakness of the opponents' arguments: unable to produce anything like the Qur'an, they invented far-fetched claims about its human origin. The next verses answer that the Qur'an was sent down by the One who knows the secrets of the heavens and the earth, so its source is divine knowledge, not human transcription.

translation: Say: It has been sent down by Him who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse answers the disbelievers' accusation that the Qur'an is a fabrication or a collection of 'tales of the ancients' dictated to the Prophet. The answer is that the Qur'an could only come from God, who knows every hidden thing in the heavens and the earth. Its contents, its knowledge of the unseen, its guidance and its laws reflect a knowledge that no human being could possess. The verse ends by mentioning God's forgiveness and mercy. Despite the gravity of their slander and denial, God does not hasten to punish. He leaves the door of repentance open, so that those who accuse the Qur'an falsely may return to Him and find forgiveness.

translation: And they said, "What is the matter with this messenger, that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he would be a warner alongside him?"
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh objected to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) because he lived an ordinary human life, eating, earning a living, and moving among people in the marketplaces. They assumed that a true messenger of God must be set apart from ordinary people, either by being an angel or by being accompanied by one who would visibly confirm his message. The verse exposes their flawed expectation: God's wisdom in choosing a human messenger is that he can be a relatable example, whose conduct people can follow and whose message they can understand and live by. Needing food and engaging in daily affairs does not diminish prophethood; it is precisely what makes the messenger a model for humanity. Their objection was therefore a pretext for rejecting the truth, not a sincere demand for proof.

translation: Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he may eat?" And the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man bewitched." (Qur'an 25:8)
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh object that the Messenger is only a human being who eats food and walks in the markets, and they demand that he be accompanied by extraordinary signs of worldly power: an angel at his side, a treasure dropped to him from the sky, or a garden to supply his sustenance. These demands reveal that they measure prophethood by wealth and status rather than by truth and the message it carries. When they cannot answer his clear proofs, they resort to slander, calling him 'a man bewitched,' that is, someone whose mind has been affected by sorcery, so that they can dismiss his message as the product of delusion. The verse shows that the Prophet's humility and simple life were no defect in his mission but part of its truth, and that the wrongdoers' accusations come from stubbornness and not from sound reasoning.

translation: See how they coin comparisons for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Furqan 25:9) addresses the Prophet about the disbelievers' habit of inventing labels and objections against him, such as calling him bewitched, a poet, or a madman, and demanding that a messenger be an angel or be given a treasure or garden. These far-fetched comparisons were not sincere attempts to understand but evasions of the truth. By choosing falsehood over clear evidence, they lost their way. Their misguidance has become so deep that they cannot find any path to guidance, because someone who rejects the truth out of arrogance and prejudice keeps contradicting himself and stumbling from one false claim to another, never reaching the straight path.

translation: Blessed is He who, if He willed, could grant you something better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He could grant you palaces.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:10) answers the disbelievers who mocked the Prophet Muhammad for eating food and walking in the markets, demanding that he have a treasure or a garden. God replies that His power is limitless and that He could easily give His messenger far more than they ask for: gardens and palaces in this world. He does not do so because prophethood is not measured by wealth or worldly splendor. The messenger is a human being sent to be an example, and his truthfulness is proven by his message and character, not by luxury. The verse also hints that the true and greater reward, the gardens and palaces of the Hereafter, is reserved for those who believe and are patient, so worldly provision is not a sign of honor in God's sight.

translation: Rather, they have denied the Hour, and We have prepared for whoever denies the Hour a blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse says that the disbelievers' objections to the Prophet, such as mocking his eating food and walking in the markets, are not sincere questions about his status. Their real problem is that they reject the Day of Resurrection and accountability. Denying the Hour removes any sense of moral answerability, so a person is free to dismiss truth, mock the messenger, and pursue desire without restraint. The verse therefore treats denial of the Last Day as the root of their rejection, and it warns that the consequence is not arbitrary. Those who deny the reckoning will meet a fierce, blazing Fire that God has already prepared for them.

translation: When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging fury and its roaring.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 25:12) portrays Hell as a living, sentient reality that perceives those condemned to it from afar and reacts with furious anger. The detail that its wrath is audible even before they reach it conveys that the punishment begins with terror and dread of anticipation: the deniers of the Hour hear the raging and roaring of the Fire from a distance, so their torment starts before they are cast in. It underscores the seriousness of rejecting the truth and warns the reader that the Fire is not a passive place but an instrument of divine justice, eager to carry out its charge against those who denied the Hour and the message.

translation: And when they are thrown into a narrow place within it, bound together in chains, they will cry out there for destruction.
interpretation: This verse describes the humiliating state of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. Being cast into a cramped, constricted place in Hellfire, with their hands tied to their necks or shackled together with their companions or devils, they will suffer both physical torment and the anguish of confinement. In that state, with no escape and no hope of relief, they will beg for annihilation, calling out 'O destruction!' as they wish death would end their suffering. The narrowness of the place signifies an intensification of punishment, since confinement increases pain, while the binding shows complete helplessness. Their cry for destruction reveals the extent of their regret and despair, yet their wish will not be granted, for they will be told not to call for a single destruction that day but for many.

translation: Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the disbelievers in the Hellfire, after they have been bound in chains in a narrow place and cry out for annihilation, hoping that death will end their torment. They are told that their wish for a single annihilation is futile, because their punishment is not a passing moment that one death could end. It is a lasting, ever-renewed suffering, so even if they were to cry out for destruction again and again, they would find no relief and no end. The verse shows that there is no escape from the consequences of their denial, not even through death.

translation: Say: Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the righteous? It will be for them a reward and a final destination.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet to put a question to the disbelievers that exposes the folly of their choice. Having just described the Fire, with its narrow places, shackles and cries of destruction, He asks whether such an end is better or the everlasting Garden promised to those who guard themselves against disobedience. The question is rhetorical, and the answer is plainly the Garden. It invites people to weigh the fleeting pleasures of disbelief and sin against the permanence of Paradise. The verse describes the Garden as a reward earned by the righteous through their piety, and as their final home, where they will dwell without end and without fear of loss. Taqwa, or God-consciousness, is thus presented as the path that leads to lasting bliss, while heedlessness leads to ruin.

translation: For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is upon your Lord a promise to be requested.
interpretation: The verse shows that the Garden is a place where the righteous receive every desire without limit or end, and that this reward is not an uncertain hope but a binding promise which God has taken upon Himself out of His generosity and truthfulness. The phrase 'a promise to be requested' is understood to mean that the believers themselves, and the angels on their behalf, ask God to fulfil what He promised, as in the supplication 'Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers.' Thus the verse teaches that God's promise is certain, that the believers should hold Him to it through prayer, and that He will surely honor it.

translation: And on the Day when He gathers them together with what they worship besides God, He will say: "Was it you who misled these servants of Mine, or did they themselves stray from the path?" (Qur'an 25:17)
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, God will gather the idolaters together with the objects of their worship, such as angels, prophets, saints, and righteous people, and will question those worshipped. The question is not meant to gain knowledge, since God already knows the answer, but to expose and shame the worshippers by having their false deities publicly disown them. It establishes that each person is responsible for their own misguidance: the worshipped beings did not call people to worship them, and the worshippers strayed by their own choice and by following their desires and their forefathers. The verse thus undermines the excuse that people were led astray by others, and affirms that worship belongs to God alone.

translation: They will say: "Glory be to You! It was not proper for us to take any protectors besides You. But You granted them and their forefathers enjoyment of worldly life until they forgot the Reminder, and they were a people doomed to perdition."
interpretation: The false deities and those who were worshipped instead of God disown the worship given to them, beginning with praise of God to affirm His perfection and their own servitude. They say they could never have taken anyone but God as a patron, so they could not have called people to worship them. The fault lies with the worshippers themselves: God's gift of comfort, prosperity and long life to them and their ancestors made them heedless. Absorbed in pleasure, they neglected the divine remembrance, meaning revelation and the call to monotheism, and lost the spiritual capacity to benefit from it. They became 'bur', a people of ruin, whose hearts were barren of good and who were destined for destruction. The verse teaches that worldly abundance without gratitude and remembrance of God leads to forgetfulness, and that responsibility for misguidance rests on those who choose it, not on those they wrongly venerate.

translation: So they have denied you regarding what you say, and you can neither avert [the punishment] nor find any help. And whoever among you does wrong, We will make him taste a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the polytheists on the Day of Judgment, after the objects of their worship (the angels, prophets and righteous people they had taken as partners with God) disown them and declare their claims false. Having been repudiated by those they relied upon as intercessors, the polytheists are left with no way to ward off God's punishment from themselves and no one to help them. The verse then lays down a general principle: whoever commits wrongdoing, the greatest form of which is associating partners with God, will taste a severe punishment. It shows that false hopes in intermediaries are shattered on that Day, and that each person is accountable for his own injustice.

translation: We did not send before you any of the messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets. And We have made some of you a trial for others: will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.
interpretation: The verse answers those who objected that the Prophet ate food and walked in the markets like ordinary people, as if true messengerhood required being removed from human life. God teaches that all earlier messengers were human beings who lived among people, earned a living, and shared in everyday needs, because a human messenger is the best model for humans to follow. The statement that God made some people a trial for others means that differences in rank, wealth, power and belief test everyone: the believer is tested by the mockery and harm of the disbelievers, the poor by the rich, the rich by the poor, and the people by their messengers, who are humans like them, so that it becomes clear who submits to the truth despite its humble appearance and who is blinded by pride. The question 'will you be patient?' calls the believers to steadfastness and good conduct in these trials, and the closing reminder that your Lord is ever Seeing assures that God knows who is patient and sincere and who is not, and will recompense each accordingly.

translation: Those who do not expect to meet Us say, 'Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?' They have certainly become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.
interpretation: This verse shows that the demand of the disbelievers for angels to be sent down or for a direct vision of God is not a sincere search for truth but a symptom of pride and denial of accountability. Because they do not anticipate standing before God for judgment, they feel no need to heed the message delivered by a human messenger, and they set impossible conditions for believing. The Qur'an says they have inflated themselves with false self-importance and have exceeded all bounds in rebellion, since asking to see God in this worldly life is an arrogant overreach that disregards the proper station of creation before its Creator. Belief therefore depends on humility and awareness of the meeting with God, not on demanding spectacular proofs, because the evidence has already been given in the revelation and signs.

translation: On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news that Day for the criminals, and they will say, 'A forbidding barrier!'
interpretation: The disbelievers had demanded to see the angels as proof of the message, but when they do see them at death or on the Day of Judgment, the sight brings no joy as it does for the believers, to whom the angels bring glad tidings of Paradise. The angels come to the wrongdoers with news of punishment and rejection. In terror they cry out the old Arab formula 'hijran mahjura', used when facing a danger to ward it off, as if begging that the angels be kept away and that mercy and safety be barred from them. Their plea is futile, and the verse shows that what they once mockingly demanded becomes the cause of their despair.

translation: And We shall turn to whatever deeds they have done, and We shall make them scattered dust.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the good deeds of those who disbelieved or who did them without faith and sincerity to God, such as charity, kindness, and good works, will be rendered worthless. Because they were not founded on belief in God or done for His sake, and were not in accordance with His guidance, they will have no weight or reward in the Hereafter. The image of floating dust particles, seen only in a ray of sunlight and impossible to grasp or gather, conveys that these deeds will have no substance, and their doers will find nothing to benefit from them when they most need it. The verse is a warning that the value of deeds depends on faith and sincerity, not on their outward appearance.

translation: The companions of Paradise, on that Day, will have the best abode and the fairest resting place.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:24) contrasts the fate of the believers with that of the wrongdoers who are held to account on the Day of Judgment. The 'mustaqarr' (abode) and 'maqeel' (midday resting place) point to a state of settled security and gentle repose: while the disbelievers face the terror of the reckoning, the people of Paradise are already at ease, free from hardship and anxiety. The comparative forms 'best' and 'fairest' do not imply that the disbelievers' end holds any goodness; rather they emphasize that Paradise's comfort is complete and unmatched, a reward for faith and righteous deeds that makes every worldly effort worthwhile.

translation: And on the Day when the heaven will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in successive descent.
interpretation: The verse describes a scene of the Day of Resurrection, when the sky will burst open and a cloud-like mass (ghamām) will emerge from it, signaling the arrival of the Divine judgment. The angels will descend in successive ranks, host after host, to surround the gathered creation. The verse conveys the overwhelming majesty and awe of that Day, when the familiar order of the cosmos is dissolved and all creation is made to face its Lord, which should move people to reflect and prepare for accountability, since on that Day true sovereignty belongs to the Most Merciful alone and the disbelievers will face it with regret.

translation: The true sovereignty on that Day belongs to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult Day for the disbelievers.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment every claim to worldly power, kingship, or authority will fall away, and it will be clear that real and lasting dominion belongs to God alone. He is named here as Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, to show that His rule is grounded in mercy and justice, so the believers will find that Day a source of safety and ease. For the disbelievers who denied Him and rejected His message, the same Day will be hard and distressing, because they will face the consequences of their denial with no ally, no authority, and no escape.

translation: And on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite upon his hands, he will say, 'Oh, I wish I had taken a path with the Messenger.'
interpretation: The verse portrays the intense remorse that overcomes a person on the Day of Judgment who wronged himself by rejecting the guidance of the Prophet and following misguiding companions or his own desires. Biting the hands is an image of extreme regret and anguish, as he finally sees the truth and realizes that the only path to salvation was the one the Messenger called to. His wish to have taken 'a path with the Messenger' shows that true success lies in following divine guidance and choosing one's companions and influences carefully, since regret will come too late once the opportunity of this worldly life has passed.

translation: Woe to me! I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:28) depicts the regret of a wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment, who bites his hands in remorse after realizing that his intimate companion led him away from the Qur'an and the Messenger's guidance after it had reached him. The point is that companionship is never neutral: close friends shape one's beliefs, choices and ultimate destiny. Befriending those who draw one away from truth and righteousness leads to bitter regret when it is too late, so a person should choose friends carefully, keeping company with those who help him obey God, and should not follow others in disobedience for the sake of friendship or social approval.

translation: "He truly led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Satan has always been a deserter of man." (Qur'an 25:29)
interpretation: This verse is the regretful cry of a wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment, who blames the bad companion he took as a close friend in worldly life. The Reminder, meaning the Qur'an and the guidance of the Messenger, had reached him clearly, so his misguidance was not from lack of knowledge but from following the influence of evil companions, who are here led by the satanic call. The verse teaches that Satan and those who act as his agents beautify falsehood and draw people away from truth, then abandon them at the moment of need, offering no help or defense when the consequences arrive. It warns that the people we choose to befriend and follow shape our relationship with revelation, and that responsibility cannot be shifted onto them, since guidance had already come. One should therefore choose companions who strengthen remembrance of God, and be wary of those who distract from it, because their promises are deceptive and their support is worthless on the Day when it matters most.

translation: And the Messenger said, "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."
interpretation: The verse portrays the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) lodging a complaint before God against those who rejected the Qur'an, which will stand as testimony against them on the Day of Judgment. To treat the Qur'an as 'mahjur' (abandoned) is not limited to outright disbelief or denial. It also covers neglecting to listen to it with attention, to reflect on its meanings, to act upon its commands and prohibitions, to seek its judgment in disputes, and to make it a guide for life. The verse is thus a warning to every community that claims to honor the Qur'an: reverence in word alone is not enough, and the book must be lived by through belief, reflection, and obedience, otherwise one risks standing among those the Messenger complains about.

translation: And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. But sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and a Helper.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by teaching that hostility from wrongdoers is a established divine pattern that every prophet faced; the truth he brings inevitably provokes those whose power, status, or desires it threatens. Such opposition is therefore not a sign of failure or of a flawed message, but part of the trial that distinguishes truth from falsehood and the sincere from the stubborn. The believer is told not to despair or lose heart, because God alone guides hearts to the right path, protecting the messenger from being misled or swayed by his adversaries, and He alone grants victory and support against them, so reliance on Him suffices.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?" Thus [it is revealed in stages] that We may strengthen your heart thereby; and We have recited it to you in a distinct, measured recitation.
interpretation: The disbelievers objected that, if Muhammad were truly a messenger, the Qur'an would have come down in a single complete book, as they believed earlier scriptures did. God answers that the gradual revelation is deliberate and a mercy: it fortifies the Prophet's heart by giving him fresh reassurance, guidance, and support at each hardship and each question he and his community face. Revealing it in stages also makes it easier to memorize, understand, and apply step by step, and lets its rulings and lessons be tied to real events. The phrase 'We have arranged it in a measured, distinct order' stresses that the gradual revelation is carefully ordered and clear, so that it settles firmly in the hearts of the believers.

translation: And they do not come to you with any parable except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation.
interpretation: God assures the Prophet that whenever his opponents raise an objection, a challenge, or a misleading analogy meant to undermine his message, the Qur'an answers it with what is true and with a clearer, more fitting explanation than their argument. The verse shows that revelation is not shaken by their criticisms. Each doubt becomes an occasion for greater clarity, and the believer can be confident that falsehood never stands against the truth without being exposed and refuted.

translation: Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell – those are the worst in position and the farthest astray in path.
interpretation: The verse describes the final state of those who denied the Prophet and mocked his message (as in the preceding verses, where they said he was merely a man sent as a messenger, and claimed he was the one who had gone astray). God reverses their charge: it is they who are in the worst place, Hell, and who have strayed furthest from the true path. Being dragged on their faces signifies humiliation and the overturning of their values; just as they turned their backs on guidance and lived with their priorities upside-down in this world, they are raised in the Hereafter in a degraded posture. The superlatives 'worst in station' and 'most astray in way' show that the true measure of status and guidance is nearness to God's truth, not worldly standing or mockery of the believers.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture and appointed with him his brother Aaron as a minister.
interpretation: God reminds of His established practice of sending messengers with revealed guidance and with human support. Moses received the Torah as a book of guidance, and because the mission of calling Pharaoh and leading the Children of Israel was heavy, God strengthened him by granting his request to make Aaron his helper and spokesman. Aaron's role as a wazir, a sharer of the burden, shows that prophetic work is supported by cooperation and trusted companionship, and it implicitly consoles the Prophet Muhammad that earlier messengers were also given scripture and aid, though their peoples denied them.

translation: Then We said, 'Go, both of you, to the people who have denied Our signs.' Then We destroyed them with utter destruction.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Furqan 25:36) shows that prophethood always follows the same pattern: God sends His messengers, here Moses and Aaron, with clear signs, and the response of the people decides their fate. The people of Pharaoh had already rejected God's signs in the sense that the evidence of His oneness was plain to them and they denied it out of arrogance. The mission of the two messengers was therefore a final call and a clear proof against them. When they persisted in denial after the message was delivered, divine justice took effect and they were wiped out completely. The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that rejection by his people is not new, and it warns the deniers that persistent rejection of clear truth brings ruin after warning has been given.

translation: And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind; and We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that denying one messenger is in effect denying all messengers, since they all bring the same core message of monotheism and accountability. The people of Noah rejected this call, so God destroyed them in the flood and made their fate a lasting lesson for later generations, showing that arrogance and persistent wrongdoing bring ruin in this world. The final clause adds that worldly punishment is not the end of the matter: those who commit injustice, above all by rejecting God's truth and oppressing others, face a painful punishment in the Hereafter as well.

translation: And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of ar-Rass, and many generations between them.
interpretation: The verse continues the account of earlier nations who denied their messengers, showing that rejecting the truth brings ruin. By naming 'Ad, Thamud and the people of ar-Rass, and by adding that there were many other generations in between, it makes clear that the fate of those who deny is a recurring divine pattern, not a single event. This is a warning and a consolation to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The Makkan deniers are not the first to reject a messenger, and their arrogance will end as the arrogance of those before them ended, while God's knowledge encompasses all generations, including those unnamed in the Qur'an.

translation: And for each of them We set forth examples, and each of them We destroyed with utter destruction.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:39) teaches that God did not punish earlier nations without first giving them full warning and clear proof. To every community He presented parables, lessons, and evidences through their messengers, so that no excuse remained for them. When they persisted in denial after receiving this guidance, destruction came upon them completely and utterly. The meaning is that divine punishment follows only after the argument has been made plain, and that rejecting truth knowingly leads to total ruin, which serves as a warning to those who deny the message of the Prophet Muhammad in later times.

translation: And they have certainly passed by the town upon which was rained the evil rain. Did they not see it? Rather, they did not expect any resurrection.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Quraysh, who on their trade journeys to Syria passed the ruins of Sodom, the town of Lot's people, destroyed by a rain of stones because of their immorality and rejection of their prophet. Those ruins stood as a visible lesson in divine punishment, yet the disbelievers took no heed. The verse explains why: it was not that they failed to see the ruins, but that they did not believe in the Resurrection and the Reckoning, so they never expected to be held accountable. Denying the afterlife blinds the heart to signs and warnings, and the one who does not fear meeting God draws no lesson from the fate of earlier peoples.

translation: And when they see you, they take you only as an object of ridicule, [saying], "Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?"
interpretation: The verse shows how the disbelievers of Makkah reacted to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): because they judged by worldly status, wealth and outward appearance, they could not accept that a man who lived among them, without power or riches, could be God's chosen messenger. Their mockery, expressed in a scornful rhetorical question, reveals arrogance and spiritual blindness rather than any real argument against his message. The verse consoles the Prophet by teaching that scorn is the habitual response of those who reject truth, and that it does not diminish the dignity of the messenger or the truth of the revelation. True honor lies in God's selection, not in people's assessment of worldly standing.

translation: He almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them. But they will soon know, when they see the punishment, who is farthest astray in path.
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh, in mockery of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), admit unwittingly how powerful and persuasive his message was: it nearly turned them from their idols, and only their stubborn clinging to ancestral worship kept them from following it. God answers this boast of 'steadfastness' by showing that it is not a virtue but obstinacy in falsehood. When they witness the punishment, whether in this world or the next, the truth will be unveiled, and they will realize that it was they, not the Prophet, who were furthest from the right path. The verse thus reverses their accusation of misguidance and warns that firmness in error leads only to ruin.

translation: Have you seen the one who has taken his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?
interpretation: The verse describes a person whose whims and appetites have become the highest authority in his life: he accepts or rejects things according to what he wants, not according to truth or revelation, so in effect he worships his own desire. Such a person has made the self a deity, and no argument or evidence can reach him while desire governs his judgment. The Prophet is told that his task is to convey the message clearly, not to force guidance on hearts or to answer for those who choose to follow their impulses. Responsibility for their choice rests with them alone, and God is the One who holds them to account. The verse also warns every believer to examine whether he submits to God's guidance or only to his own inclinations.

translation: Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand? They are nothing but like cattle; rather, they are even further astray from the path.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and warns against expecting most of those who persist in rejecting the truth to respond to his call. They have faculties of hearing and reason, but because they do not use them to listen to the message and reflect on the signs of God, they are no better than grazing animals, which hear sounds without grasping meaning and follow only their appetites. They are said to be even more astray than cattle because animals fulfill the nature God gave them and cannot be blamed, whereas humans were given intellect and free choice, and they squander it, abandon guidance, and are therefore accountable for their misguidance.

translation: Do you not see how your Lord extends the shadow? Had He willed, He could have made it still. Then We made the sun an indicator of it.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and care in the daily movement of shade. The shadow lengthens and shortens across the day in a regulated way, and it could have been fixed and motionless, which would have left the earth without the benefits of changing light and shade. Because the sun's position governs the shadow's growth and retreat, shadow is known and measured through the sun, and the sun serves as its sign. This orderly interplay of light and shadow, which people take for granted, shows deliberate design and mercy, and it should lead the reflective person to recognize the Creator's wisdom and to give thanks and worship Him alone.

translation: Then We withdrew it (the shadow) towards Us, a gentle, easy withdrawal.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 25:46) follows the preceding verse in which God lengthens the shadow over the earth. Here He gradually draws it back as the sun rises and climbs, so that the shadow shrinks and disappears little by little, not all at once. The gentleness of the withdrawal points to God's precise and merciful ordering of the daily cycle of light and shade, which is full of benefit for living things: shade is lengthened for rest and then gradually removed so that people can work, grow crops, and live by the sun's warmth and light. The shadow's gradual retreat thus stands as a sign of God's power, wisdom and care, and it invites reflection and gratitude toward the One who governs the cosmos with ease and order.

translation: And it is He who made the night a covering for you, and sleep a rest, and made the day a resurrection.
interpretation: The verse points to God's mercy and power in the daily cycle. Night is called a garment because its darkness wraps and shelters people as clothing does, giving privacy and calm. Sleep is a 'subāt', a cutting off from activity, in which the body and mind are relieved of toil and restored. The day is called 'nushūr', a spreading out or being raised to life, because people wake from sleep as if resurrected and scatter in search of their livelihood. The daily rhythm of sleeping and waking is therefore a sign of God's care for human needs, and also a reminder of the greater resurrection, since the One who revives people each morning after the 'minor death' of sleep can raise them after death. It calls for gratitude and for recognizing that He alone deserves worship.

translation: And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water.
interpretation: God points to the winds and the rain as signs of His power and care. The winds travel ahead of the rain like heralds, announcing relief and life, and the rain is called 'pure' because it cleanses and purifies, and brings life to the dead earth and sustenance to people, animals and plants. The verse invites reflection on how the natural order is a constant, merciful provision from God, and so calls people to gratitude and to worship Him alone.

translation: That We may revive thereby a dead land, and give it as drink to many of the cattle and people We have created.
interpretation: The verse presents rainwater, which God sends down pure, as a sign of His mercy and power. Its purpose is first to bring lifeless, barren earth back to life through vegetation, and then to provide drink for the animals and the many human beings He created. Life on earth depends on this continual provision, so the verse invites reflection on God's care for His creation and calls for gratitude to Him. The revival of dead land is also a reminder that the One who gives life to the earth is able to resurrect the dead.

translation: And We have certainly distributed it among them [in various ways] so that they might remember, but most of the people refused [everything] except disbelief.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Al-Furqan (25:50), follows mention of the rain that God sends down as a mercy to revive dead land and give drink to creatures. It points out that God distributes this water in varying measures across places and times, so that some regions receive it and others do not, some in abundance and others in scarcity. This variation is itself a reminder: it should lead people to reflect that the rain does not come by chance but by a wise and merciful Provider, and so to remember and thank Him. Yet most people, despite seeing these signs, respond with ingratitude and denial, attributing the blessing to natural causes, or to other than God, instead of acknowledging the Giver. The verse thus highlights how clear signs in everyday blessings call for gratitude and faith, while human heedlessness and stubbornness turn away from them.

translation: And had We willed, We would have raised up a warner in every town.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Furqan 25:51) shows that God had the power to divide the burden of warning among many messengers, one for every town.
