Instead He chose to send Muhammad (peace be upon him) as a single warner to all of humanity, which raises his rank and makes his mission universal. The verse therefore also calls on the Prophet to strive hard, using the Qur'an, in conveying the message to all people. The next verse says so directly: 'So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it a great striving.'

translation: So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it (the Qur'an) a great striving.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Furqan 25:52) instructs the Prophet, and by extension the believers, not to yield to the pressures, demands, or compromises that the deniers of truth propose, and to confront them chiefly through the Qur'an itself: by conveying its message, presenting its proofs, and answering their doubts with its clear arguments. The 'great striving' is thus primarily intellectual and moral, a patient, persistent effort of calling to truth with wisdom, steadfastness, and perseverance, which is greater in effect and reach than mere physical confrontation, since the Qur'an's guidance can transform hearts and minds.

translation: And it is He who has let loose the two seas: this one sweet and palatable, and this one salty and bitter; and He placed between them a barrier and an absolute partition.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy in how He keeps two very different bodies of water from mixing and spoiling one another, even where they meet. Fresh water, which sustains human, animal and plant life, is preserved alongside salt water, which carries ships and fills the oceans. The unseen barrier and 'forbidden partition' that God sets between them shows that natural order is maintained by His decree, so that each keeps its own character and benefit. It is a sign meant to lead people to recognize the Creator's oneness and wisdom and to be grateful to Him instead of worshipping what cannot create or sustain.

translation: And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a relative by] lineage and by marriage. And your Lord is ever Competent [Powerful].
interpretation: The verse points to God's power in the origin and organization of human life: every human being is fashioned from a humble, fluid origin, yet God shapes this being into a person embedded in a web of relationships. 'Lineage' (nasab) denotes the bonds of blood inherited through birth, while 'marriage ties' (sihr) denotes the bonds created through marriage that join different families and extend kinship beyond blood. The interpretation is that human society, with its families, kinship networks, and mutual obligations, is not accidental but part of God's design and a sign of His creative wisdom. From one simple substance He produced humanity's diversity and then bound people together in affection and mutual rights, so that the One who can do this is plainly able to do all things, including resurrecting, guiding, and holding people to account. The closing phrase, 'your Lord is ever Competent,' reassures the Prophet and believers that the One who made such an intricate order from water has full power to bring about His promises and to uphold His message despite the opposition of those who worship what cannot benefit or harm them.

translation: They worship besides God that which neither benefits them nor harms them, and the disbeliever is ever a supporter against his Lord.
interpretation: The verse condemns the folly of idolatry: those who worship idols and false deities direct devotion to things that cannot bring any benefit or avert any harm, since all power belongs to God alone. The phrase 'the disbeliever is ever a supporter against his Lord' means that the disbeliever lends aid to Satan and the forces of falsehood in opposing God and His truth, siding with His enemy against Him. In doing so he acts against his own interest, for he allies himself with weakness and misguidance against the One who created and sustains him, and whose cause will ultimately prevail.

translation: And We have not sent you (O Muhammad) except as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner.
interpretation: The verse defines the scope of the Prophet's mission: he is a messenger whose duty is to convey God's message, not to compel belief or to hold people to account. He gives good news of reward and Paradise to those who believe and do righteous deeds, and warns of God's punishment those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing. Guidance is in God's hands, and the Prophet's role is limited to clear communication, encouragement through hope, and admonition through fear, so that people may choose their path with full knowledge.

translation: Say: I ask of you no reward for this, except that whoever wishes may take a way to his Lord.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to declare that he seeks no wage or personal gain for conveying the message, so no one can suspect his motives. The only thing that comes out of his preaching is that anyone who freely chooses may find a path to God through faith, righteous deeds, and spending in His cause. In this sense, the 'reward' he asks for is the believers' own guidance and nearness to God, which benefits them rather than him. The verse affirms both the sincerity of the Messenger and human responsibility in choosing the path to the Lord.

translation: And place your trust in the Ever-Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise. And sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to anchor their reliance in God alone, because every created helper is mortal and can fail or perish, while God is eternally living and never ceases to support those who depend on Him. Trust in God is joined with praise and glorification, showing that true reliance is not passive: it is expressed through constant remembrance and gratitude, acknowledging His perfection and favors. The closing assurance that God fully knows the sins of His servants carries both comfort and warning. The Prophet and the believers need not worry about people's hidden wrongdoing or rely on others to bring justice, since nothing escapes God's knowledge, and He will hold everyone to account. So the believer rests secure in God's care and justice, and lives mindful that every deed is known to Him.

translation: He who created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, then established Himself above the Throne — the Most Merciful; so ask about Him one who is well-informed.
interpretation: The verse points to the Creator as the only One worthy of trust and worship, because His power is shown in the vast creation of the heavens, the earth, and everything between them. The command to 'ask about Him one who is well-informed' means that the true knowledge of God's nature, attributes, and majesty should be sought from those who truly know Him, namely God Himself through His revelation, and the Prophet and the people of sound knowledge who convey it, rather than from speculation, myth, or ignorant claims. The verse also contrasts the unbelievers' disregard for the Most Merciful with the reality of His absolute sovereignty and mercy, and it calls people to turn to Him alone and learn about Him from the most reliable source.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful,' they say, 'And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?' And it increases them in aversion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance and stubbornness of the disbelievers of Quraysh. When called to worship God alone under His name 'al-Rahman', they feigned ignorance of the name and rejected the command because it came through the Prophet, treating obedience as submission to a man rather than to God. Instead of softening their hearts, the reminder deepened their revulsion, showing that when a heart is closed by pride, even the invitation to mercy and truth only increases its flight from guidance. The verse is also a place of prostration for the reciter, a practical reminder that the believer answers the very call the disbelievers shun, humbling himself before the Most Merciful.

translation: Blessed is He who has placed in the heavens great constellations and placed therein a lamp (the sun) and a luminous moon.
interpretation: The verse calls us to glorify God, whose goodness and greatness are endlessly abundant, by pointing to the order of the heavens as proof of His power and wisdom. The constellations, the blazing sun that gives light and heat, and the moon that reflects a gentle light are not random but are set in precise courses that regulate day and night, months, seasons and years, and make life on earth possible. Reflecting on this harmony should lead a person from admiration of creation to recognition of the Creator, to gratitude for His favors, and to worship of Him alone.

translation: And it is He who made the night and the day succeed one another, for whoever desires to remember or desires to show gratitude.
interpretation: The constant alternation of night and day is a sign of God's wisdom and mercy, and it offers people repeated opportunities for spiritual growth. Whoever missed an act of worship, reflection, or good deed in one part of the cycle can make it up in the other, since the two stand in for one another. The turning of time is therefore a gift to those who wish to reflect on God's signs and to give thanks for His blessings. Night, with its stillness, invites contemplation and prayer, while day invites gratitude expressed through work, striving, and good conduct. The verse teaches that time is a trust, and that each cycle is a fresh chance to return to God, remember Him, and thank Him.

translation: The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth humbly, and when the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace.'
interpretation: The verse describes the character of true believers as inward humility that shows in outward conduct. Walking 'with ease' (hawnan) means moving with dignity, gentleness and modesty, without arrogance, swagger or the wish to be seen, because they know they are servants of God and not lords of the earth. Their humility is not weakness, since they also meet provocation with restraint. When the ignorant, meaning those who act foolishly or insultingly, speak to them harshly, they do not answer in kind or get drawn into quarrels. They reply with words of peace, which can mean a gentle, blameless statement or a dignified withdrawal from futile argument. The verse presents self-mastery, forbearance and calm as marks of servitude to God, and it shows that real strength lies in controlling oneself and answering ill-treatment with goodness.

translation: And those who spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing in prayer.
interpretation: This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful (Surah al-Furqan 25:64) as people whose devotion is not confined to outward conduct by day but continues in the privacy of the night. Spending the night in prostration and standing shows sincere, hidden worship, free from showing off, since night prayer is witnessed only by God. It reveals that their gentle humility toward people on earth springs from their deep humility before God, and that true servitude combines good character in public with sustained, heartfelt devotion in private.

translation: And those who say, 'Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is ever an inescapable, permanent affliction.'
interpretation: The verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful as people whose devotion and night prayers do not make them complacent. Even with good deeds they stay humble and fearful, and they ask God to protect them from Hell, because they know they cannot be saved by their own works alone. The word 'gharām' means something that clings and never lets go, so Hell's punishment is portrayed as relentless and inescapable for those who fall into it. Their fear is not despair but a sign of awareness and sincerity: true faith combines good conduct with dependence on God's mercy and constant prayer for safety from His punishment.

translation: Indeed, it (Hell) is an evil abode and resting place.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 25:66) is part of the description of the servants of the Most Merciful, who pray to be spared the punishment of Hell. It gives the reason for their plea: Hell is wretched both as a place of temporary stay (mustaqarr) and as a place of permanent residence (muqam). No condition there offers comfort, whether one is only passing through or dwelling there forever. Their awareness of how terrible this destination is deepens their fear of God and keeps them devoted to obedience, humility and repentance.

translation: And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor niggardly, but hold a just balance between the two.
interpretation: This verse, from the description of the servants of the Most Merciful in Surat al-Furqan (25:67), teaches that true devotion extends to how a believer handles wealth. Righteous spending avoids two extremes: wasteful excess (israf), which squanders resources on needless or sinful things, and stinginess (iqtar), which withholds what is rightly due to oneself, one's family, and those in need. The believer instead follows a moderate, balanced course, spending according to means and real need, giving others their rights, and treating wealth as a trust from God to be managed with wisdom, gratitude, and accountability. This reflects the broader Qur'anic ideal of moderation in all things.

translation: And those who do not invoke another god along with God, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden [to be killed] except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever does that will meet a penalty.
interpretation: This verse, describing the servants of the Most Merciful (Surat al-Furqan), presents three foundational moral boundaries that define true servitude: purity of belief (pure monotheism), protection of human life (sanctity of life, taking it only through legitimate legal right such as due judicial process), and protection of lineage and chastity (avoiding illicit sexual relations). The three correspond to the rights of God, of society, and of the family and individual honor. The warning that whoever commits these will meet 'athām' (a grave punishment and the burden of sin) indicates that violating them carries serious consequences, both in the moral harm that accumulates in this life and in the accountability of the Hereafter. The verse thus shows that real faith is expressed not only in worship but in ethical conduct that preserves life, family, and the oneness of God.

translation: His punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:69) describes the fate of those who commit grave sins such as associating partners with God, unlawful killing, and fornication. Their punishment is not a single measure but is multiplied, because each sin compounds the others and the persistence in sin deepens the guilt. The phrase 'abide therein' indicates the permanence of the punishment for the one who dies in unrepentant disbelief, while 'in humiliation' shows that the suffering is not merely physical but also a disgrace, matching the arrogance and defiance with which such people defied God's commands in this life. The verse thus serves as a warning of the gravity of these sins and prepares for the following verse, which opens the door of repentance, faith and righteous action, showing that God's mercy can replace the evil deeds of the repentant with good ones.

translation: Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:70) opens the door of redemption even to those who committed grave sins such as shirk, murder, and adultery, mentioned in the preceding verses. The condition is a threefold transformation: sincere repentance (turning away from sin with regret and resolve not to return), true faith, and sustained righteous action that proves the repentance genuine. For those who fulfil these, God does not merely erase their past wrongdoing; in His generosity He converts their record of evil into good, either by replacing the sins themselves with rewarded deeds, or by changing the person's character so that the very inclinations that once drew them to evil now draw them to obedience, with their past regret and striving being counted as good. The verse closes with God's attributes of forgiveness and mercy, reminding believers that no sin is too great to be forgiven for one who sincerely returns, and that despair of God's mercy has no place.

translation: And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns to Allah with an (accepted) repentance.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true repentance is not mere words of regret but is completed by a change in conduct, namely righteous action. Such a person turns back to God in the fullest and most meaningful way, a turning that God accepts and that carries him to God's pleasure and reward. It comes right after the mention of grave sins and their punishment, and it shows that God's door of mercy stays open to anyone who returns sincerely, abandons the sin, and replaces it with good, so that no sinner should despair of forgiveness.

translation: And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Furqan 25:72) describes the character of the servants of the Most Merciful. Their integrity shows in two ways. First, they neither give false testimony nor attend or take part in falsehood and sinful gatherings, so their words and presence always stand on the side of truth and justice. Second, when they come across idle, foolish, or vulgar speech and conduct, they do not join in, argue with it, or lower themselves to the level of those engaged in it. They turn away with self-respect and moral nobility, protecting their time, tongue, and hearts from what has no benefit. True believers are marked by honesty and by a dignified self-restraint that keeps them above worthless and harmful pursuits.

translation: And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind.
interpretation: This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful (Surah Al-Furqan 25:73) by contrasting them with those who show hollow reaction to revelation. The believers do not meet God's signs with heedless indifference, nor do they simply drop down in a show of submission while remaining deaf to the meaning and blind to the guidance. When reminded, they listen attentively, reflect with open eyes and hearts, understand what is said, and then respond with real submission and changed conduct. True faith is therefore marked by conscious awareness and action, not by blind imitation or outward ritual without comprehension.

translation: And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous." (Al-Furqan 25:74)
interpretation: This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful as people who pray not only for their own piety but for the righteousness of their families. 'Comfort to our eyes' means spouses and children whose faith and good character bring joy and peace of heart, because they obey God and help one another in worship. The final plea, 'make us leaders for the righteous,' shows that true believers aspire to be role models in piety, guiding others by example toward God-consciousness, and seek to leave behind a lasting legacy of goodness that extends through their households and communities.

translation: Those will be rewarded with the highest place in Paradise because of their patience, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Furqan 25:75) shows that the lofty ranks of Paradise are the fruit of steadfastness. The servants of the Most Merciful, described in the preceding verses, earned their reward by patience in obeying God, in refraining from sin, and in enduring hardship and the hostility of those around them. Their reward is called 'al-ghurfah', the elevated chamber, which signifies the highest station of Paradise, a status that matches the height of their perseverance. Their joy is made complete by honor: the angels and God Himself greet them with welcome and prayers for their well-being, and they live in peace, free from fear, grief, harm, or idle and hurtful speech. Thus patience is shown to be the foundation of every virtue, and its outcome is both elevated rank and lasting security and honor.

translation: Abiding therein forever. How excellent it is as a dwelling place and as a resting place.
interpretation: This verse, which describes the reward of the righteous servants of the Most Merciful (Surat al-Furqan, 25:76), teaches that Paradise is not a passing pleasure but a permanent home. Its goodness lies in both senses of settlement: it is a place of lasting rest (mustaqarr) and a place of residence and honor (muqam). The verse is meant to contrast with Hell, which the preceding verse calls an evil dwelling and resting place. It tells the believer that perseverance in humility, prayer, restraint and repentance leads to a final abode of eternal security, peace and dignity, where there is no fear of loss or removal.

translation: Say: My Lord would not care about you were it not for your prayer. But you have denied the truth, so its consequence will soon be inevitable.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human beings have worth in God's sight only through their turning to Him in worship and supplication; without faith and prayer, they hold no weight with Him. The disbelievers, by rejecting the message and the Messenger, have forfeited that standing, so the punishment that results from their denial will inevitably cleave to them, as a binding consequence they cannot escape. This was fulfilled in this world with their defeat at Badr and will be completed in the Hereafter.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta, Sin, Mim.
interpretation: These are among the disconnected letters that open several surahs, here Surah Ash-Shu'ara (The Poets). They are best understood as a signal that the Qur'an is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet familiar to the Arabs, yet it is a miraculous speech none of them could match. Their eloquence and mastery of language could not produce anything like it, which points to its divine origin. Their precise meaning is known only to God, but their opening placement calls the listener to attention and prepares them for the message that follows.

translation: These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: The verse points to the Qur'an as a Book whose signs are manifest and which makes plain the truth, distinguishing right from wrong and guidance from misguidance. It is clear in its wording, its rulings and its message, so that anyone who approaches it sincerely can grasp its guidance. Its clarity is itself a proof of its divine origin and a call to reflect on it and follow it, leaving no excuse for those who turn away.

translation: Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief because they do not become believers.
interpretation: God consoles the Prophet Muhammad, may peace be upon him, because of his intense compassion and longing for his people to be guided. He grieved so deeply over their rejection of faith that he risked harming himself. The verse reminds him that his duty is only to convey the message clearly, while guidance is in God's hands alone. He should therefore not burden his soul with sorrow over those who turn away, since God could have compelled belief by a miracle if He had willed, but He has left people free to choose and be tested.

translation: If We willed, We could send down upon them a sign from the heaven, so that their necks would remain bowed before it in humble submission.
interpretation: The verse shows that God has complete power to compel belief through an overwhelming miracle, one so manifest that the deniers' pride would break and they would submit. God does not do so because faith is meant to be a free choice, grounded in reflection on the signs already present in creation and revelation. Belief that is forced would carry no moral worth or test. The verse also consoles the Prophet, who grieved over his people's rejection, by reminding him that their disbelief is not due to any lack of divine ability. It reflects a wisdom in leaving humans free to accept or reject the guidance.

translation: And no new reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: This verse (26:5) shows that the people's rejection comes from stubborn heedlessness, not from any lack of guidance. Every fresh revelation, warning, or admonition sent to them out of God's mercy (the word 'al-Rahman' stresses that it is a gift) is met with the same habitual aversion. 'New' (muhdath) refers to the reminder's newness in being revealed or renewed for them at a given time, not to the Qur'an being created. It indicates that God keeps renewing His call to remind people, while the deniers meet each renewal with consistent turning away. The lesson is that hardened hearts are not changed by the repetition or variety of signs, and the Prophet should not grieve excessively over their denial, since the fault lies in their own disregard.

translation: They have indeed denied the truth when it came to them, but soon there will come to them the news of what they used to ridicule.
interpretation: This verse (Al-An'am 6:5) warns those who rejected the Qur'an and mocked the Messenger and his message that their scorn will not change reality. The truth they dismissed will eventually show itself, whether through the worldly triumph of the message and the defeat of its deniers, or through the certainty of the Hereafter, when the punishment and the realities they laughed at will be undeniable. Mockery of divine truth is therefore folly, because its consequences will arrive as clear tidings, and the verse also consoles the Prophet by assuring him that God will vindicate the truth in due time.

translation: Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble kinds of every species We have caused to grow in it?
interpretation: God rebukes those who deny the message and the resurrection for failing to reflect on what is plainly before their eyes. The earth, lifeless and barren, brings forth plants of every excellent, beneficial kind, in pairs and varieties, by His power and mercy. The One who brings forth such abundant, beautiful, useful life from dead soil is surely able to resurrect the dead and to send guidance to humankind. The verse therefore turns the observation of nature into evidence for God's power, wisdom, and generosity, and calls people to contemplation, faith, and gratitude rather than stubborn denial.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign; but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse, repeated after the stories of earlier prophets and their peoples (as in Surat ash-Shu'ara), teaches that the accounts of how God saved the messengers and destroyed those who denied them hold clear evidence of His power, mercy, and justice, and are lessons for anyone who reflects. Yet the verse observes that sound evidence alone does not guarantee faith: most people remain heedless or stubborn and refuse to believe, because belief depends on an open heart and a willingness to accept the truth, not merely on the clarity of the signs. It consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that the rejection he faced from his people is a recurring pattern in human history, and that it does not diminish the truth of his message.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is truly the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs at the end of the stories of the earlier prophets in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, pairs two attributes to teach that God's might and mercy work together. His 'izzah (might) is seen in how He overcomes those who deny the messengers and persist in arrogance, as He destroyed the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot, and others, so no wrongdoer can escape Him or defeat His plan. His rahmah (mercy) is seen in how He rescues the believers, sends warnings and clear signs, and gives people time to repent before punishing them. The lesson for the Prophet Muhammad and the believers is reassurance: those who reject the truth are not beyond God's reach, and the faithful who are patient will be saved and cared for by a Lord who is powerful enough to give them victory and merciful enough to guide and forgive them.

translation: And [remember] when your Lord called Moses: "Go to the wrongdoing people,"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:10) marks the start of Moses' story in Surat ash-Shu'ara' and shows that prophethood begins with a divine summons and a mission, not with personal ambition. God describes Pharaoh and his people as 'the wrongdoing people' (al-qawm al-zalimin) because their wrongdoing was twofold: they denied God and they oppressed the Children of Israel by enslaving them. The verse teaches that those who bear the message are sent to confront injustice and call the oppressors back to truth, even when they are the most powerful people on earth. Addressing the Prophet Muhammad ('your Lord') also consoles him: the rejection he faces from his own people follows the pattern of earlier prophets, and the one who sends the messenger will support him.

translation: The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God and be mindful of Him?
interpretation: God commands Moses to go to the people of Pharaoh, who had oppressed the Children of Israel and denied the truth. The rhetorical question 'Will they not fear?' expresses both divine astonishment and a call to self-reflection: despite their tyranny and arrogance, they should have feared God's punishment and restrained themselves from injustice. It signals that the mission is first and foremost a summons to God-consciousness (taqwa), giving them the opportunity to repent before judgment falls on them.

translation: He said: My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:12) records Moses' reply when God commissioned him to go to Pharaoh and his people. His words are not a refusal of the mission but an honest admission of human vulnerability and a plea for divine support. Moses knew that Pharaoh's court was arrogant and that he would be met with rejection and accusations of falsehood, and he also remembered that he had once killed an Egyptian and that his speech was not fluent. By naming his fear to God, he teaches that a believer facing a heavy responsibility should turn to God in candor and ask for help instead of hiding weakness or relying on his own strength. The verse leads into his request that God send Aaron with him, showing that seeking supporters and means is consistent with trust in God.

translation: And my chest tightens, and my tongue is not fluent, so send for Aaron.
interpretation: In this verse (Qur'an 26:13) Moses, upon being commissioned to confront Pharaoh, honestly admits his human limitations: he fears rejection and the pressure of the task tightens his chest, and his speech is not free-flowing. Rather than refusing the command, he asks God to share the mission by sending revelation to his brother Aaron, who is more eloquent, so that the message may be delivered effectively. The verse teaches that acknowledging one's weaknesses and seeking capable support is consistent with faith and submission to God's command, and that prophetic missions are carried out through cooperation, reliance on God, and the use of the best available means.

translation: And they have a charge of sin against me, so I fear that they will kill me.
interpretation: Moses, as he is commissioned to go to Pharaoh, voices his human apprehension. The 'sin' refers to the man of the Egyptians whom he had struck and killed by accident before fleeing Egypt. Moses does not refuse the mission out of disobedience but candidly acknowledges a real danger: that he would be put to death in retaliation before he could deliver the message. His words show that prophets are human, that a fear of harm does not conflict with faith, and that seeking God's reassurance and support, which God promptly grants by saying 'No, go both of you with Our signs', is the proper response to anxiety when undertaking a heavy duty.

translation: He said: "No indeed! So go, both of you, with Our signs. We are with you, listening."
interpretation: This verse is God's reassurance to Moses and Aaron after Moses voices fear that Pharaoh's people will kill him for the man he killed in Egypt and will deny him. God rejects the fear with 'No indeed' and tells them that the signs they carry are their protection and proof, so they need not be afraid. The phrase 'We are with you, listening' means God's support is constant: He hears everything between them and Pharaoh and watches over them, so no harm will reach them before they deliver the message. The lesson is that anyone who sets out in God's cause, armed with His signs and trusting Him, is under His care and protection, however powerful the opposition.

translation: So go to Pharaoh and say: 'We are the messenger of the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: God commands Moses and Aaron to confront the most powerful tyrant of their age, and the way He frames their mission shows how it should be carried out. They are not to present themselves as rivals for power or as men with a personal agenda, but as bearers of a trust from the Lord of all creation. The phrase 'Lord of the worlds' challenges Pharaoh's claim to lordship, since it places him under a sovereignty far greater than his own and makes clear that he is a created being accountable to the Creator. The singular 'messenger' for two people suggests that they share one message and one mission, which is also a sign of unity in conveying the truth. The verse teaches that the foundation of calling people to God is to state plainly who truly holds authority, and to do so with confidence that comes from God's commission rather than from worldly strength.

translation: Send the Children of Israel with us.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:17, similar to 7:105 and 20:47) records the central demand that Moses and Aaron brought to Pharaoh. It was not a request to overthrow his kingdom but a call to free the Israelites from bondage and oppression, allowing them to leave Egypt and worship God freely. The verse shows that the message of prophethood joins faith in God with the pursuit of justice. True devotion to God requires lifting the oppression of the weak, and a prophet's mission includes liberating people from tyranny so that they can serve their Lord.

translation: [Pharaoh] said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?"
interpretation: Pharaoh reminds Moses of the favor of his upbringing in the royal household in order to shame him and weaken his claim to prophethood. By recalling that Moses was cared for as an infant and lived among them for many years, Pharaoh frames him as ungrateful and as someone who owes loyalty to the very house he is now challenging. The verse shows a typical tactic of tyranny, which is to answer a message of truth with personal reproach and appeals to past benefits instead of engaging the substance of the call. It also highlights God's wisdom, since the one who would later confront Pharaoh was providentially raised in Pharaoh's own home.

translation: "And you did your deed which you did, and you were among the ungrateful." (Qur'an 26:19, Pharaoh speaking to Moses)
interpretation: Pharaoh reproaches Moses for killing the Egyptian man years earlier, calling it 'your deed' in a way that magnifies its gravity without naming it. He then accuses Moses of ingratitude (kufr in the sense of denying a favor), reminding him that he was raised in Pharaoh's household and yet repaid that upbringing with a killing. The verse shows how a tyrant tries to discredit a messenger by invoking his past and appealing to personal debt, in order to avoid facing the message of truth that Moses brought. The charge also reflects Pharaoh's view that he himself was a benefactor, while overlooking the injustice of enslaving the Children of Israel, which was the context of Moses' upbringing.

translation: He said: "I did it then, while I was among those who were astray."
interpretation: This is Moses' reply to Pharaoh, who reminded him of the Egyptian he had killed. Moses admits the act openly and does not deny it, but he places it in the time before revelation, when he lacked guidance and knowledge. The word 'ad-dallin' here means being unaware or without divine guidance, not disbelief or deliberate wrongdoing. The killing was an unintended blow, struck in defense of an oppressed Israelite, and it was a mistake made in ignorance of what the consequences would be. The verse teaches humility and honesty: a person can admit a past error without excuse or arrogance, and can recognize that guidance changes a person. Moses therefore refutes Pharaoh's attempt to discredit his message by pointing to his past, since he is no longer the person he was before God chose him as a messenger.

translation: So I fled from you when I feared you; then my Lord granted me judgment and wisdom and made me one of the messengers.
interpretation: In this verse (Qur'an 26:21), Moses answers Pharaoh's reproach about the killing of the Egyptian by admitting that he left Egypt out of fear for his life, not out of defiance. He presents his flight not as a disgrace but as the start of a path guided by God. His departure led to his being given hukm (sound judgment, wisdom and knowledge of right and wrong) and his appointment as a messenger. The point is that his standing does not come from Pharaoh's household or favor, but from God alone, who turned a moment of fear and exile into the occasion for prophethood. He thereby rejects Pharaoh's attempt to shame him with his past, and credits his mission to divine grace.

translation: And is that a favor of which you remind me — that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?
interpretation: This is Moses' reply to Pharaoh, who had reproached him for being raised in his household as a child and for the deed he later committed. Moses answers with irony and rebuke: Pharaoh calls his upbringing a favor, yet it was only the result of Pharaoh's own tyranny. Because Pharaoh enslaved the Israelites and slaughtered their male children, Moses' mother had to cast him into the river, and he ended up in Pharaoh's palace. A so-called kindness to one individual cannot justify or erase the oppression of an entire people. Moses thereby refuses to let personal debt silence his duty to deliver God's message and to demand the liberation of the oppressed, and he shows that true benevolence cannot coexist with injustice.

translation: Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"
interpretation: Pharaoh's question is one of arrogant denial and mockery rather than sincere inquiry. Moses has just announced that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, and Pharaoh, who claimed divinity and absolute authority over Egypt, responds by asking 'what' rather than 'who', treating the Creator as something unknown, trivial, or undeserving of recognition. He tries to belittle the message and shift the discussion away from Moses' claim to a matter he can dismiss. The verse shows how tyranny and pride make a ruler reject any authority above his own, and it sets the stage for Moses' reply, which points to God's lordship over the heavens, the earth, and all that lies between them, a reality evident to anyone who reflects with conviction.

translation: He said: "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, if only you would be certain."
interpretation: Moses answers Pharaoh's question about who the Lord of the worlds is by pointing to the visible order of creation. The One who made and sustains the heavens, the earth and everything between them is the only true Lord, and no human ruler can claim that title. The phrase "if you are certain" means that anyone who reflects with sincere conviction on this vast, ordered creation will recognize its Creator. Denying Him comes from stubbornness and arrogance, not from lack of evidence.

translation: He said to those around him: 'Do you not hear?'
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's reaction in Surat al-Shu'ara (26:25) after Moses described his Lord as the Lord of the heavens and the earth and all between them. Pharaoh turned to his court and asked 'Do you not hear?' in mockery and astonishment. He wanted to portray Moses' words as strange and absurd, and to stir his courtiers against the message, because Moses spoke of a Lord other than Pharaoh himself. The verse shows how tyrants answer clear proof with ridicule and with appeals to the crowd instead of reasoned argument, trying to make the truth seem laughable and to shield their own claim to authority from scrutiny.

translation: He said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:26, Ash-Shu'ara) is Moses' reply to Pharaoh, who had scoffed at the claim that there is a 'Lord of the worlds'. Moses answers by stressing that God is not a new or foreign deity but the Creator and Sustainer who has always governed every generation, including the ancestors Pharaoh's people revered. By pointing to their own forefathers, who were born, lived, and died under a power beyond themselves, Moses redirects their reliance on ancestral tradition toward the one true Lord who created them and gave them life. The point is that lordship belongs to the eternal God, who outlasts all generations and every earthly king, so Pharaoh's claim to divinity is empty, since he too is only a created being who will pass away like those before him.

translation: He (Pharaoh) said: "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman."
interpretation: Pharaoh, confronted with Moses' clear message and unable to answer it with argument, turns to ridicule and slander. By calling Moses mad and addressing his courtiers rather than Moses himself, he tries to belittle the messenger, protect his own authority, and make the people dismiss the message without considering it. The verse shows a timeless pattern of tyrants and arrogant elites: when truth overwhelms their reasoning, they discredit the bearer of truth by accusing him of insanity, since the truth would otherwise threaten their power and the people's allegiance to them.

translation: He said: "The Lord of the East and the West and all that is between them, if only you would use your reason."
interpretation: Moses answers Pharaoh's mocking question about who the Lord of the worlds is by pointing to what no one can dispute: the ordered movement of the sun and the heavens from east to west, and everything in between, shows a single, all-powerful Creator and Sustainer. The regularity and harmony of the cosmos cannot be the work of any mortal king or false deity, so anyone who reflects honestly will reach this conclusion. The closing phrase "if you would use your reason" implies that denial stems not from lack of evidence but from a failure or refusal to think, since reason leads naturally to recognizing God.

translation: He said: "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you one of the imprisoned."
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's reply to Moses (Qur'an 26:29) after Moses spoke of the Lord of the Worlds. Having no rational argument against the message, Pharaoh resorts to threat and coercion. The verse shows how a tyrant who claims absolute authority defends his power by force rather than reason. His words "a god other than me" reveal that he regarded his own rule as a claim to divinity, so that the worship of any other lord was a challenge to his political order. The threat of prison shows that falsehood, when unable to answer the truth with proof, turns to intimidation, while the prophets and their followers remain steadfast in conveying the message despite persecution.

translation: He said: "Even if I bring you something clear and convincing?"
interpretation: This is verse 30 of Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:30), in which Moses answers Pharaoh, who had threatened to imprison him if he took any god other than Pharaoh. Moses does not respond with anger or retreat. He appeals to reason and evidence, asking whether Pharaoh would still persist in his threat if he were shown a manifest proof of his truthfulness. The verse teaches that a messenger of God grounds his call in clear evidence rather than in force or mere assertion. It also shows that tyranny answers truth with threats, while the truth answers with proof and invites the opponent to judge fairly. Moses' question puts Pharaoh on the spot: to reject a clear sign would expose his refusal as arrogance and not a lack of evidence. This prepares the way for the miracles of the staff and the shining hand that follow in the next verses.

translation: He said, "Then bring it forth, if you are among the truthful."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:106, in the story of Moses and Pharaoh) shows Pharaoh's response when Moses told him he had come with a clear sign from the Lord of the worlds. Pharaoh does not engage with the message itself; he demands proof and puts the burden on Moses, as if the sign were a matter of personal boasting. His challenge 'if you are among the truthful' reflects the typical stance of arrogant rulers who treat prophetic claims as something to be tested by spectacle rather than considered with an open heart. Yet the demand ironically sets the stage for God to demonstrate the truth: Moses' staff and his shining hand, which expose the weakness of Pharaoh's power and the falseness of his claim to lordship. The verse teaches that those who reject the truth out of pride will often demand signs, and that when truth is presented, the one who denies it is left without excuse.

translation: So he threw down his staff, and behold, it became a manifest serpent.
interpretation: This verse presents the miracle given to Moses (peace be upon him) as clear, undeniable proof of his prophethood before Pharaoh. The staff, an ordinary object, was transformed by God's command into a real, visible serpent, not a trick or illusion. This shows that God's power transcends natural laws and that He supports His messengers with signs that cannot be explained away by human skill. The word 'mubin' (manifest) stresses that the sign was evident and left no room for doubt, so that those who rejected it did so out of arrogance and stubbornness, not for lack of evidence.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the beholders.
interpretation: This verse describes the second sign given to Moses (peace be upon him) when he stood before Pharaoh and his court. His hand, ordinarily of a normal complexion, shone with a brilliant, radiant whiteness visible to all who looked, not from any disease, and it returned to its normal state afterward. The miracle served as clear, public evidence that Moses was a messenger sent by God, a proof perceivable by the senses to everyone present, leaving those who denied it with no excuse but stubborn arrogance. It also shows that God can alter the natural order at will, and that His messengers are supported with signs suited to challenge the power and magic of their era.

translation: He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed, this is a knowledgeable magician."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:34) shows Pharaoh's reaction after Moses displays the signs of his prophethood, the staff and the shining hand. Pharaoh cannot refute the clear evidence, so he turns to his courtiers and labels Moses a skilled sorcerer. This is the common strategy of tyrants and those who reject the truth: they discredit the messenger instead of engaging with the message. By calling Moses a magician, Pharaoh tries to protect his authority, to cast doubt in the minds of the elite who shape public opinion, and to explain away a miracle that threatens his claim to lordship. The verse warns that stubborn arrogance and fear of losing power can blind people to obvious signs, leading them to invent false explanations for truths they cannot deny.

translation: He wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery, so what do you advise?
interpretation: These are the words of Pharaoh's chiefs, repeated by Pharaoh himself, about Moses after he showed the signs of his prophethood. Confronted with clear miracles they could not answer, the ruling elite discredited Moses by calling his signs sorcery. They also framed him as a political threat who wanted to take away their land and power. Tyrants often meet the truth this way: instead of examining its evidence, they denounce it and stir up fear for their own interests. The closing question, 'what do you advise?', shows Pharaoh's unsettled state. The man who claimed divinity had to ask his courtiers for counsel, which exposes the weakness of his claim and the fear that the message of truth stirs in the arrogant.

translation: They said: "Put him and his brother off for a while, and send summoners into the cities to gather [the magicians]."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 7:111, and similarly 26:36) shows the counsel of Pharaoh's court after Moses displays his signs. Rather than acting hastily against Moses and Aaron, the advisers urge delay and a calculated response: gather the most skilled sorcerers from across the land to confront Moses publicly. This reveals how tyrannical power responds to divine truth, not with reflection or submission, but with political strategy, mobilization of resources, and an attempt to discredit the message by pitting human skill against it. It also underlines the irony that their gathering of the magicians prepares the very stage on which God's clear sign will be made manifest and the falseness of sorcery exposed before all the people.

translation: They will bring to you every skilled and knowledgeable sorcerer.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:37, also echoed in 7:112) records the advice of Pharaoh's courtiers after Moses showed his signs. Rather than weigh the miracles honestly, they respond with a plan to summon every master magician in the land, assuming Moses' signs are simply a superior trick that other experts in the same craft can match or surpass. It shows the tyrant's establishment reducing a divine sign to mere sorcery and relying on numbers and human skill to defeat it. This sets up the confrontation in which the magicians' tricks are overcome by a real miracle, and the magicians themselves recognize the truth and submit to God.

translation: So the magicians were gathered for the appointment of a known day.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:38) shows that Pharaoh's call for the magicians was carried out and the contest with Moses was fixed for a specific, publicly known time, the day of the festival, as mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha (20:59). The appointment of a well-known day ensured that the whole people would gather and witness the confrontation, which fits Pharaoh's aim of discrediting Moses before the crowds with the combined skill of his magicians. God's decree used that very public setting to make the truth plain: when the magicians' tricks were swallowed up by Moses' staff, their defeat and their belief came before a vast audience, so the proof of prophethood was displayed openly and could not be dismissed as a private or hidden affair.

translation: And it was said to the people, 'Are you going to assemble?'
interpretation: This verse (26:39, from the story of Moses and Pharaoh) shows Pharaoh's people being summoned to gather on the appointed day of the festival, when Moses would face the magicians. The question is less a real inquiry than a call to turn out in large numbers and a means of spurring them on. They were eager to witness the confrontation and hoped to see the magicians prevail, so that they could stay loyal to their old religion. Ironically, the huge public gathering served God's purpose: when the truth was displayed in front of everyone, the defeat of the falsehood was seen by all, and the magicians themselves believed.

translation: "Perhaps we may follow the magicians, if they are the ones who prevail."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:40) records the words of Pharaoh's court as they gathered the people for the contest between Moses and the magicians. The phrase "perhaps we may follow" reveals that their loyalty was not grounded in truth but in the outcome of a show of power. Their religion followed whoever won, and they did not ask which side was right. The verse shows how tyranny and false religion depend on worldly victory and public spectacle. It also shows an irony: they hoped the magicians would win, yet when the truth was revealed, the magicians themselves became believers in the Lord of Moses and Aaron, so the outcome overturned the expectations of those who sought only to protect their own power.

translation: So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, "Will we indeed have a reward if we are the victors?"
interpretation: The verse shows how the magicians were driven by worldly gain: before they even began to confront Moses, their first concern was payment from the ruler, not the truth. It reveals the character of people who serve falsehood and tyranny for material reward, and it sets the stage for the contrast that follows, in which the same men, once they witness the clear sign of God, give up their worldly hopes, believe, and submit to the Lord of Moses and Aaron. It teaches that those who align themselves with power for profit are easily exposed when truth appears, and that sincere hearts can be transformed once the truth is made clear to them.

translation: He said, "Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:42) records Pharaoh's answer to the magicians after they asked whether they would receive a reward if they defeated Moses. By promising that they will be among his close courtiers, he offers more than payment: he offers rank and proximity to his throne. The promise shows how the magicians' skill was being used to defend the tyrant's authority, and how worldly honor and closeness to power were the bait for opposing the truth. The story then shows the contrast. When the magicians recognized the truth of Moses' miracle, they gave up this promised nearness to Pharaoh and chose real nearness to God through faith, even though it cost them his threats.

translation: Moses said to them: "Throw whatever you are going to throw."
interpretation: Moses' words come at the moment of confrontation with Pharaoh's sorcerers. His invitation to them to go first is not approval of their magic but a display of calm confidence in God's support. By letting them exhaust their tricks, he allows falsehood to reveal itself fully, so that the truth of the sign God gave him will stand out more clearly when it overcomes their illusions. The verse teaches that a person who relies on God need not fear the apparent power of falsehood, and that truth is made most evident when it is set against falsehood in open view.

translation: So they threw down their ropes and their staffs, and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we will be the victors."
interpretation: The magicians began their contest with Moses by relying wholly on worldly power and illusion, and they swore by Pharaoh's might rather than by God, which shows that their confidence rested on a tyrant's authority and not on truth. Their oath reveals how falsehood leans on human strength and prestige to assert itself. It also prepares the contrast with what follows: when Moses' staff swallowed up their contrivances, their pride in Pharaoh's might collapsed, and they recognized the truth and fell down in prostration to the Lord of the worlds. The verse teaches that those who trust in created power over God's power are sure to be disappointed, and that the claim of victory made on the basis of falsehood cannot stand against the truth.

translation: Then Moses threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up all that they were falsely fabricating.
interpretation: The verse shows that truth, when backed by God's power, overcomes falsehood no matter how elaborate or convincing it appears. The sorcerers' ropes and staffs were only illusions, products of deception, while Moses' staff was a real sign from God. When the two met, the illusions were consumed and exposed as empty. The lesson is that falsehood has no real substance or lasting power, and its apparent strength vanishes before divine truth. This is also what led the sorcerers to recognize the miracle and submit to God.

translation: And the magicians were cast down in prostration.
interpretation: When the magicians saw Moses' staff swallow up what they had fabricated, they recognized that this was no sorcery, since they knew the limits of their own craft better than anyone. The truth struck them so overwhelmingly that they fell down in prostration, as if irresistibly compelled. The passive wording 'were cast down' suggests that God's clear sign overpowered their pride, and that when truth is manifest, hearts that were once devoted to opposing it can turn at once to faith and submission to the Lord of the worlds. It shows that sincere knowledge leads to humility before God.

translation: They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Pharaoh's magicians after they witnessed Moses's miracle, shows that sincere recognition of truth can overturn even entrenched allegiance. Having come to display their mastery of sorcery, they recognized that what Moses brought was beyond trickery and was a sign from God. Their declaration of faith in the 'Lord of the worlds' is a deliberate rejection of Pharaoh's claim to lordship: they affirm that the Creator and Sustainer of all existence, not any earthly ruler, is the only one worthy of worship. The verse teaches that knowledge and expertise, when joined with honesty, can lead a person to submit to God, and that true faith is a decisive, courageous commitment that does not bow to the threats of tyrants.

translation: The Lord of Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:48, also 7:122) records the declaration of faith by Pharaoh's magicians after they witnessed the miracle of Moses. Having been summoned to defeat him with sorcery, they recognized that his staff was a sign from God and not a trick, so they fell down in prostration and professed belief in the Lord of the worlds. They then specified this Lord as the Lord of Moses and Aaron, which separates the one true God, who sent His messengers, from Pharaoh's claim to divinity. The phrase shows that true lordship belongs to God alone, who sent His prophets with guidance, and that those who sincerely recognize the truth may abandon power, fear, and worldly reward to follow it, even when threatened with punishment.

translation: He said: "Have you believed in him before I gave you permission? Surely he is your chief who taught you magic. So you will soon know! I will certainly cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you all."
interpretation: Pharaoh's reaction to the magicians' sudden faith shows the panic of a tyrant who sees his authority slipping. Because he cannot refute the evidence that convinced them, he claims that belief requires his permission, as though conscience were his to control. He then slanders Moses as the master of a magicians' conspiracy, so that their faith looks like a political plot rather than a sincere response to truth. His threat of mutilation on opposite sides and crucifixion is the last resort of power that has lost its argument. The verse teaches that oppression often follows the collapse of falsehood, and that faith, once it is truly in the heart, can stand against such threats.

translation: They said: 'No harm! Indeed, to our Lord we will return.'
interpretation: This is the reply of Pharaoh's magicians after they believed in Moses and were threatened with mutilation and crucifixion. Their faith made them steadfast: they regarded the worst Pharaoh could do as no real harm, since it only touches the body in this fleeting life. Their return to God is certain, and they trust in His forgiveness and reward. The verse teaches that a person who is certain of meeting God sees worldly threats and loss as small, and that true faith can turn fear of tyranny into calm resolve.

translation: Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers.
interpretation: These are the words of Pharaoh's sorcerers after they saw the truth in Moses' miracle and fell in prostration, declaring their faith despite Pharaoh's threats of mutilation and crucifixion. Their reply shows that faith has freed them from fear of worldly punishment. Their only concern is the forgiveness of their Lord, and they hope for it. The hope is expressed with 'we aspire' rather than certainty, which reflects humility before God, for no one can claim forgiveness as a right. They rest this hope on being the first to believe, meaning the first among Pharaoh's people to respond to the truth. This teaches that sincere and early acceptance of truth, even after a past of sin and opposition, is a means to God's mercy, and that true believers value the pardon of their sins over safety in this world.

translation: And We inspired Moses: "Set out by night with My servants, for you will surely be pursued."
interpretation: The verse shows God's guidance and protection of His believing servants at the moment of greatest danger. Moses is commanded to leave Egypt by night with the Children of Israel, and he is also told in advance that Pharaoh and his army will chase them. This foreknowledge was a mercy and a test of trust. It prepared Moses and his people to face the pursuit calmly, relying on God's plan instead of being shaken by fear. The phrase "My servants" honors the believers and places them under divine care, and it teaches that obedience to God's command, even when it leads into apparent danger, is the path to deliverance. The coming pursuit sets the stage for God's decisive intervention, in which the oppressors are defeated by means they never expected.

translation: Then Pharaoh sent summoners into the cities to gather people.
interpretation: After Moses and his brother left with the Children of Israel by night, Pharaoh was alarmed and enraged. He dispatched officers to every city of his realm to muster troops and people so that he could pursue them. The verse shows the tyrant's reliance on worldly power and numbers, and the irony that his mobilization of the whole kingdom ends only in his own destruction, since no human force can stand against God's decree. Pharaoh also belittled the fleeing Israelites as 'a small band' while insisting they were a cause of anger, which reveals how the arrogant fear the truth even when it appears weak.

translation: "Indeed, these are but a small band." (Qur'an 26:54)
interpretation: These are the words of Pharaoh's herald to the people as he gathered troops against Moses and the Children of Israel. By calling them a 'small band' he belittles them to rally his followers and to suggest that crushing them would be easy. Yet the verse shows that tyrants rely on numbers and contempt for the weak, while God's plan overturns this: the group Pharaoh considered insignificant was the one God saved, and the mighty army was destroyed. Apparent numerical and material strength does not decide the outcome; God's decree does.

translation: And indeed, they are enraging us.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:55) is spoken by Pharaoh to his assembled men about the Children of Israel who were leaving Egypt with Moses. It shows a tyrant's mindset: he presents the departure of a oppressed people as a provocation against his own pride and authority, and frames it as a grievance in order to rally his followers to pursue them. The verse reveals that his hostility was driven by wounded arrogance, not justice, and shows how oppressors often cast themselves as the wronged party. That pursuit ended in their destruction, a lesson that anger fueled by pride and injustice leads its holders to ruin.

translation: And indeed, we are all a vigilant host, wary and prepared.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:56) records the words of Pharaoh's heralds as he sent them into the cities to gather troops against the Children of Israel who had left Egypt with Moses. Pharaoh belittles them as 'a small band' who provoke his anger, and then asserts that his own side is united, alert, and fully armed. The meaning is that the tyrant relies on worldly strength, numbers and preparedness to give himself confidence and to rally his people, believing that vigilance and military might can prevent what God has decreed. The Qur'an presents this boast ironically: for all their caution and preparation, the pursuers were destroyed in the sea, teaching that human precaution and power cannot stand against God's will, and that arrogant reliance on one's own strength leads to ruin while those who trust in God are delivered.

translation: So We brought them out from gardens and springs.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:57) describes how God caused Pharaoh and his people to leave the lush gardens and flowing springs of Egypt, which they had enjoyed in comfort and pride. They left them when they pursued Moses and the Children of Israel, and it led to their destruction in the sea. The lesson is that worldly blessings and power are not lasting securities. Those who rebel against God and oppress others can be stripped of everything they cherish in an instant, so blessings should be met with gratitude and justice rather than arrogance.

translation: And treasures and a noble station.
interpretation: This verse is part of the description of what Pharaoh's people left behind: gardens, springs, treasures, and an honorable abode. It teaches that worldly wealth, status, and power are transient and cannot protect their possessors from God's decree when they persist in arrogance and oppression. Those who seemed secure in their riches and high standing were removed from them in an instant, and the verse invites reflection on the fleeting nature of worldly glory and the need to place trust in God and righteousness rather than in possessions and rank.

translation: Thus it was; and We made the children of Israel inherit them.
interpretation: The verse says that after God destroyed Pharaoh and his people and removed them from their gardens, springs, treasures and noble dwellings, He gave those same blessings as an inheritance to the Children of Israel, the people who had been oppressed and held down. The meaning is that God's power to transfer worldly dominion and wealth is complete. Tyrants who rely on their possessions and might can lose them in an instant, while the believing and patient who were once weak can be made heirs to the earth. The verse teaches that the end of oppression is the downfall of the oppressor and that reward and deliverance come from God's decree, not from human strength.

translation: So they pursued them at sunrise.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:60) recounts that after Moses and the Children of Israel left Egypt by night, Pharaoh and his army set out after them as the sun was rising. The word 'mushriqin' means they entered the time of sunrise, so the pursuit began at dawn. It shows how determined Pharaoh's host was in its tyranny and pride, and it prepares for the miracle that follows, when God parts the sea. The pursuers, confident in their power, march straight toward their own destruction, and the verse teaches that the schemes of oppressors cannot stand against God's decree and that He rescues His faithful servants at the moment of their greatest peril.

translation: And when the two hosts came within sight of each other, the companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are about to be overtaken."
interpretation: This verse shows the human reaction to a moment of extreme danger when all apparent means of escape have disappeared. With the sea ahead of them and Pharaoh's army closing in behind, the Children of Israel judged only by what they could see, and concluded that capture was certain. Their words reveal a gap between outward perception and trust in God's promise. Fear can overwhelm even those who have witnessed miracles when they look only at the apparent causes of events. The verse prepares for the answer that follows, in which Moses affirms that his Lord is with him and will guide him. It teaches that true faith means relying on God's help even when circumstances appear hopeless, because deliverance often comes exactly when human means have run out.

translation: He said: "No, never! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."
interpretation: This is Moses' reply (Qur'an 26:62) when the Children of Israel, trapped between Pharaoh's pursuing army and the sea, cried out, "We are surely overtaken!" Moses rejects their despair with an emphatic "No!" and grounds his certainty in God's presence and guidance rather than in visible circumstances. His words teach that a believer who has done what was commanded, and is following God's directive, should meet moments of apparent hopelessness with firm trust that God's support is near and that He will open a way out, just as He then commanded Moses to strike the sea with his staff and it parted.

translation: Then We inspired Moses: 'Strike the sea with your staff.' And it split, and each part became like a huge towering mountain.
interpretation: When Pharaoh's army closed in on the Children of Israel and they feared they would be overtaken, God responded not through ordinary means but through direct revelation, commanding Moses to strike the sea with his staff. The staff had no power of its own; the miracle came by God's command and will, and Moses' obedience was the occasion for it. The sea parted into twelve great walls of water, each standing firm like a mighty mountain, which shows that God can overturn the laws of nature when He wills. At the moment of utmost despair, deliverance came for the believers, and the very sea that seemed to trap them became their path to safety and the means of their enemies' destruction. The verse teaches that those who trust in God and follow His command will find a way out when every worldly means is exhausted.

translation: And We brought the others near to that place.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:64) belongs to the account of Moses and the Children of Israel at the sea. After Moses and his followers crossed, God drew Pharaoh and his army close to the same spot, drawing them into the parted waters in pursuit. The nearness was not a favor but a divine lure that led them to their doom. Their confidence in chasing the believers brought them to the place where God had prepared their destruction, so the verse shows that God's decree directs even the steps of the oppressors toward their appointed end, and that what seems to be success in pursuit may be the very path to ruin.

translation: And We saved Moses and all those who were with him.
interpretation: The verse shows God's deliverance of the faithful. When Pharaoh's army pursued Moses and the Children of Israel, God parted the sea and brought every one of Moses' followers safely through, not a single believer being lost. The word 'all' stresses the completeness of this rescue, teaching that God's protection reaches those who stay steadfast with His messenger, even when the situation seems hopeless and the enemy seems overwhelming. The salvation of Moses' people stands in contrast with the drowning of their oppressors, and it affirms that God's promise of victory over tyranny is true.

translation: Then We drowned the others.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:66) follows the account of Moses and the Children of Israel being saved when the sea parted. 'The others' are Pharaoh and his army, who pursued them into the sea and were drowned when the waters closed over them. It teaches that God's justice and power prevail over tyranny: the very pursuit by which the oppressors sought to destroy the believers became the cause of their own destruction, while those who trusted in God were delivered. It stands as a sign and a warning to every arrogant power, and as reassurance to the faithful that deliverance comes from God even when all means seem exhausted.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign; but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara after each account of a prophet and his people, teaches that the events narrated, such as the destruction of those who denied their messengers and the deliverance of the believers, contain a clear proof of God's power, justice, and mercy for anyone who reflects. Yet the verse also observes that clear signs do not by themselves produce faith: most people remain heedless or stubborn, and belief depends on an open heart and a willingness to accept the truth. It consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that the denial he meets from his people is a recurring pattern in history, and that the small number of believers does not diminish the truth of the message.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs at the end of several stories of earlier prophets in Surat ash-Shu'ara, pairs two attributes of God to show how He deals with people. As al-'Aziz, He is mighty and victorious, and He overcomes those who deny His messengers and persist in arrogance, as the fates of the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot and others show. As ar-Rahim, He is merciful: He sends messengers, grants respite, accepts repentance, and saves the believers. The verse therefore calls the listener to hold both awe of God's power and hope in His mercy, and to see that the downfall of the deniers is justice from the Almighty, while the rescue of the faithful is mercy from the Most Merciful.

translation: And recite to them the story of Abraham.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet Muhammad to relate to his people the account of Abraham, whom the Arabs claimed as their forefather and model. The command invites them to reflect on how Abraham used reason and sincere devotion to challenge his father's and his people's idol-worship, and how he placed his complete trust in God alone. By recalling this history, the verse holds up the true monotheism of Abraham as a mirror to the Quraysh's own practices, showing that their idolatry contradicts the very heritage they claim, and encouraging the believers to stand firm on the truth even when it opposes ancestral custom.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"
interpretation: The verse describes Abraham's questioning of his father and his people. He asks it not out of ignorance but as a rhetorical challenge, so that they must state their beliefs and hear how weak those beliefs are. By starting with a question rather than an accusation, he leads them to examine their idols with reason, to see that carved objects cannot hear, benefit, or harm, and to recognize that worship belongs to God alone. The verse also shows the proper way to call people to monotheism: begin with respectful but probing dialogue, even toward one's own family, and stay firm in the truth despite social pressure and inherited custom.

translation: They said: 'We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them.'
interpretation: This verse (Surat ash-Shu'ara 26:71) records the reply of Abraham's people when he asked what they worshipped. Their answer shows how entrenched and proud they were in their idolatry. They did not merely say 'we worship idols'; they added that they 'remain constantly devoted' to them, which means that their worship was a continuous, habitual practice and not an occasional one. The verse shows how people can cling to inherited customs and treat objects they made themselves as worthy of lasting devotion. Abraham's question that follows exposes the irrationality of this: idols cannot hear, benefit, or harm. The verse therefore teaches that devotion belongs only to God, and that persisting in a practice out of habit or tradition does not make it right.

translation: He said: 'Do they hear you when you call upon them?'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:72) records Abraham's question to his people as he challenges their worship of idols. By asking whether the idols can even hear their supplicants, he uses rational argument to expose the futility of idolatry: an object that cannot hear a prayer cannot answer it, grant benefit, or ward off harm. The question leads the people to confront the powerlessness of what they worship, and so to recognize that worship belongs only to God, who hears all supplication and responds to it.

translation: Or that they benefit you, or that they harm you?
interpretation: This phrase is the end of a rhetorical question in Surat ash-Shu'ara (26:73), where Abraham challenges his people about the idols they worship: 'Do they hear you when you call upon them, or benefit you, or harm you?' The meaning is that a true object of worship must be able to respond to those who call on it, bring benefit, or avert harm. Since the idols can do none of these things, the verse exposes the irrationality of worshipping them and directs the listener to worship God alone, who hears, benefits, and harms by His will.

translation: They said: "Rather, we found our fathers doing the same."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:74) records the answer of Abraham's people when he asked them whether their idols could hear, benefit, or harm. They could not claim that the idols did any of these things, so they fell back on ancestral precedent as their only justification. The verse condemns blind imitation (taqlid) in matters of belief and worship. A practice does not become true or right because earlier generations followed it, and faith must rest on evidence, reason, and revelation. Tradition is not a valid proof when it contradicts clear guidance.

translation: He said: "Have you then considered what you have been worshipping,"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:75), spoken by Prophet Abraham to his father and his people, is the opening of a challenge to their idolatry. By asking them to reflect on what they have actually been worshipping, he invites them to examine their inherited practices with reason rather than follow them blindly out of tradition. The question prepares for the verses that follow, in which he declares that these objects, along with the ancestors who worshipped them, are enemies to him except the Lord of the worlds, who alone created, guides, feeds, heals, and will resurrect. The lesson is that true worship must be directed to the Creator who has real power to benefit and harm, and that faith should rest on conscious reflection, not on imitation of forefathers.

translation: You and your earliest forefathers.
