interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:76) comes from Prophet Abraham's dialogue with his people about their idol worship. He asks them to consider what they worship, and then points out that their devotion has no better basis than inherited tradition: you and your ancestors alike follow it. The age of a practice and the number of people who have held to it do not make it true. Beliefs must be tested by reason and revelation, not accepted simply because earlier generations held them. The verse also sets up Abraham's next declaration, that these idols are enemies to him except the Lord of the worlds, who alone deserves worship.

translation: For indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: In this verse Abraham, peace be upon him, declares to his people that the idols and false gods they worship, along with everything they have set up besides God, are enemies to him, since he disowns them and refuses to take them as protectors or objects of devotion. He makes an exception only for the Lord of the worlds, the Creator and Sustainer of all existence, who alone deserves worship. The verse teaches pure monotheism: true allegiance and loyalty belong to God alone, and a believer must free himself from all false objects of worship and be wholly devoted to the One who created, guides, feeds, heals and forgives, as Abraham goes on to describe in the following verses.

translation: He who created me, and it is He who guides me.
interpretation: In this verse, spoken by Abraham (peace be upon him) as he addresses his people, he affirms that the One worthy of worship is the One who brought him into existence and continues to guide him. Creation and guidance are bound together: the One who gave him life did not leave him without direction, but guides him to what benefits him in both religion and worldly affairs. This includes guidance of the heart toward faith and truth, and guidance of daily conduct toward what is good. The verse implies that idols, which create nothing and guide no one, cannot be deserving of worship, and that true dependence for direction should be placed solely upon God.

translation: And He who gives me food and gives me drink.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Ibrahim's description of his Lord in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:79). It means that God alone is the true provider of sustenance: every meal and every drink, though it passes through apparent means such as rain, soil, plants, and human labor, ultimately comes from Him, as He created and sustains those means. By naming food and drink, the most basic daily needs, Ibrahim shows that dependence on God is constant and total, and that no created thing can claim a share in providing for life. It also teaches gratitude and trust in God, and implies that a being who provides for his servants in this way is alone worthy of worship, in contrast to idols that can neither feed nor give drink.

translation: And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:80) is part of Prophet Abraham's declaration of faith in God as the sole Provider and Sustainer. Abraham attributes illness to himself, out of courtesy toward God, even though everything occurs by God's decree, while attributing healing directly to God. The deeper lesson is that although physical causes such as medicine and doctors are real and may be used, they are only means, and true healing comes only from God. The believer should therefore maintain humility and gratitude, seek remedies while placing ultimate trust in God, and recognize that both affliction and relief are under His care and mercy.

translation: And [He is] the One who will cause me to die and then bring me back to life.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Abraham's declaration of his Lord's attributes (Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:81). It teaches that death is not an absolute end but a transition within God's control. Just as God alone gave life, He alone decrees when it ends and then resurrects human beings for accountability. Abraham mentions this as proof that only the Creator who governs life, death and resurrection deserves worship, and it expresses his calm trust that his death and return are in the hands of a merciful Lord, which should free the believer from fear of death and orient him toward the Hereafter.

translation: And who, I hope, will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: In this verse, Abraham (peace be upon him) is speaking of his Lord and expressing hope in His forgiveness. Although prophets are protected from major sins, Abraham calls his lapses 'khati'ati' out of humility and awareness of God's majesty, since even the best of people fall short of the gratitude and worship that God deserves. He uses the word 'hope' (atma'u) rather than certainty because forgiveness is God's prerogative alone and no one can claim it as a right over Him; it is a gift of His grace. The verse teaches that a believer should keep his heart between fear and hope, never presuming on his deeds, and should turn to God in lowliness, trusting in His mercy on the day when every soul is repaid for what it did.

translation: My Lord, grant me judgment and wisdom, and join me with the righteous.
interpretation: This is the prayer of Abraham (peace be upon him) in Surat al-Shu'ara' (26:83). In it he asks God for hukm, meaning sound wisdom, knowledge, and right judgment by which he can know God's truth and act upon it, and he asks to be counted among the righteous, those who obey God and are granted nearness to Him in this life and the next. The prayer teaches that true success lies in beginning with divine guidance and wisdom rather than worldly status, and in hoping to end among the righteous. Even a prophet seeks God's gift of wisdom and the company of the righteous, showing that no one is self-sufficient in guidance and that the believer's highest aspiration is a good end in the company of God's chosen servants.

translation: And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations.
interpretation: This is a supplication of Prophet Abraham (peace be upon him), in which he asks God to let his name be remembered with honor and praise by the generations that come after him. The 'tongue of truth' means a sincere, truthful reputation: people speak well of him because of his real faith and righteous deeds, not because of flattery or falsehood. His prayer was answered, as Jews, Christians, and Muslims all revere him, and Muslims invoke blessings upon him in every prayer. The verse teaches that a believer may rightly seek a lasting good legacy, so long as the aim is for truth and guidance to continue through him, not for pride or self-glorification.

translation: And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:85) is part of Prophet Ibrahim's supplication. By asking to be among the 'inheritors' of the Garden of Bliss, he shows that Paradise is a gift from God, not something earned by deeds alone, just as an inheritance is received rather than purchased. The word 'inheritance' also suggests that the believers receive Paradise as their lasting, secure possession, one that cannot be taken away. It teaches that even the greatest of the prophets turn to God in humble need, asking for the highest reward, which is eternal felicity in the Hereafter, and that a believer should hold this as the ultimate goal in prayer above worldly aims.

translation: And forgive my father; indeed, he was among those who have gone astray.
interpretation: This is Abraham's supplication in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:86), made out of filial compassion and hope that his father might be guided and so receive forgiveness. Since forgiveness of shirk is possible only through repentance and faith, the prayer is best understood as a plea that God grant his father guidance and repentance during his lifetime. Later, when it became clear that his father was a persistent enemy of God, Abraham disassociated himself from him (9:114). The verse shows that a prophet's love for his family does not conflict with submission to God's judgment, and that the prayer was conditional upon the father's turning to the truth.

translation: And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Abraham (peace be upon him) in Surat ash-Shu'ara (26:87). It expresses his awareness that on the Day of Resurrection the only true humiliation is to be exposed, rejected, or found wanting before God. Although he is a prophet, he does not rely on his rank or deeds, but humbly asks God to shield him from shame on the Day when every person's hidden record is revealed and all of creation is gathered. The verse teaches that a believer should fear the disgrace of the Hereafter more than any worldly disgrace, and should seek God's protection and mercy, since salvation depends on God's grace and not on one's own standing.

translation: The Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:88) describes the Day of Judgment, when the things people most rely on in this world for security, status, and protection, namely money and offspring, will have no power to save a person from God's reckoning. The next verse completes the thought: only the one who comes to God with a sound heart will be saved. The meaning is that true success lies not in worldly possessions or family strength but in the purity of one's heart, in sincere faith, and in freedom from shirk, hypocrisy, and arrogance. A person should therefore not let wealth and children distract them from preparing for the Hereafter.

translation: Except for him who comes to God with a sound heart.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:89) says that on the Day of Judgment, wealth and children will be of no benefit, and the only one who is saved is the person who meets God with a heart free from disease. A sound heart is one purified of polytheism, doubt, hypocrisy, pride, envy, and attachment to worldly things over God. It is wholly devoted to God, sincere in faith, and submissive to His command. What ultimately matters before God is the inner state of one's heart, which gives worth to one's deeds, and not outward status or possessions.

translation: And Paradise will be brought near to the righteous.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when Paradise will be made close and visible to those who were mindful of God, so that they can see their reward before entering it. Its being brought near, rather than the righteous having to strive toward it, expresses honor and welcome, and reassures believers that the effort and restraint of their worldly lives were worthwhile. It also serves as a warning and a motivation: the same scene confronts the misguided with what they lost, urging people in this life to cultivate God-consciousness (taqwa) so that on that Day Paradise will be near to them.

translation: And Hellfire will be brought into full view for those who went astray.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:91) describes the Day of Judgment, when Hell will be openly displayed before those who chose misguidance and rejected the truth. Its sudden, unveiled appearance is meant to heighten their dread and regret, since they can no longer deny or ignore the reality of the warnings they once dismissed. The contrast with the preceding verse, in which Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, shows that each group sees its final destination before entering it, so that the believers' joy and the misguided's anguish begin at the moment of recognition. The verse thus serves as a reminder that one's choices in this life determine which of the two scenes one will face.

translation: And it will be said to them: 'Where are those you used to worship?'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the idolaters will be rebuked and shamed with a question that exposes the emptiness of their false worship. The idols and false deities they once trusted, hoping for intercession and help, are nowhere to be found and can neither aid nor protect them. The question is not a request for information but a rhetorical reproach, showing that anything worshipped besides God is powerless and that reliance on it ends in loss and regret.

translation: "Besides Allah? Can they help you, or can they help themselves?" (Qur'an 26:93)
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical question that exposes the futility of worshipping anything other than God. Idols and false deities, and by extension anything people rely on in place of God, have no power to benefit their devotees by giving them aid or protection, and they cannot even defend themselves from harm. The question is put to the idolaters on the Day of Judgment, when their false gods are cast into the Fire with them. It shows that only God has real power to help and save, so putting trust in anything else is an error that ends in loss.

translation: Then they will be hurled into it (Hell), they and the deviators.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:94) describes the fate of those who worshipped false gods and the misguided who led them astray. The Arabic 'kubkibu' conveys being thrown headlong, one tumbling over another, which depicts the humiliation and helplessness of the damned as they are cast into the Fire. The 'ghawun' are the deviators who chose error over guidance, and the verse shows that both the leaders in misguidance and their followers share the same punishment, since each bears responsibility for abandoning the truth when it was made clear. It warns that no one can shield another from divine justice, and that falsehood, whether embraced or promoted, leads to ruin.

translation: And all the hosts of Iblis together.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:95), describes the fate of the misguided in Hell: not only those who went astray are cast into the Fire, but also the armies of Iblis, meaning all those who followed and served his cause, whether jinn or humans, and every ally and helper in his work of seduction. The word 'all together' stresses that none will escape, no follower will be spared, and none can shield another. It teaches that obeying Satan's whispers and taking part in his call to disbelief and disobedience makes one a soldier in his army, and that such allegiance leads to shared punishment on the Day of Judgment, so a believer must guard against becoming, even unknowingly, a tool of evil.

translation: They will say, while they dispute therein with one another:
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:96) depicts the misguided in Hell, quarrelling with their false gods and with those who led them astray. Their dispute shows that the bonds of falsehood which united them in the world, such as shared idolatry, blind imitation and mutual support, dissolve on the Day of Judgment. Each party then blames the other, and the verses that follow give their confession: they admit they were in manifest error when they equated their idols with the Lord of the worlds. The lesson is that following falsehood or misleading leaders brings only regret, that no one can bear another's responsibility, and that each person must base his belief on truth and not on social conformity.

translation: By Allah, we were indeed in manifest error,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:97) is spoken by the people of Hell as they quarrel with their false gods and misleaders. They confess that their error was plain and not hidden: they had the signs and the warnings of the messengers, yet they chose to follow falsehood. Their oath by Allah shows the weight of their regret and that they now see the truth. The 'error' lay in equating idols and false authorities with the Lord of the worlds (as the next verse says, 'when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds'). The verse teaches that associating partners with God is a clear and self-evident misguidance, and that recognizing it only in the Hereafter, when repentance is no longer accepted, is of no benefit.

translation: When we held you equal with the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (26:98) describes the words of the people of Hellfire, who will confess to their error as they speak to the false deities they worshipped. They admit that they were clearly misguided because they placed created beings, idols, and false gods on the same level as God, the Lord of all worlds, by giving them love, reverence, and worship that belong to God alone. The verse teaches that associating partners with God is a grave injustice, since nothing in creation can be equal or comparable to the Creator and Sustainer of all that exists. The regret expressed here warns people in this life to devote worship purely to God before the Day when such admissions come too late.

translation: And none misled us except the criminals.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:99) is spoken by the people of Hell on the Day of Judgment, as they lament their fate. They place the blame for their misguidance on the 'mujrimun', the wrongdoers who led them astray, whether leaders, elders, or corrupt companions who invited them to disbelief and idol worship and made falsehood seem attractive. Yet the verse also carries a deeper lesson: following others blindly without using one's own reason and heeding the guidance of the prophets is no excuse before God. Each soul remains accountable for its choices, and the confession exposes the regret of those who preferred the path of the sinful over the path of truth, a regret that comes too late to benefit them.

translation: So now we have no intercessors,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:100) is spoken by the people of Hell as they realize their helplessness on the Day of Judgment. In the world they relied on false gods, leaders, and worldly ties, imagining these would plead for them. Now they see that no one can intercede on behalf of those who persisted in disbelief and wrongdoing, since intercession is only by God's permission and only for those with whom He is pleased. Their cry expresses regret and the collapse of every false hope, and it warns the reader not to depend on anything besides sincere faith and righteous deeds, which alone benefit a person on that Day.

translation: Nor any close friend.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:101), spoken by the people of Hell, expresses the utter helplessness of the Day of Judgment. In the world, people rely on intercessors and close friends who will stand by them and defend them in times of hardship. On that Day, the wrongdoers realize that no worldly bond, however intimate, can avail them: no friend will show concern, offer help, or share their burden. The verse teaches that the only lasting support on that Day is faith and righteous deeds, and that friendships built on disobedience turn into regret and enmity, so a person should choose companions who lead toward God and prepare for the Hereafter.

translation: If only we had one more return (to the worldly life), then we would be among the believers.
interpretation: This verse is from Surat al-Shu'ara' (26:102), and it describes the cry of regret of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. When they face the reality they denied, they wish they could go back to the world for another chance, promising that they would then believe. Their wish exposes that faith is only of benefit when it is chosen freely in this life, while the unseen is still unseen. Once the truth becomes plain and the Hereafter is witnessed, belief no longer counts as a test and cannot be accepted. The verse warns people to use the time they have now for faith and righteous action, because there will be no return to correct what was neglected.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign; but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara after each account of a prophet and his people, teaches that the events narrated are clear signs of God's power, justice, and mercy for anyone who reflects. The destruction of the deniers and the deliverance of the believers show that truth ultimately prevails. Yet the verse also notes a sobering reality: clear evidence alone does not guarantee faith, because most people turn away through arrogance, heedlessness, or attachment to ancestral custom. Belief depends on an open heart that is willing to reflect and submit, not merely on the presence of proofs. This also consoles the Prophet, reminding him that the small number of believers does not diminish the truth of his message.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, repeated as a refrain after the accounts of the earlier prophets in Surat al-Shu'ara', pairs two attributes of God to show how He deals with people. As al-'Aziz, He is overwhelmingly powerful and able to destroy those who persistently deny the truth and reject His messengers, as He destroyed the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others. As al-Rahim, He is merciful in delaying punishment, sending warners, and saving the believers. The verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad and the faithful that they rely on a Lord whose might guarantees the vindication of truth and whose mercy embraces those who turn to Him. It also warns the deniers that His patience is not weakness, so they should return to Him before His might overtakes them.

translation: The people of Noah denied the messengers.
interpretation: By rejecting Noah, his people were in effect rejecting all the messengers, because every prophet brings the same essential message of God's oneness and the call to righteousness. Denying one messenger therefore amounts to denying the whole chain of prophethood. The verse points out that disbelief is a matter of arrogance and stubbornness rather than a lack of evidence, and it consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that rejection is a recurring pattern in the history of nations and that the truth ultimately prevails.

translation: When their brother Noah said to them: 'Will you not fear God?'
interpretation: Noah is called 'their brother' because he came from their own people, sharing their lineage and language, which shows that the prophet's call was not that of an outsider but of a trusted and compassionate kinsman who sought their good. His opening question, 'Will you not be mindful of God and guard yourselves against His displeasure?', is a gentle rebuke and invitation rather than a threat. It teaches that the foundation of every prophetic message is taqwa: awareness of God that restrains a person from idolatry and wrongdoing, and that a caller to truth should begin by awakening the conscience of his listeners with tenderness and reason.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: These words, repeated by several prophets such as Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb in Surat ash-Shu'ara', affirm that a prophet's authority rests on two pillars: that he is sent by God and not self-appointed, and that he is utterly reliable in conveying the message. The prophet is a faithful trustee of revelation, who neither adds to it, withholds any part of it, nor alters it for personal gain or to please his people. By describing himself as 'amin', he appeals to the reputation for honesty his people already knew in him, inviting them to reason that someone who never lied about people would not lie about God. This claim of trustworthiness is the basis on which he then calls them to fear God and obey him, showing that faith begins with trust in the integrity of the one who delivers the message.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This verse is the repeated call of the prophets to their peoples (for example Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb, and Jesus), joining two inseparable duties: taqwa and obedience to the messenger. Taqwa means being conscious of God and guarding oneself against His displeasure, and it is the inner foundation of faith. Obedience to the messenger is how that God-consciousness is expressed in practice, because the prophet conveys God's guidance and models how to live by it. The verse teaches that reverence for God is not complete as a private feeling alone, and that it must be shown by following the guidance of those He sent. Following the messenger is, in turn, a way of obeying God Himself, so true piety lies in uniting heartfelt awareness of God with faithful action according to His revealed way.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The prophet's refusal of any worldly wage shows that his call is sincere and free from personal gain. A person who asks for no money or status for conveying guidance cannot be accused of seeking profit or power, so his message deserves to be weighed on its truth alone. By placing his reward with God, the Lord of all the worlds, he shows that true service to faith is done for God's sake, and that those who call others to the truth should rely on God's recompense rather than on people's gratitude or payment.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, repeated by several prophets to their peoples (such as Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb), links reverence for God with obedience to His messenger. Taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that leads one to avoid what displeases Him, is not complete in the abstract. It is shown in practice by following the guidance God sent through His prophet. The messenger is not calling people to himself but to God, so obeying him is a way of obeying God. The verse teaches that true faith requires both inner God-consciousness and outward submission to divine guidance.

translation: They said, "Shall we believe in you when it is the lowliest who follow you?"
interpretation: This is the response of Noah's arrogant chieftains (Qur'an 26:111). They refuse the message not because of any flaw in its content but because of who accepted it. They measure truth by social rank and wealth rather than by evidence, treating the poor and humble believers as proof that the message was unworthy. Their pride in status blocks them from submitting to God's guidance, and the verse shows that truth is not determined by the worldly standing of its followers. The followers' sincerity and humility are what make them honorable in God's sight, while the elite's contempt exposes their own spiritual poverty.

translation: He said, "And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?" (Qur'an 26:112)
interpretation: This is Prophet Noah's reply when his people's elite objected that only the lowliest people had followed him. He does not judge people by their social rank or by their past work and standing, and he does not claim knowledge of their hidden intentions or the sincerity of their faith. His task is to convey the message, while the reckoning of hearts and deeds belongs to God alone, as the next verse says: "Their account is only upon my Lord, if you but knew." The verse teaches that a person's worth lies in faith and sincerity rather than in status, wealth, or profession. It also teaches that no one may presume to judge what is inside another's heart, and that a caller to God must accept every sincere believer without discrimination.

translation: Their reckoning is only with my Lord, if you were aware.
interpretation: This verse, from Noah's reply to his people (Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:113), teaches that judging people's inner states, sincerity, and hidden deeds is not the task of any human being but belongs to God alone. When the nobles scorned Noah's followers as lowly people and questioned the genuineness of their faith and the worth of their work, Noah answered that he is responsible only for what is outwardly apparent and for conveying the message, while their hearts and the true account of their actions are known to God, who will hold them to account. The words 'if you were aware' rebuke the disbelievers for their lack of perception: had they truly understood, they would have refrained from belittling believers on the basis of social status or profession and from presuming to judge what lies beyond their knowledge.

translation: And I am not one to drive away the believers.
interpretation: This is Prophet Noah's reply to his people, who demanded that he dismiss his poor and humble followers before they would listen to him. By refusing, Noah affirms that faith, not wealth or social rank, determines a person's worth and standing before God. A messenger of God cannot reject sincere believers to win over the arrogant. The verse teaches that the call to truth must be open to everyone equally, and that honoring believers is a matter of principle that cannot be bargained away for the approval of the powerful.

translation: I am nothing but a clear warner.
interpretation: The Prophet disclaims any role beyond conveying God's warning plainly and unmistakably. He does not claim to hold knowledge of the unseen, to control divine punishment, or to have power to compel belief. His duty is to make the message clear, warning people of the consequences of rejecting truth and persisting in error, while guidance and judgment rest with God alone. By describing himself as 'clear' (mubin), the verse stresses that the warning leaves no ambiguity and no excuse, so responsibility for accepting or rejecting it falls on those who hear it.

translation: They said: "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those who are stoned."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:116) shows how Noah's people answered his patient call to monotheism and righteousness with threats instead of reasoning. Having no argument to refute his message, they resorted to intimidation, threatening to stone him to death if he did not stop preaching. Their words reveal the typical response of arrogant establishments to reformers: when truth cannot be answered with evidence, those who hold power use force and silencing. It also consoles the Prophet Muhammad and later believers by showing that hostility and threats have always met the prophets, and that the prophets' steadfastness in the face of them is part of the divine pattern that ends with the vindication of truth and the destruction of the oppressors.

translation: He said, "My Lord, indeed my people have denied me."
interpretation: This verse, from the account of Prophet Noah (Nuh) in Surat ash-Shu'ara (26:117), shows a prophet turning to God in complaint and appeal after long, patient calling to his people. Noah does not curse them out of anger; he lays the reality of their rejection before his Lord, the One who knows it already, as a plea for divine judgment. The address 'My Lord' (Rabb) expresses intimacy and reliance, and his words acknowledge that the rejection of the message is in truth a rejection of God's guidance, not only of him personally. The verse teaches that when a believer has exhausted every means of calling people to truth and met only denial, the proper course is to entrust the matter to God, who will decide between the truthful and those who deny, as the following verses confirm by asking for a decisive judgment and for the deliverance of Noah and the believers with him.

translation: So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment, and save me and those who are with me of the believers.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Noah (Nuh) after his long call went unheeded and his people persisted in denial. The word 'fatḥ' here means a decisive ruling that settles the dispute, so he asks God to be the arbiter between the truth he brought and the falsehood they clung to. In practice, this judgment means the destruction of the deniers and the vindication of the believers. He then asks for deliverance for himself and his faithful followers, showing that the believers' salvation is bound to God's decisive judgment, and that after exhausting every means of warning, the prophet entrusts the outcome entirely to God, who answered by the flood and saved those in the ark.

translation: So We saved him and those with him in the laden ark.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:119) shows that God's deliverance comes to those who hold to faith and obey His command. After his people persisted in denying him, Noah and the believers who followed him were rescued in the ship, which was filled with believers and with pairs of living creatures, while the rest were drowned. Salvation depended on faith and trust in God, not on numbers, status, or lineage. The ark is a sign of God's mercy toward the righteous and of His justice toward those who reject the truth, and it reminds readers that perseverance in the face of ridicule and opposition ends in vindication from God.

translation: Then We drowned the others.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 26:66) describes the end of Pharaoh and his army. After God saved Moses and those with him by parting the sea, the pursuers followed them into it and the waters closed over them. The word 'the others' marks a clear separation between the believers who were delivered and the oppressors who were destroyed. The lesson is that God's deliverance of the righteous and His punishment of the arrogant come together in one event, and that worldly power and numbers offer no protection against His decree. It is also a source of reassurance for believers facing tyranny, since the tyrant's strength can be undone in a moment.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse closes the account of a people or messenger's story in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, where it recurs as a refrain. It teaches that the events just narrated, such as God's power in creation, His rescue of the righteous, and His punishment of those who denied, are clear evidence of His existence, might, and mercy for anyone who reflects. The failure of most people to believe does not come from any lack of proof. It comes from stubbornness, arrogance, and heedlessness, since signs benefit only those whose hearts are open to them. The verse also consoles the Prophet Muhammad, who should not be distressed by the denial of the majority, because truth is not measured by the number of its followers and belief has always been the path of a minority.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is truly the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, repeated at the end of several stories of earlier prophets in Surat ash-Shu'ara', teaches that God's might and mercy work together. His might (al-'Aziz) is shown in how He overcame those who denied His messengers and punished them after giving them time and warnings. His mercy (ar-Rahim) is shown in how He rescued the believers, sent guidance, and delayed punishment so people could repent. The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad and the believers: those who persist in denial will not escape God's power, and those who stay faithful can trust in His compassion and protection.

translation: The people of 'Ad denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 26:123) teaches that rejecting a single prophet is in effect rejecting all prophets, since every messenger brought the same essential message of worshipping God alone and fearing Him. The people of 'Ad denied Hud, yet the Qur'an says they denied 'the messengers' in the plural because the call to true monotheism and righteousness is one and the same across all prophets. Their denial was therefore not a rejection of one man but of the entire chain of divine guidance, and it explains why the consequence they faced was severe. The verse serves as a warning to later generations that arrogance, reliance on worldly strength, and refusal to heed revelation lead to ruin.

translation: When their brother Hud said to them: "Will you not fear God?"
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 26:124) shows the way prophets call their people. Hud is described as 'their brother', meaning he belonged to the people of 'Ad by lineage, was known to them and was sincere toward them, not an outsider. His opening question, 'Will you not be mindful of God?', is a gentle appeal to conscience. It does not begin with threats or condemnation. It invites them to reflect on their idolatry, arrogance and corruption, and to adopt taqwa, awareness of God that leads to obedience, as the basis for their reform. The verse teaches that sound guidance begins with compassion, kinship and an appeal to reverence for God before moving to further argument.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The prophet declares his credentials to his people: he is a messenger sent by God, and he is trustworthy, meaning he will convey the revelation exactly as it was given, without adding to it, omitting from it, or altering it for personal gain. By stressing his amanah (trustworthiness), he appeals to the people's own long experience of his honesty, so that they have no grounds to doubt either his character or his message. The verse thus establishes that the authority of his call rests on divine commission and on his proven integrity, and it invites the people to respond with piety and obedience.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This verse, repeated by several prophets to their peoples (such as Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb), joins two obligations: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that makes a person guard against His displeasure, and obedience to the messenger who conveys His guidance. The messenger is not asking for personal allegiance. His authority comes from being God's appointed envoy, so obeying him is a practical way of obeying God. The verse teaches that reverence for God stays incomplete unless it shows itself in following the guidance He sent through His prophets, and that true faith consists of inner God-consciousness together with outward obedience.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The prophet's refusal of any material gain shows that his call is sincere and free of self-interest. A person who seeks wealth or status through preaching invites suspicion, but one who asks for nothing gives people no reason to doubt his motives, so they can weigh his message on its truth alone. By placing his reward with God, the Lord of all worlds, he also points out that guidance is a trust to be carried out for God's sake, and that God's recompense is greater and more lasting than anything people could give. The verse thus sets a standard for all who call to God: their integrity is shown by their selflessness, and their reliance rests on God rather than on people.

translation: Do you build on every high place a monument, in vain amusement?
interpretation: This verse, from the words of the Prophet Hud to the people of 'Ad, rebukes them for raising lofty landmarks and towers on every hilltop, not out of need or benefit but for vanity, boasting, and idle display. It condemns the squandering of wealth and effort on showy, purposeless construction while neglecting worship of God, gratitude for His blessings, and care for the needy. The deeper lesson is that power and prosperity become blameworthy when they are spent on pride and frivolity rather than on goodness and the remembrance of the Creator.

translation: And you take for yourselves great fortresses and buildings, hoping that you will live forever.
interpretation: This verse, part of the admonition of the Prophet Hud to the people of 'Ad (Surah ash-Shu'ara 26:129), rebukes them for building massive, elaborate structures and water works out of a vain hope of permanence. Their construction was not for need or benefit, but stemmed from pride and an attachment to worldly life, as if their strongholds could shield them from death and make them immortal. The deeper lesson is that no worldly edifice or power can defy death or God's decree, so a person should not invest all effort into transient things while neglecting accountability before God and the everlasting life of the Hereafter.

translation: And when you seize [someone], you seize [them] as tyrants.
interpretation: In this verse (Qur'an 26:130), the Prophet Hud rebukes the people of 'Ad for their harshness and cruelty. It means that when they punished or attacked others, they did so without mercy, restraint, or justice, acting as arrogant oppressors who relied on their might. The verse condemns the abuse of power: strength is not itself blameworthy, but wielding it with brutality and haughtiness, rather than with fairness and compassion, is a moral failing that shows forgetfulness of God, to whom all power belongs, and which invites His punishment.

translation: So fear God and obey me.
interpretation: This verse is a recurring call of the prophets to their peoples (for example Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb and Jesus). It joins taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that makes a person guard against His displeasure, with obedience to the messenger. The prophet's authority is not personal. He is a trustworthy conveyor of God's guidance, so obeying him is the practical expression of fearing God. Reverence for God stays empty unless it is turned into following the revealed way, and following the messenger means following what God commanded through him. The verse therefore ties inner God-consciousness to outward obedience, and presents both as the sound response to the prophetic message.

translation: And fear Him who has provided you with all that you know.
interpretation: This verse, from the speech of the Prophet Hud to his people of 'Ad (Surah ash-Shu'ara 26:132), calls them to taqwa, consciousness of God and awe of Him, by reminding them of His favors. The blessings they themselves acknowledge, such as livestock, children, gardens, and springs (mentioned in the verses that follow), came from God alone. Gratitude for these favors should lead to obedience and reverence, not arrogance, wasteful display, or idolatry. Because the favors are known to them, they have no excuse for ingratitude and should turn to the One who gave them.

translation: He has aided you with livestock and children.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Hud's admonition to his people, the people of 'Ad (Qur'an 26:132-134). It reminds them that their prosperity, including the livestock that sustains them and the children who strengthen their families and secure their future, is not self-made but a gift from God. The implied meaning is that such favors call for gratitude and obedience to God and His messenger, not arrogance or denial. Recalling these blessings is meant to awaken their conscience and show that the One who gave them wealth and offspring is the One they should fear and worship.

translation: And gardens and springs.
interpretation: This phrase, from the account of Pharaoh's people in Surat ash-Shu'ara (26:57) and similarly in Surat ad-Dukhan (44:25-26), shows that God caused them to leave behind gardens, springs, treasures and noble dwellings. Its meaning is that worldly abundance and luxury, however lush and flowing, are not lasting and offer no protection from God's judgment when people turn to arrogance and wrongdoing. Those who rely on their wealth and comfort lose it all in a moment, so blessings are meant to be met with gratitude and obedience, not with tyranny and denial.

translation: Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a Great Day.
interpretation: These are the words of a prophet, as in Noah's address to his people (7:59, 46:21), warning them out of compassion and concern rather than hostility. The phrase shows that his call to worship God alone is not driven by self-interest; he fears that their persistence in disbelief and idolatry will bring them divine punishment on the Day of Judgment, whose gravity is such that it is called 'great'. The verse teaches that the true caller to God combines clear warning with sincere care for the people he addresses, and that rejecting the message has consequences that are real and severe.

translation: They said: 'It is all the same to us whether you admonish us or are not among those who admonish.'
interpretation: This is the reply of the people of Hud (Qur'an 26:136) when he called them to worship God alone and warned them of His punishment. Their words show a stubborn, closed-minded hardness of heart: they do not even treat his counsel as something to weigh and reject on its merits, but declare it irrelevant, whether he speaks or stays silent. Such arrogance is a sign of a heart that has sealed itself against guidance, because a person who has resolved in advance not to listen can no longer benefit from any warning or evidence, however clear. The verse teaches that the greatest barrier to guidance is not lack of proof but the willful refusal to be moved by it, and that this refusal leads people to ruin, as it did for 'Ad.

translation: This is nothing but the custom of the former peoples. (Another reading: 'khuluq' – this is nothing but the invention/habit of the ancients.)
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 26:137) records the response of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud. They dismiss his warnings of divine punishment and his call to worship God alone as nothing more than the inherited habits, myths, and fabrications of earlier generations, just as people had always spoken and behaved. By appealing to ancestral tradition, they reject the idea that his message is a fresh revelation from God and refuse to reflect on its truth. The verse shows how arrogance and attachment to inherited custom can harden hearts against guidance, and it warns that dismissing the message as 'old talk' leads to the same fate that befell earlier deniers.

translation: And we are not going to be punished.
interpretation: This is the claim of the deniers of the Hereafter, spoken in Surat al-Shu'ara' (26:138) by the people of 'Ad, who answered the Prophet Hud's warning by saying that they would not be punished. It shows a heart hardened by worldly comfort, wealth, and strength, so that it takes the present security as proof of permanent safety and dismisses divine warning as groundless. The verse teaches that rejecting accountability does not remove it. Their confidence rested on illusion rather than knowledge, and their later destruction showed that God's promise holds whether or not people believe it. It warns against mistaking worldly prosperity for divine approval, and it calls believers to take warnings seriously and to live with awareness of answerability before God.

translation: But they denied him, so We destroyed them. Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting a messenger after clear warning brings divine punishment, as happened to earlier peoples such as the people of Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb, and that the story of their destruction is a lasting lesson for later generations. Yet the evidence of history is not enough to guide people whose hearts are closed by arrogance, stubbornness, and attachment to worldly interests, so most of them still fail to believe. Faith depends on a receptive heart and sincere reflection, not merely on the presence of signs, and the believers who heed such lessons are always a minority.

translation: And indeed, your Lord — He is truly the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, repeated as a refrain after the accounts of earlier prophets and their peoples in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, teaches that God's might and mercy operate together. His 'izzah is seen in how He overcame those who denied the messengers and persisted in arrogance, so that no power could shield them from His decree. His mercy is seen in the respite He gave them, the messengers He sent to warn them, and the deliverance He granted to the believers. The verse reassures the Prophet and the faithful that the oppressed will not be abandoned, and warns the deniers that mercy delayed is not mercy denied to the wrongdoers' advantage; the door of repentance stays open until God's just decree arrives.

translation: The people of Thamud denied the messengers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:141) teaches that rejecting a single prophet is, in essence, rejecting every prophet, because all messengers bring the same core message of worshipping God alone and living righteously. Thamud denied their messenger Salih, yet the Qur'an says they denied 'the messengers' in the plural, since the truth Salih conveyed was the same truth conveyed by all who came before and after him. Their denial was therefore not just a personal rejection of one man but a rejection of divine guidance itself, which explains why they faced the consequences that followed. The verse also serves as a warning to later generations that arrogance and stubborn disbelief in the face of clear signs lead to ruin, and it consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that earlier messengers were also rejected by their peoples.

translation: When their brother Salih said to them: 'Will you not be mindful of God and fear Him?'
interpretation: The verse shows that a prophet's call begins with an appeal to God-consciousness (taqwa), the foundation of all faith and righteous conduct. By calling Salih 'their brother,' the Qur'an stresses that he came from among the people of Thamud, shared their lineage and language, and was known to them, so his warning carried sincerity and concern for their good rather than hostility. His question 'Will you not fear God?' is a gentle but pointed rebuke that invites them to reflect on their arrogance, idol-worship, and corruption, and to recognize that accountability before their Creator is the first step toward reform.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The verse, repeated by several prophets (Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb) to their peoples, is a declaration of the messenger's credibility. By calling himself 'amin' (trustworthy), the prophet appeals to his known record of honesty among his people: he has never lied or betrayed a trust, so he will not distort or add to what God has entrusted to him. The message is therefore faithfully delivered as received, without personal gain or alteration, which makes rejecting it unreasonable. It also establishes that a bearer of revelation must be morally upright, since the integrity of the messenger underpins the people's confidence in the truth of the message.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This verse, which the Qur'an places on the lips of several prophets such as Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb when they addressed their peoples, joins two duties that depend on each other. Taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that makes a person guard against His displeasure, is the inner foundation of faith. Obedience to the messenger is how that awareness is put into practice, because the messenger conveys God's guidance and shows how to live by it. The prophet is not asking for obedience to himself as a person. He asks it as God's appointed envoy, so obeying him is a way of obeying God. The verse teaches that reverence for God is incomplete without following the guidance He sent, and that true obedience to the messenger comes from a heart that fears and honors its Creator.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The prophet who repeats this statement, as in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, shows that his call is free of any worldly motive. Because he asks his people for no wages, wealth, or status, they cannot accuse him of seeking personal gain, and his sincerity becomes a sign of the truth of his message. By placing his reward with the Lord of the worlds, he teaches that conveying guidance is an act of devotion done for God alone, and that those who call to the truth should rely on God's recompense, not on people's payment or approval.

translation: Will you be left secure in what is here, in gardens and springs, and fields and palm trees with tender spadices?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:146) is the prophet Salih's rebuke to the people of Thamud. He asks whether they imagine that the blessings they enjoy, their security, gardens, springs, crops and palms, will last forever without accountability. It warns that worldly comfort is a trust and a test, not a permanent guarantee. Ingratitude, arrogance and disobedience to God can bring those blessings to an end. The people should therefore use their prosperity with gratitude, obey God, and be mindful of the Hereafter instead of being lulled into false security.

translation: Amid gardens and springs.
interpretation: This phrase describes the reward of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) in the Hereafter, as in Surat al-Hijr (15:45) and Surat al-Dhariyat (51:15). It portrays their final abode as a place of lasting comfort, abundance and tranquility, where gardens and flowing springs symbolize God's generosity and the fulfillment of every need and desire. The reward is the fitting outcome of their piety and good deeds in this world, in contrast to the torment prepared for the deniers.

translation: And [amid] crops and palm trees whose spathes are fine and delicate.
interpretation: This verse, part of Prophet Salih's address to the people of Thamud (Qur'an 26:148), reminds them of the abundant blessings God had granted them: fertile fields and date palms whose clusters were tender, soft, and heavily laden. The word 'hadim' conveys fruit so ripe and plentiful that it is delicate and pressed together. Salih points to this bounty to show that their security and prosperity came from God, not from their own power, and to call them to gratitude, piety, and obedience rather than arrogance and corruption. The blessings are meant to be a cause for thankfulness, and he warns that ingratitude and rejection of the message place those blessings at risk.

translation: And you carve out houses from the mountains, skillfully and with great exuberance.
interpretation: This verse is part of the prophet Salih's address to the people of Thamud, reminding them of God's favors. Their ability to hew dwellings from solid rock was a gift of strength, skill, and prosperity, yet they used it with arrogance and heedless pride rather than gratitude. The word 'farihin' conveys both skill and a boastful, self-satisfied joy, suggesting that blessings become a trial when enjoyed in forgetfulness of the Giver. The verse calls believers to recognize their abilities and achievements as trusts from God, to respond with thankfulness, humility, and obedience, and not to let worldly accomplishment breed arrogance or corruption.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This verse is a call made by the prophets to their peoples (as in the accounts of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb, and Jesus). It joins two duties: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that leads a person to avoid what displeases Him, and obedience to the messenger, who conveys God's guidance. Taqwa is the inner root of faith, and obeying the messenger is its outward expression, because the messenger shows in practice how God's commands are to be followed. A person cannot claim to fear God while disregarding the guidance He sent through His messenger, and obeying the messenger is in effect obeying God. The verse therefore presents reverence and obedience as inseparable, and as the basis for a righteous life and for deliverance from God's displeasure.

translation: And do not obey the command of the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:151) is part of Prophet Salih's address to his people of Thamud, urging them to fear God and obey him. The 'musrifin' are those who exceed all bounds in disobedience, arrogance, corruption, and indulgence, whether leaders or influential elites who lead others astray. The verse teaches that obedience belongs to God and His messenger alone, and that following those who violate moral and divine limits makes one complicit in their corruption. It calls believers to use their own moral judgment and not follow the powerful or the majority into wrongdoing, since the consequence of such obedience is the same ruin that befalls the transgressors themselves.

translation: Those who cause corruption in the land and do not set things right.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:152) describes the character of the extravagant transgressors whom people are warned not to obey. Their defining fault is that their corruption is total and unmixed with any reform: their influence, whether through oppression, injustice, idolatry, or the abuse of wealth and power, spreads disorder in society and the earth, and they never contribute anything to its betterment. The phrase 'and do not set things right' stresses that these are not people who err occasionally and then repent or repair, but people whose conduct is consistently destructive. The lesson is that those who lead others into harm should not be followed, and that true righteousness means actively promoting good and justice, not merely refraining from some evils.

translation: They said: 'You are only one of those who are bewitched.'
interpretation: This verse (26:153, said by the people of Thamud to the Prophet Salih; similar words are said to Shu'ayb in 26:185) shows a typical response of those who reject a prophet: instead of weighing his message and evidence, they dismiss it by claiming his mind has been affected by sorcery. By calling him 'bewitched', they explain away his call to monotheism and righteousness as the product of delusion rather than divine revelation. The interpretation is that arrogant disbelief often resorts to personal accusation and ridicule to avoid confronting the truth, and that such slander does not diminish the prophet's sincerity or the validity of his message.

translation: You are nothing but a human being like us. So bring a sign, if you are among the truthful.
interpretation: This is the response of Thamud to their prophet Salih (Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:154). Their words show a common attitude of disbelief: they assume that a messenger must be of a different, superhuman nature, and so they treat his humanity as grounds for doubting his claim. They demand a miraculous sign as proof of his truthfulness. The verse shows that rejecters often set conditions for faith while ignoring the signs already evident in his message and character. In response God gave them the she-camel as a sign, which also served as a test: if they harmed it, punishment would follow. The lesson is that prophets were chosen from among human beings so that people could follow their example, and that a demand for miracles out of stubbornness does not lead to faith but increases accountability when the sign arrives and is still rejected.

translation: He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a right to drink (water), and you have a right to drink, each on a appointed day."
interpretation: The Prophet Salih sets a fair rule for sharing the community's limited water: the she-camel, sent as a miraculous sign, drinks on one day and the people drink on another. The verse teaches that divine signs come with moral responsibility, and that the people's faith would be tested by whether they would respect a fair, God-ordained boundary and let others have their due rights rather than monopolize a shared resource out of greed or arrogance. The clear, known schedule leaves them no excuse for harming the camel, so any later violation would be willful transgression.

translation: And do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you the punishment of a great day.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:156) is the warning of the Prophet Salih to his people of Thamud concerning the miraculous she-camel that God sent as a sign. Salih commands them not to harm her in any way, whether by hurting, hamstringing, or killing her, since she was a trial and a divine sign whose rights to water and pasture were to be respected on her appointed day. The meaning is that violating a clear sign of God, after the proof has come, is not a minor offense but an act of open defiance that invites collective divine punishment. The 'great day' refers to the day on which the punishment would come, so terrible that the day itself is described as great. The verse teaches that rejecting and mistreating what God has set up as a sign, and doing so with arrogance, brings destruction upon a whole community that consents to or participates in the wrongdoing.

translation: But they hamstrung her, and in the morning they became regretful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:157) refers to the people of Thamud, who defied their prophet Salih by killing the she-camel that God had sent as a sign. Their regret was not true repentance that leads to forgiveness; it was the remorse of those who see the consequences of their sin closing in on them, since the promised punishment had come after the three-day respite. The lesson is that regret which comes only after the warning has been ignored and the sin committed, when the chance to amend has passed, does not save a person. Real repentance must come before the consequences become unavoidable, and rejecting a clear sign of God out of arrogance or collective complicity leads to ruin.

translation: So the punishment seized them. Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment is the just consequence of persistent denial of the truth after clear warning, and that the fate of earlier peoples is a lasting lesson for those who reflect. Yet signs and historical examples benefit only those whose hearts are open to faith; most people, despite witnessing evidence of God's power and justice, remain unmoved by it. The refrain calls the reader not to be among those who see the sign but fail to take heed, and to treat past destruction as a warning to turn to God in belief and obedience.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is truly the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, repeated at the end of several stories of earlier prophets in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, pairs God's might with His mercy. It teaches that God's power ('Aziz) is exercised in justice, so that He overcomes and punishes those who persist in denial and wrongdoing, as happened to the peoples who rejected their messengers. Yet His mercy (Rahim) shows in His patience, in sending warnings and guidance, in giving people time to repent, and in saving the believers. The believer should therefore feel both reverent fear and hopeful trust: no tyrant can escape God, and no sincere servant is forgotten by Him.

translation: The people of Lot denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting one prophet is rejecting all of them, because every messenger brought the same core message of tawhid, moral uprightness and accountability before God. Lot's people are said to have denied 'the messengers' (plural) even though Lot was sent to them, since denying the truth he brought meant denying the message common to all prophets. Their rejection was rooted in persistence in shameless acts and in contempt for moral admonition. The verse warns that denying revelation out of stubborn attachment to desires leads to the ruin that befell them, and it consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that earlier prophets faced the same denial.

translation: When their brother Lot said to them, "Will you not fear God?"
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 26:161) shows that Lot was sent as a messenger from among his own people, and that is why he is called their 'brother', meaning a kinsman who shares their lineage and cares for them. His opening question is a gentle but pointed rebuke: it appeals to their conscience and calls them to taqwa, the God-consciousness that would restrain them from their shameful practices and from transgressing the limits set by their Lord. The prophetic message begins not with threats but with a compassionate reminder that accountability before God is real, and that true brotherhood means warning one's people against what will bring about their ruin.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The prophet speaks these words to his people (as in the stories of Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb in Surat ash-Shu'ara) to establish his credibility before calling them to worship God. By calling himself a trustworthy messenger, he asserts two things: that he is sent by God and not speaking from himself, and that he will convey the message faithfully, neither adding to it, omitting from it, nor altering it. The claim also appeals to his people's own experience of his honesty, since he lived among them as a known and reliable person. His trustworthiness is therefore the foundation on which they are expected to accept his warning and his command to fear God and obey him.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This verse is the refrain of the prophets in the Qur'an, notably Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, when they address their peoples. It joins two duties: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that leads one to avoid disobeying Him, and obedience to the messenger. The messenger is not asking for loyalty to himself. He conveys God's revelation, so obeying him is the practical way of obeying God. Taqwa is the inner foundation, a reverent consciousness of God's majesty and accountability before Him, and obedience is its outward fruit, shown by following the guidance the prophet brings. Faith is therefore not complete with belief in the heart alone. It requires acting on the message and following the one God sent to teach it.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse, repeated on the tongues of several prophets (as in Surat ash-Shu'ara), shows that the messenger's call is free of worldly self-interest. By refusing any payment for delivering the message, the prophet shows his sincerity and removes any grounds for suspicion that he seeks wealth, status, or power. It teaches that those who call to truth should work for God's pleasure alone, trusting that He is the One who rewards, and that guidance should not be turned into a means of profit. It also strengthens the message's credibility, since a person who gains nothing materially and who endures hardship is far more likely to be speaking truthfully.

translation: Do you approach males among all the people of the world?
interpretation: This verse is the prophet Lot's rebuke of his people, in which he condemns their practice of male-male sexual relations as a shameful act. By saying 'among all the worlds' (min al-'alamin), he stresses that they were the first to invent this deviation, which no earlier nation had committed, and that they had abandoned the natural disposition (fitrah) God created in humankind, which is lawful union between husband and wife. The question is not a request for information but an expression of disapproval and astonishment, calling them to return to what is natural and upright and to turn away from transgression.

translation: And you leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses? Rather, you are a transgressing people.
interpretation: The Prophet Lut (Lot) rebukes his people for turning away from the natural, lawful union that God created between men and women in marriage, and for seeking men instead. Their act is not a mere preference but a deliberate violation of the bounds set by God and of the natural disposition (fitra) He placed in human beings. By calling them 'a people who transgress,' he shows that their sin is a habitual overstepping of limits, which is a defining character of their whole community, not just a single lapse.

translation: They said: 'If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be among those expelled.'
interpretation: The people of Lot, unable to answer his call to abandon their immoral practices with argument, resort to threat and force. They menace him with exile from the city, the typical response of a corrupt society that cannot bear a voice of conscience. His purity and moral admonition become intolerable to them, so they seek to remove him rather than reform themselves. The verse shows how persistent wrongdoers treat the righteous as the problem, and how banishment from one's homeland is a common trial faced by prophets who stand firm on truth. It also prepares for the divine deliverance of Lot and his family and the destruction of those who rejected him.

translation: He said: 'Indeed, I am of those who despise your deed.'
interpretation: This is Prophet Lot's reply to his people (Qur'an 26:168). He does not reject them as people or abandon his duty to call them, but distances himself from their act of lewdness and declares his hatred of it. The verse teaches that a believer must openly and firmly disapprove of grave wrongdoing, hating the sin itself while remaining concerned for the sinners' guidance. Lot's words mark a clear moral separation between himself and his people's conduct, and his emphatic phrasing ('of those who despise') shows that his rejection was deep and settled, not a passing displeasure.

translation: My Lord, save me and my family from what they do.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Lot (Lut) in Surat ash-Shu'ara (26:169), made after he had warned his people and they persisted in their shameful deeds and rejected his call. It shows that when a prophet's patient admonition is exhausted, he turns to God, seeking deliverance not only from the punishment that will befall the wrongdoers but also from the corruption of their conduct and its moral contagion. By asking for his family to be saved with him, Lot shows that a believer's concern extends to his household's safety and faith, while recognizing that salvation ultimately comes from God alone. The prayer teaches that dissociating oneself from sin and its people, and relying on God for protection, is the proper response when one cannot reform an entrenched society.

translation: So We saved him and his family, all of them.
interpretation: This verse, which speaks of Lot (Lūṭ) in the context of the punishment that befell his people, shows that God's deliverance comes to those who remain steadfast in faith and righteousness amid widespread corruption. The rescue of Lot and his household is a mark of divine care for the believers: when God's judgment descends on wrongdoers, He distinguishes between the corrupt and the faithful and preserves the latter. The word 'all of them' stresses the completeness of the rescue of the righteous household, while the exception of his wife, mentioned in other verses, shows that salvation depends on one's own faith and deeds rather than on mere kinship with a prophet.

translation: Except an old woman who was among those who remained behind.
interpretation: This verse comes in the accounts of Lot (Lut) and his people, where God says He saved Lot and all his family except an old woman, understood to be his wife, who stayed behind and was destroyed with the wrongdoers. The lesson is that salvation depends on one's own faith and deeds, not on kinship or closeness to a prophet. Although she lived in the household of a messenger, she sided with the wicked in heart and conduct, so she shared their fate. Being related to the righteous brings no protection to someone who does not follow their path.

translation: Then We destroyed the others.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:172, repeated in similar form elsewhere in Surat ash-Shu'ara') comes after God relates how He saved Lot and his family, except for an old woman who stayed behind. 'The others' are Lot's disobedient people, who persisted in their transgression and rejected their prophet's warnings. The verse teaches that divine deliverance of the righteous goes together with the just destruction of those who stubbornly refuse guidance after clear warning. It reminds listeners that arrogance and persistent wrongdoing lead to ruin, while faith and obedience bring salvation, and it consoles the believers of every era that God's justice will prevail.

translation: And We rained upon them a rain [of stones]; and evil was the rain of those who had been warned.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment is the certain outcome for those who persist in sin after clear warning. The people of Lot were warned by their prophet and ignored him, so the rain that fell on them was not a mercy that revives the earth but a rain of baked clay stones that destroyed them. The word 'evil' stresses how terrible that end was, and it is meant as a lesson: those who hear the warning and reject it have no excuse, and the fate of earlier peoples should lead later generations to heed their prophets and turn back to God before it is too late.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This refrain, repeated after the accounts of earlier prophets and their peoples in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, teaches that the stories of God's power, mercy, and the fate of those who denied are clear proofs for anyone who reflects. Yet the existence of clear signs does not guarantee faith, because belief depends on a heart that is open to guidance. Most people stay unmoved by evidence out of arrogance, heedlessness, or attachment to inherited customs and worldly interests. The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that the rejection of the majority is no reflection on the truth of his message or on his efforts, and it warns later generations not to repeat the pattern of those who saw the signs but did not learn from them.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is truly the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, repeated as a refrain after the stories of the earlier prophets in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, teaches that God's might and mercy work together. His might (al-'Aziz) is seen in how He overcame the deniers who rejected their messengers, such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, so that no power can withstand His decree. His mercy (ar-Rahim) is seen in how He sent warners, gave people time to repent, and saved the believers. The lesson for the Prophet and the believers is that opposition from the arrogant will not defeat the truth. They can trust that God will ultimately support the righteous, while His patience with wrongdoers is a mercy that invites them to return to Him before His justice overtakes them.

translation: The dwellers of the Wood (Al-Aykah) denied the messengers.
interpretation: The people of Al-Aykah, understood to be the people of Shu'ayb who lived among dense thickets and were known for dishonest trade, rejected their prophet. Because all the messengers bring the same core message of worshipping God alone and living with justice, rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them. The verse therefore teaches that denial of truth is a single stance of arrogance and attachment to worldly gain, and that it brings the same fate on every generation that persists in it.

translation: When Shu'ayb said to them: 'Will you not be mindful of God and fear Him?'
interpretation: Shu'ayb, sent to the people of the Thicket (Aykah), opens his mission with a gentle rhetorical question rather than a harsh command. By asking 'Will you not be God-fearing?' he appeals to their conscience and sense of accountability, implying that their dishonest dealings, such as cheating in weights and measures and spreading corruption, ought to be restrained by awareness of God. The verse shows that the core of every prophet's message is taqwa: recognizing that God sees and will judge, and letting that awareness govern one's conduct in worship and in daily transactions.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The prophet addressing his people affirms that he is not speaking from personal interest or invention but conveys what God has entrusted to him, neither adding to it nor withholding any part. By stressing his trustworthiness (amīn), a quality his people already knew in him, he grounds his call to fear God and obey him in his proven honesty. The verse teaches that the credibility of the messenger's character supports the truth of the message, and that prophethood is a trust (amāna) which the messenger faithfully delivers.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This verse is the call that Qur'anic prophets, such as Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb, and Jesus, give to their peoples. It joins two duties: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that makes a person guard against His displeasure, and obedience to the messenger. The prophet is the means by which God's guidance reaches people, so obeying him is a practical expression of fearing God. Reverence for God is incomplete if it is not shown in following the guidance He sent, and it is that reverence which leads a person to accept and follow the messenger.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The prophets who speak in this verse (as in Surah Ash-Shu'ara) show that their call is sincere and free of any worldly motive. By refusing payment, wealth or status from their people, they remove any suspicion that they preach for personal gain, which makes their message more credible and leaves their listeners no excuse of cost or ulterior motive. They place their hope entirely in God, who alone can give a reward worthy of their effort, and who is the Lord of all the worlds, so His recompense is vast and certain. The verse also teaches that those who call to God should do so purely for His sake, not for material gain or praise from people.

translation: Give full measure, and do not be among those who cause loss to others.
interpretation: This verse, part of the Prophet Shu'ayb's call to his people (Qur'an 26:181), commands absolute honesty and fairness in all dealings. It is not limited to the marketplace: anyone who shortchanges others, whether in trade, wages, trust, or rights, causes loss to people and corrupts the social order. Believers are urged to give what is due in full, and even to give a little extra, so that justice, mutual trust, and God-consciousness govern economic and social life. Those who cheat may seem to profit, but in truth they are the real losers, since they forfeit blessing, integrity, and their standing before God.

translation: And weigh with an even and straight balance.
interpretation: The verse commands absolute honesty and justice in all dealings, especially in trade and commerce. The 'straight balance' (al-qistas al-mustaqim) stands for fairness that goes beyond literal scales: giving each person their full due, neither cheating nor exploiting, and keeping integrity in measure, contract and judgment. Such uprightness protects the rights of others, builds trust in society, and is a sign of fearing God, since it is a duty owed to people and to Him together. It is also linked to the best outcome, as justice in dealings yields lasting benefit and social harmony.

translation: And do not deprive people of their due, and do not roam the earth spreading corruption.
interpretation: This verse, from the words of the Prophet Shu'ayb to his people of Madyan, forbids defrauding people of their rights in any form, not only short-changing in weights and measures but also withholding wages, belongings, dignity, or fair treatment. It then links such injustice to wider corruption: when economic cheating and wrongdoing become normal, trust and social order break down. The verse teaches that justice in dealings with others is a basic duty of faith, and that protecting people's rights keeps the earth in a state of integrity and peace.
