God was the One who made Makkah a safe sanctuary for them while they were still polytheists, and He sends them the produce of every land as sustenance. The One who protected and fed them in a state of disbelief can surely protect and provide for them if they believe and obey. Their real mistake is ignorance: most of them fail to see that security and provision come from God alone and not from their own tribal power or their idols, so they fear people more than they trust God.

translation: How many a town have We destroyed that exulted in its way of living! Those are their dwellings, which have scarcely been inhabited after them, except a little. And it is We who were the inheritors.
interpretation: The verse warns that prosperity without gratitude leads to ruin. The destroyed peoples were not punished for being wealthy, but for becoming arrogant and ungrateful, treating their comfort as a source of pride and heedlessness instead of a trust from God to be met with thankfulness and obedience. Their abandoned, empty homes stand as lasting evidence that worldly security does not last and cannot protect those who reject God's guidance. By saying 'We are the Inheritors,' God shows that He alone remains after all creation passes away, and that all wealth and property eventually return to Him. People should therefore stay humble, use their blessings responsibly, and learn from the fate of earlier nations.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would never destroy the towns unless their inhabitants were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse expresses God's justice: He does not punish communities arbitrarily or without first establishing proof against them. A messenger is sent to the central, most influential town (the 'mother' of the surrounding settlements), so that his message spreads widely from the hub of the region and no one can claim ignorance. Destruction comes only after the warning has been delivered clearly and the people persist in injustice, meaning disbelief, oppression, and rejection of the truth. Thus ruin is the consequence of the people's own wrongdoing and willful refusal after guidance, not an act of unjust severity from God.

translation: Whatever thing you have been given is only the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment. But what is with God is better and more lasting. Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: The verse tells people that wealth, status, children and every other worldly gain are temporary, and that they only decorate a short earthly life and then end. The reward God has prepared in the Hereafter is better in quality and lasts forever, so it is foolish to trade the lasting for the fleeting. The closing question, 'Will you not then use your reason?', appeals to the listener's sense. A sound mind weighs both sides and sees that effort and sacrifice should go toward what lasts, while worldly goods should be held lightly and used as a means to earn God's pleasure, not as the goal of life.

translation: Is, then, one to whom We have made a good promise, which he will surely meet, like one whom We have allowed to enjoy the provision of worldly life, and who then, on the Day of Resurrection, will be among those brought forward for punishment?
interpretation: The verse draws a decisive contrast between two outcomes: a believer who has been promised Paradise and will certainly attain it, and a person who has been granted only fleeting worldly enjoyment and then will be summoned to account and punishment. The rhetorical question stresses that they cannot be equal. Worldly comfort is brief and deceptive, while God's promise is true and lasting. Therefore a sensible person should not exchange the enduring reward of the Hereafter for the transient pleasures of this life, and should measure success by the final destination, not by present ease.

translation: And on the Day when He will call out to them and say, "Where are My partners, those whom you used to claim?"
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment God will publicly confront those who associated others with Him, asking where the idols, false deities, and powers they worshipped and imagined to be His partners are now. The question is not a request for information but a rebuke that exposes the emptiness of their claims. Those objects of worship are absent and powerless to help, so the polytheists are left with no defense and no intercessor, and they are forced to recognize that all dominion and the only true claim to worship belong to God alone.

translation: Those against whom the word has become due will say: "Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray just as we ourselves went astray. We declare ourselves innocent before You. It was not us that they worshipped."
interpretation: This verse portrays a scene on the Day of Judgment in which the leaders of misguidance, those against whom God's sentence of punishment has been justly confirmed, try to distance themselves from their followers. They admit that they misled others in the same way they were misled, as though sharing in error lessens their guilt, and then disown any responsibility. Their claim that the followers were not really worshipping them points to the fact that obeying and following desires, tyrants, and false leaders in opposition to God is itself a form of worship. In truth, the followers were really following their own whims and passions, which these leaders only beautified. The verse teaches that no one can shift blame onto others on that Day: leaders and followers are each accountable for their own choices, and any alliance built on falsehood in this world will turn into mutual disavowal in the hereafter.

translation: And it will be said, "Call upon your partners [whom you associated with God]." So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, those who worshipped others besides God will be publicly exposed as having placed their hope in nothing. Being told to summon their false deities is a form of rebuke, since the idols, saints, or powers they depended on cannot hear, answer, or help. The silence of these 'partners' shows that all the support they relied on in this world was an illusion. When the punishment becomes visible and certain, they will realize that guidance was available to them in life through reason and revelation, and that only by following it could they have avoided this outcome. The closing phrase expresses regret: had they truly been guided to the worship of God alone, they would not now face this humiliation and suffering.

translation: And on the Day when He will call them and say, "What answer did you give to the messengers?"
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qasas 28:65) describes the Day of Resurrection, when God will question all people about how they responded to the prophets sent to them. The question is not about their beliefs in the abstract, but about their concrete response to the divine message: whether they accepted it, rejected it, or ignored it. This shows that every person is accountable for the guidance that reached them, and that the messengers' call is a binding proof against humankind. It also implies that the real measure of a person on that Day is their answer to revelation, not their lineage, status, or worldly claims, and that no excuse will remain for those who turned away.

translation: But the news will be obscured to them on that Day, so they will not ask one another.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when God asks the disbelievers what answer they gave to the messengers, all arguments and excuses will vanish from their minds. They will have no proof to offer and will be struck dumb with confusion. Even those who might once have turned to one another for advice or help will not ask each other, because everyone will be equally lost, preoccupied with their own plight, and unable to bring to mind any defense. The verse shows how helpless those who rejected the truth will be on that Day, when neither reasoning nor mutual support can rescue them.

translation: But as for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, then perhaps he will be among the successful. (Qur'an 28:67)
interpretation: The verse opens the door of return to everyone, including those who have been steeped in polytheism and disobedience. It sets out three connected conditions for salvation: sincere repentance, which means turning away from wrongdoing and back to God; faith, which means correcting one's inner belief; and righteous action, which means proving that change through conduct. The word 'perhaps' ('asa) does not express doubt about God's generosity. It reflects the way God's promises are phrased with grace: success is not something a person can claim as an entitlement, and it depends on God's acceptance. So the believer lives between hope and humility. He is encouraged to hope for felicity in this world and the next, and he is also reminded not to be complacent about his deeds, because falah, true success, is a gift granted by God to those who return to Him sincerely.

translation: And your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses; they have no choice. Exalted is God and high above whatever they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation and selection belong to God alone, because only He knows what is truly best for His creatures. He chooses whom to favor, whether prophets, messengers, places, times, or paths, and no human preference, status, or wealth can override His choice. Those who objected that revelation should have come to some prominent man, or who set up partners alongside God, were claiming a right of choice that was never theirs. The right response is submission and trust in His wisdom, and recognition that He is far above any partner or rival that people ascribe to Him.

translation: And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 28:69) affirms that God's knowledge encompasses both the hidden and the manifest in human beings: the secret intentions, grudges, denial, or sincerity that hearts hold, as well as what people say and do openly. It consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the face of his opponents' concealed hostility and open mockery, assuring him that nothing escapes God, and that every person will be held to account with perfect knowledge and justice. It also warns believers and deniers alike that outward appearances cannot hide inner realities from God, calling for sincerity of heart as well as conduct.

translation: And He is God; there is no deity but Him. To Him belongs all praise in the first life and the last, and to Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone is worthy of worship and that every good, blessing, and perfection in this world and the next ultimately calls for praise directed to Him, since He is the source of all favor. Because He alone holds absolute authority, His decree governs both creation and law, and no ruler, power, or ideology can rival it. Since all people will return to Him for reckoning, human life has moral accountability and purpose: one should live in gratitude and submission to His command, knowing that final justice rests with Him and that nothing escapes His judgment.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if God were to make the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than God could bring you light? Then will you not hear?
interpretation: The verse invites people to reflect on how completely they depend on God for the alternation of night and day, which they usually take for granted. If the night were made endless, no power besides God, whether an idol, a created being, or a human invention, could restore daylight. Light here means more than illumination: it is the condition that makes work, sustenance, movement, and life itself possible. Since every blessing they enjoy rests on God alone, worship and gratitude belong to Him alone. The closing question, 'Will you not hear?', reproaches those who ignore this clear reminder and urges them to listen with understanding and heed the call to monotheism.

translation: Say: 'Have you considered: if God were to make the day everlasting over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?'
interpretation: The verse directs the listener to reflect on the alternation of night and day as evidence of God's sole lordship and mercy. Night is not merely the absence of light but a provision that allows rest, recovery, and stillness; endless daylight would exhaust people and disrupt life. Since no being besides God has the power to change this order or to supply the night, no one else deserves worship. The closing question, 'Will you not see?', rebukes those who observe these daily signs yet remain blind to their meaning, and urges them to perceive with insight and recognize God's unique power and favor, and so to thank Him and worship Him alone.

translation: And it is out of His mercy that He made for you the night and the day, so that you may rest in it and seek of His bounty, and so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: The alternation of night and day is presented as a deliberate act of divine mercy, designed around human needs. Night, with its darkness and stillness, gives the body and mind rest and recovery, while day, with its light, makes possible work, trade, and the pursuit of livelihood, which the verse calls seeking God's bounty. Because both rest and provision come through this arrangement, people should not take it for granted, since it is a gift they did not create. The verse ends by naming its purpose: that reflection on this daily rhythm should lead people to gratitude, expressed in acknowledging God as the source of these blessings, worshipping Him alone, and using His gifts rightly.

translation: And on the Day when He will call to them and say, 'Where are My partners, those whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 28:62) shows that on the Day of Judgment God will publicly confront those who associated others with Him in worship. The question is not a request for information, since God knows all things. It is a rebuke that exposes the falsehood of their claims. The idols, saints, and false authorities they relied on in the world will be absent and unable to help them, so the idolaters are left with no excuse and no intercessor. The lesson is that worship and trust belong to God alone, and that reliance on anything besides Him proves empty when the truth becomes plain.

translation: And We shall draw out from every nation a witness, and say: 'Bring your proof.' Then they will know that the truth belongs to God, and what they used to invent will abandon them.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, God will bring forth a witness from every community, namely its prophet, who will testify to what the people did with the message they were sent. The disbelievers will then be challenged to produce any evidence for their beliefs and their worship of others besides God. They will have none, and in that moment of helplessness they will recognize with certainty that all truth and all authority belong to God alone. The false gods, lies, and claims they once fabricated will vanish and fail them, leaving them without any defense or intercessor.

translation: Indeed, Qarun was among the people of Moses, but he oppressed them. And We had given him of treasures so much that its keys would burden a group of strong men. When his people said to him, 'Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not like the exultant.'
interpretation: The verse shows how wealth, when it breeds arrogance, leads to transgression against others. Qarun's abundant riches, so vast that merely carrying the keys to his treasures was a heavy burden for a band of strong men, made him haughty and unjust toward his own people. The warning 'do not exult' does not condemn ordinary joy or gratitude for God's blessings; it condemns the proud, heedless, boastful exultation that forgets the Giver, attributes wealth to one's own merit, and neglects the duties of gratitude, humility, and justice. God's dislike of such exultation is a lesson that worldly abundance is a trial and not a sign of worth or divine favor.

translation: And seek, through what Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and do not forget your share of this world. And do good as Allah has done good to you. And do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, Allah does not like the corrupters.
interpretation: This is the counsel given to Qarun by the righteous among his people, and it lays out a balanced way of using wealth. Worldly blessings are not ends in themselves but means to earn the Hereafter, so wealth should be spent in obedience to God, in charity, and in supporting the needy. Islam does not demand renouncing the world: a person may enjoy lawful pleasures, provide for himself and his family, and take his rightful portion of life's good things without extravagance or arrogance. Gratitude for God's generosity must be shown by generosity toward others, since God has been kind to you and you should be kind to His creatures. Wealth should also never be used to oppress, cheat, boast, or spread injustice, because those who spread corruption lose God's love.

translation: He said, 'I was only given it because of knowledge I possess.' Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were stronger than him in power and greater in accumulation of wealth? And the criminals will not be asked about their sins [because Allah already knows them].
interpretation: This verse describes Qarun's arrogant claim that his wealth was the product of his own skill and knowledge, not a gift from God. The Qur'an rebukes this attitude by reminding that history is full of earlier nations who had greater strength and riches yet were annihilated when they became ungrateful and corrupt. Wealth and power are therefore not proof of merit or divine favor, nor do they protect from God's judgment. The closing clause teaches that God has full knowledge of the wrongdoers' sins, so they will not be questioned in order to inform Him; rather, they will be held to account and punished with certainty, and no excuse or claim of self-sufficiency will avail them.

translation: So he came out before his people in his adornment. Those who desired the life of this world said, "If only we had the like of what Qarun has been given! Indeed, he is possessed of great fortune."
interpretation: The verse shows how worldly display dazzles those whose hearts are fixed on this life alone. Qarun's showy procession reveals the shallow standard by which they judge success: wealth, luxury and status. Because their ambitions end with this world, they mistake abundant riches for a 'great portion' and wish to be like him, without considering how he acquired and used his wealth, or the accountability and ruin it could bring. The passage warns that the true measure of fortune is faith, righteous action and gratitude to God. It also shows how outward splendor can seduce the heedless and distort their sense of what is worth desiring, preparing for the sharp contrast with the knowledgeable believers who follow, and with Qarun's downfall.

translation: But those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of God is better for whoever believes and does righteous deeds, and none will attain it except the steadfast."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 28:80) describes how people of true knowledge responded to those who envied Qarun's worldly wealth. Real knowledge is shown by the ability to see beyond the glitter of this life and to value what God has prepared for the believers. The scholars rebuke the covetous with 'Woe to you' because they have confused temporary riches with real success. They teach that the reward of God is better than any treasure, but that it is attained only through faith joined with righteous action. Such a reward is granted only to the patient, those who stay steadfast in obeying God, who refrain from sin, and who stay content with God's decree and do not envy the worldly gains of others. Thus, knowledge in the Qur'anic sense is not only information but the insight that orients a person toward the hereafter and produces patience.

translation: So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling; and he had no group to help him besides God, nor was he among those who could defend themselves.
interpretation: The verse shows the end of Qarun, whose wealth and pride made him feel self-sufficient and superior to others. His destruction came by God's decree, and neither his riches, his followers, nor his own power could save him. It teaches that worldly resources and social support are worthless against God's command, that arrogance and ingratitude toward the One who bestowed blessings lead to ruin, and that true help and protection come only from God.

translation: And those who had wished for his position only the day before began to say: "Ah, indeed! God extends provision to whom He wills of His servants, and restricts it. Had God not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us too. Ah, indeed! The disbelievers never succeed."
interpretation: After witnessing Qarun's destruction, those who had envied his wealth and worldly splendor realized that riches are not a sign of divine favor or a measure of a person's worth, but a matter of God's wisdom and will, who gives abundantly or sparingly as He chooses, as a test. Their envy turned into gratitude and humility, as they recognized that their own safety from a similar fate was only through God's mercy, not their own merit. They concluded that those who deny God and are arrogant in their wealth may enjoy a temporary prosperity, but they will not ultimately attain true success. The verse teaches that real success lies in faith and humility before God, not in worldly possessions.

translation: That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who do not seek exaltation upon the earth, nor corruption. And the best outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the felicity of the Hereafter is not granted to those driven by pride, domination, or the wish to elevate themselves above others, nor to those who spread wrongdoing. It is reserved for people whose hearts are humble and who do not use power or status to oppress or corrupt. Such people live with God-consciousness (taqwa), seeking God's pleasure rather than worldly superiority, and the final, lasting success belongs to them. The verse thus makes the criterion for salvation inner humility and righteous conduct rather than worldly rank, and it follows the example of Pharaoh's arrogance in the preceding story, in which tyranny and corruption end in ruin.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have something better than it; and whoever comes with an evil deed—those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse sets out the principle of divine justice and mercy on the Day of Judgment. A good deed is rewarded with more than its worth: it is multiplied, and God grants it a reward greater than the deed itself. An evil deed is repaid only with its exact equivalent, with no added penalty and no injustice. This shows that God's grace outweighs His strict justice. It encourages believers to do good and to hope for His generosity, and it warns wrongdoers that they will face only the consequences of their own actions.

translation: Indeed, He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to a place of return. Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error.
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet Muhammad that the One who entrusted him with conveying and living by the Qur'an will not abandon him: just as He sent him out in hardship, He will bring him back to his homeland, Mecca, in victory, as happened at the conquest of Mecca. The 'place of return' also carries a deeper sense, that every person ultimately returns to God for reckoning. When the disbelievers accuse him of being misguided, he is told not to argue endlessly but to leave the judgment to God, who knows perfectly who follows true guidance and who is plainly astray. The outcome will vindicate the truth and its bearers.

translation: You did not expect that the Book would be conveyed to you, but it came as a mercy from your Lord. So never be a supporter of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that revelation was not something he sought, earned, or even anticipated; it was a pure gift of divine mercy. Because his prophethood and the Qur'an are a favor from God alone, the fitting response is gratitude expressed through steadfast loyalty to the truth. That means he must never lend support, aid, or alliance to those who reject God's message, nor ease their opposition by compromising the call. The command is addressed to him to show how serious the matter is, and it applies by extension to every believer: those who have received guidance as an undeserved mercy should not become helpers of falsehood or of those who oppose it.

translation: And let them not turn you away from the verses of Allah after they have been sent down to you. And call people to your Lord, and never be among the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse is a firm directive to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and by extension to every believer, to hold fast to divine revelation despite the pressure, mockery, or opposition of the disbelievers. Once the truth has been revealed and its proof established, nothing should divert one from it or weaken one's commitment to conveying it. The command to call people to the Lord means that steadfastness is not merely personal: it must be joined with active invitation to the worship of God alone. The final warning against being among the polytheists affirms the absolute purity of monotheism. Although addressed to the Prophet, who was already protected from idolatry, it serves to emphasize the gravity of the matter and to instruct the community that no compromise in tawhid is permissible under any circumstances.

translation: And do not invoke any other god along with God. There is no god but Him. Everything is perishing except His Face. His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse commands absolute devotion to God alone, grounding it in the contrast between created and Creator: everything in existence is transient and subject to annihilation, with only God, referred to by His 'Face' (His own essence, or that which is done seeking Him), remaining eternal. Since only the Everlasting is worthy of worship, turning in prayer or hope to anything else is futile. God alone holds ultimate authority over creation and over the final judgment, and every person will return to Him to be held accountable, so one should live in awareness of this return and direct all worship and trust to Him alone.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Mim.
interpretation: These disconnected letters, which open Surah Al-Baqarah and several other surahs, are best understood as a challenge to the Arabs and a pointer to the Qur'an's miraculous nature. The Qur'an is made of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs used in their eloquent speech, yet they could not produce anything like it. The letters are placed at the start of the revelation to awaken the listener's attention and to show that a Book composed of familiar elements carries an inimitable message. Their true meaning is known fully only to God, and their presence reminds believers to approach the Book with humility, recognizing that its source lies beyond human ability.

translation: Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and will not be tested?
interpretation: Faith is not established by a verbal declaration alone; it has to be proven through trials. God tests believers with hardship, loss, temptation, and difficulty so that the sincere are distinguished from those who merely claim belief, and so that faith is purified, strengthened, and made real in action and steadfastness. Trials are therefore a divine norm applied to every community, and a believer should expect them and meet them with patience rather than take them as a sign of God's neglect or displeasure.

translation: And We certainly tested those who came before them, so Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful, and He will surely make evident those who are liars.
interpretation: Trials are a consistent divine practice applied to every community, including earlier nations and prophets' followers, so believers should not be surprised or shaken when hardship comes. The purpose of testing is not to give God new knowledge, since He already knows all things, but to bring what is within hearts into plain, observable reality. Hardship separates sincere faith, which stays firm in word and deed under pressure, from false claims that crumble when faith costs something. Claiming belief is therefore not enough; its truth is established through steadfastness in the face of difficulty, and the outcome of the test exposes each person's real standing before God and before others.

translation: Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us? How evil is what they judge!
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who persist in wrongdoing while imagining they can escape God's reach, whether by evading accountability in this life or by avoiding punishment in the next. Nothing and no one can slip beyond God's power, knowledge, or timing, so the delay of punishment is no sign of impunity but a respite and a test. Their assumption that evildoers and believers will end up equal, or that wrongdoing will go unanswered, is a corrupt judgment that contradicts divine justice. The verse calls the reader to sober self-examination: to take moral accountability seriously, to abandon false security, and to align one's expectations with God's justice rather than with wishful thinking.

translation: Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then indeed the term appointed by God is sure to come. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse offers reassurance to the believer who longs to meet his Lord: the appointed time of death and the Resurrection, when that meeting takes place, is certain and cannot be delayed or missed. Hoping for the meeting is not idle wishing; it should motivate a person to prepare through faith and righteous deeds, since the moment is fixed and approaching. The closing names, the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, indicate that God hears the sincere supplications and longings of those who hope for Him and knows their intentions and actions, so He will reward them justly when the promised time arrives.

translation: And whoever strives, strives only for his own soul. Indeed, Allah is free of need from all the worlds.
interpretation: Every effort made in God's cause, whether struggling against one's own desires, persevering in obedience, defending the faith, or striving to do good, ultimately benefits the one who makes it. God gains nothing from human striving, since He is entirely self-sufficient and has no need of any creature. Worship and sacrifice are therefore not favors done for God but investments in one's own salvation, moral growth, and eternal reward. The verse removes any sense of pride or entitlement from the believer, who should see their striving as a grace and opportunity granted to them, and not as something God owes them thanks for.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove from them their misdeeds, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ankabut 29:7) promises that faith joined with righteous action brings two blessings from God: the erasure of past sins, so that a believer's slate is wiped clean through sincere belief and good works, and a recompense measured by the best of their deeds rather than their average or weakest ones. God's generosity thus exceeds strict justice, since He rewards even modest acts at the level of the finest act the believer performed. It encourages believers to persevere through the trials mentioned in the surrounding verses, assuring them that faith and good works are never wasted and that divine mercy outweighs human shortcomings.

translation: And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that kindness and good treatment toward parents is a divine command, ranking just after the duty owed to God. That duty is bounded, though: obedience to any creature, even parents, ends where it would require disobeying God, here by committing shirk, which has no basis in knowledge or proof. Even then, the believer is not released from treating parents well in worldly matters; he refuses their command on belief while keeping up his kindness and respect toward them. The closing reminder that all will return to God, who will inform each person of their deeds, teaches that final accountability is to God alone. Loyalty to family must therefore never override loyalty to the Creator, and each person will answer for their own choices.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely admit them among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ankabut 29:9) teaches that true faith joined with good works earns the highest honor: not just entry into Paradise but companionship with the righteous, the prophets and the pious. Salvation depends on the combination of sincere belief and deeds that confirm it. The emphatic oath-like wording ('We will surely admit them') is a firm divine promise that reassures believers who endure hardship and trials, as the surrounding verses describe, that their reward is certain and their company in the hereafter will be among the best of people.

translation: And among the people are those who say, 'We believe in God,' but when they are harmed for the sake of God, they regard the persecution of people as if it were the punishment of God. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, 'Indeed, we were with you.' Is not God best aware of what is in the breasts of all the worlds?
interpretation: The verse exposes the weak, hypocritical type of faith that is professed only in times of ease. Such a person declares belief with the tongue, but when he meets hardship or persecution for the sake of God, he cannot bear it and treats the harassment of human beings as though it were God's own punishment, so he gives in to people's pressure and abandons his commitment, fearing their torment more than God's. Yet when God grants victory and gain to the believers, he rushes to claim solidarity with them and says 'we were with you,' seeking a share of the spoils. The closing rhetorical question reminds us that no pretense can deceive God, who knows exactly what lies in every heart, including the true sincerity of the believers and the hidden insincerity of the hypocrites. Real faith is thus proven by steadfastness under trial, not by words spoken in times of safety and success.

translation: And Allah will surely make evident those who have believed, and He will surely make evident the hypocrites.
interpretation: The verse teaches that trials and hardships are a divine means of sifting people, so that the reality hidden within hearts becomes manifest in action. God's knowledge is complete and eternal, so the point is not that He gains new information; rather, the tests expose each person's true state so that it becomes an established fact for all, and so that reward or reckoning rests on demonstrated conduct rather than on claims. The sincere believer remains steadfast under affliction and shows faith through patience and perseverance, while the hypocrite, whose profession of faith is only verbal, wavers, retreats, or sides with the opposition when difficulty arrives. Thus hardship serves as a criterion that separates genuine faith from pretense.

translation: Those who disbelieved said to those who believed, 'Follow our way, and we will carry your sins.' But they will not carry any of their sins at all. Indeed, they are liars.
interpretation: The verse exposes the false promises of the disbelievers of Makkah, who urged believers to abandon Islam and return to their ancestral religion, claiming that if there were any punishment in the Hereafter, they would bear the sins on the believers' behalf. The Qur'an refutes this, affirming the principle of individual accountability: no soul bears the burden of another, and no one can shoulder even a small part of someone else's sins on the Day of Judgment. Their offer is a lie, as it is beyond their power and each will be preoccupied with their own fate. The lesson is that one must not be swayed by empty assurances from those who call to misguidance, because responsibility for one's choices rests solely on oneself before God.

translation: And they will surely bear their own burdens, and other burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ankabut 29:13) warns those who urge believers to abandon faith and promise to bear their sins for them. They cannot actually relieve anyone of their own guilt, since each person is accountable for their own deeds. But because they misled others and invited them to falsehood, they will carry the weight of their own sins plus the added burden of having caused others to go astray, without lessening the burden of those who followed them. On the Day of Resurrection they will be held to account for the lies they invented, including their false promises and their claims about God and religion. Responsibility for leading others into error is a real, additional moral weight.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, and the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad and the believers by pointing to Noah's extraordinary patience: he called his people to God for 950 years, yet only a few believed. It teaches that the apparent delay of divine punishment is no sign of God's approval of the oppressors, and that persistence in wrongdoing, in this case idolatry and rejection of the message, ends in ruin. The flood came upon them because of their own injustice, not because of any lack of warning or time to repent. Believers are therefore called to remain steadfast in conveying the truth without being discouraged by how few respond or how long it takes, trusting that God's promise will be fulfilled.

translation: So We saved him and those who were with him in the ship, and We made it a sign for all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation comes from God to those who obey Him and persevere in faith, while the arrogant deniers perish. The ship that carried Noah and the believers through the flood was not merely a means of rescue but a lasting sign for all peoples and generations. It reminds humanity that God's power controls nature, that His promise to the righteous is true, and that the fate of past nations who rejected their prophets is a warning and a lesson for those who come after them.

translation: And [We sent] Abraham, when he said to his people: Worship God and be mindful of Him. That is better for you, if only you knew.
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's call as the core message of all prophets: true worship belongs to God alone, joined with taqwa, a conscious awareness of Him that restrains a person from wrongdoing. Abraham tells his people that this path is better for them, and the words 'if you knew' suggest that people cling to inherited idol-worship out of ignorance, not because it benefits them. Real knowledge, in this reading, shows that devotion to the one God brings lasting good in this world and the next, while false worship yields only loss. The call also invites reason: whoever reflects honestly will see that serving the Creator is wiser than serving what cannot help or harm.

translation: You only worship idols besides God, and you invent a falsehood. Indeed, those whom you worship besides God do not possess for you any provision. So seek provision from God, and worship Him, and be grateful to Him. To Him you will be returned.
interpretation: In this verse Abraham exposes the emptiness of idol worship by showing that the idols are lifeless objects fashioned by human hands, and that the claims made about their power and divinity are fabrications. Since they cannot provide sustenance or meet any real need, they have no claim on anyone's devotion. Provision, the most basic human need, comes only from God. So a person should seek livelihood from Him alone, by turning to Him in prayer and trust while also striving by lawful means. The proper response to His provision is worship and gratitude, which means obeying Him and acknowledging His favors. The closing reminder that all will return to God adds moral weight: those who direct their worship and thanks elsewhere will have to answer to Him for it.

translation: And if you deny [the message], then nations before you have already denied. And the Messenger's duty is only to convey the clear message.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and warns his people: rejection of divine truth is not new, since earlier nations denied their prophets and met the consequences of their denial. Your denial therefore does not harm the message or the messenger; it harms only you. The Messenger's responsibility is limited to delivering God's message plainly and unmistakably, leaving no excuse for ignorance. Guidance itself, and the reckoning that follows, rest with God, so once the message has been clearly conveyed, accountability falls on those who hear it and choose to reject it.

translation: Have they not seen how Allah originates creation and then repeats it? Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse (al-Ankabut 29:19) answers those who deny resurrection by pointing to what they can already observe. Creation is brought into being from nothing, and life renews itself continually in plants, animals, human generations and the changing seasons. Anyone who can see that Allah starts creation has no rational basis for thinking He cannot bring it back after death, since repeating something is easier for the mind to accept than first producing it. Resurrection is therefore not an impossible claim but a natural consequence of the power already on display in the world. Nothing is difficult for Allah, whose will needs only the command 'Be'. The verse urges people to reflect on the signs around them and let that reflection strengthen their belief in the Hereafter and in accountability.

translation: Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation; then God will bring about the final creation. Indeed, God has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse invites people to learn from the natural world and from the traces of earlier creation. If they reflect on how God brought life into being from nothing, and on the stages by which living things first came to exist, they will see that resurrection is no more difficult for Him than the first creation. Beginning creation is evidence of the ability to renew it, so the verse links observation and reasoning to belief in the afterlife, and it closes by stressing that God's power is unlimited.

translation: He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ankabut 29:21) affirms that God's judgment is absolute and perfectly just: punishment and mercy are His alone to give, and He does so according to His knowledge and wisdom, as those who persist in rebellion and wrongdoing earn His punishment, while those who turn to Him in faith and repentance receive His mercy. No one can escape His authority, because every human being will be brought back to Him after death. The verse calls the listener to sober awareness of accountability, to fear God's punishment, to hope for His mercy, and to live in preparation for the return to Him.

translation: And you cannot escape Him on earth or in the heaven, and you have besides God no protector and no helper.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's total dominion: no one can place themselves beyond His reach, whether by hiding, fleeing, or resisting, anywhere in creation. It also teaches that no one other than God can shield a person from His decree or help them against it. A believer should therefore stop relying on false powers, accept accountability before God, and turn to Him alone for protection and support.

translation: And those who disbelieved in the signs of God and in the meeting with Him — those have despaired of My mercy, and those will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: Denying God's signs and the reality of standing before Him in the Hereafter cuts a person off from the very path through which mercy is received. Because such people reject accountability and the One who forgives, they never turn to Him in repentance or hope, so they despair of His mercy by their own choice. Their despair is not because God's mercy is lacking, since it encompasses all things, but because their disbelief closes the door to it. The painful punishment is the consequence of this self-imposed severance from the source of mercy.

translation: But the answer of his people was only that they said, 'Kill him or burn him.' Then God saved him from the fire. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: When Abraham called his people to worship God alone and gave them clear proofs, they had no argument left, so they turned from reason to violence and chose to silence him by killing or burning him. This shows that falsehood, when defeated intellectually, resorts to force. God then rescued Abraham from the fire he was thrown into by making it harmless to him, showing that no human plot can harm one whom God protects. The event is a sign only for believers, because they alone reflect on it, accept God's power over natural causes, and take from it trust in God and steadfastness in the truth.

translation: And he said: 'You have taken idols besides God only as a bond of affection among yourselves in the life of this world. Then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another and curse one another, and your abode will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers.'
interpretation: Abraham tells his people that their idol-worship is not grounded in truth but in social convenience: they cling to shared false gods to preserve unity, tradition, and mutual approval in worldly life. Such bonds built on falsehood are temporary and hollow. When the Day of Judgment comes and the consequences become plain, the same companions who encouraged one another in error will repudiate and curse each other, each blaming the others for misleading him. No ally or intercessor will rescue them from the Fire, since the idols they trusted have no power, and only sincere devotion to God offers real protection and lasting companionship.

translation: And Lot believed him. And [Abraham] said, "Indeed, I will emigrate to [the place commanded by] my Lord. Indeed, it is He who is the Exalted in Might, the Wise."
interpretation: The verse shows that true faith demands sacrifice and trust in God. When Abraham's people rejected his message and sought to harm him, only Lot believed him, which shows that truth is not measured by the number of its followers. Abraham's decision to emigrate was an act of obedience: he left his homeland not in defeat but in reliance on his Lord, so his migration was a migration 'to my Lord' and not merely away from his people. By affirming that God is the Almighty and the All-Wise, he expresses confidence that God can protect and support those who leave everything for His sake, and that He directs their journey with wisdom, so that hardship and displacement become part of a purposeful divine plan that leads to a better outcome.

translation: And We granted him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed prophethood and the Scripture among his descendants, and We gave him his reward in this world; and indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse describes how God honored Abraham for his faith and sacrifice when he left his people and homeland for God's sake. His reward came in this world through righteous offspring (Isaac and Jacob), through the lineage in which the prophets and revealed books continued, and through lasting good repute and the love and respect of the nations after him. Yet this worldly reward does not diminish his reward in the next life, where he is counted among the righteous. The lesson is that sincere devotion to God is never lost: God may reward the believer in both worlds, and the greatest honor is to be among the righteous in the Hereafter.

translation: And [We sent] Lot, when he said to his people: "Indeed, you commit such immorality as none among the worlds has preceded you in."
interpretation: The verse presents Lot's message as a moral rebuke grounded in the novelty of his people's sin. Calling it 'al-fāḥisha' marks it as an extreme, shameless transgression against human nature and the order God established. The claim that no one in all the worlds had done it before shows that they did not merely follow a common human weakness. They invented and institutionalized a corruption, and so bore the responsibility of originating it and setting a harmful precedent for others. The lesson is that when a society normalizes flagrant immorality and takes pride in it, a prophet's duty is to confront it plainly and call people back to their innate disposition (fiṭra) and to obedience to God.

translation: Do you indeed approach men, and cut off the road, and commit in your gatherings the abominable act? But the answer of his people was only that they said, 'Bring us the punishment of God, if you are among the truthful.'
interpretation: Lot (Lut) rebukes his people for three compounding crimes: a sexual practice contrary to the natural order God created, highway robbery that spread insecurity and cut off travel and trade (and, in a broader sense, severing the natural path of procreation and the social bonds that sustain a community), and the open, shameless practice of vice in their public assemblies without any sense of guilt. The last point shows that sin becomes most dangerous when it is normalized and committed publicly, since society then loses its moral conscience. Their reply shows hardened arrogance: instead of reflecting or repenting, they mock the warning and dare the prophet to bring down God's punishment, treating it as an empty threat. The verse teaches that persistent wrongdoing, public indecency and the rejection of sincere admonition lead hearts to blindness, and that mocking God's warnings does not make them any less real.

translation: He said: "My Lord, help me against the corrupting people."
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Lot (Lut) in Surat al-Ankabut (29:30), made after his people persisted in their shameless acts, highway robbery, and rejection of his warnings. By calling upon his Lord and describing his people as 'those who spread corruption', he shows that he has exhausted every means of guidance and no longer hopes for their reform. He turns to God alone for victory, acknowledging that true help comes only from Him. The verse teaches that when corruption becomes entrenched and advice is rejected, the believer's refuge is sincere prayer for God's intervention, and that God answers the plea of His righteous servants by sending His decree against the wrongdoers.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Abraham with the glad tidings, they said: 'Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town. Indeed, its people have been wrongdoers.'
interpretation: The angels sent to Abraham brought him the good news of the birth of Isaac, and then disclosed the second part of their mission: the destruction of the people of Lot's town (Sodom). The verse shows that divine punishment is not arbitrary but is a just consequence of persistent wrongdoing, namely disbelief, transgression, and moral corruption. It also shows God's honoring of Abraham by informing him of what was about to happen, so that mercy and warning stand side by side: the believers are given glad tidings while the unjust are met with a decreed, deserved destruction.

translation: Abraham said, "But Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is of those who stay behind."
interpretation: Abraham, concerned for his nephew Lot and hoping the punishment might be delayed or averted, raises the fact that a righteous man lives in the town. The angels reassure him that God's knowledge encompasses every person there, so Lot's presence has not been overlooked. Divine judgment discriminates precisely: the believer and his household are saved, while the one who shares the community's disbelief is not spared merely through kinship. Lot's wife, though married to a prophet, remained behind with the doomed and perished with them, showing that salvation depends on one's own faith and conduct, not on family ties or proximity to the righteous.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them. They said, 'Do not fear and do not grieve. We will surely save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind.'
interpretation: The verse shows how the angels came to Lot in the form of handsome young men, and Lot was anxious because he knew how depraved his people were and feared for the safety of his guests, yet he could not protect them. At the moment of his greatest helplessness, God's messengers revealed who they were and brought reassurance: they told him not to fear the people who threatened him nor to grieve over what would befall them. Divine rescue comes to the righteous at the point when human means are exhausted. Salvation depends on faith and not on kinship, since Lot's own wife, who sided with the wrongdoers in heart, was excluded from deliverance and counted among those left behind to be destroyed. The lesson is that God protects His believing servants, and that closeness to a prophet cannot save someone who does not share his faith.

translation: Indeed, We are going to bring down upon the people of this town a punishment from the heaven because they have been defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse is the angels' message to Lot (Lūṭ) about the fate of his people, the inhabitants of Sodom. It shows that divine punishment is not arbitrary but follows persistent, open transgression: they had abandoned obedience to God and openly committed immoral acts. The 'rijz' sent from heaven stands for a decisive, overwhelming chastisement that falls on a community after its moral corruption has become entrenched and warnings have been rejected. It teaches that persistent, unrepentant defiance of God's guidance brings about the downfall of a society, and that the cause of ruin is the people's own wrongdoing ('bi-mā kānū yafsuqūn'), not injustice from God.

translation: And We have certainly left of it a clear sign for a people who use reason.
interpretation: This verse (29:35) refers to the ruined remains of the people of Lot after God's punishment. Their devastated land, which travelers in Arabia could still see, stands as a lasting and evident warning. God says the lesson is plain, but only those who use their intellect, reflecting on the fate of wrongdoers and the consequences of immorality and rejecting the prophets, will actually draw a lesson from it. Those who do not reflect pass by it unmoved, so the sign benefits only those who reason.

translation: And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb. He said: 'O my people, worship God, hope for the Last Day, and do not roam the earth as agents of corruption.'
interpretation: The verse shows that every prophet's message joins right belief to right conduct. Shu'ayb first calls his people to worship God alone, then to live with the Last Day in mind, hoping for its reward and fearing its reckoning, and finally to stop spreading corruption on earth. In Madyan this corruption was chiefly cheating in weights and measures and wronging people in their dealings. The verse implies that faith in God and accountability in the Hereafter are what restrain a society from injustice and exploitation, so worship and social righteousness cannot be separated.

translation: But they denied him, so the earthquake seized them, and by morning they were lying prostrate, lifeless in their homes.
interpretation: The verse shows that persistent rejection of a prophet's clear message ends in divine judgment. Those who denied Shu'ayb (the verse appears in the context of Madyan, and similar wording is used for Thamud) did not fall through chance. Their denial was met with a sudden and overwhelming tremor that destroyed them where they lived. The image of them 'crouched' or 'fallen on their knees' in their dwellings means they were struck so suddenly that they had no chance to flee, repent, or defend themselves. Their homes, which had been symbols of their security and pride, became their graves. The lesson is that worldly strength and comfort give no protection from God's decree when people persist in arrogance and rejection of truth, and that the fate of earlier nations is a warning to later ones.

translation: And (We destroyed) 'Ad and Thamud; and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. Satan made their deeds attractive to them and averted them from the path, though they were endowed with insight.
interpretation: The verse points to the ruined homes of 'Ad and Thamud as visible, lasting evidence that nations who rejected God's messengers were destroyed. Their downfall did not come from lack of intelligence or ability, since they were people of perception and skill. It came because Satan made their wrongdoing look appealing, so they mistook falsehood for right and turned away from God's path. The lesson for the listener is that worldly cleverness and strength do not protect anyone if the heart is deceived by desire and arrogance, so one should learn from the ruins of the past and not let Satan's embellishment blind one to the truth.

translation: And [We also destroyed] Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman. Moses came to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly in the land, and they were not able to outstrip [Us].
interpretation: The verse warns that wealth, political power, and worldly authority offer no protection from God's judgment. Qarun (representing riches), Pharaoh (representing royal power), and Haman (representing the machinery of state) each rejected the clear signs brought by Moses, not for lack of evidence but out of arrogance. Their pride made them refuse to submit to truth. The closing phrase, 'they were not able to outstrip Us,' means that they could not escape or outrun God's punishment, so every arrogant power that defies divine guidance ultimately meets its appointed downfall, however secure it appears.

translation: So each We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those who were seized by the Blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah would never have wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment is never arbitrary but is a just consequence of a people's own wrongdoing. The earlier nations, such as 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun, Pharaoh and others, were each punished in a way that fit their sin and arrogance, showing that God has many means of seizing the wrongdoers, and that no worldly power, wealth or strength can protect against them. The closing statement affirms God's perfect justice: He did not oppress them, rather they brought ruin upon themselves by rejecting the truth and persisting in disobedience, so that the blame lies on their own choices and not on their Lord. This serves as a warning for later generations to heed the message and repent before the same fate overtakes them.

translation: The likeness of those who take protectors other than God is like that of the spider, which makes for itself a house; and indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse teaches that anything people rely on besides God for protection, provision, or security, whether wealth, status, power, or other people, gives only the appearance of safety. Like a spider's web, it looks like a shelter but cannot shield against heat, cold, wind, or even a light touch. Those who place their ultimate trust in created things build their lives on something that collapses when real hardship comes. Real, lasting security comes only from relying on God, who alone has power over benefit and harm. The closing phrase, 'if only they knew,' suggests that this misplaced trust stems from ignorance: if people truly understood the weakness of what they depend on, they would turn to God alone.

translation: Indeed, God knows whatever they invoke besides Him of anything; and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse is a warning to those who worship idols and other false deities: God is fully aware of everything they call upon instead of Him, and He knows how powerless and worthless those objects are, as well as the true motives behind the worshippers' devotion. Nothing they invoke has any real existence as a partner to God or any power to benefit or harm. Because God is Almighty, He can bring them to account and render their false gods useless. Because He is All-Wise, His judgment and His dealings with them are perfectly just and purposeful. The verse therefore both exposes the emptiness of polytheism and reassures believers that God's knowledge and power overshadow every false claim.

translation: And these examples We strike for the people, but none will understand them except those who have knowledge.
interpretation: God teaches through parables to bring abstract truths closer to human understanding, yet the benefit of them is not automatic. Only those with true knowledge, meaning deep insight and reflection joined with awareness of God, grasp the wisdom behind them and apply it. Merely hearing a parable is not enough; understanding it is a mark of the people of knowledge, so the verse elevates the status of the learned and calls everyone to contemplate the Qur'an's parables rather than pass over them heedlessly.

translation: God created the heavens and the earth with truth. Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers.
interpretation: The creation of the heavens and the earth was not random or purposeless play, but was established upon truth, wisdom, order, and purpose. Its precise design and harmony point to a Creator who is wise, powerful, and just, and who holds creation accountable to a meaningful end. Those who believe are the ones who reflect on this and benefit from it, because faith opens the heart to read creation as evidence of God's existence, oneness, and wisdom, which strengthens their certainty and moves them to live purposefully and responsibly.

translation: Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prevents immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of God is greater. And God knows what you do.
interpretation: The verse links two acts of devotion, engaging with revelation and keeping up prayer, as the foundation of moral transformation. Prayer, when performed with presence of heart and consistency, acts as an inner restraint: it renews a person's awareness of God several times a day, shaming them away from indecency and from what conscience recognizes as wrong. Yet the verse says that the remembrance of God is greater than prayer's outward form. The ultimate purpose of prayer is a living, constant consciousness of God, which shapes behavior, and which is also greater in that God's remembrance of His servants surpasses all else. The closing reminder that God knows everything people do reinforces accountability: one cannot merely perform rituals while neglecting their fruit, because God sees whether prayer truly restrains a person from wrong.

translation: And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the way that is best, except for those of them who commit injustice. And say: 'We believe in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to you; our God and your God is one, and to Him we submit.'
interpretation: This verse lays down the ethics of interfaith dialogue. Muslims are instructed to engage Jews and Christians with courtesy, wisdom, and fairness, using arguments that are gentle, honest, and aimed at clarifying the truth rather than winning or humiliating. The only exception is those who show injustice, such as aggression, persecution, or obstinate hostility, for whom a firmer response may be warranted. The believers are to ground the discussion in common ground: faith in the revelation sent to both communities, and in the oneness of God. By affirming that the God of Muslims and the People of the Book is the same one God, the verse stresses shared monotheistic roots, while ending with the distinctive Muslim commitment of total submission to Him. Dialogue should therefore combine respectful engagement with a confident and clear statement of one's own faith.

translation: And thus We have sent down the Book to you. Those to whom We gave the Book believe in it, and among these (people) are some who believe in it. And none denies Our signs except the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ankabut 29:47) affirms that the Qur'an is a revelation from God in continuity with earlier scriptures, sent down to Muhammad just as previous books were sent to earlier prophets. Those among the People of the Book who sincerely held to their own scripture recognize the truth of the Qur'an because it confirms what they already know, and so they believe in it. Likewise, some of the people of Makkah and the Arabs ('these') will come to believe in it. Rejection of God's signs does not stem from any lack of clarity in them but from stubborn, willful concealment of the truth; only those whose hearts are settled in disbelief knowingly deny signs that are plain, since 'jahd' means denying something one recognizes to be true.

translation: And you did not recite any book before it, nor did you write one with your right hand; in that case, those who follow falsehood would have had cause for doubt.
interpretation: God points to the Prophet Muhammad's unlettered state as proof of the Qur'an's divine origin. His community knew that before revelation he had never read scripture or written anything, so he could not have learned these accounts of earlier prophets and nations from books or composed the Qur'an himself. Had he been a reader and writer, those who reject the truth could have plausibly claimed he copied it from earlier writings or authored it. Because he was unlettered, that claim has no basis, and his being unlettered is itself evidence that the revelation came from God alone.

translation: Rather, it is clear signs preserved in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge. And none denies Our signs except the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The Qur'an is not a mere book dependent on writing, as the Prophet's opponents imagined; it is a set of manifest, self-evident proofs that God has lodged in the hearts of the scholars who understand and memorize it, so that its truth is secure and recognizable to people of knowledge. Its clarity and its preservation in the minds of the learned bear witness to its divine origin. Those who reject these clear signs do so not from any lack of evidence but out of injustice: they wrong themselves and the truth by arrogance, stubbornness and refusal to submit to what they know to be right.

translation: And they say, "Why are not signs sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The signs are only with God, and I am only a clear warner."
interpretation: The verse teaches that miracles are not at the command or disposal of any prophet; they belong to God alone, who sends them when and if His wisdom decrees. Those who demand ever more signs are usually not seeking truth but evading it, since the Qur'an itself and the signs in creation are already sufficient for a sincere seeker. The Prophet's role is limited to delivering a clear warning and conveying the message plainly, while guidance and the timing of any sign remain with God. It thus reminds believers to keep a proper sense of the limits of human messengers and to respond to the evidence already given rather than setting conditions for faith.

translation: Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them? Indeed, in that is a mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse answers those who demanded further miraculous signs as proof of the Prophet's truth. God points out that the Qur'an is itself a sufficient and enduring miracle: it is not a one-time event that fades with those who witnessed it, but a living revelation recited to people in every age, whose eloquence, guidance, and truth stand as proof. Whoever reflects on it with sincerity will find in it mercy, since it guides the heart, heals the soul, and shows the path to salvation, and also a reminder that renews awareness of God, of one's purpose, and of the Hereafter. Yet only those inclined to believe benefit from it, because faith opens the heart to receive its light, while those who are determined to reject it remain unmoved however many signs they see.

translation: Say: "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth. Those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah - it is they who are the losers."
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to rest his case with God as the ultimate and all-knowing witness over the dispute between him and those who deny his message. Since God knows everything in the heavens and the earth, He knows the truth of the Prophet's claim and the real motives of his opponents, so no further proof is needed beyond His testimony. The verse then warns that those who place their faith in falsehood, such as idols, false deities, and baseless claims, while rejecting the one true God, have made the worst exchange. They trade truth for illusion and so forfeit their own souls, their purpose, and their eternal reward, which is true loss.

translation: They ask you to hasten the punishment. Had it not been for a term already appointed, the punishment would certainly have come to them. But it will surely come upon them suddenly, while they are unaware.
interpretation: The disbelievers mockingly challenge the Prophet to bring down God's punishment, taking its delay as proof that the warning is empty. The verse answers that the delay is not weakness or falsehood but mercy and wisdom: God has fixed a specific term for each people, and punishment comes only when that term is complete. Their time is limited, and when it expires the punishment will arrive without warning, while they are heedless and unprepared. The lesson is that a reprieve is a chance to repent, not a sign of safety, and that mocking God's warnings only increases the danger of being taken by surprise.

translation: They ask you to hasten the punishment, while indeed Hell will surely encompass the disbelievers.
interpretation: The disbelievers mock the Prophet by demanding that God's threatened punishment come immediately, taking its delay as proof that it is false. The verse answers that the delay does not mean the punishment will never come. Hell already surrounds them in the sense that it is certain and inescapable, and they are heading toward it with no way out. Their deeds and disbelief are bringing them to it, and what they treat as a joke is a reality that will enclose them completely. God postpones the punishment out of His mercy and wisdom, not because He is unable to bring it.

translation: On the Day when the punishment will envelop them from above them and from beneath their feet, and He will say: 'Taste what you used to do.'
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment when the disbelievers' punishment will surround them completely, with no direction of escape and no refuge, so that they are fully engulfed in it. The command 'Taste what you used to do' teaches that the torment is not an arbitrary imposition but the direct and just consequence of their own deeds, which they now experience as a bitter reality. Their earlier rejection of the truth and their wrongdoing return to them as the very thing they must taste, reminding the reader that actions carry real moral weight and that each person will be held accountable for them.

translation: O My servants who have believed, indeed My earth is spacious, so worship Me alone.
interpretation: This verse tells believers that no place or circumstance can excuse them from serving God. If they are oppressed or prevented from practicing their faith in one land, they should not resign themselves to humiliation or compromise their religion, because God's earth is wide and offers other places where they can live in safety and worship freely. Migration for the sake of faith is therefore encouraged, and the verse teaches that devotion to God takes priority over homeland, comfort, and worldly attachments, since sincere worship belongs to Him alone wherever one may be.

translation: Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse reminds us that death is a certain fate for every living being, with no exception, and that it is not the end of existence but a passage to accountability. Because every person will return to God after death to be judged for their deeds, life should be lived with awareness, sincerity, and responsibility, without being deceived by worldly attachments, since the final destination is God alone.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty dwellings in Paradise beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of the doers [of good].
interpretation: This verse affirms that faith joined with righteous action leads to a lasting and honorable reward. God promises the believers not merely entry into Paradise but exalted homes within it, a sign of high rank and comfort, with rivers flowing beneath them and eternal residence free from fear of loss or removal. By calling it the 'reward of the doers,' the verse shows that Paradise is granted in recognition of sincere effort and patient perseverance, including steadfastness under hardship and the willingness to migrate or sacrifice for faith, as the surrounding verses address. It encourages believers that no good deed is wasted, and that the temporary difficulties of this world are far outweighed by the everlasting reward God has prepared.

translation: Those who are patient and who put their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 16:42 and 29:59) describes the quality of the believers who earn God's reward: they combine steadfast patience with reliance on God. Their patience means holding firm to obedience, abstaining from sin, and enduring hardship and persecution for the sake of their faith without despair or compromise. Their trust (tawakkul) means that, after doing their part and taking the means available, they hand the outcome over to God, confident that He alone controls results and will not let their efforts be lost. The two qualities complete each other: patience sustains a person through the trial, while trust in God gives the heart peace and certainty that relief and recompense come from Him.

translation: And how many a creature there is that does not carry its own provision; Allah provides for it and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse comforts believers who feared poverty or hardship if they emigrated for the sake of their faith, as in the context of leaving Makkah. It teaches that sustenance does not depend on one's homeland, wealth, or storing up resources, because many creatures neither store nor carry their food, yet God sustains them each day wherever they are. So the believer should not let worry about livelihood hold them back from obeying God or from what is right, while still striving by lawful means. The closing names, the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, assure that God hears their prayers and knows their needs and circumstances, so He will provide for them as He provides for all His creation.

translation: And if you were to ask them, 'Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?' they would surely say, 'Allah.' Then how are they deluded away from the truth?
interpretation: The verse points out a contradiction in the polytheists' belief: they acknowledge by their own nature and reason that Allah alone is the Creator and the one who governs the order of the cosmos, including the regular courses of the sun and moon. Yet in worship and devotion they turn to others besides Him. Since recognizing that Allah is the sole Creator logically requires devoting worship to Him alone, the closing question, 'Then how are they turned away?', is a rebuke. It shows that their denial of tawhid in worship is not based on ignorance or lack of evidence, but on perversity and the diversion of their hearts from what they themselves already know to be true.

translation: God extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it for whomever He wills. Indeed, God is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The abundance or scarcity of a person's livelihood is not a measure of their worth or of God's love or anger toward them, but flows from God's wise and all-encompassing knowledge. He gives or withholds according to what He knows to be best for each individual, since wealth may be a test of gratitude and poverty a test of patience. A believer should therefore strive lawfully for provision while trusting that the outcome is governed by a wisdom beyond human sight, and should respond to whatever portion they receive with gratitude, contentment, and reliance on God rather than envy or despair.

translation: And if you ask them, 'Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?' they will surely say, 'Allah.' Say, 'Praise be to Allah.' But most of them do not use reason.
interpretation: The verse points out a contradiction in the idolaters' belief. They admit that Allah alone is the Creator and Sustainer who revives dead land with rain, yet they still worship others besides Him.
