Human tools for recording are finite: every tree turned into a pen and oceans, replenished sevenfold, turned into ink would run out before the meaning and effects of God's words could be fully written down. The number seven stands for abundance, not a literal limit. The lesson is that human beings should be humble about how little they know compared with God's infinite knowledge, and should recognize that His creation holds endless signs to reflect on. The closing names, 'Almighty' and 'Wise', explain why His words are inexhaustible: nothing can overpower His will, and everything He decrees is set in perfect wisdom.

translation: Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse stresses the limitless power of God: creating and resurrecting all of humanity requires no more effort, time, or means than creating or raising one individual. God needs only to will, and it is, so the disbelievers' doubt that the resurrection of countless generations is possible rests on a false, human measure of ability. The closing names, All-Hearing and All-Seeing, add that God knows every word and deed of every person and therefore will hold each one to account, with nothing escaping His perception despite the vast numbers involved.

translation: Do you not see that God causes the night to merge into the day and causes the day to merge into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running its course for a specified term, and that God is fully Aware of what you do?
interpretation: The verse points to the precise, orderly system of the cosmos as proof of God's power, wisdom, and unity. The gradual lengthening and shortening of night and day, and the fixed courses of the sun and moon, never fail or fall into disorder, and each is bound for an appointed end, which is a reminder that the world is created, dependent on God, and temporary. The verse then draws a moral conclusion: the One who governs the heavens with such exactness is also fully aware of every human deed, so people should not be heedless. They should reflect on these signs, worship God alone, and act with accountability, knowing that nothing they do escapes Him and that, like the sun and moon, they are heading toward an appointed term and a return to Him.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse grounds the preceding divine help and justice in the nature of God Himself: He alone is the real, self-existent and unchanging Truth, so His promises, judgments and support for the wronged always come to pass. Everything people call upon besides Him, whether idols, powers, or false hopes, has no independent reality or power and is therefore empty and doomed to fail. Since God is supreme above all things and greater than anything that can rival Him, He can grant victory, sustain what is right and bring falsehood down. The believer is thus called to place trust and worship in God alone, and not to be awed by any worldly force that opposes the truth.

translation: Do you not see that the ships sail through the sea by the favor of God, that He may show you some of His signs? Indeed, in that are signs for everyone who is steadfastly patient and deeply grateful.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection on something familiar: ships moving over vast, powerful waters. Their sailing is possible only because God has set the laws of buoyancy, wind, and currents and made the sea subservient to people, so it is a blessing rather than a human achievement alone. Such blessings are meant to point the heart toward the Creator and Sustainer. Only those who are 'sabbar' (very patient, steady in hardship and in the face of the sea's dangers and life's trials) and 'shakur' (very thankful, recognizing God's favor in ease) truly benefit from these signs. Believers hold both states at once: patience when tried, and gratitude when blessed. Those two qualities open the mind and heart to perceive God's power and mercy in everyday phenomena.

translation: And when waves cover them like canopies, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them remain moderate. And none denies Our signs except every treacherous, ungrateful person.
interpretation: The verse shows how human nature turns to God with pure, undivided devotion when worldly means fail and death seems near, which reveals that awareness of God's lordship is innate. Yet once safety returns, people divide: some stay between gratitude and heedlessness, partially holding to the sincerity they pledged at sea, while others abandon it. The ones who persist in rejecting God's signs are described as 'khattar' (those who break covenants and betray their pledges) and 'kafur' (those who are deeply ungrateful). Their denial is therefore not from lack of evidence, since they themselves experienced the truth in their hour of need, but from betraying the promise they made to God and from ingratitude for His rescue.

translation: O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will be able to compensate for his child, nor will a child be able to compensate for his father in anything. Indeed, the promise of God is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you about God.
interpretation: The verse calls all people to God-consciousness by reminding them of the Day of Judgment, when even the closest family bonds cannot bring relief, since each soul bears its own responsibility and no one can bear another's burden. Because the resurrection and reckoning are certain, people should not postpone repentance or rely on relatives, status, or wealth. The verse warns of two sources of delusion: the allure of worldly life, which makes people forget the hereafter, and Satan, who tempts people to sin by inflating their hopes in God's mercy while neglecting obedience. The believer is thus urged to prepare sincerely for the meeting with God through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: Indeed, with Allah alone is the knowledge of the Hour; He sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse affirms that certain domains of the unseen are held by Allah alone, so that human beings are reminded of the limits of their knowledge and of their total dependence on Him. The timing of the Last Hour, the coming of rain at its appointed time and place, the condition of the unborn child in the womb, what one will earn or experience in the future, and where and when one will die all lie beyond human certainty, even though people may make estimates or use means to anticipate some of them. Because no one can be sure of tomorrow or of the place of their death, the believer should live in constant readiness: acting righteously now, not putting off repentance, trusting in Allah's decree, and avoiding arrogance about one's plans. The closing names, 'Alim (All-Knowing) and Khabir (All-Aware), stress that His knowledge encompasses both the outer and the hidden details of every matter, so nothing in creation escapes Him.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Mim.
interpretation: These disconnected letters, which open Surah Al-Baqarah and several other surahs, are best understood as a challenge to the Arabs, whose eloquence was unmatched. The Qur'an is composed of the very same letters of the alphabet that they use in their own speech, yet they cannot produce anything like it. The letters therefore point to the miraculous nature of the Revelation and its divine origin. They also draw the listener's attention, preparing the heart to receive the message that follows, while their true and complete meaning remains with God alone.

translation: The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is not a human composition but a revelation sent down by God, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. Its source is certain, so it is free of any falsehood, contradiction, or legitimate cause for doubt. Because the One who revealed it is the Lord of all the worlds, its guidance is universal. It is meant for all humankind, and its authority rests on divine origin rather than on any human claim. A person who approaches it sincerely can therefore trust it fully as a guide in belief and conduct.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has invented it'? Rather, it is the truth from your Lord, that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, so that they may be guided.
interpretation: The verse answers the accusation of the disbelievers that Muhammad forged the Qur'an. God rejects the claim and affirms that the revelation is the truth from the Lord, which a mere human could not have fabricated. Its purpose is to warn the Arabs, a people who had no prophet sent to them for a long time, reminding them of accountability before God, so that through this warning they may turn from heedlessness and polytheism and find the right path. The verse shows that revelation is a mercy whose aim is guidance, and that the Prophet's role is to warn and convey, not to invent.

translation: It is God who created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six days, then established Himself on the Throne. You have no protector or intercessor besides Him. Will you not then take heed?
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to worship God alone in His power as Creator and Sovereign. Because He alone brought the whole of creation into being and governs it from the Throne, no other being has any real authority to protect or help people, and no one can intercede except by His leave. Turning to other patrons or intermediaries is therefore irrational and futile. The closing question rebukes human heedlessness and invites reflection: if people considered who made and sustains the universe, they would see that dependence and devotion belong to God alone.

translation: He regulates the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day the measure of which is a thousand years of those which you count.
interpretation: The verse says that God alone governs all of creation. His decrees and commands descend from the highest realm to the earth, and then every matter, including deeds, outcomes, and accounts, returns to Him. This happens on a scale of time that is vastly beyond human reckoning, so what seems long to us is a single day for Him. The lesson is that God is in complete control, and that human haste and limited time-perception should not lead anyone to doubt His wisdom, His timing, or the certainty of the return to Him and the Day of Judgment. People should therefore be patient, trust His management of affairs, and live mindful that all things end with Him.

translation: That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse points to the One who has just been described as the Originator and Sustainer of all things, and affirms that His knowledge is total: nothing hidden from creatures and nothing apparent to them escapes Him. Yet this complete knowledge is joined with two qualities that shape how humans should relate to Him. He is al-'Aziz, whose power and dominion cannot be resisted, so He is able to enact what He knows and wills; and He is al-Rahim, whose mercy tempers that might, so His full awareness of people's secret intentions and open deeds is a basis for hope and not only for fear. The believer is thus called to live with the awareness that God sees both inner and outer life, to reverence His authority, and to trust in His compassion.

translation: He who perfected everything He created, and began the creation of the human being from clay.
interpretation: The verse points to the excellence and harmony in all of God's creation: each thing is made with fitting proportion and purpose, so that nothing He fashioned is flawed or without wisdom. Even the human being, whose origin is humble clay, was brought into existence by the same perfect craftsmanship. This is meant to cultivate humility in people by reminding them of their lowly beginnings, and to cultivate gratitude and awe toward the Creator, whose power turned simple earth into a conscious, honored being. It also invites reflection that the One who could create so beautifully from clay is fully able to resurrect and hold humans to account.

translation: Then He made his progeny from an extract of a despised fluid.
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Sajdah, 32:8) points to how God, after originating the first human from clay, established the continuation of mankind through reproduction. Human offspring come from a drop of fluid, the 'extract' (sulala) being the essence drawn from a lowly, insignificant liquid. The description 'despised' (mahin) is meant to humble the human being and remind him of his modest physical origins, so that he does not grow arrogant. It also highlights God's power and wisdom: from such a humble beginning He fashions a complete, hearing, seeing, reasoning person, which should lead one to gratitude, humility, and belief in the Creator and in the resurrection.

translation: Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit, and made for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little is the thanks you give.
interpretation: The verse (Surat As-Sajdah 32:9) describes how God perfected the human being after creating him from clay: He shaped him in balanced proportion and breathed into him a soul that He honored by attributing it to Himself, which gives humans life, consciousness, and a dignity above other creatures. He then endowed humanity with the faculties of knowledge: hearing and sight, which receive information from the world, and the hearts (minds), which reflect, understand, and discern truth from falsehood. These faculties are trusts and blessings meant to lead a person to recognize the Creator and to worship Him. The closing rebuke, 'little is the thanks you give,' means that most people fail to use these gifts for their intended purpose, neglecting gratitude through belief, obedience, and reflection on God's signs, so true thankfulness is shown by using hearing, sight, and intellect to acknowledge God and follow His guidance.

translation: And they say, "When we have become lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse shows that the deniers' rejection of resurrection is not really a rational objection about the possibility of recreating bodies that have decayed and mixed into the soil. God, who created them the first time, is able to bring them back. Their real problem is a denial of accountability: they disbelieve in meeting their Lord because acknowledging that meeting would oblige them to answer for their deeds. Their mocking question is a pretext covering a deeper refusal to submit to moral responsibility before God.

translation: Say: The Angel of Death, who has been put in charge of you, will take your souls; then to your Lord you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse answers those who deny the resurrection by affirming that death is not random or the end of existence. It is an ordered process carried out by an angel appointed by God, who has no independence and acts only by God's command. Human life is therefore bounded and managed by a higher authority, and death is a transition, not annihilation. After the soul is taken, every person is returned to their Creator and Sustainer, who will hold them accountable for their deeds. The verse calls people to remember their mortality, to prepare for the meeting with God, and to live with responsibility and awareness that they will be answerable to Him.

translation: If only you could see when the guilty hang their heads before their Lord: 'Our Lord, we have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do righteous deeds; we are now certain.'
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Resurrection, when those who denied the resurrection and persisted in sin stand before God in utter shame and humiliation, heads bowed. What they once rejected in the world has become plain to their eyes and ears, so they plead for a second chance to live righteously, claiming that their doubt has turned into certainty. Their plea comes too late, because faith and good works are only of value when they come from free choice and trust in the unseen in this life. Once the truth is seen directly, belief is no longer a test, and the chance to act has passed. The verse warns the heedless to reflect and repent now, before regret becomes useless.

translation: And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance; but the word from Me has come into effect: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together.'
interpretation: God's power is absolute, and He could have compelled every soul to be guided, leaving no room for disbelief. But He created humans and jinn with free will, so that faith would be a matter of real choice and accountability. Those who knowingly choose rejection and persist in denial, despite the clear signs and warnings sent to them, bring upon themselves the decree that was already spoken. Hell will be filled with those who chose to disbelieve. The verse therefore does not excuse misguidance as divine compulsion; it affirms that guidance is offered while the final outcome rests on human choice, and that God's warning is certain to be fulfilled.

translation: So taste [the punishment], for you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours; indeed, We have forgotten you. And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse is the address of God to the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment. Their punishment is a fitting consequence of their conduct: because they neglected the reality of standing before God and lived as though no reckoning would come, they are now treated as those who are forgotten. God does not literally forget, since forgetfulness is impossible for Him. The phrase is a rhetorical mirroring of their deed, meaning that He leaves them in the Fire and withholds His mercy and care from them, just as they abandoned obedience and ignored His warnings. The verse closes by stressing that the lasting punishment is not arbitrary but the just recompense for their own deeds, which shows that the denial of the Hereafter in this life leads directly to enduring loss in the next.

translation: Only those truly believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration and glorify their Lord with praise, and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: True faith is shown through humble responsiveness to God's revelation, not through a mere claim to belief. A real believer is moved by the reminder of God's verses to bow in worship, to exalt God above all imperfection while praising Him, and to put aside the pride that makes people refuse the truth. Arrogance is the barrier that keeps people from submitting to divine guidance, while humility is the sign of sincere belief, so a person's reaction to being reminded of God's signs reveals the true state of their heart.

translation: Their sides draw away from their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and in hope, and they spend from what We have provided for them.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who sacrifice the comfort of sleep in the night to stand in prayer and supplication. Their hearts are balanced between fear of God's punishment and hope for His mercy and reward, so neither despair nor false security overtakes them. Their devotion is not only private worship but also shows in generosity, since they give charity from the provision God has granted them. True faith is thus shown in both night-time devotion to God and in compassion toward His creatures, and it is this combination that earns the great reward promised in the following verse.

translation: No soul knows what has been hidden for them of joy and delight for the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the reward Allah has prepared for the sincere believers, especially those who rise at night in worship, is beyond human imagination and knowledge. It is a concealed treasure of delight that no creature, not even angels or prophets, can fully comprehend in this world. Just as these believers hid their devotion in the privacy of the night, away from people's sight, God hides their reward and then discloses it only in the Hereafter, so the recompense matches the deeds in kind and exceeds them in splendor. The phrase 'joy of the eyes' conveys lasting happiness and contentment, and it assures believers that the reward is a just recompense from God's generosity for their deeds, not a mere wage.

translation: Is then one who is a believer like one who is a transgressor? They are not equal.
interpretation: The verse (Surat As-Sajdah, 32:18) rejects the idea that faith and defiance of God can end up with the same result. Since God is just, He cannot treat the one who believed and did righteous deeds the same as the one who rebelled against Him and disobeyed His commands. The rhetorical question stresses that moral choices have real consequences, and that the believer and the transgressor differ in their standing with God, in their conduct, and in their final destiny: the believer is promised the gardens of refuge, and the transgressor the Fire. The verse therefore affirms divine justice and calls people to recognize that a person's faith and actions determine their ultimate fate.

translation: As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Refuge, as a welcome (hospitality) for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse shows that true faith is completed by righteous action, and that God honors such people with an entertainment fit for honored guests. 'Jannat al-Ma'wa' (Gardens of Refuge) are called so because they are the final dwelling and shelter where the believers find rest and security after the hardships of this world. The word 'nuzul' signifies the hospitality prepared for a guest on arrival, which implies that what God has in store beyond this initial welcome is even greater. Paradise is thus presented not as a mere wage but as a gracious reception, which God bestows in recognition of the believers' deeds, while those deeds themselves remain a means made possible by His grace.

translation: But as for those who defied God and disobeyed, their refuge is the Fire. Every time they want to come out of it, they are returned into it, and it is said to them: 'Taste the punishment of the Fire, which you used to deny.'
interpretation: The verse sets the fate of the willful transgressors against that of the believers who are given the Gardens just before it. Those who 'fasaqu' have stepped outside obedience to God and rejected His warnings, so the Fire becomes their abode, not a passing stop. The picture of them trying to escape and being driven back shows that no way out exists and that their hope is crushed again and again, which makes the torment psychological as well as physical. The closing rebuke, 'Taste the punishment which you used to deny,' says their suffering is the direct result of their own mockery and disbelief. In life they treated the warnings of the Hereafter as lies, and now they face the reality they dismissed. The verse works as a moral warning: denial does not cancel the truth, and every act of defiance has a consequence that cannot be avoided.

translation: And We will surely let them taste the nearer punishment before the greater punishment, so that perhaps they will return.
interpretation: God declares that before the ultimate punishment of the Hereafter, He sends lesser, worldly trials such as hardship, illness, loss, and calamity to those who persist in defiance. These are not mere vengeance but a merciful warning and a call to awaken: they are meant to shake people out of heedlessness, humble their arrogance, and lead them to repent and return to faith and obedience before the opportunity is lost and the far graver punishment becomes inescapable.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord and then turns away from them? Indeed, We will take retribution from the criminals.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest wrongdoing is not mere ignorance but willful rejection after clear guidance. When a person is reminded of God's signs, whether in revelation or in the created world, and understands them yet deliberately turns away out of arrogance or desire, he wrongs himself and truth in the worst way, because he had the means to be guided and chose heedlessness. Such persistent turning away makes a person among the 'mujrimun', those who sever themselves from their Lord's guidance and commit crimes against His truth, and God promises to hold them to account with just retribution. This is both a warning that rejecting divine reminders carries real consequences, and an urging to respond to guidance with humility and openness before it is too late.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, so do not be in doubt about meeting him. And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel.
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet Muhammad that revelation is not a novelty: just as Moses received a divine Book, so too has Muhammad received one, and the two missions are connected. The command not to doubt 'meeting him' is read as a reference to the Prophet's meeting Moses, as in the Night Journey, or to the certainty that Moses truly received revelation and that Muhammad will experience the same kind of encounter with God's guidance. The Torah was meant as a guide for the Children of Israel, showing that revelation always aims at guiding people to the right path. The verse therefore strengthens the Prophet's confidence and affirms the continuity of prophecy across communities.

translation: And We made from among them leaders who guided by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs.
interpretation: This verse (Surat as-Sajdah, 32:24) teaches that spiritual and moral leadership is not an inherited privilege but a reward earned through two qualities: steadfast patience and firm certainty. Among the Children of Israel, those who endured hardship, obeyed God's commands, and refrained from wrongdoing were raised by God as guides whose direction came from divine revelation, not personal whims. Patience gave them the strength to hold to the truth through trials, while certainty in God's signs gave them clear insight and conviction. Together these made their guidance credible and effective. The lesson for believers is that anyone who wishes to lead others toward goodness must first be tested and remain firm, and must ground their knowledge in sure faith.

translation: Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.
interpretation: The verse teaches that disputes over religion and truth, which people cannot settle in this world because of pride, envy, and rivalry, will be settled by God alone with perfect knowledge and justice on the Day of Resurrection. It offers reassurance to the believer, here addressed through the Prophet, that he need not despair over the persistence of disagreement or take on the burden of forcing a final settlement. His duty is to convey the truth and remain steadfast, while the final decisive judgment belongs to God, before whom every claim will be exposed and every person held accountable.

translation: Is it not a guidance for them how many generations We destroyed before them, in whose dwellings they walk about? Indeed in that are signs. Then will they not hear?
interpretation: God reproaches the deniers among the Quraysh and others for failing to learn from history. The ruined homes of earlier peoples such as 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Lot lay along their own trade routes, and they pass through them with no concern. Those ruins are plain proofs that rejecting the messengers brings destruction, and that the same fate may befall those who persist in denial. The closing question, 'Then will they not hear?', rebukes them for being deaf to the warning. These signs speak to anyone who listens and reflects, yet the heedless pass them by and gain no guidance. The verse calls people to take lessons from the fate of past nations and to respond to the message before the time to repent is gone.

translation: Do they not see that We drive water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops from which their livestock and they themselves eat? Then do they not see?
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy in reviving dead, parched earth with rain so that it yields food for both animals and humans. The revival of lifeless land is a visible, everyday sign that the One who brings vegetation out of barren soil is able to resurrect the dead and to sustain His creatures. Those who deny the Resurrection or the divine origin of the message are rebuked for ignoring evidence in front of their eyes: if they reflected on how their very sustenance depends on God's gift, they would recognize His power, be grateful, and accept the truth.

translation: And they say, "When will this decision come, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Sajdah 32:28) shows the mockery of the disbelievers, who ask the believers and the Prophet about the 'fath', the final judgment or decisive ruling between truth and falsehood, which the believers had been promised. They ask 'when' not out of sincere inquiry but out of denial and ridicule, supposing that a delay in the promised judgment proves it to be false. The following verses answer them: on the Day of that decision, their belief will no longer benefit them and they will be given no respite. The lesson is that God's promise is certain, but its timing belongs to God's wisdom alone. Delay is a test and an opportunity to repent, and it is no evidence that the warning is untrue.

translation: Say: On the Day of the Decision, their faith will be of no benefit to those who disbelieved, nor will they be granted respite.
interpretation: The verse (Surah As-Sajdah 32:29) teaches that faith has value only while a person is still free to choose it. On the Day of Judgment, when God decides between truth and falsehood, the truth becomes undeniable. Belief at that moment is forced by sight rather than freely chosen through reflection and trust in the unseen. It therefore cannot undo a lifetime of denial, and no further time will be given to repent or make amends. The verse urges people to turn to God and act on their faith now, while repentance is still accepted, instead of putting it off until the opportunity is gone.

translation: So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are waiting.
interpretation: The Prophet is told to stop arguing with those who obstinately reject the message, since they have already been given clear warning, and to leave their affair to God. He is to wait patiently for God's promise of vindication, while the deniers wait for what they hope will be his downfall. The verse closes with a quiet warning: the outcome they are awaiting will in fact turn against them, because God's decree will prevail and truth will be made manifest.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, be mindful of God and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, God is ever All-Knowing and All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse calls the Prophet to hold fast to God-consciousness (taqwa) as the guiding principle of his leadership, and not to yield to the pressure, bargaining, or suggestions of those who reject faith openly or feign it while opposing it in secret. If the Prophet is commanded this way, then all believers are even more bound by it: when worldly pressure, social influence, or the desire for compromise would lead them to abandon truth and justice, they should refuse and remain loyal to God's guidance. The closing statement gives the reason: God knows the true intentions and the hidden schemes of all people and is wise in what He commands, so following His direction is safer and better than following the counsel of those who oppose Him.

translation: And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah is ever Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet, and through him every believer, to hold fast to divine revelation as the sole guide for conduct, without bending it to the pressures, desires, or opinions of people, whether opponents or hypocrites. The reminder that God is fully aware of all that people do grounds this obedience in accountability: no action, intention, or compromise is hidden from Him. So a believer should be sincere and steadfast in following revelation, trusting that God knows their efforts and will deal with them justly.

translation: And put your trust in God; and God suffices as a Guardian (Disposer of affairs).
interpretation: The verse calls the believer, first the Prophet and by extension every Muslim, to rely fully on God after taking the means available, without fearing opposition, hostility, or the schemes of hypocrites and enemies. Trust in God is not passivity but a settled confidence that outcomes lie in His hands. Since God alone is sufficient to manage and protect one's affairs, there is no need to seek security or support from anyone else, and whoever entrusts their matters to Him will not be left without help.

translation: Allah has not placed two hearts within the body of any man. Nor has He made your wives whom you declare to be like your mothers' backs (zihar) truly your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons truly your sons. That is merely your saying with your mouths, but Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the right way.
interpretation: The verse teaches that reality is determined by what Allah has established, not by human claims or empty words. Just as a person cannot have two hearts, a person cannot hold two contradictory realities at once: a wife cannot become a mother simply by a verbal formula, and an adopted child cannot become a biological son simply by being called one. These pre-Islamic customs were mere utterances with no real basis, so they cannot carry the legal consequences of true motherhood or true sonship, such as inheritance rights, prohibited marriage, and lineage. Allah alone speaks the truth and guides to the straight path, so legal and family relationships must be grounded in truth and in His revealed rulings rather than in invented customs. This prepared the ground for the following command to call adopted children by their real fathers' names, preserving true lineage while still encouraging kindness and care toward them.

translation: Call them by their fathers' names; that is more just in the sight of God. But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in faith and your close associates. There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake, but only for what your hearts deliberately intend. And God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse sets the rule that people must be identified by their true lineage, which ends the pre-Islamic practice of adoption in which an adopted child was treated as a biological son, with the inheritance and family-law consequences that followed. Justice and truthfulness require that a person be named for his real father. Where the father is unknown, the Qur'an does not leave the person without a place in society. He is addressed as a brother in faith or a mawla (a freed associate or close friend), so he keeps his dignity and belongs to the community. The verse also states a principle of moral responsibility. Accidental slips, such as mistakenly calling someone by the wrong father's name, are not sinful, because accountability rests on the intention of the heart and not on an unintended error. God's forgiveness and mercy ease the burden on believers who err without intending to.

translation: The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers. And those related by blood are closer to one another in the Decree of God than the believers and the emigrants, except that you may do some kindness to your close friends. That has been written in the Book.
interpretation: The verse sets out the rank of the Prophet and the order of rights and duties in the new Muslim community. The Prophet's authority and care for the believers come before their own desires and personal choices, so obeying him takes priority over what they would choose for themselves, and his concern for their salvation exceeds their own. His wives are called 'mothers of the believers' as a mark of respect, which means they are honored and may never be married by anyone after him. The verse also corrects the early practice in Medina of inheriting through pledged brotherhood between emigrants and helpers. Inheritance and the rights that go with it now belong to blood relatives, who have priority over others. Even so, the door to goodness stays open: a person may still give gifts, help, or leave a bequest to friends and allies. The verse ends by saying that this ordering is a fixed, recorded decree of God and not a passing arrangement.

translation: And [remember] when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you [O Muhammad], and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary; and We took from them a solemn covenant.
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet Muhammad and the believers that every prophet was bound by a weighty pledge to faithfully convey the divine message, to uphold the religion, to avoid division in it, and to support one another's truth. The five named messengers, who are the greatest of the resolute ones, are singled out for honor, with Muhammad mentioned first to show his rank. The description of the covenant as 'solemn' (ghalīẓ) stresses its gravity and binding force. If the prophets themselves, the best of humanity, were held to such a firm commitment, then their followers are all the more obliged to be sincere in fulfilling their duties, obeying God, and delivering the message without compromise or fear of people.

translation: That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness. And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment.
interpretation: God holds even the sincere to account: the truthful will be asked about the honesty of their words, their covenants, and their conduct, so that their sincerity is made manifest and rewarded, and no claim of faith or loyalty stands without proof. If the truthful are examined this way, the disbelievers who denied the truth and broke faith have no escape, and God has readied for them a painful punishment as the just consequence of their rejection.

translation: O you who believe, remember the favor of God upon you when armies came to you, and We sent against them a wind and armies you did not see. And God is ever Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse recalls the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), when confederate tribes besieged Medina and the believers were in great fear. Their deliverance did not come through their own strength but through God's direct intervention: a fierce, cold wind that overturned the enemy's camp, and unseen forces (angels) that shook their resolve. The believers are told to remember this favor so that gratitude and trust in God replace fear in later hardships, and to understand that victory ultimately belongs to God. The closing reminder that God sees all they do carries both reassurance and accountability: He sees their patience and sincerity in trial and rewards them, and He also sees their wavering or hypocrisy, so they should keep their conduct true to their faith.

translation: When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes turned away in fear and the hearts reached the throats, and you harbored various thoughts about God.
interpretation: The verse recalls the terror of the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), when the Muslims of Medina were besieged by confederate tribes advancing from the higher eastern side and the lower western side of the city. The fear was so intense that eyes wavered and hearts seemed to leap into the throats. In that trial, people's inner states were exposed: the sincere believers kept their trust in God's promise of help, while the weak in faith and the hypocrites entertained doubts and despairing thoughts about whether God would grant victory. The verse teaches that times of extreme hardship test the quality of one's trust in God, and that a believer should hold fast to good expectation of God even when circumstances appear hopeless.

translation: There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Ahzab, describes the siege of Medina in the Battle of the Trench, when enemy forces gathered from above and below and fear reached the hearts. God says the believers were put to a real test there: their faith, steadfastness and trust in Him were tried, and they were shaken inwardly by fear, hunger, cold and uncertainty. The meaning is that hardship is a divine means of sifting sincere believers from the weak of faith and the hypocrites. True belief is proven not in times of ease but in severe trials, and those who remain firm through such shaking are purified and strengthened, while God's help follows for those who endure.

translation: And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, 'Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion.'
interpretation: This verse, from the account of the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), shows how severe trial exposes the real condition of hearts. When the Muslims were besieged by the confederate armies, and fear and hardship were at their peak, the hypocrites and those with weak, doubt-ridden faith began to doubt the promises of divine help and victory made to the believers. They dismissed these promises as deception and empty illusion, judging by the apparent circumstances of the siege rather than trusting in Allah's decree. The verse teaches that hardship distinguishes sincere faith, which holds firm in trust in Allah's promise even when circumstances seem dire, from hypocrisy and spiritual sickness, which collapse into doubt and accusation when ease is removed. It also warns that a heart diseased by doubt or weak certainty reads Allah's promises through fear and worldly calculation, and so falls into despair and ill thoughts about Allah.

translation: And when a group of them said, 'O people of Yathrib, there is no standing for you here, so go back.' And a party of them sought leave of the Prophet, saying, 'Our houses are exposed,' while they were not exposed. They only wished to flee.
interpretation: The verse exposes how fear and hypocrisy surface during the siege of Medina (the Battle of the Trench). Some wavering people tried to demoralize the believers by saying they could not hold their ground and should retreat, and others hid behind a pretext of unprotected homes to seek permission to leave the battle line. God reveals that their excuse was false, since their houses were not vulnerable; their true motive was escape from the duty of defense. The lesson is that weak faith produces spurious excuses to avoid hardship, and God knows the real intentions behind outward claims.

translation: And if it (Madinah) were entered upon them from all its sides, and then they were asked to commit sedition (to renounce faith and return to disbelief), they would surely have done it, and they would not have hesitated over it except for a little.
interpretation: The verse exposes the weakness of the hypocrites' commitment during the Battle of the Trench. Their faith was so shallow that if the enemy armies had breached Madinah from every side and then demanded that they abandon Islam and join in fighting the believers, they would have complied almost at once, delaying only briefly, and then only for the sake of appearances or a pretext, not out of any firm loyalty to their faith. Their fear of worldly danger outweighed their attachment to the truth, which shows that their professed belief was merely on the tongue and not rooted in the heart.

translation: And they had already pledged to God before that they would not turn their backs [in flight]. And a covenant with God will surely be asked about.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, having earlier promised God that they would stand firm and not flee in battle, now seek excuses to abandon their posts. It teaches that a vow made in God's name is a binding trust, not a casual word: every person will be questioned about it and held accountable on the Day of Judgment. Faithfulness to one's pledges, especially those made before God, is a mark of true faith, and breaking them out of fear or weakness is a serious failing that cannot be hidden behind pretexts.

translation: Say: Fleeing will not benefit you if you flee from death or from being killed, and even then you would not be allowed to enjoy life except for a little while.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:16) addresses those who shirked fighting and sought excuses to flee from battle, fearing death. God teaches that every person's lifespan is already decreed, so running away from the battlefield cannot extend life or avert an appointed end; death or killing will come at its set time wherever one is. Even if flight granted some added time, worldly enjoyment is brief and fleeting compared with the Hereafter. The lesson is that cowardice and desertion bring no real gain, so a believer should trust in God's decree, stand firm in duty, and not trade the lasting reward for a short-lived, uncertain safety.

translation: Say: Who is it that can protect you from God if He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you? And they will not find for themselves, besides God, any protecting friend or helper.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all benefit and harm are in God's hands alone. Nobody, whether a person, a tribe, or an invented deity, can shield anyone from what God decrees, and nobody can block His mercy. The hypocrites in the context of the verse were hoping that human alliances or evasion of duty would keep them safe, but the verse tells them that real protection and help come only from God. The right response is to turn to Him in trust and obedience, and to stop depending on created beings who have no power to benefit or harm anyone without His permission.

translation: Indeed, Allah knows those among you who hinder others, and those who say to their brothers, 'Come along with us,' while they themselves come to battle only a little.
interpretation: This verse, revealed about the Battle of the Trench, exposes the hypocrites in Medina who discouraged believers from supporting the Prophet. They tried to dissuade others from fighting by urging them toward comfort and safety, saying 'Come to us,' meaning leave the front and join the security of home. They themselves took part in the fighting only in a token, half-hearted way, either to keep up appearances or because they had no real conviction. The verse teaches that nothing is hidden from Allah: He knows both those who openly obstruct the cause of truth and those who quietly weaken the resolve of others. It also shows that real faith is proven through steadfastness and sacrifice in hardship, whereas hypocrisy shows itself in fleeing from difficulty and pulling others away from duty.

translation: Being miserly toward you. Then when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one who is fainting from death. But when the fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues, being greedy for good things. Those have not believed, so God has made their deeds fruitless, and that is ever easy for God.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' inconsistent character. In the face of danger they are cowardly and cling to the Prophet for protection, overcome with terror like a dying man. Once safety returns they become bold and abusive, attacking the believers with harsh words to claim a share of the spoils, because of their stinginess in sacrifice and their greed for worldly gain. Since their professed faith was only on their tongues and not in their hearts, their deeds carry no weight with God. He nullifies them, and doing so is easy for Him. Outward religion without sincere belief and steadfastness earns no reward.

translation: They think that the confederates have not gone away. And if the confederates should come [again], they would wish they were in the desert among the Bedouins, asking for news about you. And if they were among you, they would not fight except a little.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:20) exposes the cowardice of the hypocrites during the Battle of the Trench. Even after the confederate armies withdrew, their fear was so deep that they still imagined the enemy was camped outside Medina. Should the confederates return, they would prefer to flee the city and live among the nomadic Bedouins, safe at a distance and only inquiring about the believers' fortunes from afar, rather than share in the hardship and danger. Even if they stayed among the believers, their fighting would be minimal and for show, not for God's sake. The verse teaches that real faith is revealed in times of trial, and that hypocrisy shows itself through fear, evasion of sacrifice, and lack of sincere commitment to the community.

translation: Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have an excellent example for whoever hopes in God and the Last Day and remembers God often.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Prophet Muhammad is the model for believers to follow in his words, actions, character, patience, and steadfastness, especially in hard times. It was revealed in the context of the Battle of the Trench, when some faltered while the Prophet remained firm. This example benefits those whose hearts are truly oriented toward God and the Hereafter and who constantly remember God. Such hope and remembrance move a person to emulate the Prophet sincerely, and so give them strength, conduct, and resolve in all circumstances, not only in hardship.

translation: And when the believers saw the confederates, they said: 'This is what God and His Messenger promised us, and God and His Messenger spoke the truth.' And it only increased them in faith and submission.
interpretation: The verse shows that the same trial can lead to opposite outcomes depending on the state of the heart. While the hypocrites saw the massing of the enemy armies at the Battle of the Trench and lost hope, the true believers recognized in the hardship the fulfillment of what God had forewarned, namely that they would be tested, and that after the test comes help and victory. Their trust in the divine promise turned a moment of terror into a source of certainty, so the danger did not weaken them but deepened their faith (iman) and their inner and outward surrender (taslim) to God's decree. The lesson is that real faith is confirmed and strengthened under pressure, and that believers interpret hardship through God's promise rather than through the apparent strength of their enemies.

translation: Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to God. Among them are those who have fulfilled their vow by death, and among them are those who are still waiting; and they have not changed in the least.
interpretation: The verse honors the steadfast believers who kept their covenant with God to stand firm in His cause, as many Companions did at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. Some of them were martyred and so completed their pledge with their lives, while others live on, awaiting either martyrdom or the chance to keep faith. Neither group altered or weakened its commitment through hesitation, fear or worldly gain. The verse holds them up as a model of loyalty to God and sets them against the hypocrites, whose pledges proved false. True faith is measured by faithfulness to one's word with God, and by consistency in keeping it until the end of life.

translation: So that Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness, and punish the hypocrites if He wills, or accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The trials and events described in the surrounding verses, especially the testing of the believers during the siege of the Confederates, serve to separate sincere faith from feigned faith. Those who were true to their covenant with God are rewarded for their honesty and steadfastness, while the hypocrites, whose inner reality contradicts their outward words, are left under God's will: if they persist in hypocrisy they deserve punishment, but the door of repentance remains open to them. Their fate is not sealed, because God's nature is defined by forgiveness and mercy, so He pardons whoever turns back to Him sincerely. The verse teaches that truthfulness is the basis of reward, that hypocrisy is a serious wrong deserving punishment, and that God's mercy always precedes His punishment.

translation: And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they attained no good. And Allah sufficed the believers in battle. And Allah is ever Strong and Mighty.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), where the confederate tribes besieged Medina intending to destroy the Muslim community but were driven back, filled with frustrated anger, gaining neither victory nor spoils. The believers were spared a decisive military clash because Allah sent a violent wind and unseen forces that scattered the enemy camp, showing that victory comes from divine support rather than from numbers or strength alone. The closing attributes, Strong and Mighty, ground this outcome in God's power, teaching that those who trust and persevere in faith will find that Allah suffices them against forces that seem overwhelming.

translation: And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who had supported them from their fortresses and cast terror into their hearts; some you killed, and some you took captive.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Banu Qurayzah, the Jewish tribe of Medina who broke their covenant with the Muslims and aided the confederate armies during the Battle of the Trench. God caused them to leave their strongholds by casting fear into their hearts, which shows that their defeat came from divine help rather than from the strength of the Muslims alone. Their fortified positions gave them no protection once God willed their downfall. The outcome was that their fighting men were killed and their women and children were taken captive, a consequence of their betrayal and the danger it posed to the Muslim community. The lesson is that breaking trust and siding with the enemy in a time of crisis brings ruin, and that God's support for the believers can overcome even well-defended opponents by striking fear into them.

translation: And He made you inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever Able to do all things.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:27) recalls God's favor to the believers after the siege of the Confederates, when the Banu Qurayza, who had betrayed their covenant, were defeated. God gave the Muslims their lands, fortresses, and property as an inheritance, along with yet another land they had never set foot on, which many commentators understand as a promise of future conquests such as Khaybar, or lands conquered later. The closing statement, that God has power over all things, teaches that victory and the transfer of wealth and territory come from His will and not from human strength alone. Believers who stay steadfast and trust Him can see even what seems impossible become reality, and they should respond with gratitude and obedience.

translation: O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a gracious release.
interpretation: This verse presents the Prophet's wives with a clear choice between worldly luxury and a life devoted to God and His Messenger. Because they share the household of the Prophet, they are held to a higher standard of detachment from worldly comforts, as their lives are an example for the community. If any of them prefers the world's pleasures and ornaments, she is free to leave, and the Prophet will give her a fair provision and part from her kindly, without bitterness, harm, or injustice. The verse shows that service to God's cause cannot be built on reluctance or divided desires, and that even separation must be carried out with generosity and dignity.

translation: But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the home of the Hereafter, then indeed Allah has prepared for the doers of good among you a great reward.
interpretation: The verse makes clear that closeness to the Prophet is not honored by lineage or marriage alone but by sincere intention and righteous conduct. The wives of the Prophet, offered a choice between worldly adornment and a life of simplicity beside the Messenger, are told that choosing God, His Messenger and the Hereafter is the path to lasting honor. The promised great reward is not for all who merely hold the title, but specifically for the 'muhsinat', those who excel in devotion, patience, contentment and good deeds. Thus, true status before God is measured by sincerity and ihsan, and giving up worldly comforts for the sake of the Hereafter is richly repaid.

translation: O wives of the Prophet, whoever among you commits a blatant immorality, her punishment will be doubled twofold, and that is ever easy for God.
interpretation: The verse establishes that closeness to the Prophet brings greater responsibility, not immunity. Because the Prophet's wives are models for the believing community and their conduct reflects on the message itself, any clear and flagrant wrongdoing from them would carry a heavier penalty than the same act from an ordinary person. Moral accountability rises in proportion to one's rank, knowledge and proximity to revelation. The closing phrase, that this is easy for God, removes any notion that their status could shield them or that God would be hindered from enforcing His justice. It warns that kinship or social standing cannot substitute for righteous conduct, and it urges them to guard their behavior carefully.

translation: And whoever among you [wives of the Prophet] is devoutly obedient to God and His Messenger and does righteous deeds, We shall give her reward twice over, and We have prepared for her a generous provision.
interpretation: The verse shows that closeness to the Prophet does not in itself bring privilege; what counts is sincere devotion and good action. Because the Prophet's wives live in the midst of revelation and are held to a higher standard, their obedience carries a double reward: one for the deed itself and another for the added burden and example of their position, and for their care of the Messenger's household. Alongside this, God promises them a noble and honorable provision in the Hereafter, a lasting bounty that suits their patience and steadfastness. The principle is that greater responsibility brings greater accountability and also greater reward.

translation: O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women. If you are mindful of God, then do not be soft in speech, lest one in whose heart is a disease should feel desire, but speak with appropriate, honorable words.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet's wives as women of elevated status, whose conduct is a model for the whole community, which is why they are held to a higher standard of propriety than other women. Their special rank lies not in lineage or privilege but in taqwa, God-consciousness, and the greater responsibility that comes with their closeness to the Prophet. The instruction not to be soft or alluring in speech when addressing men outside their household does not mean harshness or rudeness. It means avoiding a tone, whether tender, coquettish, or flirtatious, that could stir improper thoughts in someone whose heart is diseased with lust or moral weakness. Instead, they are to speak plainly, firmly, and respectfully, with words that are good, well known to be fitting, and free of suggestion. The verse thus establishes a principle of modesty and dignity in social interaction, protecting the integrity of the Prophet's household and the community's moral life by closing the door to temptation and slander.

translation: And stay in your houses, and do not display yourselves as with the display of the former times of ignorance. And establish prayer, give zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Allah only intends to remove from you impurity, O members of the household, and to purify you thoroughly.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet's wives, calling them to a dignified, modest life centered on their homes, to avoid the flaunting and immodest public display typical of pre-Islamic society, and to anchor themselves in worship, charity, and obedience to God and His Messenger. Their special closeness to the Prophet places a greater responsibility on them to be moral exemplars for the community. These commands are not meant as burdens but as means by which God wishes to keep moral and spiritual defilement away from the Prophet's household and to purify them completely, so that the home of prophethood remains a model of purity and righteous conduct for all believers.

translation: And remember what is recited in your homes of the verses of God and the wisdom. Indeed, God is Subtle and All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet's wives to keep in mind, treasure, and act upon the revelation and the Prophet's teaching (the Sunnah, here meant by 'wisdom') that is recited in their homes, because their homes are places where revelation descends. It makes them witnesses and transmitters of the faith to the community, so their guidance should be carried from private households into public knowledge. The closing names, Latif (Subtle, Gentle) and Khabir (All-Aware), indicate that God has kindly chosen them for this honor and knows their deeds and intentions, so He knows who is worthy to preserve and convey His message, and He gently guides His servants toward what is good for them.

translation: Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the devout men and devout women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men and women who guard their chastity, and the men and women who remember God often — God has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse affirms that spiritual standing and divine reward depend on faith and conduct, not gender. Men and women are addressed in parallel across ten qualities: outward submission (Islam), inner conviction (iman), obedient devotion, honesty, perseverance, humility before God, generosity, self-discipline through fasting, moral purity, and constant remembrance of God. Together these describe a complete character in which inner belief, worship, ethics, and social responsibility are joined. Those who embody them are promised forgiveness for their shortcomings and a great reward, showing that God's mercy and recompense are open equally to every sincere servant who strives toward these virtues.

translation: It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith requires submission to divine judgment. Once God and His Messenger have issued a clear ruling, a believer has no right to weigh it against personal preference, desire, or custom, as if free to accept or reject it. It was revealed in the context of Zaynab bint Jahsh and Zayd ibn Haritha, when her family was reluctant to accept the marriage the Prophet proposed. The lesson is general: faith is shown by willing obedience, not mere verbal profession, and those who knowingly set their own choice above a clear command have left the path of guidance and fallen into manifest misguidance. This does not forbid consultation or reasoning in matters where no decisive ruling exists, but it forbids opposing a decided command.

translation: And [remember, O Prophet] when you said to the one upon whom Allah had bestowed favor and upon whom you had bestowed favor: 'Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah,' while you concealed within yourself what Allah was going to bring to light, and you feared the people, though Allah has more right that you should fear Him. Then when Zayd had fulfilled his need of her [by divorcing her], We married her to you, so that there would be no discomfort for the believers regarding the wives of their adopted sons when they have fulfilled their need of them. And the command of Allah is always executed.
interpretation: The verse addresses the case of Zayd ibn Haritha, the Prophet's freed slave and adopted son, and his wife Zaynab bint Jahsh. Zayd, whose marriage to Zaynab was troubled, came to consult the Prophet, who advised him to keep his wife and be mindful of God. Yet God had already revealed to the Prophet that Zaynab would become his wife after Zayd divorced her, in order to abolish the pre-Islamic custom of treating adopted sons as real sons, which forbade marrying their former wives. The Prophet kept this revelation private, not out of doubt about God's command but out of natural human concern over how people would react, since marrying the ex-wife of one's adopted son was seen as scandalous. God gently reminds him that He alone is most deserving of fear, not public opinion. When Zayd divorced Zaynab, God Himself arranged the marriage, making it a legal precedent that removes any blame from believers in marrying the former wives of their adopted sons. This shows that divine law overrides social custom, that adoption does not create the legal bonds of blood kinship, and that God's decree will inevitably be carried out.

translation: There is no blame upon the Prophet concerning what Allah has made obligatory for him. This is the way of Allah with those who passed away before; and the command of Allah is a decree determined.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:38) removes any fault or reproach from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for carrying out what God has ordained for him, which in context refers to his marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh after her divorce from Zayd, an act that abolished the pre-Islamic custom that an adopted son's former wife was forbidden to his adoptive father. People's talk and social taboos must not hinder obedience to God's legislation. God affirms that this is His consistent practice with the prophets before him: they were given lawful matters and commands to carry out without being blamed for them, as with David and Solomon, who were granted what was lawful. Whatever God decrees is a settled, measured, and wise decision that must come to pass, so the believer should carry out the divine command with confidence, not fearing the criticism of people.

translation: Those who convey the messages of God and fear Him, and fear none but God. And God suffices as a Reckoner.
interpretation: The verse describes the character of the prophets before the believers: they deliver God's message in full, without concealing or altering any part, because their fear is directed to God alone. Fear of people, of their power, their ridicule or their disapproval, therefore has no hold on them and does not hinder them from declaring the truth. The closing phrase, 'God suffices as a Reckoner,' means that God alone keeps the account of all deeds and will judge them with perfect knowledge and justice, so the messenger needs no other protector or judge. The lesson for believers is that anyone who conveys the truth should do so with sincerity and courage, relying on God and not on the approval of others.

translation: Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of God and the Seal of the Prophets. And God has ever been Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse clarifies that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) has no legal fatherhood over any grown man in the community, which settles the matter of Zayd ibn Haritha, whom he had adopted and whose former wife Zaynab he married after her divorce, showing that adoption does not create the legal bonds of true lineage. His relationship to the believers is of a higher order: he is God's Messenger and the final prophet, so no prophet will come after him and his message completes and seals revelation. The closing statement that God is All-Knowing of everything indicates that this ruling and the finality of prophethood stem from God's perfect wisdom and knowledge of what suits humanity until the end of time.

translation: O you who believe, remember Allah with much remembrance.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:41) calls believers to make remembrance of God a constant, abundant part of their lives and not merely an occasional ritual. Such remembrance includes the tongue through glorification, praise, and recitation, the heart through awareness of God and reverence, and the conduct through acting in obedience to Him and mindful of His commands. The command to remember 'much' indicates that, unlike prescribed acts of worship with fixed limits and times, dhikr has no set boundary, so a believer should keep God present in every state, whether standing, sitting, or lying down. This continual consciousness nurtures sincerity and steadfastness, protects against heedlessness and sin, and brings inner tranquility and God's mercy and remembrance in return.

translation: And glorify Him morning and evening.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ahzab 33:42) calls believers to make the remembrance and glorification of God a constant habit, marking the beginning and the end of the day as anchors for it. Naming the two ends of the day signals continuity: a believer's whole day should be framed by awareness of God's perfection and freedom from any deficiency, so that the hours between are lived in that consciousness. Glorification (tasbih) here is both verbal, by saying 'Subhan Allah', and a lived acknowledgment of God's transcendence. Through it the heart is kept attached to its Creator, protected from heedlessness, and made ready for the blessings and mercy that God promises to those who remember Him often.

translation: It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels as well, so that He may bring you out from the darkness into the light. And He is ever Merciful to the believers.
interpretation: God's 'blessing' (salat) upon the believers is His mercy and care for them, and the angels' blessing is their prayer for forgiveness and goodness on the believers' behalf. The purpose of this divine and angelic attention is to lift believers out of the darkness of disbelief, ignorance, misguidance, and sin into the light of faith, knowledge, and righteous action. This guidance is not a result of human effort alone but of God's grace, which is why the verse closes by affirming that He is always merciful to the believers, both in this world, by guiding and sustaining them, and in the Hereafter, by granting them forgiveness and reward.

translation: Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be 'Peace,' and He has prepared for them a generous reward.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:44) describes the honor given to the believers when they meet God in the Hereafter: they are received with words of peace and safety, a sign that they are free from fear, punishment and distress. Some commentators hold that God Himself greets them with peace, others that the angels do so, and the meaning is that the meeting is one of welcome and security rather than reckoning and dread. Beyond the greeting, God has prepared for them a noble reward, one that is generous, abundant and lasting, granted out of His bounty and exceeding what their deeds alone would merit. The believers' faithfulness in this world, especially their constant remembrance of God and gratitude, is thus answered by honor, tranquility and bounty in the next.

translation: O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good tidings, and a warner.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ahzab 33:45) defines the threefold mission of the Prophet Muhammad. As a witness, he testifies to the truth of God's oneness and to the conduct of his community, and he will bear witness against or for them on the Day of Judgment, so his life becomes the living standard by which the message is understood. As a bearer of good tidings, he gives hope and encouragement, promising God's mercy, forgiveness, and Paradise to those who believe and do good, so that faith is sustained by hope. As a warner, he alerts people to the consequences of disbelief, injustice, and heedlessness, so that they turn back before it is too late. Together these roles show that the prophetic message balances hope and fear, and that the Prophet's task is to convey the truth clearly and faithfully, not to compel belief.

translation: And as one who calls to God by His leave, and as a shining lamp.
interpretation: The verse describes the Prophet Muhammad's mission as a caller to God, one who invites people to worship the One God and to follow His path, not by his own authority but only by God's permission and commission. He is likened to a luminous lamp because, just as a lamp dispels darkness and lets people see their way, the revelation and guidance he brings remove the darkness of ignorance, idolatry and misguidance, and show humanity the clear road to faith, righteousness and God's pleasure.

translation: And give glad tidings to the believers that they will have from God a great bounty.
interpretation: God commands His Prophet to bring joy to those who truly believe, assuring them that their reward does not rest merely on what their deeds strictly earn but flows from God's own generosity, a grace far greater than their efforts deserve. The 'great bounty' includes success and guidance in this world and, above all, the lasting favor of Paradise and God's pleasure in the next. The verse thus teaches that faith is the ground of hope, and that the believer should look to God's abundant grace, not to his own merit, with confidence and gratitude, especially when facing the opposition of disbelievers and hypocrites.

translation: And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and disregard their harm, and put your trust in God. And God suffices as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet, and through him every believer, not to yield to the pressure, demands, or compromises urged by those who reject the truth openly or feign faith while opposing it. Obedience belongs to God's guidance alone. The command to leave aside their harm means not to be preoccupied with their insults, plots, and hostility, nor to retaliate in a way that distracts from the mission, but to carry on with steadfastness. The believer's source of strength is reliance on God, because He is sufficient to protect, support, and manage all affairs, so one who entrusts matters to Him need not fear the schemes of any opponent.

translation: O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period (iddah) that you can require of them. So provide them with a gift of consolation and release them in a gracious manner.
interpretation: The verse establishes that a woman divorced before the marriage has been consummated owes no waiting period, since the purpose of the iddah is to ascertain whether she is pregnant and to allow for possible reconciliation, and neither concern arises here. It then teaches that the end of a marriage must not be a occasion for harm or bitterness. The husband is obliged to give her a gift (mut'ah) as compensation for the hurt of divorce and to honor the bond that existed, and to part from her with dignity, kindness, and good words, without reproach, injury to her reputation, or withholding of what is due. The verse thus joins legal clarity with moral refinement, showing that even in separation the believer must act with generosity and decency.

translation: O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives to whom you have given their dowries, and those your right hand possesses from what Allah has granted you [of captives of war], and the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts, the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts who emigrated with you, and a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her, as a privilege for you alone, to the exclusion of the believers. We know what We have imposed upon them concerning their wives and those their right hands possess, so that there may be no difficulty upon you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse sets out the categories of women lawful for the Prophet Muhammad in marriage, and it shows that his marital situation came with special provisions to serve his mission and to lift hardship from him. Most believers are bound by the general limits revealed to them, such as the number of wives, the requirement of a dowry, and the rules for marrying a woman who offers herself. The Prophet is granted certain exceptions, notably that a believing woman who gives herself to him may be married without a dowry if he chooses, a privilege that belongs to him alone. These allowances were meant to give him room in establishing family ties, honoring women who sacrificed by emigrating, and fulfilling the social and legal purposes of his prophetic role without constraint. The closing statement that God is Forgiving and Merciful reassures him and the community that these rulings stem from divine mercy and wisdom, and that the community should receive them with trust rather than doubt.

translation: You may defer whomever you will of them, and take to yourself whomever you will; and there is no blame upon you if you seek one whom you had set aside. That is more likely that their eyes will be comforted and they will not grieve, and that all of them will be satisfied with what you have given them. And God knows what is in your hearts. And God is ever Knowing and Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse grants the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) discretion in arranging the turns and times he spends with his wives, relieving him of the strict obligation of equal rotation that applies to other believers. He may postpone one and keep another close, and may return to one he had set aside without sin. The wisdom is that the wives, knowing this is a divinely granted allowance and not a personal slight, will feel at ease, will not grieve, and will be content with whatever share he gives them.
