Though the allowance is there, he continued to treat them fairly out of his own good character. The closing reminder that God knows what is in people's hearts warns that inner feelings, such as inclinations, jealousy, or resentment, are known to God, while His forbearance shows mercy toward human weakness and gives people room to correct themselves.

translation: It is not lawful for you, [O Prophet], to take more women after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty impresses you, except what your right hand possesses. And Allah is, over all things, an Observer.
interpretation: This verse sets a limit on the Prophet's marriages after the wives whom God had already made lawful to him, and it affirms the dignity and security of the wives he already had. They had chosen God, His Messenger and the Hereafter over worldly life, and God rewards that choice by guaranteeing their position: they are not to be replaced or added to out of attraction to another woman's beauty. The only exception is a slave woman who comes into his possession, which was permitted under the norms of that time. The closing phrase, 'And Allah is Observer over all things,' reminds believers that God is aware of every inclination of the heart and every action, so the limits He sets must be respected in private as well as in public. The verse thus joins a legal ruling with moral accountability: desire and glances are not outside God's watchful knowledge.

translation: O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission for a meal, without waiting for its preparation. But when you are invited, then enter; and when you have eaten, disperse, without settling in to talk. Indeed, that used to hurt the Prophet, and he is shy of dismissing you, but God is not shy of the truth. And when you ask his wives for something, ask them from behind a screen. That is purer for your hearts and their hearts. And it is not for you to hurt the Messenger of God, nor to marry his wives after him, ever. Indeed, that would be an enormity in the sight of God.
interpretation: The verse sets out rules of etiquette and respect for the Prophet's household. Believers must not treat his homes as public spaces: they may enter only by invitation, arrive when the meal is ready rather than lingering beforehand, and leave promptly after eating instead of prolonging conversation. The Prophet's modesty kept him from asking guests to leave, so God Himself states the rule plainly, since truth and proper conduct should not be neglected out of shyness. The instruction to speak to his wives from behind a screen protects privacy and keeps relations between the community and his family pure and free of suspicion, which is why it is described as purer for both men's and women's hearts. The prohibition on ever marrying his widows honors his unique status as Messenger and protects his dignity, and God declares that violating it would be a grave offense.

translation: Whether you reveal anything or conceal it, indeed Allah has always been, of all things, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 33:54) teaches that nothing escapes God's knowledge, whether it is spoken openly or kept hidden in the heart. Coming after instructions about proper conduct toward the Prophet and his household, it reminds believers that outward compliance is not enough: intentions, private thoughts, and secret feelings are all known to God and will be accounted for. It calls the believer to sincerity and inner integrity, and to be mindful of God (taqwa) in private as much as in public.

translation: There is no blame upon them (the women of the Prophet) concerning their fathers, their sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, or those their right hands possess. And fear God. Indeed, God is ever a Witness over all things.
interpretation: After the command of hijab and of speaking to the Prophet's wives from behind a screen (Q 33:53), this verse sets out the exceptions: women may appear unveiled before their close male relatives (mahrams), before fellow believing women, and before those under their care, since the risk of temptation is absent and ease of family life is needed. The verse then reminds the women that these permissions do not remove personal accountability. The command to be mindful of God means that modesty is, at root, a matter of inner God-consciousness and not only of outward rules, because God witnesses everything, both what is seen and what is hidden. Observing the limits in private and in public is therefore an act of reverence for God, not merely social convention.

translation: Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with worthy greetings of peace.
interpretation: The verse establishes the Prophet Muhammad's exalted rank by showing that his honor is affirmed at the highest level: God praises him before the angels and showers him with mercy, and the angels pray for him. Believers are then called to join this universal act of honoring him. To send blessings upon him is to ask God to exalt his mention and grant him mercy, while to greet him with peace is to submit to his guidance wholeheartedly, to honor him in speech and conduct, and to follow his teachings without resistance or doubt. Honoring him in this way is an expression of gratitude for the guidance he conveyed, and it draws the believer into harmony with what God and His angels already do.

translation: Indeed, those who annoy and offend Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter and has prepared for them a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:57) shows how seriously God takes any offense against the Prophet. Harming God means disobeying Him and attributing to Him what is unfitting, such as partners, children, or falsehood, while harming the Messenger means insulting, slandering, or opposing him and his mission. By linking the Messenger's honor to His own, God makes hurting the Prophet a grave sin that brings exclusion from His mercy in this life and the next, followed by a punishment that humiliates, which fits the arrogance of those who sought to demean the Prophet. The lesson for believers is to honor the Prophet, avoid whatever hurts him, and guard their tongues and conduct toward him.

translation: And those who harm believing men and believing women for something they have not earned have certainly borne upon themselves slander and a manifest sin.
interpretation: The verse warns that falsely accusing or harming believers, whether by spreading lies about them, defaming them, or punishing them for faults they did not commit, is a grave moral offense. Such a person commits two wrongs: buhtān, which is fabricating a falsehood that leaves an innocent person disgraced, and a clear sin (ithm mubīn), because the wrong is evident and cannot be excused. The Qur'an thus sets the dignity and honor of every believing man and woman as protected, and makes slander and unjust harm a burden of guilt that the offender carries personally before God. Harm is blameworthy only when it is undeserved, since the phrase 'for what they have not earned' stresses that the victims are innocent of the charge or deed attributed to them.

translation: O Prophet, tell your wives, your daughters, and the women of the believers to draw their outer garments closer around themselves. That is more suitable so that they will be recognized and not be harassed. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse sets out a measure of protection and dignity for believing women in the society of Medina, where women who went out, especially at night, were sometimes harassed by wrongdoers who could not tell free women from slaves. By drawing their outer cloaks (jalabib) over themselves, Muslim women would be visibly marked as respectable free women, which would discourage molestation. The command is given first to the Prophet's own household, so that they serve as the example for the rest of the community. The reason given is recognition and protection from harm, not restriction for its own sake. The closing words, 'Allah is Forgiving and Merciful,' assure believers that past lapses before this instruction are forgiven and that the rule comes out of divine mercy and care for the community's safety.

translation: If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and those who spread rumors in Medina do not desist, We shall surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors in it except for a little while.
interpretation: This verse is a firm warning to three groups who harmed the Muslim community in Medina: the outwardly pious but inwardly faithless hypocrites, those whose hearts were diseased with lust and moral corruption and who harassed believing women, and the rumor-mongers who spread alarming false news to weaken morale and sow discord. God declares that if they persist in their harmful conduct, He will empower the Prophet against them and give him authority over them, so that they will be expelled or removed and will not be able to live alongside the Muslims in Medina except briefly. The meaning is that public order and the safety and dignity of the community cannot be left at the mercy of those who undermine it through hypocrisy, harassment, and the spreading of falsehood, and that persistent offenders face being cut off from the society they harm.

translation: Accursed, wherever they are found they shall be seized and killed in a massacre.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 33:61) describes the fate threatened for the hypocrites and rumor-mongers in Medina, who spread false reports and harassed the believers, if they did not desist (as stated in the preceding verse). Being 'accursed' means they are distanced from God's mercy and from the community's protection, and the verse warns that persistent sedition and subversion would leave them exposed to the full force of legal and communal punishment wherever they were found. Many commentators read it as a conditional warning that lapses upon cessation of the harmful conduct, emphasizing that threatening public order and the security of the believers through treachery and sowing fear is a grave offense with severe consequences, rather than a general license for violence.

translation: That is the way of God with those who passed away before; and you will never find any change in the way of God.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God governs human history by fixed, consistent laws. Just as earlier nations met the consequences of their choices, with truth and the believers ultimately upheld and arrogant wrongdoing and opposition to God's messengers brought to ruin, so the same moral order applies in every era. The outcome of conflict between faith and disbelief is not random or subject to whim; it follows established principles that neither shift nor can be replaced. This should reassure believers that God's promise of support is dependable, and it warns the wrongdoers that they cannot escape the consequences by changing circumstances or times.

translation: People ask you about the Hour. Say: 'Knowledge of it is only with God.' And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the timing of the Day of Judgment is a matter of the unseen that God has kept to Himself, so not even the Prophet is given it. Questioners, whether sincere or mocking, are redirected from idle speculation about when it will come. The closing phrase, 'perhaps the Hour is near,' does not give a date. It urges people to treat the Hour as always imminent, to prepare through faith and righteous deeds, and not to postpone repentance. Since each person's own death could come at any moment and begins their accountability, the practical concern is readiness, not calculation.

translation: Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and has prepared for them a blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ahzab 33:64) teaches that those who persist in rejecting God and His truth place themselves outside His mercy. The 'curse' means banishment and deprivation from God's mercy and guidance, a state that begins in this world through hardness of heart and spiritual blindness. The 'blazing Fire' that God has already 'prepared' signifies that the consequence of stubborn disbelief is not arbitrary but a settled, certain reality in God's decree, serving as both a warning to the heedless and a reminder to believers of the gravity of faith and obedience.

translation: They will abide therein forever; they will find no protector and no helper.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ahzab 33:65) describes the fate of the disbelievers in Hellfire: their punishment is not temporary, and every source of rescue they relied on in the world will fail them. The wealth, tribes, leaders, and false gods they trusted cannot shield them or intercede for them. The point is that true protection and help belong to God alone, and whoever turns away from Him and His Messenger leaves himself with no refuge on the Day when only God's judgment remains. The verse thus warns against depending on created means for salvation and calls the believer to seek guardianship and support from God through faith and obedience.

translation: On the Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say, "If only we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ahzab 33:66) depicts the disbelievers' regret in the Hereafter. Their faces, the most honored part of the body, are turned about in the Fire, which expresses their humiliation and unceasing torment. Only then do they wish they had obeyed God and His Messenger, a wish that comes too late. The lesson is that obedience to God and the Prophet must be chosen now, while repentance and change are still possible, because regret on the Day of Judgment brings no benefit.

translation: And they will say: "Our Lord, we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the path." (Qur'an 33:67)
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the people of Hellfire will try to shift blame onto those they followed blindly, such as powerful chiefs and elders who shaped their beliefs and choices. The verse teaches that taking responsibility for one's faith and conduct cannot be handed over to others. Each person is given reason and clear guidance and will be accountable for choosing to follow falsehood, so imitating authority without examining whether it accords with truth is no valid excuse before God.

translation: Our Lord, give them double the punishment, and curse them with a mighty curse.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ahzab 33:68) is the plea of the people of Hellfire against the leaders and elders they followed. They say that these leaders led them astray from the truth, so they ask God to multiply the leaders' punishment, because the leaders were guilty twice: once for their own disbelief and again for misguiding others. They also ask that the leaders be removed from God's mercy by a great and severe curse. It shows that blind imitation of leaders and elders is no excuse on the Day of Judgment, and that each person is accountable for the choices he made. It also warns that those who lead others into error will bear a heavier burden, since they carry their own sins as well as a share of the sins of those who followed them.

translation: O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, and God cleared him of what they said. And he was, in the sight of God, honorable and held in high esteem.
interpretation: The verse warns the believers against hurting the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, through slander, suspicion, or false accusation, as some of the Children of Israel did to Moses by spreading baseless rumors about him and his character. God vindicated Moses and exposed the falsehood of what they claimed, showing that He defends His messengers and protects their honor. The reference to Moses being 'wajīh' (honored and esteemed) with God teaches that a prophet's true standing is determined by God, not by people's gossip. The lesson for believers is to guard their tongues, to show respect and loyalty toward God's messenger, and to know that slandering the righteous is a serious wrong that God Himself will answer by clearing His chosen servants.

translation: O you who believe, fear God and speak words that are straightforward and true.
interpretation: The verse links inner God-consciousness (taqwa) to the discipline of speech. Believers are told that fearing God is not only a matter of private devotion but must show in how they talk: words should be honest, just, and to the point, free of lies, slander, deception, or careless speech. The phrase 'qawl sadid' suggests speech that hits the mark, being truthful in content and fitting in its purpose, so that it neither harms others nor distorts the truth. The following verse in the Qur'an (33:71) promises that this integrity of speech leads God to set right the believers' deeds and forgive their sins, showing that upright speech is the foundation of upright conduct overall.

translation: He will amend for you your deeds and forgive you your sins. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly attained a great success.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ahzab 33:71) presents the reward that follows from fearing God and speaking words that are upright. When a believer guards their speech and keeps God in mind, God responds in two ways. He sets their deeds right, by making them sound, accepted and easier to do well, and He erases their past wrongdoing. The verse then defines true success. It is not worldly gain or status but obedience to God and His Messenger, which leads to forgiveness and to salvation from punishment and entry into God's pleasure. Such a person has won the greatest triumph, because it is a success that lasts into the next life.

translation: Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and were afraid of it; yet the human being undertook to bear it. Indeed, he has been very unjust and very ignorant.
interpretation: The 'Trust' (amanah) is moral responsibility: the obligation to know and obey God freely, with the accountability of reward and punishment that comes with free choice. The heavens, earth and mountains serve God by natural compulsion and have no choice to disobey, so they shrank from a burden that carries the risk of failure. Humans, endowed with reason and free will, accepted it, which gives them a unique dignity and the capacity to rise above the angels or fall below the beasts. Yet most people prove 'unjust' to themselves by neglecting the Trust and 'ignorant' of the weight of what they took on, underestimating its consequences. The verse is thus both an honor and a warning: humans should recognize the gravity of their responsibility, remain faithful to it through faith and righteous conduct, and not betray it through heedlessness.

translation: So that God may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, and that God may turn in mercy to the believing men and believing women. And God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 33:73) explains the outcome of the trust (amanah) mentioned in the preceding verse, which humankind undertook. Because humans accepted the burden of moral responsibility and obedience to God, they divide into groups according to how they carry it. Those who feign faith while concealing disbelief (the hypocrites) and those who openly associate partners with God (the polytheists) betray the trust, and so they deserve punishment. Those who sincerely keep faith and obedience are the believers, and God turns toward them with acceptance, forgiving their lapses and shortcomings. The verse closes with God's attributes of forgiveness and mercy, which show that human weakness in fulfilling the trust is met with pardon for those who sincerely return to Him, and that the real dividing line is sincerity of faith, not perfection of conduct.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise belongs to God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; and to Him belongs all praise in the Hereafter. And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse teaches that praise is due to God alone because He is the true owner and sovereign of everything in creation, so every blessing people enjoy in this world originates from Him. His praise does not end with this life: in the Hereafter, when worldly powers and illusions of independence fall away, the believers will glorify Him for the fulfillment of His promise and the justice of His judgment. The closing names, the All-Wise and the All-Aware, ground this praise in His perfect wisdom in ordering the universe and His complete knowledge of all hidden and apparent matters, so that nothing He decrees is without purpose and nothing in creation escapes His awareness. Gratitude and praise are therefore the fitting response of the human being to a Lord whose ownership, wisdom, and knowledge are absolute.

translation: He knows what penetrates into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends therein. And He is the Most Merciful, the Most Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's knowledge is all-encompassing and reaches every hidden movement in creation: the seed and the water that sink into the soil, the plants, springs, and treasures that emerge, the rain, revelation, and decrees that come down from above, and the deeds, words, and angels that rise up. Nothing escapes Him, whether it is unseen or seen, small or great. Yet the verse ends by pairing this total awareness with His names 'the Most Merciful' and 'the Most Forgiving', teaching that the One who knows every secret of His servants is also the One who treats them with mercy and forgives their shortcomings when they turn to Him. His complete knowledge should therefore inspire both watchfulness in conduct and hope in His forgiveness, rather than despair.

translation: Those who disbelieve say, 'The Hour will never come upon us.' Say, 'Yes indeed, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you—He is the Knower of the unseen. Not even the weight of an atom escapes Him, in the heavens or on the earth; nor is there anything smaller than that or larger, except that it is in a clear Record.'
interpretation: The verse answers the disbelievers' denial of the Resurrection by having the Prophet swear an oath by his Lord that the Hour is certain. The proof for its certainty is God's perfect, all-encompassing knowledge: since He knows the unseen and nothing, however minute, is hidden from Him or left unrecorded, He knows every deed and every body part to be recompensed and is able to gather and resurrect them. Their denial stems from imagining that things decay, vanish and are lost after death, but nothing is lost to God, since all is preserved in a clear Record. Thus the Hour's coming is a matter of divine knowledge, power and justice, requiring that each person be held to account for what they did.

translation: That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds. Those will have forgiveness and a noble provision.
interpretation: The verse explains the wisdom behind the Hour and the divine knowledge of all things: God's purpose in bringing about the final reckoning is to give just recompense to those whose faith was joined with good works. Faith alone is not the whole of the matter, nor are deeds without faith; the two together earn God's favor. Their reward is twofold: forgiveness, meaning that their sins and shortcomings are wiped away so that they are spared punishment, and a noble provision, meaning generous, honorable and lasting bounty in Paradise, given without humiliation or deficiency. It shows that salvation rests on God's mercy and generosity, which exceed the believers' deeds, and it encourages them to remain steadfast in faith and righteous action.

translation: And those who strive against Our verses, seeking to defeat them, for such there will be a painful punishment of wrath.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who exert effort to undermine, discredit, or obstruct God's revelation, imagining they can outwit God or render His message ineffective, are not merely mistaken but accountable. Their opposition is futile because God's truth cannot be overcome, and their scheming brings a punishment that is both morally fitting and severe. Just as those endowed with knowledge recognize the revelation as truth that guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, those who actively fight it earn a torment of defilement and agony, showing that deliberate hostility to divine guidance carries grave consequences.

translation: Those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, and that it guides to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: People of true knowledge, whether scholars among the earlier People of the Book or believers who reflect deeply, recognize through reason and evidence that the Qur'an is the truth from God. Their knowledge makes the proofs of its message clear to them: its teachings agree with sound reason, with what earlier revelation affirms, and with the order seen in creation. They also see that it leads to the way of God, who is Almighty (al-'Aziz), so that whoever follows His path is never humiliated, and who is Praiseworthy (al-Hamid), so that this path is the one that earns praise and ends in a good outcome. The verse sets the testimony of the knowledgeable against the denial of those who disbelieve and who mocked the promise of resurrection in the preceding verses.

translation: Those who disbelieved said, "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that, when you have been utterly torn to pieces, you will indeed be in a new creation?"
interpretation: The verse shows the mocking disbelief of the Quraysh and other deniers toward the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the message of resurrection. They deride him by calling him 'a man' and presenting his claim as a strange rumor, as if it were absurd that bodies completely scattered into dust could ever be remade. Their sarcasm reveals a failure to reflect on God's power: the One who created them the first time from nothing is surely able to bring them back. The verse thus exposes how arrogance and ridicule are used to dismiss the truth of the Hereafter, when the real issue is their unwillingness to accept accountability.

translation: Has he invented a lie about God, or is there madness in him? No! Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in the punishment and in far-reaching error.
interpretation: This verse records the disbelievers' mocking charge against the Prophet after he told them of resurrection: they said he was either deliberately lying about God or was possessed by madness. The Qur'an rejects both accusations with 'Bal' (No!), and turns the charge back on them. The Prophet is neither a liar nor insane; he is a truthful warner. The ones truly in danger are those who deny the Hereafter, because their denial leaves them in a state of deep error now, having strayed far from truth and reason, and it leads them to punishment later. Their rejection of accountability is itself the real madness and misguidance, while the punishment they dismiss is what awaits them.

translation: Do they not see what lies before them and what lies behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We willed, We could cause the earth to swallow them, or cause fragments of the sky to fall upon them. Indeed in that is a sign for every servant who turns back to God in repentance.
interpretation: The verse calls the deniers of the resurrection and the message to reflect on the vast creation that surrounds them on every side: the sky above and the earth beneath, which enclose them wherever they turn. These are signs of God's power and of how completely He encompasses them, and they are also a warning. The same earth that supports them and the same sky that shelters them are under God's command, and He could turn them into instruments of punishment, by making the ground swallow the people or by dropping pieces of the sky upon them. That this does not happen is not because they are safe by their own strength, but because of God's forbearance and mercy, which gives them time to repent. Only the person who is oriented toward God, who constantly returns to Him in repentance and reflection (the 'munib'), draws a lesson from this: he recognizes God's power, fears His punishment, and is grateful for His patience, so he turns from heedlessness and arrogance to obedience.

translation: And We certainly gave David from Us bounty: 'O mountains, echo [Our praises] with him, and the birds.' And We made iron soft for him.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's favor to David was a gift that came directly from Him, not from David's own power. God made creation join David in glorifying Him, so the mountains and birds responded to his devotion and echoed his praise. God also made iron pliable in his hands, so that he could work it without fire or heavy tools and use it for beneficial crafts such as armor. The lesson is that every talent and power is a trust from God, and the proper response is gratitude, worship, and using one's abilities for good.

translation: Make full-length coats of mail, and measure well the links in their weaving. And do righteous deeds, for indeed I am All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: After God softened iron for David, He guided him to use that gift skillfully: to forge complete, protective armor and to make its rings balanced and well-proportioned, neither so thin that they break nor so thick that they are unwieldy. This teaches that using one's God-given gifts and craft requires precision, diligence, and excellence. The verse then links worldly skill to moral purpose: the capacity to craft and to benefit others must be joined to righteous action, and a person should remain conscious that God observes every deed, so that work done well becomes a form of gratitude and worship.

translation: And to Solomon We subjected the wind: its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey. And We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him. And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord. And whoever among them deviated from Our command, We would make him taste of the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse shows that God granted Solomon extraordinary power over the natural and unseen worlds as a favor and a trial, yet all of it remained under divine authority. The wind carried him on journeys that would normally take two months in a single day, the molten copper gave him material for building and craftsmanship, and the jinn labored for him only by God's leave, not by any power of their own. The warning that any jinn who disobeyed would be punished with the blazing fire reminds us that even the most powerful beings are accountable to God's command, and that Solomon's dominion was a gift to be met with gratitude and obedience, not a source of pride.

translation: They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries, statues, basins like reservoirs, and fixed cauldrons. [We said:] 'Work, O family of David, in gratitude; and few of My servants are truly grateful.'
interpretation: God reminds us that the power He gave Solomon over the jinn was a blessing, to be answered with thankfulness shown in deeds rather than words alone. The command 'Work, O family of David, in gratitude' teaches that real gratitude is to use God's gifts in obedience to Him and in service of what is good: worship, justice, and benefit to people. The closing statement, 'few of My servants are truly grateful,' warns that even though blessings are plentiful, sincere and constant gratitude is rare, because most people are distracted by the gifts or take credit for them instead of recognizing the Giver. The verse therefore calls every believer to examine whether their abilities, wealth, and position are being used as an expression of thanks to God.

translation: And when We decreed death upon him, nothing indicated his death to them except a creature of the earth eating away his staff. Then when he fell down, it became clear to the jinn that, had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes how Solomon died while leaning on his staff, and the jinn, who were working under his command, continued their hard labor without knowing he was dead, since he remained propped upright. Only when a termite gnawed through the staff and his body fell did they realize he had died. The point is that the jinn, whom people imagined to have knowledge of hidden matters, could not perceive even the death of someone right in front of them. This shows that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone, and that claims of jinn or soothsayers knowing the unseen are false. Had the jinn truly known the unseen, they would not have spent that long period in degrading toil.

translation: There was indeed a sign for the people of Sheba in their homeland: two gardens, one to the right and one to the left. 'Eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him: a good land and a Forgiving Lord.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's blessings are meant to awaken gratitude and recognition of the Giver. The people of Sheba lived in Yemen, in a land made fertile by the Ma'rib dam, with orchards stretching on both sides of their valley. The abundance was not merely a comfort but a 'sign' (ayah), a reminder pointing to God's generosity and care. They were called to respond with thankfulness and obedience, since their pleasant land and healthy living were gifts and not self-earned entitlements. The phrase 'a good land and a Forgiving Lord' links outward prosperity with spiritual mercy: God gave them good living, and if they fell short, He was ready to forgive them when they turned back to Him. The verse sets up the lesson of the following verses, which show that ingratitude and turning away lead to the loss of blessings, while gratitude secures them.

translation: But they turned away, so We sent upon them the flood of the dam, and We replaced their two gardens with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote trees.
interpretation: This verse describes how the people of Saba', after being given abundant provision and gardens on both sides of their land, neglected gratitude and turned away from the message of their messengers. Their punishment came through the very source of their prosperity: the dam that held their water broke and the flood destroyed their orchards. What replaced their lush, fruitful gardens was wild, worthless vegetation: bitter-tasting fruit, tamarisk, and scant thorny lote trees. The lesson is that blessings are tied to gratitude and obedience, and that persistent ingratitude can turn a means of abundance into a cause of ruin. Worldly prosperity is therefore not a guarantee of permanence, but a trust from God that can be withdrawn when it is met with heedlessness.

translation: That is how We repaid them for their ingratitude and disbelief. And do We repay [with such punishment] anyone but the ungrateful disbeliever?
interpretation: The verse refers to the people of Saba (Sheba), whom God had blessed with fertile gardens and security but who turned away from Him and were ungrateful, so He sent upon them the flood of the dam and replaced their gardens with bitter, barren growth. The meaning is that this punishment was not arbitrary but a just consequence of their persistent denial of God's favors and their rejection of His guidance. The rhetorical question 'Do We repay any but the ungrateful?' stresses that God's retribution falls specifically on those who persist in kufr, meaning both disbelief and ingratitude, whereas the grateful and believing are treated with mercy and are rewarded or pardoned. It teaches that gratitude preserves blessings, while ingratitude brings about their loss.

translation: And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed [other] towns easily visible, and We made the journey between them measured and well-regulated: 'Travel through them by night and day, secure.'
interpretation: The verse recalls the favor God gave to the people of Saba'. Their land in Yemen was linked to the blessed lands of the Levant by a continuous chain of connected, visible towns, each within sight of the next and spaced at measured stages. Travelers needed no heavy provisions, could not lose their way, and feared neither thirst nor robbers, so they could journey at any hour in safety. The verse presents this ease, security and prosperity as a blessing meant to elicit gratitude. The following verses show that the people of Saba' turned ungrateful and even wished for longer, harder journeys, and so lost the blessing. The lesson is that security and ease of life are gifts from God, and that gratitude preserves them while ingratitude puts them at risk.

translation: But they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys longer." And they wronged themselves, so We made them (mere) tales, and We scattered them in complete dispersal. Indeed, in that are signs for everyone who is steadfastly patient and grateful.
interpretation: The people of Saba', who had been given safe, easy travel between flourishing towns and abundant blessings, grew tired of ease and ungratefully asked for hardship and distance, which showed their arrogance and their failure to value God's favor. By turning away from gratitude they wronged themselves, and the consequence was the loss of their prosperity and unity: they were scattered and became a story told to later generations as a warning. The verse teaches that blessings last through gratitude and are lost through ingratitude, and that only the person who is patient in hardship and thankful in ease reflects on such histories and draws lessons from them.

translation: And indeed, Iblis proved true his estimation of them, so they followed him, except for a group of the believers.
interpretation: When Iblis vowed to lead humankind astray, he was acting on a conjecture about human weakness, and in most people that conjecture was borne out, because they yielded to his whispers and followed desire over guidance. His success came only through their own choices, since he has no power to compel anyone. The verse also makes clear that the believers who held firm were exempt, which shows that sincere faith and reliance on God protect a person from Satan's influence. Their safety came from steadfastness and God's protection, not from any inability on Satan's part to tempt them.

translation: And he (Iblis) had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter as distinct from who is in doubt about it. And your Lord is, over all things, a Guardian.
interpretation: Satan's power over people is only the power to whisper and tempt, never to compel. God permits this temptation as a test through which what is hidden in hearts becomes manifest in reality: those who truly believe in the Hereafter and hold themselves accountable resist him, while those who doubt the Hereafter follow him. The phrase 'that We might know' does not imply that God gains new knowledge, since He knows all things beforehand; rather it means that the knowledge becomes realized in outcomes and actions, so that proof stands for or against each person. The closing statement that God is Guardian over all things reassures believers that He preserves and watches over everything, including His servants and their deeds, and that Satan cannot exceed the limits God has set.

translation: Say: Call upon those whom you claim to be gods besides Allah. They do not possess even the weight of an atom in the heavens or in the earth, nor do they have any share in either of them, and He has no helper from among them.
interpretation: The verse challenges the polytheists to summon the beings they worship besides God and see whether they can help, and it then dismantles every possible ground for worshipping them in descending steps. These beings own nothing, not even an atom's weight, anywhere in creation. They hold no partnership in the heavens or the earth. And God does not rely on any of them as a supporter or aide. Since worship is justified only by ownership, partnership, or the power to help, and all three are denied, the verse establishes that no created being deserves devotion and that divine power belongs wholly to God, who is self-sufficient and needs no assistance. The command to call upon them is a rhetorical challenge that exposes their helplessness and calls people to pure monotheism.

translation: And intercession with Him benefits not, except for one whom He has permitted. Until, when terror is removed from their hearts, they say, 'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'The truth. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.'
interpretation: The verse affirms that no being, however exalted, can intercede with God by its own authority; intercession is valid only for those whom God permits, and only by His leave. It then depicts the awe of the angels when God's command is revealed: they are struck with fear and stunned at the majesty of His speech, and when the fear lifts from their hearts they ask one another what their Lord has said. The answer comes that He has said the truth, for His word is always right and just. This shows that all power and decree belong to God alone, that even the closest of creatures stand before Him in reverent dread, and that any false deity or intercessor claimed by the polytheists has no independent standing. The closing words, 'He is the Most High, the Most Great,' affirm His absolute transcendence over all creation.

translation: Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: God. And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse uses the argument of shared reality to expose the weakness of polytheism. The Prophet is told to ask who provides sustenance from the heavens (rain, sunlight) and the earth (crops, water, minerals), then to answer the question himself, because the idolaters cannot honestly name anyone but God. Since the sole Provider is God, only He deserves worship, so the two camps cannot both be right. The closing statement is a courteous and fair way of debating: it does not name who is guided and who is misguided, and it leaves the listener to reason for himself. The structure of the sentence nevertheless makes the answer evident, since the one who worships the true Provider is on guidance, and the one who worships others beside Him is in clear error. This invites sincere reflection and avoids hostility.

translation: Say: You will not be asked about what we have committed of sin, and we will not be asked about what you do.
interpretation: This verse (Saba' 34:25) establishes the principle of individual moral responsibility. The Prophet is instructed to address the disbelievers with fairness and gentleness, even attributing the word 'crime' to himself and the believers by way of courtesy and to avoid provocation, while they were in fact the ones in error. The meaning is that each person is accountable only for his own deeds before God, and no one will bear the burden of another. By removing accusation and rhetorical heat, the verse invites the opponents to reflect honestly and independently on the truth of the message, leaving final judgment to God, who will decide between the two parties with justice.

translation: Say: Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth; and He is the Knowing Judge (the Opener, the All-Knowing).
interpretation: The verse teaches the Prophet how to answer the disagreement between believers and those who associate partners with God: the dispute will not be settled by argument in this world but by God Himself on the Day of Resurrection. All people will be brought together before their Lord, and He will decide between them with perfect justice, exposing who was on guidance and who was in error. The names 'al-Fattah' (the One who opens, decides, and judges) and 'al-'Alim' (the All-Knowing) show that His judgment rests on complete knowledge of every hidden intention and deed, so no one will be wronged. It also reassures the believers and calls the opponents to reflect, since the final verdict belongs to God alone and not to human claims.

translation: Say: Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners. Never! Rather, He is God, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The Prophet is told to challenge the polytheists to produce any real evidence that their idols deserve a share in divinity. The challenge is rhetorical, since they cannot show any attribute of lordship, creation, or power in them, and the emphatic 'Never!' rejects the claim outright. Divinity belongs to God alone, who is mighty and cannot be overcome or need any associate, and who is wise in all He creates and legislates, so no partner could have a place in His rule.

translation: And We have not sent you except to all of mankind as a bearer of good tidings and a warner, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse affirms the universality of the Prophet Muhammad's mission: unlike earlier prophets who were generally sent to their own peoples, his message is addressed to all humanity across every place and era. His role is twofold: to give glad tidings of reward and mercy to those who believe and do good, and to warn those who reject truth and do wrong of its consequences. The closing phrase observes that most people fail to grasp the truth of his mission and its scope, whether through heedlessness, arrogance, or attachment to inherited ways, so they deny or overlook the guidance offered to them for their own benefit.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The disbelievers mock the warning of resurrection and judgment by demanding a date for it, as though the lack of an immediate answer proves the message false. Their question is not an honest search for truth but a way to deflect the call to repentance. The verse shows how people who are heedless treat the unseen: they mistake God's delay for impossibility, when the delay is mercy and a chance to reform, and the exact time of the Hour is known only to God. What matters for a person is not when it will come but being prepared for it.

translation: Say: For you is the appointment of a Day which you can neither delay by a single hour nor bring forward.
interpretation: The verse answers the disbelievers' mocking question about when the promised Day will come. It teaches that the Day of Judgment is fixed by God's knowledge and decree, with a precise appointed time that no one can change, whether by hastening it through challenge or postponing it through denial or delay. Their mockery therefore has no effect on its arrival. The verse warns them to prepare for a certain reckoning instead of scoffing, because time is in God's hands alone and every soul will meet its appointed term.

translation: Those who disbelieve say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in what came before it." If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, casting blame back and forth upon one another. Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant, "If not for you, we would have been believers."
interpretation: The verse shows how stubborn denial of truth, which rejects revelation outright and even the earlier scriptures that confirm it, ends in a moral reckoning in which no one can escape personal responsibility. In this world, the disbelievers harden themselves against the Qur'an and its message. On the Day of Judgment, when they stand before God stripped of every pretense, their worldly alliances collapse into mutual blame. The followers who surrendered their reasoning and conscience to the powerful blame their leaders, saying they would have believed but for them. The verse warns that blind conformity to arrogant authority is no excuse, since each person was given the ability to recognize truth and is accountable for the choice made. It also exposes the emptiness of the arrogant, whose influence in life offers neither protection nor benefit before God.

translation: Those who were arrogant will say to those who were deemed weak: "Did we hinder you from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Saba (34:32), depicts a scene on the Day of Judgment in which the leaders who had been arrogant reject the blame placed on them by their followers. The followers had claimed that, were it not for the leaders, they would have been believers. The leaders answer that they did not use force or remove the followers' free will: guidance had plainly reached them, and they themselves chose to turn away from it. The leaders say the followers were 'mujrimin' (wrongdoers) by their own choice. The lesson is that every person is personally accountable for accepting or rejecting the truth after clear guidance has come. Following the powerful, the majority, or tradition blindly is no excuse, since a person's decision is his own, even though those who misled others also bear their own burden of guilt.

translation: Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Rather, it was your scheming by night and day, when you commanded us to disbelieve in God and to set up rivals to Him." And they will conceal their remorse when they see the punishment. And We will place shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved. Are they recompensed for anything other than what they used to do?
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when followers who were led astray blame their leaders, saying the leaders' relentless, ceaseless deception, night and day, drew them into disbelief and the worship of partners alongside God. Yet blaming others will not absolve them, for each person bears responsibility for the choices made. Both leaders and followers are overcome by regret, which they hide out of shame or helplessness once the reality of the punishment appears. The shackles on their necks symbolize the binding consequences of their own rejection of faith, and the closing question affirms divine justice: no one is punished unjustly, for the recompense exactly matches their deeds.

translation: And We did not send into any town a warner except that its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent." (Qur'an 34:34)
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in human history: those who enjoy wealth, luxury, and social status are usually the first to reject prophetic reform, because the message of God's oneness, justice, and accountability threatens the privileges and power they hold. Their comfort breeds arrogance and self-reliance, so they dismiss the truth openly and lead others to do the same. This is meant to console the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the believers, since opposition from the elite is not a sign that the message is false but the normal response to every messenger. It also warns that prosperity without gratitude and humility can blind the heart to guidance.

translation: And they said: "We have more wealth and more children, and we will not be punished." (Qur'an 34:35)
interpretation: The verse exposes the flawed reasoning of those who treat worldly abundance as proof of divine favor and as a guarantee against accountability. The affluent among the disbelievers used their wealth and numerous offspring as evidence that God was pleased with them, so they felt safe from punishment in the Hereafter. The Qur'an teaches that wealth and children are tests and not signs of honor or nearness to God. The following verses explain that God expands and restricts provision according to His wisdom, and that what brings a person close to Him is faith and righteous action, not possessions or status. The verse warns believers against measuring worth or truth by material success, and against the arrogance that makes people dismiss the warnings of the prophets.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth and scarcity are not signs of divine favor or rejection but results of God's wisdom and will, working as tests and trials for people. Most people misunderstand this and assume that abundance proves they are honored by God while hardship proves they are disgraced. The believer is therefore urged to look beyond material circumstances: to be grateful and generous when given plenty, patient and trusting when provision is restricted, and to judge a person's standing before God by faith and righteous deeds rather than by worldly possessions.

translation: It is not your wealth or your children that bring you closer to Us in nearness, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds. For those, there will be a double reward for what they did, and they will be secure in the lofty chambers (of Paradise).
interpretation: The verse overturns worldly measures of status: wealth and offspring, which people treat as signs of divine favor, have no weight in themselves in securing nearness to God. Nearness is earned only through faith joined with righteous action. Wealth and children become valuable only when they are put to the service of faith, for example by spending in charity or raising children in righteousness. The believer who does this is rewarded multiplied many times over, beyond the strict measure of the deeds, and enjoys lasting safety in the high places of Paradise, free from the fear, loss and anxiety that accompany worldly possessions.

translation: But those who strive against Our verses, seeking to defeat them and to escape accountability, those will be brought into the punishment.
interpretation: The verse draws a contrast with those who believe and are rewarded. People who work to undermine God's revelation, by rejecting it, casting doubt on it, or obstructing others from it, imagine they can thwart God's message or outrun its consequences. They cannot. The word 'brought' (muhdarun) suggests they will be compelled to appear for punishment without any means of escape, just as they once tried to evade the truth. Their efforts at opposition are futile, and their end is a certain, inescapable reckoning.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it for whom He wills. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it; and He is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth and sustenance are entirely in God's control, so abundance or scarcity is not a measure of a person's worth or of God's favor, but a matter of His wisdom and trial. Knowing this should free believers from the fear that giving will impoverish them. Whatever is spent in obedience to God, especially in charity and on good causes, is never truly lost: God replaces it, whether through worldly means, through blessing in what remains, or through reward in the Hereafter. Because He is the best of providers, all other means of earning are only causes, while He is the true source, and trust in Him should make a person generous rather than miserly.

translation: And on the Day when He gathers them all together, then He will say to the angels, "Was it you that these people used to worship?" (Qur'an 34:40)
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection God will assemble all of humanity, including those who worshipped angels, and will address the angels before them. The question is not asked because God needs an answer. It is meant to expose the falsehood of idolatry in front of its followers, and to have the angels themselves, whom the idolaters claimed as intercessors and partners, publicly disown that worship. The angels will respond by declaring God's glory and saying that He alone is their protector, and that the people were really following the jinn, meaning the devils who led them astray. The verse teaches that worship belongs to God alone, that no created being, however honored, can share in it or accept it, and that on the Day of Judgment every false object of devotion will be disavowed and the worshippers will have no excuse.

translation: They (the angels) said: "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."
interpretation: The angels, when asked on the Day of Resurrection whether the idolaters had worshipped them, declare God's transcendence above any partner and affirm that their only allegiance and guardianship is to God, not to those who worshipped them. They disown the idolaters' worship, explaining that what the polytheists were actually obeying were the jinn, meaning the devils who beautified idolatry and whispered to them to take angels as objects of devotion. Most of them believed in the jinn, trusting and following them. The verse shows that worship is not merely ritual but includes obedience and belief in whatever one submits to, and that those who are claimed as partners with God reject such worship, leaving the idolaters with no defender.

translation: So today none of you has power over benefit or harm for another, and We will say to those who wronged themselves: 'Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.'
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection all the false supports people relied on in this world, such as idols, false deities, leaders, and allies, are stripped away. No one, whether the worshipped or the worshipper, the leader or the follower, can bring a benefit to another or ward off a harm from them, because all power belongs to God alone. The wrongdoers, whose gravest wrong was associating partners with God and rejecting the revelation and the Hereafter, are then told to taste the Fire they used to dismiss as a lie. The punishment is thus the realization of the very reality they denied, and it comes with the humiliating recognition that nothing they trusted in can help them.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, they say: 'This is nothing but a man who wishes to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship.' And they say: 'This is nothing but a fabricated falsehood.' And those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them: 'This is nothing but obvious magic.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the reflexive hostility of the Quraysh and similar disbelievers toward revelation. Instead of weighing the clear evidence in the verses on its own merits, they attack the messenger's motives, claiming he only wants to divert people from their ancestral religion, so inherited tradition becomes their yardstick for truth. They then deny the source of the message by calling it a fabricated lie, and finally, when the truth fully reaches them, they dismiss it as sorcery. These shifting accusations (a self-interested man, a forgery, magic) show that their rejection stems from stubborn attachment to custom and pride, not from any rational objection, since clear signs leave them with no real argument and so they resort to slander.

translation: And We had not given them any scriptures which they could study, nor did We send to them before you any warner.
interpretation: The verse refutes the idolaters of Makkah by showing that they have no revealed basis for their beliefs and practices. They possessed no divine book that they could study and use as proof for their claims of denying the Qur'an and the Prophet, and no messenger had come to them in the recent past to warn them and give them a standard to rely on. Their rejection of Muhammad is therefore baseless: the only revelation and warning that has reached them is the one he brings, so they ought to be the first to accept it rather than deny it. This highlights both the lack of any evidence in their position and the great mercy of God in sending them a warner, who is the sole source of guidance for them.

translation: Those before them also denied, and these have not attained even a tenth of what We gave those earlier peoples. Yet they denied My messengers, so how was My rejection of them?
interpretation: God warns the Meccan deniers by pointing to earlier nations who were far stronger, wealthier and more established than they were, yet their power could not protect them once they rejected the prophets. The verse teaches that worldly strength and abundance do not shield anyone from divine justice when they are met with arrogance and denial of truth. The closing rhetorical question, 'how was My rejection?', invites reflection on the ruin of those peoples as a lesson: if mighty nations were destroyed for their denial, the weaker deniers of Muhammad have even less reason to feel secure, and should heed the message before the same fate overtakes them.

translation: Say: I advise you of one thing only: that you stand up for God, in pairs and individually, and then reflect. There is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse invites the Meccan opponents to settle the question of the Prophet's truthfulness through sincere, unbiased reflection rather than through crowd emotion, prejudice, or social pressure. 'Standing for God' means approaching the matter with sincere devotion to truth, free of partisanship. 'In pairs and individually' means that people should deliberate in small groups, where they can exchange ideas and check one another honestly, or alone, where they can examine their own conscience. In a large crowd, passions tend to override reason. If they reflect in this way, they will see that Muhammad, whom they have known for years as a person of sound mind, honesty, and good character, is not possessed or mad. His message is not the product of delusion. He is simply a warner, sent to alert them to a coming severe punishment so that they may change course before it arrives.

translation: Say: Whatever reward I may have asked of you, it is for yourselves. My reward is only from God, and He is a Witness over all things.
interpretation: The Prophet is told to declare that he seeks no worldly payment for delivering the message. If he ever asked anything of them, such as love for kin or following the right path, the benefit returns to them and not to him, since guidance serves their own salvation. His only recompense is with God, who sees his sincerity, his conveying of the message, and everything people do, so no deed or intention is hidden or goes unaccounted for. The verse shows that a true messenger is selfless and that those who call to God should not be motivated by material gain.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord hurls the truth; He is the Knower of the unseen.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Saba 34:48) teaches that God casts the truth against falsehood, as one might throw a projectile, so that falsehood is shattered and cannot stand against it. The Prophet is told to declare this to those who deny him, as an assurance that the message does not rest on human power or argument but on God's own action, so the truth will inevitably prevail over disbelief. The mention of God as 'Knower of the unseen' explains why: because God alone knows what is hidden in hearts and in the future, He knows precisely how and when to send down revelation and bring truth to victory, and no deception or concealment by the deniers can escape Him or defeat His plan.

translation: Say: The truth has come, and falsehood neither originates anything nor restores anything.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Saba 34:49) declares that the revelation brought by the Prophet Muhammad, which is the truth, has arrived and prevailed, while falsehood, and by extension Satan, who stands behind it, has no creative or regenerative power. Falsehood can neither begin anything of lasting benefit nor bring anything back once the truth has overcome it. It is therefore powerless and doomed to vanish, and whatever its followers hope to gain from it will come to nothing. Only the truth, backed by God, endures and has real effect.

translation: Say: If I go astray, I go astray only to my own loss; and if I am guided, it is only by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to answer those who accuse him of error by stating a principle of personal accountability: the consequences of misguidance fall only on the one who strays, and no one can harm the truth by rejecting it. Guidance is not credited to one's own intellect or power but is a gift from God through revelation, so even the Messenger depends on his Lord for right direction. The verse closes by assuring that God hears every word and is close to every person, so He knows the sincerity of the seeker and the claims of the deniers alike, and is near to answer and to hold each soul to account.

translation: If you could only see when they are terrified, with no escape, and they are seized from a place close by.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of divine reckoning for the deniers, whether at death, at the sudden punishment in this world, or at the Resurrection. Overcome by terror, they will find no way to flee or hide, because God's grasp reaches them wherever they are. The phrase 'from a place close by' means that no distance separates them from God's power: they cannot outrun their fate, and the punishment will seize them from where they stand, as near as the ground beneath their feet. It warns that the arrogance and heedlessness of deniers will collapse in an instant, when repentance and escape are no longer possible.

translation: And they will say, "We believe in it." But how can they attain [faith] from so far a place?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Saba 34:52) describes the disbelievers at the moment of death or the Day of Resurrection, when they finally declare belief in the truth they once denied. Their declaration comes too late. Faith is accepted only in this worldly life, the place of trial and choice, which the verse likens to a place near at hand. Once they have left it and entered the Hereafter, a far-off place, they cannot reach faith or reclaim the opportunity, just as a person cannot grasp something that is far beyond his reach. The verse warns that repentance and belief must come while one is still able to act, since the door closes when the truth becomes unmistakable and the chance for choice has passed.

translation: And they had already disbelieved in it before, and they cast conjecture about the unseen from a distant place.
interpretation: The verse (Saba 34:53) describes the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, when they claim belief after it is too late. They had rejected the truth in the worldly life, when faith was still possible and beneficial. Their present declaration of belief is like trying to grasp something from a far-off place, unreachable for them now. In the world they used to hurl baseless guesses about the unseen, calling the Messenger a poet, a sorcerer or a liar and denying resurrection and the Hereafter, without any knowledge or evidence. The lesson is that faith must be embraced in this life, while the opportunity exists, and that speculating about the unseen without revelation leads to ruin.

translation: And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their likes before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.
interpretation: This verse describes the moment of death or the Day of Judgment, when the disbelievers who were arrogantly engrossed in worldly pleasures are cut off from everything they craved: faith, repentance, a return to life, and the comforts of the world. Just as earlier nations who denied the messengers were suddenly seized and denied any chance to make amends, so will these be. The cause of this deprivation is stated at the end: they lived in a doubt that was unsettling and suspicious, rejecting revelation without sound reason. Their persistent uncertainty about resurrection and accountability led them to squander the opportunity for belief, so when the time of certainty arrived, it was too late to benefit from it.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers having wings, two, three, or four. He increases in creation whatever He wills. Indeed, God is over all things capable.
interpretation: The verse opens Surah Fatir by directing praise to God as the one who brought the heavens and earth into being without precedent, and so alone deserves gratitude and worship. The angels, though powerful and exalted, are only created servants and carriers of God's commands, each equipped with wings suited to the task He assigns, which shows that they are not partners or intercessors with independent authority. The statement that He adds to creation whatever He wills shows that His creative power is not limited to what we know. It may include wings, beauty, strength, voice, intellect, or any other attribute, and human beings are meant to see in this the boundless power and wisdom of God. The closing affirmation that He has power over all things reminds believers that nothing He wills is beyond His ability, which should lead them to trust Him and to give praise to Him alone.

translation: Whatever mercy God opens to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all provision, guidance, health, security and every form of mercy are controlled solely by God's will. When He grants a blessing, no creature, however powerful, can block it, and when He withholds something, no one can bring it about against His decree. The believer should therefore place hope and trust in God alone and not fear or depend on people or created means as if they held independent power over benefit or harm. Gifts and denials alike flow from His might (al-'Aziz), so nothing overcomes Him, and from His wisdom (al-Hakim), so nothing He gives or withholds is without purpose, even when its wisdom is hidden from us.

translation: O people, remember the favor of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? There is no deity except Him, so how are you deluded?
interpretation: The verse calls humanity to move from heedlessness to gratitude by reflecting on the blessings they enjoy every day: rain and sunlight from above, and crops, water and resources from the earth. Because these are plainly gifts they did not create or secure for themselves, the rhetorical question shows that no other being shares in creating or sustaining them. Gratitude and worship therefore belong to God alone. Turning to other deities despite this evidence is irrational, and the closing question 'how are you deluded?' rebukes those who let falsehood, habit or desire turn them away from the truth that stands before them.

translation: And if they deny you, then indeed messengers before you were denied. And to God all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, by reminding him that rejection is the common lot of God's messengers, so the denial of his people is neither a sign of failure nor a reflection on the truth of his message. It teaches that patience is the proper response, since the prophets before him endured the same and remained steadfast. The closing clause, 'to God all matters are returned,' assures believers that the final judgment belongs to God alone: He will vindicate the truthful, hold the deniers to account, and set right every wrong, so the messenger need not grieve over those who reject him.

translation: O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you about Allah.
interpretation: God warns people that His promises of resurrection, reckoning, reward and punishment are certain, and that they must not let the pleasures, wealth and status of this fleeting life distract them from preparing for the Hereafter. Nor should Satan, the great deceiver, or any false hope, lead them to sin by persuading them that God's mercy and forbearance mean there will be no accountability. The verse calls for sober awareness: enjoy lawful worldly goods without being enslaved by them, and combine hope in God's mercy with fear of His justice, acting with obedience and repentance rather than complacency.

translation: Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party to be among the companions of the Blaze.
interpretation: God warns that Satan's hostility toward humankind is real and constant, so it is not enough to avoid him casually: believers must treat him as a true enemy by rejecting his whispers, distrusting his embellishment of sin, and resisting the paths he opens. His aim is not to benefit those who follow him but to drag them into the same fate he has earned, the Blaze. Every call to disobedience, however attractive it seems, is a recruitment into his party, whose end is ruin. The verse thus calls for vigilance and for a deliberate stance of opposition to Satan, expressed through obedience to God.

translation: Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment, but those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse sets out a divine principle of justice: the outcomes of the afterlife follow from one's stance toward truth and how one acts on it. Rejecting faith, with the arrogance and wrongdoing that usually come with it, leads to a severe reckoning. Faith that is proven by righteous action brings two gifts. The first is forgiveness, which wipes away past shortcomings and shows that God's mercy outweighs human failings. The second is a great reward, a generous recompense far beyond what the deeds alone would earn. The verse also teaches that belief must be joined with action, and that the believer's hope rests on God's mercy and not on a flawless record.

translation: Is he, then, to whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive so that he sees it as good, (like one who is guided)? Indeed, God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So let not your soul be consumed in regret over them. Indeed, God is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a person who persists in wrongdoing can fall into self-deception, so that his moral sense becomes inverted and he regards his evil deeds as good. This state is not something a preacher can repair by force or by grief, for guidance and misguidance come through God's will, which follows His wisdom and the choices people make. The Prophet is therefore consoled and told not to torment himself with sorrow over the refusal of his people to believe. His duty is to convey the message, while their reckoning belongs to God, who knows fully everything they do and will requite it with justice.

translation: And it is God who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus will be the Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse points to a process people witness every year as proof of the Resurrection. God sends winds that gather clouds, and drives the rain to land that is barren and lifeless, so that plants spring from it. In the same way, God can bring dead bodies back to life on the Day of Resurrection. The one who revives dry earth with rain is fully able to revive the dead, so denying the afterlife is unreasonable. The natural order shows His power and mercy, and it should lead people to believe in the Hereafter and to prepare for it.

translation: Whoever desires honor and power [should know that] all honor and power belong to God. To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it up. As for those who plot evil deeds, for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will come to nothing.
interpretation: True honor cannot be obtained by flattering the powerful, following falsehood, or scheming against others; it is wholly God's to give, so anyone who truly wants dignity must seek it through obedience to Him. The path to that honor is faith expressed in pure speech, such as remembrance of God and truthful words, which is accepted by Him only when it is joined to righteous action that lifts it up, showing that words without deeds lack weight. By contrast, those who devise evil schemes, whether to undermine truth, harm believers, or gain status unjustly, seek a false power and will face severe punishment, and their plots will perish and fail, because what is built on falsehood has no lasting foundation.

translation: And Allah created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then made you pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one grows old who is granted a long life, nor is anything reduced from his life, except that it is in a Record. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse points to God's complete power and knowledge over human life from beginning to end. He began humanity from dust, then carried it through the stages of the sperm-drop and the creation of male and female pairs, so the origin of life is wholly in His hand. Nothing in the course of any life escapes Him: every conception and birth occurs with His knowledge, and the length of each person's life, whether extended or shortened, is already written in a Record. Since this all-encompassing knowledge and ordering is effortless for God, the verse invites people to recognize His lordship, to trust that their lifespan and affairs are measured and not random, and to be mindful of Him and of the resurrection, which is just as easy for the One who created them in the first place.

translation: And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty, bitter. Yet from each you eat tender meat and extract ornaments which you wear. And you see the ships plowing through them, so that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: The verse uses the contrast between fresh and salt water as a sign that things which differ greatly in nature and quality can still come from one Creator and still serve human beings. Believer and disbeliever are no more equal than the sweet and the bitter sea, just as guidance and misguidance are not equal. Yet God's mercy and provision reach people through both: fresh meat from fish, jewels such as pearls and coral, and the sea routes that carry ships for trade and livelihood. The verse points to the natural world as evidence of God's power and generosity, and calls people to respond with gratitude by recognizing the Giver, worshipping Him alone, and using His gifts in ways that please Him.

translation: He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for an appointed term.
