That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those whom you invoke besides Him do not possess even the thin skin of a date-stone.
interpretation: The verse argues from the order of the cosmos to God's exclusive right to be worshipped. The steady alternation of night and day, with each gaining on the other through the seasons, and the sun and moon moving by a precise, fixed course until an appointed end, show a single Designer who governs creation without partner or interruption. Because He alone controls these vast systems, the dominion belongs to Him alone. By contrast, the idols and beings people call upon besides Him own nothing, not even a qitmir, the tiniest membrane on a date stone. Beings who own nothing cannot answer prayers or benefit anyone, so directing worship to them is irrational. Worship is due only to the Lord who rules the universe.

translation: If you call upon them, they do not hear your call; and even if they were to hear, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disown your associating them with God. And none can inform you like One who is All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse exposes the futility of worshipping anything besides God. The idols and false deities that people invoke are powerless: they cannot hear a prayer, and even if they could hear, they lack any ability to answer or help. Their uselessness is not only in this world; on the Day of Resurrection they will themselves repudiate those who made them partners with God, so the very objects of devotion will become witnesses against their worshippers. The closing phrase affirms that this is the truth told by God, the One who is All-Aware of the reality of all things, so His report about the helplessness of false gods is more reliable than any human speculation or inherited belief, and it calls the listener to turn to God alone, who truly hears and responds.

translation: O mankind, you are the ones in need of God, while God is the Self-Sufficient, the Worthy of all praise.
interpretation: The verse states a basic truth about the relationship between human beings and their Creator. All people, whatever their wealth, power, or knowledge, depend on God at every moment for their existence, sustenance, health, guidance, and survival. This need is constant and part of their nature, not an occasional condition. God, by contrast, needs nothing from His creation. Their worship, obedience, and gratitude add nothing to Him, and their disobedience takes nothing from Him. The name 'the Praiseworthy' (al-Hamid) adds that God's self-sufficiency is not cold detachment. He gives generously and acts with wisdom, so He deserves praise in every circumstance. The verse therefore calls people to humility and gratitude, and to turn to God alone rather than relying on themselves or on other created beings. It also teaches that worship benefits the worshipper, not God.

translation: If He wills, He can remove you and bring forth a new creation.
interpretation: The verse reminds humankind that God has no need of them, while they depend wholly on Him. Their existence and continuity are not guaranteed by their own power but rest entirely on God's will. He could end the present generation and replace it with another whenever He wished. This should humble people, turn them away from arrogance and heedlessness, and lead them to gratitude, obedience and return to their Creator, since their worship benefits only themselves and adds nothing to His sovereignty.

translation: And that is not difficult for God.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute power: nothing is hard or beyond Him. It is stated in several places (e.g., 14:20, 35:17) after God warns that He can remove the disobedient and bring a new creation in their place. The point is that humanity's rejection of faith does not diminish God in any way, and His will is never obstructed. People depend entirely on Him, while He is free of need of them. The verse is therefore both a warning to those who defy Him, since He can replace them whenever He wills, and a reassurance to believers that His promises will be fulfilled with ease.

translation: No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if one heavily laden calls for help with its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he be a close relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for his own good. And to God is the final return.
interpretation: The verse establishes individual moral responsibility on the Day of Judgment: each soul answers for its own deeds, and no one, however close in kinship, can take on another's sins. This removes false reliance on family, ancestry, or intercessors in place of one's own faith and conduct. The Prophet's warning benefits only those whose hearts are receptive, who revere God though He is unseen and who keep up prayer. Self-purification through faith, repentance, and good deeds is not a favor to anyone else but an investment in one's own salvation, since every person will return to God for judgment. The verse thus urges personal accountability and spiritual effort now, before the time when no one can help another.

translation: And the blind and the seeing are not equal.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 35:19) draws a contrast between the one who is spiritually blind, who refuses to perceive the signs of God and the truth of revelation, and the one who sees, whose heart is open to guidance and who recognizes his Creator. The two cannot be alike in their state, their path, or their end, because the believer walks in light, understanding and purpose, while the disbeliever stumbles in ignorance and heedlessness. The verse affirms that insight, not mere physical sight, is what distinguishes people in God's sight, and that their differing outcomes in the Hereafter will reflect this difference.

translation: Nor are the darknesses equal to the light.
interpretation: This verse (Surat Fatir 35:20) continues a series of contrasts: the blind and the seeing, the darkness and the light, the shade and the scorching heat, the living and the dead. Darkness stands for disbelief, ignorance, and misguidance, which leave a person confused and unable to find the way. Light stands for faith and revealed guidance, which show the path to truth and salvation. The two cannot be placed on the same level, and so the believer and the disbeliever cannot share the same state or fate. The verse calls people to choose the clarity of faith over the confusion of unbelief.

translation: Nor are the shade and the scorching heat alike.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Fatir 35:21) continues a series of contrasts: the blind and the seeing, darkness and light, shade and burning heat. Together they illustrate that belief and disbelief, guidance and misguidance, can never be equal in nature or outcome. The shade stands for the comfort, mercy and tranquility that believers find in faith and, in the next life, in Paradise, while the scorching heat stands for the distress and torment of disbelief and its consequence in the Fire. The verse calls people to recognize this clear difference and to choose the path that leads to God's mercy.

translation: Nor are the living and the dead alike. Indeed, God makes hear whom He wills, and you cannot make hear those who are in the graves.
interpretation: The verse uses life and death as a metaphor for spiritual states. Those whose hearts are alive with awareness and receptiveness to truth are not equal to those whose hearts have died through stubbornness and heedlessness. Guidance is ultimately in God's hands: He grants the ability to hear and accept the message to whoever is open to it. The Prophet's task is only to convey the message, and he cannot make people respond if their hearts are as lifeless as the dead in their graves, who cannot hear any call. This consoles him about the disbelievers' rejection and reminds him that results rest with God alone.

translation: You are nothing but a warner.
interpretation: This phrase, which appears in the Qur'an in the address to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) (e.g., Surah Fatir 35:23), defines the limits and nature of his mission. His role is to convey the message clearly and warn people of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, not to compel anyone to believe or to control their hearts and destinies. Guidance, judgment, and reckoning belong to God alone. The verse comforts the Prophet when his people reject him, reminding him that his responsibility is fulfilled once the warning is delivered, and it teaches that the duty of a caller to truth is sincere communication, not forcing results.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner. And there is no community but that a warner has passed among them.
interpretation: God affirms that Prophet Muhammad was sent with the truth, to give glad tidings of reward to those who believe and obey, and to warn those who deny and persist in wrongdoing. The verse then places his mission within a universal pattern of divine guidance: no nation has been left without a messenger or warner who reminded it of God and of accountability. This means that the message of warning is not new or unique to one people, that God's justice requires clear notice before judgment, and that those who reject the truth do so after guidance has reached them. It also consoles the Prophet, since rejection of the warners has been the fate of earlier communities as well.

translation: And if they deny you, then those before them also denied; their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with the scriptures, and with the enlightening Book.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by reminding him that rejection of truth is a recurring pattern in human history and not a sign of any deficiency in his message. Earlier messengers brought undeniable evidence: miracles and clear signs, books of wisdom and admonition, and illuminating scripture that guides. Yet their peoples still denied them out of stubbornness, arrogance, and attachment to worldly interests, not for lack of proof. The lesson is that he should remain steadfast and patient, as denial does not diminish the truth, while those who reject clear guidance bear the responsibility and consequences of their choice.

translation: Then I seized those who disbelieved, and how [terrible] was My denial [of them].
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 22:44) reminds the listener that God does not hasten to punish deniers at once. He gives them respite, and they are lulled into thinking their disbelief carries no consequence. Then, when the appointed time comes, He seizes them suddenly with His punishment. The rhetorical question 'how was My nakir?' invites the hearer to reflect on the fate of earlier nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Madyan, who rejected their messengers. The ruins and the memory of their destruction show how severe and just God's disapproval of their denial was. The lesson is a warning to the present deniers to learn from history and repent before they meet the same end, and a consolation to the Prophet and the believers that God's judgment will surely overtake those who reject the truth, however long it seems delayed.

translation: Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and with it We bring forth fruits of varying colours? And among the mountains are streaks of white and red, of varying shades, and others intensely black.
interpretation: The verse points to the diversity of creation as evidence of God's power and wisdom. A single source, rain from the sky, yields fruits of many colours, and the mountains, though made of the same earth, show different layers and hues, from white to red to deep black. This variety is no accident but the work of a deliberate Creator who gives each thing its own character. It prepares the following verses, which say that people and animals also differ in their colours, and that those who truly fear God are the knowledgeable, the ones who reflect on such signs and so recognise His greatness.

translation: And among people, and moving creatures, and grazing livestock are various colors likewise. Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Forgiving.
interpretation: After pointing to the diversity of colors in fruits, mountains, and other created things, the verse says that humans and animals also differ in color and kind, and that this variety is a sign of the Creator's power and wisdom. Those who truly reflect on creation and know Allah through His signs are the ones who stand in awe of Him, because their knowledge brings them to recognize His greatness, majesty, and accountability. Knowledge here is not mere information but the insight that produces reverence and obedience, so the more one knows of Allah and His creation, the greater one's fear and humility. The closing names remind the believer that Allah is Almighty, so He is to be feared, and Forgiving, so He is to be hoped in and turned to in repentance.

translation: Indeed, those who recite the Book of God, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, are hoping for a trade that will never perish.
interpretation: The verse portrays true believers as those whose faith is expressed in action: they constantly recite and follow God's Book, maintain their prayer as their link with their Lord, and give generously of their wealth both in private, to protect the dignity of the recipient and keep their sincerity, and in public, to set an example and encourage others to do good. The Qur'an calls this conduct a 'trade' because the believer offers time, effort, and wealth and expects a return from God. Unlike worldly commerce, which is uncertain and can end in loss or ruin, this trade with God can never fail or decay, for its profit is God's lasting reward and His abundant favor in the Hereafter.

translation: So that He may give them their full rewards and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is Forgiving and Appreciative.
interpretation: This verse (Fatir 35:30) explains the purpose of the believers' recitation of God's Book, their establishing prayer, and their spending in secret and in public, as mentioned in the preceding verse: God will give them the full recompense for their deeds without any diminishment, and then add to it out of His pure generosity beyond what they have earned. The closing names show why: God forgives their shortcomings and flaws, and He is Shakur, who appreciates and rewards even small acts of obedience with abundant return. Thus the believer's salvation rests not on the strict measure of deeds alone but on divine forgiveness and gratitude that magnify the reward.

translation: And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what came before it. Indeed, Allah is, of His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.
interpretation: The Qur'an is the truth because it agrees with the core message of the earlier revealed scriptures, such as the Torah and the Gospel, and does not contradict their original teachings of monotheism and righteousness. This agreement shows that it comes from the same divine source. God sends it with full knowledge of the inner and outer condition of His servants. He knows what guidance they need and what will reform them, so the revelation is perfectly fitted to humanity's needs. It is therefore the final and most reliable guidance for people to follow.

translation: Then We made those whom We chose from among Our servants inherit the Book. Among them are those who wrong themselves, among them are those who follow a middle course, and among them are those who are foremost in good deeds by God's permission. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: The verse says that God gave the Qur'an as an inheritance to the community He chose, and that this community falls into three ranks according to how they carry the Book. The first is the one who wrongs himself: he believes but falls short, sometimes neglecting duties or committing sins, so he harms his own soul while remaining within the fold of faith. The second is the moderate one, who fulfills the obligations and avoids what is forbidden but does not go beyond that. The third is the one who races ahead in good deeds, who does the obligatory and the recommended and leaves even doubtful matters, and does so only through God's enabling grace, not by his own power. Being counted among the chosen heirs of the Book, and especially being given the ability to reach the highest rank, is the 'great bounty,' a favor from God that no one earns by his own merit alone.

translation: Gardens of Eden, which they will enter, adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be of silk.
interpretation: The verse portrays the reward of the righteous who were chosen and who strove in good deeds: they will dwell permanently in the Gardens of Eden, a name signifying lasting residence. The adornments of gold and pearl and the clothing of silk, which are signs of honor, dignity and ease, are given to them as a fitting recompense for the restraint they practiced in this world. The worldly pleasures they gave up for God's sake, or used only within what is lawful, are returned to them in perfected and lasting form, showing that God's honoring of His faithful servants is complete, outward as well as inward, and is a mark of God's generosity and of the bliss that has no end.

translation: And they will say: 'Praise be to God, who has removed grief from us. Indeed, our Lord is truly Forgiving and Appreciative.'
interpretation: This verse describes the speech of the people of Paradise upon entering it. The 'grief' they praise God for removing encompasses every kind of sorrow: fear of the Hereafter, anxiety over their sins and their final destiny, and the worries and hardships of worldly life. Their relief is credited entirely to God's grace, not their own deeds. They call Him 'Forgiving' because He pardoned their shortcomings, which is what spared them from punishment, and 'Appreciative' (Shakur) because He accepts even small good deeds and repays them with abundant, lasting reward. The believer is thus taught that salvation rests on a balance of divine forgiveness of faults and divine gratitude for good works, and that gratitude and praise to God are the fitting response to His mercy.

translation: He who, out of His bounty, has settled us in the Abode of permanence, wherein no toil touches us and no weariness touches us.
interpretation: This verse is the speech of the people of Paradise after they are relieved of grief. They credit their entry into the eternal abode to God's grace and not to their own deeds alone, since no deed could by itself earn such a reward. Their dwelling is permanent, with no moving on and no death. Life there is free of both kinds of hardship: 'nasab' is the exertion and fatigue of effort, and 'lughub' is the exhaustion and languor that follows from it. Paradise is therefore a state of complete, lasting rest, in contrast to worldly life, where every pleasure is bought with labor and ends in tiredness. Their gratitude is the proper response to a gift that is both unearned and unending.

translation: And those who disbelieve will have the fire of Hell; it will neither finish them off so that they die, nor will any of its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful disbeliever.
interpretation: The verse presents the fate of persistent denial of truth as a just and fitting consequence rather than an arbitrary punishment. Those who reject faith after being given reason, signs, and time to reflect have chosen to close themselves off from God's guidance, so the afterlife confirms the state they chose. The severity is described as a condition with no relief: they are denied both death, which would end the suffering, and any easing of it. This conveys that the consequence of willful ingratitude (kufr means both disbelief and ingratitude) toward the Creator is lasting and serious. The closing phrase, 'Thus do We recompense every ungrateful disbeliever,' stresses divine justice: the recompense is universal and consistent, applied to every person who knowingly denies and is thankless for God's favors, and it serves as a warning to turn back to faith and gratitude while there is still opportunity.

translation: And they will cry out therein: 'Our Lord, take us out; we will do righteousness, other than what we used to do.' [Allah will respond:] 'Did We not grant you life long enough for whoever would remember to remember therein? And the warner came to you. So taste [the punishment], for the wrongdoers there is no helper.'
interpretation: The verse portrays the despair of the disbelievers in Hell, who scream loudly and plead for a second chance on earth, promising to do good deeds instead of their former evil ones. Their plea is rejected because they were already given ample time in life, long enough for anyone willing to reflect and be guided, and they were also sent a warner, the Prophet bringing the Qur'an, who made the truth clear. Having no excuse, they must taste the consequences of their own choices. The closing statement means no one can rescue or intercede for those who wronged themselves and others through disbelief and sin, since the opportunity for repentance exists only in this worldly life and ends at death.

translation: Indeed, God is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of what lies within the hearts.
interpretation: The verse teaches that nothing is hidden from God, neither the vast unseen realities of the cosmos nor the most private inner states of a person, such as intentions, secrets, and beliefs. Since God knows what hearts conceal, outward claims and appearances carry no weight with Him, and human accountability rests on sincerity. It is a call to be mindful of God and to purify one's intentions, because the believer lives under the awareness that his inner life is as open to God as his outward deeds.

translation: He it is who made you successors on the earth. So whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is against him. And the disbelief of the disbelievers adds nothing with their Lord except abhorrence, and the disbelief of the disbelievers adds nothing except loss.
interpretation: God reminds humankind that He entrusted them with the earth, generation succeeding generation, as a trust and a test, so they are accountable for how they live on it. Rejecting God and His guidance does not harm Him or diminish His sovereignty; its entire burden falls on the one who disbelieves. Far from bringing any gain, persistence in disbelief only increases God's displeasure toward the disbeliever and deepens his spiritual and ultimate ruin, since he squanders the purpose of his stewardship and loses both his standing before God and his own salvation.

translation: Say: Have you considered your partners whom you call upon besides God? Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens? Or have We given them a Book so that they stand upon clear evidence from it? Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion.
interpretation: The verse is a challenge to idolatry that demands proof. The Prophet is told to ask the polytheists to produce evidence for their false deities by three kinds of proof: a rational proof (have these partners created anything on earth?), a proof of ownership or partnership (do they share in governing the heavens?), and a proof from revelation (has God given them a scripture that authorizes worshipping them?). Since none of these can be shown, the worship has no basis. What leads people into it is mutual deception: the leaders and elders among the wrongdoers promise their followers that these idols will intercede and bring benefit, but these promises are only illusion and false hope. Only God, who creates and owns everything and sends revelation, deserves worship.

translation: Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease to be. And if they were to cease, no one could hold them back after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the continued existence and order of the whole cosmos is not self-sustaining but depends moment by moment on God's power and will. Those who ascribe divinity to anything besides Him, whether idols, angels, or created forces, are shown that none of these can uphold even a single star or the ground beneath our feet, so they have no claim to worship. The closing attributes add a moral lesson: human beings persist in ingratitude, denial, and sin, which might seem to merit the collapse of creation, yet God in His forbearance does not hasten punishment, and in His forgiveness He opens the door of repentance. The stability of the universe is therefore both a proof of His oneness and power and a sign of His mercy and patience toward people, calling them to turn back to Him.

translation: They swore by God their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be better guided than any of the other nations. But when a warner did come to them, it only increased them in aversion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the gap between what people claim about themselves and how they actually behave. The Quraysh, seeing the misguidance of earlier communities such as the Jews and Christians, boasted with strong oaths that if a messenger came to them they would follow him more readily than any of those peoples. Yet when Muhammad (peace be upon him) came with clear guidance, their response did not improve. They fled from the truth and grew more averse to it, out of arrogance and attachment to their own status and interests. The lesson is that good intentions voiced before a test are no proof of sincerity. A heart that is not truly willing to submit to the truth will only be hardened further when the truth arrives, so that the warning itself exposes the stubbornness already within it.

translation: [They did so] out of arrogance in the land and the plotting of evil; but the evil plot encompasses only its own people. Then do they await anything but the way [God dealt with] the former peoples? You will never find any change in the way of God, and you will never find any alteration in the way of God.
interpretation: The verse explains that the root of the disbelievers' rejection of the truth was pride and scheming against the believers and the messenger, yet God has established a fixed moral law: evil plots ultimately recoil upon those who devise them, destroying the plotters rather than their targets. Those who persist in arrogance and deceit are therefore merely awaiting the same fate that befell earlier nations who denied their prophets. This divine pattern of consequences is constant and reliable: God does not substitute a different outcome for the wrongdoers (no 'tabdil'), nor divert the punishment from them to others or turn it away from its deserving recipients (no 'tahwil'). The believer is thus reassured that justice is certain, and the wrongdoer is warned that arrogance and conspiracy lead to self-destruction.

translation: Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them, who were greater than them in power? And Allah is not such that anything in the heavens or on the earth could frustrate Him. Indeed, He is ever All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: The verse calls the deniers of the Prophet's message to learn from history: the ruined dwellings and traces of earlier nations, such as 'Ad and Thamud, who had more strength, wealth and influence, show that worldly power did not protect them once they rejected the truth and defied God's messengers. If they could not escape God's punishment, those who come after them, weaker and less established, have even less reason to feel secure. The verse then gives the underlying reason for this: nothing in the heavens or the earth can thwart God's will or escape His reach, because His knowledge encompasses every deed and intention, and His power is able to carry out what He decrees. The verse is therefore both a warning to the arrogant and a reassurance to the believers that wrongdoing will not triumph forever.

translation: If God were to hold people to account for what they have earned, He would not leave on its surface a single living creature. But He defers them until a appointed term. And when their term arrives, then surely God is ever Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: The verse points to God's forbearance and mercy: the wrongdoing of humankind is grave enough that immediate punishment would devastate the whole earth, even the innocent creatures that share it, yet God delays judgment and gives people time to repent and amend. This delay is not neglect or indifference, nor a sign that deeds go unnoticed; every soul has a fixed, known term, and when it arrives, each will be judged by the One who sees all His servants perfectly, knowing their deeds and intentions, and who will requite them with full justice.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ya, Sin.
interpretation: Ya Sin is one of the 'muqatta'at', the disconnected letters that open several surahs. The most fitting reading is that these letters are a divine mark of the Qur'an's miraculous nature: the revelation is composed of the very letters the Arabs use in their speech, yet they cannot produce anything like it. Their placement at the start of the surah draws the listener's attention and prepares the heart to receive the message that follows, which affirms the Prophet's mission, the truth of revelation, and the certainty of resurrection. Their precise meaning is known fully only to God, so the believer accepts them with reverence and without speculation.

translation: By the Qur'an, full of wisdom.
interpretation: God takes an oath by the Qur'an, describing it as 'al-Hakim' (the Wise), meaning that it is perfectly firm, free of contradiction and falsehood, and that every command, prohibition, report and law within it is set in its right place with wisdom. By swearing by it, God affirms its exalted status and the truth of what follows in the surah: that Muhammad is truly one of the messengers, so those who deny him have no valid ground, since the very Book he brings bears the mark of divine wisdom and guides to what is right.

translation: Indeed, you are one of the messengers.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:3) is a divine affirmation of the Prophet Muhammad's authenticity, following the oath by the wise Qur'an in the preceding verse. God Himself testifies that Muhammad is not a poet, soothsayer, or self-appointed claimant, but a true messenger sent in the line of earlier prophets. The emphasis, through the particles 'inna' and 'la', answers the denial of the disbelievers and consoles the Prophet, assuring him that his mission is divinely commissioned and that the message he brings is truth, so he should remain steadfast despite rejection.

translation: On a straight path.
interpretation: This phrase, found in Surah Ya-Sin (36:4) following the affirmation that the Prophet Muhammad is among the messengers, means that the messengers are upon a path that is upright, with no crookedness, deviation, or contradiction. The path is God's religion of monotheism and righteousness, which leads those who follow it safely to God and to His pleasure. By describing it as straight, the verse affirms that the guidance brought by the Prophet is true, balanced, and free of error, so that whoever walks it will reach his destination, while those who stray from it are lost.

translation: This is a revelation sent down by the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an does not originate from the Prophet or any human being but is sent down from God. It pairs two attributes deliberately: 'the Almighty' (al-'Azīz) indicates that this revelation is backed by irresistible power and cannot be overcome, altered, or successfully opposed by those who deny it, while 'the Most Merciful' (al-Raḥīm) shows that its purpose is mercy, as it guides people out of misguidance toward salvation. The revelation is thus both a warning from a mighty Lord and a gift of compassion, and its authority rests on God's might while its content flows from His mercy.

translation: That you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless.
interpretation: The verse explains the purpose of the Prophet's mission: to bring a warning to the Arabs, to whom no messenger had come in the recent generations before him. Because they had lacked prophetic guidance for so long, they had drifted into forgetfulness of God, the Hereafter, and their accountability. Their heedlessness is therefore not a settled rejection after clear warning, but a state of neglect that the Qur'an's message comes to rouse them from, so that they awaken, reflect, and return to the truth.

translation: The word has already been justified against most of them, so they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:7) means that God's decree of warning and punishment has become binding upon most of those to whom the Prophet was sent, not because God compelled them to disbelieve, but because He knew in advance, through His eternal knowledge, that they would persist in arrogance and stubborn rejection after the truth was made clear to them. Their repeated denial hardened their hearts until they lost the openness needed to accept guidance, so the outcome foretold by the divine word came to pass: they remain unbelieving. It consoles the Prophet, teaching him that their refusal is not a failure of his message but the result of their own chosen obstinacy.

translation: Indeed, We have placed shackles around their necks, reaching up to the chins, so their heads are held up, unable to bend them.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of neck-shackles that lock the head upward to describe the spiritual condition of those who stubbornly reject the message. Just as a person with a collar up to the chin cannot lower his head or look at the ground, these people are prevented by their own arrogance and persistent denial from submitting, reflecting, or humbly accepting the truth. Their obstinacy becomes a self-imposed restraint, and God's decree confirms it as a consequence of their choice, so guidance does not enter their hearts even though the warning reaches them.

translation: And We have set a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and We have covered them, so they do not see.
interpretation: The verse describes the spiritual state of those who persistently reject the truth after the warning has reached them. The barriers before and behind them are an image of being hemmed in by their own stubbornness, pride and heedlessness: they cannot move forward toward guidance, and they cannot turn back to reflect on the signs they have already ignored. God veils their insight as a consequence of their persistent refusal, so even though their eyes see, their hearts cannot perceive the truth in front of them. The blindness is moral and spiritual rather than physical, and it is the result of their own choices, which God then confirms by closing off their perception.

translation: And it is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet by showing that the disbelief of certain people does not come from a failure in his message. Those described here have so hardened themselves in stubborn denial, after the truth was clear to them, that warning has no effect on them. Their refusal is the result of their own persistent arrogance and rejection, which closes their hearts to guidance, so the Prophet should not grieve over them or blame himself. His duty is only to convey the message; guidance rests with God. The warning still has value because it establishes the proof against them and benefits those who are receptive.

translation: You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful in the unseen. So give them good news of forgiveness and a generous reward.
interpretation: The Prophet's warning benefits only those whose hearts are open to receiving it. Those who follow the Qur'an and hold God in awe even when no one sees them, which shows sincere faith that does not depend on public observation, are the ones who actually take the warning to heart and change. The verse consoles the Prophet that those who persist in rejecting the message are not his responsibility, and it directs him to give the sincere believers glad tidings of God's forgiveness for their shortcomings and a noble reward in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forth and their traces. And everything We have enumerated in a clear register.
interpretation: God affirms His power to resurrect the dead and declares that nothing a person does is lost: both their deeds done in life and the lasting effects they leave behind, whether good, like beneficial knowledge, charity, and good example, or evil, like corrupting practices others follow, are recorded. Every person is therefore accountable not only for their direct actions but also for the consequences that continue after death, and all of it is precisely preserved in a clear, comprehensive record (the Preserved Tablet or book of deeds), so that on the Day of Resurrection each soul will find its full account, which should motivate one to leave a righteous legacy.

translation: And present to them an example: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it.
interpretation: God instructs the Prophet to give the Meccan disbelievers a parable drawn from history, showing that rejecting messengers is a repeated pattern with a consistent outcome. The 'town' is commonly understood as Antioch, where messengers were sent to call its people to God's oneness, and they were denied. The lesson is that the Meccans' denial of Muhammad is not new, that the truth of a message does not depend on the number of its supporters or the acceptance of its audience, and that those who reject warnings bring upon themselves the fate of earlier deniers. It also consoles the Prophet, reminding him that earlier messengers faced the same rejection and remained steadfast.

translation: When We sent to them two messengers, they denied them both; so We reinforced them with a third, and they said, 'Indeed, we are messengers sent to you.'
interpretation: The verse shows that God's call to truth is not abandoned when people reject it, but is strengthened with further support and proof. The townspeople's denial of the first two messengers did not cause God to withdraw the message; He reinforced it with a third, so that the argument would be established ever more firmly against them. The messengers speak with united, confident voice, stating plainly that they are sent by God, which teaches that the bearers of truth should remain steadfast and cooperative in the face of denial, and that rejection by the majority does not diminish the truth of the message.

translation: They said: "You are nothing but human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has not sent down anything. You are only lying."
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:15) records the response of the townspeople to the messengers sent to them. They rejected the message because they assumed that prophethood is incompatible with ordinary humanity: since the messengers ate, drank, and lived as they did, they reasoned that these men could not be recipients of divine revelation. Their objection reveals a stubborn arrogance and a false standard for judging truth, one based on the outward form of the messenger rather than the content of the message and its signs. By saying that God, the Most Merciful, has revealed nothing, they denied revelation altogether and accused the messengers of fabrication, a common excuse of those who refuse guidance. The verse teaches that rejection of the truth often stems from pride and preconceived notions, and that God's mercy, shown in sending guidance through humans who can be understood and followed, is wrongly treated as grounds for disbelief.

translation: They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you."
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:16) records the reply of the messengers to the people of the town who denied them. Having been accused of being mere mortals and liars, the messengers do not argue endlessly or swear by worldly proofs; they appeal to God's knowledge as the ultimate witness to their truthfulness. Their words show the confidence of those who are sincere: when people reject the truth, the believer's final recourse is that God knows his true state, and no denial can alter the reality of his mission. It also teaches that the duty of a messenger is to convey the message, while acceptance or rejection rests with those addressed and the judgment rests with God.

translation: And we are responsible only for the clear delivery of the message.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:17) is the reply of the messengers to the people of the town who rejected them. It shows that the prophets' duty is limited to communicating God's message plainly and unambiguously, with no ambiguity left. They are not charged with forcing belief or with deciding the outcome. Guidance lies with God alone, and once the message has been clearly conveyed, the messengers have discharged their trust and the responsibility for accepting or rejecting it passes to the listeners. The verse also teaches the believers who call to God to be patient and steadfast, to focus on conveying the truth with clarity and sincerity, and to leave the results to God.

translation: They said, "Indeed, we see an evil omen in you. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment from us will surely touch you."
interpretation: In this verse (Ya-Sin 36:18), the people of the town answer the messengers sent to them with superstition and threats instead of reflection. Blaming the messengers for their misfortunes, they claim the message has brought bad luck, which shows how people who reject the truth shift responsibility for their own state onto those who call them to God. When they have no rational argument against the message, they turn to intimidation and the threat of violence, stoning and torture, to silence the call. The verse illustrates a recurring pattern in the history of prophets: those who refuse guidance respond with ill omens, hostility and persecution, while the true cause of their misfortune lies in their own disbelief and deeds, as the messengers reply in the next verse.

translation: They said: "Your omen is with you. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a transgressing people."
interpretation: The messengers reply to the townspeople who blamed them for bad luck: the cause of any misfortune lies in the townspeople's own deeds and disbelief, not in the messengers or their message. The verse rebukes them for treating admonition as an evil sign. Being reminded of God and warned should lead to repentance, but they respond with superstition and threats. Their real fault is that they are people who exceed all bounds, in rejecting the truth and in persecuting those who bring it.

translation: And there came from the farthest part of the city a man, running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers."
interpretation: The verse shows that truth does not depend on status, power, or proximity to the centre of influence. A man from the far edge of the city, who had perhaps nothing to gain and much to lose, hurried out of sincere concern once his heart recognized the truth of the messengers' call. His urgency ("running") reflects how genuine faith moves a person to act at once, and not to keep the message to himself. He addresses the people tenderly as "my people," which shows that sincere advice is given with compassion and with a sense of belonging to those who are being advised. His call to follow the messengers teaches that those who accept the truth first are often ordinary, humble people, and that standing up for the truth in the face of widespread denial is an act of courage and sincerity.

translation: Follow those who ask of you no reward, and who are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse (Ya-Sin 36:21) gives a practical test for recognizing a true messenger of God: sincerity and selflessness. A person who calls others to the truth without demanding wealth, status, or any worldly gain shows by his disinterest that his message is not a means to profit, and the soundness of his guidance can be seen in what he teaches and how he lives. The believer who speaks these words urges his people to accept the messengers because they combine two qualities that rarely occur together in false claimants: freedom from greed, and a path that leads to God. Those who benefit from a message they preach have a motive to distort it, but those who ask for nothing have no reason to deceive, so their call deserves to be followed.

translation: And why should I not worship the One who created me, and to Whom you will all be returned?
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the believing man in Surah Ya-Sin (36:22), presents worship as the natural and rational response to the Creator's rights over His creation. The man asks why he would turn away from the One who brought him into being, when that same One is the final destination of all people, including those who reject him. By framing the argument in the first person, he gently invites his people to reflect on their own situation without accusing them directly. The message is that origin and destiny both lead to God alone, so devotion belongs to Him and not to idols that neither created nor will judge. Accountability on the Day of Return makes sincere worship in this life a matter of wisdom as well as gratitude.

translation: Shall I take besides Him gods whose intercession will not avail me at all, if the Most Merciful intends some harm for me, and who cannot rescue me?
interpretation: The verse (Ya-Sin 36:23) is the believing man's rational argument for rejecting idol worship. Worshipping anything besides God makes no sense, because false deities have no power of their own. If God decrees harm for a person, those gods cannot intercede, since intercession belongs only to those God permits, and they cannot save him by their own strength. Only the One who holds benefit and harm in His hand deserves worship, so devotion to Him alone is the only reasonable course.

translation: "Indeed, then I would be in clear error."
interpretation: This is the declaration of the believing man in Surah Ya-Sin (36:24), who stood up for the messengers sent to his town. He has just argued that it would be senseless to worship gods that cannot intercede for him or rescue him from harm, and that he has no reason not to worship the One who created him. He then says that if he were to take such powerless beings as gods beside Allah, he would be plainly and unmistakably astray. The verse shows that worshipping anything besides the Creator is clear misguidance, evident to anyone who reasons soundly. It also shows the believer's courage in stating the truth openly, even to a hostile community, and in clearly distinguishing tawhid from error.

translation: Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.
interpretation: This is the declaration of the believing man in Surah Ya-Sin (36:25), who came from the farthest part of the city urging his people to follow the messengers. Having been threatened by his people, he publicly and fearlessly affirms his faith in the Lord of all of them, not merely his own private Lord, to show that the Creator they all owe worship to is the One he believes in. By saying 'so listen to me,' he calls on them to heed his sincere counsel and bear witness to his stance. The verse teaches that true faith must be proclaimed with courage and conviction even in the face of persecution, and that a sincere believer cares for guiding others even at the risk of his own life.

translation: It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "If only my people knew,
interpretation: This verse describes the believing man of Ya-Sin who called his people to follow the messengers and was killed for it. On his death he was honored with entry into Paradise, and rather than feeling bitterness or a desire for revenge against those who killed him, his first thought was for the very people who had wronged him. He wished they could know the forgiveness and honor God had granted him, so that they would believe and be saved. The verse shows the ideal character of a true caller to God: sincere compassion for people even when they are hostile, and a concern for their guidance that outlasts life itself.

translation: Of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured ones.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:27) is the wish of the believing man who came running to warn his people and urge them to follow the messengers. After he was killed for his faith, he was admitted to Paradise and wished that his people could know what he now knew: that God's forgiveness of his sins and His honouring of him came because of his faith and steadfastness. The verse shows that salvation and honour rest on God's mercy and forgiveness, and that the true believer, even after death, still wants good for those who wronged him, hoping that they will learn from his fate, believe, and gain the same reward.

translation: And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever to send one down.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:28) speaks of the people who killed the believing man who urged them to follow the messengers. It shows that God had no need to mobilize angelic armies or cosmic forces to destroy them; their punishment was a matter of a single, simple act of His will, as the next verse says, 'It was but one cry, and they were extinguished.' The verse underlines the insignificance of the wrongdoers in the sight of God and His absolute power. Destruction of the arrogant requires no grand display of force, and the believer's cause is never in need of elaborate means to be vindicated, for God's decree alone suffices.

translation: It was nothing but one single Blast, and behold, they were extinguished (utterly still and lifeless).
interpretation: The verse (Ya-Sin 36:29) shows how effortless God's punishment is for those who reject His messengers. The people of the town who denied the messengers were not destroyed by armies of angels or a prolonged affliction. A single cry was enough to end them, so that they fell silent and lifeless like a fire that dies out. The word 'khamidun' evokes a flame that has been put out, as if their life and defiance were a fire that vanished at once. The lesson is that worldly power and numbers offer no protection against God's decree, and that His command needs no elaborate means, since He has only to will something for it to be.

translation: Alas for the servants! No messenger ever comes to them but they ridicule him.
interpretation: The verse expresses deep sorrow and lament over humanity's persistent stubbornness. Despite God's mercy in sending guides to lead people toward truth, they repeatedly respond to each messenger with mockery rather than reflection. This mockery is the cause of their own ruin, since they reject the very means of their salvation. The 'regret' is voiced over their folly: they are the ones who lose out, because ridiculing divine guidance brings them nothing but loss in this world and the next, and it serves as consolation to the Prophet Muhammad that earlier messengers faced the same treatment.

translation: Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that those (generations) will not return to them?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny the truth for failing to draw a lesson from history. Whole generations that were once powerful and prosperous were wiped out by God because of their arrogance and disbelief, and none of them came back to the living, so they cannot return to warn, help, or intercede for their descendants. Their end shows that this worldly life is brief and that death is final as far as returning to this world is concerned. The people of Makkah, therefore, should not rely on their strength or numbers or assume they will escape the same fate, but should reflect, repent, and prepare for the return to God in the Hereafter, where everyone will be held to account.

translation: And indeed, all of them together will be brought before Us.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:32) affirms that no community or generation will escape accountability: every nation that has lived and perished, however great or numerous, will be gathered on the Day of Judgment and presented before God. The earlier verses remind people of the many generations destroyed before them who never return to this world, and this verse completes the thought by stating that they are not lost to oblivion but are held for a final reckoning. Its purpose is to rouse the heedless to remember that worldly power and survival are temporary, and that each person will stand before God to answer for deeds, so they should live with awareness of this certain meeting.

translation: And a sign for them is the dead earth: We give it life and bring forth from it grain, and from it they eat.
interpretation: The verse points to the revival of barren land as clear evidence of God's power and mercy. Just as lifeless soil is made to bloom and yield grain, the staple of human sustenance, so God can raise the dead to life on the Day of Resurrection. The daily bread people eat comes from a process they cannot create themselves, which should lead them to recognize the Giver of life, thank Him, and acknowledge that the resurrection they deny is no harder than the renewal of the earth they see every year.

translation: And We placed therein gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth within it.
interpretation: The verse points to God's deliberate provision for human life: the earth is not merely inhabited but prepared with sustenance. Gardens of date palms and grapevines represent food that is both a staple and a delight, while the springs are the hidden water that makes all growth possible. Water is brought forth from within the earth, so fruitfulness is not an accident of nature but a sign of divine design, mercy and power. Reflecting on this should lead a person to gratitude and to recognizing that the One who revives dead land with water is able to resurrect the dead, as the surrounding verses on the signs of creation and resurrection suggest.

translation: So that they may eat of its fruit, though their hands did not make it. Will they not then be grateful?
interpretation: The verse (Ya-Sin 36:35) points out that the gardens, date palms and vines God causes to grow exist so that people may eat their fruit, yet the fruit is not the product of human effort alone: people may plant and tend, but it is God who creates the seed, the soil, the water and the growth. Recognizing that this provision is a gift beyond their own labor, the verse rebukes human ingratitude and calls for thankfulness to God, expressed by acknowledging Him as the true provider and worshipping Him alone.

translation: Glory be to Him who created all the pairs—from what the earth grows, and from their own selves, and from what they do not know.
interpretation: The verse declares God's absolute transcendence above any flaw or partner by pointing to a universal law of creation: duality and pairing. Plants, humans, and countless things unknown to people at the time of revelation exist as complementary pairs, such as male and female, positive and negative. Only the Creator is One, without a mate or equal, while everything else is created in pairs and so depends on something beyond itself. The ordered, harmonious design of creation, including realms human knowledge has not yet reached, is a sign of the Creator's perfect wisdom, and it calls people to glorify Him and to recognize that He alone is the single source of all that exists.

translation: And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are plunged in darkness.
interpretation: God points to the nightly cycle as clear evidence of His power and wisdom. Day is the original covering of the world, and night is what remains when the light is drawn away, like a skin peeled from a body, leaving people suddenly in darkness. The ordinary rhythm of night and day is not self-sustaining or accidental. It is governed moment by moment by the Creator, who can withdraw the light whenever He wills. This should lead people to reflect on their complete dependence on Him, to recognize His power to bring about the Resurrection and other unseen realities, and to respond with gratitude and faith rather than heedlessness.

translation: And the sun runs on course toward a resting place for it; that is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse points to the sun's ordered, unceasing motion as a sign of God's power and wisdom. The sun moves along a path set for it until it reaches a appointed term or place, whether this is understood as its daily course, its yearly cycle, or the final end of the world when its movement stops. Nothing in this motion is random. It follows a precise measure fixed by the One who is Almighty (al-'Aziz), so no one can disrupt it, and All-Knowing (al-'Alim), so everything about it is set with perfect knowledge. The verse invites reflection that the regularity of the cosmos, on which human life and time-keeping depend, is evidence of a Creator who governs it, and that the universe is moving toward a destined end under His command.

translation: And the moon We have determined for it phases, until it returns like the old, dried-up palm stalk.
interpretation: The verse points to God's precise ordering of the cosmos: the moon moves through fixed stages, or mansions, each night, growing from a thin crescent to fullness and then waning until it appears thin, curved, and pale like an aged date-palm stalk (the 'urjun) that has dried and bent. This regular cycle is a sign of God's wisdom and power. It gives people a natural calendar for reckoning months and times of worship, and it invites reflection that everything in creation follows a measured decree set by the Creator, and that nothing in the heavens moves by chance.

translation: It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each floats along in an orbit.
interpretation: The verse points to the precise order God has set in the cosmos: the sun and moon each move along their own appointed course, so neither collides with or overtakes the other, and night and day follow one another in a fixed sequence without either coming early or encroaching on the other. This balance, in which every celestial body glides in its own path, is presented as a sign of the Creator's power, wisdom and meticulous planning, calling people to reflect and acknowledge that a perfectly regulated universe cannot be the product of chance and that it is He alone who deserves worship.

translation: And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.
interpretation: The verse points to God's mercy and power as seen in the ship of Noah, and in ships generally, in which humankind is borne safely over the sea. The 'laden ship' was filled with believers, animals and provisions, and its survival amid the flood was not due to human skill alone but to God's decree. Their 'offspring' were carried because the later generations of humanity descend from those saved in the ark, so the very existence of mankind is a favor from God. Likewise, the ability to sail the seas with cargo is a continuing sign that He subjected the water and made it bear heavy vessels. The verse therefore calls people to reflect, recognize the Creator's care and control over the natural world, and respond with gratitude and worship rather than heedlessness.

translation: And We have created for them the like of it (the ark) that which they ride.
interpretation: After recalling how God carried the offspring of humankind in the laden ark, the verse points to His further favor: He has given people other means of transport patterned on that ship, such as the vessels and ships that have followed it, and by extension the animals and conveyances they ride on land. The meaning is that human travel and carrying of burdens is not their own achievement but a gift from God, who provided the materials, the knowledge, and the natural laws that make such vessels float and move. This should lead people to gratitude and to recognition of His power, since He who preserves them in their ships can also cause them to drown if He wills.

translation: And if We willed, We would drown them; then there would be no one to respond to their cry for help, nor would they be rescued.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:43) reminds people that their safety at sea, and in every journey and endeavor, depends wholly on God's mercy and not on their own skill or technology. The ships that carry them are only secure because God allows the waters to bear them. If He willed otherwise, no helper or savior could intervene and no power could rescue them. Seen this way, the verse calls human beings to gratitude and humility, to recognize their total dependence on their Creator, and to turn away from arrogance and heedlessness, because the same Lord who grants safety can withdraw it in an instant.

translation: Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a while.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ya-Sin (36:44), speaks of God's mercy toward humankind: people are not drowned or destroyed despite the dangers around them, such as the sea, and are saved only because of God's compassion. Their survival and their time of enjoyment in this life are not due to their own power or entitlement but are a gift from God, granted for an appointed term. This reminds the believer that life is a temporary respite given by mercy, calling for gratitude, humility and preparation for the moment when that term ends.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Beware of what is before you and what is behind you, that you may receive mercy,' [they turn away].
interpretation: The verse (Ya-Sin 36:45) describes the stubborn disregard of the disbelievers when they are called to take heed. 'What is before you' refers to the punishments and consequences awaiting them in the Hereafter, while 'what is behind you' refers to the fate of earlier nations and the sins and punishments of this worldly life that preceded them. They are urged to learn from past destructions and to fear the coming reckoning so that God may have mercy on them. Mercy is thus presented as the fruit of God-consciousness and reflection on both history and the future, and the verse implies that those who ignore such admonition forfeit that mercy by their own heedlessness.

translation: And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: The verse points to a stubborn habit of heart: the deniers' rejection does not come from a lack of evidence but from a settled unwillingness to heed it. Whether the sign is a verse of revelation, a wonder in the heavens and the earth, or a warning in the events of history, they treat it with heedlessness and avoidance rather than reflection. Their turning away is a chosen attitude, which is why each new sign leaves them unmoved, and why guidance depends on a willing and attentive heart as much as on the clarity of the proof. The verse warns that persistent neglect of God's signs hardens a person against truth, so that even the clearest evidence stops having any effect.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided for you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed? You are not but in manifest error."
interpretation: The verse exposes a false argument that disbelievers use to excuse their stinginess: they invoke God's will and decree to justify refusing charity, claiming that if God wished the poor to be fed, He would have fed them Himself. This reasoning is flawed because God has made the wealthy a means of provision for the needy and has tested them through their wealth, commanding them to give. Divine decree does not cancel human responsibility; God also gave wealth and could have made all people rich, yet He established the differences between people as a trial, so that the generous are distinguished from the miserly. The disbelievers then turn the charge on the believers, accusing them of manifest error, when in truth the error lies with those who use theology as a pretext to avoid compassion and obedience.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The deniers of the Resurrection and the Judgment pose this question not out of a sincere search for truth but out of mockery and disbelief, treating the warning as an empty threat that must be proven by an immediate date. They assume that because the promised punishment has not yet come, it will never come. The verse exposes how disbelief hides behind demands for a timetable, when the real issue is the denial of accountability. The knowledge of when the Hour will arrive belongs to God alone, and the Messenger's task is only to warn clearly. Delay is not evidence of falsehood, but a respite and a test, and people should prepare for it rather than ridicule it.

translation: They await nothing but a single Blast that will seize them while they are disputing with one another.
interpretation: The verse (Ya-Sin 36:49) warns that the Hour will arrive suddenly, with the first blowing of the Trumpet, and that no warning or preparation will precede it. The people it describes are heedless deniers who keep mocking the promise of resurrection and judgment ('When will this promise come to pass?'). The Hour will catch them at their ordinary worldly business, absorbed in arguing, haggling and quarreling, so they will have no chance to repent, make a will or return to their families (as the next verse says). The lesson is that people should not postpone faith and repentance, because death and the end of the world come without notice, and a heart consumed by worldly disputes is easily caught unprepared.

translation: So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their own families.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:50) describes the sudden blast of the Last Hour, which will seize people while they are absorbed in their worldly affairs. It will come so abruptly that no one will have time to make a will, give final advice, settle debts, or even return home to say farewell. The meaning is a warning that death and the Hour arrive without notice, so a person should not postpone repentance, repairing wrongs, or preparing for the Hereafter, because the opportunity for action will be cut off in an instant and each person will be left alone to face accountability.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown, and behold, they will rush out from their graves to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse points to the second blast of the Trumpet, which ends the sleep of death and brings the resurrection. The word 'yansilun' describes people hurrying out of their graves in swift, urgent streams, like a mass moving at once with no ability to delay or resist. Their destination is 'their Lord', which shows that the resurrection leads to being brought before God for reckoning, with no other authority or refuge. The verse stresses that God's power to raise the dead is immediate and total. A single blast is enough to bring all of humanity from their resting places to stand before their Creator, which should move the listener to remember accountability and prepare for that meeting.

translation: They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our place of sleep? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when the trumpet is blown a second time, the people will rise from their graves bewildered and terrified. Because the interval between death and resurrection will seem to them like a short sleep, they call their graves a 'place of sleep' and cry out in distress. Then they, or the believers who answer them, recognize the reality they had denied or doubted: this is the very resurrection that God, in His mercy, had promised, and the messengers had told the truth about it. The verse shows that the truth of the resurrection becomes undeniable when it happens, but then acknowledgement comes too late to benefit those who rejected it, and it urges the hearer to believe now, while belief is still of use.

translation: It was nothing but a single Blast, and behold, they were all brought together before Us.
interpretation: The verse shows how effortless the resurrection is for God. No long preparation or elaborate process is needed. A single cry, the blast of the trumpet, is enough to gather every human being at once, however many generations have passed and however scattered their remains. The phrase 'before Us' stresses that all of humanity will stand in God's presence for reckoning, with no escape and no intercessor except by His leave. The verse warns the heedless who deny the Hereafter or think it far off, and it reassures believers that divine justice is certain and will arrive in a moment.

translation: So today no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ya-Sin (36:54), announces the perfect justice of the Day of Judgment. Nothing will be added to a person's punishment unjustly, and no good deed will be left unrewarded or reduced. Each person's outcome follows directly from their own conduct in this life, so the reckoning is a mirror of what they chose and did, not an arbitrary decree. The verse tells believers that every deed counts and urges them to hold themselves accountable now, since on that Day no one can blame another or claim unfair treatment.

translation: Indeed, the companions of Paradise, on that Day, are occupied in joyful engagement, delighting in themselves.
interpretation: The verse portrays the state of the people of Paradise on the Day of Judgment: they are so absorbed in the bliss that God has granted them that they are free of all worry, reckoning, and fear. The 'occupation' (shughl) is not burdensome labor but a pleasant preoccupation with divine favor, such as companionship with their spouses, feasting, and fellowship, which keeps them content and joyful (fakihun). It stands in contrast to the anxious, distressed state of the disbelievers, and signals that the believers' reward is a complete, carefree happiness that distracts them from any sorrow or any concern about the fate of others.

translation: They and their spouses will be in shade, reclining on couches.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:56) describes the honor and peace of the people of Paradise. Being in shade signifies comfort and freedom from hardship, as shade stands for relief from the heat and toil of this world. Reclining on couches is the posture of those who are at ease, served and secure, with no labor or worry. The mention of their spouses beside them shows that Paradise's joy is shared with loved ones, so that companionship and family closeness complete their bliss. The verse contrasts the lasting tranquility of the believers with the distress of those who denied the message, and it reminds the reader that faith and righteous deeds lead to rest and honor in the Hereafter.

translation: For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for.
interpretation: The verse describes the generosity of Paradise for its people: they will have fruit in abundance, and beyond that, every wish they voice will be granted at once. Their joy is not limited to a fixed portion of provisions, because whatever they ask for or desire will be present for them. This shows that the bliss of the people of Paradise is complete and unrestricted, and that God honors them with fulfillment of every desire, so nothing they long for will be withheld.

translation: "Peace!" – a word spoken from a Lord Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:58) describes the highest honor granted to the people of Paradise: beyond all the bounties of gardens and enjoyment, they are greeted directly by God with a word of peace. It shows that the greatest reward is not merely material comfort but divine acceptance and honor. The greeting comes from a Lord described as 'Rahim' (Most Merciful), signifying that their entry into Paradise and the security they enjoy there are the fruit of God's mercy, and that this peace is complete, free of any fear, loss, or sorrow, and will never be withdrawn.

translation: And [it will be said]: 'Separate yourselves today, O you criminals!'
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:59) describes the Day of Judgment, when God commands the wrongdoers to be set apart from the believers. In this life the righteous and the sinful live side by side, but on that Day all mixing ends and each group is distinguished by its record. The criminals are cut off from the company and mercy of the righteous, left isolated, and gathered toward their reckoning. The command carries humiliation and finality, showing that no ties, status, or fellowship will shield anyone from accountability. It warns people to take stock of their deeds now, so that they may be counted among those who are honored on that Day.

translation: Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment God reminds humanity of the primordial covenant He took from them, which was embedded in their natural disposition and renewed through the messengers: that they should obey and serve God alone. 'Worshipping Satan' here means not ritual prayer to him but obeying his whispers and following his path of disobedience, idolatry, and vice, since obedience in what contradicts God's command is a form of servitude. The verse is a rebuke that leaves no excuse: Satan's enmity was openly declared from the time of Adam's creation, so those who followed him did so knowingly and by their own choice, and are accountable for having taken as a guide the one who was plainly their enemy rather than the Lord who created and sustained them.

translation: And that you worship Me. This is a straight path.
interpretation: God calls people to devote their worship to Him alone, free from any partner or intermediary, and declares that this exclusive devotion is the straight path. It is the single, clear, balanced road that leads a person to God's pleasure and to salvation. Unlike the crooked paths of following Satan, who is the open enemy of humankind, it has no deviation. Worship here is more than ritual: it means obeying God in belief, action, and conduct. A life in which the heart and the limbs are aligned with His guidance reaches its destination safely.

translation: And he had already led astray a great multitude of you. Then did you not use reason?
interpretation: This verse is God's rebuke to humanity regarding Satan's enmity (following the preceding call not to worship Satan). It reminds people that Satan has a long history of misleading countless generations before them, and the evidence of the ruin of those who followed him is plain in history. Anyone who reflects on the fate of earlier nations should recognize the danger of obeying him and recoil from his path. Following Satan's whispers is therefore not a matter of ignorance but of failing to use the intellect God gave, so the verse calls people to reflect, learn from the past, and turn to worship of God alone, which is the straight path.

translation: This is Hell, which you were promised.
interpretation: This verse (Ya-Sin 36:63) is spoken to the criminals on the Day of Judgment as Hell is brought before them. It is a rebuke, not merely an announcement: the warnings the messengers delivered, which they denied or ignored, are now a visible reality. Its meaning is that God's promises and warnings are true, that denial in this world cannot change what is coming, and that the punishment is the direct result of their own rejection of the truth after the warning had been made clear to them. The words add to their torment by confronting them with the reality they once mocked, leaving them no excuse.

translation: Enter it (Hellfire) today to burn in it, because of what you used to disbelieve.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 36:64) is spoken to the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment when Hell is brought before them. It teaches that the punishment is not arbitrary but a just consequence of their own persistent denial of God and His messengers. The command to 'taste its heat today' contrasts with their worldly heedlessness: the denial they practiced in life, despite clear warnings, returns to them as a lived reality. It affirms divine justice, that every person is recompensed according to their beliefs and deeds, and warns that postponing faith in this life leaves no remedy in the next.

translation: Today We shall seal their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the deniers who made excuses and denied their wrongdoing will be stripped of the power of speech, so their own bodies will testify against them. Their mouths will be sealed so they cannot lie, while their hands will tell what they did and their feet will bear witness to the places they walked in sin. The verse shows that nothing can be concealed from God, and that a person's own limbs, which he used in this world as tools of disobedience, will become the most truthful and irrefutable witnesses against him. It is a warning to guard every faculty in this life, since each will be questioned and made to testify.

translation: And if We willed, We could have effaced their eyes, so they would race to find the path, but how would they see?
interpretation: The verse reminds the stubborn deniers that their sight, and the ability to find the right path, is a gift from God that He can remove at any moment. Having refused guidance despite clear signs, they are shown how helpless they would be if He took away their physical sight: they would grope toward the road and never find it. It suggests that the same is true spiritually. God's delay in punishing them is mercy, and they should use their faculties of perception and reason to see the truth and follow the straight path before the chance is taken from them.

translation: And if We willed, We could have transformed them where they stood, so they would be unable to go forward, nor could they return.
interpretation: The verse shows God's complete power over those who persist in denial and stubbornness. Their ability to move, to act, and to choose a path is a gift from God and not something they own.
