What is manufactured by people cannot be a creator, provider, or deserving of worship, since the maker is plainly above the thing he made. The question is rhetorical and calls people to use their reason and recognize that worship belongs only to God, who created both them and what they make, as the next verse states: "While God created you and what you do."

translation: While Allah has created you and what you do.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:96) comes in the context of Prophet Ibrahim's rebuke of his people for worshipping idols they themselves had carved. It teaches that the Creator alone deserves worship, since He is the source of both the human being and the material and abilities with which people fashion things. Whatever people make or do exists only by His creation and enabling power, so it is irrational to worship what is made by human hands rather than the One who created the makers and the means of their work. The verse also affirms that human actions, though carried out by human choice and effort, take place within Allah's creation and power, which calls people to humility, gratitude, and exclusive devotion to Him.

translation: They said, "Build for him a structure and cast him into the blazing fire."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:97) shows how falsehood turns to brute force once it loses the argument. After Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) dismantled the logic of idol-worship, his people had no rational reply, so they resorted to violence and chose a public, humiliating punishment: an enormous enclosure in which a fire would be kindled and Ibrahim thrown into it. The verse teaches that tyrants and those clinging to inherited error often answer proof with persecution, and that their scheming is ultimately powerless against God's will. The following verse confirms this: they wanted to harm him, but God made them the lowest, so their plot failed and the believer's steadfast trust in God was vindicated.

translation: They intended a plot against him, but We made them the lowest (the defeated and humiliated).
interpretation: The verse refers to the people of Abraham, who sought to harm him by casting him into the fire after he rejected their idols. God turned their scheme against them: the fire became cool and safe for Abraham, and his opponents were left vanquished, their plan failed and their argument refuted. It teaches that when the believers rely on God, the plots of those who oppose truth rebound upon them, and that true elevation and victory belong to those who stand with God, while the arrogant wrongdoers end up abased, whatever power they appear to hold.

translation: And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me." (Qur'an 37:99)
interpretation: Abraham, after God delivered him from his people's hostility and the fire, declares that he is leaving the land of idolatry in migration for the sake of God, turning wholly toward his Lord. His words show complete trust: he does not know the destination or what lies ahead, yet he is certain that God will guide him to what is right, both in the path he travels and in the place where he will settle. The verse teaches that true faith means leaving what opposes one's devotion to God, relying on Him alone, and expecting His guidance with confidence even when the way is unclear.

translation: My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah As-Saffat (37:100), made after he left his homeland to follow God's path. Having separated from his people and family, he asks God for a righteous son who would be a companion, a support, and a continuation of his mission of monotheism. The verse teaches that the believer's hope for offspring should be tied to their righteousness and service to God rather than worldly desire alone, and that prayer is the proper recourse when seeking blessings that lie beyond human power. God's response, giving him glad tidings of a forbearing boy, shows that sincere supplication made in sacrifice for God's sake is answered.

translation: So We gave him glad tidings of a forbearing boy.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:101) announces God's response to Abraham's prayer for a righteous child, after he left his people and asked for a son from among the righteous. The son promised is described as 'forbearing' (halim), a quality that foreshadows his character: patience, gentleness, and self-restraint, which appear in the trial that follows, when he calmly submits to God's command. The verse teaches that God answers sincere supplication with a gift that fits the one who prays, and that the child's greatest distinction is the moral and spiritual quality of forbearance, not just his birth.

translation: Then, when he reached the age of walking and working with him, he said: 'O my son, I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so consider what you think.' He said: 'O my father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.'
interpretation: The verse shows that submission to God's command is the highest test of faith, and that it is best met through a willing, trusting heart rather than coercion. Ibrahim, knowing that a prophet's dream is revelation, does not impose the command on his son but consults him gently, seeking his consent so that the act becomes a shared offering. Ismail's reply shows a faith inherited and made his own: he treats the dream as God's command, tells his father to carry it out, and attributes any steadfastness to God's will by saying 'God willing', not to his own strength. Patience here means giving up what one loves most in obedience to God, and relying on Him for the strength to do so.

translation: Then when they had both submitted [to God's will], and he laid him down upon his forehead,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:103) captures the climax of the trial of Ibrahim and his son: both yielded completely to God's command, the father by proceeding to carry out the order he had received in a dream, and the son by accepting it patiently. The phrase 'aslama' means that true islam is total surrender of the will to God, even when what is asked seems to be the dearest thing one has. Laying the son down 'upon his forehead' shows that Ibrahim carried his obedience to the very threshold of the act, so that the test was fulfilled in intention and deed. The verse teaches that God's real aim is the sincerity and readiness of the heart, not the bloodshed itself, which is why the next verses record that God ransomed the son and rewarded Ibrahim for his proven devotion.

translation: And We called out to him: "O Abraham!"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:104) comes at the climax of the trial in which Abraham was prepared to sacrifice his son in submission to God's command. The divine call, addressing him by name, marks the moment when God halts the act, because Abraham has already shown complete obedience in heart and intention. The lesson is that God tests His servants not to harm them but to prove and elevate their faith, and that sincere readiness to surrender to Him is what He values. Once that submission is demonstrated, mercy and relief follow, as the verses that come next confirm.

translation: You have already fulfilled the vision. Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This is God's address to Abraham after he moved to sacrifice his son in obedience to the vision he had seen. God declares that Abraham's willing submission and readiness to act on the command had already fulfilled the vision's purpose, since the real test was the surrender of his heart and will, not the shedding of blood. The verse then states a general principle: God rewards those who excel in devotion and obedience (muhsinin) by lifting hardship from them, relieving them of the trial, and honoring them. Sincere, complete submission to God is thus met with mercy, deliverance, and lasting distinction.

translation: Indeed, this was surely a clear trial.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:106) comes after the story of Ibrahim and his son, when Ibrahim was commanded to sacrifice him and both submitted to God's command. It describes the command as a manifest, unmistakable test, and it reveals how severe the test was. The test showed that Ibrahim's love for God outweighed his love for the thing he cherished most, his long-awaited son. Both father and son showed complete obedience and trust in God. The verse teaches that true faith is proven by willingness to surrender to God's will even when it is hardest, and that God's trials expose the sincerity of His servants and are followed by relief and reward for those who pass them.

translation: And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.
interpretation: This verse describes God's mercy toward Abraham and his son after they both showed complete submission in the test of sacrifice. God spared the son by providing a ram in his place, teaching that what God asks of the believer is sincere obedience and readiness to give up what is dearest, not human bloodshed. The sacrifice is called 'great' because God Himself provided it, because it redeemed a human life, and because it became a lasting rite of remembrance, commemorated each year in the sacrifice of Eid al-Adha. The verse shows that trust in God's command is rewarded with relief and a way out of hardship.

translation: And We left for him a lasting memory among later generations.
interpretation: This verse (37:78, which recurs for Noah, Abraham, and others in Surat as-Saffat) means that God granted His righteous servant an enduring good reputation and praise among the generations that came after him. Because of his patience, faithfulness, and perseverance in calling people to God despite hardship, his name remained honored on people's tongues, and later communities continued to invoke peace and blessings upon him. The verse teaches that sincere devotion to God is rewarded not only in the hereafter but also with a lasting legacy of honor in this world, and that true remembrance is a gift bestowed by God rather than something gained by worldly power.

translation: Peace be upon Abraham.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:109) comes at the end of the passage recounting Abraham's trials and his willing submission to God, including the command to sacrifice his son. The greeting of peace is a divine honor: God Himself bestows salutation and lasting security upon Abraham as a reward for his steadfast faith, obedience, and sincerity. It signals that those who surrender fully to God and pass His tests are granted enduring praise among later generations, and that their legacy is marked by God's own peace and approval, which is why believers continue to invoke blessings and peace upon him.

translation: Thus do We reward those who do good.
interpretation: The verse affirms a consistent divine principle: those who perform ihsan, meaning excellence in worship and in conduct, doing good sincerely as though in God's sight, will be recompensed in kind and with generosity. God does not let their goodness go unnoticed, and just as He honored and rescued His righteous servants in the preceding narrative, He will deliver and elevate every person who acts with such sincerity. The reward is not an accident of circumstance but a certain law of God's justice and mercy.

translation: Indeed, he was one of Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse, which closes the account of several prophets such as Ibrahim, Musa, Harun, Ilyas and Lut in Surat As-Saffat, gives the reason for their honor and their deliverance. Their high rank before God did not come from lineage, power, or miracles, but from two qualities: servitude to God ('ibadah') and true faith (iman). By calling the prophet 'from Our servants' God ties him to Himself in a relationship of honor and protection, and by describing him as 'believing' God shows that faith is the foundation of every reward and victory. The lesson for the reader is that the highest status a human can reach is to be a sincere, believing servant of God, and that those who hold to this are saved and remembered with praise in later generations.

translation: And We gave him glad tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.
interpretation: After Abraham submitted completely to God, even to the point of being ready to sacrifice his son, God rewarded him by announcing the birth of another son, Isaac, who would himself be a prophet. The verse shows that God's gifts are not limited to worldly blessings but extend to a lasting spiritual legacy: the prophetic mission continues through Abraham's descendants. Describing Isaac as 'from among the righteous' places him among those whose faith and conduct are exemplary, which teaches that sincere obedience and sacrifice for God's sake are met with generous recompense, often beyond what the believer expected.

translation: And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their offspring are those who do good, and those who plainly wrong themselves.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine blessing granted to prophets like Abraham and Isaac does not automatically pass on to every descendant, because lineage confers no guarantee of righteousness or salvation. Each person is judged by their own conduct: some of their offspring are righteous and fulfil the covenant, while others openly wrong themselves through disbelief and sin. Honor before God rests on faith and good deeds, not on noble ancestry.

translation: And We certainly bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse (Surat as-Saffat, 37:114) affirms that God granted Moses and Aaron special grace, chiefly prophethood, revelation, and guidance, and later rescued them and their people from Pharaoh's oppression. It teaches that all blessings come from God's pure generosity and not from any merit of the recipients, and it reminds the believer that God supports those who serve His cause, raising the righteous and delivering them from tyranny despite their apparent weakness.

translation: And We saved them both and their people from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:115) refers to Moses and Aaron, and God's deliverance of them and the Children of Israel from the great affliction of Pharaoh's oppression, which included enslavement, the killing of their sons, and the pursuit that ended at the sea. The 'great distress' signifies not only physical bondage but the overwhelming terror and helplessness of their situation. The verse teaches that God rescues His chosen servants and the believers who follow them, and that deliverance, however impossible it seems, comes by His decree as a mark of His favor upon those who are patient and faithful.

translation: And We helped them, so it was they who were the victors.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:116) refers to Moses, Aaron and their people, the Children of Israel, after God mentions delivering them from great distress and the tyranny of Pharaoh. It teaches that victory comes from God's support alone, not from numbers or material strength. The oppressed who remain steadfast in faith are given divine aid, and the outcome is reversed: those who were once overpowered become the dominant ones, while the arrogant oppressors are drowned and defeated. It reassures believers that God's help follows patience and trust in Him, and that the final triumph belongs to the righteous.

translation: And We gave them both the Book that makes things clear.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:117) refers to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them, and the Torah that was revealed to them. It is called 'clear' (al-mustabīn) because it set out the law, the lawful and the forbidden, and the guidance that the Children of Israel needed, without ambiguity or obscurity. It shows that God's favor to His prophets lay not only in raising their rank but in giving them a revealed scripture that makes the truth plain, so that guidance reaches their people and the proof against them is established.

translation: And We guided them both to the straight path.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:118) refers to Moses and Aaron, upon whom God bestowed the clear Scripture. Its meaning is that guidance is a divine gift: beyond giving them revelation, God kept them firm on the path of truth, free from deviation and excess, which leads to His pleasure. The 'straight path' is the way of sincere monotheism and obedience, and the verse teaches that those chosen as leaders and teachers must themselves first be guided by God, and that true steadfastness in righteousness comes through His grace and support.

translation: And We left for them (Moses and Aaron) a lasting good mention among later generations.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat as-Saffat, shows that God honored Moses and Aaron after their mission by preserving their names with praise and esteem among the people who came after them. Their faithful service, patience, and steadfastness in calling their people to God were rewarded with a good reputation that endures through the ages. The verse teaches that sincere devotion to God is repaid not only in the Hereafter but also with a lasting, honorable legacy in this world, in which later generations remember and invoke the righteous with respect and blessing.

translation: Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse from Surah As-Saffat (37:120) is God's own declaration of honor for Moses and Aaron, granting them lasting peace and safety from the disparagement of later generations. It shows that their faithful service in delivering the message to Pharaoh and guiding the Children of Israel earned them a permanent place of respect, so that believers who mention them should do so with reverence and invoke peace upon them, just as they do for every prophet.

translation: Thus indeed do We reward those who do good.
interpretation: This verse, which appears in several places in the Qur'an (for example in Surat al-Saffat), affirms a consistent divine principle: God honors those who perfect their conduct, whether in worship, in their dealings with people, or in steadfastness under trial. The word 'muhsinin' refers to people who act with excellence (ihsan), doing good sincerely as though they were in God's sight. The phrase 'thus' points back to the preceding example of a servant who was tested, remained faithful and was then rescued and honored. It teaches that God's reward is not random but follows a pattern: those who are sincere and patient receive relief, a good name and ultimately Paradise. The verse thus gives reassurance to believers that no good deed is lost and encourages them to strive for excellence.

translation: Indeed, they were among Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse, which closes the accounts of Moses and Aaron (and is also used of Noah, Abraham, Elias and Lot in the same surah, As-Saffat), is a divine testimony of praise. It teaches that the highest rank a person can attain, even for prophets who were given scripture, miracles and leadership, is true servitude to God joined with faith. Their greatness did not lie in status or power but in their sincere submission and belief, so God honors them by attributing them to Himself with the words 'Our servants'. The lesson is that faith and devoted servitude are the real measure of honor in God's sight, and that the believer should aspire to this same description.

translation: And indeed, Elias (Elijah) was among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse opens the brief account of Elias in Surat as-Saffat and affirms his prophethood as part of the single chain of divine messengers sent to guide humanity. By stating that he was truly one of the messengers, the Qur'an places him alongside Noah, Abraham, Moses and Aaron mentioned before him, and shows that his message was the same call to worship God alone. It also reassures the Prophet Muhammad and the believers that the struggle of earlier prophets against their peoples' rejection is a recurring pattern, and that God honors and vindicates His messengers.

translation: When he said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: This verse presents the opening of a prophet's address to his community, as in the stories of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and others in Surat ash-Shu'ara' (the phrase here is associated with Noah's call in 26:106). The rhetorical question 'Will you not be mindful of God?' is a gentle but firm rebuke: rather than starting with threats, the prophet appeals to their conscience and their awareness of accountability. It shows that the foundation of every prophetic message is taqwa, the God-consciousness that restrains a person from idolatry, injustice and arrogance, and that true reform begins by awakening the heart to reverence for its Creator before demanding any change in outward behavior.

translation: Do you call upon Baal and abandon the Best of creators?
interpretation: This verse is the prophet Elias (Ilyas) rebuking his people for worshipping Baal, an idol they venerated, while neglecting God, who alone brings all things into being. The phrase 'Best of creators' does not concede that others truly create; it affirms that God's creation is incomparably perfect, so that whatever others are said to fashion falls infinitely short. The rebuke points to the folly of the people's choice: they turn from the Creator, Sustainer and Provider of their lives to a lifeless idol that can neither create, benefit, nor harm. It teaches that devotion belongs only to the One who creates and sustains, and that abandoning Him for something powerless is both irrational and ungrateful.

translation: Allah is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earlier ones.
interpretation: The verse affirms that lordship belongs to Allah alone, and that this truth is not a new doctrine but the constant reality across all generations. By pointing to the earlier ancestors, it answers those who cling to inherited customs and idol-worship merely because their forefathers practiced them: the very forefathers they follow were themselves created and sustained by Allah, so their ancestors' example is no proof for associating partners with Him. The One who created and nurtured the earlier generations is the same One who created and nurtures the present one, so worship is due to Him alone, and loyalty to the truth should outweigh loyalty to ancestral tradition.

translation: But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth [for punishment].
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:127) speaks of the people of Prophet Ilyas (Elijah), who rejected his call to worship God alone and abandon Baal. Their denial of the messenger was not a trivial error but a rejection of truth after it had been clearly conveyed, and so it carries a certain consequence: they will be made to stand before God and be brought into the punishment they earned. The word 'muhdarun' (those brought forth) implies that they will be compelled and will have no way to escape or evade, in contrast to the sincere servants of God, who are exempted from this fate in the next verse. The lesson is that denying the prophets leads inevitably to accountability, and that no one can avoid appearing before God to face the result of their choices.

translation: Except for the sincere and devoted servants of God.
interpretation: This verse sets apart those whom God has purified and chosen for Himself from the fate that befalls others. Because they have devoted their worship and their hearts purely to God, they are protected from the deception and misguidance of Satan and from the punishment awaiting the wrongdoers. Salvation is thus tied not to mere outward belonging but to inner sincerity (ikhlas), and God's favor safeguards those who give Him exclusive devotion.

translation: And We left for him [a good remembrance] among the later generations.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat As-Saffat (37:78), follows the account of Prophet Noah (peace be upon him). It means that God preserved Noah's name and honor among the generations that came after him. Despite the rejection and mockery he endured from his people, his steadfast patience and devotion to God earned him lasting praise, so that believers in every later era mention him with respect and invoke peace upon him, as the next verse says: 'Peace be upon Noah among all the worlds.' The lesson is that those who remain faithful to God and endure hardship for His sake are rewarded with enduring honor and a good legacy, while the worldly standing of their opponents fades away.

translation: Peace be upon Ilyasin (the family of Ilyas).
interpretation: This verse closes the account of the Prophet Ilyas (Elijah) in Surah As-Saffat (37:130). After describing how he called his people away from worshipping Baal and how God preserved him, God honors him with a lasting greeting of peace. The form 'Il Yasin' is understood as a variant name of Ilyas, as the Qur'an also says 'Tur Sina' and 'Sinin' for the same mountain, so the verse means peace and divine safety upon Ilyas himself. It teaches that God grants His faithful messengers enduring praise among later generations, and that steadfastness in calling people to worship God alone is rewarded with His peace.

translation: Indeed, it is thus that We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse affirms a divine principle: those who act with excellence (ihsan), whether by worshipping God as though they see Him or by doing good to others with sincerity, are rewarded by God in the way He rewarded the righteous before them. It means that God's recompense is not arbitrary, as He consistently lifts, protects, and vindicates people who persist in goodness, especially under trial. The reward is not limited to the hereafter, since God may also grant such people honor, relief from hardship, and a good standing in this life, while the verse reassures believers that their steadfast good conduct will never be lost.

translation: Indeed, he was one of Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs in Surat as-Saffat in the accounts of Ibrahim, Musa and Harun, Ilyas, and Lut, gives divine testimony to the standing of the prophets. God describes them as His 'servants' (ibad), which is a title of honor and closeness, and then qualifies them as 'believing', which shows that their greatness lies in their sincere faith and complete submission to God and not in any lineage or worldly rank. The verse teaches that true faith, expressed in obedience and servitude to God, is the highest distinction a person can attain, and that God rewards His faithful servants by praising them and keeping their remembrance among later generations.

translation: And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:133) opens the account of Prophet Lot by affirming his divine commission. It establishes that his call to his people was not personal reform or opinion but a mission entrusted by God. By placing him in the unbroken chain of messengers, it teaches that the message of pure monotheism and moral uprightness is one across all times, and that those who reject God's messengers bear responsibility for the consequences that follow. It also prepares the listener for the deliverance of Lot and his family and the destruction of the transgressing people, showing that God vindicates His messengers and saves the faithful.

translation: When We saved him and his family, all of them,
interpretation: This verse recalls God's deliverance of Lot (Lūṭ) and his household from the punishment that befell his people, who persisted in immorality and rejected his warnings. It shows that God's salvation is the reward for steadfast faith and obedience in the midst of a corrupt society: when divine judgment arrives, the righteous are rescued by God's mercy and care, while the wrongdoers are destroyed. The word 'all of them' stresses the completeness of this rescue for those who believed and followed him, which demonstrates that God fulfills His promise to protect His servants. The verse also gives reassurance to believers of every age that patience and loyalty to the truth will not be lost with God, and that deliverance, however delayed, will come from Him.

translation: Except an old woman among those who remained behind.
interpretation: This verse, which appears in the account of Lot (Lūṭ) in Sūrat al-Shu'arā' (26:171), excepts Lot's wife from the salvation granted to him and his family. Though she was part of his household, her closeness to a prophet could not save her, because she sided with the wrongdoing of her people and did not share his faith. She lingered behind with those who were doomed and perished with them when the punishment came. The lesson is that deliverance depends on belief and righteous conduct, not on family ties or proximity to the righteous, and that each soul is judged by its own stance toward the truth.

translation: Then We destroyed the others.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 26:172, repeated in similar form in the story of Lot) conveys that after God rescued Lot and his family, He annihilated the rest of his people who persisted in rejecting the message and in their transgression. The meaning is that divine deliverance and divine punishment are both certain: the believers are saved, while those who stubbornly deny the truth and persist in wrongdoing meet a decisive end. It serves as a warning to later generations that worldly power or numbers do not protect against God's judgment once the warnings of the prophets are ignored.

translation: And indeed, you pass by them (the ruined towns of Lot's people) in the morning.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Quraysh and the Arabs that the remains of Sodom, the destroyed cities of Lot's people, lie along their trade route to the Levant, and they pass by them at daybreak on their journeys. These ruins are standing evidence of the fate of those who persisted in immorality and rejected their prophet. The verse calls on people to reflect on that visible, historical proof, to learn from it rather than pass heedlessly, and to recognize that the same consequences await those who deny God's messengers.

translation: And by night. Then will you not use reason?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 37:138) completes the address to the Quraysh about the ruined towns of Lot's people: they pass by those ruins in the morning on their trade journeys, and at night as well. The question 'Then will you not use reason?' is a rebuke. Seeing these remains of a destroyed people day and night should lead a thinking person to draw a lesson. The punishment that struck those who denied their prophet and persisted in wrongdoing is an enduring sign, and ignoring it shows a failure to reflect. Reason, properly used, should lead to heeding the warning, accepting the truth, and avoiding the fate of earlier nations.

translation: And indeed, Jonah was surely among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:139) opens the account of Prophet Yunus (Jonah) by affirming his status as a divinely chosen messenger before narrating his trial in the fish. By stating this at the outset, God makes clear that his momentary departure from his people without permission and the hardship that followed did not diminish his rank of prophethood. It teaches that prophets, though human and subject to testing and correction, remain honored by God, and that God's trials are meant to refine and purify His servants, who return to Him in repentance and are restored to favor.

translation: When he fled to the laden ship.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:140) refers to the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who left his people in anger before receiving God's permission to depart. The word 'abaqa' is used for a slave running away from his master, which conveys that Yunus left his post of duty without leave, even though he did so out of distress at his people's persistent denial. The 'laden ship' suggests a vessel so heavy with cargo and passengers that it was at risk of sinking, and this sets the scene for the lots being cast and his being thrown into the sea. The lesson is that even a righteous messenger must remain steadfast and patient in carrying out his mission until God commands otherwise. Leaving the duty of conveying the message without God's leave brings trial, and the trial in turn leads to repentance and mercy.

translation: Then he cast lots (with the ship's people), and he was among those who were defeated.
interpretation: This verse, from the account of Prophet Yunus (Jonah) in Surat as-Saffat, describes how, when his ship was overloaded and its people feared sinking, they cast lots to decide who should be thrown overboard, and the lot fell upon Yunus. It shows that his departure from his people without awaiting God's permission was a lapse for which he was tested, and that he submitted to the outcome of the lots rather than resisting it. His being 'among the defeated' signals that God's decree overruled his own course of action: he lost the draw not by mere chance but by divine design, bringing him into the trial of the great fish, during which he turned to God in repentance and glorification, and was thereby saved. The lesson is that no servant, even a prophet, escapes accountability, and that humble submission and repentance lead to deliverance.

translation: Then the great fish swallowed him, while he was blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:142) describes the Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after he left his people without awaiting God's permission and boarded the ship. When the lots were cast, he was thrown into the sea and a great fish swallowed him. The word 'muleem' means one who has done something deserving of blame, and he was blameworthy for abandoning his mission in frustration before God authorized it. The lesson is that even a prophet is accountable for hastiness and lack of patience in fulfilling a divine task; the swallowing was a corrective trial rather than mere punishment, drawing him back to humble repentance, as shown in the following verses, where his glorification of God (tasbih) leads to his rescue.

translation: Had he not been among those who glorify God,
interpretation: The verse refers to Prophet Yunus (Jonah) in the belly of the fish. It teaches that his constant remembrance and glorification of God, both before his trial and while in the darkness, was the means of his deliverance. Sincere devotion and consistent worship in times of ease become a source of rescue in times of hardship, because God cares for those who habitually turn to Him. His cry, 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers,' joined repentance with praise, showing that humility and tasbih open the door to divine mercy.

translation: He would surely have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: The verse describes the Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after the great fish swallowed him. It teaches that his salvation came only through his glorification of God, as the preceding verse says, 'Had he not been of those who glorify God.' His constant remembrance and sincere repentance in the depths of darkness earned him God's mercy and rescue. The lesson is that sincere turning to God, remembrance of Him, and praising Him in times of hardship can avert even a seemingly inescapable fate, and that deliverance is in God's hands alone. The phrase 'until the Day they are resurrected' stresses how complete the confinement would have been, to the point that the fish would have become his grave until the Resurrection.

translation: Then We cast him onto the bare shore, while he was ill.
interpretation: This verse describes how God, after Jonah (Yunus) was delivered from the belly of the fish, caused him to be thrown onto an open, barren stretch of land with no shelter or vegetation, weakened and sick from his ordeal. It teaches that divine rescue from a trial does not always come with immediate comfort: Jonah, who had left his people without permission, was brought out of the darkness yet left vulnerable and exposed, so that he would experience his total dependence on God. His frailty becomes a stage of humbling and renewal, after which God provides mercy and care, as the following verses show with the gourd plant that shaded him, illustrating that God restores those who turn to Him in repentance.

translation: And We caused to grow over him a gourd-bearing plant.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:146) describes God's mercy to the Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after the fish cast him onto the barren shore, weak and ill. God provided a broad-leaved gourd plant whose shade shielded his sensitive body from the sun and whose fruit nourished him as he recovered. It shows that after repentance and sincere turning to God, divine care follows hardship, and that God sustains and heals His servants through simple, natural means. Yunus's trial ended in restoration, reminding believers that no distress is beyond God's relief when a servant returns to Him.

translation: And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah As-Saffat (37:147), speaks of the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), whom God sent as a messenger to the people of Nineveh after his ordeal in the belly of the fish. The phrase 'a hundred thousand or more' conveys the great size of the population to whom he was sent, and the 'or more' signals that the number was at least a hundred thousand and likely exceeded it. The point is that despite the vast numbers, his mission bore fruit: the next verse says they believed, and God granted them enjoyment of life for a time. It teaches that a prophet's task is not diminished by the size of the audience, that repentance can be accepted from an entire community, and that God's mercy reaches those who turn back to Him, as it also restored Yunus after his trial.

translation: So they believed, and We let them enjoy life for a time.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:148) refers to the people of Yunus (Jonah), who, after he left them, saw the signs of impending punishment, repented sincerely, and believed as a whole community. Their faith, though it came late, was accepted by God, so the punishment was lifted and they were granted continued life and prosperity until their appointed term. The lesson is that sincere repentance and faith can avert divine punishment and open the door of God's mercy, and that worldly enjoyment is only temporary, lasting 'for a time' until each one's appointed end.

translation: So ask them [O Muhammad], 'Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?' (Qur'an 37:149)
interpretation: The verse challenges the idolatrous Arabs over their own contradiction. They claimed the angels were God's daughters, yet they themselves despised having daughters and preferred sons. By asking them to consider this, the verse exposes how unjust and irrational their claim was: they assigned to God the very offspring they considered inferior for themselves. It also shows that God is far above having children at all. Such a claim has no rational or revealed basis, and it rests only on baseless conjecture and cultural prejudice.

translation: Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical challenge to those who claimed the angels were daughters of God. Knowledge of how something was created can come only from direct witness or from revelation, and the claimants had neither: they were not present at the creation of the angels, and no revelation told them such a thing. Their claim is therefore baseless conjecture. It also ascribes to God a lineage and gender that do not befit Him and demeans the angels, who are honored servants. In matters of the unseen, belief must rest on sound evidence from God, not on inherited assumptions or speculation.

translation: Behold! It is out of their own falsehood that they say:
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:151) exposes the claim of the idolaters that God has begotten offspring, or that the angels are God's daughters, as a fabricated lie rather than knowledge. The phrase 'out of their own falsehood' shows that the statement did not come from revelation, evidence, or reason, but from their own invention and corrupted imagination. By introducing it with 'Behold!' the Qur'an draws the listener's attention to the gravity of what follows, which is a blasphemous statement attributing to God what is unworthy of Him, and it makes clear that such beliefs are rooted in deliberate deception and self-made delusion.

translation: God has begotten offspring — and indeed, they are liars. (Qur'an 37:152)
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that God has children, a claim made by the Arabian polytheists who called the angels daughters of God. It declares this a fabrication with no basis in revelation, reason, or witness. God is absolutely One, self-sufficient, and free of any need for offspring, since begetting implies likeness, need, and origin in time, all of which contradict divine perfection and transcendence. Those who attribute offspring to God are therefore deliberate or deluded inventors of falsehood, and their assertion is a grave deviation from pure monotheism.

translation: Has He chosen daughters over sons?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question of rebuke (Qur'an 37:153), addressed to those who claimed that the angels were God's daughters. It points out the contradiction in their position: they themselves disliked having daughters and favored sons, yet they ascribed to God what they considered inferior for themselves. The verse exposes the absurdity of attributing offspring to God, who is far above having children, and shows that their claim rested on prejudice and baseless speculation rather than knowledge or evidence.

translation: What is the matter with you? How do you judge?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:36) is a rebuke aimed at those who deny the truth. They claim that God would treat the believers and the wrongdoers alike, or that they would enjoy favor in the Hereafter as they do in this world. The question is not asking for information. It exposes how absurd and unjust their reasoning is. Anyone with a sound mind and a sense of justice can see that the obedient and the disobedient cannot be equal in God's sight. Judgment must rest on evidence and fairness, not on desire, arrogance, or baseless assumption. The verse calls people to reflect on the standards by which they judge and to bring their conclusions into line with reason and divine justice.

translation: Will you not then remember?
interpretation: This brief rhetorical question, which appears in several places in the Qur'an, is a gentle rebuke to people who ignore clear signs and reminders. It suggests that the truth about God's oneness, His power, and the accountability of human beings is already known to the human conscience and to what people observe in creation. The problem is not that evidence is lacking but that people are heedless. The verse therefore calls the listener to stop being negligent, to reflect, and to bring back to mind what the innate nature (fitra) and revelation have already taught, so that this recollection leads to right belief and right action.

translation: Or do you have a clear authority?
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:156) is a rhetorical challenge to those who made false claims about God, such as attributing daughters or offspring to Him. It asks whether they hold any clear, demonstrable proof or divine warrant for their assertions. The point is that beliefs about God cannot rest on conjecture, inherited custom, or desire. They must be grounded in clear evidence, either rational demonstration or revelation from God. Since the claimants have no such proof, their claims are baseless.

translation: So bring your scripture, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse is a challenge to those who make claims about God, such as that He has partners or offspring, or that they hold special divine favor, without evidence. It teaches that religious claims must rest on proof, whether revealed scripture or sound knowledge, and not on inherited habit, conjecture, or desire. Those who assert such things are asked to produce a clear, authentic source from God. Since they cannot, their claims are exposed as baseless, and truthfulness in matters of faith is shown to require demonstrable evidence.

translation: And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth for judgment.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the idolaters who claimed a lineage between God and the jinn, such as that the angels or jinn were His daughters or that He had partners among them. It rejects this by pointing out that the jinn themselves know they are created beings who will be brought before God for reckoning. Beings who are summoned, held accountable, and subject to His judgment cannot be related to Him as kin, since they are servants under His authority. The claim is therefore false by the testimony of the very creatures it exalts, and it shows that divinity belongs to God alone, who is far above having offspring, kin, or equals.

translation: Glory be to God, far above what they attribute to Him.
interpretation: This verse (found in Surah al-Mu'minun 23:91 and similar in other places) declares God's absolute transcendence and purity from every deficiency. It rejects the claims of those who ascribe to Him offspring, partners, or any limitation that belongs to created beings. The affirmation of tasbih here teaches that human descriptions, shaped by imagination and limited experience, cannot capture or define the divine reality. God alone is worthy of praise, and only what He has revealed about Himself is a sound basis for describing Him, so the believer's response to false claims is to exalt God above them and hold fast to pure monotheism.

translation: Except for the sincere servants of God.
interpretation: This verse sets apart a group from the fate or judgment described in the preceding verses: those whom God has purified for Himself and who devote their worship and obedience to Him alone. Because their devotion is free of showing off, association of partners with God, and the corruption of base desires, they are shielded from the punishment, deception, and misguidance that overtake others. Their safety comes from God's favor in choosing and protecting them, together with their own sincerity, which shows that salvation depends on purity of intention and wholehearted servitude rather than on outward claims.

translation: So indeed, you and what you worship —
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:161) opens a declaration addressed to the disbelieving Quraysh and the idols they worship besides God. It is completed by the next verse: 'You cannot cause anyone to go astray from Him, except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire.' The meaning is that neither the idolaters nor their false gods have any power to lead God's servants away from the truth or to harm their faith. Their falsehood can influence only those whom God has already known to be set on the path to the Fire by their own choice. The verse thus reassures believers, exposes the impotence of idols, and affirms that guidance and misguidance occur only within God's knowledge and decree.

translation: You cannot tempt away anyone from Him (by what you worship), except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:162) is the continuation of 37:161, 'So indeed, you and what you worship'. It declares that the disbelievers and their false gods have no power to lead astray any servant of God whom God has guided. Misguidance takes hold only of those who, through their own persistent choice of disbelief, are already bound for Hell. The verse teaches that human beings cannot be seduced from the truth by the idols and false deities of the polytheists unless God's decree of misguidance has already been established against them due to their own willful rejection. Faith is therefore protected by God's will, and the deceptions of falsehood have influence only over those who incline toward them.

translation: Except for him who will burn in the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse (37:163) follows the preceding one, which says that the disbelievers cannot lead anyone astray from God. The point is that the only people who can be seduced by the devils and the misleaders are those whom God has already decreed will enter Hellfire because of their own persistent choice of disbelief and wrongdoing. Misguidance has no power over the sincere, since a person is led astray only by his own inclination to follow falsehood. Responsibility therefore rests with the individual who chooses the path that ends in the Fire, and God's knowledge of that outcome does not remove the person's accountability.

translation: And there is none among us except that he has a known station.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:164) is spoken by the angels, who declare that each of them has a fixed rank and assigned duty in the order of creation which he does not exceed. It affirms that they are servants of God, not partners or daughters of His as the polytheists claimed. Each stands in his appointed place in worship and obedience, submitting to God's command, which is a lesson that true honor lies in humble service and in keeping to the role God has set.

translation: And indeed, we are those who stand in rows.
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:165) is spoken by the angels, describing themselves as ranked in orderly rows in worship and obedience to God, awaiting His command. It teaches that the angels' existence is defined by discipline, humility, and servitude: they claim no divinity and no share in God's authority, but stand in disciplined devotion. By implication, it also invites believers to emulate this order and unity, as in the congregational prayer where worshippers align themselves in straight rows before their Lord.

translation: And indeed, we are those who glorify (God).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:166) is spoken by the angels, who declare that they are the ones who constantly exalt God and proclaim His perfection, free from every flaw and from the false attributes the disbelievers ascribe to Him. In context, it follows the angels' statements that each has an appointed station and that they stand in ranks. Together these affirm that the angels are servants of God, not His daughters or partners, as the polytheists claimed. Their ceaseless glorification shows that true greatness lies in humble worship and submission to the Creator, and it invites human beings to join in that same praise and obedience.

translation: And indeed they used to say,
interpretation: This is the opening of Surah As-Saffat 37:167, 'And indeed they used to say,' which continues in the next verse, 'If only we had a reminder from the earlier peoples, we would have been servants of God, sincere.' It refers to the Quraysh and the idolaters among the Arabs before the Prophet Muhammad's mission. They claimed that if God had sent them a scripture like those of earlier nations, they would have been devoted and sincere believers. The interpretation is that their claim was a pretext and a boast, since when the Qur'an did come to them, they rejected it. This exposes their insincerity and shows that disbelief comes from stubbornness and arrogance, not from lack of guidance.

translation: "If we had a reminder (a scripture) from the earlier peoples, we would surely have been servants of God, sincere and devoted." (Qur'an 37:168-169)
interpretation: The verse records what the Arabs of the Prophet's time used to claim before revelation came to them: that had they been given a divine book like the earlier communities of Jews and Christians, they would have been the most sincere and obedient worshippers of God. It exposes the emptiness of this boast. When the Qur'an, a clear reminder, actually came to them, they rejected it, which shows that their disbelief was not due to a lack of guidance but to arrogance and stubbornness. The verse teaches that people often promise they would respond better to guidance than others did, yet the real test is how they act once the guidance is in front of them.

translation: But the chosen servants of God (would have been saved).
interpretation: This verse comes in Surat As-Saffat (37:40) as an exception to the punishment of the wrongdoers described before it. After the Qur'an describes the fate of those who denied the truth and will taste the painful punishment, it excludes the sincere servants of God, those whom God purified and chose for Himself through sincere devotion. The point is that salvation depends not on lineage or outward claims but on ikhlas, wholehearted sincerity in worship and obedience to God alone. Those whose faith and deeds are purified for God are protected by His grace from the torment that befalls the deniers, and they are granted honor and lasting bliss in the Garden.

translation: But they disbelieved in it (the Qur'an/the Message), so soon they will know.
interpretation: After the truth came to them, the deniers chose to reject it out of arrogance and stubbornness rather than because of any lack of proof. The phrase 'so soon they will know' is a warning: the consequences of their denial are certain, and when the reality of God's promise appears, whether in the defeat of falsehood in this world or in the reckoning of the Hereafter, their doubts and mockery will give way to certain knowledge, but too late for them to benefit from it.

translation: And Our word has already gone forth to Our servants, the messengers.
interpretation: God declares that His decree is firm and unalterable: those He sent as messengers are promised, by a prior and binding divine decision, that they will be given victory and support. The following verses state the content of this word, that they will surely be helped and that God's host will prevail. The verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad and the believers that the apparent hardship and rejection faced by the prophets is temporary, and that the final outcome is already settled in God's knowledge and will, whether the triumph appears through clear worldly victory or through the vindication of their message and the defeat of their opponents.

translation: Indeed, they will be the ones given victory.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:172) is part of God's promise concerning His messengers, affirming that those sent by Him will ultimately be supported against their opponents. Their triumph is not necessarily measured by worldly or immediate success, but by the vindication of the truth they carry: their message prevails, their opponents' falsehood is exposed, and God's decree of aid is fulfilled in His appointed time. The verse offers reassurance to believers that persistence on the path of truth, even amid hardship and rejection, ends in divine victory.

translation: And indeed, Our soldiers will be the ones who prevail.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:173) affirms that God's party, made up of the messengers and the believers who follow them, will ultimately triumph over those who deny the truth. The victory may be one of clear evidence and proof, or one of eventual worldly success and support from God, even if believers face hardship or apparent defeat along the way. It comforts the Prophet and the believers by assuring them that the outcome rests with God's promise, not with the apparent strength of their opponents, and that steadfastness in obedience to Him leads to final success.

translation: So turn away from them for a while.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:174) instructs the Prophet Muhammad to withdraw from the disbelievers who persist in denying the message, leaving them to their stubbornness and entrusting their affair to God. It is a consolation and a call to patience: his duty is only to convey the message, not to compel belief. The phrase 'for a while' implies that the time of God's decisive judgment and the vindication of the believers will surely come, so he need not be distressed by their rejection or hasten the outcome.

translation: And watch them, for soon they will see.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:179) consoles and instructs the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to observe patiently how his opponents behave and to await the outcome of their denial. It carries a promise that the truth of his message and the consequences of their disbelief will soon become plain to them. What they now reject, they will witness with their own eyes, whether as defeat in this world or as the reckoning of the Hereafter. The verse calls the believer to steadfast patience and trust in God's decree, assured that falsehood does not endure and that clear vision of reality will inevitably come.

translation: Is it, then, for Our punishment that they are asking to be hastened?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:176) is a rhetorical question of rebuke. The disbelievers of Quraysh mockingly challenged the Prophet to bring down the punishment he warned them about, saying in effect, 'Bring it on, if you are truthful.' God responds by expressing astonishment and censure at their foolishness: they are making light of a punishment that is real and terrible, and they fail to grasp what its arrival will mean. The next verses explain that when it descends upon their courtyards, the morning of those who were warned will be evil. The verse teaches that scoffing at divine warnings does not delay or nullify them, and that this attitude reflects heedlessness and arrogance rather than strength or insight.

translation: But when it descends upon their courtyard, how evil will be the morning of those who were warned.
interpretation: The verse portrays God's punishment as an army that suddenly encamps in the open ground of the disbelievers' own home, a moment they never prepared for. The morning is the time of the attack, when they expected another ordinary day. They had been warned through the messengers and had mocked those warnings, so the day of reckoning is truly dreadful for them. It teaches that ignoring clear admonition does not delay the consequence. When it comes, it arrives without escape and at an hour people think they are safe.

translation: So turn away from them for a while.
interpretation: This verse (37:174, from Surat as-Saffat) instructs the Prophet Muhammad to disengage from the disbelievers of Quraysh who persisted in denying the message, and to stop being distressed by their stubbornness. He is to be patient and leave them for a appointed time, until God's promise is fulfilled and the matter is decided, whether by their defeat and the Prophet's victory, as happened at Badr and the conquest of Mecca, or by the time of their reckoning. The command is not to abandon conveying the message, but to withhold anxious preoccupation with their rejection and entrust their outcome to God, who will bring about the vindication He has promised to His messengers.

translation: And watch them, for soon they will see.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah As-Saffat (37:175), consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the face of his people's denial and hostility. He is told to observe patiently what they do and to await God's promised outcome, for the truth of the message will soon become plain to them. The 'seeing' they will experience is the realization of the consequences of their disbelief: defeat and humiliation in this world, and punishment in the next. The command to watch implies that the believer's role is steadfast patience and trust in God, while the vindication of truth and the downfall of falsehood are certain and in God's hands.

translation: Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Honour and Power, above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse declares God's absolute transcendence over every false claim made about Him, such as that He has offspring or partners. Since all honour and might belong to Him alone, He is utterly free of the weakness, need, and limitation that such claims would imply. The believer is taught to answer slander against God's nature not with argument alone but with tasbih, affirming His perfection and holding Him far above human imagination and invention.

translation: And peace be upon the messengers.
interpretation: This verse, Surah As-Saffat 37:181, closes the surah by extending God's salutation of peace to all the prophets and messengers. It affirms their honor and their safety from God's displeasure, and it acknowledges that the message they brought, the worship of One God, was true and was vindicated over the claims of those who denied them. Believers are thereby taught to hold all the messengers in respect and to send peace upon them, and to see their mission as secure in God's protection and favor, regardless of the rejection they met in the world.

translation: And all praise is due to God, Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse teaches that praise in its fullness belongs to God alone, because every blessing in creation, whether seen or unseen, comes from Him. He is Rabb, the Creator, Owner, Sustainer, and Nurturer of all the worlds, so everything that exists depends on His continuous care. Praising Him is therefore not a mere formula but an acknowledgment of His perfection and generosity, and it calls the believer to gratitude, humility, and an awareness that every favor, and every outcome ultimately returns to Him.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.
interpretation: The disconnected letter 'Sad' is among the mysterious opening letters whose true meaning is known to God alone, though it also draws attention to the fact that this Book is composed of the very letters familiar to the Arabs, yet is inimitable. God then swears by the Qur'an, described as 'dhi al-dhikr', meaning it is the bearer of reminder, honor, and lasting renown: it reminds people of their Lord, of the Hereafter, of lessons from earlier nations, and of what is lawful and unlawful. The oath affirms the Qur'an's truth and its elevated status, preparing the listener for the message that follows, namely that those who disbelieve do so out of arrogance and opposition, not from any lack of clear proof in the Book.

translation: Nay, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition.
interpretation: The verse explains that the disbelievers' rejection of the Qur'an does not come from any lack of proof or clarity in the message. It comes from their arrogance (izzah), which keeps them from submitting to the truth, and from their hostility and schism (shiqaq), which leads them to oppose the Prophet and the believers. Their obstinate pride and their habit of opposing the Messenger out of stubbornness, not rational conviction, is what keeps them from heeding the reminder.

translation: How many a generation We destroyed before them! They cried out [for mercy], but it was no longer a time of escape.
interpretation: The verse warns the Quraysh who were arrogantly rejecting the Prophet by pointing to the fate of earlier nations. Those peoples persisted in disbelief and pride until punishment overtook them. Only then did they call out in desperation and repentance, but repentance at the moment of punishment is not accepted, because the opportunity to turn back and be saved had already passed. The lesson is that one should respond to God's call and repent while there is still time, rather than delay until the point where no escape remains.

translation: And they marvelled that a warner from among themselves had come to them; and the disbelievers said, "This is a magician, a liar."
interpretation: The verse (Sad 38:4) shows that the disbelievers of Quraysh rejected the message not because of any flaw in the evidence but because of pride and prejudice. They could not accept that God would choose a human being, one they knew from among their own people, as His messenger. Unable to refute the clear truth of his message and his well-known honesty, they resorted to slander, calling him a 'magician' to explain away the powerful effect of the Qur'an on hearts, and a 'liar' to discredit his claim to prophethood. The point is that arrogance and attachment to inherited customs blind people to the truth, and that those who oppose true guidance often attack the messenger's character rather than answer his argument.

translation: "Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!" (Qur'an 38:5)
interpretation: This verse records the astonishment of the Meccan polytheists when the Prophet called them to worship God alone. Their reaction shows how deeply inherited custom had shaped them: because they had grown up with many deities, the simple truth of one God sounded strange to them, while their own idolatry seemed normal. The Qur'an thus points to the power of habit and tradition in blinding people to clear truth. What is truly astonishing is not the oneness of the Creator but the worship of many lesser beings who can neither benefit nor harm. The verse invites the reader to question inherited assumptions and recognize that pure monotheism is the most natural and rational belief.

translation: And the chiefs among them went off, saying: 'Go on, and remain steadfast to your gods. Indeed, this is a thing intended.'
interpretation: This verse shows the leaders of Quraysh, alarmed when the Prophet called them to worship God alone, urging their people to leave the gathering and cling stubbornly to their idols. By saying 'this is a thing that is intended', they mean that Muhammad's message is not a sincere call to truth but a scheme with a hidden purpose, such as seeking leadership, power, and dominion over them. In this way they try to discredit the message by questioning the messenger's motives instead of answering its evidence. The verse also shows how the elite of a society often protect their status and inherited customs by pressing others to endure and persist in falsehood, and by labeling the call to monotheism as an ulterior worldly ambition.

translation: We have not heard of this in the latest religion; this is nothing but a fabrication.
interpretation: This is the response of the Quraysh leaders to the Prophet's call to the oneness of God (Surah Sad 38:7). They claim they never heard of pure monotheism in 'the last creed', which most commentators take to mean the Christianity of their day with its Trinity, or the final religion they knew of, or the religion of their forefathers. Since the idea contradicted their inherited polytheism and nothing like it was familiar to them, they dismissed it as an invention made up by Muhammad. The verse shows how people rooted in ancestral tradition reject truth by appealing to unfamiliarity rather than evidence, treating the novelty of a message as proof of its falsehood.

translation: Has the Reminder been sent down to him out of all of us? Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh object that God would not have singled out Muhammad, a man like them with no special wealth or rank, to receive the revelation. Their objection is not a sincere intellectual difficulty, because the real cause is doubt and denial of the Qur'an itself, which comes from arrogance and envy. They persist in this doubt only because they have not yet experienced God's punishment. Once the punishment touches them, their doubt will vanish and they will be forced to recognize the truth they now reject. The verse shows that denial often rests on stubborn pride and heedlessness rather than a lack of evidence, and that certainty is often reached only when the consequences become undeniable.

translation: Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:9) rebukes the disbelievers who objected that revelation was sent to Muhammad rather than to one of their own notables. God asks rhetorically whether they hold the storehouses of His mercy, so that they could decide who is chosen for prophethood and favor. The answer is plainly no: mercy, including the gift of prophecy, belongs wholly to God, who is al-'Aziz (the Almighty, whom none can overrule) and al-Wahhab (the Bestower, who gives freely and without compulsion). He grants it to whom He wills according to His wisdom, and human envy or status has no say in His choice.

translation: Or do they own the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them? Then let them ascend by whatever means.
interpretation: The verse challenges the disbelievers who dismiss the Prophet's message and who question why revelation was sent to him and not to them. It asks whether they hold sovereignty over the cosmos and thus have the right to decide who receives prophethood and mercy. Since they plainly do not, the command to 'ascend by the means' is ironic and rhetorical: if they claim such power, let them climb up to the heavens and take control of its affairs, or block the decree of God. Their inability to do so shows that authority belongs to God alone, and so it is for Him, not them, to choose whom He will for His message. The verse exposes the weakness of their arrogance and the folly of objecting to God's wisdom.

translation: A host of the confederates, there, is bound to be defeated.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:11) is a divine response to the Quraysh's arrogant mockery and denial of the Prophet's message. It declares that those who band together against God's messenger, however numerous and confident, are only a small, insignificant force destined for defeat. The word 'there' (hunalik) points to their position of opposition, which is the very place where they will be humbled. It also carries a promise of consolation and certainty to the Prophet and the believers: the truth will prevail, and the alliances of falsehood, like earlier peoples who rejected their prophets, will collapse regardless of their numbers or strength.

translation: Before them, the people of Noah denied the truth, as did 'Ad, and Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and warns his opponents among the Quraysh by reminding them that rejecting messengers is an old pattern, and that it has always ended in ruin. The people of Noah were destroyed by the flood, 'Ad by a fierce wind, and Pharaoh by drowning, despite their great numbers, physical strength, and worldly power. The description of Pharaoh as 'lord of the stakes' points to his firmly established, unshakeable-seeming authority and his brutality, since he is said to have staked down those he tortured, and also to his mighty armies and monuments, which stood like tent-pegs holding his kingdom fast. Yet none of this protected him from God's decree. The lesson is that power and arrogance cannot shield those who deny the truth, so the Quraysh should take heed and not expect a different outcome.

translation: And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the dwellers of the Thicket. Those were the factions.
interpretation: The verse points to the peoples of Thamud, Lot, and the Thicket (the people of Shu'ayb) as the 'confederates' or 'factions' who banded together against their messengers. The term 'al-aḥzāb' signals that denial of the truth is not an isolated act but a collective alliance of the powerful against God's prophets. By naming them, the Qur'an reminds the Prophet Muhammad and his opponents that the Quraysh's hostility is just the latest episode in a recurring pattern. Just as those mighty coalitions, despite their numbers and strength, were destroyed when they rejected their messengers, so too will any group that unites in opposition to the truth meet the same fate. The verse consoles the believers and warns the deniers that numerical or political strength cannot shield against divine judgment.

translation: Every one of them did nothing but deny the messengers, so My punishment became due.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment is not arbitrary but the just consequence of rejecting revelation. Each of the earlier nations, despite differences in power and numbers, shared one fault: they denied the messengers sent to guide them. To deny one messenger is in effect to deny the message of all, since they brought the same call to worship God alone. Because they persisted in this denial after clear warning, God's promised penalty became inevitable. The verse also warns later generations, including those who opposed the Prophet Muhammad, that the same fate awaits any people who persist in rejecting truth.

translation: And these [disbelievers] await nothing but a single Blast, which will have no pause or delay.
interpretation: The verse warns the persistent deniers of the Prophet's message that their mockery and defiance will not last forever. The Hour will come suddenly, with one mighty cry (the blowing of the Trumpet), and once it begins it cannot be paused, postponed, or repeated, just as the milk of a she-camel cannot be held back between milkings. The lesson is that the chance to repent and mend one's ways exists only in this life, and there is no extra time or reprieve once the decreed moment arrives, so a person should not be deceived by the delay of punishment but should return to God while there is still time.

translation: And they say, "Our Lord, hasten for us our share (our record of deeds) before the Day of Reckoning."
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:16) shows the mocking disbelief of the Quraysh and the deniers. The word 'qitt' means a portion, share, or written record, and here refers to their allotted punishment. By demanding it be hastened before the Day of Reckoning, they ridicule the Prophet's warnings, feeling sure that no punishment is coming. Their taunt exposes their heedlessness and arrogance, as they treat a grave warning as a joke. The verse also implies that God's delay of punishment is mercy and a respite, not proof that the warning is false. Those who mock it are only increasing their own accountability, and the reckoning will come at its appointed time, not when they demand it.

translation: Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant David, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was ever turning back to God in repentance.
interpretation: God consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the face of the denial, mockery, and accusations of his opponents, and directs him to find steadfastness in the example of earlier prophets. David is held up as a model because he combined outward power, as a king, a warrior, and a devoted worshipper with great physical and spiritual strength, with constant inward humility and return to God. The lesson is that true strength is not arrogance or retaliation but patience joined with repeated turning to God: someone who has power yet keeps returning to his Lord in repentance and obedience is best able to endure hostility, and the believer should therefore meet harsh words with patience and remembrance of God rather than despair or anger.

translation: Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify Our praise along with him (David), at evening and at sunrise.
interpretation: The verse shows God's special favor to David: his devotion was so sincere and his remembrance of God so strong that creation itself joined him in worship. The mountains, which seem silent and lifeless, are in truth part of a universe that constantly glorifies its Creator, and God allowed David to share in that praise at the beginning and end of the day. The mention of morning and evening points to steady, regular devotion, and it teaches that a servant who turns to God with sincerity and consistency is in harmony with all of creation, while the strength and power of a prophet-king are put to the service of worship, not arrogance.

translation: And the birds assembled; all turned to Him in repentance and obedience.
interpretation: The verse portrays the extent of God's favor to David: the birds were gathered to him, and they joined him in glorifying God whenever he praised. Each of them, like the mountains mentioned just before, was 'awwāb', constantly returning to God in devotion. The point is that David's remembrance of God was so sincere and powerful that all creation echoed it, showing that the whole of creation naturally inclines toward worship of its Creator, and that those who sincerely turn to God find the world in harmony with them.

translation: And We strengthened his kingdom, and gave him wisdom and decisive speech.
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:20) describes God's favors upon the Prophet David (Dawud). God made his rule firm and secure, through military strength, awe among his people, and protection of his authority. He gave him hikmah, meaning sound understanding, right judgment, and prophetic insight into religion and worldly affairs. He also granted him 'faslul-khitab', the ability to speak and judge with clarity, separating truth from falsehood and bringing disputes to a decisive end, whether by his eloquent, to-the-point speech or by his sound judgment between litigants. The verse shows that true leadership rests on both power and wisdom, and that both are gifts from God used to establish justice.

translation: Has the news of the disputants reached you, when they climbed over the wall into the private chamber of worship?
interpretation: The verse opens the account of David's trial. Two disputants entered his place of worship unexpectedly by climbing over the wall rather than through the door, and this surprised him. The unusual entry shows that the test was sudden and unforeseen. It also teaches that a ruler or judge is accountable even in his most private moments of devotion, and that he must be ready to hear anyone who comes seeking justice, however and whenever they come. God draws the Prophet's attention to this story so that he and the believers may learn from it about judgment, humility and turning back to God.

translation: When they entered upon David and he was alarmed by them, they said, 'Do not fear. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not be unjust, and guide us to the right path.'
interpretation: The verse shows that justice requires a judge to be accessible and to hear grievances openly, even when the circumstances are startling. David was in his private place of worship, and the unexpected entry of the two men over the wall frightened him, yet they calmed him by explaining that they were only disputants seeking a verdict. Their request has three parts: judge with truth, do not overstep or lean toward either side (la tushtit), and guide us to the middle of the path, meaning the fair and balanced resolution. The lesson is that a judge must remain impartial and act with fairness, and that those who seek judgment should ask for truth rather than favor. It also serves as the opening of a trial in which David himself is tested and led to turn back to God in repentance.

translation: Indeed, this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes, and I have a single ewe. Yet he said, 'Entrust her to me,' and he overcame me in argument.
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable brought before the prophet-king David (Dawud) in Surah Sad.
