Through the case of the man with ninety-nine ewes who covets his brother's only one, the verse illustrates the injustice of the powerful who, despite having abundance, seize the little that the weak possess, using pressure and forceful speech to prevail. Its deeper lesson is that David was being reminded, through this analogy, to judge with absolute justice and to guard against taking more than one's rightful share at another's expense. It leads him to reflect on his own conduct and to turn to God in repentance.

translation: He said: "He has certainly wronged you by asking that your ewe be added to his ewes. Indeed, many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And David realized that We had only tested him, so he asked forgiveness of his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance.
interpretation: David gives his judgment after hearing only one litigant's complaint, condemning the other man's greed and observing that injustice commonly arises among business partners and associates, with only the faithful and righteous few restraining themselves. As he speaks, he realizes that the case was a trial from God meant to make him reflect on his own conduct and the need for care and fairness in judgment, perhaps on a lapse of his own. His response is the model for a servant who errs: he immediately asks God's forgiveness, prostrates in humility, and returns to God in sincere repentance. The verse teaches that even prophets are tested, that a judge should hear both sides before ruling, and that the right answer to a mistake is swift repentance, which is why this verse is a place of prostration in recitation.

translation: So We forgave him that; and indeed, he has with Us a place of nearness and a good final return.
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:25), spoken of the Prophet David after he turned to God in repentance, shows that sincere repentance is met with divine forgiveness and honor. God not only erases the lapse but raises the repentant servant to closeness with Him ('zulfa') and promises a beautiful destination in the hereafter ('husn ma'ab'). Even prophets with great authority remain human servants who turn back to God, and the door of mercy stays open to everyone who does the same: forgiveness is followed by elevation, not lingering disgrace.

translation: O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between people in truth and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of God. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of God will have a severe punishment because they forgot the Day of Account.
interpretation: The verse teaches that authority is a trust delegated by God, not a personal privilege, and that the one who holds it must rule by justice and truth. The greatest threat to just judgment is personal whim, since following desire gradually draws a ruler away from God's path. The root of that deviation is forgetting accountability: a person who loses awareness that he will answer for his actions on the Day of Account becomes careless with justice, and that heedlessness is why the punishment is severe. Remembering the Day of Reckoning is therefore what keeps power and judgment upright.

translation: We did not create the heaven and the earth and all that is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve; so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the cosmos is the product of wisdom and purpose, not of chance or futility. Creation is ordered toward a moral end: humans are accountable, justice will ultimately be established, and the wrongdoer will not be treated the same as the righteous. To think that existence is aimless, with no resurrection or reckoning, is the baseless conjecture of those who reject faith, and since such denial leads people to live without accountability, their end is the Fire. The warning of 'woe' shows that denying the purposeful design of creation is not a harmless opinion but a grave error with serious consequences in the Hereafter.

translation: Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption in the earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question whose answer is plainly no. It argues that divine justice and wisdom require a final reckoning. If the believer who strives for righteousness and the corrupter who spreads injustice both ended the same way, with no recompense after death, creation would be pointless and God's justice meaningless. Since the wrongdoer often prospers in this world while the righteous suffer, the verse points to the Hereafter as the place where each receives what they deserve, which gives moral meaning to human choices and comfort to those who remain steadfast in faith and piety.

translation: [This is] a blessed Book which We have sent down to you, so that they may ponder its verses, and so that those of understanding may take heed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an's purpose is not mere recitation or blessing-seeking but active reflection (tadabbur) on its meanings, which leads to remembrance and practical guidance. Its blessedness lies in the abundant, lasting good it brings to those who contemplate it and act on it. Those with sound intellect (ulu al-albab) are the ones who truly benefit, because they use reason to move from understanding the verses to being reminded of the truth and living by it.

translation: And We granted to David [a son], Solomon. What an excellent servant he was! Indeed, he was ever turning back [to Allah].
interpretation: The verse presents Solomon as a gift from God to David, showing that children and blessings are favors bestowed by Him. Solomon's praise as an 'excellent servant' teaches that true honor lies in servitude to God rather than in kingship or power, even though he was given a vast kingdom. The reason given for this praise is that he was 'awwab', meaning one who constantly returns to God in repentance, remembrance, and obedience, whether in times of ease or trial. The verse thus holds up constant turning back to God as the hallmark of a righteous servant.

translation: When there were displayed before him, in the afternoon, the poised, swift steeds.
interpretation: The verse describes Prophet Solomon being absorbed in reviewing his magnificent warhorses, standing gracefully on three legs with one hoof lifted, as evening came. It introduces a lesson about how love of worldly goods, even lawful and noble ones kept for jihad, can distract the heart from the remembrance of God. In the following verses Solomon realizes that the sun has set and he has missed his prayer or remembrance, and so he returns to God in repentance. The point is that a believer must keep the love of God above all possessions, honors and power, and must quickly turn back to Him when heedlessness occurs.

translation: So he said, 'Indeed, I have preferred the love of good things over the remembrance of my Lord, until the sun disappeared behind the veil (of darkness).'
interpretation: Solomon, upon being shown the swift, noble horses in the evening, realizes that his absorption in reviewing them caused him to miss his prayer or remembrance of God until the sun had set. His words express that his love for good things, which was lawful and even intended for God's cause, momentarily distracted him from remembrance of his Lord. He then acknowledges the lapse humbly and turns back to God, showing that even a permissible attachment must never take precedence over devotion to God, and that a prophet's response to heedlessness is immediate self-reproach and return to Him.

translation: "Bring them back to me." Then he began stroking their legs and necks.
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:33) follows the episode in which Solomon was distracted by his fine horses until the sun had set and the time of prayer had passed. He asks for the horses to be brought back, then lovingly passes his hand over their legs and necks. On this reading, which many exegetes such as al-Tabari favor, he does so as an act of kindness and care for the animals, or to inspect them and tend to them. The act shows that his attachment to worldly goods did not turn him away from God. He returns to remembrance of God, and the moment shows both his tenderness toward creatures and his repentance, since he put worship above worldly possessions.

translation: And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (in repentance).
interpretation: The verse shows that even a mighty prophet-king like Solomon was put through a trial meant to remind him of his complete dependence on God. The 'body' on his throne signals that power and royal authority are fragile and passing: a lifeless form sitting where the king sat is a reminder of how quickly a ruler can be reduced to nothing without God's sustaining will. Solomon's response was immediate: he turned back (anāba) to his Lord in humility, repentance, and renewed reliance on Him. The lesson is that trials humble even the greatest, and the mark of true nobility is to return to God at once, acknowledging that all sovereignty belongs to Him alone.

translation: He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."
interpretation: This is the supplication of the Prophet Solomon (Sulayman), who begins by seeking forgiveness before asking for worldly favor, which teaches that spiritual purification comes before requests for power or blessings. His request for a unique kingdom is best understood not as greed or rivalry, but as a plea for a distinctive sign confirming his prophethood, a dominion (including command over the wind, the jinn, and the language of birds) that would serve as a miracle and a means of establishing God's truth. He ends by invoking God as al-Wahhab, the Ever-Bestowing, acknowledging that all power is a pure gift from God, given without being earned, and that only He can grant such a sovereignty.

translation: So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command wherever he directed.
interpretation: The verse shows that God granted Solomon (peace be upon him) authority over the wind as a special favor after he turned to God in repentance and asked for a kingdom unlike any other. The wind carried him and his forces gently and smoothly, never harsh or destructive, to whatever place he intended. This teaches that when a servant turns sincerely to God, God can make even the mightiest natural forces tame and beneficial for him, and that all power ultimately belongs to God, who bestows it as a gift and a test of gratitude, not as something humans own independently.

translation: And [We subjected to him] the devils, every builder and diver.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Sad (38:37), shows the extent of the authority God granted Solomon: even the rebellious jinn were made to serve him. They were put to work according to their abilities. Some built for him, raising great structures such as fortresses and monumental buildings, while others dived into the seas to bring up pearls and other treasures. The point is that Solomon's power was a divine gift, not a human achievement. It also shows that God can restrain even the most defiant forces and turn them to useful purposes, so that they could not harm him and could only obey by God's leave.

translation: And others bound together in shackles.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Sad (38:38), continues the account of the favors God granted Prophet Sulayman (Solomon), whom He gave authority over the jinn. Besides those jinn who built and dived for him, there were others, the rebellious and mischievous among them, whom he restrained by binding them together in pairs or groups in chains. The meaning is that God gave Sulayman such complete dominion that even defiant beings were subdued and prevented from causing harm, showing that his power was a gift from God and not something he achieved on his own.

translation: This is Our gift, so bestow it generously or withhold it, without any reckoning.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Sad (38:39), comes after God's account of the gifts given to Prophet Sulaymān (Solomon), including dominion over the wind and the jinn. It conveys that his power and wealth were a pure grace from God, not something earned or owed. God gave him full discretion to give to others or to hold back, without being held accountable for how he used it. This freedom did not make him arbitrary, because it came from a servant who was upright and trusted. The verse teaches that all blessings come from God, and that a righteous person entrusted with them can be relied upon to use them with wisdom and justice.

translation: And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good place of return.
interpretation: This verse, spoken of Prophet Dawud (David) in Surah Sad (38:25), affirms that God's forgiveness after his repentance did not merely erase his error but raised his standing. The 'nearness' (zulfa) signifies closeness to God and honor in the Hereafter, and the 'good place of return' (husn ma'ab) signifies a blessed final destination in Paradise. The lesson is that sincere repentance and turning back to God restore a servant to favor, and that a person who errs and then humbly returns may attain a rank higher than before.

translation: And remember Our servant Job, when he called upon his Lord: 'Indeed, Satan has afflicted me with hardship and suffering.'
interpretation: The verse presents Job as a model of patient endurance and humble reliance on God. Facing severe illness, loss, and pain, he does not complain against God or despair, but turns to his Lord in supplication. By attributing his affliction to Satan's touch, he shows good manners with God: the whispering and despair that accompany suffering come from Satan, while the trial itself is permitted within God's wisdom. Job's call is a lesson that a believer should respond to hardship by seeking God's help, remaining patient, and guarding against the despair that Satan tries to instill, trusting that relief will come from God alone.

translation: Strike the ground with your foot: here is a cool spring to wash in and to drink.
interpretation: This verse is God's answer to Job's (Ayyub's) prayer in his long affliction. God commands him to stamp the earth, and in response a spring wells up beneath his foot. Bathing in its cool water washes away the illness and hardship from his body, and drinking from it heals him from within. The verse shows that relief comes from God after patient endurance, that He can make means of healing appear where none seemed to exist, and that the believer's part is to act in obedience, here by the simple act of striking the ground, while the cure itself is God's gift.

translation: And We granted him his family and the like of them along with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: This verse describes God's restoration of Prophet Job (Ayyub) after his long trial of illness and loss. God did not merely end his suffering but replaced what he had lost, giving him back his family and doubling them, as a pure act of divine mercy rather than something earned by right. It also serves as a lasting lesson for people of reason: those who endure hardship with patience, gratitude and constant turning to God will find that relief and generous compensation come from Him, so that believers should never despair in times of affliction and should remember that God's mercy follows patience.

translation: "And take in your hand a bundle of grass and strike with it, and do not break your oath." Indeed, We found him patient, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was ever turning back to God in repentance.
interpretation: This verse describes God's relief for Prophet Job (Ayyub) after his long trial. During his illness he had sworn in a moment of distress to strike his wife a set number of lashes, likely because of something she had done. God did not want him to break his oath, and He did not want his faithful wife, who had stayed loyal and cared for him, to be harmed. So He gave him a gentle way out: gather a bundle of thin stalks, with the number of stalks matching the number of lashes, and strike once with it. That fulfills the oath without causing injury. The verse shows that God provides an exit for those who are patient and mindful of Him, and that the law favors mercy and wise solutions over harshness. It also affirms that vows should be taken seriously. The closing praise, that Job was patient, an excellent servant, and constantly turning to God, shows that true patience is not silent suffering alone but steady return to God in every state, and that such devotion is rewarded with ease and honor.

translation: And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men of strength and insight.
interpretation: God holds up these three prophets as models of devotion by describing them as possessing 'hands' and 'eyes'. The 'hands' stand for strength and capability in obeying God and performing righteous deeds, and the 'eyes' stand for spiritual insight and clear understanding of the truth. They did not merely hold correct beliefs, they put them into action with energy and perseverance, and they perceived reality with discernment. The verse teaches that true servanthood joins sound knowledge and vision with committed, effective action, and that the believer is called to follow their example in both.

translation: Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Home (of the Hereafter).
interpretation: God chose these prophets (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, mentioned in the preceding verses) and made them His sincere servants by granting them one distinctive and unalloyed trait: their hearts were wholly devoted to remembering the Hereafter. Their thoughts, deeds and calling to others were centered on the abode of the next life rather than on worldly attachments, so they constantly worked for it and reminded people of it. This single-minded orientation toward the Hereafter is what set them apart as chosen and purified in God's sight.

translation: And indeed, in Our sight they are among the chosen, the best of men.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the mention of Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Yaqub in Surah Sad (38:47), affirms that God Himself selected these prophets and purified them for His service. Their excellence is not a matter of human praise but of divine election: they were chosen to carry His message and were preserved in goodness, so they stand as the finest examples of righteousness. The phrase 'in Our sight' stresses that the true measure of a person's worth is God's judgment, which rests on sincere devotion and remembrance of the Hereafter, as the preceding verse describes.

translation: And remember Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhul-Kifl; and each of them was among the best of people.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet, and every believer after him, to recall these three figures as models of moral excellence. It is not enough to know their names; remembering them means taking lessons from their patience, steadfastness, and fidelity to their covenant with God. Ishmael is known for truthfulness and submission, Elisha for carrying on the prophetic mission with devotion, and Dhul-Kifl for upholding his responsibilities and trust. The closing phrase, 'each of them was among the best (al-akhyar)', teaches that true goodness is measured by obedience to God and by consistent righteous conduct. Those who walk in their way can aspire to the same rank among the chosen and virtuous.

translation: This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is a good place of return.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an, and the preceding account of the prophets in Surah Sad, is a source of remembrance and admonition that revives the heart's awareness of God. It also states that those who guard themselves against disobedience and keep God in mind will have the best final destination, Paradise, so that a person is encouraged to take heed now and prepare for the return to God, since piety is what makes the ultimate homecoming a good one.

translation: Gardens of Eden, whose gates are opened wide for them.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:50) describes the reward of the God-fearing (al-muttaqin) as everlasting gardens of permanent residence. The phrase 'whose gates are opened for them' signifies honor and ease: the righteous will not wait, knock, or be denied entry, as the gates stand open to welcome them. It conveys that Paradise is a gracious welcome from God, in contrast to the locked, harsh reception of the people of Hell, and that their entry is dignified, immediate, and free of hardship or anxiety.

translation: Reclining therein, they will call for abundant fruit and drink.
interpretation: The verse portrays the ease and honor of the people of Paradise. To recline is the posture of those who are secure, comfortable and free of toil, and it shows they have no worry or need to exert themselves. They need only ask, and whatever they desire of fruit and drink is brought to them in abundance without scarcity or end. This conveys the completeness of divine generosity, in which every wish is fulfilled with dignity and rest, as a reward for their faith and righteous deeds in the world.

translation: And with them will be maidens of modest gaze, of equal age.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards promised to the righteous in Paradise: companions who restrain their eyes, looking only at their spouses out of chastity and contentment, and who are all of the same youthful age. The 'modest gaze' signifies purity, loyalty, and faithfulness, while 'equal age' signifies harmony, companionship, and shared vitality, so that the joy of the believers in the Hereafter is complete and free from jealousy, discord, or the decline that comes with aging.

translation: This is what you are promised for the Day of Account.
interpretation: The verse is addressed to the righteous who are received in Paradise (Surah Sad 38:53). It tells them that the blessings they see, such as gardens, open gates, rest and companionship, are the fulfillment of God's promise, which He kept after they lived in faith and obedience. It confirms that the Day of Reckoning is real, that no good deed is lost, and that their patience and restraint in the world have ended in lasting honor and reward. The wording is also a quiet reassurance for believers now: the promise holds, and it will be fulfilled when accounts are settled with justice.

translation: Indeed, this is Our provision; it will never run out.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:54) is addressed to the God-fearing who enter Paradise, and it affirms that what they receive there is a gift directly from God. Unlike worldly blessings, which are limited, decay and come to an end, the bounties of the Hereafter are everlasting. Their pleasure is never cut off by scarcity, loss or death, so the believers can enjoy their reward with complete security and without fear of its ending. It also teaches that all provision, in this life and the next, comes from God alone, and that the permanence of the reward is part of the honor and completeness of the blessing.

translation: This is (the reminder for the righteous). And indeed, for the transgressors there will be an evil place of return.
interpretation: After describing the honor and the beautiful final destination awaiting the God-fearing, the verse draws a stark contrast: those who exceed all bounds in disobedience, arrogance and oppression will return to a wretched end. The word 'maab' (place of return) reminds that every soul ultimately goes back to God, and the destination is determined by one's conduct in this life. The verse serves as a warning that defiance of God's limits, however empowered or unchecked it may seem now, leads to the worst outcome in the Hereafter, which is Hell, while obedience and humility lead to lasting honor.

translation: Hell, in which they will burn, and wretched is that resting place.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Sad 38:56) describes the fate of the rebellious transgressors, who are denied a place of rest in the Hereafter. The word 'mihad' means a bed or a prepared place of repose, a thing people expect to be comfortable. By calling Hell their 'mihad', the verse turns the idea of comfort upside down: instead of ease and rest, the arrogant who defied God find the fire spread out beneath them as their dwelling. The lesson is that anyone who chooses rebellion and pride in this world is preparing for themselves a terrible abode, so a person should consider what kind of resting place their conduct is preparing for them.

translation: This! So let them taste it: boiling scalding water and a foul, freezing discharge.
interpretation: The verse describes the fitting recompense awaiting the transgressors in Hell, whose torment will be twofold and extreme. They will suffer both the opposite extremes of scalding water that burns them from within and without, and ghassaq, a bitterly cold, putrid fluid flowing from the bodies of the damned. The command 'let them taste it' stresses that they will experience this punishment directly and personally, as the just consequence of their arrogance, rejection of the truth, and oppression in worldly life, and it serves as a warning that no part of the punishment will offer relief, since even what is meant to quench or soothe becomes a source of suffering.

translation: And other torments of similar kind, in pairs (various kinds of the like).
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:58) describes the punishment of the transgressors in Hell, following the mention of boiling water (hamim) and foul, freezing fluid (ghassaq). It means that besides these two torments there are yet other punishments of a similar nature, existing in pairs or varieties that match one another in severity and bitterness. The meaning is that the suffering of the wrongdoers will not be limited to a single form of pain but will come in multiple, mutually reinforcing kinds, so that they are afflicted from every side, each torment complementing the other, as a just recompense for the various forms of their disbelief and rebellion in this world.

translation: This is a troop rushing headlong with you; no welcome for them. Indeed, they will burn in the Fire.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Sad 38:59) depicts the dwellers of Hell, where the leaders of misguidance see a new group of their followers being driven into the Fire after them. The leaders speak to one another, announcing that this crowd is plunging in alongside them, and they greet it with a curse instead of a welcome, since those who followed them in error share their fate. It shows how in the Hereafter the ties of false allegiance turn into mutual rejection and blame, and how those who led others astray and those who followed them will end up sharing the same punishment.

translation: They (the followers) will say: 'Rather, it is you! No welcome to you! It is you who brought this upon us (prepared it for us), and what an evil place to settle!'
interpretation: This verse depicts the dispute among the people of Hell. The followers answer the leaders who misled them by turning the blame back on them, rejecting any greeting of welcome. They say that the leaders' false guidance, their invitation to disbelief and wrongdoing, is what brought them to this punishment, so the leaders bear responsibility for it. Each side is cursing the other, and all of them are left in the miserable abode of Hell. The lesson is that blind following of misguided leaders is no excuse on the Day of Judgment, since each person is accountable for the choices they made, and that companionship built on falsehood in this world turns into mutual blame and hostility in the Hereafter.

translation: They will say: "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase for him a double punishment in the Fire."
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:61) shows the followers in Hell blaming those who led them astray. By "whoever put this before us" they mean the leaders and those who introduced disbelief and misguidance, whose false teachings and example led to their present torment. They ask God to double the leaders' punishment, which expresses their bitterness and wish to shift responsibility. The verse teaches that people are accountable for their own choices, and that blaming others will not excuse them on the Day of Judgment. It also warns that those who lead others into error bear a heavier burden, since they carry both their own sin and a share of the sins of those who followed them.

translation: And they will say: "What is the matter with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?"
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:62) describes the inhabitants of Hell, the arrogant disbelievers, searching for the poor and humble believers, such as Bilal, Suhayb, Ammar and others, whom they used to despise and consider wicked and of no worth in the world. When the disbelievers find themselves in the Fire, they look around and cannot find these believers among them, because the believers have been admitted to Paradise. Their question reveals their regret and the collapse of their worldly standards: the people they ridiculed and judged as evil were in truth the righteous and successful, while the ones who deemed themselves superior are the losers. The verse teaches that true worth lies in faith and righteous conduct, not in status, wealth or the opinions of the arrogant, and that God's judgment on the Day of Resurrection overturns false worldly valuations.

translation: Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:63) is spoken by the people of Hellfire as they search for the believers they used to ridicule in the worldly life. Finding themselves in the Fire, they do not see those whom they had belittled and called wicked, so they ask in bewildered regret whether they were wrong to mock them, or whether the believers are indeed present but their eyes have failed to spot them. The verse shows the reversal of fortunes on the Day of Judgment: those who scorned the righteous discover that the ones they derided are in honor and bliss, while the mockers are left in humiliation and doubt over their own earlier arrogance.

translation: Indeed, that is the truth: the disputing of the people of the Fire with one another.
interpretation: The verse closes the passage in Surah Sad (38:59-64) that describes how the leaders and followers among the people of Hell will quarrel and curse one another as they are cast into the Fire. God affirms that this scene is certain and will surely happen, and is not a figure of speech or an exaggeration. The verse warns that the bonds of worldly allegiance, such as following leaders in disbelief and arrogance, will turn to mutual blame and enmity on the Day of Judgment, since no one can help another escape accountability. Hearers are therefore urged to examine whom they follow and what they follow now, and to take responsibility for their own choices while there is still time to turn to God.

translation: Say, "I am only a warner; and there is no god except God, the One, the Subduer."
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to define his role as a warner who alerts people to the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, not as one who controls or compels their guidance. The verse then grounds this warning in the foundation of the message: absolute monotheism. God alone is worthy of worship because He is the One without partner, and al-Qahhar, the Subduer, whose power overcomes all things. Since everything in creation is subject to His will, worshipping anything else is futile, and the warning has real weight, because no one can escape the reckoning of the One who dominates all.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that lies between them, the Almighty, the Ever-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to monotheism in God's lordship over the whole of creation. The One who sustains and governs everything between and beyond the heavens and earth alone deserves worship, not idols or created beings. The pairing of 'the Almighty' (al-'Aziz) with 'the Ever-Forgiving' (al-Ghaffar) holds two attributes together: His power is absolute and no one can resist Him, yet He uses it with mercy, forgiving those who turn back to Him. This invites the listener both to revere Him and to hope in Him, and to see repentance as an open door because the One who has total authority is also the One who forgives repeatedly.

translation: Say: It is a great news.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:67) directs the Prophet to declare that the message he brings, especially the Qur'an and its central truths of tawhid (God's oneness), prophethood, and the resurrection and accountability in the Hereafter, is an event of immense consequence. It is not a trivial matter to be dismissed. The people's heedless turning away from it (as the next verse says) reveals their neglect of the most weighty reality that will decide their ultimate fate, so they are urged to take it seriously and reflect on it.

translation: You are turning away from it.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Sad (38:68), follows the declaration that the Qur'an is 'a great news' (naba' 'azim). It rebukes those who hear the message of resurrection, accountability, and the oneness of God, yet ignore it. The reproach is not that they failed to understand, but that they willfully turn their backs on a truth of the gravest consequence. Neglecting something so momentous is a serious fault, and the verse invites the listener to reflect on whether he too, through heedlessness or pride, avoids the message instead of facing it and responding to it.

translation: I had no knowledge of the exalted assembly (the highest chiefs) when they were disputing.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:69) is spoken by the Prophet Muhammad as a proof of his prophethood. He had no means of knowing about the debate among the angels, the 'highest assembly', over the creation of Adam, except through divine revelation. Since he was unlettered and had no access to earlier scriptures or to the unseen, his accurate report of that heavenly discussion shows that the Qur'an is revealed to him by God, and that what he conveys does not originate from himself.

translation: It is revealed to me only that I am a clear warner.
interpretation: The Prophet declares that the whole of his mission, and everything revealed to him, comes down to a single purpose: to warn people plainly about the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing. He makes no claim to knowledge of the unseen, to divine powers, or to any authority beyond conveying what God reveals. The word 'clear' (mubin) means his warning is explicit and free of ambiguity, leaving his audience without excuse. Revelation is therefore not a source of personal status for him but a trust to deliver, and his role is to make the truth unmistakable, while guidance and judgment remain with God.

translation: When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay."
interpretation: The verse announces the creation of humankind as a deliberate act of God's will, made known to the angels before it happened. By stating that the human is made from clay, the lowest and most humble of materials, it points to the human being's earthly and dependent nature. This humble origin is a reminder against arrogance. It also sets up the contrast with the dignity that follows, when God breathes of His spirit into the human being and commands the angels to prostrate. The human being's true worth therefore lies not in his material origin but in the divine breath and in obedience to his Creator. Pride, such as Iblis showed when he judged by origin alone, is the root of disobedience.

translation: So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration.
interpretation: The verse shows that human dignity comes from God's own act of creation, not from the clay. After the body is proportioned and perfected, God breathes into it a spirit that He honors by ascribing it to Himself. This gives humans life, awareness, reason and moral capacity. The angels' prostration is not worship of Adam. It is obedience to God's command, and it acknowledges the rank God gave to humanity as His vicegerent on earth. The verse also sets up the test of Iblis, whose refusal comes from arrogance and from judging by origin (fire versus clay) instead of submitting to God's wisdom.

translation: So the angels prostrated themselves, all of them together.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 15:30, also 38:73) shows the angels' complete and immediate obedience to God's command to honor Adam after He created him and breathed His spirit into him. The emphatic wording 'all of them' and 'together' stresses that not a single angel held back and that they acted at once, with no delay or dissent. Their prostration was not worship of Adam but an act of obedience to God and an acknowledgment of the dignity He gave humanity. It also sets up the contrast with Iblis, who alone refused out of arrogance, and so teaches that true submission means yielding to God's command without pride or objection, and that rank or origin gives no excuse for disobedience.

translation: Except Iblis; he was arrogant and became one of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse shows that the root of Iblis's downfall was not ignorance of God's existence or power but pride. When commanded to prostrate to Adam, he considered himself superior and refused the divine order out of arrogance, so his disobedience grew into disbelief. The Qur'an presents arrogance as a spiritual disease that blinds a person to truth, makes him reject rightful authority, and turns a rank of nearness to God into expulsion. The lesson for believers is to guard their hearts against self-exaltation and to submit humbly to God's commands even when they do not fully see the wisdom behind them.

translation: He said: 'O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My own two hands? Were you arrogant, or were you among the exalted ones?'
interpretation: God confronts Iblis with a question that exposes the root of his disobedience. The command to prostrate to Adam was not a command to worship a creature but to honor one whom God had specially distinguished, having created him 'with My hands', a phrase that signals particular honor and care. Iblis's refusal was therefore not a matter of misunderstanding but of pride. The question 'Were you arrogant, or were you among the exalted ones?' is rhetorical: it leaves Iblis with no defense, since if he was not truly of a higher rank by God's own decree, then his refusal could only come from arrogance, which is the first sin, the belief that one's own status entitles one to question God's command. The verse teaches that arrogance blinds a person to the honor God has bestowed on others and leads to rebellion against divine orders, and that true rank is determined by God's judgment and not by self-estimation.

translation: He said: I am better than him; You created me from fire and You created him from clay.
interpretation: This verse exposes the root of Iblis's disobedience: arrogance grounded in a false standard of worth. Instead of obeying God's direct command to prostrate to Adam, Iblis judged by origin and substance, reasoning that fire is nobler than clay. He thereby set his own reasoning against divine command and, in effect, blamed God's act of creation. The lesson is that true virtue lies in submission and obedience to God, not in lineage, material, or status. Pride that elevates oneself over others and rejects a command because it does not suit one's self-image is the first sin, and it leads to expulsion from God's mercy.

translation: He said: 'Then get out of it, for indeed you are expelled (accursed).'
interpretation: This verse records God's judgment on Iblis after he refused to prostrate to Adam out of arrogance. His expulsion from the heavenly station is the direct consequence of pride and disobedience: rank and nearness to God are not secured by origin or nature, but by humility and submission to His command. The word 'rajim' means one cast away, driven off in disgrace, so Iblis loses his place of honor and is branded with rejection. The verse teaches that arrogance before divine command removes a being from God's mercy, and that status is forfeited when obedience is replaced by self-exaltation.

translation: And indeed, upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Sad 38:78) is God's declaration to Iblis after he refused to prostrate to Adam out of arrogance. It shows that arrogance and disobedience toward God's command bring banishment from His mercy. The curse is not arbitrary; it is a consequence of Iblis's own pride and his claim of superiority. The phrase 'until the Day of Judgment' marks the period in which he is respited and remains expelled from mercy, after which his final punishment, which is Hell, will follow. It warns humankind that the same pride that led to Iblis's downfall can lead anyone away from God's mercy, and that humility and submission to God's commands are the way to remain within it.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, then grant me respite until the Day they are resurrected.'
interpretation: Iblis, having been expelled for refusing to prostrate to Adam, does not repent but instead asks God to delay his death until the Day of Resurrection. His request reveals that his rebellion springs from pride and a determination to take revenge on humankind, not from ignorance of God. He acknowledges God's lordship and the reality of resurrection, yet this knowledge does not lead him to obedience. The verse teaches that belief in God's existence and power is worthless without humble submission. It also shows that the respite he was given is a test and a trial for humanity, not a sign of divine favor to him. Those who follow his path and refuse to heed guidance bear responsibility for their own choices.

translation: He said: "Then indeed, you are among those granted respite."
interpretation: In this verse God answers Iblis's request to be delayed until the Day of Resurrection, and grants him a reprieve. The respite is not a sign of honor or divine approval. It is part of God's wisdom and a test for humankind: Iblis is allowed time to tempt people, so that those who follow him are distinguished from those who stay faithful to God. The reprieve also shows God's forbearance, because He does not hasten punishment even for the rebellious. Human beings are given free choice and are accountable for whether they yield to temptation or resist it, and Iblis has no power to compel anyone.

translation: Until the Day of the known time.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Hijr (15:38) and also Surah Sad (38:81), completes God's reply to Iblis, who asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection. God grants him a delay, but only until a time fixed and known to Him alone. The phrase teaches that even Iblis's reprieve is bounded by divine decree: his ability to tempt humankind is a temporary test, not an independent power, and it ends at an appointed moment when all creatures are held to account. The unknown timing also reminds believers that every respite is a trial in which they should choose obedience and not follow Satan's misguidance.

translation: He (Iblis) said: "Then by Your might, I will surely mislead them all,"
interpretation: In this verse (Surah Sad 38:82), Iblis responds to being cast out for refusing to bow to Adam by swearing by God's own power and honor that he will lead all human beings astray. His oath shows that he does not deny God's existence or might, yet his pride and envy drive him to rebellion and to making humanity the target of his enmity. It also shows that his power is not independent: he swears by the very might of God, acknowledging that his ability to tempt exists only by God's permission. The verse is a warning that temptation is a real and constant test, and the next verse makes an exception for God's sincere servants, whom Iblis cannot mislead. The believer is therefore taught to seek protection through sincerity, remembrance, and reliance on God.

translation: Except, among them, Your chosen, sincere servants.
interpretation: This verse is Iblis's declaration (Qur'an 15:40 and 38:83) that he will lead all of humanity astray, with the single exception of those whom God has purified and drawn to Himself (al-mukhlaṣīn). The meaning is that sincerity is a gift from God as much as an effort of the servant: those whose worship is made purely for God, free from showing off and hidden idols of the self, are placed beyond the reach of Satan's deception. Their protection lies not in their own strength but in God's choosing and safeguarding them. The verse teaches that the way to be safe from Satan's whispering is wholehearted devotion and reliance on God, since Satan's power is limited to those who open themselves to him.

translation: He said: "Then the truth it is, and the truth I speak." (Qur'an 38:84)
interpretation: In this verse God, in answer to Iblis's defiance and his request to mislead mankind, binds Himself and His speech to the truth. The verse stresses that divine decree and judgment rest on absolute justice. Iblis's rebellion will not overturn God's wisdom, so the punishment of Hell for Iblis and for those who follow him is a just and certain outcome. Everything God says and decides is true, and nothing He does is arbitrary. The oath-like phrasing underlines the certainty that the promised consequences will come.

translation: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those of them who follow you, all together.
interpretation: This is God's declaration to Iblis (Satan) after he refused to prostrate to Adam and vowed to lead humanity astray (Surah Sad 38:85, similar to al-A'raf 7:18). It shows that God's justice is certain: Satan and those who willingly choose to follow his path and reject guidance will share the same fate. Satan has only the power to tempt, not to compel, so those who follow him are accountable for their own choice. The verse is a warning that obedience to desire and falsehood leads to ruin, and that the safeguard is sincere devotion to God, since those who are sincere servants are beyond Satan's mastery.

translation: Say: I do not ask you for any payment for it, and I am not among those who pretend or impose themselves.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to affirm his sincerity: he conveys the message purely for God's sake, seeking no worldly reward from his people, so no one can suspect him of ulterior motives. He also declares that he does not fabricate or claim what he has not been given, nor burden himself with inventing speech or knowledge beyond the revelation entrusted to him. The verse thus shows that a true messenger is marked by selfless devotion and honesty, and that his message stands on its own truth rather than on any personal gain or affectation.

translation: It is nothing but a reminder for all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur'an is not the speech of a poet, soothsayer, or devil, nor is it limited to one people or era. It is a universal reminder (dhikr) addressed to all of humankind and the jinn, awakening in them the innate awareness of their Creator, recalling the purpose of their existence and their accountability, and guiding them to what brings honor and salvation. Its message transcends ethnic, geographic, and temporal boundaries, so that whoever receives it has no excuse to remain heedless.

translation: And you will surely know its news after a while.
interpretation: This verse (Sad 38:88) declares that the truth of the Qur'an and the message it brings, including its warnings and promises, will become clear to the disbelievers with the passage of time. Its veracity will be proven by events in this world, such as the triumph of Islam and the fulfillment of what it foretold, and finally in the certainty of death and the Day of Resurrection, when doubt will no longer be possible. It is both a consolation to the Prophet in the face of denial and a warning to those who reject the message that they will come to know its reality when it is too late to benefit from that knowledge.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The revelation of the Book is from God, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes the divine origin and authority of the Qur'an before anything else is said. By attributing the Book's revelation to God rather than to any human author, it calls the reader to approach it with reverence and to accept its guidance as truth. The two names chosen are significant: 'the Almighty' (al-'Azīz) indicates that the revelation is backed by power that no one can overcome or nullify, so its promises and warnings will come to pass, while 'the All-Wise' (al-Ḥakīm) indicates that every command, ruling, and story in it is placed with perfect wisdom and purpose. Together they teach that the Qur'an is both irresistible in authority and flawless in guidance, and that obedience to it is therefore both necessary and beneficial for the one who submits.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, so worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zumar 39:2) links the truthfulness of revelation to the obligation of pure worship. Because the Qur'an is sent down in truth, its central demand is that worship be directed to God alone, without partners or intermediaries, and that the inner intention and outward devotion be free from showing off and from any hidden devotion to others. In other words, true knowledge of the revealed truth must lead to sincerity (ikhlas): obedience and devotion performed purely for God's sake, which is the essence of the religion He has prescribed.

translation: Surely, sincere religion is due to God alone. And those who take protectors besides Him say, "We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to God in position." Indeed, God will judge between them concerning that in which they differ. Indeed, God does not guide one who is a liar and persistently ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that worship and obedience must be purified of every partner and offered to God alone, because He is the only one who deserves devotion and needs no intermediary. The idolaters' excuse that they venerate saints, angels, or idols merely as means of nearness to God is rejected, because seeking nearness through created beings is itself the very act of associating partners with Him, and God has never authorized such a path. Nearness to God is gained only by directly worshipping Him in the way He has prescribed. On the Day of Judgment God will settle the disagreement between the people of pure monotheism and those who associate others with Him, exposing the falsehood of the latter. The closing warning teaches that one who fabricates lies about God and is stubbornly ungrateful for His favors, by attributing divine rights to others, forfeits His guidance, since guidance is withheld from those who persist in deliberate falsehood and denial.

translation: Had God willed to take a son, He could have chosen whatever He wished from what He creates. Glory be to Him! He is God, the One, the Irresistible.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that God has offspring by arguing from His absolute power and oneness. Anything that exists apart from God is created, and so cannot share His nature as a son would share a father's. Even if God had willed to take a son, which is inconceivable, the one chosen would still have come from among His creatures and would be a servant, not a partner in divinity. The notion of a son is therefore impossible in itself. It implies need, likeness, and multiplicity, all of which contradict God's perfection. Because He is the One, unique in essence and attributes, and the Irresistible, who subdues all things to His will, nothing can be equal to Him or be a part of Him. Everything else is subject to His command.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a term appointed. Truly, it is He who is the All-Mighty, the Ever-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the universe is not the product of chance or play but is built on purpose, order, and truth, and that its precise rhythms point to a Creator who governs it with wisdom. The alternating night and day, and the sun and moon moving along fixed courses toward an appointed end, show that creation is finite and accountable to a divine decree, just as human life has an appointed term after which people will return to answer for their deeds. Since God is the All-Mighty, no one can escape His reckoning or resist His command; yet since He is also the Ever-Forgiving, the door of repentance stays open. The reader is therefore called to reflect on the cosmos, recognize the oneness and power of God, and turn to Him in humility and hope for His forgiveness before the appointed term ends.

translation: He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate, and He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses. That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. There is no god but Him. So how are you turned away?
interpretation: The verse argues from God's continuous, intimate acts of creation and provision to the conclusion that He alone deserves worship. Humanity's common origin in one soul and its pairing into male and female shows a single purposeful Creator behind human unity. The livestock, sent down as a gift in their paired kinds, show His provision for human needs. The staged formation of the embryo in the womb, hidden within three layers of darkness (commonly understood as the belly, the womb, and the membrane enclosing the fetus), shows that no one but God oversees a human life from its very beginning, unseen by any other creature. From this the verse draws its conclusion: the One who creates, nurtures, and sustains is the Lord who holds all dominion, so there is no god besides Him. The closing question, 'So how are you turned away?', is a rebuke. Given such clear signs, it is irrational and ungrateful for people to turn from the Creator to worship created things or to deny Him.

translation: If you disbelieve, then indeed God is free of need of you, and He does not approve of disbelief for His servants. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of what lies within the hearts.
interpretation: The verse establishes that God's relationship with humanity is one of complete self-sufficiency on His part and need on ours: human unbelief cannot diminish Him, nor can faith add to Him, so the moral consequences of belief and gratitude fall wholly on people themselves. God's disapproval of disbelief is an expression of His care for His servants, since ingratitude harms them, while He is pleased with gratitude because it leads to their own benefit and salvation. The principle that no soul bears another's burden affirms individual accountability: on the Day of Judgment no one can offload their sins onto others, nor be punished for another's wrongdoing, so each person must take responsibility for their own choices. All will return to God, who will disclose the true reality of their deeds, and nothing can be concealed from Him because He knows even the secret intentions and hidden beliefs in the heart. This calls the believer to sincerity, gratitude and self-examination, not mere outward conduct.

translation: When harm touches a human being, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He grants him a favor from Himself, he forgets what he used to call upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to God to lead others astray from His path. Say: Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed, you are among the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inconsistency of the ungrateful human heart: in hardship, the natural disposition (fitra) recognizes that only God can relieve distress, so a person turns sincerely to Him; yet once relief comes, heedlessness returns and he attributes his deliverance to other causes or false deities, even inviting others to that error. This shows that the denial of God's oneness is not based on real conviction but on forgetfulness and ingratitude, since the person's own moment of need testified to the truth. The command to 'enjoy your disbelief a little' is a stern warning, not permission: worldly enjoyment is brief, and persisting in ingratitude and in misleading others leads to the Fire. The lesson for the believer is to remain as mindful and devoted to God in times of ease as in times of hardship.

translation: Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord, (like one who is not)? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know? Only those endowed with understanding will remember.
interpretation: The verse sets the believer who devotes his nights to worship against the heedless disbeliever, and shows that real knowledge is not mere information but a living awareness of God that appears in action. The one who stands and prostrates at night balances fear and hope: he fears the account of the Hereafter and does not rest on his deeds, yet he hopes for God's mercy and does not despair. This balance comes from true knowledge of God, His majesty and His mercy. Those who know in this way cannot be equal to those who do not, because knowledge that leads to humility, devotion and preparation for the afterlife differs from ignorance that leaves a person careless about his end. The closing statement says that only people of sound intellect, those whose reason is not clouded by desire or arrogance, take heed and draw lessons from such comparisons and from God's signs.

translation: Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and God's earth is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to live in constant God-consciousness and promises that righteousness is rewarded both now and in the hereafter. The statement that God's earth is spacious means that when believers are oppressed or blocked from practicing their faith in one place, they are not trapped. They may move elsewhere, such as by emigrating, to preserve their religion rather than yield to persecution. Those who endure hardship, whether in obedience, against sin, or in the trials of exile and persecution, will receive a reward so generous that it is beyond measure or reckoning, which shows that patience is among the most richly rewarded virtues.

translation: Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.
interpretation: The Prophet is told to declare publicly that his mission begins with his own submission: worship is valid only when it is purified of every partner, show, or hidden motive, and directed to God alone. The verse teaches that sincerity (ikhlas) is the foundation of religion, since outward acts without exclusive devotion to God lack worth. By stating that he himself is under this command, the Prophet shows that no one is exempt from it, and that calling others to pure monotheism must be matched by living it first.

translation: And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit [to God].
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 39:12) shows that the Prophet Muhammad was commanded not only to worship God with sincere devotion but also to lead by example in submission. A true guide does not merely instruct others to obey; he is the first to practice what he preaches. Being 'the first of the Muslims' means being foremost in surrender to God's will, in sincerity, and in action, so that his own conduct serves as the standard for his community. It teaches that leadership in faith rests on personal precedence in obedience and humility before God.

translation: Say: Indeed, I fear, if I were to disobey my Lord, the punishment of a mighty Day.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to declare that no one is above accountability before God, not even the messenger himself. By stating that he too would fear the punishment of the Great Day (the Day of Judgment) if he disobeyed his Lord, he shows that his call to worship God alone and to reject associating partners with Him is not driven by personal interest or authority but by sincere reverence and submission. It teaches that true faith combines obedience with fear of God's judgment, and that the truthfulness of a messenger is shown by his holding himself to the same standard he sets for others, which leaves his opponents no excuse to dismiss the message.

translation: Say: 'It is God alone I worship, being sincere to Him in my religion.'
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 39:14) tells the Prophet to declare that his worship is directed to God alone, with no partners and no mixed motives. Sincerity (ikhlas) means that devotion is purified of showing off, of seeking worldly approval, and of any rival object of reverence. The verse also places worship ahead of any claims or pressures from others. Faith is therefore not just an inherited label or a social identity but an inner orientation of the heart, expressed in action, in which God is the sole aim of one's obedience and love.

translation: So worship whatever you wish besides Him. Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the clear loss.
interpretation: The command 'worship what you will besides Him' is not permission but stern warning, a rhetorical challenge that exposes the folly and consequences of idolatry. Those who turn away from God's exclusive worship may follow their whims, but the true bankruptcy is not loss of wealth or worldly status; it is the loss of one's own soul, by being condemned to punishment, and the loss of one's family, either because they are separated from them, with no kin to intercede or share their fate in Paradise, or because they led them astray. On the Day of Judgment, all worldly attachments that were preferred over God dissolve, leaving the polytheist with total and unmistakable ruin that no later gain can repair.

translation: They will have canopies of fire above them, and canopies beneath them. That is what God warns His servants with: 'O My servants, so be mindful of Me.'
interpretation: The verse portrays the punishment of the disbelievers as total enclosure: fire surrounds them from above and from below, so that there is no escape, no shelter, and no protection on any side. The layers beneath them are called 'canopies' because the fire below also covers and engulfs them, just as the fire above does. God describes this scene out of mercy rather than cruelty. It is a warning meant to awaken His servants, and He ends it with a tender address, 'O My servants,' calling them to piety (taqwa), that is, to guard themselves against this fate by obeying Him and avoiding disobedience while they still have the opportunity.

translation: And those who avoid the worship of Taghut and turn in repentance to God – for them is good news. So give good tidings to My servants,
interpretation: The verse teaches that true salvation requires both a rejection and an affirmation: abandoning every false object of devotion, whether idols, tyrants, desires, or Satan's whisperings, and turning back to God with sincere repentance and devotion. Those who do both are promised glad tidings, which come in this life through inner peace and God's guidance, and in the next through His mercy and Paradise. The command to give good news to God's servants shows that His message is one of hope and encouragement for those who sincerely choose Him over every false object of worship.

translation: Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse praises believers who are discerning in what they hear: they weigh every saying, teaching, or counsel and then choose and act upon what is best, most truthful, and most righteous, rather than following blindly, whim, or custom. It means that real guidance comes from combining open-minded listening with sound judgment and a sincere desire for the good. Such people choose the better course, for example forgiveness over retaliation, or the clearest and most beneficial teaching over what is merely familiar. The verse says that this readiness is itself a sign that God has guided them, and that it shows they possess true intellect (ulu al-albab), meaning minds that are purified and able to reach the core of truth, not just the surface of things.

translation: Then is he against whom the word of punishment has been justly decreed (to be saved)? Can you, then, rescue the one who is in the Fire?
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and affirms that guidance rests with God alone. Those who persist in disbelief and arrogance, and thereby deserve the sentence of punishment that God has already decreed, cannot be saved by the Prophet's eagerness or effort. The rhetorical question stresses that his task is only to convey the message; he has no power to turn a hardened heart or to deliver anyone from the consequences of their own choices. It is a reminder that salvation depends on responding to the truth before it is too late, and that those who have sealed their fate by rejecting it are beyond human rescue.

translation: But those who fear their Lord will have lofty chambers, above which are more chambers built, beneath which rivers flow. This is the promise of God; God never breaks His promise.
interpretation: The verse sets the fate of the God-fearing against that of the disbelievers, who are described in the preceding verse as enveloped by layers of fire above and below them. The righteous, who guarded themselves against disobedience out of reverence for their Lord, are given tiered mansions in Paradise, storey upon storey, with rivers running beneath them. This describes a lasting and ever-rising honor, in contrast to the layered torment of the Fire. The phrase 'the promise of God' stresses that this reward is certain and not merely hoped for. Because God never fails to keep His promise, believers can place full trust in the unseen reward and stay patient and upright in this world, knowing their effort will be fulfilled.

translation: Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky and causes it to penetrate the earth as springs, then brings forth with it crops of various colors; then they wither and you see them turn yellow; then He makes them debris. Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse uses the life cycle of vegetation as a lesson about the transience of worldly life. The same water that God sends down and stores in the earth gives rise to fresh, colorful crops, yet they dry, yellow, and crumble into chaff. In the same way, worldly life, with its beauty, youth, and power, flourishes briefly and then declines to nothing. Those with sound intellect take this as a reminder not to be deceived by the world, to recognize God's power and providence in creating and ending life, and to prepare for the lasting afterlife with faith and righteous deeds.

translation: Is he whose breast God has opened to Islam, so that he walks in a light from his Lord, like one who does not? So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of God. Those are in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse contrasts two states of the heart. When God expands a person's heart to receive submission to Him, it becomes open to truth and is guided by a light that comes directly from God, a light that lets the person see right from wrong, accept the revelation with ease, and act on it. Hearing God's remembrance softens such a heart. By contrast, the heart that grows hard when God is mentioned has shut itself off from guidance through its own persistent heedlessness and stubbornness. Instead of being moved by the Qur'an, it becomes more distant from it. The verse warns such people of ruin and declares that their hardness is itself clear proof that they are in plain misguidance, since a heart unmoved by the remembrance of its Creator has lost the very faculty by which truth is recognized.

translation: God has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent in its parts, oft-repeating: the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God. That is God's guidance, by which He guides whom He wills; and whoever God leaves to stray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as the most excellent discourse, harmonious in its message, free of contradiction, and repeating its lessons, stories, promises and warnings so that they sink in. Its effect on the God-fearing is both awe and tenderness: hearing warnings of God's majesty and judgment makes them tremble, and hearing of His mercy and promises calms and softens their hearts, drawing them to the remembrance of God. This balance of reverent fear and hopeful serenity is the mark of true faith, in contrast to hardened hearts that are unmoved. The verse then explains that such receptivity is itself a gift of divine guidance, granted to those who sincerely seek it, while those who persistently turn away are left in their misguidance, and no one else can guide them.

translation: Is, then, he who must shield his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection (like one who is safe)? And it will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn.
interpretation: The verse portrays the humiliating helplessness of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. Their hands are bound, so the face, the noblest part of a person, is the only thing left to ward off the blaze, and it takes the full force of the punishment. This stands in stark contrast to the believer, who is secure and honored. The wrongdoers are told to taste the consequences of their own deeds, which teaches that the punishment is no arbitrary injustice but the exact result of what they chose and accumulated in life. Every action carries a recompense, so a person should consider now which of the two positions they are preparing for.

translation: Those before them also denied, so the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.
interpretation: The verse warns that denying God's messages brings ruin, and that this ruin does not arrive in a way people expect or can guard against. The earlier nations were complacent in their security, strength and worldly confidence, and they assumed that the punishment could only come from a direction they could see and defend. It struck them suddenly, from an unforeseen source, and left them no chance to prepare or escape. The lesson for the present deniers is that their apparent safety is deceptive. Divine justice is not bound by human calculations, and delay in punishment is no proof of immunity, so they should take heed from history and turn back to faith before it is too late.

translation: So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine justice may bring humiliation and disgrace upon those who reject the truth and persist in wrongdoing even in this worldly life, as a warning and a visible consequence of their deeds. Yet this worldly disgrace is only a small foretaste; the real and far heavier reckoning awaits in the Hereafter, which is lasting and severe. The closing phrase, 'if only they knew', indicates that their heedlessness stems from a lack of true awareness of the gravity of the afterlife; had they grasped this reality, they would have turned from their denial and corrected their conduct.

translation: And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, so that they may remember.
interpretation: God has made the Qur'an a book that teaches through parables and illustrations drawn from every area of human experience, including the fates of earlier nations, the order of the natural world, and the realities of the afterlife. The purpose is not to entertain or impress but to turn abstract truths into concrete images that the heart can grasp and keep. By making guidance clear and familiar, the verse implies that people have no excuse for heedlessness. The aim of these examples is tadhakkur, a reawakening of what is already innate in human nature, such as recognition of God, moral awareness, and accountability, so that a person returns to the truth they already know deep down.

translation: An Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, so that they may become mindful of God.
interpretation: The verse stresses that the Qur'an was revealed in clear Arabic so its audience can understand it directly, and that it is free of any contradiction, distortion, or deviation in its wording, its message, and its rulings. Because it is straight and consistent, it leaves people no excuse for confusion or doubt. Its purpose is to awaken God-consciousness (taqwa), leading people to guard themselves against disobedience and to live with awareness of accountability before God.

translation: God sets forth a parable: a man owned by several partners who quarrel with one another, and a man belonging wholly to one master. Are the two equal in comparison? Praise be to God! But most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse illustrates the difference between the polytheist and the monotheist. The polytheist is like a slave shared among quarrelsome masters, each pulling him in a different direction and demanding his service, so he is torn, anxious and never at rest, unable to satisfy them all. The monotheist is like a slave who belongs to a single master; he knows what is required of him, serves one lord, and enjoys peace, clarity and security. The two cannot be equal, so worshipping many gods leads to confusion and distress while worshipping the One God brings inner unity and tranquility. The exclamation 'Praise be to God' affirms that all praise and the clear proof belong to Him alone, and the closing remark notes that most people, through ignorance, fail to grasp this obvious truth and so persist in associating partners with God.

translation: Indeed, you [O Muhammad] will die, and indeed, they will die.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Az-Zumar 39:30) reminds everyone, including the Prophet himself, that death is a certain fate for all human beings. No one is exempt, not even the best of creation. It levels all people before the reality of mortality and directs them to the Hereafter, where they will stand before God and be held to account for their disputes and deeds. Therefore, a person should not place their hope in worldly life or in any mortal, but should prepare for the meeting with their Lord with faith and righteous action.

translation: Then, on the Day of Resurrection, you will dispute with one another before your Lord.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the reminder that every soul will taste death (Q 39:30), teaches that death is not the end of human affairs but a passage to accountability. Differences, grievances and mutual accusations that were left unresolved in this world, such as those between believers and disbelievers, oppressors and oppressed, leaders and followers, will be brought before God, the only Judge whose verdict is perfectly just. The verse warns that no wrong will be forgotten or escape settlement there. It urges people to act justly, to make amends and seek forgiveness now, and it consoles the wronged that their cause will be heard and rightly decided.

translation: Who, then, is more unjust than one who invents lies about God and denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest form of wrongdoing is a double offense: ascribing falsehood to God, such as attributing partners or children to Him or claiming to speak for Him without warrant, and then rejecting the truth, namely the revelation and the Prophet's message, at the very moment it reaches him. Such a person has corrupted both belief and response to guidance, since he fabricates falsehood and spurns truth when it is clear. The closing rhetorical question affirms that justice requires a fitting outcome: Hell is the lodging prepared for those who stubbornly reject, so their punishment is not arbitrary but the natural consequence of their deliberate denial.

translation: And the one who brought the truth and [those who] believed in it - those are the righteous.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 39:33) honors both the bearer of truth and those who confirm it. The first group is the Prophet Muhammad, who brought the message of truth (the Qur'an and tawhid), and the second is the believers who affirm it, accepting and living by it rather than rejecting it. Righteousness (taqwa) is therefore not only delivering the truth but also believing it sincerely and acting on it. Those who stand firmly with truth, in conveying it or in affirming it, earn the name of the God-fearing, who guard themselves against disobedience out of awareness of God. The verse is a contrast with the preceding verse, which condemns those who lie about God and deny the truth when it comes to them.

translation: They will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward of the muhsinin, those who worship God as though they see Him and who excel in sincerity and righteous conduct. Their reward is not limited to a fixed portion but is open-ended: whatever they desire will be theirs in the presence of their Lord, which signifies both the fulfillment of every wish and the honor of nearness to God. Because the verse calls this the reward of those who do good, it teaches that excellence in faith and action is answered with generosity beyond measure. The reward matches the quality of the deed, as the one who strives to give his best in this world is granted the fulfillment of every longing in the next.

translation: So that God may remove from them the worst of what they did, and reward them their recompense according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 39:35) explains the outcome of those who were truthful and affirmed the truth, the righteous mentioned in the preceding verses.
