God's grace towards them is twofold: first, He wipes out and forgives even the worst of their deeds, so that their past sins do not stand against them; second, He does not weigh their reward by the average or the lesser of their deeds, but rewards them by the standard of their best deeds. This shows the vastness of divine generosity: the believer's faults are covered by mercy, while their good works are raised and valued at their highest degree, so that even ordinary good acts are recompensed as though they were of the finest quality.

translation: Is not God sufficient for His servant? Yet they try to frighten you with those besides Him. And whoever God lets go astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet, and every believer after him, that God alone suffices to protect, support, and sustain whoever sincerely serves Him, so there is no reason to fear anyone else. The idolaters tried to intimidate the Prophet with threats from their false gods and from the power of those who worshipped them, but these have no power to harm or benefit. Fear that belongs only to God is misplaced when it is directed at created things, and trust in God frees a person from dread of others. The closing statement explains why some people remain deaf to this truth: when a person persistently chooses falsehood and turns away from guidance, God leaves him to his own course and withholds guidance from him. Once that happens, no one else can set him right, because guidance is ultimately in God's hands.

translation: And whoever God guides, for him there is no one who can lead him astray. Is God not Almighty, the Lord of retribution?
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is ultimately in God's hands: when God grants a person guidance because of their sincerity and openness to the truth, no force, whether human or satanic, can pull them away from it. Believers should therefore rely on God alone and not fear the threats or schemes of those who oppose them, as the surrounding verses mock the idolaters for trying to frighten the Prophet with their false gods. The closing rhetorical question reassures the faithful that God is mighty and will take retribution against wrongdoers and those who persist in denial, so the believers' trust is well placed and the oppressors' power is empty.

translation: And if you were to ask them, 'Who created the heavens and the earth?' they would surely say, 'Allah.' Say: 'Then have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah intended some harm for me, could they remove His harm; or if He intended for me mercy, could they withhold His mercy?' Say: 'Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely those who rely.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the inconsistency of polytheism: the idolaters themselves admit that Allah alone is the Creator of the universe, yet they direct worship and hope toward beings that create nothing. The Prophet is told to challenge them with a simple test of power: if the One who created everything decrees harm or mercy for a person, no idol, saint, or created being can avert the harm or hold back the mercy. Since benefit and harm lie wholly in Allah's hands, worship, supplication, and dependence are due to Him alone. The closing declaration, 'Allah is sufficient for me,' teaches that true reliance (tawakkul) means placing one's full trust in Allah, with a heart free from fear of or hope in anything else, and that this is the path of all those who truly trust in Him.

translation: Say: O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. Then soon you will know.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to answer those who persist in rejecting the message with calm confidence rather than argument or force: let each side carry on according to its own ability and path, for he will remain steadfast in his mission. The verse is a gentle warning that outcomes are not decided by present power or status but by the truth of one's course, and time will reveal who was right, who receives God's help, and who gains the final good end in this world and the next. It teaches that after the message has been conveyed clearly, the believer should persevere in righteous action and leave the verdict to God.

translation: To whom a punishment will come that disgraces him, and upon whom an everlasting punishment will descend.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who persist in denial and opposition to the truth will face a twofold fate: first a humiliating punishment that exposes and shames them, which may occur in this world, as happened to the deniers at Badr, and then a lasting punishment in the Hereafter that never ends. The disgrace shows that arrogance and mockery of the messengers end in dishonor, while the permanent torment shows that the consequences of rejecting God are not temporary. It encourages believers to be steadfast against ridicule, since the outcome belongs to God, and it reminds everyone that the one who mocks the truth will ultimately be the one humiliated.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own soul; and whoever goes astray, only goes astray to its detriment. And you are not a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an is a truthful, purposeful revelation meant for all people, and that guidance or misguidance has consequences that fall entirely on the individual. Whoever accepts the guidance benefits himself, since God has no need of anyone's belief, and whoever rejects it harms only himself. The Prophet's role is limited to conveying the message clearly and faithfully; he is not responsible for compelling hearts to believe or for controlling their choices, so he should neither grieve excessively over those who turn away nor force faith on them. Accountability is personal and rests with each soul before God.

translation: God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died, during their sleep. He then keeps those for which He has decreed death, and sends the others back until a appointed term. Surely in that are signs for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse shows that life, sleep and death are wholly in God's hands and differ only in degree: in sleep He takes hold of a person's soul and releases it again when He wills, while in death He keeps it and does not return it. Every night, then, a person experiences a small foretaste of death and a small resurrection when waking, which should remind him that his waking life is a loan with a fixed term he does not control. Those who reflect will see in this daily cycle the power of God to give life and take it away, His mercy in granting another day, and the reality of the resurrection, and so will turn to Him with gratitude, humility and readiness for the meeting with Him.

translation: Or have they taken intercessors besides God? Say: "What! Even if they possess nothing and have no understanding?"
interpretation: The verse rebukes the idolaters who worship idols, saints, or other beings, claiming these will intercede for them with God. The Prophet is told to challenge them: can intercession come from beings that own no power at all and have no intellect or awareness? Intercession is a right belonging to God alone and is granted only by His permission to whom He wills, as the following verse affirms ("Say: To God belongs all intercession"). Lifeless idols, or any created being acting independently, cannot hold such authority. So relying on them is irrational as well as a form of shirk, and the proper course is to turn directly to God alone in worship and supplication.

translation: Say: To God belongs all intercession. His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse refutes the idea that false deities, idols, or saints hold independent power to intercede with God. Intercession is wholly God's: no one can intercede except by His permission and for those with whom He is pleased, because He alone owns the heavens and the earth and everything in them. Since all authority is His, seeking help from anyone besides Him is futile. The closing reminder that all people will return to Him warns that each will face Him in person, so a person should turn to God alone and prepare for that meeting rather than rely on imagined intermediaries.

translation: And when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink with aversion; but when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice.
interpretation: The verse exposes a telling test of what a person's heart truly loves and trusts. Those who deny the Hereafter feel no accountability before God, so the pure call to His oneness, without any partners or intermediaries, constricts their hearts and irritates them, because it demands exclusive devotion, submission and answerability. When their idols, false deities, or other objects of reverence are named, they feel delight, since these ask nothing of them morally and fit their desires. Their reaction reveals that their attachment is to their own whims and inherited customs rather than to truth. Conversely, the believer's heart finds peace and joy at the remembrance of God alone, so a person's response to hearing God mentioned alone is a measure of the health of their faith.

translation: Say: O Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to turn to God in supplication, invoking Him by names that show His complete authority: He originated the heavens and the earth from nothing, and He knows both what is hidden and what is apparent. Because of this perfect power and knowledge, only He can judge justly between people in their disputes. The verse comforts the believer who faces denial and stubborn disagreement from those who reject the truth: there is no need to settle every dispute in this world, because the final ruling belongs to God, who knows every intention and every hidden fact and will render a verdict free of error or injustice. It calls for patience, reliance on God, and leaving the final judgment to Him.

translation: And if those who have done wrong possessed all that is on the earth, and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from Allah what they had never reckoned.
interpretation: The verse shows how worthless worldly wealth becomes before divine judgment. The wrongdoers, who spent their lives hoarding and chasing possessions as though these could secure them, will on the Day of Resurrection find that even the whole earth doubled could not purchase their release, and they would gladly pay it all to escape the torment. The final clause warns that the reality they meet will exceed every expectation: they had presumed their deeds, their false beliefs, or their reliance on intercessors and on Allah's leniency would somehow protect them, or they had never imagined the severity of the reckoning. They will be confronted with the truth of their deeds and the punishment they had dismissed, so the verse urges people to correct their beliefs and actions now, while repentance still counts, rather than rely on illusions that will collapse when it is too late.

translation: And the evils of what they earned will become manifest to them, and that which they used to mock will encompass them.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the wrongdoers will see their deeds laid bare, with every sin they once committed or concealed exposed for what it truly was, so they can no longer deny or excuse it. The punishment and the reality of the Hereafter, which they used to ridicule and dismiss as empty threats when warned by the messengers, will surround them completely from every side, leaving no escape. Their mockery turns into the very thing that overwhelms them, showing that scorning God's warnings does not cancel their truth but only brings about one's own ruin.

translation: When harm touches a human being, he calls upon Us; then when We grant him a favor from Us, he says, 'I was only given it because of knowledge I have.' Rather, it is a trial, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zumar 39:49) exposes a common human inconsistency: in hardship a person turns sincerely to God, fully aware that only He can relieve him, but once relief and blessings arrive he forgets that they are gifts and attributes them to his own skill, knowledge, or cleverness. This arrogance is a form of ingratitude and self-deception. God corrects this claim by saying that the blessing is not proof of personal merit or of divine favor; it is a fitna, a test of whether the person will respond with gratitude, humility, and obedience or with pride and heedlessness. Most people fail to grasp this, mistaking trial for entitlement, so the verse calls believers to recognize every blessing as coming from God and to use it in thankfulness.

translation: Those before them said it as well, but what they used to earn did not avail them.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 39:50) points out that the arrogant claim of ascribing blessings to one's own knowledge or ability is nothing new: earlier nations said the same when favors came to them after hardship, yet their wealth, power, and accomplishments could not shield them from God's punishment when it came. The lesson is that worldly means and self-reliance offer no real protection against divine decree, and that a person should attribute blessings to God with gratitude and humility rather than to his own cleverness, since pride in one's own earnings leads to the same ruin that overtook earlier peoples.

translation: So the evil consequences of what they earned struck them. And those who have wronged among these [present people] will also be struck by the evil consequences of what they earned, and they cannot escape [Allah's plan].
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment is not arbitrary but the natural and just outcome of people's own deeds. The earlier nations who boasted of their wealth and power, claiming their success was due to their own knowledge, were seized by the consequences of their own wrongdoing. The same law applies to the wrongdoers of the Prophet's own time and to every generation after: no one can outrun or frustrate God's decree, and arrogance and injustice always return upon the one who commits them. It is a warning to take lessons from past peoples and to turn to God in gratitude and repentance, rather than attributing blessings to one's own cleverness.

translation: Do they not know that God extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it? Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth and scarcity are not measures of a person's worth or of God's favor, but come from God's wisdom and will. He gives abundantly to some and sparingly to others as a test and for reasons He knows best. Those who grasp this do not let prosperity make them arrogant, as if their riches came from their own knowledge or skill. They also do not despair in hardship, because provision is in God's hands, not in the hands of people or circumstances. Only people with faith reflect on this and recognize in it a sign of God's power and justice, and so they respond with gratitude in ease and patience in difficulty, relying on Him.

translation: Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, God forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse is an open invitation to hope and repentance. However heavy or numerous a person's sins, including grave ones, despair is never warranted, because God's mercy is greater than any wrongdoing. Despair of God's mercy is itself a harmful state that keeps people from turning back to Him. The verse teaches that forgiveness is available to every sinner who sincerely repents, turns back to God, and abandons the sin, and that God, who is named al-Ghafur and ar-Rahim, welcomes such return. It balances fear of God's judgment with confidence in His compassion, urging believers to move toward Him rather than away from Him in shame.

translation: And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, then you will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse is an urgent call to act while there is still time. Turning to God (inabah) means a sincere return in repentance, leaving sin and heedlessness and re-orienting the heart and conduct toward Him. Submitting (islam) means yielding fully to His commands, outwardly in obedience and inwardly in trust. Both must be done before the punishment arrives, whether in this world or at death and the Hereafter, because once it comes the opportunity is lost: no one will be able to avert it or defend the guilty, and no power or intercessor will help. The lesson is that repentance is valuable only while a person is still free to change, so delay is dangerous and a believer should hurry back to God now.

translation: And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you are not aware.
interpretation: The verse urges people to act promptly on the guidance God has revealed, choosing its most excellent teachings: obeying His commands, avoiding His prohibitions, and preferring the noblest course in every matter, such as pardon over retaliation and the obligatory together with the commendable. Life is uncertain and the end may come without warning, whether through death or a divine punishment in this world or the next. No one knows when it will arrive, so repentance and righteous action must not be put off. Heedlessness is dangerous because the punishment strikes at a moment when people expect it least, when it is too late to amend their ways.

translation: Lest a soul should say: 'Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah, and indeed I was among the mockers.'
interpretation: The verse warns people to turn back to God and follow His guidance before death or the Day of Judgment, when regret will be useless. On that day a person will lament the time and opportunities squandered in neglecting the duties owed to God, His rights, His path, and His revelation. The regret is made worse by the confession of having mocked the truth and those who followed it. The verse teaches that neglect and scorn of faith are not harmless; they bring painful remorse that cannot be undone once the chance to act is gone, so a person should act sincerely and promptly while there is still time.

translation: Or it (the soul) should say: 'If only God had guided me, I would have been among the righteous.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 39:57) shows a person on the Day of Judgment trying to excuse their failure by shifting blame onto God, claiming that lack of divine guidance, not their own choices, kept them from piety. The Qur'an rejects this excuse, since God had already sent clear guidance through revelation and messengers and gave people the will and ability to choose. The verse therefore teaches that humans are accountable for what they do with the guidance they receive, and that wishing for guidance only after death is useless because the time for action in this world has already passed.

translation: Or lest it say, when it sees the punishment, 'If only I had another chance, I would be among those who do good.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 39:58) is the third of three regrets voiced by a soul on the Day of Judgment. Once the punishment is plainly seen, the sinner no longer denies it but begs to return to the world, claiming that a second chance would make him a righteous person. The verse teaches that the time for action is now, in this life. Regret after the unseen becomes visible is of no use, because the test of faith depends on believing before the proof is beyond doubt. Such a wish is also not sincere repentance but a plea made under duress, and the Qur'an elsewhere says that if such people were sent back they would return to what they were forbidden. The verse is therefore a warning to turn to good deeds and repentance while there is still opportunity, rather than putting off reform in the hope of a later chance.

translation: Yes, My signs did come to you, but you denied them, acted arrogantly, and were among the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse is God's reply to a soul on the Day of Judgment that wishes it had been guided or had another chance. God rejects the excuse: guidance was not lacking, because clear signs had already reached it. The soul's failure was not ignorance but a deliberate response of rejection and pride. Denial of the truth began with refusing to accept it, then grew into arrogance, which means looking down on the truth and on those who bring it. That arrogance settled into a lasting disbelief. The verse teaches that people are accountable once clear proof reaches them, and that pride is a main barrier to accepting the truth, so the punishment is a just consequence of their own choices and not a wrong done to them.

translation: And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about God with their faces blackened. Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the arrogant?
interpretation: The blackening of the faces on the Day of Resurrection is the outward sign of inner disgrace, exposing what the liars concealed in this world. Their lie against God, whether by ascribing partners or children to Him or by declaring lawful and unlawful what He has not, was rooted in arrogance: they refused to submit to His guidance and preferred their own claims to His revelation. The verse ends with a rhetorical question, whose answer is certainly yes, to show that Hell is a just and fitting abode for arrogance, since those who exalted themselves above the truth will be brought low.

translation: And God will save those who were mindful of Him by their attainment (of success); no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 39:61) promises that those who guard themselves against God's displeasure through faith and righteous deeds will be delivered from the terror and punishment of the Day of Judgment because of the success they earned through their piety. Their deliverance is not arbitrary but tied to their taqwa, which becomes the means of their triumph. On that Day they will be safe from every harm and from the distress of the Fire, and they will feel no sorrow over the past or fear for the future, enjoying complete security and lasting peace in God's mercy.

translation: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, a Disposer of affairs (Guardian).
interpretation: This verse, Surat az-Zumar 39:62, teaches that nothing exists independently of God: every being, power, and event owes its existence to Him alone, so no created thing can rightfully share in divinity or be worshipped beside Him. Because He originated everything, He also sustains and governs it, and the word 'wakil' conveys that He manages every affair with perfect knowledge and wisdom. The believer is therefore called to rely on God completely, to be at peace with His decree, and to put trust in Him rather than in created means, while still making an effort, since the One who created all things is able to take care of them.

translation: To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. And those who disbelieve in the signs of God—it is they who are the losers.
interpretation: The 'keys' (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth express God's absolute control over all treasures, provisions, and affairs of creation: nothing is opened or withheld, given or taken, except by His will. Since everything rests in His hand, those who reject His signs have cut themselves off from the only source of true provision, guidance, and mercy. Their loss is therefore complete: they forfeit the benefits of this world's blessings as they were meant to be used, and they lose their standing in the Hereafter, having exchanged certain guidance for denial.

translation: Say: Is it other than God that you order me to worship, O you ignorant ones?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 39:64) rebukes the pagans who pressed the Prophet to compromise by worshipping their gods. By calling them ignorant, it shows that turning to anything besides the Creator, Sustainer, and sole Sovereign of all things is irrational, a failure to grasp who is truly worthy of devotion. Worship belongs to God alone, so no social pressure or bargaining can justify it. The question is rhetorical and expresses amazement that anyone would make such a demand. It teaches the believer to hold firmly to pure monotheism and to answer pressure to compromise with clarity and confidence.

translation: And it has already been revealed to you, and to those before you: 'If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely come to nothing, and you will surely be among the losers.'
interpretation: The verse affirms that the rejection of shirk is a universal principle in every divine revelation, binding even upon the prophets, who are the most noble of people. Its purpose is to show how grave associating partners with God is: it nullifies all good works, since deeds are accepted only when grounded in pure monotheism, and it leaves the person at a total loss in the Hereafter. The address to the Prophet is a warning to his community, since if the best of creation is warned in this way, others are even more in need of heeding it. It teaches that sincerity of worship to God alone is the foundation on which the worth of every deed depends.

translation: Rather, worship God alone, and be among the grateful.
interpretation: The verse comes after the warning that associating partners with God nullifies one's deeds (Qur'an 39:65). The word 'rather' (bal) rejects shirk and calls for pure monotheism. Placing 'God' first in the sentence ('Rather, it is God you must worship') restricts worship to Him alone. The command to be among the grateful follows because gratitude is the natural response to God's blessings and is itself an act of worship. Worship is therefore not only ritual obedience but also a conscious acknowledgment of God's favors, shown through devotion, obedience, and right use of His gifts. A believer's relationship with God is meant to rest on exclusive devotion and heartfelt thankfulness.

translation: They did not esteem Allah with the esteem due to Him, while the whole earth will be within His grip on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who worship others besides God, because they have not grasped His true greatness. If they had appreciated His majesty, they would never have set up partners with Him. The images of the whole earth held in His grip and the heavens rolled up in His right hand convey that what people find vast and enduring is, in relation to God's power, small and completely under His control. On the Day of Resurrection the apparent powers of this world will vanish and all sovereignty will be seen to belong to Him alone. Such a God cannot have equals or partners, and the verse ends by declaring His transcendence above every form of shirk. The lesson is that proper knowledge of God's might should lead to exclusive worship, humility, and awareness of accountability before Him.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall dead, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.
interpretation: The verse portrays the absolute sovereignty of God over life and death on the Day of Resurrection. The first blast of the Trumpet brings the extinction of all creation, showing that no being, however exalted, has power of its own apart from God's will, and the exception 'except whom God wills' affirms that only God decides who is spared. The second blast restores everyone to life at once, so that they rise bewildered and watching, awaiting judgment. The lesson is that the One who can end and re-create all beings with a single blast is fully able to resurrect and hold humankind accountable, so people should prepare for that moment with faith and righteous deeds rather than heedlessness.

translation: And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, and the Book will be set in place, and the prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward, and judgment will be passed between them with truth, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the ordinary order of the world gives way to the manifest presence of divine justice. The earth is illuminated not by sun or moon but by God's own light, which signals that every veil is lifted and nothing remains hidden. The record of each person's deeds is laid open, and the prophets and witnesses are called to testify. The prophets bear witness that the message was delivered, and the witnesses testify to how people responded. Because the verdict rests on complete knowledge, clear evidence, and testimony, no one can claim ignorance or unfairness. Each soul receives exactly what it earned, with no good deed ignored and no wrong added unjustly. The verse is meant to instill accountability and trust in God's perfect justice, urging people to live now as those who know they will be called to account.

translation: And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and He is best aware of what they do.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 39:70) affirms perfect divine justice on the Day of Judgment. No soul will be wronged, and no deed will be overlooked or reduced: each person will receive full recompense, whether reward or punishment, exactly matching what they earned. The closing phrase explains why this judgment is flawless. God needs no witnesses, records, or reminders, for His knowledge encompasses every action, intention, and hidden detail of human conduct. This should instill in the believer both hope, since no good deed is lost, and accountability, since nothing can be concealed from God, urging sincerity and righteous conduct in this life.

translation: Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates are opened and its keepers say to them, "Did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?" They will say, "Yes, but the word of punishment has been realized against the disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse shows that Hell's punishment is a matter of justice, not arbitrary harshness. The disbelievers are herded in separate groups, humiliated and without dignity, and the gates open only when they arrive. The keepers' question is not a request for information but a rebuke that makes them face the proof already given: God sent messengers from their own people who spoke their language, recited His signs, and warned them of this very Day. Their answer, 'Yes', is a forced admission that they have no excuse, since the warning reached them. Their further words, 'the word of punishment has been realized', show them acknowledging that their own stubborn rejection, after the truth was made clear, brought the decree of punishment on them. The ruling was fulfilled because of what they chose, not because of any deficiency in the guidance.

translation: It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein forever." How wretched is the abode of the arrogant!
interpretation: The verse shows that arrogance is the root cause of the punishment described. The arrogant refused to submit to God's truth and looked down on His messengers and on other people, so their final dwelling is fitting recompense: those who exalted themselves above the truth are brought low in humiliation. The command to enter 'the gates' suggests that each person is led to the particular gate matching their deeds, and the word 'abiding' signifies that their rejection was a settled disposition of the heart rather than a passing lapse. The verse warns that pride before God and against His guidance is among the gravest spiritual diseases, and that true safety lies in humility and submission.

translation: And those who feared their Lord will be led to Paradise in groups, until, when they arrive at it and its gates are opened, its keepers will say to them: 'Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, to abide eternally.'
interpretation: The verse shows that Paradise is a place of honor and welcome for the God-fearing. Unlike the disbelievers, who are driven roughly to Hell, the righteous are 'led' gently and respectfully, in groups arranged according to their ranks and deeds. The gates are opened for them in advance, a sign of hospitality and eagerness to receive them. The keepers greet them with 'peace' and tell them they are 'good' (tibtum), meaning they have been purified of sins, wrongdoing, and the burdens of the world through faith, piety, and God's forgiveness. Purity is thus the condition for entering Paradise, and the closing words, 'enter it, to abide eternally', declare that their bliss will be everlasting and free of any fear of loss or removal.

translation: And they will say: Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the land, so that we may settle in Paradise wherever we please. How excellent is the reward of those who labor.
interpretation: This verse describes the inhabitants of Paradise as they enter it, acknowledging that their salvation is due to God's grace and His faithfulness to His promise made through the prophets. Their first response is gratitude, not boasting about their deeds. The 'land' they inherit is the realm of Paradise, which God grants to the righteous as an inheritance, and they are free to dwell wherever they wish within it, a sign of complete freedom, security, and contentment. The closing phrase affirms that the effort of faith and righteous action in this world, though small and temporary, is repaid with an excellent, everlasting reward, teaching believers that patient striving for God is never wasted.

translation: And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying their Lord with praise. And judgment will have been passed between them (all creation) in truth, and it will be said: 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse closes the scene of the Day of Judgment in Surat az-Zumar by showing that when God's judgment is complete, the whole of creation recognizes His perfect justice. The angels encircling the Throne are not fearful or idle but fully absorbed in glorifying God, which conveys that all majesty and authority belong to Him alone. The judgment is 'in truth' because no one is wronged: the righteous are rewarded and the wrongdoers are held to account with full fairness. Once the outcome is final, it is not only the believers but all existence that responds with praise, 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds', acknowledging that God's wisdom, mercy, and justice have been vindicated. The verse teaches that the ultimate end of creation is the praise of God, and that believers should anticipate that day by praising Him now and living in awareness of His just reckoning.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Meem.
interpretation: Ha-Meem is one of the disconnected letters (al-muqatta'at) that open several surahs, and its precise meaning is known only to God. The most sound reading treats these letters as a signal of the Qur'an's miraculous nature: the revelation is composed of the very same letters that the Arabs use in their own speech, yet no one can produce anything like it. They also serve to arouse the listener's attention before the message of revelation is delivered, reminding the believer that this Book comes from God, whose knowledge exceeds human grasp, and that some of its depths call for humility and submission rather than speculation.

translation: The revelation of this Book is from God, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes the divine origin and authority of the Qur'an: it is not the product of the Prophet's own mind or of any human source, but a revelation sent down by God. The two attributes chosen here, 'the Almighty' (al-'Azīz) and 'the All-Knowing' (al-'Alīm), are meaningful for the Book's purpose. Because God is Almighty, His word cannot be overpowered, altered, or defeated by those who reject it, and His warnings and promises will certainly come to pass. Because He is All-Knowing, His guidance is perfectly suited to human nature, needs, and circumstances, free from error, ignorance, or contradiction. The believer is thus invited to receive the Qur'an with trust and submission, recognizing it as guidance that combines irresistible power with complete wisdom and knowledge.

translation: Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Owner of abundant bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return.
interpretation: The verse presents God's attributes in a balance of mercy and justice, so that the believer lives between hope and fear. He forgives sins and accepts the repentance of those who turn back, which keeps the door of return open to every sinner. Yet He is also severe in punishing those who persist in rebellion and arrogance, so His mercy must not become a reason for complacency. His vast bounty (al-tawl) means His favors and generosity exceed what anyone deserves, and forgiveness itself is an act of grace, not a debt. Because there is no god but Him, no one else can forgive, punish, or grant favor, and since every soul will return to Him, a person should hasten to repent, obey Him, and prepare for the meeting with Him.

translation: None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve, so let not their moving about freely in the land deceive you.
interpretation: The verse teaches that arguing against God's revelations out of stubbornness and a desire to refute the truth, rather than to seek understanding, is the conduct of those who have rejected faith. The believer, and the Prophet first among them, is told not to be impressed or misled by the apparent prosperity, power, and freedom of movement that such deniers enjoy through trade, travel, and worldly success. Their worldly ease is no sign of God's approval or of the soundness of their position. It is only a temporary respite, after which God's judgment will come, as it did upon earlier nations who denied their messengers.

translation: Before them, the people of Noah denied the truth, and so did the factions after them. Every nation plotted against its messenger to seize him, and they disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth thereby. So I seized them, and how was My punishment!
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that rejection of prophets is an old pattern, not something unique to the Quraysh. Nations before them, from Noah's people to the later factions, did not merely disbelieve but actively schemed to capture, harm or kill their messengers, and they used false arguments, sophistry and baseless disputation in an attempt to defeat the truth. God's response was to seize them with punishment, and the closing rhetorical question, 'how was My punishment?', invites the listener to reflect on how severe and just that punishment was. The lesson is that falsehood, however loudly or cleverly argued, cannot overcome the truth, and those who persist in opposing God's messengers will meet the same end as earlier deniers, while the believers should remain patient and confident in God's support.

translation: And thus has the word of your Lord been justly fulfilled against those who disbelieved: that they are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse (Ghafir 40:6) consoles the Prophet by pointing to the fate of earlier nations who denied their messengers, plotted against them, and argued falsely to refute the truth. Just as the punishment of this world came upon those past peoples, God's decree of punishment in the Hereafter is established against all who persist in disbelief after the truth has come to them. The 'word of your Lord' is His just, prior decree that persistent rejection of the truth leads to the Fire. This outcome is not arbitrary but the consequence of their own choice to reject guidance, so the disbelievers of every age are fittingly described as 'companions of the Fire,' meaning those who are inseparably bound to it as the natural result of their deeds.

translation: Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise, believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for those who believe: 'Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Hellfire.'
interpretation: The verse shows the exalted rank of the angels closest to God, whose worship never makes them neglect the believers on earth. Their glorification and faith are bound together with sincere care for humanity, because faith creates a bond among all who believe, even across the divide between the unseen and the seen world. Their prayer begins by acknowledging God's all-encompassing mercy and knowledge, which is the proper way to make supplication: they appeal to His mercy as the grounds for forgiveness and to His knowledge as the guarantee that He knows who truly repents. They ask forgiveness only for those who combine repentance with following God's path, teaching that forgiveness is tied to turning back to God and living by His guidance. The verse also comforts believers, assuring them that they are remembered in the prayers of the noblest of creation, and it encourages them to pray for one another as the angels do.

translation: Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, along with the righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their offspring. Indeed, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse is part of the supplication of the angels who bear the Throne and those around it, who seek forgiveness for the believers. After asking God to protect the repentant from Hellfire, they pray that He grant them eternal Gardens, fulfilling His promise. Their request extends to the righteous relatives of the believers, so that families may be reunited in Paradise and their joy completed. The inclusion of relatives is conditioned on their own righteousness (faith and good deeds), showing that kinship alone does not earn salvation, though God may elevate the rank of the lesser to join their kin out of His generosity. The closing description, 'the Almighty, the All-Wise,' affirms that God's promise cannot be thwarted and that He grants and distributes reward with perfect wisdom, placing each person where they deserve.

translation: And protect them from evil deeds and their consequences. Whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have indeed shown them mercy. And that is the supreme triumph.
interpretation: The angels who bear the Throne pray for the believers, asking that God shield them from the consequences of their sins, especially on the Day of Judgment. The verse teaches that salvation from punishment is not earned by deeds alone but is a sign of God's mercy: whoever is spared the evil results of their wrongdoing has received divine compassion. This deliverance is the greatest success, greater than any worldly gain, because it secures eternal safety and nearness to God. It also teaches believers to rely on God's mercy while striving to avoid sin.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to: 'God's hatred of you was greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were invited to faith and you refused.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers will be consumed with self-loathing as they face the consequences of their choices, blaming and despising themselves. They will then be told that God's abhorrence of their disbelief, which they persisted in after being repeatedly called to faith through the messengers and signs, was far greater than the anger they now feel toward themselves. Their regret comes too late. The verse stresses that the fault lies in their own deliberate rejection of a sincere invitation, not in any lack of guidance or any injustice from God.

translation: They will say: "Our Lord, You have made us die twice and given us life twice, and now we acknowledge our sins. So is there any way out?"
interpretation: This verse depicts the disbelievers in the Hereafter, humbled and admitting their guilt. Their reference to two deaths and two lives points to the stages of existence: they were lifeless before being created, then given life in this world, then made to die, and then resurrected on the Day of Judgment. By invoking these stages they affirm God's power to give life and death, and so to resurrect, which they denied in the world. Their confession comes too late, since belief in the Hereafter, when the truth is plainly seen, no longer benefits. Their question, 'Is there any way out?', expresses desperation and a faint hope of escaping punishment. The verse is a warning to acknowledge the truth, repent, and turn to God while there is still time in this life, because regret in the Hereafter will not change the outcome.

translation: That is because, when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but if partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to God, the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse explains why the disbelievers are suffering in the Hellfire, where they will beg to be brought out. Their punishment is justified by their own disposition: they rejected the pure call to the oneness of God and were repelled by it, yet they eagerly accepted belief in idols and false deities when others were joined with Him. This shows that their disbelief was not rooted in a lack of evidence but in stubborn attachment to polytheism and rejection of exclusive devotion to God. The verse closes by affirming that final judgment belongs only to God, the Exalted above all and Greater than all, so His sentence is just, no one can overturn it, and none of the false deities they worshipped can intercede or alter it.

translation: It is He who shows you His signs and sends down provision for you from the sky. But none takes heed except one who turns to God in repentance.
interpretation: The verse points to God's signs in creation, such as the order of the heavens, the rain and the sustenance that grows from it, as evidence of His power, mercy and oneness. These signs are visible to everyone, yet only the person who returns to God with a humble and attentive heart actually reflects on them and draws a lesson from them. Those who are heedless or stubborn see the same signs but remain unmoved. Receiving guidance depends on inner openness and the willingness to turn back to God, not merely on the presence of evidence.

translation: So call upon Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, even if the disbelievers dislike it.
interpretation: This verse (Ghafir 40:14) commands the believer to direct all supplication and worship to God alone, purifying the intention and practice of faith from any partner, show, or seeking of people's approval. Calling upon God here includes both asking Him and worshipping Him, and sincerity (ikhlas) means that the heart's turning is exclusively for Him. The closing phrase teaches that this devotion must not be compromised or diluted to win the approval of those who reject the truth: even if the disbelievers resent and oppose the believers' pure monotheism, the believer must remain steadfast, since God's pleasure outweighs the displeasure of any creature.

translation: He is the Exalter of ranks, the Owner of the Throne. He sends the Spirit [revelation] by His command upon whomever He wills among His servants, so that he may warn of the Day of Meeting.
interpretation: God, whose majesty is far above all creation and who rules over the Throne, chooses certain servants as prophets and sends them revelation, which gives life to hearts just as the soul gives life to bodies. The purpose of this selection is not honor for its own sake but warning: the messenger is to alert people to the Day of Meeting, when all creatures will meet their Lord and each other and will be held accountable for their deeds. The verse teaches that prophethood is a divine gift granted by God's will alone, and that its central message is to prepare people for that encounter with God.

translation: The Day when they will come forth, nothing about them being hidden from God. To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To God, the One, the Irresistible.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, people will emerge from their graves exposed and fully visible, with no building, mountain, or veil to conceal them, and none of their deeds, secrets, or intentions will be hidden from God, whose knowledge encompasses everything. On that Day, all worldly pretensions of kingship and power will vanish. The question 'To whom belongs the dominion today?' is answered by God Himself: it belongs to Him alone, the One without partner, the Subduer to whom all creation is subject. The verse teaches that absolute sovereignty has always belonged to God, but on that Day it becomes undeniably manifest, leaving every tyrant and arrogant person stripped of illusions, and calling the believer to humility, accountability, and sincere awareness of God's constant watchfulness in this life.

translation: This Day every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned. There is no injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Day of Judgment is the Day of perfect justice, when every person receives exactly what their own deeds merit, whether good or evil, with nothing added to their burden and nothing of their good taken away. Because Allah's knowledge encompasses everything, He needs no lengthy investigation, so His reckoning of all creation is swift. The verse therefore calls believers to self-accountability in this life, since every choice, however small, is being recorded and will be repaid in full, and it reassures the oppressed that wrongs unrighted in this world will be set right.

translation: Warn them of the Day of the Impending (the Approaching One), when hearts will be at the throats, choking with suppressed anguish. The wrongdoers will have no close friend and no intercessor who would be obeyed.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to warn people about the Day of Judgment, which is called 'al-Azifah' because it is ever drawing near and is certain to arrive. On that day fear will be so overwhelming that hearts seem to rise into the throats, and people will be filled with grief that they can only swallow and cannot voice or relieve. In that moment the wrongdoers, those who associated partners with God and oppressed others, will find no loyal ally to defend them and no intercessor whose word is accepted, since intercession belongs to God alone and is granted only by His permission to those He approves. The meaning is a call to repent and prepare for the Hereafter now, because worldly ties, status, and false deities will be of no benefit then.

translation: He knows the stealthy glance of the eyes and whatever the hearts conceal.
interpretation: This verse (Ghafir 40:19) stresses that God's knowledge reaches even the subtlest and most hidden human acts. The 'treachery of the eyes' is a furtive look, such as a glance at what is forbidden or a secret signal that conveys a hidden meaning, which no other person would notice. 'What the breasts conceal' refers to the inner intentions, secret thoughts and feelings that a person never voices. By pairing an outward, almost imperceptible act with a purely inward one, the verse shows that nothing in a person's visible conduct or hidden heart escapes God. The lesson is that the believer should cultivate sincerity and moral vigilance, because he will be held to account before an All-Knowing Judge who judges with perfect justice, and the wrongdoer should not feel secure in concealment.

translation: And Allah judges with truth, while those whom they invoke besides Him judge nothing. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse affirms that only God has real authority to decide matters, because His judgment rests on perfect knowledge, justice, and power. Whatever people worship or call upon besides Him, whether idols, false deities, or created beings, has no ability to judge, decide, or bring about any outcome, so devotion to them is futile. God's judgment is never mistaken or unjust because He hears every word and sees every deed, so nothing is hidden from Him. The believer is thus invited to trust God's decree, to seek justice from Him alone, and to be mindful that every action is witnessed and will be weighed with truth.

translation: Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those who were before them? They were stronger than them in power and in the traces they left upon the earth, yet God seized them for their sins, and they had no protector against God.
interpretation: The verse calls the deniers of the message to learn from history rather than rely on their own strength or worldly standing. Earlier nations surpassed them in might, buildings, and lasting monuments, yet none of that shielded them once they persisted in sin and rejected their messengers. Their ruin shows that worldly power and legacy give no immunity from divine justice, and that destruction comes as a consequence of wrongdoing, not from weakness. Reflecting on the ruins and fates of past peoples should therefore produce humility, repentance, and acceptance of the truth before the same fate overtakes those who repeat their errors.

translation: That was because their messengers kept coming to them with clear proofs, yet they disbelieved, so God seized them. Indeed, He is Strong, severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse explains that the destruction of earlier nations was not arbitrary but a just consequence of their own choice. God did not punish them without warning: He sent messengers with clear, undeniable evidence, and they persisted in rejecting the truth despite that clarity. Their punishment came only after the proof had been established against them. The closing description of God as Strong and severe in punishment is a warning that no power, status, or numbers can shield a people from His seizing once they knowingly reject His guidance, and it urges the present audience to heed the messengers rather than repeat the errors of those before them.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: God affirms that Moses was not sent empty-handed or on his own initiative, but was commissioned with undeniable miracles (such as the staff and the shining hand) and with clear, compelling proof that left no room for legitimate doubt. The verse shows that true prophethood is always supported by evidence from God, so that those who reject the message, like Pharaoh and his court, do so out of arrogance and not for lack of proof. It also consoles the Prophet Muhammad, reminding him that earlier messengers came with clear proofs and were still denied, so he should be steadfast.

translation: To Pharaoh, Haman and Korah; but they said, "A lying sorcerer." (Qur'an 40:24)
interpretation: The verse shows that Moses was sent with clear signs to the three pillars of tyranny: political power (Pharaoh), state administration and influence (Haman), and wealth (Qarun). Faced with undeniable proofs, these arrogant elites could not answer with reason, so they resorted to slander, branding the messenger a 'lying sorcerer' to discredit him and turn people away from his message. It teaches that those who are entrenched in worldly power, authority and riches are often the first to reject the truth out of pride and fear of losing their status, and that accusing prophets and reformers with false labels is a common tactic of the arrogant when they have no real argument. It also consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that the denial he faced from the Quraysh leaders was the same as that faced by earlier messengers.

translation: So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, "Kill the sons of those who believed with him and spare their women." But the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in vain (in error).
interpretation: The verse shows how tyranny responds to clear truth with violence rather than reason. Pharaoh and his circle, having been shown Moses's proofs, could not refute them, so they turned to a renewed campaign of oppression: killing the male children of the believers to weaken and humiliate the community and sparing the women for servitude. The closing statement is a divine assurance that such schemes are doomed. Plotting against God's message is lost effort that goes astray and cannot achieve its aim, because God's will prevails over the cunning of those who reject the truth. The lesson for believers is that persecution is a sign of the opponents' weakness and that patience and trust in God will be vindicated.

translation: And Pharaoh said: 'Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land.'
interpretation: This verse shows the tyrant's logic when confronted with a truth he cannot refute. Pharaoh, unable to answer Moses's clear signs with argument, resorts to threatening violence while mocking Moses's reliance on God, as if he does not fear any divine consequence. He also inverts right and wrong: he disguises his fear of losing power as concern for the people's religion and public order, accusing the prophet of bringing 'corruption' when it is Pharaoh himself who is the corrupter. The verse thus illustrates how oppressive rulers justify suppressing reformers by claiming to protect the community's faith and stability, when they are truly protecting their own authority.

translation: And Moses said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Account."
interpretation: Moses answers Pharaoh's threat to kill him by turning to God rather than to any human power. He says that what he fears is the arrogant disposition itself: the pride that refuses to accept truth and a higher authority. The root of such tyranny is disbelief in the Day of Reckoning. A person who does not expect to be held accountable feels free to oppress and kill. By calling God 'my Lord and your Lord', Moses reminds his opponents that the same Lord who protects him also holds them accountable. The verse teaches believers to seek God's protection against oppressors, relying on Him instead of fearing the threats of the powerful, and it presents belief in the Hereafter as the true restraint on injustice.

translation: A believing man from among Pharaoh's people, who concealed his faith, said: "Would you kill a man merely because he says, 'My Lord is God,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? If he is a liar, his lie will fall upon him; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed, God does not guide one who is a transgressor and a habitual liar."
interpretation: The verse shows the wisdom of the concealed believer in Pharaoh's court, who defends Moses with calm, fair argument instead of confrontation. He first exposes the injustice of killing someone only for affirming that God is his Lord, especially when clear signs have been shown. He then reasons that Moses is either a liar or truthful. If he is lying, the consequences rest on him alone, so there is no need to kill him. If he is truthful, the warnings he brings may strike them, so they would be foolish to risk harming him. He closes by noting that God does not guide the transgressor and compulsive liar, which implies that Moses, given such clear proofs and divine support, is not such a person, and that Pharaoh's oppression and falsehood may be what leaves him unguided. The verse teaches the value of courageous, tactful speech for truth and justice, even from someone in a position of weakness or concealment.

translation: O my people, yours is the dominion today, being prevalent in the land. But who will help us against the punishment of God if it comes to us? Pharaoh said: I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct.
interpretation: The verse sets a believing man of Pharaoh's household against Pharaoh himself. The believer warns that worldly power and security are temporary and give no protection once God's punishment comes, so no earthly authority can defend anyone from divine judgment. Pharaoh answers with the typical arrogance of a tyrant. He claims that his own opinion is the only correct one, that he alone has the right guidance, and that he does not need counsel from anyone else. His claim to be guiding people to 'the path of right conduct' is deceptive. It shows how despotic rulers present their own desires and self-interest as wisdom and public good, and so close their ears to sincere advice and to the warnings of revelation.

translation: And the one who believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you the like of the day of the factions."
interpretation: This is the believer from Pharaoh's household, who had concealed his faith and now speaks openly to his people to avert their destruction. He does not threaten them from a position of hostility but warns out of genuine concern, addressing them tenderly as 'my people.' By invoking 'the day of the factions,' meaning the fate that befell earlier communities such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud, who banded together against their prophets and were annihilated, he teaches that persistent denial and collective opposition to God's messengers bring divine punishment. The verse shows that sincere advice to those in error is rooted in compassion, and that history's examples of ruined nations should serve as a warning against repeating their rebellion.

translation: Like the fate of the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not intend any injustice for His servants.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the punishment that befell the deniers was not arbitrary but the consistent outcome of a divine law: when nations reject the message and persist in wrongdoing after clear warnings, ruin follows, just as it did for earlier peoples. Their destruction was the consequence of their own choices and sins, not an act of oppression by God, who is perfectly just and wills no wrong for His creatures. It is thus both a warning to later generations to learn from history and a reassurance that divine judgment is always rooted in justice.

translation: And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling (the Day of Summoning).
interpretation: This verse (Ghafir 40:32) is the warning of the believing man from Pharaoh's household, who urges his people to heed the message of Moses. The 'Day of Mutual Calling' is the Day of Judgment, when people will cry out to one another in distress and regret: the inhabitants of Paradise and Hell will call to each other, the wrongdoers will cry out for help and wail 'woe to us', and the angels will call people to their reckoning and their records. The believer's point is that this is a day on which no one can escape or help another, so denying the truth and persisting in disbelief and tyranny leads to a terrifying outcome. His concern is a sincere, compassionate one: he addresses them as 'my people' and fears for them, which teaches that the caller to God should be motivated by genuine care for others' ultimate fate, reminding them to prepare for accountability before it is too late.

translation: The Day you turn back, fleeing, you will have no protector from God. And whoever God leaves to go astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse describes the terror of the Day of Judgment, when people will flee in panic and discover that no power, ally, or means of escape can shield them from God's decree; the protection they relied on in this world, such as wealth, status, or false deities, will vanish. It then affirms that guidance rests with God alone: those who persistently reject truth and choose arrogance and wrongdoing are left by God in their misguidance, and once that happens no one else can guide them. The lesson is to seek guidance and refuge in God now, while the opportunity remains, rather than depend on anything else.

translation: And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, but you continued in doubt about what he brought you, until when he died you said, 'Never will God send a messenger after him.' Thus does God leave astray one who is a transgressor and a doubter.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a pattern of stubborn disbelief across generations: the people of Egypt rejected the clear signs of the Prophet Joseph while he lived, staying in doubt about his message. Once he died, they did not repent but turned their disbelief into a rationalization, claiming that God would never send another messenger, which let them dismiss any future prophet in advance. The Qur'an shows that their denial was not a lack of evidence but a flaw in their hearts: they were wasteful in transgression (musrif) and habitually doubting (murtab). Guidance is withheld from those who persist in excess and cultivate suspicion toward clear proofs, so God lets them go astray as a consequence of their own choices. The lesson is that a person who rejects truth out of arrogance and doubt will keep finding excuses to reject it, whoever brings it and whenever it comes.

translation: Those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority having come to them—greatly hateful is that in the sight of God and in the sight of those who believe. Thus does God seal up every heart that is arrogant and tyrannical.
interpretation: The verse teaches that arguing against divine revelation is blameworthy when it is driven by pride and not by evidence. Honest questioning that seeks truth is not condemned. What is condemned is obstinate disputation that rests on no proof from reason or scripture and is meant only to defeat the truth. Such behavior earns the strong disapproval of God and of the believers. The sealing of the heart is the consequence of persistent arrogance. When a person keeps rejecting the truth out of haughtiness and oppression of others, their heart gradually hardens and loses the ability to recognize guidance. This is a just result of their own choices, not an arbitrary act. The verse therefore warns that arrogance is the root of rejection and that humility before the truth is the way to keep the heart open to guidance.

translation: And Pharaoh said: 'O Haman, build for me a lofty tower so that I may reach the ways,
interpretation: Pharaoh's order to Haman expresses his arrogant denial of God and his mockery of Moses' message. By demanding a towering structure to reach 'the ways' of the heavens, he pretends that God's existence can be settled by physical, worldly means, as though the Lord of the heavens were a being one could climb to and inspect. The verse shows how tyranny and pride blind a person to the obvious signs of God, reducing the unseen to the measurable and trusting political power and engineering over revelation. Its deeper lesson is that human might and cleverness cannot reach or challenge the Creator, and that those who rely on them in defiance of truth are heading toward ruin.

translation: The means of reaching the heavens, so that I may look upon the God of Moses; and indeed I think he is a liar. And thus the evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the path. And the scheming of Pharaoh led only to ruin.
interpretation: Pharaoh's demand that Haman build him a tower shows how arrogance and stubborn denial blind a person to clear truth. He treats God's existence as a physical question that a tall building could settle, and he slanders Moses as a liar to shield his own authority. The verse teaches that when someone persists in wrongdoing, God lets him see his evil as good, and this self-deception closes the way to guidance. Every plot against God's message is bound to fail and bring about the plotter's own destruction, however powerful he appears.

translation: And the one who believed said, "O my people, follow me, and I will guide you to the way of right conduct."
interpretation: This verse (Ghafir 40:38) records the call of the believing man from Pharaoh's household, who had concealed his faith and now publicly urged his people to leave Pharaoh's path of arrogance and disbelief. By saying 'follow me,' he invites them to heed the sincere counsel of someone who seeks their welfare, in contrast to Pharaoh, who had claimed that he was guiding them only to the 'path of right guidance' while leading them to ruin. The believer's words show that true guidance (rashad) is found in submission to God and the message of Moses, not in obedience to tyrants. It also teaches that a believer should speak the truth with compassion, addressing people as 'my people' and presenting guidance as a benefit to them, not a personal gain.

translation: O my people, this worldly life is only a fleeting enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanent settlement.
interpretation: The believing man in Pharaoh's household urges his people to see the world in its true proportion. Life here is temporary provision, like a traveler's supplies, which is enjoyed for a while and then ends, so it should not be the ultimate goal or a reason to rebel against God. The Hereafter is the only home of lasting stability, where there is no moving on, decline or death. A wise person therefore treats this world as a path to the next, spending its brief span on faith and righteous deeds that will determine where he settles forever.

translation: Whoever does an evil deed will be repaid with only its equivalent, but whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, where they will be provided for without measure.
interpretation: The verse sets out a principle of divine justice and generosity. Wrongdoing is answered strictly in proportion, with no added punishment, which shows God's fairness. Good deeds are treated differently. They are not rewarded by strict measure but with limitless bounty, and God's favor far exceeds what the believer earned. The reward depends on two conditions: righteous action and faith. Gender makes no difference, since men and women stand equal before God and are judged by their faith and deeds alone. The phrase 'without measure' tells believers that Paradise brings unending provision beyond reckoning or imagination. This should encourage people to turn away from sin, to do good, and to hope for God's mercy.

translation: And O my people, how is it that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?
interpretation: The believer of Pharaoh's household voices his astonishment at the contradiction between the two invitations. He summons them to the path of safety, which is faith in God alone and obedience to His messenger, and the reward and deliverance that follow. They in turn summon him to shirk and to following Pharaoh's falsehood, which ends in Hellfire. His rhetorical question exposes the unreasonableness of their response: a sincere advisor offers them rescue and receives nothing in return but pressure to join them in the way of destruction. The verse teaches that true guidance leads to deliverance in this life and the next, while the call to disbelief and wrongdoing, however attractive or powerful its advocates, leads to ruin.

translation: You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Almighty, the Perpetually Forgiving.
interpretation: The believing man of Pharaoh's household contrasts the two invitations. His people summon him to deny God and worship partners for which there is no knowledge or proof, so their call rests only on blind imitation and desire. His own call is to God, who is Almighty (al-'Aziz), so nothing can overcome Him, and who is Perpetually Forgiving (al-Ghaffar), so He pardons those who return to Him. The verse teaches that true faith rests on knowledge and evidence rather than on inherited custom, and that the one who calls to God offers both awe of His power and hope in His mercy, while the call to idols offers neither certainty nor benefit.

translation: Without doubt, that to which you call me has no claim to be invoked, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter; and indeed our return is to God, and indeed the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: This is the believer of Pharaoh's household speaking to his people (Surah Ghafir). He tells them that the idols and false deities they urge him to worship have no real power to answer anyone's call: they cannot benefit or harm in this life, and on the Day of Resurrection they will disown their worshippers and have no authority or intercession. Since every soul must return to God alone, only He deserves worship. Those who exceed all bounds, by associating partners with God, tyrannizing, and shedding blood, will be the inhabitants of Hell. The verse calls people to recognize that false gods are powerless, to prepare for the certain return to God, and to avoid the transgression that leads to the Fire.

translation: So you will remember what I am telling you, and I entrust my affair to God. Indeed, God is All-Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: These words are the believer of Pharaoh's household's final statement after warning his people. He knows that they now dismiss his counsel, but a day will come, whether in this world through punishment or in the Hereafter, when they will recall his warning and regret ignoring it. Having delivered the truth, he does not rely on his own status, cleverness, or any human protection against their threats; he places the outcome entirely in God's hands. This is true tawakkul: doing one's duty to advise sincerely, then leaving the results to God. His closing confidence that God sees all His servants means that God knows who is sincere and who is arrogant, and will protect the righteous and hold the wrongdoers to account. The verse thus teaches that a believer should speak truth without fear and rely on God alone, certain that nothing escapes His sight.

translation: So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and the worst of punishment befell the people of Pharaoh.
interpretation: The verse shows that Allah safeguards the believer who trusts in Him and stands for truth, even when he is alone against a tyrannical power. The schemes of the oppressors, however strong they appear, cannot harm those whom Allah protects, and their own plotting rebounds on them. Pharaoh's people, who intended harm to the believing man from among them, were themselves overtaken by a terrible punishment, which teaches that deliverance rests with Allah and that evil plots ultimately ruin their authors.

translation: The Fire: they are exposed to it morning and evening. And on the Day the Hour is established [it will be said], "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment."
interpretation: The verse points to two stages of punishment for Pharaoh's people. The first begins at death and lasts through the intermediate life of the grave (barzakh). In it their souls are shown their place in the Fire each morning and evening, a foretaste that shows them where they are headed and keeps the dread of it before them. The second stage begins on the Day of Resurrection, when they are cast into the Fire itself and suffer its worst torment. This shows that the consequences of tyranny and rejecting God's message start immediately after death, and that the final judgment will bring a greater and more complete punishment for those who persist in arrogance and oppression.

translation: And [mention] when they will dispute with one another in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, we were following you, so will you relieve us of a share of the Fire?" (Qur'an 40:47)
interpretation: The verse shows that blind imitation of powerful and arrogant leaders offers no protection on the Day of Judgment. In the world, the weak surrendered their reason and conscience to the arrogant, following their falsehood out of fear, convenience, or admiration. In the Fire, each person bears individual responsibility, so the followers' plea for relief from even a portion of the punishment is futile. The leaders cannot help them, as the next verse says: they too are in it, and God has judged between His servants. The lesson is that people must examine the truth for themselves and must not hand their faith and moral choices over to those who lead them astray, because excuses such as 'we were only following' will not be accepted.

translation: Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed, all of us are in it (the Fire). Indeed, God has already judged between His servants."
interpretation: This verse shows the arrogant leaders in Hell answering their former followers, who had asked them to lighten the punishment. The leaders disclaim any power to help, saying that they and their followers share the same fate, since all of them are suffering in the Fire. Their reply to the plea for help acknowledges that God's judgment is final and just, and that no one can alter or intercede against it once it has been issued. Arrogance and the blind following of arrogant leaders in this world bring no benefit in the next, and each person is accountable for his own choices before God's decree.

translation: And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us one day of the punishment."
interpretation: The verse portrays the despair of the inhabitants of Hell, who no longer dare to address God directly and so appeal to the angelic guardians as intermediaries. They ask only for one day of relief, not for release, which shows how severe their suffering is and how far their hopes have shrunk. Their wording, 'your Lord' instead of 'our Lord', also reveals their recognition of their own distance from God because of their denial in worldly life. The verse warns that the time for repentance and effective supplication is in this life, and that after death, pleas for mercy will not be answered.

translation: They (the keepers of Hell) will say: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" They will say: "Yes, indeed." They will say: "Then supplicate yourselves." But the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in futility (misguidance).
interpretation: This verse shows that God's justice is complete: no one is punished without clear warning. The guardians of Hell remind the condemned that messengers had brought unmistakable evidence, and the condemned have no defense, so they admit it.
