This admission shows that their disbelief was a willful rejection of truth rather than ignorance. The guardians then refuse to intercede for them, telling them to make their own supplication, which is a sorrowful rebuke, since the angels know that it will be useless. The final statement says that the plea of disbelievers on that Day is wasted and misdirected: when the time for repentance has passed and they stand without faith, their prayers cannot reach acceptance. The verse warns that the opportunity to respond to guidance exists in this life, and that after death regret and calling out bring no benefit.

translation: Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe, in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses will stand.
interpretation: God's promise of support is a firm law that unfolds in ways beyond immediate appearances. In this world, victory comes through vindication of truth, the survival of the message, the refutation of falsehood, and often the downfall of the oppressors, even if individual believers are harmed or killed along the way, since their cause prevails and their reputation endures. On the Day of Judgment, when angels and prophets stand as witnesses, the support becomes complete and open: the believers are vindicated, honored, and rewarded, while the wrongdoers' excuses are of no benefit. The verse therefore consoles the faithful that apparent worldly weakness does not mean abandonment, and that true and final triumph is guaranteed to those who hold to faith and steadfastness.

translation: The Day when their excuses will not benefit the wrongdoers; for them will be the curse, and for them the evil abode.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, those who persisted in injustice, whether by associating partners with God, oppressing others, or rejecting the truth, will find that no plea or justification can rescue them. Excuses work in worldly life, where truth can be obscured, but before God, who knows all that is hidden, they carry no weight, and the wrongdoers' own limbs and deeds will testify against them. Their punishment is twofold: banishment from God's mercy, which is the curse, and the wretched final home of the Fire, which is the evil abode. The verse warns that the time to repent and make amends is now, before it is too late to do so.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the guidance, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture.
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet Muhammad and his audience that guidance is a divine gift and not a human achievement. Moses was given the guidance, meaning the revelation, the law, and the signs that showed the way to truth, and this guidance did not remain confined to him. It passed to his people as an inheritance in the Scripture, the Torah, which they received, preserved, and carried from generation to generation. The verse stresses that possessing revealed knowledge is a trust and a responsibility: those who inherit the Book are bound to act on it, and it should serve as a source of guidance and reminder for people of understanding. The previous communities were given the same kind of divine guidance that the Qur'an now confirms, so the Prophet is not bringing something unprecedented, and he should be patient as Moses was in conveying the message despite opposition.

translation: As guidance and a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 40:54) describes the scriptures given to Moses as a source of guidance and remembrance. It teaches that revelation benefits those who use their intellect sincerely: people of sound reason, not mere cleverness, reflect on divine signs, recognize the truth, and let it direct their conduct. Guidance shows the right path, while remembrance keeps it alive in the heart and guards against forgetfulness and heedlessness. In this way, true intelligence is measured by a person's readiness to accept and act on God's guidance.

translation: So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And ask forgiveness for your sin, and exalt Allah with praise of your Lord in the evening and in the morning.
interpretation: The verse calls the believer, first addressed in the person of the Prophet, to steadfast patience in the face of hostility and delay, because God's promise of victory for the truthful and of reckoning for the deniers is certain and will be fulfilled in its appointed time. Patience is then joined with two inner and devotional supports: seeking forgiveness, which acknowledges human shortcomings and keeps the heart humble and purified even in the midst of a righteous struggle, and constant glorification of God with praise at the beginning and end of the day. Together these practices anchor the soul in trust in God, so that endurance does not harden into despair or pride, and the believer remains connected to God while waiting for His promise to come true.

translation: Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority having come to them—there is nothing in their breasts but pride, which they will never attain. So seek refuge in God; indeed, it is He who is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse explains that the root of the arguing against divine revelation is not a sincere intellectual difficulty or a proof they possess, but arrogance in their hearts: they refuse to submit to the truth, and especially to accept that a messenger and a message have come from among others rather than themselves. They desire greatness and leadership, yet they will never reach the status they covet, because God abases the arrogant and raises the truth. The command to seek refuge in God directs the believer to protect himself from the evil of such proud disputers and from the whispers of pride and arrogance in his own self, relying on God alone, who hears what they say and sees what they conceal and what they do, and who will deal with them justly.

translation: The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse points to the vastness and complexity of the cosmos as evidence of God's power. If God created the heavens and the earth, which are far greater in scale and majesty than human beings, then raising humans back to life after death is clearly no difficult matter for Him. Those who deny the Resurrection fail to reflect on this. Most people do not truly know or ponder it, because heedlessness and arrogance veil their reasoning, so they underestimate God's power and dismiss the promise of the Hereafter.

translation: And not equal are the blind and the seeing, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds equal to the evildoer. Little do you remember.
interpretation: God draws a parallel between physical sight and spiritual insight. Just as a blind person and a sighted person can never be the same, the believer who perceives the truth and expresses faith through righteous action cannot be compared with the wrongdoer who is blind to the signs of God and sinks into evil. The verse reasons that if the Creator can bring about the heavens and earth and will resurrect the dead, then the moral order demands a reckoning in which these two groups are not treated alike. The closing rebuke, 'little do you remember,' points out that people rarely reflect on this obvious truth, and it urges them to heed the reminder, open their inner eyes, and choose the path of faith and good works before the Hour comes.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt about it; but most of the people do not believe.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Day of Judgment is a certain reality, not a matter open to speculation, and that its coming will not fail even though people may deny or neglect it. The denial of the majority does not alter the truth, because truth is not measured by numbers or popular opinion. The Hour is the moment when all accounts are settled and justice is fully realized, and the verse reminds believers that belief in it is the foundation of moral responsibility: if one knows that every deed will be weighed, one lives with accountability, patience in the face of injustice, and sincerity toward God. The remark about most people's disbelief consoles the Prophet and the faithful, teaching them not to be discouraged or shaken by the prevalence of heedlessness, but to hold firm to what is certain.

translation: And your Lord has said: "Call upon Me, and I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation."
interpretation: In this verse God invites people to approach Him directly through supplication, promising to answer, and he treats du'a as itself an act of worship. Calling on God expresses humility, dependence, and recognition that He alone has power to give and to withhold. Answering may take different forms: granting the request, averting some harm, or storing the reward for the Hereafter. The verse then warns of the opposite attitude. Those who refuse to call upon God or worship Him out of arrogance, imagining themselves self-sufficient, will be brought low in Hell. The humiliation of the next world is the fitting outcome of the pride they showed in this one, so the verse sets submissive turning to God against arrogant self-reliance.

translation: It is God who made the night for you so that you may rest in it, and the day to give sight. Indeed, God is full of bounty to people, but most people do not give thanks.
interpretation: The verse points to the alternation of night and day as an everyday sign of God's mercy and care. Night brings stillness and rest for the body and mind, and day is bright so that people can see, work, earn a living and move about. These blessings are constant and so easily taken for granted, and that is why most people fail to give thanks. True gratitude means recognizing that every benefit comes from God alone, acknowledging it in the heart, praising Him with the tongue, and using these blessings in obedience to Him instead of heedlessness or ascribing partners to Him.

translation: Such is God, your Lord, the Creator of everything. There is no god but Him. So how are you being turned away?
interpretation: The verse argues that the One who creates every single thing is the only one who deserves to be worshipped and obeyed, since lordship and divinity cannot be separated. If everything in existence, including the people themselves and whatever they might venerate besides God, was brought into being by Him, then no created thing can share in His authority or merit devotion. The closing question, 'how are you being turned away?', is a rebuke. It points out how irrational it is for people to abandon clear evidence of God's oneness in creation and be diverted, by their own desires, by inherited custom, or by deceptive influences, toward worshipping what has no power to create or benefit them. It calls the listener to reflect and return to pure monotheism.

translation: Thus are deluded those who used to reject the signs of God.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 40:63) teaches that turning away from the truth is a consequence of deliberate denial. Those who knowingly reject God's clear signs in the universe and in revelation are gradually deprived of guidance and led astray from the straight path, so their minds and hearts are diverted from truth toward falsehood. Their delusion is not random; it follows from their persistent obstinacy, just as the disbelievers of earlier communities were misled after rejecting the evidence before them. The verse warns that arrogance toward clear proofs blinds a person's perception, and it invites the believer to remain humble and receptive to God's signs so as to avoid being turned away from the truth.

translation: It is God who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy, and who shaped you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things. Such is God, your Lord; so blessed is God, Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse argues that the very conditions of human life point to a single Lord who alone deserves worship. The earth is stable and fit for dwelling, the sky is a protective, ordered roof above, and human beings are given a well-proportioned, dignified form, along with wholesome sustenance. Each of these is a continuing gift that no created being or false deity can claim to have given. Gratitude and exclusive devotion are therefore the proper response. The closing words, 'blessed is God, Lord of all the worlds', affirm that His goodness and greatness are abundant and constant, and that His lordship extends over everything that exists, not over humanity alone.

translation: He is the Ever-Living; there is no god but Him. So call upon Him, being sincere to Him in religion. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse grounds sincere worship in the nature of God: because He alone is eternally alive and never dies or changes, only He deserves to be invoked. Everything else that people turn to is perishable and dependent, so supplication and devotion must be directed to Him alone, free from showing off, hidden idolatry, or reliance on intermediaries. Such sincerity is completed by gratitude, for the verse ends by acknowledging that all praise belongs to God as the Lord who creates, sustains, and nurtures all the worlds. True faith therefore joins pure devotion in calling upon God with thankful recognition of His lordship.

translation: Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God, now that clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to declare that his rejection of idol worship is not a matter of inherited custom or personal preference but is grounded in knowledge: clear evidence from God, in the form of revelation and the signs of creation, has made it plain that nothing besides God deserves devotion. Worship directed to anything other than the Creator is therefore irrational and unjustified. The verse also shows that true faith has two aspects: the negation of false deities and the positive act of surrender to God, who alone is Lord of all creation. Submission is thus a conscious choice made on the basis of evidence, not blind imitation, and the Prophet models it for his people by publicly stating his own position.

translation: He it is Who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot; then He brings you forth as a child, then [He lets you live] so that you reach your full strength, then so that you become old—though some of you are taken in death before that—and so that you reach an appointed term, and perhaps you will understand.
interpretation: The verse traces the stages of human life, from humble origins in dust and the first stages of the embryo, through birth, childhood, maturity and old age, to show that every phase is shaped by God's power and wisdom and not by human control. Since some die before reaching old age, life's length is fixed by a term God has appointed and no one can advance or delay it. The purpose of recounting these stages is to make people reflect: a being who is formed from lowly beginnings, who grows weak and strong in turn, and who cannot determine his own end should recognize his total dependence on his Creator, acknowledge His oneness, and prepare for the return to Him, including the resurrection, which is no harder than the first creation.

translation: He is the One who gives life and causes death. So when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone holds absolute authority over life and death, and that nothing limits His power to bring anything into being. His will is carried out immediately, without need for tools, helpers, time, or effort; the command 'Be' expresses the perfect effectiveness of His will rather than a literal process of speech that takes time. Since creation and the cycle of life and death are so easily within His power, the verse calls people to recognize His oneness, to abandon any dependence on other powers, and to trust that resurrection and every divine promise are certain to occur just as He decrees.

translation: Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of God? How are they turned away?
interpretation: The verse (Ghafir 40:69) expresses astonishment at people who, instead of reflecting on God's clear signs in revelation and creation, argue against them out of stubbornness and arrogance rather than a sincere search for truth. The rhetorical question 'how are they turned away?' points out that their deviation is irrational, since the evidence is plain. Their turning from guidance is the result of their own pride and hardened hearts, which lead them away from the truth despite its clarity.

translation: Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers — they will soon come to know.
interpretation: The verse warns that rejecting the Qur'an, and the guidance brought by all earlier messengers, is not a harmless difference of opinion but a denial of the one truth God has sent through every prophet. Those who reject it may feel secure and unaccountable now, but 'they will soon know' signals that reality will become undeniable: when they face the Day of Judgment and its consequences, the truth they dismissed will be made plain to them, and their denial will be shown to have been a grave and costly error.

translation: When the iron collars will be around their necks and the chains; they will be dragged along.
interpretation: The verse portrays the humiliating and helpless state of those who denied God's revelations (as described in the preceding verses of Surah Ghafir). In this world they were arrogant and free to dispute the signs of God, but on the Day of Judgment they will be bound with collars and chains and pulled along, with no power or dignity left. The scene is a just reversal: those who refused to submit willingly to God's guidance are made utterly subject to His command, showing that arrogance in denying the truth ends in complete powerlessness and disgrace.

translation: In the boiling water, then in the Fire they will be burned.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ghafir 40:72) describes the escalating torment of those who denied God's revelations and associated partners with Him. They are first dragged with chains and shackles through scalding boiling water (hamim), then thrust into the Fire to be fueled and kindled. The word 'yusjarun' conveys that they themselves become the fuel that feeds the flames, which shows that their punishment is complete and all-encompassing and fits their arrogance and denial in this life. The movement from boiling water to fire shows that there is no rest or relief, because they are carried from one torment to another.

translation: Then it will be said to them: 'Where are those you used to associate (with God) in worship?'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 40:73) describes a scene on the Day of Judgment in which the idolaters are confronted with the emptiness of their false worship. The question 'Where are they?' is not a request for information but a rebuke and exposure: the idols, saints, and false powers that people trusted in and called upon besides God are absent and powerless when they are needed most. It teaches that all reliance on anything other than God collapses at the moment of truth, and that only God, the One who truly holds power over benefit and harm, can be depended upon. It is a warning to reflect now, while there is still time, on where one places hope, devotion, and trust.

translation: “Besides God?” They will say: “They have abandoned us; rather, we were not calling upon anything before.” Thus does God lead the disbelievers astray.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment the disbelievers will be asked where the idols and false deities are that they used to worship besides God. They will have no answer, and they will say the false gods have vanished and left them. Then they will deny or retract their worship, saying they were never really calling upon anything of substance, for they will realize that those objects were nothing and had no power to help. The verse ends by saying that just as their false gods failed them and their schemes were exposed as futile, God leaves the disbelievers astray, because they chose falsehood over guidance and so lose their way on that Day, as they had lost it in this world.

translation: That is because you used to rejoice on earth without right, and because you used to behave with insolent exuberance.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment the people of the Fire are told that their punishment is the direct consequence of their worldly conduct. They took pride and delight in falsehood, in denying the truth, in oppressing others, and in their disbelief and sins, and they exulted in these things as if they were achievements. Their arrogant, boastful and heedless merrymaking made them forget accountability to God. The verse teaches that joy rooted in wrongdoing and arrogance is blameworthy, whereas rejoicing in God's guidance and mercy is the proper kind of happiness. It also shows that the punishment is just, being matched to inner attitudes as well as outward deeds.

translation: Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein forever; and wretched is the dwelling-place of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse shows that arrogance, meaning the refusal to submit to truth and the contempt for God's signs and for other people, is the root of the punishment, not merely a side fault. Those who looked down on the message in this world are now brought low by being driven to the gates of Hell, where each group is assigned its own entrance according to its deeds. The word 'mathwa' (abode) implies a place of settled, lasting residence, so the verse conveys that their punishment is a permanent dwelling fitting their pride: those who exalted themselves over truth end in the lowest and most humiliating place. It also warns believers to guard against pride in knowledge, status or wealth, since it can close the heart to guidance.

translation: So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And whether We show you some of what We promise them [of punishment] or We cause you to die [before that], to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and calls him to steadfastness in the face of the denial and hostility of his opponents, assuring him that God's promise of victory for the believers and punishment for the deniers is certain. Whether the Prophet lives to witness part of that punishment in this world, as happened with the defeat of the Quraysh at Badr, or dies before it unfolds, it makes no difference to the final outcome, because all people will return to God for judgment. Justice is therefore guaranteed either in this life or the next, and the believer's task is to remain patient and trust in God's timing rather than hurry for results.

translation: We have already sent messengers before you; among them are those whose stories We have related to you, and among them are those whose stories We have not related to you. It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by God's permission. Then when God's command comes, judgment will be passed with truth, and the falsifiers will be the losers there and then.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that he belongs to a long line of messengers, known and unknown, who faced the same denial and the same demands for miracles. It teaches that no messenger controls miracles or the timing of events; signs are God's alone to give, so the unbelievers' challenges to produce them on demand are misplaced. The verse also stresses that God has a fixed time for His decisive command, when He will judge between truth and falsehood with perfect justice. On that day those who built their lives on falsehood and denied the message will be utterly lost, while the truth and its bearers will be vindicated.

translation: It is God who made the livestock for you, so that you may ride some of them, and some of them you eat.
interpretation: The verse points to animals as a deliberate gift from God, not a product of human effort or chance. A single creature serves several needs: transport that carries people and burdens over distances they could not otherwise cross, and nourishment that sustains them. The verse is meant to turn people from simply using these blessings to recognizing the Giver. Noticing such everyday provision should lead to gratitude and to worship of God alone, who subjected these animals to human use. Animals that are far stronger than their handlers submit to being ridden and fed upon only because God made them tractable.

translation: And you have in them (the cattle) other benefits, and so that through them you may reach a need that is in your breasts; and upon them, and upon ships, you are carried.
interpretation: The verse reminds people that God subjected livestock to them for more than food and milk: they provide wool, hides, and strength for work, and above all they carry people and their loads to distant places where they have pressing needs, such as trade, pilgrimage, visiting kin, or seeking livelihood, journeys that would otherwise be too hard to complete. By pairing the animals that carry people on land with ships that carry them on the sea, the verse shows that every means of travel, on land or water, is a mercy and a sign of God's power and provision, so it should lead a person to gratitude and to recognizing the Creator who made these means available, rather than to heedlessness.

translation: And He shows you His signs. So which of the signs of Allah do you deny?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical challenge to those who reject faith. God's signs are visible everywhere, in the natural world, in the human self, and in the revelation, and they are shown continually and not once. Because the evidence is so plain and so varied, no one can honestly claim that all of it is unconvincing. The question exposes denial as stubbornness and not as a lack of proof. It calls people to reflect on what they already see and to admit that rejecting any one sign has no sound basis.

translation: Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them, and greater in strength and in the traces they left upon the earth, yet what they used to earn did not avail them.
interpretation: The verse calls the deniers to learn from history through observation and reflection. Earlier nations surpassed them in population, power, and lasting monuments such as buildings and civilizations, yet when they rejected the truth and the messengers, God's decree overtook them and neither their wealth, their numbers, nor their achievements could protect them. The lesson is that worldly strength and accumulated gains give no security against divine judgment when a people persists in arrogance and disbelief, so those who now reject the message should heed the ruins and records of the past and turn to faith before suffering the same fate.

translation: But when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they exulted in what they had of knowledge, and there encompassed them that which they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse (Ghafir 40:83) shows how past nations met the clear signs brought by their prophets not with humility but with arrogant self-satisfaction. They considered their own worldly knowledge, skills, and customs sufficient and looked down on divine revelation, so they ridiculed the warnings of punishment. The verse teaches that pride in human knowledge, when it shuts the heart to guidance, is a form of ignorance. The very punishment they had scoffed at then surrounded them and left no escape, showing that mockery of God's warnings does not stop them from coming true.

translation: Then, when they saw Our might, they said: 'We believe in God alone, and we reject what we used to associate with Him.'
interpretation: The verse (Ghafir 40:84) teaches that faith professed only when divine punishment is actually witnessed comes too late and is not accepted. Belief is valuable when it is a free choice made in the realm of the unseen, through reflection on the signs and the messengers' warnings. Once the punishment becomes visible, the person is no longer choosing but compelled by what they see, so the confession is not an act of sincere faith but an expression of desperation. The next verse confirms this by stating that their belief did not benefit them after they saw Our might, and that this has been God's established way with His servants. The lesson is to turn to God and renounce false worship while there is still time for repentance, rather than delaying until the moment of certain doom.

translation: But their faith was of no benefit to them once they saw Our punishment. This is Allah's established way which has already taken place among His servants, and there the disbelievers were lost.
interpretation: Faith professed only when divine punishment is already visible is the faith of compulsion, not of free choice, so it cannot rescue the one who professes it. Allah has set a constant law for all nations: repentance and belief are accepted while the matter of the unseen remains a test and a person can still choose, but once the punishment is seen the time for choosing has passed. The disbelievers who postponed belief until the moment of certain doom lose everything at that point, because they discovered the truth only when it could no longer change their fate.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha-Mim.
interpretation: The disconnected letters 'Ha-Mim' that open this chapter are best understood as a divine signal marking the Qur'an as a revelation composed of the very letters of human speech, yet beyond human capacity to imitate. They summon the listener's attention before the message begins and challenge the audience to recognize that a scripture made from familiar letters bears an inimitable origin. Their true meaning is known fully only to God, while their function is to affirm the Qur'an's miraculous nature and to prepare the heart to receive the revelation that follows, which is introduced under the banner of God's mercy and compassion through the opening basmala.

translation: A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Fussilat 41:2) affirms that the Qur'an does not originate from human invention but is sent down by God, whose defining attributes in this context are mercy and compassion. The choice of the names ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim presents revelation itself as an act of divine mercy: God sends guidance out of care for humanity, so that people may find direction, healing, and a path to felicity in this life and the next. Accordingly, the proper response to the Qur'an is to receive it as a gift of grace and to approach it with gratitude, trust, and openness to its guidance.

translation: A Book whose verses have been set out in detail, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse stresses that the Qur'an's message is made clear and distinct: its rulings, stories, promises, warnings and proofs are explained point by point, so nothing essential is left ambiguous. Because it came in clear Arabic, its first audience could understand it directly, with no barrier of language. Yet its benefit is bound to those who use knowledge and reflection. Those who think, seek understanding and are open to the truth will recognize its clarity and gain guidance from it, while those who are stubborn or heedless will not benefit, however clear it is.

translation: A bearer of good news and a warner; yet most of them turned away, so they do not hear.
interpretation: The Qur'an, revealed in clear Arabic, comes both to give glad tidings of mercy and reward to those who believe and act righteously, and to warn of God's punishment for those who persist in denial. Despite this clarity, most of the people addressed turned away out of arrogance and stubbornness. Their 'not hearing' is not a lack of physical hearing but a refusal to listen with the heart and to heed and accept the message. Hearing in the true sense means attentive reception that leads to obedience, so whoever closes his heart to the truth is like one who is deaf to it.

translation: And they said: 'Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you call us, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier. So act; indeed, we are acting.' (Qur'an 41:5)
interpretation: The verse shows the stubborn self-sealing of the disbelievers' hearts. By claiming their hearts are veiled, their ears blocked and a screen stands between them and the Prophet, they declare that they have no intention of understanding or accepting his message, and they turn their rejection into an excuse. Their challenge to him to 'act' while they 'act' is a defiant declaration of separation: he may continue his mission and they will continue their opposition. The verse shows how persistent arrogance and refusal to listen make the heart insensitive to guidance, and how people may blame their own willful rejection of the truth on inability.

translation: Say: I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed that your God is One God. So take the straight path to Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to those who associate partners with Him.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to affirm that his role is not divine: he shares in human nature and differs from others only in being chosen to receive revelation. This removes any basis for exalting him or any created being to a rank of worship, and it makes the core of the message pure monotheism. Since God is One, the believer's whole life must be directed to Him without deviation, meaning sincere faith and obedience in belief, worship, and conduct. Because no one can keep that straight course perfectly, the verse joins it with seeking forgiveness, which repairs lapses and keeps the servant returning to the right path. The closing warning of woe to those who associate partners with God shows that shirk is the gravest deviation, since it denies the very truth on which uprightness and forgiveness depend.

translation: Those who do not give zakat, and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse (Fussilat 41:7) describes the idolaters as those who neither purify their souls and wealth by giving zakat nor believe in the Hereafter. Withholding zakat reflects greed and attachment to this world, and it stems from denying that people will be held accountable and rewarded in the next life. Belief in the Hereafter is what motivates a person to spend generously for God's sake, because they expect a greater return from Him. Those who deny it therefore cling to their possessions and neglect the rights of the poor. The verse links moral conduct with faith: lack of charity is presented as a sign and consequence of disbelief in the Day of Judgment, and giving zakat as an expression of true belief.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that is never cut off.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith is only complete when joined with righteous action, and that God's recompense for such people is not a fleeting or measured wage that can be reduced, interrupted, or held over them as a favor. Their reward is everlasting and unfailing, a pure gift from God with no reproach attached, which encourages believers to remain steadfast in good works, trusting that no effort done for God's sake will ever be lost.

translation: Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke that exposes how irrational it is to deny God or to worship others beside Him. The One who brought the earth into being, in a measured and purposeful process, is the only one who has authority over everything in existence. Whatever is created, dependent and limited cannot be an equal to its Creator, so setting up rivals to Him, whether idols, powers, desires or any object of ultimate devotion, contradicts the evidence of creation itself. By ending with 'That is the Lord of the worlds', the verse says that the Creator of the earth is also its Sustainer and Master, and that He alone deserves worship and obedience, because all creation depends on Him.

translation: And He placed on the earth firmly set mountains rising above it, and blessed it, and measured out its sustenance within four days, equal for all who ask.
interpretation: The verse points to God's deliberate provision in creating the earth. The mountains stabilize it, and the blessing in it means abundant, lasting benefit: water, soil, plants, and minerals. The phrase 'measured its sustenance' means that God set the nutriments and resources for every creature in precise proportion, so the earth sustains life without lack. The 'four days' are best read as the total span of the earth's formation and preparation (the two days of its creation plus two more for the mountains, blessing and provision), not as ordinary days. The words 'equal for those who ask' mean that this provision suffices for all who need it, whether they ask in words or through their need, so that the world's resources are enough for everyone. The verse invites reflection on God's wisdom, mercy, and power, and calls for gratitude and worship of Him alone.

translation: Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: 'Come, willingly or unwillingly.' They both said: 'We come willingly.'
interpretation: The verse shows that all creation is wholly subject to God's will and command. After creating the earth and setting its provisions in place, God directed His creative will to the heavens, which were then in a primordial, vaporous state, and ordered both heaven and earth to submit to the roles He assigned them. Their answer, 'We come willingly,' expresses that the cosmos by its very nature obeys its Creator, and nothing in it can resist or deviate from the divine decree. Whether the exchange is understood literally or figuratively, the lesson is that the whole universe is in a state of submission (islam) to God, so human beings, who are given the choice, should freely and gladly obey Him as the rest of creation does.

translation: So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and He revealed to each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse shows that the creation of the heavens was a deliberate, ordered act carried out by God's will, not by chance. After the earth was prepared in four days, the heavens were shaped into seven layers in two days, and each was given its function and the laws that govern it, so that it runs according to the purpose God assigned. The nearest heaven was adorned with stars that serve two purposes: beauty for those who look up at the night sky, and protection, since according to the commentators they guard it against eavesdropping devils. The closing words, 'the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing,' ground this whole design in two attributes: power, since nothing can resist or disrupt His creation, and knowledge, since every part of it is arranged with complete wisdom. The lesson is that a universe so precisely governed points to one Creator, who alone deserves worship and obedience.

translation: But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt that struck 'Ad and Thamud."
interpretation: This verse (Fussilat 41:13) tells the Prophet that after the Qur'an has been clearly presented, those who still refuse to accept it have no excuse left. His duty is only to warn them, and the warning is of a sudden, devastating punishment like the one that destroyed 'Ad and Thamud, who were once powerful and proud but were wiped out for denying their messengers. The mention of these two peoples is a historical lesson: material strength and worldly success give no protection from God's decree when a people persists in arrogance and rejection of the truth. The verse therefore combines a reassurance to the Prophet that he has fulfilled his task with a stern reminder to the disbelievers that their situation is no different from that of earlier nations that perished.

translation: When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying: 'Worship none but Allah,' they said: 'Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels. So indeed, we are disbelievers in what you have been sent with.'
interpretation: The verse describes how the peoples of 'Ad and Thamud, like many nations before them, were approached by prophets from every direction, meaning the messengers pursued them with the call to pure monotheism by every possible means and at every time, with the message consistent across generations, both those who came before and those who came after. Their rejection was not based on any flaw in the message but on arrogance and a mistaken notion of prophethood: they argued that if God truly wanted to send a message, He would have sent angels rather than human beings like themselves. By saying they disbelieved in what the messengers were sent with, they exposed that their objection was a pretext for refusing to submit to God alone. The lesson is that the call to worship God alone is constant and universal, and that stubborn pride, not lack of evidence, is what leads people to reject divine guidance.

translation: As for the people of 'Ad, they behaved arrogantly in the land without any right, and said, 'Who is mightier than us in strength?' Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they continued to deny Our signs.
interpretation: The verse shows that arrogance rooted in material power is a delusion. 'Ad mistook their physical strength and worldly achievements for self-sufficiency and used them as grounds for oppression and for rejecting divine guidance. The Qur'an answers with a simple point of reasoning: the One who created them and gave them their strength must possess far greater power, since any strength a creature has is only a gift from the Creator and can be withdrawn at will. Pride in one's power therefore ignores its true source, and it naturally leads to denying God's signs, because accepting them would mean accepting accountability. The verse warns that power without humility and gratitude leads to injustice and to ruin.

translation: So We sent upon them a furiously roaring, bitterly cold wind during days of misfortune, so that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgraceful, and they will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse describes the fate of the people of 'Ad, who arrogantly claimed 'Who is mightier than us in strength?' and rejected their prophet Hud. God humbled their pride through the very thing they could not resist: a violent, freezing wind, a natural force beyond human control. The punishment was fitting, since arrogance is answered with disgrace and helplessness. The 'days of misfortune' mark a period of ruin for them as wrongdoers, not a belief that time itself is unlucky. The verse also teaches that worldly punishment is only a foretaste. The disgrace awaiting those who persist in denial and arrogance in the Hereafter is greater and more lasting, and on that day no power, ally, or strength will rescue them. It is a warning to every people that material power and pride offer no protection against God's decree.

translation: As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: God's guidance came to Thamud clearly, through the prophet Salih and the sign of the she-camel, so the truth was made plain to them. Guidance in this sense means clear direction, not forced acceptance. They knowingly chose the blindness of disbelief and stubborn arrogance over the light offered to them. Preferring error to guidance was their own free choice, and the punishment was not an injustice but the direct consequence of their deeds. Their sin was not ignorance but a deliberate preference for misguidance after the way had been shown. The humiliating punishment matched their pride, since those who arrogantly rejected God's guidance were brought low and destroyed by a thunderbolt.

translation: And We saved those who believed and who were mindful of God.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 41:18, and similarly 27:53) teaches that deliverance from divine punishment is tied to two qualities together: sincere faith in the heart and consistent God-consciousness (taqwa) in conduct. When destruction struck the disbelieving peoples such as Thamud, God did not leave the righteous to share their fate. Salvation is therefore not granted by lineage or by claims of belonging, but by true belief joined with continuous caution against disobedience. The verse also offers reassurance to believers that God protects those who remain faithful, even when they live among wrongdoers.

translation: And on the Day when the enemies of God are gathered to the Fire, they will be driven in ranks, held together.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when those who denied God and opposed His message are assembled for punishment. The word 'yuza'un' conveys that the first of them are held back until the last catch up, so they are arranged in orderly groups and driven together, none able to escape or stray. This shows that their reckoning is controlled and inescapable, and that their numbers and worldly power give them no protection before God's authority. It is a warning that enmity toward God, expressed through disbelief and wrongdoing, ends in a humiliating, compelled gathering toward the Fire.

translation: Until, when they reach it (the Fire), their hearing, their sight, and their skins will bear witness against them for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when the deniers are brought to the Fire and can no longer hide behind excuses or denial. The very faculties through which they received guidance and acted in the world — hearing, sight, and skin (the sense of touch and the body as a whole) — are made to testify against them. These faculties were entrusted to them as means of knowing and obeying God, yet they used them in disobedience, believing their deeds were hidden. On that Day God gives these faculties speech, so the evidence comes from within the sinners themselves, leaving no room for denial. The lesson is that a person is constantly accountable and should be mindful of how every part of the body is used, since nothing done in secret is truly unobserved.

translation: And they will say to their skins, 'Why did you testify against us?' They will say, 'God, who gives speech to everything, has made us speak. He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers will be shocked that their own bodily organs bear witness against them, and they will reproach their skins for betraying them. The skins' reply shows that their testimony is not an act of treachery or free choice but the result of God's power: the One who gave speech to every created thing, and who brought them into being from nothing, can make any part of creation speak. This also serves as an argument for resurrection, since the One who created humans the first time is able to return them to Him for reckoning. The verse warns that no sin can be hidden, for one's own body is a witness, and it urges believers to be mindful of God in private as well as in public.

translation: You did not used to conceal yourselves out of fear that your hearing, your sight, or your skins would testify against you; rather, you assumed that God did not know much of what you were doing.
interpretation: The verse reproaches the deniers on the Day of Judgment for lacking true God-consciousness. They hid their sins from other people and never imagined that their own bodies, which they used to commit those sins, would become witnesses against them. Their deeper error was a corrupt belief about God: they assumed that He does not know much of what they do, so they felt free to disobey in private. The lesson is that awareness of God's all-encompassing knowledge should restrain a person from sin even when alone. Heedlessness of this, and the thought that deeds can stay hidden, leads to ruin.

translation: And that [very] thought of yours, which you thought about your Lord, has ruined you, so you have become among the losers.
interpretation: The verse (Fussilat 41:23) addresses the disbelievers who imagined that God did not know much of what they did in secret, so they were unafraid to sin when unseen. Their false and negligent assumption about God's knowledge, power, and justice was not harmless; it was the very cause of their destruction. A wrong belief about God removes the sense of accountability, leads to corruption in conduct, and ends in ruin in the Hereafter. By contrast, a right opinion of God joined with fear and obedience leads to salvation, so the verse teaches that one's conception of God shapes one's deeds and ultimate fate.

translation: So if they endure patiently, the Fire is their abode; and if they ask for favor and pardon, they will not be among those granted it.
interpretation: The verse says that on the Day of Judgment the deniers will find no way out of their punishment, whether they bear it with patience or plead for mercy. Patience, which brings relief in this world, will not change their fate in the Hereafter, because the time for repentance and amends has ended. Nor will their pleas to be restored to God's favor be accepted, since the chance to earn it was in worldly life, and they wasted it through disbelief and denying the signs of God and the testimony of their own hearing, sight and skins. The point is a warning to act while there is still time to repent, for in the Hereafter neither endurance nor appeals will alter the outcome.

translation: And We assigned to them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the word [of punishment] became due against them among nations of jinn and mankind that had passed on before them. Indeed, they were losers.
interpretation: The verse explains that the disbelievers' persistent rejection of truth led God to leave them to the companions they chose, evil associates from among jinn and humans who embellished their present worldly pursuits and their view of the past and the future, so that they saw falsehood as beautiful and became heedless of the Hereafter. Because of this, the decree of punishment became justly due on them, just as it had been on earlier communities of jinn and mankind who followed the same path. Their loss is total: they squandered their souls, their purpose, and their eternal prospects, so the verse teaches that bad company and self-deception, combined with willful turning away from guidance, lead to ruin.

translation: Those who disbelieve say, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise and talk idly during its recitation, so that you may overcome."
interpretation: The verse shows that the opponents of the Prophet could not answer the Qur'an's message with argument, so they resorted to drowning out its recitation. Their tactic is an implicit admission of its power: they feared that anyone who heard it with an open heart would be moved and persuaded by it. Silencing it through noise and disruption was their only hope of 'winning'. The verse thus shows how falsehood often avoids honest hearing and reasoned debate, relying on distraction and obstruction because it cannot withstand the clear truth when it is heard.

translation: So We will surely cause those who disbelieve to taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them for the worst of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse (Fussilat 41:27) is a firm divine promise that disbelief, especially the active obstruction of the truth, will not go unanswered. Those who rejected the message and tried to drown out the Qur'an by noise and ridicule, as the preceding verse describes, will not only suffer a harsh punishment but will be judged by the measure of their worst deeds. The wording shows divine justice: the consequence matches the gravity of the wrongdoing, and their most evil actions become the standard of their recompense. It serves as a warning to the arrogant and as reassurance to the believers that oppression and denial of truth will ultimately meet accountability.

translation: That is the recompense of the enemies of God: the Fire. For them therein is the home of eternity, as a recompense for their having denied Our signs.
interpretation: The verse explains that the punishment of the Fire is not arbitrary but a just consequence of the stance the disbelievers took toward God. By rejecting His signs knowingly and stubbornly, they placed themselves in enmity with Him, and so their deserved outcome is an abode from which there is no exit. Calling the Fire their 'home of eternity' stresses that their rejection was not a passing error but a settled disposition, so the consequence is lasting. The phrase 'recompense for denying Our signs' teaches that the root of this ruin is the deliberate refusal of truth after it has become clear, and that divine justice matches the penalty to the nature of the deeds.

translation: And those who disbelieved will say: 'Our Lord, show us those who misled us from among the jinn and mankind, that we may place them beneath our feet so that they will be among the lowest.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers, seeing the reality of their punishment, will turn their anger against those who led them astray, whether devilish jinn who whispered to them or human leaders and companions who beautified falsehood. Their wish to trample them underfoot shows how bitter their regret is and how they try to shift blame onto others, even though they themselves chose to follow misguidance. The verse warns that false allegiances in this world turn into enmity on the Day of Judgment, and that each person is accountable for whom they follow. The desire to place them in the lowest depths of the Fire reflects the collapse of worldly alliances and the futility of blaming others for one's own choices.

translation: Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, saying: 'Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of the Paradise which you were promised.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith is not merely a declaration but a declaration upheld by lasting steadfastness: affirming Allah's lordship and oneness, then staying firmly on the straight path through obedience, patience, and avoidance of deviation despite trials and temptations. Those who do so are rewarded with divine reassurance, as the angels come to them, most strongly at death and in the moment of resurrection, and also as a comforting inspiration in life. The angels' words remove the two great burdens of the human heart: fear of what lies ahead (the hereafter, punishment, the unknown) and grief over what has been left behind (family, worldly possessions, past shortcomings). In their place comes the glad tiding of Paradise, which God had promised through His messengers. The verse thus shows that consistent perseverance in belief and righteous action leads to security, comfort, and eternal joy.

translation: We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. And you will have therein whatever your souls desire, and you will have therein whatever you ask for.
interpretation: This verse (Fussilat 41:31) describes the angels addressing the righteous believers who stayed steadfast, after they have said 'Our Lord is God.' The angels reassure them that they were companions and supporters to them in this world, guiding them, strengthening their hearts, and inspiring them to good, and that this protection continues in the Hereafter: at death, in the grave, at the Resurrection, and until they enter Paradise. In Paradise, the believers are promised complete fulfilment: every desire their souls feel will be granted, and whatever they request will be given to them, which shows the totality of divine generosity and the removal of all want, fear, and sorrow.

translation: As a welcoming gift of hospitality from the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Fussilat 41:32) describes the honor given to the believers who said 'Our Lord is Allah' and stayed upright. Paradise and what they are granted in it are likened to a generous reception prepared for an honored guest. The giver is described by two names, Ghafur and Rahim, which shows that their entry into this bounty is due to God's forgiveness of their sins and His mercy toward them, not simply to their own deeds. The believer's final reward is therefore a gift of divine grace, offered with the care and generosity a host shows to a welcomed guest.

translation: And who is better in speech than one who calls to God, does righteous deeds, and says, 'Indeed, I am of those who submit (the Muslims).'
interpretation: The verse teaches that the most excellent speech belongs to the person whose words are matched by sincere faith and action. Inviting others to God is not enough on its own; the caller must live out what he calls to through righteous deeds, and must openly and humbly affirm his own submission to God, without arrogance or claiming credit for himself. Thus true da'wah combines three things: the invitation, the practice, and the declaration of one's identity as a servant of God. This makes the caller a model of integrity, whose message is credible because his character and conduct support it, and whose aim is to please God rather than to elevate himself.

translation: The good deed and the evil deed are not equal. Repel evil with that which is better; then behold, the one between whom and you there was enmity will become as though he were a close, devoted friend.
interpretation: The verse teaches that responding to harm with kindness is a powerful moral and social strategy. Good and evil differ in worth and in effect, so a believer should not answer an insult or wrong in kind but with patience, forgiveness, and good conduct. Such conduct disarms hostility, softens hearts, and can turn an enemy into a sincere friend. It presents gentleness not as weakness but as a deliberate force that changes people and ends cycles of animosity, a quality that takes steadfastness and spiritual maturity.

translation: But none will be granted it except those who are patient, and none will be granted it except one possessed of a great share of good fortune.
interpretation: This verse comes after God's instruction to repel evil with what is better, so that the one who was once an enemy becomes like a close friend. It teaches that responding to harm with kindness, forgiveness, and restraint is not easy or natural; it requires deep self-discipline. Only those who have trained themselves in patience, by controlling anger, resisting the urge for retaliation, and holding firm to God's guidance, are enabled to attain this noble character. The 'great share' is the immense spiritual good and divine favor bestowed on such people, showing that this high moral conduct is both a result of perseverance and a gift from God.

translation: And if an evil suggestion from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that no one, even a person of firm faith and good character, is free from Satan's whispers, which may stir anger, hasty reactions, or temptation to respond to evil with evil. The remedy is not to rely on one's own willpower alone but to turn to God for protection, because Satan's influence is subtle and only God can fully guard against it. The closing names, 'the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing,' give reassurance: God hears the believer's plea for refuge and knows the inner struggle and the unseen whisperings of Satan, so seeking refuge in Him is both sincere and effective. In context, following the command to repel evil with what is better, it shows that gentle, patient conduct in the face of provocation is sustained by constant reliance on God.

translation: And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun nor to the moon, but prostrate to God who created them, if it is Him that you truly worship.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the great and awe-inspiring bodies of creation, the alternation of night and day and the sun and moon, are not deities but created signs pointing to their Creator. Their regularity, usefulness, and subjection to a fixed order show that they are themselves governed and dependent, so they cannot deserve worship. Worship and prostration belong exclusively to God, who brought them into being. The closing condition, 'if it is Him you worship', means that real devotion to God cannot coexist with directing acts of worship to any creature; claiming to worship God while prostrating to His creation is a contradiction, so true monotheism requires reserving all worship for Him alone.

translation: But if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him by night and by day, and they never tire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has no need of human worship, so a person's arrogance and refusal to submit harms only himself and takes nothing from God's majesty. The angels who dwell in His presence glorify Him constantly without weariness, which shows that creation is full of devoted worshippers and that the proud deniers are not missing from God's kingdom but from their own salvation. It consoles the Prophet and the believers over the rejection they meet, and it calls every listener to humble prostration, which is why the verse is a place of prostration in recitation.

translation: And among His signs is that you see the earth barren and still; but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who gives it life is the Giver of life to the dead. Indeed, He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection on a familiar natural cycle as proof of resurrection. Dry, lifeless land that revives, trembles and grows once rain falls shows that God's creative power is not bound by apparent death. Because the One who brings dead earth back to life without any visible cause can equally bring human beings back to life after death, the renewal of the earth becomes an everyday sign pointing to the Hereafter. The closing statement, that He has power over all things, grounds this claim in God's unlimited ability, so that doubt about resurrection is answered by what people already witness in the world around them.

translation: Indeed, those who deviate from the truth concerning Our verses are not hidden from Us. Is one who is cast into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do what you will; indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse warns those who twist, distort, or deny God's revelations, whether by misinterpreting their meanings, mocking them, or turning people away from them, that their schemes are fully known to God and nothing can be concealed from Him. The rhetorical question sets two destinies side by side: the one who is thrown into the Fire as a consequence of his deviation, and the believer who comes safe on the Day of Judgment because of his faith and obedience. The answer is obviously the second. The command 'Do what you will' is not a permission but a stern threat, in the style of warning: you are free to choose your path, yet God sees every deed and will hold you to account. It stresses human moral responsibility and the certainty of divine justice.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved in the Reminder when it came to them [will be called to account]; and indeed, it is a mighty Book.
interpretation: The verse declares that those who rejected the Qur'an, the Reminder, when it reached them will face the consequences of their denial, and it affirms that the Qur'an is an invincible and honored Book. It is 'mighty' because it is protected from corruption, falsehood cannot enter it from any side, and no one can produce its like or overcome its truth. Their rejection does not diminish its authority or dignity; the loss falls on those who turned away from a guidance that is inherently powerful, precious, and preserved by God.

translation: Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation sent down from One who is All-Wise and Worthy of all praise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is protected from corruption in every direction and across all time. 'Before it' and 'behind it' signify that no falsehood preceded it that could invalidate it, and none will come after it to abrogate, alter, or discredit it. Its protection rests on its source: it is revealed by God, who is Hakim (perfectly wise in all He legislates and decrees) and Hamid (worthy of praise for all His acts). Because its Author is flawless in wisdom and deserving of praise, His Book is free from contradiction, error, and distortion, which makes it a trustworthy guide that those who reject it cannot undermine.

translation: Nothing is said to you [O Muhammad] except what was already said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness and the Possessor of painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that the denial, mockery, and abuse he receives from his people are not unique to him; every earlier messenger faced the same accusations of sorcery, madness, and falsehood. It teaches him to be patient and steadfast, since this is the way of the prophets. The verse then balances hope and fear: God is abundantly forgiving to those who repent and believe, yet He inflicts a painful punishment on those who persist in rejection and wrongdoing. The outcome therefore depends on how people respond to the message, and believers should remain between hope in God's mercy and fear of His punishment.

translation: And had We made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not made clear? What! A non-Arabic book and an Arab audience?" Say: "For those who believe it is guidance and healing; but those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness upon them. Those are being called from a far-off place."
interpretation: The verse answers the disbelievers' habit of finding fault with revelation whatever form it takes. God sent the Qur'an in clear Arabic so that its first audience could understand it. Had He sent it in a foreign tongue, the same people would have objected that a message in an incomprehensible language, addressed to Arabs, makes no sense. Their objections therefore come from stubbornness, not from any real search for truth. The verse then says that the Qur'an's effect depends on the receptiveness of the heart. For believers it guides them to the right path and heals the spiritual illnesses of doubt, ignorance and moral corruption. For those who reject it, it is as if they were deaf to its words and blind to its signs, so that it only increases them in error. Their state is like that of someone called from a great distance, who hears nothing distinctly and cannot respond, because their hearts are far from understanding and accepting the message.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but differences arose concerning it. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt about it.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by showing that disputes over revelation are nothing new: even the Torah given to Moses was accepted by some and rejected or disputed by others, so the disagreement over the Qur'an should not distress him. The 'word that preceded from your Lord' is God's prior decree to grant humankind a respite until an appointed term, with final judgment deferred to the Day of Resurrection; were it not for this, those who denied the truth would have been punished and the dispute settled at once. The closing phrase describes the deniers' state: their rejection does not come from certain knowledge but from unsettling, suspicious doubt about the Book, which shows that their denial rests on stubbornness and uncertainty rather than evidence.

translation: Whoever does righteous deeds, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it. And your Lord is never unjust to His servants.
interpretation: Every person bears the consequences of his own conduct: the benefit of good deeds returns to the one who does them, and the harm of wrongdoing falls upon the wrongdoer, since God has no need of anyone's worship and is not harmed by anyone's disobedience. God's judgment is perfectly just: He does not wrong anyone by increasing their punishment beyond what they earned, by reducing the reward they deserve, or by holding them accountable for what others have done. The verse calls people to take responsibility for their own actions and to trust in the fairness of divine recompense.

translation: To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruits emerge from their coverings, and no female conceives or gives birth, except with His knowledge. And on the Day He calls to them, 'Where are My partners?' they will say, 'We declare to You, there is not among us any witness.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone. When people ask about the timing of the Last Hour, the answer is that only God knows it, just as only He knows the hidden processes of the natural world, such as fruit developing in its sheath and the conception and birth of every child. If God's knowledge encompasses even these small hidden details, then no created being, and no idol or false deity, can share in His divinity or in His knowledge. On the Day of Judgment, God will confront the polytheists with the question 'Where are My partners?' exposing the emptiness of their claims. They will disown their false gods and say that none of them can bear witness to any such partnership. The lesson is that associating partners with God is baseless, and that people should turn to the One whose knowledge and power encompass all things, preparing for the Hour whose time He alone knows.

translation: And what they used to invoke before will fail them, and they will realize that they have no place of escape.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment the false gods and idols the polytheists used to call upon and rely on will vanish and prove useless, unable to help or intercede. Stripped of every false support, the disbelievers will become certain that there is no refuge, no escape, and no way to avoid God's judgment, so their worldly hopes collapse into total helplessness before Him.

translation: Man never tires of praying for good things; but if evil touches him, he becomes despairing and hopeless.
interpretation: The verse (Fussilat 41:49) exposes a weakness in human nature: people persistently and eagerly seek wealth, health, and comfort, never growing weary of asking for them, yet when hardship strikes they quickly lose hope in God's mercy and sink into despair. It teaches that a believer should not let adversity break their trust in God, since relief and wisdom lie in His hands. Just as one asks God in times of ease, one should remain patient, hopeful and reliant on Him in times of difficulty, recognizing that despair is a flaw of character incompatible with true faith.

translation: And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, 'This is due to me, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. And even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him.' But We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a harsh punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes the ingratitude and arrogance of a disbelieving human who, when relief and blessing follow a period of suffering, does not recognize it as God's grace but claims it as something he earned or deserved. This entitlement leads him to deny or doubt the Day of Judgment, and even if he allows the possibility of returning to God, he presumptuously assumes he would be favored there too, judging his standing before God by worldly prosperity. The verse teaches that worldly comfort is not proof of divine approval, and that gratitude and humility are the proper responses to blessings. It warns that such false confidence will be shattered when the deniers are confronted with the true record of their deeds and meet a severe punishment.

translation: And when We bestow favor upon the human being, he turns away and withdraws to his side; but when evil touches him, then he is full of lengthy supplication.
interpretation: The verse exposes a common weakness in human nature: in times of ease and blessing, a person grows heedless and arrogant, forgetting God, turning away from remembering and thanking Him, and distancing himself as though he has no need of his Lord. But when hardship strikes, he suddenly becomes insistent and prolonged in prayer, pleading at length. The 'broad' supplication signifies its abundance and persistence. The lesson is that true servitude means remembering and being grateful to God in prosperity just as one calls upon Him in adversity, rather than treating Him as a mere refuge in times of need.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if this (Qur'an) is from God and yet you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one who is in deep opposition?
interpretation: The verse (Fussilat 41:52) challenges the deniers to reason honestly: if the Qur'an truly is a revelation from God, then rejecting it without examination puts them in the gravest peril. It appeals to prudence and fairness, since mere doubt or suspicion should lead a rational person to investigate the signs rather than dismiss them. Persisting in stubborn hostility toward a message that may be divine, without weighing the evidence, is the deepest form of misguidance, because such a person has placed himself far from truth and willingly widened the gap between himself and God.

translation: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. Is it not enough concerning your Lord that He is a Witness over all things?
interpretation: God promises that evidence for the truth of the Qur'an and of His oneness will keep unfolding, both in the vast external world (the heavens, the earth, the natural order, and the rise and fall of nations) and in the human self (the body's design, the mind, the conscience, and the innate disposition toward God). As knowledge grows and events unfold, those who doubt will increasingly recognize that the revelation is true. The closing question teaches that, even apart from such signs, the believer should find it sufficient that God witnesses and knows everything: He sees every deed and every denial, and nothing escapes Him. This brings reassurance to the faithful and a warning to the deniers, because they will be held accountable before the One who is aware of all.

translation: Behold! They are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Behold! He encompasses all things.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of the disbelievers' heedlessness and misconduct: they doubt that they will stand before God for reckoning, and this doubt lets them live without accountability. It then answers that doubt by reminding them that God encompasses everything in His knowledge, power, and dominion. Nothing they hide or do escapes Him, and no one can flee from His grasp. Their uncertainty therefore changes nothing: the meeting with Him is certain, and He will bring every deed to account with full knowledge.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Mim.
interpretation: Ha-Mim is one of the 'disjointed letters' (al-muqatta'at) that open several surahs, and its precise meaning is known fully only to God. The most persuasive reading is that these letters are a challenge and a reminder: the Qur'an is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs used in their eloquent speech, yet they cannot produce anything like it. The letters thus draw the listener's attention to the miraculous, inimitable nature of the revelation that follows, and prepare the heart to receive its message with awe and humility, while the opening basmala places the whole revelation under God's mercy and grace.

translation: 'Ayn, Sīn, Qāf.
interpretation: These are among the disconnected letters (al-muqaṭṭaʿāt) that open Surah Ash-Shura (42:2), following the opening Ha Mim. Their true meaning is known only to God. The most sound understanding is that they are a divine challenge and a reminder of the Qur'an's miraculous nature: the revelation is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs knew and used, yet they could not produce anything like it. The letters thus direct the listener's attention to the source of the revelation and call for reverence and reflection on the message that follows.

translation: Thus does God, the Almighty, the All-Wise, reveal to you and to those before you.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelation given to Prophet Muhammad is not a novelty but part of one continuous divine tradition. The same God who sent guidance to earlier prophets sent it to him, with the same core message of tawhid, accountability, and righteousness. The names 'the Almighty' (al-'Aziz) and 'the All-Wise' (al-Hakim) show that this revelation comes from a source of absolute power that cannot be overcome or frustrated, and of perfect wisdom, so its guidance is purposeful and fitted to human need. The believer is therefore reassured that the Qur'an belongs to the lineage of true prophecy and should be received with trust, while those who deny it are in effect denying the unified message that all earlier prophets brought.

translation: To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone is the true owner and sovereign of all creation, so nothing exists independently of His will, and no created being holds any real power apart from what He permits. His names 'the Most High' and 'the Most Great' mean that He is exalted above all creatures in His essence, power and authority, and that nothing He has made can rival or approach His majesty. The believer should therefore recognize their complete dependence on Him, give Him sole devotion, and take comfort in knowing that the One who owns and governs everything is also the One to whom they turn.
