translation: The heavens almost burst apart from above them, while the angels glorify their Lord with praise and seek forgiveness for those on earth. Truly, it is God who is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse conveys the overwhelming majesty of God. The heavens nearly split apart out of awe at His greatness, and also at the burden of the shirk and disbelief that people on earth commit against Him. The angels, who are closest to God and best know His grandeur, respond with constant praise and with intercession, asking forgiveness for the inhabitants of the earth rather than calling for their destruction. The verse closes by affirming that forgiveness and mercy belong to God alone, so that people understand that they are spared and given the chance to repent only through His clemency, not through their own merit.

translation: And those who take protectors besides Him—Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and sets the limits of his role. Those who worship or follow others instead of God, trusting them for protection, help, or intercession, are not hidden from God. He watches over their deeds and preserves a precise record of them, and He alone will call them to account and requite them. The Prophet is not responsible for forcing them to believe, nor is he their keeper or the one who answers for what they do. His task is only to convey the message clearly. Guidance and reckoning belong to God, so the Prophet should not grieve over their rejection or burden himself with their outcome.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Mecca) and those around it, and warn of the Day of Gathering about which there is no doubt: a party will be in Paradise and a party in the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse explains that the Prophet's mission rests on a revelation in clear Arabic, the language of the people he first addressed, so that the message could be understood directly and then spread outward. Mecca, the 'Mother of Cities', was the religious and cultural center of Arabia, so warning it and its surroundings was the starting point for a message that would reach beyond. The warning centers on the Day of Gathering, when all of humanity will be brought before God and held to account. Its certainty is stressed ('no doubt about it') to urge people to take their present choices seriously. On that Day people will divide into two groups according to their belief and deeds: one that enters Paradise and one that enters the Blazing Fire. The verse thus presents life as a moral test whose outcome matters, and it calls people to faith and righteous action before that Day arrives.

translation: If God had willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whomever He wills into His mercy. And the wrongdoers have neither protector nor helper.
interpretation: The diversity of belief among people is not an accident or a lapse in God's power. He could have compelled everyone into a single religion, but He created humans with choice and tests them. Entry into His mercy is therefore a gift He gives to those who turn to Him and are fit to receive it, not something people can claim by lineage, power, or argument. The wrongdoers, who persist in injustice, idolatry, and rejection of the truth, shut themselves out of that mercy. On the Day when all worldly allies fail, they will find no guardian to defend them and no helper to rescue them, because true protection comes only from God.

translation: Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But God alone is the Protector, and it is He who gives life to the dead, and He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who turn to false patrons, such as idols, saints, or powerful people, for help and guidance in place of God. It argues that real guardianship belongs only to the one who can actually give life and who holds power over everything. Beings who cannot even revive the dead, and who themselves depend on God, cannot truly protect, help, or judge between people. The believer's loyalty and trust should therefore rest on God alone, since only He has the ability and authority that true guardianship requires.

translation: And whatever you differ about in any matter, its judgment rests with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; in Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when people disagree over matters of religion or worldly affairs, the final and decisive ruling belongs to God alone, so believers should refer their disputes to His revelation rather than to desires or human opinion. The Prophet then affirms this principle in his own stance: God is his Lord, so he relies on Him completely for support and outcomes, and he continually returns to Him in obedience and repentance. Reliance on God and turning back to Him are thus presented as the proper response to disagreement and uncertainty.

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you mates from among yourselves, and mates of the cattle too, by which He multiplies you. There is nothing whatsoever like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse presents God as the original creator who brought the heavens and earth into being without precedent, and it points to the pairing of male and female in humans and animals as a sign of His design for sustaining life and increasing generations. Its climax is the affirmation of absolute transcendence (tanzih): nothing in creation resembles God in His essence, attributes, or acts, so the mind should not reduce Him to any created likeness or imagine Him in human terms. Yet He is not remote or unknowing, for He hears and sees all things. The verse thus balances God's utter uniqueness with His constant awareness of and involvement with His creation, calling believers to worship Him alone with reverence and trust.

translation: To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The 'keys' (maqalid) signify absolute control and ownership over all the treasures and affairs of creation: nothing in the heavens or the earth is opened, closed, given or withheld except by God's authority. Hence, variation in people's provision, whether abundance or scarcity, is not random or a sign of worth or worthlessness, but flows from God's wise and all-encompassing knowledge, who knows what is best for each person and what each can bear. The believer should therefore seek sustenance by lawful means while relying on God alone, accepting His apportioning with contentment and trust, and not putting hope in created beings who hold none of these keys.

translation: He has ordained for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you [O Muhammad], and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: to establish the religion and not be divided therein. Grievous to the polytheists is that to which you call them. God chooses for Himself whoever He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance.
interpretation: The verse affirms that all the prophets shared one essential core of religion: the worship of God alone, belief in His revelation, and obedience to Him. The details of law may differ between communities, but the foundation does not change. Believers are therefore commanded to uphold this shared faith sincerely and in practice, and not to split into factions that turn differences into division, since disunity usually arises from rivalry and transgression, not from ignorance of the truth. The polytheists find the call to pure monotheism hard to bear because it challenges their inherited customs and their pride. Yet guidance is not a matter of status or lineage: God selects whom He wills for His favor, but He guides in particular those who sincerely turn back to Him, so the door to divine guidance depends on repentance and inward return to God.

translation: And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord for a specified term, judgment would have been decided between them. And indeed, those who were made to inherit the Scripture after them are in disquieting doubt about it.
interpretation: The verse explains that religious division among earlier communities did not arise from lack of clear guidance or ignorance, but occurred after the knowledge had reached them, driven by mutual envy, rivalry, and the desire for superiority and leadership. Its cause was human transgression, not any defect in the revelation. God's delay in punishing them is due to His prior decree granting respite until an appointed time; otherwise, they would have been judged and destroyed immediately. The later generations who inherited the Scripture received it only as an inherited tradition rather than with true conviction, so they remain in unsettling doubt about it, following their forebears' disputes instead of holding firm certainty in the truth. The lesson is a warning to the believers not to fall into the same pattern of dividing over the truth out of envy and worldly motives.

translation: So to this [faith] then call, and stand firm as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires, and say: 'I believe in whatever Book God has sent down, and I have been commanded to establish justice among you. God is our Lord and your Lord. For us are our deeds and for you your deeds. There is no argument between us and you. God will gather us together, and to Him is the final return.'
interpretation: After the previous verses describe how earlier communities fell into division and doubt about their scriptures, this verse instructs the Prophet (and, through him, every believer) on how to respond: invite people to the one true religion of unity, remain steadfast and balanced on the straight path without deviating or yielding to the whims of those who dispute, and affirm faith in all revealed scripture without partisan division. His mission includes upholding justice even toward opponents. The verse sets out the basis of coexistence once the truth has been clearly conveyed: the Creator is the same Lord of all, each party is accountable for its own deeds, and further wrangling is pointless since the evidence has been made plain. The final judgment belongs to God, who will gather all people on the Day of Return and settle their differences, so the believer should present the message with firmness, fairness, and without hostility or compromise of principle.

translation: Those who dispute concerning Allah after He has been responded to, their argument is invalid in the sight of their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shura 42:16) warns those who argue against Allah and His religion and try to turn believers away from it after people have already answered His call and accepted Islam. Their arguments carry no weight: they are futile and void before their Lord however clever they may seem in worldly debate. Because they obstruct the truth out of stubbornness, not sincere inquiry, they incur divine anger and are promised a severe punishment. The verse reassures believers that the falsehood of such disputers will not undermine the truth, and it cautions against contentious opposition to clear guidance.

translation: It is God who sent down the Book with the truth, and the Balance. And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.
interpretation: God sent revelation as a standard of truth, and with it the balance of justice by which human conduct, rights, and obligations are weighed. The verse reminds people that the Book and the Balance are given so that they may order their lives with fairness and truthfulness before they are weighed on the Day of Judgment. The question 'what will make you know?' stresses that no one knows when the Hour will come, and that it may be nearer than people think. This calls for urgency: believers should hold themselves to account now by the Qur'an's standard of justice and prepare for the reckoning, instead of putting off repentance and good deeds.

translation: Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are fearful of it and know that it is the truth. Indeed, those who dispute concerning the Hour are certainly in profound error.
interpretation: The verse contrasts two attitudes toward the Day of Judgment. The disbelievers demand that it come quickly, out of mockery and denial, because they do not think it will ever happen and so feel no accountability. The believers, by contrast, are anxious about it. Their fear comes from knowing it is real, from awe of standing before God, and from concern about falling short in their deeds. The more certain a person is of the Hour, the more seriously they take it, so fear is a sign of true faith and mocking impatience a sign of heedlessness. The verse ends by saying that those who persistently argue and doubt the Hour have strayed far from the truth. The evidence for resurrection is clear, and rejecting it means missing the purpose of life, which is accountability before God.

translation: God is Subtle and Kind toward His servants; He provides for whom He wills. And He is the Strong, the Almighty.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's care for His creatures operates in ways so fine and hidden that people often do not perceive them: He brings benefits through unseen means, gives each person sustenance in the measure and manner that accords with His wisdom, and may bless or test them through ways they do not expect. Provision is therefore not a product of human cleverness or power alone, nor is its unequal distribution a sign of neglect. It is a gentle, purposeful gift from a Lord who knows what is best for each servant. The closing names, the Strong and the Almighty, add that this gentleness is not weakness: God's kindness is joined with complete power, so no one can obstruct what He decides to give, and believers can trust Him fully, rely on Him for their needs, and be content with what He apportions.

translation: Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We will give him of it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse likens deeds to farming, in which every person sows according to his aim and reaps what he sowed. One who works with the Hereafter as his goal, seeking God's pleasure, is rewarded with growth: his good deeds are multiplied, he is helped to do more good, and he receives provision in this world as well. One whose striving is only for worldly gain receives only what God has decreed for him from it, not necessarily all that he wanted, and he is left with nothing in the Hereafter because he never sought it or worked for it. The verse urges believers to set their intentions and priorities on the lasting life, treating this world as a means and not the final aim.

translation: Or do they have partners [in disbelief] who have legislated for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted? And if not for the decisive word [of postponement until the appointed time], it would have been judged between them. And indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who accept human or false authorities as lawgivers in matters of faith and worship. Making things lawful or unlawful, or inventing rites and beliefs, is a right belonging to God alone, and whoever grants it to anyone else has in effect set up partners with Him. Divine justice is not hasty: God has already decreed that final judgment be deferred to the appointed Day, which is why such wrongdoers are not destroyed immediately. This delay is not approval, and it does not mean escape, for the wrongdoers will certainly face a painful punishment when the time comes.

translation: You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned, while it is bound to befall them. But those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the meadows of the Gardens; they will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the fates of the two groups on the Day of Judgment. The wrongdoers, who persisted in disbelief and injustice, will be seized by dread when they see the consequences of their own deeds, yet their fear will bring no relief because the punishment is certain and unavoidable. By contrast, the believers whose faith was matched by righteous action will dwell in the loveliest part of Paradise, the lush meadows of the Gardens, where every desire is granted by their Lord. The verse presents this reward not as something earned by deeds alone but as God's immense grace and favor, which is why it is called the great bounty.

translation: That is what God gives glad tidings of to His servants who believe and do righteous deeds. Say: 'I ask of you no reward for it except affection among kin.' And whoever earns a good deed, We will increase for him good therein. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Appreciative.
interpretation: The verse explains that the great gardens and bounties promised to the believers are the sure good news of God for those whose faith is proven by righteous action. The Prophet is told to declare that he seeks no worldly wage for delivering the message; the only thing he asks is that people honor the bonds of kinship and treat one another with affection, beginning with the ties between him and Quraysh, who were his relatives, so that they would not harm him and would let the message reach people. This shows the sincerity and selflessness of the prophetic mission and the high value Islam places on family bonds. The verse then adds that every good deed a person earns is multiplied by God with further goodness, and that God forgives shortcomings and thanks His servants by rewarding even small efforts generously, which encourages believers to keep doing good and to hope for His forgiveness.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has invented a lie about God'? But if God willed, He could seal your heart. And God erases falsehood and establishes the truth by His words. Indeed, He is Knowing of what lies within the hearts.
interpretation: The verse answers the disbelievers' charge that the Prophet fabricated the revelation. The charge is absurd, because if he had invented lies about God, God would have sealed his heart, taking away his understanding and his ability to speak, as He does with those who falsely attribute things to Him. That the Prophet's heart remains open to revelation, and that the message keeps prevailing, shows he is truthful. The verse also states a lasting principle: God does not let falsehood endure, but removes it and confirms the truth through His decrees and the revelation He sends down. Nothing the Prophet or his accusers conceal in their hearts is hidden from God, who knows their real motives and intentions. The verse thus comforts the Prophet and warns his opponents that their slander will be erased while the truth stands.

translation: And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants, pardons evil deeds, and knows what you do.
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shura 42:25) shows God's mercy and perfect awareness together. He accepts sincere repentance and wipes out the consequences of sins for those who turn back to Him. This is not because He is ignorant of what people did, since He knows everything they do, outwardly and inwardly. So a person should never despair of forgiveness, because the door of return is always open, and should never grow careless or hypocritical, because nothing is hidden from God. Repentance is accepted by One who knows the true state of the heart, so only sincere repentance counts, and it should be accompanied by a real change in conduct.

translation: And He answers those who believe and do righteous deeds, and increases them from His bounty; but the disbelievers will have a severe punishment.
interpretation: God grants the prayers of sincere believers whose faith is proven by righteous action, and He does not stop at fulfilling what they ask: out of His generosity He adds to it, giving more than they requested or deserved, whether in this life or the next. Faith joined with good deeds thus makes a person worthy of divine response and surplus favor. By contrast, those who reject the truth have closed themselves off from this mercy and are left with a severe punishment, showing that the outcome of each group results from its own stance toward God.

translation: And if Allah were to extend the provision for His servants, they would surely transgress upon the earth; but He sends down in due measure whatever He wills. Indeed, He is, of His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.
interpretation: Human nature tends toward arrogance and oppression when it is given unlimited wealth and power, since abundance can make people feel self-sufficient and lead them to wrong one another and spread corruption. God, who knows the inner states and outward conditions of every person, therefore distributes provision in measured amounts that suit what is good for each one and for society as a whole. Seen this way, limited provision is not neglect or stinginess but an expression of divine wisdom and mercy, protecting people from the harm they might do to themselves and others, and calling them to trust that God knows better than they do what suits them.

translation: And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy. And He is the Protecting Guardian, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse points to God's care for people at their lowest moment. When drought has lasted so long that hope is gone, He sends rain that revives the dead land, and through it He spreads His wider mercy in provision, relief and renewal. The lesson is that despair has no place in a believer's heart, because relief comes in God's time, not according to human expectations. His timing is wiser than people's calculations. He is the Walī, the Protector who manages the affairs of His servants, and the Ḥamīd, who is praised for all He does, since His acts of giving and even of withholding are rooted in wisdom and goodness. Gratitude and trust in Him are therefore the fitting response.

translation: And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and whatever living creatures He has spread throughout them. And He is able to gather them together whenever He wills.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader to read the created order as evidence of God's power and lordship. The vast heavens and earth, along with the countless forms of life dispersed across them, could not have come about without a Creator who is both all-powerful and all-knowing. The verse then makes a logical step: the One who originated and scattered all this life can also gather it again. This points to the Day of Resurrection and Judgment, when every creature will be brought together before Him. The dispersal of life is thus not random or purposeless. It is part of a plan that ends in return to God, and the reminder is meant to strengthen belief in the resurrection and to encourage humility and accountability before the One whose power over all creation is complete.

translation: Whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned, and He pardons much.
interpretation: The verse teaches that hardships and calamities in this life are often consequences of human wrongdoing, whether they serve as a recompense, a warning, or a means of purification and a call to repent. Yet God's mercy is wider than His reckoning, for He forgives and overlooks many sins without bringing any consequence for them. A believer should therefore respond to affliction with self-examination and repentance rather than blame or despair, recognizing that the trouble they experience is far less than what their deeds might merit.

translation: You cannot frustrate His plan anywhere on earth, and you have no protector or helper besides God.
interpretation: The verse reminds people that no one can escape God's power or outrun His decree, whether by hiding, by fleeing, or by relying on worldly strength. When God's judgment or trial comes, no created being can shield a person from it or give real help against it. The verse therefore calls the believer to give up false reliance on wealth, status, allies, or schemes, to turn to God alone for protection and support, and to live with humility and awareness that ultimate security is found only in Him.

translation: And among His signs are the ships sailing through the sea like mountains.
interpretation: The verse points to the great ships that glide across the open sea, towering like mountains, as a sign of God's power and mercy. Their ability to float and move is not the work of humans alone but depends on laws God placed in nature: the buoyancy of water and the winds that drive them. He can still the wind so that they lie motionless, or wreck them for the sins of their people, as the following verses say. The verse therefore calls people to reflect on how their safety and livelihood depend on God's grace, and to respond with patience in hardship and gratitude in ease.

translation: If He wills, He stills the wind, and then they (the ships) remain motionless on its surface. Indeed in that are signs for everyone who is patient and grateful.
interpretation: The verse shows that the ships' movement across the sea depends entirely on God's will, not on human skill or on the wind itself. The same wind that carries sailors to safety can be stopped at His command, leaving them stranded and helpless. This teaches that every moment of ease or hardship is under divine control. A person who is steadfast (sabbār) in times of difficulty, when the wind falls and progress halts, and thankful (shakūr) in times of ease, when the ships sail smoothly, is the one who truly perceives these signs and draws lessons from them, turning in humility and gratitude to God in both conditions.

translation: Or He may destroy them [the ships] for what they have earned, while He pardons much.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ash-Shura (42:34), follows the mention of ships sailing upon the sea by God's command, which He can still by calming the wind. It adds that He could also wreck and drown those vessels and their passengers because of the sins people have committed. The point is that disasters at sea, as elsewhere, are linked to human wrongdoing, yet God's mercy is far greater than His punishment: He overlooks most sins and does not seize people for every one. Safe passage is therefore a sign of His forbearance and grace, and it calls people to gratitude, patience and repentance.

translation: And let those who dispute concerning Our signs know that they have no place of escape.
interpretation: This verse (Ash-Shura 42:35) warns those who argue against God's revelations out of stubbornness and denial that when God's judgment comes, there will be no refuge, no shelter, and no way to flee from it. Their disputation may seem to give them power in this world, but it will not save them from accountability. The verse teaches that arrogance toward divine truth ends in helplessness before God's authority, and it calls the believer to humility and sincere submission rather than argumentation aimed at rejecting the truth.

translation: Whatever you have been given is but a passing enjoyment of the life of this world; but what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and who put their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: The verse reminds people that wealth, status, and comforts in this world, however abundant, are temporary and cannot be relied upon, so they should not become the goal of life or a source of pride. The reward God has prepared in the Hereafter is superior in quality and never ends. This lasting reward is reserved for those who combine sincere faith with true reliance on God: they do their part and strive, but their hearts rest on God rather than on worldly possessions, which frees them from anxiety over loss and from attachment to what will pass away.

translation: And those who avoid the major sins and indecencies, and when they are angry, they forgive.
interpretation: The verse describes the character of true believers as marked by self-restraint at two levels: outwardly, they keep away from grave sins and shameful deeds, and inwardly, they master the surge of anger. Forgiveness at the moment of anger is a sign of moral strength rather than weakness, since anger is the point at which people are most inclined to retaliate or transgress. By pairing the avoidance of major wrongdoing with the willingness to pardon others, the verse teaches that faith is shown in both purity of conduct and gentleness toward people, and that those who overcome their own impulses for God's sake earn what is with God, which is better and more lasting than worldly gain.

translation: And those who respond to their Lord, establish prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation, and spend out of what We have provided for them.
interpretation: The verse describes the character of true believers as a balanced union of devotion to God and responsible community life. Answering their Lord means they submit to His call in faith and obedience, and establishing prayer keeps their bond with Him alive. Their affairs being decided by consultation means that collective matters are settled through shared deliberation, not by the whim or tyranny of one person, which fosters justice, humility, and unity. Spending from what God has provided shows that wealth is a trust to be shared, so generosity and social solidarity are part of faith. Together, worship, consultative governance, and charity form the foundation of a righteous, cohesive society.

translation: And those who, when tyranny and oppression afflict them, defend themselves and help one another.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 42:39) describes believers whose character combines humility with dignity. They do not submit passively to injustice or aggression. When wronged, they stand up for themselves and seek redress, whether by their own effort or by the support of their community. Their faith does not mean weakness. Islam recognizes the right to resist oppression and to defend one's rights and honor, while keeping that response within just limits. The verses that follow set those limits: retaliation must be proportionate to the wrong, and forgiveness and reconciliation are better still. The verse therefore affirms that standing against tyranny is a virtue, and that it must be guided by justice and restraint rather than vengeance or excess.

translation: The recompense for an evil deed is an evil like it; but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is due from God. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse sets out justice as the limit of lawful retaliation: a person wronged may respond only in equal measure and may not go beyond it. It also raises forgiveness above retaliation, since the one who pardons and thereby mends the relationship, rather than feeding hatred, is promised a reward that God Himself guarantees, a reward greater than any compensation a person could take. The closing warning shows that wrongdoing includes both the one who starts the injustice and the one who exceeds the proper measure in taking revenge, so the right to retaliate is bounded by fairness, and mercy remains the better course.

translation: And whoever defends himself after having been wronged – for those there is no blame upon them.
interpretation: The verse affirms that a person who has suffered injustice is permitted to seek redress and retaliate in a measured way, equal to the wrong done to him, and he bears no blame, sin, or legal liability for doing so. Standing up against oppression is not condemned; what is blameworthy is the aggression of the wrongdoer. The following verse makes this clear by placing the path of blame only on those who wrong people and transgress on earth without right. Thus, Islam upholds the right to self-defense and justice while still encouraging forgiveness as the higher virtue, as the preceding verses indicate.

translation: The blame is only against those who wrong people and transgress in the earth without right. Those will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes that legitimate grounds for blame, reproach, or legal action lie only against aggressors: those who commit injustice against others and spread corruption and oppression on earth without any rightful claim. It implies that someone who defends himself or seeks redress in proportion to a wrong done to him bears no blame, while the real culpability rests with the initiators of oppression. The promise of a painful punishment warns that wrongdoing against people and arrogant transgression are grave sins that will not escape divine justice, even if they escape worldly accountability.

translation: But whoever is patient and forgives, indeed, that is among the matters requiring firm resolve. (Qur'an 42:43)
interpretation: The verse teaches that patience in the face of harm and the choice to forgive, even when one has the right to retaliate, are marks of strong character and spiritual determination. Responding to wrong with restraint is harder than taking revenge, because it requires mastery over the anger and ego of the self. The verse presents forgiveness not as weakness but as a high moral resolve that God commends and rewards, one that reflects trust in God's justice and a desire for His reward rather than personal vindication.

translation: And whomever God leaves to go astray has no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, 'Is there any way to return?'
interpretation: Guidance and misguidance rest with God's wisdom: those who persistently choose arrogance and wrongdoing are left to their chosen path, and then no one can rescue or protect them from the consequences. The verse shows that on the Day of Judgment the illusion of worldly power and self-sufficiency collapses. When the wrongdoers see the punishment with their own eyes, they are humbled and plead for a second chance to return to the world and amend their ways. But the time for action has passed, so the request comes too late. It is a warning to act on guidance and repent now, while repentance is still accepted.

translation: And you will see them being exposed to it, humbled by disgrace, looking with a furtive glance. And those who believed will say: 'Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.' Truly, the wrongdoers will be in a lasting punishment.
interpretation: The verse portrays the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment as they are brought before the Fire: their arrogance in this world is replaced by humiliation, so that they cannot look at it directly and can only steal timid, fearful glances at it. At that moment the believers declare what true loss is. It is not the loss of wealth or status in this life, but the loss of one's own self through ruin in the Hereafter, and the loss of one's family, either because they are separated from them or because they led them astray and are now cut off from them forever. The verse closes by affirming that the wrongdoers, meaning those who associated partners with God and persisted in injustice, face an unending punishment, which shows that the ultimate failure is to forfeit eternal salvation.

translation: And they will have no protectors to help them besides God. And whomever God leaves to stray, for him there is no way out.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment, the wrongdoers will find that every source of support they relied on in this world, whether wealth, status, allies, or false deities, is powerless to protect them from God's decree. Real help and guardianship belong to God alone. It also teaches that guidance is in God's hands: when a person persistently chooses arrogance and rejection of truth, God withdraws His guidance and lets them remain in error, as a just consequence of their own choices. Such a person then has no path to salvation, since no one can open a way that God has closed because of their stubborn denial. The verse is a call to turn to God humbly, seek His guidance, and rely on Him alone rather than on created things.

translation: Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from God that cannot be turned back. You will have no refuge on that Day, and you will have no means of denial.
interpretation: The verse is an urgent call to answer God's summons through faith, obedience, and repentance while one still has the opportunity, because the Day of Judgment is certain and nothing can postpone or avert it. On that Day a person will have nowhere to hide from God's reckoning, and no way to deny the sins recorded against them, since their deeds, their own limbs, and the record of their life will testify. The wise course is therefore to act now, in this life, because after death the chance to turn back and amend one's ways is gone.

translation: But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey the message. And when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have forwarded, then indeed man is ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet by limiting his role to delivering the message: he is not accountable for forcing belief or for guarding people from their own choices, since guidance and reckoning belong to God. It then describes a common human flaw: when people receive God's blessings, such as health, wealth, or security, they exult in them, often forgetting the Giver. When hardship strikes as a consequence of their own deeds, they forget all earlier favors and complain or deny God's kindness. The verse thus warns against shallow gratitude that depends on circumstances, and teaches that people should recognize their own responsibility for their conduct, remain thankful in ease, and turn back to God with patience and repentance in hardship.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He grants females to whom He wills, and grants males to whom He wills.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's sovereignty is absolute, and that human offspring are entirely His gift, not something people control. Whether a couple is given daughters or sons is an act of divine will and wisdom, so no one should take pride in one kind of child or resent another. Both are equally His bounty. This corrects the pre-Islamic prejudice against baby girls, since the verse names females first and presents each kind as a favor from the One who owns all creation.

translation: Or He gives them both males and females, and He makes whomever He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: The verse completes the account of how God distributes offspring: some receive only daughters, some only sons, some both, and some none at all. This variety shows that having children is not within human control or a matter of merit; it is a pure gift of God's will. Because He is All-Knowing, He gives or withholds according to perfect wisdom regarding what is best for each person, and because He is All-Powerful, nothing can prevent what He decrees. The believer should therefore accept whatever lot God has given with gratitude and patience, and turn to Him in supplication, recognizing that apparent deprivation is part of a wise design and a test.

translation: It is not granted to any human being that God should speak to him except through revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who then reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, Most Wise.
interpretation: The verse explains that God's communication with human beings is limited to three modes, because human beings cannot bear direct, unmediated encounter with the divine majesty. The first is inspiration (wahy), a direct casting of meaning into the heart or through true dreams, as happened with prophets. The second is speech from behind a veil, where the human hears God's word without seeing Him, as with Moses at the mountain. The third is the sending of an angelic messenger, such as Gabriel, who conveys God's revelation precisely by His leave. All three modes show God's transcendence: He is 'Ali, too exalted to be encountered face to face in this world, and Hakim, so His chosen way of addressing each prophet fits what is wise and suitable for the recipient and for the message. The verse thus affirms that true revelation comes only from God's will and not from human effort or claim, and it places the Qur'an within this established divine pattern of guidance.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was; but We have made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse explains that the Qur'an is a divine 'spirit' that gives life to hearts, just as the soul gives life to bodies, and that it came to the Prophet Muhammad purely by God's revelation and not through his own learning, effort, or prior knowledge. Before revelation he did not know the details of scripture or the laws and fullness of faith, which shows that prophethood is a gift from God and not something earned. God made the revelation a light that clarifies truth from falsehood, yet guidance is granted by His will to those who are receptive and sincere. The Prophet's role is to convey and show the way, calling people to the straight path of Islam, the path of God, while the success of that guidance in hearts remains with God alone.

translation: The path of God, to whom belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth. Truly, to God all matters return.
interpretation: The straight path to which the Qur'an guides is not a human invention but the way of God Himself, the sovereign Owner of everything in creation. Because all that exists belongs to Him, His guidance carries absolute authority and wisdom, and following any other way means turning away from the One who owns and governs all things. The verse ends with a reminder that every affair, whether of individuals or nations, will finally be referred to God for judgment and resolution. This should lead the believer to hold firmly to the path of God, take accountability seriously, and trust that justice will ultimately be established by Him.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Meem.
interpretation: Ha-Meem is one of the disjointed letters that open several surahs (the Ha-Meem series, 40–46), and their precise meaning is known only to God. The most sound reading is that these letters are a challenge and a reminder: the Qur'an is composed of the very letters the Arabs used in their eloquent speech, yet they could not produce anything like it, which affirms that it is a revelation from God and not the work of a human being. Opening with the basmala places everything that follows under God's mercy and authority, signaling that the revelation is a mercy to humankind.

translation: By the clear Book.
interpretation: God swears by the Qur'an, a Book that makes plain its guidance, its rulings, and its truth to those who reflect on it. The oath draws attention to the Book's clarity and its status as proof: its message is not obscure or confused, and it distinguishes truth from falsehood. By swearing by it, God affirms that what follows, the truth of the revelation and the Prophet's mission, rests on a source whose evidence is manifest and which leaves people no excuse for ignoring its guidance.

translation: Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: God sent revelation in the clear Arabic language of the people to whom it was first addressed, so that its message could not be dismissed as foreign or obscure. The purpose is rational comprehension: the Qur'an invites reflection, not mere recitation. By removing the barrier of language, God leaves no excuse for failing to grasp its guidance, and people are called to use their intellect to understand its signs, accept its truth, and act on it.

translation: And indeed, it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, truly exalted and full of wisdom.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is preserved in the Preserved Tablet, the original source of all revelation, in God's presence, safe from alteration or corruption. Its being 'exalted' means it is high in rank and status, above any speech of human beings and beyond the ability of any rejecter to diminish or challenge it. Its being 'wise' means it is filled with sound judgments, precise guidance, and wisdom that sets right matters of belief, law, and morals. So the disbelievers' mockery and heedlessness cannot lower its dignity, because its authority comes from its heavenly origin with God and not from the acceptance of people.

translation: Shall We then turn the Reminder away from you and ignore you, because you are a people who transgress?
interpretation: This rhetorical question stresses God's mercy and patience. Even though the people were excessive in disbelief and sin, God does not withdraw revelation and guidance from them or leave them without admonition as a punishment for their transgression. The Qur'an continues to be sent to them as a mercy, calling them back to the truth. The verse implies that withholding guidance would be a fitting consequence of their excess, but God in His grace keeps reminding them, so the responsibility rests with them to accept the message rather than persist in heedlessness.

translation: How many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:6) reminds the Prophet Muhammad and his audience that sending messengers is God's constant way with humanity, not a novelty of Muhammad's mission. Divine guidance has been offered to every community in every age, so the Quraysh have no ground to be surprised at or to reject a warner from among them. It also consoles the Prophet: earlier prophets were met with the same denial and mockery, which shows that opposition does not disprove a message and that patience is the proper response. It further warns the deniers that they are following the path of earlier peoples who rejected their prophets and met a bad end.

translation: And no prophet ever came to them but that they used to mock him.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in human heedlessness: when people are bound to their habits, status, and desires, they meet divine guidance not with sincere inquiry but with ridicule. Mockery is a defense mechanism. It lets them dismiss the message without having to answer its claims or change their lives. The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that the scorn he faced was no sign of his message's weakness, since every earlier messenger met the same response. It also warns that persistent mockery of truth hardens the heart and leads to the ruin that befell earlier nations.

translation: So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might, and the example of the earlier peoples has already passed.
interpretation: The verse warns the Quraysh and every later generation that worldly power offers no protection from God's judgment. Earlier nations such as 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh's people had greater strength, wealth and military force, yet they were destroyed when they denied the truth and rejected their messengers. Their fate has become a proverbial lesson, a pattern in God's dealings with humanity. Those who persist in arrogance and denial should expect the same end, because that pattern does not change. Anyone with sense should therefore heed the warning, reflect on history, and turn to faith and humility before it is too late.

translation: And if you were to ask them, 'Who created the heavens and the earth?' they would surely say, 'The Almighty, the All-Knowing created them.'
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:9) shows that the idolaters of Makkah did not deny that God is the Creator of the cosmos; their own innate nature (fitrah) and reason led them to acknowledge that only a Mighty and Knowing Being could have brought the heavens and earth into existence. This admission becomes an argument against them: if they accept that God alone created everything with power and knowledge, then it is inconsistent and unjust to worship others besides Him or to deny His right to be obeyed, to send revelation, and to resurrect the dead. Acknowledging God's lordship in creation obliges one to devote worship to Him alone.

translation: He who made the earth for you a cradle, and made for you therein pathways, so that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse points to God's care for humankind in preparing the earth as a settled, comfortable place to live, like a cradle that is stable and hospitable, and in opening routes across it, such as roads, valleys, and mountain passes, so that people can travel, trade, and reach their needs. These pathways carry a double meaning: they guide people physically from place to place, and they should lead the reflective person spiritually to recognize the Creator behind such provision. The ease and order of the world is a sign calling people to gratitude and to follow the right path to God alone.

translation: And He who sends down water from the sky in due measure, and by it We revive a dead land. Likewise you will be brought forth.
interpretation: The verse points to the renewal of barren, lifeless earth through rain as evidence that resurrection is possible. The rain comes down in a measured amount, neither so little that the land stays dead nor so much that it floods and destroys, which shows deliberate wisdom and power. The God who brings dead soil back to life with this water can just as easily bring human beings out of their graves after death. Resurrection is therefore not an unfamiliar or impossible event, but one comparable to a process people see every year in the natural world around them.

translation: And He who created all the pairs, and made for you from the ships and the cattle that which you ride.
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:12) points to God's power and generosity as the Creator of everything in complementary pairs, such as male and female, and the many kinds of opposites and counterparts that make up creation, which shows that He alone is One and without partner. It then points to a specific favor: He made ships for travel on the sea and livestock for travel on land, and so put the means of transport and burden-bearing at human disposal. The meaning is that these provisions are signs of divine care and should lead people to gratitude and the acknowledgment of His oneness, not to heedlessness or ingratitude. Every journey and every benefit drawn from creation should remind a person of the One who subjected these things, as the following verses say when mounting a ride: 'Glory to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have done it ourselves.'

translation: That you may settle firmly upon their backs, then remember the favor of your Lord when you have settled upon them, and say: 'Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, for we could never have subdued it ourselves.'
interpretation: God has made animals and vessels obedient to people so that they may ride them, and this ease is a blessing to be acknowledged rather than taken for granted. When a person mounts a steed or boards a ship, he should recall that his control over a creature far stronger than himself is not his own power but a gift of God. He should respond by declaring God's glory and confessing his own limitation. Every journey and every use of the creation thus becomes an occasion for gratitude, humility, and awareness that all ability comes from God, which also guards against arrogance and heedless enjoyment of His favors.

translation: And indeed, to our Lord we will surely return.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:14) is part of the supplication taught to travelers when they mount their rides, after praising God for subjecting these means of transport. It reminds the believer that every journey, however ordinary, echoes the final journey back to God. Gratitude for God's blessings should be joined with awareness of accountability, so that one's travels, comforts, and worldly gains are held with humility and do not lead to arrogance or heedlessness. The believer is thus prompted to keep the afterlife in view, to act righteously, and to see all worldly movement as passing toward a final return to the Creator.

translation: Yet they have ascribed to Him a part of His servants as offspring. Truly, man is clearly ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who attribute offspring to God, such as claiming the angels are His daughters or that some creature is His son, as if a portion of His creation shared in His divine essence. This is a grave falsehood, because God is One, self-sufficient and in need of no child, and everything in the heavens and earth is His servant and possession, so no created being can be part of Him. The closing statement says that people who make this claim, despite being sustained by God's countless blessings, show open and obvious ingratitude, since they repay His favors by denying His oneness and assigning Him partners and lineage.

translation: Or has He taken daughters from among what He creates, and chosen you to have sons?
interpretation: This verse of Surat az-Zukhruf (43:16) rebukes the idolaters of Arabia, who claimed that the angels were God's daughters. It is a rhetorical question that exposes how illogical their claim is. They themselves disliked having daughters and were ashamed of them, yet they attributed to God the very offspring they considered inferior, while reserving the more prized sons for themselves. The verse shows that the claim is both unjust and absurd. God is far above having offspring, and anything He might supposedly take as a child is only a created being, so it could never share in His divinity. The verse also draws attention to the contradiction in their standards, since they assigned to the Creator what they would not accept for themselves.

translation: And when one of them is given news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.
interpretation: This verse, Qur'an 43:17, exposes the contradiction in the pagan Arabs' beliefs. They claimed the angels were daughters of God, thereby assigning to the Most Merciful the very kind of offspring they despised for themselves. When one of them was told that a baby girl had been born to him, which is the same kind of child he attributed to God, his face darkened with shame and he choked back his anger and sorrow. The verse rebukes this hypocrisy and injustice. They ascribed to God what they themselves found unbearable, and in doing so they showed their prejudice against women and the absurdity of attributing offspring to God, who is far above any likeness to His creation.

translation: Is one who is brought up amid ornaments and adornment, and who in disputation is unable to make himself clear, [to be attributed to God]?
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:18) rebukes those who ascribed daughters to God while despising daughters for themselves. It points out the inconsistency of attributing to the Creator a kind of offspring they viewed as lesser: one raised in luxury and jewelry, who in a heated dispute cannot argue her case clearly. This portrays how the pre-Islamic Arabs regarded women, as ornamental and unable to defend themselves in debate. The verse's point is that it is absurd and unjust to assign to God what they considered deficient, and the claim that angels are God's daughters is therefore baseless. The rebuke is aimed at the polytheists' flawed reasoning, not at women, whose dignity Islam elsewhere affirms.

translation: And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the idolaters who claimed that the angels were daughters of God, because it ascribes to honored servants of God a status and gender that no one has any knowledge of. Belief about the unseen realm cannot rest on conjecture or inherited fancy; it needs either revelation or direct witness. The rhetorical question 'Did they witness their creation?' exposes that they had no basis at all, since they were not present when the angels were created. The warning that their testimony will be written down and that they will be questioned teaches that making false claims about God and His creation is a grave matter for which every person will be held accountable on the Day of Judgment. It also affirms the angels' true nature as humble, obedient servants of God, not partners, offspring, or intercessors with any independent divine standing.

translation: And they say, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only conjecture.
interpretation: The verse refutes the polytheists' excuse that their worship of angels, whom they claimed to be daughters of God, was by God's will and therefore approved by Him. They confuse God's universal will, by which He allows people the freedom to choose belief or disbelief, with His approval and command. That God permits something to happen does not mean He is pleased with it or has sanctioned it. They have no revealed or rational knowledge to support the claim that God approves of their idolatry. They are merely guessing and speculating, using fatalism as a pretext to justify their false practices and escape responsibility for their choices.

translation: Or have We given them a Book before this (Qur'an), so that they are holding fast to it?
interpretation: This verse challenges the idolaters' claims and practices by asking whether they have any prior revealed scripture that authorizes their worship of others besides God. The rhetorical question implies a negative answer: they possess no divine book that sanctions their beliefs. Their religion rests only on inherited custom and conjecture, not on revealed proof. The verse teaches that true religious claims must be grounded in authentic revelation from God rather than ancestral tradition or desire, and it exposes the groundlessness of their opposition to the Qur'an.

translation: Rather, they say: 'Indeed, we found our fathers following a certain way, and we are guided by following in their footsteps.'
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:22) exposes the argument of those who reject the message: they have no proof from revelation or reason, so they rest their religion on blind imitation of ancestral custom. They equate the longevity and familiarity of a tradition with truth, and claim to be rightly guided merely because they follow their forefathers. The Qur'an condemns this stance because guidance is measured by evidence and divine revelation, not by inherited habit; a path being old or popular does not make it right. The verse calls people to examine what they inherit, using reason and revelation, rather than clinging to it out of social loyalty or pride.

translation: And likewise, We did not send before you any warner into a town except that its affluent ones said, 'Indeed, we found our forefathers upon a way, and we are following in their footsteps.'
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet by showing that rejection of divine guidance is a recurring pattern, rooted in blind imitation of ancestors rather than in reason or evidence. It singles out the 'mutrafūn', the wealthy and comfortable elite, because their privileges, status and power depend on the established order, so they are the first to resist a message that calls for change, justice and accountability to God. Their appeal to ancestral custom is not a real argument but a way to protect their position and to avoid scrutinizing their beliefs. The verse thus warns that clinging to inherited tradition simply because it is inherited, especially when comfort and status are at stake, closes the heart to truth, and that every person must judge a message by evidence and sound reasoning, not by the habits of those who came before.

translation: He said, "Even if I bring you something better guided than that which you found your fathers upon?" They said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent."
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:24) exposes the stubbornness of blind ancestral imitation. The warner offers a rational challenge: if guidance clearer and truer than inherited custom is placed before them, would they not at least weigh it? Their reply shows that their rejection is not based on evidence or reflection but on pride and attachment to tradition, so they reject the message outright without examining it. The lesson is that tradition has no authority against clear truth, and that people who put inherited habit above revealed guidance close the door to correction and remain in disbelief even when shown a better path.

translation: So We took retribution from them. Then see how was the end of those who denied.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent denial of God's messengers and signs is not left without consequence: after warnings and respite, divine justice overtakes the deniers. The call to 'see' invites the reader to reflect on the fate of earlier nations as historical lessons, showing that arrogance and rejection of truth lead to ruin, while the call of the prophets is vindicated. It consoles the believers and the Prophet that falsehood, however powerful it seems, has a doomed end, and warns later generations to heed the truth before they suffer the same outcome.

translation: And [remember] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free from what you worship."
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's declaration of tawhid as a complete and public break with his community's idolatry. His use of the word 'bara'' (free of, disassociated from) shows that faith in the One God requires clear inner and outward separation from false worship, even when the objects of that separation are one's closest kin and the surrounding society. His loyalty rests on truth rather than on lineage or custom, and his stance becomes a model for believers who must hold fast to monotheism with conviction and courage, without compromising it to preserve social ties.

translation: "Except for Him who created me; indeed, He will guide me." (Qur'an 43:27)
interpretation: In this verse Abraham declares his freedom from the idols his people worshipped and makes a single exception: his Creator. Because God originated him (fataranī), he draws the logical conclusion that only the One who brought him into being has the right to be worshipped and the ability to direct his life. His confidence that God 'will guide me' shows that guidance is not something a person earns by his own cleverness or inherits from his forefathers, but a gift that flows from the Creator to the one who turns to Him alone. The verse thus ties pure monotheism to dependence on God: the One who created is the One who guides, so nothing else deserves devotion or trust.

translation: And he made it a word enduring among his descendants, so that they might return.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 43:28) refers to Abraham's declaration of pure monotheism, 'I am free of what you worship, except He who created me' (43:26-27). By this declaration, Abraham made the creed of worshipping God alone a lasting legacy in his progeny. It was passed on through generations of prophets and righteous people after him, so that whenever his descendants strayed into error, the enduring message would be there to call them back to God and to the worship of Him alone. The verse shows that true faith is a trust to be handed down, and that the reminder of tawhid always remains available for people to return to the truth.

translation: Rather, I let these people and their forefathers enjoy worldly life until the truth came to them, and a clear Messenger.
interpretation: The verse shows that Allah's delay in punishing the idolaters was not approval of their beliefs but a mercy and a test. He granted them and their ancestors long life, provision, and safety, and this ease lulled them into heedlessness and arrogance instead of leading them to gratitude. When the Qur'an (the truth) and Prophet Muhammad, whose message is plain and whose proofs are evident, finally came, their excuse of ignorance was removed. The worldly enjoyment they had received therefore became a proof against them, and it shows they were responsible for how they responded to clear guidance.

translation: But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 43:30) exposes how stubborn arrogance leads people to reject clear guidance. The Quraysh had earlier boasted that they would be more rightly guided than any other community if a warner came to them, yet when the Qur'an and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived with the truth, they dismissed it as sorcery rather than examine it. Calling it magic was an excuse to discredit what they could not refute, and their declaration of disbelief shows that the rejection came from pride, envy, and attachment to their status and inherited ways, not from any lack of evidence. The lesson is that truth, when it comes plainly, demands humility, and those who refuse it will invent labels to avoid submitting to it.

translation: And they said: Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from one of the two towns?
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh objected to the Prophet Muhammad's receiving revelation because he lacked the worldly rank they admired. By the 'two towns' they meant Mecca and Ta'if, and they had in mind men of wealth and status such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira in Mecca or 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi in Ta'if. Their objection shows that they measured honor by wealth and social standing, whereas God chooses His messengers by their sincerity, character, and fitness for the trust of prophethood. The following verses answer them: if people cannot even divide worldly provision among themselves, they have no authority to decide who receives God's mercy and prophethood. God alone knows where to place His message.

translation: Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? It is We who have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others into service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.
interpretation: The verse answers those who objected that prophethood should have gone to a wealthy and prominent man instead of Muhammad. God says that people have no authority over His mercy, which includes prophethood and guidance, since even the means of worldly livelihood are apportioned by God and not by them. The differences in wealth, rank, and ability are part of a divine wisdom: they make people interdependent, so that each uses the labor and skills of others and society functions. Worldly riches are therefore no measure of closeness to God or of fitness for His message. The mercy of God, meaning revelation, faith, and the reward of the hereafter, is far better than all the wealth people hoard, so the believer should value it above worldly status.

translation: And were it not that people would become one community [of disbelief], We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and stairways of silver upon which they ascend.
interpretation: This verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:33) teaches that worldly wealth has little worth in God's sight. If giving abundant riches to disbelievers did not risk leading people to follow disbelief en masse out of love for the world, God would have given the deniers of the Most Merciful extravagant luxury, with silver roofs and stairways. He withholds this because it is a mere passing enjoyment, and wealth is neither a sign of God's favor nor a measure of a person's true standing. Real honor and lasting reward belong to the Hereafter and to those who are God-fearing, so believers should not be dazzled by the prosperity of the disbelievers.

translation: And [We would have made] for their houses doors and couches upon which they could recline.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:34) continues a thought from the preceding verses, which say that if it were not for the fear that all people would become one community of disbelievers, God would have given those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver and stairways to ascend. The verse adds doors and couches of silver and gold for their homes. The meaning is that worldly luxury and abundance are of trivial worth in God's sight, and are not a sign of His honor or favor toward anyone. The wealth that people covet is merely the fleeting enjoyment of this present life, whereas the Hereafter with its lasting reward belongs to the God-fearing. Believers should therefore not be deceived by the apparent prosperity of the disbelievers, nor measure a person's worth by material possessions.

translation: And adornments of gold. Yet all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world; and the Hereafter, with your Lord, is for those who are mindful of Him (the God-fearing).
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly wealth, luxury, and splendor, however dazzling, are only fleeting goods that have no lasting worth in God's sight, and so they are not a sign of divine favor or of a person's true standing. Real and lasting honor lies in the Hereafter, which God reserves for those who are conscious of Him and guard themselves against sin. The believer should therefore not be dazzled by the wealth of the disbelievers or measure success by material abundance, but should seek the eternal reward through piety.

translation: And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he becomes his constant companion.
interpretation: Whoever willfully turns a blind eye to the Qur'an and the remembrance of God, out of heedlessness and preference for worldly desires, God punishes him by assigning a devil to accompany him inseparably. This devil adorns evil for him, misleads him, and hinders him from guidance, while he comes to believe he is rightly guided. The verse shows that persistent neglect of God's reminder leads to a spiritual consequence: a person's own rejection of guidance opens the way for misguidance to take hold of him as a close, constant companion.

translation: And indeed, they (the devils) turn them away from the path, while they think that they are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse shows how deception works: those who turn away from remembering the Most Merciful are given a devil as a close companion (as the preceding verse says), and these companions keep obstructing them from the path of truth and guidance. The tragedy is that the misguided do not know they are lost. Because falsehood has been made attractive to them, they take their deviation for guidance and feel confident in it. So they have no urge to repent or change course. This warns the believer to guard against self-deception, to keep up remembrance of God, and to measure his beliefs and actions by revelation rather than by his own feelings of certainty.

translation: Until, when he comes to Us, he says: 'O would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts—what an evil companion!'
interpretation: The verse describes the Day of Judgment, when a person who turned away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful and was accompanied by an assigned devil arrives before God. He realizes that the devil, who made misguidance appear attractive and kept him from the truth, has led him to ruin. In regret and disgust he wishes for the greatest possible distance between himself and that companion, expressed as the distance between the two easts (the farthest points of sunrise and sunset). The verse teaches that evil companionship, whether from devils or from people who lead one away from God, brings only remorse in the end, and it warns that heedlessness of God's remembrance leaves one exposed to such a companion.

translation: And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are partners in the punishment.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, the wrongdoers will find no relief in sharing their torment with their misleading companions and devils. In worldly life, shared hardship can lighten grief, since people console one another that others suffer the same. But the pain of the Hereafter is so overwhelming that each person is consumed by his own suffering and cannot feel any comfort from the company of others. Their wrongdoing in turning away from the remembrance of God and clinging to the devil as a companion has sealed this outcome, so having partners in punishment neither lessens it nor excuses them.

translation: Can you, then, make the deaf hear, or guide the blind, and those who are in manifest error?
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and reminds him that his duty is to convey the message, not to force hearts to accept it. Those who have willfully shut their ears to the truth and closed their eyes to its signs are likened to the deaf and the blind, and their stubbornness has plunged them into clear misguidance. Guidance in the sense of opening hearts and bringing about faith lies with God alone, who grants it to whoever is receptive; the Prophet is not to grieve or exhaust himself over those who persist in rejecting the truth after it has become clear.

translation: So whether We take you away [in death], We will surely take retribution from them.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:41) consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and warns those who deny him. Divine justice does not depend on his presence among them: if God causes him to die before the punishment comes, the wrongdoers will still not escape. Their retribution is certain, whether it is carried out in this world or in the Hereafter. The Prophet's task is to convey the message faithfully, and the outcome of the opposition is in God's hands, so he need not grieve over their obstinacy or fear that their wrongdoing will go unanswered.

translation: Or We shall show you that which We have promised them, for indeed We are fully capable over them.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet that God's promised punishment of the deniers is certain and does not depend on any human timetable. Whether God lets him witness it in his lifetime or takes him before it happens, it will not fail, because God's power over them is complete and they cannot escape or resist it. The Prophet's task is therefore to remain patient and steadfast and to leave the timing and manner of the outcome to God, whose promise will be fulfilled in this world or the next.

translation: So hold fast to that which has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet Muhammad, and by extension every believer, to cling firmly to the revelation and not be swayed by the denial of the disbelievers or by the worldly success of those who reject it. Revelation is the sole dependable guide, and holding to it is what keeps a person on the straight path, the way that leads without deviation to God and to success. The assurance 'you are on a straight path' gives reassurance and confidence: steadfastness on what God revealed is itself proof of being rightly guided, whatever the opposition or the number of those who disagree.

translation: And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you will be questioned.
interpretation: The Qur'an is a source of honor and remembrance for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and for his people, the Quraysh and the Arabs, since it was revealed in their language and through one of their own, raising their standing among nations if they hold to it. But this honor carries responsibility: on the Day of Judgment they will be asked whether they upheld the Book, acted by its guidance, and conveyed it, or whether they neglected it and denied the favor God bestowed on them. The verse teaches that receiving divine revelation is both a distinction and a trust for which one will be held accountable.

translation: And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint gods other than the Most Merciful to be worshipped?
interpretation: This verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:45) affirms that the call to pure monotheism is the same message brought by every prophet. The Prophet Muhammad is told to 'ask' the earlier messengers, meaning to consult their teachings and the revealed scriptures they left behind, or to ask their followers who preserved those teachings. All of them will testify that God never authorized the worship of any deity besides the Most Merciful. The question is rhetorical, and its answer is a firm no. It shows that polytheism has no support in any divine revelation and is a human invention, while tawhid is the consistent foundation of all true religion. This silences the idolaters of Quraysh, who could produce no divine authority for their idols.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "Indeed, I am the messenger of the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse affirms that prophethood comes with clear evidence from God, and that Moses' mission was not a personal claim to authority but a delegated message. By addressing Pharaoh and his ruling elite, who held political and social power, Moses confronted the center of arrogance directly. His declaration that he is the messenger of the 'Lord of the worlds' challenges Pharaoh's claim to supreme lordship and teaches that sovereignty belongs to God alone over all creation, not to any earthly ruler. It also shows the pattern of divine guidance: God sends messengers with proofs, and the messenger's task is to convey the truth plainly to even the most powerful, leaving them accountable for their response.

translation: But when he came to them with Our signs, behold, they laughed at them.
interpretation: This verse, describing Moses and Pharaoh's people (Surat az-Zukhruf 43:47), shows how arrogance and hardness of heart lead people to meet clear proofs with mockery rather than reflection. The miracles Moses brought, such as the staff and the shining hand, were meant to awaken faith, yet the people dismissed them with ridicule because ridicule is an easy way to avoid the burden of admitting the truth. The verse warns that scorning divine guidance is a sign of spiritual blindness, and that such scorn invites the consequences that followed, as God then seized them with successive afflictions.
