translation: And We did not show them any sign except that it was greater than its fellow; and We seized them with the punishment so that perhaps they would return.
interpretation: The verse refers to the successive signs and plagues that God sent to Pharaoh and his people through Moses, such as the staff, the flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood. Each new sign was more compelling and more severe than the one before it, so that the evidence for Moses' truthfulness kept growing, leaving them without excuse. God did not punish them all at once but gradually afflicted them with famine, loss of crops, and plagues as a form of warning and mercy, hoping they would reflect, abandon their arrogance and disbelief, and turn back to the truth. It teaches that divine punishment in this world often comes as a corrective call to repentance, and that persistent denial after clear signs reflects stubbornness rather than lack of proof.

translation: And they said, 'O sorcerer, call upon your Lord for us by the covenant He has made with you; indeed, we will be guided.'
interpretation: When the plague struck Pharaoh's people, they turned to Moses in desperation and addressed him as 'sorcerer', a title that reflects their habitual contempt and their failure to grasp his prophethood, even as they begged for his help. Their plea shows that they recognized, in their hour of hardship, that Moses had a special bond with his Lord and that his prayers would be answered. Yet their promise to be guided was not sincere faith but a bargain made under duress, for once the punishment was lifted they broke their word, as the following verses show. The verse thus illustrates how arrogance and disbelief can persist in the heart even when the truth is plainly seen, and how people may seek God only in times of distress while forgetting Him in times of ease.

translation: But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:50) shows how fickle people can be when they are in distress. They plead for relief and promise to believe and obey, but the moment God lifts the hardship, they go back on their pledges, as if the suffering had taught them nothing. The word 'idha' (behold/suddenly) stresses how immediately they revert, with no interval of gratitude or reflection. The lesson is that hardship alone does not produce real faith. Sincere repentance needs a lasting change of heart, and relief that is followed by betrayal of one's promises invites more serious accountability.

translation: And Pharaoh called out among his people, saying: 'O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Then do you not see?'
interpretation: Pharaoh, faced with the message of Moses, resorts to boasting of worldly power and wealth as proof of his superiority and legitimacy. He measures truth and honor by material possession, sovereignty, and the abundance of the Nile's canals, and he appeals to his people's eyes and worldly perception rather than reason or revelation. The verse shows how arrogance and attachment to dominion blind a tyrant, and how rulers manipulate the masses by pointing to outward splendor to dismiss a prophet who comes with guidance. The irony is that the very rivers he claims as his own were a bounty from God, and they would become the means of his destruction when he was drowned.

translation: Or am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself clearly?
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's boast to his people (Qur'an 43:52), in which he tries to discredit Moses by comparing himself to him. He judges worth by worldly power, wealth and the kingdom of Egypt, and he mocks Moses for his lowly status and for the hesitation in his speech. The verse shows how tyrants undermine a messenger by attacking his appearance, social standing or manner of speaking instead of answering the truth he brings. It also shows that true worth lies in faith, truthfulness and the guidance of God, not in outward authority or eloquence. Pharaoh's arrogance was deceptive, and the Qur'an goes on to show his downfall, which proves that the one he despised was the one favored by God.

translation: Why then have no bracelets of gold been cast upon him, or angels come with him accompanying him?
interpretation: This verse records Pharaoh's boast against Moses (Qur'an 43:53). Pharaoh measured worth by outward display of wealth and power. Gold bracelets were worn by kings and nobles in Egypt, so he argued that a true messenger of the Lord of the worlds would be adorned with royal insignia or attended by an angelic escort. Because Moses came in plain clothes with only a staff, Pharaoh treated him as a lowly man with no real authority. The verse shows a recurring pattern in how the arrogant reject prophets: they confuse worldly status with truth and ignore the message itself. Divine authority is shown by the clarity of the guidance and the signs that confirm it, not by wealth or pageantry. Pharaoh's demand was an excuse for his refusal to believe, not a sincere request for proof.

translation: So he (Pharaoh) made light of his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:54) explains how tyranny takes hold: Pharaoh did not rule by the strength of his argument but by manipulating a people who were already morally compromised. He belittled their intellects and deceived them with displays of power, wealth, and ridicule of Moses, and they, lacking firm conviction and sound judgment, followed him. Their obedience was not an excuse, because the Qur'an places the cause in their own corruption: they were 'fasiqin', people who had already departed from obedience to God, so they were ready to submit to a tyrant's falsehood. The lesson is that a people who abandon clear thinking and devotion to God become easy prey for oppressors, and they share responsibility for the injustice they enable.

translation: So when they provoked Our wrath, We took retribution from them and drowned them all together.
interpretation: The verse (Q 43:55) speaks of Pharaoh and his people, who, after witnessing clear signs through Moses, persisted in arrogance and denial. Divine punishment does not strike at the first offense: God gives repeated warnings, signs, and respite. But when a people persists in tyranny and rejection until they have exhausted every chance to repent, they bring upon themselves God's justice. Their drowning in the sea shows that the very power they boasted of, the waters of the Nile and the sea they thought they controlled, became the means of their destruction. It is a warning that worldly might offers no protection against God's decree, and that persistent oppression ends in a just and total downfall.

translation: So We made them a precedent and an example for later generations.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:56) refers to Pharaoh and his people, who were drowned after persisting in arrogance and rejecting the message of Moses. God made them a 'precedent' (salaf), meaning a people who went before and whose fate stands as a warning that later deniers will follow the same path and face the same consequence if they persist in the same disbelief. He also made them a 'parable' (mathal), an exemplary lesson that is recalled to teach that wealth, power and dominion cannot protect those who defy God's signs. The verse thus teaches that the fate of past oppressors is a moral lesson for every generation, urging people to reflect, humble themselves and heed divine guidance before the consequences of their arrogance overtake them.

translation: And when the son of Mary was presented as an example, behold, your people raised an outcry (turned away in clamor) at it.
interpretation: The Quraysh seized upon the comparison between the Prophet's message and the worship of Jesus, arguing that if Jesus, who is worshipped by Christians, could be honored alongside God, then their own idols deserved similar status. They raised a clamor of mockery and disputation, not out of sincere search for truth but out of stubborn argumentativeness. The verse shows how opponents twist a lesson meant to illustrate God's power and the servanthood of Jesus into a pretext for ridicule and for resisting the call to worship God alone.

translation: And they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They did not present this comparison to you except for argument. Rather, they are a contentious people.
interpretation: After the example of Jesus, son of Mary, was mentioned (that he was worshipped by some though he was only a servant), the disbelieving Quraysh seized on it to argue that if Jesus can be worshipped and still be honored, then their own gods must be at least as good as Muhammad or Jesus. The verse exposes this as a sophistic trick: they did not raise the comparison out of any sincere search for truth, but merely to win a debate and avoid submission. It shows that their opposition stemmed from stubbornness and love of disputation, not from honest inquiry, which is why God calls them a people given to quarrelsome contention.

translation: He was nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel.
interpretation: The verse refers to Jesus, son of Mary, and rejects the claim that he was divine or a son of God. He was only a human servant of God, honored with prophethood, miracles, and blessings. God made his extraordinary birth and life a sign and a lesson for the Children of Israel, showing God's power to create as He wills and calling them to worship God alone and to follow the straight path.

translation: And if We willed, We could have made from among you angels on the earth, succeeding one another.
interpretation: The verse points to God's absolute power and to the wisdom behind how humanity was created. God could easily have made angels, who are obedient by nature and have no free will to disobey, inhabit and inherit the earth in place of human beings. He chose instead to place humans there as successive generations, each inheriting from the one before. This means people are given free will and are tested by it. They are not forced into obedience, and the value of their faith and good deeds lies in choosing them. The verse also rebukes those who exaggerate the status of angels or demand that angels be sent down as messengers, because human beings are best suited to be guided by a messenger of their own kind. It reminds people that their place on the earth is a trust and a trial, not a right they own.

translation: And indeed, he is a sign for the Hour, so do not doubt it, and follow Me. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse refers to Jesus, son of Mary, whose miraculous birth, his miracles, and his return near the end of time are a sign that the Day of Resurrection is coming. Since God, who created him without a father and gave life to the dead through him, has power over all things, resurrection and the Hour are not to be doubted. The people are therefore called to give up their hesitation and follow God's guidance by worshipping Him alone and obeying His messenger, which is the straight path leading to Him, free from the exaggeration and denial that people showed concerning Jesus.

translation: And let not Satan hinder you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse warns believers not to let Satan turn them away from the path of truth, obedience to God, and the good that He commands, whether through temptation, doubt, fear of poverty, or the lure of desires. It reminds them that Satan's hostility is open and certain, not hidden, so there is no excuse for following him. Recognizing him as a manifest enemy calls for constant vigilance, seeking refuge in God, and holding firmly to what God has prescribed, since Satan's aim is always to lead people away from guidance and toward ruin.

translation: And when Jesus came with clear proofs, he said: "I have come to you with wisdom, and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ. So fear God and obey me."
interpretation: This verse presents Jesus as a prophet whose mission was to guide his people through divine wisdom, not to found a rival to God. His clear signs confirmed that his message was true. His role was to settle some of the religious disagreements that had split the Children of Israel, by clarifying what they had distorted or disputed. His closing command, 'fear God and obey me', shows the logic of prophethood in the Qur'an: obeying the messenger is a way of obeying God, since the messenger conveys God's guidance. Piety (taqwa) comes first, which makes Jesus's authority derive from God and keeps it subordinate to Him. The verse also implies that the sound resolution of religious disputes lies in accepting prophetic guidance with a God-conscious heart, not in following whims or sectarian rivalry.

translation: Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Jesus (peace be upon him) in Surat Al 'Imran 3:51 and Maryam 19:36, affirms that he himself is a servant and not divine: the One he calls Lord is the very same Lord of all people, so no intermediary or partner shares in His lordship. Because God alone is the Creator and Sustainer, He alone deserves worship, and devoting worship purely to Him, without associating anything with Him, is the straight path that leads without deviation to God's pleasure and to salvation. Pure monotheism is thus presented as the unchanging message of all the prophets.

translation: But the factions differed among themselves; so woe to those who did wrong from the punishment of a painful Day.
interpretation: After Jesus brought clear teaching about God's oneness and worship of Him alone as the straight path, the groups that followed him split into sects and disputed over his nature. Some exaggerated and called him God or the son of God, while others denied his message and slandered him. The verse shows that the disagreement came not from any lack of clarity in the message but from the rivalry and wrongdoing of the people themselves. Those who wronged themselves by distorting the truth and associating partners with God are warned of a painful punishment on the Day of Judgment, when each will be held to account for turning away from the clear guidance.

translation: Are they waiting for anything other than the Hour, that it should come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who persistently deny the truth and delay repentance, as if the only thing that could convince them is the Last Hour itself. Their stubborn refusal, despite clear signs and warnings, leaves them in effect awaiting the Hour, which will come without notice and with no chance to prepare or amend. The message is that people should not put off faith and good deeds in the hope of having more time, since the end, whether the world's final hour or one's own death, arrives suddenly, and by then repentance no longer helps.

translation: On that Day, close friends will be enemies to one another, except for the righteous (those who are mindful of God).
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 43:67) teaches that friendships built on worldly interests, shared heedlessness, or mutual encouragement of wrongdoing will turn into bitter enmity on the Day of Judgment, as each person blames the other for leading them astray and seeks to save himself. Only bonds grounded in taqwa, namely friendships formed for the sake of God and upon faith, righteousness, and mutual encouragement to good, will endure and even be a source of benefit and honor in the Hereafter. The verse thus invites believers to choose their companions carefully, since the companionship one keeps in this life either becomes a cause of regret or a lasting blessing in the next.

translation: O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when others are seized by terror and regret, God addresses the sincere believers with tender assurance. He calls them 'My servants,' an honor that signals His nearness and approval. He removes from them fear of what lies ahead, such as judgment, punishment, and the horrors of that Day, and grief over what they left behind, such as worldly losses and missed opportunities. Their faith and devotion in life have earned them complete security and lasting peace, so they enter the Hereafter with neither anxiety about the future nor sorrow over the past.

translation: Those who believed in Our verses and were Muslims (submitting themselves to God).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:69) describes those who will be addressed on the Day of Resurrection with the words 'O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve.' It teaches that true faith is not mere intellectual assent to revelation but must be joined with outward submission and obedience to God. Belief in God's signs (iman) is the inner conviction of the heart, while being 'muslimin' is the practical surrender of the will, shown in deeds and conduct. Only those in whom both the inner affirmation and the outward submission are united attain security from fear and sorrow, and enter the Garden promised to the righteous.

translation: Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted and joyful.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Az-Zukhruf (43:70), is the divine welcome given to the righteous believers who had faith in God's signs and submitted to Him. It shows that the reward of Paradise is not a solitary one: the believers are honored together with their righteous spouses, so that their joy is complete through companionship and family bonds sustained by faith. The word 'tuhbarun' conveys a joy that is visible and overflowing, a happiness that shows on the face and fills the heart, which includes delight, honor, and lasting bliss. The verse teaches that faith and righteous conduct in this world lead to a state of complete contentment in the next, in which the believer is free from the fear and grief that marked earthly life.

translation: Platters of gold and cups will be passed around among them, and therein will be whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse describes the fullness of Paradise as a state in which every pleasure, both of the body and of the senses, is granted without effort or want. The golden platters and cups signify honor, abundance, and the dignity of the believers, who are served rather than serving. The phrase 'whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in' means that nothing the heart longs for will be withheld and nothing pleasing to the sight will be lacking, so that joy is complete inwardly and outwardly. The closing words, 'and you will abide therein forever,' give the crowning blessing: this bliss is never interrupted by fear of loss, decay, or death, because a pleasure that must end is incomplete, while eternity perfects it.

translation: And that is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:72) is addressed to the righteous on the Day of Judgment. It teaches that Paradise is described as an inheritance, which signals that it is a gift from God that passes to its people as of right, not something that human effort could ever purchase at its true price. At the same time, the verse ties entry into it to the good deeds believers performed in the world. The meaning is that deeds are the cause and sign of God's acceptance, while the reward itself is a result of His grace and mercy. The believer is therefore encouraged to act with sincerity and righteousness, relying on God's generosity rather than on his own merit.

translation: There are for you therein many fruits, from which you eat.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:73) is addressed to the people of Paradise as a closing note on their reward. It stresses that their bliss is abundant and unending: the fruits are many and varied, not scarce or limited, and they are free to eat from them as they wish. In contrast to worldly fruit, which is seasonal, perishable, and gained by toil, the fruit of Paradise is ever-present and effortless. The phrase 'from which you eat' signals ongoing enjoyment and reassures believers that the blessings promised for their faith and righteous deeds are real, plentiful, and a source of lasting honor and contentment from their Lord.

translation: Indeed, the criminals will abide eternally in the punishment of Hell.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 43:74) teaches that those who persist in grave wrongdoing, especially by rejecting God and His message and by corrupting themselves and others, have chosen a path whose natural consequence is lasting punishment. The word 'mujrimin' refers to people who have cut themselves off from truth and righteousness through stubborn, deliberate sin, and the term 'khalidun' stresses that their torment will not end or be lightened. It serves as a moral warning, set in contrast to the believers' reward in the preceding verses, that there is real accountability and justice, so a person should reflect, repent, and align their conduct with faith while there is still time.

translation: It will not be lightened for them, and therein they will be in despair.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:75) describes the state of the criminals in Hellfire: their punishment will never be eased or paused, not even for a moment. Because of this unrelenting torment, they will be plunged into utter despair, with every hope of relief or mercy cut off. The word 'mublisun' conveys a silent, crushed hopelessness, a fitting consequence for those who persisted in denying the truth and rejected the chance to repent while they were in the world.

translation: We did not wrong them, but it was they who were the wrongdoers.
interpretation: God clarifies that the punishment and ruin that overtook earlier peoples was not an act of injustice on His part. They had been given messengers, clear signs and time to repent, yet they chose denial, arrogance and oppression. Their destruction was the natural and just consequence of their own choices, so the real wrong lay in what they did to themselves by rejecting the truth and transgressing, not in any unfair act by their Lord.

translation: And they will call out, 'O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us.' He will say, 'Indeed, you will remain.'
interpretation: This verse portrays the despair of the people of Hell, who, after realizing that their torment is unbearable, plead to the keeper of the Fire, Malik, to ask God to end their lives so they may find relief in death. His reply, 'You will remain,' shows that there is no escape, not even through annihilation: the punishment is lasting, and death, which they once feared in the world, is now something they long for but cannot obtain. The verse warns that the consequences of rejecting truth in this life are fixed in the next, and it urges people to take their accountability seriously while repentance is still possible.

translation: We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 43:78) shows that rejection of the truth is not caused by any lack of clarity or proof in the message, but by the state of the hearts that hear it. The truth has been delivered plainly, yet most people dislike it because it conflicts with their desires, inherited customs, pride, and worldly interests, since accepting it would demand that they change their beliefs and conduct and give up status or comfort. The verse teaches that aversion to the truth is a moral and psychological barrier rather than an intellectual one, and it calls each person to examine whether their resistance to a teaching stems from real doubt or from reluctance to submit to what is right. It also consoles the believers by reminding them that the truth is not measured by the number of its followers, because the majority may dislike it while it remains the truth.

translation: Or have they determined upon some matter [against the Prophet]? Then indeed, We are determining [what will counter it].
interpretation: The verse warns the disbelievers of Quraysh that their plotting against the Prophet Muhammad and the believers will not succeed. They may settle on a scheme to harm the message or its bearer, but God has already decided His own firm plan, which will overturn theirs. Their cunning cannot overcome divine will, and their schemes will recoil upon them, as the rest of the surah shows in its warnings of their ultimate defeat and punishment.

translation: Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private counsels? Yes indeed, and Our messengers are with them, writing it down.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who assume that what they hide in their hearts or whisper privately escapes God's notice. Nothing remains concealed from Him: He hears even their secret thoughts and private conversations. Beyond His knowledge, the angels assigned to each person are present and record every word and deed, so there is both perfect divine awareness and a written record to be presented on the Day of Judgment. The verse is a reminder to be mindful of God in private as in public, and to know that no plotting or secret speech goes unaccounted for.

translation: Say: 'If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.'
interpretation: The verse (Q 43:81) negates, by way of a conditional that is impossible, any offspring for God. The Prophet is commanded to declare that if the claim of divine sonship had any basis, he, as the most devoted servant of God, would be the first to honor and worship such a son, since his whole life is submission to what God truly has. Yet he does not worship any such being, which shows that the claim is false and that God has no child. The verse thus uses the Prophet's known devotion as proof that the claim is baseless, and it affirms that worship belongs to God alone, who is above needing offspring.

translation: Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, far above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse declares God's absolute transcendence above every flaw, limitation, and false attribution that people ascribe to Him, such as having children, partners, or needs. Because He is the Lord of the heavens, the earth, and the Throne, the very seat that signifies supreme sovereignty, nothing within creation can resemble or share in His divinity. The mention of His lordship over all creation is itself the proof of His uniqueness: whoever originates, sustains, and governs the entire cosmos cannot be matched by anything He has made, so any description that diminishes Him or likens Him to creation is baseless, and the believer's proper response is to glorify Him and keep their conception of Him pure.

translation: So leave them to indulge in their falsehood and amuse themselves until they meet their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: The verse is a warning wrapped in an instruction to the Prophet: he should stop pressing those who persistently reject the truth after the message has been clearly conveyed. Their immersion in vain talk and frivolous pursuits is not harmless, because it leads them toward a fixed appointment, the Day of Judgment. When they meet it, their heedlessness will give way to certain knowledge and accountability. The command to 'leave them' is thus not approval of their conduct but a sign of impending consequence. The Prophet is relieved of the burden of their stubbornness, and they are left to the outcome of their own choices.

translation: And it is He who is God in the heavens and God on the earth; and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing. (Qur'an 43:84)
interpretation: The verse affirms that divinity belongs to God alone in every realm of existence. He is not a deity confined to the heavens while other powers govern the earth, as pagans imagined when they assigned lesser gods to different domains. The same One is worshipped and obeyed by those above and those below. The closing attributes explain why this worship is rightful: His wisdom means that He orders creation and legislates with perfect purpose, and His knowledge means nothing in any realm is hidden from Him. So devotion is due to Him alone, and His commands and judgments are to be trusted.

translation: Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God alone is the source of all lasting goodness and sovereignty. Since the whole of creation, seen and unseen, belongs to Him, no created being, whether saint, angel, or idol, can share in His authority or intercede without His leave. The knowledge of the Hour is kept exclusively with Him, which reminds people that they cannot know when their time or the world's time will end, so they should not delay repentance or put off preparing for the Hereafter. The closing words, 'to Him you will be returned', make the message a call to accountability: those who have lived under His dominion will finally stand before Him to answer for their beliefs and deeds, so a person should align life with worship of God alone and with awareness of the Day of Return.

translation: Those whom they invoke besides Him possess no power of intercession, except those who testified to the truth knowingly.
interpretation: The verse refutes the belief that false deities, saints, angels, or other created beings can intercede for their worshippers. Such beings have no authority to intercede, since all intercession belongs to God alone and is granted only by His leave. The only exception is those who bore witness to the truth, namely the oneness of God, with sincere knowledge and conviction rather than blind imitation or mere words. This includes figures like the angels, the prophets, and the righteous believers, who may intercede by God's permission for those who likewise held to the truth. Hence the objects of idolatrous worship cannot help their devotees, while true intercession is a mercy that God grants to people of sound faith and knowledge.

translation: And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded away from the truth?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 43:87) points out a contradiction in the belief of the idolaters of Makkah. They themselves admitted that Allah alone is their Creator, which acknowledges His lordship and power over all existence. Yet they directed worship, devotion, and intercession to idols and other beings that created nothing. The rhetorical question 'how are they turned away?' rebukes this inconsistency: if the Creator is One, then He alone deserves worship. Their own innate recognition of the Creator (fitrah) should have led them to pure monotheism, so turning away from it is a sign of misguided reasoning, inherited habit, and heedlessness, not a lack of evidence.

translation: And [He has knowledge of] his saying, 'O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe.'
interpretation: The verse shows that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) complained to God about the stubborn disbelief of his people after he had called them for a long time and they kept refusing. It is not a curse but a sorrowful appeal, and it shows that God hears the cry of His messenger and knows his grief. The 'saying' is joined to God's knowledge of the Hour in the previous verse, meaning that God knows both the hidden matters and the Prophet's plea, and so He will judge between them with perfect justice. The verse also comforts the Prophet by reassuring him that his words and distress are not lost with his Lord, who is aware of the state of those who reject faith.

translation: So turn away from them, and say, 'Peace.' For soon they will know.
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to meet the hostility and denial of his opponents with forbearance and dignified restraint rather than retaliation or bitter argument. The 'peace' he is to say is not agreement with their beliefs but a courteous farewell that rises above insult and ignorance, protecting the believer's character and leaving the matter in God's hands. The closing warning, 'soon they will know,' reminds that the truth will become undeniable, whether in this world or the next, so the believer need not waste himself in disputes, since the consequences of rejection will make themselves plain in time.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Meem.
interpretation: Ha-Meem is one of the disconnected letters (al-muqatta'at) that open several surahs, and its precise meaning is known only to God. The most sound reading is that these letters are a challenge and a reminder: the Qur'an is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs used in their eloquence, yet they could not produce anything like it. By opening with them, God draws the listener's attention to the divine origin of the revelation that follows and to its inimitability, calling the heart to attentive and humble listening before the message is delivered.

translation: By the clear Book.
interpretation: God swears by the Qur'an, the Book that makes things plain, to affirm its status and the truth of what it brings. It is called 'clear' because its guidance, its rulings, and its proofs are made evident to those who reflect, and it distinguishes truth from falsehood and guidance from misguidance. By taking an oath on it, God directs attention to its greatness and makes it a witness to the truth of the message and the Messenger who conveys it.

translation: Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night. Indeed, We are ever warning.
interpretation: God declares that the Qur'an was revealed on a night of great blessing, which most commentators identify with Laylat al-Qadr in Ramadan. The night is blessed because of the immense good that came with the guidance descending upon humanity, and because mercy, forgiveness and divine decrees are abundant in it. Revelation was not a random event but an act of divine mercy, rooted in God's constant concern for His creation. The phrase 'We are ever warning' explains why it was sent down: God, out of compassion, warns people of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing so that no one can claim ignorance, and so that they may turn to faith and righteous action before the Day of Judgment.

translation: In it every wise matter is made distinct and decreed. (Qur'an 44:4)
interpretation: The verse refers to the blessed night mentioned just before it, the night in which the Qur'an was sent down, which is commonly understood as Laylat al-Qadr. It teaches that on this night God's wise decrees for the coming year, such as provisions, life spans, and events, are detailed and set out from the preserved Tablet to the angels charged with carrying them out. Every matter is described as 'hakim' because nothing in God's ordering is arbitrary or in vain: each decree rests on perfect wisdom and purpose. The night is therefore marked by the combined weight of revelation and divine ordainment, which shows the Qur'an's exalted status and calls the believer to reverence, worship, and trust in God's wise governance of all things.

translation: As a command from Us. Indeed, We have always been sending messengers.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ad-Dukhan, 44:5) continues the description of the blessed night in which every wise matter is distinguished. It means that the wise decree and the revelation of the Qur'an come as an authoritative command issued from God's own presence, not from any created being. It also affirms that sending messengers with revelation is God's constant practice, grounded in His mercy toward humankind. The Qur'an sent through Muhammad is thus part of a continuing divine pattern of guidance, so people are called to heed it as a binding command and a mercy from their Lord.

translation: A mercy from your Lord. Indeed, it is He who is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's sending of revelation and messengers is itself an act of pure mercy, not something owed to humanity. God sends guidance because He hears the cries and supplications of His servants and knows precisely what they need, so His mercy is perfectly fitted to their condition. The divine attributes of hearing and knowing show that this mercy is neither random nor blind but is directed with complete awareness of every word spoken and every state of the heart.

translation: The Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, if only you were certain in faith.
interpretation: The verse calls people to recognize that the One who created, owns and sustains the entire cosmos is the only true object of worship. Certainty (yaqin) is the condition for benefiting from this recognition: whoever reflects on the order and vastness of creation with sincere conviction will be led from mere acknowledgment of a Creator to complete devotion to Him, so that denial or doubt persists only where a person's certainty is lacking, not where evidence is lacking.

translation: There is no god but He; He gives life and causes death; He is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old.
interpretation: The verse grounds the exclusive right to worship in God's exclusive power over life and death. Since only God brings people into existence and ends their lives, no created being or idol can share in divinity. By calling Him the Lord of the earlier generations as well, the verse tells its hearers that tradition and ancestry cannot justify associating partners with God. The lordship that sustained their forefathers is the same lordship that sustains them, so worship that is owed to Him cannot be set aside for inherited customs. Every generation is equally accountable to the one Creator, who gives life, causes death, and is the only source of true guidance.

translation: Nay, they are in doubt, amusing themselves.
interpretation: This verse (Surah ad-Dukhan, 44:9) describes the deniers of Makkah: their rejection of the message does not stem from certain knowledge or sound reasoning, but from lingering doubt about the truth of resurrection, revelation, and accountability. Rather than treating these matters with the seriousness they deserve, they trifle with them, mocking the warnings and dismissing the Prophet's call as a jest. Their doubt is not an honest search for truth but heedless play, which shows that their disbelief is rooted in negligence and indifference to the consequences that await them.

translation: So watch for the Day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 44:10) commands the Prophet to wait and watch for a day of divine reckoning when a clear, unmistakable smoke will envelop the sky. One reading, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, links it to the severe famine that struck the Quraysh after the Prophet supplicated against their persistent denial, when hunger was so intense that people saw a haze of smoke between heaven and earth. In this sense the verse is a warning that rejecting the truth brings tangible consequences, and that God's punishment, when it comes, will be manifest and impossible to deny, leaving the disbelievers without excuse.

translation: It will envelop the people: 'This is a painful punishment.'
interpretation: This verse follows the mention of the 'clear smoke' (dukhan) that the sky will bring forth in Surah Ad-Dukhan (44:10-11). It says that this smoke will cover and overwhelm all the people, leaving no escape from it, and that they will be told, 'This is a painful punishment.' Many commentators read it as a warning to the deniers of truth: when divine punishment comes, it will surround them completely, and they will then recognize and admit the reality of what they had rejected. The statement is meant to shake the heedless into repentance and faith before it is too late, since acknowledging the punishment when it arrives brings no benefit.

translation: Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:12) depicts the plea of the disbelievers when hardship and punishment overtake them. Having denied the truth while living in ease, they cry out to God in distress and promise to believe if He relieves them. The verse shows how adversity strips away denial and arrogance, and how a sudden profession of faith driven only by the wish to escape suffering is not a sincere, lasting commitment. The following verses make this plain, asking how such a reminder can benefit them when a clear messenger had already come and they turned away from him. True faith must be chosen freely and acted on in times of ease, not just invoked when punishment is already at hand.

translation: How can the reminder avail them, when a clear Messenger had already come to them?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 44:13) addresses those who, when struck by affliction, cry out for relief and promise to believe. God points out that their sudden willingness to take heed comes too late and is not sincere. The time for reflection was when the clear Messenger came to them with plain proofs, an honest character, and an unambiguous message, and they turned away from him. Seeking guidance only once punishment is at hand is not true remembrance but a reaction to fear, and it carries no weight, because faith is meant to be chosen freely in response to clear evidence, not forced out by hardship.

translation: Then they turned away from him and said, "A tutored one, a madman!"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:14) exposes the contradictory and insincere way the disbelievers answered the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Although clear signs and a plain messenger had come to them, they turned their backs on his message and tried to discredit him with two accusations that cannot both be true. By calling him 'taught' (mu'allam) they claimed that a human being was coaching him with the revelation, and by calling him 'mad' (majnun) they claimed that he was out of his mind. A person who is being taught by others cannot be insane, and a madman cannot produce such a coherent and profound message. The contradiction shows that their rejection came from stubbornness and arrogance, not from real doubt. The lesson is that people who refuse the truth often resort to mutually inconsistent slander, because they have no sound argument to refute it.

translation: Indeed, We will remove the punishment for a little while; indeed, you will return [to your disbelief].
interpretation: The verse shows that the relief God grants is only a temporary respite and a test, not proof that the disbelievers have sincerely changed. When hardship is lifted, those who pleaded for relief out of fear do not hold to their promise of belief. They go back to denial and defiance, which shows that their earlier turning to God was driven by distress rather than conviction. God knows what is in their hearts and what they will do, so their relapse exposes the insincerity of their pledges and leaves them without excuse when the greater punishment comes.

translation: On the Day when We seize them with the greatest seizure, We will surely take retribution.
interpretation: The verse warns that a day will come when God's overwhelming power will strike those who persist in denial and arrogance, and that this punishment is a just recompense for their rejection of truth and their oppression. The 'greatest seizure' signifies a decisive, unavoidable judgment—understood by many commentators as the Day of Resurrection (or, in another reading, the defeat at Badr)—in which no one can resist or escape God's justice. It reminds the believer that apparent delay of punishment is not neglect, and that wrongdoing will ultimately be answered.

translation: And indeed, before them We tested the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble messenger.
interpretation: God reminds the Quraysh who rejected Prophet Muhammad that earlier nations were also tried with ease, power, and prosperity, and that Pharaoh's people, despite their might, were tested by the arrival of Moses, a messenger honorable in character and standing before God. The verse warns that being given a noble messenger is a trial of one's response: Pharaoh's people arrogantly rejected him and met destruction, so those who now reject Muhammad risk the same fate if they persist in denial.

translation: [Saying]: 'Hand over to me the servants of God. Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.'
interpretation: Moses addresses Pharaoh and his people with a demand rooted in justice: the Children of Israel, who are God's servants, must be released from bondage and allowed to follow him. Pharaoh had no rightful claim over them, since true servitude belongs to God alone. Moses then affirms the authority and integrity of his mission by describing himself as an honest, trustworthy messenger, one who conveys God's message faithfully without alteration, concealment, or personal gain. So the verse joins a call to end oppression with a declaration that the prophet's word is reliable and he can be trusted.

translation: And do not exalt yourselves against God. Indeed, I come to you with a clear authority.
interpretation: Moses tells Pharaoh and his people not to act arrogantly toward God, whether by rejecting His signs, disobeying His commands, or scorning His messenger, because arrogance is the root of disbelief and tyranny. Such pride sets a creature against its Creator and makes a person refuse the truth. Moses supports his call by saying he brings 'a clear authority', meaning evident proofs and miracles, such as the staff and the shining hand, which show that he is truly sent by God. So the verse sets humble submission to God against haughty defiance, and it grounds the prophet's call in clear, demonstrable evidence rather than in personal claim.

translation: And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me.
interpretation: Moses declares that he has placed himself under the protection of God, who is the Lord of both him and his opponents, so no threat of violence from Pharaoh and his people can truly harm him. By appealing to the shared Lordship of God, he reminds them that they too are answerable to the same Creator, and that any attempt to stone him or kill him by stoning or by harsh words would be a transgression against the One whose protection he has sought. The verse teaches that a believer facing intimidation turns first to God as refuge, trusting in Him rather than in worldly power.

translation: And if you do not believe me, then withdraw from me.
interpretation: This is Moses's words to Pharaoh and his people (Surat al-Dukhan, 44:21). Having brought clear signs and shown that he is a trustworthy messenger from God, he asks them to believe in him. If they will not, he asks them at least to leave him alone, neither harming him nor standing in the way of his mission. The verse shows the fair and restrained manner of a prophet's call. He does not force belief or answer hostility with hostility, and he asks only that he be allowed to deliver his message in peace. It also shows that faith cannot be compelled, and that those who reject the truth should at least not persecute those who convey it.

translation: So he called upon his Lord, saying: 'These are a people who are wrongdoers (criminals).'
interpretation: This verse (Surat ad-Dukhan, 44:22) shows that Moses, after delivering his message and being met with persistent denial and oppression from Pharaoh and his people, turned to God in supplication. His complaint is not an act of personal vengeance but a formal appeal to God, the ultimate Judge, declaring that their crimes had reached a point where they no longer deserved respite. The plea marks the end of the opportunity for guidance and the point at which divine judgment becomes due, as God then commanded him to leave with the believers by night and promised the drowning of the pursuing host. It teaches that when the message has been fully conveyed and rejected through arrogance and injustice, the believer's recourse is to entrust the matter to God, who responds with justice in His own timing.

translation: "Then set out with My servants by night, for you will surely be pursued."
interpretation: This is God's command to Moses (peace be upon him) at the climax of his mission in Egypt, after Pharaoh and his chiefs had rejected every sign. Moses is to lead the believers out secretly under cover of night. The words 'My servants' honor the believers by attributing them to God, marking them as under His protection. The warning 'you will surely be pursued' is not meant to frighten but to prepare them. God discloses in advance that Pharaoh's forces will chase them, so that their hearts stay steady and they know the escape is under divine control. The pursuit will end in the sea with the deliverance of the believers and the destruction of their oppressors. The verse teaches that believers must take practical steps, such as leaving at night and in secret, while trusting that the outcome rests with God, and that God often foretells a trial so that His servants meet it with certainty in His help.

translation: And leave the sea parted (calm and still), for indeed they are an army that will be drowned.
interpretation: God commands Moses, after he has crossed the sea with the Children of Israel, not to strike the sea again to restore it to its former state, but to leave it open and still as a dry path. This is so that Pharaoh and his army will see the passage and plunge into it in pursuit. The verse shows that what seems a means of escape for the oppressors is in fact the very instrument of their destruction, because God has already decreed their drowning. It teaches that the downfall of the arrogant comes by God's precise planning, and that deliverance for the believers and ruin for the tyrants can come through the same event.

translation: How many gardens and springs they left behind!
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:25) describes the people of Pharaoh after their destruction in the sea. It teaches that worldly luxury, wealth and power offer no lasting protection against God's judgment. Those who were absorbed in the blessings of this world, and who arrogantly transgressed, had to abandon everything in an instant, taking nothing with them. The verse warns the reader not to be deceived by the comforts of this life or to become heedless of the Giver of those blessings, and urges gratitude, humility and preparation for the Hereafter.

translation: And crops, and noble dwellings.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:26) continues the description of what Pharaoh's people left behind when they were destroyed: gardens, springs, fields of crops, and splendid, honorable residences and stations of status. The meaning is that all the worldly abundance, prosperity, and rank they relied on and took pride in could not protect them from God's punishment. It is a reminder that material wealth and social standing are fleeting, and that arrogance and tyranny lead to ruin however much comfort a people enjoys, so a believer should hold worldly blessings with gratitude and humility rather than pride.

translation: And [how many] comforts in which they used to delight!
interpretation: This verse, from Surat ad-Dukhan (44:27), completes the description of what Pharaoh's people left behind when they perished: gardens, springs, fine estates, and a life of ease in which they took joyful pleasure. The word 'fakihin' suggests a carefree, merry enjoyment of blessings, without gratitude to the Giver. The point is that worldly bounty is no protection from God's punishment when it is met with arrogance and denial. All of that abundance vanished in an instant, a warning that blessings should lead to thankfulness and obedience, not heedless indulgence.

translation: So it was; and We made it an inheritance for another people.
interpretation: The verse closes the account of the fall of Pharaoh's people, who left behind gardens, springs, fields and noble dwellings. It teaches that worldly power and luxury do not last and are held only as a trust from God. When a people persist in arrogance and oppression, God removes their blessings and passes them to others, with no lasting claim for the wrongdoers. It is a reminder that every nation is tested by what it has been given, and that fortunes change by God's decree and justice, not by human strength.

translation: Neither heaven nor earth wept for them, nor were they granted any respite.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:29) describes the fate of Pharaoh and his people after they were drowned and stripped of all the gardens, springs, crops and comfortable dwellings they had enjoyed. It says that the heavens and the earth did not mourn their passing, because they left behind no righteous deeds that ascended to heaven and no worship upon the earth that would make their absence felt. Weeping for someone is a mark of honor reserved for the believer, whose places of prayer on earth and whose good deeds rising to heaven are missed when he dies. The tyrants who persisted in arrogance and disbelief were so insignificant in God's sight that their destruction passed unnoticed by creation, and when their appointed time came they were given no extra delay to repent or set things right. The verse teaches that worldly power and wealth earn no lasting esteem, and that true worth lies in faith and righteous action.

translation: And We certainly saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:30) recalls God's deliverance of the Israelites from the oppression of Pharaoh, who enslaved them, killed their sons and degraded their women. The punishment is called 'humiliating' because it stripped them of dignity as well as inflicting physical suffering. The verse teaches that God's help comes to the oppressed when they remain steadfast, and that tyrants, however powerful, cannot stop God's decree. It serves as a warning to the Quraysh who persecuted the believers, and as reassurance to the Prophet and his followers that deliverance and honor follow patience and faith.

translation: From Pharaoh. Indeed, he was a tyrant, one of the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse recalls that the Children of Israel were delivered from the humiliating punishment inflicted by Pharaoh. It explains that his torment was so severe because he was arrogant and haughty in the land, exalting himself above others and claiming lordship. He was also among the extravagant transgressors, a man who went beyond all limits in oppression, bloodshed, and disbelief. The lesson is that God rescues the oppressed from tyrants whose pride and excess lead them to ruin.

translation: And We chose them, knowingly, above all peoples of the world.
interpretation: This verse (Ad-Dukhan 44:32) refers to the Children of Israel, whom God favored in their time by sending them prophets, scripture, and deliverance from Pharaoh. The phrase 'with knowledge' means God chose them with full awareness of their merit and of what they would later do, so the choice was neither arbitrary nor a sign of inherent racial superiority. It was a distinction tied to their historical role and responsibility, and it applied 'above the worlds' of their own era. That favor was conditional on faithfulness, and it could be lost through disobedience, as the Qur'an shows elsewhere.

translation: And We gave them of the signs that in which there was a clear trial.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ad-Dukhan, 44:33) refers to the Children of Israel, and teaches that the miracles and favors God granted them, such as the parting of the sea, the shading clouds, manna and quails, and deliverance from Pharaoh, were not mere honors but also a manifest test. Each sign placed responsibility upon them: it revealed whether they would respond with gratitude, faith and obedience, or with ingratitude and stubbornness. Divine blessings and clear proofs are thus a trial of the heart, and the greater the evidence given, the greater the accountability of those who receive it.

translation: Indeed, these (people) say:
interpretation: This phrase, found in Surat ad-Dukhan (44:34), refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh who denied the resurrection. The verse introduces their claim, completed in the next verse: 'There is nothing but our first death, and we will not be resurrected.' The interpretation is that their denial stems from arrogance and heedlessness rather than evidence, and the Qur'an draws attention to the baselessness of their speech by opening with emphatic particles ('inna' and the lam of emphasis), showing how firmly they held to a position that had no proof. It serves as a reminder that rejecting the afterlife is a conviction held by assertion, not by knowledge, and that God is aware of what they claim.

translation: There is nothing but our first death, and we will not be resurrected.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ad-Dukhan 44:35) records the claim of the disbelievers of Makkah, who denied the afterlife. They held that existence consists only of life in this world followed by one death, after which there is no return to life and no judgment. Their statement shows a worldview that rejects accountability, and the Qur'an answers it in the surrounding verses by pointing to the purposeful creation of the heavens and earth and the certainty of the Day of Decision. The denial rests on their limited experience rather than on any proof, since the One who created them the first time is able to bring them back, and a creation made with purpose implies a reckoning for how people lived.

translation: So bring our forefathers back, if you are truthful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:36, in Surah ad-Dukhan) records the challenge of the disbelievers who denied the Resurrection. They said that there is only the first death and that they will not be raised again, and demanded that the believers prove otherwise by bringing their dead ancestors back to life as evidence. Their demand reveals a faulty line of reasoning: they assume that a claim about the Hereafter can be true only if it is demonstrated in this worldly life on their terms. The Qur'an teaches that the resurrection takes place at God's appointed time, according to His wisdom, and not at the whim of those who mock it. Resurrection is not a spectacle to be staged on demand, but a promise tied to the Day of Judgment, when all will be gathered for accountability. The One who created humankind from nothing is certainly able to recreate them, so the disbelievers' challenge shows stubbornness and arrogance, not a genuine search for truth.

translation: Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them; indeed, they were criminals.
interpretation: The verse warns the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection and persecuted the Prophet that their worldly strength and standing give them no immunity. The people of Tubba' in Yemen were a mighty and wealthy nation, and earlier peoples such as 'Ad and Thamud were mightier still, yet God destroyed them because of their crimes, chiefly disbelief, wrongdoing and denial of the truth. If those stronger nations did not escape God's punishment, the Quraysh have no reason to think they will escape it while following the same path. Destruction comes from persistent sin, not from weakness, and the verse calls on them to take heed and repent before the same fate overtakes them.

translation: We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in jest.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation is purposeful and grounded in wisdom and truth, not in idle play or randomness. The ordered cosmos points to a Creator who intends meaning for it, which implies human accountability: life is a trust with a moral goal, and people will be called to account for how they lived. Seeing the universe as purposeful should lead a person to take life seriously, act justly, and avoid treating existence, or its Creator's commands, as a game.

translation: We did not create the two of them (the heavens and the earth, and all that is between them) except in truth, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation is not a game or an aimless accident but is grounded in wisdom, purpose, and justice. The heavens and the earth were made with a meaningful end: to manifest God's power and knowledge, to serve as a testing ground in which human beings are held accountable, and to lead to a Day of Judgment when right is distinguished from wrong and each soul is recompensed. Most people, absorbed in heedlessness and denial of the Hereafter, fail to grasp this purpose, and so they live as though existence had no moral consequence.

translation: Indeed, the Day of Decision is the appointed time for all of them.
interpretation: This verse (Surah ad-Dukhan 44:40) teaches that no wrongdoing goes unanswered and no one escapes ultimate accountability. The Day of Judgment is called the 'Day of Decision' because on it God separates truth from falsehood and the righteous from the wicked, settling every dispute that was left unresolved in worldly life. The words 'all of them' stress that this appointment is universal and inescapable: the arrogant who denied the resurrection, their followers, and every other person will gather at a fixed, predetermined time that cannot be advanced or delayed. The verse thus counters the deniers' claim that death is final, and it reminds believers that the world has a purposeful moral order, so that they should live with awareness of the meeting with their Lord and prepare for it.

translation: The Day when no friend or patron will be of any benefit to another friend or patron in the least, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:41) describes the Day of Judgment, the 'Day of Decision', when all worldly ties of loyalty, kinship, tribal protection, and patronage lose their power. In this life people rely on allies, relatives, and protectors to shield them from consequences, but on that Day no one will be able to avert from another even the smallest portion of God's judgment, and no outside power will come to their aid. The meaning is a warning that each soul stands alone before God, accountable for its own deeds, so a person should not place false hope in worldly support or in those they follow and depend upon, but should prepare through faith and righteous action while there is still time. The only exception, as the following verse indicates, is those upon whom God shows mercy.

translation: Except for those on whom God has had mercy. Indeed, it is He who is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation from the consequences of conflict, falsehood, and divine judgment is not earned by power, lineage, or worldly standing, but is granted only through God's mercy. Those whom God shields, by guiding them to faith and righteous action, are the ones who escape what befalls others. The closing names pair His might with His compassion: He is able to enforce justice upon all, yet He chooses to extend mercy to those who turn to Him, so believers should live between awe of His power and hope in His mercy.

translation: Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum
interpretation: This verse opens a description of the food of the people of Hellfire. Zaqqum is a bitter, loathsome tree that grows in the depths of Hell, and God mentions it as a warning that the sinners' sustenance in the Hereafter will be a source of torment rather than nourishment. The disbelievers mocked the idea of a tree growing in fire, so the verse presents it as a trial for the wrongdoers and a reminder that God's power extends beyond human expectations, so that people take heed and avoid the path that leads to such a fate.

translation: The food of the sinner (Qur'an 44:44).
interpretation: This short verse follows the mention of the Tree of Zaqqum in Surah ad-Dukhan and identifies who will eat from it: the habitual, persistent sinner (al-athim), meaning one who stubbornly rejects faith and persists in wrongdoing and disbelief. The verse teaches that the punishment fits the offense. Those who consumed the world's sustenance while denying their Lord and oppressing others will be given, in the Hereafter, a bitter, scalding food that boils in the belly like molten brass. It is a warning that sin carries a real, lasting consequence, and a reminder to avoid the arrogance and persistent disobedience that lead to such an end.

translation: Like molten brass, it boils in the bellies (Qur'an 44:45).
interpretation: The verse describes the punishment of the people of Hellfire, who are given the fruit of the Zaqqum tree to eat. It is like murky molten metal or dregs of oil, and when it enters the stomach it seethes and boils violently. The image conveys an intense, inward torment: the sinner's very food becomes a source of burning agony from within, a fitting recompense for those who denied the Day of Judgment and lived in heedless indulgence. It warns the reader to consider the lasting consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, and to turn toward faith and righteousness before that Day arrives.

translation: Like the boiling of scalding water.
interpretation: This phrase completes the description of the 'muhl' (molten dregs of oil or metal) in Surah Ad-Dukhan (44:45-46), which the food of the sinner, the tree of Zaqqum, is likened to as it boils in the bellies of the damned. The meaning is that the tree's fruit will not nourish but will seethe and burn inside them with a violent, scalding heat, just as boiling water churns. It conveys that the punishment of the Hereafter is internal as well as external: the very thing a person consumes to satisfy hunger becomes a source of agonizing torment, a fitting recompense for those who consumed what was unlawful and denied the truth in this life.

translation: "Seize him and drag him by force into the midst of the Hellfire."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:47) records the command that God will give to the angels of punishment on the Day of Judgment, addressed to the angels who guard Hellfire, concerning the arch-sinner, described in the preceding verses as the one who is a sinner and who denied the Day of Decision. The command shows the humiliation and utter helplessness of the one who in life was arrogant and thought himself mighty and noble. The word 'i'talūhu' conveys being dragged roughly and forcefully, as one drags a heavy, unwilling person, which stands in stark contrast to the pride he displayed in the world. The phrase 'to the midst of Hellfire' signifies that he will be thrown into its very center, where the punishment is most intense and there is no escape from any side. The verse teaches that disbelief in the Hereafter and arrogance toward God's signs lead to a just recompense, and that worldly status will offer no protection before divine judgment.

translation: Then pour over his head some of the torment of the boiling water.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ad-Dukhan 44:48) describes the command given to the angels of punishment on the Day of Judgment regarding the arrogant disbeliever, represented by Abu Jahl or those like him, who once boasted of being mighty and noble. After he is seized and dragged into the midst of Hellfire, the punishment is intensified by scalding water poured upon his head, the most honored part of the body and the seat of pride and arrogance. The verse teaches that divine recompense matches the offense: those who carried their heads high in defiance of God and mocked the warnings of the Hereafter will be humbled and tormented in the very place that symbolized their haughtiness, and that no worldly status can protect anyone from God's justice.

translation: Taste this! Indeed, you were the mighty, the honored!
interpretation: This verse (Surat ad-Dukhan 44:49) is spoken by the angels of punishment to a disbeliever, likely Abu Jahl, as he is dragged into the Fire. It is bitter mockery: he used to boast of his power and nobility and to think himself above accountability, and now those very claims are turned against him to expose how hollow they were. Worldly status, wealth and pride offer no protection before God's justice, and arrogance that rejects the truth ends in humiliation.

translation: Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.
interpretation: This verse is spoken to the deniers on the Day of Judgment, when the punishment they mocked is made real before them. In the world they disputed and doubted the resurrection, the reckoning, and the Hereafter, dismissing the warnings of the prophets as unproven. Now that the truth stands in front of them, their doubt is exposed as baseless and there is no room left for denial. The verse stresses that the Hereafter is certain and that the time for doubt and excuses has ended, so that the unbelievers meet the consequences of their own disbelief with full awareness. It also warns people to take the signs of God seriously while they still have the chance to believe and act.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure station.
interpretation: This verse (Ad-Dukhan 44:51) describes the reward of those who are mindful of God (al-muttaqin): in the Hereafter they will dwell in a place of complete safety, free from fear, grief, harm, expulsion, and death. The word 'amin' (secure) shows that their abode is not only pleasant but also permanently protected, which stands in contrast to the dread and punishment awaiting the wrongdoers described just before it. Taqwa, the God-consciousness that led them to guard themselves against sin in this life, is thus rewarded with lasting peace and security in the next.

translation: Amid gardens and springs.
interpretation: This verse describes the final abode of the God-conscious (al-muttaqin), who are promised a secure and blissful dwelling in Paradise. The gardens and flowing springs symbolize lasting comfort, abundance and tranquility, in contrast to the hardships of worldly life. It conveys that the reward for those who guarded themselves against sin and obeyed God is not only material delight but a state of peace and honor in His presence, where their lives are free from fear, want and sorrow.

translation: They will wear garments of fine silk and heavy brocade, sitting face to face.
interpretation: The verse describes the honor given to the God-fearing in Paradise (Surat al-Dukhan, 44:53). Their clothing of fine silk (sundus) and rich brocade (istabraq) shows that they are given the finest and most dignified attire, a reward for the modesty and restraint they practiced in the world. Their sitting face to face (mutaqabilin) shows that Paradise is a place of companionship, mutual affection, and equality. No one turns his back on another or feels contempt or resentment toward him, because hearts there are cleansed of hostility. Their joy is thus complete in both outward splendor and inward harmony.

translation: Thus it will be; and We will pair them with fair maidens with large, beautiful eyes.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 44:54) describes the culmination of the bliss granted to the God-fearing in Paradise, after mention of gardens, springs, fine silks, and security. Being 'paired' with 'hur 'in' signifies that the blessings of the Hereafter include perfect, pure companionship, free from the flaws of worldly life. The phrase 'Thus it will be' affirms that this reward is certain and complete, matching the description just given. Many commentators understand the 'hur' as pure, beautiful companions whose wide, lustrous eyes symbolize purity and beauty, indicating that Paradise fulfils every legitimate human longing for love, harmony and joy, as a recompense for righteousness and restraint in this world.

translation: They will call therein for every kind of fruit, in security.
interpretation: The verse describes the ease and security of the people of Paradise: whatever fruit they desire is theirs the moment they ask, without scarcity, effort, or delay. They call for it freely, and it comes with no fear of running out, of harm, sickness, or satiety, or of the blessing ever being taken away. The word 'secure' shows that the greatest part of Paradise's bounty is peace of heart, since the enjoyment is complete and permanent and is free from every worry that spoils worldly pleasures.

translation: They will not taste death therein, except the first death; and He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse describes the dwellers of Paradise, the God-fearing, as living in eternal life with no further death awaiting them. The only death they ever experienced was the one in this worldly life, which is already behind them. The exception 'except the first death' underscores that nothing remains of death for them, so their bliss is permanent and untroubled by fear of ending. Beyond this, God's greatest favor is that He shielded them from Hellfire, so their success is both the attainment of Paradise and salvation from punishment, which the Qur'an elsewhere calls the supreme triumph.

translation: A bounty from your Lord. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 44:57) closes the description of the righteous in Paradise, who are protected from the punishment of Hell. It teaches that entering Paradise and being saved from the Fire is not earned by deeds alone, as though deeds put God under an obligation, but is first of all a gift of God's grace and generosity. The believer's greatest success is therefore not worldly gain but receiving God's favor and mercy, which brings lasting safety and joy. This should lead believers to act with humility and gratitude, hoping in God's bounty rather than relying on their own merit.

translation: So We have only made it (the Qur'an) easy in your tongue, that perhaps they may remember.
interpretation: God explains that He revealed the Qur'an in the clear Arabic language of the Prophet Muhammad so that its message would be easily understood by those he addressed. The purpose of this ease is not mere recitation but reflection: when people grasp the warnings, promises, and guidance in plain words, they are more likely to take heed and turn back to God. The verse implies that those who still reject it have no excuse, since the barrier is not the difficulty of the message but their own heedlessness.

translation: So wait and watch; indeed, they too are waiting.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ad-Dukhan 44:59) closes the surah by urging the Prophet to patiently await God's decision between him and his opponents. The disbelievers wait for the Prophet's downfall, expecting him to fail and his message to vanish, but the outcome they are actually heading toward is divine judgment and the vindication of truth. The Prophet is told to wait with confidence and patience, because God's promise will be fulfilled, while the deniers are waiting, unknowingly, for their own punishment.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Meem.
interpretation: Ha-Meem is one of the 'disjointed letters' (al-muqatta'at) that open several surahs, and its precise meaning is known only to God. The most reasonable reading is that these letters point to the Qur'an's miraculous nature: the revelation is composed of the very letters of the Arabic alphabet that the Arabs used in their eloquent speech, yet they could not produce anything like it. The letters thus call the listener to attention and underline that the Book that follows is of divine origin, not human authorship. The Basmala preceding them places the whole revelation under God's mercy, signaling that the guidance to come is itself an expression of divine compassion.

translation: The revelation of the Book is from God, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is not a human composition but a revelation sent down from God. Two of His names are chosen to ground its authority. His might (al-'Aziz) means that no one can overpower His will or nullify His message, so the Book's guidance and warnings stand firm. His wisdom (al-Hakim) means that all He reveals is placed with perfect judgment, so its commands, stories, and laws serve real purposes and benefit human beings. The reader is therefore called to receive the Book with trust and obedience, recognizing it as the word of One who is both powerful enough to enforce what He says and wise enough to say only what is right.

translation: Indeed, in the heavens and the earth are signs for the believers.
interpretation: The order, vastness, and harmony of creation are not random but point to a Creator who is wise, powerful, and merciful. The verse says these signs are for the believers because faith opens a person's heart and mind to reflect on them sincerely: someone who already acknowledges God sees in the sky, the earth, and everything within them clear evidence of His oneness, knowledge, and care, which in turn deepens his certainty and gratitude. Contemplating the natural world is therefore an act of worship that strengthens faith.

translation: And in your creation and in all the living creatures He scatters throughout the earth are signs for a people who have firm faith.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection on the intricate design of human beings, from their origin in a drop of fluid through their stages of development, with their senses, intellect, and capacity for speech, and on the astonishing variety of animal life spread across the earth, each kind perfectly equipped for its environment and needs. Such order, wisdom, and purposeful balance cannot be the result of blind chance; they point to a single Creator who is All-Knowing, All-Powerful, and Merciful. The signs are said to be for those who have certainty (yuqinun), because conviction grows when a person moves beyond casual observation to deliberate contemplation. The one who is sure of God's existence and power sees in his own body and in every creature a proof that strengthens his faith, deepens his gratitude, and affirms that God alone deserves worship.

translation: And in the alternation of night and day, and in the provision God sends down from the sky by which He revives the earth after its death, and in the shifting of the winds, are signs for a people who use their reason.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the ordered rhythms of nature are not random but point to a single, wise, and merciful Creator. The succession of night and day, the rain that brings dead land back to life, and the changing directions and qualities of the winds all operate with precision and purpose, sustaining life. The revival of barren earth also serves as a reminder that God can resurrect the dead. Yet only those who reflect and use their intellect will read these phenomena as signs leading to faith, gratitude, and acknowledgment of God's oneness, while the heedless see them merely as routine events.

translation: These are the verses of God, which We recite to you in truth. In what statement, then, after God and His verses, will they believe?
interpretation: The verse points out that the revelation is self-evidently true, so a person who rejects it has no better source to turn to.
