The verse also warns that an open, attentive heart is what allows the Qur'an to bring about understanding and change.

translation: Indeed, those who have turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them—Satan has enticed them and prolonged their hopes.
interpretation: The verse explains that apostasy or turning away from the truth does not come from lack of evidence, since the guidance was already plain to them, but from the whispering of Satan, who makes their wrong path appear attractive and fills them with false hopes of a long life and of escaping accountability. Their retreat is thus a deliberate yielding to temptation and wishful delay of repentance, and it warns believers that knowing the truth is not enough unless they hold firmly to it and guard against self-deception.

translation: That is because they said to those who disliked what God has revealed, "We will obey you in some of the matter." And God knows their secrets.
interpretation: The verse explains why the hypocrites will meet such a terrible end at death: they secretly conspired with those who rejected the revelation, promising to side with them in part of their opposition to the Prophet and the Qur'an. Even a partial pledge of loyalty to the enemies of God's guidance, while outwardly professing faith, is a betrayal of faith itself, because faith demands wholehearted submission rather than selective obedience. Their secret conversations and private compromises are hidden from people but not from God, who knows all that they conceal. The verse warns that no concealed alliance or half-hearted allegiance against God's revelation escapes His knowledge or accountability.

translation: Then how will it be when the angels take their souls at death, striking their faces and their backs?
interpretation: The verse is a warning to the hypocrites (Surah Muhammad 47:27) who outwardly professed faith while secretly siding with those who opposed God's revelation and promising to obey them in some matters. Having described their hidden betrayal, the verse asks a rhetorical question: what will their condition be when death comes and they can no longer hide behind pretense? The angels who take their souls will strike their faces and backs, a vivid image of humiliating, painful punishment that begins at the moment of death. The blows to the face recall how they turned toward falsehood and confronted the truth, and the blows to the back recall how they turned away from obeying God. The verse teaches that duplicity and aligning oneself with falsehood bring a reckoning that cannot be avoided, and that the time to correct one's faith and conduct is now, while one still has life.

translation: That is because they followed what angered God and disliked His pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 47:28) explains why the souls of the hypocrites and disbelievers meet such a terrible fate at death: their own choices. They pursued paths that provoke God's anger, such as disobedience, disbelief, and secret opposition to the Prophet, and they found God's pleasure, which lies in faith and obedience, burdensome and distasteful. Because their hearts turned away from what God loves and toward what He hates, whatever good they may have done lost its value, since deeds are accepted only when they rest on sincere faith and the aim of pleasing God. The lesson is that a person's actions are only as sound as the orientation of the heart behind them, and that seeking God's pleasure is the foundation which preserves the worth of all deeds.

translation: Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will never bring to light their malice?
interpretation: The verse addresses the hypocrites, whose hearts are sick with doubt and hidden hatred toward the Prophet and the believers. It rebukes their false confidence that their concealed spite and ill will can stay secret forever. God's knowledge encompasses what is inside hearts, and He will expose it, whether through their slips of speech, their conduct, or events that reveal their true allegiance. The verse is a warning that outward pretense cannot hide inner corruption from God, and that He will eventually make it plain to others.

translation: And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their marks; but you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech. And Allah knows your deeds.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Muhammad (47:30), addresses the Prophet regarding the hypocrites in Medina. Allah tells him that He could have exposed them openly by outward signs, yet He left their identity partly veiled in His wisdom, giving them room to repent and preserving the community's order. Even so, their inner disbelief inevitably leaks out in how they speak: their innuendo, ambiguity, mockery, and evasiveness when faith, jihad, or the Prophet are mentioned. The verse teaches that speech reveals the heart, and that the real measure of a person is not outward appearance but what their words and conduct disclose. It closes with a reminder that Allah knows everyone's deeds, so judgment rests with Him, who knows hidden intentions perfectly, and the believers should neither be deceived by show nor judge beyond what is evident.

translation: And We will surely test you until We make evident those among you who strive and those who are steadfast, and We will test your reports.
interpretation: God declares that testing is a fixed divine practice for the believing community, not a sign of His displeasure. Hardship, fear, loss and the demands of struggle sift real commitment from mere claims. The phrase 'until We know' does not mean God gains new knowledge, since He knows all things beforehand. It means that what He knows becomes manifest in actual deeds and can be held to account. The test separates those who exert themselves in God's cause (the mujahidun) from those who endure with patience (the sabirun), so faith is shown in action and perseverance. 'Testing your reports' means that people's claims and the news about them are verified by how they behave under trial. The hypocrite's professions are exposed, and the sincere believer's loyalty is confirmed. The verse thus calls believers to strive and to be patient, and to expect that tests are the way sincerity is proven.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved and turned people away from the path of Allah and opposed the Messenger after guidance had become clear to them will never harm Allah in any way, and He will render their deeds worthless.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting the truth knowingly and actively obstructing others from it harms only the one who does so. Allah is entirely self-sufficient, so neither disbelief nor hostility toward His Messenger diminishes His power or the progress of His religion. The real loss falls on the opponents: because they chose defiance after the proof was plain, their deeds, including any apparent good or efforts to extinguish the message, will be nullified and bring them no reward. It is both a warning to those who persist in opposition and a reassurance to believers that Allah's cause will not be defeated by those who oppose it.

translation: O you who believe, obey God and obey the Messenger, and do not render your deeds void.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the worth of a believer's deeds depends on sincere, ongoing obedience to God and to His Messenger, whose guidance shows how God is to be served. Deeds are not safe merely because they were done; they can be nullified by things that contradict faith and obedience, such as hypocrisy, showing off, disbelief, turning away from the Messenger's guidance, or opposing him. The believer is therefore urged to protect their good works by remaining faithful to revelation and the Prophet's example, so that their efforts are not lost and bear fruit on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved and turned people away from the path of God, then died while they were disbelievers, God will never forgive them.
interpretation: The verse (Muhammad 47:34) teaches that forgiveness is withheld not merely because of past unbelief, but because of persisting in it to the very end. Those who rejected the truth and also obstructed others from the way of God compounded their guilt, and then died without repentance. Since God's mercy and forgiveness remain open to anyone who turns back to Him before death, the denial of forgiveness here is tied to dying in a state of disbelief, when the chance for repentance has ended. The verse thus underscores the seriousness of both rejecting faith and hindering others from it, and it stresses the importance of repentance while there is still time.

translation: So do not weaken and call for peace while you are the uppermost, and Allah is with you and will never deprive you of the rewards of your deeds.
interpretation: The verse urges believers not to lose heart or seek a humiliating truce out of fear or weakness when they hold the upper hand, whether through the truth of their cause, their moral and spiritual standing, or their actual strength. Seeking peace from a position of weakness and surrender, when one is in the stronger position, would be a failure of resolve. The believers are reassured by two promises: that Allah's support is with them, and that He will not diminish or waste the reward of their efforts and sacrifices. Steadfastness is therefore grounded in trust in divine help and in the certainty that no good deed is lost with Him.

translation: The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement. But if you believe and are mindful of God, He will give you your rewards, and He does not ask you for your wealth.
interpretation: The verse tells believers not to treat worldly life as the goal. Its pleasures, rivalries and accumulations are passing diversions that distract people from what is lasting, so they should not stake their lives on them. Real worth lies in faith and God-consciousness, and God promises full reward for these in the Hereafter. His call is also gentle. He does not demand all of your wealth, and He is not in need of it. What He asks of you, such as charity and spending in His cause, benefits you and is a means to your own reward. So the verse urges people to put the world in its proper place and to invest in what will last.

translation: If He were to ask you for it (all your wealth) and press you, you would withhold, and He would bring out your ill feelings.
interpretation: The verse (Muhammad 47:37) explains God's mercy in prescribing only a small portion of wealth, such as zakat and charity, instead of demanding all that people own. Human nature is inclined to miserliness, and if God demanded everything and pressed people for it, they would cling to their wealth, and their hidden resentment and spite would come to the surface, exposing the weakness of their faith. The legislation is therefore a kindness that takes human frailty into account, and it also serves as a test that reveals who is truly sincere in giving.

translation: Here you are, those who are called to spend in the cause of God, yet among you are those who withhold. And whoever withholds only withholds from himself. God is the Self-Sufficient, and you are the needy. And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charitable giving and sacrifice for God's cause are not favors done for God, who has no need of anything, but are for the benefit of the giver. A miser's stinginess harms only his own soul, since he forfeits reward, spiritual growth and God's pleasure. Human beings are wholly dependent on God, while He depends on none. The closing warning is that God's religion does not rely on any particular community: if believers abandon their duty, He can replace them with a people more devoted and obedient, so being among the first Muslims confers no guarantee of favor unless it is matched by action.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory.
interpretation: The 'clear opening' is most commonly understood as the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which seemed to many a setback but which God declares a manifest triumph. By ending hostilities, it opened the way for the free spread of Islam, for people to meet Muslims and hear the message, and for the later peaceful conquest of Mecca. The verse teaches that true victory is measured by God's wisdom and its outcomes, not by outward appearances, and that patience and trust in God's plan can turn what looks like concession into a lasting success.

translation: That Allah may forgive for you what preceded of your sin and what will follow, and complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, revealed after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, shows that the clear victory granted to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) carries four divine gifts: forgiveness covering all his shortcomings, past and future, which reflects his protection and high standing with God and the removal of any burden of blame; the completion of God's favor through prophethood, the spread of Islam, and eventual triumph; and continued guidance on the straight path, meaning steadfastness and success in his mission. The 'sins' are understood as the lapses and lesser slips that befit his high rank, since for the closest servants even the best of actions may be seen as falling short of what is due to God. Forgiveness here is therefore a mark of honor and assurance, and a sign that patience and trust in God's plan, even when events seem like setbacks, lead to the fullest blessing.

translation: And that God may help you with a mighty help.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Fath (48:3), completes the blessings God promises the Prophet Muhammad after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The 'mighty help' (nasran 'aziza) is a victory that is honorable, decisive and unassailable, one that no enemy can overturn or humiliate. It teaches that true triumph comes from God alone, and that what appeared on the surface to be a concession in the treaty was in reality a clear opening toward dignity and strength for the believers. Such help is granted to those who remain patient, trusting and obedient to God, even when circumstances seem unfavorable.

translation: It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers so that they would increase in faith along with their faith. And to God belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and God is ever All-Knowing and All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, teaches that inner calm and steadiness of heart are a gift from God that He places in the believers at moments of fear, uncertainty, and apparent setback. This sakina is not mere emotional comfort but a means of spiritual growth: when believers accept God's decree with trust and patience, as the Companions did in accepting terms that seemed unfavorable, their faith deepens beyond what it was before. The reminder that God commands the forces of the heavens and the earth shows that He needs no human strength to achieve His purposes, and that He can bring about victory or restraint by whatever means He wills, whether seen or unseen. The closing attributes, All-Knowing and All-Wise, assure the believer that every event, even one that looks like a loss, unfolds according to perfect knowledge and wise planning, so the proper response is trust, composure, and growing faith rather than anxiety or hasty action.

translation: That He may admit the believing men and the believing women into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and remove from them their misdeeds; and that is, in God's sight, a great triumph.
interpretation: The verse explains the purpose behind the tranquility and divine support God sent down upon the believers (as in Surat al-Fath): He strengthens their hearts and faith so that their steadfastness is rewarded with the highest outcome. Admission to Paradise, together with the erasure of their sins, shows that salvation has two sides: being cleansed of past faults and being given lasting bliss. Mentioning believing women alongside men affirms that both are equally accountable and equally rewarded, with reward depending on faith and deeds rather than gender. Calling this a 'great triumph in God's sight' teaches that true success is not worldly victory or gain but God's approval and the eternal home He grants, and that its worth is measured by God's own judgment.

translation: And that He may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, who think evil thoughts about God. Upon them is the turn of evil; God is angry with them, has cursed them, and has prepared Hell for them — and what an evil destination!
interpretation: The verse explains that one purpose of the believers' victory (Surah al-Fath) is divine justice against those who harbored false beliefs about God. Their gravest sin is 'thinking ill of God': they assumed God would not help His Messenger and the believers, and that the Muslim cause would be wiped out. This reveals a lack of true faith and trust in God's promise and power. The 'turn of evil' means the misfortune and ruin they anticipated for the believers rebounds upon themselves. Beyond worldly defeat, they face God's wrath, being cast far from His mercy, and the punishment of Hell. The verse teaches that a person's inner assumptions about God, whether trusting or suspicious, carry real moral weight and consequences, and that hope in God's help is part of faith.

translation: To God belong the soldiers (hosts) of the heavens and the earth, and God is ever Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that all forces in creation, whether angels, natural powers, or human beings, are instruments under God's command, so He needs no help from anyone and can bring about victory, calm, or punishment however and whenever He wills. Because He is Almighty, nothing can resist His decree; because He is All-Wise, He employs His forces with perfect wisdom, delaying or hastening events according to a purpose that may not be apparent to people. Believers are therefore meant to find reassurance and trust in His plan, and to understand that outcomes depend on His power and wisdom rather than on numbers or material strength.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner.
interpretation: God addresses the Prophet Muhammad, defining his threefold mission. As a witness, he testifies before God about the message he delivered and about the conduct of his community, and he stands as a model whose truthfulness and example bear witness to the truth of revelation. As a bearer of good news, he gives glad tidings of mercy, forgiveness and Paradise to those who believe and do righteous deeds. As a warner, he cautions those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing about the consequences of that path in this life and in the Hereafter. Together these roles show that the Prophet's task is to convey, guide and call people to account through clear communication, balancing hope and fear, not to compel anyone to believe.

translation: That you [people] may believe in Allah and His Messenger, and honor him and respect him, and glorify Him morning and evening.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Fath, 48:9) states the purpose of sending the Prophet as witness, bearer of good news and warner: to bring people to a faith that shows itself in conduct. Belief in God and His Messenger is not merely verbal but carries obligations. Supporting and honoring the Messenger (ta'zir and tawqir) means defending his mission and revering his status and message, which is a form of obedience to God Himself since he conveys God's guidance. Glorifying God 'morning and evening' (tasbih) points to constant remembrance of Him, so that the whole day is framed by worship. The verse thus joins right belief, due respect for the Prophet, and continuous devotion to God as the foundation of a believer's life, with the glorification belonging to God alone while the honor and support are owed to the Messenger as His servant.

translation: Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, [O Muhammad], are actually pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is over their hands. So whoever breaks his pledge only breaks it to the harm of himself; and whoever fulfills what he has promised Allah, He will grant him a great reward.
interpretation: The verse, revealed regarding the Pledge of Ridwan at Hudaybiyyah, teaches that swearing loyalty to the Prophet is in truth a covenant with God Himself, since the Prophet acts as God's messenger and his command is God's command. The phrase 'the hand of God is above their hands' conveys that God witnesses, supports, and guarantees the pledge, so it carries the gravity of a sacred oath. Consequently, betraying the pledge harms only the betrayer, because he forfeits God's help and incurs the consequences of covenant-breaking, while God cannot be harmed. Whoever remains faithful to his promise, even amid danger and uncertainty, will be rewarded by God with an immense recompense, in this world and the next.

translation: Those of the Bedouin Arabs who stayed behind will say to you, "Our possessions and our families kept us occupied, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say, "Who then can avail you anything against God if He intends harm for you or intends benefit for you? Rather, God is ever Aware of what you do."
interpretation: The verse exposes the insincerity behind the excuses of those hypocritical desert Arabs who avoided going out with the Prophet (peace be upon him) at the time of Hudaybiyyah. They claimed that worldly duties, wealth and family prevented them, and then asked him to seek forgiveness for them, though they did not truly feel remorse and did not believe that their absence was a sin. Their words were only on their tongues and not in their hearts. God teaches that faith is measured by inner conviction and not by polished speech, and that no excuse can deceive Him. The rebuke 'Who can avail you anything against God?' reminds them that neither property nor family can protect them from harm or secure any benefit unless God wills it, so fear of losing them was no justification for abandoning obedience. The verse closes by affirming that God is fully aware of their deeds and intentions, so they cannot hide the real reason for their staying behind, which was doubt and the assumption that the Prophet and the believers would never return.

translation: Rather, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, ever. That was made attractive in your hearts, and you harbored an evil thought, and you became a people ruined.
interpretation: This verse rebukes the hypocrites among the desert Arabs who stayed behind from the journey that led to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Their excuse of being busy with property and families was not the real reason. They were convinced that the Prophet and the believers would be wiped out by Quraysh and never come home, so they chose safety over loyalty. Satan beautified this despairing assumption in their hearts until they accepted it as certain. Their thinking was an evil thought about God, since it denied His promise to support His Messenger and rested on doubt in His power and wisdom. Because of this corrupt belief and the choice that followed from it, they became a people 'bur', meaning spiritually barren and destined for ruin, with no good in them and no deeds of value. The verse teaches that thinking ill of God and abandoning the believers in times of trial is a sign of weak faith and brings loss in this world and the next.

translation: And whoever does not believe in God and His Messenger — then indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 48:13) makes faith in God and in His Messenger together the criterion of salvation, so that neither outward claims nor mere association with the believing community are enough. Those who reject this belief, or who pretend to it while inwardly doubting, as the hypocrites and the Bedouin who lagged behind from the Prophet's journey did, cannot hide their true state from God, who knows what hearts conceal. The words 'We have prepared' indicate that the punishment is already ready and certain, and not merely a possibility. The word 'blazing Fire' (sa'ir) conveys its intensity. The verse serves as both a warning and a call: sincere belief is required, and hollow excuses or hypocrisy will not protect anyone from the consequences of disbelief.

translation: To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse grounds God's judgment in His absolute sovereignty over all creation: since everything belongs to Him, He alone decides matters of forgiveness and punishment, and no one can claim a right against Him. Yet His will is not arbitrary or harsh, because it is closely tied to His own attributes. The closing words, 'ever Forgiving, Merciful,' show that mercy and forgiveness are the dominant themes of His dealings with people. This should lead believers to fear His justice while placing great hope in His mercy, to turn to Him in repentance, and never to despair of His forgiveness.

translation: Those who were left behind will say, when you set out to take the spoils of war: "Let us follow you." They wish to change the word of God. Say: "You shall not follow us; thus God has said beforehand." Then they will say: "Rather, you envy us." Nay, but they understand only a little.
interpretation: The verse exposes the opportunism of the Bedouins who shunned the Prophet's march to Hudaybiyyah when danger loomed, yet will eagerly ask to join the expedition to Khaybar once easy booty is certain. God had already decreed that the spoils of Khaybar were reserved for those who had pledged allegiance and been present at Hudaybiyyah, so their request amounts to an attempt to alter God's decree. The Prophet is told to refuse them firmly, citing God's earlier ruling. Their retort that the believers merely envy them shows their distorted outlook: they blame others for their own forfeited reward, because their understanding is confined to worldly gain and they grasp little of faith, sincerity, and the consequences of abandoning the Messenger in time of trial.

translation: Say to the Bedouins who lagged behind: 'You will be called against a people of great military might; you will fight them, or they will submit. If you obey, God will give you a good reward; but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment.'
interpretation: The verse offers the Bedouins who stayed behind from the Hudaybiyyah expedition a chance at redemption. Their earlier excuses exposed weak faith, and God now tests their sincerity with a future call to fight a formidable people. Whether that call is read as referring to the Hawazin and Thaqif, to the campaigns against the apostates, or to the Persians and Byzantines, the point is the same: the people in question would either be fought or would submit. The verse ties reward and punishment to obedience. Those who answer the call sincerely will earn a good reward, while those who turn away again, repeating their former desertion, will face a painful punishment. In this way it teaches that repentance is open to those who failed before, but it is proven only by real obedience when the next test arrives, not by words or excuses.

translation: There is no blame on the blind, nor any blame on the lame, nor any blame on the sick. And whoever obeys God and His Messenger, He will admit him into Gardens beneath which rivers flow; but whoever turns away, He will punish him with a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse (al-Fath 48:17) lifts the obligation of military campaigning from those with genuine physical disabilities, showing that God's law accounts for human capacity and does not burden anyone beyond what they can bear. Their excuse is accepted because the inability is real, not a pretext. The verse then moves to a general principle: reward and punishment depend on obedience to God and His Messenger, not on outward ability alone. Those who obey, including the disabled who are sincere in intention, receive Paradise, while those who deliberately turn away, using no valid excuse, face a painful punishment. The verse therefore distinguishes between legitimate inability, which is forgiven, and willful disobedience, which is held to account.

translation: Indeed, God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquility upon them and rewarded them with an imminent victory.
interpretation: This verse, revealed after the Hudaybiyyah episode, shows that God's pleasure was earned by the sincerity of the Companions' hearts and not by the outward act of the pledge alone. They swore loyalty to the Prophet, even to the point of fighting, when they feared that Quraysh had killed 'Uthman, and their pledge was made with no guarantee of success. God knew the true state of their hearts, so He granted them sakinah, an inner calm and steadfastness, which let them accept the seemingly unfavorable treaty with patience and discipline. As a reward for their loyalty, He gave them a near conquest, understood as the victory of Khaybar and, more broadly, the way opened to the conquest of Mecca. The lesson is that sincere trust and obedience bring God's approval, inner peace, and success that comes sooner than expected.

translation: And abundant spoils which they will take. And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Fath, 48:19) continues God's promise to the believers who pledged allegiance under the tree at Hudaybiyyah. Besides the nearby victory mentioned just before it, God promises them many future gains of war, understood mainly as the spoils of Khaybar and later conquests, as a reward for their sincerity and loyalty. The closing attributes explain why this promise can be trusted: God is 'Aziz (Mighty), so no power can stop what He has decreed for His servants, and Hakim (Wise), so He distributes victories and gains according to perfect wisdom and timing. This teaches that apparent setbacks, like the treaty of Hudaybiyyah that seemed unfavorable, can conceal great blessings, and that obedience and patience are rewarded in both spiritual and worldly ways.

translation: God has promised you abundant spoils which you will take, and He has hastened this one for you, and has restrained the hands of people from you, so that it may be a sign for the believers and that He may guide you on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse, revealed after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, reassures the believers that God's promises are true and that what seemed like a setback was in fact a blessing. The 'hastened' gain is commonly understood as the spoils of Khaybar, or the peace and security of the treaty itself, while the many future gains point to later conquests. God held back the hostile hands of the Quraysh and their allies, who might have attacked the Muslims and their families, and this protection became a visible sign confirming the Prophet's truthfulness and showing believers that God's care surrounds those who trust Him. Through such events, as trust deepens and obedience to the Prophet is tested and vindicated, God increases the believers' guidance and keeps them firm on the straight path, the path of certainty, patience, and reliance on God's wisdom even when outward circumstances appear unfavorable.

translation: And there is another [victory] which you were not able to attain; Allah has already encompassed it. And Allah is ever Able to do all things.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Fath 48:21) tells the believers that besides the spoils and victories already granted to them, there is a further gain that was beyond their capacity to achieve by their own strength, such as the later conquest of Mecca or the lands of Persia and Byzantium. Allah has already encompassed it in His knowledge and decree, so it is secured for them in due time and will come only by His will, not by their power. The closing phrase affirms that nothing is beyond Allah's ability, so the believers should trust His promise, remain patient, and not measure what is possible by their own limited means.

translation: And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs in flight; then they would find neither protector nor helper.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Fath 48:22) assures the believers that their strength comes from God's support rather than from numbers or equipment. Had the disbelievers of Quraysh chosen to fight at Hudaybiyyah, God would have given the believers victory and the enemy would have fled in defeat. They would then have had no ally to shield them and no helper to reverse the outcome, since those who oppose God's cause are left without real support. The restraint of fighting at Hudaybiyyah was therefore a mercy and wisdom from God, not a sign of Muslim weakness, and the treaty that followed opened the way to a greater victory.

translation: [Such is] the established way of God which has passed before; and you will never find any change in the way of God.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God governs human history by fixed, consistent laws: truth ultimately prevails over falsehood, and those who persist in denial and hostility toward the faithful meet defeat, just as earlier nations did. These patterns do not shift to favor any group because of its power, lineage or claims; outcomes follow moral and causal principles that God has set. This should reassure believers that divine justice is dependable, and warn wrongdoers that the fate of previous peoples awaits them if they follow the same path.

translation: And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Mecca after He had given you victory over them. And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse recalls the events around Hudaybiyyah, when armed Quraysh men approached the Muslims and were overpowered and captured, then released without a battle. God shows that this restraint was His favor and wisdom: He held back both sides from bloodshed near the Sacred Precinct so that peace could take hold, believers still living in Mecca would not be harmed unknowingly, and the way would be opened for Islam to spread through the treaty. Though the Muslims had the upper hand, they showed discipline and obedience, and God, who sees all their deeds, notes their restraint and guides events toward the best outcome.

translation: They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and prevented the offering from reaching its place of sacrifice. And had it not been for believing men and believing women whom you did not know—that you might trample them and thus incur guilt on their account without knowledge—(Allah would have permitted you to enter Makkah). This was so that Allah may admit into His mercy whomever He wills. Had they been distinguishable, We would have inflicted on those among them who disbelieved a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse refers to the events of Hudaybiyyah, when the Quraysh blocked the Prophet and the Muslims from performing the pilgrimage and stopped the sacrificial animals from reaching Makkah. It explains the divine wisdom behind restraining the Muslims from fighting their way in: Makkah still contained hidden believers, men and women who concealed their faith, and an armed clash would have caused the believers to unknowingly kill them and bear the distress and blame of that harm. God's restraint was therefore a mercy that protected those vulnerable believers and left the door open for others to enter Islam, as indeed happened after the treaty. Had the believers and disbelievers been separate and distinguishable, God would have allowed the disbelievers to be punished at the believers' hands with a painful punishment.

translation: When those who disbelieved set in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance, Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and bound them to the word of piety, for they were most deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse recalls the day of Hudaybiyyah, when the Quraysh, driven by tribal pride and stubborn arrogance, barred the Prophet and his companions from the Sacred Mosque and refused even to let the treaty be written with 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' or to call him 'Messenger of Allah'. It contrasts two responses to provocation: the disbelievers acted from the blind, ego-driven fury of pre-Islamic tribalism, while the believers, though angered, were given divine calm (sakinah) that kept them from rash retaliation and let them accept the treaty's apparent humiliation for the sake of a greater good. This restraint reflects the 'word of piety', the declaration of faith and the God-consciousness that goes with it, which Allah fixed firmly in their hearts because He knew they were truly fit for it. Real strength lies in disciplined, God-conscious composure rather than in pride-driven reaction, and Allah's perfect knowledge of hearts means He grants His peace and guidance to those who are deserving.

translation: Indeed, Allah has fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and hair cut short, not fearing. He knew what you did not know, and He ordained besides that a near victory.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Prophet's dream that he and his Companions entered Mecca and performed the pilgrimage. When the Muslims were turned back at Hudaybiyyah and some doubted the dream, God affirmed that it was true and would come to pass, but in His appointed time, not in that year. The phrase 'if Allah wills' teaches that all future events depend on God's will and wisdom. God knew the benefits hidden in the treaty that the believers did not see: the peace that allowed Islam to spread, and the people who would enter the faith. So before the promised entry into Mecca, He gave a near victory, which is the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, and, according to many commentators, the conquest of Khaybar. The verse teaches trust in God's promise and wisdom even when events seem to contradict expectations.

translation: He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion. And sufficient is God as a Witness.
interpretation: God declares that Muhammad was sent with true guidance and a just, truthful way of life whose proofs, clarity, and moral soundness will ultimately rise above every other creed, whether through argument and evidence, or through historical success and spread. This outcome does not depend on human approval or on the objections of opponents, because God Himself bears witness to the Messenger's truthfulness and to the promise of the religion's triumph. His testimony is enough to settle the matter, which reassures believers facing hardship and rebukes those who deny.

translation: Muhammad is the Messenger of God; and those with him are firm and severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration. That is their description in the Torah. And their description in the Gospel is like a seed that sends forth its shoots, then strengthens them, so they grow thick and stand firm upon their stalks, delighting the sowers, that He may enrage the disbelievers through them. God has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse portrays the ideal community formed around the Prophet: its members combine firmness in defending their faith against hostility with tenderness and compassion toward one another, and their inner devotion shows in constant worship and sincere seeking of God's favor rather than worldly gain. The luminous mark of humility and piety from prostration is visible in their demeanor. Their growth is likened to a seed that begins small and weak, then gradually strengthens, thickens, and stands firm, so that onlookers admire it. This signifies that the believers began few and vulnerable, but through mutual support and God's help they matured into a powerful, flourishing community, a sight that provokes the rage of the disbelievers. The verse ends by making the promised forgiveness and great reward conditional on genuine faith and righteous action, so that merely belonging to the community is not enough without sustained sincerity and good deeds.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger, and fear God. Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse sets out the basic etiquette of faith: believers must not rush ahead of divine revelation or the Prophet's guidance by issuing rulings, forming judgments, or acting on personal opinion or custom before God and His Messenger have spoken. True faith means submitting one's own judgment to revealed guidance and waiting upon it with humility. The command to be mindful of God supports this by reminding believers that their intentions and conduct are always observed, and the closing description of God as All-Hearing and All-Knowing warns that every word and hidden motive is known to Him, so presuming to lead where He has not permitted is a serious matter.

translation: O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds become void while you are unaware.
interpretation: This verse teaches that faith must be expressed through reverence and good manners toward the Messenger. Respect for him is part of respect for the revelation he carries, so treating him as an equal in conversation, or letting one's own opinion drown out his guidance, shows a heart that does not truly honor his station. Such disrespect can grow unnoticed into arrogance and disregard for his authority, which can erode a person's good deeds without their realizing it. The warning that deeds may be nullified 'while you are unaware' shows that spiritual harm often begins with small lapses in humility, and that believers must keep watch over their hearts and their conduct toward the Prophet, in his lifetime and in honoring his teachings after his death.

translation: Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of God are the ones whose hearts God has tested for righteousness. For them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward conduct reveals the state of the heart. Lowering one's voice before the Prophet is not mere etiquette but a sign of reverence and awareness of God, and it shows that inner piety (taqwa) has taken root. God 'tested' their hearts, refining and purifying them until they were fit for righteousness, so their restraint reflects a tried and sincere devotion. Because they honored the one God sent as His messenger, they are promised forgiveness for their shortcomings and a great reward. In a broader sense, the verse affirms that respect for the Prophet, his words, and his legacy is an expression of faith, and that humility in speech and manner is a mark of a God-conscious heart.

translation: Indeed, those who call out to you [O Muhammad] from outside the private chambers — most of them do not use reason.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 49:4) rebukes those who, in ignorance of proper manners, shouted for the Prophet from outside his wives' private rooms rather than waiting patiently for him to come out. The Qur'an attributes this to a lack of 'aql (sound judgment): a person who truly understands the Prophet's station and the sanctity of his home would recognize that such behavior is disrespectful and would restrain himself. The lesson is that reverence toward the Messenger and respect for people's privacy are signs of wisdom and understanding, while rudeness and impatience reveal a failure to reflect. It also teaches believers to observe etiquette when seeking an audience with those deserving honor, and to wait with patience until they are received.

translation: And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 49:5) teaches proper conduct toward the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Those who called out to him impatiently from outside his private quarters would have done better to wait calmly until he came out on his own. Patience here expresses respect for the dignity of the Messenger and for his time and privacy, and it is better for the believers in this world and the next because it reflects good manners and reverence. The closing words, 'God is Forgiving and Merciful,' reassure those who erred out of ignorance or haste: God does not condemn them harshly but pardons them when they learn and correct themselves, while still guiding them toward better etiquette. The lesson extends beyond this incident to a general principle of courtesy, restraint, and humility toward those whom one should honor, such as the Prophet, scholars, and elders.

translation: O you who believe, if a wrongdoer comes to you with a piece of news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and then become regretful over what you have done.
interpretation: This verse sets out a principle of due diligence in how a community handles information. Believers are not to act on a report simply because it has been delivered, especially when the source is known for unreliability or moral corruption (fasiq). They must investigate and confirm it before reacting. Acting on unverified claims can lead to unjust harm against innocent people, whether through violence, punishment, slander, or broken relationships, and the damage cannot always be undone, leaving only regret. The verse thus protects social justice and trust by requiring that judgments rest on verified knowledge rather than rumor, suspicion, or the word of untrustworthy people. It also implies that a person's reliability bears on how far their testimony can be trusted.

translation: And know that among you is the Messenger of God. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would surely suffer hardship. But God has endeared faith to you and made it pleasing in your hearts, and has made disbelief, defiance, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse reminds the believers that the Prophet is a divinely guided leader living among them, so they should not press their own opinions or impulses on him, because human judgment is limited and acting on whims would bring them hardship and harm. His guidance, grounded in revelation, is the safeguard of their welfare. It then reminds them that their love of faith, and their inner aversion to disbelief, wrongdoing, and disobedience, is not their own achievement but a grace from God, who places faith in the heart and makes it beautiful there. Those whose hearts have been shaped in this way, who love what God loves and dislike what He dislikes, are the truly rightly guided. The proper response is humility toward the Prophet and gratitude to God.

translation: A favour from God and a blessing. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 49:8) comes after the description of believers whom God has endeared to faith and made averse to disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. It teaches that their right guidance is not something they earned by their own power or merit; it is purely a grace and bounty from God. The closing names, 'All-Knowing, All-Wise,' show that God grants this favour with perfect knowledge of who is sincere and deserving of guidance, and with wisdom in how and when He bestows it. The believer should therefore respond with humility and gratitude, and credit any inclination toward faith and righteousness to God's gift rather than to personal achievement.

translation: And if two parties of the believers fight each other, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of God. Then if it returns, make peace between them with justice and act equitably. Indeed, God loves those who act equitably.
interpretation: This verse lays down a path for settling conflict within the Muslim community, and the path has stages. Believers must first try to reconcile the two sides, because the bond of faith continues even when fighting breaks out. If one side refuses reconciliation and persists in aggression, the community, through its legitimate authority, is obliged to restrain that side, by force if needed, but only until it returns to God's command, meaning it stops its aggression and accepts the ruling of truth. The aim is to end injustice and restore peace, not to destroy the wrongdoers or take revenge. Once the aggressor yields, the fighting must stop and the settlement must be fair, free of favoritism, punitive excess, or settling scores. The verse ends by stressing that God loves those who are just, so justice is the standard even toward a party that has just been fought.

translation: The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.
interpretation: The verse establishes that faith creates a bond of brotherhood stronger than tribe, lineage, or interest, so a quarrel between two believers is a family matter that the wider community must not ignore. Those who are not party to the dispute are obliged to step in and reconcile the two sides with justice, which preserves the unity and security of the community. The command to fear Allah reminds believers that reconciliation must be done sincerely and fairly, free of partiality or personal motives. It also promises that those who uphold these bonds of brotherhood and peacemaking place themselves within Allah's mercy.

translation: O you who believe, let not one group of men ridicule another group, for perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule other women, for perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another, nor call each other by offensive nicknames. How evil is the name of wickedness after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse lays down the ethics of respect that hold a believing community together. Mockery rests on the false assumption that outward status, wealth, or appearance shows a person's real worth, yet true standing belongs to God, who alone knows hearts, so the one mocked may be better in His sight than the mocker. Because believers form one body, defaming or insulting a fellow believer is like defaming oneself, and giving someone a demeaning nickname wounds their dignity. To behave this way after accepting faith is a contradiction: it earns the label of 'wickedness' (fusuq), which is a shameful name for someone who has professed belief. The way out is sincere repentance, and whoever refuses to repent and persists in humiliating others commits injustice against both others and himself.

translation: O you who believe, avoid much suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sin. And do not spy, nor let some of you backbite others. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear God; indeed, God is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse sets out ethics for protecting the dignity and trust of the believing community, moving step by step from the heart to the tongue. It begins with inner thoughts: believers should avoid baseless, ill-founded suspicion of others, because assuming the worst without evidence can become a sin and leads to injustice. Suspicion then drives people to investigate hidden faults, so the verse forbids spying, which means probing into the private affairs and concealed failings of others. The last step is backbiting, which means speaking of someone in their absence in a way they would dislike. The Qur'an gives a vivid image of how ugly this is: it is like eating the flesh of your own dead brother. The victim cannot defend himself, the act violates the bond of brotherhood, and any natural sense would recoil from it. The verse then calls for taqwa, consciousness of God, as the inner safeguard for these behaviors. It ends with hope: whoever has fallen into these faults can repent, and God accepts repentance and is merciful. The believer should therefore stop, seek forgiveness, and, where possible, make amends.

translation: O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse establishes the fundamental equality of all human beings, who share a single origin, and presents the diversity of nations, tribes, and lineages not as grounds for pride or superiority but as a means of mutual recognition, cooperation, and understanding. True honor and worth are not determined by race, ancestry, wealth, or status, but solely by taqwa, that is, God-consciousness, moral integrity, and righteous conduct. Since God is All-Knowing and All-Aware of what lies within hearts and of people's real standing, only He can truly judge who is most noble, so people should abandon arrogance and boasting of lineage and instead strive for piety and good character.

translation: The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts. But if you obey God and His Messenger, He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful." (Qur'an 49:14)
interpretation: The verse distinguishes between outward submission (islam) and inward faith (iman). Some desert Arabs, newly joining the Muslim community, claimed full faith, perhaps seeking status or benefits. God teaches that true faith is a settled conviction of the heart that shows itself in sincere obedience, sacrifice, and trust, while mere verbal or outward acceptance is only the first step of submission. The Bedouins are not condemned for their submission, which is accepted and protects them in the community, but they are corrected for overstating their spiritual rank. The path is left open: if they sincerely obey God and His Messenger, none of their good deeds will be diminished, and God will forgive their shortcomings and show mercy as their faith deepens. The lesson is humility in self-assessment: faith is not a claim to be announced but a reality to be cultivated and proven through conduct.

translation: The believers are only those who have believed in God and His Messenger and then have not doubted, and who strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of God. Those are the truthful ones.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hujurat 49:15) defines true faith as more than a verbal claim. It begins with inward certainty, belief in God and His Messenger that stays firm and is never shaken by doubt, and it is proven by outward sacrifice, giving up one's wealth and one's self in striving for God's cause. The preceding verses rebuke the Bedouins who said 'we have believed' while faith had not yet entered their hearts. The verse therefore sets the real standard: sincere faith is unwavering conviction, shown through costly action. Those who meet it are the 'truthful' (as-sadiqun), because their deeds confirm their words and their claim of faith is true.

translation: Say: Would you inform Allah about your religion, while Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth? And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who claim faith by their words alone, as the desert Arabs did when they said 'We believe.' Faith is not established by a verbal declaration that one presents to God as if He needed to be informed or persuaded. God already knows what is in every heart and everything in creation, so a profession of belief means nothing unless it is matched by sincere conviction and action. Claims of piety cannot deceive the One whose knowledge encompasses all things, and a person's true standing with God depends on the reality of their inner faith, not on what they announce.

translation: They count it as a favor to you that they have submitted. Say: Do not count your submission as a favor to me. Rather, it is God who confers a favor upon you in that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who treat their embrace of Islam as a kindness to the Prophet, as if he owed them gratitude. It teaches that guidance is a gift from God alone. Whoever accepts faith has received a blessing and has not done anyone a service, so a believer should respond with humility and thanks to God and not with pride or a sense of entitlement. The phrase 'if you are truthful' makes the point that sincere faith shows itself in gratitude for having been guided, while claiming to have done a favor by believing exposes a flaw in one's claim to faith.

translation: Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse reminds believers that nothing is hidden from God, neither the unseen realities beyond human perception nor the hidden intentions behind visible deeds. Because God's knowledge encompasses what is secret in the cosmos and His sight encompasses every action, a person is called to sincerity and accountability. Outward claims, private motives, and concealed conduct are equally known to Him, so one should act with integrity, whether observed by people or not, and be mindful that every deed will be weighed with perfect knowledge and justice.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.
interpretation: The isolated letter 'Qaf' opens the chapter as a reminder that the Qur'an is composed of the very letters and sounds familiar to the Arabs, yet its eloquence is beyond human imitation. God then swears by the Qur'an, describing it as 'majid' (glorious, noble, abundant in goodness and guidance), to affirm its exalted rank and the truth of what the chapter will go on to establish: that Muhammad is a true warner, and that resurrection and the final reckoning, which the disbelievers find astonishing, are certain. The oath by the Qur'an thus asserts that the book's own majesty is itself a proof of the truth of its message.

translation: Rather, they marvel that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, 'This is a strange thing.'
interpretation: The verse shows that the disbelievers' rejection of the Prophet Muhammad was rooted in pride and prejudice rather than in reason or evidence. They could not accept that God would choose a mortal man from their own community, someone they knew well and saw as no better than themselves, to warn them of the Hereafter and accountability. Their astonishment reveals a closed mindset: instead of weighing the message on its merits, they dismissed it as strange because it disturbed their inherited beliefs and social standing. The verse thus teaches that the truth is often resisted not for lack of proof but because of arrogance and attachment to familiar customs, and that a warner coming from among the people is itself a mercy and a proof against them, since his honesty and character were known to them.

translation: "When we have died and become dust, [shall we be resurrected]? That is a distant return."
interpretation: The verse (Qaf 50:3) records the disbelievers' astonished denial of bodily resurrection. They judge God's power by human limits, reasoning that once the body has decayed into dust, bringing it back to life is impossible and unthinkable. The Qur'an answers this objection in the verses that follow: God knows precisely what the earth diminishes of them, and a record preserving everything is with Him. The One who created them in the first place is able to recreate them, so what they consider far-fetched is easy for God, and the resurrection is certain.

translation: We have already known what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a book that preserves everything.
interpretation: The disbelievers denied resurrection, asking how bodies that have disintegrated into dust could ever be brought back. The verse answers that God's knowledge encompasses every particle of their bodies that the earth consumes after death. Nothing is lost or hidden from Him, and there is also a preserved record with Him in which all things are written and guarded. Since He knows exactly what has decayed and where it has gone, He can reassemble and resurrect each person, so the doubt about resurrection rests on a misunderstanding of God's knowledge and power.

translation: Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused and troubled state.
interpretation: This verse (Qaf 50:5) explains that rejecting the truth, here the Prophet's message and the revelation, leaves people without any stable ground. Those who deny the truth once it has plainly reached them cannot settle on a coherent belief. Their views shift and contradict one another: they call the Prophet a poet, a soothsayer or a madman, and they cannot agree on any one account. The word 'marij' conveys something mixed up and entangled, like a ring that turns back on itself. This describes the inner and outer turmoil that follows from abandoning the clear truth. Whoever holds to the truth finds clarity and steadiness, while whoever rejects it is left in doubt and contradiction.

translation: Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it and adorned it, and how it has no cracks?
interpretation: The verse invites the deniers of resurrection to reflect on the heavens as evidence of God's power and wisdom. The sky is a flawless structure, raised without rifts or flaws and adorned with stars and celestial beauty. The One who could create something so vast, ordered and beautiful is certainly able to bring the dead back to life. Looking at creation should therefore lead a person from heedlessness to recognition of the Creator's might, and to accepting the truth of revelation and the Hereafter.

translation: And the earth We have spread out, and cast therein firmly set mountains, and caused to grow therein every beautiful kind of plant.
interpretation: The verse points to God's deliberate design of the earth as a place fit for human life: He extended it and made it broad and habitable, anchored it with mountains so that it stays stable and does not shake beneath its inhabitants, and filled it with plants of every pairing and variety, pleasing to the eye and beneficial for sustenance. These blessings are signs of God's power, wisdom and mercy, meant to move people to reflect on the Creator who brings forth such order and beauty, to be grateful to Him, and to accept that the One who gives life to the dead earth is able to resurrect the dead.

translation: An insight and a reminder for every servant who turns (to God) in repentance.
interpretation: This verse (Qaf 50:8) follows the mention of the heavens built without flaw, the earth spread out with firm mountains, and the growth of every beautiful pair of plants. It teaches that these signs in creation are meant to open the inner eye and awaken remembrance, but only the one who turns back to God with a humble and attentive heart actually benefits from them. Reflecting on the order and beauty of the universe leads such a person to recognize the Creator's power, including His ability to resurrect the dead, and to return to Him in repentance and obedience. The one who is heedless or stubborn sees the same signs yet gains no lesson, while the penitent servant draws insight and reminder from them.

translation: And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens and the grain of the harvest.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy in sustaining life: rain is called blessed because it brings abundant good, reviving dead land and producing both orchards that give fruit and staple grains that people harvest for their food. It invites reflection that the regular cycle of rain and growth is not a mere natural accident but a sign of the Creator's deliberate provision, and therefore of His ability to resurrect the dead, as the following verses link this renewal of the earth to the resurrection. Gratitude, trust in God, and recognition of His signs in everyday blessings are the lessons to draw.

translation: And the tall palm trees, having layered clusters of dates.
interpretation: The verse, part of a passage in Surah Qaf that lists signs of God's power in creation, points to the palm tree as evidence for resurrection. Its towering height and its orderly, tightly packed spadices of fruit show deliberate design and generous provision. The One who brings forth such abundance from dry, lifeless soil can just as easily bring the dead back to life, so the natural world becomes a reminder to reflect on God's creative power and to accept the reality of the afterlife.

translation: As provision for the servants; and We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence [from the graves].
interpretation: God points to the rain that makes gardens, grain, and tall palm trees grow as sustenance for His servants, and to the barren, lifeless earth that revives after the rain. The same power that brings dead soil back to life with no difficulty can raise the dead from their graves on the Day of Resurrection. The verse invites people to read the natural world as a daily sign of resurrection, so that denying the afterlife appears unreasonable when the renewal of life is visible all around them.

translation: Before them, the people of Noah, the Companions of ar-Rass, and Thamud also denied the truth.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and warns his opponents: rejecting a messenger is not a new phenomenon but a recurring pattern in human history. Earlier nations such as the people of Noah, the Companions of ar-Rass, and Thamud all denied the messengers sent to them, and each met the consequences of their denial. The Meccan disbelievers are thus reminded that their stubborn rejection places them in the same line as those destroyed communities, and that the Prophet's patience in the face of denial follows the path of the earlier prophets, with God's promise of ultimate vindication for the truth and accountability for those who reject it.

translation: And [the people of] 'Ad, and Pharaoh, and the brethren of Lot,
interpretation: This verse belongs to the passage in Surah Qaf that lists earlier nations who denied their messengers, including 'Ad, Pharaoh and the people of Lot, who are called his 'brethren' because they were his kin by their shared community and dwelling, not because they shared his faith. The verse stands as a warning to the Makkan deniers. It teaches that the denial of prophets is a recurring pattern in history, and that each of these peoples met the consequence promised to them. So those who reject the Messenger and the Resurrection should not expect a different outcome, since God's way with deniers does not change.

translation: And the Companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubba'. Each of them denied the messengers, so My warning was fulfilled.
interpretation: The verse recalls peoples of the past, such as the community of Shu'ayb (the Companions of the Thicket) and the people of Tubba', who were powerful and prosperous yet rejected the prophets sent to them. The warning of punishment came true against every one of them. The lesson is that divine justice follows a constant pattern: denying God's messengers, whatever a nation's strength, wealth, or era, leads to the fulfillment of God's threatened consequences. This should warn those who deny the Prophet Muhammad that they are not exempt from this pattern, and it also reassures the Prophet and the believers that the outcome of truth and falsehood is certain.

translation: Were We then exhausted by the first creation? Rather, they are in confusion and doubt about a new creation.
interpretation: The verse answers those who deny the resurrection by appealing to their own experience of creation. God, who brought humankind and the universe into being from nothing, was not wearied or made powerless by that first act, so recreating them after death is no harder for Him. Their denial does not come from any real proof. It comes from bewilderment and doubt, because they measure God's power by human limits and cannot imagine life returning after death. The verse invites them to reason from the first creation to the certainty of the second.

translation: We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.
interpretation: God stresses His complete and intimate knowledge of every human being. The Creator knows not only a person's outward actions but also the most hidden inner thoughts and impulses that pass through the heart before they are ever spoken. The phrase 'closer than the jugular vein' is a metaphor for God's nearness through knowledge, awareness, and power, not physical proximity: nothing in a person's inner life is concealed from Him. The verse is meant to instill mindfulness (taqwa) and sincerity, reminding believers that they are always observed and that their intentions are known, and it also reassures them that God is near to those who call upon Him.

translation: When the two receivers receive [his deeds], seated on the right and on the left.
interpretation: Every human being is accompanied by two angels who are assigned to record his words and deeds, one sitting on the right and the other on the left. The angel on the right records good deeds and the one on the left records evil deeds. Nothing is omitted or forgotten, so a person is never left alone or unobserved, and he will be confronted with an exact record when he is held to account. The verse is a reminder that God's knowledge of a person is complete and that he should be mindful of his speech and conduct at every moment.

translation: He does not utter a single word except that beside him is a ready observer [angel] recording it.
interpretation: This verse (Qaf 50:18) teaches that human speech is never lost or unaccounted for: every word a person says is observed and written down by an angel who is always present and prepared, so nothing escapes the record that will be presented on the Day of Judgment. It calls the believer to constant mindfulness of God, to guard the tongue from falsehood, backbiting, and idle or harmful talk, and to speak only what is good, since each utterance carries moral weight and will be weighed in the final reckoning.

translation: And the stupor of death will come in truth: "That is what you used to shun."
interpretation: This verse says that death is an undeniable reality, not an illusion. Its agony overwhelms a person and dulls his senses and mind, and it brings him face to face with the truth he ignored in life: the end of worldly life and the beginning of accountability. Throughout life people try to avoid the thought of death, flee from it, and live as though it will never reach them. The verse tells them that this flight was futile. Death comes at its appointed time, and no one can escape it. It is a warning to heedless people to remember their end and prepare for the Hereafter with faith and righteous deeds before the moment arrives when regret no longer helps.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown; that is the Day of the Warning.
interpretation: The verse says that the blowing of the Trumpet, which signals the resurrection and the start of the final reckoning, is the day on which every warning given by God and His messengers is fulfilled. The threats that the deniers dismissed as empty or far off become real and unavoidable. The verse calls on the listener to take the warning seriously now, while repentance and change are still possible, because after the Trumpet sounds, heedlessness no longer helps anyone and each person faces what was promised.

translation: And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.
interpretation: This verse, Surah Qaf 50:21, describes the Day of Resurrection, when each person is brought to account accompanied by two angels. One angel drives them forward to the place of reckoning, so that no one can evade standing before God. The other bears witness to everything the person did in life, as recorded in their deeds. The meaning is that no one will be left unattended or able to deny their record on that Day, and each person will face full accountability. It is a reminder to live with awareness that every action is observed and will be testified to.

translation: You were indeed heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and today your sight is sharp.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, God addresses the human being who lived in heedlessness of the reality of resurrection and accountability. In the worldly life, the veil of distraction, desires, pride, and attachment to material things covered the heart and mind, so the person did not truly perceive the truth of the Hereafter. When death and resurrection come, that veil is lifted and the unseen becomes plain. The person's insight, once dull toward the truth, becomes keen and penetrating, so he sees clearly what he denied or neglected, but at a time when it is too late to act. The verse is a warning to awaken from heedlessness now, while repentance and righteous action are still possible.

translation: And his companion (the angel assigned to him) will say: 'This is what I have ready with me (of his record).'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the angel who was appointed to accompany a person in the world and record his deeds (the qarīn) will present the complete, preserved record of that person's actions, declaring that it is ready and present for the reckoning. Nothing has been omitted or altered; every word and deed has been meticulously written down and kept in readiness, so the person has no room to deny or dispute what he did. The verse stresses divine justice and accountability, reminding that each person's life is under constant, precise record-keeping that will be laid out before him on that Day.

translation: Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Qaf (50:24), is a divine command addressed on the Day of Judgment to the two angels who accompanied each soul, the driver and the witness. It declares that those who persistently denied the truth and stubbornly resisted it, knowing it was right, will be thrown into Hell. The word 'anid' denotes someone who opposes the truth out of arrogance and obstinacy, not out of ignorance. The verse teaches that the severity of punishment is tied to willful rejection of clear guidance, and that on that Day God's justice is executed with decisive authority, with no escape or intercession for those who persisted in obstinacy.

translation: A preventer of good, a transgressor, a doubter (given to suspicion and causing doubt).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 50:25) describes the one who is cast into Hell in the Day of Judgment, and it identifies the moral roots of his ruin: he withheld good, whether by refusing to give of his wealth, to fulfill the rights of others, or to accept and support the truth and guidance; he transgressed all bounds set by God and wronged people by oppression and sin; and he lived in persistent doubt and suspicion, rejecting clear signs and spreading uncertainty about faith in God and the Hereafter. The verse teaches that disbelief is not merely an intellectual error but a character that shows itself in stinginess, aggression, and stubborn skepticism, and that such a character earns accountability.

translation: He who set up another god alongside God – cast him, then, into the severe torment.
interpretation: The verse is part of God's command, in Surah Qaf, to the two angels who accompany every soul, the driver and the witness, concerning the one who is a stubborn denier. After the earlier description of such a person as one who obstructs good, transgresses and is full of doubt, this verse names the gravest of his crimes, shirk, which is to set up a partner with God in divinity, worship or devotion. The verse teaches that associating partners with God is the root of every other wrong, since it denies the One who alone deserves worship and thereby opens the way to injustice and denial of accountability. The punishment fits the crime, and it is severe because the offense is the greatest of offenses. The command to cast him into the torment shows that judgment on the Day of Reckoning is decisive and no one can resist or escape it.

translation: His companion (the devil assigned to him) will say: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he himself was in far-gone error." (Qur'an 50:27)
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the disbeliever will try to shift blame onto the devil who accompanied him in life, and the devil will disown responsibility. The verse teaches that the devil's whispering is only an invitation and has no power to compel. Real responsibility lies with the human being, who chose to follow it. The phrase 'far-gone error' shows that the person's misguidance came from his own long-standing choices, his persistent heedlessness and rejection of truth, until his heart became distant from guidance. Therefore no one can excuse their wrongdoing by blaming Satan or companions, since each person is accountable for what he freely chose.

translation: He (Allah) will say: 'Do not dispute in My presence, for I had already sent you the warning beforehand.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, when the disbeliever and his companion (the devil) blame one another before Allah, the Lord cuts short their wrangling and excuses. Quarrelling is pointless at the place of final judgment because Allah had already given the people full notice through the messengers and revealed Books, warning them of the punishment awaiting those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing. No one can therefore claim ignorance or say that they were not warned; the proof against them is complete, and the judgment that follows is just, being the fulfillment of a warning that was clearly delivered in advance.

translation: The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants.
interpretation: This verse (Qaf 50:29) is God's declaration on the Day of Judgment, after the disputes among people have been settled.
