interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 54:35) comes after the mention of Lot's household being saved from the punishment that struck his people. It teaches that their deliverance was not a matter of chance or merit earned independently, but a pure grace from God. It also sets out a general principle: God consistently rewards those who are grateful, meaning those who acknowledge His favors with faith, obedience, and right action. Gratitude is thus presented as a path to salvation and divine favor, while ingratitude and denial lead to ruin, as happened to Lot's people.

translation: And he had already warned them of Our seizure, but they doubted the warnings and disputed them.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 54:36) refers to the people of Lot, whose prophet had cautioned them that God's punishment would strike if they persisted in their transgression. Instead of heeding the warning, they argued over it, casting doubt and denying its truth. The lesson is that divine warnings come with clear notice and ample opportunity to repent, and that disputing and mocking them out of arrogance or desire does not avert the consequence; it only hardens the heart, so that when God's seizure comes, no one can claim ignorance.

translation: And they had certainly demanded of him his guests, so We blinded their eyes, [saying], "Taste My punishment and My warnings."
interpretation: The verse recalls the people of Lot, who pressed him to hand over the angels who had come to him in the form of human guests, intending to commit their indecent acts against them. Their shamelessness in violating the sacred duty of hospitality and protection of guests showed how far they had sunk in sin. God then struck them with blindness as an immediate punishment, which was a sign and a prelude to the greater destruction that followed at dawn. The words 'Taste My punishment and My warnings' show that the warnings sent through Lot had been clear, that they had ignored them, and that the punishment came as a just consequence of persistent rejection. The lesson is that God protects His righteous servants and that disregard for divine warnings leads to ruin.

translation: And certainly, early in the morning there came upon them a settled (lasting) punishment.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Qamar, refers to the people of Lot. After they rejected his warnings and persisted in their immoral conduct, the punishment struck them at dawn. It is called 'mustaqirr' (settled or fixed) because it was decisive and irreversible: it could not be turned back or lifted, and its consequences remained over them, beginning in this world with their destruction and continuing into the Hereafter. The verse teaches that divine warning, when persistently ignored, ends in a definitive reckoning, and that the fate of earlier deniers stands as a lasting lesson for those who would repeat their conduct.

translation: So taste My punishment and My warnings.
interpretation: This verse, repeated like a refrain in Surah Al-Qamar after the accounts of the destroyed peoples such as Noah's people, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot's people and Pharaoh's folk, is God's rebuke to those who denied the messengers. It teaches that the suffering they received was not arbitrary but the direct and just consequence of ignoring clear warnings. The word 'taste' conveys that they experienced the punishment fully and personally, while 'My warnings' reminds the reader that God sent admonition before every punishment, leaving no excuse. The repetition is meant to awaken the listener, so that the reader draws a lesson from past nations and heeds the warnings of the Qur'an before facing a similar fate.

translation: And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?
interpretation: God has made the Qur'an accessible for understanding, memorization, and heeding admonition, with clear language, vivid lessons, and guidance suited to human nature, so that no one has an excuse for turning away from it. The repeated question is an invitation and a gentle reproach: since the means of reflection and reform have been made easy, the only remaining barrier is the heedlessness or stubbornness of the listener, and the verse calls each person to take the Book to heart and act on its guidance.

translation: And indeed, there came to the people of Pharaoh the warnings.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 54:41) recalls that Pharaoh and his people were not destroyed without prior notice: God sent them Moses and Aaron with clear warnings, signs, and miracles, such as the staff, the plagues, and the parting of the sea, calling them to faith and justice. They rejected these warnings out of arrogance, so the punishment that followed was a result of their own stubborn denial rather than any lack of guidance. In the context of Surah al-Qamar, it serves as a caution to the Quraysh and to all later people that God's warnings are a mercy and a proof against them, and that ignoring clear admonition brings the same fate that befell earlier nations.

translation: They denied all of Our signs, so We seized them with the seizing of One who is Almighty, All-Powerful.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 54:42) refers to Pharaoh and his people, who, despite being shown clear miracles through Moses, rejected every sign without exception, driven by arrogance and stubbornness rather than lack of evidence. Their punishment was therefore not arbitrary but a just consequence of persistent denial. The description of God's seizure as that of One who is 'Aziz (Almighty, unable to be overcome) and Muqtadir (All-Powerful, with complete ability to carry out His will) emphasizes that no power, army, or worldly strength could shield them or delay the decree. It serves as a warning to later deniers that rejecting God's signs invites a inescapable reckoning, and as reassurance to believers that God's might ultimately prevails over tyranny.

translation: Are your disbelievers better than those (earlier destroyed peoples), or do you have an exemption (immunity) in the Scriptures?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 54:43) is a rhetorical challenge to the Quraysh of Mecca. After the Qur'an recounts how the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot, and Pharaoh were destroyed for denying their messengers, God asks whether the disbelievers of Quraysh are superior in strength, status, or virtue to those nations, such that they would be spared the same fate. Or, God asks, do they hold some written guarantee in earlier divine scriptures granting them immunity from punishment? The implied answer to both questions is no. The meaning is that disbelief and persistent denial bring about divine consequences regardless of who commits them, that there is no special exemption by lineage, power, or wealth, and that the fate of past nations is a warning meant to make the Quraysh reconsider their rejection of the Prophet before similar punishment overtakes them.

translation: Or do they say, 'We are a united host, [able to] defend ourselves'?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Qamar, 54:44) rebukes the disbelievers of Quraysh for their arrogant confidence in their numbers, unity, and strength. They imagined that their collective power would shield them from God's punishment and ensure victory over the Prophet and the believers, as it had in worldly conflicts. The verse exposes the emptiness of this reliance: no alliance or military might can protect anyone from divine decree. The next verse promises that their multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs in flight, a prophecy fulfilled at Badr. The lesson is that true victory comes from God and not from numbers, and that those who reject truth out of pride deceive themselves about their own security.

translation: Soon their multitude will be defeated, and they will turn their backs in flight.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 54:45) is a promise of divine victory for the believers and a prophecy of the downfall of the Quraysh and their allies, who were united in numbers and strength against the Prophet. It teaches that sheer numbers and material power cannot withstand God's decree. The prophecy was fulfilled at the Battle of Badr, where the much larger Meccan force was routed and fled. Its lesson is that truth, backed by God's support and patience, ultimately prevails over arrogant opposition, and that those who persist in denial will face humiliating defeat.

translation: Rather, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour will be most grievous and most bitter.
interpretation: The verse tells the disbelievers of Quraysh that the defeat and worldly punishment they are warned about are not the end of their reckoning. Their true appointed meeting is the Day of Judgment, when the full consequences of their denial will come. That day will be more calamitous (adha) and more bitter (amarr) than anything they could suffer in this world, or any affliction they now mock. The verse thus serves as a stern reminder that postponing or dismissing the warning does not cancel it, and that the real measure of loss and gain lies in the Hereafter, so a person should prepare for it by faith and obedience rather than rely on temporary worldly strength or numbers.

translation: Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness (or: in misguidance and blazing Fire).
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Qamar, 54:47) declares that those who persist in sin and reject the messengers are lost in a deep deviation from the truth, and that this deviation is not harmless: it carries its own punishment. Their straying in this world, in which they follow desires and doubt in place of guidance, leads to the blazing Fire in the next. The word 'sa'ir' can be understood as the flaming Fire of Hell, so the verse links the criminals' error in life directly to their destined torment. It serves as a warning that persisting in rejection ends in ruin, and that what appears to be freedom from divine guidance is in fact confusion and a path to burning.

translation: On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces, [it will be said to them]: "Taste the touch of Saqar (Hell)."
interpretation: The verse describes the humiliation of those who denied God's decree and persisted in wrongdoing. Just as they turned away from the truth and were proud in this world, they are dragged on their faces in the Hereafter, so the punishment matches their arrogance and rejection. The command 'Taste the touch of Saqar' is a rebuke, not an invitation: the word 'taste' implies they will feel the pain directly, and 'touch' shows that even the slightest contact with Hell's heat is severe. The verse warns that denying divine destiny and disbelieving in God's signs lead to disgrace and just recompense, urging people to humble themselves before God now rather than face humiliation later.

translation: Indeed, We have created everything in due measure and proportion.
interpretation: The verse teaches that nothing in creation exists by chance or without purpose. Everything has been brought into being according to a precise measure set by God, with its appointed nature, quantity, time, and course, and this measure is known to Him and written in His prior knowledge. This means the universe is governed by order and wisdom rather than randomness, so a believer should see in the harmony of creation the sign of a knowing Creator, and should accept that events unfold within His decree while still being responsible for their own choices and actions.

translation: And Our command is but one word, like the blink of an eye.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qamar 54:50) expresses the absolute power of God and the immediacy of His will. When God wills something, He needs only to say "Be," and it comes to pass instantly, as swiftly as a glance of the eye, without effort, delay, preparation, or any need for assistance. Within its context, it warns the deniers that the fulfillment of God's decree, including the Hour and His punishment, is as effortless for Him as a blink, so they should not mistake the delay for impossibility or take His patience as weakness.

translation: And We have already destroyed the likes of you, so is there anyone who will take heed?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Qamar, 54:51) warns the disbelievers of the Prophet's time that they are not the first to deny the truth. Earlier peoples who shared their disbelief and arrogance, such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and Lot, were wiped out when they rejected their messengers. Their fate is a lesson and a precedent, and God asks whether anyone will reflect on it, change course, and return to faith before the same judgment overtakes them. The rhetorical question stresses that the evidence is plain and the warning clear, so only heedlessness or stubbornness keeps people from learning from history.

translation: And everything they have done is in the records.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 54:52) teaches that nothing done by earlier wrongdoing nations, or by anyone, escapes God's knowledge and recording. Every deed, great or small, is written in the records (the books of the angels who record deeds, and the preserved record with God), and it will be brought forth on the Day of Judgment for reckoning. It is both a warning to the deniers that their actions are not lost or forgotten and that they will be held accountable, and a reassurance to the believers that no good deed will go unnoticed or unrewarded.

translation: And every small and great thing is written down.
interpretation: This verse, Surah Al-Qamar 54:53, affirms that nothing escapes God's record: every deed, word and event, however minor or major, is inscribed in a register that is preserved. It warns that people will be held to account for all they have done, since even the smallest action is recorded with precision. It is a reminder to act with awareness, hope for reward for even slight good, and fear consequences for even slight wrongdoing, because the final reckoning will be based on a complete and exact record.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be amid gardens and rivers.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Qamar 54:54) promises those who guard themselves against disobedience and live in awareness of God a place of lasting comfort and honor in the Hereafter. Gardens and flowing rivers signify abundance, peace, and delight, the opposite of the destruction suffered by the earlier peoples who denied their prophets, as described earlier in the surah. The word 'nahar' (river), used in the singular, conveys the idea of generality and vastness, indicating that the believers' blessings will be boundless and unending. Taqwa in this life, then, is shown to be the means to a secure and joyful eternal life.

translation: In a seat of truth, in the presence of an Omnipotent Sovereign. (Qur'an 54:55)
interpretation: This verse describes the final reward of the God-fearing: a place of honor and true standing, free from vanity, falsehood, or loss, unlike the fleeting positions of this world. It is called a 'seat of truth' because it is real, lasting, and granted to those who were truthful in faith and deed. Being 'in the presence of' the Sovereign shows that their greatest honor is nearness to God, whose perfect power guarantees that this reward cannot be taken away, diminished, or obstructed by anyone. The verse thus gives believers reassurance and sets the permanent security of the righteous against the temporary power of the deniers mentioned earlier in the surah.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Most Gracious.
interpretation: Beginning every act with the name of God places it under His authority and seeks His help and blessing, acknowledging that nothing happens except by His will. The opening of Surah Ar-Rahman, 'The Most Gracious,' then uses one of His names as the entire first verse, which signals that mercy is the foundation of all that follows in the surah: He is the one who teaches the Qur'an, creates humankind, and gives order to the universe. By naming Him as Ar-Rahman before any other statement, the verse invites the listener to read every blessing in creation and revelation as an expression of His boundless, all-encompassing mercy, and to respond with gratitude and reverence.

translation: He taught the Qur'an. (Qur'an 55:2)
interpretation: This verse presents teaching the Qur'an as the first of God's gifts named in Surah Ar-Rahman, right after His name 'the Most Merciful.' It means that the Qur'an is not a human invention but a revelation which God Himself taught, first to the Prophet Muhammad through Gabriel and then through him to humanity. Placing it before the creation of the human being (verse 3) suggests that guidance is the highest mercy, since it gives life its purpose and direction, and that God's compassion shows itself above all in not leaving people without knowledge of how to know Him and live rightly.

translation: He created man.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman, 55:3) points to God's creation of the human being as one of His great blessings, following the mention of teaching the Qur'an. It means that the Merciful, who sent revelation, also brought humanity into existence, giving him intellect, form, and the capacity to receive guidance. Human existence is therefore not accidental but a purposeful gift, which calls the human being to gratitude and to recognize the Creator's mercy and his own responsibility to live in accordance with the guidance revealed.

translation: He taught him clear expression.
interpretation: This verse (Surat Ar-Rahman, 55:4) points to the gift of articulate speech and the ability to convey thought. God did not only create the human being; He also equipped him with the power to explain what is in his mind, to understand others, and to learn. Language and reasoned communication are what make knowledge, law, and moral guidance possible. They are a divine favor that sets humanity apart and enables people to receive and understand revelation, and so the verse calls the human being to gratitude and to use speech for truth rather than falsehood.

translation: The sun and the moon follow precise courses, according to a exact reckoning.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman, 55:5) points to the perfect order God has set in the heavens. The sun and the moon move by a fixed, measured calculation that never errs or falters, and by them people reckon days, months, years, seasons, and times of worship. The precision of these celestial motions is a sign of the Creator's wisdom, power, and mercy, and a reminder that the universe is governed by a deliberate design rather than chance, which should lead people to gratitude and to recognizing the One who ordained it.

translation: And the stars and the trees prostrate themselves.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Ar-Rahman, 55:6) teaches that all of creation, whether the heavenly bodies above or the plants of the earth below, submits to God's will and order. Their prostration is not a ritual act like human prayer but a complete obedience to the laws God set for them: the stars follow their appointed courses and the trees grow, cast shadows and bear fruit as they were ordained. By pointing to the greatest and humblest of created things alike, the verse reminds humans, who have been given free will, that they should submit to their Lord in gratitude for His favors, since everything around them already does so.

translation: And the heaven He raised high, and He set up the balance.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman 55:7) points to the order God built into creation. The heaven is raised in grandeur and precision, and the 'balance' (mizan) is the principle of justice and equilibrium that runs through the cosmos and human life alike. Just as the heavens and the universe are held in exact measure, humans are meant to live by that same justice in their dealings, their rights and duties, and their moral choices. The raising of the sky and the setting of the balance are mentioned together to show that the physical order and the moral order come from one Creator, and that upholding fairness is in harmony with the very design of existence.

translation: So that you do not transgress in the balance.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman, 55:8) teaches that the balance God set in creation and in human dealings must not be violated. It means that people should not exceed the limits of justice, whether in weighing and measuring in trade or in judging, giving rights, and conducting affairs. Transgressing in the balance means cheating, favoring one's own interest, or leaning toward injustice. Just as God established order and equilibrium in the heavens and the earth, humans are commanded to uphold fairness and equity in their own conduct, giving each person his due without excess or deficiency.

translation: And establish weight with justice, and do not make the balance deficient.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman 55:9) commands uprightness and honesty in all dealings, not only in the marketplace. Having stated that God set up the balance as a cosmic principle of order and equity, it calls on people to mirror that order in their own conduct. Giving full and fair measure, and never cheating or shorting others, is a mark of faith and a safeguard of social trust. By extension, the verse calls on a believer to weigh their words, judgments, rights and duties with fairness, because injustice upsets the harmony God built into creation and ultimately causes loss to the one who commits it.

translation: And the earth He laid out for living creatures.
interpretation: God made the earth a prepared and stable home for all created beings, humans and other creatures alike. It is level enough to live on, and it supplies provision, shelter, and the means of life. This points to God's care and generosity, and it invites people to be grateful and to use the earth with justice, without corruption or wrongdoing, because they are guests who have been given a trust rather than absolute owners.

translation: In it are fruits and palm trees having sheaths (clusters covered by their spathes).
interpretation: The verse points to God's generous provision for humankind on the earth, listing fruit and the date palm as signs of His care. The palm's fruit grows enclosed in protective sheaths that burst open when ripe, showing the precision of His design: sustenance is wrapped, protected, and delivered in perfect time. Such blessings are meant to awaken gratitude and reflection, leading people to recognize the Provider rather than take His bounty for granted.

translation: And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat ar-Rahman (55:12), continues the list of God's blessings on earth. Grain in its husk is the staple food of humans, while the husk and stalks serve as fodder for animals, so the provision reaches both people and livestock. 'Rayhan', the fragrant plants, adds scent and pleasantness to life beyond mere survival. The verse teaches that God provides for need and for delight, and that sustenance is a favor to be met with gratitude, which is why the surah keeps asking: 'Which of your Lord's favors will you deny?'

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surat ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn and confronts them with the reality of God's countless blessings, from creation, teaching of the Qur'an, and the order of the heavens and earth to the rewards of the Hereafter. Its meaning is that every one of these gifts is a sign of divine mercy and power, so denying or ignoring them is ingratitude and unreasonable. The repeated question awakens conscience, urges reflection and thankfulness, and leaves the listener with no excuse, calling them to acknowledge God and live in gratitude and obedience.

translation: He created man from dry, sounding clay like pottery.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 55:14) points to the humble, earthly origin of the human being: his physical nature is drawn from dry clay that resonates when struck, like fired pottery. It is mentioned among God's favors in Surah Ar-Rahman to remind people that they are formed from lowly material and that their dignity comes not from their substance but from the breath of life and the faculties God bestowed on them. This should lead to gratitude and humility before the Creator, who shapes inert earth into a living, reasoning being.

translation: And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman 55:15) points to the origin of the jinn as a distinct order of creation, made from the pure, intense flame of fire just as humans were made from clay in the preceding verse. Its meaning is that God is the Creator of every kind of being, shaping each from a different substance according to His wisdom and power. Because both humans and jinn are addressed together in this surah, the verse reminds them that, despite their different natures and origins, both are created and dependent on God, and so both are accountable to Him and owe Him gratitude for His favors.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat al-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn and confronts them with the reality of God's countless blessings, from creation, revelation, and the ordering of the cosmos to the rewards promised in the Hereafter. Its repetition after each mention of a blessing or a warning is a rhetorical question that exposes the unreasonableness of ingratitude: since every gift is plainly from God, denial is without excuse. It calls the listener to reflect, acknowledge God's bounty, and respond with gratitude, faith, and obedience, recognizing that even warnings and the reminders of judgment are themselves mercies that guide toward salvation.

translation: Lord of the two Easts and Lord of the two Wests.
interpretation: The verse (Surat ar-Rahman, 55:17) points to God's absolute lordship over the cosmos, the two risings and two settings of the sun, understood as its farthest points in summer and winter. The sun rises and sets at different points through the year, and this precise, ordered shifting is a sign of God's power and mercy: the alternation of seasons, day and night, and the sustenance of life on earth all depend on it. By invoking the cosmic order right after mentioning the creation of humankind and the balance of the world, the verse calls people to recognize the One who governs these vast, regulated movements and to respond with gratitude and worship rather than denial of His favors.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surat al-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn and calls them to recognize that every blessing they enjoy, from creation, speech and the order of the cosmos to the promised rewards of the hereafter, comes from God alone. After each mention of a divine favor or sign, the verse works as a rebuke: since the blessings are so evident and so many, denying them or giving thanks to anything other than God is ungrateful and unreasonable. It invites the listener to reflect, acknowledge the Giver, and answer with gratitude, faith and obedience.

translation: He released the two seas, meeting side by side (Qur'an 55:19).
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy in setting the two great bodies of water in motion so that they meet and flow alongside one another, yet, as the next verse says, a barrier lies between them so that neither overwhelms the other. The meaning is that the Creator maintains balance and order in nature, keeping apart waters of different qualities, such as fresh and salt, where they meet, which is a sign of His wisdom and a favor to humankind that calls for gratitude and reflection.

translation: Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 55:20) points to God's power in keeping the two seas, one fresh and one salty, side by side without one overwhelming or mixing with the other. The barrier (barzakh) is a divinely set boundary that holds each in its own limits, and neither oversteps it. It is a sign of the order God has placed in creation and a reminder that nature runs by His measure and wisdom. Reflecting on such precise balance should lead people to gratitude and acknowledgment of their Lord, as the surah repeatedly asks: 'Which of your Lord's favors will you deny?'

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surah Ar-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, and it confronts them with the denial that their own lives contradict. Every blessing mentioned before it, such as the teaching of the Qur'an, the creation of humankind, the order of the heavens and the earth, and the provision of sustenance, is a sign of God's mercy and a reason for gratitude. The question is rhetorical. It does not seek information but exposes the unreasonableness of ingratitude. Its repetition after each blessing and each warning keeps the listener's conscience awake, so that gratitude becomes an active response in belief and obedience. Denial of God's favors is not just a spoken rejection. It also includes heedlessness toward them and failing to acknowledge their Giver.

translation: From both of them come forth pearls and coral.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman, 55:22) points to the bounty God places in creation, even in the seemingly ordinary elements of the seas. Pearls and coral are precious treasures hidden in the depths, and they are brought out for human benefit, adornment, and admiration. The verse invites reflection on God's generosity and wisdom: He conceals beauty and value in places people would not expect, and He enables them to discover and enjoy it. It is meant to awaken gratitude, which is why it sits within the surah's recurring question, 'Which of your Lord's favors will you deny?'

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain of Surat ar-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, and it asks each of them to recognize that everything they enjoy comes from God: creation, the gift of reason and speech, the order of the sun, moon, and heavens, provision on earth, and the promised rewards of the Hereafter. Its repetition after each blessing, and after each warning, works as a gentle but firm rebuke. It reminds the listener that denying God or ignoring His signs is a form of ingratitude, and that the fitting response to such abundant generosity is thankfulness, humility, and obedience. Even the warnings are counted as favors, because they guide people away from ruin.

translation: And to Him belong the ships, raised high upon the sea like mountains.
interpretation: The verse points to ships as a sign of God's power and favor. Vessels that tower over the water like great landmarks float and sail only because God has set the laws of nature in place: the buoyancy of water, the movement of the winds and currents, and the ability He gave humans to build and steer them. So even the most imposing human achievement depends wholly on God's command. The same God who keeps these huge ships afloat can, if He wills, still the wind or let them sink, as the surrounding verses say. The verse therefore calls people to gratitude, humility and awareness of His dominion rather than pride in their own ingenuity.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat Ar-Rahman, addresses both humankind and jinn, confronting them with the abundance of God's blessings, from creation, revelation, and the order of the universe to the promised rewards of the Hereafter. By repeating the question after each blessing or warning, it awakens gratitude and shows that denial is unreasonable. Even the warnings are counted among God's favors, since they guide people toward righteousness and spare them from loss. The verse invites the listener to reflect and respond with thankfulness, faith, and obedience instead of ingratitude.

translation: Everyone upon it (the earth) will perish.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman, 55:26) declares that every created being on earth is transient and destined for death and annihilation. Human life, power, and worldly possessions are temporary, and no creature has permanence. It reminds the believer not to attach the heart to this fleeting world, but to turn toward God, since only He is eternal, as the following verse affirms: 'And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.' The verse therefore calls for humility, preparation for the Hereafter, and reliance on the Ever-Living who does not die.

translation: And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.
interpretation: This verse, Qur'an 55:27, teaches that everything on earth is subject to perishing, while God alone is eternal. The 'Face' of the Lord signifies His own Self and everlasting existence, which is described as full of majesty (jalal), reflecting His greatness and supreme authority, and honor (ikram), reflecting His generosity and the honor He bestows on His righteous servants. The reminder calls the believer to detach from transient worldly things, to place hope and devotion in the One who never ceases, and to live with awe of His majesty and gratitude for His bounty.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain, addressed to both humans and jinn, is a rebuke that calls each listener to honest self-examination. After each description of God's gifts, such as creation, teaching the Qur'an, the order of the cosmos, and the blessings of this world and the next, the verse asks whether anyone can truthfully reject them. Denial here is not only a spoken rejection but also ingratitude and failure to acknowledge the Giver. The question has no valid answer except gratitude, so it urges the listener to recognize that every blessing comes from God and to respond with faith, thankfulness, and obedience.

translation: Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him; every day He is engaged in some affair.
interpretation: All created beings, in every realm of existence, depend entirely on God and continually petition Him, whether in words or through their very need, for sustenance, guidance, forgiveness, and mercy. God is never idle or exhausted by this: in every moment He is actively governing creation, giving life and death, raising some and lowering others, answering needs, relieving distress, and bringing about His decrees. The verse teaches that creation is not a finished mechanism left to run on its own, but is sustained moment by moment by God's ongoing, limitless will and care, so a believer should turn to Him alone in every need and trust His constant management of all affairs.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surah Ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn, calling them to recognize that every aspect of existence, from creation, revelation, and the order of the heavens and earth to the promised reward in the Hereafter, is a gift from God. Having each blessing enumerated, the listener is confronted with the absurdity of ingratitude: since nothing they enjoy comes from any source but God, denying or ignoring His favors is unreasonable. The repetition drives home that gratitude and acknowledgment of the Lord's mercy is the fitting response, and that denial is a failure of both reason and conscience.

translation: We will soon attend to you, O two weighty beings (humans and jinn).
interpretation: This verse from Surah Ar-Rahman (55:31) is a solemn warning of the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'We will attend to you' does not imply that God is ever occupied or distracted with anything else, since nothing diverts Him from anything; rather, it is an idiom of eloquent Arabic expressing that the time of reckoning is now at hand and will be given full, undivided attention. After listing His countless blessings upon humans and jinn (the 'two weighty beings', so called because of their burden of responsibility and moral accountability), God turns to remind them that they will be brought to account for how they responded to those blessings, whether with gratitude and obedience or with denial and ingratitude. The verse thus shifts the tone of the surah from reminders of divine favor to the certainty of accountability, urging both humans and jinn to reflect and act rightly before that Day arrives.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is the refrain of Surat al-Rahman, addressed to both humankind and jinn. It reminds them that everything described before it, including creation, revelation, the order of the cosmos, and the provision of sustenance, is a blessing from God. Since these gifts are clear and undeniable, the verse invites the listener to feel gratitude and to recognize God's lordship. Denying them, whether by words, by ingratitude, or by living as if they came from someone else, is unreasonable and unjust. The repetition makes this question strike the heart anew after each mention of a blessing or a warning, because even warnings and the reality of judgment are mercies that guide one toward righteousness.

translation: O company of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. You will not pass except with authority.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, God challenges jinn and humankind to try to escape His dominion and reckoning. The challenge shows how powerless they are: no one can flee the bounds of the heavens and the earth, because all of creation is under God's sovereignty. The only way to cross those bounds would be with a 'sultan', meaning a power or authority that God alone grants, and He will not grant it to anyone seeking to escape His judgment. The verse therefore teaches human and jinn helplessness before God, and that the only refuge from Him is to return to Him in submission.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat Ar-Rahman is addressed to both humans and jinn. It reminds them that all existence, guidance, creation, and the rewards and warnings of the Hereafter are signs of God's grace and mercy. Even warnings are a mercy, because they steer people away from ruin. Since the blessings are so clear and so many, denying them is ingratitude and a lapse of reason. The verse calls the listener to reflect, acknowledge God's bounty, and respond with gratitude and obedience instead of denial.

translation: There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and smoke (or molten copper), and you will not be able to defend yourselves.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Rahman, 55:35) warns the two accountable groups, jinn and humans, that if they try to escape God's dominion they will fail. Just as no one can pass beyond the heavens and the earth without authority from God, no one can escape His judgment. Any attempt to flee will be met with blazing flames and scorching smoke, and no power or ally will help them. The point is that human and jinn power is limited and wholly dependent on God, and that the right response to this reality is humble submission and gratitude toward the Lord whose favors the surah enumerates.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surat Ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn and calls them to honest reflection. Every blessing, from creation, revelation and the order of the cosmos to the promised reward and even the warnings that guide people away from ruin, comes from God's mercy. Denying any of them is therefore ingratitude. The verse asks the listener to recognize God's generosity, to respond with thankfulness and obedience, and to see that no one has a reasonable excuse for rejecting the Giver of these gifts.

translation: And when the sky is split open and becomes rose-colored, like (melting) red leather or oil.
interpretation: This verse describes a terrifying sign of the Day of Judgment: the heavens will crack apart and their familiar blue calm will give way to a glowing, rose-red hue that flows and shimmers like molten oil or tanned red hide. The image conveys that the seemingly fixed, immovable order of the cosmos will dissolve at God's command, so that human beings realize that nothing in creation is permanent or beyond God's power, and that they should heed the warning and prepare for the reckoning, when denial of their Lord's favors and warnings will no longer be possible.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat al-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, calling on them to reflect on the countless blessings God has granted: creation, revelation, the order of the cosmos, and the promised rewards of the hereafter. It is a rhetorical question that exposes the unreasonableness of ingratitude. Because every blessing points to the Lord's mercy and power, denying any of them is shown to be irrational and unjust. The repetition after each listed favor and warning keeps the listener's conscience engaged, moving them from heedlessness to gratitude, faith, and obedience.

translation: On that Day, neither human being nor jinn will be asked about his sin.
interpretation: This verse (Ar-Rahman 55:39) means that on the Day of Judgment, when the guilty are known by their marks (as the next verse indicates, they will be recognized by their faces), there will be no need to question them in order to learn of their sins. God's knowledge is complete and the evidence of their wrongdoing will be plainly visible, so the guilty will be seized by their forelocks and feet without any inquiry to establish what they did. The questioning of reproach and accountability occurs elsewhere, but here the point is that God needs no information from them: nothing is hidden from Him, and the judgment will be decisive, certain, and just. This should instill awareness and sincere fear of God in humans and jinn alike, since no deed can be concealed or denied on that Day.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat Ar-Rahman is addressed to both humans and jinn, and it asks them to reflect on how much they have been given. Because the verses before each repetition describe creation, teaching, the order of the cosmos, and the rewards and warnings of the Hereafter, the question implies that every one of these, including the warnings, is a form of divine mercy. Warnings guide people away from ruin, and the promised rewards motivate good conduct. Denying any of these favors is therefore ingratitude, since all of them come from God alone. The repeated question is meant to wake the heart from heedlessness and lead it to gratitude, humility, and obedience.

translation: The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by their forelocks and their feet.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman, 55:41) says that on the Day of Judgment no one will need to ask who the wrongdoers are, because their sins will show on their faces: the darkness, gloom, and humiliation of their countenances will betray them. The angels of punishment will then seize them by the hair at the front of the head and by the feet, folding them together and hurling them into Hell. This is a picture of total helplessness and public disgrace. Those who were arrogant and held their heads high in defiance of God are now dragged down in utter abasement, with no power to resist and no chance to hide what they did.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat al-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, and it confronts them with the many blessings God has given: creation, revelation, the order of the cosmos, provision, and the promise of reward. Every gift comes from God alone, so denying any of them, whether by disbelief, ingratitude, or living as though they were not from Him, is unreasonable and unjust. The repetition after each blessing or warning works as a gentle rebuke that calls the listener to reflect, acknowledge God's generosity, and answer with thankfulness and obedience. Even the warnings count as favors, because they guide people away from ruin.

translation: This is Hell, which the guilty used to deny.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the angels of Hell will say these words to the wrongdoers as they are brought before the Fire. They are shown the very reality they dismissed in the world, so that denial can no longer shelter them. What they once mocked as a fable or a threat meant only to frighten them is now in front of their eyes. The verse is a rebuke that adds moral and psychological pain to the physical punishment, since it shows that rejecting a truth does not cancel it. It also warns that the warnings of the Qur'an are real and that arrogance in the face of revelation ends in certain, visible accountability.

translation: They will go back and forth between it (Hellfire) and boiling, scalding water.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman 55:44) describes the fate of the criminals who denied God's signs: they are not left in one place of torment but are driven in circuits between the blazing Fire and a spring of water heated to the utmost limit. The 'ānin' (water that has reached extreme heat) shows that even the thing which normally relieves thirst becomes another source of agony. The image conveys the unrelenting, inescapable nature of divine justice for those who persisted in denial, with no rest or relief, in contrast to the cool gardens and flowing springs promised to the righteous in the verses that follow.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat ar-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, and it asks them to reflect on how much they have been given. Every blessing, from creation, revelation and the order of the natural world to the promise of reward in the Hereafter, comes from God alone. Denying these gifts through ingratitude, arrogance or turning to other than God has no justification. Its repetition after each blessing and warning stirs the conscience again and again. It calls the listener to acknowledge God's generosity with gratitude, faith and obedience instead of heedlessness.

translation: But for him who fears the standing before his Lord there will be two gardens.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman 55:46) promises that the person who is conscious of standing before God for judgment, and who therefore restrains himself from disobedience and strives in obedience, will be rewarded with two gardens in the Hereafter. The fear meant here is not mere dread but a lasting awareness of God's watchfulness and of accountability, which shapes conduct in private and in public. The dual gardens signify abundant and complete reward, a blessing above blessing, granted in recompense for the inner discipline of having held back from sin out of reverence for the Lord.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat Ar-Rahman addresses both humankind and jinn, calling each to recognize that every blessing they enjoy, from creation, revelation, and sustenance to the order of the heavens and earth and the promise of reward in the Hereafter, comes from God alone. The rhetorical question is meant to awaken gratitude and shame the conscience. Since the favors are so plain and so many, denying them would be ingratitude and willful blindness. The verse thus urges the listener to turn from denial to thankfulness, humility, and obedience to the Lord who gave these gifts.

translation: Both abounding in branches (or varieties of delights).
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman 55:48) describes the two gardens of Paradise prepared for those who feared standing before their Lord. The word 'afnan' is understood to mean spreading branches laden with fruit and shade, signifying lushness and abundance. It conveys that the gardens are full of beauty, shade, and diverse kinds of fruits and delights, so that the inhabitants enjoy endless variety and comfort, a reward that reflects God's generosity toward the God-fearing.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surah Ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn, calling them to recognize that every blessing they enjoy, from creation, revelation, and the order of the cosmos to the promised rewards of the Hereafter, comes from God alone. Its repetition after each mention of a divine favor or a warning serves as a rhetorical challenge: since the blessings are so evident and so numerous, denying them is unreasonable and ungrateful. The verse thus invites the listener to reflection, gratitude, and acknowledgment of God's lordship, and to see even the warnings of judgment as a mercy that guides people toward the right path.

translation: In both of them are two springs flowing.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman 55:50) describes the two gardens prepared for the righteous who feared standing before their Lord. The two flowing springs signify continual, unfailing abundance and life in Paradise: unlike earthly water that may run dry, these springs never cease, watering the gardens and refreshing their dwellers. Their flowing is a sign of beauty, comfort and perpetual divine bounty, and it reminds the believer that the reward of Paradise is both a physical delight and an unending mercy from God, which calls for gratitude, as in the surah's refrain, 'Which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?'

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is the refrain of Surat Ar-Rahman, addressed to both humans and jinn. It reminds them that every aspect of existence, including creation, revelation, the balance of the cosmos, sustenance, and the promise of reward, is a gift from God. Since these blessings are so clear and so many, denying them or ignoring the One who gave them is unreasonable and ungrateful. The repeated question works as a gentle rebuke that pushes the listener to reflect, acknowledge God's generosity, and answer with gratitude and obedience, because no honest person can find any blessing that did not come from the Lord.

translation: In both of them there are two kinds of every fruit.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat ar-Rahman (55:52), describes the two gardens promised to those who fear standing before their Lord. It means that every fruit in them comes in two varieties, which conveys the abundance and diversity of Paradise's provision. The 'pair' signals that the blessings are not monotonous or limited: each fruit appears in more than one kind, perhaps one familiar to people from this world and another unfamiliar and beyond what they have known, so that the believers' enjoyment is renewed and completed. It teaches that God's reward for the righteous surpasses worldly pleasures in both quantity and variety.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat Ar-Rahman, addresses both humankind and jinn, calling each to recognize that every aspect of existence, from creation, revelation, and the ordered cosmos to the provision of sustenance and the promise of reward and warning, is a grace from God. Even the warnings and descriptions of judgment are mercies, since they guide souls toward salvation. The repeated question is rhetorical: it exposes the irrationality and ingratitude of denial, and it invites the listener to reflect, acknowledge God's blessings, and respond with gratitude, faith, and obedience.

translation: They will be reclining on furnishings whose linings are of rich brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within easy reach.
interpretation: The verse (Ar-Rahman 55:54) shows the perfect comfort and honor of the people of Paradise. If the inner lining of their couches is of heavy silk brocade, which is normally hidden, then the outer surface must be even more splendid, which hints at a beauty beyond human imagination. Reclining is the posture of ease and security, free from toil and fear. The fruit hanging close enough to be picked while sitting or lying down means they need not exert any effort, so provision comes to them without hardship, in contrast to the labor of earning in this world. Together, these images describe a reward that is complete in both rest and sustenance, granted to those who feared standing before their Lord.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat Ar-Rahman is addressed to both humans and jinn, and it asks them to reflect on how many blessings they have received from God: creation, speech, the order of the heavens and the earth, provision, and the promise of reward in the Hereafter. Each blessing is a sign of God's mercy and power, so denying it, whether by ingratitude, by disbelief, or by attributing it to something other than God, is unreasonable and unjust. The verse is repeated after each mention of a favor or warning, and it works as a reminder that even God's warnings and the descriptions of judgment are mercies, because they guide people toward gratitude, faith, and righteous conduct before it is too late.

translation: In them are maidens of restrained glances, whom no man or jinn has touched before them.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Rahman, 55:56) describes the companions awaiting the righteous in the two gardens of Paradise. 'Restrained glances' means they are modest and content with their spouses, looking at no one else, which points to purity of character and faithful devotion. Their not having been touched by any human or jinn before signifies that they are pristine and unblemished, so the joy of the believers is complete and fresh. The mention of both humans and jinn reflects the surah's address to both categories of accountable beings, and it shows that Paradise's rewards are pure and perfect, a fitting recompense for those who feared standing before their Lord.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat Ar-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, calling them to recognize that everything around them, from creation, revelation, and sustenance to the promise of reward and the warning of reckoning, is a grace from God. Even warnings and reminders of judgment are mercies, because they steer a person toward salvation. Denying any of these blessings, whether by words, by ingratitude, or by living as though they came from someone else, is therefore unreasonable. The verse is a rhetorical question that calls for gratitude, humility, and acknowledgment of the Lord's generosity, and it is repeated to stir the heart after each description of divine favor so that the listener cannot escape reflecting on it.

translation: As if they were rubies and coral.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Rahman 55:58) describes the maidens of Paradise who restrain their glances. The comparison to rubies and coral points to their purity, radiance, and flawless beauty. Ruby suggests a clear, glowing brilliance, while coral suggests a smooth, fine whiteness tinged with rosy color. Together the images convey that the blessings of the people of Paradise are perfect, untouched, and of a beauty far beyond ordinary worldly things, as a reward for those who feared standing before their Lord.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat ar-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, the two accountable creations. It makes denial of God's blessings a matter of conscience. Every gift, from the order of creation and the gift of speech and revelation to the promise of reward in the Hereafter, is a sign of God's mercy and power. Because none of these can be credited to anyone else, rejecting them is unjustifiable ingratitude. The repeated question is a rhetorical challenge that moves the listener from heedlessness to reflection, gratitude and obedience, and it leaves no defensible grounds for disbelief.

translation: Is there any reward for good other than good? (Qur'an 55:60)
interpretation: The verse sets out a universal divine principle: kindness and righteous conduct are always met with goodness in return. It is posed as a rhetorical question, so the answer is clearly 'no'. In context, after Surat al-Rahman lists God's blessings upon the righteous in Paradise, the verse tells us that these blessings are the fitting return for faith and good deeds done in this world. It also carries a moral call to humans: those who have received good should answer it with good, and above all should answer God's countless favors with gratitude and devoted obedience. Goodness, then, is never wasted. Whoever sows it will reap its like, in this life and the next.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain from Surat Ar-Rahman addresses both humans and jinn, and it is repeated after each blessing and sign of God's power that the surah lists, from teaching the Qur'an and creating the cosmos to the rewards of Paradise. Its meaning is that every good thing, whether natural, moral, or spiritual, comes from God's mercy and not from human merit, so denying or ignoring it is ingratitude. The question is rhetorical and leaves no room for an honest denial. It calls the listener to reflect on these blessings, to acknowledge the Giver, and to answer with gratitude, faith, and obedience.

translation: And besides these two there are two other gardens.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Ar-Rahman (55:62) begins the description of a second pair of gardens, which are lesser in rank or nearer in position than the first two gardens described earlier (55:46-61), which were for those who feared standing before their Lord. The most reasonable reading is that Paradise has levels, and God rewards people according to their degrees of fear of Him, devotion, and excellence in faith. The first two gardens are for the foremost, the muqarrabun, while these two are for the righteous who come after them, showing that divine reward is graded and fully just, and that every believer receives blessings fitting their deeds while all of it remains an immense favor from God.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is the refrain of Surat ar-Rahman, addressed to both humankind and the jinn. It reminds them that every blessing they enjoy, including creation, revelation, the order of the heavens and the earth, sustenance, and the promise of recompense, comes from God's mercy alone. It is therefore a rhetorical question that exposes the irrationality and ingratitude of denial. Its repetition after each mention of a blessing or a warning calls the listener to reflect and acknowledge the Giver, to respond with gratitude, obedience, and awareness of accountability, and to see that even God's warnings are a mercy because they guide people away from ruin.

translation: Dark green with foliage.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman 55:64) describes the two lesser gardens of Paradise as so lushly vegetated that their deep green verges on blackness. Such intense greenness signals abundant water, fertility, and freshness, so the verse conveys that the inhabitants of these gardens will enjoy lasting, vibrant, ever-flourishing bounty, lush and restful, which is a mercy and a reward from God for the righteous.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is the refrain of Surat Ar-Rahman, addressed to both humans and jinn. It calls on them to look honestly at the blessings God has given them: creation, revelation, the order of the heavens and earth, and the rewards promised in the Hereafter. After each blessing is mentioned, the question reminds the listener that denying God or being ungrateful is irrational and unjust. The repetition awakens the heart to gratitude and to responsibility. Every favor points to the Giver, so acknowledging His gifts should lead to faith, thankfulness, and obedience.

translation: In both of them are two springs, gushing forth.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman 55:66) describes the two gardens that lie below the two highest gardens, and it presents their springs as ever-flowing, surging fountains. The word 'naddakhatan' conveys water that gushes abundantly and continuously, not a mere trickle. The meaning is that the people of Paradise are given a lavish, living bounty: its water never runs dry, it renews itself, and it brings freshness, beauty and delight. This reflects God's generosity in rewarding the righteous with blessings that are active and overflowing, far beyond the stillness or scarcity known in worldly life.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn and calls them to recognize that everything they enjoy, from creation, revelation, and provision to the order of the cosmos and the promise of reward in the Hereafter, is a gift from God. Denying these blessings, whether by word, by ingratitude, or by living as though they came from someone else, is unreasonable. The repeated question is meant to stir the conscience, so that the listener answers inwardly that none of God's favors can be denied, and responds with gratitude, faith, and obedience.

translation: In both of them are fruit, date palms, and pomegranates.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ar-Rahman, 55:68) describes the two gardens of Paradise reserved for the believers, and it singles out date palms and pomegranates for special mention even though they fall under the general category of fruit. Their separate mention honors them and signals their excellence. In Paradise they are not merely sustenance, as they are in this world, but are given as lasting delight and honor, free of scarcity, decay, or toil. The verse thus shows God's generosity to the righteous by promising them familiar blessings in a perfected form, and it invites the believer to see the bounties of this world as pointers to the greater bounties of the next. It also belongs to the surah's refrain, 'Which of your Lord's favors will you deny?'

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surat ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn, calling each to recognize that every blessing they enjoy, from creation, revelation, and the order of the heavens and earth to the promised rewards of the Hereafter, comes from God alone. The rhetorical question carries gentle reproach: since the signs of His mercy and power are so evident, denying them is ingratitude and unreasonable. The verse invites reflection and thankfulness, and leads the listener to acknowledge God's lordship and respond with faith and obedience rather than denial.

translation: In them are good and beautiful ones.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ar-Rahman 55:70) describes the companions of Paradise, who are gifted with excellent character (khayrat) and beauty (hisan). The meaning is that the reward of the God-fearing in the gardens is not merely physical delight but wholesome perfection: those who dwell there are blessed with inner goodness, moral purity, and outward loveliness, so that nothing in the bliss of the hereafter is marred by the faults or deficiencies known in worldly life.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you two deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn and confronts them with the reality of God's countless blessings, in creation, revelation, provision, and the promised reward of the Hereafter. Its repetition after each blessing or warning is a rhetorical question that leaves no room for a sound excuse: every gift, and even every warning that guides one away from ruin, is a mercy from God. Denying them is therefore ingratitude and a denial of the obvious. The verse calls the listener to reflect, acknowledge God's favor, and respond with gratitude, faith, and obedience.

translation: Fair maidens with lovely eyes, secluded and sheltered in pavilions.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise: companions of pure beauty who are kept in honored seclusion within lofty, splendid tents. Their being 'maqsurat' (confined or reserved) does not signify imprisonment but rather modesty, dignity, and chastity: they are guarded and cherished, their gaze and affection reserved for their spouses alone, and not roaming about or displayed to others. The imagery of tents conveys privacy, honor, and luxurious comfort, showing that the bliss of Paradise is not merely sensory delight but a state of purity, security, and dignified fulfillment granted by God to those who were faithful.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat al-Rahman (55:13), addresses both humans and jinn and holds them to account for ingratitude. After each reminder of God's gifts, whether the creation of the heavens and the earth, the teaching of the Qur'an, the balance, the fruits and the seas, or the promises and warnings of the Hereafter, the question is repeated. Its purpose is to awaken the conscience: every blessing, and even the warnings that turn people from ruin, comes from God's mercy, so denying them is baseless. The right response is to recognize the favors, give thanks through faith and obedience, and not deny the One who gave them.

translation: No human has touched them before them, nor any jinn.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 55:56, repeated in 55:74) describes the maidens of Paradise as pure and untouched. They are virgins whom no man or jinn has ever had relations with, so they are given to the people of Paradise in perfect purity and chastity, and this is part of the honor and completeness of the reward prepared for the righteous. The mention of both humans and jinn fits the surah's address to both groups, showing that the blessings of Paradise are open to believers from either, and that the purity of its companions is absolute.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat Ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn, calling each to recognize that every blessing they enjoy, from creation, revelation, and the order of the cosmos to the promised rewards of the Hereafter, comes from God alone. Its repetition after each blessing and each warning works as a gentle rebuke that awakens the conscience. Since the favors are so clear and so many, denying them is ungrateful and unreasonable. The proper response is gratitude, humility, and obedience to the Giver, and even the warnings of judgment are counted among His favors because they guide people away from ruin.

translation: Reclining on green cushions and beautiful, fine carpets.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Rahman 55:76) describes the comfort and honor of the people of the two lesser gardens, who recline in ease upon lush green cushions and exquisitely wrought carpets. The posture of reclining signifies complete rest, security, and dignity, free from toil or worry. The green color, associated with life, freshness, and tranquility, and the finest craftsmanship of the carpets, show that Paradise's blessings are of the highest beauty and luxury, far surpassing worldly comforts. God thus rewards the believers with a state of lasting peace and honor that appeals to both the senses and the soul, calling humanity to be grateful for His favors.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, the refrain of Surat Ar-Rahman, addresses both humans and jinn, and it asks them to reflect on how much of what they have is a gift from God. Each blessing, whether the creation of the heavens and earth, the teaching of the Qur'an, the balance of the universe, or the rewards promised in the Hereafter, comes from the Lord's mercy rather than from anything they earned. The rhetorical question carries gentle reproach. Denying or ignoring such favors is ingratitude, and no reasonable being can justify it. The verse calls the listener to acknowledge God's bounty, give thanks, and respond with faith and obedience.

translation: Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour.
interpretation: The verse closes Surat ar-Rahman by affirming that everything good and abundant flows from God, so that even His name is a source of blessing and exaltation. If His mere name carries such blessing, then He Himself is infinitely greater. The two attributes named, Majesty (jalal) and Honour or Generosity (ikram), pair awe with kindness: God is exalted above all creation, beyond need and beyond comparison, yet He honours His servants and bestows His favours upon them. After the surah has listed His countless gifts and the fate of the believers and the deniers, this ending directs the reader to respond with reverence, gratitude and constant remembrance of His name, and to ask Him through these attributes, since He is both to be feared in His majesty and loved for His generosity.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the Inevitable Event occurs,
interpretation: The verse opens Surah al-Waqi'ah by announcing the arrival of the Day of Resurrection, called 'the Event' because its occurrence is certain and cannot be averted or denied. The conditional 'when' leaves the result unstated and so builds suspense. The verse is meant to shake the listener out of heedlessness and to confront the human conscience with the fact that a moment is coming that no one can doubt or postpone. It prepares the ground for the sorting of people into distinct ranks according to their faith and deeds, and it urges the listener to take stock and to prepare for that day while there is still time.

translation: There is no denying its occurrence (Qur'an 56:2).
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Event, the Day of Resurrection, is absolutely certain. When it comes, no soul will be able to deny it, turn it back, or claim it was a lie. Today people may doubt or dismiss it, but its occurrence will be so undeniable and overwhelming that all uncertainty will vanish. The verse is a reminder to take the Hereafter seriously and to prepare for it while there is still time, since its coming is a settled truth, not a possibility.

translation: It will bring down some and raise up others.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:3) describes the Day of Resurrection as a great reversal of worldly standing. On that Day, people who were exalted in this life through wealth, power, and status, but who rejected faith and righteousness, will be brought low and humiliated in the Fire. Those who were despised or considered insignificant in the world, but who were sincere and godly, will be elevated to high ranks in Paradise. Only true worth in God's sight, measured by faith and deeds, will determine a person's station, and worldly hierarchies will hold no weight.

translation: When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking,
interpretation: This verse opens Surat al-Waqi'ah and describes the first great event of the Day of Resurrection. The earth, which people regard as the symbol of stability and permanence, will be convulsed violently and everything built upon it will be thrown into upheaval. The repetition of the verbal form with its emphatic cognate (rajja rajjan) stresses the severity and totality of the quake, which is beyond any earthquake known in this world. The lesson is that worldly security, power and monuments are fragile and temporary, and that on that Day only a person's faith and deeds will give stability. The verse calls the listener to reflect and prepare for the certain event, whose occurrence no one can deny.

translation: And the mountains are crumbled to pieces,
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah, 56:5) describes one of the cosmic upheavals of the Day of Resurrection. The mountains, which people regard as the most stable and enduring features of the earth, will be pulverized and reduced to fine powder or loose dust, and will then become scattered like dust particles in the air, as the next verse states. The lesson is that nothing in creation is permanent or secure except by God's will. If mountains cannot withstand the Hour, human power, wealth and status can offer no protection, so a person should turn to God and prepare for the Day of Judgment, when the earth is leveled and all creation stands before its Lord.

translation: And they become scattered dust.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes the mountains on the Day of Resurrection: after being crushed and set in motion, they are reduced to fine dust dispersed in the air. The lesson is that even the firmest and most enduring things of this world, which people regard as symbols of permanence and strength, will utterly lose their substance when God's command arrives. This should lead the believer to recognize that only God is truly lasting, to place no ultimate trust in worldly might or possessions, and to prepare for the Day when all created stability is undone.

translation: And you will be [divided into] three groups.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:7) declares that on the Day of Resurrection, all of humanity will be sorted into three distinct categories according to their faith and deeds. The following verses identify them: the Companions of the Right (ashab al-yamin), who receive their record in the right hand and are destined for Paradise; the Companions of the Left (ashab al-shimal), who are destined for punishment; and the foremost (as-sabiqun), who surpassed others in faith and good works and are the nearest to God. The verse teaches that human destiny is not uniform, and that a person's standing in the Hereafter is determined by their belief and conduct in this life, urging the listener to reflect on which group they are striving to join.

translation: Then the companions of the right: what are the companions of the right?
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, uses a rhetorical question to magnify the status of those who receive their record of deeds in their right hand on the Day of Judgment. The repetition ('what are the companions of the right?') is a device of awe and exaltation, signaling that their honor, bliss, and good fortune are so great that they exceed ordinary description. They are the believers whose faith and righteous deeds earn them salvation and Paradise, and the verse invites the listener to contemplate and aspire to their rank, in contrast to the companions of the left who follow.

translation: And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Waqi'ah, 56:9) uses a rhetorical question to magnify the horror of the fate awaiting those who are given their record in the left hand, the people of misfortune who rejected faith and persisted in wrongdoing. The repetition, 'what are the companions of the left?', is not a request for information but a way of stirring awe and dread, suggesting that their state on the Day of Judgment is so terrible that human words cannot fully capture it. It serves as a warning that reflecting on the consequences of one's deeds now should move a person to repent and choose the path of the people of the right before the matter is decided.

translation: And the foremost, the foremost [in faith and good deeds].
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah, 56:10) singles out those who raced ahead in responding to God's call, hastening to belief, obedience, and righteous works before others did. The repetition of 'the foremost' stresses how elevated and distinguished their rank is: their precedence in this world, in embracing truth and striving in good, is matched by precedence in the Hereafter, where they are the nearest to God and enjoy the highest stations of Paradise. The verse teaches that the true measure of honor with God lies in eagerness to do good and in not delaying to answer His guidance.

translation: Those are the ones brought near [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Waqi'a, 56:11) describes the foremost in faith and righteousness, those who raced to believe and to do good in the world. Because they were first in obedience, they are rewarded with the highest nearness to God in the Hereafter, a closeness of honor, rank, and divine favor. It teaches that proximity to God is earned through sincere, prompt devotion and striving in good deeds, not through lineage or claims.

translation: In the Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: This phrase describes the final abode of the foremost and the righteous believers, who are brought near to God. It teaches that their reward is a place of complete and lasting delight, free from the hardship, fear, and sorrow of worldly life. The word 'bliss' (na'im) conveys that the blessings are not only material but also spiritual, including God's pleasure and nearness to Him. The verse thus affirms that faith and good deeds are ultimately rewarded with perfect peace and joy in the Hereafter.

translation: A multitude from the earlier generations.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Waqi'ah 56:13) describes the foremost ones (as-sabiqun), the nearest to God in Paradise. It tells us that a large group of them come from the earlier communities, those who preceded the Muslim nation, such as the followers of the previous prophets. The word 'thullah' signifies a great company, and the verse affirms that excellence and hastening to righteousness were widespread among the early peoples, so the highest ranks of Paradise are filled with many from them. The following verse, 'and a few from the later ones,' contrasts this by indicating that the truly foremost are fewer in the later generations, which encourages believers to strive to join the ranks of those who race toward good deeds.

translation: And a few from the later generations.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:14), describes the foremost ones (as-sabiqun), the highest rank of believers who will be nearest to God in Paradise. It says that the foremost among the earlier communities will be many, whereas among the later generations they will be few. The point is that outstanding spiritual distinction, being first in faith, sincerity and good deeds, is rare in later times as piety weakens and worldly distractions grow, though the Qur'an leaves the door open for any individual to strive for that elite rank. It is a call to aim for the highest level of devotion rather than settling for the ordinary.

translation: On couches woven [with gold and precious stones].
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:15), describes the resting places of the foremost ones (al-sabiqun) in Paradise. The word 'mawdunah' means closely woven or interlaced, as in thickly plaited with threads of gold and studded with gems.
