The meaning is that their seats are crafted with extraordinary artistry and splendor, signifying the honor and perfect comfort God bestows upon them. Reclining on such couches, as mentioned in the next verse, shows their state of complete ease, rest, and dignity, free from the toil and hardship of worldly life.

translation: Reclining upon them, facing one another.
interpretation: The verse describes the bliss of the people of Paradise, who recline on couches in a state of complete rest and honor. They sit facing one another rather than with their backs turned, which shows mutual affection, harmony, and the absence of malice or division among them. Their fellowship is complete: each enjoys the company of the others and sees them face to face in love and peace, a contrast to the strained and hostile gatherings often found in worldly life.

translation: Immortal youths will go around among them, serving them.
interpretation: This verse, describing the people of Paradise (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:17), shows that the blessings of the Hereafter include not only pleasures but also dignity and ease. The believers are served by youths who never age or perish, which signifies that the bliss of Paradise is eternal and unspoiled by decay or change. The youths remain forever in the freshness and beauty of boyhood, so the comfort of the dwellers is complete and lasting. Being attended in this way is a reward for those who, in the world, served God with devotion and exerted themselves in obedience, and it shows that in Paradise they are honored guests who have no need to labor.

translation: With cups, pitchers, and a goblet filled from a flowing spring.
interpretation: The verse describes the hospitality of Paradise, in which the vessels of service are paired with a drink that never runs dry. The 'flowing spring' (ma'in) shows that the drink is drawn from an ever-gushing source rather than from a stored supply that could be exhausted. The people of Paradise are therefore served in complete abundance and honor, with nothing to diminish their joy. Unlike the intoxicating wine of this world, this drink brings only pure delight, as the following verses make clear when they say it causes neither headache nor loss of reason.

translation: They will suffer neither headache from it, nor will they be intoxicated (or have their minds depleted).
interpretation: This verse, describing the pure drink of Paradise (Surat al-Waqi'ah 56:19), means that unlike worldly wine, which harms the body and mind, the drink offered to the people of Paradise brings only pleasure. It causes no headache or pain, and it does not drain their reason or strength, so the dwellers of Paradise enjoy complete and lasting well-being, with their minds and bodies unimpaired.

translation: And fruit of whatever they choose.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'a (56:20), describes the blessings of the foremost believers in Paradise. They will not be restricted to what is served to them; they will be able to select whatever fruit they desire from an abundance of varieties. The wording 'mimma yatakhayyarun' (of what they choose) points to complete freedom and honor in the next life, where every wish is met with the best of what is available. The choice itself is a part of the bliss, because it reflects their dignity and God's generosity toward those who were devoted to Him in this world.

translation: And the flesh of birds, from whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'a (56:21), describes part of the bounty awaiting the foremost believers (the muqarrabun) in Paradise. It teaches that their provision there is not limited or fixed, but is granted according to their own desire: whatever kind of bird meat their souls long for will be available to them. The point is that Paradise fulfills longing itself, so that God's generosity answers the wishes of the righteous completely, with no scarcity, effort, or dissatisfaction, as a reward for their faith and good deeds in the life of this world.

translation: And [there will be] companions with beautiful, large eyes.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:22), describes one of the rewards of the foremost believers in Paradise. The 'hur' are pure, beautiful companions whose eyes are wide and lustrous, a sign of beauty and purity. The verse is read as part of a larger picture of Paradise's blessings, which meet human longing for companionship, beauty and joy. By pairing these companions with the other delights of the Garden, it shows that the believers' reward is complete and fulfilling, free from the flaws and sorrows of worldly life, and a gift from God's generosity in return for their faith and good deeds.

translation: Like unto pearls well-guarded (hidden within their shells).
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:23) describes the maidens of Paradise (the hur al-'in) as being like pearls carefully preserved in their shells, untouched by hands or exposure. The image conveys their perfect purity, flawless beauty, and freshness: just as a pearl kept in its oyster is unblemished by dust, sunlight, or handling, so they remain pristine and unspoiled. It teaches that the rewards of Paradise are of unmatched purity and value, beyond any worldly blemish or decay.

translation: A recompense for what they used to do.
interpretation: This phrase, which appears in several places such as Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:24), teaches that the rewards of the people of Paradise are not arbitrary but are the fruit of their own deeds. Everything God grants them of bliss, honor, and joy is a just and generous return for the faith and righteous actions they carried out in the world. The verse underscores the moral link between action and consequence: what a person does in this life is never lost, and God, out of His grace, repays even small efforts with immense reward. It encourages believers to persevere in good works, trusting that each deed is recorded and will be answered with fitting recompense.

translation: They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech.
interpretation: This verse describes the atmosphere of Paradise as one wholly purified of the moral ills of worldly gatherings. In this life, even pleasant company is often marred by vain chatter, backbiting, lies, insults, and speech that provokes sin or accuses others of wrongdoing. In Paradise, the inhabitants will be free from all of this: no meaningless words that waste the heart and mind, and no speech that incites sin or leaves anyone burdened with guilt. Their conversation will instead be filled with peace, remembrance of God, and gratitude, as the verse that follows in Surah al-Waqi'a indicates ('only the saying: Peace, peace'). The verse thus conveys that the reward of the righteous is not only physical delight but also complete spiritual and social serenity, where the tongue and ear are honored and preserved from all that degrades the human soul.

translation: Only the saying: 'Peace, peace!'
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:26), describes the blessed state of the people of Paradise. It means that in Paradise they will hear no idle talk or sinful speech, and the only speech that reaches them is the greeting of peace. The angels greet them with salaam, they greet one another with salaam, and their Lord's greeting to them is peace. The repetition of 'salaam' stresses that peace and security will fill every exchange and every moment there, free from the quarrels, insults, and vain talk that mark worldly life. It shows that the people of Paradise are purified in heart and tongue, and that their company is one of harmony, safety, and honor.

translation: And the companions of the right — what are the companions of the right?
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:27), uses a rhetorical question to magnify the status of the righteous who receive their records of deeds in their right hands. By asking 'what are the companions of the right?' without answering at once, the Qur'an signals that their honor and bliss exceed human imagination and ordinary description. It prepares the listener for the detailed account that follows of their reward: thornless lote trees, layered banana trees, extended shade, flowing water, abundant fruit, and elevated couches. The verse therefore stirs longing for the state of those saved by faith and righteous deeds, and encourages the reader to seek to be among them.

translation: [They will be] among thornless lote trees,
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes the companions of the right hand in Paradise. The lote tree (sidr) in this world is known for its thorns, which make it unpleasant to approach, but in Paradise its thorns will be removed (makhdud), so that it offers only shade and fruit without harm. The meaning is that Paradise transforms what is troublesome in worldly life into pure comfort, and that the believers will enjoy every blessing free from hardship, pain, or annoyance.

translation: And banana trees (or acacia trees) arranged in layers, piled tightly one upon another.
interpretation: This verse, part of the description of the companions of the right in Paradise (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:29), points to the abundance and perfection of the blessings given to the people of Paradise. The talh, a tree known for its shade and fruit, is shown in a state of beauty and fullness, its fruits or leaves stacked in orderly layers from base to crown. Whereas the thorny, harsh trees of the world may bring discomfort, in Paradise the same kind of tree is transformed into a source of comfort, shade, and delight, showing that God removes every hardship from the believers' dwelling and replaces it with ease, richness, and harmony.

translation: And [they will dwell] in extended shade.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes one of the blessings awaiting the People of the Right Hand in Paradise: a shade that is vast, constant, and unending. It does not shift or shrink as shade does in this world with the movement of the sun, and it brings lasting comfort without the burden of scorching heat or cold. The Arabs, who knew the harshness of desert sun, regarded continuous shade as a great luxury, so the image conveys complete and enduring ease and serenity in the Hereafter, in contrast to the scorching wind and black smoke of the People of the Left.

translation: And water poured forth.
interpretation: This phrase from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:31) describes one of the blessings of Paradise for the People of the Right. The water is ever-flowing and abundant, gushing continuously without interruption, effort, or scarcity. Unlike water in this world that must be drawn from wells or carried and can run dry, the water of Paradise is always available and always at hand. It stands for the complete provision and comfort granted to the dwellers of Paradise, who never have to labor for their needs or fear their loss.

translation: And abundant fruit.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:32), describes the blessings of the people of the Right Hand in Paradise. The fruit is called abundant because it is plentiful and unfailing: it is never cut off by season and never denied by prohibition, unlike the fruits of this world, which are limited by time, place, and scarcity. It conveys the Qur'an's picture of Paradise as a place of lasting, effortless provision, where the believer's enjoyment is complete and free from the anxiety of loss or depletion.

translation: Neither cut off nor forbidden.
interpretation: This phrase from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:33) describes the fruits of Paradise. Unlike the fruits of this world, which are seasonal and can be out of reach, the fruits of Paradise never run out at any time of year, and nothing prevents the people of Paradise from enjoying them. They are always available and within easy reach, so the believers can take what they desire without hardship, fear of scarcity, or any barrier. This shows the perfection and permanence of the blessings God has prepared for the righteous.

translation: And [they will be] on raised couches.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah, 56:34) describes the blessings of the people of the right hand in Paradise. The 'raised couches' signify elevated, luxurious resting places that reflect honor, comfort, and dignity, and they are a sign of the complete ease granted to the believers. Many commentators also understand the raised height as indicating the exalted rank and status of the dwellers of Paradise, whose rest is never disturbed by toil or hardship, as the surrounding verses speak of fruits that are neither cut off nor forbidden.

translation: Indeed, We have created them (the maidens of Paradise) in a special new creation.
interpretation: The verse refers to the companions of the people of the Right Hand in Paradise. God says He brings them into being in a perfect, fresh creation that is not like their earthly form. Whether they are women of this world restored or the maidens of Paradise, they are made flawless, free of age, defect and decay, so that their beauty and purity are fitting for the everlasting bliss of the believers. The emphasis on 'We created them' shows that this is a direct act of God's power, and that the blessings of the Hereafter are not mere continuations of worldly life but a renewed, perfected existence.

translation: And We made them virgins.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:36), follows the re-creation of the women of Paradise mentioned in the preceding verse. It means that God restores them to a state of perpetual purity and youthfulness, so that whenever their husbands come to them, they find them as virgins, untouched and renewed. The meaning is that the blessings of Paradise are never marred by age or decay, and that this renewal includes even those who were old in the worldly life, who are raised in a perfected, youthful form.

translation: Loving companions, of equal age.
interpretation: This phrase from Surat al-Waqi'a (56:37) describes the maidens of Paradise as 'urub, meaning women who are devoted to their spouses, affectionate and endearing in their manner, and atrab, meaning companions of the same age as one another and as their spouses. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will enjoy perfect companionship: their partners will be full of love and charm, and matched with them in youthful vigor, so that harmony, affection and delight are complete, free of the gaps in age, temperament or affection that can trouble earthly relationships.

translation: For the companions of the right.
interpretation: This phrase from Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:38) describes those who will enjoy the gardens of Paradise, with their blessings of fruit, shade, and companions of equal age. The 'companions of the right' are the righteous believers who receive their book of deeds in their right hand on the Day of Judgment, a sign of their salvation and God's acceptance. The verse teaches that these blessings are reserved as a reward for those who lived in faith and obedience, so it encourages the believer to strive for the rank of the people of the right through sincere belief and good works.

translation: A multitude from the earlier generations,
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:13) describes the People of the Right Hand, the foremost (as-sabiqun) who will be nearest to God in the Gardens of Bliss. It says that a large group of them come from the earlier communities, those of past prophets and nations, who were ahead in faith and righteous deeds. The word 'thullah' denotes a great company, showing that nearness to God was attained by many in earlier ages, and that the highest rank is open to every generation through sincere faith and good works, not limited to one community.

translation: And a multitude from the later generations.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Waqi'a, 56:40) describes the Companions of the Right Hand, the people of Paradise who are the second category after the foremost ones (as-sabiqun). While the foremost are described as a large group from the earlier generations and a few from the later ones (verses 13-14), the Companions of the Right are described as many from the earlier generations and likewise many from the later generations, including the later followers of the Prophet Muhammad. The meaning is that salvation and reward in the Hereafter are not confined to the early believers, but a great number of the later community will also attain Paradise through faith and righteous deeds, which reflects God's abundant mercy toward this community.

translation: And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'a (56:41), uses a rhetorical question to stress how dreadful the condition of those given their record in the left hand is. By asking 'what are the companions of the left?' without answering at once, it makes the listener's imagination reach for the scale of their misery and prepares the mind for the description that follows: scorching wind, boiling water, and the shade of black smoke. They are the people who rejected faith and persisted in wrongdoing and arrogance, and the verse warns that their fate is terrible beyond what words can easily convey.

translation: In scorching wind and scalding water.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'a (56:42), describes the condition of the People of the Left in the Hereafter. They are surrounded by a burning, penetrating wind and boiling water, which stand as the fitting recompense for the life they lived. Having sought comfort and indulgence in this world, heedless of God and the Day of Judgment, they find no relief or shade in the next, only searing torment that reaches every part of them. The verse teaches that worldly luxury without faith and gratitude ends in a reversal of fortune, and it urges the believer to cultivate awareness of the Hereafter and to submit to God before that Day comes.

translation: And a shade of black smoke.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes the torment of the People of the Left in the Hereafter. They will be in scorching wind and boiling water, and the only 'shade' they will have is a shade of yahmum, thick, dark, suffocating smoke. Ordinary shade offers relief from heat, but this shade offers none, and instead adds to their suffering. The verse shows that what seems to be a comfort in the next life becomes a source of torment for those who denied the truth and lived in heedless indulgence, as the following verses make clear: it is neither cool nor pleasant.

translation: Neither cool nor pleasant.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Waqi'ah 56:44) describes the shade of the people of the Left, who dwell in scorching wind and boiling water, and who are given a shade of black smoke. The shade is denied the qualities that make shade a mercy: it brings no coolness to relieve the heat, and it offers no generosity, comfort or benefit. The verse thus shows that what looks like relief in the Hereafter is only another form of torment for those who denied the truth and lived in heedless luxury. The worldly shade they enjoyed had been a means of comfort and ease, while the shade of Hell is bitter and hurtful.

translation: Indeed, before this they were living in luxury and indulgence.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Waqi'a 56:45) explains why the people of the left hand suffer punishment in the Hereafter: in worldly life they were immersed in comfort and pleasure, absorbed in wealth and self-indulgence. Their luxury made them heedless of God, ungrateful for His blessings, and dismissive of the message of resurrection and accountability, so that they neglected their duties to God and to others. The verse does not condemn lawful wealth in itself, but warns that unchecked affluence, when it breeds arrogance and forgetfulness of the Hereafter, leads to rejecting the truth and so to a fitting punishment.

translation: And they used to persist in the great sin.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Waqi'a, 56:46) describes the people of the left hand, who were living in comfort and luxury before their downfall. Their central fault was not a passing lapse but a stubborn, repeated insistence on the 'great sin' (al-hinth al-'azim), which the commentators chiefly understand as shirk, associating partners with God, and denial of resurrection and judgment. The word 'yusirruna' (they persisted) shows that their wrongdoing was deliberate and habitual, a settled refusal to repent or turn back even after the signs and warnings had reached them. Their punishment is thus the consequence of obstinately clinging to disbelief and defiance of God, not of mere human error.

translation: And they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we really be resurrected?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogant disbelief of those who lived in heedless luxury and persisted in grave sin: they judged the possibility of resurrection by their limited, material reasoning, assuming that once the body has decayed into dust and bones, restoring it is impossible. Their question is rhetorical denial rather than sincere inquiry. The Qur'an's answer, given elsewhere, is that the One who created them from nothing the first time is fully able to recreate them. Their denial of the afterlife freed them from accountability and fueled their persistence in wrongdoing, so the verse shows that rejecting the Day of Judgment is the root of moral corruption and that divine power is not constrained by human notions of what is possible.

translation: "And our forefathers, the earlier ones, too?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 37:17 and 56:48) records the incredulous question of the deniers of resurrection. After asking how they could be raised once they have died and become dust and bones, they add their ancestors, as if the idea becomes even more absurd the further back in time one goes. Their skepticism rests on the assumption that decay and the passage of generations place the dead beyond any possibility of being restored. They also lean on ancestral tradition as a standard of truth, treating what their forefathers did not know or believe as automatically false. The Qur'an presents this as a flawed form of reasoning. God, who created humankind the first time from nothing, is fully able to bring back every generation, the earliest as well as the latest, for judgment. Remoteness in time or the extent of decomposition places no limit on His power.

translation: Say: Indeed, the earlier peoples and the later ones (Qur'an 56:49).
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet to declare that every generation of humankind, from the first to the last, is included in God's knowledge and power. No one is left out of the gathering on the appointed Day. The time that separates one generation from another, however long, does not limit God. The One who created the first generation can resurrect all of them together, so no one can escape being held to account. This should lead the listener to take the Day of Judgment seriously and to prepare for it with faith and good deeds.

translation: Surely they will all be gathered together at the appointed time of a known Day.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:50) declares that all of humanity, from the first generations to the last, will be resurrected and assembled at a time fixed by God and known to Him. The people who denied the Resurrection and said, 'When we are dead and turned to dust and bones, will we be raised?' are answered by the assurance that the Day of Judgment is a certain, predetermined appointment that cannot be advanced or delayed. Its timing is hidden from people but precisely known to God. The verse reminds us that no one will escape being brought to account, and that the world is moving toward a fixed meeting with the Creator, which calls for preparation through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: Then indeed you, O those who have gone astray and denied the truth,
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:51) addresses the deniers of the Resurrection and the Message directly, after the Qur'an has divided humanity on the Day of Judgment into three groups. It names the two defining faults of the people of the left: 'ad-dallun', who strayed from the path of guidance by following desire and misguided assumptions, and 'al-mukadhdhibun', who rejected the revelation and the promise of resurrection when it came to them. The address prepares for the punishment that follows in the next verses, where they will eat from the tree of Zaqqum and drink boiling water. It teaches that denial of the truth is not merely an intellectual error but a moral and spiritual failing with grave consequences, and that every person will ultimately face what he used to deny.

translation: You will surely eat from a tree, from Zaqqum.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the deniers on the Day of Judgment, who are told they will be made to eat from the tree of Zaqqum, a bitter and foul tree that grows in the depths of Hell. The repetition of 'from a tree, from Zaqqum' stresses the horror of it: their food will be the very thing that tortures them. It is a fitting recompense for those who indulged in worldly desires and denied the resurrection, for what they once consumed without gratitude is replaced by a bitter, painful meal that deepens their punishment rather than relieving their hunger.

translation: And you will fill your bellies with it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:66) describes the people of Hellfire eating from the tree of Zaqqum. Though the fruit is bitter, foul and harmful, they will be compelled by intense hunger to eat from it until their bellies are full. The meaning is that the torment is increased through the very thing they turn to for relief: instead of nourishment, they find that their only food is a source of further suffering, a fitting recompense for those who indulged in worldly appetites and denied the truth.

translation: And drink on top of it from the scalding water.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes the punishment of the deniers who go astray. After they fill their bellies with the bitter fruit of the Zaqqum tree, they will be given boiling water to drink on top of it. The intended meaning is that their torment is compounded: instead of relief from the burning hunger and the harshness of the Zaqqum, they receive more suffering, since the scalding water, rather than quenching thirst, tears at their insides. It serves as a stark warning that those who reject the truth and persist in sin will face a fitting and agonizing recompense, the opposite of the comfort and refreshment promised to the righteous.

translation: And you will drink it as thirsty camels drink.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Waqi'ah 56:55) completes the description of the deniers of the truth in the Hereafter, who will eat from the tree of Zaqqum and fill their bellies with it, then drink scalding water upon it. The 'hīm' are camels afflicted with an unquenchable thirst, so the image conveys that the people of Hell will gulp the boiling water greedily and ceaselessly, driven by a raging thirst that can never be satisfied. It shows how their punishment fits their state: they who neglected the true source of nourishment and guidance are given a drink that torments rather than relieves, and their craving only grows the more they consume.

translation: This will be their hospitality on the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:56), concludes the description of the 'companions of the left' who will be fed from the tree of Zaqqum and made to drink boiling water. The word 'nuzul' normally means the welcome or lodging prepared for a guest, so using it here is deeply ironic: what is offered as their 'hospitality' is torment. If this is only the initial reception, the reader is invited to imagine how severe the rest of their punishment will be. The verse is a warning that those who denied the resurrection and persisted in arrogance and sin will meet on the Day of Judgment the very reality they rejected, and that their treatment will be the opposite of the honor given to the righteous.

translation: We created you, so why do you not believe?
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:57) argues from the reality of human origins to the truth of resurrection and God's oneness. Since it is God alone who brought people into existence from nothing, and no one else claims credit for creating them, denying that He can recreate them after death is illogical. The question 'why do you not believe' is a gentle rebuke: the evidence of one's own existence should lead to acknowledging the Creator, accepting His messengers, and affirming that the Hereafter is possible and certain, since the second creation is easier than the first for the One who began it.

translation: Have you considered the semen that you emit?
interpretation: This verse opens a series of questions (Surat al-Waqi'ah, 56:58-59) that direct human beings to reflect on the origin of their own existence. The sperm-drop is something people emit without any real control over what becomes of it. They do not design it, give it life, or shape it into a human being. The question is rhetorical: if humans cannot claim to create the child that develops from it, then the Creator is God alone. That same power can also resurrect the dead, so the verse answers those who denied the Resurrection by pointing to the wonder of creation they already witness in themselves, and it calls them to humility and gratitude.

translation: Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:59) follows the question about the sperm that humans emit, and it challenges people to consider the origin of their own existence. The point is that human beings only take part in the outward means of procreation, and they have no power to turn a drop of fluid into a fully formed human being, with sight, hearing, intellect, and life. The shaping of the embryo, its growth, and the breathing of life into it are acts beyond human capacity, so only God can be the true Creator. The rhetorical question is meant to lead the denier of resurrection to admit that the One who created them the first time is able to recreate them after death, and that He alone deserves gratitude and worship.

translation: We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outstripped.
interpretation: God reminds humankind that death is not a matter of chance but a measured decree He has ordained for every person, each with an appointed time. Nothing can outpace or thwart His will, so no one can delay death or escape it, and no power can prevent Him from replacing people with others or recreating them in forms they do not know. The verse calls people to reflect on their mortality and to accept that the One who governs life and death is fully able to resurrect them, so they should prepare for the return to Him rather than being heedless.

translation: [We are able] to replace you with others like you and to recreate you in a form that you do not know.
interpretation: The verse stresses God's absolute power over human life and death. Death is not a limit on His ability: He can remove one generation and replace it with similar ones, and He can bring people into being again in a new mode of existence beyond human experience and knowledge. This answers those who deny resurrection. If God can replace entire peoples and fashion them in forms unknown to us, then raising people after death is easy for Him. It is also a warning to the arrogant that they are not indispensable, since God can substitute others for them whenever He wills.

translation: And you have already known the first creation, so why do you not remember?
interpretation: God reminds humanity that they already know, from their own experience and reason, that He brought them into existence the first time from nothing, out of a drop of fluid, and then shaped them in stages. Whoever was able to originate them initially can surely bring them back to life again at the resurrection, which is easier by comparison. The verse reproaches those who deny the resurrection for failing to reflect on this clear evidence in themselves, and urges them to take heed, acknowledge God's power, and prepare for the Hereafter.

translation: Have you considered what you cultivate?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:63) invites people to reflect on farming. Humans plough the soil, scatter the seed and tend the land, but they do not create the seed, make it sprout, or cause it to grow into a crop. The growth of plants, and the sustenance that comes from it, is God's work alone. The verse leads into the next one, which asks 'Is it you who make it grow, or are We the Grower?' It aims to make people humble and grateful, and to show that the One who brings plants out of dead earth is able to bring the dead back to life. Human effort is only a means; the real power over provision belongs to God.

translation: Is it you who make it grow, or are We the Grower?
interpretation: The verse (Al-Waqi'a 56:64) directs human attention to the seed they sow in the earth. People only plant the seed and tend the soil; they do not create life within the seed, split it open, push forth the shoot, or bring it to fruit. Those processes belong to God alone. The rhetorical question moves the listener to acknowledge that daily sustenance is a gift from God's power and mercy rather than the product of human effort alone. This acknowledgment should lead to gratitude and to recognition of God's ability to resurrect the dead, since the One who brings plants out of lifeless earth can also bring life back to the dead.

translation: If We willed, We could make it crushed debris, and you would remain wondering and lamenting.
interpretation: After calling attention to the crops that people sow and that God alone causes to grow, the verse shows how completely human beings depend on Him. The harvest is not secured by their effort; it is a gift that God can withdraw at any moment. If He willed, He could turn the ripening crop into dry, broken stubble, useless as food, and the people would be left astonished and grieving over their loss, trading regrets and complaints. The verse is meant to awaken gratitude and to lead people to acknowledge the Provider, whose mercy preserves their sustenance, and so to recognize His power and to reflect on resurrection as well, since the One who brings life from dead soil can raise the dead.

translation: "Indeed, we are burdened with debt (or: we are ruined)."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 56:66) records what the people of Paradise's opposites, the deniers, would say when they see their harvest turned to dry chaff: after toiling to plant and cultivate, they realize their labor has come to nothing and they are left with loss and debt. The meaning is a reminder that all sustenance comes from God alone, not from human effort; the farmer only sows, while it is God who makes the seed grow. When He wills, He can destroy the crop, leaving people in regret and ruin. The verse calls people to gratitude and to recognize God's power over provision, which in turn supports belief in His power to resurrect.

translation: Rather, we have been deprived.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:67) is the retort of the people who, after seeing their crops ruined, say that they are not merely burdened with debt but are people denied any provision at all. It shows that they realize the produce they relied on was not under their control. The sowing was their effort, but the growth, ripening and preservation of the harvest belong to God alone. He can withhold sustenance whenever He wills. Their cry of loss is meant to lead them to acknowledge His power and to be grateful for His provision, rather than to take credit for their own labor.

translation: Have you considered the water that you drink?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 56:68) invites people to reflect on water, the most basic requirement of their survival, and to recognize that they did not create it and have no power to produce it. The next verses ask whether they send it down from the clouds or whether God does. The point is that the daily provision people take for granted is a continuous gift from God. It should lead them to acknowledge His power and lordship and to be grateful. It also supports the belief in resurrection: the One who sustains life with water can bring the dead back to life.

translation: Is it you who sent it down from the rain clouds, or are We the Sender?
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Waqi'a, 69) is a rhetorical question that draws attention to God's sole power over water, the basis of all life. People drink rain water that falls from the clouds, but none of them can gather the clouds, make the water descend, or control its amount, timing, or place. Since no human or natural cause acts independently of God's will, the verse calls the reader to acknowledge that the Creator alone sends down the rain as a mercy. This recognition should lead to gratitude and worship, and to the conviction that the One who sustains life with water is able to bring the dead back to life.

translation: If We willed, We could make it bitter; so why do you not give thanks?
interpretation: After reminding people of the rain that falls from the clouds, the verse shows that sweet, drinkable water is a mercy from God and not something people secure for themselves. Had He willed, He could have made the water salty and bitter, so that it could not quench thirst or sustain crops and life. That it stays fresh and wholesome is therefore a favor that calls for gratitude, and the verse rebukes people for taking it for granted and failing to thank the Provider through faith, obedience, and acknowledgment of His oneness and power.

translation: Have you considered the fire that you kindle?
interpretation: God directs people to reflect on something so familiar that it is easily taken for granted: the fire they strike from wood or flint for cooking, warmth, and light. Humans can use the materials, but they did not create the property by which fire is held within them or the power by which it comes forth. This everyday experience is meant to awaken gratitude and humility, and to point to a Creator who brings forth fire from green wood and who is therefore able to bring the dead back to life. The verse turns an ordinary benefit into a sign of divine power, mercy, and the truth of resurrection.

translation: Is it you who created its tree, or are We the Creator?
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:72), refers to the tree from which fire is kindled, in the preceding verses about the fire people strike from green wood. It is a rhetorical question that draws attention to human dependence on God. People use fire daily and benefit from it, yet they have no power to bring into being the tree that supplies its fuel. The tree grows only by God's will, power, and provision, so the verse is meant to make people recognize that every resource they use is a gift from the Creator. This should lead to gratitude and acknowledgment of His oneness, and to the recognition that the One who can bring forth fire from a green tree is also able to resurrect the dead.

translation: We have made it a reminder and a provision for the travelers of the desert.
interpretation: The verse refers to the fire that people kindle (mentioned in the preceding verses). God made this fire a reminder of the greater Fire of Hell, prompting people to fear God's punishment and take heed, and at the same time a benefit and means of livelihood for the muqwin, those who journey through or camp in the barren wilderness, who rely on fire for warmth, cooking, light, and guidance. Thus the same blessing serves both as a spiritual admonition and a practical mercy, pointing to God's power and generosity and calling people to gratitude and reflection.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surat al-Waqi'ah, is a call to respond to everything the surah has shown: God's power in creation, in resurrection, and in the final judgment of humankind. The fitting response to these signs is tasbih, declaring God free of all imperfection and partners, and praising Him with the heart, tongue, and conduct. Glorifying 'the name' of the Lord indicates that His names and attributes are themselves worthy of reverence, and that remembering Him with awe should shape how a person lives. The description 'the Most Great' reminds the believer that nothing compares to God's majesty, so gratitude and humility before Him are the proper stance in light of the truths of revelation and the afterlife.

translation: So I swear by the setting places of the stars.
interpretation: God opens an oath by the places where the stars set, or fall, a sign of His power and order in the cosmos. By swearing by something so vast and precisely ordered, He draws attention to the solemn truth that follows in the next verses: that the Qur'an is a noble recitation and a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. Just as the stars follow exact courses and positions that point to a wise Creator, the gradual descent of the Qur'an to the heart of the Prophet, in its proper times and places, is a guidance of equal order and majesty. The oath calls the listener to reflect on the signs in creation as a way to recognize the truth of revelation.

translation: And indeed, it is a mighty oath, if only you knew.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 56:76) comes after God swears by the setting places of the stars (56:75), and it stresses how weighty that oath is. The parenthetical 'if you only knew' suggests that people overlook the greatness of what is being sworn by: the order, precision and power seen in the heavens, which point to the Creator's wisdom and might. God swears this oath to affirm that the Qur'an is a noble, protected revelation (56:77-78), so the grandeur of the oath underlines how certain and authoritative the revelation is. Anyone who grasped the scale of the cosmic signs would approach the Qur'an with awe rather than denial.

translation: Indeed, this is a noble Qur'an.
interpretation: The verse affirms the Qur'an's honor and excellence: it is 'karim' because it is rich in benefit, guidance and wisdom, and because it elevates those who hold to it and act by it. Its nobility lies in its source, as the speech of God, and in its content, which calls people to what is best in belief, character and conduct. It is not the poetry or soothsaying that the disbelievers claimed, but a generous, abundant revelation whose guidance never runs dry, and which deserves to be received with reverence, respect and sincere obedience.

translation: In a Book well-guarded (concealed and protected).
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:78), describes the Qur'an as preserved in a protected Book, which most commentators understand to be the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) in the heavens. The word 'maknun' means hidden, shielded, and safeguarded from any alteration, corruption, or tampering. The verse affirms the Qur'an's honor and its divine origin: its source is guarded by God, kept beyond the reach of Satan and of human interference, and so its message reaches people exactly as it was revealed. The verse also invites reverence toward the Qur'an and confidence in its authenticity.

translation: None shall touch it except the purified.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 56:79) refers to the Noble Qur'an, which is preserved in a well-guarded Book (al-Kitab al-Maknun) mentioned in the preceding verse. Its true meaning is that this heavenly record is shielded from corruption and from the touch of any but the angels, who are pure and free of sin. Thus the revelation reached the Prophet ﷺ unaltered, untouched by devils or by the impure influence of falsehood. By extension, it teaches that the Qur'an's reality and guidance are opened only to hearts purified of arrogance, hypocrisy and desire, and it calls the believer to approach the Book with reverence, outward cleanliness and inward sincerity.

translation: A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is not the composition of Muhammad or any created being, but a revelation sent down by God, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. By describing God as Lord of the worlds, it stresses that this Book carries divine authority and mercy for all humanity and every realm of existence, so its guidance is universal, truthful, and binding, and those who doubt or reject it are in fact disputing a message that originates with the Creator and Sustainer Himself.

translation: Is it this discourse that you hold in contempt and treat with indifference?
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Waqi'a rebukes those who receive the Qur'an with laxity, flattery, or disdain instead of faith and sincere acceptance. The word 'mudhinun' implies compromising or dissembling: pretending to be neutral or accommodating toward the truth while inwardly rejecting it, or neglecting its commands out of heedlessness. Having just affirmed the Qur'an's honor, its preservation in a protected book, and its being a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, God expresses astonishment that anyone would treat such a weighty message lightly. The verse calls people to take the Qur'an seriously, to believe in it, and to act on it, rather than trifling with it or accommodating falsehood at the expense of the truth.

translation: And you make your denial of the truth your means of livelihood (or: you make it your share of provision that you deny).
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, instead of expressing gratitude to God for the provision He sends down, such as the rain and the Qur'an's guidance, which are the source of life and sustenance, turn the blessing into an occasion for ingratitude. They attribute God's gifts to other causes, such as the stars or seasons, so that their only portion of His bounty is to deny it. The interpretation is that a person's proper response to provision is thankfulness, and whoever responds to God's favors with denial has made ingratitude the very thing he lives by, and thus forfeits the true benefit of the blessing.

translation: Then why, when the soul reaches the throat [at the moment of death],
interpretation: This verse opens a challenge to those who deny God's power and the Resurrection. It pictures the dying person at the final moment, when the soul rises to the throat and life is slipping away. Family and attendants stand helpless, unable to hold the soul back. The point is that human beings, for all their pride and self-reliance, cannot control life and death. If they cannot stop their own loved one from dying, they have no ground to deny that God alone governs life, death, and the return to Him for judgment.

translation: And you at that moment are looking on.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 56:84) belongs to the passage describing a dying person whose soul reaches the throat. Those gathered around the deathbed can only watch helplessly as the person slips away. They see the signs of death but can do nothing to prevent it. The verse points to human powerlessness before God's decree over life and death. Since people cannot hold back a soul at its final moment, they should recognize that God alone has authority over life, death, and the return to Him, and that this should lead them to humility, gratitude, and preparation for the Hereafter.

translation: And We are nearer to him than you are, but you do not see.
interpretation: The verse speaks of a dying person at the moment of death, as those gathered around him watch helplessly. God's knowledge, power, and decree encompass the dying person more closely than the family and friends at his bedside, who can only look on. God is aware of his inner state and controls the departure of his soul, while the angels of death, whom the onlookers cannot perceive, are present to take it. The verse reminds people that nothing escapes God's authority at the decisive moment of death, and that human perception and ability are limited before the unseen realities that God alone governs.

translation: Then why do you not, if you are not to be held to account (not subject to recompense),
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:86) challenges those who deny the Resurrection and Judgment. It continues the argument begun in the previous verses about the moment of death, when the soul reaches the throat and the onlookers stand helpless. God asks: if you truly believe you will never be judged or recompensed, and that there is no Lord with authority over you, then why can you not bring back the departing soul to the body when it reaches the throat? The verse points out that human beings are utterly powerless in the face of death, which demonstrates that they are under a higher power who gives life, takes it away, and will bring them to account. Their inability to prevent death exposes the hollowness of their denial and affirms God's absolute dominion and the certainty of the Reckoning.

translation: Then bring it back [the soul to the body], if you are truthful.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 56:87) completes the challenge begun in 56:83-86. When a dying person's soul reaches the throat and those around can only watch, God asks the deniers of resurrection and divine authority: if you are truly independent, not subject to any judgment or higher power, then restore the departing soul to its body. Their inability to do so exposes their helplessness before death. It follows that the One who takes life holds power over it and can bring it back at the resurrection, so their denial of accountability has no basis. The verse is meant to humble human pride and lead the hearer to acknowledge God's sovereignty over life, death and the return to Him.

translation: So if he [the dying person] is one of those brought near [to Allah],
interpretation: This verse begins the account of the soul's fate at the moment of death, which the passage describes as the time when the soul reaches the throat and everyone present watches helplessly. It tells that whoever departs this life among the muqarrabun, the foremost who raced to obedience and good deeds in the world, will be met with honor from the very start of the next life. The muqarrabun have the highest rank among believers because they were nearest to God in faith, devotion, and sincerity, so their closeness in this world is rewarded with closeness in the Hereafter. The verse points out that a person's end follows from the course of their life, and that the dying hour is when the reality of one's standing with God becomes clear. The following verses elaborate on this reward as rest, fragrance, and a garden of bliss.

translation: Then [for him is] rest and bounty, and a Garden of Delight.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:89) describes the reward of those brought near to God at the moment of death and in the hereafter. 'Rawh' is relief, comfort and freedom from the burdens and anxieties of worldly life; 'rayhan' is sweet fragrance and God's provision and bounty; and 'jannat na'im' is the Garden of bliss where delight is complete and lasting. Together they show that the believers drawn near to God receive ease of soul, pleasing provision, and eternal joy, so that their reward is both spiritual peace and sensory delight.

translation: And as for him who is of the companions of the right,
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah (56:90), begins the final division of humankind at death and in the Hereafter. Those who are 'companions of the right' are the people of faith and righteousness who receive their record of deeds in their right hands, a sign of acquittal and salvation. They are a rank below the foremost (al-muqarrabun) but are still among the successful. The verse points to the fact that a person's destiny at the moment of death is determined by their faith and conduct in life, and that those who die in a state of belief and good works are met with honor, which the following verse expresses as greeting of peace: 'Then peace be to you from the companions of the right.' The verse thus offers reassurance to believers and encourages steadfastness, since the dying person's end is decided by the path they have walked.

translation: Then peace be upon you from the companions of the right.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Waqi'a 56:91) describes the dying person who was among the Companions of the Right, those who are saved. At the moment of death, or in the afterlife, he is greeted with peace and assurance of safety, and is told that he is among the righteous whose record is received in the right hand. The greeting signals that he is free from fear and punishment, and that God's mercy and the salutations of the angels and fellow believers accompany him as he enters his promised honor and rest.

translation: But if he is one of the deniers who have gone astray,
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes the third category of people at death and in the Hereafter: those who rejected the truth of resurrection, revelation and the Messengers, and who strayed from the path of guidance out of ignorance and arrogance. Denial (takdhib) and misguidance (dalal) are joined here to show that their error was both a rejection of the truth when it came and a loss of the way. The verse prepares for the next verses, which announce their punishment: a welcome of boiling water and the burning of Hellfire. The lesson is that a person's final destiny depends on his faith and his response to God's guidance, and that persistent denial of the truth leads to ruin.

translation: So an abode of scalding boiling water awaits them.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:93) describes the fate of those who denied the truth and went astray: their welcome and lodging in the Hereafter will be boiling water. The word 'nuzul' denotes the hospitality prepared for a guest, so the verse speaks with bitter irony. Instead of the honor a guest receives, the deniers are given scalding water as their reception, which shows the severity of their punishment and the justice of recompense for their rejection of the Resurrection and persistence in sin.

translation: And the burning in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:94) completes the description of the deniers who went astray, who are given boiling water as hospitality and then are cast into Hellfire. It means that their final destiny is not merely discomfort but to be engulfed and roasted in blazing fire, a just recompense for their denial of the truth and the Day of Judgment. The word 'taṣliyah' conveys total immersion in the flames, showing that the punishment is complete and inescapable, and that the one who rejected God's signs will taste the full consequence of that rejection.

translation: Indeed, this is the certain truth.
interpretation: This verse, which comes at the close of Surat al-Haqqa (69:51), affirms that the Qur'an and the message it carries, including the reality of the Day of Judgment, reward and punishment, and the divine origin of the revelation, are not conjecture or poetry or the speech of a soothsayer but absolute truth. The phrase 'haqq al-yaqin' joins truth with certainty to stress that this is knowledge beyond all doubt: it is the truth in itself, and for the one who accepts it, it brings a conviction that is firm and cannot be shaken. The believer is therefore called to base their beliefs and actions on this certainty and to respond with worship and glorification of God, as the following verse commands.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surah al-Waqi'ah (and also appears in Surah al-Haqqah), is a call to respond to everything that has been described before it: the power of God in creation, the certainty of resurrection, the reckoning, and the fate of the believers and the deniers. After such evidence of God's majesty, the fitting human response is tasbih, declaring God free of any imperfection, partner, or incapacity, and praising Him with heart, tongue, and conduct. The phrase 'the name of your Lord' teaches that even His name deserves reverence, and that the believer should remember Him with honor in worship, in speech, and in daily life. The attribute 'the Most Great' reminds the believer that nothing is greater than God, so gratitude, humility, and devotion belong to Him alone. The address to the Prophet also extends to every believer, making glorification of God the conclusion and purpose of reflection on His signs.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all of creation, in its very existence and order, bears witness to God's perfection and declares Him free of any flaw or partner. This glorification is not limited to humans: every being by its nature and design points to its Creator. The closing names, Al-'Aziz (the Almighty) and Al-Hakim (the All-Wise), explain why the glorification is deserved. His power is unrivaled, so nothing can resist or overcome Him, and His wisdom is flawless, so nothing He creates or decrees is without purpose. Believers are therefore invited to join the rest of creation in praising Him, to trust His commands, and to submit to Him in the knowledge that His might is always joined with wisdom.

translation: To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death, and He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms that absolute sovereignty over the whole of creation rests with God alone, so nothing happens outside His authority. Life and death, the most basic realities every creature experiences and none can control, are in His hand alone, which shows that humans and all other beings depend entirely on Him for their existence and its end. Because His power extends to everything without exception, He is able to create, sustain, bring death and raise to life again. The believer should therefore place trust in Him, submit to His command, and fear no created power, since all power is delegated from Him and returns to Him.

translation: He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He has full knowledge of all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God transcends time and space: nothing precedes Him and nothing outlasts Him, so He is the origin and final end of all existence. He is the Manifest because His signs and His supremacy are evident in creation and nothing is above Him, and He is the Hidden because His essence cannot be perceived or encompassed by the senses and nothing is closer to creation than His knowledge. Because His being envelops every beginning and end and every outward and inward reality, His knowledge encompasses all things, including what people conceal in their hearts. The believer is therefore invited to live with constant awareness of God, trusting in Him and holding himself accountable in both public and private conduct.

translation: He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne. He knows what penetrates into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you may be. And God is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty as Creator and His comprehensive, all-encompassing knowledge. His being above the Throne denotes His majesty and transcendence over creation, yet this does not distance Him from it: His knowledge covers everything that enters the earth, like seeds, rain and the dead, and everything that emerges from it, like plants, springs and treasures, as well as what comes down from the sky, like revelation, rain and decrees, and what rises to it, like angels, deeds and supplications. The phrase 'He is with you wherever you are' is understood as His being with His creatures through knowledge, observation and power, so no one can be hidden from Him. The verse ends with a moral reminder that, since God sees all deeds, a believer should live with constant awareness of Him, doing good and avoiding wrongdoing even in private.

translation: To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to God all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone holds true and absolute sovereignty over the whole of creation, so whatever power humans or any other beings seem to have is only entrusted and temporary. Since every matter, whether its origin, course, or outcome, ultimately returns to Him for final judgment, no injustice will remain unaddressed and no deed will be lost. This should lead the believer to rely on God, hold fast to responsibility and righteousness, and be content that the ultimate decision rests with the One who is perfectly wise and just.

translation: He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He is Knowing of what lies within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse points to the gradual, precisely ordered alternation of night and day, with the lengthening of one at the expense of the other through the seasons, as a sign of God's total control over time and creation. The One who governs these vast cosmic cycles with perfect precision and wisdom also knows the innermost secrets of human hearts: intentions, beliefs, and hidden thoughts. Just as nothing in the cosmic order escapes His management, nothing in the inner life of a person escapes His knowledge. This calls the believer to sincerity, to awareness of God's constant watchfulness, and to gratitude and humility before a Lord whose power is outward in nature and inward in awareness of the soul.

translation: Believe in God and His Messenger, and spend out of that in which He has made you successors. For those among you who believe and spend, there is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth is not truly owned by people but is a trust from God, who has made them temporary custodians of it, having belonged to others before them and destined to pass to others after them. Since a person is only a steward, spending in God's cause is not a loss but the proper fulfillment of that trust, and the real proof of faith. Belief must therefore be accompanied by generosity, and those who combine the two are promised a great reward from God.

translation: And what is the matter with you that you do not believe in God, while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are indeed believers?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke that exposes the inconsistency of claiming faith while holding back from its demands. Every excuse for disbelief or hesitation has already been removed: the Messenger is present among them, calling them clearly and directly to faith, and God has already taken a covenant from them. That covenant is the natural disposition (fitra) and the innate recognition of their Lord's lordship, together with the pledge they gave in accepting Islam. The phrase 'if you are indeed believers' means that real faith cannot coexist with turning away from the Messenger's call. Belief must show itself in trust, obedience, and sacrifice for God's cause, which is the theme of the surrounding verses on spending and striving. Anyone who truly believes has no reasonable ground for hesitating.

translation: It is He who sends down upon His servant clear verses to bring you out from the darknesses into the light. And indeed, Allah is to you Compassionate and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse presents revelation as an act of divine mercy. The clear signs sent down to the Prophet Muhammad are a means of guidance, lifting people out of the darkness of disbelief, ignorance, doubt, and moral confusion into the light of faith, knowledge, and certainty. Darkness is spoken of in the plural because misguidance has many forms, while light is singular because the path of truth is one. The closing statement explains the reason for this guidance: God's compassion and mercy toward His creation. He did not leave people lost in error but gave them clear proofs and a way to follow.

translation: And what is the matter with you that you do not spend in the cause of God, while to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent before the Conquest and fought; those are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought. But to each God has promised the best reward. And God is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse rebukes hesitation in giving for God's cause by reminding believers that everything they hold is only a trust: God is the ultimate inheritor of all things, so what they withhold will pass from them anyway, and spending it for God is the only way to secure lasting benefit. It also teaches that moral and spiritual worth is measured by sacrifice and timeliness: those who gave and struggled when the community was weak, vulnerable, and the outcome uncertain, before the Conquest (of Mecca, or the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah), hold a higher rank than those who gave once victory was secure, because their sincerity was tested under greater hardship. Yet God does not deny the later believers, promising all sincere givers the 'best' reward, while He knows precisely the intentions and efforts behind every deed, so each is recompensed with perfect justice.

translation: Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him, and he will have a generous reward?
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a loan to encourage spending in God's cause. Whatever a person gives sincerely and from lawful earnings, to support the needy, to serve the community, or to defend the faith, is treated by God as a debt He owes the giver. God needs nothing, since everything belongs to Him, so the image is an act of grace that shows how much He honors charity. A loan is 'goodly' when it comes from pure wealth, is given with sincere intention and without reproach or expectation of praise, and goes to a worthy cause. God promises to multiply such giving many times over, and beyond that the giver receives a generous reward in the Hereafter. The believer should therefore give freely, trusting that nothing given for God's sake is lost.

translation: On the Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running ahead of them and on their right sides: 'Your glad tidings today are gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein you will abide forever. That is the great triumph.'
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the faith and righteous deeds that believers cultivated in this world take shape as a radiant light guiding them across the darkness of that Day. The light before them marks their guidance and steady progress toward Paradise, while the light on their right signifies that their record of deeds is given in the right hand, a sign of acceptance and success. The angels greet them with good news of eternal gardens, showing that the reward is both honor and lasting security. The verse concludes that this outcome is the true and supreme success, since every worldly gain is fleeting by comparison, and the light of the hereafter is the fruit of the light of faith and obedience in this life.

translation: On the Day when the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say to those who believed: 'Wait for us, that we may take some light from your light.' It will be said: 'Go back behind you and seek light.' Then a wall will be set up between them, with a gate; on its inner side is mercy, and on its outer side, facing it, is punishment.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the light of faith and righteous deeds that guided believers in the world will become a visible light guiding them across the Hereafter, while the hypocrites, who outwardly joined the believers but inwardly lacked sincere faith, will find themselves in darkness. They will plead to borrow some light, but they will be told to go back and seek it, a rebuke meaning that light cannot be acquired then, since it is earned only through sincere faith and deeds in this life. A barrier will then separate the two groups: the side of the believers is mercy and safety, leading to Paradise, while the side where the hypocrites stand is torment. The verse teaches that hypocrisy brings no benefit in the Hereafter, that outward association with the faithful cannot substitute for genuine belief, and that the separation between truth and falsehood, hidden in this world, will be made plain and final on that Day.

translation: They (the hypocrites) will call out to them (the believers): "Were we not with you?" They will say: "Yes indeed, but you led yourselves into temptation, you waited and watched, you doubted, and your false hopes deluded you until God's decree came; and the Deceiver deceived you about God."
interpretation: The verse describes a scene on the Day of Judgment in which the hypocrites, separated from the believers by a barrier and left in darkness, plead that they had outwardly shared the believers' community, prayers, and life. The believers answer that outward association was worthless because the hypocrites' inner state was corrupt. They ruined themselves by yielding to temptation and sin, by waiting for misfortune to strike the believers, by doubting the truth of the message and the resurrection, and by clinging to vain wishes such as the idea that God would overlook their conduct or that repentance could always be postponed. This self-deception lasted until death or God's judgment arrived suddenly, and Satan, the great deceiver, made them feel secure about God's mercy while neglecting His commands. The lesson is that membership in a community and outward conformity do not save a person; sincere faith, certainty, and action are what count, and one should beware of false hope and of using God's mercy as an excuse for heedlessness.

translation: So today no ransom will be accepted from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire; it is your protector, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites on the Day of Judgment, after they have been left in darkness and separated from the believers. It declares that the chance for redemption has ended: no payment, however great, and no excuse can buy their release, and the same is true of the open disbelievers. The Fire is called their 'mawla' to mean it is the only thing left to claim them and the place that suits them, as a consequence of how they lived. Having chosen doubt, deception and worldly desire over sincere faith, they are given the Fire as their final home, which is a terrible end. The verse warns that salvation must be sought now through sincere faith and righteous action, because on that Day nothing will be accepted in exchange.

translation: Has the time not yet come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves at the remembrance of God and at what has come down of the truth, and that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture before, for whom the term grew long, so their hearts became hardened? And many of them are defiant transgressors.
interpretation: The verse is a gentle but firm reproach to believers whose spiritual fervor may have weakened. It asks whether it is not high time for their hearts to soften and submit when God is mentioned and when the Qur'an is recited. The warning is that long familiarity with revelation, and the passage of time since receiving guidance, can breed heedlessness and then hardness of heart, as happened to earlier communities who drifted from the spirit of their scripture into ritual routine and disobedience. Faith therefore needs constant renewal through reflection, remembrance, and sincere humility. Otherwise, complacency over time can lead to spiritual deadness and, eventually, open defiance of God's commands.

translation: Know that God gives life to the earth after its death. We have made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse points to the renewal of barren land by rain as a visible sign of God's power to restore life, and in particular to revive hearts that have grown hard through heedlessness and forgetfulness of Him. Just as lifeless earth is brought back to fertility, a hardened heart can be softened and revived by remembrance of God and by the guidance of revelation. God has made His signs plain in both creation and scripture, so that people will use their reason, draw the lesson from what they observe, and respond with humility, faith, and obedience.

translation: Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and have lent Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity given sincerely for God's sake is treated by God as a loan He Himself guarantees to repay. Calling spending in His cause a 'goodly loan' (qard hasan) shows His generosity: although He owns everything and needs nothing, He honors the giver as a creditor and promises to multiply the gift many times over. The 'goodly' quality means the gift comes from lawful wealth, is given willingly and without reproach or expectation of worldly return, and is offered purely for God's pleasure. Besides the multiplied return, the giver is promised a 'noble reward' (ajr karim), meaning Paradise and God's pleasure, a recompense that is generous, lasting and free of deficiency. The verse also names men and women equally, showing that both share the same standing and the same reward before God for their good deeds.

translation: Those who believe in God and His messengers — it is they who are the truthful (siddiqun), and the witnesses (martyrs) before their Lord will have their reward and their light. But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith, when it is sincere and wholehearted, raises a person to the highest rank of truthfulness. Belief in God and in all His messengers without distinction is not just a claim but a conviction that is confirmed by conduct, so the believer becomes a 'siddiq', one whose words, inner state, and deeds agree. Alongside them, those who bear witness to the truth through sacrifice, even to the point of giving their lives, are promised a special reward and a light that will guide them on the Day of Judgment. In contrast, rejecting God's signs and denying revelation is a deliberate turning away from the truth, and its consequence is a lasting place in Hell. The verse sets two clear paths before people: a faith that brings light and honor, and denial that ends in darkness and punishment.

translation: Know that the life of this world is but play, amusement, adornment, boasting among yourselves, and rivalry in wealth and children. It is like rain whose growth delights the farmers; then it dries up, and you see it turn yellow, then it becomes debris. And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment, and forgiveness from God and approval. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.
interpretation: The verse portrays worldly life as a passing stage that moves through phases like a plant's life cycle: childlike play, then amusement, then adornment, then pride and competition in wealth and offspring. Like crops that flourish after rain, impress people, then wither into chaff, worldly achievements are attractive but short-lived and cannot be relied upon. Its purpose is to loosen the heart's attachment to the world and redirect effort toward what lasts. The Hereafter brings serious consequences: severe punishment for those who were absorbed in delusion and forgot God, and forgiveness and divine pleasure for those who kept their priorities right. The world is therefore a deceptive commodity that tricks people if treated as the final goal, but it can be a means to earn God's forgiveness and approval if used with awareness of the Hereafter.

translation: Race one another toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is like the width of the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who believe in God and His messengers. That is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse urges believers to treat the pursuit of salvation as a competition, hastening to righteous deeds, repentance, and sincere faith without delay, because forgiveness and Paradise are the true goals worth striving for, unlike the fleeting pleasures of worldly life mentioned in the preceding verses. The description of Paradise as vast as the heavens and the earth conveys its immense scale and the abundant room for all who strive. Yet entry is not earned by deeds alone: faith in God and His messengers is the condition, and the final attainment is a gift of God's grace, which He grants to whomever He wills. This balances human effort with dependence on divine generosity, encouraging action while preventing pride in one's own works.

translation: No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being. Indeed, that is easy for God.
interpretation: The verse teaches that everything that happens, whether a widespread disaster in the world or a personal hardship, is within God's prior knowledge and decree, recorded in the Preserved Tablet before creation. Nothing occurs by chance or outside His wisdom, and recording and bringing all events into being is effortless for Him. Believers are thus meant to meet trials with patience, trust, and acceptance, knowing that their afflictions are neither random nor beyond God's care. This understanding steadies the heart in loss and guards against despair and grief, as the following verses make clear, and equally against arrogance in times of gain.

translation: So that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you. And God does not love any arrogant, boastful person.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Hadid 57:23) teaches that since everything is already decreed by God, believers should hold a balanced attitude toward worldly fortune. Loss and missed opportunities should not crush the soul with despair, because they were written and come with wisdom. Gains and blessings should not lead to giddy pride, because they are gifts from God and not the result of one's own power or merit. Grief that denies God's decree and joy that breeds arrogance both stem from attachment to the world and forgetfulness of the Giver. The verse ends by warning that God dislikes the conceited and boastful, who treat blessings as personal achievements and look down on others. The believer is meant to respond to hardship with patience and to ease with gratitude and humility.

translation: Those who are stingy and enjoin upon people stinginess. And whoever turns away – then indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.
