interpretation: The verse condemns those who refuse to spend what Allah has given them and who go further by encouraging others to be miserly too, so that their stinginess becomes a corrupting influence on society. It warns that turning away from the command to spend and obey harms only the one who turns away, because Allah is completely self-sufficient and has no need of anyone's wealth or worship, and He remains worthy of all praise whether or not people thank Him. Giving in charity is therefore a benefit to the giver, not to Allah, and withholding it brings loss only upon the withholder.

translation: We sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the Balance so that people may uphold justice. And We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people, so that God may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, God is Powerful, Almighty.
interpretation: The verse presents justice as the goal of revelation and shows how it is achieved. Prophets bring clear evidence, the Book supplies divine guidance, and the Balance supplies a just standard by which rights and wrongs are weighed. But moral guidance alone is not always enough, because some people will resist justice. Iron, a symbol of power, law enforcement, and material strength, is therefore described as a means of restraining oppression and protecting the social order, and also as a source of many benefits such as tools, industry, and civilization. The verse also says that using such strength in the cause of truth is a test of sincerity. God does not need human help, being Powerful and Almighty, but He tests who supports His religion and messengers out of faith in the unseen. Real faith is therefore shown in working for justice, with both principle and strength, without having seen the unseen.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham, and We placed in their descendants prophethood and scripture; among them are those who are guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's choice of Noah and Abraham as the two great ancestral lines of prophethood and revelation (every later prophet and scripture came from their offspring) did not make their descendants righteous automatically. Guidance is a matter of each person's own response, not of lineage or inherited privilege. Even within families honored with revelation, only some follow the right path, while many depart from obedience to God (fisq). The lesson is that nobility of descent offers no protection from accountability, and that being rightly guided depends on one's own faith and conduct; it also consoles the Prophet Muhammad that most people's rejection of the message is nothing new in the history of prophetic missions.

translation: Then We caused Our messengers to follow in their footsteps, and We followed them with Jesus, son of Mary, and gave him the Gospel. And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy. But monasticism they invented – We did not prescribe it for them – only seeking the pleasure of God; yet they did not observe it with the care due to it. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse traces the succession of prophets culminating in Jesus, whose true followers were distinguished by gentleness and mercy toward people. It then addresses monasticism: it was not a divine obligation but a practice the Christians devised themselves, initially out of a sincere desire to please God. However, they did not maintain it properly, either by abandoning its discipline or corrupting its purpose and straying from the true teachings of Jesus, including later rejecting the final Prophet Muhammad. The lesson is that innovation in worship, even with good intentions, is risky, since people cannot sustain what God has not required of them, and that sincerity must be matched by faithful adherence. Those who truly believed and stayed faithful receive their full reward from God, while many of them fell into transgression and disobedience.

translation: O you who believe, be mindful of God and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy, and will make for you a light by which you walk, and will forgive you. And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse calls those who already profess faith to deepen it: to renew and perfect their God-consciousness (taqwa) and their sincere trust in the Messenger. Doing so brings three gifts. First, a twofold share of divine mercy, a generous multiplication of reward that honors both their earlier faith and their faithful following of the final Messenger. Second, a guiding light of inner insight and right conduct that illuminates their path through life and on the Day of Judgment. Third, forgiveness of their shortcomings. The closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, assure believers that God's generosity exceeds their deserving, so that sincere faith joined with obedience is met with pardon and abundant grace.

translation: So that the People of the Scripture may know that they have no power over anything of God's bounty, and that all bounty is in God's Hand; He grants it to whom He wills. And God is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse closes Surat al-Hadid's discussion of the double reward promised to believers who accept the final message. It teaches that divine favor, including prophethood, guidance, and reward, is not an inherited privilege of any community or something people can claim, monopolize, or restrict by lineage or pride. The People of the Book had assumed that God's grace was confined to them, but God shows that He alone controls His bounty and gives it to whomever He wills, in this case by sending Muhammad to a new community and granting its sincere believers a great share. The lesson is humility and gratitude: favor is a gift from God, not an entitlement, and His generosity is vast and unconstrained by human expectations.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. God has indeed heard the speech of the woman who disputes with you concerning her husband and complains to God. And God hears the dialogue between you both. Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse shows that God is intimately attentive to the pleas of the wronged, especially the weak and those who have no one else to turn to. The woman, Khawla bint Tha'laba, had been subjected to the pre-Islamic pronouncement of zihar, in which a husband declared his wife to be like his mother's back as a way of cutting her off without freeing her. Rather than being dismissed, her complaint was heard from above the seven heavens and became the occasion for revelation that changed the law. The lesson is that no cry for justice goes unheard, that bringing one's grievances to God is an act of faith and not a sign of weakness, and that God's hearing is not mere awareness but a hearing that leads to relief and to the establishment of justice. The closing description of God as All-Hearing and All-Seeing assures believers that He knows both what is said and the circumstances of those who say it.

translation: Those among you who declare their wives to be like their mothers' backs (zihar) - they are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them. Indeed, they say an evil word and a falsehood. But indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse abolishes the pre-Islamic practice of zihar, in which a man would swear that his wife was as forbidden to him as his mother's back, effectively leaving her in limbo, neither a wife nor free to remarry. The Qur'an declares that a verbal formula cannot change reality: a wife does not become a mother by words, since motherhood is established only by childbirth. Such a statement is therefore condemned as a reprehensible utterance and a lie, because it misrepresents the truth and harms the woman. Yet the verse closes with mercy: Allah pardons and forgives those who repent and turn back from this wrongdoing, which paves the way for the expiation (kaffarah) prescribed in the following verses, restoring the marital relationship on just and lawful terms.

translation: Those who pronounce zihar against their wives and then wish to go back on what they said, must free a slave before the couple touch one another. This is what you are admonished to do, and God is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse sets out the expiation (kaffara) for zihar, the pre-Islamic practice in which a man declared his wife to be as forbidden to him as his mother's back. Islam treats this as a wrongful and false utterance that does not actually end the marriage or make the wife a mother. A man who then wants to resume married life must first make amends by freeing a slave, and until he does, marital intimacy is forbidden to him. The ruling aims to discourage the harmful, demeaning practice and to protect women from being left in limbo, neither truly married nor divorced. It also teaches that serious words carry moral consequences, and that repairing a wrong requires an act of generosity and liberation. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of everything people do stresses sincerity: the expiation should be carried out as an act of true repentance and obedience, not as a mere formality.

translation: But whoever does not find a slave to free, then [let him fast] two consecutive months before the couple touch one another. And whoever is unable, then [let him] feed sixty poor people. That is so that you may believe in God and His Messenger. And those are the limits set by God. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse completes the atonement (kaffarah) for zihar, the pre-Islamic practice of declaring one's wife as forbidden as one's mother's back. The expiation is graded according to ability: freeing a slave first, then, for one who cannot, fasting two consecutive months before resuming marital relations, and for one unable even to fast, feeding sixty poor people. The gradation shows God's mercy and that the law is tailored to a person's capacity. The verse stresses that obeying these rulings is an expression of faith, a sign of submission to God and His Messenger over old tribal customs. It also warns that these rulings are divine boundaries not to be transgressed, and that those who reject and disregard them out of disbelief face a painful punishment.

translation: Indeed, those who oppose God and His Messenger will be humbled as those before them were humbled. And We have sent down clear verses, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that opposing God and His Messenger, by setting oneself against the divine command and the authority of the Prophet, leads to disgrace and defeat, just as earlier nations who resisted their prophets were brought low and their arrogance broken. This outcome is not arbitrary, because God has already made the truth plain through clear signs and verses, so no one has an excuse for rejecting it. Those who knowingly reject this clear guidance out of pride will face a punishment that humiliates them, which is fitting for those who sought honor through defiance rather than through submission to God.

translation: On the Day when God will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. God has recorded it, while they have forgotten it; and God is Witness over all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that nothing a person does is lost or overlooked. On the Day of Resurrection, everyone will be raised together and confronted with the full truth of their deeds, including those they have long forgotten or dismissed as trivial. God's perfect knowledge has preserved every action, word, and intention, while human memory is weak and heedless. Because God is a witness over everything, the judgment will be perfectly just, leaving no room for denial or excuse. The believer is thus urged to live with constant awareness of accountability, to do good, and to repent of wrongs before the day when all is laid bare.

translation: Have you not seen that God knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? No secret conversation takes place among three but that He is the fourth of them, nor among five but that He is the sixth of them, nor among fewer than that or more but that He is with them wherever they may be. Then on the Day of Resurrection He will inform them of what they did. Indeed, God is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's all-encompassing knowledge and constant awareness of His creatures. Even the most private consultations, whether among a few people or many, are fully known to Him, for He is 'with them' by His knowledge, hearing, and observation, not by being physically mixed with creation. This reminds believers to be conscious of God in secret as well as in public, to avoid plotting sin, injustice, or evil whispering, and to know that nothing is lost: every deed will be disclosed and accounted for on the Day of Resurrection, since His knowledge encompasses everything.

translation: Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conspiracies, then return to what they were forbidden, and conspire together in sin, aggression, and disobedience to the Messenger? And when they come to you, they greet you with a greeting with which God has not greeted you, and they say within themselves, 'If only God would punish us for what we say.' Hell is sufficient for them; they will burn in it, and what an evil destination.
interpretation: The verse exposes the behavior of hypocrites and hostile groups in Medina, who held secret meetings meant to spread sin, hostility, and defiance of the Prophet, even after being told to stop. Their disobedience was compounded by mockery: they twisted the greeting, as some Jews said 'as-sāmu ʿalayka' (death be upon you) instead of 'salām', while privately reasoning that if the Prophet were truly God's messenger, God would have punished them at once. The verse answers that God's delay in punishment is not proof of their rightness or of the Prophet's falsehood; it is forbearance, and their real recompense is Hell, a wretched end. It teaches that outward words and secret schemes alike are known to God, that using speech to harm, deride, or defy is a grave wrong, and that postponed punishment should never breed false security.

translation: O you who believe, when you confer privately, do not confer in sin, aggression, and disobedience to the Messenger; but confer in righteousness and piety. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse teaches believers that private conversation is not morally neutral: secret talk is judged by its purpose. It warns against whispered plotting that harms others, transgresses against them, or undermines the Prophet's guidance, as the hypocrites and some of the Prophet's opponents did when they held secret meetings to cause suspicion and distress among the Muslims. In their place it directs believers to use confidential counsel for good works and God-consciousness, such as reconciling people, helping the needy, and encouraging obedience. By ending with the reminder that all will be gathered before God, the verse says that hidden speech is never truly hidden, and that awareness of accountability on the Day of Gathering should govern what a believer says in private as much as in public.

translation: Secret counsels are only from Satan, that he may grieve those who believe; but he cannot harm them in the least except by Allah's permission. And in Allah let the believers put their trust.
interpretation: The verse teaches that secret whispering and conspiratorial conferring, especially when aimed at the believers, is a tool of Satan, who inspires it so as to fill the hearts of the faithful with sadness, suspicion, and fear. Yet this scheming holds no real power, for nothing can bring harm to a believer unless God has permitted it within His decree. The proper response is therefore not anxiety or retaliation but reliance on God, since whoever entrusts their affairs to Him finds reassurance that no plot can overcome what He has willed, and the believer's grief is replaced with confidence and peace.

translation: O you who believe, when it is said to you, 'Make room in the gatherings,' then make room; God will make room for you. And when it is said, 'Rise up,' then rise up; God will raise those among you who believe, and those who have been given knowledge, by degrees. And God is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches good manners in communal gatherings, especially in the assembly of the Prophet. Believers are asked to be generous and accommodating, making space for others and yielding when asked to leave or stand so that others may sit or the gathering may end. Such generosity is rewarded in kind: whoever makes room for others, God will make room for them, in this world through ease and in the hereafter through mercy. The verse also affirms that true rank with God is not determined by where one sits or how early one arrives, but by faith and knowledge. Those who combine sincere belief with knowledge are elevated in status, and humility in obeying such requests does not lower a person but raises them. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of all deeds assures that every act of courtesy, as well as every show of reluctance or pride, is known and will be justly recompensed.

translation: O you who believe, when you consult the Messenger privately, offer a charity before your private consultation. That is better for you and purer. But if you do not find the means, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mujadila 58:12) set a temporary rule meant to discipline and purify the believers' manner of seeking private audience with the Prophet. By requiring a charitable gift before a private talk, it tested the sincerity of those who wanted his time and attention. It spared the Prophet needless, trivial private conversations that burdened him, and it gave the poor a share. It also separated those truly devoted to the faith from those who sought private talks out of vanity or for show. The charity purified hearts from attachment to wealth and from self-importance, and it taught reverence toward the Prophet's time and station. The final clause shows divine mercy: those who had nothing to give were not burdened and were forgiven, so the rule never shut anyone out of access to the Messenger.

translation: Are you afraid of offering charities before your private consultations? Then, since you did not do so and God has turned to you in forgiveness, establish prayer, give zakah, and obey God and His Messenger. And God is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse comes after the command in Surah Al-Mujadila (58:12) to give charity before a private conversation with the Prophet. That command was a test of sincerity. It also curbed excessive private meetings that burdened the Prophet. When the believers hesitated, whether from fear of poverty or from stinginess, God eased the ruling and forgave them. The verse then replaces that temporary, specific obligation with the lasting core duties of faith: establishing prayer, paying zakah, and obeying God and His Messenger. Its point is that God lifts hardship out of mercy, and that He wants real devotion shown in steady, constant worship and obedience rather than in a burdensome requirement that people shrink from. The closing words, 'God is All-Aware of what you do,' remind believers that their intentions and deeds are fully known to Him. They should therefore act sincerely, not just outwardly.

translation: Have you not seen those who take as allies a people with whom God is angry? They are neither of you nor of them, and they swear to falsehood while they know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites of Madinah, who secretly allied themselves with the Jews, a people who had incurred God's wrath, while outwardly professing loyalty to the believers. Their allegiance is divided and belongs to no one: they are not sincere members of the Muslim community, nor do they truly belong to those they secretly side with, since they flatter both sides for their own advantage. They compound this by swearing oaths that they are loyal and have said nothing wrong, knowing full well that they are lying. The lesson is that duplicity and false oaths, used to shield oneself while undermining the believing community, are condemned, and that real faith requires consistent, sincere loyalty to God and His community rather than opportunistic shifting of allegiances.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. Indeed, evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment is not arbitrary but the just outcome of a person's own conduct. The severity of the torment matches the gravity of their deeds, which the verse calls evil. Their wrongdoing was not a passing lapse but a persistent pattern, as 'they used to do' implies habitual practice. Their actions carried real moral weight and had real consequences, and the punishment was prepared for them in advance because their choices led there. It serves as a warning to the reader to examine their own conduct and not to treat sinful habits lightly.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a shield, so they turn people away from the path of God, and for them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes the hypocrites, who swear false oaths of loyalty and faith to protect themselves from the consequences of their disbelief, such as being treated as enemies or being punished. They use religious pledges as a cover for their real intentions, and by doing so they mislead others and hinder them from following God's path, since their outward claims of belief make people trust them and doubt the truth. Because they misused sacred oaths for deception and obstructed others from guidance, their punishment is humiliating, a fitting recompense for their pretense of honor and their abuse of God's name to preserve their standing.

translation: Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against God. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the things people most rely on for security and status in this world, such as riches and offspring, have no power to protect or save the disbelievers from God's judgment on the Day of Reckoning. Worldly assets can shield a person from hardship only within the limits of this life; once God's decree is issued, neither possessions nor family ties can ransom, defend, or intercede for someone who persisted in disbelief and rejected the truth. Their fate is the Fire, where they remain, because their disbelief closed the way to the only thing that could have saved them: faith and righteous deeds. The verse is therefore a warning to place trust in God and in preparing for the hereafter, rather than in worldly means that will ultimately fail.

translation: On the Day when God resurrects them all, they will swear to Him just as they swear to you, thinking that they stand on something firm. Beware! They are indeed the liars.
interpretation: The hypocrites' habit of lying is so deeply rooted in their character that it does not leave them even in the Hereafter. In this world they swear false oaths to believers to shield themselves and to pass off their insincere faith as genuine. On the Day of Resurrection, when every secret is exposed and God knows all that is hidden, they will still swear to Him, as they swore to people, imagining that their oaths will benefit them and save them, just as deception served them in this life. The verse shows that habitual falsehood becomes second nature and a self-deception, so that the liar comes to believe his lies have some worth. God ends by declaring that they are the true liars, confirming that their oaths carry no weight with Him and that no deceit can avail against His complete knowledge.

translation: Satan has gained mastery over them and made them forget the remembrance of God. Those are the party of Satan. Truly, it is the party of Satan who are the losers.
interpretation: The verse explains that hypocrisy and persistent heedlessness are not only moral failings but a gradual surrender of the heart to Satan. When people habitually follow their whims, lie, and break their oaths, they lose their awareness of God, their accountability to Him, and their reverence for His commands. Satan's mastery over them is a result of their own choices: each act of neglect weakens their remembrance of God and strengthens his hold on them, until they become his partisans, who share his aims and carry out his work. The final warning that Satan's party are the true losers means that whatever worldly gain, status, or security such people seem to obtain by deceit is worthless, since they forfeit their own souls and their ultimate success in the Hereafter. The verse therefore urges believers to guard their remembrance of God as the protection against Satan's domination.

translation: Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger — they will be among the most humiliated.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who set themselves against God and His Messenger, by rejecting the divine limits and deliberately working against the guidance, place themselves on the opposite side of the source of all honor and might. Since true dignity belongs to God, His Messenger and the believers, anyone who stands in hostile opposition cuts himself off from that source and is therefore destined for abasement. This humiliation may appear in this world through defeat and loss of standing, and it is surely realized in the Hereafter. The wording 'among the lowest' shows that their disgrace is complete: they are placed with the most degraded of all peoples, however powerful or proud they may seem for a time.

translation: Allah has decreed: 'I and My messengers will surely prevail.' Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Almighty.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mujadila 58:21) affirms that the ultimate triumph of truth over falsehood is a divine decree that cannot fail. The victory of the messengers is not necessarily measured by immediate worldly outcomes, but is guaranteed in terms of the vindication of their message through proof, argument, and eventual dominance of their cause, even if individual messengers were opposed or killed. The assurance is grounded in two of God's attributes, strength (qawiyy) and might (azeez): since He possesses all power and nothing can overcome Him, His promise to support those who convey His guidance must come to pass. The verse consoles believers who face hostility and urges them to remain steadfast, trusting that aligning with God's cause means aligning with the side destined to prevail.

translation: You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose God and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred. For those, He has inscribed faith upon their hearts and supported them with a spirit from Him. And He will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein eternally. God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of God. Truly, it is the party of God who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine faith sets a believer's ultimate loyalty and love with God and His Messenger, above even the strongest natural bonds of family and tribe. Sincere belief is incompatible with warm, intimate allegiance to those who actively set themselves against God and His Messenger in hostility and enmity. It does not forbid kindness, justice or maintaining family ties as such, but rules out aligning one's heart and loyalty with the cause of those who fight the truth. Those who hold to this priority, even at the cost of painful separation, are rewarded: faith becomes firmly engraved in their hearts, God strengthens them with inspiration and support from Him, and He grants them eternal gardens and mutual pleasure with Him. They form 'the party of God,' whose true success lies in this nearness and acceptance rather than in worldly attachments.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies God, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: All creation, in its very existence and order, bears witness to God's perfection and declares Him free of any flaw or partner, whether through speech, as with those who can speak, or through the state and design of things that cannot. This universal glorification is grounded in two of His attributes: His might (al-'Aziz), meaning that nothing can overpower His will, and His wisdom (al-Hakim), meaning that nothing He creates or commands is without purpose. The verse invites the believer to join the rest of creation in praising God, with trust that His power is always exercised with wisdom.

translation: It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave, and they thought that their fortresses would protect them from God. But God came upon them from where they had not expected, and cast terror into their hearts; they destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take a lesson, O people of insight.
interpretation: The verse recounts the expulsion of the Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadir from Medina as a demonstration that victory and defeat rest solely with God, not with material strength. The tribe trusted in their fortified strongholds, and the Muslims themselves thought their removal unlikely, yet God's decree reached them through an unforeseen channel: inner dread that undermined their resolve before any battle was fought. Their self-inflicted demolition of their homes, partly to carry off the timber and partly to deny them to the Muslims, shows how those who rely on worldly defenses against God's will bring about their own ruin. The closing command, 'take a lesson, O people of insight,' urges reflective people to draw a general principle: arrogance, defiance of God and reliance on power or fortifications lead to downfall, while the believers should place their trust in God and not in apparent means.

translation: And had God not decreed exile for them, He would have punished them in this world; and in the Hereafter they will have the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Hashr about the Banu al-Nadir, teaches that their expulsion from Medina was an act of divine mercy and wisdom, not the full extent of what their betrayal deserved. God had written exile as their fate, which spared them the harsher worldly punishment, such as killing and captivity, that other treaty-breakers faced. Yet this leniency in the world does not absolve them: their persistent opposition to God and His Messenger means that the real and enduring reckoning awaits in the Hereafter, where the punishment of the Fire is certain. The lesson is that delay or lightness of worldly punishment is no sign of divine approval, and that ultimate justice is in the next life.

translation: That is because they opposed God and His Messenger; and whoever opposes God, then indeed God is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse explains the reason behind the humiliation and punishment that befell the disbelievers: they did not merely err, but deliberately took a stance against God and His Messenger, splitting into a separate camp in hostility and defiance of the divine guidance. The word 'shāqqū' conveys the image of placing oneself on one side while the truth is on the other, so opposition is portrayed as willful separation from the divine path. The closing statement turns the specific incident into a general principle: anyone who persists in such opposition, in any era, will face God's severe retribution. It serves both as a warning to those who would oppose the Prophet's message and as reassurance to believers that God's justice is certain, and that the consequences of the disbelievers' defeat were a direct result of their own choice, not of injustice.

translation: Whatever palm trees you cut down, or left standing on their roots, it was by the permission of God, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse was revealed in the context of the siege of the Banu al-Nadir, when some Muslims cut down or burned some of their palm trees while others objected and left theirs standing. The verse settles the dispute by teaching that both actions fell within God's permission and will: neither group sinned, since cutting the trees served a legitimate military purpose of pressuring and humiliating the enemy, and sparing them was equally permissible. Its deeper meaning is that events in war unfold under divine decree and sanction, and that God uses even such acts to humiliate those who persist in treachery and wrongdoing, so the believers should not be troubled over whether they acted rightly when they acted in good faith within the bounds God allowed.

translation: And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur on any horses or camels for it, but Allah gives His messengers authority over whomever He wills. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes the ruling on fay', the property that passes to the Muslims from their enemies without actual fighting, such as the lands and wealth of Banu al-Nadir, who surrendered after being besieged. Because the Muslims did not exert themselves with cavalry or riding beasts to obtain it, it is not distributed like battle spoils (ghanimah) among the fighters. Instead, its disposal is entrusted to the Messenger, who allocates it according to Allah's direction, as the following verses specify for the Messenger, his kin, orphans, the poor, and travelers. The verse teaches that victory and its gains come from Allah's decree and power, not from human strength or numbers, since He grants His messengers dominance over whomever He wills, and nothing is beyond His ability.

translation: Whatever Allah has bestowed as spoils upon His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah, to the Messenger, to the relatives, the orphans, the poor, and the wayfarer, so that it may not become a circulating benefit only among the rich among you. Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: This verse lays down a foundational principle of Islamic economic justice: wealth acquired by the community without fighting (fay') is not to be monopolized by the powerful or affluent, but must be directed to the Messenger (for public affairs), his relatives, and the vulnerable—orphans, the poor, and travelers in need—so that wealth keeps flowing throughout society rather than circulating only among the rich. The verse then broadens into a general rule of religious authority: whatever the Prophet commands or allocates must be accepted and whatever he prohibits must be avoided, making obedience to his guidance binding in all matters. It closes by joining social fairness and obedience to taqwa (God-consciousness), warning that Allah severely punishes those who violate these rights and commands.

translation: [Some of the spoils are] for the poor emigrants who were driven out of their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from God and His approval, and supporting God and His Messenger. Those are the truthful ones.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hashr 59:8) identifies the first group entitled to the spoils taken without fighting (fay'): the poor Muhajirun, who left Makkah. They lost their homes and wealth because of their faith and not out of any worldly motive, since they sought God's bounty and pleasure. They proved the sincerity of their belief by sacrificing everything for it and by supporting God and His Messenger with their efforts and their lives. The verse ends by calling them 'the truthful' (as-sadiqun), which shows that true faith is demonstrated by costly action and not just by words. They therefore deserve the community's care and honor, and their sincerity is a model for all believers.

translation: And those who were settled in the abode [Medina] and in faith before them love those who emigrated to them, and find in their hearts no need for what the emigrants were given, and prefer them above themselves even though they themselves are in poverty. And whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul – it is those who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse praises the Ansar of Medina as a model of selfless community: they welcomed the Muhajirun with sincere love, felt no envy or resentment when the emigrants were given a share of the spoils, and even gave them priority over themselves while in need. This generosity springs from overcoming 'shuhh', the miserly, grasping greed of the self, which the verse identifies as the root of selfishness and envy. Real success, in this life and the next, belongs to those whom God guards against that inner stinginess, so that they give, share, and prefer others out of faith rather than calculation.

translation: And those who came after them say: 'Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful.'
interpretation: The verse describes the ideal attitude of later generations of believers toward earlier ones, especially the Companions of the Prophet: they do not look back with envy, blame, or hostility, but with prayer and love. Faith creates a bond of brotherhood that spans time, so a true believer asks forgiveness for those who preceded him in faith and asks God to cleanse his heart of ghill, the hidden rancor and malice that can poison relations within the community. Such a heart-level purity is a mark of sound faith, and the believer relies on God's gentleness and mercy to keep him free of it, since only God can purify the inner self.

translation: Have you not seen those who practice hypocrisy, how they say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture: 'If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you; and if you are fought, we will surely help you.' But Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Hashr 59:11) exposes the hypocrites of Medina, such as Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his circle, who secretly allied with the Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadir against the Prophet. They made grand promises of solidarity: to leave Medina alongside them if they were banished, to defy anyone who urged them to abandon the tribe, and to fight on their side if attacked. God reveals that these pledges were empty and insincere, and He testifies to their lying. The deeper lesson is that hypocrisy produces unreliable allegiances: words of loyalty that are not rooted in true conviction or courage collapse when real hardship comes, while God, who knows what hearts conceal, sees through such false assurances.

translation: If they are expelled, they will not go out with them; and if they are fought, they will not help them; and even if they were to help them, they would surely turn their backs in flight, and then they would not be helped.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Hashr 59:12) exposes the emptiness of the hypocrites' promises to the Jews of Banu al-Nadir. Their pledges of solidarity rest on self-interest, not real loyalty or courage, so they abandon their allies when tested. Even if they did fight, they would flee at the first confrontation, and no one would be given victory, because the support of God belongs to the believers and is not won by falsehood. The lesson is that alliances built on hypocrisy and opposition to the truth are fragile and bring defeat to everyone involved, and that true strength lies in faith and sincerity, not in worldly partnerships.

translation: You are more feared in their hearts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' misplaced fear: in their hearts they dread the believers' power and the worldly consequences of confronting them more than they dread God, who holds all real power and judgment. This inverted fear comes from their lack of true understanding. They judge by outward, visible forces and do not grasp the reality of God's might, His power over all affairs, or the ultimate accountability before Him. Had they understood, their reverence and fear would be directed to God alone, and the believers' strength would not overawe them.

translation: They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls. Their violence is severe among themselves. You think they are united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not use reason.
interpretation: The verse describes the hypocrites and the People of the Book who opposed the believers (referring to the Banu Nadir and their allies). Their courage is hollow: they dare not meet the believers in open battle and only fight when sheltered behind fortifications and walls, which shows their fear and weakness. Although they appear fierce and unified from the outside, they are actually fierce against one another, and their hearts are scattered by rivalries, conflicting interests and desires. Real unity comes from shared faith and a shared purpose in God, and they have neither. Their disunity and cowardice come from a lack of understanding: had they reasoned, they would have recognized the truth and the folly of relying on worldly defenses and alliances instead of God. The believers should therefore not be intimidated by the apparent strength of their opponents.

translation: Like those who were shortly before them: they tasted the evil consequence of their conduct, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hashr 59:15) refers to the Banu Nadir, whose fate is likened to that of the idolaters of Quraysh defeated at Badr, or to the Jewish tribe of Banu Qaynuqa, who had defied the Prophet shortly before them. The point is that those who oppose God and His Messenger, relying on their own schemes and on false allies, bring ruin upon themselves. Their disobedience carries its own bitter consequence in this world, whether through defeat, humiliation, or exile, and beyond that they face a painful punishment in the Hereafter. The lesson is that history repeats its pattern: rejecting guidance leads to a bad end, and people should take warning from the fate of those who came just before them rather than repeat their mistakes.

translation: Like the Satan when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.' Then when he disbelieves, he says, 'Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: The verse (Al-Hashr 59:16) likens the hypocrites who urged the People of the Book to resist and promised them support, then abandoned them at the moment of trial, to Satan's conduct toward humankind. Satan entices a person to disbelief with false promises, and once the person has fallen into it and faces its consequences, Satan disowns him and pretends to fear God. The lesson is that those who call to falsehood offer no real protection and betray their followers when it counts, so a person should not trust the empty assurances of deceivers, whether Satan or his human allies, and should hold firmly to faith in God.

translation: So the end of both of them is that they will be in the Fire, abiding therein forever. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent disobedience and injustice carry a fixed, just consequence. Those who wrong themselves and others, here the two who obeyed Satan's whispering to deceive and sin, do not escape the result of their choices, and the outcome of their path is the Fire, not worldly gain. The word 'wrongdoers' (zalimin) widens the lesson beyond these two, making it a general law: whoever places things where they do not belong, by disobeying God, oppressing others, or following evil counsel, will receive a recompense that matches their wrongdoing. It is a warning to avoid the beginnings of such conduct and a reminder that God's justice is certain even when the wrongdoing seems profitable at first.

translation: O you who believe, fear God, and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow. And fear God; indeed, God is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to continual self-accountability: since the Day of Judgment, 'tomorrow', is certain, each person should examine their deeds before they are reckoned, asking whether their deeds are worthy of being presented before God. The command to fear God is repeated, first to urge sincere devotion and obedience in preparing good deeds, and then to urge vigilance in avoiding sin and neglect. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of everything one does removes any hope of concealment and makes a person conscious of God's watchfulness in both private and public conduct.

translation: And be not like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against heedlessness of God, because forgetting the Creator leads to forgetting one's own true self and interests. Those who neglect God's commands and the remembrance of Him lose awareness of their purpose and of what benefits their souls for the Hereafter. They stop preparing good deeds for themselves, and they squander their lives on fleeting worldly matters. As a result they are left estranged from their own spiritual well-being, and this is a fitting recompense for their abandonment of God. Such people are described as fasiqun, those who step outside obedience to God. The lesson is that remembering God is the foundation of self-awareness and self-preservation, and that the believer should constantly prepare for the Day of Judgment, as the preceding verse commands, rather than follow the path of the negligent.

translation: Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise. The companions of Paradise are the ones who are the victorious.
interpretation: The verse denies any moral or ultimate equivalence between those who forgot God and lived heedlessly and those who remained mindful of Him. Since God's justice means that deeds have consequences, a life of obedience and awareness cannot end in the same place as a life of neglect and disobedience. Success (fawz) is therefore defined not by worldly gain, status, or comfort, but by salvation from the Fire and entry into Paradise. The verse invites the reader to weigh daily choices against the final outcome and to pursue what leads to lasting triumph rather than passing benefit.

translation: Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart out of fear of God. Such are the parables We set forth for people, so that they may reflect.
interpretation: The verse stresses the immense weight and power of God's revelation. A mountain, the very emblem of hardness and firmness, would crumble in awe if it were charged with this Qur'an and grasped its meaning. Human beings, who have been given intellect and the capacity to understand, are therefore even more in need of a heart that trembles before God's words. If a heart stays unmoved, hard, and heedless when the Qur'an is recited, it is blameworthy, because the fault lies in its own negligence and arrogance, not in any lack in the message. The parable is meant to rouse people to reflect, soften their hearts, humble themselves before their Lord, and act on what they hear instead of merely listening.

translation: He is God, other than whom there is no god; Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse grounds true worship in God's unique divinity: because He alone knows everything hidden from creatures as well as everything they can perceive, no other being has the knowledge or authority to share in divinity or deserve devotion. His knowledge is complete, so nothing in the heart or the world escapes Him. Yet this absolute knowledge is joined to mercy: the One who knows every secret of a person is also the One whose compassion embraces all creation in this life (Rahman) and whose mercy is especially bestowed on the believers (Rahim). Believers are thus invited to hold both awareness of God's all-seeing presence and hope in His mercy, so that reverence and trust go together.

translation: He is God, other than whom there is no god: the Sovereign, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supreme in Greatness. Glory be to God, far above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Hashr 59:23) teaches that divinity belongs to God alone, and it grounds this in His attributes. He is the true King whose dominion is absolute and needs no one. He is utterly free of any flaw, deficiency or injustice. He is the Source of peace, safe from all defect, and the one who gives safety to His creation. He gives security to the believers and is the watchful Guardian over all things and over all that His servants do. His might cannot be overcome, His will prevails and He mends what is broken, and His greatness belongs to Him alone, so creatures have no right to arrogance. Since these attributes belong to God exclusively, associating any partner with Him is baseless, and the verse closes by declaring Him exalted above everything the polytheists ascribe to Him. The believer is thus called to worship Him alone, to find security and trust in Him, and to be humble before His majesty.

translation: He is God, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner; to Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation unfolds through three distinct stages, each tied to a divine name: God as al-Khaliq plans and determines all things, as al-Bari' brings them into existence free of any flaw or disproportion, and as al-Musawwir gives each being its particular form and character. The diversity of shapes, faces, and natures in the universe is therefore no accident but the work of a deliberate, wise will. Because every excellent attribute belongs to God alone, His names are 'most beautiful' and are a means by which believers know and call upon Him. The whole of creation, in its very existence and order, testifies to His perfection and declares Him free of any deficiency, which is its glorification. This is grounded in His might, since nothing can resist His will, and His wisdom, since nothing He does is without purpose. The believer is thus led from reflecting on creation to knowing the Creator, and to worship, humility, and trust in Him.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, extending to them affection, while they have disbelieved in the truth that has come to you, expelling the Messenger and yourselves because you believe in God, your Lord. If you have come out to strive in My cause and seeking My pleasure, [how can you] confide to them affection in secret, while I know best what you conceal and what you declare? And whoever of you does that has certainly strayed from the right path.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mumtahanah 60:1) warns believers that true faith is incompatible with giving one's deepest loyalty and affection to those who actively oppose God and persecute the faithful. It was revealed in connection with a companion who secretly wrote to the Quraysh of Mecca to warn them of the Prophet's planned advance, hoping to protect his family there. The verse teaches that loyalty (walāʾ) must be anchored in belief, not in kinship, personal interest, or fear. The believers' own sacrifice, having been driven from their homes for their faith, and their claim to strive for God's pleasure contradict secretly befriending those same persecutors. Since God knows both what is hidden and what is open, no secret correspondence escapes Him. Whoever does this has lost the straight path, meaning that betraying the community's cause for the sake of enemies of the faith is a serious moral and spiritual deviation, even if it arises from understandable human concerns.

translation: If they gain the upper hand over you, they will be enemies to you, and will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Mumtahanah 60:2) warns believers against taking hostile disbelievers as close allies. It says their hidden enmity would become open once they had power over the believers: they would attack physically with their hands and verbally with slander, insult and abuse with their tongues. Their deepest desire is not only to harm Muslims in this world but to pull them away from their faith, which is the greatest loss. The lesson is that believers should not be deceived by outward friendliness or put their trust in those who hold ill will toward them and their religion. They should keep their loyalty for God and the believers, and recognize that the hostility of such people would show itself fully as soon as they had the chance.

translation: Neither your blood relations nor your children will benefit you. On the Day of Resurrection He will separate between you. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that family ties and offspring, which people often put before obedience to God, cannot rescue anyone on the Day of Judgment. Believers are warned against betraying their faith or breaking their commitments to God out of loyalty to relatives, as Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah did when he wrote to the Quraysh to protect his family in Mecca. On that Day, God will separate people according to their faith and deeds, not their lineage, so salvation depends on one's own conduct. Since God sees everything people do, including hidden motives, each person should give priority to God's command over kinship and worldly attachments.

translation: There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people: 'Indeed, we are free of you and of whatever you worship besides God. We have rejected you, and enmity and hatred have appeared between us and you forever, until you believe in God alone' — except for the saying of Abraham to his father: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to do anything for you against God.' 'Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the final destination.'
interpretation: The verse holds up Abraham and his companions as a model for believers in how to handle loyalty and disassociation: when a community's polytheism is clear, a believer must openly part ways with its false worship and refuse to let family or social ties override faith in God alone. Enmity here is principled and tied to belief, and it is meant to end if the others accept faith ('until you believe in God alone'). The exception, Abraham's promise to seek forgiveness for his father, is not a model to follow, since it was a hope voiced before it became clear that his father was an enemy of God, and Abraham himself disavowed it afterward. Believers should not pray for forgiveness for persistent polytheists, because no one can avert God's decree. The closing supplication shows the right inner stance behind such separation: total reliance on God, repentance to Him, and awareness that all return to Him. The believer's stand rests on trust in God, not on personal hostility.

translation: Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This is a supplication of the believers, following Abraham's example, asking God not to let disbelievers gain the upper hand over them or afflict them in a way that would make the disbelievers think they are on the truth and the believers on falsehood, thereby hardening them in their disbelief. It also asks that God not allow the believers' shortcomings or hardships to become a stumbling block that turns people away from faith. They then seek forgiveness for their sins, which are a cause of such trials, and conclude by affirming God's might, by which He can protect them and grant them victory, and His wisdom, by which He orders all matters, including trials, with perfect justice and purpose.

translation: Indeed, there has been for you in them an excellent example for whoever hopes in God and the Last Day. And whoever turns away, then surely God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the mention of Abraham and those with him in Surah al-Mumtahanah, teaches that the believers' steadfastness, their open disavowal of idolatry, and their devotion to God alone are a model for all who truly hope for God's reward and fear the Day of Judgment. Following such examples is presented as a mark of sincere faith, because real hope in God and the Hereafter shows itself in conduct and loyalty, not in words alone. The closing warning says that anyone who rejects this guidance harms only themselves: God has no need of anyone's obedience and is worthy of praise whether or not people give it, so the benefit of following righteous examples returns entirely to the follower.

translation: It may be that God will bring about affection between you and those of them with whom you are now at enmity. God is All-Powerful, and God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: After commanding believers to sever ties of loyalty with those who fight them, the verse offers hope instead of permanent hostility. Enmity between people is not fixed, because hearts are in God's hands and He can turn hatred into love, as happened when many of the Meccan opponents later embraced Islam and became brothers in faith. Believers are therefore to hold firm to their principles without despairing of reconciliation, and to keep their hostility measured, leaving room for mercy. God's power makes this change possible, and His forgiveness and mercy are open to those who turn from their opposition and to believers who erred in the past.

translation: God does not forbid you from those who have not fought you because of your religion and have not driven you out of your homes, that you deal kindly with them and act justly toward them. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mumtahana 60:8) sets out the ethic Muslims are to follow toward people of other faiths. The prohibition on taking enemies as close allies, mentioned just before it, applies only to those who actively wage war against the believers, fight them over their faith, or expel them from their homes. It does not apply to peaceful non-Muslims who have not harmed them. Toward these, kindness (birr) and fairness (qist) are not merely permitted but encouraged: Muslims may treat them with good conduct, honor their rights, keep their agreements, and deal with them equitably in trade, neighborliness, and justice. The closing phrase, that God loves those who act justly, makes fairness a universal principle of faith that does not depend on the religion of the other party, and it shows that hostility is reserved for aggression, not for difference of belief.

translation: Allah only forbids you from taking as allies those who fought you because of your religion, expelled you from your homes, and aided in your expulsion. And whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse sets the limit of the preceding permission to deal kindly and justly with non-Muslims who do not harm the believers. The prohibition on close alliance and loyalty is not general toward all non-Muslims, but is specific to those who actively persecute Muslims for their faith, drive them from their homes, or help others do so. Such people have shown real hostility, so aligning with them, by giving them support, trust, or backing against the believers, betrays the community and the faith. The Qur'an calls those who do this wrongdoers because they place their loyalty in the wrong place, supporting oppression against their own brothers and sisters in faith and undermining justice. The verse therefore ties the ruling to conduct and not to mere difference of religion: peaceful non-Muslims are to be treated with kindness and fairness, while aggressors who wage war and persecute are not to be taken as allies.

translation: O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, test them. God is most knowing of their faith. If you ascertain that they are believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are the disbelievers lawful for them. And give the disbelievers what they have spent [as dowers]. There is no blame upon you if you marry them when you have given them their bridal due. And do not hold on to the marriage bonds of disbelieving women, but ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of God; He judges between you. And God is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse sets out a legal and ethical arrangement following the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when women who embraced Islam fled from Makkah to Madinah. The believers are to examine the sincerity of the emigrant women, for instance that they came out of faith and not out of worldly motives such as escaping a husband or seeking material gain, while leaving the true state of the heart to God. Once their faith is established, they must not be sent back to the disbelieving community, because the difference in religion dissolves the marital bond between a believing woman and a disbelieving husband. Justice is nonetheless preserved: the Muslims must compensate the former husbands for the dowers they paid, and Muslim men may marry these women after giving them their own dowers. Likewise, Muslim men must not remain bound to their disbelieving wives, and may claim back what they paid, so that the same standard applies on both sides. The verse concludes that this is God's judgment, grounded in His knowledge and wisdom, which balances protection of faith and conscience, fairness in financial rights, and the preservation of peace agreements.

translation: And if any of your wives escape from you to the disbelievers, and you then have your turn (of gain, in war or reprisal), then give those whose wives have gone away the equivalent of what they had spent. And fear Allah, in Whom you are believers.
interpretation: This verse sets out a principle of fairness after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The preceding verse required Muslims to return to the disbelievers the dowries of women who had emigrated and become believers. This verse covers the reverse case: if a Muslim's wife defects to the disbelievers and they refuse to refund her dowry, the Muslim should not be left with the loss. When the believers later obtain spoils or compensation from that same enemy, the husband who lost his wife is to be repaid the amount of the dowry he had given from what has been gained. The rule makes obligations mutual between the two sides and protects the believers' property rights. The closing command to fear Allah, in Whom they believe, reminds Muslims to apply this justice with integrity and without greed, favoritism or transgression.

translation: O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you, that they will not associate anything with God, will not steal, will not commit unlawful sex, will not kill their children, will not bring forth a slander they invent between their hands and their feet, and will not disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge and ask God to forgive them. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse sets out the foundational covenant of the believing women who joined the Muslim community, establishing them as full moral agents who pledge allegiance in their own right. The pledge covers the core ethical pillars of the faith: pure monotheism, protection of property, sexual chastity, protection of life (including the practice of killing children, as in pre-Islamic Arabia), and honesty. The phrase 'a slander they invent between their hands and their feet' is commonly understood as forbidding a woman from attributing a child to a husband who is not its father, or more generally from fabricating falsehoods. The condition of obedience 'in what is right' (ma'ruf) teaches that obedience to the Prophet, and by extension to any authority, is bound by goodness and justice. The closing instruction to seek forgiveness for them and the description of God as Forgiving and Merciful show that the pledge is accompanied by divine mercy: past failings are pardoned, and the new believers are encouraged to begin a life of moral responsibility.

translation: O you who believe, do not take as allies a people upon whom God's wrath has fallen. They have despaired of the Hereafter, just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves.
interpretation: The verse closes Surat al-Mumtahanah by forbidding believers from befriending or giving their loyalty to those who have incurred God's anger by rejecting His guidance and who have lost all hope in the afterlife. Such people do not expect resurrection or reckoning, so they lack the moral restraint that comes from accountability before God, and close alliance with them endangers the believers' faith and community. The comparison to the disbelievers who despair of those in the graves can be read as saying that, just as the disbelievers have lost hope that the dead will ever return to life, these people have lost hope of any reward or good in the Hereafter. The verse therefore teaches that a believer's deepest loyalties should be to God and to those who share belief in the Last Day, and that trust and intimacy should not be placed in those who deny the Hereafter and are hostile to the faith.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies God, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents the whole of creation as engaged in a continuous act of praise, whether through speech, through its very existence, or through its complete submission to God's decree. Every created thing, by its order and dependence, bears witness that its Creator is free of any flaw or partner. The closing names tie this universal praise to its reasons: God is 'al-Aziz', so His power cannot be resisted and all things yield to Him, and He is 'al-Hakim', so every command and act of His is grounded in wisdom and purpose. The believer is thus reminded to join creation in glorifying God, and to trust that His might and wisdom govern both the cosmos and the believer's own affairs.

translation: O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 61:2) calls believers to match their words with their actions. Faith is not proved by declarations, promises, or claims of virtue alone, but by conduct that confirms them. A gap between what a person professes and what they practice is a moral failing that damages integrity and trust, and it is deeply disliked by God, as the next verse says. The believer should therefore be sincere: make only promises they intend to keep, and call others to only what they themselves are willing to do.

translation: It is most hateful in the sight of God that you say what you do not do.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 61:3) teaches that a gap between a person's words and deeds is a grave moral failing in God's eyes. Promising, professing, or advocating virtue while failing to act on it is a form of hypocrisy and breach of integrity that provokes God's strong displeasure. Faith must be shown through consistent action, so a believer should speak only what he intends to fulfill and should fulfill what he has pledged or preached.

translation: Indeed, God loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as though they were a solid structure cemented together.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's love is gained not merely by striving in His path, but by doing so with discipline, unity, and cohesion. The image of a 'solidly cemented structure' means that each believer is like a brick that supports the others: no gaps, no disorder, no individual rivalry. Strength comes from being aligned in purpose and action, with each person holding their place and fulfilling their role. It follows that sincere commitment to a just cause must be joined with organization, mutual reliance, and steadfastness, since a divided community is weak while a united one is firm and resilient.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people: 'O my people, why do you harm me while you know that I am the Messenger of God to you?' Then when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate. And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse recalls how the Israelites persisted in hurting Moses, through accusations, stubbornness and disobedience, even though they had clear knowledge of his truthfulness as God's messenger. Their harm was therefore willful rejection and not ignorance. When they deliberately turned away from the truth after it was clear to them, God left them to the consequence of their choice and let their hearts swerve further from guidance, so that their deviation became a settled state. The lesson is that guidance is withheld from those who knowingly and persistently defy God (the fasiqun), and that abusing a prophet after recognizing his truth brings a spiritual punishment of hardening of the heart. It also consoles Prophet Muhammad, who faced similar harm from his own people, and warns his community not to follow that path.

translation: And [remember] when Jesus, son of Mary, said: 'O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of God sent to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah, and giving glad tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad.' But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said: 'This is plain magic.'
interpretation: The verse presents the unity of the prophetic message across history: Jesus did not bring a new religion in opposition to earlier revelation but affirmed the Torah, and he in turn prepared his people for the coming of a final messenger, named Ahmad, understood by the Muslim tradition as the Prophet Muhammad. This shows that true prophets confirm one another and that belief in them is a continuous chain. The closing part reveals a recurring human response: when clear signs and evidence arrive that challenge people's pride, expectations, or interests, they dismiss them as mere trickery rather than honestly reflect. The verse thus both affirms the legitimacy of Muhammad's mission as foretold and warns against rejecting manifest truth by labeling it deception.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents falsehood about God while he is being invited to Islam (submission to God)? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the gravest form of wrongdoing is to attribute lies to God, such as denying His revelation, calling the Qur'an sorcery, or claiming partners and false teachings for Him, especially when one is being offered the path of submission and salvation. Such a person closes the door of truth with his own hands: he has been shown the way and has chosen falsehood out of arrogance and stubbornness. God's refusal to guide the wrongdoers is not an arbitrary denial but a consequence of their persistent injustice. Those who knowingly reject the truth and obstinately persist in their wrongdoing forfeit the divine guidance that is available to anyone who sincerely seeks it.

translation: They want to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect His light, even if the disbelievers detest it.
interpretation: The verse likens the opponents of the faith to people who try to blow out a great light with their breath. The light is God's guidance, the message of Islam and the truth brought by the Prophet, and the 'mouths' stand for their empty words, slander, mockery and false claims against it. Such efforts are as futile as trying to put out the sun by blowing on it. God has decreed that His guidance will be completed and made manifest, so it will spread and endure however much the deniers resent it. The verse reassures believers that the truth does not depend on human approval and that hostility to it will fail.

translation: It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may cause it to prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it.
interpretation: God declares that the mission of Muhammad is backed by divine purpose and promise: the guidance he brought and the true way of life (submission to the One God, Islam) are destined to stand supreme over every other creed and system, not necessarily through coercion, but through the strength of its proof, its clarity, and its moral and spiritual superiority, as well as through God's support for it in history. The opposition of those who associate partners with God, however fierce, cannot reverse this outcome, because it rests on God's will rather than on human approval. The verse thus offers reassurance to believers that truth will ultimately prevail, while reminding them that their task is to carry the message faithfully and trust in God's promise.

translation: O you who believe! Shall I guide you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?
interpretation: God addresses the believers using the language of commerce to show that faith is not merely a claim but an exchange in which a person invests the self for an everlasting return. The verses that follow define this trade as true belief in God and His Messenger and striving in God's cause with one's wealth and one's life. The 'profit' is deliverance from the Hellfire and entry into Paradise, so the believer who gives up fleeting worldly comfort in obedience and sacrifice gains a far greater and lasting reward. The verse thus calls believers to measure their deeds by their eternal gain and to renew their faith through action and sacrifice, not words alone.

translation: You believe in God and His Messenger, and you strive in the cause of God with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if only you knew.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 61:11) explains the 'trade' that saves from a painful punishment, mentioned in the preceding verse. It defines true faith as more than a verbal claim: it is belief in God and His Messenger that is proven through sacrifice. Striving 'with wealth and lives' means devoting one's resources and one's very self, whether through struggle in defense of the faith, perseverance in obedience, or effort in spreading good, to the path of God. Wealth is mentioned first because giving it up is often the first and most constant test of sincerity. The phrase 'that is better for you, if only you knew' signals that this exchange of worldly things for the pleasure of God is the most profitable bargain, since worldly wealth and life are fleeting while the reward of God is lasting. The verse urges the believers to see through the apparent loss of sacrifice to the real gain of salvation and eternal reward.

translation: He will forgive you your sins and admit you into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, and into pleasant dwellings in the Gardens of Eternity. That is the great success.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward promised to those who believe in God and His Messenger and strive in His cause (as in Surat As-Saff). God's reward has two stages: first, cleansing, as He erases the believers' sins and removes the burden of past wrongs; then, honoring, as He admits them to Gardens of lush beauty with flowing rivers, and to pleasant dwellings in Gardens of Eden, the abode of permanent stay. The 'pleasant dwellings' point to comfort, purity and lasting contentment that are free from the troubles of worldly life. The verse ends by declaring that this, not worldly gain, is the true and supreme triumph, since it brings salvation from punishment and the attainment of eternal bliss.

translation: And [He will give you] another thing that you love: help from God and a swift victory. And give glad tidings to the believers.
interpretation: After describing the profitable trade of faith and striving for God's cause, which brings salvation from a painful punishment and entry into gardens in the Hereafter, God adds a further reward that people naturally desire in this world: His support against their enemies and a near conquest, understood by many commentators as the conquest of Mecca. The verse acknowledges that believers love tangible, worldly success, and affirms that God grants it as a gift to those who are sincere and steadfast, while the command to give glad tidings makes this a source of hope and reassurance. It teaches that true commitment to God brings both lasting reward in the next life and, in His wisdom and timing, help and relief in this one.

translation: O you who believe, be supporters of God, as Jesus son of Mary said to the disciples: 'Who will be my supporters in the way to God?' The disciples said: 'We are God's supporters.' Then a group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved. So We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to make their faith active rather than merely verbal: being 'supporters of God' means standing firmly for His religion, upholding His truth, and obeying His messenger with sincerity and sacrifice, just as the disciples answered Jesus's call to help him convey his message. The example of Jesus shows that every prophetic mission divides people into those who accept and those who reject, and that God's help does not come by numbers or status but by faith and steadfastness. Those who believed in Jesus were granted support and ascendancy over their opponents through the clear proof of the truth they held, so the verse promises the present believers that if they support God's cause as the disciples did, God will support and strengthen them in turn.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies God, the Sovereign, the Most Holy, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surat al-Jumu'ah teaches that all of creation, through its very existence, order, and obedience to divine laws, continually declares God's perfection and freedom from any flaw.
