The four names given here explain why such glorification is fitting: He is the Sovereign whose dominion is absolute, so nothing exists outside His authority; He is the Most Holy, utterly pure of any defect or partner; He is the Almighty, whose will cannot be thwarted; and He is the All-Wise, who places everything in its proper place with purpose. The verse thus invites human beings, who alone may be heedless, to join the rest of creation in conscious worship and submission, and it prepares the reader for the surah's themes of prophetic guidance, responsibility toward revelation, and devotion to God in daily life.

translation: It is He who raised among the unlettered people a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and the wisdom, although before this they were in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet Muhammad's mission as an act of divine grace to a people with no prior scripture. He came from their own community, so they knew his character and lineage and had no ground to dismiss him as a stranger. His work had three connected parts: reciting revelation so that guidance reaches people through God's own words; purifying them of idolatry, moral corruption and inner vices so that faith changes character; and teaching the Book and the wisdom, meaning both the text and the understanding of how to apply it in belief, law and conduct. The closing phrase shows how great the transformation was. A community that had been plainly lost became a people of knowledge, discipline and moral purpose, and this shows that guidance comes from God's favor and not from the people's own prior merit.

translation: And [He has sent the Messenger also to] others among them who have not yet joined them. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Jumu'ah 62:3) extends the Prophet Muhammad's mission beyond the Arabs of his own time to all later generations who would come after the first community and follow his guidance, whatever their race or language. His message is therefore universal and lasting, and later believers are spiritually joined to the Companions through shared faith even though they come after them in time. The closing names, the Almighty and the All-Wise, teach that God has the power to carry this message to every people and to the end of time, and that choosing an unlettered Messenger and spreading his teaching across the ages reflects His perfect wisdom.

translation: That is the bounty of God, which He grants to whom He wills; and God is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every blessing, whether guidance, faith, knowledge, provision, or high standing with God, is a gift from Him and not something people earn by their own power or merit. God grants it according to His wisdom to those He knows are fit to receive it. This should lead believers to humility and gratitude, not pride or envy toward others who have been favored. It also gives hope, because God's generosity has no limit and no one should despair of receiving it. The right response is to seek His bounty through sincere devotion and good deeds, trusting that what He gives is vast.

translation: The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not bear it faithfully is like that of a donkey carrying volumes of books. Wretched is the likeness of the people who deny the signs of God. And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that knowledge of revelation is worthless unless it is understood and acted upon. Those given the Torah, who learned its words but did not live by its commands or recognize what it foretold, are compared to a donkey that carries heavy books on its back: it bears the burden but gains no benefit, wisdom, or guidance from them. Carrying scripture as mere memorization, ritual, or a source of pride, without submission to its message, brings only the weight of responsibility and not its light. Such people, by denying God's signs, wrong themselves, and God withholds guidance from those who persist in injustice and willful rejection of the truth.

translation: Say, 'O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are the favored friends of God to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: The verse challenges a claim of spiritual exclusivity. Those who believed that they alone were God's chosen friends, and that the Hereafter was guaranteed to them, ought to long to meet God, since a true friend of God would prefer the nearness of His presence over the hardships and attachments of this world. Their reluctance to wish for death exposes the hollowness of the claim and shows that they were aware of their own deeds and shortcomings. Closeness to God is therefore proven by sincere faith and righteous action, not by lineage or by a self-proclaimed status.

translation: But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forth; and God is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse says that those who claim the abode of the Hereafter is exclusively theirs will never truly long for death, because they know the sins and wrongs they have stored up for themselves and fear the reckoning that follows death. Their reluctance exposes the emptiness of their claim: someone confident of a favored place with God would welcome meeting Him, while those who know their record shrink from it. The closing phrase reminds them that God knows the wrongdoers fully, including their hidden fears and deeds, so no pretense or boast can conceal the truth from Him, and He will hold them to account.

translation: Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse tells those who cling to worldly life and run from death, whether from fear of dying or from the duties that might lead to it, that flight is useless because death is a fixed appointment that no one can avoid. Since it is certain, the real concern should be what comes after it. Every person will be brought before God, who knows both what is hidden in the heart and what is openly done, so nothing can be concealed or denied. He will then confront each person with the true account of their deeds. The verse therefore turns fear of death into accountability, urging people to prepare for the meeting with God through sincere faith and righteous action instead of trying to escape what cannot be escaped.

translation: O you who believe, when the call to prayer is made on the day of Friday, hasten to the remembrance of God and leave off trade. That is better for you, if only you knew.
interpretation: The verse teaches believers to put the worship of God ahead of worldly business at the appointed time of the Friday congregational prayer. The 'hastening' (sa'y) means moving toward the prayer with seriousness and diligence rather than running, and the 'remembrance of God' refers to the sermon and the prayer. Trade is singled out because it is the most common pursuit that distracts people from obligation. Setting it aside briefly is not a loss, because the spiritual and communal benefits of gathering in remembrance, unity, and reminder outweigh any passing gain, and obedience also brings blessing to one's livelihood. The closing phrase, 'if you only knew,' invites believers to recognize through reflection and faith that true benefit lies in putting God first.

translation: And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often that you may succeed.
interpretation: After the Friday congregational prayer ends, the restriction placed on buying and selling during the call to prayer is lifted, and believers may return to their work and seek lawful livelihood, which the verse calls God's bounty. Yet worldly pursuits must not displace devotion: the verse teaches that remembrance of God should accompany a believer throughout daily life, in the marketplace as in the mosque. True success lies in balancing worship and work, keeping the heart mindful of God while engaged in earning, so that business becomes an act of gratitude rather than heedlessness.

translation: But when they saw some trade or a diversion, they rushed to it and left you standing. Say: 'What is with Allah is better than diversion and than trade, and Allah is the best of providers.'
interpretation: The verse refers to an incident during the Friday sermon, when a trade caravan arrived in Medina and some of the congregation hurried out to it, leaving the Prophet standing in the middle of his address. It rebukes them for letting worldly gain and amusement pull them away from remembering God and from the collective worship. The Prophet is told to remind them that the reward and blessing with God, in the form of spiritual benefit, divine favor and the hereafter, are far better than any passing profit or entertainment. Since God is the true Provider who sustains all creatures, a believer need not fear losing sustenance by putting obligations to Him first. Livelihood should be sought, but never at the expense of devotion, and a person should trust that provision comes ultimately from God.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the hypocrites come to you, they say, 'We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of God.' And God knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and God bears witness that the hypocrites are surely liars.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith is not established by words alone but by sincerity of the heart. The hypocrites uttered a statement that was true in content, since Muhammad is indeed God's Messenger, yet God declares them liars because their tongues contradicted their inner convictions; they did not truly believe what they professed. Thus a claim is judged by the agreement of speech with belief and action, and God's knowledge of hidden intentions is the final measure of truthfulness. The verse also reassures the Prophet that his status rests on God's own testimony, not on the endorsement of people, least of all insincere ones.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they have turned people away from the path of God. Truly, evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' habit of using solemn oaths as a cover to protect themselves from suspicion and punishment. By swearing that they are loyal believers, they shielded their hidden disbelief and kept their standing among the Muslims. This deceit did more than shelter them. It also misled others and weakened the community's resolve. Their false assurances sowed doubt and confusion, which in effect hindered people from following God's path. The closing judgment, that their deeds are evil, teaches that sacred oaths must never serve as tools of deception, and that hypocrisy harms both the hypocrite and those around him.

translation: That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed, and so they do not understand.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 63:3, about the hypocrites) explains the cause of their spiritual state: they outwardly professed faith, then returned to disbelief once the truth conflicted with their interests, and in doing so repeatedly rejected the truth after it became clear to them. God's sealing of their hearts is a consequence of their own choice, not an arbitrary act: persistent hypocrisy and rejection hardens the heart until it loses the capacity to perceive guidance, so they no longer grasp the reality and warnings that sincere believers understand. The lesson is that trifling with faith and repeatedly turning away from the truth gradually deadens one's moral and spiritual insight.

translation: And when you see them, their bodies please you; and if they speak, you listen to their speech. They are like pieces of timber propped up. They think every cry is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. May God destroy them! How deluded they are!
interpretation: The verse portrays the hypocrites (munafiqun) as outwardly impressive but inwardly empty. Their physical appearance and eloquent speech attract admiration, yet they are like propped-up wooden planks: lifeless, hollow, and without the substance of real faith, courage, or understanding. Because of their guilty consciences and constant fear of being exposed, they imagine every shout or alarm is directed at them. This makes them a real danger to the believers, since they hide enmity behind a pleasing face and smooth words, so the believers are told to stay vigilant. The curse 'May God destroy them' expresses condemnation of their treachery, and the closing question, 'How deluded they are,' marvels at how they are turned away from truth and guidance despite the clear signs before them.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Come, the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you,' they turn their heads aside, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' pride as the real obstacle to repentance. They are offered an easy path back, which is to come to the Prophet, admit their fault, and have him pray for their forgiveness. Yet they twist their heads in scorn and walk away in conceit. Their refusal shows that their problem is not ignorance but arrogance: they will not admit wrongdoing or submit to the guidance and authority of God's messenger. A heart that regards itself as too great to seek forgiveness shuts the door to mercy on itself, and so the verse warns that arrogance is what blocks people from repentance and from accepting the truth.

translation: It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; God will never forgive them. Indeed, God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Munafiqun, 63:6) addresses the Prophet regarding the hypocrites who outwardly professed faith while inwardly rejecting it, and who showed arrogance when invited to seek forgiveness. It means that forgiveness is not obtained merely through the intercession or prayer of another, even one as noble as the Prophet, when the person himself persists in insincerity, hypocrisy, and obstinate rebellion. Their hearts have closed themselves to repentance, so asking forgiveness on their behalf is futile. God's refusal to guide them is the consequence of their own persistent defiance (fisq): when a people deliberately turn away from the truth despite clear signs, God leaves them to their chosen path, and thus no guidance or pardon reaches them unless they themselves sincerely turn back to Him.

translation: They are the ones who say, 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse.' But to God belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, yet the hypocrites do not understand.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' mistaken belief that provision lies in their own hands, so that withholding money could starve the Prophet's companions into abandoning him. It answers that all sustenance comes from God, who owns every treasury of the heavens and the earth and gives to whom He wills, so no human can cut off what He has decreed. The hypocrites fail to grasp this because their hearts are fixed on worldly means and not on God's power. This lack of true understanding (fiqh) is why they rely on material pressure, while believers trust in God's provision.

translation: They say: 'If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely drive out from it the more humble.' But to Allah belongs all honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 63:8) records the boast of the hypocrites, led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who threatened that the supposedly mighty townspeople would expel the Prophet and the poor Muslim emigrants from Medina. The Qur'an overturns this claim by teaching that true honor and might do not come from wealth, tribe, or social standing, but belong ultimately to God, and by His grant to His Messenger and the believers, who gain dignity through faith, obedience, and reliance on Him. The hypocrites, blinded by worldly measures of power, fail to grasp this reality, so their threat is empty, and the humiliation they intended for others falls back upon themselves.

translation: O you who believe, let not your wealth and your children distract you from the remembrance of God. And whoever does that, those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse warns believers that the things they naturally love and strive for, such as property, earnings, and family, are blessings that become a danger when they take over the heart and crowd out devotion to God. 'Remembrance of God' covers the obligatory prayers, gratitude, obedience, and constant awareness of Him. The verse does not condemn wealth or children in themselves. It condemns letting them become the ultimate concern, so that a person neglects duties to God for their sake. Such a person is called 'the loser' because he trades lasting, eternal gain for fleeting worldly benefit, and he ends up losing the very things he preferred, since they offer no benefit in the Hereafter if they led him away from his Lord.

translation: And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, 'My Lord, if only You would delay me for a little while, so I could give charity and be among the righteous.'
interpretation: The verse urges believers to use their wealth in charity and good works now, while they still have the time and ability to do so, because opportunity ends abruptly at death. At that moment, when the reality of the Hereafter becomes clear, a person will wish for even a short extension of life to make up for neglect, but that plea will not be granted. The lesson is that a person should not postpone generosity and righteousness, and should not let worldly wealth distract him from remembering God, since regret at the time of death comes too late to change one's record.

translation: And Allah will never delay a soul when its appointed time has come. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every person's lifespan is fixed by God, and when the appointed moment of death arrives it cannot be postponed by wealth, effort, or any means. This should move believers not to be heedless or to put off acts of charity and obedience, since the opportunity to do good ends suddenly and without warning. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of all that people do links the certainty of death to accountability: each person will meet their end with a record of deeds known to God, so one should act now in a way that will stand before Him.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies God. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the whole of creation, by its very existence, order, and dependence, bears witness to God's perfection and declares Him free of any flaw or partner. Because He alone holds true sovereignty, every blessing and every admirable quality ultimately originates from Him, so He alone deserves complete praise. His power is unlimited, so nothing escapes His will or lies beyond His ability. The believer is thus invited to join the rest of creation in glorifying Him, to recognize that all authority and gratitude belong to God, and to place trust in His complete power over every matter.

translation: He it is who created you; and among you is the disbeliever, and among you is the believer. And Allah, of what you do, is All-Seeing.
interpretation: God created human beings with a shared origin and a natural capacity for recognizing Him, yet He granted them the freedom to choose their path, so some turn to faith and others to disbelief. Neither outcome is forced on them, and each person's stance is the result of their own choice. Because God sees everything they do, every choice and action is recorded and will be accounted for, and people are responsible for the direction they take.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth, and He shaped you and perfected your forms; and to Him is the final return.
interpretation: The verse teaches that creation is purposeful and not a product of play or chance: the cosmos was made 'in truth', meaning with wisdom, order and a goal. Humans, shaped in the finest form, are among the clearest signs of this purpose, and their physical and intellectual endowment is a gift that calls for gratitude and responsibility. Since existence has a purpose, it must also have an end in which that purpose is fulfilled, so all return to God and are accountable to Him. Belief in a purposeful creation and in the final return should therefore shape how a person lives, leading him to honor the gift of his form and faculties by worshipping God and acting justly.

translation: He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose. And God is All-Knowing of what lies within the hearts.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine knowledge is total and leaves no gap between the outward and the inward: nothing in the cosmos, no private secret, no public declaration, and no hidden intention escapes God. Its purpose is to cultivate God-consciousness (taqwa) and sincerity. Because God knows even the unspoken contents of the heart, a person cannot deceive Him with outward displays of piety, and cannot find refuge in secrecy when tempted toward wrongdoing. The believer is therefore called to align inner intention with outward action, to hold themselves accountable in private as in public, and to take comfort that God also knows their hidden sincerity, struggles, and hardships, even when no one else does.

translation: Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before? They tasted the evil consequence of their conduct, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse is a warning drawn from history. God reminds people that earlier nations who rejected the truth did not escape the results of their own choices. Their disbelief and defiance brought ruin in this world, which is the 'evil consequence of their affair', and a painful punishment awaits them in the next. The lesson is that disbelief and rejecting God's messengers lead to destruction by a settled divine law, so a person should learn from the fate of earlier peoples and not repeat their mistakes, rather than wait to experience the same outcome.

translation: That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they said, 'Shall mere human beings guide us?' So they disbelieved and turned away, and God did without them. And God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse identifies the root cause of the ruin of earlier nations: not a lack of evidence, but arrogance. The messengers brought unmistakable signs, yet the people rejected them because they could not accept that guidance would come through someone of their own human kind, whom they saw as no better than themselves. This disdain led them from disbelief to active turning away. The statement that God 'did without them' teaches that faith and obedience benefit only the human being, while rejecting them does no harm to God. He is free of any need for His creatures and is worthy of praise in Himself, whether or not anyone praises Him. Their destruction was therefore a just consequence of their own choice, not a loss to God.

translation: Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say: 'Yes indeed, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that, for God, is easy.'
interpretation: The verse refutes the disbelievers' denial of life after death by commanding the Prophet to answer with an emphatic, oath-sworn affirmation. Resurrection is not a matter of speculation but a certain truth, and its purpose is moral: every person will be confronted with the full reckoning of their deeds, so life is a trust for which one is accountable. The closing phrase answers the objection that raising decayed bodies is impossible. What seems inconceivable to limited human reasoning is effortless for the One who created them in the first place, since God's power is not bound by human limits.

translation: So believe in Allah and His Messenger and in the light which We have sent down. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls people to move from mere awareness of the truth to real commitment: to trust Allah, to follow His Messenger, and to take the Qur'an as their guiding light, since it lifts people out of the darkness of ignorance, doubt, and moral confusion. Faith here is not only an inner claim but a way of life that must show itself in action, which is why the verse ends by reminding believers that Allah knows everything they do, outwardly and inwardly. This awareness is both a warning against hypocrisy and negligence and a reassurance that sincere effort is never lost.

translation: On the Day when He gathers you for the Day of Gathering—that is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain. And whoever believes in God and does righteous deeds, He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: The Day of Gathering is when all people, from the first to the last, are assembled for reckoning. It is called the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain (yawm at-taghābun) because the true value of every life is revealed on it: the believers who invested in faith and good deeds are shown to have gained, while the disbelievers and heedless, who traded the eternal for the fleeting, are shown to have lost. Worldly appearances of success and failure are reversed, and the dwellers of Paradise take the places and benefits that would have been the share of the losers. The verse then states the way to real gain: sincere faith in God joined with righteous action. God promises that such a person will have their sins erased and be given gardens of lasting bliss. This, not wealth or status in this world, is the greatest success, so the believer should measure their choices by the standard of that Day.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein forever; and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse presents disbelief joined with active denial as a single moral failing, and it names its consequence. Rejecting the truth is not merely a passive lack of faith. It is a deliberate refusal to accept clear signs, whether the revealed verses or the signs of God in creation. Calling them 'companions of the Fire' implies an enduring bond: the choices they made and the way they lived in this world have become inseparable from them, so the Fire is their fitting and lasting abode. The warning about 'a wretched destination' is meant to jolt the listener into reflection. Life is a journey with a final end, and the reader is urged to weigh whether their present stance toward God's guidance leads somewhere they would want to arrive, while there is still time to turn back toward faith.

translation: No calamity befalls except by the permission of God. And whoever believes in God, He guides his heart. And God is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: Every hardship that strikes a person happens only within God's knowledge, decree, and allowance, so it is neither random nor outside His control. The believer who truly trusts in God is granted inner guidance: when affliction comes, God steadies and directs his heart to accept it with patience, to say 'we belong to God and to Him we return,' and to see wisdom and a path to reward in it, rather than falling into despair or protest. This is because God knows everything, including what is best for His servants, and so the believer's heart finds peace in submitting to His all-encompassing knowledge.

translation: And obey God, and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon Our Messenger is only the clear delivery of the message.
interpretation: The verse ties true faith to practical obedience: obeying God means following His commands, and obeying the Messenger means following the guidance he brings, since the Messenger conveys and explains God's will. It also makes clear the limits of the Messenger's role. His duty is only to deliver the message plainly and unambiguously, not to force anyone to accept it. If people turn away after the message has been clearly conveyed, the responsibility and consequences fall on them, not on the Messenger, who has fulfilled his trust. The verse therefore serves as both a call to obedience and a warning that rejecting clear guidance leaves people accountable before God.

translation: Allah – there is no god but Him. And in Allah let the believers place their trust.
interpretation: The verse joins a statement of pure monotheism to a practical consequence. Since divinity belongs to God alone, and He alone holds power over benefit and harm, provision and outcome, the believer's reliance should rest on Him and on no one else. Trust in God (tawakkul) is not passivity: a believer takes the lawful means and makes the effort, then entrusts the result to God, knowing that no created thing can give or withhold anything without His leave. The placing of 'upon Allah' first in the sentence stresses exclusivity, so that trust is directed to God alone. Tawakkul is thus presented as a mark of true faith, which brings the believer inner calm, steadfastness in hardship, and freedom from fear of or dependence on other people.

translation: O you who believe, indeed among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon, overlook, and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse warns that family love can sometimes pull a believer away from obedience to God, for instance by keeping him from emigrating, from striving in God's cause, or from lawful earning, or by tempting him toward wrongdoing for their sake. In that sense a spouse or child can act as an 'enemy' of one's faith, even though no ill will is intended. The command to 'beware' means guarding one's religious commitments and not letting attachment to family override duties to God. Yet the verse does not tell believers to be harsh or to cut ties. It urges pardoning, overlooking, and forgiving their faults and shortcomings, and it promises that as one is gentle with one's family, God will deal with one's own failings with forgiveness and mercy. The believer is therefore asked to balance firm vigilance over faith with compassionate, forgiving treatment of loved ones.

translation: Your wealth and your children are only a trial, and with God is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the things people love most, their property and their offspring, are tests of faith and not ends in themselves. Attachment to them can pull a person away from obedience, honesty, and duty to God, whether by tempting them to earn unlawfully, to hold back charity, or to neglect obligations out of excessive love. The verse reminds the believer to keep priorities in order: use wealth and family as means for doing good and not let them become masters of the heart, because the lasting and far greater reward is with God, and it outweighs any worldly gain or comfort that wealth and children can offer.

translation: So fear Allah as much as you are able, and listen, and obey, and spend in charity for the benefit of your own souls. And whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul, it is those who will be the successful.
interpretation: The verse sets out a path to success that rests on realistic, sincere devotion. God does not burden anyone beyond capacity, so piety (taqwa) is required according to one's ability, not by an impossible standard. This piety shows itself in attentive listening to divine guidance, obedience to it, and generous spending in God's cause. Such spending is not a loss for the giver. It is a good that returns to the giver's own soul, purifying it and bringing reward. The central obstacle is the soul's stinginess (shuhh), a deep-rooted greed and clinging to wealth. Whoever is shielded from it by God's help and by self-discipline has overcome the main barrier to obedience and generosity, and so is truly successful (muflih) in this life and the next.

translation: If you lend to God a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And God is Most Appreciative, Most Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse presents spending in God's cause, whether on the poor, on relatives, or on good public causes, as a loan to God that is given with sincere intention, from lawful wealth, and without reproach or expectation of worldly return. Calling it a loan means that God guarantees its repayment and returns it many times over in reward, and that He also forgives the giver's sins because of it. God is Shakur, so He appreciates and rewards even a small deed far beyond its worth. He is Halim, so He does not hasten to punish people for their shortcomings and gives them time to repent and do good. The believer should therefore give with confidence and trust that nothing given for God's sake is lost.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's knowledge is complete and unbounded: nothing is hidden from Him, whether beyond human perception or plainly visible. This knowledge is joined with His might and wisdom, so His power is never arbitrary and His decrees are always grounded in perfect understanding. The believer is thus called to trust that God sees every intention and circumstance, and that His rule over creation is just and purposeful even where human understanding falls short.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet! When you (believers) divorce women, divorce them at the start of their prescribed waiting period, and count the period accurately, and be mindful of God, your Lord. Do not expel them from their homes, nor should they leave, unless they commit a clear indecency. These are the limits set by God; whoever transgresses God's limits has wronged his own soul. You do not know: perhaps God will bring about a new matter after that.
interpretation: The verse sets out a framework of mercy and responsibility for divorce, so that it is not carried out in anger or haste. Divorce should be pronounced in a way that lets the waiting period ('idda) begin properly, which is understood as a time when the wife is not menstruating and no intimacy has taken place. The husband must keep an accurate count of that period. During it the wife stays in the marital home rather than being cast out, since the home preserves her dignity and security and keeps open the chance of reflection and reconciliation. The only exception is a flagrant, proven misconduct. Observing these boundaries is an act of taqwa, and breaking them harms the transgressor himself. The closing phrase, 'perhaps God will bring about a new matter,' points to hope: while the couple stays under one roof in a period of calm, God may soften their hearts, restore affection, and let them return to each other, so divorce is treated as a last and reversible step rather than a sudden break.

translation: Then when they have reached their term, either retain them in a fair manner or part with them in a fair manner, and call to witness two just persons from among you, and establish the testimony for God. That is what is enjoined upon whoever believes in God and the Last Day. And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out.
interpretation: This verse addresses the end of a divorced woman's waiting period (iddah). The husband faces a clear choice at that point: either take her back with kindness and honest intention, or let her go with dignity, without harming her, withholding her rights, or using the waiting period as a means of pressure. Calling two upright witnesses protects both parties from later disputes and false claims, and the command to give testimony sincerely 'for God' means witnesses must speak truthfully and impartially, without favoring either side. The verse presents these rules as a moral reminder for those who truly believe in God and the Day of Judgment, since faith shows itself in just treatment of others even in the painful moment of separation. The closing promise teaches that whoever is conscious of God and keeps within His limits in a hard, emotionally charged situation like divorce will find God opening a path out of hardship and distress, so that fearing God becomes the practical way to relief.

translation: And He will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a measure.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who are mindful of God are granted sustenance through means they never anticipated, because provision is not bound by human calculation but by God's will. True reliance (tawakkul) means doing one's part while entrusting the outcome to God, and such trust brings sufficiency, since God needs no helper and nothing can obstruct His decree. Yet this reliance does not mean that matters will unfold according to one's own timetable: God has assigned every event, hardship, and relief a fixed measure and appointed time. The believer should therefore remain patient and confident, knowing that difficulty has a defined limit and that relief will arrive at its decreed moment.

translation: And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, then their waiting period is three months, and likewise those who have not yet menstruated. And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden. And whoever fears God, He will make matters easy for him.
interpretation: This verse completes the rulings on the waiting period ('idda) after divorce for categories of women not covered by the rule of three menstrual cycles. Women past menopause, if uncertain about how to count, and girls who have not yet begun to menstruate, observe three lunar months, so that a clear and fixed measure replaces the cycles by which waiting is otherwise reckoned. A pregnant woman's waiting period ends with childbirth, however short or long the pregnancy, because the purpose of the 'idda is to confirm that the womb is clear and to protect lineage and the rights of the child. The closing sentence ties these legal details to God-consciousness: whoever is mindful of God in observing these limits, treating a divorced wife justly and fulfilling her rights, will find God easing his affairs and relieving him of hardship in this world and the next.

translation: That is the command of God, which He has sent down to you. And whoever fears God, He will remove from him his misdeeds and will magnify for him his reward.
interpretation: The rulings just mentioned about divorce and waiting periods are not human customs but binding divine guidance revealed for people's benefit, so they should be honored and not treated lightly. Those who keep God-consciousness (taqwa) in applying them, by being just, fair, and avoiding harm to others, especially in sensitive family matters, are promised two gifts: God erases their past faults and shortcomings in this life and the next, and He greatly increases their reward. Taqwa is thus presented as both a means of purification from sins and a path to abundant divine recompense.

translation: Lodge them (the divorced women) where you yourselves dwell, according to your means, and do not harm them in order to put them in difficulty. And if they are pregnant, spend on them until they deliver their burden. Then if they suckle the child for you, give them their due payment, and consult together in a fair and just manner. But if you find yourselves in difficulty with one another, then another woman may suckle the child for him.
interpretation: The verse sets out the rights of a divorced woman during her waiting period ('idda) and the care of the child. The husband must give her housing at the standard of his own residence and within his means, and must not harass her or pressure her to leave or to bring about hardship. If she is pregnant, he must support her fully until she gives birth, even if the divorce was final. After birth, if she nurses the child, she is entitled to fair wages for it, and both parents should settle the matter by mutual consultation with kindness and fairness, without harm to either side or to the child. If they cannot agree, for instance over payment or terms, the father may have the child nursed by another woman, so that the child's welfare is protected and neither parent uses the child as a means of pressure.

translation: Let the man of means spend according to his means, and let him whose provision is restricted spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden any soul except with what He has given it. Allah will bring about ease after hardship.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Talaq 65:7) lays down the principle that financial obligations, especially maintenance of divorced wives and nursing children, are measured by each person's actual capacity. The wealthy must be generous in proportion to their wealth, while the poor are required only to give what they can afford, and neither is held to a standard beyond his means. This reflects God's justice and mercy: no one is charged with what is beyond his capacity, so obligations never become a source of oppression. The closing promise, that God will bring ease after hardship, consoles those in financial difficulty, encouraging patience, trust in God, and hope that their circumstances will improve, while also reminding others not to exploit or look down on those who are struggling.

translation: How many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We held it to a severe reckoning and punished it with a terrible, unheard-of punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that no community is exempt from divine accountability. When a society arrogantly defies God's guidance and rejects the messengers sent to it, it does not simply escape; its deeds are strictly audited and it meets a grave and unprecedented punishment. The 'severe reckoning' shows that God's justice is exacting and takes into account every act of disobedience, while the 'terrible punishment' shows the seriousness of persistent rebellion. The verse invites the reader to learn from earlier nations, to obey God and His messengers, and to treat the fate of past peoples as a warning rather than a mere story.

translation: So it tasted the evil consequence of its conduct, and the outcome of its affair was loss.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 65:9) teaches that rebellion against God's commands and His messengers carries its own punishment. The communities that defied their Lord did not suffer an arbitrary fate. They tasted the ill result of their own choices, and their end was utter ruin in this world and the next. The word 'wabal' suggests a heavy, unwholesome burden, so the harm they suffered was the direct fruit of their own deeds. The verse is a warning to later generations that disobedience brings loss, while obedience and piety lead to safety and success.

translation: God has prepared for them a severe punishment. So be mindful of God, O people of understanding who have believed. God has sent down to you a Reminder.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the consequences of defying God's commands are real and grave, as shown by the fate of earlier communities who rejected His messengers. Because of this, God calls on the believers, who are described as people of intellect, to use their reason and hold to taqwa, which means consciously guarding themselves against His displeasure by obeying Him. Intelligence is shown to be proven by heeding warnings and learning from history, not by mere cleverness. The 'Reminder' (dhikr) that God has sent down is the Qur'an, together with the Messenger who conveys it, and it serves as the means of awakening the heart, guiding believers to what pleases God, and keeping them from heedlessness and ruin.

translation: A Messenger who recites to you the clear verses of God, so that he may bring those who believe and do righteous deeds out of the darkness into the light. And whoever believes in God and does righteousness, He will admit him into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God has indeed made for him an excellent provision.
interpretation: This verse explains the purpose of sending the Prophet Muhammad with revelation: his recitation of God's clear signs is a means of guidance that lifts people out of the darkness of ignorance, disbelief, and moral confusion into the light of true knowledge, faith, and right action. Light and darkness stand for guidance and misguidance, and the verse ties deliverance to both faith and righteous deeds, so that belief must show itself in conduct. It then promises the believer who lives this way eternal Gardens, and describes that reward as the finest provision God grants, which surpasses any worldly sustenance in quality and permanence. The message is that revelation is a mercy intended to transform the believer inwardly and lead to everlasting felicity.

translation: It is Allah who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them. His command descends among them, so that you may know that Allah is Able to do all things, and that Allah has indeed encompassed all things in knowledge.
interpretation: The verse points to the vastness and order of creation as evidence of God's attributes. The seven heavens and the corresponding earths, with divine command continually descending through them, show that all creation is governed moment by moment by God's will and decree. The purpose is to ground belief in two truths: God's absolute power, since nothing is beyond His ability, and His all-encompassing knowledge, since nothing escapes Him. Realizing this should lead the believer to reverence and obedience, to trust in God's decree and justice, and to awareness that every action, whether open or hidden, is known to Him and will be accounted for.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, why do you forbid yourself what God has made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives? And God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse is a gentle divine admonition addressed to the Prophet over a personal vow to deny himself something lawful, which was commonly understood to be honey or, in another report, his relationship with a slave woman, made out of a wish to please his wives. It teaches that no one, not even the Prophet, has the authority to make unlawful what God has permitted; the power to declare things lawful or forbidden belongs to God alone. Seeking the contentment of family is a good thing, but it must not lead a person to restrict what God has allowed or to alter the boundaries of the religion. The closing words, 'God is Forgiving and Merciful', soften the reproach: the matter was a minor lapse of judgment prompted by kindness, not a sin of disobedience, and God lovingly corrects it while pardoning it, showing both the Prophet's dignity and the mercy by which believers are guided back to what is right.

translation: Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths. And Allah is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tahrim 66:2) teaches that a believer is not trapped by an oath that binds him to abandon something lawful. Allah has legislated expiation (kaffarah) as a way out: when a person swears to forbid himself what Allah has made permissible, he should break the oath and make the prescribed atonement, rather than persist in a vow that restricts what Allah has allowed. This reflects the mercy and ease of the law, and underscores that no one has the right to make unlawful what Allah has made lawful. The closing reminder that Allah is the believers' Protector (mawla), All-Knowing and All-Wise, assures them that His rulings, including this relief, come from perfect knowledge of human circumstances and from wisdom, and that He guides and supports them in their affairs.

translation: And when the Prophet confided a certain matter to one of his wives, and she then divulged it, and God made it known to him, he made known part of it and refrained from part. Then when he informed her of it, she said, 'Who told you this?' He said, 'The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that confidences are a trust and that betraying one, even within the closest household relationship, is a serious matter. God, who knows what is hidden in private chambers, informed the Prophet that his secret had been disclosed. The Prophet's response also models noble character: when confronting his wife he mentioned only part of what had happened and graciously overlooked the rest, which shows forbearance and magnanimity and avoids exposing every fault. His reply, 'The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me,' affirms that his knowledge came through divine revelation and that nothing people conceal escapes God, so believers should be mindful of Him in private as well as in public.

translation: If you two repent to God, then your hearts have indeed inclined; but if you support one another against him, then indeed God is his Protector, and Gabriel and the righteous among the believers, and moreover the angels are his supporters.
interpretation: This verse of Surat at-Tahrim addresses two of the Prophet's wives, who by the common reading are Aisha and Hafsa, after they acted in a way that troubled him. It invites them to repent and to correct hearts that had leaned away from what is right, so the door to forgiveness remains open. It also warns that collusion against the Messenger will not harm him. God Himself is his guardian and helper, and Gabriel, the righteous believers, and all the angels stand behind him. The verse teaches that those closest to the Prophet bear a greater responsibility to respect his position, that turning back to God is the proper response to wrongdoing, and that whoever is under God's protection has a support that no human opposition can overcome.

translation: It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you: submitting (Muslim) women, believing, devoutly obedient, repentant, devoted in worship, given to fasting (or travelling for the sake of God), previously married and virgins.
interpretation: This verse is a warning addressed to the Prophet's wives after some of them caused him distress. It reminds them that their standing depends on their own faith and conduct, not merely on being married to the Prophet. If they persisted in behavior that harmed him, God could replace them with women who surpass them in the qualities that matter: sincere submission, true belief, humble obedience, regular repentance, devotion in worship, and self-discipline shown in fasting or in forsaking comfort for God's sake. The mention of both previously married women and virgins shows that God's replacement would be fully adequate and varied, so the Prophet would lack nothing. The lesson is that closeness to the Prophet brings greater responsibility, and that worth in God's sight is measured by piety and righteous action.

translation: O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are appointed angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them but do what they are commanded.
interpretation: This verse places on every believer a personal duty of moral and spiritual stewardship: salvation is not only about one's own conduct but also about guiding one's household through teaching, good example, encouragement to worship, and discouragement of wrongdoing. Protection from the Fire is achieved in this world by obedience to God and by nurturing faith and righteousness in those under one's care. The description of the Fire, fueled by people and stones, and guarded by stern angels who carry out God's commands without fail, underscores the seriousness and inescapability of divine justice, reminding believers that no one can bribe, resist, or escape it, so the time for responsibility and reform is now.

translation: O you who disbelieve, make no excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, when they are brought before the fire. It tells them that the time for excuses has passed: in this world they were given reason, guidance, messengers, and time to repent, so no justification will be accepted or will help them now. Their punishment is not an arbitrary injustice but the direct and fair consequence of their own deeds and choices. The lesson for the believer is to take account of oneself and repent now, while excuses and repentance still have value, because on that Day only the outcome of one's own actions remains.

translation: O you who believe, turn to God in sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will run ahead of them and on their right sides; they will say, 'Our Lord, perfect our light for us and forgive us. Indeed, You are over all things competent.'
interpretation: The verse calls believers to a repentance that is genuine and purifying: leaving the sin at once, regretting it, and resolving firmly not to return to it, so that the repentance is free of hypocrisy and half-heartedness. Such repentance is tied to a hopeful promise of God's mercy: the erasing of past wrongs and entry into Paradise. The verse then pictures the Day of Judgment, when the faithful will be honored rather than shamed, and the light of their faith and good deeds will go before them and on their right as a guide across the darkness of that Day. Even so, they will keep asking God to complete their light and forgive them, which shows that believers never feel self-sufficient in their deeds and always depend on God's mercy, knowing that He alone has power over all things.

translation: O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be firm and harsh upon them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to exert full effort in resisting those who reject the truth openly and those who feign faith while working against it, using the means suited to each. Against the disbelievers who waged war this meant resistance, and against the hypocrites, who professed Islam outwardly, it meant argument, exposure of their duplicity, and the application of the law's limits. 'Be firm' means not yielding to their pressure or compromising the clear principles of the faith, and not letting mercy become weakness in matters of truth and justice. The verse ends by reminding that the ultimate consequence of persistent opposition is Hell, so firmness in this world reflects the seriousness of the stakes in the next.

translation: God sets forth an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so their husbands could not avail them against God in the least, and it was said, 'Enter the Fire with those who enter.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation depends on one's own faith and deeds, not on kinship or closeness to righteous people, even prophets. Noah's and Lot's wives lived in the intimacy of prophetic households, yet their betrayal was a betrayal of the message: they did not share their husbands' faith and sided with the disbelievers, not an act of immorality. Their proximity to prophets therefore gave them no protection from God's judgment. The example warns disbelievers that they cannot rely on family ties or the status of righteous relatives to rescue them, and each soul is accountable for its own belief and conduct.

translation: And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse holds up Asiya, Pharaoh's wife, as a model showing that a believer's faith is not determined by their surroundings or by the wickedness of those closest to them. Though she lived in the household of the most tyrannical ruler, with every luxury available, she preferred nearness to God and a home in the Hereafter over worldly comfort. Her prayer teaches the right order of a believer's priorities: she first sought closeness to God ('near You'), then asked for deliverance from the evil of oppression and from complicity in it. It shows that one can remain firm in belief and disown corruption even when unable to change one's environment, and that sincere reliance on God in such circumstances is a path to salvation and honor.

translation: And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into it of Our spirit; and she believed in the words of her Lord and His Scriptures, and she was among the devoutly obedient.
interpretation: God presents Mary as a model for believers, men and women alike, of steadfast faith in the face of a society that would doubt her. Her guarding of her chastity shows moral purity and self-restraint, and the divine breathing of the spirit into her garment's opening, by way of the angel Gabriel, shows that the birth of Jesus was a miracle willed by God and not the result of any human act. Her affirming of God's words and Scriptures means she accepted His decrees and revelation without doubt, even when they were difficult to bear. Her being among the qanitin, the devoutly obedient, shows that her faith was expressed in constant worship, humility and submission to God. The verse teaches that true righteousness joins purity of conduct, sincere belief, and lasting devotion, and that such a person is raised in rank by God whatever the person's circumstances.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion, and He has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone holds absolute sovereignty over the whole of creation, seen and unseen. 'Blessed' (tabāraka) conveys that His goodness, greatness and majesty are abundant, enduring and beyond measure, so that every blessing in existence flows from Him. 'In whose hand is dominion' means that kingship, authority and the ordering of all affairs, including life, death, provision and judgment, are ultimately His, and that human power and worldly rule are only entrusted and temporary. The closing statement that He has power over all things grounds this sovereignty in limitless capacity: nothing escapes His will or ability. The believer is therefore invited to respond with reverence, trust and accountability, recognizing that the One who owns everything and can do everything is the One to whom they must turn and answer, which prepares the ground for the surah's coming themes of testing in life and the reckoning to come.

translation: He who created death and life to test you [as to] which of you is best in deed; and He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse teaches that life and death are not random or purposeless but are part of a divine test. Life is an opportunity to act and death is the reckoning point that ends the chance to act, so human existence is framed by accountability. What God looks for is not the greatest quantity of deeds but the best quality of deed: actions done sincerely for God's sake and in line with what is right. The verse closes with two names of God that balance each other. Being the Almighty (al-'Aziz) means that He is fully able to hold people to account and no one can escape His judgment. Being the Forgiving (al-Ghafur) means that He pardons the shortcomings of those who strive and repent, so the believer should neither despair nor be complacent, but live between awe and hope.

translation: He who created seven heavens in layers. You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency. So return your vision to the sky: do you see any flaws?
interpretation: The verse points to the perfect order and harmony in God's creation as proof of His power, wisdom, and mercy. The heavens are layered and balanced, with no disproportion, discord, or defect in them. By inviting the observer to look again and again, the verse challenges human skepticism: however hard one searches for a crack or flaw, none will be found, so the flawless design must have a single, all-wise Creator who deserves belief and worship. The use of the name 'the Most Merciful' hints that this precise order is itself a form of mercy, since it sustains life and makes the universe a stable, intelligible home for humankind.

translation: Then look again, and yet again; your sight will return to you humbled and exhausted.
interpretation: After the previous verse invites the reader to scan the heavens for any flaw in the Merciful's creation, this verse intensifies the challenge: repeat your inspection as many times as you wish, and your eyes will return without having found any defect or incongruity. The sight comes back 'khasi'an' (repulsed, humiliated at its failure to find fault) and 'hasir' (weary and dazed from straining at the flawless perfection). The point is that the order, harmony and precision of creation point to the wisdom and power of its Creator, and humbling the critic's gaze should lead the observer to acknowledge God's perfection and to reflect on faith.

translation: And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and We made them [missiles] to stone the devils, and We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and wisdom in creation: the stars that beautify the lowest sky and guide people are also instruments of His protection of the heavens, repelling the rebellious devils who try to eavesdrop on the unseen. It teaches that the cosmos is under divine order, that no evil force can breach what God has guarded, and that the devils, who seek to mislead humanity, face disgrace in this world and a fierce fire in the next. This serves as a warning to those who follow them and a reminder to the believer to rely on God's design and to look at the heavens with reflection and gratitude.

translation: And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 67:6) teaches that rejecting God, after the clear signs and warnings He has sent, is not a matter without consequence. Disbelief here means more than lack of knowledge; it is a deliberate denial of the Creator's lordship and of the guidance that came from Him. The verse presents Hell as the just outcome of that denial, since a person who rejects the One who created and sustained him has broken the most basic bond of gratitude and accountability. The closing phrase, 'wretched is the destination,' stresses that the afterlife is the final place every soul returns to, so the real measure of a choice is where it ultimately leads. The verse serves as a sober warning that makes a person weigh his beliefs and actions against his final end rather than against passing worldly gains.

translation: When they are thrown into it, they will hear from it a dreadful roaring (like the braying of a donkey) as it boils up.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mulk 67:7) shows how terrifying Hell is for those who denied the truth. It is portrayed as a living, raging presence. When the disbelievers are cast into it, it draws in breath with a harsh, horrifying gasp and seethes with fury, as if eager to punish. The scene is meant to stir fear in the listener and to warn that denying God's messengers and signs leads to a punishment that is not only physical but also overwhelming in its awe and dread. Hearing the sound before feeling the full torment adds to the terror, and it urges people to reflect and to mend their ways while there is still time.

translation: It almost bursts with rage. Every time a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them: 'Did no warner come to you?'
interpretation: The verse portrays Hell as a living, furious force that seethes against the disbelievers, almost splitting apart in its wrath at those who rejected God. The question posed by its keepers is not a request for information but a rebuke that establishes divine justice: no one is punished without first having been warned. Each group entering the Fire is confronted with the fact that God's messengers had reached them and that their punishment results from their own denial, leaving them without any excuse.

translation: They will say: 'Yes indeed, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, "God has not sent down anything; you are only in great error."'
interpretation: This verse shows the people of Hell admitting their guilt when the keepers of the Fire ask whether no warner came to them. They concede that God's justice was fully established, because warning came through the messengers and the revelation. They rejected it out of arrogance and mocked the warners by accusing them of being lost. The verse means that no one will have a valid excuse on the Day of Judgment. Punishment follows a clear message that people knowingly refused, and the real error lay with those who denied, not with those who warned. The admission also teaches that people are accountable for how they respond to guidance, and that dismissing revelation and insulting those who convey it leads to ruin.

translation: And they will say: 'If only we had listened or used our reason, we would not have been among the companions of the Blazing Fire.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the people of Hellfire will acknowledge that their downfall came from neglecting the two means of guidance God gave them: receptive hearing of revelation and the messengers' warnings, and independent reasoning that reflects on the signs in creation. The verse teaches that true guidance requires both listening to divine revelation and using reason to understand it. Whoever shuts off both, preferring arrogance or inherited habit, bears responsibility for their own end, and their regret will come too late to help them.

translation: So they will confess their sin; then away with the companions of the Blaze!
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 67:11) describes the people of Hell when they finally admit that they rejected the warners and the truth that came to them. Their confession comes too late to benefit them, because the time for acting on belief and repentance has passed. The prayer 'away with them' (suhqan) is a decree of distance from God's mercy, signifying that their own persistent denial and arrogance led them to their fate, and that their punishment is just. The lesson is that a person should acknowledge the truth and repent while it is still of use, rather than waiting for the Day when recognition will bring no relief.

translation: Indeed, those who fear their Lord in the unseen will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mulk, 67:12) teaches that true reverence for God is proven when no one is watching. Fearing God 'in the unseen' means being mindful of Him in private, where there is no social pressure, reputation, or worldly accountability, and where only faith and conscience restrain a person. Such sincere, inner God-consciousness is the foundation of real righteousness, and it is rewarded in two ways: forgiveness, which erases the sins and shortcomings that even the sincere commit, and a great reward, the generous recompense of Paradise. The verse encourages believers to cultivate integrity and sincerity in their hidden lives, assuring them that God, who knows what is unseen, values and richly repays what no other person ever witnesses.

translation: Whether you conceal your speech or proclaim it openly, indeed He is All-Knowing of what lies within the hearts.
interpretation: The verse teaches that there is no difference before God between what people say secretly and what they say aloud, since His knowledge reaches beyond words to the innermost intentions, thoughts, and feelings hidden in the heart. Human speech may be hidden from other people, but nothing can be hidden from the Creator. This should lead a believer to constant God-consciousness (taqwa): sincerity in intention, honesty in private as in public, and caution against plotting, hypocrisy, or harboring ill will, because every inner state is known and will be accounted for.

translation: Does He who created not know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse uses a rhetorical question to affirm that God's knowledge is complete and all-encompassing. The One who brought creation into being, with all its hidden details, must know what He created, including the secret thoughts and intentions in people's hearts that are mentioned in the preceding verse. His being 'al-Latif' means His knowledge reaches the most delicate and unseen matters, and His being 'al-Khabir' means He is fully aware of the inner realities of all things. The lesson is that no one can hide anything from God, so a person should be mindful of Him in secret as well as in public, and should trust that His subtle care and wisdom run through all that He decrees.

translation: It is He who made the earth tame and manageable for you, so walk in its tracts and eat of His provision; and to Him is the resurrection.
interpretation: God has made the earth submissive and suitable for human life, so that people can settle it, travel across it, and pursue their livelihood. This is a call to take action: to strive and seek lawful sustenance with effort, while recognizing that every provision ultimately comes from God and not from one's own power. The verse ends by reminding that this ease and enjoyment of the earth carries accountability, since all people will be raised and return to Him, and so one should use the earth's blessings with gratitude, honesty and awareness of the Day of Judgment.

translation: Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up, while it is shaking and heaving?
interpretation: The verse warns people who have grown heedless because of the apparent stability of their lives. The earth that seems firm beneath their feet is entirely under God's command, and He can turn it from a place of safety into a source of destruction in an instant. The phrase 'He who is in the heaven' points to God's supremacy and absolute authority over creation, not to His being confined to a place. Security therefore rests on His mercy and not on the natural order, and the verse calls the arrogant and the neglectful to humility, gratitude, and awareness of their dependence on Him.

translation: Or do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not send upon you a storm of stones? Then you will know how [true] was My warning.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny the message for their false sense of safety. Their security rests on nothing, because God holds absolute power over them and over everything above them. He could turn the very sky they rely on into a source of destruction, as He did with earlier peoples such as the people of Lot, who were struck by a rain of stones. Their heedlessness does not protect them. The warning brought by the Prophet is not an empty threat, and when the punishment arrives, those who ignored it will know with certainty that it was true. The verse calls people to drop their complacency, to recognize God's sovereignty, and to heed the warning while there is still time to repent.

translation: And those before them also denied [the truth]; so how was My denial (disapproval and punishment)?
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and warns his opponents. Rejection of divine messages is not new: earlier nations denied their messengers as the Quraysh now deny him. God then answers the question 'how was My nakir?' by pointing to history: His response was severe, as shown by the ruin of Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and others. The rhetorical question invites the listener to recall those fates and conclude that persisting in denial brings the same end, while patience and steadfastness are for the believers. Divine justice may be delayed but is not forgotten.

translation: Have they not looked at the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is All-Seeing of everything.
interpretation: The verse directs people to reflect on the flight of birds as a sign of God's mercy and power. A bird glides with wings outstretched, then draws them in, and yet it stays aloft in the air, held there by the order God has set in nature: the shape of its body, the laws of the air, and the gravity that would otherwise pull it down. Nothing sustains it except the Most Merciful, whose mercy is the reason creatures are preserved and are not left to fall. The verse names God as 'al-Rahman' to stress that this sustaining is a gift of grace, not something creatures achieve by their own power. Those who deny or feel secure in their disbelief should recognize that they too are upheld by God at every moment and could be undone by Him if He willed. The closing words, 'He is All-Seeing of everything', affirm that God's knowledge and care reach the finest detail of creation, so He orders each thing with wisdom and precision, and nothing escapes His awareness. The proper response is gratitude, humility, and turning to Him alone for protection.

translation: Or who is it that could be an army for you to help you, other than the Most Merciful? The disbelievers are in nothing but delusion.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Mulk, 67:20) challenges the disbelievers' false sense of security. They rely on their numbers, strength, wealth, and allies, or on false deities, imagining these will protect them from God's punishment. The rhetorical question shows that no force exists that can defend or give victory against God's will, since He alone holds all power and mercy. Their confidence in anything besides Him is only deception and illusion, planted by Satan and their own desires, and it will vanish when His decree comes upon them. The verse teaches that true protection and victory come only from God, and that trusting in created means apart from Him is self-deceit.

translation: Or who is this that could provide for you if He withheld His provision? Rather, they persist in arrogance and aversion.
interpretation: The verse challenges the disbelievers to consider where their sustenance really comes from. Rain, crops, and every means of livelihood depend on God's will, and if He withheld them, no idol, power, or person could restore them. Despite this clear proof, the deniers do not reflect or turn back. They persist in stubborn pride (ʿutuw), refusing to submit to the truth, and in aversion (nufūr), recoiling from the message. The point is that their rejection stems not from a lack of evidence but from arrogance and an unwillingness to acknowledge their dependence on their Provider and to thank Him with worship.

translation: Is he who walks prone on his face better guided, or he who walks upright on a straight path?
interpretation: The verse (Al-Mulk 67:22) uses two images to contrast the disbeliever with the believer. The one who stumbles along with his face bent to the ground cannot see where he is going, so he blunders, loses his way and ends in ruin. This is the person who is heedless of the truth and absorbed in worldly desires and falsehood. The one who walks upright on a straight path sees his way, knows his destination and moves with purpose and steadiness. This is the believer who follows divine guidance and the path of monotheism and righteousness. The rhetorical question makes the answer obvious: guidance belongs only to the one who lives with open eyes and an upright heart, following God's straight path, while the one who ignores revelation wanders aimlessly and will be raised in the Hereafter in the same state, humbled and misguided.

translation: Say: He it is who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little do you give thanks.
interpretation: The verse reminds human beings that their very existence and their faculties of perception and understanding are gifts from God, not products of their own power. Hearing, sight, and the heart (the seat of reason and reflection) are the means by which a person can recognize truth, contemplate creation, and arrive at faith. Since these faculties are entrusted to people, gratitude is owed to the Giver, and true gratitude is shown by using them for what they were given for: listening to revelation, observing the signs of God in the world, and reflecting with an open heart, ultimately worshipping God alone. The closing phrase rebukes human ingratitude, since most people enjoy these blessings while neglecting to acknowledge their Source or to use them in obedience, and so fall short of the thankfulness that is due.

translation: Say: He it is who multiplied you throughout the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse reminds humanity that the One who scattered and propagated people across the earth, in their many nations, languages and lands, is the same God to whom all will return. Their dispersal in this world is temporary and purposeful, and it is not a sign of separate destinies. The same Creator who brought them into being and spread them out will gather them in a single assembly on the Day of Judgment, where each will be held accountable. This calls the listener to gratitude for creation and to moral awareness, since life on earth is a passage toward a certain return to God.

translation: And they say: "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The disbelievers mock the warning of resurrection and judgment by demanding a specific date for it, not out of a sincere search for truth but out of scorn and denial. Their challenge treats the lack of an immediate answer as proof that the warning is false. The Qur'an's response to this question elsewhere is that knowledge of the Hour rests with God alone, and the Messenger's task is only to warn clearly. The verse shows that the issue is not the timing of the promise but their refusal to prepare for it. A warning's truth does not depend on whether its date is announced, and delay is a mercy, giving people time to repent, not evidence that the promise will fail.

translation: Say: 'The knowledge [of the Hour] is only with God, and I am only a clear warner.'
interpretation: The verse draws a clear boundary around the Prophet's role.
