Knowledge of unseen matters such as the exact timing of the Hour belongs to God alone, so the Prophet does not claim it and people should not demand it from him. His task is to warn plainly and convey the message, and the right response to the warning is to prepare through faith and righteous action instead of asking when the Hour will come. The verse teaches humility before God's absolute knowledge and shows that a messenger's authority lies in conveying what he has been given, not in knowing everything.

translation: But when they see it close at hand, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed, and it will be said, "This is that which you used to call for."
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the punishment the disbelievers used to mock and demand in haste becomes a visible reality, close upon them. Their faces darken with grief, fear, and disgrace as their denial collapses before the evidence of what they rejected. They are then rebuked with the words 'This is what you used to call for', meaning the very torment they challenged the Prophet to bring about, saying 'When will this promise come, if you are truthful?' The verse teaches that mockery and denial of God's warnings cannot postpone or cancel the truth, and that those who treat the warnings as a joke will face their reality with regret and humiliation when no chance to repent remains.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if God destroys me and those with me, or has mercy on us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to turn the disbelievers' hopes away from his own fate. They awaited his death or the ruin of the believers as though it would relieve them of the message. Whether God takes the believers' lives or shows them mercy, the believers are secure in either outcome, since both lead to God's reward. The disbelievers, by contrast, have no protector from the painful punishment their denial has earned. The question shows that the believers' fate does not decide the disbelievers' fate, and that each person must secure his own salvation by faith instead of waiting on the fortunes of others.

translation: Say: He is the Most Merciful; we believe in Him, and in Him we have put our trust. So you will soon know who is in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to answer those who wish him and the believers ill by declaring that their security lies in faith and reliance on God, whose mercy encompasses all things. Belief and trust go together: faith is the inward acceptance of God, and tawakkul is entrusting one's affairs to Him while still striving. Naming God as ar-Rahman reminds the believers that He is the source of true protection and sustenance, unlike the disbelievers' reliance on numbers, power, or worldly means. The closing warning is that truth and falsehood will be made plain over time and on the Day of Judgment, so the disbelievers will come to see who was truly astray, and it consoles the believers by assuring them that the outcome rests with God.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if your water were to sink away into the earth, who then could bring you flowing water?
interpretation: The verse reminds people that their most basic necessity, water, is entirely a gift from God and not something they control. The springs and wells they rely on could vanish deep into the earth at any moment, and no human power, wealth or technology could bring them clear, flowing water again. By asking a question whose only answer is God, it calls on people to acknowledge His power and mercy, to be grateful for His provision, and to turn to Him in faith rather than being heedless or arrogant.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe.
interpretation: God swears by the pen and by what is written with it, which elevates writing, knowledge, and the recording of deeds as among His great signs. The oath prepares the ground for the next verses, which affirm that the Prophet Muhammad is not mad. Just as the pen preserves truth and makes knowledge lasting, the revelation he brings is a reasoned, recorded, and trustworthy message, and no accusation of madness can stand against it. The isolated letter Nun is one of the mysterious letters whose exact meaning is known to God alone; it also draws attention to the Qur'an's miraculous character, since it is composed of the same letters the Arabs used in their own speech.

translation: By the grace of your Lord, you are not a madman.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:2) is God's direct reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad, answering the accusation of the disbelievers of Quraysh who called him mad because of the revelation he brought. The phrase 'by the grace of your Lord' signals that the Prophet is favored with prophecy, sound intellect, and noble character, so the charge of madness is false and falls away of itself. The verse treats his rational, balanced conduct and the wisdom of the message as evidence of that favor, and it comforts him against the insults of his opponents, assuring him that God's blessing upon him refutes their slander.

translation: And indeed, for you is a reward that is never cut off.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:3) consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ after the disbelievers accused him of madness. God assures him that his patience, steadfastness, and perseverance in conveying the message will be met with a reward that is unending and never diminished or reproached. The meaning is that the worth of his work is measured by God, not by the slander of his opponents, so their insults cannot erase or reduce what awaits him. The promise also extends as encouragement to every believer who endures hardship for the sake of truth, since God's recompense for sincere effort remains constant and lasting.

translation: And indeed, you [O Muhammad] are of a great moral character.
interpretation: God affirms the Prophet Muhammad's exalted moral excellence, showing that his noble conduct, such as patience, forbearance, honesty, mercy, and humility, was not a passing quality but an established disposition. This testimony comforts him against the accusations of madness made by his opponents, and it presents his character as the highest model for believers, whose embodiment of the Qur'an's teachings in daily life is itself evidence of the truth of his message.

translation: So you will see, and they will see.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:5) addresses the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, after the disbelievers accused him of madness. It assures him that the truth will become plain: when reality is unveiled, whether in this world through the vindication of his mission or on the Day of Judgment, both he and his opponents will clearly see who was truly sound of mind and on the right path, and who was misguided and afflicted. The verse consoles the Prophet, calling for patience in the face of slander, and warns his detractors that their accusations will be exposed as baseless.

translation: Which of you is the afflicted one (the one bereft of sanity)? (Qur'an 68:6)
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet's opponents who accused him of madness. God turns the accusation back on them: on the Day when truth is revealed, it will become clear which party is truly afflicted, whether the Prophet, who embodies sound character and a great moral standard, or those who reject the truth, persecute their guide, and follow error. Madness is thus redefined as the loss of moral and spiritual insight, not the possession of divine guidance.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is the Most Knowing of who strays from His path, and He is the Most Knowing of the rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance and misguidance are matters known perfectly to God, who knows the inner state of every person: their intentions, sincerity, and capacity to accept truth. The Prophet is therefore consoled and relieved of the burden of judging or forcing people to believe. His duty is to convey the message with wisdom, while the final reckoning and the discernment between those who go astray and those who are guided rest solely with God. It also cautions believers against arrogantly claiming to know who is saved or lost, since only God knows the true standing of hearts and the ends to which people will come.

translation: So do not obey those who deny the truth.
interpretation: This verse from Surat Al-Qalam (68:8) instructs the Prophet Muhammad, and by extension every believer, not to yield to or compromise with those who reject the truth of the message. The deniers sought to pressure him into softening his call or meeting them halfway, as the following verse indicates ('They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise'). The command affirms that faith and integrity cannot be traded for social approval or peace with those who reject God's guidance, and that steadfastness in truth requires refusing to follow the wishes of those whose disbelief is rooted in arrogance and worldly interest.

translation: They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise.
interpretation: The disbelievers of Quraysh desired that the Prophet soften his stance and make concessions in his call, such as ceasing to criticize their gods or accepting part of their way, in return for which they would ease their opposition and appear to accept part of his message. The verse reveals that their offer was not sincere conviction but a bargain of mutual accommodation in matters of faith. Truth cannot be diluted or traded, and the believer must not yield principle to win the favor of those who oppose it. Such compromise would only erode the integrity of the message, which is why the surrounding verses command him not to obey those who deny the truth.

translation: And do not obey every worthless, habitual swearer of oaths.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:10) warns the Prophet, and through him every believer, against yielding to or taking guidance from people whose character is marked by constant, careless oath-swearing. Such a person swears readily because his word carries no real weight, and he is 'mahin', meaning base and contemptible in his moral worth, since he lacks truthfulness and inner integrity. The verse teaches that obedience, deference and trust should not be given to those who cheapen God's name to win people over or to push their own interests. Leadership and influence must rest on honesty, and compromising with the morally despicable weakens one's firmness upon the truth.

translation: A slanderer, going about spreading malicious gossip.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:11) describes a character trait of the one who is not to be obeyed: someone who habitually insults and defames others, and who actively moves among people carrying tales in order to sow discord between them. The Qur'an treats backbiting and talebearing as grave moral diseases, because they destroy trust, break bonds of kinship and friendship, and corrupt the social fabric. By linking verbal abuse with the deliberate act of carrying harmful speech from person to person, the verse teaches that a believer's integrity is measured in part by how they guard their tongue, and that those who spread division through slander are unworthy of obedience or deference.

translation: A preventer of good, a transgressor, a sinner.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:12) continues the description of the type of person the Prophet is told not to obey (68:10-13). It characterizes such a person by his harmful conduct toward others and toward God's limits: he withholds good, whether by refusing his wealth to the needy, by obstructing people from faith and righteous deeds, or by hindering kindness in general. He also oversteps the bounds of justice and divine law, and is steeped in sin. The lesson is that moral worth is measured by one's contribution to the good of others and by respect for God's limits, and that those who obstruct goodness and habitually transgress must not be followed or given authority over one's conscience, however wealthy or influential they may be.

translation: Harsh and cruel, and moreover of doubtful lineage (an ignoble upstart).
interpretation: The verse completes the description of the type of person warned against in Surat al-Qalam: beyond the vices already named (swearing oaths readily, slander, obstructing good, transgression), he is 'utul'—coarse, hard-hearted, and violent toward others—and 'zanim', one who is attached to a people without truly belonging to them, which points to a base and disreputable character. The Qur'an thus teaches that a person's worth is not measured by wealth or status but by moral character, and that cruelty and ignobility of conduct expose the one who rejects truth and the believers, so believers should not obey or yield to such a person.

translation: Merely because he possessed wealth and sons.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:14) gives the reason for the warning in the preceding verse (68:10-13), which forbids obeying the despised, oath-swearing slanderer. It also reproves the person who meets God's revelation with arrogance. When the verses of God are recited to such a person, he dismisses them as 'tales of the ancients' only because God has given him wealth and children. His worldly prosperity makes him self-important and blinds him to gratitude. Instead of thanking the Giver of blessings, he uses them as a basis for pride and for rejecting the truth. Wealth and offspring are trials and favors from God, not proof of one's worth or of being right, so they must never be a reason to deny God's message or to look down on others.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients."
interpretation: This verse exposes the arrogance and willful denial of the person who rejects revelation, as described in the preceding verses (Surah Al-Qalam 68:10-14, and also Al-Mutaffifin 83:13). When the clear signs of God are recited to him, he does not engage with them honestly or reflect on their truth, but dismisses them as mere legends handed down from past generations. His dismissal is not the result of sound reasoning but of a heart hardened by wealth, status, and sin, which prevents him from recognizing truth. The verse teaches that rejection of divine guidance often stems from pride and moral corruption rather than a lack of evidence, and that mocking revelation as 'old stories' is a way to evade the accountability and moral demands it places on a person.

translation: We will brand him upon the snout.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Qalam 68:16) refers to the arrogant, sinful man described in the preceding verses, who is a swearer, slanderer, hinderer of good, and transgressor. The 'snout' (khurtoom) is a word normally used for the nose of an animal, so the verse mocks him by likening him to a beast. God declares that He will mark him with an indelible sign of disgrace, so that his shame becomes plain and visible to all. The meaning is that the pride he carried on his face will be turned into lasting humiliation, whether in this world through public disgrace or in the Hereafter through a mark that exposes his wickedness.

translation: Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the owners of the garden, when they swore they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning,
interpretation: God explains that the wealth and blessings given to the Quraysh of Mecca are a test, not a sign of divine favor or a guarantee of lasting security. Like the owners of the garden, who took their produce for granted and resolved to pick it at dawn, they assumed that their plans were certain and that they were in control. By swearing without saying 'if God wills' and by planning to keep the poor from their share, those garden owners showed arrogance and stinginess, and their garden was destroyed overnight. The verse warns that ingratitude, forgetting God, and withholding the rights of the needy can bring loss of blessings, and that a person's plans succeed only by God's will.

translation: And they did not make an exception (by saying "If Allah wills").
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat al-Qalam (68:18), describes the owners of the garden who swore they would harvest its fruits in the morning, without saying "insha'Allah" (if God wills). Their oath was made in self-reliance, as though the outcome was entirely in their own control and not subject to God's will. The verse teaches that human plans are always contingent on God's decree, and that forgetting to link one's intentions to His will reflects arrogance and heedlessness. Their garden was then destroyed overnight, showing the consequence of relying on oneself while ignoring God's power and of withholding the rights of the poor.

translation: Then a visitation from your Lord came upon it (the garden) while they were asleep.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qalam 68:19) describes how God's decree struck the orchard of the men who had resolved to harvest it at dawn while deliberately excluding the poor. During the night, as they slept unaware, a calamity sent by God enveloped the garden and destroyed it. The meaning is that human plans built on stinginess, arrogance, and the denial of the rights of the needy cannot withstand God's will; divine punishment can arrive suddenly and unseen, when people feel most secure and heedless, and wealth is a trust whose blessing is lost when its due charity is withheld.

translation: And by morning it had become like a harvested, barren field, as if cut down and stripped bare.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the owners of the garden in Surat al-Qalam (68:20), teaches that no plan or possession is secure against God's command. The men had resolved to pick their fruit at dawn in secret, so that no poor person could claim a share. During the night a calamity from God struck the garden and left it blackened and stripped, like a field already reaped or like darkness itself, since 'sarim' can mean both 'cut off' and 'night'. The verse presents this as divine justice for their stinginess and their arrogant confidence in their own scheme, and as a warning that wealth withheld from those in need can be lost entirely, while gratitude and generosity protect blessings.

translation: And they called out to one another at morning time.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:21) comes in the story of the owners of the garden, who had sworn to harvest its fruit at dawn without giving the poor their share. As morning came, they eagerly urged one another to go early and carry out their plan. Their haste shows how fully they had committed to their selfish scheme, relying on their own planning and forgetting that God controls all outcomes. The verse sets up the lesson that stinginess and neglect of the rights of the needy bring loss and ruin, since what they planned in secret and rushed to do was undone by God's decree before they arrived.

translation: Saying: "Go early in the morning to your tilth (your fruit-bearing garden), if you are determined to pick its fruit."
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Qalam (68:22), describes the owners of the garden who called to one another at dawn to hurry to their orchard and harvest it before the poor could come. The word 'harth' (tilth) refers to their crops and fruit, and 'sarimin' means those resolved to cut or pluck the fruit. The verse reveals their scheming intention: they dressed a selfish plan in the language of diligence and early effort, planning to deny the needy their rightful share, as their father had previously allowed. The lesson is that human planning which is rooted in greed and in withholding the rights of the poor, and which forgets reliance on God's will ('in sha' Allah'), is doomed to ruin, as the following verses show when the garden was destroyed overnight.

translation: So they set off, whispering to one another.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:23) describes the owners of the garden who resolved to harvest their fruit at dawn so that the poor would not get any of it. They went off speaking in hushed voices, hiding their plan out of stinginess and fear that a needy person would hear and ask for a share. Their secrecy shows the greed in their hearts. They thought they could conceal their intentions from people, yet God was fully aware of them, and He destroyed the garden before they arrived. The verse teaches that withholding the rights of the poor and plotting in secret to deny them is a grave wrong, and that no scheme against God's commands can succeed.

translation: "Let no poor person enter it upon you today."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:24) records what the owners of the garden said to one another as they went out early in the morning to harvest their fruit in secret, so that no needy person would come and claim a share. It exposes their stinginess and their disregard for the right of the poor, which their forefathers had honored by letting the needy share in the harvest. The point is that wealth is a trust from God, and withholding the due share of the poor out of greed invites divine punishment. The garden was destroyed overnight as a result, showing that hoarding blessings and scheming against the needy leads to the loss of those very blessings.

translation: And they went out early in the morning, determined and resolved, believing they were able to carry out their plan.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the owners of the garden in Surah Al-Qalam (68:25), shows people who set out at dawn with fixed intent to harvest their garden's fruit secretly so that no poor person could share in it. They felt fully capable and in control of their plan, and relied on their own strength and scheming rather than on God, never adding 'if God wills'. The verse teaches that human confidence in one's own ability, joined to stinginess and denial of the rights of the needy, is blind to God's power. What they thought they could secure was already destroyed by God's decree, so the lesson is that wealth is a trust, and that those who withhold the due share of the poor risk losing the blessing entirely.

translation: So when they saw it (their garden ruined), they said, "Indeed, we must have lost our way."
interpretation: The owners of the garden had resolved to harvest it secretly at dawn so the poor would get nothing. When they arrived and saw it burnt and barren, they did not at first recognize it, because it looked so unlike the lush orchard they knew. Their first reaction was to assume they had come to the wrong place. This shows how complete the devastation was, and how the outcome of their scheming, which God had thwarted, was beyond their expectation. Only afterward, when they understood that this was truly their garden, did they realize they had been deprived of it as a punishment for their stinginess and their plan to withhold the rights of the needy.

translation: Rather, we have been deprived [of our harvest].
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:27) records the final words of the owners of the garden in Surah al-Qalam. After they had resolved to harvest their fruit at dawn in secret so that no poor person could share in it, they found the garden utterly ruined. At first they thought they had lost their way and said, 'Indeed, we are astray.' Then they realized it was their own garden and said, 'Rather, we have been deprived.' Their deprivation was a just consequence of their stinginess and their plan to withhold the rights of the needy, since God removed the blessing from the very thing they sought to monopolize. The lesson is that wealth is a trust from God and that the poor have a right in it. Greed and scheming to deny that right bring loss, and what people try to hoard can be taken from them entirely.

translation: The most moderate (best) of them said: 'Did I not say to you, why do you not glorify (God)?'
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of the owners of the garden (Surah Al-Qalam, 68:28). The fairest and most upright among the brothers had warned them against their plan to harvest the fruits at dawn in secret and deny the poor their share. His reminder to glorify God (tasbih) meant that they should remember God, acknowledge that their wealth is His gift, and give thanks by sharing it with those in need, rather than relying on their own power and scheming. When their garden was destroyed, his earlier counsel was recalled as a reproach: remembrance of God and gratitude would have protected them from arrogance and from the loss that came as a consequence of their greed and stinginess.

translation: They said: 'Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the owners of the garden in Surat al-Qalam (68:29), shows the moment their pride collapses. After they schemed to harvest their garden at dawn so the poor would get nothing, and then found it ruined, they turn to praising God and confessing their own wrongdoing. By declaring God's perfection first, they clear Him of any injustice in what befell them, and they place the fault on themselves: their selfishness, their stinginess toward the needy, and their arrogant reliance on their own plans. The verse teaches that admitting one's guilt and exonerating God is the first step of repentance. It also warns that denying the rights of the poor in one's wealth brings loss, and that blessings can be taken away when they are met with greed instead of gratitude.

translation: Then some of them turned to others, blaming one another.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:30, in the story of the owners of the garden, and similarly 37:50 about the people of Paradise/Hell) shows the moment after the disaster, when the owners of the garden realize their wrongdoing. They had resolved to harvest their garden at dawn so as to deny the poor their share, and when they found it destroyed they began to blame each other instead of taking responsibility alone. The deeper meaning is that sinful plans made together end in mutual recrimination: each person who took part in the scheme tries to shift guilt onto others, until they finally admit their own transgression and turn back to God in repentance. It teaches that injustice and stinginess bring ruin, and that true accountability lies in recognizing one's own fault and returning to God rather than blaming others.

translation: They said: 'Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors.'
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Qalam 68:31) records the response of the owners of the garden after they saw it ruined. They had sworn to harvest its fruit at dawn and deny the poor their due, and they had made no exception by saying 'if God wills.' When they found the garden destroyed, they cried out in distress and, for the first time, admitted their wrongdoing. Their confession of being 'transgressors' (tāghīn) shows that they recognized the root of their loss was not bad luck but their own arrogance, greed and exceeding the bounds God had set by withholding the rights of the needy. The point is that blessings can be lost through ingratitude and stinginess, and that honest self-reproach and repentance, even after a calamity, is the beginning of returning to God, and it is better to heed that warning before the loss occurs.

translation: Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it; indeed, to our Lord we turn in earnest desire.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qalam 68:32) is the repentant cry of the owners of the garden, who had resolved to harvest their orchard at dawn without giving the poor their due, and found it ruined. After admitting their wrong, they express hope, not certainty, that God might replace their loss with something better, and they show that their hope rests on turning to Him alone. The verse teaches that sincere repentance means acknowledging one's fault and then placing one's longing and trust in God, who can restore and exceed what was lost, while keeping the humility of hope rather than presuming a guaranteed reward.

translation: Such is the punishment [in this world]; but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Qalam 68:33) comes after the story of the owners of the garden, whose crop was destroyed in one night as a result of their stinginess and their scheme to deny the poor their share. It teaches that the worldly calamities God sends on arrogant, ungrateful people are only a mild warning and a call to repent. They are a small foretaste of the far more severe and lasting punishment in the next life. If people truly understood this, they would turn back to God, be grateful, give what is due to others, and not be deceived by the temporary security of their wealth.

translation: Indeed, for the righteous, God-fearing ones, there are with their Lord Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The verse teaches that taqwa, a conscious reverence for God that shows itself in obeying Him and avoiding what He forbids, is the key to lasting reward. The phrase 'with their Lord' makes the reward more than a place of pleasure. It signals honor, nearness and divine favor, and it shows that God Himself prepares and guarantees what awaits the righteous. 'Gardens of Bliss' (jannat al-na'im) points to a fulfilled, untroubled happiness that lacks the hardship and decay of worldly pleasures. By contrasting the fate of the God-fearing with that of the wrongdoers described around it, the verse urges the believer to place hope in the hereafter and to accept present restraint and patience, since what God holds in store far outweighs any fleeting enjoyment in this life.

translation: Then shall We treat those who submit (the Muslims) like those who are criminals?
interpretation: This rhetorical question, from Surat al-Qalam (68:35), denies that divine justice could make no distinction between the obedient believers and the wrongdoers who persist in sin and denial. If God treated both alike in their final outcome, moral choice and accountability would have no meaning. The verse affirms that a just Lord must reward those who submit to Him and hold the guilty to account, so the believers can be certain of a good reward and the disbelievers should fear the consequences of their crimes.

translation: What is the matter with you? How do you judge?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:36) is a rebuke to those who deny the truth. After God has established that the God-fearing will have gardens of bliss and that He would not treat the Muslims like the criminals, He asks the disbelievers how they can arrive at such a baseless judgment. The question exposes the irrationality and injustice of believing that those who submit to God and those who persist in wrongdoing would share the same fate. It calls people to reason soundly and uphold moral accountability, since a just God will not treat the righteous and the wicked alike.

translation: Or do you have a book in which you study?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question that rebukes the disbelievers for their baseless claims. Having just claimed that they would enjoy a favored status with God, they are challenged to produce any revealed scripture they have studied that supports it. The implication is that no such book exists, and that judgments about reward and punishment rest on divine revelation, not on wishful thinking or personal assumptions.

translation: Indeed, you will have therein whatever you choose.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 68:38) rebukes the disbelievers who claimed they would enjoy favor with God in the Hereafter just as the believers would. It mocks their presumption by asking whether they hold a divine book in which they study, and in which they are promised whatever they desire. The meaning is that such a claim has no basis in revelation: salvation and reward are not determined by human wishes or self-serving assumptions, but by God's guidance and justice. Those who deny the truth cannot dictate their own destiny by merely choosing what pleases them; reward belongs only to those who have faith and righteous conduct.

translation: Or do you have oaths binding upon Us, extending until the Day of Resurrection, that you shall have whatever you judge for yourselves?
interpretation: God challenges the disbelievers who claim they will enjoy the same or better rewards as the believers in the Hereafter. He asks whether they hold any binding covenant or solemn guarantee from Him, valid until the Day of Resurrection, that entitles them to whatever they decree for themselves. The rhetorical question exposes their claim as baseless wishful thinking: divine reward is determined by God's promise and justice, not by human assumption, and since they possess no such pledge, their confident expectations are groundless.

translation: Ask them: which of them will vouch for that?
interpretation: After the preceding verses ask the disbelievers whether they think believers and wrongdoers will be treated alike in the Hereafter, the Prophet is told to challenge them: which of them can guarantee this claim? The word 'zaim' means a guarantor who takes responsibility for an assertion. The verse exposes the emptiness of their presumption, since they have no revealed scripture, no covenant from God, and no one who can stand surety for such a claim. A judgment that equates the obedient with the criminals is baseless, and nobody can underwrite it, because justice belongs to God alone, who will not treat the two groups as equal.

translation: Or do they have partners (in godhood)? Then let them bring forth their partners, if they are truthful.
interpretation: This verse is a challenge to those who ascribe partners to God. It asks them to produce proof, since a claim of divinity needs evidence, and those they worship have no power to create, to benefit, to harm, or to intercede. Because they cannot produce any such proof, their worship rests on baseless assumption and inherited custom, not on knowledge, and the verse makes clear that only God is worthy of worship.

translation: On the Day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostrate, but they will be unable to.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when a moment of overwhelming terror and severity is unveiled. The phrase 'uncovering of the shin' is an Arabic idiom for the intensity of a calamity, as people tuck up their garments and bare their legs when a grave matter arises. On that day, those who refused to prostrate to God out of arrogance, hypocrisy, or heedlessness in the world will be summoned to prostrate, but their backs will become rigid and they will be unable to bend. This inability is a fitting recompense: they withheld sincere worship when they were able and it was accepted, so on that day, when prostration would be a sign of true faith, they are deprived of it, and they are left in humiliation and regret.

translation: Their eyes will be downcast, and disgrace will cover them. They had been called to prostrate themselves [in worship] while they were sound and healthy, [but they refused].
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the deniers on the Day of Judgment: their humbled gaze and the disgrace overwhelming them are the direct consequence of their earlier arrogance. In life, when they were healthy and fully able to bow in worship, they were repeatedly invited to submit to God but turned away, thinking there would always be time. On that Day, when they will be unable to prostrate, their lost opportunity becomes their regret. The lesson is that health and ability are trusts, and one must answer God's call to worship and obedience while still capable, rather than postponing it until the chance is gone.

translation: So leave Me alone with those who deny this message. We will lead them on, step by step, from where they do not know.
interpretation: God tells the Prophet to leave the matter of the deniers of the Qur'an to Him, for He will deal with them Himself. Their punishment comes through gradual drawing-in (istidraj): God lets them keep enjoying blessings, health, and worldly success while they persist in sin, so they take these as a sign of divine favor and grow more arrogant and heedless. Each new blessing without gratitude draws them closer to a sudden and unavoidable reckoning that they never saw coming. The verse is both a warning to the arrogant not to be deceived by their comfort, and a consolation to the Prophet and believers to be patient and trust in God's justice rather than worry over the deniers' apparent prosperity.

translation: And I give them respite. Indeed, My plan is firm.
interpretation: God grants those who deny the truth time and ease, allowing them to continue in their wrongdoing, which may lead them to think they are safe or even favored. This respite is not neglect or approval but a gradual means of drawing them toward their downfall, for His plan is strong and cannot be thwarted or escaped. When their appointed time comes, nothing will protect them, so the verse warns against being deceived by the delay of punishment and calls people to repent while they still have the opportunity.

translation: Or do you ask them for a payment, so that they are weighed down by debt?
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that his call is free of any worldly motive. He asks nothing from people for conveying the message, so no one can excuse their rejection by claiming that following him would burden them with costs or debts. The verse thus removes every pretext for turning away. The messenger is sincere and disinterested, the guidance is a pure gift from God, and refusal can come only from stubbornness and pride, not from any hardship the message imposes.

translation: Or do they have access to the unseen, so that they write it down?
interpretation: This verse, Surah At-Tur 52:41, is a rhetorical challenge to those who denied the Prophet's message. It asks whether they possess knowledge of the unseen, held with God or in the Preserved Tablet, which they record and then rely on to justify their disbelief and their rejection of the resurrection and the Prophet's warnings. The implied answer is no. Knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone, so the deniers have no revealed or independent basis for their claims. Their stance rests on conjecture and stubbornness, and the only trustworthy knowledge of the unseen is what God reveals through His messengers.

translation: So be patient with the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish [Jonah], when he called out while he was choked with distress.
interpretation: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is told to remain steadfast in conveying the message and to endure the denial and harm of his people until God's judgment comes, without giving way to haste or anger. The example of Jonah warns against leaving one's mission out of frustration before receiving God's permission. Jonah called upon God from within the belly of the fish, overwhelmed with grief, and was only relieved after turning back in repentance. The lesson is that patience in the face of hardship, and trust in God's timing and wisdom, are the way of the prophets and the path to deliverance.

translation: Had a favour from his Lord not reached him, he would surely have been cast onto the barren shore, while blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after he was swallowed by the fish. It teaches that his deliverance came solely through God's grace and mercy, accepting his repentance and his glorification of God from within the depths. Had that divine favour not reached him, he would have been thrown onto the bare, empty shore in a state of censure for having left his people without permission. Because mercy encompassed him, he was cast out ill but forgiven, restored, and made among the righteous. The lesson for the Prophet Muhammad, who is being told to be patient with his people's rejection, is not to be hasty or distressed like the Companion of the Fish, and to recognize that every rescue from hardship, and every state of honour, is ultimately a gift of God's grace rather than the result of one's own deeds.

translation: Then his Lord chose him and made him one of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse (al-Qalam 68:50) comes after the story of Yunus (Jonah), who left his people in anger and was then tested in the belly of the whale, where he called out in repentance. It shows that sincere repentance and patient turning back to God restore a person to divine favor. God did not abandon His prophet over a lapse in judgment. He drew him close again, chose him for Himself, and reinstated him among the righteous. The lesson is that human error, even in the best of people, does not close the door of mercy, and that trials can purify a servant and raise his rank. It also consoles the Prophet Muhammad, who is told to be patient with his Lord's decree and not to be like the one of the whale, impatient and hasty.

translation: And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is surely mad."
interpretation: The verse shows how intense the disbelievers' hatred and envy of the Prophet were. When they heard the Qur'an being recited, they glared at him with such fierce, hostile looks that they seemed ready to make him stumble or destroy him, as if their eyes could knock him off his feet. Unable to refute the message, they turned to slander and called him mad. The verse comforts the Prophet and tells him that God protects him from their malice. Their accusation is baseless, because the Reminder they heard is a sign of wisdom and guidance, not of madness. The next verse says so directly: the Qur'an is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds.

translation: And it is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (found at the end of Surat al-Qalam, 68:52, and similarly in Surat al-Takwir) affirms that the Qur'an is not the speech of a madman, as the disbelievers accused the Prophet of being, but a universal reminder. Its message is not limited to one tribe, people, or era; it is addressed to all of humankind and jinn, awakening their innate nature (fitra) to remember their Creator, their purpose, and their accountability. The verse thus refutes the slander against the Prophet by pointing to the nature of what he brought: a guidance of such wisdom, breadth, and benefit for all creation that it could only come from divine revelation, not from a deranged mind.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Inevitable Reality.
interpretation: The opening word 'al-Ḥāqqah' names the Day of Resurrection as the certain, undeniable truth whose occurrence is beyond doubt. It is called 'the Reality' because everything the prophets warned about, including reckoning, reward and punishment, will be proven true on that Day. By opening the surah with this single, weighty word, the Qur'an stirs awe and urgency in the listener, pressing them to stop denying the Hereafter and to prepare for the moment when truth will be fully and inescapably revealed.

translation: What is the Inevitable Reality?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical question that heightens awe and anticipation. 'Al-Haqqah' refers to the Day of Resurrection, the hour whose occurrence is certain and which makes real every truth that people denied, including reward, punishment, and God's promise. By asking 'What is it?', the Qur'an signals that its magnitude exceeds ordinary comprehension, preparing the listener to reflect on the fate of those who denied it, such as Thamud and 'Ad, and to take the warning seriously.

translation: And what will make you comprehend what the Inevitable Reality is?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Haqqah 69:3) magnifies the awe of the Day of Resurrection by posing a rhetorical question. By asking what could possibly let the Prophet grasp the true nature of the Inevitable Reality, God signals that its terror and certainty exceed human imagination and ordinary description. The phrase invites the listener to reflect and be humbled, understanding that the Hour is not a mere possibility but a truth that will undeniably come to pass, when every soul will meet the consequences of its deeds. Its purpose is to awaken the heart to fear God and prepare for the Hereafter before knowledge of it comes too late.

translation: Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity (the Day of Resurrection).
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 69:4) recalls that two mighty ancient peoples rejected the warning of the Day of Judgment, called 'al-Qari'ah' because it strikes hearts with terror and shatters the order of the world. Their denial did not delay or change that reality; instead it brought upon them the very punishment they mocked, as the following verses describe: Thamud were destroyed by a mighty blast, and 'Ad by a furious, roaring wind. The lesson is that disbelief in accountability, however powerful the people who hold it, ends in ruin, and that the destruction of past nations is a sign and a warning that the final reckoning is certain.

translation: As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming blast.
interpretation: The verse says that the people of Thamud, who denied their prophet Salih and hamstrung the she-camel that was sent as a sign, were wiped out by a terrible, overpowering cataclysm, a thunderous cry or scream from the sky. The word 'al-taghiyah' points to something that exceeds all bounds in its force, which parallels the way Thamud themselves exceeded bounds in their transgression and arrogance. Their punishment matched their crime: because they overstepped all limits in rebellion, they were seized by a power that went beyond anything they could withstand. The lesson is that persistent tyranny and denial of God's messengers leads to a ruin that no human strength or number can avert.

translation: And as for 'Ād, they were destroyed by a furiously roaring, violent wind.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment fits the nature of the sin. 'Ād were proud of their physical might and boasted that no one was stronger than they were. God destroyed them with something that seems weak and unseen, the wind, but which He made fierce, icy and uncontrollable ('ātiyah, a wind that overstepped all bounds and could not be held back by any guard or defense). Their strength was no protection against a force they could not see or resist. The lesson is that arrogance in worldly power is futile before God's command, and that the created world, down to the very air, serves His will to bring down the rebellious.

translation: He imposed it upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you could see the people therein lying prostrate, as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees.
interpretation: The verse describes how God's punishment of the people of 'Ad was total and relentless: the destructive wind blew without pause for a full cycle of days and nights, leaving no chance of respite or escape. The mighty, arrogant people who boasted of their physical strength were reduced to lifeless bodies sprawled on the ground, like decayed, hollow palm trunks, toppled and empty. The image teaches that human power and pride are fragile before God's decree, and that those who reject the divine message and transgress cannot be saved by their strength, since the very creation they thought they could master becomes the instrument of their ruin.

translation: Then do you see of them any remnant?
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Haqqah, 69:8) concludes the account of the people of 'Ad, who were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind that struck them for seven nights and eight days. The rhetorical question stresses how total the destruction was: no trace of the tyrants remained, no survivor and no lasting legacy to protect them. Their strength, their buildings and their pride did not save them once God's decree came. The verse is a warning to later generations that denying the messengers and persisting in arrogance and wrongdoing leads to ruin, and that worldly power cannot withstand God's command.

translation: And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities (the towns of Lot's people), with sinful deeds.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in human history: nations that rejected God's messengers and persisted in wrongdoing met their ruin. Pharaoh, earlier peoples, and the towns of Lot's people (al-mu'tafikat, 'those overturned') were not destroyed arbitrarily. Each arrived at its fate carrying its own sin, which here means disbelief, denial of the prophets, arrogance, and moral corruption. The word 'khati'ah' (sinful deed) shows that these were deliberate transgressions, not honest mistakes. The verse warns that the same accountability applies to every generation, and that worldly power, as with Pharaoh, and entrenched social corruption, as with Lot's people, offer no protection from God's judgment.

translation: But they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so He seized them with a seizure exceeding [in severity].
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting a messenger is rejecting the Lord who sent him, and that this carries a heavy consequence. The word 'rābiyah' (growing, swelling, increasing) suggests that God's punishment was greater and more intense than their wrongdoing appeared to be, building in force beyond anything they could resist or escape. It is a warning that persistent defiance of divine guidance, as seen in the earlier peoples of Pharaoh, Lot, and others mentioned in the context, leads to a punishment that overwhelms the offenders, and that no power or status can shield them from it.

translation: Indeed, when the water overflowed beyond its limits, We carried you in the floating ship.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Haqqah 69:11) reminds humanity that its survival from the Flood of Noah was an act of God's mercy, not the result of human strength or planning. When the waters rose in defiance of all natural bounds, only God's command preserved the believers, and the ship became a means of salvation by His will. The address 'We carried you' speaks to all later generations as descendants of those saved, so they owe Him gratitude and should heed the warning that the same power which destroyed the rebellious can save the obedient. The lesson is that human existence depends wholly on God, and that arrogance and denial bring ruin while faith and obedience bring deliverance.

translation: So that We may make it a reminder for you, and that a retaining ear may retain it.
interpretation: The verse explains the purpose behind the saving of the believers in the Ark while the disbelievers were drowned in the Flood: God preserved this event as a lasting lesson and admonition for later generations. Yet its benefit reaches only those who listen attentively. The 'retaining ear' is the heart that hears with understanding, remembers what it has heard, and acts on it. Merely hearing the story is not enough; only the person who reflects, preserves the lesson in memory, and lets it shape their conduct truly benefits from God's signs.

translation: Then when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast,
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:13) announces the onset of the Day of Resurrection. The single blast of the Trumpet, blown by the angel Israfil at God's command, marks the sudden end of the present order: it is not a drawn-out or gradual process but an instantaneous event that no one can delay or resist. By stressing that the blast is only one, the verse shows the effortless, absolute power of God, for whom bringing the whole universe to its end requires no more than a single command. It serves as a warning to those who denied the Hereafter, as the verses that follow describe the earth and mountains being crushed and the Event befalling all creation, so that every person is made to face the reckoning with nothing able to avert it.

translation: And the earth and the mountains are lifted up and crushed with a single crushing.
interpretation: The verse describes the second blast of the Trumpet on the Day of Judgment, when God's power overturns the most solid and seemingly permanent features of creation. The earth and mountains are shattered in one instant, with no repetition or delay, because God's command needs only a single utterance to take effect. This shows that nothing in the physical world is truly lasting or able to resist God, and it warns people not to rely on worldly stability or strength. Since even mountains cannot stand on that Day, only faith and righteous deeds will provide security.

translation: On that Day, the Inevitable Event will come to pass.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Haqqah 69:15) teaches that the Day of Judgment is not a distant possibility but a certain reality that will surely occur. It follows the blowing of the Trumpet and the shattering of the earth and mountains described in the preceding verses. 'The Inevitable Event' (al-Waqi'ah) names the Hour as something whose occurrence cannot be averted or denied. The verse reminds the believer that worldly power and denial will count for nothing when this moment arrives, urging humility, accountability, and preparation for meeting God.

translation: And the heaven will be split asunder, for on that Day it will be frail and weak.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the cosmic upheavals of the Day of Judgment, found in Surat al-Haqqah (69:16). The heavens, which people regard as a symbol of strength, stability and permanence, will lose their firmness and fall apart. It teaches that all created things, however immense and secure they appear, are temporary and subject to God's command alone. The collapse of the sky reminds the believer that only God is truly enduring and all-powerful, so a person should not place ultimate trust in the apparent solidity of the world, but should prepare for the Day when God's authority will be manifest to all.

translation: And the angels will be on its sides, and eight will bear the Throne of your Lord above them on that Day.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment after the heavens have split open: the angels stand at the edges and borders of the torn sky, awaiting God's command, while eight mighty angels carry the Throne of the Lord above all creation. The image stresses God's absolute sovereignty and majesty on that Day, when every earthly power vanishes and all creatures stand in awe before the One who alone judges. The number eight and the manner of bearing the Throne belong to the unseen, so the believer should affirm them without speculation and let the scene deepen reverence, humility, and readiness for accountability.

translation: On that Day you will be presented for judgment, and none of your secrets will remain hidden.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:18) describes the Day of Resurrection as a day of complete accountability. People will be brought before God, the All-Knowing, and nothing they concealed, whether deeds, intentions, or hidden thoughts, will stay secret. It warns that the privacy and deception possible in this world will not work before divine judgment, and it urges people to practice sincerity and self-accountability now, since every inner and outer act will be exposed and weighed with perfect justice.

translation: As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: 'Here, take and read my record!'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the believer who receives his book of deeds in his right hand is a sign of salvation and honor. His overwhelming joy and certainty of success make him eager to show it to everyone around him and invite them to read it, since he has nothing to hide. This reveals that he lived in awareness of the Reckoning, so his good deeds are now a source of pride and relief rather than fear, and he is confident of God's acceptance and mercy.

translation: Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning.
interpretation: This is the declaration of the person who receives his record in his right hand on the Day of Judgment (Qur'an 69:20). The word 'ظننت' here carries the sense of firm conviction rather than doubt, as is common in Arabic usage when speaking of unseen realities. He explains why he is saved: in the worldly life he firmly believed that he would be brought to account for his deeds, so he prepared for it with faith and righteous action, and lived with accountability in mind. His belief in the Hereafter shaped his conduct, and thus he is granted joy and a pleasant life in an elevated Garden. The verse teaches that conviction in the certainty of the final reckoning is the foundation of righteousness and the cause of salvation.

translation: So he will be in a life of contentment.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:21) describes the person who receives his record of deeds in his right hand. His reward is a life in Paradise that is itself 'pleasing': it is a state of lasting satisfaction in which he lacks nothing and fears no loss, sorrow, or end. The wording suggests that the life is so complete in its comfort and blessing that the one living it is wholly content with it, and this contentment is the fruit of the faith and righteous deeds he sent ahead in this world, as a result of his certainty that he would meet his reckoning.

translation: In a lofty Garden.
interpretation: This verse describes the final abode of the righteous on the Day of Judgment. The Garden is called 'lofty' in both physical and spiritual senses: it is high in rank and station, raised above the lowly trials and afflictions of worldly life, and far removed from the humiliation and suffering of the Fire. Its elevation signifies the honor, dignity, and nearness to God that the believers who had faith and did good works will enjoy, a stark contrast to the disgraced faces and toil of the people of Hell mentioned earlier in the surah.

translation: Its fruits will be within easy reach.
interpretation: This phrase from Surat al-Haqqah (69:23) describes the Garden of the righteous, whose clusters of fruit hang so low and near that the dwellers can pick them with no toil or strain, whether standing, sitting, or reclining. It teaches that the reward of Paradise is complete ease and honor: in contrast to the labor and hardship of earning provision in this world, the believers receive their blessings effortlessly, as a mark of God's generosity and the fulfillment of their striving in obedience.

translation: Eat and drink with wholesome enjoyment for what you sent forth in the days gone by.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:24) is spoken to the people of Paradise, who are given their record in their right hands. Their blissful food and drink is not an unearned gift but a reward for the righteous deeds they advanced during their worldly lives, the 'days gone by'. Their patience, restraint from desires, fasting, and obedience in the brief life of this world are what have earned them the lasting delight of the next. The word 'hani'an' signifies pleasure free of any harm, worry, or end, and the verse teaches that what a person sends ahead through faith and good works determines the quality of their eternal life.

translation: But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, 'Oh, I wish I had never been given my record!'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the person handed his book of deeds in his left hand knows from this sign that he is among the condemned. Seeing his sins laid bare with nothing to defend them, he is overcome by shame and regret and wishes he had never been shown the record. The verse shows that the reckoning exposes every deed, and that the pain of that exposure is so great that he longs for non-existence rather than facing the consequences of a life lived in heedlessness of God.

translation: And I had not known what my account was.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:26) describes the wretched person who receives his record of deeds in his left hand and wishes he had never been given it. His regret reveals that he lived heedlessly, never preparing for the Day of Reckoning. Now that his deeds are laid bare, he finds that what he neglected in life has become a heavy, inescapable reality, and he wishes he had never faced it.

translation: If only it [death] had been the end of me.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Haqqah, 69:27) voices the despair of the one handed his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgment. Seeing his deeds exposed and the punishment awaiting him, he wishes that the death he experienced in the world had been final, a complete end with no resurrection and no reckoning. Whereas he once denied the Hereafter, he now longs for annihilation as an escape from the horror before him. The verse shows that the disbeliever's greatest regret on that Day is not merely the loss of reward but the realization that there is no way out, so that death, once feared above all else, becomes the thing he most desires.

translation: My wealth has been of no benefit to me. (Qur'an 69:28)
interpretation: This is the lament of the person handed his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgment. He realizes that the wealth he hoarded and trusted in during worldly life cannot save him from God's reckoning or punishment. The verse teaches that possessions, which people often rely on for security and status, become worthless on the Day of Judgment, and that only faith and righteous deeds bring benefit.

translation: My authority has perished and left me.
interpretation: This is the lament of the one who receives his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgment (Surat al-Haqqah, 69:29). He realizes that the wealth, power, status, and influence he relied on in the world, and the arguments he used to justify himself, were of no use to him before God. Everything he trusted has vanished at the moment he needs it most, leaving him helpless and exposed. The verse teaches that worldly power is transient and that only faith and righteous deeds remain of any benefit on that Day.

translation: "Seize him and bind him." (Qur'an 69:30)
interpretation: This verse is the command God gives to the angels of Hell concerning the one who was handed his record of deeds in his left hand and who denied faith and neglected charity. It shows that on the Day of Judgment, the unbeliever is stripped of all honor and power, which he relied on in this world. He is seized without resistance and bound in shackles, as the beginning of a just punishment that fits his arrogance and rejection of God. The swift, forceful command conveys that no wealth, status, or protection can save him once divine judgment has been decreed.

translation: Then cast him into the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Haqqah 69:31) follows the command to seize and bind the one who was given his record of deeds in his left hand. It conveys that his punishment does not end with disgrace and shackling: after being humiliated, he is made to burn in Hell. The ordering shows that the sinner, who rejected faith in God and neglected feeding the poor, is held to full account for arrogance and injustice. Hell is his final and just recompense, since he denied the Day of Judgment and lived heedless of God's commands.

translation: Then into a chain whose length is seventy cubits, insert him (bind him).
interpretation: The verse portrays the severity and inescapability of divine punishment for the one who denied God and failed to feed the poor. After being seized and fettered and cast into Hellfire, he is further bound in a chain of seventy cubits, a number that signals great length and intensity rather than a mere measurement. The word 'fasluku-hu' (thread him through) suggests the chain is passed through and around him so that he is utterly confined, with no possibility of movement, escape, or relief. This fitting retribution humbles the arrogant who once felt free and unbound by accountability, teaching that deeds of disbelief and cruelty carry real, proportionate consequences in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, he used not to believe in Allah, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 69:33) gives the reason for the punishment of the one who receives his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgment. His fate is not an arbitrary harshness but the result of his core failure: denying the Almighty Lord, whose greatness demands faith, gratitude, and obedience. By describing God as 'the Most Great,' the verse shows that rejecting Him is the gravest of wrongs, because it denies the rightful Sovereign of all creation. That denial corrupts a person's conduct and leads to the neglect of the poor, which the following verse mentions. Disbelief in God removes the foundation of moral responsibility and accountability, and so it leads to the severe judgment described.

translation: And does not urge the feeding of the needy.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Haqqah (69:34), describes the grave failing of the one who denied God and was condemned to the Fire. His sin is not only disbelief but also a moral callousness toward society's weakest. He did not feed the poor himself, and he did not even encourage others to do so. The Qur'an treats concern for the hungry as an expression of true faith, so neglecting it shows a heart that does not truly fear God or believe in accountability. Indifference to another's hunger, even without actively harming them, is counted as a serious wrong, and faith is meant to show itself in compassion and social responsibility.

translation: So today he has here no close friend.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:35) describes the fate of the one who is given his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgment. The worldly bonds he relied on, such as friends, family, allies and supporters, are all severed. In the world, a person may have sought protection or help from close companions, but on that Day no friend can intercede, defend, or share the burden of punishment. The word 'hamim' denotes a loyal, warm and caring friend, so its negation stresses total abandonment and helplessness. The lesson is that human relationships built on worldly interests, and not on faith and obedience to God, offer no benefit in the Hereafter, and that a person should invest in righteous deeds and in friendships grounded in piety, since only these will endure.

translation: And no food except from ghislīn (the filthy discharge of the washed wounds of the inmates of Hellfire).
interpretation: This verse completes the description of the punishment of the one who is given his record in his left hand (Surat al-Ḥāqqa 69:25-37). Having lost every friend who could help him and every means of protection, he is also deprived of any real nourishment. The only 'food' left for him is ghislīn, the foul runoff from the wounds and bodies of those being punished. The lesson is that someone who denied God and did not urge the feeding of the poor (as the preceding verses mention) is repaid in kind: he withheld nourishment and compassion from the needy in this life, so in the Hereafter he receives nothing wholesome, only loathsome filth that adds to his torment and humiliation.

translation: None eat it except the sinners.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 69:37) describes the food of the people of Hell, the foul pus-like discharge (ghislin) mentioned just before it. It makes clear that this fate belongs to those who deliberately persisted in wrongdoing. The word 'khati'un' refers to those who knowingly and intentionally commit wrong, rather than those who merely err by mistake, so the verse stresses that the punishment is just and is earned by willful denial of God and by neglecting the rights of the poor, as the preceding verses indicate. The food is thus a fitting recompense: those who refused to nourish the needy and rejected faith are given a loathsome nourishment that only such deliberate transgressors must consume.

translation: So I swear by what you see,
interpretation: This verse opens the oath in Surat al-Haqqah (69:38), where God invokes the visible, observable creation as a witness to the truth of the Qur'an and the message of the Prophet. The phrase 'fa-la uqsimu' is an emphatic form of swearing, meaning the matter is so clear that it hardly needs an oath. By pointing to everything perceptible to human eyes, the signs in the heavens and the earth, the blessings and the order of the world, the verse directs people to see in creation evidence of its Creator's power and wisdom. The visible world thus testifies that the revelation is true and that the Messenger is not a poet or soothsayer, as the following verses go on to affirm.

translation: And [I swear] by what you do not see.
interpretation: This verse, Surah Al-Haqqah 69:39, follows the oath 'So I swear by what you see' (69:38). Together the two verses embrace the whole of creation, visible and invisible. The unseen includes Allah, the angels, the soul, the Hereafter, and the many realities beyond human perception. By swearing by both realms, the verse affirms that the Qur'an is the true word of a noble Messenger, revealed from the Lord of the worlds, and not the speech of a poet or a soothsayer. It teaches that human perception is limited, that reality extends far beyond what the senses can grasp, and that a believer should accept truths conveyed by revelation even when they cannot be witnessed.

translation: Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is a revelation delivered through a noble messenger, understood by many commentators as Gabriel in Surat at-Takwir (81:19), or Muhammad in Surat al-Haqqa (69:40). The messenger is only the trustworthy bearer and conveyor of the message, not its author. The Qur'an originates from God, and the messenger's nobility vouches for the honesty and integrity of its transmission. This answers the charge that it is the invention of a poet or soothsayer, and it points to the reliability and elevated source of the divine message.

translation: And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe.
interpretation: The verse refutes the accusation that Muhammad was a poet and that the Qur'an is mere poetry. Its message is not the product of poetic imagination or rhetorical embellishment but a revelation from God, grounded in truth, guidance, and moral clarity. The remark that the disbelievers believe only a little points to their stubbornness: despite clear signs, they accept very little of the truth, and their rejection stems from obstinacy, not from any lack of evidence.

translation: Nor is it the speech of a soothsayer; how little you remember.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Haqqah 69:42) continues the denial that the Qur'an is human invention. Having rejected the claim that Muhammad is a poet, it also rejects the charge that he is a soothsayer (kahin). Soothsayers of Arabia delivered rhymed, obscure utterances claimed to come from jinn and demons, filled with guesswork, falsehood and self-interest. The Qur'an differs from this in its clear guidance, its moral call to worship God alone, and the upright character of the Prophet who brought it. The closing phrase, 'how little you remember,' rebukes the disbelievers for failing to reflect. If they considered the Prophet's honesty, the coherence of the message, and its difference from the soothsayers' speech, they would recognize it as a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The fault lies in their heedlessness, not in any lack of evidence.

translation: A revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is not the composition of Muhammad or of any poet or soothsayer, but a revelation whose source is God Himself, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. By describing God as Lord of the worlds, it ties the Book's authority to His universal lordship: the One who created and sustains all things is the One who sent down this guidance, so its message is binding and trustworthy for all of humanity, not for one people or era alone. The word 'tanzil' (a sending down) also conveys that the revelation descended from on high, gradually and with purpose, as an act of divine mercy and care for His creatures.

translation: And if he (Muhammad) had invented some sayings and attributed them to Us,
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:44) establishes the truthfulness of the Prophet's message by describing the grave consequence that would follow had he falsely ascribed any words to God. The point is that a messenger carries a trust: he must convey revelation exactly as it was sent, adding nothing and altering nothing, not even a small part ('some sayings'). The following verses speak of God seizing him by the right hand and severing his life-vein, which shows that God would not allow a false claimant to prophethood to continue and prosper. Since Muhammad was preserved, supported, and his message continued, the verse argues that the Qur'an is genuine revelation from the Lord of the worlds and not the composition of a poet, soothsayer, or the Prophet himself.

translation: We would have seized him by the right hand.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 69:45) is part of the warning that if the Prophet Muhammad had falsely attributed any statements to God, God would have dealt with him with decisive force. The 'right hand' symbolizes strength and power, so the meaning is that God would have seized him with full might and overpowered him, leaving him no means of resistance. The verse stresses that the Qur'an is truly divine revelation and that the Messenger is utterly faithful in conveying it, since any fabrication in God's name would have met immediate and severe divine retribution.

translation: Then We would have severed from him the aorta (the vital artery of the heart).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Haqqah (69:46), completes a warning about what would have befallen the Prophet had he fabricated any saying and attributed it to God. It teaches that the Prophet's message is a trust that he conveys exactly as revealed and that he has no authority to add to it or alter it. The 'severing of the aorta' is an image of sudden, decisive destruction: just as life cannot continue once the main artery of the heart is cut, a false claimant of prophethood would be cut off from life and denied any chance to continue his deception. That the Prophet continued to live and his mission was sustained is therefore taken as a sign of his truthfulness and of divine protection over the revelation.

translation: And not one of you could have shielded him (the Prophet) from it.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Haqqah 69:47) concludes the warning that if the Prophet Muhammad had falsely attributed any statement to God, God would have seized him by the right hand and severed his aorta. The verse stresses that no one, neither the Prophet's followers nor his opponents, would have had the power to hold back or protect him from God's punishment. The point is that divine authority is absolute and the Qur'an is not the Prophet's own invention. His steadfast delivery of the message, even at the cost of hardship and persecution, shows that it is a true revelation from the Lord of the worlds, and that no created power can stand between God and His decree.

translation: And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 69:48) says that the Qur'an is a source of remembrance and admonition whose benefit is realized by those who possess taqwa, meaning conscious awareness of God and a desire to avoid His displeasure. Although the Qur'an is addressed to all of humanity, only those whose hearts are receptive and humble let its warnings and promises awaken them, and so it works as a reminder that turns them toward obedience, mindfulness of the Hereafter, and moral restraint. For those who are heedless or stubborn, it does not have this effect, which makes the verse a statement about the receptivity of the listener as much as about the power of the message.

translation: And indeed, We know that among you there are those who deny.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 69:49) is a divine warning that God has full knowledge of those who reject the Qur'an's message, even though it is a clear reminder for the God-fearing. Their denial is neither hidden nor unnoticed. It carries an implicit threat of accountability: their rejection will be met with a just reckoning, while the verse also consoles the Prophet and the believers that the denial of some does not diminish the truth of the revelation.

translation: And indeed, it (the Qur'an) is a source of regret for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 69:50) teaches that on the Day of Judgment, when the truth of the Qur'an is made undeniable and the reward of those who believed in it is seen, those who rejected it will be overcome by anguish and remorse. The Qur'an, which was offered to them as guidance and mercy in this life, will become the cause of their grief, since they will realize that they had the chance to accept it and squandered it. Its truth, which they denied, will stand as evidence against them, and their regret will come from recognizing what they lost through their own denial.

translation: And indeed, it is the truth of certainty.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Haqqah 69:51) affirms that the Qur'an, and the message it brings about the Day of Judgment, the reckoning and the reward and punishment, is not conjecture or poetry but absolute truth beyond any doubt. The phrase 'haqq al-yaqin' signifies certainty in its highest degree: knowledge so firmly established that it is the very reality of what is known, not just hearing about it or seeing signs of it. The verse calls on the listener to move from doubt and denial toward full conviction and to live by what has been revealed, since its truth will ultimately be witnessed in reality.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surat al-Waqi'ah, calls the believer to respond to all the signs of God's power described in the chapter—creation, rain, provision, death, resurrection, and the final judgment—with active worship. Glorifying (tasbih) means declaring God free of any imperfection, partner, or inability, and doing so with His name signifies praising Him with a heart and tongue that acknowledge His greatness. Having seen that He alone gives life, sustains, and brings every soul to account, the fitting response is to exalt Him, remember Him constantly, and live in humble submission to the Lord whose majesty is beyond measure.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A questioner asked about a punishment that is bound to occur.
interpretation: The verse points to the mocking disbelief of those who challenged the Prophet to bring down the punishment he warned of, as if its coming were doubtful or could be hurried on demand. The Qur'an answers that the punishment is not hypothetical: it is certain and will fall upon those who deny, and no one can avert it when God decrees it. The question is thus turned into a warning that scornful demands for divine judgment reflect heedlessness, and that God's justice arrives in His own time, not at the whim of those who doubt it.

translation: For the disbelievers, there is none to avert it.
