interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 52:2 in some readings of the context, 70:2: 'For the disbelievers, there is none to repel it') teaches that the punishment decreed by God for those who reject faith is certain and inescapable. No power, ally, wealth, or intercession can prevent it once God's command comes to pass. The verse is meant to instill awareness of divine justice and the finality of God's judgment, urging people to turn to faith and righteous action before the Day when no one can ward off what God has ordained.

translation: [This punishment is] from Allah, the Lord of the ways of ascent.
interpretation: The verse says the punishment that the disbelievers ask to be hurried (Q 70:1-2) comes from Allah and no one can repel it. Calling Him 'Dhu al-Ma'arij,' Owner of the ascending stairways, points to His exalted majesty and absolute authority. Angels and the Spirit rise to Him through these levels (Q 70:4), and so do commands, deeds, and the realities of the unseen. Whatever He decrees, including the punishment, therefore comes from the highest source of power and wisdom, and the unbelievers' scorn cannot stop it.

translation: The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years.
interpretation: The verse conveys the immense majesty of God and the vastness of the divine realm compared with human experience of time. The angels and the Spirit (Gabriel) ascend to God in a Day so long that it is reckoned at fifty thousand years, which signals that the Day of Judgment, when all affairs are returned to God, will be overwhelming in its weight and duration, especially for those who denied it. Time as humans measure it does not bind God or His angels, and the verse invites the believer to reflect on God's transcendence, to be patient with the delay of promised justice, and to take seriously the accountability that awaits, a Day that is long and hard for the disbelievers yet, as other traditions of exegesis note, may feel light for the faithful.

translation: So be patient with a beautiful patience.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 70:5) urges the Prophet to endure the denial and mockery of those who reject the message, and by extension calls every believer to a patience free of complaint, bitterness, or hasty resentment. 'Beautiful patience' is steadfastness that is carried with dignity and trust in God, keeping the heart at peace and the tongue restrained, because the outcome rests in God's wisdom and the promised justice will certainly come, even when those who deny it see it as far away.

translation: Indeed, they see it as distant.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ma'arij 70:6) refers to the Day of Judgment and the punishment that the disbelievers are asking to be hastened. They regard its coming as far-fetched and improbable, either because they deny resurrection and accountability altogether or because they imagine it to be a remote event. Their denial rests on a misjudgment of reality: what they consider distant is in truth near, as the following verse says, 'And We see it as near.' The verse teaches that human disbelief and heedlessness do not change the certainty of what God has decreed. Anything that is sure to come is near, however long it may seem, so a person should prepare for the Hereafter instead of being lulled into complacency by the false sense that it is far away.

translation: But We see it as near.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:7) follows the previous verse, in which the disbelievers see the Day of Judgment as far-off and improbable. God answers that what they deem distant is in fact near, because everything that is certain to come is close, and no matter how long the world lasts, its span is short compared with eternity. The verse warns people not to be lulled into heedlessness by delay, and urges them to prepare for the meeting with their Lord, since death and the Hour could arrive at any moment.

translation: On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:8) describes a scene from the Day of Judgment, when the firm and seemingly unshakable order of the heavens will break down and dissolve like molten metal or the dregs of oil. The image teaches that even the grandest, most stable features of creation are temporary and wholly subject to God's command. If the sky itself will melt and lose its form, then human power, wealth, and worldly security offer no protection, so a person should prepare for that Day with faith and righteous action rather than rely on this fleeting world.

translation: And the mountains will be like carded wool.
interpretation: This verse describes the upheaval of the Day of Judgment, when the mountains, which people regard as the firmest and most immovable features of the earth, will lose their solidity. They will be shattered, loosened and made weightless, drifting like tufts of dyed wool that are carded and scattered by the wind. The image shows that if even the mightiest and most stable parts of creation cannot withstand God's command on that Day, human beings should recognize their own frailty, abandon arrogance and heedlessness, and prepare for the reckoning by faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And no close friend will ask about [the condition of] a close friend.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Ma'arij 70:10) describes the terror of the Day of Judgment. The horror of that day will be so overwhelming that every person will be consumed by his own fate. Even the closest of friends, who in this world would anxiously inquire after one another and offer help, will not ask about each other, because each will be preoccupied with his own reckoning. They will not be prevented from seeing one another, since the next verse says they will be made to see them, but the severity of the moment will leave no room for concern for anyone else. The lesson is that worldly bonds of companionship cannot benefit a person on that Day, and one should prepare for it with righteous deeds.

translation: They will be made to see one another. The criminal will wish he could ransom himself from the punishment of that Day by his own children,
interpretation: The verse describes the terror of the Day of Judgment. Close relatives and friends will see and recognize one another, yet nobody will be able to help or ask after anyone else, because each person's own punishment consumes them. The wrongdoer will be so desperate to escape the torment that he would offer even his dearest possession, his own children, as a ransom, though it is natural to protect them at all costs in this world. This shows that worldly bonds and attachments offer no protection on that Day, and that only faith and righteous deeds can save a person.

translation: And his wife and his brother.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:12) belongs to the description of the Day of Judgment, when a guilty person will wish to ransom himself from the punishment by offering his closest loved ones: his children, his wife, and his brother. The point is that the terror of that Day is so overwhelming that the bonds of family and companionship, which people hold dearest and would normally defend at any cost, lose all value. A person would be willing to give up even those nearest to him in order to save himself, yet no ransom will be accepted. This teaches that on that Day only one's faith and deeds will avail, not kinship or worldly attachments.

translation: And his kin who sheltered him.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:13) describes the horror of the Day of Judgment, when a guilty person would wish to ransom himself with his own children, his spouse, his brother, and even his closest clan, the family that gave him refuge and support in this world. The meaning is that the strongest worldly ties of protection and belonging will offer no help on that Day. Someone who relied on his tribe for security will find that nothing can shield him from God's reckoning, and that he will be so consumed by his own fate that he would give up even those dearest to him to escape punishment. The verse teaches that salvation depends on one's faith and deeds, not on kinship or worldly support.

translation: And (if he could ransom himself with) all who are on the earth, so that this might then save him.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Ma'arij (70:14), describes the Day of Judgment, when a guilty person will wish to ransom himself from the punishment by offering everything dear to him: his children, spouse, brother, family, and even all the people on earth. The meaning is that on that Day no worldly bond, wealth, or relationship can save anyone, and the wrongdoer would sacrifice all of humanity just to escape, yet this wish will be futile. It warns that salvation depends only on faith and righteous deeds done in this life, not on anything one might offer or depend on when it is too late.

translation: No! Indeed, it is the Flame (Lazā), blazing fiercely.
interpretation: The verse rejects the false hope of the denier who imagines that he could ransom himself from punishment on the Day of Judgment by offering his children, spouse, kin, and everything on earth. 'Kallā' is a firm repudiation: no ransom will ever save him. The fire he will face is no ordinary fire but a raging, flaming blaze that burns with relentless intensity, and its fierceness is such that no worldly bond or wealth can avert it. The lesson is that salvation depends on faith and righteous action in this life, not on attachments or possessions that people lean upon, and that reliance on them against God's judgment is an illusion.

translation: Snatching away the scalps (or extremities) as it strips them off.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:16) describes the Hellfire, called 'Lazā' in the preceding verse, as a flame that violently tears away the outer parts of the body, such as the skin of the head and limbs. The meaning is that the punishment of the Fire is not a mere touch of heat but a total, agonizing assault that strips and peels away flesh, leaving the sinner in unrelenting pain. It serves as a warning to the disbelievers who turned away and hoarded wealth, reminding them that the consequence of rejecting truth is a severe and unavoidable torment.

translation: It calls (to itself) whoever turned his back and turned away.
interpretation: The verse speaks of Hellfire (as in the preceding verse about Hell being a 'blazing fire that strips away the skin'), which will summon those who in this life turned their backs on the truth and turned away from faith and obedience. The meaning is that the punishment is not random: Hell is, by God's command, drawn to and seizes those who knowingly rejected the call of the message, so that their own deliberate turning away from God in the world becomes the cause that brings them to Hell in the hereafter.

translation: And amassed [wealth] and hoarded it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ma'arij 70:18) describes the person who turned away from the truth: he gathered wealth and then stored it away in vessels, holding on to it out of greed and attachment to the world. He neither spent it in the cause of God nor gave the rights due from it to the poor and needy, such as zakat and charity. The verse condemns the hoarding of wealth and the love of accumulation that distracts a person from the remembrance of God and from preparing for the Hereafter. It teaches that wealth is a trust to be used rightly, not an end in itself to be hoarded.

translation: Indeed, mankind was created anxious and impatient.
interpretation: The verse describes a basic trait of human nature: left to himself, without faith and discipline, a person is restless and driven by fear of loss and craving for gain. This is not a fixed condemnation but a diagnosis of the raw disposition that must be trained and refined. The verses that follow show the remedy: those who pray steadfastly, give from their wealth, and hold firm to belief in the Day of Judgment overcome this panic and greed, and become steady in both hardship and ease.

translation: When evil touches him, he is anxious and impatient.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:20) describes a trait of human nature when left undisciplined by faith: a person tends to panic, complain and lose composure at the first touch of hardship, poverty, illness or loss. It is not a fixed condemnation of humanity but a diagnosis of the untrained self, and the verses that follow (70:22-23) show the remedy, which is steadfast prayer and a heart anchored in trust in God. Faith turns hardship into a test to be borne with patience, so that a believer is not broken by adversity or hurried into despair.

translation: And when good touches him, he withholds it grudgingly.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Ma'arij 70:21) continues the description of the human being's innate nature, created restless and impatient. When wealth, health, or any blessing reaches a person, he becomes miserly and clings to it, refusing to share it with the poor and needy or spend it in the way of God. It points to the weakness of the untrained self, which turns anxious in hardship and tight-fisted in ease. The following verses make clear that only those who are devoted to prayer, give a known right from their wealth to the beggar and the deprived, and believe in the Day of Judgment are freed from this trait. The verse thus teaches that generosity and gratitude are the cure for the selfishness and greed that are natural to human beings.

translation: Except those who pray.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ma'arij 70:22) follows the description of human nature as anxious, impatient in adversity, and miserly in prosperity. It makes an exception for the true worshippers, showing that sincere and steadfast prayer reforms the character: it cures restless anxiety, instills patience and trust in God, and frees the heart from stinginess. The verse implies that prayer is not a mere ritual but a transformative discipline that elevates a person above the base tendencies of their nature, as the following verses show by describing these worshippers as constant in their prayer, generous toward the needy, and mindful of the Day of Judgment.

translation: Those who are constant in their prayer.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:23) describes the believers who are steadfast in their prayer: they do not neglect it, delay it without excuse, or perform it only when convenient. Constancy here means that prayer becomes a lasting rhythm of their lives, observed at its appointed times with humility and presence of heart. Such persistence reflects an unbroken bond with God, and it is this steadiness, more than occasional bursts of devotion, that shapes character and shields a person from the restlessness, anxiety, and stinginess that the preceding verses attribute to human nature.

translation: And those in whose wealth there is a known, rightful share.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Ma'arij (70:24), describes a quality of the truly devout who remain steadfast in prayer: they regard part of their wealth as a defined right belonging to others, not as a favor they bestow. The phrase 'a known right' points to a share that is fixed and recognized, such as the obligatory zakat, so giving is a duty owed rather than a matter of mood or generosity. In the next verse the right is said to be for the beggar and the deprived. The verse teaches that wealth is a trust from God, and that a person's faith is shown in how they meet the claims of the needy upon what they own, which purifies the giver from greed and builds social solidarity and justice.

translation: For the one who asks and the one who is deprived.
interpretation: This phrase comes in the Qur'an's descriptions of the righteous, who set aside a known, recognized right in their wealth (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:24-25; also Surah adh-Dhariyat 51:19). It teaches that charity is not a favor but a due owed to two kinds of needy people: the as-sa'il, who openly asks for help, and the mahrum, who is deprived yet refrains from asking out of dignity or modesty, or who has been cut off from sustenance through misfortune. The believer is therefore called not only to respond to those who plead, but also to seek out and discreetly assist those whose need is hidden, recognizing that wealth is a trust from God in which the poor have a share.

translation: And those who affirm the truth of the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who do not merely say they believe in the Hereafter but live in constant awareness that they will be held accountable for their deeds. Their certainty that a Day of Recompense will come shapes their conduct: it restrains them from wrongdoing, motivates them toward prayer, charity, and justice, and keeps their hearts humble before God. Their belief in the Day of Judgment is the foundation of their moral discipline and of their steadfastness in worship.

translation: And those who, of the punishment of their Lord, are fearful.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:27) describes a quality of the true believers who are exempt from the restless, impatient nature of mankind: they live in constant, reverent awareness of God's punishment. Their fear is not despair or paralysis but a mindful apprehension that keeps them humble despite their prayer, charity, and good deeds. They never assume they are safe from God's reckoning, so this fear moves them to remain steadfast in obedience, guard against sin, and keep hoping for God's mercy. The verse teaches that genuine faith combines worship with inner watchfulness, and that a heart which trembles before its Lord is protected from complacency and arrogance.

translation: Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not something one can feel secure from.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:28) describes the believers who pray steadfastly and are marked by humility. Even with their devotion and righteous deeds, they never feel safe from God's punishment, because no one can be certain of being spared it by their own deeds alone. Their awe of God keeps them from complacency and self-righteousness, so they remain between fear and hope, relying on God's mercy rather than on their own works. True faith is therefore a constant state of reverent vigilance, not false security.

translation: And those who guard their private parts.
interpretation: This verse, which describes the believers who succeed (Surat al-Mu'minun 23:5), presents sexual chastity as a defining trait of true faith. To guard one's private parts is to restrain desire and keep it within what God has made lawful, namely marriage, as the following verses clarify. It means avoiding fornication, adultery, and every unlawful form of sexual conduct. Chastity here is an act of conscious self-discipline and God-fearing awareness, and it protects the individual's dignity, the integrity of the family, and the moral health of society. The verse treats this restraint as a mark of spiritual strength, not mere suppression of natural instinct, because it directs a natural human drive toward its rightful and responsible place.

translation: Except from their spouses or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse (23:6 and 70:30) follows the description of the believers who guard their private parts, and it sets the boundary of lawful sexual relations: they are permitted only within the bond the divine law recognizes, namely marriage, or the then-existing legal status of those under a slave-owner's right hand. Within this framework, a person incurs no blame, because the desire itself is natural and is not condemned. What the verse stresses is that chastity does not mean suppressing human nature but channeling it through lawful, responsible, and accountable relationships, while anything outside these bounds is transgression, as the following verse states. Classical scholars understood the reference to 'those whom their right hands possess' as belonging to the social and legal conditions of that time, which Islam sought to regulate and gradually reduce through the encouragement of emancipation.

translation: But whoever seeks anything beyond that, then those are the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mu'minun 23:7, and also Al-Ma'arij 70:31) follows the description of the believers who guard their chastity except with their spouses or those whom their right hands possess. It teaches that the lawful bounds of sexual relations are clearly set by God, and anyone who seeks fulfillment of desire outside those limits has crossed the boundary set by God. The word 'al-'adun' (transgressors) conveys that such people are not merely mistaken but have willfully overstepped divinely drawn limits, thereby wronging themselves and violating the moral order. The verse thus affirms that true faith includes self-restraint and submission to God's boundaries in the most powerful of human desires.

translation: And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenants.
interpretation: The verse describes believers as people of integrity who honor every form of trust and commitment placed upon them. This includes trusts entrusted by others, such as property, secrets, and responsibilities, as well as the trust of duties owed to God. It also covers promises and agreements made with God and with people. The word 'ra'un' (observing, shepherding) suggests more than avoiding betrayal: they actively guard, protect, and fulfill these obligations with care, as a shepherd tends a flock. Reliability in trust and word is presented as a mark of true faith and good character, and a foundation of a trustworthy society.

translation: And those who stand firm in their testimonies.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:33) describes a quality of the true believers who are saved from anxious, impatient human nature: they uphold truthfulness and justice in bearing witness. They do not conceal testimony, alter it, or let kinship, wealth, enmity, or fear sway them, but give it exactly as they know it, even against themselves, their parents, or their relatives. This steadfastness shows their integrity and their accountability before God, since witnessing is a trust whose fulfillment secures rights and sustains justice in society.

translation: And those who are ever mindful of guarding their prayers.
interpretation: This verse, which closes the description of the successful believers in Surah Al-Mu'minun (and Al-Ma'arij), teaches that true faith is shown by steadfast care for prayer. Their prayer is not occasional or careless: they observe its proper times, its conditions, its pillars, and its inner presence and humility. The description opens with humility in prayer (khushu') and ends with guarding it, so prayer frames the believer's whole character. The one who preserves the link with God through regular, careful worship is thereby helped to keep trust, fulfill promises, and maintain moral discipline in the rest of life, and so becomes worthy of the inheritance of Paradise promised in the verses that follow.

translation: Those will be in Gardens, honoured.
interpretation: The verse describes the final reward of God's sincere servants, mentioned just before it as those who are given known provision and sustenance. Their honour is twofold: they dwell in the Gardens of Paradise, and they are held in esteem there. Their honour is not only physical comfort and abundance but also dignity and respect from God and His angels, free from the humiliation and distress that marks the fate of the deniers. It shows that salvation and sincere devotion in this world are repaid in the hereafter with lasting bliss joined to true honour.

translation: So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, that they rush hastily toward you, with necks stretched out in fear and bewilderment?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the disbelievers of Makkah for the contradiction in their conduct. They crowd around the Prophet, ﷺ, stretching their necks and fixing their eyes on him, as if eager to listen. Yet they do not take his message to heart or act on it. They come close to hear the Qur'an but only to mock it, find fault with it, or be entertained, while their hearts stay hardened. The verse teaches that physical nearness to revelation and outward interest in it are worthless without sincere belief and obedience, and that hearing the truth without responding to it is only evidence against the one who hears.

translation: [Seated] on the right and on the left, in separate groups.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:37) describes the disbelievers in the Prophet's time who rushed toward him with outstretched necks, staring in hostility and mockery, then gathered around him in scattered, huddled bands from every side. Their dispersal into factions on his right and left shows a lack of unity and sincerity: they came as onlookers who listened without any intention to believe or act, so their nearness to the Prophet brought them no benefit. The verse rebukes this attitude and warns that hearing the message while scorning it leads only to accountability, in contrast to the believers described earlier in the surah, who are steadfast in prayer and faithful to their trusts.

translation: Does every one of them hope to be admitted into a Garden of Bliss?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 70:38) rebukes the disbelievers of Makkah who turned away from the Prophet and the message, crowding around him in mockery, yet still expected to enter Paradise. It teaches that Paradise is not gained by wishful thinking or by lineage, status, or wealth, but by faith, humility before the truth, and righteous action. Those who scorn revelation and reject accountability have no ground for expecting divine reward, and the question is rhetorical, implying that such hope is baseless and absurd.

translation: No! Indeed, We have created them from that which they know.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ma'arij 70:39) rebukes those disbelievers who presumed they would enter the Garden of bliss without faith and righteous deeds. God rejects their claim with 'No!' and reminds them of their humble origin: they were created from a despised fluid, a drop of fluid, which they themselves know well. The point is that human beings have no inherent merit or status by which to claim Paradise; their origin is lowly, and entry into Paradise is only through faith, obedience, and God's mercy. Since the One who created them from such a source is able to resurrect them and hold them to account, they should abandon arrogance and prepare for the Day of Judgment.

translation: So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests that We are certainly able.
interpretation: God swears by His lordship over every point where the sun and stars rise and set, and over their changing positions through the seasons, to affirm that He has full power to replace the disbelievers with people better than them, and to resurrect them after death. The ordered motion of the heavens, with its endless variety of risings and settings, shows a power and wisdom that cannot be defeated. A Lord who governs the whole cosmos with such precision is not incapable of recreating human beings or of substituting one generation for another. The oath therefore answers the deniers of resurrection and warns the arrogant that their disbelief does not place them beyond His reach.

translation: [We are able] to replace them with better than them, and We cannot be outstripped.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:41) affirms God's absolute power over the deniers who mock the Day of Judgment. Those who reject the warning are reminded that their existence depends wholly on God's will. If He wished, He could remove them and bring forth in their place a people better than they, more grateful and obedient, and no one can escape or thwart His plan. The verse is a warning that human arrogance has no basis, for no one can outrun God's decree, and that God's favors are not tied to any particular people but are bestowed on those who respond to the truth with faith and righteous action.

translation: So leave them to indulge in their false talk and play until they meet their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: The verse is a warning to those who deny the truth and mock the message. God tells the Prophet not to exhaust himself in arguing with people who treat serious matters as a game and immerse themselves in idle disputation and worldly amusement after the proof has been made clear to them. Leaving them is not approval but a threat, since their heedlessness is not free of consequence: their time is running out, and they will be confronted on the Day of Judgment with the reality they denied, when play and frivolous talk will be of no use and they will face the full accountability they were promised.

translation: The Day when they will emerge from the graves hastening, as if they were rushing toward an erected goal.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 70:43) describes the Day of Resurrection, when people will rise swiftly and without delay at the summons of God, unable to hesitate or resist. The comparison to people racing toward a nusub, a standing marker or goal, evokes the eager speed of runners heading to a finish line or of idol-worshippers hurrying to their stone idols. It teaches that those who denied the resurrection in this world, and who once dawdled or mocked, will on that Day be driven by an irresistible compulsion toward the place of reckoning. It is meant to instill awareness of accountability and to turn the heedless toward preparing for the meeting with their Lord.

translation: Their eyes humbled, humiliation will cover them. That is the Day which they had been promised.
interpretation: The verse describes the condition of the disbelievers when they rise from their graves on the Day of Resurrection. Those who once carried themselves with arrogance and mocked the warnings of the Hereafter will lower their gaze in fear and shame, because they now see the reality they used to deny. Humiliation will overwhelm them, a fitting recompense for their pride and for having refused to bow before God in the world. The closing phrase, 'That is the Day which they had been promised,' points out that the Day is no surprise: the messengers warned of it repeatedly, and the disbelievers dismissed it. Its arrival confirms the truth of the promise and leaves them with no excuse, and it teaches the reader to humble themselves before God now, before humility is forced upon them then.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, saying: 'Warn your people before a painful punishment comes upon them.'
interpretation: The verse presents prophethood as an act of divine mercy and justice: God does not let punishment fall on a people without first sending a clear warning. Noah's mission is framed as preventive, since the command is to warn 'before' the punishment arrives, which leaves a real chance for repentance and change. The task is first of all to call people back to sincere worship of God and to correct their course while there is still time. The mention of a 'painful punishment' shows that the consequences of persistent denial are serious, but the emphasis on warning beforehand shows that God's way is to offer guidance and opportunity first, so that those who are punished later have no excuse.

translation: He said: "O my people, indeed I am to you a clear warner."
interpretation: This verse (Nuh 71:2 is the same phrase pattern as in Hud 11:25 and al-A'raf 7:59) shows the Prophet Noah opening his mission by addressing his people with affection, calling them 'my people', which signals that his warning comes from care and not from hostility or personal interest. By describing himself as a 'clear warner' (nadhir mubin), he affirms that his role is not to invent or obscure anything but to plainly convey a divine message about the consequences of persisting in disbelief and idolatry. The clarity of the warning leaves no excuse for those who reject it, establishing that the duty of every prophet is to give open, unambiguous notice of the truth, while guidance itself remains in God's hands.

translation: [Saying]: Worship God, fear Him, and obey me.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 71:3) captures the threefold core of Prophet Noah's message to his people. 'Worship God' calls for exclusive devotion to the One God, rejecting idols. 'Fear Him' (taqwa) means living with constant awareness of God, guarding oneself against His displeasure by avoiding sin and doing good. 'Obey me' shows that obedience to God is made concrete through following His messenger, since the prophet conveys God's guidance and models how to live by it. Together, faith in God, moral consciousness, and following divinely sent guidance form one inseparable path to salvation.

translation: He will forgive you some of your sins and grant you respite until a set term. Indeed, when the term appointed by God comes, it cannot be delayed, if only you knew.
interpretation: The verse (Nuh 71:4) is part of Prophet Noah's call to his people to worship God, fear Him and obey him. Those who respond receive two blessings: forgiveness, which clears the burden of their past wrongs, and a life lived out to its appointed length rather than being cut short by punishment or destruction. The verse then warns that the fixed term God has decreed, whether the death of an individual or the doom of a people who persist in denial, is absolute and cannot be postponed once it arrives. So the time for repentance and obedience is now, while there is still respite. Delaying until the end is in sight is useless, because at that point no plea or regret will extend the time. People who truly grasped this would hurry to turn to God instead of putting it off.

translation: He said, "My Lord, indeed I have invited my people night and day."
interpretation: This verse (Nuh 71:5) shows Prophet Noah turning to God to report on his mission and acknowledge his own sincere effort. His calling of his people 'night and day' signifies tireless, uninterrupted persistence: he did not wait for convenient times or give up when met with rejection, but used every available moment to call them to worship God alone. It teaches that a caller to truth must exert his full effort and then entrust the outcome to God, since guidance is in God's hands. It also serves as a plea and a testimony before God that the people's persistent refusal was not due to any shortcoming in the delivery of the message, thereby establishing the proof against them.

translation: But my call only increased them in flight (running away from the truth).
interpretation: In this verse, Noah complains to God about the result of his persistent preaching to his people. Rather than softening their hearts, his invitation to faith made them withdraw further. Their aversion hardened when the truth was presented to them clearly. The verse shows that a heart already inclined toward arrogance and stubbornness can react to guidance by fleeing from it, so the message itself is not at fault. The failure lies in the listeners' rejection, and it makes plain how much Noah endured as a prophet whose sincere effort met increasing hostility.

translation: And indeed, every time I called them to Your forgiveness, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted in their stubbornness, and became extremely arrogant.
interpretation: Noah is lamenting to God that his people met his call to repentance with total rejection. Stopping their ears and wrapping themselves in their clothes were physical gestures of refusing to hear or even to look at him, showing that they did not want to listen to the truth. Their persistence in disbelief and sin, joined with intense pride, reveals that the barrier to guidance was not a lack of proof but arrogance. The call to seek God's forgiveness was an offer of mercy to them, and they rejected the very means of their own salvation, which is why they deserved the consequence that followed.

translation: Then indeed, I called them openly.
interpretation: In this verse (Nuh 71:8) Prophet Nuh reports to God how he escalated his call after private appeals failed. Having first summoned his people by night and day without success, and finding that they fled from him, he turned to public preaching and addressed them aloud in open gatherings. The lesson is that a caller to God should use every wise means and adapt his method to the situation, moving from one approach to another with persistence, without giving up and without compromising the message, so that no excuse remains for those who reject it.

translation: Then indeed, I proclaimed to them openly, and I confided to them privately in secret.
interpretation: In this verse (Nuh 71:9), Prophet Noah describes to God the full range of methods he used in calling his people to monotheism. After inviting them by night and day and finding them fleeing from the truth, he tried addressing them publicly before gatherings and then approached them individually in private. The meaning is that he exhausted every approach, adapting to different circumstances and temperaments, so that no excuse remained for them. It teaches that a caller to God should be persistent and wise, using varied means and appropriate settings to convey the message, while the outcome of guidance remains in God's hands.

translation: And I said, 'Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He has always been Most Forgiving.'
interpretation: Noah presents repentance as the first step toward renewal. By asking his people to return to God and seek pardon for their disbelief and wrongdoing, he shows that the door of mercy is never closed to those who sincerely turn back, however long they have persisted in error. The description of God as 'Ghaffar' (One who forgives again and again) tells us that His forgiveness is abundant and continual, so no sin is too great and no one should despair. The verse also links turning to God with the blessings that follow in the next verses, such as rain, wealth, and children. Spiritual reform and inner purification are thus the foundation of both moral and worldly well-being.

translation: He will send down rain from the sky upon you in abundance.
interpretation: This verse, from Nuh's call to his people (Surah Nuh 71:11), presents seeking forgiveness from God as a means of material blessing as well as spiritual renewal. When people turn back to their Lord in repentance, He opens the gates of sustenance, sending abundant, continuous rain that revives the land, brings crops and prosperity, and relieves hardship. The word 'midrar' conveys rain that falls repeatedly and in due season, a lasting mercy rather than a passing shower. The verse teaches that obedience and repentance are linked to God's generosity, and that rain, on which all life depends, is a sign of His favor toward those who return to Him.

translation: And He will provide you with wealth and children, and will grant you gardens, and will grant you rivers.
interpretation: This verse, part of Noah's address to his people (Nuh 71:12), presents repentance and seeking God's forgiveness as a path to worldly blessing as well as spiritual cleansing. The blessings named are the main pillars of a prosperous, stable life: wealth for sustenance, children for continuity and strength, and gardens and flowing rivers for agricultural abundance. The point is that God's mercy extends to this life as well as the next, and that gratitude and return to Him open the door to His generosity. Material sufficiency is a gift from God, not a result of self-reliance or of persisting in disbelief, so Noah's people are invited to see obedience as the cause of their flourishing rather than an obstacle to it.

translation: What is wrong with you that you do not hope for dignity and reverence from God? (Qur'an 71:13)
interpretation: Prophet Noah rebukes his people for showing no awe of God. Their refusal to revere Him, to fear His majesty and to recognise His right to be obeyed, is unreasonable, since He is the Creator who has shaped them in stages and sustains them. The verse points out that hope in God's reward and fear of His punishment both rest on esteeming His greatness. A person who denies Him that esteem has no sound basis for rejecting His message, and the lack of reverence is the root of their disobedience and ingratitude.

translation: While He has created you in stages.
interpretation: The verse points to God's creative wisdom in shaping the human being step by step: from dust and a drop of fluid, to a clinging clot, to a lump of flesh, to bones clothed in flesh, then birth, childhood, maturity, and old age. Since God brought each person through these varied, carefully ordered phases of existence, which no one could have arranged for himself, it is unreasonable for people not to hold Him in awe and revere His majesty. The one who can create and transform humans in such stages is clearly deserving of reverence, gratitude, and obedience, and is fully able to raise them again after death.

translation: Do you not see how Allah has created seven heavens, one above another?
interpretation: The verse (Nuh 71:15) invites people to reflect on the order and grandeur of creation as evidence of God's power, wisdom, and oneness. Nuh addresses his people, pointing to the layered heavens, ordered in harmonious tiers, as a sign that the One who created such a vast, precisely structured cosmos is worthy of worship and obedience alone, and is fully able to resurrect and hold humans to account. Rather than a detailed description of astronomy, the verse directs the heart from observing creation to recognizing the Creator, and to repenting and seeking forgiveness, as the surrounding verses urge.

translation: And He made the moon therein a light, and made the sun a lamp.
interpretation: This verse (Nuh 71:16) points to God's deliberate design of the heavens as a source of benefit and guidance for humankind. The moon is described as a reflected, gentle light (nur) that illuminates the night and marks months and years, while the sun is a blazing lamp (siraj) that is the source of both light and heat, sustaining life and making day possible. The distinction between the two teaches that the lights in the sky are not independent deities but created instruments placed in the service of people, so they are signs of the Creator's wisdom, power, and mercy. The verse calls on a person to reflect on the order of the cosmos and to respond with gratitude and worship of God alone, rather than denying Him as the people of Noah did.

translation: And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.
interpretation: The verse (Nuh 71:17) points to the human origin in the earth: Adam was created from clay, and all of his descendants are sustained by what the earth produces, so that their bodies are in effect formed from it. The Qur'an likens this to the growth of plants, as God brings humans into being and develops them stage by stage just as He brings forth vegetation from the soil. The verse is meant to remind people of their humble beginnings and of their complete dependence on God's power and provision. The One who brought them forth from the earth is able to return them to it in death and to bring them out of it again at the resurrection (as the next verse says), so denying Him or associating partners with Him is unreasonable and ungrateful.

translation: Then He will return you into it, and bring you forth [again] with a full bringing forth.
interpretation: This verse (Nuh 71:18) affirms resurrection after death. The 'it' is the earth from which humans were created: after they die and are buried, they return to it, and on the Day of Judgment God will bring them out of their graves in a real, certain, and unmistakable way. The emphatic 'ikhrajan' (a bringing forth) removes any doubt that the second creation is as real as the first. It reminds people that their origin, their death, and their rising are all in God's hands, so they should be accountable to Him and heed the call to worship and obey Him.

translation: And God has made the earth a wide expanse for you.
interpretation: This verse (Nuh 71:19) points to God's favor in preparing the earth for human life: He made it spread out, stable, and easy to live on, so that people can walk upon it, settle, build, farm, and travel its paths. The image of a carpet or spread conveys comfort and suitability rather than a claim about the earth's literal shape. It calls people to recognize the Creator's care and to respond with gratitude and worship, since everything they depend on has been laid out for them as a gift, not as something they produced themselves.

translation: So that you may travel along its spacious roads (paths).
interpretation: This verse (Nuh 71:20) completes the blessing of the earth that Noah mentions to his people: God made the earth a spread-out expanse for them. The 'wide paths' (fijaj) are the open valleys and mountain passes through which people can move, trade, seek sustenance and journey from place to place. The verse points to God's favor in shaping the earth so it is not an impassable barrier but a land with ways that ease human travel and livelihood. Such a provision is a sign of His power and mercy, and it calls people to recognize their Creator and be grateful to Him rather than deny Him or associate partners with Him.

translation: Noah said: "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and have followed one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss."
interpretation: Noah turns to his Lord after long, patient preaching and reports the outcome of his mission: his people rejected his call and instead followed their wealthy, powerful leaders, those whose riches and offspring became a source of arrogance and a barrier to faith rather than a blessing. The verse teaches that worldly possessions and children, when they lead a person away from obedience to God, are not real gain but ruin. The true measure of success is faith and righteous conduct, and following misguided elites out of admiration for their status leads only to loss in this world and the next.

translation: And they plotted a mighty plot.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Nuh (71:22), describes how the leaders of Noah's people schemed on a vast scale against him and his message. Their plotting went beyond rejecting his call: they incited the masses to cling to their idols, turned people against Noah, and may have plotted to harm him and the believers. The word 'kubbar' (immense), an intensive form, stresses how great and relentless their deceit and opposition were. The verse teaches that those with power and status often use cunning and manipulation to defend falsehood and keep their privileges, and that such scheming, however great, cannot defeat a truth that God supports.

translation: And they said, 'Do not abandon your gods, and do not abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, and Ya'uq, and Nasr.'
interpretation: The verse shows how the people of Noah answered his call to worship God alone. Their leaders urged the masses to hold fast to their inherited idols and named the five best known. According to the commentators, these had begun as righteous men whose memory was honored, and over generations that reverence was turned into statues and then into worship. The verse therefore warns how excessive veneration of the pious can slide into polytheism. It also shows that the stubborn pull of ancestral tradition and the influence of elites can lead people to reject the message of pure monotheism.

translation: "And indeed they have led many astray. And (O Lord) do not increase the wrongdoers in anything except misguidance." (Qur'an 71:24, from the prayer of Noah)
interpretation: Noah, after long and patient preaching, supplicates against his people only once it is clear they will never turn back. The chiefs and elders of his community, through their influence, wealth, and idols, drew the masses away from the truth. His plea that God not increase the wrongdoers except in misguidance is understood as a recognition of the consequence of persistent injustice: when people knowingly and stubbornly reject guidance, God leaves them to the path they have chosen, so their error deepens and hardens, culminating in their deserved destruction. The verse teaches that wrongdoing is not only a personal fault but a corrupting force that harms others, and that willful rejection of truth can bring about a spiritual blindness that is itself a form of divine justice.

translation: Because of their sins they were drowned, then made to enter a Fire, and they found for themselves besides God no helpers.
interpretation: The verse, from the account of Noah's people (Nuh 71:25), teaches that destruction comes as the direct consequence of persistent wrongdoing and rejection of the prophet's call. Their drowning in the flood was only the first stage of punishment, followed by the Fire of the grave and the hereafter. When God's decree arrives, no false god, idol, power, or ally they relied on can protect them. Only God can help, and those who turn away from Him in this life find no supporter in the next.

translation: And Noah said, "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any dwelling place of the disbelievers." (Qur'an 71:26)
interpretation: This is Noah's supplication after centuries of calling his people with patience, in public and in private, while they met him with arrogance, mockery and ever-deepening rejection. His prayer is not an outburst of personal anger but a judgment grounded in knowledge given to him by God that none of them would believe (11:36). The word 'diyar' (a dwelling, or anyone who stays in a home) expresses a plea that not a single household of those persistent deniers remain, so that their corruption would not spread to the believers or to later generations, as he explains in the next verse: if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and beget only wicked, ungrateful offspring. The verse teaches that a prophet's call for divine punishment comes only after the proof has been fully delivered and hope of guidance has been exhausted, and that the destruction of a stubborn people is an act of divine justice and mercy toward the believers and the earth itself.

translation: Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants, and they will beget none but wicked, persistent disbelievers.
interpretation: This is part of Prophet Noah's supplication after centuries of calling his people to God. He had come to know, through divine revelation that no more of them would believe, and through his long experience that their corruption was entrenched and self-perpetuating. His plea is therefore not born of personal anger but of concern for the faith of the righteous believers: if the unbelievers remained, they would continue to lead God's servants astray, and their children, raised in that environment of disbelief and moral corruption, would inherit and deepen it, producing only generations of sinners who knowingly and stubbornly reject the truth. The verse shows that when a society becomes irredeemably corrupt and a threat to the guidance of others, divine judgment becomes a mercy to the believers and to the future of humanity.

translation: My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house as a believer, and all believing men and believing women, and do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction.
interpretation: This closing supplication of Noah, after he endured a long and fruitless call to his people, shows that a true prophet's concern is first for salvation through divine forgiveness. He begins with himself, then his parents, then those who join him in faith, and finally the whole community of believers across all times, which reflects the bond of faith that goes beyond family and generation. His prayer against the wrongdoers is not born of personal anger. It comes after they stubbornly rejected the truth and after God had told him that no more of his people would believe. The verse teaches that faith is the real basis of belonging, that seeking forgiveness and praying for fellow believers is a duty, and that persistent injustice and denial of truth lead to a people's ruin.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened, and they said, 'Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an.'
interpretation: The verse opens Surat al-Jinn by showing that the Prophet Muhammad did not witness the jinn's listening himself, but learned of it only through divine revelation, which affirms that his knowledge of the unseen comes from God alone. It also shows that the Qur'an's message is universal and not limited to humankind: when a group of jinn heard it, they recognized its extraordinary eloquence, guidance and power, and described it as 'wondrous' because it was unlike any speech they had known. Their immediate and sincere reaction presents a model of receptive listening, in which hearing the truth with an open heart leads to recognition and then to faith, while it also quietly rebukes those humans who heard the same recitation and stubbornly rejected it.

translation: It guides to the right course, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.
interpretation: This verse, from the jinn's account in Surat al-Jinn, shows that hearing the Qur'an led them to faith because they recognized that it leads to what is right: sound belief, truth, and good conduct. Their belief is not mere admiration but a commitment, and they pledge never to attribute any partner to God. Faith in the Qur'an thus naturally results in pure monotheism, and the guidance of the Book is shown to be self-evident to every sincere listener, whether human or jinn.

translation: And that He - exalted is the majesty of our Lord - has taken neither a wife nor a son.
interpretation: This verse, part of the jinn's declaration in Surah Al-Jinn (72:3), affirms that God's greatness, glory and sovereignty are so supreme that He is utterly free from needing any companion or offspring. Taking a spouse or child implies need, dependence, limitation, and likeness to created beings, all of which contradict divine perfection. By acknowledging this, the jinn who heard the Qur'an renounce the false beliefs of those who attributed consorts or children to God, and affirm pure monotheism: God is self-sufficient, unique, and beyond any resemblance to His creation.

translation: And that the foolish one among us used to speak about God an outrageous falsehood.
interpretation: This verse is part of the jinn's account after hearing the Qur'an (Surah Al-Jinn). They confess that their earlier belief in a partner or child for God came from the ignorance of their foolish ones, whom they had followed uncritically. The word 'shatata' means exceeding all bounds in injustice and falsehood, so attributing a consort, child, or partner to God is portrayed as a transgression beyond reason and truth. The verse teaches that such claims arise from folly rather than knowledge, and that blind imitation of foolish leaders is no excuse. Once truth becomes clear, one should acknowledge past error and return to pure monotheism.

translation: And we had thought that neither mankind nor the jinn would ever speak a lie about God.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Jinn (72:5), voices the jinn's admission of why they had earlier accepted false beliefs, such as attributing a consort or son to God or following foolish ones among them. They trusted that no one, human or jinn, would dare to fabricate lies about God, so they assumed what they heard from others must be true. After hearing the Qur'an, they realized that their assumption was naive: falsehood about God can be spoken by anyone, and trust in people's claims about religion is not a substitute for verifying truth. The lesson is that beliefs about God must rest on sound revelation and evidence rather than on presuming the sincerity of those who speak in His name, and that blind imitation is no excuse once the truth has come.

translation: And that there were persons among mankind who used to seek refuge with persons among the jinn, but they only increased them in burden, folly and wrongdoing.
interpretation: The verse points to the pre-Islamic Arab practice of seeking protection from the jinn. When travelers stopped in a desolate valley at night, they would say they sought refuge with the master of that valley from the foolish ones of his people. Instead of gaining safety, those people were left worse off. The jinn grew arrogant and bold, believing humans feared them and that they had power over them. The humans were afflicted with more fear, anxiety, and misguidance, and sank deeper into polytheism and error. The lesson is that seeking refuge in anyone other than God does not bring security. It leads to humiliation and spiritual loss, because only God can truly protect and benefit, so refuge must be sought in Him alone.

translation: And indeed, they thought, as you thought, that God would never resurrect anyone.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Jinn (72:7), is part of the jinn's speech to their people about what they learned from hearing the Qur'an. It acknowledges that some among the jinn had denied resurrection and accountability, just as many humans did. It shows that disbelief in the Hereafter is an old error shared by both jinn and humans, and that this denial lets them live heedlessly and transgress, since they imagine no reckoning follows. The Qur'an's message corrects this by affirming that God will raise all beings to account for their deeds, so the believer is urged to live with responsibility and awareness of the final judgment.

translation: And we (the jinn) reached for the heaven, but found it filled with stern guards and flaming meteors.
interpretation: The jinn speak of how they used to try to approach the lowest heaven to overhear the divine decrees, as they had done before. After the coming of the Prophet Muhammad and the revelation of the Qur'an, they found the heavens heavily protected by powerful angelic guards and by shooting flames that strike any who approach. This protection safeguards the revelation from being contaminated or distorted by the eavesdropping and claims of soothsayers, and affirms that the unseen belongs to God alone. The jinn's testimony led them to recognize that something momentous had occurred, which is why they went on to believe in the Qur'an.

translation: And we used to sit in stations therein (in the heaven) to listen; but whoever listens now will find a flaming meteor lying in wait for him.
interpretation: The jinn are describing how things changed once the Qur'an began to be revealed. Before that, they were able to take up positions near the lower heaven and overhear fragments of the unseen matters decreed there, which they would pass on to soothsayers and fortune-tellers. Now the heavens are heavily guarded, so any jinn who tries to eavesdrop is met by a blazing shooting star kept ready to strike him. This protection preserves the revelation from being mixed with the claims of soothsayers, and it shows that the unseen belongs to God alone. It is also a sign marking the arrival of the Prophet Muhammad's mission.

translation: And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the jinn, who after hearing the Qur'an acknowledge the limits of their knowledge of the unseen. Having lost their ability to eavesdrop on heavenly news because the heavens became guarded with fierce guards and meteors, they recognize that this change signals something momentous. They do not presume to know whether God's purpose is to bring harm to humankind or to guide them. Their humility shows that knowledge of God's plans belongs to Him alone, and the verse hints that the sending of the Qur'an and the guarding of the heavens is, in fact, a sign of divine guidance (rushd) for humanity. The wording also teaches good manners in speech: evil is mentioned in the passive ('is intended') without attributing it to God, while guidance is attributed directly to 'their Lord,' affirming that goodness is ascribed to God while evil is not ascribed to Him as a matter of courtesy.

translation: And among us are the righteous, and among us are others less than that; we were (of) different ways, divided into various paths.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the jinn (Surah Al-Jinn 72:11), acknowledges that their community was not uniform: some were truly righteous, while others fell short of righteousness in varying degrees. By saying they followed 'different paths,' they admit that before hearing the Qur'an they were split into diverse beliefs, inclinations, and moral standards. The deeper lesson is that people, whether jinn or humans, differ in their spiritual states and choices, and that guidance comes through hearing and accepting the truth, which moves one from scattered, divergent paths to the single path of faith and righteousness.

translation: And we have come to realize that we can never frustrate God on earth, nor can we frustrate Him by fleeing.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the jinn after hearing the Qur'an (Surah Al-Jinn, 72:12), expresses a conviction born of faith: God's power encompasses everything, so no created being can escape His decree or hold Him back from carrying out His will, whether by standing their ground or by running away. The meaning is that real security lies only in submitting to God and turning to Him, because there is no refuge from Him except with Him. Recognizing this inescapable divine sovereignty should lead a person to humility, obedience, and accountability for their actions, rather than to arrogance or the false hope of evading God's judgment.

translation: And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it. So whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither deprivation nor oppression.
interpretation: The jinn speaking here show that sincere faith is the natural response to hearing truth: they did not delay or argue but believed at once. Their closing statement is a promise of security for every believer. Whoever puts trust in God will not be cheated of the reward for his good deeds, nor have any of it reduced, and he will not be burdened with wrongs he did not commit or be overcome by humiliation or injustice. The verse teaches that a person's relationship with the Lord is one of perfect justice and mercy, so the believer has no reason to fear loss or tyranny, either in this world or on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And among us are those who have submitted (to God), and among us are the unjust deviators. Whoever has submitted—those have sought out the right path.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the jinn after hearing the Qur'an (Surah Al-Jinn 72:14), shows that the jinn, like humans, are morally accountable beings who divide into the obedient and the wrongdoers. It teaches that true guidance is found only through submission to God: those who surrender themselves to Him have deliberately and wisely chosen the path of rectitude and salvation, while those who deviate from justice and truth, the qasitun, have chosen a path that leads away from it.

translation: And as for the unjust (those who deviate from the truth), they will be firewood for Hell.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Jinn (72:15), declares that those who abandon justice and swerve from faith and righteousness, by rejecting the truth and wronging themselves and others, will not merely enter Hell but become the very fuel that feeds it. The image of firewood conveys the utter degradation and the fitting consequence of their crookedness: just as dry wood is cast into a fire to be consumed, so those who turned away from the straight path of God will be cast into the Fire. It stands in deliberate contrast to the preceding verse, which promises those who submit (the Muslimun) that they have sought out right guidance, so the verse teaches that the destiny of every being, whether human or jinn, depends on whether it chooses submission and justice or deviation and injustice.

translation: And (it has been revealed to me) that if they had remained straight upon the path, We would surely have given them abundant water to drink.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 72:16) teaches that steadfastness upon the path of truth and obedience to God is a cause of divine blessing and sustenance. 'Abundant water' symbolizes plentiful provision and prosperity, since water is the source of life, growth and livelihood. The verse affirms that righteousness brings ease and abundance in worldly life as well as spiritual reward, while the following verse indicates that such abundance is also a trial, to test whether people remain grateful and obedient or turn away from the remembrance of their Lord.

translation: That We might test them thereby. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter into a severe, ever-increasing punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that blessings such as abundant provision, which God grants to those who are upright, are also a trial: God observes whether people respond with gratitude and obedience or with arrogance and heedlessness. Whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, whether by neglecting the Qur'an, worship, or the awareness of God's commands, will be led into a punishment that grows ever harder and more overwhelming, one that will leave him no relief. Turning away is not a minor fault but a path whose consequence intensifies the longer one persists in it.

translation: And [know] that the places of worship belong to God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 72:18) teaches that worship in its entirety, whether in the physical mosques or in the acts of prostration through which a person submits, is owed exclusively to God. Because the sacred spaces and the acts of devotion belong to Him alone, it is unfitting for anyone to pray to, call upon, or seek help from any other being, whether angel, prophet, saint, or idol, in the same place or in the same act of worship. The verse calls believers to pure monotheism: when they stand in prayer, their hearts and supplications must be directed to God alone, with no partner associated with Him.

translation: And that when the servant of God stood up calling upon Him, they almost became about him a dense crowd, pressing one upon another.
interpretation: The verse describes the reaction of the jinn who heard the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) reciting the Qur'an and calling to his Lord in prayer. They were so moved and astonished by the beauty and power of the recitation that they crowded tightly around him, layer upon layer like clustered tufts, eager to listen. It shows that the Qur'an's message captivates sincere hearts, and that the jinn, like humans, are addressed by revelation and can respond to it with attentiveness and awe. Some commentators add that it may also allude to the pagans crowding against him in hostility, yet the primary sense is the eager, wonder-filled gathering of listeners drawn to the call of God's servant.

translation: Say: I only call upon my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with Him.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to declare that the heart of his message is pure monotheism: worship, supplication, and reliance belong to God alone. When people reject him or fear the consequences of following him, he answers that he has not come to invent a new cult or to make himself an object of devotion, but only to call upon his Lord with undivided devotion. The verse shows that true faith lies in directing all prayer and ultimate hope to God, with no partner, intercessor, or power sharing in what is due to Him alone. It also reminds believers that, however much opposition or pressure they face, their stance should remain a plain and firm affirmation of God's oneness.

translation: Say: Indeed, I have no power to bring any harm upon you, nor to guide you to what is right.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet Muhammad to declare the limits of his own role: he is a human messenger who cannot cause harm or bring benefit, nor can he compel anyone to guidance. Harm, benefit, and the opening of hearts to the truth are in God's hands alone. His task is only to convey the message, so no one should attribute divine powers to him or expect him to control their fate. This reaffirms strict monotheism and the principle that guidance is granted by God, while the messenger only delivers the warning and the good news.

translation: Say: Indeed, no one can protect me from God, and I will never find any refuge besides Him.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to declare that even he, the bearer of the message, is wholly dependent on God and has no power to save himself from God's judgment should he disobey or fail to convey the message. If the Messenger himself has no protector or shelter apart from God, then no one else can have one. The verse thus affirms pure monotheism, stripping away any claim that a human being, however exalted, could intercede independently, protect, or serve as a refuge from divine decree. The only true place of safety from God is in God Himself, through obedience, trust, and sincere devotion to Him alone.

translation: But I only convey a proclamation from God and His messages. And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.
interpretation: The Prophet's role is limited to delivering God's message faithfully; he has no power to bring benefit or harm by his own authority, for guidance and judgment belong to God alone. Having conveyed the message, the responsibility passes to those who hear it. Whoever knowingly rejects the commands of God and His Messenger after the truth has been made clear has chosen his own destruction, and the verse warns that persistent defiance of this kind, especially in the form of disbelief, leads to the eternal punishment of Hell. The verse thus joins the duty of the messenger to deliver the message with the accountability of every person who receives it.

translation: Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Jinn, 72:24) answers the disbelievers who belittled the Prophet and his followers as few and weak. They will persist in their denial until the promised punishment, in this world or on the Day of Judgment, comes upon them. At that moment the reality will be reversed: they will see that the true weakness lies with those who rely on numbers, wealth, and false patrons, because no one can aid them against God's decree. The believers, though few and seemingly powerless, have God as their protector and are therefore the stronger party. The verse teaches that true strength and support belong to God alone, and that worldly appearances of power are deceptive.

translation: Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a distant term.
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to tell those who deny the warning of punishment and the Hour that the knowledge of its timing belongs to God alone. He does not know whether it will come soon or whether God has appointed a long span before it. The verse stresses that the unseen is known only to God and that the messenger's task is to convey the warning, not to fix dates. It also teaches humility in the face of divine knowledge, and shows that the delay of the promised event is no proof that it will not happen, because its timing rests wholly with God's wisdom.

translation: [He is] the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His [knowledge of the] unseen to anyone.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Jinn, 72:26) affirms that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone, as an attribute unique to Him. No created being, whether a prophet, an angel, or a jinn, has independent access to it, and no one can claim to know the future or the hidden realities by his own power. Whatever glimpses of the unseen people receive come only through God's will and permission, as the following verse clarifies in the case of messengers chosen for revelation. The verse therefore guards against fortune-telling and false claims to hidden knowledge, and it teaches that humans must depend wholly on God and on the revelation He has sent.

translation: Except for a messenger whom He has approved; then He sends before him and behind him guardians.
interpretation: God alone knows the unseen and discloses none of it to anyone, except what He chooses to reveal to a messenger with whom He is pleased. Because revelation is a sacred trust, God surrounds the messenger with protective watchers, namely angels, who guard him on every side. They keep the revelation from being stolen, distorted, or tampered with by devils or anyone else before it reaches him and before he delivers it to the people. The verse shows that knowledge of the unseen is a privilege granted only through prophethood, and that God protects both the messenger and the message so that it is conveyed intact.

translation: So that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord; and He encompasses all that is with them, and He has counted everything in number.
interpretation: The verse explains the purpose of God's protecting the messenger who receives revelation, with guardians placed before and behind him: it is so that the reality of the delivery is established, that the messengers have indeed conveyed their Lord's messages intact, unaltered and uninterrupted by any interference. God's knowledge is not limited to what is apparent, for He encompasses everything the messengers possess and everything around them, and He has numbered and recorded every single thing down to its smallest count. The lesson is that revelation is guarded by God's complete and precise knowledge, so no part of it can be lost, corrupted, or hidden, and all creation remains fully accounted for before Him.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who are wrapped in your garments.
interpretation: God addresses the Prophet Muhammad with an affectionate, intimate title rather than by name, calling him as one who has wrapped himself in his cloak, whether from the chill and awe of receiving the first revelation or from rest at night. The address gently moves him from a state of cover and repose toward the weighty responsibility of prophethood, which the following verses spell out as night prayer and measured recitation of the Qur'an. It teaches that carrying a great mission requires spiritual readiness, discipline, and devotion in the stillness of the night before engaging with the demands of the day.

translation: Stand [in prayer] through the night, except for a little.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet Muhammad to devote most of the night to prayer and recitation of the Qur'an, resting only during a small part of it. The night vigil is presented as spiritual preparation for the heavy responsibility of prophethood: in the stillness of the night the heart is most attentive, free from distraction, and best able to absorb revelation and gain the strength and steadfastness needed for the mission ahead.

translation: Half of it, or reduce it a little.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Muzzammil 73:3) follows the command to the Prophet to stand in prayer through the night, and it gives him flexibility in how long he prays. The night prayer may be about half the night, or somewhat less than half. The verse shows that night devotion is a serious discipline with a suggested measure, but it is not rigid. Its length is adjusted to a person's capacity, so that worship stays sustainable and does not become a crushing burden.

translation: Or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in a slow, measured manner.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the command to stand in prayer at night for about half of it or somewhat less, permits adding to that time and then gives the main instruction: to recite the Qur'an with tartil. Tartil means more than slow reading. It means pronouncing each letter clearly, observing the rules of recitation and the places to pause, and reflecting on the meaning so that the words reach the heart. The Qur'an is meant to be pondered and lived by, not just rapidly voiced, and a measured recitation prepares the believer to receive the weighty word described in the following verses.

translation: Indeed, We will cast upon you a weighty word.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Muzzammil announces to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that the revelation of the Qur'an, with its commands, prohibitions, and the responsibility of conveying the message, is a heavy burden. The 'weighty word' refers to the Qur'an itself, which is heavy in its authority, in the obligations it imposes, and in the physical and spiritual strain of receiving it, as reports describe the Prophet sweating on cold days when revelation came. Placed after the command to rise for night prayer, the verse suggests that standing in prayer, reciting the Qur'an slowly, and drawing close to God in the quiet of the night is the preparation of heart and soul needed to bear this great trust.

translation: Indeed, the rising by night is more effective for concentration and more suitable for speaking clearly.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Muzzammil, 73:6) teaches that worship in the night, after one wakes from sleep, has a special power to shape the soul. At that hour the world is quiet and distractions fall away, so the heart and tongue are brought into harmony: the worshipper's presence of mind is stronger and more firmly rooted, and the recitation of the Qur'an is clearer, more reflective, and better understood. The night prayer is thus presented as a means of training the self in sincerity, focus, and deep engagement with God's words, preparing the believer, and the Prophet in particular, for the weighty message and the burdens of the day ahead.

translation: Indeed, for you during the day is prolonged occupation.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Muzzammil 73:7) explains why the Prophet is told to rise for prayer at night. His daytime is filled with a long round of activity: calling people to God, teaching, dealing with people's affairs, and earning a living. Because the day leaves little room for undistracted devotion, the quiet of the night is the time set aside for focused worship and communion with God. It carries the lesson that a believer should reserve a time of solitude and spiritual renewal that worldly duties cannot crowd out, and that this inner strengthening prepares one for the burdens of public life.

translation: And remember the name of your Lord, and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion.
interpretation: This verse of Surat al-Muzzammil (73:8) commands the Prophet, and every believer after him, to make the remembrance of God a constant presence in the heart and on the tongue, and to turn away wholeheartedly from worldly distractions toward Him. 'Tabattul' means to cut oneself off and detach: it does not call for abandoning life or society, but for freeing the heart from dependence on created things so that one's deepest attachment, hope, and reliance rest on God alone.
