It is tempered with kafur, which here denotes not the bitter substance known in this world but a spring in Paradise whose water is cool, fragrant, and white in purity. This mixture signifies the coolness, serenity and freshness of the believers' reward, for it cleanses the heart and body, leaving no intoxication, harm or heaviness. The verse conveys that the righteous, who restrained themselves from forbidden desires and endured hardship in worship, will be rewarded with a refined, tranquil and wholesome pleasure that fits their purity.

translation: A spring from which the servants of God will drink, making it gush forth abundantly.
interpretation: The verse describes a fountain in Paradise reserved for the sincere servants of God, the righteous who were devoted to Him in the world. That they 'make it gush forth' means the spring is subject to their will: they can direct it wherever they wish, and it flows freely to whatever place they want, without effort or scarcity. This suggests that those who submitted their wills to God in this life are honored in the next with ease, dominion and unending abundance, so that the blessings they enjoy are never withheld from them.

translation: They fulfil their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Al-Insan, 76:7) describes the righteous as people of integrity who honour even the obligations they took upon themselves voluntarily. If they keep their vows to God, they will be all the more faithful to what He made obligatory. Their faithfulness is rooted in awareness of accountability: they fear the Day of Judgment, whose terror and hardship will spread and envelop everyone except those God shelters. This fear is not paralysing but motivating. It drives them to sincere worship, keeping their word, and generosity, as the following verses show by describing how they feed the needy for God's sake alone.

translation: And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive.
interpretation: The verse praises the righteous for a generosity that costs them something: they give away food while they themselves love it and need it, whether because they are hungry, because food is scarce, or because they cherish it. Their giving is therefore a real sacrifice, not the handing over of surplus. It also reaches the most vulnerable groups in society: the poor who lack provision, the orphan who has lost his protector, and the captive who is helpless and dependent on others. The verse teaches that true righteousness lies in putting the needs of the weak ahead of one's own desires, and in showing mercy without regard to a person's status, so that kindness becomes a mark of faith and a means of drawing near to God.

translation: "We feed you only for the sake of God. We desire from you neither reward nor thanks."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 76:9) expresses the purity of intention (ikhlas) of the righteous. Their charity is not a transaction or a means of gaining gratitude, status, or reciprocation from people; it is done solely seeking God's countenance and pleasure. By renouncing any expectation of repayment or even verbal thanks, they free the recipient from any sense of indebtedness and free their own deeds from showing off or seeking praise. The verse teaches that the true worth of a good deed lies in the sincerity behind it, and that real generosity is given for God alone, leaving the reward entirely to Him.

translation: Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day that is austere and distressful.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Insan, 76:10) gives the true motive behind the righteous people's generosity in feeding the poor, the orphan, and the captive. They give not for thanks or reward from people but out of reverent fear of God and of the Day of Judgment. That Day is called 'abusan (frowning, grim) and qamtarir (extremely severe and distressing) because its terror makes faces scowl and contract in anguish. The verse teaches that awareness of accountability before God is the root of sincere charity and good conduct, and that such fear leads the believer to act now so as to be spared the hardship of that Day.

translation: So Allah protected them from the evil of that Day, and gave them radiance and joy.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Insan 76:11) shows that the righteous, who fed the needy, the orphan and the captive purely for God's sake and out of fear of a grim and distressing Day, are rewarded in kind. Because they feared the Day's hardship, God shields them from its terror and distress. He then gives them 'nadrah', a radiance and joy in their faces, and 'surur', a joy in their hearts. Their inner gladness and outward brightness together mark the fullness of divine favor: security from harm first, then happiness of body and soul.

translation: And He will reward them for their patience with a Garden and silk.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Insan, 76:12) teaches that God repays the patience of the righteous, who endured hardship while fulfilling their vows, feeding the poor, orphan and captive for God's sake alone, and restraining themselves from disobedience, with the lasting bliss of Paradise. The Garden stands for their eternal dwelling and security, while silk, forbidden or discouraged for men in worldly life, symbolizes the comfort, honor and dignity granted in the Hereafter. Their brief endurance of hunger, hardship and self-restraint in this world is answered by a reward of abundant ease and luxury, showing that patience is the means to the highest and most complete recompense.

translation: Reclining therein on raised couches, they will see therein neither a burning sun nor bitter cold.
interpretation: The verse portrays the perfect comfort of the people of Paradise: they rest in dignified ease, free from toil, and their environment is perfectly temperate. Because there is no scorching heat or biting cold, the two extremes that cause hardship in worldly life, the verse teaches that the believers' reward is a state of complete and lasting well-being, in which nothing can disturb their peace or cause them discomfort.

translation: And near above them are its shades, and its clusters of fruit are made easily within reach.
interpretation: This verse describes a blessing of Paradise for the righteous: the shade of the garden's trees lowers itself over them and stays close, so that they enjoy comfort and coolness, and the fruits hang so low and are so submissive that a person can pick them whether standing, sitting, or reclining, without strain or difficulty. It shows that Paradise offers effortless, complete bliss, in contrast to the toil of worldly life, and that God's reward fulfills both comfort and provision together.

translation: And they will be served around with vessels of silver and goblets that are of crystal-clear glass.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Al-Insan, 76:15) portrays the honor and luxury granted to the righteous in Paradise: they are waited on by attendants carrying vessels and cups. The phrase 'qawarira' (glass) signals that the cups possess the transparency and purity of glass, while being made of silver, as the next verse clarifies ('qawarira min fiddah'). This combination of two precious qualities, the brightness of silver and the clarity of crystal, which are never joined together in this world, shows that the bliss of the hereafter surpasses worldly experience, and that the believers are granted effortless, refined comfort as a reward for their patience and devotion.

translation: Crystal-clear vessels of silver, which they have measured out according to their exact measure.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Al-Insan 76:16) describes the refined wonder of Paradise: its drinking vessels combine the transparency of glass with the purity and brilliance of silver, something unknown in this world, where these qualities do not come together in one material. The phrase 'they have measured it out exactly' means that the people of Paradise, or those serving them, have determined the contents of each cup to match precisely the desire and capacity of the one who drinks, so that it neither exceeds nor falls short of what he wants. This shows that God's bounty in the Hereafter is perfectly fitted to the wish of each person, free from waste, deficiency, or the burden of measuring that marks worldly pleasures.

translation: And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is of ginger.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 76:17) describes a blessing for the righteous in Paradise. The Arabs prized ginger blended into their drinks for its warmth and pleasant, lively taste, so the image conveys a delight that is familiar yet perfected. Unlike the camphor-mixed drink mentioned earlier in the same passage, which evokes coolness and calm, the ginger-mixed cup adds a stimulating, savory sweetness. Together these give the dwellers of Paradise a full range of pure pleasures. The cup is a reward for their faithfulness, charity, and fear of the Day of Judgment, and it shows that God's bounty is both complete and tailored to what the soul finds most pleasing.

translation: A spring therein named Salsabil.
interpretation: The verse describes a spring in Paradise whose name, Salsabil, conveys water that is sweet, smooth, and easily flowing, pleasant to drink and effortless to swallow. The believers will drink from it, and its mention, together with the cups mixed with ginger in the preceding verse, shows that the blessings of the next life are of a purer and more refined kind than anything known in this world. The fact that the spring is given a name signals its distinction and honor, and that the reward promised to the righteous is real, specific, and abundant.

translation: And around them will go about eternal youths; when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls.
interpretation: The verse describes the honor and delight of the people of Paradise, who are served by youths who never age or change, remaining forever in the freshness of youth. Likening them to scattered pearls conveys their radiant beauty, purity, and brilliance. Pearls that are scattered, rather than strung, shine from every direction as the youths move about swiftly and attentively in service, so the beholder sees luminous beauty all around. The image shows that Paradise's blessings include both perfect service and a lasting, unfading beauty that delights the eye.

translation: And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Insan 76:20) describes the inhabitants of Paradise. When the believer looks around in the Garden, whichever way he turns his eyes, he sees boundless delight and a vast dominion that surpasses anything known in this world. The 'great kingdom' signifies that even the lowest of the people of Paradise will possess expansive realms, servants, palaces, and authority, with no decline or end to it. It conveys that God's reward for the righteous is not merely comfort but honor, grandeur, and abiding sovereignty, inspiring believers to patience and good deeds in this life in hope of that everlasting favor.

translation: Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and heavy brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them a pure drink.
interpretation: The verse portrays the honor God grants the righteous in Paradise in three ways: outward dignity, adornment, and inner purification. The green silk and brocade show comfort, luxury, and the lasting freshness of the next life, and the silver bracelets show their elevated status, as ornaments once worn by the honored. The most important blessing is that their Lord Himself serves them a 'pure drink' (sharaban tahura). The drink is pure in itself and also purifies those who drink it, cleansing hearts of envy, rancor, and every blemish, unlike worldly intoxicants that corrupt the mind and body. The drink comes directly from their Lord, which shows that the final reward is His nearness and pleasure, and that it is complete: bodily delight accompanied by spiritual cleansing.

translation: Indeed, this has been for you a reward, and your striving has been appreciated.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Insan 76:22) is God's address to the people of Paradise, completing the description of their blessings. By calling it a 'reward,' it affirms that their bliss is the fruit of their faith and righteous deeds in this world, such as fulfilling vows, feeding the poor out of love for God, and fearing the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'your striving has been appreciated' means that God accepts and honors their efforts, and that He is the One who thanks His servants, rewarding even their modest deeds generously. This brings them honor and joy, since the highest fulfillment is hearing that their Lord is pleased with what they did, and it encourages believers to remain sincere and steadfast in their efforts, knowing that no good deed is wasted.

translation: Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Qur'an to you, [O Muhammad], progressively, in stages.
interpretation: God emphasizes with the doubled pronoun 'We, indeed We' that the Qur'an is not authored by Muhammad but is a revelation from God Himself, sent down gradually in portions over time rather than all at once. This reassures the Prophet amid the accusations and pressure of the Meccan opponents: the message is divinely guaranteed, and its gradual unfolding strengthens his heart, allows the believers to absorb and apply it step by step, and responds to events as they arise. It prepares him to be patient and steadfast in conveying the message and awaiting God's judgment, since the One who revealed it is the One who protects and supports him.

translation: So be patient with the decree of your Lord, and do not obey among them any sinner or ungrateful disbeliever.
interpretation: The verse (Surah al-Insan 76:24) instructs the Prophet, and by extension every believer, to hold firm and endure with steadfastness whatever God has ordained, including the delay of relief and the hardships of conveying the message, trusting that God's wisdom governs the outcome. It also warns against yielding to those who push toward wrongdoing or rejection of truth, whether by temptation, pressure, or compromise. The 'sinner' (athim) is one who invites to immorality and transgression, while the 'ungrateful disbeliever' (kafur) is one who denies God's truth and His favors. Spiritual strength comes from patience in God's decree and uncompromising loyalty to His guidance rather than to the demands of those who oppose it.

translation: And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 76:25) commands constant remembrance of God through the day, with morning and evening marking its beginning and end. It means that a believer's life should be framed by devotion: prayer, glorification, and awareness of God. Such remembrance gives steadfastness and spiritual strength, especially in the face of hardship and opposition, as the surrounding verses instruct the Prophet to be patient with his Lord's decree and not to obey the sinful or ungrateful among the disbelievers.

translation: And during part of the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him for a long night.
interpretation: After commanding the Prophet to be patient with his Lord's decree and to remember the name of his Lord morning and evening, the verse directs him to devote a portion of the night to worship, through prayer and prostration and extended praise of God. The night is the time of stillness and freedom from worldly distractions, so worship then strengthens the heart, fortifies the believer against the hostility and burdens of calling people to the truth, and builds the steadfastness that patience requires. The verse teaches that endurance in the face of hardship is sustained by long, sincere devotion to God in private, especially in the depths of the night.

translation: Indeed, these love the fleeting life of this world and leave behind them a heavy Day.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Insan 76:27) diagnoses the moral failing of those who reject the message: their hearts are bound to immediate gratification, wealth, and status, so they neglect preparing for the Day of Judgment. The 'heavy Day' is heavy in its gravity, its terrors, and the weight of accountability it brings. By casting the Day 'behind their backs', the verse portrays a deliberate turning away, treating the Hereafter as something to be ignored rather than faced. It warns that attachment to what is quickly gone, at the cost of what is lasting, is a misplaced priority that will be exposed on that Day.

translation: We created them and strengthened their constitution; and whenever We will, We can replace them with others like them, a complete replacement.
interpretation: God reminds human beings that their existence, the soundness of their bodies and the strength of their joints and makeup are all gifts from Him, not something they achieved on their own. Because they owe their very being and strength to Him, they have no grounds for arrogance or for turning away from the truth. The verse also warns that He has full power to remove those who persist in denial and replace them with another generation who would be obedient, so the human being's continued existence is not guaranteed but depends on God's will, and gratitude and submission are the fitting response.

translation: Indeed, this is a reminder; so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an, with its warnings and its promises, is a reminder that awakens the heedless heart and clarifies the truth. Guidance is therefore open to every person: no one is compelled, and the way to God is made clear through faith, sincere worship, and righteous deeds. Whoever wishes to draw near to God must choose the path of obedience and strive along it, so the responsibility for taking or neglecting this path rests on the individual's own choice, and this choice is itself made possible by God's grace and enabling.

translation: And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: Human choice and willpower do not operate independently of God: a person's ability to will good or to choose a path exists only because God permits and enables it. This does not cancel human responsibility, since God has given people real capacity to choose, but it reminds them that their will falls within God's greater will, so they should not be arrogant about their guidance or despair of it, and should ask Him for success. The closing names, Knowing and Wise, show that God's will is never arbitrary: He knows who is fit for guidance and who is not, and He places every decree, including who is guided and who is left to stray, in accordance with perfect wisdom.

translation: He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but as for the wrongdoers, He has prepared for them a painful punishment.
interpretation: Entry into God's mercy is a matter of His sovereign will and grace, which He grants to those who respond to His guidance with faith and righteous deeds; it is not something anyone can claim by right or earn by their own power. The wrongdoers, namely those who persist in disbelief, associating partners with God, and oppressing others, have by their own choices placed themselves outside that mercy. For them God has already prepared a painful punishment, a reminder that divine mercy and divine justice both operate, and that a person's destiny follows from the path he chooses.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By those sent forth in succession.
interpretation: God opens Surat al-Mursalat with an oath by those forces that are sent forth one after another, which many early commentators understood as the winds sent in gentle, continuous succession, bringing mercy and rain. By swearing by them, God draws attention to His power and wisdom in directing creation, and prepares the listener for the oath's purpose: that the promised Day of Judgment is certain to come. Just as the winds arrive in an ordered sequence beyond human control, so the promised resurrection will arrive at its appointed time, and its coming cannot be averted or denied.

translation: By those [winds] sent forth in succession, then those raging violently in a tempest.
interpretation: This verse opens Surat al-Mursalat's series of oaths (v. 2 in the sequence). God swears by the powerful winds that blow with fierce force, sweeping away whatever lies in their path. The oath draws attention to God's unrestrained power over nature: if winds under His command can uproot and scatter all things, then He can surely bring about the Day of Judgment that the surah promises. The imagery reminds the listener that the order of the world is subject to the divine will, and that the warning of the coming Day is as certain and irresistible as a storm.

translation: And [by] those that spread [far and wide], spreading.
interpretation: This oath in Surah Al-Mursalat (77:3) is by the angels or the winds that spread things abroad. On the interpretation of the angels, they spread the revelation, mercy and the divine command across the earth, scattering guidance among people just as the winds scatter clouds and rain. God swears by these forces to affirm that the Day of Judgment promised to humanity is certain and will surely come to pass. The oath draws on powerful, ordered forces in creation, which operate entirely by God's command, as evidence that the One who directs them is able to resurrect the dead and hold them to account.

translation: And those [angels] that distinguish [truth from falsehood] with a clear distinction.
interpretation: The verse is an oath by the angels who bring down revelation and separate truth from falsehood, and lawful from unlawful. By swearing by them, God stresses that the promised Day of Judgment is certain, and that revelation is a decisive criterion by which people's paths are divided into guidance and misguidance, so that no one has an excuse. This is the reading of those who take the 'separators' to be angels who deliver God's decisive word to the messengers.

translation: And those [angels] who deliver the Reminder,
interpretation: This verse, which opens Surat al-Mursalat (77:5), is an oath by God by the angels who bring down revelation and cast the divine message into the hearts of the prophets. Their task is to deliver the Reminder, whether as a warning or as an excuse for those who reject it, so that no one has an argument against God. By swearing by these beings, the verse stresses that revelation is a real, authoritative communication from God, and that the promised Day of Judgment, which the surah goes on to affirm, is certain to come.

translation: As an excuse or a warning.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 77:6) follows the oath by the angels who bring down revelation ('those who cast the Reminder'). It explains the purpose of that revelation: God sends it so that no one will have an excuse on the Day of Judgment, and so that people are warned of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing. The message gives the believers and the repentant an 'excuse' in the sense of removing blame and establishing God's justice, since He has made the truth clear and so no one can claim ignorance. It also acts as a 'warning' to the heedless, so that they may turn back before accountability arrives. Revelation therefore serves as clear proof from God (hujjah) and as mercy, leaving each person responsible for their response.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised will surely come to pass.
interpretation: This verse, which opens a divine oath in Surat al-Mursalat (77:7), affirms that the Day of Judgment, resurrection, and the reckoning that God has promised are certain and unavoidable. It is not a possibility to be debated but a coming reality. Its meaning is that denial or heedlessness cannot delay or cancel it, so a person should live with awareness of accountability, prepare through faith and righteous action, and not be deceived by the apparent delay of that promised Day.

translation: When the stars are obliterated.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mursalat 77:8) describes one of the signs of the Day of Judgment: the stars, whose light guides travelers and seems permanent and orderly, will be effaced and their light extinguished. It signals the complete collapse of the present cosmic order, reminding people that nothing in creation endures except God's command, and that the promised Day is certain, so those who deny it should reflect and prepare for it.

translation: And when the heaven is split open.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mursalat, 77:9) is the second in a series of cosmic signs that herald the Day of Judgment, where the stars are effaced and the mountains are blown away like dust. The splitting open of the sky signifies the collapse of the ordered universe as we know it, with its firmament breaking apart and opening into gates. It reminds the listener that the heavens, which appear to be a fixed and unshakable canopy, are wholly subject to God's command, and that the world's apparent stability is temporary. The message is one of accountability: just as the sky yields to God's will, every human being will be brought before Him, so the verse calls on people to reflect and prepare for the promised Day rather than deny it.

translation: And when the mountains are blown away as dust.
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Mursalat (77:10) describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection: the mountains, which in this world symbolize firmness, stability and permanence, will be uprooted, pulverized and scattered like dust. The meaning is that nothing in creation, however massive and immovable it appears, can withstand God's command when the appointed Hour comes. If the mightiest of the earth's features are reduced to nothing, then human power, wealth and status will certainly count for nothing before God, and only one's deeds will remain. The verse thus awakens the listener to the reality of the Hereafter, urging humility, accountability and preparation for the Day of Judgment.

translation: And when the messengers are given a appointed time.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mursalat 77:11) describes one of the signs of the Day of Judgment: the messengers will be gathered at their appointed time to testify against their peoples. The word 'uqqitat' means that a fixed time has been set for them, so that on the Day of Resurrection they will bear witness regarding how their nations responded to the message. The verse stresses that the Day of Decision is precise and certain, with every messenger and community brought together at the moment God has decreed, so that judgment is established upon clear testimony.

translation: For what day was it postponed?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mursalat 77:12) is a rhetorical question about the messengers whose affairs were delayed. It points to the Day of Decision, when judgment is made between people. The question is meant to stir awe and awareness, and its answer follows in the next verse: 'For the Day of Decision.' It reminds the listener that postponing the reckoning in this world does not mean it will not happen. Every promise of justice and accountability is held for a fixed, certain day, so a person should prepare for it rather than be heedless.

translation: For the Day of Decision.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mursalat (77:13), answers the question of what day the warnings and deferred judgment are meant for. It points to the Day of Judgment, called the Day of Decision (Yawm al-Fasl) because on it God will separate truth from falsehood, the righteous from the wrongdoers, and settle every dispute with final justice. The verse stresses that the delay of consequences in this world is not neglect: all deeds are being held for a definite day when the ambiguity of worldly life is removed and each soul receives its decisive, irreversible outcome.

translation: And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?
interpretation: This verse, repeated in Surah Al-Mursalat, uses a rhetorical question to magnify the awesomeness of the Day of Judgment. It is called the Day of Decision because on it Allah will separate truth from falsehood, the righteous from the wicked, and will judge between all people with perfect justice. The phrasing signals that its true magnitude lies beyond human comprehension, which should awaken the listener to take it seriously, repent of denial, and prepare through faith and righteous deeds before the final judgment arrives.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, His messengers, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and grievous punishment on the Day of Judgment. The word 'woe' (wayl) conveys destruction and severe suffering, and its repetition after each description of God's power and His signs in creation underscores that denial is without excuse. Each time it is repeated, it confronts the denier with another proof that was ignored, so that the ruin they face is shown to be the consequence of their own willful rejection of clear evidence.

translation: Did We not destroy the former peoples?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mursalat 77:16) is a rhetorical question meant to remind the deniers of the Day of Judgment that God's power and justice are established in history. Earlier nations such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud rejected their messengers and were annihilated for it. The verse warns that the same fate can befall those who reject the truth and the Resurrection, and it shows that the One who destroyed earlier generations is able to bring about the Hereafter and hold everyone to account.

translation: Then We shall make the later generations follow them.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mursalat 77:17) follows the mention of the destruction of the earlier peoples who denied their messengers, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. It teaches that God's way with deniers is consistent: those who come after and persist in the same disbelief and wrongdoing will meet the same fate as those who came before. Divine punishment is not a unique event of the past but a standing law, and later generations who reject the truth are warned that they will be made to follow the earlier ones into ruin, just as the Day of Judgment awaits all deniers.

translation: Thus do We deal with the criminals.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mursalat 77:18) comes after the mention of the destruction of earlier nations who denied the truth. It affirms that God's way of dealing with wrongdoers is consistent and just. Those who persist in denial, injustice, and sin will meet the same fate as those before them, since divine law does not change or show favoritism. It serves as both a warning to those who reject the message and a reminder that no one is exempt from accountability, while the believer takes comfort that justice will ultimately prevail.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the message of the prophets, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and severe punishment on the Day of Judgment. The word 'woe' (wayl) expresses doom and utter destruction. The repetition after each set of reminders, such as the evidence of creation, the fate of earlier nations, and the certainty of the promised Day, emphasizes that denial in the face of such clear proofs is inexcusable. The verse calls the listener to reflect, drop arrogance and heedlessness, and accept the truth before the time when regret will bring no benefit.

translation: Did We not create you from a despised fluid?
interpretation: The verse reminds human beings of their humble physical origin in a base, insignificant fluid, the sperm-drop, in order to cultivate humility and gratitude, and to refute arrogance and denial of resurrection. The One who brought them into being from such lowly beginnings and shaped them into complete, living, reasoning persons is surely able to recreate them after death. Their existence is a gift from God's power and care, not from any merit of their own, so it calls for thankfulness and acknowledgment of His authority.

translation: Then We placed him in a firm and secure resting place.
interpretation: The verse refers to the stage of human creation in which the drop of fluid (nutfah) is lodged in the womb, which is described as a secure and well-protected place. The womb is a safe haven, shielded by the body's structures and surrounded by protective layers and fluids, where the developing human is sheltered from external harm. This shows God's care and precise design in sustaining human life at its most vulnerable stage, and it points to His power and mercy, which should lead a person to gratitude, humility, and recognition of the Creator who nurtures him from the very beginning.

translation: Until a known, appointed term.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Mursalat (77:22), completes the thought of the preceding verse about how God created human beings from a despised fluid and placed it in a secure resting place (the womb). The meaning is that the period of gestation is fixed by God with precise knowledge and measure. Nothing about the beginning of human life is left to chance: God has decreed the length of time each person develops in the womb, just as He has decreed each person's lifespan and destiny. This points to His power and wisdom in creation, and serves as a reminder that the One who originated humans from such humble beginnings and sustains them with precision is certainly able to resurrect them.

translation: For We determined [it] with precision, and how excellent are We as Determiners.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 77:23) points to God's perfect power and wisdom in shaping human creation, from a drop of fluid through each stage of development until birth. It teaches that nothing in a person's origin or growth is accidental, because every stage is measured and ordained by God with exact proportion. Since the One who fashioned humans so precisely is fully capable of resurrecting them, those who deny the Day of Judgment have no grounds for their denial. The verse also invites reflection and gratitude, because it affirms that God's decree is flawless and that He is the best of all who measure and ordain.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, His messengers, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and destruction when the Day of Decision arrives. Having been shown clear evidence of God's power in creation and in the fate of earlier peoples, their denial leaves them without excuse. The repetition drives home that every proof they dismissed will count against them, and that the consequence of persistent denial is a doom that no one can avert on that Day.

translation: Have We not made the earth a receptacle that gathers and holds together,
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 77:25) points to God's favor in making the earth a vessel that draws humankind to itself and holds them: the living are lodged and sustained upon its surface, and the dead are gathered and laid within its depths. The word 'kifat' conveys containing and gathering. The earth is thus a constant sign of God's power and wisdom, since it is perfectly suited to hold both the living and the dead. A God who fashioned the earth to contain all of creation is certainly able to bring the dead back to life on the Day of Resurrection, which the deniers in this surah reject.

translation: The living and the dead.
interpretation: This phrase is from Surah Al-Mursalat (77:26), where God points to the earth as a vessel that gathers people, both the living and the dead. The living dwell and move upon its surface, while the dead are laid to rest within it. The verse reminds people of God's favor and power in making the earth a home and a final resting place. It also points to the resurrection: the One who made the earth hold all humankind in life and in death can bring them forth again for judgment.

translation: And We placed therein lofty, firmly set mountains, and We gave you sweet, fresh water to drink.
interpretation: The verse points to God's providence in preparing the earth for human life. The towering mountains are fixed so that the earth is stable and its crust is balanced, and they also serve as reservoirs and sources: they gather clouds and rain, store water as snow and in underground channels, and release it as springs and rivers. The 'sweet, fresh water' is thus a deliberate gift made possible by this design, and not a chance occurrence. Mentioning mountains and drinkable water together invites reflection on how the grandeur of creation and the daily provision of life's necessities both come from one Creator, which should lead people to gratitude and to acknowledging the truth of resurrection and the divine power that can bring about all things.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the Messengers, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and destruction on the Day of Judgment. The word 'woe' (wayl) expresses severe doom and anguish, and it is directed at the deniers because on that Day the truth they dismissed will be undeniably clear, while their denial will leave them with no excuse or defense. The repetition serves to jolt the conscience, urging the listener to reflect on each sign of God's power and each warning mentioned, and not to be counted among those who deny them.

translation: Go forth to that which you used to deny.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mursalat 77:29) is spoken to the deniers on the Day of Judgment. It is a rebuke and a command: the Hellfire and the punishment they mocked and rejected in the world, dismissing the warnings of the messengers, are now a present reality. They are driven toward it by the very thing they once denied, which shows that denial cannot change truth, and that the Hereafter, which they treated as a fable, stands before them in full certainty. The wording stresses that their punishment corresponds to their disbelief: what they refused to believe in is exactly what they are now made to face.

translation: Proceed to a shadow having three branches.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 77:30) is said to the deniers on the Day of Judgment, after they are told to go toward what they used to deny, namely the Fire. The 'shadow with three branches' is understood as the thick smoke of Hell that rises and splits into three columns. It is a mocking inversion of true shade: it gives no coolness and no protection from the flame, as the next verse says, 'Neither shady nor availing against the blaze.' The verse therefore teaches that those who rejected the truth will find no refuge from God's judgment, and that what looks like relief in the Hereafter will itself be a form of punishment.

translation: Neither shady nor of any avail against the flame.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mursalat, 77:31) describes the 'shadow' of smoke that the deniers will be told to take shelter beneath on the Day of Judgment. Unlike a true shade, which gives coolness and protection from the sun's heat, this shadow of black smoke offers no relief and does not shield anyone from the blazing fire. The point is a stark reversal of expectation: what appears to promise refuge turns out to be a further torment, underscoring that there will be no escape or comfort for those who denied the truth, and mocking their false reliance on worldly protections that could not save them from God's judgment.

translation: Indeed, it throws up sparks as huge as a castle.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mursalat (77:32), describes the terrifying scale of Hellfire. Its sparks are not like the small embers of worldly fires but are as massive as great fortresses or palaces, conveying the immense power and dread of the punishment awaiting those who denied the truth. By comparing the sparks to a towering building, the verse stirs awe and fear, urging the listener to reflect on the severity of the Hereafter and to take heed now, while there is still opportunity to believe and act righteously.

translation: As if they were yellowish camels (or: bright, tawny cables/ropes).
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mursalat 77:33) completes the description of the sparks thrown up by Hellfire, which are likened to great castles in the preceding verse and here to tawny, yellowish camels. It conveys both the immense size of the sparks and their color and restless, scattered movement as they leap and fly about in every direction, as a herd of dark-yellow camels would. The image is meant to instill dread in those who deny the Day of Judgment, showing that even the mere sparks of the Fire are terrifying in magnitude and appearance, so how much more terrible the Fire itself.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the Messengers, and the truth of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and grievous punishment on the Day of Judgment. Its repetition after each reminder of God's power, His favors, and the certainty of the Hereafter serves to strike the heart and show that denial is without excuse. Every sign of creation and revelation is a proof, so rejecting it after clear evidence brings inescapable loss. The 'woe' signifies destruction and misery, and may also refer to a place of torment in Hell. The verse calls the reader to reflect, believe, and prepare for accountability before that Day arrives.

translation: This is a Day on which they will not speak.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 77:35) describes the Day of Judgment, when those who denied the truth will be unable to speak in defense of themselves. Speech will be of no use to them: the evidence against them is clear, their deeds are recorded, and no excuse remains. Their silence reflects the helplessness of the deniers before divine justice. It shows that the final judgment rests on truth and not on argument or pretext, and that the chance to offer excuses and make amends belongs to this life, not to the Hereafter.

translation: And they will not be permitted to offer excuses.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mursalat 77:36) describes the Day of Judgment, when the deniers will be rendered speechless. No pretext will be accepted from them, and they will not even be given leave to make one, because the truth will be fully manifest and the proof against them complete. Their deeds and the clear signs they rejected in the world leave no ground for excuse. This shows that the final judgment is absolutely just: it is not a moment for argument or negotiation, since the time for repentance and making amends was this worldly life, which they squandered in denial. The verse is a warning to use the present opportunity to turn to God, before a day comes when no plea can be made.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the Messengers, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and severe punishment on the Day of Decision. Having been given clear evidence in creation and revelation, their denial is without excuse, and the refrain drives home that the Day's truth will be undeniable, turning their former mockery into regret and destruction.

translation: This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you together with the earlier generations.
interpretation: The verse announces that the Day of Judgment is the moment when all disputes are finally settled and truth is separated from falsehood. Those who denied the message in the present era are brought together with the nations before them, showing that no one escapes accountability through the passage of time. Every generation, from the first to the last, stands in a single assembly before God, so the justice of that day is complete and universal, and the denial and mockery of the deniers is answered by a reality they can no longer avoid.

translation: So if you have any scheme, then scheme against me.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 77:39) will be said to the deniers on the Day of Judgment. It is a challenge that exposes their helplessness. In the world they plotted against the truth, against the messengers and against believers, and relied on their own cunning and power. Now, standing before God for judgment, they are told to use whatever strategy they have to escape the punishment. The command is not an invitation but a rebuke. It makes clear that every means they relied on has vanished, that no plan can save them from God's decree, and that sovereignty on that Day belongs to God alone. It also reminds listeners now to abandon arrogance and reliance on their own schemes, and to submit to God before the time for plotting is gone.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the message of the prophets, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and destruction on the Day of Judgment. The word 'woe' (wayl) expresses severe doom and anguish, and its repetition after each reminder of God's power, His favors, and the proofs of the Hereafter stresses that denial is inexcusable. Once the truth they dismissed becomes undeniable, their regret will be too late to help them.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be amid shades and springs.
interpretation: This verse contrasts the fate of the God-fearing with that of the deniers, who in the preceding verses are told to depart to the shadow of smoke that offers no coolness or protection. The righteous, who guarded themselves against God's displeasure through faith and obedience, are rewarded in the Hereafter with true, refreshing shade and flowing springs, which signify comfort, security, and lasting mercy. The reward mirrors the believers' own restraint in the world: those who shielded themselves from sin are themselves sheltered by God's grace on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And fruits of whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mursalat (77:42), describes part of the reward awaiting the God-fearing (al-muttaqin) in Paradise. Alongside the cool shades and springs mentioned in the preceding verse, they will have fruits of every kind they long for. The point is that the bounty of the next life is not fixed or limited but follows the wishes of its dwellers: whatever fruit the heart craves is available, without effort, scarcity, or fear of running out. This stands in contrast to the fate of those who denied the Day of Judgment, who are threatened with a shadow that gives no shade. The phrase 'whatever they desire' also shows that Paradise fulfills the inner longings of the believers, offering them complete satisfaction and honor as the fruit of their piety in this world.

translation: Eat and drink with enjoyment, for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the people of Paradise (as in Surat at-Tur, 52:19, and Surat al-Mursalat, 77:43). It means that the blessings given to the righteous are not arbitrary but are a reward for their faith and good deeds in the worldly life. The word 'hanī'an' conveys food and drink that is pure, pleasant, and free of any harm, burden, or worry. Being told that this is 'for what you used to do' adds to their joy by affirming that their efforts were recognized and honored by God, even though entry into Paradise ultimately comes through His mercy and grace.

translation: Indeed, this is how We reward those who do good.
interpretation: This verse affirms a consistent divine principle: God honors those who excel in faith and conduct (the muhsinun) by rescuing them, elevating them, and granting them a good outcome, as He did with the prophets and righteous servants mentioned before it. The word 'kadhalika' (thus) shows that the favor they received was not an exception or a coincidence but an example of a lasting law of divine justice and generosity. The verse encourages believers to strive for ihsan, doing good with sincerity and awareness that God sees them, and to trust that no good deed goes unrewarded, whether in this world through relief and a lasting good reputation, or in the Hereafter through greater reward.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's revelation, the Messenger, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and severe punishment on the Day of Judgment. 'Woe' (wayl) expresses doom, destruction, and grief, and its repetition after each reminder of God's power, His signs in creation, and the fate of earlier nations underscores that denial is without excuse. Once the truth they dismissed becomes manifest, their rejection will bring only regret, and no argument or intercession will rescue them.

translation: Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while; indeed, you are wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 77:46) is a warning addressed to those who deny the Day of Judgment. It says that the worldly enjoyment they take pride in is brief and insignificant compared with the eternal life to come. Their indulgence does not show that God approves of them. Because of their denial and their wrongdoing, they are criminals whose short-lived pleasure will end in a grave reckoning. The command to eat and enjoy is not a permission but a rebuke: take your small share now, since your end is already decided by your own deeds.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the message of the prophets, and the reality of resurrection will face ruin and destruction on the Day of Judgment. The word 'woe' (wayl) expresses severe doom and anguish, and the repetition after each reminder of God's power and creation presses the point that denial is inexcusable. Having seen clear evidence of God's might in creation and in the fate of earlier nations, the deniers will have no defense, and their rejection will turn into regret and punishment when the truth they denied becomes undeniable.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Bow down in prayer,' they do not bow down.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mursalat, 77:48) condemns those who deny the truth: when they are called to submit to God through worship, symbolized by ruku' (bowing), they refuse out of arrogance and stubbornness. Their refusal shows that the problem is not a lack of evidence but a hardened heart that resists humbling itself before its Creator. It teaches that real faith requires obedient submission, and that pride is what keeps people from responding to divine guidance. For this reason the verse is followed by a warning of woe to the deniers on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, a refrain repeated throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the Messenger, and the reality of resurrection will face ruin and severe punishment on the Day of Judgment. It is a pronouncement of doom: when the truth they denied becomes plainly visible, denial offers no protection, and their regret will be unavoidable. Its repetition after each of God's signs and mentions of His power drives home that every proof of His power and every warning of the Hereafter increases the culpability of those who deny them, so the moral call is to accept the truth and prepare for accountability before that Day comes.

translation: In what statement, then, after this will they believe?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 77:50, and similarly 7:185) is a rhetorical question that expresses astonishment at the disbelievers. If the Qur'an, with its clear proofs, warnings, and guidance, does not move them to faith, then no other speech can. The Qur'an is presented as the final and most truthful discourse, so rejecting it leaves no other source of guidance that could persuade a heart that is closed to truth. The verse calls on the listener to reflect and accept the Qur'an, since refusing it means persisting in misguidance.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. About what are they asking one another?
interpretation: The opening of Surah An-Naba' poses a rhetorical question that is meant to magnify the importance of what follows. The disbelievers of Quraysh were debating among themselves, with mockery and doubt, about the message of the Prophet Muhammad, especially the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment. By asking 'About what are they asking one another?' without yet naming the subject, God stirs the listener's anticipation and signals that the matter is so momentous and undeniable that it should never have been treated as a subject of ridicule or dispute. The following verses go on to identify it as the 'great news' (an-naba' al-'azim), pointing to the certainty of resurrection and accountability.

translation: About the Great News.
interpretation: This verse (Surat An-Naba', 78:2) answers the question posed in the preceding verse, 'About what are they asking one another?' The 'Great News' is most commonly understood as the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment, along with the message of the Qur'an that announces it. The disbelievers of Makkah were disputing and mocking this news, doubting that the dead could be raised and held to account. By calling it 'great', God stresses its immense weight and consequence: it is the pivotal truth that gives meaning to human life and moral responsibility, and no one can remain indifferent to it, since every person will ultimately face it.

translation: About which they are in disagreement.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah An-Naba (78:3), describes the Great News (An-Naba' al-Azim) that the people were questioning one another about. It points to the Day of Resurrection and the afterlife, a matter on which people were divided: some firmly believed in it, while others denied it or doubted it. The verse highlights that human disagreement does not change the reality of the event, and it prepares the listener for the next verses, which warn that they will soon come to know the truth of what they dispute.

translation: No! They will soon come to know.
interpretation: This verse, Qur'an 78:4, is a stern rebuke that rejects the disbelievers' denial and mockery of the Day of Resurrection, which they argued about in the preceding verses. The word 'kallā' (No!) firmly refutes their doubt, and the promise that they will 'soon know' warns that the truth will become undeniable when they witness the Hour and face the consequences of their disbelief. Knowledge that they refused to accept through reflection and revelation will be forced upon them by direct experience, when denial no longer helps.

translation: Then, no indeed! They will soon come to know.
interpretation: This verse repeats and intensifies the warning of the preceding verse ("No indeed! They will soon know"), addressing those who doubt or deny the Great News of resurrection and the Day of Judgment in Surah An-Naba. The repetition with 'then' (thumma) signals a graver, more emphatic stage of knowledge: if the first warning refers to the realization they will have at the moment of death and in the grave, this one points to the fuller, undeniable certainty they will face on the Day of Resurrection when the reality is unveiled and the consequences of their denial become clear. Their present arguing and disbelief will give way to certain knowledge, but at a time when it will be too late to benefit them.

translation: Have We not made the earth a resting place?
interpretation: This verse (Surat An-Naba', 78:6) opens a series of rhetorical questions that point to God's power and care as evidence that He is able to resurrect the dead. The earth is described as a 'mihad', a smooth, prepared bed or cradle, like the one laid out for a child. God made it stable, level, and hospitable, so that people can settle on it, walk, build, farm, and rest. This ease of life is not accidental. It is a deliberate gift from a Creator who planned for human needs. Whoever can prepare the earth so carefully can certainly bring people back to life for judgment, and the proper response is gratitude and acknowledgment of His lordship.

translation: And the mountains as stakes?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 78:7) points to the mountains as divine design: just as tent pegs anchor a tent and keep it from shifting, the mountains are set deep into the earth to steady its crust and keep it stable, so that it does not shake with those who live on it. This reflects God's power and care in preparing the earth as a secure dwelling for humankind. It is one of several signs in the opening of Surat an-Naba' that call people to reflect on creation, and so to accept that the One who created and ordered the earth with such precision is able to resurrect the dead and bring them to account.

translation: And We created you in pairs.
interpretation: This verse, Surah An-Naba 78:8, points to the divine wisdom in how humanity was made: male and female, formed as complementary partners. This pairing is a sign of God's power and mercy, since it creates companionship, tranquility, affection, and the continuation of human life through procreation. In the context of the surah, which argues for the reality of the Resurrection, it is one of several signs in creation, alongside the earth, mountains, sleep, night, and day. The One who could bring forth life in such an ordered and balanced way can certainly raise the dead, and humans are meant to reflect on this design with gratitude and recognition of their Creator.

translation: And We made your sleep a rest.
interpretation: God made sleep a means of cutting off the body's constant activity and toil, so that people may recover from fatigue and regain strength. The word 'subat' implies a cessation or severance from movement, so sleep is a mercy and a deliberate design: a regular, restorative pause that renews body and mind for the next day's work. That such a profound and necessary state of rest is built into human nature points to the wisdom and power of the Creator, who is able also to bring about the greater 'awakening' of resurrection.

translation: And We made the night a covering.
interpretation: The night is likened to a garment that wraps and conceals. Its darkness envelops people like a cloak, giving them privacy, stillness and rest from the toil of the day, so that body and mind can recover. It is a mercy from God: the night shields people from view and gives them a time of calm, in which they can sleep, worship and reflect, and it prepares them for the livelihood and activity of the day that follows. The verse points to God's care in arranging the natural order for human benefit, and calls people to gratitude and to recognition of His power.

translation: And We made the day for livelihood.
interpretation: God made the daytime a period of light and activity, in which people rise from sleep to seek their sustenance, work, trade, and manage their worldly needs. The verse presents the alternation of night and day as a deliberate act of divine mercy and wisdom: the night brings rest and the day brings renewed energy for earning a living. This is a sign that should lead a person to gratitude, and a reminder that seeking lawful provision is part of a life ordered by God's design, to be pursued with thankfulness toward the One who arranged it.

translation: And We have built above you seven strong (heavens).
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and design in creating the heavens as a firm, well-ordered structure above humankind. The 'seven strong ones' are the seven heavens, which are described as 'shidād' (strong and solid) because they are stable and do not fall or crumble, and they are kept in place and order by God's command. The verse is meant as a sign for reflection: the One who built such a mighty and enduring cosmos is certainly able to resurrect the dead, which is the argument of the surrounding verses in Surat an-Naba'. It invites people to recognize God's might and to be grateful and mindful of the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We made a blazing lamp.
interpretation: The 'blazing lamp' refers to the sun, which God created as a radiant source of intense light and heat. Unlike the moon, which reflects light, the sun blazes by its own power, and through it day is illuminated, life is sustained, plants grow, and the seasons turn. The verse points to the sun as a sign of God's power and mercy, inviting reflection on the Creator who set such a vital source of light and warmth in the heavens for humankind's benefit.

translation: And We sent down from the rain-clouds water pouring forth in abundance.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power and mercy in the natural world: the clouds laden with moisture release rain in copious, continuous streams by His command. This abundant water is a sign that the One who gives life to dead earth through rain is able to resurrect people after death, and it is a provision for humankind and their livestock, bringing forth grain, plants and lush gardens, as the following verses explain. It should therefore move people to gratitude and to reflection on the truth of the Resurrection.

translation: That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:15) points to the purpose of the water sent down from the rain clouds: God sends it so that the earth yields both grain, which is the staple food for people and livestock, and green plants and herbage. The verse presents the revival of dead land as a sign of God's power and care. He who brings forth life, sustenance, and diversity from lifeless soil through a single act of rain is certainly able to resurrect human beings after death. It also reminds people to be grateful for the provision that sustains them, and to see in nature's ordered cycle evidence of a purposeful Creator rather than chance.

translation: And gardens thickly intertwined.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Naba (78:16), completes a list of signs of God's power in creation, following the mention of grain and vegetation brought forth by rain. It points to orchards whose trees grow so dense that their branches and foliage overlap and entwine. The image shows that the One who sustains life with such abundance, beauty, and order is able to resurrect the dead, and so it calls people to reflect on God's bounty, to be grateful, and to recognize that the Day of Judgment is certain.

translation: Indeed, the Day of Decision is a appointed time.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Naba', 78:17) affirms that the Day of Judgment, when God will decide between all people and separate the righteous from the wrongdoers, is a fixed and predetermined appointment in God's knowledge. It is not random or subject to delay by human wishes or denial. The disbelievers questioned and disputed the Great News of resurrection, and this verse answers them: the day has a set time that all creation is moving toward, so accountability is certain, and people should live mindful of that meeting.

translation: The Day when the Trumpet is blown, and you will come forth in crowds.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Naba 78:18) describes the Day of Resurrection, when the angel blows the Trumpet and all of humanity is raised from the dead. People will not rise as isolated individuals but will come in large groups, each community gathered with its own kind, following its prophet or its deeds. The meaning is that the Day of Decision is a certain, collective event: every person will be summoned and driven to the place of reckoning, and no one can escape being brought to account for what they did in this world.

translation: And the heaven will be opened, so it will become gateways.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:19) describes the Day of Judgment, when the ordered structure of the sky will be undone. The heaven, which now appears as a sealed and unbroken canopy, will be split open so completely that it becomes like many gateways, as if the whole expanse were made of doors. The meaning most commonly given is that these openings are the passages through which the angels will descend to carry out God's command. The verse shows that the cosmos is wholly subject to God's will, and that what seems fixed and permanent will give way when the promised Day arrives. It is a reminder that the Day of Decision, which the disbelievers doubted, is certain.

translation: And the mountains will be set in motion and become a mirage.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:20) describes the cosmic upheaval of the Day of Judgment. The mountains, which people regard as the most solid and permanent features of the earth, will be uprooted and moved, then dissolve until they are only the appearance of mountains, like a mirage that looks like something real but has no substance. The lesson is that if even the mountains lose their firmness on that Day, then the worldly things people rely on, such as power, wealth and status, offer no real security. Only the reality of God's judgment remains, so a person should prepare for it and not be deceived by the apparent permanence of this world.

translation: Indeed, Hell has been lying in ambush.
interpretation: Hell is not a passive place but is ever-watchful and prepared, like a trap set in wait for those who transgress. It stands in readiness for the rebellious, who will not be able to evade or escape it, for it lies in wait on the path every soul must traverse. This warns that the oppressors and deniers are heading toward an appointed end that is already prepared and certain, and that no one can slip past God's reckoning.

translation: For the transgressors is a place of return (an evil destination).
interpretation: This verse from Surat An-Naba (78:22) follows the mention of Hell lying in ambush (v. 21). It means that Hell is the appointed destination and final refuge of those who exceeded all bounds in rebellion against God, denying the Day of Judgment, oppressing others, and rejecting His signs. The word 'ma'ab' implies the place to which one inevitably returns, so the verse warns that their arrogance and tyranny in this world will end not in lasting power but in a certain, just recompense, from which there is no escape.

translation: They will remain therein for ages (aḥqāb).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:23) describes the state of the transgressors who expected no reckoning, saying that they will dwell in Hell for long, successive periods of time. The word 'aḥqāb' denotes extended epochs, and its mention conveys the severity and prolonged duration of the punishment, as a warning that rejecting the Day of Judgment and denying God's signs carries grave consequences. Many scholars understand the verse not as setting a limit after which the punishment ends, but as emphasizing that these ages follow one upon another without a foreseeable end, since the following verses speak of them tasting no coolness or drink and being increased only in punishment, as a just recompense for their deeds.

translation: They will taste therein neither coolness nor drink (Qur'an 78:24).
interpretation: The verse describes the condition of the transgressors who denied the Reckoning: in Hell they find nothing to soothe them. 'Bard' can mean coolness that relieves the heat of the fire, and it can also mean sleep or rest, which is the relief that eases a suffering body. The verse therefore teaches that their punishment is complete, because they are denied both the comfort that cools the body and the drink that quenches thirst. What they are given in its place is boiling water and foul discharge, as the following verses state. The point is that the punishment fits the deeds of those who rejected the truth and never hoped for an accounting, and that no mercy or respite will reach them there.

translation: Except for scalding water and foul, freezing pus.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Naba 78:25) describes the only 'refreshment' awaiting the transgressors in Hell, who in the preceding verse are said to taste neither coolness nor drink there. Instead of relief, what they receive is itself a form of torment: boiling water that burns and a fetid, bitter-cold discharge that disgusts and pains. The verse teaches that divine recompense mirrors the deeds of those who denied the Day of Reckoning and disregarded God's signs, so that the very things that normally sustain life and bring comfort become sources of suffering for them. It serves as a solemn warning to awaken the conscience to accountability and to encourage people to seek God's mercy and forgiveness before the Day of Judgment.

translation: A fitting recompense.
interpretation: This phrase from Surat An-Naba (78:26) describes the punishment of the transgressors in Hell: it is not arbitrary or excessive but exactly matches their deeds. Their torment is a just and proportionate requital for the disbelief, denial of the Day of Reckoning, and wrongdoing they practiced in life, showing that God's judgment is perfectly balanced and that every person receives a consequence in harmony with what they earned.

translation: Indeed, they did not expect any reckoning.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:27) gives the reason for the punishment of the transgressors in Hell. Their gravest fault was not merely sinning, but living with no fear of being held to account. Because they denied or disregarded the Day of Judgment, they had no moral restraint and no sense of answerability to God for their deeds. The belief that life ends without accountability leads a person to disregard justice and truth, and so their torment is the fitting consequence of a life lived heedless of the Hereafter.

translation: And they denied Our signs with [intense] denial.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:28) describes the people of Hell who did not expect a reckoning. The intensive form 'kidhdhaba' stresses that their rejection of God's revelations and proofs was not a passing doubt but a persistent, wholehearted and obstinate denial. They did not merely neglect the signs in the Qur'an and in creation; they actively and repeatedly called them lies. Their punishment in the following verses is therefore a just recompense for deliberate and sustained denial of the truth after it was made clear to them.

translation: And everything We have recorded in a book.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Naba 78:29) affirms that God's knowledge is all-encompassing and that nothing a person does, says, or intends escapes His notice. Every deed, big or small, is precisely enumerated and written down in a record. It is a reminder that human beings are accountable, and that on the Day of Judgment, when the reckoning takes place, no one will be wronged and no action will be forgotten. It calls the believer to constant self-awareness and to live with the consciousness that all of their conduct is being preserved for the day they meet their Lord.

translation: So taste [the punishment], for We will never increase you except in torment.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Naba (78:30), is God's address to the transgressors in Hell who denied the Day of Reckoning and rejected His signs. They are told to taste the consequences of their own deeds, and the verse declares that their punishment will never ease or stay the same but will keep growing, each state of torment followed by a harsher one. The scholars note that it is among the most severe verses in the Qur'an for the people of Hell, because it removes any hope of relief. This reflects divine justice: the penalty matches their persistent disbelief and denial, and their stubborn rejection of guidance in the world leads to an ever-increasing recompense in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, for the righteous there will be a place of triumph.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Naba' (78:31), follows the description of the punishment awaiting the transgressors in Hell and sets against it the reward of those who were mindful of God. The 'muttaqun' are those who guarded themselves against God's displeasure through faith, obedience, and avoiding sin. For them, 'mafaz' is a station of success and salvation, meaning deliverance from the Fire and attainment of Paradise. The verse teaches that true victory is not worldly gain but safety from God's punishment and arrival at His lasting pleasure, and that this outcome is secured through God-consciousness in this life. It also gives comfort and motivation to believers, affirming that the effort of piety will not be lost, and that the final outcome belongs to those who fear God.

translation: Gardens and grapevines.
interpretation: This phrase is part of the description of the bounties God has prepared for the God-fearing in the Hereafter (Surah An-Naba 78:32), following the mention of 'a place of triumph' (mafaza). It specifies what that triumph consists of: lush, enclosed orchards and vineyards that signify abundance, rest, and delight. Grapes are singled out as one of the most cherished fruits of the Arabs, so naming them conveys that the reward fulfills what people most desire, a lasting, tangible fulfillment of the believers' patience and piety in this world.

translation: And full-breasted maidens of equal age,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:33) belongs to the description of the rewards awaiting the God-fearing (al-muttaqin) in Paradise. It speaks of companions who are in the prime of youth and beauty, all of one age, which signifies that the blessings of the Hereafter are perfect and free from the decline of aging. The 'equal age' implies harmony, companionship, and mutual affection among the people of Paradise, so that their joy is complete. The verse conveys that Paradise fulfills the purest human desires for love, beauty, and companionship in a dignified and everlasting form, as a reward for righteousness in this life.

translation: And a full cup, brimming over.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Naba' (78:34), describes one of the rewards awaiting the God-fearing in Paradise. The 'full cup' (ka's dihaq) is understood as a cup of pure drink, filled to the brim and flowing continuously, without ever running short. It signifies the abundance and completeness of the bliss granted in the Hereafter: the people of Paradise will not suffer scarcity or lack, and their drink will bring pure delight without the intoxication, harm, or idle speech associated with wine in this world. The image conveys generous, unending divine hospitality and the fulfillment of every desire of the righteous.

translation: They will hear therein no idle talk and no falsehood.
interpretation: This verse, describing the people of Paradise (Surah An-Naba 78:35), means that their abode is free from all the defects of worldly speech. There is no vain or purposeless talk, no lying, and no one denying or accusing another of falsehood. The verse conveys that Paradise is a place of complete purity and peace, where hearts and tongues are cleansed of malice and deceit, and where speech is only truthful, wholesome, and filled with greetings of peace and the praise of God. The blessing of a pure social environment is thus presented as a reward just as great as its physical delights.

translation: A reward from your Lord, a sufficient gift.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 78:36) concludes the description of the God-fearing's rewards in Paradise. It teaches that their blessings are not merely wages earned by deeds, but a recompense that comes from their Lord as a generous gift, given out of His grace. The word 'hisaban' means sufficient or fully proportioned: God gives them what suffices them, an abundant and precisely measured reward that leaves no need or desire unfulfilled. Thus, the believers' deeds are met with divine generosity that exceeds what the deeds alone would merit, while still being accounted with perfect justice.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, the Most Merciful; none of them has the power to address Him.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty and lordship over all creation, joined with His mercy as the Most Merciful. On the Day of Judgment, no one, whether angels, prophets, or any other being, will have the ability or authority to speak before Him or intercede, except by His leave. Every created being stands in complete submission and awe before the Creator, so that nobody can claim a right to question His judgment or to initiate speech in His presence unless He permits it.

translation: On the Day when the Spirit and the angels will stand in ranks, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who says what is right.
interpretation: The verse portrays the awe and absolute authority of the Day of Judgment. Even the Spirit (commonly understood as Gabriel) and the angels, the most honored of creatures, stand in orderly rows in silent humility before God. If the noblest beings cannot speak without divine permission, then no human can speak, plead, or intercede on their own authority. Speech on that Day is allowed only for those whom God grants leave, and only when what they say is true and just, such as a sincere intercession for those God is pleased with. The lesson is that dominion belongs wholly to God, and every person should prepare now with faith and righteous deeds and with truthful speech, since on that Day only truth will be heard.

translation: That is the True Day. So whoever wills, let him take a path of return to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Day of Resurrection, when the spirit and the angels stand in ranks and none speaks except by the leave of the Most Merciful, is an undeniable reality, not a myth or a possibility. Because it is certain, the verse turns to the listener's responsibility: the way back to God is open to everyone, and each person is invited to choose it by faith and righteous action in this life. The 'return' (ma'ab) is not merely a destination that all will reach, but a journey one prepares for, so the wise person lives now in a way that makes the meeting with his Lord a place of safety and honor rather than of regret.

translation: Indeed, We have warned you of a punishment that is near, on the Day when a person will look at what his hands have sent forth, and the disbeliever will say, 'Oh, I wish I were dust!'
interpretation: The verse says the Day of Judgment is close and certain, so that no one can claim they were not warned. On that Day every person sees their own record of deeds with nothing hidden and no one to blame. The disbeliever, facing the full consequences of rejecting faith and the harm of his own actions, is overcome by regret and despair.
