He wishes he had never been created, or had been mere dust like the animals, which are turned to dust after being judged and so face no further reckoning. The verse urges people to take stock of their deeds now, while repentance and change are still possible, because the only thing that will matter later is what they have already sent ahead.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By those [angels] who pull out [souls] with force.
interpretation: God opens the surah with an oath by the angels of death who extract the souls of the disbelievers and the wicked, tearing them out harshly and thoroughly, drawing them from the depths of the body. The oath underscores the certainty of death, resurrection, and the Day of Judgment that the surah goes on to affirm: just as these angels carry out God's command without fail, the promised Hour will surely come, and everyone will be brought to account.

translation: And [by] those that draw out [gently and] swiftly.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Nazi'at (79:2), continues the oath begun in the opening verse. God swears by angels who withdraw the souls of the believers with ease and gentleness, as though loosening a knot. The word 'nashitat' conveys the idea of drawing out with agility. The oath points to the certainty of death and resurrection: the same angels who take souls at death are under God's command, and just as they carry out their task precisely, the promised Day of Judgment will come to pass without fail. It reminds the listener that death is an appointed, orderly process carried out by God's servants, and that every soul will be called to account.

translation: And by those that glide swiftly, gliding along.
interpretation: This verse is an oath in Surat An-Nazi'at, following the oaths by the angels who pull out souls and those who draw them out gently. Most commentators understand 'as-sabihat' as the angels who, after seizing the souls, glide swiftly through the heavens and the space between heaven and earth, carrying them and executing God's commands with ease and speed. The oath draws attention to the power, obedience and precision of the angels, and affirms that the Resurrection and the reckoning, which the surah goes on to describe, are certain and will be carried out exactly as God ordains.

translation: And those that race ahead, outstripping [one another] in a race.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nazi'at, 79:4) continues the oath begun in the opening verses of the surah, swearing by angels who carry out God's commands. According to the most widely held interpretation, it refers to the angels who speed ahead to carry out the commands of God, or who hasten with the souls of the righteous to Paradise, outstripping one another in obedience. The oath points to the certainty of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment: just as these angels swiftly and faithfully execute God's will, so the promised Hour will arrive without fail, and its coming cannot be delayed or resisted.

translation: And those that arrange and direct each affair.
interpretation: In this verse (Surat an-Nazi'at, 79:5), God swears by the angels who carry out His commands in governing creation. After having been given their instructions, they manage the affairs of the world by His leave: delivering His decrees, sending down provision and mercy, and executing His decisions. The oath points to the order and precision of the unseen realm, showing that nothing in creation is left to chance but is arranged by God's will through those He appoints. It is also a reminder that the Resurrection, which the surah goes on to affirm, is just as certain and just as easy for the One who directs all affairs.

translation: On the Day when the quaking one shall quake,
interpretation: The verse refers to the first blast of the Trumpet on the Day of Judgment, when the earth and everything in it will be violently shaken and all life will be struck down. It reminds the listener that the world's apparent stability is temporary and fully subject to God's command. This should awaken the heart from heedlessness, since an overwhelming event is certain to come, after which a second blast follows and all are resurrected to be held accountable. Hearing of it should lead a person to repent and prepare for that Day before it arrives.

translation: The second blast follows it.
interpretation: This verse (79:7) describes the Day of Resurrection, in which the first blast of the trumpet, which shakes and annihilates all creation, is immediately followed by a second blast that brings the dead back to life. The verse conveys the swift, inescapable succession of events at the end of time: no interval of relief separates the destruction of this world from the rising of humankind for judgment, reminding the believer that the Hour comes suddenly and that preparation for it must be made now.

translation: On that Day, hearts will be trembling (anxious and throbbing with fear).
interpretation: This verse from Surah An-Nazi'at (79:8) describes the inner state of people on the Day of Resurrection. When the great event of resurrection occurs, hearts will shake with dread and anxiety, especially the hearts of those who denied the resurrection and lived heedlessly. Their fear is not merely outward but a deep, inner agitation, as they realize the truth they once rejected and anticipate the reckoning. The verse teaches that the true weight of that Day is felt first in the heart, and it calls the listener to reflect and prepare through faith and righteous action, so that the heart may be at peace on that Day.

translation: Their eyes will be humbled.
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surat an-Nazi'at (79:9), where it describes the hearts of the deniers on the Day of Resurrection, hearts that tremble, and eyes that are lowered in humiliation and fear. The meaning is that those who were arrogant in this world and scoffed at the promise of resurrection will find their pride completely broken. Their lowered, downcast gaze shows the inner terror and shame they feel when they face the reality they once denied, and it shows that on that Day no one can hold on to arrogance or deny the truth.

translation: They say: 'Shall we really be returned to our former state of life?'
interpretation: This verse (An-Nazi'at 79:10) records the mocking disbelief of those who deny the resurrection. They ask in astonishment whether, after dying, they could be restored to the condition they were in before, that is, to life as they knew it. The word 'al-hafirah' refers to the previous state, like footprints marking the path one has already walked. Their question is not sincere inquiry but ridicule, resting on the assumption that once a body has decayed, bringing it back is impossible. The verse exposes the shortsightedness of denying the afterlife, since the One who created them the first time is fully able to recreate them, and the following verses answer this doubt by showing how easily it will occur through a single blast.

translation: "What! When we have become decayed, hollow bones?"
interpretation: This verse (An-Nazi'at 79:11) records the disbelievers' mocking denial of bodily resurrection. They regard it as absurd that people whose bodies have rotted away to brittle, hollow bones could ever be restored to life. Their question comes from judging God's power by the limits of human experience. The Qur'an answers this elsewhere: the One who created them from nothing the first time can recreate them, and doing so is no difficulty for Him. The verse shows how disbelief in the Hereafter often rests on arrogant incredulity rather than on any rational proof, and it calls the reader to reflect on the Creator's boundless power over life and death.

translation: They say: "That, then, would be a losing return!"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 79:12) voices the disbelievers' mocking reaction to the idea of resurrection. When told they will be brought back to life after death, they sneer that if such a return were real, it would be a ruinous one for them, since by their own logic it would mean accountability for lives spent denying it. Their jest unwittingly concedes that they are on the path of loss, and it exposes how ridicule is used to evade facing the truth of the Hereafter. The verse shows that a person's denial does not alter reality: the return will come, and the real loss belongs to those who disbelieved in it.

translation: For it will be but a single cry (a single blast), and at once they will be looking on.
interpretation: The verse teaches that resurrection, which the deniers regard as impossible, will require no elaborate process or effort from God. A single mighty blast, understood as the blowing of the Trumpet, will be enough to bring all of creation out of their graves and set them standing in bewilderment before their Lord. It reminds the reader that God's power over life and death is absolute and instantaneous, that what seems remote and improbable to human reasoning is effortless for Him, and that the deniers' mockery will give way to helpless awareness when the Day arrives.

translation: And behold, they are on the surface of the earth, wide awake.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Nazi'at (79:14), describes the instant of resurrection that follows the single mighty blast. The word 'sahira' denotes the open face of the earth, a plain where no one sleeps. The people who were dead and buried in their graves are suddenly brought up and standing on the earth's surface, fully awake and aware, ready for reckoning. The verse stresses how effortless resurrection is for God: it takes just one cry, and humanity is transformed from death to a state of alert presence before Him. Those who denied the return to life will see that what they scoffed at has come about, with no chance of escape or delay.

translation: Has the story of Moses reached you?
interpretation: This rhetorical question, which opens the account of Moses in Surah Ta-Ha (20:9), is not asking for information but is meant to draw the Prophet Muhammad's attention and prepare him for an important lesson. It invites him, and every listener, to reflect on how God supported Moses through hardship, called him to prophecy, and carried out His plan despite the power of Pharaoh. In this way it comforts the Prophet in the opposition he faces, reminding him that the path of the messengers before him was also one of trial, patience, and eventual divine help.

translation: When his Lord called out to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
interpretation: The verse recalls the moment Moses was summoned by God directly, in a valley made holy by the divine presence. It shows that prophethood is a gift of God's choosing, not something a person earns by his own effort. The call to Moses came as a solemn command that required him to leave his ordinary state and answer with humility and reverence. The setting also teaches that places touched by divine revelation are to be honored, and that a person approaching God must put aside pride and worldly attachments. The call came as a preparation for sending Moses to confront Pharaoh's tyranny, so it links worship and inner purification with the duty to speak truth to power.

translation: Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed all bounds.
interpretation: This verse is God's command to Moses (peace be upon him) at the start of his mission, and it shows that prophetic duty is directed first at the source of oppression and corruption. Pharaoh is described as having 'transgressed' (tagha), meaning he exceeded the limits set for a created being by claiming absolute authority, even divinity, and by oppressing his people. The command teaches that tyranny calls for confrontation with truth, and that those who rebel against God must still be addressed with a message and an opportunity to repent, as the following verses show by instructing Moses to speak to him gently. Moses is sent not out of hostility but as a warner to call the powerful back to servitude to God and justice toward people.

translation: And say to him: 'Would you be willing to purify yourself?'
interpretation: In this verse, God instructs Moses on how to approach Pharaoh, the most arrogant tyrant of his age. Rather than commanding or confronting him harshly, Moses is told to pose a gentle question that offers a choice: 'Would you like to purify yourself?' The word 'tazakka' implies growth and cleansing of the soul from disbelief, arrogance, and wrongdoing, so that it may flourish in faith and good character. The lesson is that calling people to God should begin with courteous, soft speech that appeals to a person's own desire for betterment and respects their dignity, even when addressing someone who has transgressed greatly, because such an approach is most likely to open the heart to guidance.

translation: And that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him.
interpretation: In this verse (Qur'an 79:19) Moses is told to offer Pharaoh a path to purification and guidance. Guidance toward the Lord is described as leading to khashyah, a reverent awe that comes from true knowledge of God. Fear of God is therefore the fruit of knowing Him rightly, not of ignorance or terror. Whoever recognizes the greatness, power and mercy of his Creator becomes conscious of Him, and that consciousness restrains him from arrogance and wrongdoing. Pharaoh's tyranny came from heedlessness of his Lord, so the remedy begins with being guided to Him, after which humility and obedience follow.

translation: So he showed him the greatest sign.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nazi'at 79:20) refers to Moses, peace be upon him, who after being sent to Pharaoh presented him with clear proof of his prophethood. The 'greatest sign' is most commonly understood as the staff that turned into a serpent (and the hand that shone white), a miracle meant to convince Pharaoh that Moses came from God. The verse shows that God sends guidance accompanied by undeniable evidence, so that rejection stems from stubborn arrogance and not from lack of proof, as Pharaoh's response in the next verse shows: he denied and disobeyed.

translation: But he denied and disobeyed.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Nazi'at (79:21), describes Pharaoh's response after Moses showed him the great sign. Despite clear proof, he rejected the truth of the message and defied God's command out of arrogance. It teaches that disbelief is not for lack of evidence but often stems from pride and stubbornness, and that rejecting the truth in the heart naturally leads to disobedience in action: denial of belief is followed by defiance in deed.

translation: Then he turned his back, striving hard.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 79:22) describes Pharaoh after he saw the great sign that Moses brought. He did not turn to God in belief; he turned away from the truth and hurried off, devoting his effort to opposing it. His striving was not toward guidance but toward plotting against Moses, gathering his magicians, and rallying his people against him. The verse shows that someone who is shown clear proof and still refuses it does not stay neutral. Arrogance pushes him to use his energy and power to resist the truth and to harm those who carry it.

translation: Then he gathered [his people] and called out.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 79:23) describes Pharaoh's response after Moses showed him the great sign. Rather than submitting, he assembled his magicians and courtiers and proclaimed to them in a public declaration. This shows how arrogance leads a ruler to use his power and public platform to rally people against the truth instead of heeding it. The gathering and the proclamation that follows ("I am your lord, the most high") reveal that his rebellion was not merely private disbelief but an open attempt to mislead others and establish his own false claim to lordship.

translation: And he said, "I am your lord, the most high."
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 79:24) records Pharaoh's climactic claim to absolute divinity after he gathered his people and called out to them. It shows how unchecked political power, when joined with arrogance, can lead a person to claim a status that belongs to God alone. Pharaoh's words go beyond ordinary tyranny: he claims supreme authority over the lives, laws and destinies of his subjects, and he demands that they submit to him as their ultimate master. The Qur'an presents this as the height of transgression (tughyan), which is why God seized him with a punishing example in this world and the next. The lesson is that any claim to ultimate sovereignty by a created being is false, and that true lordship belongs only to God, so human power is accountable and cannot be absolute.

translation: So God seized him with an exemplary punishment for the last and the first [transgression].
interpretation: This verse describes how God punished Pharaoh by drowning him, making him a deterrent for all who come after. The punishment answered both his earlier sin of denying Moses and claiming to be the 'highest lord' (his last statement), and his earlier defiance in saying 'I know of no god for you other than myself.' In this reading, his punishment in this world through drowning was an example to others, while the chastisement of the Hereafter awaits him as well. The lesson is that tyranny and arrogance toward God's messengers bring a just and exemplary recompense, and that rejecting truth after it has been clearly shown leads to ruin in both worlds.

translation: Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears [God].
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 79:26, following the account of Pharaoh's defiance of Moses and his punishment in this world and the next) teaches that the downfall of arrogant tyrants is not mere history but a moral warning. Only those whose hearts are alive with awe of God, who are humble and receptive, will draw benefit from such events. They reflect on how rebellion and claims of lordship end in ruin, and so they are moved to obedience, humility, and accountability before their Lord, whereas the heedless and proud pass over the same signs without being changed.

translation: Are you more difficult to create, or the heaven? He built it.
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical question addressed to those who denied the resurrection, and it argues from the greater to the lesser. The heavens are vast, ordered, and sturdy, and God brought them into being and built them. If He could create something so immense, then re-creating human beings after death is far easier for Him and well within His power. The denial of resurrection is therefore unreasonable, because it underestimates the power of the Creator. The verse invites people to reflect on the grandeur of the cosmos as evidence of God's omnipotence and of the certainty of the Hereafter.

translation: He raised its vault high and proportioned it perfectly.
interpretation: The verse (An-Nazi'at 79:28) speaks of the heavens, which God raised high above the earth without any visible support, and made them flawless, balanced and harmonious, free of flaws or cracks. The 'raising' points to the vastness and height of the sky, and the 'proportioning' points to the precise order God placed in it. This is offered as evidence of His power: One who can build such a vast and ordered creation can certainly bring people back to life after death, which is the argument the surrounding verses are making against those who denied the resurrection.

translation: And He darkened its night and brought forth its daylight.
interpretation: The verse points to God's power in ordering the heavens: He made the night dark and covered the world in its shade, then brought out the bright morning light. Day and night follow each other in a precise rhythm, and this rhythm is not accidental. It is a sign of a deliberate Creator who sustains life and gives people time for rest and for work. Anyone who sees how reliably the darkness yields to light should be led to recognize that a power able to arrange the cosmos in this way can also resurrect the dead, which is the argument the surrounding verses make to those who denied the afterlife.

translation: And the earth, after that, He spread out (made smooth and expanded it for habitation).
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 79:30) teaches that after creating the heavens, God prepared the earth as a place fit for human life. The word 'dahaha' conveys spreading out and making smooth and ready, which many commentators understand as God extending the earth, causing its waters and pastures to emerge (as the next verse states), and fixing its mountains. The verse points to God's deliberate care in preparing a home for humankind, and it serves as a sign of His power and favor, supporting the argument that the One who created such vast and ordered creation is fully able to resurrect people after death.

translation: He brought forth from it its water and its pasture.
interpretation: The verse points to God's provision in shaping the earth for living beings: after spreading out the earth, He made springs, rivers and rain-fed waters gush from it, and caused plants, grasses and fodder to grow, so that people may eat and their livestock may graze. It is meant as a sign of His power and care, and as a reminder that this sustenance is a blessing that calls for gratitude, and that the One who brings life out of lifeless earth is able to resurrect the dead.

translation: And the mountains He set firmly in place.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nazi'at 79:32) points to God's power in creation: after spreading out the earth, He fixed the mountains in it like pegs so that the earth would be stable and not shake or sway with its inhabitants. The mountains are therefore both a sign of divine might and a mercy, giving the earth balance and making it a secure home for humankind and animals, which should lead people to reflect on the One who created and ordered all this and to recognize that resurrecting them is easy for Him.

translation: As provision for you and for your livestock.
interpretation: This phrase (from Surah An-Nazi'at 79:33, and similarly 'Abasa 80:32) concludes the mention of God's gifts of water, pasture, and vegetation from the earth. It teaches that these blessings are not accidental but a deliberate divine provision for the sustenance and enjoyment of both humans and the animals that serve them. The verse points to God's care and generosity in creating an interdependent natural order, calling people to recognize the Provider through His favors, to be grateful, and to reflect that the One who brings life from dead land is also able to resurrect the dead and hold humanity accountable.

translation: But when the greatest calamity (the Overwhelming Event) comes to pass,
interpretation: The 'greatest calamity' (al-Ṭāmmah al-Kubrā) is the Day of Resurrection and Judgment, an event so overwhelming that it overtops every misfortune a person has known in this world. The verse is a solemn warning that this Day will inevitably arrive, and that all the ease, defiance and heedlessness of the worldly life will be eclipsed by it. It prepares the listener for the verses that follow, which divide humanity by their conduct: those who transgressed and preferred the worldly life, and those who feared standing before their Lord and restrained the self from desire. The verse therefore calls the believer to live with the awareness that every deed will be weighed on that Day.

translation: On the Day when man will remember what he strove for.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 79:35) says that on the Day of Resurrection, when the great overwhelming event (al-Tammah al-Kubra) arrives, every person will recall all of his deeds, good and bad, that he worked for in worldly life. What he had forgotten or neglected will come back vividly to his mind, and he will see that his life was a striving whose outcome now stands before him. The verse is a warning that our efforts are never lost: each person should therefore examine what he is striving for now, and direct his effort toward what will bring him benefit on that Day, since the record of his own striving will be his proof or his reproach.

translation: And Hellfire will be brought into full view for whoever sees.
interpretation: This verse (an-Nazi'at 79:36) describes the Day of Judgment, when Hell will no longer be a hidden or distant reality but will be openly displayed before all people. The words 'for whoever sees' indicate that every person will behold it with their own eyes, so that denial becomes impossible and the warning given by the messengers is confirmed as fact. The sight is meant to awaken fear and heedfulness: those who transgressed and preferred the worldly life will witness the destination awaiting them, while the God-fearing who restrained themselves from desires will see it as a danger they were spared. Thus the verse urges the reader to reflect now, while there is still time, on the reality of the Hereafter and to prepare through faith and righteous conduct.

translation: As for he who transgressed,
interpretation: This verse, from Surat An-Nazi'at (79:37), opens the description of those destined for Hellfire. 'Tagha' means to overstep all bounds set by God: to rebel against Him through arrogance, disbelief, and persistent disobedience, treating one's own desires and worldly power as supreme. The verse teaches that the root of ruin is not mere human weakness or occasional error but a defiant exceeding of limits, in which a person refuses to recognize their Creator's authority and their own accountability. It sets up the verses that follow, which show that this transgression is joined with preferring the life of this world over the Hereafter, and that such a path leads to the blazing Fire.

translation: And preferred the life of this world.
interpretation: This verse (An-Nazi'at 79:38) describes the one who transgressed all bounds: he chose the fleeting pleasures, status, and gains of worldly life over the life to come. His preference was not a mere oversight but a deliberate prioritizing of immediate desire over obedience to God and preparation for the Hereafter. The Qur'an presents this misplaced priority as the root of his rebellion, since whoever makes this world his chief goal becomes willing to violate divine limits to secure it, and his end, as the following verse says, is the Hellfire as his abode.

translation: Then indeed, Hellfire will be the refuge.
interpretation: This verse (Surah An-Nazi'at 79:39) concludes the description of the one who transgressed and preferred the life of this world. It teaches that whoever rebels against God and gives priority to worldly desires over the Hereafter will find that his final destination and lasting abode is Hell. The word 'refuge' (ma'wa) is used with stern irony: the place where such a person ends up seeking shelter is not one of safety and rest, but of punishment, showing that unchecked arrogance and attachment to worldly gain lead ultimately to ruin.

translation: But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from vain desire,
interpretation: The verse describes the person who is saved: one who is conscious that he will one day stand before God for reckoning, and that awareness becomes a real inner restraint. Fear of God's judgment is not mere emotion but produces action, namely the daily struggle to hold the self back from whatever its whims urge against God's guidance. The verse suggests that the root of transgression is the unchecked desire of the soul, and that the root of salvation is the union of two things: awareness of accountability and disciplined self-control. Whoever lives with this awareness chooses obedience over impulse, and in the following verse is promised Paradise as his abode.

translation: Then indeed, Paradise will be the refuge.
interpretation: This verse (An-Nazi'at 79:41) is the outcome promised to the person who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from base desire (79:40). It teaches that real success comes from self-mastery: whoever keeps his desires in check out of awareness of accountability before God will find his lasting home in Paradise. It stands in contrast to the one who transgressed and preferred worldly life, whose abode is Hellfire. The point is that the final resting place of humankind is decided by whether a person's reverence for God governs his inclinations or his appetites govern him.

translation: They ask you about the Hour: when will its arrival take place?
interpretation: The verse (Al-A'raf 7:187) shows that the people kept pressing the Prophet to name the time of the Last Hour, some out of mockery and some out of curiosity. The answer that follows in the same verse is that knowledge of its timing belongs to God alone, and that it will come suddenly. The question is therefore redirected: the believer's task is not to calculate when the end will come but to prepare for it through faith and righteous action. Hiding the timing of the Hour keeps people mindful and accountable at every moment, and it affirms that some matters of the unseen are reserved for God alone, even the Prophet does not know them.

translation: In what are you concerned with mentioning it? (Qur'an 79:43) — that is, what part do you have in stating when the Hour will come?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who keep asking the Prophet Muhammad about the exact time of the Final Hour. Knowledge of its timing belongs to God alone, and even the Prophet has no share in it, so it is not his role to specify it. His task is to warn people of its certainty and prepare them for it, as the next verse says, 'To your Lord is its final term.' The lesson is to turn from speculation about the unseen hidden by God to the practical duty of readiness through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: To your Lord belongs its final term (the knowledge of its appointed time).
interpretation: This verse (Surat An-Nazi'at 79:44) answers those who kept asking the Prophet about the exact time of the Hour. It teaches that the knowledge of when the Hour will come ends with God alone. Neither the Prophet nor any angel or human being has been given that knowledge. The Prophet's role is only to warn those who fear it, so people should stop asking about its timing and prepare for it with faith and righteous deeds.

translation: You are only a warner for those who fear it (the Hour).
interpretation: The Prophet's role is to warn, not to compel belief or to bring about the Hour's timing, which belongs to God alone. Though his warning is addressed to all people, only those who hold the Hour in awe and are mindful of being held to account actually benefit from it. A heart that fears the reckoning is receptive to reminder and moves toward guidance, while those who are heedless remain unmoved however clear the warning. The verse thus redirects attention from idle questions about when the Hour will come to preparing for it through reverence and righteous conduct.

translation: On the Day they see it, it will be as if they had stayed in the world only an evening or the morning following that evening.
interpretation: The verse says that when people witness the Hour, the long span of worldly life, and of their time in the grave, will seem to them extremely brief, no more than part of a single day. Measured against the endless life to come and the gravity of the reckoning, all the pleasures, delays, and worries of this world shrink to almost nothing. This should make the listener stop treating the world as the goal and prepare for the Hereafter, which is real and lasting, rather than being deceived by the apparent length of worldly time or by doubts about when the Hour will come.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. He frowned and turned away.
interpretation: The verse opens Surah 'Abasa with a gentle divine rebuke. According to the widely accepted account, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was engaged in inviting the leaders of Quraysh to Islam when the blind man Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum came and asked to be taught. The Prophet, hoping the influential men might accept the message, showed displeasure at the interruption and turned away. The verse conveys that sincere seekers, regardless of their status or disability, must never be slighted in favor of the powerful, and that worth in God's sight rests on sincerity and the desire for purification, not on rank. The use of the third person ('he frowned') rather than direct address is understood as a tender form of reproach that preserves the Prophet's honor while still teaching him and the community an enduring lesson about equality and humility in calling to God.

translation: Because the blind man came to him.
interpretation: This verse, the second of Surah 'Abasa, gives the reason for the Prophet's frowning and turning away in the first verse. The blind man, Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came seeking guidance while the Prophet was occupied with inviting some leading men of Quraysh to Islam. The Qur'an gently reproaches the Prophet for giving priority to the powerful and influential over a sincere seeker, even a humble and disabled one. The lesson is that sincerity in seeking truth matters more than status, that no sincere seeker should be slighted, and that the worth of a person lies in his eagerness for faith and purification, not in rank or wealth. Even the Prophet is held to the highest standard of attentiveness and fairness in conveying the message.

translation: And what would make you know that perhaps he might be purified?
interpretation: The verse comes from Surat 'Abasa, where God gently rebukes the Prophet for turning away from the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum, who came seeking guidance, because he was occupied with the leaders of Quraysh. The rhetorical question reminds the Prophet that he cannot know the hidden state of hearts or who will benefit from his teaching. The seeker who comes humbly, wanting to learn, may be the one who grows in faith and moral purity, so no sincere seeker should be slighted for the sake of those who appear more influential. Worth in God's sight depends on sincerity and openness to purification, not on status, and a teacher should give his care to the one who is eager to be purified.

translation: Or that he might be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah 'Abasa (80:4), explains what might have come of the blind man's request to the Prophet ﷺ. It suggests that he might have taken heed and gained real benefit from the teaching. The verse stresses that a sincere seeker of guidance is worth far more attention than the prestige of the powerful who show indifference. The worth of a person is measured by readiness to learn and to be moved by admonition, not by rank or status. Those who come in earnest humility should be given priority in the work of calling people to God.

translation: As for him who considers himself self-sufficient (Qur'an 80:5)
interpretation: The verse describes a person who regards himself as free of need for guidance, for God, and for the people around him, because of his wealth, status, or pride. Such a person turns away from the message and from those who offer it, and he shows disdain toward it. In context (Surah 'Abasa), the Prophet was giving his attention to such a man, one of the powerful Quraysh leaders, while a blind man who sincerely sought guidance was left waiting. The verse teaches that a person's sense of self-sufficiency is a spiritual illusion, since every human being depends on God. It also teaches that the call to truth should be directed first toward those who sincerely seek it, and not toward those who are arrogantly indifferent.

translation: Yet you give him your attention.
interpretation: This verse is from Surat 'Abasa (80:6). It gently rebukes the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) for turning his attention to a wealthy, influential man of Quraysh, hoping he would accept Islam, while he was inattentive to the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum, who came sincerely seeking guidance. The lesson is that a person's worth lies in sincerity and eagerness for truth, not in status or wealth. A preacher's concern should go first to those who truly seek to learn and purify themselves, rather than being drawn to the powerful out of eagerness for their approval or the hope of their following.

translation: And you are not accountable if he does not purify himself.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:7) consoles and clarifies the limits of the Prophet's responsibility. His duty was to convey the message clearly, while guiding hearts and bringing about self-purification lies with God alone. The verse addresses the case of the arrogant, self-sufficient leaders of Quraysh whom the Prophet had been eager to win over. It teaches that a caller to God must not exhaust himself over those who turn away, nor give them priority over sincere seekers, such as the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum, who came eager to learn. Success in calling people to faith is not measured by their response, since the caller is responsible for conveying the truth, not for their acceptance of it.

translation: But as for him who came to you striving earnestly,
interpretation: This verse, from Surah 'Abasa (80:8), contrasts with the preceding verses that rebuke the Prophet for turning away from the blind man, Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum. It describes the sincere seeker who comes eagerly, motivated by a genuine desire for guidance and purification. The word 'yas'a' (striving) conveys earnestness and effort, teaching that true value lies in a person's sincerity and spiritual yearning, not in social rank, wealth, or influence. Those who actively seek knowledge and righteousness deserve the greatest attention and care from those who teach and guide.

translation: While he fears [Allah].
interpretation: This phrase from Surah 'Abasa (80:9) describes the blind man, Ibn Umm Maktum, who came to the Prophet seeking guidance. His fear of Allah (khashyah) is the mark of a sincere seeker whose heart is ready to benefit from reminder. The verse teaches that true worth before Allah is measured by sincerity, humility, and God-consciousness rather than by status, wealth, or influence, and that those who come eagerly with fear of Allah deserve priority and attention in receiving guidance over those who are indifferent and self-sufficient.

translation: So you are distracted from him (paying him no attention).
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:10) gently rebukes the Prophet ﷺ for turning his attention away from the blind man, Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, who came sincerely seeking guidance, while the Prophet was occupied with inviting the notables of Quraysh. The verse teaches that a sincere seeker of knowledge and purification deserves priority and care over those who are prominent but indifferent, and that the worth of a person lies in the eagerness of his heart for truth, not in his rank, wealth, or status. It also sets a principle for the caller to faith: not to be so preoccupied with winning over the powerful that he neglects the humble who truly come with fear and yearning for God.

translation: No! Indeed, it is a reminder.
interpretation: The verse is a firm rebuke to the attitude of 'Abasa, where the Prophet was drawn to the wealthy notables while turning away from the blind man who came seeking guidance. The word 'No!' corrects that conduct: the Qur'an's message is not to be pursued by courting the powerful or measured by their status. It is a reminder, a gift of admonition for anyone who sincerely wishes to be mindful. Its worth does not depend on the importance of those who accept it, and those who are eager to learn deserve the most attention, since the Qur'an exists to awaken hearts that are open to it, not to be pressed on those who feel self-sufficient and turn away.

translation: So whoever wills may remember it.
interpretation: This verse (Surat 'Abasa, 80:12) stresses that the Qur'an is a reminder whose benefit depends on a person's own free choice. God has made the message clear and sufficient, so anyone who wants guidance can take it to heart and act on it, and no one is forced. This places moral responsibility on each person: those who choose to heed the reminder gain its benefit, while those who turn away have only themselves to blame. It also implies that the Qur'an's dignity does not depend on whether people accept it, since its value is intrinsic, and the choice to remember affects only the one who makes it.

translation: In honored scrolls,
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:13) describes the Qur'an's exalted status and protected origin. The 'honored scrolls' signify that its message is held in a noble, revered state in the heavenly record, free from any corruption or alteration. This teaches that the revelation is not an ordinary or insignificant text to be treated lightly, but a dignified reminder whose source is lofty and pure, so those who receive it should approach it with reverence, respect, and sincere attention rather than disregard, as the preceding verses rebuke the one who turned away from it.

translation: Exalted and purified.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Abs (80:14), describes the pages of the Qur'an recorded in honored scrolls. 'Exalted' means these revelations hold a lofty rank with God and in the highest heavens, above any worldly text; 'purified' means they are kept free from every trace of falsehood, corruption, doubt, and the touch of Satan or impure hands. The verse affirms that the Qur'an's source and message are sacred and protected, which calls for reverence toward it and for approaching it with sincerity and a clean heart.

translation: By the hands of scribes (angelic emissaries),
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 80:15) describes the noble honored Qur'an as being carried by the hands of angelic scribes or messengers who transmit revelation from God. It affirms the purity and elevated status of the revelation: it passes through trustworthy, righteous intermediaries, so no corruption or alteration can touch it between its heavenly source and the Prophet. The word 'safara' conveys both writing and acting as an envoy who brings about reconciliation, suggesting that these angels faithfully convey God's message and bring people closer to Him.

translation: Noble and virtuous (scribes).
interpretation: This phrase (Qur'an 80:16) describes the angels who carry and record the revelation and the deeds of people. They are 'kiram', meaning honorable and elevated in rank with God, and 'barara', meaning obedient, pure and righteous, never disobeying Him. The verse underscores the dignity and purity of the Qur'an's transmission: the Message is preserved in sacred pages carried by hands that are pure and trustworthy, so it is free from corruption or falsification, and it calls humans to honor and respect the revelation.

translation: May man be destroyed! How ungrateful he is!
interpretation: The verse (Abbasa 80:17) rebukes the human being for his stubborn denial and ingratitude toward his Lord. Despite being created from a humble drop of fluid, provided for, and sustained at every stage of life, he turns away from God and refuses to acknowledge His favors. The phrase 'may he be destroyed' is an expression of strong censure, not a literal wish, conveying astonishment at how one so dependent on God's care can be so persistent in disbelief and thanklessness. The verses that follow, which recount his creation, his path through life, his death, and his resurrection, show that gratitude and humility are the fitting response to his Creator.

translation: From what thing did He create him?
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:18) is a rhetorical question that points human beings to their humble origin so as to curb arrogance and ingratitude. The next verse answers it: He created man from a mere sperm-drop and shaped him in due measure. The meaning is that a being formed from such lowly matter, who owes his existence, form, and every faculty entirely to God, has no grounds for pride or for turning away from his Creator's guidance, and should instead respond with humility, gratitude, and obedience.

translation: From a sperm-drop He created him, then proportioned him.
interpretation: The verse points to the humble origin of the human being: a tiny drop of fluid, which God shaped and measured out with precise stages, form, lifespan, provision, and destiny. This is meant to humble human arrogance, for one who began as a minute drop has no ground for pride or for turning away from his Creator, and it shows that every aspect of a person's existence is governed by God's deliberate measure and wisdom rather than by chance or by his own power.

translation: Then He made the way easy for him.
interpretation: The verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:20) points to God's grace in guiding a human being through life from the moment of creation. The most widely held reading is that God made the path of birth easy, bringing a person out of the womb with ease after shaping and measuring him. Another reading takes the path to be the way of guidance, meaning that God has made it clear and accessible through reason and revelation. In either case the verse is a reminder of the human being's total dependence on God's care. It stresses that nothing in one's life is self-made, and it makes ingratitude and arrogance toward the Creator all the more unjustified.

translation: Then He caused him to die and provided a grave for him. (Qur'an 80:21)
interpretation: The verse points to death as a mercy and honor for human beings: God did not leave the dead body exposed like the bodies of animals, but ordained that it be buried in a grave. Death is therefore not an end in itself but a stage in a divinely ordered journey, running from creation to death to burial and then resurrection. It reminds people that their life and death are in God's hands, and that this should humble them and keep them from arrogance and ingratitude toward their Creator.

translation: Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:22) completes the account of the human life cycle: after God creates a person, causes him to die, and has him buried, He will raise him back to life at the time of His own choosing. The phrase 'when He wills' stresses that the timing of resurrection belongs to God alone, not to any human calculation or demand. Resurrection is thus presented as certain, yet its hour is hidden, and it is as easy for the One who originated creation as the first creation was. The verse is meant to remind the heedless and ungrateful human being that he is wholly dependent on his Lord, who gave him life and will bring him back to account for his deeds.

translation: No! Man has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 80:23) rebukes the disbelieving, ungrateful human being described in the preceding verses, who is quick to deny despite being created from a drop of fluid and having his path made easy. The word 'No!' rejects his arrogance and any claim that he has rendered due thanks. Despite all of God's favors, no person has fully discharged the duties of gratitude and obedience that God has required. The verse humbles human pride: instead of boasting or denying, a person should recognize his shortcomings, acknowledge his dependence on his Creator, and strive to fulfill God's commands.

translation: Let man then look at his food.
interpretation: The verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:24) invites a person to reflect on the origin of the food he eats every day and to see in it a sign of God's power and care. What seems an ordinary routine depends on a chain of events no human controls: rain falls, the earth splits open, and grain, fruits, and pasture grow, as the following verses describe. The one who brought this sustenance into being out of lifeless earth is able to bring man back to life after death. The verse therefore calls for gratitude and humility, and for acknowledging that one's provision is a gift from God, so that the believer is led from material blessings to faith in the Creator and the Resurrection.

translation: We poured down water in abundance.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:25) is part of a passage inviting the human being to reflect on his food and the divine care behind it. The pouring of water in abundance refers to the rain that God sends from the sky, which softens and revives the lifeless earth. It points to the fact that sustenance does not originate in human effort alone: before any plowing or planting, there is a gift from God that makes growth possible. Recognizing this should lead a person to gratitude and humility, and strengthen belief in God's power to bring life from barren ground, just as He is able to resurrect people after death.

translation: Then We split the earth, splitting it open.
interpretation: The verse describes a stage in God's provision of sustenance for humankind. After sending down water in abundance from the sky, God cleaves the earth open, so that the soil breaks apart and allows seeds to sprout and plants to rise through it. It points to God's deliberate design in the natural world, in which the earth is made yielding and fertile, and the emergence of plants from the ground is not chance but a blessing from the Creator. Human beings are meant to reflect on their food as a gift from God and respond with gratitude and faith, remembering that the same power that brings life from dead soil can bring them back to life on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: And We caused to grow therein grain.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:27) is part of a sequence in which God points human beings to His provision and power. After the earth is split open by water, He brings forth grain from it, the staple on which human life depends. Its meaning is that the sustenance people take for granted comes from God's deliberate care and not from chance, so reflecting on the food in front of them should lead to gratitude, to recognition of His power to give life, including resurrection, and to obedience to Him.

translation: And grapes and vegetables (fresh edible plants).
interpretation: This verse belongs to the passage in Surah 'Abasa (80:24-32) where God directs humanity to reflect on their food and how it comes to be. After describing the splitting of the earth and the growing of grain, God lists grapes and qadb, which is understood as fresh green plants and vegetables that are cut repeatedly for eating or fodder. The meaning is that these varied provisions, from fruit to greens, are signs of God's power and care, intended to provoke gratitude and to remind the human being of the Creator who sustains life, and thus of His ability to resurrect the dead and to hold people accountable.

translation: And olives and palm trees,
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:29) belongs to a passage in which God lists the blessings He causes the earth to produce for human beings and their livestock: grain, grapes, vegetables, olives, and date palms. The olive provides food and oil, and the palm provides fruit and shade. Mentioning them is a reminder of God's power and care. The One who brings life from barren soil is able to resurrect people after death, and the sustenance He provides is a reason for gratitude and obedience rather than heedlessness.

translation: And gardens dense with trees.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah 'Abasa (80:30), continues the list of God's provisions for human beings in the growth of the earth. The word 'ghulb' describes orchards whose trees are thick, lush, and tall with intertwining branches. It points to God's generosity in creating not only the staple foods of grain and vegetables but also abundant, beautiful groves that give fruit, shade, and delight. The verse is meant to make a person reflect on the care and design behind the sustenance they take for granted, so that they will recognize the Creator's power and grace, be grateful, and be convinced that the One who brings life from dead earth is able to resurrect them and hold them accountable.

translation: And fruit and pasture (fodder).
interpretation: This verse, from Surah 'Abasa (80:31), completes the list of blessings God causes the earth to bring forth after the rain. It points to God's care in providing sustenance for both humans and animals: fruit is for people's enjoyment, and pasture is for livestock. The verse invites reflection on divine power and generosity, and since the One who makes dead earth yield such provision is able to resurrect humanity, it calls people to gratitude, humility, and readiness for the Hereafter.

translation: As provision for you and for your livestock.
interpretation: This phrase (from Surah 'Abasa 80:32, following the description of how God brings forth grain, grapes, vegetation, olives, date palms, dense gardens, fruits and pasture) explains the purpose of these blessings: they are sustenance and benefit given by God for human beings and their animals. The verse teaches that the earth's produce is not accidental but a deliberate act of divine care, meant to sustain life. It calls people to reflect on God's provision and to respond with gratitude and obedience, and it reminds them that the One who nourishes them in this world is also able to resurrect them, which is the larger theme of the passage.

translation: But when the Deafening Blast comes,
interpretation: The 'Deafening Blast' (as-Sākhkhah) is a name for the second blowing of the trumpet on the Day of Resurrection, a sound so overwhelming that it pierces the ears and stuns every hearer. The verse opens a conditional clause whose consequence follows in the next verses: on that day a person will flee from brother, mother, father, spouse and children, each consumed by their own fate. The verse teaches that the Hereafter will arrive suddenly and with such intensity that worldly bonds lose their power to help. It calls the believer to prepare now with faith and righteous deeds, since on that day no one's relationships can substitute for their own accountability before God.

translation: On the Day when a man will flee from his brother,
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:34) describes the terror of the Day of Judgment, when the overwhelming gravity of the moment will dissolve even the closest bonds of kinship. A person will run away from his own brother, the very one he would have relied on for support in this world, because each soul will be consumed with its own reckoning and fear for its own fate. The verse teaches that on that Day worldly relationships and loyalties offer no refuge, and only a person's faith and deeds will matter. It is a warning to prepare for the Hereafter now rather than depend on family ties or companions.

translation: And his mother and his father,
interpretation: This phrase is from Surat 'Abasa (80:35), part of a description of the Day of Resurrection, when a person will flee from his brother, his mother and his father, his wife and his children. The mention of the mother and father, the closest and most cherished bonds, shows how terrifying that Day will be. Each person will be so consumed by his own reckoning that even the strongest ties of love and duty will not draw him to help others, and that is why one must prepare in this life with faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And his wife and his children.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:12) belongs to the description of the Day of Judgment, when a guilty person will wish to ransom himself from the punishment by giving up even his closest loved ones: his wife, his sons, and his brother. The meaning is that on that Day, the terror of the reckoning will be so overwhelming that the bonds of love and kinship, which people hold dearest in this world, will count for nothing against the instinct of self-preservation. A person who clung to family ties and put them ahead of obedience to God will be willing to sacrifice them just to escape the punishment, yet no ransom will be accepted. The lesson is that nothing in this world, including family, wealth, or status, can save a person from accountability, and that only faith and righteous deeds will be of benefit.

translation: On that Day, every one of them will have a concern that suffices to occupy him.
interpretation: This verse (Abasa 80:37) describes the terrifying atmosphere of the Day of Resurrection, when the blast of the trumpet sounds and a person flees from his brother, mother, father, spouse, and children. Each soul will be so consumed by the weight of its own reckoning, fear for its fate, and anxiety over its record of deeds that it has no capacity to attend to anyone else. The lesson is that worldly bonds of kinship and companionship cannot shield a person on that Day, so one should prepare now through faith and righteous action, since each individual will stand alone before God answerable for himself.

translation: Some faces, on that Day, will be bright and shining.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:38) describes the state of the believers on the Day of Resurrection. Their faces will be radiant and illuminated, which shows an inner joy and peace that comes from faith and righteous deeds in this world. The brightness of their faces is an outward sign of God's acceptance and the good news of reward awaiting them, in contrast to the dust-covered, darkened faces of the disbelievers described a few verses later.

translation: Laughing, rejoicing at good news.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah 'Abasa (80:39), describes the faces of the people of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection. It follows the verse 'Some faces on that Day will be bright' (80:38). Their faces shine with laughter and joy because they have received the good news of God's pleasure and their reward. The inner state of certainty and contentment shows outwardly as cheerfulness, in contrast to the faces of the disbelievers, which are covered with dust and darkness in the verses that follow.

translation: And other faces, on that Day, will have dust upon them.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa 80:40) begins the description of the fate of the disbelievers and wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment, in contrast to the radiant, joyful faces of the believers described just before. The 'dust' (ghabarah) upon their faces symbolizes the gloom, shame, and humiliation that come from their disbelief and sinful conduct. Their outward state mirrors their inner state: just as they soiled their souls in worldly life through denial and transgression, their faces now bear the visible mark of disgrace, and the following verse adds that darkness will cover them as well. The verse serves as a warning that the inner reality of a person's deeds will become manifest on the Day when nothing can be hidden.

translation: Darkness will cover them.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 80:41) describes the faces of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. While the faces of the believers are bright, laughing, and joyful, the faces of the wicked will be overcast with gloom, blackness, and disgrace. The word 'qatara' denotes a dark dust-like gloom that envelops the face, signifying the outward manifestation of inner despair, shame, and the dread of the punishment they know awaits them. Their inward state of ingratitude and defiance in this world will appear openly on their faces, so that all will recognize them by it.

translation: Those are the disbelievers, the wicked ones.
interpretation: This verse (Surah 'Abasa, 80:42) concludes the description of the Day of Judgment, when some faces will be bright, laughing and joyful, and others will be covered with dust and darkness. It teaches that the second group, whose faces are veiled in gloom, earn that fate through their own conduct. They are people who denied God's truth and rejected His signs (kufr), and who also openly violated His limits and gave themselves over to moral corruption (fujur). The pairing of the two words shows that disbelief in the heart and immorality in action reinforce each other: denying accountability leads to shamelessness in sin, and persistent sinning hardens the heart against faith. Their punishment is therefore a just recompense for both their rejection of belief and their corrupt deeds.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sun is wrapped up (folded and extinguished).
interpretation: The verse opens the description of the Day of Resurrection with the collapse of the cosmic order. The sun, which people see as the most dependable source of light and life, will be rolled up like a turban or cloth and its light removed. This shows that even the greatest created things are subject to God's command and are not self-sustaining or worthy of worship. The universe was created with a term, and when that term ends, the signs people took for granted will be undone. The verse calls the listener to reflect on the transience of this world and to prepare for the accounting that follows, since if the sun itself will be extinguished, human power and worldly attachments are far more fragile.

translation: And when the stars are dimmed and fall scattered.
interpretation: This verse, Surah At-Takwir (81:2), describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection. The stars, which people see as fixed and orderly features of the heavens, will lose their light and be thrown down in disarray, as the cosmic order that sustains this world is dismantled. Its meaning is that all of creation is subject to God's command, and that nothing in the universe is eternal except Him. The stars that people may admire, rely on for navigation, or even venerate will be extinguished, which reminds the believer that this worldly life is temporary and that every created thing will pass away. This should lead a person to prepare for the Hereafter and to place their trust in the Creator rather than in His creation.

translation: And when the mountains are set in motion.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat at-Takwir (81:3), describes one of the cosmic upheavals that mark the Day of Judgment. Mountains, which people regard as the most solid and permanent features of the earth, will be uprooted and made to move, first crumbling and then dissolving into dust. The message is that nothing in creation is permanent except God. The verse reminds the listener that the apparent stability of this world is temporary and wholly dependent on God's will, so a person should not be deceived by worldly power or permanence, but should prepare for the Day when all things are brought to account.

translation: And when the pregnant she-camels are neglected,
interpretation: This verse is among the signs of the Day of Resurrection in Surat at-Takwir (81:4). The 'ishar were the ten-month pregnant she-camels, the most prized possession of the Arabs, guarded with great care and valued above other wealth. Their being abandoned and left unattended shows the overwhelming terror of that Day: people will be so stunned by the cosmic upheaval that they will forget even their most treasured property and have no concern for it. The lesson is that worldly wealth and attachments, however precious they seem now, lose all meaning before the Judgment, so a person should not let them distract him from preparing for the Hereafter.

translation: And when the wild beasts are gathered together.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takwir, 81:5) describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection. Wild animals, which normally flee from humans and from one another, will be herded together in terror and bewilderment as the order of the world collapses. Their gathering shows how overwhelming that Day will be: even creatures that live apart by instinct will be brought together by the upheaval, so humans should realize that no one will be able to escape or remain independent of God's command, and should prepare for the Day of reckoning by turning to God now.

translation: And when the seas are set ablaze.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat At-Takwir, describes one of the cosmic upheavals that will mark the Day of Judgment. The seas, which seem to be the most stable and vast bodies of water, will be ignited or made to overflow and burn. This shows that nothing in creation is permanent or beyond God's power: the very element that extinguishes fire will itself become fire. The verse reminds people that the present order of the world is temporary, and it urges them to prepare for the Hereafter instead of relying on the apparent permanence of this life.

translation: And when the souls are paired (joined together).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat At-Takwir (81:7), describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection: every soul will be joined with its like or counterpart according to its deeds and faith. The righteous will be grouped with the righteous and placed among the people of Paradise, while the wicked will be grouped with the wicked and gathered with those like them in belief and conduct. It signals that on that Day, worldly distinctions of lineage and status fall away, and people are reunited with those who match their inner reality and actions, as well as, in another understanding, with their bodies when souls are returned to them for judgment.

translation: And when the girl who was buried alive is asked,
interpretation: This verse, from Surat At-Takwir, describes a scene of the Day of Judgment in which the infant girl buried alive, a practice of pre-Islamic Arabia, is questioned about the crime committed against her. The question is in effect directed at her killers, since she is the victim, so it exposes the gravity of the crime and affirms that God holds every person accountable for wrongs done to the innocent. Nothing is overlooked on that Day, and the weak and voiceless will be given justice. The verse also condemns the killing of children and the devaluing of female life, and it establishes the sanctity of every human soul.

translation: For what sin was she killed?
interpretation: This phrase from Surat at-Takwir (81:9) belongs to the scenes of the Day of Judgment, where the girl buried alive is asked why she was killed. The question is not meant to gather information, since God knows everything. It is a rebuke aimed at her killers and a public vindication of the victim. It condemns the pre-Islamic Arab practice of burying infant daughters alive out of shame or fear of poverty. It also affirms that no innocent life is taken without being called to account, that the wronged will have their rights restored, and that even the weakest and most voiceless people are seen and defended by God.

translation: And when the pages (records of deeds) are spread open.
interpretation: This verse, Qur'an 81:10 from Surat at-Takwir, describes a scene on the Day of Judgment when the written records of every person's deeds, which the angels have kept throughout life, are laid open. Nothing is concealed anymore: each person will face a complete and accurate account of what they did, whether great or small, public or private. The verse is a reminder that human actions are never lost or forgotten, and that every individual will be held personally accountable before God. It calls the believer to self-examination in this life, to sincerity in secret as well as in public, and to prepare for the day when the truth of one's conduct is made fully manifest.

translation: And when the sky is stripped away.
interpretation: This verse (Surat at-Takwir, 81:11) describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection: the sky, which people now see as a fixed and protective canopy, will be peeled back like a skin or covering removed from a slaughtered animal, revealing what lies behind it. The meaning is that the ordered cosmos is wholly subject to God's command; what seems permanent will be removed in an instant, and the hidden realities of the unseen, including the Divine reckoning, will be laid bare. It reminds the listener that this world's apparent stability is temporary, and that they should prepare for the moment when every veil is lifted and nothing remains concealed.

translation: And when the Blaze is set ablaze (Qur'an 81:12).
interpretation: This verse describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection: Hell is kindled and its fire intensified to a fierce, raging blaze. It stands as a warning that Hell is a real and terrible destination prepared for those who reject God and persist in wrongdoing. The verse is meant to awaken the heart to accountability, so that a person reforms his conduct, repents, and seeks refuge in God's mercy before that Day arrives, when every soul will know what it has brought forth.

translation: And when Paradise is brought near.
interpretation: This verse (Surat at-Takwir, 81:13) is one of the scenes of the Day of Resurrection. Paradise will be drawn close to the God-fearing, so that they see their reward before entering it. This nearness is a source of joy and honor for the righteous, and a reminder to every soul that the promised abode is real and close at hand, which should motivate people to strive in obedience now, before the cosmic upheavals of that Day unfold and each soul comes to know what it has brought forth.

translation: Then every soul will know what it has brought forth.
interpretation: This verse (Surat at-Takwir, 81:14) is the answer to the series of conditional clauses describing the cosmic upheavals of the Day of Resurrection: the sun folded up, the stars falling, the mountains set in motion, the seas set aflame, and the souls joined together. When these events occur, each person will fully realize the reality of their own deeds, whether good or evil, which they have presented before God. The point is that on that Day no one will be able to deny, forget, or excuse their record, because every act will be present and its consequence plain. The verse therefore calls a person to self-accountability now, to examine what they are preparing for their meeting with God before the moment when such knowledge comes too late to change anything.

translation: So I swear by the retreating stars.
interpretation: The verse opens an oath (Surat at-Takwir 81:15) by the stars that withdraw from sight, which most commentators take to mean those that recede and hide in the daytime or at their setting. By invoking the regular, ordered disappearance and reappearance of the heavenly bodies, God points to His precise control over the cosmos and to the reliability of the oath's subject, which is that the Qur'an is the true word delivered by a noble messenger. Just as the stars vanish and return by a fixed decree, so the revelation is firmly established and its truth cannot be concealed or denied. The oath invites reflection on creation as a sign that the One who governs the heavens with such order is also the source of this message.

translation: By the planets that run their courses and hide (set).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 81:16, from Surat at-Takwir) continues an oath begun in the preceding verses, swearing by the heavenly bodies, most commonly understood as the stars or planets that move along their orbits (al-jawār) and then withdraw from sight, like gazelles retreating into their dens (al-kunnas). God swears by these awe-inspiring signs of the cosmos to affirm the truth of the Qur'an and the revelation delivered by the noble messenger. The point is that the same Creator who governs the precise, unfailing motion of the heavens has sent a trustworthy message, and that the order and regularity of creation testify to divine power, wisdom, and the certainty of the Day of Judgment described in this surah.

translation: And by the night as it departs (or: as it falls in darkness).
interpretation: This verse is an oath by the night at the moment it withdraws and gives way to dawn. The verb 'asas carries the sense of the night's darkness turning away, so the verse points to the passing of darkness and the arrival of light as a sign of God's power. It is a reminder that no darkness lasts, that God governs the cycles of time with precision, and that the One who ends the night and brings forth the morning can also bring about the resurrection and the unveiling of truth described in the surrounding verses of Surat at-Takwir. Swearing by this moment draws the listener's attention to the order and purpose in creation, and invites reflection that the Qur'an's message is itself a light dispelling heedlessness.

translation: And by the morning when it breathes.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takwir, 81:18) is part of an oath by God invoking signs of the natural world. The dawn is pictured as a living being that breathes: as night recedes, the morning gradually draws in life, light, and movement, spreading across the horizon like a breath released after confinement. The image points to the steady, certain unfolding of God's order, in which darkness is always followed by light. It serves as a reminder that the One who brings the day to life with such precision is able to bring about the resurrection and the revelation of truth, and that the message of the Qur'an, like the dawn, is a clear and inevitable light dispelling the darkness of ignorance and denial.

translation: Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is conveyed through a noble, trustworthy messenger who delivers it faithfully from God. The Messenger is described as 'noble' (karim) to stress his integrity, honor and reliability as a bearer of revelation, so that what he conveys is not his own invention nor the product of a poet or soothsayer. Attribution of the words to the messenger is one of delivery and not authorship: he transmits the message entrusted to him, and the surrounding verses make clear that it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The verse thus defends the authenticity and divine origin of the Qur'an by pointing to the exalted character of the one who brings it.

translation: Possessed of power, and held in high standing with the Lord of the Throne.
interpretation: This verse, describing the noble messenger angel (Gabriel) who brings the revelation, affirms his dual qualification as a bearer of the divine message: he has great strength, so that no one can overpower him or tamper with what he conveys, and he holds an honored, secure rank in the presence of God, the Lord of the Throne. His power guarantees that the revelation is protected from corruption or interference, and his high station with God guarantees that he is trustworthy and that his message carries true divine authority, so the Qur'an reaches the Prophet exactly as God sent it.

translation: Obeyed there, and trustworthy.
interpretation: This verse (Surat at-Takwir, 81:21) describes the noble angelic messenger, Jibril (Gabriel), as one who is obeyed in the heavenly realm, where the angels follow his command, and who is also entrusted with the revelation. Being 'obeyed' points to his high rank and authority among the angels, while 'trustworthy' affirms his integrity in carrying God's message: he conveys it to the Prophet Muhammad exactly as received, without alteration, addition, or omission. Together these qualities assure the listener that the Qur'an is a reliable revelation, delivered by a faithful and honored messenger of God.

translation: And your companion is not a madman.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takwir 81:22) affirms the sanity and truthfulness of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who lived among the Meccans for years and was known to them. By calling him 'your companion' (sahibukum), God reminds the people that they knew his character, wisdom, and honesty from long association, so the accusation of madness leveled against him by his opponents was baseless. The message he brought, particularly the revelation delivered through the noble angel Gabriel as described in the preceding verses, could not be the product of a deranged mind but is a sound, authentic and divinely inspired guidance.

translation: And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takwir 81:23) affirms that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, truly saw the angel Gabriel, the bearer of revelation, in his real angelic form on the clear, open horizon. It is meant to refute the claim that the Qur'an was the product of a madman or a devil, as the preceding verses assert. The vision was not an illusion or inner imagining but a real, unobstructed sighting in the open sky, which establishes the trustworthiness of the messenger and the divine origin of the message he received from the noble, powerful, and trusted angel.

translation: And he is not stingy concerning the unseen (what has been revealed to him).
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet Muhammad does not withhold or conceal any part of the revelation he receives from God. What God discloses to him of the unseen, such as matters of faith, the Hereafter, and divine guidance, he conveys fully and faithfully to people without hoarding, altering, or demanding a price for it. This establishes his trustworthiness as a messenger and refutes the accusation that he was a soothsayer or that his message was fabricated, since a true messenger delivers the entirety of what he is entrusted with.

translation: And it is not the word of an accursed Satan.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 81:25) completes the Qur'an's defense of its divine origin, answering the claim that the revelation was inspired by jinn or devils. The Qur'an is not the speech of any satan driven away from God's mercy, because its message calls to worship of One God, moral accountability, justice, and purification of the soul, which is the opposite of what satanic whispering seeks. Satan is described as 'rajim' (accursed, cast out) and is barred from access to the heavenly realm, so he cannot bring down or corrupt the revelation. Its guidance, its protection by God, and its transmission through the trustworthy angel Gabriel to the truthful Prophet Muhammad all prove it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

translation: So where are you going?
interpretation: This verse (Surat at-Takwir, 81:26) is a rhetorical question addressed to those who deny the Qur'an. After God has affirmed that the Qur'an is the speech of a noble messenger and not the word of a possessed man or an accursed devil, He asks where they think they are heading. The question points out that every other path they might take, such as rejecting the revelation, following conjecture, or relying on false explanations, leads away from the truth. The only sound course is to accept the Qur'an, which is a reminder for all the worlds and the guidance for whoever wishes to walk straight.

translation: It is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 81:27, also echoed in 38:87 and 68:52) affirms that the Qur'an is not the speech of a poet, soothsayer, or devil, but a universal reminder whose purpose is to awaken people's innate awareness of God, their accountability, and the right way to live. The word 'worlds' shows that its message is not confined to one tribe, nation, or era: it addresses all humankind and jinn, in every time and place. It is a reminder because it recalls truths already imprinted in human nature and conscience, and it calls everyone, whatever their background, to benefit from its guidance and to choose the straight path.

translation: For whoever among you wills to take the straight path.
