interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 81:28) follows the declaration that the Qur'an is a reminder for all the worlds, and it specifies who actually benefits from it: those who choose to walk uprightly. Guidance is offered to everyone, but its fruit belongs to those who intend and strive for steadfastness in faith and righteous action. The verse affirms human responsibility and choice: each person has the will to pursue the straight path, so no one can excuse a deviation by blaming fate. The very next verse then adds that this will operates only within God's greater will, so that a person neither boasts of self-sufficiency nor falls into fatalism, but seeks God's help to remain steadfast.

translation: And you do not will except that Allah wills, the Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takwir 81:29) teaches that human choice and will operate only within the bounds of God's greater will. When a person wishes to take the path of guidance and uprightness mentioned in the preceding verse, even that desire and the capacity to act on it come from God's permission and enabling. It does not cancel human responsibility; rather, it humbles the believer, directing him to seek God's help and guidance, and to recognize that no ability exists independent of the Lord who sustains and governs all creation.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is split apart.
interpretation: The verse opens Surat al-Infitar by announcing one of the great signs of the Day of Judgment: the heavens, which appear firm and unbreakable, will be cleaved and torn open at God's command. Its meaning is that the whole created order is temporary and entirely subject to God's power. If the vast, seemingly stable sky cannot endure when God's decree comes, human beings should not be deceived by worldly permanence. They should recognize their accountability, remember that the Hereafter is certain, and prepare for it with sincere faith and righteous action.

translation: And when the stars are scattered,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 82:2) describes one of the cosmic signs of the Day of Judgment. The stars, which people perceive as fixed and ordered in the heavens, will lose their arrangement and fall and disperse. Its meaning is that the whole system of the universe, which seems permanent and unshakable, depends entirely on God's command, and when He wills its end it will be dismantled. The verse reminds the believer that this world is temporary, that its apparent stability should not breed heedlessness, and that one should prepare for the Day when every soul will know what it has sent forward and left behind.

translation: And when the seas burst forth.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Infitar (82:3), describes one of the cosmic upheavals that will signal the Day of Judgment. The seas, which now are held within their bounds by God's decree, will break through their barriers and spill over into one another, mixing their fresh and salt waters and overflowing the earth, or they will erupt and be set ablaze. The collapse of the order of the natural world, which people consider stable and permanent, is meant to awaken the heart to the fragility of this world and the certainty of the Hereafter, so that a person is moved to reckon with his deeds before the day when each soul will know what it has sent forward and left behind.

translation: And when the graves are overturned and their contents scattered.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Infitar (82:4), describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection: the graves will be turned upside down and emptied of their dead, who will rise to be brought before God. It stresses that death is not an end but a passage to accountability. No one can remain hidden in the earth, and every soul will be raised to face what it has done. The verse calls the believer to wake from heedlessness and prepare for that meeting with sincere faith and righteous deeds.

translation: Each soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Infitar, 82:5) declares that on the Day of Judgment, when the heavens split and the stars scatter, every person will be fully aware of the record of their deeds. 'What it sent forward' means the good and bad deeds it performed during life, and 'what it left behind' means what it neglected or failed to do, as well as the lasting effects of its actions, such as a good tradition or a corrupt one that others continue to follow after death. Nothing will be hidden or forgotten, so each person will face the full account of their life. The verse is a reminder to take stock of one's actions now, while there is still time to correct them.

translation: O mankind! What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?
interpretation: This verse (Al-Infitar 82:6) is a gentle yet probing rebuke addressed to every human being. God's generosity is not a license for heedlessness. Rather than punishing people immediately, God grants them life, provision, and time to repent, and some mistake this forbearance for a sign that they will not be held accountable. The verse uses the name 'the Most Generous' (al-Karim) to show that this very generosity should awaken gratitude, shame, and obedience, not arrogance or disobedience. A person who reflects on God's kindness should be moved to return it with faithfulness, and should not be lured by false hopes, desires, or Satan's whispers into neglecting the coming Day of Judgment.

translation: He who created you, then proportioned you, then made you well-balanced.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Infitar, 82:7) reminds human beings that their very existence and the harmony of their bodies and faculties are signs of God's care and power. Having been formed from nothing, shaped with proper proportion, and given balanced limbs, senses, and intellect, a person has no justification for being heedless of or ungrateful to the Creator. The verse functions as a gentle reproach to the question in the preceding verse, 'What has deceived you concerning your generous Lord?': the One who fashioned you so perfectly deserves your gratitude, obedience, and awareness of accountability, and the very fact of such careful creation implies that life has purpose and that one will answer for how it is lived.

translation: In whatever form He willed, He assembled you. (Qur'an 82:8)
interpretation: This verse completes the reminder of God's favor on humankind begun in the previous verse, which says that God created, fashioned and proportioned you. Here, the verse stresses that your particular form, whether in features, build, color, resemblance to parents or distinctiveness from them, was not a matter of chance or of natural forces acting blindly, but the result of God's sovereign will and wisdom. Every person is composed in the exact shape God chose for them, so the verse points to His power and care and to humanity's duty of gratitude. It is also a rebuke to the one who is heedless and denies the Day of Judgment: the One who so deliberately shaped you is surely able to resurrect you and hold you accountable, and it is unfitting to be deceived about such a generous Lord by disobeying Him.

translation: No! Rather, you deny the Judgment (the Religion).
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human tendency to rely on false excuses and pretensions. After the preceding verses invoke the greatness of God's creation and bounty, this verse rejects any justification for being deceived about the Creator. The real cause of human arrogance and heedlessness is not a lack of evidence but a willful denial of the Day of Recompense. People reject accountability because acknowledging it would require them to change how they live, so they dismiss the Judgment in order to follow their desires without restraint.

translation: And indeed, over you are keepers (guardian recorders).
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 82:10) affirms that God has appointed angels to watch over every human being and preserve a precise account of their deeds. It reminds people that no action, word, or intention is lost or hidden, so that they live with moral awareness and accountability, knowing their record will be presented on the Day of Judgment, and are thereby urged to deny the false belief that there is no reckoning.

translation: Noble ones, writing down [everything].
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Infitar 82:11) describes the guardian angels appointed over every human being as 'kiraman' (noble, honorable) and 'katibin' (recorders). It means that all of a person's words and deeds are being faithfully and precisely documented by honorable angels who would never wrong, forget, or falsify anything. The point is to instill accountability and God-consciousness: since nothing escapes being recorded, a person should live mindfully, avoid denying the Day of Judgment, and prepare for the reckoning in which this record will be presented.

translation: They know whatever you do.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Infitar (82:12), refers to the noble recording angels (al-kiram al-katibin) who are appointed over every human being. It means that nothing a person does, whether open or secret, great or small, escapes their knowledge, so that every deed is faithfully known and recorded for the Day of Judgment. The verse is a reminder to live with constant awareness of accountability, to keep one's conduct upright even in private, and to avoid denying the Final Judgment, since one's entire record of deeds is preserved and will be presented before God.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Infitar 82:13) promises that those who were truly devoted to God, faithful in their belief and sincere in their obedience and good deeds, will be placed in a state of lasting delight in the Hereafter. The word 'abrar' denotes people of piety and goodness who fulfilled their duties to God and to others. The word 'na'im' conveys a complete and comprehensive happiness, in which the soul, heart, and body are all at ease, free from any sorrow or fear. The verse stands in deliberate contrast to the following verse about the wicked who will be in Hellfire, and so it emphasizes that the Hereafter is a place of just recompense in which a person's final state mirrors their moral and spiritual conduct in this world.

translation: And indeed, the wicked will be in a Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the promise of bliss for the righteous (al-abrar) in Surat al-Infitar, sets out the opposite end of divine justice. The fujjar are those who burst through the bounds of God's law by persistent disbelief and open sin, and it is they who are destined for Jahim, a fiercely burning Hell. The point is that the moral choices people make in this life are not lost or meaningless: each leads to a real outcome in the next. The verse is meant to awaken the heedless, who deny the Day of Judgment, to the fact that the reckoning is certain and that a life of defiance toward God ends in the punishment it has earned.

translation: They will burn in it on the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 82:15) speaks of the wicked (al-fujjār) mentioned in the preceding verse, who will be in a blazing Hell. It means that they will enter the Fire and endure its heat on the Day of Recompense, when each soul is repaid for what it did. The verse stresses that the consequences of deliberate wrongdoing and denial of accountability are not escaped, and that the Day of Judgment is the moment when divine justice becomes fully manifest, so that those who lived heedless of God's commands face the outcome of their choices.

translation: And they will not be absent from it.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Infitar (82:16), speaks of the wicked who will enter the Hellfire on the Day of Judgment. It means that once they are cast into it, they can never escape, withdraw, or hide from its punishment. Their punishment is constant and unending. They will not be absent from it even for a moment, nor will death or any other means remove them from it. The verse stresses the certainty and permanence of the consequences of rejecting God and living in sin.

translation: And what will make you realize what the Day of Judgment is?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Infitar 82:17) uses a rhetorical question to stress the immense gravity of the Day of Judgment. By asking 'what will make you realize,' God signals that its reality is so vast and awe-inspiring that human minds cannot fully grasp it through ordinary experience or imagination. The verse calls the listener to reflect seriously on accountability, to recognize that this Day is a certainty far beyond comprehension, and to prepare for it by living with awareness of God and responsibility for one's deeds.

translation: Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 82:18) repeats the rhetorical question to heighten the awe and terror of the Day of Judgment. By asking 'what will make you know?', it signals that the reality of that Day is so vast and overwhelming that human minds cannot fully grasp it through ordinary experience. It calls the listener to sober reflection and to prepare through faith and righteous deeds, since on that Day every soul will stand accountable before God and no one will have power to help another, for all command belongs to God alone.

translation: The Day when no soul will have power to do anything for another soul, and the command on that Day belongs entirely to God.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 82:19) describes the Day of Judgment as a day when all worldly forms of power, kinship, rank, and intercession lose their effect. In this life people appear to hold authority over one another, and they rely on family, wealth, or status to help them. On that Day, no one can avert punishment from another or grant a benefit to them, because every soul is occupied with its own reckoning. Absolute and unchallenged sovereignty belongs to God alone. Any intercession that occurs happens only by His leave. The verse is meant to instill awareness of personal accountability and to turn the believer away from dependence on created beings toward sincere devotion to God and righteous action now, while there is still time.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Woe to the defrauders (those who give short measure).
interpretation: The verse opens Surat al-Mutaffifin with a stern warning of ruin and divine punishment for those who cheat in trade, taking full measure when they receive from others but giving less when they measure or weigh for others. It teaches that honesty and justice in dealings are matters of faith, not mere social convention, and that even small acts of cheating, often hidden from people, are known to God and will be called to account. By extension, the warning covers any form of unfairness in rights and obligations, such as demanding full due from others while denying them theirs.

translation: Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 83:2) describes the defrauders mentioned in the opening of Surat al-Mutaffifin. Their wrong lies in a double standard: when they are the ones receiving their due from others, they insist on full measure and guard their own rights with great exactness. Yet, as the following verse shows, when they measure or weigh for others they give less. The verse therefore exposes injustice rooted in self-interest, where a person demands from others a standard of fairness that he refuses to uphold himself. The broader lesson is that faith requires one consistent standard of honesty and justice, applying to others what one expects for oneself, in trade and in every dealing.

translation: And when they measure or weigh for them, they cause loss.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:3), describes the dishonesty of the cheaters: when they are the ones giving goods to others, whether by measure or by weight, they shortchange the buyer and deprive people of their due. Together with the preceding verse, which describes them taking their full right when they buy, it exposes a double standard in which a person demands strict justice for himself but denies it to others. The Qur'an treats this as a grave moral corruption in dealings, rooted in heedlessness of accountability before God on the Day of Judgment, and it teaches that honesty and fairness in trade and in all social relations are a binding duty, requiring a person to give others exactly what he would want for himself.

translation: Do those people not think that they will be resurrected?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mutaffifin, 83:4) is a rebuke aimed at those who cheat in weights and measures, taking full measure from others while giving less than what is due. It implies that such dishonesty can only come from heedlessness of the Hereafter. If they truly believed they would be raised from the dead and made to stand before God for a full reckoning, they would not dare to defraud people. Fear of accountability on the Day of Resurrection is the foundation of honesty and justice in dealings, and the verse suggests that corruption in daily transactions is rooted in weak certainty about the afterlife.

translation: For a Mighty Day.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mutaffifin, 83:5) completes the rhetorical question that begins in the previous verse: 'Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a Mighty Day?' The 'Mighty Day' is the Day of Judgment, when all people will stand before the Lord of the worlds to be held accountable. The verse rebukes those who cheat in weights and measures, showing that if they truly reckoned with this momentous day, when every deed, however small, will be weighed and reckoned, they would never defraud others. Its greatness lies in the terror of the occasion and the absolute justice of God's reckoning, so awareness of it should restrain a person from injustice and instill honesty and God-consciousness in all dealings.

translation: The Day when all people will stand before the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 83:6) describes the Day of Judgment, when every human being will rise from the grave and stand in humble submission before God, with no intermediary, status, or wealth to shield them. It appears in the context of a warning to those who cheat in weights and measures, reminding them that dishonesty in even small worldly transactions will be accounted for before the One who governs all creation. The verse calls the believer to constant awareness of ultimate accountability, so that justice, honesty, and fear of God shape conduct in this life.

translation: No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.
interpretation: God rebukes those who deny the Day of Judgment and live in transgression, declaring that the register of their deeds is kept in Sijjin, a place of confinement and lowliness, which signifies that their deeds are recorded in a state of degradation and that their destiny is a narrow, abased place of punishment. The word 'Sijjin' is linked with the idea of imprisonment, indicating that the wicked, who exceeded the limits set by God, will have their record and their fate sealed beneath, far from the elevation granted to the righteous.

translation: And what will make you know what Sijjīn is?
interpretation: The verse uses a rhetorical question to stress how grave and terrible Sijjīn is, a reality beyond ordinary human understanding. Sijjīn is the record in which the deeds of the wicked and the disbelievers are written, and it also stands for the lowest, most confined place of ruin to which they are destined. By asking 'what will make you know', God makes the listener pause and fear the fate of those who persist in sin and deny the Day of Judgment, and urges them to reform before their record is sealed in humiliation and punishment.

translation: A written record, clearly inscribed.
interpretation: This phrase, which appears in Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:9 and 83:20), describes the book of deeds as something fixed and inscribed, so that nothing in it can be altered, erased, or forgotten. In verse 9 it explains what Sijjin is, the register of the wicked, whose deeds are recorded and who are bound for ruin. In verse 20 it describes the record of the righteous (Illiyyun), which is likewise written down and preserved. The message is that every deed, good or bad, is recorded with precision and will be brought forth on the Day of Judgment, so people should be mindful of their conduct and honest in their dealings. Because the record is complete and cannot be disputed, each person will receive full and just recompense.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surat al-Mursalat, warns that those who rejected God's signs, the Messenger, and the reality of resurrection and judgment will face ruin and destruction on the Day of Judgment. When the truth they denied is plainly revealed, their denial offers no protection, and their regret comes too late. The repetition after each reminder of God's power, His creation, and His favors stresses that denial is especially grievous because the evidence was clear and the warnings abundant. It calls the listener to reflect, believe, and prepare for accountability before that Day arrives.

translation: Those who deny the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 83:11, following 'Woe that Day to the deniers') identifies the deniers as those who reject the reality of accountability in the Hereafter. Their denial is not merely intellectual disbelief but the root of moral corruption: because they do not expect to answer for their deeds, they feel free to cheat, oppress, and transgress, as the surrounding verses about defrauding in weights and measures show. Belief in the Day of Judgment acts as the inner restraint that keeps a person just and conscientious, while denying it removes that restraint and leads to heedlessness and injustice.

translation: And none denies it except every transgressor, sinful one.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 83:12) refers to the Day of Judgment mentioned in the preceding verses. It teaches that denial of the Day of Reckoning does not stem from sound reasoning or lack of evidence, but from moral corruption. Only one who habitually oversteps the limits set by God and indulges in sin has an interest in rejecting the idea of accountability, because belief in it would restrain his injustice and wrongdoing. Thus the person who denies the Hereafter does so to preserve the freedom to transgress, while the upright heart, which is conscious of answerability before God, readily accepts the truth of the Judgment.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says: "Tales of the ancients."
interpretation: The verse portrays the arrogant denier who, when confronted with divine revelation, does not engage with its message or weigh its truth, but dismisses it as mere inherited folklore, no different from old myths and legends. This dismissal is a defense mechanism: by reducing revelation to human storytelling from the past, he excuses himself from accountability, moral change, and belief in resurrection and judgment. The root of such rejection is not a lack of evidence but pride and attachment to wealth, status, and desires, which makes the heart deaf to guidance. The verse warns that mocking or belittling God's words, rather than reflecting on them, is a sign of a heart hardened by sin and heedlessness.

translation: No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered their hearts like rust.
interpretation: The verse rejects the disbelievers' claim that the Qur'an is merely 'tales of the ancients' (verse 13). Their denial does not come from a lack of evidence. It comes from the accumulated effect of their own sins and wrongdoing, which built up on their hearts like rust on iron until it covered them. Repeated sin darkens the heart and blunts its ability to perceive truth, so that guidance can no longer penetrate it. Their blindness to the truth is therefore a consequence of their own deeds, and they are responsible for it.

translation: Nay! Indeed, on that Day they will be veiled from their Lord.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mutaffifin 83:15) declares that those who persistently denied the truth and wrapped their hearts in the rust of their own sins will, on the Day of Judgment, be barred from the nearness and vision of God. Their hearts were veiled in this world by their wrongdoing and heedlessness, so the veil is their just recompense in the Hereafter: as they shut out God's guidance and refused to see Him in this life, He shuts them out from His grace and the joy of meeting Him. This deprivation is a spiritual punishment even before the physical punishment of Hell, showing that the greatest loss for a human being is separation from their Lord, and that the believers, by contrast, are honored with His closeness.

translation: Then indeed, they will surely enter and burn in the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 83:16) follows the preceding verse, which says the wrongdoers will be veiled from their Lord on the Day of Judgment. It teaches that the punishment of the deniers has two stages: first, the disgrace of being barred from God's nearness and mercy, and then the physical suffering of entering Hell. The word 'thumma' (then) marks a progression in severity. Being shut out from God is already a profound loss, and yet the fire comes after it. The verse warns that persistent sin and denial of the Day of Recompense lead to a just consequence, one that affects both the soul and the body.

translation: Then it will be said to them: "This is what you used to deny."
interpretation: This verse (83:17) describes the disbelievers' fate on the Day of Judgment. After they enter Hell, the angels, or the keepers of Hell, will rebuke them. The rebuke is a moral and psychological punishment added to the physical one. The people who mocked the warnings of the Hereafter, dismissed the Resurrection and the Reckoning as myths, and lived as though they would never be held accountable now face what they denied. The verse teaches that denying a truth does not make it go away, and that arrogance toward revelation leads only to regret when reality appears. It also reminds believers to take God's warnings seriously now, while there is still time to repent and change.

translation: Nay! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the deeds of the righteous are recorded and preserved in an exalted, honored place, 'Illiyyin, which signifies the highest ranks. This elevation of their record points to their elevated standing with God and their eventual place in the highest levels of Paradise. It stands in contrast to the record of the wicked, which is kept in a low and confined place (Sijjin), teaching that a person's end is determined by the character of their deeds, and that God preserves every act of goodness and honors those who performed it.

translation: And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is?
interpretation: The verse uses a rhetorical question to magnify the station of 'Illiyyun, the exalted register or high place where the deeds of the righteous (al-abrar) are recorded and where their souls are honored. By saying that its true nature is beyond ordinary human knowledge, the Qur'an points to the grandeur of the reward awaiting the believers. Its loftiness stands in deliberate contrast to Sijjin, the low and confined place for the record of the wicked. The lesson is that a life of righteousness raises a person in rank with God, and that its true worth will be fully known only in the Hereafter.

translation: A written record, clearly inscribed.
interpretation: This phrase, which appears in Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:9 and 83:20), describes the record of deeds, which is written and sealed so that nothing in it can be altered, added to, or erased. In verse 9 it explains what Sijjin is: the ledger of the wrongdoers, whose deeds are registered and preserved for their reckoning and lead to their ruin. In verse 20 it describes the book of the righteous, the 'Illiyyun, which is likewise fully documented and kept for their reward. Both uses stress that God's recording of human actions is precise and complete, so that every person should be mindful of accountability and that justice on the Day of Judgment will rest on a fixed record, not on guesswork.

translation: Those brought near [to God] bear witness to it.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:21), refers to the 'Illiyyin, the register in which the deeds of the righteous are recorded. It means that the angels nearest to God attend and witness this record, guarding it and testifying to it. Their witnessing shows the high honor of the righteous, whose good deeds are preserved, secure from alteration or loss, and affirmed by the highest company in the unseen realm. The register is thus a sign of certain reward and elevated rank in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Infitar, 82:13) promises that those who were truly devoted to God and faithful in obedience, the abrar, will be in a state of lasting delight in the Hereafter. The word 'na'im' conveys a comprehensive felicity, covering physical comfort, inner peace, and nearness to God's favor. It follows the earlier reminder that every deed is recorded, and it implies that goodness practiced in this life is not lost but is rewarded with a blessing that exceeds earthly pleasure. The verse also sets up a contrast with the fate of the wicked, which follows in the next verse, so that people will take stock of their conduct and choose righteousness.

translation: On couches, they will be gazing.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:23), describes the state of the righteous (al-abrar) in Paradise. They recline in comfort and honor on adorned couches, and from there they gaze at the bounties around them, at the humiliation of their former mockers, and, according to many commentators, at the Face of their Lord. Their reclining signifies complete security, rest, and royal ease, while their gazing signifies the fulfillment of every desire and the joy of seeing what God has promised them. It stands as a contrast to the disbelievers, who are veiled from their Lord and who once laughed at the believers in this world; now the believers rest and look on in peace.

translation: You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Mutaffifin 83:24) describes the righteous in Paradise. Their inner contentment and the honor God has granted them show outwardly on their faces, so that anyone who sees them knows at once, without being told, that they are in a state of lasting joy, safety, and divine favor. The radiance is a sign that the blessings are not merely external pleasures but have transformed them fully, in contrast to the faces of the wicked, which are marked by distress and humiliation.

translation: They will be given to drink from a sealed pure wine.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward of the righteous (al-abrar) in Paradise: they are served a pure, unadulterated drink that is 'sealed,' meaning it is preserved from any impurity or corruption, and its seal is musk, as the following verse says. The sealing signifies the drink's perfect purity, its high value and honor, and that it is reserved exclusively for them. Unlike worldly wine, it brings no intoxication, harm, or loss of reason, but only delight and lasting pleasure, a gift matching the sincerity and patience they showed in this world.

translation: Its seal is musk. So for that let the competitors compete.
interpretation: The verse describes the pure drink of the righteous in Paradise (al-Raḥīq al-Makhtūm), whose final taste and residue is fragrant musk, signifying its perfect purity and delight, unlike the dregs of worldly drinks. It then directs people's aspirations: if they must vie and strive against one another, let it be for this everlasting reward through faith, obedience, and good deeds, not for the fleeting pleasures and gains of this world, which are unworthy of such rivalry.

translation: And its mixture is from Tasnim.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 83:27) describes the pure drink of the righteous in Paradise, which is sealed and then blended with Tasnim. Tasnim is a spring of Paradise whose name comes from the Arabic root meaning 'elevation', so it is a drink of the highest rank. The next verse says it is a spring from which those brought near to God drink. The meaning is that the righteous receive a pure and noble drink, and those nearest to God enjoy the finest and unmixed form of it, while the other righteous receive it mixed. This shows that Paradise has degrees of reward, which match the degrees of nearness to God earned in this world.

translation: A spring from which those brought near [to God] will drink.
interpretation: The verse describes the highest drink of Paradise, reserved for the muqarrabun, those who drew nearest to God through sincere devotion and excellence in faith and deeds. Elsewhere the drink of the righteous (al-abrar) is said to be mixed with this spring, which suggests that the nearest ones receive it pure and unmixed while others receive it only in part. The message is that the rewards of the hereafter are graded according to nearness to God, and that those who strove most in drawing close in this world are given the purest and most exalted delight in the next.

translation: Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Mutaffifin 83:29) shows that the disbelievers and wrongdoers in this world treated the believers with scorn and mockery, regarding their faith, humility and piety as foolishness or weakness. It exposes arrogance as the root of their rejection: they judged truth by worldly status and power rather than by God's standard. The verse also consoles believers, teaching them that ridicule is an old trial faced by the faithful, that it carries no weight with God, and that the mockers' laughter is temporary, since the following verses reverse the scene on the Day of Judgment, when the believers will laugh at the disbelievers.

translation: And when they passed by them, they would wink at one another (mockingly).
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mutaffifin, 83:30) describes the disbelievers who used to ridicule the believers. When the wicked passed by the believers, they exchanged winks and gestures of contempt, belittling their faith and sincerity. It shows that the mockery of the righteous is a mark of arrogance and a sign of those who deny the truth. It also serves as consolation for believers, who are reminded that the scorn of the wrongdoers is temporary, and that on the Day of Judgment the roles will be reversed, with the believers laughing at the disbelievers from their places of honor.

translation: And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting and delighting.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 83:31) exposes the arrogance of those who mocked the believers. After ridiculing the faithful, they went home to their families in a mood of self-satisfied amusement, treating the believers' sincerity as a source of entertainment. Their delight shows hearts that have grown heedless of accountability, taking pleasure in the humiliation of others rather than reflecting on the truth. The verse warns that mockery of righteous people is a sign of spiritual blindness, and it prepares for the reversal in the Hereafter, when the believers will laugh at the disbelievers (83:34).

translation: And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are truly astray."
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:32) describes how the wrongdoers who mocked the believers in this world judged them by worldly measures. Because the believers gave up the pursuit of worldly pleasure and pride, and held to faith, restraint and devotion to the Hereafter, the disbelievers took them to be misguided and foolish. The verse shows that the disbelievers' ridicule rested on a false standard, since they took their own path to be right and the believers' path to be error. The surrounding verses reverse this judgment: on the Day of Judgment the believers will laugh at the disbelievers, so true guidance is shown to lie with those who were mocked. The verse consoles believers who face scorn for their faith, and warns against judging people's guidance by worldly success or popular opinion.

translation: And they were not sent as guardians over them.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:33), speaks of the wrongdoers who mocked the believers. It stresses that those mockers had no authority or appointed role to supervise, judge, or control the believers' conduct or faith. They were never made keepers of the believers' deeds or of their guidance, so their ridicule was baseless presumption. Judgment belongs to God alone, and on the Day of Judgment the believers will be vindicated while the mockers see how unfounded their arrogance was.

translation: But today, those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Mutaffifin, 83:34) reverses the scene of worldly mockery. In the life of this world the wrongdoers used to scoff at the believers, winking at one another when the believers passed by and treating their faith as foolishness. On the Day of Judgment the roles are overturned: the believers, now secure and honored, laugh at those who once derided them as they see the disbelievers' humiliation and the true outcome of their choices. The laughter is not petty revenge but a sign of vindication and divine justice, showing that patience under ridicule for the sake of faith is never wasted and that final victory belongs to those who stayed faithful to God.

translation: On adorned couches, they will be looking on.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Mutaffifin 83:23) describes the righteous in Paradise, reclining in comfort and dignity on raised, canopied couches. Their gaze is free and untroubled: they look upon the bounties around them, upon their honored station, and, according to many commentators, upon the face of their Lord. It stands in deliberate contrast to the disgrace of the wrongdoers, who are veiled from their Lord. The 'looking' signifies security, honor, and joy, as they behold with satisfaction the reward promised for their faith and righteous deeds in this world, after having been mocked by the disbelievers.

translation: Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?
interpretation: This closing verse of Surat al-Mutaffifin (83:36) is a rhetorical question. It asks the believers, who are enjoying their blessings on couches and watching the disbelievers who used to mock them, whether those disbelievers have now received full recompense for their deeds. The implied answer is yes: the disbelievers' mockery, scorn and wrongdoing in the world have been matched by a just and exact requital in the Hereafter. The verse affirms God's perfect justice, assuring the believers that no deed goes unrewarded or unpunished, and that the reversal of fortunes on the Day of Judgment is a fair repayment rather than an injustice.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is split open.
interpretation: This verse opens Surat al-Inshiqaq with a depiction of the cosmic upheaval that will mark the Day of Judgment. The splitting of the sky, which appears to humans as a fixed and secure canopy, signals that the entire order of the created world is entirely subject to God's command and will come to an end when He wills. It serves as a reminder that nothing in creation is eternal or independent, and that the heavens themselves submit to their Lord, so human beings, who are far weaker, should likewise prepare for the moment when they will return to Him and be held accountable for their deeds.

translation: And has listened to its Lord, as it must do.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Inshiqaq 84:5) describes the sky on the Day of Judgment: when it splits apart, it submits entirely to God's command, hearing and obeying without resistance. The phrase 'and it was bound to do so' (wa huqqat) means that obedience is the sky's rightful duty, since it is a created thing wholly subject to its Creator. The lesson is that if the vast heavens yield willingly to God's will, then human beings, who are given choice, should all the more heed their Lord and submit to Him before the day when all creation is made to do so.

translation: And when the earth is stretched out.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Inshiqaq 84:3) describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection: the earth will be flattened and extended, its mountains, valleys, and buildings leveled, so that it becomes a vast, even plain. Many commentators explain that it will be spread out like a leather sheet to make room for all of humanity, gathered for reckoning on a single open expanse where nothing remains hidden or sheltered. It conveys that the familiar world will be transformed by God's command, and that every created thing will submit to His decree, just as the sky is split open and obeys its Lord in the preceding verses.

translation: And it casts out what is within it and becomes empty.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Inshiqaq, 84:4) describes the Day of Resurrection, when the earth will cast out everything it holds within it, including the dead in their graves and the treasures and hidden things buried in its depths, until it is completely emptied. The word 'takhallat' (becomes empty) stresses that nothing remains hidden inside the earth. This signifies that all humankind will be raised for reckoning, and that no deed or secret will remain concealed, since the earth, which was a witness and a keeper of what was entrusted to it, will surrender it in submission to its Lord's command.

translation: And has listened to its Lord, as it must do.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Inshiqaq (84:5), describes the sky on the Day of Judgment: when it splits apart, it obeys its Creator's command completely and without resistance, because it is bound by duty to obey. The point is that even the vast heavens submit to God's will as soon as He commands, so human beings, who are far smaller and weaker, should submit willingly in this life rather than resist, since every created thing will ultimately yield to its Lord.

translation: O mankind, you are laboring toward your Lord with great exertion, and you will meet Him.
interpretation: Every human being is in constant striving throughout life, whether in pursuit of livelihood, status, pleasure, or righteousness, and all of this effort is moving inexorably toward death and then standing before God. The verse reminds people that no labor is without a destination: since the end of every path is meeting the Lord and being held accountable for one's deeds, a person should direct their exertion toward what will benefit them in that encounter, namely faith and righteous action, rather than wasting it on what perishes.

translation: As for he who is given his record in his right hand,
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, every person will receive the record of his deeds. Receiving it in the right hand is a sign of salvation and honor, showing that the person was among the righteous whose good deeds outweighed their wrongs by God's mercy. It is a public declaration of success that brings joy, as the following verses describe the person happily inviting others to read his book, since he had always believed in the reckoning and prepared for it through faith and good works.

translation: Then he will be judged with an easy reckoning.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Inshiqaq, 84:8) describes the believer who receives his record of deeds in his right hand. His reckoning will be gentle: his deeds are simply presented to him, his good is acknowledged, and his shortcomings are overlooked through God's mercy without harsh interrogation or exposure. It teaches that salvation on the Day of Judgment rests on God's forgiveness and generosity, not on strict scrutiny, and that those who live in faith and righteousness will be spared the terror of a difficult accounting.

translation: And he will return to his people joyfully.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Inshiqaq 84:9) describes the person who receives his record of deeds in his right hand and is reckoned with an easy reckoning. Having been saved, he goes back to his family, meaning his relatives and spouses among the people of Paradise or the household prepared for him there, in a state of joy and delight. The verse shows that true happiness is the fruit of faith and righteous action: the believer who is spared a strict accounting, and whose deeds are accepted, returns with a gladness that no worldly pleasure can equal, and he is reunited with those he loves in lasting security and bliss.

translation: But as for him who is given his record from behind his back,
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 84:10) describes the fate of the one who is condemned on the Day of Judgment. Receiving the record of deeds behind the back signifies rejection and disgrace: such a person turned away from God's guidance and cast His revelation behind him in the worldly life, so he is handed his book in a manner that mirrors his conduct. It is a sign of loss and foreshadows the punishment that follows, in which he will wish for destruction and enter the blazing fire. The believer receives his record in his right hand openly and with honor, while the denier receives it in shame, showing that the manner of receiving the record reflects one's relationship with the truth in this life.

translation: He will soon call out for destruction.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 84:11) describes the person who is handed his record of deeds behind his back on the Day of Judgment. Realizing the gravity of his misdeeds and the punishment awaiting him, he will cry out 'Woe, ruin!' wishing for annihilation as an escape from his torment. The call for destruction is an expression of utter despair: he sees no way out except to wish for death, yet that wish cannot be granted. It reveals that the true horror of the Hereafter lies in the full awareness of one's own responsibility, and that those who turned away from God's guidance in this life will find their regret inescapable when the truth is made plain.

translation: And he will enter a blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Inshiqaq 84:12) describes the final fate of the one who was given his record of deeds behind his back. Having rejected the truth and lived heedlessly in the world, he will not merely pass near the Fire but will be cast into it and burn in its intense, flaming blaze. The word 'yasla' conveys being immersed in and tasting the heat of the fire, and 'sa'ir' denotes its fierce, roaring flame. It stands as a just recompense for denying the Hereafter and for his arrogance, in contrast to the believer who returns to his family in joy, and it is a warning that deeds in this life determine one's eternal outcome.

translation: Indeed, he used to be among his family in joy.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Inshiqaq 84:13) explains why the person who receives his record in his left hand faces a grim fate. In the worldly life he lived heedlessly, delighting in his family and pleasures and arrogantly content with himself. His joy was that of someone absorbed in the present life, who did not fear God, did not prepare for the Hereafter, and did not think he would be called to account. His worldly delight was unaccompanied by gratitude or awareness of accountability, so it now stands in sharp contrast to the sorrow and distress he will experience. By comparison, the believer, who may have felt fear and concern in this life, is granted lasting joy in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, he thought that he would never return (to God).
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Inshiqaq, 84:14) explains why the person who receives his record in his left hand meets such an end. In worldly life he lived heedlessly and arrogantly among his family, believing that there would be no resurrection, no return to God, and no reckoning. The word 'yahur' means to return or to go back, so his error was a denial of accountability. Because he never expected to stand before his Lord, he felt free to do wrong without restraint. The verse teaches that disbelief in the Hereafter is the root of moral corruption, and that belief in returning to God is what disciplines conduct and keeps a person mindful of justice.

translation: Yes indeed! His Lord was ever All-Seeing of him.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 84:15) answers the person who is handed his record in his left hand and thought he would never return to God (84:14). The word 'Yes' firmly refutes that assumption: he will indeed return and be resurrected. God had full knowledge of him throughout his life, including his deeds, his intentions, and what he concealed, so nothing is lost and his account will be exact and just. The verse is both a warning and a reminder that human beings are always observed by God and are accountable before Him, so they should live with awareness of that accountability.

translation: So I swear by the twilight glow after sunset.
interpretation: Here God draws attention to the shafaq, the redness that lingers on the horizon after the sun has set, as a sign of how things pass from one state to another. Day gives way to night in stages, and this points to the stage-by-stage progression that human beings themselves will go through, from life to death to resurrection (as the following verses on the night and the moon, and on 'stage after stage,' suggest). The oath is meant to awaken reflection: the One who governs the changing sky with such precision is able to carry people through the changing stages of existence and to bring them to account. The opening 'fa-la uqsimu' is an emphatic form of oath, which stresses that the matter is so certain it hardly needs an oath, yet the oath is given to arouse the listener's attention.

translation: And by the night and all that it envelops and gathers in.
interpretation: In this oath (Surah Al-Inshiqaq, 84:17), God swears by the night and everything it draws together: when darkness falls, people return to their homes, animals to their shelters and birds to their nests, and creatures that scattered by day are gathered and brought into rest. This daily gathering points to a greater gathering, since the God who orderly collects all things under the cover of night is able to gather humankind on the Day of Resurrection, when every soul will be brought together to face its account and move from one state to another, stage after stage.

translation: And [I swear] by the moon when it becomes full.
interpretation: God swears by the moon at the moment it reaches completion and fullness, after growing night by night from a thin crescent. This oath points to the gradual progression that marks all of creation, including the human being, who passes through successive stages of life and states before meeting his Lord. The moon's steady journey from crescent to full light under a divinely set order is a sign of God's precise design and a reminder that nothing moves except by His decree, so a person should reflect on his own course and prepare for the stages that lie ahead, ending in the return to God.

translation: You will surely ride stage after stage (or: pass from one state to another, level upon level).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Inshiqaq (84:19), reminds human beings that their existence is a journey through successive stages and conditions: from creation, to childhood, to maturity, to old age, then death, the barzakh, resurrection, and finally reckoning. No one remains in a fixed state, and each stage is harder or more serious than the one before. The point is that, since life is a continual transition ending in standing before God, a person should not be deceived by present ease or power, but should prepare for the coming stages with faith and righteous deeds.

translation: So what is the matter with them that they do not believe?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 84:20) is a rhetorical question of astonishment and rebuke. After God points to clear signs in creation, such as the twilight, the night and what it gathers, and the full moon, and reminds people that they will pass from one stage to another until they return to Him, the verse asks what excuse the disbelievers could possibly have. The evidence for God's power and for the Resurrection is plain, so their refusal to believe has no rational justification and stems from stubbornness and heedlessness, not from any lack of proof.

translation: And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate?
interpretation: The verse, from Surat al-Inshiqaq (84:21), rebukes those who hear God's words yet remain unmoved. Prostration here means more than the physical act: it stands for humility, submission and acknowledgment of God's majesty. A heart that is alive responds to the Qur'an with awe and obedience. Those who hear its warnings, promises and signs and still show no reverence, no change of conduct and no surrender to God reveal hardness of heart and a refusal to believe. The verse also teaches that recitation should lead to action and devotion, not mere listening, which is why this is a place of prostration in recitation.

translation: Nay, those who disbelieve persist in denial.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 84:22) tells us that the refusal of the disbelievers to prostrate or submit when the Qur'an is recited to them does not come from any lack of evidence or clarity. It comes from a settled attitude of rejection and stubborn denial. The word 'bal' (nay) turns away from asking why they do not believe and gives the real reason: their disbelief is an active, ongoing habit of calling truth a lie. Their denial is deliberate and arises from arrogance and the hardness of their hearts, not from ignorance. The verb in the present tense ('yukadhdhibun') suggests continuity, meaning they persist in this denial and do not relent despite the signs and warnings placed before them.

translation: And God knows best what they keep within themselves.
interpretation: The verse says that God has complete knowledge of what the disbelievers hold inside their hearts and minds, including their hidden denial, envy, and ill intentions, even when they show something different outwardly. Nothing they conceal escapes Him, so their inner state will be accounted for, and no outward pretense can protect them from His judgment. It also reminds believers to purify their intentions, since God judges the heart as well as the visible deed.

translation: So give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse uses the Arabic idiom of 'glad tidings' (bushra) ironically. Good news would normally mean something pleasant, but here it is applied to a grievous punishment. This irony is a form of rebuke: those who reject God's guidance, hoard wealth without fulfilling their obligations, or persist in wrongdoing are told that the only 'good news' left for them is the consequence of their own choices. The verse serves as a moral warning that actions have a reckoning, and that sincere repentance and a change of conduct are the way to avoid this outcome.

translation: Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward that is never cut off.
interpretation: This verse sets apart those whose faith is joined with righteous action from the general condition of human decline described just before it, where people are brought low after being created in the best form. Faith alone is not enough, and neither are deeds without faith. Together they lift a person above that decline. Their reward from God is 'ghayr mamnun', meaning it will never be interrupted, diminished, or spoiled by reproach. It is a perpetual and unending recompense, given purely out of God's generosity, without the taint of grudging favor, and it makes up for the weakness and trials of this worldly life.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the heaven containing great constellations.
interpretation: God swears by the sky with its vast stars and celestial formations, calling attention to His power and the order of creation. The oath prepares the listener for the surah's message: the One who built and governs such a magnificent, ordered cosmos is fully able to hold the oppressors accountable, to protect and vindicate the steadfast believers, and to bring about the Day of Judgment promised in the verses that follow.

translation: By the Promised Day.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Burooj 85:2) is an oath by God swearing by the Day of Resurrection, the day He has promised to gather all creation for reckoning and recompense. By swearing by it, God stresses that the Day is certain and will come without fail, so that the oppressed may take comfort that justice will be done, and the oppressors, like those who persecuted the believers in the story that follows, be warned that their deeds will not go unanswered.

translation: And [by] the witness and the witnessed.
interpretation: God swears by two realities, the one who bears witness and that which is witnessed, to stress the gravity of what follows in Surat al-Buruj. The most widely held reading is that the witness is Friday, or the Prophet and the community who testify, and the witnessed is the Day of Arafah or the Day of Judgment, when all creation will be gathered and every deed will be testified to. The oath reminds believers that every act is observed and recorded, that the persecutors of the faithful, such as the People of the Trench, will be held to account before a witnessing assembly, and that no oppression escapes divine justice.

translation: Destroyed were the companions of the trench.
interpretation: This opening of the account in Surah Al-Burooj is a condemnation and a curse upon the tyrants who dug trenches, kindled fires, and cast the believers into them because of their faith in God alone. The verse teaches that oppressors who persecute people for their belief earn God's wrath and destruction, however powerful they seem. It also consoles the faithful of every age: their steadfastness in the face of persecution is witnessed and honored by God, and the final defeat belongs to those who torment them, while the believers' reward is secure with Him.

translation: The fire full of fuel.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Buruj 85:5) describes the pit of fire in which the believers were burned by their persecutors, the People of the Trench (Ashab al-Ukhdud). The phrase 'full of fuel' conveys how intensely and fiercely the fire was stoked, showing the extent of the oppressors' cruelty and the severity of the crime they committed. It serves to console the believers by affirming that God knows exactly what was done to them, and it warns the tyrants that their cruelty is recorded and will be answered with a punishment even more terrible than the fire they kindled.

translation: When they were sitting by it (the fire pit),
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 85:6) continues the account of the People of the Trench (Ashab al-Ukhdud), describing the persecutors who sat beside the pit of fire into which they had thrown the believers. Their sitting there shows they were not reluctant executioners but cold-blooded onlookers who took pleasure in watching the believers burn, as the next verse says they were witnesses to what they did to the believers. The verse stresses the depth of their cruelty and their personal involvement in the crime, and so it warns that God, who sees such oppression, will hold the oppressors to account while the steadfast believers are vindicated.

translation: And they were, to what they were doing to the believers, witnesses.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Buruj (85:7), describes the oppressors known as the People of the Trench, who burned believers for their faith. They sat by the fire and watched, fully aware of and personally taking part in the cruelty, so they cannot claim ignorance or say they were forced. Their watching shows deliberate, willing participation in the crime. The verse also hints that on the Day of Judgment they will be held accountable, with their own deeds and presence at the scene standing as testimony against them, while God, the true Witness over all things, saw what they did and will requite it.

translation: And they resented them for nothing except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Buruj 85:8) shows how senseless and unjust the persecutors were. The believers had committed no crime and no wrong that could justify the torture inflicted on them. Their only 'offense' was holding faith in God, who is Almighty (Al-'Aziz), so no one who relies on Him is truly defeated, and Praiseworthy (Al-Hamid), so He is worthy of worship and gratitude in every condition. Faith is therefore the very thing that tyrants hate, and the believers' steadfastness shows that their loyalty to the Mighty and Praiseworthy God outweighs any worldly threat. This also consoles the believers of every era who are oppressed for their belief: their cause is honorable, and God, whose attributes of might and praiseworthiness are invoked here, will vindicate them and hold their persecutors to account.

translation: He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; and God is Witness over all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone holds true sovereignty over all creation, so nothing in the heavens or the earth lies outside His authority or knowledge. Because He is witness to everything, no deed, intention, or event, whether open or hidden, escapes Him. This should give the believer reassurance that God sees their patience and sincerity even when no one else does, and it should warn the wrongdoer that their oppression is observed and will be accounted for. It calls people to live with constant awareness of God, to be just and to trust in His justice.

translation: Indeed, those who persecute the believing men and believing women and then do not repent will have the punishment of Hell, and they will have the punishment of the Burning Fire.
interpretation: The verse warns those who tortured and tempted the believers, men and women alike, to abandon their faith, whether by physical harm, coercion, or trials, as the people of the trench did and as the Quraysh did to the early Muslims. If they persist in their oppression and die without turning back to God in repentance, they face a double punishment: the torment of Hell for their disbelief and wrongdoing, and the specific torment of burning, a fitting recompense for those who burned or tortured the faithful. The verse also shows that the door of repentance stays open even for the worst persecutors, since the threat is conditional on their not repenting. It affirms God's mercy and His justice together: He protects the oppressed, and He gives the oppressors a chance to return before the punishment becomes certain.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true success is not worldly gain or status but the pairing of sincere faith with righteous action. Belief alone is not enough, and deeds without faith are not enough. God promises those who combine the two an eternal home of lush gardens with flowing rivers, an image of lasting peace, abundance, and God's acceptance. By calling this 'the great triumph,' the verse tells believers to measure success by what endures in the hereafter, and to stay steadfast in faith and good conduct even when it costs them in this life.

translation: Indeed, the seizing (grip) of your Lord is severe.
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Buruj warns that when God takes wrongdoers to account, His punishment is overwhelming and none can resist or escape it. It comes after the account of the persecutors who tortured believers, and serves both as a warning to tyrants that their power is insignificant before God's might, and as consolation to the faithful that the oppressors will not go unpunished. The word 'your Lord' addresses the Prophet with reassurance, indicating that the One who nurtures and protects him is the One whose reckoning is certain and severe.

translation: Indeed, it is He who originates creation and then repeats it.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 85:13) affirms God's complete power over creation and resurrection. Since He brings creatures into existence from nothing at the beginning, He is surely able to bring them back to life after death for judgment. In its context, following the warning of the severe seizure of the oppressors who persecuted the believers, it is both a warning and a consolation: no wrongdoer can escape accountability, because the One who began creation will also restore it and recompense every soul with perfect justice. The believers can therefore trust that their suffering is not forgotten, and the tyrants should know that their reckoning is certain.

translation: And He is the Most Forgiving, the Most Loving.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 85:14) presents two attributes of God that offer deep hope to believers. God forgives sins for those who sincerely turn back to Him, and His forgiveness is joined with active love toward His servants. Coming right after the warning of punishment for those who persecuted the believers and did not repent (85:10), the verse shows that even the worst wrongdoers are invited to repent, because the door of mercy remains open. It also teaches that God's relationship with those who return to Him is not merely the pardoning of faults but one of affection and closeness: He loves those who obey Him and repent, and He draws them near, so that fear of His power is balanced by confidence in His mercy.

translation: Owner of the Throne, the Glorious.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 85:15) describes God as the Lord of the Throne, the sovereign seat of His dominion, and as Al-Majid, the Glorious, whose greatness, nobility, and generosity are limitless. By linking His possession of the Throne, the highest of all created things, with His glory, the verse stresses that His power is absolute and that no tyrant or persecutor can escape His reach. It is a reassurance to the believers who suffer for their faith, as in the story of the People of the Ditch in this surah, that the One they trust is supreme in authority and majesty, and that His justice will certainly prevail over those who oppress them.

translation: He is the Doer of whatever He intends.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 85:16) affirms God's absolute and unrestricted will and power. Nothing can hinder, compel, or overrule what He wills, and whatever He decides comes to pass according to His perfect wisdom. It follows the mention of His mercy and love for believers and His severe seizing of the oppressors, assuring the faithful that their Lord's promise is certain and warning the tyrants who persecuted believers that they cannot escape His decree. His acts are never arbitrary but grounded in wisdom and justice, so believers should trust His plan and hold fast to patience and hope.

translation: Has there reached you the story of the armies?
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Burooj 85:17) opens a rhetorical question that draws the Prophet's attention to the fate of earlier tyrannical hosts. The next verse names them as Pharaoh and Thamud. The question is not asking for information. It reminds the listener that arrogant power, however large its numbers and strength, cannot stand against God's decree. It consoles the believers, who were being persecuted in Makkah, with the assurance that the oppressors of the past were destroyed and that the Quraysh, who were opposing and tormenting the believers, face the same end if they persist in disbelief.

translation: Pharaoh and Thamud.
interpretation: This phrase comes from the Qur'anic passage that recalls earlier peoples who rebelled against God and were destroyed (cf. Surah al-Buruj 85:17-18: 'Has the story of the hosts reached you, of Pharaoh and Thamud?'). It names two proud, defiant powers, Pharaoh with his armies and Thamud with their might and rock-hewn dwellings, as historical examples that worldly strength, authority and numbers do not shield anyone from God's punishment when they deny His messengers. It serves as a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah and a reassurance to the believers that tyranny and denial of the truth end in ruin, however powerful the oppressors seem.

translation: Rather, those who disbelieve are engaged in denial.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Burooj 85:19) describes the disbelievers as being immersed in rejection of the truth. Even after the lessons of earlier nations, such as the people of Pharaoh and Thamud, and the stories of those who persecuted the believers, the disbelievers do not take heed. Their denial is not from a lack of evidence but from stubbornness and arrogance, so they remain absorbed in it, as though denial surrounds and occupies them completely, and they persist in it despite clear warnings.

translation: And God encompasses them from behind.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Buruj (85:20), tells us that those who persecute the believers and deny the truth are never beyond God's reach. Although they may think they act freely and escape accountability, God surrounds them completely with His knowledge, power, and authority, so that nothing they do is hidden and they cannot flee His judgment. It is both a warning to the oppressors that their reckoning is inescapable and a consolation to the believers that God sees what they endure and will bring justice.

translation: Rather, it is a Glorious Qur'an.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Buruj, 85:21) answers the disbelievers who denied the revelation and called it poetry, sorcery, or the words of men. It affirms that the Qur'an is majestic and honored: lofty in its rank, abundant in goodness and guidance, and unmatched in its eloquence and truth. Its glory comes from its divine source, and it is preserved from alteration, as the next verse says it is in a Preserved Tablet. The Qur'an's worth is therefore not diminished by the rejection of those who deny it.

translation: In a Preserved Tablet.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Buruj, 85:22) completes the preceding verse, 'Nay, it is a Glorious Qur'an,' and declares that the Qur'an is recorded in a Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), a heavenly record kept safe from any alteration, corruption, addition, omission, or tampering by devils or humans. It affirms that the Qur'an's origin is divine and its text is protected by God's knowledge and decree, so the message remains authoritative and secure regardless of the denial or plotting of those who reject it, just as the tyrants mentioned earlier in the surah could not extinguish the faith of the believers.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the heaven and the night-comer (the Tariq).
interpretation: God opens the chapter with an oath by the heaven, the vast and ordered dome above us, and by the 'night-comer', which the following verses identify as the piercing star. Swearing by these signs draws attention to the precision and power of the Creator's design. The oath prepares the listener for the main message of the chapter: that every soul has a guardian recording over it, and that the One who created and sustains the heavens and its brilliant stars is fully able to create humans and to resurrect them for accountability. The sudden appearance of a star piercing the darkness of night also symbolizes how truth and divine reckoning arrive unexpectedly and cut through heedlessness, urging people to reflect and be mindful of their ultimate return to God.

translation: And what will make you know what the Night-Comer is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question, found in Surah At-Tariq (86:2), is meant to stir the listener's attention and signal the greatness of what comes next. The 'Tariq' is the one who comes at night, and the next verse identifies it as the piercing star. By asking 'what will make you know,' God shows that the reality of this star and what it points to goes beyond ordinary human knowledge and cannot be fully grasped without divine revelation. The verse leads the reader to reflect on the signs God has set in the heavens, and to see that these signs bear witness to a Watcher who guards every soul, a theme the surah develops afterward in the reminder that every soul has a guardian over it.

translation: The piercing star.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat At-Tariq (86:3), describes the star that pierces through the darkness of the night with its brilliant light. It points to the idea that God's creation bears witness to His power and to His watchful care over every soul, since the surah goes on to say that no soul is without a guardian. Just as the bright star cuts through the night's darkness and cannot be hidden, so the truth and God's knowledge penetrate all concealment, and nothing a person does is hidden from Him. The image invites reflection on the heavens as a sign that every human being is observed, accountable, and sustained by their Lord.

translation: There is no soul but has a guardian watching over it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tariq, 86:4) teaches that every human being is under constant, precise watchfulness. Most commentators understand the 'guardian' (hafiz) as angels appointed by God to record and preserve each person's deeds, words, and intentions, so that nothing is lost and everything will be presented on the Day of Judgment. It also carries the sense that God's protection and knowledge encompass every soul, guarding it through its appointed term. The verse thus instills moral accountability: a person should live consciously, knowing that no action goes unrecorded, and that the One who created them from a fluid and can return them to life is fully aware of all they do.

translation: So let man consider from what he was created.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 86:5) invites human beings to reflect on their humble origin. Man, who may grow arrogant or deny resurrection, is urged to look at the stages of his own creation: he was made from a despised, small fluid, not from anything of his own power. Recognizing this lowly beginning should instill humility and awareness of dependence on the Creator. It also serves as proof of resurrection, since the One who brought humans into being from such an origin is surely able to bring them back to life and hold them accountable, as the following verses affirm.

translation: He was created from a gushing fluid.
interpretation: The verse points humans to the humble origin of their existence: each person was created from a fluid that is ejected with force, namely the seminal fluid. By reminding a person of this lowly beginning, the Qur'an cultivates humility and counters arrogance and denial of the resurrection. The One who brought a human being into existence from such a fluid is plainly able to bring them back to life after death and hold them to account. The verse thus moves from reflection on one's origin to certainty about one's return to God.

translation: It issues forth from between the backbone and the ribs.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 86:7) describes the origin of the fluid from which a human being is created, mentioned in the preceding verse as water gushing forth. It points to the place from which the seed emerges, between the loins (the back) and the ribs or chest area, and it stresses that human life begins from a humble, fluid origin. The interpretation I give is that this reminds humans of their weak and lowly beginnings, so that they will recognize the power of the One who created them from such a source and is therefore fully able to bring them back to life on the Day of Resurrection, which is the argument the surah builds toward in the following verse: 'Indeed, He is able to return him.'

translation: Indeed, He is able to bring him back (to life).
interpretation: The verse (86:8) affirms God's power to resurrect humankind after death. Having just reminded people of how they were created from a gushing fluid emitted from between the backbone and the ribs, the Qur'an argues that the One who originated them from so humble a beginning can surely recreate them. Resurrection is thus presented not as something improbable but as easier to conceive than the first creation, and it serves as a reminder that every person will be brought back to account for their deeds on the Day when secrets are laid bare.

translation: On the Day when all secrets will be examined and laid bare.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tariq 86:9) means that on the Day of Resurrection, what people concealed in their hearts, such as their true intentions, beliefs, hidden deeds, and sincerity or hypocrisy, will be tested, exposed, and brought to light. In this world people are judged by outward appearances and can hide their inner realities, but on that Day nothing will stay concealed, and a person's inner state will determine their standing before God. The verse is a reminder to purify one's intentions and be mindful of God in private as well as in public, since the Almighty, who is able to bring humans back to life, also knows and will account for every secret.

translation: Then he will have no power, and no helper.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 86:10) describes the human being on the Day of Resurrection, when secrets are laid bare and all hidden deeds are examined. On that Day, the person will be unable to rely on any strength of his own to protect himself from accountability or punishment, and no one else will come to his aid or defend him. The worldly supports people lean on, such as wealth, status, kin, and allies, will be void. This is a reminder that the God who created humans from a fluid and is able to bring them back to life holds absolute authority, so a person should prepare for that Day with faith and righteous action rather than trusting in false sources of security.

translation: By the sky that returns [rain].
interpretation: God swears by the sky, which sends back what is placed in it. The 'raj'' (returning) is most commonly understood as rain that returns again and again, season after season, falling from the sky to revive the dead earth. The oath draws attention to a sign of God's power: just as He sends life-giving water down in a repeating cycle and brings forth growth from lifeless ground, He is able to bring man back to life after death. This prepares for the surah's central message that the Creator who originated man can return him for resurrection and reckoning, and that every soul has a guardian recording its deeds.

translation: And [by] the earth which splits open [with vegetation].
interpretation: God swears by the earth that cracks open as plants and springs burst forth from it.
