The oath points to the power that brings life out of the lifeless ground, just as He is able to bring people back to life after death. The splitting of the soil to release new growth is a visible sign of resurrection, so the verse affirms that the Qur'an's message about the Hereafter is true and that the One who revives the barren earth can raise humankind for judgment.

translation: Indeed, it is a decisive word.
interpretation: This verse (At-Tariq 86:13) affirms that the Qur'an is a final, decisive statement that separates truth from falsehood. It is not idle talk or a matter of jest, as the next verse confirms. Its judgments are binding and its message is clear and authoritative, so a person must take it seriously and decide to accept it and live by it, since it distinguishes guidance from misguidance and right from wrong.

translation: And it is not a thing of jest.
interpretation: This verse (At-Tariq 86:14) affirms that the Qur'an is the decisive word that separates truth from falsehood, and that its message is serious and not frivolous. Its warnings, promises, and rulings are real and binding, so people must receive it with earnest attention and obedience rather than treat it with mockery or indifference, because it will bear on their account before God.

translation: Indeed, they are plotting a scheme.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tariq 86:15) describes the disbelievers of Makkah who schemed against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the message of truth, plotting to extinguish the light of revelation through deceit, ridicule, persecution, and conspiracies against his life. It reminds the believer that falsehood always organizes itself and exerts effort to oppose the truth, yet their plotting is ultimately weak and futile in the face of divine will. The verse sets up the following verse, 'And I am planning a plan,' which assures that God's wisdom and power overturn the schemes of wrongdoers, so the believer should remain steadfast and place trust in God rather than fear the machinations of those who oppose the truth.

translation: And I am planning a plan.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tariq 86:16) is God's response to the disbelievers who scheme against the Prophet and the message of truth. It affirms that while they plot to extinguish the light of revelation, God devises a perfect, unseen strategy that overturns their schemes and brings them to failure. The 'plan' of God is not deception in a human, immoral sense but a just and wise counter-measure: He gives the wrongdoers respite, lets their own plotting lead them to ruin, and ensures the ultimate victory of truth. It consoles the believers that no human scheme can prevail against divine will, and warns the arrogant that their apparent success is only a temporary delay before their downfall.

translation: So give the disbelievers respite; give them a little time, gently.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 86:17) comforts the Prophet and warns the deniers. After the preceding verses describe their scheming against the truth and God's counter-plan, the Prophet is told not to hurry for their punishment or be distressed by their delay. Their respite is brief and measured by God's wisdom, not a sign of neglect or approval. It is a test and a stage before the justice that will certainly overtake them, either in this world or the next. Believers are therefore urged to be patient and trust that God's timing is perfect and that the triumph of truth over falsehood is certain.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.
interpretation: The verse commands the believer to declare God free of every imperfection, weakness, and partner, and to honor His name with reverence. Glorifying His name means mentioning it only with veneration, never using it casually or in association with anything false, and it extends to glorifying God Himself in prayer and daily life. The attribute 'the Most High' points to His absolute supremacy over all creation in essence, power, and rank, so that nothing is above Him and nothing resembles Him. The verse therefore calls for a heart and tongue that keep God exalted above every created thing, which is the foundation of sincere worship.

translation: [He] who created, then proportioned [what He created].
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-A'la, 87:2) describes the Lord as the One who brought every creature into existence and then perfected its form, making it well-proportioned and fit for its purpose. It points to the order and harmony in creation, especially in the human being, whose limbs and faculties are balanced and suited to their functions. This shows that such precision could only come from a Creator of absolute power and wisdom, who alone is worthy of glorification and worship.

translation: And who has determined [all things] and then guided [them].
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-A'la 87:3) points to God's complete mastery over creation: He measured out and ordained for every creature its nature, purpose, and appointed measure, and then guided each to fulfill its role. Fish are guided to swim, birds to fly, infants to seek the breast, and human beings are guided to what benefits them in life and, above all, to the path of truth through reason and revelation. Creation is therefore neither random nor left without direction; every being is given both its design and the inner or revealed guidance to carry out that design, which calls the believer to glorify the Lord Most High with trust in His wisdom.

translation: And who brought forth the pasture.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-A'la, 87:4) points to God's power and providence in sustaining life: He causes the green vegetation and grazing land to spring from the barren earth, providing food for animals and, through them, for humankind. It is offered as a visible sign that the One who creates and perfects, determines and guides, is also the One who nourishes. Seeing the earth's greenery emerge from lifeless soil should lead a person to reflect on God's gracious care and to glorify Him, and it also hints that the same power that revives dead land can bring the dead back to life.

translation: And then made it dark, dried-up stubble.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-A'la (87:5), completes the image begun in the preceding verse, where God brings forth the green pasturage. After its freshness and vitality, He reduces it to withered, blackened debris that the flood carries along. The verse points to the transience of worldly life: whatever flourishes in it, however lush and beautiful, is destined to decay and fade by God's decree. The same Power that creates and gives growth also brings things to their end, so a person should not be deceived by the passing splendor of this world but should turn to the Creator and prepare for the lasting life of the Hereafter.

translation: We will make you recite, so you will not forget.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 87:6) is God's assurance to the Prophet Muhammad that the revelation is secured by divine guarantee rather than by human effort alone. God Himself will teach him the Qur'an and fix it in his heart, so that nothing of what is revealed will slip from his memory. The Prophet need not hurry or anxiously repeat the verses out of fear of losing them, because preserving the message is God's responsibility. This reflects the broader Qur'anic theme that the revelation is protected by God and that the Prophet's role is to receive and convey it with calm trust in His promise.

translation: Except what God wills. Indeed, He knows what is declared openly and what is hidden.
interpretation: This verse (Al-A'la 87:7) follows the promise to the Prophet that he will be made to recite and will not forget. The exception 'except what God wills' affirms that retention of revelation depends entirely on God's will, so even the Prophet's memory is not independent of Him. If God wills that something be forgotten or abrogated, it is so, and the Prophet cannot claim any power of his own. The verse then grounds this in God's perfect knowledge: He knows what is spoken aloud and what is concealed in hearts, so His decisions about what is preserved, abrogated, or made easy are based on complete wisdom and awareness of what benefits His servants. It teaches humility and total reliance on God, whose knowledge and will govern all things.

translation: And We will ease you toward the easy path.
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-A'la promises the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that God will make the path of revelation, its retention, and its implementation smooth for him, and will facilitate for him every good matter and the way of the religion, which is easy and free of hardship. It carries a broader lesson that when a servant is sincere and entrusts his affairs to God, God makes goodness and obedience easy for him and removes obstacles from his way, so that following the straight path becomes natural and light rather than burdensome.

translation: So remind, if the reminder should benefit.
interpretation: God commands the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to keep admonishing and teaching people, and the condition 'if the reminder benefits' does not make reminding contingent on guaranteed success. It points to where reminding is worthwhile: it should be directed to those in whom there is some hope of benefit, and it should be given at the right time and place and with the right wisdom. The mission is to convey and remind, while guidance itself rests with God. The verse also implies that those who are receptive, who fear God and are open to being reminded, will take heed, while the stubborn will turn away from the message and bear its consequences.

translation: The one who fears [God] will take heed.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-A'la, 87:10) teaches that the capacity to benefit from admonition depends on the state of the heart. A person who fears God, and is conscious that he will be held accountable, is inwardly open to reminders and responds to them by reflecting, repenting, and changing his conduct. Reverent fear is therefore the gateway to guidance: it makes the heart attentive to warnings and signs, while the heedless and arrogant, who feel no such awe, turn away from the same message and gain nothing from it. The Prophet is thus consoled that his task is only to remind, and that those whose hearts are alive with taqwa will be the ones who heed.

translation: But the most wretched will avoid it.
interpretation: The verse refers to the admonition (al-dhikra) mentioned just before it, in Surah Al-A'la (87:11). The one who is most wretched, meaning the person whose heart is hardened by disbelief and stubborn arrogance, keeps away from the reminder and turns from it. He avoids it because he does not want to be bound by its truth or to change his way of life. His wretchedness is therefore not an arbitrary fate but the outcome of his own deliberate rejection of guidance. The next verse adds that he will enter the great Fire, which shows that turning away from the reminder leads to the worst end.

translation: He who will enter the greatest Fire.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-A'la, 87:12) describes the wretched person who turns away from the reminder and avoids admonition, as mentioned in the preceding verse. His fate is to burn in the 'greatest Fire', the Fire of the Hereafter, which is far more severe than any fire known in this world or any lesser punishment. The word 'greatest' stresses the intensity and terrible nature of the torment of Hell, serving as a warning that rejecting guidance has consequences that dwarf worldly hardships, and urging the listener to heed the reminder before it is too late.

translation: Then he will neither die therein nor live.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-A'la 87:13) describes the state of the most wretched person who rejects the warning and will be cast into the great Fire. His torment is so severe that he longs for death, yet death will not come to relieve him; and he cannot enjoy true life, which is one of ease, peace and benefit. He is held in a suspended existence of unending suffering, neither dying and thereby escaping the pain, nor living a life worthy of the name. The verse stresses the severity and permanence of divine punishment for those who turn away from faith, and warns that there is no escape or relief through death.

translation: He who purifies himself has indeed succeeded.
interpretation: True success is not measured by wealth, status, or worldly gain, but by the purification of the soul. The one who cleanses his heart from disbelief, arrogance, and sin, and refines his character through faith, sincere worship, and good deeds, attains lasting triumph in this life and the next. The verse teaches that inner purity is the foundation of salvation, and that every person is responsible for working on his own self-purification.

translation: And mentions the name of his Lord and prays.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-A'la 87:15) describes the one who attains success through purification: he keeps his heart conscious of God by invoking His name, and that remembrance leads him to formal prayer. Remembrance of God is the inner source of worship, and prayer is its outward expression. A person truly prospers when awareness of his Lord comes first and moves him to establish regular prayer, rather than prayer being an empty ritual disconnected from the heart.

translation: Yet you prefer the life of this world,
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-A'la, 87:16) rebukes human beings for choosing the fleeting pleasures, gains, and comforts of worldly life over the lasting good of the Hereafter. After the preceding verses speak of the one who purifies himself, remembers his Lord, and prays, this verse exposes the root of neglect: a preference for the immediate and visible over the unseen and eternal. It calls the listener to re-examine priorities, since favoring the world is a matter of choice, and to give the Hereafter, which the next verse describes as better and more enduring, its rightful precedence.

translation: And the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-A'la, 87:17) sets the fleeting pleasure of worldly life against the lasting reward of the next life. It teaches that the world's wealth, status and comforts are temporary and perishable, while what God prepares for the believers in the Hereafter is greater in quality and never ends. The verse calls the believer to put first what lasts, and to work for the Hereafter through purification of the soul, remembrance of God and prayer, as the preceding verses describe. It does not demand abandoning the world. It asks that the world never take priority over the eternal life to come.

translation: Indeed, this is in the earlier scriptures,
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-A'la, 87:18) affirms that the core message just stated in the preceding verses, namely that true success belongs to those who purify themselves, remember their Lord, and pray, and that the Hereafter is better and more lasting than worldly life, is not a new or isolated teaching. It is the same eternal truth that God revealed in the earlier scriptures. The point is that the call to purification, devotion, and prioritizing the Hereafter has been consistent across divine revelation, which strengthens the Qur'an's credibility and shows the unity of the prophetic message through history.

translation: The scriptures of Abraham and Moses.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-A'la 87:19) completes the preceding statement that the message of success through purification, remembrance of God, and prayer, and the preference of the eternal Hereafter over the fleeting world, was already present in the earlier scriptures. It affirms that the Qur'an does not bring a new or isolated teaching but renews the one enduring truth revealed to earlier prophets such as Abraham and Moses. The core of divine guidance, belief in God, self-purification, and priority of the Hereafter, remains constant across all revelations, which links the Prophet Muhammad's message to a continuous chain of prophecy.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Has there reached you the report of the Overwhelming Event?
interpretation: The verse opens with a question that is not meant to gather information but to arouse attention and awe. It points to the Day of Resurrection, called al-Ghashiyah because its terror will envelop and overwhelm all creation, leaving no one untouched. By asking the Prophet and every listener whether this news has reached them, the Qur'an urges them to reflect seriously on the certainty of the Hereafter and to prepare for it, since what follows in the surah describes the contrasting fates of those humbled in punishment and those joyful in reward.

translation: Faces on that Day will be humbled,
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Ghashiyah (88:2), describes the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. 'Faces' stands for the whole person, since the face is where fear, shame, and inner states show first. On that Day their arrogance and heedlessness in worldly life will give way to visible abasement and humiliation, because they will see the reality they denied and will know the punishment awaiting them. Their lowered, downcast faces reveal an inner state of dread and regret that can no longer be hidden.

translation: Toiling, weary.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Ghashiyah, 88:3) describes the faces of the people of the Fire on the Day of Judgment. It means that they labored and exhausted themselves in deeds in this world, yet those deeds were not founded on true faith or sincere devotion, or were done in misguidance, so their effort brought them no benefit. Their toil and weariness in this life, wasted because it was not grounded in truth, is mirrored by the weariness and humiliation they suffer in the Hereafter, as the verses that follow describe them entering a blazing fire.

translation: They will enter upon a scorching Fire.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ghashiyah, 88:4) describes the fate of the faces that will be humbled and weary on the Day of Resurrection. The word 'tasla' means to be thrown into and burned by the fire, not merely to approach it, and 'hamiyah' means intensely hot, blazing. The meaning is that those who spent their lives in arrogance, disbelief, or misdirected striving, whose labor was not grounded in true faith and submission to God, will be made to endure the full, unrelenting torment of Hell. The fire's extreme heat conveys the severity of divine justice, and the verse serves as a warning to turn back to sincere belief and righteous action while there is still time.

translation: They will be given to drink from a boiling spring.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the people of Hellfire (Surat al-Ghashiyah, 88:5). After entering a blazing fire, they are given water that offers no relief, because the spring is at the peak of boiling heat. The water, which people normally seek in order to quench thirst and cool themselves, becomes another instrument of torment, scalding their mouths and insides. The verse shows that the punishment is complete and suited to its purpose: even the means of relief turn into suffering for those who turned away from the truth in this world.

translation: They will have no food except from a bitter, thorny plant (dari').
interpretation: This verse describes the torment of the people of Hell, whose only nourishment is dari', a foul thorny plant. It is a food that neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger, as the following verse states. The meaning is that the inhabitants of Hell are denied any comfort or benefit even in the basic need of eating, so that their physical hunger is added to their punishment. It stands in deliberate contrast to the abundant, pleasant provisions promised to the people of Paradise in the same passage, underscoring the consequences of rejecting God's guidance.

translation: It neither nourishes nor avails against hunger.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat al-Ghashiyah (88:7), describes the bitter thorny plant (dari') that will be the only food of the people of Hell. Its meaning is that this food gives none of the benefits real food gives: it does not fatten or strengthen the body, and it does not relieve the pain of hunger. The people of Hell are thus left in a state of unending deprivation, with their food adding to their torment instead of easing it. This is a sharp contrast with the Garden, where provisions are abundant and satisfying. It also reminds the reader that sustenance and relief come only by God's grace, and that those who turn away from Him find no real fulfillment in what they pursue.

translation: On that Day, some faces will be joyful.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ghashiyah, 88:8) describes the state of the righteous on the Day of Judgment. The word 'faces' stands for the whole person, since the face is where inner feelings show. Their faces will glow with delight and serenity because they know their efforts in this world were accepted and that they have been given Allah's mercy and the reward of Paradise. It stands in contrast to the humiliated, weary faces of the disbelievers mentioned just before it, and it reminds the believer that the trials of faith and obedience in this life lead to lasting joy in the next.

translation: [On that Day, faces will be] pleased with their striving.
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Ghashiyah (88:9) describes the faces of the people of Paradise, which on the Day of Judgment will be radiant with joy. They are content with the fruit of their own efforts in this world, their faith and righteous deeds, because they now see the great reward that those efforts earned. The verse teaches that whatever a person strives for in this life will be met with a recompense on the Last Day, and that sincere striving for God's sake ends in lasting satisfaction, unlike the weariness and toil that marked the faces of the disbelievers mentioned earlier in the surah.

translation: In a lofty Garden.
interpretation: The verse describes the final abode of the righteous, who will be in a Garden that is exalted in rank and in physical height. It is elevated above all the troubles, lowliness, and humiliation of this worldly life. This loftiness points to the dignity and honor granted to its inhabitants, who dwell in a place of peace, security, and nearness to God's mercy, in contrast to the low and humiliating state of the people of the Fire.

translation: You will hear in it no idle talk.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Ghashiyah (88:11), describes the people of Paradise. It means that their abode is wholly free from vain, harmful, or offensive speech: no lies, insults, slander, or empty chatter will reach their ears. Because hearing is a primary way the heart is disturbed in this world, the removal of all such speech signals a state of complete inner peace and dignity. Their company and conversation will be pure and wholesome, filled only with words of goodness, peace, and remembrance of God, which is part of the perfect honor and tranquility granted to the believers.

translation: In it is a flowing spring.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Ghashiyah (88:12), describes one of the blessings of Paradise for the people of faith. The 'flowing spring' signifies a source of continual, unfailing abundance: unlike worldly water that can dry up or run short, the spring of Paradise runs without ceasing, so its inhabitants never fear loss or scarcity. Coming after the description of the Fire's inhabitants who are given boiling spring water to drink (88:5), it offers a deliberate contrast: where the wrongdoers receive scalding thirst-torment, the believers receive refreshing, flowing water that brings comfort, joy, and lasting satisfaction as a reward for their faith and righteous deeds.

translation: In it are raised couches.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Ghashiyah, describes the Garden promised to the believers. The 'raised couches' signify honor, dignity, and lofty status: the dwellers of Paradise recline upon elevated seats of repose, free from toil and anxiety. Their height conveys both elevated rank in the sight of God and the believers' ability to look out over the blessings surrounding them, such as flowing springs, cups set in place, and cushions arranged in rows, so that comfort and tranquility are perfected for them.

translation: And cups set in place.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Ghashiyah (88:14), describes the blessings awaiting the people of Paradise. The cups are already laid out and ready, so the inhabitants need not wait or exert any effort to have them prepared. Their drinking vessels stand at hand, set down in readiness beside the couches and springs mentioned in the preceding verses. This conveys the completeness of divine hospitality: every comfort is provided in advance, and the believers enjoy lasting ease and honor as a reward for their faith and striving in the world.

translation: And cushions arranged in rows,
interpretation: This verse is part of the description of Paradise in Surah Al-Ghashiyah (88:15). It portrays the comfort and honor awaiting the believers, who will recline on cushions set out in neat rows, ready for them. The orderly arrangement suggests that everything in Paradise is prepared in advance, so nothing has to be sought or arranged, and that the blessed enjoy complete ease, dignity, and companionship in a place of lasting peace and serenity, in contrast with the toil and humiliation of the people of Hell described earlier in the surah.

translation: And carpets spread out.
interpretation: This verse completes the description of the blissful state of the people of Paradise (Surah Al-Ghashiyah, 88:16). The 'zarabi' are fine, luxurious carpets or rugs, and 'mabthutha' means they are scattered and laid out in abundance in every place, ready for the dwellers to sit and recline upon wherever they wish. It signifies that comfort, honor, and luxury in the Hereafter are not scarce or confined to a single spot, but are available everywhere, so that the believers may enjoy complete ease as a reward for their faith and good deeds.

translation: Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?
interpretation: This verse (88:17) invites people who deny the resurrection and the power of God to reflect on the world around them, beginning with an animal familiar to the Arabs of the time. The camel is wonderfully suited to its environment: its body can endure thirst and heat, it carries heavy loads over long distances, it provides milk, meat, and hair, and it is easily managed despite its size. Such precise design cannot be accidental, and points to a wise and powerful Creator. The verse teaches that contemplating creation leads to recognition of God's power, wisdom, and mercy, and that the One who made such wonders is able to resurrect the dead and hold humanity to account. Faith, in this view, is not blind but is nourished by observation and thoughtful reflection.

translation: And at the sky, how it has been raised high?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Ghashiyah 88:18) invites people to reflect on the sky as a sign of God's power and wisdom. Its vast, towering expanse, held aloft without visible pillars, points to a Creator who designed and sustains it with precision. The verse follows the call to consider the camel and precedes the mountains and the earth, directing the believer from what is near to what is vast, so that contemplating creation leads to recognizing God's oneness, His power to resurrect, and the truth of the message He sent.

translation: And at the mountains, how they have been set firmly in place?
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Ghashiyah (88:19), invites human beings to reflect on the mountains as a sign of God's power and wisdom. The mountains are not random features of the earth: they are raised and fixed in place with deliberate design, giving the earth stability and serving as sources of water, shelter, and minerals. Placed alongside the camel, the sky, and the earth in the neighboring verses, the mountain is an everyday sight that people, especially the Arabs addressed first, knew well. The verse teaches that such ordinary sights, when contemplated, point to a Creator who is capable of all things. That Creator must also be able to bring about the Day of Resurrection, which the surah's earlier verses describe, and He alone deserves to be worshipped.

translation: And at the earth, how it was spread out?
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Ghashiyah (88:20), is part of a call to reflect on visible signs of God's creative power, following the mention of camels, the sky, and the mountains. The earth has been laid out and made level and habitable, with its plains, paths, and fertile ground suited to human life, agriculture, travel, and shelter. Such an arrangement is not accidental but reflects deliberate design and mercy. By contemplating the ordinary world around them, people are led to recognize the Creator's wisdom and power, to acknowledge His oneness, and to accept the truth of the Resurrection and the message that the Prophet brings. The one who can fashion and prepare the earth so perfectly is certainly able to bring the dead back to life and hold humanity to account.

translation: So remind, for you are only a reminder.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Ghashiyah (88:21) instructs the Prophet Muhammad to keep on conveying the message and admonishing people, because his appointed role is to remind and convey, not to compel belief or control hearts. The outcome of guidance lies with God alone, so the Prophet should not grieve or burden himself over those who turn away. It establishes that the duty of a caller to the truth is sincere reminding, with patience and gentleness, while leaving the response to people and the final judgment to God.

translation: You are not a controller over them.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ghashiyah 88:22) clarifies the limits of the Prophet's role: his task is to remind people and convey the message with wisdom and clarity, not to compel hearts to believe. Faith cannot be forced, because it is a matter of free conviction and choice, and guidance lies in God's hands alone. The Prophet is therefore relieved of the burden of people's acceptance or rejection, and the reckoning of those who turn away belongs to God, to whom all will return.

translation: But whoever turns away and disbelieves.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 88:23) sets apart those who, after the Prophet's reminder, deliberately turn their backs on the truth and reject faith. It teaches that the Prophet's task is only to remind, not to compel, and that people are accountable for their own choice. The exception marks those who persist in turning away and denying despite clear guidance, and the verses that follow make clear that God will hold them to account and inflict the greatest punishment, since their rejection was willful rather than out of ignorance.

translation: Then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 88:24) completes the warning about those who turn away and disbelieve: whoever rejects the truth after the reminder has been conveyed will face, in the Hereafter, the severest chastisement. It is called 'the greatest' in contrast to the lesser punishments of this world, such as hardship, defeat, or loss, which are only minor warnings. The greatest punishment is the eternal torment of Hell, and the verse stresses that final judgment belongs to Allah alone, since the Prophet's task was only to remind, not to compel.

translation: Indeed, to Us is their return.
interpretation: This verse, Surah Al-Ghashiyah 88:25, affirms that every human being will ultimately return to God after death, with no escape from this final destination. It carries a warning to those who turn away from the truth and a reassurance to the believers, since the One to whom all return is the same One who will judge with perfect knowledge and justice. The Prophet's task is only to remind, while the final reckoning of each soul belongs to God alone.

translation: Then indeed, upon Us is their account.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Ghashiyah 88:26) concludes the passage in which the Prophet is told that his task is only to remind, not to compel. It means that after the return of all creatures to God, the final reckoning of their deeds belongs to God alone. The Prophet and the believers are not responsible for forcing faith on those who turn away, nor for judging their final outcome. Their duty is to convey the message, while God will bring every soul to account with perfect justice, requiting each according to what it did, so that no one is wronged.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the dawn.
interpretation: God opens Surah Al-Fajr with an oath by the dawn, the moment when darkness gives way to light. This image invites reflection on God's power to bring order, renewal, and clarity out of obscurity, and it prepares the listener for the surah's themes: that just as night inevitably yields to day, oppression and arrogance of past nations ended in their downfall, and every human being will be brought to account. Swearing by the dawn draws attention to a daily sign of divine design as evidence that the promised Day of Judgment and the triumph of justice are certain.

translation: And by ten nights.
interpretation: In this oath (Qur'an 89:2), God swears by ten special nights, which most commentators identify as the first ten nights of Dhul-Hijjah, the sacred month of pilgrimage. These nights are singled out because they are among the most virtuous days of the year, a time when worship, remembrance of God, fasting, and righteous deeds are especially beloved to Him, culminating in the Day of Arafah and the sacrifice at Eid al-Adha. By swearing by them, the verse draws attention to the sanctity of sacred time and calls believers to seize such blessed opportunities for devotion and nearness to God, in contrast to the heedless tyrants of past nations mentioned later in the chapter.

translation: And [by] the even and the odd.
interpretation: In this oath from Surat al-Fajr (89:3), God swears by the 'even' and the 'odd', which is best understood as pointing to the whole of creation, which comes in pairs and in singles. Everything created is characterized by duality or pairing, such as heaven and earth, night and day, male and female, while the Creator alone is the One, the Odd (al-Witr), unique and without partner. The oath therefore draws attention to God's oneness and the order that runs through all creation, inviting reflection on the signs that testify to His power and to the truth of the accountability and judgment that the surah goes on to warn of.

translation: And by the night when it passes on.
interpretation: God swears by the night as it moves along and departs, drawing attention to the order He has set in the cycle of night and day. The night's passing is a sign of His power and wisdom: darkness does not last forever, and every hardship and period of concealment is followed by dawn. Taking this oath alongside the others in Surah al-Fajr (the dawn, the ten nights, the even and the odd), the verse urges reflection on time as a trust and a witness. It tells people that life passes just as the night does, and that they will be held to account for what they did in it, so they should use their time in obedience and remembrance of God before it is gone.

translation: Is there not in that an oath for one who has intellect?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Fajr, 89:5) comes after God swears by the dawn, the ten nights, the even and the odd, and the night as it passes. It asks whether these oaths are enough to convince a person of reason (the one with 'hijr', meaning intellect that restrains one from error). The meaning is that these oaths are weighty and sufficient. They point to God's power, wisdom, and order in creation, and a sensible person who reflects on them will be restrained from denial and wrongdoing and will submit to the truth that God alone deserves worship and that accountability follows.

translation: Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad,
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical question addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, and through him to every listener, calling attention to the fate of the people of 'Ad, a mighty and arrogant nation to whom the Prophet Hud was sent. They denied their messenger, relied on their strength and their towering buildings, and were destroyed by a fierce, roaring wind. The phrase 'your Lord' gives reassurance to the Prophet that God supports His messenger and will defeat the arrogant who reject the truth, just as He destroyed those before them. The 'seeing' here means certain knowledge, since the story was so well known that it was as if it had been witnessed. The verse serves as a warning that worldly power, wealth and civilization cannot protect those who rebel against God and reject His guidance, and that divine justice will overtake the oppressors however strong they may appear.

translation: Iram, possessor of lofty pillars.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 89:7) refers to the ancient people of 'Ad, whose city or lineage, Iram, was renowned for its towering columns and grand architecture. The verse points to their great power and material magnificence, which was part of a warning: despite their strength and monumental buildings, they were destroyed when they rebelled against God and rejected their prophet Hud. Worldly might and splendor offer no protection from divine justice, and they should lead people to gratitude and humility rather than arrogance.

translation: The like of which had never been created in all the lands.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 89:8) completes the description of the people of 'Ad and their city of Iram with its lofty pillars. It stresses that their civilization was unmatched in its time for architectural grandeur, strength, and power. The point is that material might and worldly splendor do not protect a people from God's punishment when they turn arrogant, reject the message of their prophet, and spread corruption. Their destruction serves as a warning that true standing before God lies in faith and righteousness, not in achievements, wealth, or dominion.

translation: And [with] Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Fajr (89:9), continues the list of earlier peoples whom God destroyed despite their power, after mentioning 'Ad and Pharaoh. Thamud were famed for their extraordinary skill in cutting and hewing massive rock into dwellings and buildings in the valley (Wadi al-Qura), as the Qur'an elsewhere says they carved homes out of mountains. The point is that technical mastery, architecture, and material strength do not protect a people who rebel against God and reject His prophet Salih. Their great works could not save them from His punishment, so the verse warns that worldly power and achievement are fleeting and that true security lies in faith and righteousness.

translation: And [He dealt with] Pharaoh, the possessor of the stakes.
interpretation: The phrase 'possessor of the stakes' points to the might and firm establishment of Pharaoh's rule. The 'stakes' symbolize the strength of his armies and the stability of his kingdom, which were held fast like a tent secured by pegs. The verse teaches that even a tyrant whose power seemed unshakable and whose dominion seemed firmly anchored could not escape God's punishment once he transgressed and spread corruption. Worldly strength offers no protection against divine judgment.

translation: Those who transgressed all bounds in the lands.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 89:11) describes the peoples of 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, mentioned just before it, as those who rebelled against God's limits and exceeded all bounds in arrogance and tyranny across the lands. Their power, strength, and worldly stability led them to arrogance rather than gratitude, so they oppressed people and rejected the guidance of their messengers. The verse teaches that power and prosperity without humility before God and justice toward others lead to transgression, and that such tyranny, however widespread, invites divine retribution, as the following verses show: 'and increased corruption therein,' so your Lord unleashed upon them a scourge of punishment.

translation: And spread much corruption therein.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 89:12) completes the description of the tyrants of earlier nations such as 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who transgressed in the lands. Their rebellion against God did not stay a private fault but became a public evil: they multiplied injustice, oppression, and moral and social ruin on the earth, so that wrongdoing spread through their cities and affected the lives of others. The verse teaches that arrogance and disobedience, when unchecked, grow into widespread corruption, and it prepares for the next verse, where God sends down upon them a scourge of punishment, showing that He does not leave persistent oppression and corruption without account.

translation: So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Fajr, 89:13) shows that divine punishment comes decisively once a people persist in tyranny and corruption. The image of a whip (sawt) being poured out portrays the punishment as abundant, overwhelming and inescapable, descending on them like a downpour rather than as a light or passing chastisement. It follows the mention of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who transgressed in the land and spread much corruption, and it teaches that God's justice may be delayed but is never absent. Worldly power and strength give no protection against Him, and a society that oppresses and ignores warnings will face a consequence that is complete and proportionate to its wrongdoing.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful (lying in ambush, keeping close watch over all).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Fajr (89:14), affirms that God observes every deed of every person and no oppressor or wrongdoer can escape His reckoning. Coming after the account of tyrannical nations such as 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, who spread corruption and were seized by punishment, it serves as a warning that divine justice is certain and that nothing is hidden from God. It reassures the oppressed that justice will be done, and it calls on everyone to act with accountability and to be mindful of God, since He is ever-present in watching over and recording what people do.

translation: As for man, whenever his Lord tests him by honoring him and favoring him with blessings, he says, "My Lord has honored me."
interpretation: The verse shows a mistaken human outlook on wealth, status, and comfort. When God grants a person abundance, the person takes it as proof of his own worth and of God's special favor, forgetting that these blessings are a trial of gratitude and obedience, not a measure of nearness to God. True honor in God's sight lies in faith, righteous deeds, and how one uses what one is given, such as caring for orphans and the poor, as the following verses stress. Prosperity and hardship are both tests, so neither should be mistaken for a sign of God's approval or disapproval.

translation: But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says, 'My Lord has humiliated me.'
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human tendency to treat wealth and hardship as proofs of a person's standing with God. Just as ease and honor are not necessarily signs of divine favor (the preceding verse), constricted provision is not a sign of divine disgrace; both are trials. The person who despairs and concludes that God has humiliated him misreads the test. Worth before God is measured by faith, gratitude, patience, and righteous conduct, not by material abundance or scarcity. The proper response to hardship is patience, trust in God, and generosity toward others, rather than complaint or a false conclusion about one's value.

translation: No! But you do not honor the orphan.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the notion that wealth is a sign of God's favor and poverty a sign of His disfavor. The true failing lies in the moral conduct of people: they neglect the orphan, who is the most vulnerable member of society, by failing to treat him with generosity, dignity and care. Honoring the orphan means more than providing material needs; it includes kindness and protecting his rights. Neglecting him reveals a hardened heart and a misplaced sense of values, so a person's standing before God depends on compassion and social responsibility rather than on worldly abundance or scarcity.

translation: And you do not urge one another to feed the poor.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 89:18) condemns not only personal stinginess but also social indifference: those who fail to encourage others to feed the needy share in the guilt of neglecting them. Because the Qur'an says 'urge' rather than just 'give', it makes care for the poor a shared communal duty. A healthy society actively builds a culture of generosity, reminding and motivating one another to relieve hunger, and a community that leaves its poor unfed without even calling for their relief shows a hardened heart and excessive love of wealth.

translation: And you devour the inheritance greedily, consuming it all without distinction.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Fajr 89:19) rebukes people for their greed in wealth, especially the inheritance of orphans and the weak. The phrase 'aklan lamma' suggests gathering and swallowing everything indiscriminately, mixing lawful with unlawful and not caring where the money comes from or who has a right to it. It condemns an insatiable attachment to worldly property that overrides justice and compassion, and it shows that this moral failing is a reason for accountability on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And you love wealth with an immense love.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Fajr (89:20), rebukes human beings for their excessive attachment to material possessions. It follows the criticism of those who neither honor the orphan nor urge the feeding of the poor, and it shows the root of those failings: a consuming, insatiable greed for wealth. The phrase 'hubban jamma' (abundant, overflowing love) suggests a love that has no limit and is never satisfied, so that wealth becomes the goal of life rather than a means to serve God and help others. The verse warns that when love of money takes over the heart, it hardens it against generosity, justice, and mindfulness of the Hereafter, and so one should keep wealth in its proper place and spend it in ways that please God.

translation: No! When the earth is pounded and crushed, again and again, into powder.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who are heedless of the Hereafter and who love wealth and neglect the orphan and the poor, as in the preceding verses of Surat al-Fajr. The word 'No!' rejects their misplaced priorities and false sense of security. It warns that the apparent stability of the world, which people rely on for their power and possessions, will be shattered. The earth, which seems firm and permanent, will be pounded repeatedly until it is leveled, showing the terrifying completeness of the Day of Judgment. On that day, worldly attachments will be worthless, and every person will face their Lord and their own deeds alone. The verse calls people to reflect on this inevitable end and to live with accountability, generosity, and awareness of God before it is too late.

translation: And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Fajr 89:22) describes the Day of Judgment, when God comes in a manner befitting His majesty to judge among creation, with the angels standing in orderly, successive rows. It conveys the overwhelming gravity and solemnity of that Day, when all worldly power and illusion of autonomy vanish, and every soul stands in awe before its Creator. The image of ranked angels underscores divine order and authority, reminding the believer to live with accountability and reverence, since the reckoning is certain and no one can escape it.

translation: And on that Day Hell will be brought forth. On that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment Hell will be made visible and brought near to the gathered creation, so that its reality is no longer a matter of belief but of sight. At that moment a person will remember what he neglected: the warnings of the prophets, his heedlessness, and the chances he wasted for repentance and good deeds. Yet this remembrance comes too late, because the worldly life was the place for heeding and acting, while the Hereafter is the place of reckoning and recompense. The verse teaches that the one who is wise remembers and takes heed now, while repentance is still accepted, rather than waking to regret when the time for action has passed.

translation: He will say: "Oh, if only I had sent ahead something for my life!" (Qur'an 89:24)
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the person who neglected the hereafter will be overcome with regret. He will realize that the real, everlasting life is the one after death, and that the worldly life was only a brief opportunity to prepare for it. His cry shows that deeds done now are the only provision that can be sent ahead, and that when the chance to act has passed, regret will bring no benefit. The verse is a warning to use the present life to do good, so that one is not left empty-handed when true life begins.

translation: So on that Day none will punish as He punishes.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Fajr 89:25) says that on the Day of Judgment God's punishment of those who denied Him and loved wealth while neglecting the orphan and the poor will be unmatched in its severity. No earthly ruler or power can inflict anything like it, and no created being has the power to punish in this way. The verse is a warning that real justice and real accountability belong to God alone, and that the consequences of heedlessness in this world are far graver than any worldly suffering, so a person should turn back to God before that Day arrives.

translation: And none will bind as He binds [on that Day].
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Fajr 89:26) describes the Day of Judgment, when God's punishment of the disbelievers will be unmatched. No human or created being can inflict a chastisement as severe as His, nor shackle the wrongdoers as firmly as He will. The verse stresses that all power and authority belong to God alone on that Day, and that the retribution of the Hereafter is far beyond any punishment known in this world, serving as a warning to turn back to Him before it is too late.

translation: O tranquil soul!
interpretation: This verse (Al-Fajr 89:27) is God's address to the believing soul at death and on the Day of Resurrection. The 'tranquil soul' (al-nafs al-muṭma'inna) is the soul that has found peace through faith, remembrance of God, trust in His promise, and acceptance of His decree, so it is no longer restless with doubt, fear, or the pull of base desires. By calling it with the intimate address 'O', God honors it and announces that its struggle is over, preparing it for the words that follow: to return to its Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, and to enter among His servants and His Paradise. The verse teaches that the goal of spiritual life is a heart that is settled and secure in God, and that such a soul receives a gracious welcome from Him.

translation: Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him].
interpretation: This verse is the divine call to the soul at peace (al-nafs al-mutma'inna) at the moment of death and in the Hereafter. It means that the believing soul, having trusted in God and submitted to His decree throughout life, returns to its Lord content with what God has prepared for it of reward and mercy, while God, in turn, is pleased with it for its faith and righteous deeds. The mutual pleasure signifies the highest state of spiritual fulfillment: the servant is satisfied with God's decree and bounty, and God accepts the servant, welcoming the soul into the company of His righteous servants and into His Paradise, as the following verses affirm.

translation: "Enter among My servants." (Qur'an 89:29)
interpretation: This is the Lord's invitation to the soul at peace (al-nafs al-muṭma'inna) after it returns to Him well-pleased and well-pleasing. To be admitted among God's servants is to be given a place in the company of the righteous, the prophets, the truthful, and the martyrs, and to share in their honor and nearness to Him. The verse shows that the highest reward is not only individual salvation but acceptance into the community of those whom God has chosen as His own servants, which is the true station of devotion and the gateway to Paradise that follows in the next verse.

translation: And enter My Paradise.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 89:30) is the closing of the call to the soul at peace (an-nafs al-mutma'inna), and it marks the culmination of the believer's journey. After the soul is addressed as returning to its Lord, pleased and pleasing, and being admitted among His righteous servants, it is finally invited into God's own Paradise. The phrase 'My Paradise' is an honor in itself, because the garden is attributed directly to God. This suggests that the greatest reward is not only the pleasures of the garden but being welcomed into a place of nearness to God, security, and lasting peace. The verse teaches that a soul which finds tranquility in faith, trust in God's decree, and obedience in this life is rewarded with a gracious welcome into eternal bliss in the next.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. I swear not by this city.
interpretation: The opening of Surat al-Balad uses the phrase 'I do not swear' as an emphatic form of oath, a rhetorical device in Arabic that stresses how certain and weighty the matter is, as if it needs no oath to be believed. The 'city' is Mecca, the sacred land where the Prophet Muhammad was living and preaching. By invoking its sanctity, the verse draws attention to the honor of the place and sets up the surrounding verses, which stress that the Prophet is a dweller of this city who is nonetheless being wronged within its sanctuary. This points to the contrast between the city's inviolable status and the way its people treated the Messenger, and it prepares the listener for the surah's central theme: that humanity is created in struggle and hardship, and must choose the steep path of good deeds, such as freeing slaves, feeding the hungry, and showing mercy, rather than boasting of wealth.

translation: And you, [O Muhammad], are a resident of this city.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:2) follows the oath by the sacred city of Mecca. God swears by the city and notes that the Prophet dwells in it as a free, honored resident whose presence adds to its sanctity. The point is the irony that the Meccans, who revere the city as inviolable, nonetheless harm and oppose the very Messenger who lives among them and makes it more sacred, violating the sanctity they claim to uphold. The verse also carries a consoling promise to the Prophet that the city where he is now persecuted will become lawful for him to enter and prevail in, a sign of the coming conquest of Mecca.

translation: By the begetter and what he begot.
interpretation: This is the oath at the opening of Surat al-Balad (90:3). The most widely held reading takes the 'begetter' to be Adam and 'what he begot' to be his descendants, or more generally every parent and child. God swears by the continuity of human generation, which shows His power in creating and sustaining humankind, to draw attention to the toil and struggle that characterize human life. The oath points to the sign in procreation: humans come into being in hardship, grow through effort, and are accountable for how they use their faculties. It therefore leads into the declaration that follows, that man was created in distress (kabad), so he should recognize his Creator and strive through righteous deeds rather than arrogance.

translation: We have certainly created man in hardship (toil and struggle).
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:4) teaches that human life is by its nature a path of struggle and exertion. From birth through growth, work, loss, illness, and the facing of death, a person is constantly subjected to trials and effort, and no one lives free of difficulty. The verse reminds humans not to be deluded by their own strength or wealth, as in the preceding and following verses where someone boasts of squandering vast wealth, thinking no one has power over him. Since hardship is the universal human condition, a person should direct his striving toward what is worthy, namely faith, freeing slaves, feeding the hungry, and showing mercy, and so be rewarded for his toil, rather than wasting it on vanity and arrogance. The hardship is thus both a reminder of human weakness before God and a call to give struggle a purpose that leads to lasting success in the hereafter.

translation: Does he think that no one has power over him?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:5) rebukes the arrogant human being who, deceived by his wealth, strength, and status, imagines that no one can overpower him or call him to account. The question is a rebuke: his sense of security is an illusion. God has complete power over him, and He will hold him accountable for his deeds, so he should not be heedless or rebellious.

translation: He says: "I have squandered abundant wealth." (Qur'an 90:6)
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance of a person who boasts of having spent vast amounts of wealth, whether on showing off, on opposing the truth, or on seeking status and fame. The word 'lubad' suggests wealth piled up in heaps. His boast reveals that he measures his worth by what he spends and not by the sincerity of his heart. He forgets that God sees his intentions and knows what he spent, and why. Wealth spent for vanity or for resisting the truth is a loss and no source of honor. Real value lies in spending for God's sake, such as freeing slaves and feeding the hungry and the orphan, as the following verses indicate.

translation: Does he think that no one has seen him?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:7) is a rebuke to the arrogant person who boasts of having squandered vast wealth. He wrongly imagines that his deeds, his spending, and his intentions go unseen. In truth, God sees everything he does and the motives behind it, so nothing escapes His knowledge and every action will be accounted for. The rhetorical question exposes the delusion of heedlessness and reminds the believer to live with constant awareness that God is watching.

translation: Have We not made for him two eyes?
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Balad (90:8) is a rhetorical question that reminds the human being, who boasts of his strength and wealth, of the blessings God has given him. The gift of sight is among the clearest signs of God's power and care, for through it a person perceives the world, distinguishes truth from falsehood, and reflects on the signs of the Creator. The one who has been given such a faculty is accountable for using it in gratitude and guidance, not in arrogance or heedlessness, and he cannot imagine that no one sees or holds him to account, since the One who created his eyes sees him fully.

translation: And a tongue and two lips?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:9) continues a series of rhetorical questions that remind humans of God's favors upon them. The tongue and lips are the instruments of speech, expression, and communication, through which a person conveys thought, learns, teaches, and calls to good. The verse points out that these faculties are a trust and a blessing: the One who gave them is aware of how they are used, so a person should be grateful by employing speech in truth, guidance, and kindness rather than in falsehood or harm. It also shows that God's creation of the human being is purposeful, with abilities that carry moral responsibility.

translation: And We have shown him the two ways.
interpretation: God has given every human being the moral awareness and rational capacity to distinguish between the two paths of life: the path of good and righteousness, and the path of evil and wrongdoing. Through innate conscience, reason, and the guidance of revelation, the choice is made clear, so people bear responsibility for which path they take. The verse stresses that no one can claim ignorance, since both ways have been plainly shown, and it leads into the following verses that urge climbing the steep path of righteousness through freeing slaves, feeding the hungry, and having faith.

translation: But he has not attempted the steep path.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Al-Balad, 90:11) rebukes the person who boasts of having spent abundant wealth, yet has not undertaken the difficult, uphill road of true righteousness. The 'steep path' (al-'aqabah) is a metaphor for the hard moral struggle against the self's greed and desire. Following verses explain it as freeing a slave, feeding the hungry on a day of famine, and caring for orphans and the needy, joined with faith, patience, and mutual compassion. The lesson is that real virtue lies not in claims or display but in costly, selfless acts of service that demand effort and sacrifice.

translation: And what will make you know what the steep path is?
interpretation: This verse from Surat al-Balad uses a rhetorical question to stress how weighty and demanding the 'steep path' (al-'aqaba) is. The Qur'an presents it as a moral ascent that requires real effort and self-denial, in contrast to the easy path of wealth-boasting and heedlessness. The verses that follow define it through concrete acts of compassion: freeing a slave, feeding the hungry in times of famine, and caring for orphans and the destitute. Salvation is therefore won by costly, practical service to others and by overcoming the self's selfishness, not by claims of status or empty words.

translation: The freeing of a slave (literally: the releasing of a neck).
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat al-Balad (90:13), names one of the steep, demanding acts of righteousness that the verse sets against mere wealth and boasting. It teaches that true virtue lies in costly deeds of mercy rather than in status. Freeing a person from bondage, whether by liberating a slave or paying to release someone from captivity or crushing debt, is among the most elevated ways to serve God, because it restores human dignity and freedom. The Qur'an presents it as a means of climbing the 'steep path' to salvation, calling the believer to sacrifice personal means to lift burdens from others.

translation: Or the feeding, on a day of hunger, of
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:14) continues the description of the 'steep path' (al-'aqabah), which is the way of real moral striving. It names one act of freeing the soul from selfishness: giving food at a time of famine or severe hardship, when food is scarce and generosity costs the giver something. Charity is most valuable when the giver is himself in need and gives despite his own hunger. Real spiritual ascent therefore lies in sacrificial compassion for others, not in wealth or boasting.

translation: An orphan near of kin.
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Al-Balad (90:15) names the first of the people to whom a free, charitable meal should be given on a day of hunger (90:14). It urges believers to give food especially to an orphan who is also a relative. Such an act earns a double reward, one for charity and one for upholding family ties. It teaches that real spiritual effort, which Surah Al-Balad calls 'climbing the steep path' (al-'aqaba), means sacrificing wealth for the vulnerable, especially in times of hardship, and beginning with those closest to us who have lost their protector.

translation: Or a needy person lying in the dust (in extreme poverty).
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad, 90:16) completes the description of the 'steep path' (al-'aqaba) that a person is urged to take, which is the freeing of a slave or feeding, on a day of hunger, an orphan of one's kin or a destitute person. The phrase 'dha matraba' describes someone so poor that he has nothing to cover him but the dust, clinging to the earth in hardship and homelessness. The verse teaches that true spiritual ascent lies not in wealth or boasting but in compassionate action, particularly in relieving the most desperate members of society, and that the neediest deserve priority in charity, especially in times of scarcity.

translation: Then he is among those who believe and urge one another to patience and urge one another to compassion.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Balad 90:17) completes the description of the 'steep path' (al-'aqaba): freeing a slave or feeding the hungry are acts of charity, but they only reach their full worth when joined to sincere faith. True ascent to God is not merely individual good deeds but the formation of a believing community whose members are bound together by mutual counsel. Such a community encourages steadfastness (sabr) in obeying God, avoiding sin, and enduring hardship, and fosters mercy (marhama) by inspiring kindness toward the weak, the orphan, and the poor. Faith thus becomes both inward conviction and a social ethic, in which believers strengthen one another in perseverance and soften one another's hearts with compassion.

translation: Those are the Companions of the Right.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Waqi'ah, describes the people who receive their record of deeds in their right hands. They are the righteous believers whose faith and good works earned them Allah's pleasure and Paradise. The 'right' signals honor, blessing and safety: those who are grouped on the right side on the Day of Judgment are saved from punishment and are granted lasting felicity in the Gardens of Bliss, in contrast to the Companions of the Left, who are destined for torment.

translation: But those who disbelieved in Our signs - they are the companions of the left (the people of misfortune).
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Balad 90:19) draws a sharp contrast with the 'companions of the right' mentioned just before it. It teaches that rejecting God's signs, whether the revelations in scripture or the evidences in creation and the conscience, is the root cause of a person's ruin. Such denial hardens the heart, so that one fails to take the 'steep path' of freeing slaves, feeding the hungry in times of famine, and being among those who believe and encourage patience and compassion. Because they refuse guidance, their record is given in the left hand, which signifies misfortune and loss on the Day of Judgment. The verse thus links faith with moral responsibility: belief is not mere words but a transformative commitment, and its rejection leads to a destiny of wretchedness.

translation: Upon them will be a fire closed in all around.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Humazah (104:8), describes the fate of the slanderer and backbiter who hoards wealth and thinks it will make him immortal. The word 'mu'sadah' means sealed or vaulted over, so the fire is shut upon its inmates with no door open and no escape and no relief. The verse stresses the totality of their confinement: just as the miser locked up and counted his wealth, he is himself locked in, and the torment is inescapable and enduring.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the sun and its brightness.
interpretation: God swears by the sun and its morning radiance to draw attention to His signs in creation. The sun's light, warmth and regular movement sustain life on earth, so the oath invites reflection on the Creator's power, wisdom and mercy. It also opens a surah whose theme is moral responsibility: just as the sun's light clearly separates day from darkness, God has made clear the paths of guidance and wrongdoing, and each person must choose between purifying the soul and corrupting it.

translation: And [by] the moon when it follows it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ash-Shams, 91:2) is part of an oath God takes by His creation. The moon 'follows' the sun in that it rises after the sun sets, or in the days of the lunar month it trails the sun and reflects its light, especially when it is full. The oath draws attention to the order and precision of the heavens: the moon's light is borrowed from the sun, and each has its appointed course and role. By swearing on these signs, God directs people to reflect on His power and wisdom, and prepares the ground for the oath's subject, that the soul is shaped and guided, and that success lies in purifying it.

translation: And by the day when it displays the sun's brightness (or: when it reveals it).
interpretation: This verse is an oath by the day at the moment it brings the sun's light into full clarity. Daylight is the means by which the sun's radiance is made manifest, so the day is shown as a sign of God's power and mercy: it lifts the darkness, exposes the world, and makes life, movement and sustenance possible. By swearing by it, the verse directs the listener to reflect on how the regular cycle of light is evidence of a wise Creator who governs the cosmos, and prepares the mind for the moral point of the surah, that the soul is accountable and that success lies in purifying it.

translation: And by the night when it covers it (the sun) in darkness.
interpretation: God swears by the night at the moment it veils the sun, hiding its light and spreading darkness over the world. The oath points to the regular alternation of light and dark as a sign of divine order and power. The sun's brightness, mentioned in the preceding verses, is not permanent: it is followed by the night that conceals it, a reminder that both are subject to the Creator's command. Just as day and night are opposites that nonetheless serve a purpose together, human beings are called to reflect on their own conduct, with guidance and error each having consequences, as the surah goes on to say when it speaks of the soul and its purification or corruption.

translation: And [by] the heaven and He who built it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ash-Shams 91:5) is part of a series of divine oaths in which God swears by the sun, the moon, the day, and the night, and then by the heaven and its Builder. The phrase 'wa ma banaha' is understood to refer to God Himself as the Maker who constructed the heavens with perfect order, balance, and wisdom. By swearing by the sky together with its Builder, the verse directs the human mind from the created marvel to the Creator, reminding us that the vast, ordered, pillarless canopy above is a sign of God's power and design. This sets the stage for the surah's central message: the One who orders the cosmos so precisely also fashioned the human soul, inspired it with awareness of right and wrong, and holds each person accountable for purifying or corrupting it.

translation: And [by] the earth and He who spread it out.
interpretation: God swears by the earth and by its Creator, who stretched it out and made it broad and level so that it could be inhabited, cultivated, and traveled upon. The oath points to the Creator's power and mercy: the earth is laid out as a place of provision and trial for human beings. It prepares for the verses that follow, which stress that the soul is shaped and guided by its Maker, and that success lies in purifying it.

translation: And by the soul and Him who proportioned it,
interpretation: God takes an oath by the human soul and by the One who fashioned it in perfect balance, endowing it with reason, natural disposition, and the capacity to distinguish right from wrong. The oath draws attention to the soul's dignity and to its moral responsibility: since God created it sound and balanced, and then inspired it with awareness of its wickedness and its piety (verses 8-10), each person is accountable for either purifying it through faith and righteous deeds, or corrupting it through sin. The soul is thus presented as the arena where human success or failure is decided.

translation: And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness.
interpretation: God has placed in the human soul an innate awareness of right and wrong, so that every person recognizes by inner moral intuition what leads to corruption and what leads to God-consciousness. This does not remove human responsibility: because the soul has been given this knowledge and the freedom to choose, each person is accountable for which path they follow. The verses that follow (91:9-10) confirm this, declaring that whoever purifies the soul succeeds and whoever corrupts it fails.

translation: He has succeeded who purifies it (the soul).
interpretation: True success and ultimate salvation belong to the one who cleanses his soul from sin, corrupt beliefs, and base character, and nurtures it with faith, sincere worship, and righteous deeds. The verse follows the oath by the sun, moon, day, night, heavens, and earth, and the statement that God inspired the soul with its wickedness and its piety. It teaches that each person bears responsibility for the moral state of his own self, and that prosperity in this world and the next is found not in wealth or status but in inner purification and obedience to God.

translation: And he who corrupts it has failed.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ash-Shams 91:10) completes the oath-based declaration that true success belongs to the one who purifies his soul. Its opposite is the one who 'dassāhā': who buries, suppresses, or smothers his soul, burying its natural inclination toward God under layers of sin, heedlessness, and corruption. Just as a seed buried in the ground cannot grow, the soul that is stifled by disobedience loses its capacity for goodness and guidance. Such a person is truly lost, for he has squandered the one thing entrusted to him and forfeited his happiness in this world and the next. The verse teaches that each person is responsible for the state of his own soul, and that spiritual ruin is not imposed from outside but results from one's own choices to smother the conscience and the innate disposition toward truth.

translation: Thamud denied [the truth] through their transgression.
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 91:11) explains that the people of Thamud rejected their prophet Salih not out of lack of evidence, but because of their own arrogance and rebellion. Their tyranny and overstepping of limits blinded them to the clear sign of the she-camel and led them to deny the message. The lesson is that pride and transgression are what drive people to reject divine guidance, and that this kind of denial leads to ruin, as the verses that follow show. A soul is purified by obedience and humility, and corrupted by defiance.

translation: When the most wretched of them rose up (in zeal to hamstring the she-camel).
interpretation: This verse recounts the moment the people of Thamud's act of defiance reached its climax: the most wretched man among them, identified in the tradition as Qudar ibn Salif, rose with determination and eagerness to slaughter the camel that God had sent as a sign. The word 'inba'atha' conveys a swift, willing surge of energy toward evil, showing that the crime was not accidental but deliberate and zealous. He is called 'the most wretched' because he became the instrument of his people's destruction, and the others, by approving and supporting him, shared in his guilt. The verse teaches that when a community consents to wrongdoing, the sin is attributed to all, and that the one who acts most eagerly against God's signs earns the worst fate.

translation: But the Messenger of God said to them: "This is the she-camel of God, so let her drink."
interpretation: The Prophet Salih warns his people, Thamud, not to harm the she-camel that God sent them as a miraculous sign. By calling her "the she-camel of God," he marks her as sacred and under divine protection. By telling them to respect her "drinking," he refers to the agreed arrangement in which the water of the town was divided: one day for her and one day for the people. The verse teaches that divine signs must be honored and that agreements about shared resources must be respected with justice. Thamud's disregard of this warning, when they hamstrung the she-camel, showed their arrogance and brought God's punishment upon them.

translation: But they denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord crushed them for their sin and leveled them all alike.
interpretation: The verse shows that rejecting a messenger and committing open transgression bring divine punishment. The people of Thamud denied the Prophet Salih and killed the she-camel that God had sent as a sign. Their collective crime was a deliberate defiance of God's clear warning, so the punishment was not arbitrary but a direct consequence of their own wrongdoing ('for their sin'). The punishment struck them all together and left no distinction among them, which implies that those who took part in or approved of the crime shared the guilt. Its lesson is that arrogance and denial of revealed truth end in destruction, however strong a nation may be.

translation: And He does not fear its consequence.
interpretation: This closing verse of Surat ash-Shams describes God's judgment upon the people of Thamud after they hamstrung the she-camel and defied their prophet Salih. Unlike a human ruler who may hesitate to punish a people out of fear of retaliation, rebellion, or later harm, God acts with absolute power and perfect justice. He destroyed them for their transgression without any dread of what might follow, because nothing can threaten His sovereignty or hold Him to account. The verse stresses that the punishment was deserved, was precisely measured, and was carried out by One whose authority is unchallengeable, warning those who persist in arrogance and wrongdoing that no one can escape the consequences of defying God.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the night when it covers [the world with darkness].
interpretation: God opens Surat al-Layl with an oath by the night as it envelops the earth, drawing attention to a sign of His power and wisdom. Night, with its cloaking darkness, stillness and rest, stands as the first half of a pair that the next verses complete: the brightness of day. The oath sets up the surah's central theme that human efforts and paths are as different from one another as night is from day. Just as night and day are opposites that nonetheless work together in a single ordered creation, people's striving diverges between generosity and God-consciousness on one side and miserliness and heedlessness on the other, and their outcomes will diverge accordingly.
