The covering darkness also suggests how heedlessness and wrongdoing veil the heart, while the sign of night invites reflection on the Creator who governs time and all that happens within it.

translation: And by the day when it appears in brilliance.
interpretation: In this oath (Surah Al-Layl, 92:2), God swears by the day when it unveils itself and shines forth, dispelling the darkness of night. Paired with the oath by the night that covers, it points to the contrast between concealment and clarity, and between the different paths people take in life. Just as day and night differ in nature and function, human efforts differ: some strive toward generosity, piety, and truth, which bring light and ease, while others incline to miserliness and denial, which bring hardship. The day's radiance is a sign of God's power and mercy in ordering creation, and a reminder that guidance, like daylight, makes the right path plain for those who choose to see it.

translation: And [by] He who created the male and the female,
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl, 92:3) is part of an oath in which God swears by the Creator's act of bringing into being the two sexes. The interpretation is that God draws attention to the wisdom and power evident in creating humankind in complementary pairs, differing in form, nature, and roles, yet issuing from a single origin. Just as these two kinds are different but complementary, the oath prepares for the statement that follows, that human striving and efforts are likewise diverse in their paths and outcomes: some strive toward good and God-consciousness, others toward stinginess and heedlessness. The diversity within creation thus points to the diversity in human deeds, and to the fact that each person will be held accountable for the path they choose.

translation: Indeed, your efforts and pursuits are diverse and divergent.
interpretation: God swears by the night, the day, and the creation of male and female, and then affirms that people's strivings lead in different directions and toward different ends. Some strive in giving, piety, and belief in the best reward, which eases their path toward goodness and ultimate felicity; others strive in miserliness, self-sufficiency, and denial of the truth, which eases their path toward hardship and ruin. Just as night and day, and male and female, are opposites, so are human endeavors, and each person's deeds determine his final destiny. The verse therefore calls every person to examine what he is working for, since the outcome of the effort is as different as the effort itself.

translation: As for him who gives (in charity) and is mindful of God,
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl, 92:5) begins the description of the path of ease. It teaches that real success comes from two joined qualities: generosity, meaning spending one's wealth and effort for the sake of God and for the good of others, and taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that makes a person avoid what He forbids and fulfill what He commands. Giving purifies the heart of greed and attachment to the world, while taqwa gives that giving sincerity and direction. The verse implies that a person who combines open-handed charity with God-consciousness is being prepared for ease in life and in the hereafter, because good deeds open the way to further good deeds.

translation: And believes in the best reward (al-husna).
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Layl, 92:6) describes the person who gives, is mindful of God, and affirms the truth of al-husna, the 'best' that God has promised: the finest reward in the hereafter, Paradise, and by extension the truth of the good word of faith. The belief is not mere intellectual assent but a conviction that shapes conduct. Because he is certain that God will repay every good deed with something better, he gives freely and does not fear loss. This certainty is the root of his generosity and piety, and it is why God promises to ease his path toward ease and goodness.

translation: We will facilitate for him the path to ease.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl 92:7) refers to the one who gives in charity, is mindful of God, and affirms the best reward. God promises that He will make goodness easy for such a person: obeying Him will become light on the heart, righteous deeds will come naturally, and the way to success and ultimate felicity in this life and the next will be smoothed. The meaning is that sincere effort toward good invites divine assistance, so each good act opens the door to further good and strengthens the believer's inclination toward righteousness.

translation: But as for him who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient,
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl, 92:8) describes the opposite of the generous, God-fearing person. The miser withholds what he owes of his wealth and good deeds, and he thinks himself independent of God's guidance and reward, so he neglects the hereafter and feels no need for God's grace. His withholding springs from arrogant self-reliance: he believes his wealth and his own power suffice, and he forgets that everything he has is a gift from God. The verse thus warns that stinginess is not merely a financial failing but a spiritual disease rooted in heedlessness and pride, and that it leads, as the following verses state, to the path of hardship.

translation: And denies the best (reward).
interpretation: This verse (Al-Layl 92:9) describes the person who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient, and who rejects al-husna, the best, meaning the truth of the promise of Allah's good reward in the Hereafter, or the testimony that there is no god but Allah. By denying it, he sees no value in giving or in striving for the afterlife, and so he withholds his wealth and follows the path of disbelief and heedlessness. His denial is the root of his miserliness and of the hardship toward which Allah will ease his way, because whoever does not believe in a reward for good deeds has no motive to do them.

translation: We will ease him toward hardship.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Layl 92:10) describes the end of the one who is stingy, considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best reward (the truth). God will make the path of difficulty easy for him, meaning that persistent wrongdoing and rejection of guidance harden the heart and steer a person step by step toward actions that lead to ruin. Each evil choice makes the next one easier and good harder, until the person is drawn toward a hard outcome and punishment, as a consequence of his own choices and not an arbitrary decree.

translation: And what will his wealth avail him when he falls (into the Fire/perishes)?
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl 92:11) warns the miser who considers himself self-sufficient and denies the best reward that his accumulated wealth will be of no use to him at the moment of his downfall, whether in death, in the grave, or in being cast into Hellfire. Wealth that was withheld from righteous causes cannot ransom or protect him; only faith, piety, and generosity in the way of God bring true benefit on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Indeed, upon Us rests the guidance.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl 92:12) affirms that God has taken it upon Himself to make the path of truth clear to humankind. He does so by sending messengers, revealing scripture, and placing in people the capacity to distinguish right from wrong, so that no one can claim they were left without direction. Guidance in the sense of showing and explaining the way is God's responsibility, which establishes His proof over His creation and leaves each person accountable for choosing to follow that path or turn away from it.

translation: And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the former (this world).
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl, 92:13) declares that God alone holds absolute sovereignty over both this life and the next. Guidance is therefore His to give, and no one's disobedience or denial diminishes His dominion, just as no one's obedience adds to it. The one who turns away from the guidance gains nothing, because both realms are in God's hands, and the only true path to success in either world is to seek Him and submit to His guidance.

translation: So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes fiercely.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Layl, 92:14) shows that divine warning is an act of mercy and an establishment of proof: God, through His Messenger and revelation, has made the consequence of disbelief and wrongdoing plain before it occurs, so that no one can claim ignorance. The fire is described as 'talazza', meaning flaring and burning with intense, ever-rising flames, which conveys the severity of the punishment and its vivid, present reality. The warning is meant to awaken the conscience and push a person toward the path of giving, God-consciousness, and truthfulness described in the surrounding verses, so that one takes the opportunity to change course while there is still time, rather than discovering the truth only when it is too late.

translation: None shall burn in it except the most wretched,
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl, 92:15) speaks of the Fire that was just warned of in the preceding verse. Only the one who is most wretched will enter and be scorched by it in a lasting, deserved way. The next verse identifies this person as the one who denied the truth and turned away from faith and obedience. The meaning is that damnation is not arbitrary; it is the consequence of a person's own persistent rejection of divine guidance and refusal to submit, which makes them the most unfortunate of people. By contrast, the God-fearing are spared it, as the following verses state.

translation: The one who denied [the truth] and turned away.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl 92:16) describes the person destined for the Fire: one who rejects the message brought by the Prophet and then turns his back on obedience to God. The verse shows that damnation stems from two linked failings, denial in the heart and abandonment in action. Belief is not merely an inner conviction, nor is disbelief merely a lack of knowledge. Rather, a person is held to account when truth has become clear and he knowingly rejects it and then refuses to act upon it. The verse warns that arrogance and heedlessness toward divine guidance lead to ruin, while sincere acceptance and practice of faith lead to salvation.

translation: And the most righteous will be kept away from it.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl, 92:17) promises that the one who is most conscious of God, who guards himself against disobedience and gives his wealth to purify himself, will be spared and distanced from the Fire described in the preceding verse. Salvation here is a result of taqwa: the person who fears God and acts upon that fear is protected by God's grace from the blazing Fire, while the wretched one who denies and turns away is the one who will burn in it.

translation: He who gives his wealth to purify himself.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Layl, 92:18) describes the God-fearing person (al-atqā) who spends his wealth not out of vanity or for show, but seeking to purify his soul and cleanse it of stinginess, greed, and sin. Giving is an act of self-purification (tazkiyah): by freeing the heart from attachment to worldly possessions, the believer grows spiritually and draws nearer to God. Wealth is thus a means of inner growth, and charity done for God's sake is what elevates a person and distinguishes him from the miser who withholds.

translation: And he has no one with him who has done him a favor that must be repaid.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-Layl, 92:19) describes the true believer who gives his wealth to purify himself. His giving is not a repayment for any favor or a calculated exchange of benefits. He does not give in order to return a kindness or to gain something from people. His generosity is pure and free from worldly motives, directed only to God, as the next verse says: 'except seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High.' The verse teaches that real charity is sincere and is measured by the intention behind it, not by social obligation or reciprocity.

translation: Except for seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Layl 92:20) describes the righteous person who gives his wealth to purify himself, not in order to repay any favor owed to him by anyone, but solely out of a desire for the pleasure of his Lord, the Most High. It teaches that the true worth of charity lies in sincere intention: giving that is free from show, expectation of worldly reward, or obligation, and directed purely to God, is what elevates the giver and earns divine acceptance. The phrase 'seeking the Face of his Lord' conveys longing for God's good pleasure and nearness to Him, and the attribute 'the Most High' reminds the giver that God is exalted above all human recompense and thus worthy to be the sole object of one's devotion.

translation: And soon he will be satisfied.
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surah Al-Layl (92:21), promises the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, seeking only the Face of his Lord and not repayment for any favor, that God will grant him such abundant reward that he will be fully content. The satisfaction is a divine gift: it begins with ease in this life and comes to completion in the Hereafter. Contentment is thus presented as the fruit of sincere generosity and God-consciousness, and the sincere giver's own hearts are filled with joy in return for what he gave for God's sake alone.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the morning brightness.
interpretation: God opens Surah Ad-Duha with an oath by the bright forenoon, the time when the sun has risen and the world is filled with light and activity. The oath draws attention to a sign of His power and mercy: just as the daylight returns after the darkness of night, so relief, guidance, and comfort follow periods of hardship and apparent silence. In the context of the surah, which was revealed to console the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ during a pause in revelation, the oath assures the believer that God has not abandoned him, and that times of difficulty are followed by ease and divine support.

translation: And by the night when it grows still and calm.
interpretation: God swears by the night when it settles and covers the world in darkness and stillness, after the brightness of the forenoon mentioned in the preceding verse. The pairing of day and night points to the order and wisdom in God's governance: just as the light of day and the calm of night alternate by His will and neither signifies abandonment, so the pause in revelation that the Prophet Muhammad experienced was not a sign that his Lord had forsaken or despised him. It was a temporary stillness within a purposeful design, to be followed by renewed guidance and mercy, as the verses that follow affirm.

translation: Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He become displeased with you.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ad-Duha, 93:3) was revealed to comfort the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ after a pause in revelation led the disbelievers to taunt him that his Lord had abandoned him. God answers with an oath-backed reassurance that the silence was not abandonment or dislike but part of His wisdom and timing. The verse teaches that periods of apparent divine distance, hardship, or delayed guidance are not signs of God's rejection of a faithful servant, and that His care and love for His chosen ones remain constant even when they do not feel His nearness.

translation: And surely the Hereafter is better for you than the present life.
interpretation: This verse (93:4), from Surah Ad-Duha, consoles the Prophet Muhammad during a time when revelation paused and he felt distressed. It assures him that whatever hardship, opposition, or apparent loss he faces in this world is temporary, and that the everlasting life to come holds far greater honor, reward, and nearness to God than anything this world offers. It teaches believers to measure success by eternal outcomes rather than by passing worldly conditions, and to remain patient and hopeful in God's promise.

translation: And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ad-Duha, 93:5) is a divine assurance to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that God's generosity toward him will be continuous and ever-growing until he reaches complete contentment. It consoles him after the pause in revelation and the hardships he faced, promising that what awaits him exceeds what he has now. The giving is left unspecified, so it encompasses every kind of good: success of his message, victory over opposition, honor in this world, and in the Hereafter the station of intercession and elevated rank. The result is not mere receiving but 'you will be satisfied': a settled inner peace and fulfillment. This teaches that God's care for His servants is never abandoned, and that patient trust in His timing is rewarded with contentment.

translation: Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, of His care for him from the earliest stage of life. He lost his father before birth and his mother in childhood, then was sheltered first by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and afterward by his uncle Abu Talib. The verse shows that divine providence was with him when he had no worldly protector, and it reassures him that the One who sheltered him in vulnerability will not abandon him now. It also lays the moral foundation for the commands that follow in the surah to treat orphans kindly, since gratitude for God's mercy is shown by extending the same mercy to others.

translation: And He found you lost, and guided you.
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet Muhammad of His favor upon him: before revelation he did not know the path of faith and the details of the divine law, though he was never an idolater, and he was bewildered about the truth his people had strayed from. God then guided him by choosing him as a prophet, sending down the Qur'an, and setting him on the straight path. The verse shows that guidance is wholly a gift from God, not something earned by human effort, and it consoles the Prophet that the One who guided him in the past will not abandon him now.

translation: And He found you in need, and made you self-sufficient.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ad-Duha, 93:8) reminds the Prophet Muhammad of God's care for him: he had been poor and without abundant means, and God relieved his need. This enrichment came through means such as his honest trade and his marriage to Khadijah, and above all through the contentment God placed in his heart, which is the truest wealth. The verse shows that the one who is provided for in hardship should respond with gratitude and with compassion toward others in need, as the surrounding verses command care for the orphan and the beggar.

translation: So as for the orphan, do not oppress him.
interpretation: This verse (Surat ad-Duha, 93:9) commands the believer not to harshly overpower, humiliate, or wrongfully seize the rights of the orphan. It follows God's reminder to the Prophet Muhammad that He found him an orphan and gave him shelter. The point is that gratitude for divine mercy should be expressed through compassion toward the vulnerable. Those who have no father to protect them are especially exposed to injustice, so a person who has been sheltered by God must in turn offer kindness, protect the orphan's dignity and property, and never exploit the orphan's weakness.

translation: And as for the one who asks, do not repel him harshly.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat ad-Duha, teaches that gratitude for God's favor is shown through kindness toward those in need. Having reminded the Prophet that God sheltered him as an orphan and guided and enriched him, the verse commands that he never scold, drive away, or treat harshly anyone who comes asking, whether for money, help, or knowledge. If one cannot give, one should at least refuse gently with kind words. Remembering one's own former need should cultivate humility, compassion, and respect for the dignity of the person asking.

translation: And as for the favor of your Lord, proclaim it.
interpretation: This verse from Surat ad-Duha instructs the believer, first addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, to acknowledge and speak openly of God's blessings, whether they are guidance, provision, security, or knowledge. Such speech is not boasting but an expression of gratitude, recognizing that every blessing comes from God. By mentioning the favors received, the believer honors the Giver, strengthens thankfulness in his own heart, and encourages others to turn to God. It follows the earlier reminders in the surah, where God recalls how He sheltered the orphan, guided the one who was lost, and enriched the one in need. The fitting response to those gifts is to give thanks and share their benefit, through words of praise, through sharing guidance, and through generosity toward others.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Have We not expanded for you your chest?
interpretation: The 'expanding of the chest' signifies God's opening of the Prophet's heart to receive revelation, wisdom, and faith, and freeing it from anxiety, constriction, and grief. It is a reminder of divine favor: the One who prepared his heart with serenity, patience, and capacity to bear the heavy burden of prophethood will not abandon him in his hardships. The rhetorical question affirms that this blessing has already been granted, offering reassurance and encouragement that relief and ease accompany difficulty.

translation: And We removed from you your burden.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Ash-Sharh 94:2) reminds the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that God lifted from him the heavy weight of anxiety and responsibility that pressed upon him, whether the grief over his people's misguidance, the burden of the message before revelation was made clear to him, or the weight of the hardships of prophethood. God's relief came through guidance, revelation, and the strengthening of his heart, so that the task which once felt crushing became bearable. It is a divine consolation, showing that God does not leave His servant alone under a burden He has asked him to carry, and that relief is a mercy bestowed from Him.

translation: Which weighed down your back.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat Ash-Sharh (94:3), continues God's reminder to the Prophet Muhammad of the favor of relieving his burden. The 'burden' that 'weighed down his back' is understood as the heavy load of anxiety, grief, and responsibility he bore regarding his people's rejection, the weight of delivering the message, and the sense of concern over past shortcomings. The image of a load so heavy that it makes the back creak conveys how intense this distress was, and God's mention of lifting it assures the Prophet that divine support, ease, and relief accompany hardship, as the surah goes on to affirm: 'Indeed, with hardship comes ease.'

translation: And We raised high for you your remembrance.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), is a reminder of the honor God bestowed on him: his name is exalted and joined with God's own name in the call to prayer (adhan), in the testimony of faith (shahada), in prayers, and in the sermons, and it is blessed and invoked by believers across the world and through the ages. The meaning is that even when he faced rejection, hardship and mockery in Makkah, God had already assured him that his standing would be elevated by divine decree rather than by human approval, so that his mission would endure and his reputation would be honored. It consoles him and strengthens his resolve, showing that sincere service to God brings lasting honor and relief after difficulty.

translation: For indeed, with hardship comes ease.
interpretation: The verse offers reassurance that difficulty is never permanent or unaccompanied: ease is bound up with hardship itself, arriving alongside it rather than only after it. It teaches the believer to meet trials with patience and trust in God, since relief is part of the divine design of every difficulty, and hardship often carries within it the means of its own resolution, such as growth, reliance on God, and new opportunities.

translation: Indeed, with hardship comes ease.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 94:6) offers reassurance that hardship is never without relief. The word 'with' (ma'a) rather than 'after' suggests that ease accompanies difficulty and is bound up with it, so that relief is already unfolding within the trial itself. For the believer, this means that adversity is not a final state but a passing phase carrying within it the seeds of its own resolution. The verse calls on a person to meet trials with patience, trust in God, and hope, knowing that God's mercy is present even in the hardest moments.

translation: So when you have finished [your duty], then strive on [in worship].
interpretation: This verse from Surat Ash-Sharh (94:7) teaches that a believer should never fall into idleness. When one completes a task, whether it is the work of daily life, the duties of teaching and calling to God, or an act of worship, one should immediately turn with renewed energy to another beneficial endeavor, above all devoted worship and supplication to the Lord. Rest is not an end in itself; life is a continual movement from one act of obedience and good work to the next, and the verse, following the promise that with hardship comes ease, directs the gratitude for relief into further striving toward God, to whom one should turn with longing in the next verse.

translation: And to your Lord turn your longing and desire.
interpretation: After completing a task, act of worship, or duty, one should not settle into idleness but should turn wholeheartedly to God, directing all hope, desire, and aspiration toward Him alone. The verse teaches that true fulfillment and reliance lie with God rather than in people or worldly means, so that one's efforts in this life remain purposeful and one's heart stays attached to the Creator who eases hardship and grants relief.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the fig and the olive.
interpretation: God opens Surah At-Tin with an oath by the fig and the olive, two blessed fruits that stand for the lands and the prophetic message tied to them, notably the Holy Land of Syria-Palestine, where Jesus was sent and where many prophets lived. By swearing by these symbols of blessing, nourishment, and sacred history, God draws attention to the dignity of human beings and the continuity of divine guidance. The oath prepares the ground for the surah's central teaching: humans were created in the best form, yet their final standing depends on faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And [by] Mount Sinai.
interpretation: This is an oath in which God swears by the mountain where He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him, and revealed the Torah to him. By swearing by this blessed place, the verse points to the dignity of divine revelation and the prophetic missions that guide humanity. Together with the oaths before and after it, it prepares the ground for the declaration that God created the human being in the best form, and that the one who keeps faith and does good deeds will be rewarded, while the one who falls away from that guidance is brought low.

translation: And by this secure land.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tin, 95:3) is an oath by God, swearing by Mecca, the city that is safe and secure. It is called 'secure' because God made it a sanctuary since the time of Ibrahim, where people are protected from violence and bloodshed, and where those who enter find safety. By joining it in an oath with the fig, the olive, and Mount Sinai, the verse links the places where revelation and prophethood were centered, culminating in Mecca, the place of the final message sent to Muhammad. The oath underscores the sanctity and dignity of these sites, and prepares for the declaration that follows: that God created the human being in the best form, so that humans should honor that gift by faith and righteous deeds.

translation: We have certainly created man in the best of stature (in the finest form and proportion).
interpretation: The verse affirms the dignity God has bestowed on human beings: they are fashioned with a balanced physical form, upright bearing, intellect, speech, and moral awareness, which equips them for knowing and worshipping their Creator. This excellence of creation is a trust and a responsibility, not a license for pride. The verses that follow show that a person who abandons faith and righteous deeds sinks to the lowest of the low, while those who believe and do good keep their elevated status and receive an unending reward. The verse therefore calls people to live up to the high nature in which they were created.

translation: Then We reduced him to the lowest of the low.
interpretation: After creating the human being in the best of forms (Qur'an 95:4), God says that humans can sink to the lowest state when they abandon faith and righteousness. On this reading, the 'lowest of the low' is a moral and spiritual degradation, in which a person who has been given reason, dignity and a sound nature misuses these gifts and falls below even the animals in the sight of God. The next verse supports this by excepting those who believe and do righteous deeds, who keep their dignity and receive an unending reward. The verse is therefore a warning that human honor depends on faith and good conduct, not on outward form.

translation: Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward that will never be cut off.
interpretation: This verse, which appears in Surah At-Tin (95:6) and Surah Fussilat (41:8), sets apart the believers from the rest of humanity, who may sink to the lowest of the low or fall into disbelief. It teaches that faith alone is not enough, and neither are deeds without faith. Salvation requires both sincere belief and righteous action. Those who combine them are promised a reward from God that is endless and uninterrupted, and that is never diminished, withdrawn, or followed by reproach. The word 'ghayru mamnun' conveys a gift that is pure and lasting, which points to the eternal bliss of Paradise, a recompense that does not end, in contrast to worldly rewards that fade.

translation: So what causes you [O man] to deny the Recompense (the Judgment) after this?
interpretation: After God has shown the clear signs of His power and wisdom, above all the creation of man in the best form and the proof that He can bring him back to life, no sound argument remains for denying the Day of Judgment. The verse is a rhetorical challenge to the human being: since the evidence points plainly to resurrection and accountability, denial can come only from stubbornness, heedlessness, or a wish to live without answering for one's deeds. It calls the person to reflect honestly and to accept that moral responsibility and a final reckoning are rational and necessary.

translation: Is not God the most just of all judges?
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Tin, 95:8) closes the surah with a rhetorical question whose answer is an emphatic yes. After describing how humans were created in the best form, how some sink to the lowest of the low, and how those who believe and do good are promised an unfailing reward, the verse affirms that God's judgment is perfectly wise and just. Nothing escapes His knowledge, and no wrong goes unaccounted for. It calls the reader to trust that the final reckoning will give each person what they deserve: the believers their reward, and the wrongdoers the consequences of their deeds. In turn, this should inspire accountability in how one lives, and patience and reassurance when facing the injustices of the world, since the ultimate Judge is the wisest and fairest.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Read in the name of your Lord who created.
interpretation: This opening command of the first revelation to the Prophet Muhammad makes knowledge and reading a religious act, not a neutral skill. Reading is to be done 'in the name of your Lord,' meaning that learning should begin with the awareness of God and be directed by His guidance, seeking His help and serving His purposes. The description of God as the One 'who created' grounds this in the most basic truth: the Creator of all things is also the source of all true knowledge. Reflecting on creation, including oneself and the world, is thus a path to recognizing the Lord, so that seeking knowledge becomes an act of worship and gratitude rather than arrogance or self-sufficiency.

translation: He created man from a clinging clot.
interpretation: The verse points to the humble origin of human beings: man begins as a tiny, clinging embryonic form attached to the womb, not as something self-made or self-sufficient. By recalling this lowly beginning, God shows that the Creator who shaped a complex, knowing and speaking being from something so small is fully able to teach, guide and hold him accountable. It is meant to cultivate humility and gratitude, and to remind people that their intellect and capacity to learn, which the following verses mention, are gifts from God and not grounds for arrogance.

translation: Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous.
interpretation: This verse repeats the command to read and ties it to God's boundless generosity. The Prophet, who was unlettered, is assured that the ability to recite and convey the message does not come from his own skill but from the bounty of his Lord. God's generosity exceeds all measure: He gives knowledge, guidance and capacity without being asked, and He gives more than any person deserves. So the believer should approach reading, learning and the revelation with trust in God's generosity rather than fear of personal inadequacy, since the One who commands is the One who enables.

translation: He who taught by the pen.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 96:4) points to the pen as a great means by which God conveys knowledge to humankind. Through writing, knowledge is recorded, preserved, and passed from one generation to the next, so that what one person learns can benefit people far beyond their own time and place. By naming the pen as the instrument of teaching, the verse presents literacy and learning as divine gifts and honors the pursuit of knowledge as an act bound to gratitude toward the Lord. It also shows that all human knowledge ultimately comes from God, who taught humans what they did not know, with the pen as the means of that teaching.

translation: He taught man that which he did not know.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 96:5), from the first revelation to the Prophet Muhammad, presents knowledge as a pure gift from God. Human beings begin in ignorance, and whatever they come to understand, whether through revelation, reason, the senses, or the skills of writing and learning, ultimately originates from God's teaching. It calls for humility, since no one's knowledge is self-made, and for gratitude, since it is a mark of God's generosity toward humanity. It also encourages people to seek knowledge and use it responsibly, in recognition of the One who taught it.

translation: No! Indeed, man transgresses all bounds.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-'Alaq, 96:6) comes right after the verses that stress God's gift of knowledge and the pen, and it warns that human beings, once they feel self-sufficient, tend to rebel against their Creator. The next verse says, 'because he sees himself as self-sufficient.' Wealth, power, knowledge, or status can create an illusion of independence from God, and that illusion leads to arrogance, injustice, and disobedience. The word 'kalla' (No!) firmly rejects the expectation that gifts such as knowledge and provision would naturally lead to gratitude. The verse teaches that blessings are a test: unless a person stays humble and aware of dependence on God, they can become a source of transgression instead of thankfulness.

translation: Because he sees himself as self-sufficient.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 96:7) explains the cause of man's transgression mentioned in the preceding verse, 'Indeed, man transgresses.' When a person perceives himself as independent of others and of God, because of his wealth, power, status, or knowledge, he becomes arrogant and rebels against divine guidance and moral limits. The verse teaches that the feeling of self-sufficiency is a spiritual danger. Human beings are in constant need of God, and forgetting this need leads to pride, injustice, and defiance. True humility comes from remembering that all provision and ability come from God and that to Him is the final return, as the next verse states.

translation: Indeed, to your Lord is the return.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 96:8) reminds that every human being, however much wealth, power, or self-sufficiency has led them to transgress, will ultimately return to God for judgment. It serves as a warning to the arrogant who consider themselves independent of their Creator, and a call to humility, accountability, and awareness that no worldly status can place one beyond God's reckoning.

translation: Have you seen the one who forbids
interpretation: This opening of a rebuke (Surat al-'Alaq, 96:9) points to the astonishing conduct of a man, traditionally identified with Abu Jahl, who tried to stop the Prophet Muhammad from praying. The rhetorical question 'Have you seen?' is meant to provoke wonder and condemnation: how brazen it is to obstruct a servant of God from worshipping his Lord. The verse carries a wider moral lesson: anyone who uses power or status to hinder others from worship and goodness is guilty of arrogance and transgression, and God sees and will hold him to account.

translation: A servant when he prays? (Qur'an 96:10)
interpretation: This verse belongs to the passage in Surat al-'Alaq that rebukes the one who forbids a servant of God from praying. The verse expresses astonishment and condemnation at such a prohibition. Prayer is the most basic act of devotion and a servant's direct link to his Lord, so hindering someone from it is a grave transgression. Tradition applies the verse to Abu Jahl, who threatened the Prophet Muhammad for praying at the Ka'ba. Its wider lesson is that no one has the right to obstruct a believer's worship or freedom of conscience, and that those who do so face God's knowledge and judgment, since God sees all.

translation: Tell me, what if he (the one who forbids a servant of God from praying) is upon guidance?
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 96:11) is part of a rebuke directed at the one who tries to prevent a servant of God from praying. It poses a rhetorical question that exposes the absurdity of his behavior. If the person he obstructs is truly rightly guided, then to hinder him is a grave wrong, since he is standing in the way of someone who follows the truth. The verse invites the opponent to reflect on his own position and warns that opposing guidance, whether by force, mockery, or intimidation, leaves him answerable to God, who sees all that people do. It teaches that the one who stands on guidance must not be hindered, and that those who obstruct worship cannot justify themselves.

translation: Or enjoins piety (God-consciousness)?
interpretation: This phrase is from Surah Al-'Alaq (96:12), part of a rhetorical series addressed to the one who forbids a servant of God from praying. The verse asks: have you considered if the one you obstruct is upon guidance, or commands righteousness and God-consciousness? The meaning is that the person being hindered from worship is not harming anyone but is rightly guided and calls others to taqwa, which is awareness of God expressed in obedience and avoidance of wrongdoing. The condemnation of the one who forbids him is therefore all the more severe, for he opposes both sincere worship and the call to goodness, and he forgets that God sees all that he does.

translation: Have you considered if he denies the truth and turns away?
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-'Alaq (96:13), continues a rebuke of the one who forbids a servant of God from praying. It asks the listener to reflect on the condition of such a person: he not only rejects the message and calls it a lie, but also turns his back on faith and obedience. The rhetorical question carries amazement and censure, since a person who denies the truth and turns away is in no position to hinder those who worship. It also prepares for the warning in the next verse, that God sees all that he does and will hold him accountable.

translation: Does he not know that God sees?
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-'Alaq, 96:14) is a rhetorical question addressed to the one who denies the truth and tries to prevent the believer from praying. It reminds him that nothing he does is hidden from God, who sees every action and intention and will hold him accountable. The verse offers reassurance to the believer who is oppressed for his worship, and it warns the oppressor that God's knowledge and observation of his conduct should make him fearful and restrain him from wrongdoing.

translation: No! If he does not desist, We will surely drag him by the forelock.
interpretation: The verse warns Abu Jahl, or anyone like him, who forbids the servant of God from praying and obstructs the truth. It is a strong rebuke that rejects his arrogance and threatens that if he persists in his defiance, God will seize him by the forelock, the front of the head that symbolizes pride and authority. This means he will be humbled, overpowered, and dragged in disgrace to punishment, in this world or the next. The seeming power of the oppressor is nothing before God's might.

translation: A lying, sinful forelock.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 96:16) describes the forelock of Abu Jahl, or of any arrogant person like him, who forbids the servant of God from praying. The forelock stands for the whole person, since it is the front part of the head and the part by which someone is seized and dragged. The verse says that the person is characterized by lying, because he denies the truth, and by sinfulness, because he knowingly commits wrong. It is therefore a warning that such a person will be seized by that very forelock and dragged to account, as the preceding verse threatens, so that his pride and defiance of God end in humiliation.

translation: Then let him call upon his council (his associates and supporters).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-'Alaq (96:17), is a challenge to Abu Jahl, who threatened and tried to prevent the Prophet ﷺ from praying at the Ka'ba. If he thinks his tribe and companions can protect him or defeat the truth, let him summon them. The verse exposes the weakness of worldly support against God's power, and the next verse answers it: 'We will call the guards of Hell (az-zabaniyah).' Whatever human backing the arrogant oppressor can gather is nothing compared with the forces of God, so the believer need not fear such threats.

translation: We will call the Guards of Hell (the angels of punishment).
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-'Alaq (96:18), is God's reply to the arrogant man who threatened the Prophet and tried to stop him from praying, relying on his supporters and his club. The Qur'an says that if he summons his gang, God will summon the stern angels of punishment, who are the zabaniyah. They push and seize with irresistible force. The verse shows that worldly power and numbers are weak before divine power, and that those who oppose the truth and hinder the worshippers of God will meet a force far greater than anything they can gather. It also comforts the believer, who is told that God defends those who obey Him and that the oppressor's end is humiliation.

translation: No! Do not obey him. Prostrate yourself, and draw near [to God].
interpretation: The verse (Qur'an 96:19) closes Surat al-'Alaq as a firm command to the Prophet, and through him to every believer, not to yield to the pressure of those who oppose truth and try to hinder worship, as Abu Jahl did when he threatened the Prophet for praying. Real nearness to God comes through humble submission, and the closest a servant is to his Lord is in prostration. The believer therefore answers intimidation and arrogance not with compliance but with greater devotion, finding strength, security, and closeness to God in sincere worship, however much the powerful may threaten.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr).
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an was first revealed on a single, uniquely honored night, and in doing so it elevates both the Book and the time of its descent. The 'Night of Qadr' is understood as a night of both 'decree' (when divine wisdom orders the affairs of the coming year) and 'honor' (a night of immense worth). By having God speak in the first person plural ('We'), the verse stresses His majesty and His direct, deliberate agency: guidance for humanity was not an accident of history but a purposeful act of divine mercy, timed on a night whose significance signals that receiving the Qur'an is the greatest event in human spiritual life. The implied lesson is that believers should revere the Qur'an and seek this night through worship, since a moment connected to God's revelation can carry more blessing than an ordinary lifetime of days.

translation: And what will make you know what the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr) is?
interpretation: The rhetorical question, 'And what will make you know?', is a Qur'anic device for emphasizing the immense greatness of something beyond ordinary human grasp. By posing it, God directs the listener to see that the Night of Decree is no ordinary night: it is the night on which the Qur'an began to be revealed and on which divine decrees for the coming year are made manifest to the angels. Its worth cannot be measured by human reckoning, which is why the next verses explain that it is better than a thousand months. The verse invites believers to honor this night, seek it in devotion, and appreciate the guidance whose revelation gave the night its exalted status.

translation: The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 97:3) teaches that the Night of Power, the night on which the Qur'an began to be revealed, carries a spiritual worth beyond measure. Worship, prayer, remembrance and seeking forgiveness on this one night are rewarded more than devotion over a thousand months, roughly eighty-three years, a span approaching a whole lifetime. Its excellence lies in the descent of divine mercy, the angels and the Spirit, and in God's decreeing of matters for the year. God thus shows His generosity to the community of Muhammad, whose lives are short, by giving them a chance to gain, in a single night of sincere devotion, a reward that could outweigh a lifetime of deeds. The believer is encouraged to seek this night with earnestness and not to treat it lightly.

translation: The angels and the Spirit descend therein, by the leave of their Lord, with every decree.
interpretation: This verse, describing the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), means that on this night the angels descend to earth in great numbers, together with Jibril (the Spirit), carrying out God's permission and bringing the decrees that He has ordained for the coming year, including matters of provision, life, and events. Their descent is not by their own will but solely by their Lord's command, which shows the night's immense sanctity and blessing. The earth is filled with mercy and peace as the heavenly host draws near to the believers who spend the night in worship, which is why a single night of devotion is described as better than a thousand months.

translation: Peace it is, until the rising of the dawn. (Qur'an 97:5)
interpretation: The verse describes the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) as a night wholly filled with peace and security. Because the angels and the Spirit descend with their Lord's permission, the night is free of harm and evil, and it brings tranquility and mercy to the believers who spend it in worship. This peace is not momentary but lasts without interruption from the beginning of the night until the break of dawn, showing that the night's blessing is complete and continuous.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to depart from their state until the clear proof came to them.
interpretation: The verse says that the disbelievers among the Jews and Christians, together with the idolaters of Arabia, were fixed in their disbelief and divisions, and nothing short of a manifest, decisive proof would move them from it. That proof is the Messenger Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the Qur'an he recited, which clarified truth from falsehood. The verse thus presents the revelation as God's wise and merciful way of ending a deadlock in human guidance: people had reached a point where reasoning alone and inherited custom had not freed them from error, so God sent a clear proof as a decisive means of removing their excuse and drawing a clear line between those who accept the truth and those who persist in rejecting it.

translation: A Messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures.
interpretation: The verse describes the clear proof that was to come to the People of the Book and the idolaters: the Prophet Muhammad, sent by God and not speaking from himself, who recites revealed pages free from falsehood, corruption, doubt and impurity. The scriptures are 'purified' because they are protected from the distortions and contradictions found in earlier altered writings, and contain only truth, upright guidance and sound laws. The Messenger's authority therefore rests on his divine commission and on the purity of the message he conveys, which is itself evidence of its source.

translation: Wherein are correct and upright writings.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 98:3) describes the purified scriptural pages recited by the Messenger in the preceding verse. It means that the revelation contains scriptures that are straight, just, and free of crookedness or error: its commands, teachings, and rulings are firmly established and truthful, guiding people to what is right in belief and conduct. Because these writings are upright and everlasting in value, they leave the clear proof (al-bayyina) fully sufficient, so that people have no excuse for remaining in disbelief or division once it has come to them.

translation: And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear proof had come to them.
interpretation: The verse (Surat al-Bayyinah, 98:4) teaches that the disagreement among the People of the Book was not caused by any lack of guidance or by ambiguity in the truth. Division arose after clear evidence, namely the Prophet Muhammad and the revelation he brought, which confirmed what they already knew in their own scriptures. Their splitting into factions and their rejection of him stemmed from envy, stubbornness, and worldly desires, not from ignorance. The lesson is that disunity in religion often comes from arrogance and self-interest after the truth has become plain, and that clear proof leaves those who turn away from it without excuse.

translation: And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth, and to establish prayer and to give zakah. And that is the correct religion.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Bayyinah 98:5) teaches that the essence of what all revealed scripture asked of its followers is simple and consistent: devote worship purely to God, free of any partner or show, turn away from falsehood in the way of Abraham, and express that faith through two pillars—prayer, which binds a person to God, and zakah, which binds a person to society. It implies that true religion is not mere ritual or sectarian identity but sincere, God-centered devotion joined with moral and social responsibility. This upright, balanced path is what the verse calls 'the correct religion' (dīn al-qayyimah), in contrast to the divisions the People of the Book fell into after clear proof came to them.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever. Those are the worst of creatures.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting the truth after clear proof has come is a grave moral failing, not a mere difference of opinion. The preceding verses speak of a 'clear evidence' (the Messenger and the revelation) that came to both Jews and Christians and the idolaters. Those who knew the truth or had it plainly presented yet persisted in denying it, out of stubbornness, envy, or attachment to their own ways, have squandered the highest capacity God gave humans: reason and the ability to recognize and accept guidance. Their punishment, abiding in Hell, reflects the gravity of willfully turning away from God after the proof is established. Calling them 'the worst of creatures' means that humans, who were granted intellect and moral choice and could have been among the best of creation, fall below even other creatures when they knowingly reject their Creator. The verse is thus a warning that honor lies in responding to truth, and that responsibility grows with the knowledge one has received.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds - they are the best of creatures.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true honor and rank in God's sight are not based on lineage, wealth, or status, but on the union of sincere faith and righteous action. Belief alone, without deeds that embody it, is incomplete, and good deeds without faith lack their foundation. When the two are joined, a person fulfills the purpose of human existence and attains the highest station among all created beings. The verse thus sets a standard of excellence open to everyone, and it contrasts with the preceding description of the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists, who are called the worst of creatures, showing that moral and spiritual choices, not identity, determine one's ultimate worth.

translation: Their reward with their Lord is Gardens of Eternity beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. That is for whoever fears his Lord.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the believers who do righteous deeds receive a reward that is not merely material but supremely spiritual: the lasting Gardens are a blessing, yet the greatest honor is the mutual pleasure between God and His servants. God's pleasure with them is the fruit of their faith and obedience, and their pleasure with Him means they are fully content with His decree in this life and with His generous reward in the next. The closing phrase makes clear that this high station is not gained by lineage or outward claims, but by khashyah, a reverent awe of God that is aware of His greatness and presence. This fear restrains a person from sin and moves him toward good deeds, so it is the root of the whole path that leads to the eternal reward.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the earth is shaken with its [final, violent] quaking,
interpretation: This verse opens Surat az-Zalzalah by describing the first sign of the Day of Resurrection: the earth will be convulsed with a quake proper to its magnitude, one that befits the power of its Creator and is unlike any tremor known in this world. The phrase 'its quaking' signals a shaking of ultimate severity, which shatters the apparent stability and permanence of the ground people trust and live upon. The verse is meant to jolt the listener out of heedlessness, reminding them that everything in this world is fragile and temporary and that the Hereafter, where all deeds will be weighed, is certain. It prepares the heart for the verses that follow, in which the earth will bear witness to what was done upon it, and so calls the believer to self-accountability and to doing good before that day arrives.

translation: And the earth brings out its burdens.
interpretation: This verse (Surat az-Zalzalah, 99:2) describes the Day of Judgment, when the earth is violently shaken and casts out everything it holds within it. The 'burdens' (athqal) are understood as the dead who will be raised from their graves, and also the buried treasures and hidden things within the earth. The earth, which has silently carried humanity's remains and secrets, is made to release them all, so that nothing remains concealed. This signals the total exposure of all that was hidden and the beginning of the reckoning, when every person will face the deeds they did.

translation: And man says, "What is the matter with it?"
interpretation: This verse (Surah Az-Zalzalah 99:3) describes the shock of the Day of Judgment, when the earth is violently shaken and gives up its burdens. Human beings, startled and bewildered by something they have never witnessed, cry out in astonishment, asking what has happened to the earth that was once stable beneath their feet. The question reveals the sudden collapse of worldly certainty and heedlessness: what people took for granted as fixed and lifeless is now shaking, and they are forced to confront the reality of the Hereafter they had denied or neglected. It serves as a reminder to prepare for that day before the question is asked in fear rather than reflection.

translation: On that Day, the earth will report all its news.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat az-Zalzalah, means that on the Day of Judgment, after the earth is shaken violently and casts out its burdens, it will bear witness and tell everything that was done upon it. Every deed, good or evil, that people performed on its surface will be declared by the earth itself, as though it speaks by God's command. The meaning is that nothing a person does is hidden or forgotten, since even the ground beneath their feet is a witness that testifies for or against them. It is a reminder to live with awareness of accountability and to do good deeds, even those done in private, knowing that they are recorded and will be revealed before God.

translation: Because your Lord has inspired it (to the earth).
interpretation: This verse (Surah Az-Zalzalah 99:5) explains why the earth will speak on the Day of Judgment and report all that was done upon it. Its testimony is not by its own will but by divine command: God has instructed it, and it obeys. The meaning is that all creation, even what seems lifeless, is subject to God's will and serves as a witness to human deeds, so no action, however hidden or small, can escape accountability.

translation: On that Day, people will come forth in separate groups to be shown their deeds.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Zalzalah, 99:6) means that on the Day of Resurrection, after the earth is shaken and gives up its burdens, people will emerge from their graves and from the place of reckoning scattered and divided, not as one mass: the believers separated from the disbelievers, and the righteous from the wicked, each heading toward their own destiny. They are brought forth so that each person is shown the record of what they did in life, with nothing hidden or lost. The point is individual accountability: every person will face their own deeds, which leads into the following verses about seeing even an atom's weight of good or evil. It is a call to self-examination now, to act with awareness that no deed, however small, will be overlooked.

translation: So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it.
interpretation: This verse (Surat az-Zalzalah, 99:7) teaches that on the Day of Judgment no good deed will be lost or overlooked, however small it may seem. Every act of kindness, sincerity, or righteousness, even one as tiny as the weight of a speck of dust, is recorded and will be shown to the person, who will find its reward with God. The verse encourages believers never to belittle any good deed and to value even the smallest acts of goodness, since divine justice is exact and nothing is wasted.

translation: And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.
interpretation: This verse affirms perfect divine justice on the Day of Judgment: no wrongdoing, however small or hidden, is overlooked or lost. Every person will be confronted with the full record of their deeds and will see its consequences. It calls the believer to constant self-awareness and moral vigilance, avoiding even seemingly trivial sins, since small wrongs accumulate and nothing escapes God's knowledge, while also leaving room for repentance and God's mercy to erase sins before that reckoning.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the racing steeds that run panting,
interpretation: God opens the chapter by swearing an oath by war horses charging at full speed, so out of breath that they pant, in order to draw attention to the truth that follows. The oath points to the horses' loyalty, effort and endurance in serving their riders, a quality the chapter then contrasts with the human being's ingratitude toward his Lord, who gave him every blessing. The animal's faithful striving is held up as a mirror to human failure: if a horse gives everything for its master, the human being, who has been given so much more, should not be ungrateful to the One who sustains him.

translation: By the strikers of sparks, striking fire.
interpretation: In this oath, God swears by the war horses that, when galloping hard over rocky ground, strike sparks of fire from the stones with their hooves. It points to the force, speed and determination of the horses in the charge, and it prepares for the verses that follow, which describe the raid at dawn and the dust it raises. The oath draws attention to the power of these animals as a blessing from God, and it leads to the reminder that the human being is ungrateful to his Lord and is a witness to his own ingratitude.

translation: And those that raid at dawn,
interpretation: This verse is part of an oath in Surah Al-Adiyat, continuing the description of the charging war horses. After swearing by the galloping, panting horses that strike sparks with their hooves, God swears by those that launch raids at the break of dawn, the time when enemies are unprepared and attacks were customarily carried out. The oath draws attention to the intensity, speed and force of the horses and their riders, and sets the stage for the surah's real point: that despite all the energy and daring humans show in worldly pursuits, man is ungrateful to his Lord and intensely attached to wealth, so he should be mindful of the Day when what is in the graves is scattered and what is in hearts is revealed.

translation: And raise thereby a cloud of dust,
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-'Adiyat, 100:4) continues the oath by the charging horses of battle. After they race and strike sparks of fire, they stir up dust in the early morning, which shows the intensity and speed of their charge. The vivid image is meant to draw attention to the power and urgency of the scene, preparing the listener for the point of the oath: that the human being is ungrateful to his Lord, and that he will be held accountable when what is in the graves is overturned and what is in the hearts is brought out. Just as the horses give everything in their charge, dust rising behind them, the verse implies that humans, who are given far greater blessings, should be loyal and grateful to their Lord rather than ungrateful.

translation: And penetrate thereby into the midst of a throng.
interpretation: This verse (Surat al-'Adiyat, 100:5) describes the charging war-horses that, after raising dust with their galloping, plunge into the very center of the enemy gathering. Beyond the literal image, it is an oath by these steeds that underscores the intensity and force of their charge. The oath prepares the listener for the point of the surah: human beings are ungrateful to their Lord and attached to wealth. Just as the horses rush fearlessly and relentlessly into the heart of the crowd, driven by loyalty to their master, a person should be even more loyal and thankful to the Lord who provided for him, and not be heedless of the Day when what is in the graves is scattered and what is in the hearts is exposed.

translation: Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Al-'Adiyat, 100:6) says that the human being, by his unrefined nature, tends to deny the favors of his Lord. The word 'kanud' describes one who forgets or ignores countless blessings and remembers only hardship and loss. A person receives life, health, provision, and security from God, yet often responds with complaint, heedlessness, or misuse of these gifts instead of gratitude and obedience. The verse is a reproach that calls people to self-examination, to recognize God's favors, and to overcome this tendency through thankfulness, faith, and righteous action, as the surah goes on to remind them of accountability when graves are overturned and what is in hearts is made known.

translation: And indeed, he is a witness to that [ingratitude] himself.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Adiyat, refers to the human being who is ungrateful to his Lord (as stated in the preceding verse: 'Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord'). The meaning is that the person's own conscience and conduct testify against him: he knows deep down, and his actions and behavior make evident, that he is ungrateful for God's blessings. He cannot deny or excuse his ingratitude, because he is a self-witness to it, and so it stands as a proof against him on the Day of Judgment. An alternative reading takes the 'he' to refer to God as witness, but the most fitting understanding is that man himself bears witness to his own denial of his Lord's favors, which should prompt him to repent and be thankful.

translation: And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth.
interpretation: The verse closes the Surah's rebuke of ungrateful humankind, who deny their Lord's favors. It explains the root of that ingratitude: an overpowering attachment to worldly goods, here called 'khayr' (wealth). This attachment makes a person stingy and heedless of duty, and it distracts him from gratitude and from remembering the Hereafter. The verse does not condemn wealth in itself. It warns against letting love of it dominate the heart so that it displaces obedience to God and the fulfillment of what is owed to Him and to others.

translation: Does he not know that when what is in the graves is overturned and scattered out,
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human being who is ungrateful and attached to worldly wealth, reminding him that his heedlessness is rooted in forgetting the Resurrection. The 'overturning' of the graves signifies the dead being raised and brought out of the earth in a sudden upheaval. If a person truly grasped that he will be raised and called to account, he would restrain his greed and ingratitude toward his Lord and live with awareness that every deed will be examined on the Day when what lies hidden is brought to light.

translation: And that which is within the breasts is brought out and made known.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-'Adiyat (100:10), speaks of the Day of Resurrection, when nothing remains hidden. The intentions, beliefs, secrets, and motives that people concealed in their hearts in this world will be extracted, laid bare, and separated out, just as the grain is separated from the husk. The meaning is that on that Day judgment will rest not only on outward deeds but on the inner reality behind them, such as sincerity, hypocrisy, gratitude, or ingratitude. This should lead a believer to purify their heart and intentions now, knowing that God, who is fully aware of what lies within, will hold everyone to account with perfect justice.

translation: Indeed, their Lord, on that Day, will be fully Aware of them.
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surah Al-Adiyat, teaches that on the Day of Resurrection nothing about human beings will be hidden from God. He knows all their deeds, intentions, and what their hearts concealed, so reckoning will be perfectly just and exact. It follows the surah's rebuke of the ungrateful human being, who is stingy toward his Lord and fiercely attached to wealth, and it works as a warning: whoever knows that God is fully aware of his inner state should be grateful, restrain his greed, and prepare for the Day when what is in the graves is scattered and what is in the breasts is brought out.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Striking Calamity.
interpretation: Al-Qari'ah is a name for the Day of Resurrection, called 'the Striking' because it strikes hearts with terror and shatters the order of the world with its overwhelming force. By opening the chapter with this single, abrupt word, the Qur'an jolts the listener into awareness, making them feel the shock of that Day before any description is given. It signals that the Hour is a real, imminent event of immense gravity, and that every person should awaken from heedlessness and prepare for the reckoning where deeds will be weighed.

translation: What is the Striking Calamity?
interpretation: This opening verse of Surat al-Qari'a uses a rhetorical question to awaken awe and heighten anticipation. 'Al-Qari'a' is the Day of Judgment, so named because it strikes hearts with terror and shatters the order of the world with its overwhelming events. By asking 'What is it?' without immediately answering, God signals that its magnitude exceeds human comprehension, urging the listener to reflect on its seriousness and to prepare for it through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qari'ah, 101:3) uses rhetorical questioning to heighten the sense of awe and dread surrounding the Day of Resurrection. By posing the question 'what will make you know?', the Qur'an signals that the true nature of the Striking Calamity lies beyond ordinary human comprehension or imagination. The repetition of the term, first in verse 1 and then again here, magnifies its gravity and prepares the listener's heart to be shaken before the description that follows. The meaning is that the Hour is so overwhelming that no earthly analogy can fully convey it, so a person should reflect seriously and prepare for it through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: It is a Day when people will be like scattered moths.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 101:4) describes the Day of Resurrection, the opening scene of 'Al-Qari'ah' (The Striking Calamity). Moths fly in all directions without order or purpose and are drawn blindly toward a flame. In the same way, on that Day people will rise from their graves bewildered and terrified, dazed by the magnitude of the event, and rush in confusion toward the summons of the caller to the reckoning. The image strips away all worldly rank, strength, and self-direction, showing humans as helpless and disoriented before God's command, and it urges the listener to prepare now for the Day when no one will be able to find their own way except by the guidance they followed in this life.

translation: And the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Qari'ah, describes the terrifying upheaval of the Day of Resurrection. Mountains, which people regard as the most solid and immovable features of the earth, will lose their firmness and be shattered and scattered until they resemble carded, colored wool that is loose and drifts in the wind. If the mightiest and most stable parts of creation are reduced to such weightlessness, then human beings, in their frailty, should recognize the immense power of God and the gravity of that Day, and should prepare for it with faith and righteous deeds rather than rely on worldly strength or status.

translation: As for the one whose scales are heavy [with good deeds],
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 101:6, Surat al-Qari'a) teaches that on the Day of Judgment a person's standing is determined by the moral weight of their deeds. Heaviness of the scales signifies the abundance and sincerity of righteous actions, those done with faith and for God's sake, so that even small acts carry great weight when they are sincere. Such a person is assured of a pleasant, contented life in the Hereafter, as the following verses say. It is a call to measure life by lasting good works rather than by worldly status, wealth, or appearances, and to fill one's record with deeds that will count for something in the divine balance.

translation: So he will be in a life of pleasure, well-pleasing.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the person who receives his record of deeds in his right hand (Surat al-Haqqah, 69:19-21). His reward is a life in Paradise so complete in its contentment that the life itself is described as 'pleased': nothing in it is lacking, and no sorrow, fear, or decline can touch it. The verse teaches that true fulfillment is granted by God to those who prepared for the Day of Reckoning with faith and righteous deeds, and that the final state of the believer is an enduring satisfaction that leaves no desire unmet.

translation: But as for him whose scales are light,
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qari'ah 101:8) describes the person whose good deeds weigh little on the Day of Judgment, either because he has few righteous deeds or because his faith and sincerity were lacking, so that falsehood and sin outweighed whatever good he did. On that Day, worth is measured by the truth and sincerity of one's deeds, not by outward appearance, status, or wealth in this world. The verse warns that a life spent in heedlessness and disbelief leaves a person empty-handed before God, and it leads into the next verses, which reveal that such a person's destination is the abyss, a consequence of neglecting to prepare for the Hereafter.

translation: Then his refuge (literally, his mother) will be the Abyss.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Qari'ah (101:9), describes the fate of the one whose good deeds weigh lightly on the Scale on the Day of Judgment. Calling the Abyss (Hawiyah) his 'mother' means it will be his final shelter and place of return, just as a mother is the one a child turns to and clings to for refuge. The irony is deliberate: instead of a comforting home, the one who is found wanting will be gathered into a deep, falling pit of Hellfire, from which there is no escape. It conveys that his ruin is total and that this destination will envelop him as a mother embraces her child.

translation: And what will make you know what it is?
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qari'ah 101:10) closes the description of the one whose scales are light and whose home is the Abyss (Hawiyah). It is a rhetorical question that raises the listener's awareness of the Abyss's terrifying nature, a reality beyond ordinary human comprehension and imagination. The verse prepares the mind for the stark answer that follows in the next verse, 'A raging Fire,' showing that the punishment is so severe that only God's revelation can convey its true nature. It is meant to stir fear and urge people to live righteously so that their scales will be heavy on the Day of Judgment.

translation: A scorching Fire.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surat al-Qari'a (101:11), describes what Hellfire truly is, after the Qur'an asks, 'And what will make you know what it is?' The answer is that it is a fire of intense, blazing heat, far beyond any fire known in this world. The verse is a warning meant to stir awe and fear in the hearer. Those whose good deeds are light on the Scale will meet this fate, so a person should strive to do righteous deeds and keep away from what leads to it.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Rivalry in worldly increase distracts you.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human tendency to become so absorbed in competing for more wealth, children, status, and followers that the deeper purpose of life is forgotten. This endless striving keeps people heedless of their duty to God and preparation for the Hereafter, and it continues until death arrives and exposes how fleeting these pursuits were. The verse is a call to wake up before it is too late and to measure life by what lasts rather than by what accumulates.

translation: Until you visit the graves.
interpretation: The verse completes the warning of the preceding verse, which says that rivalry in worldly gain and increase distracts people. This distraction does not leave them until death overtakes them and they end up in their graves. It teaches that the pursuit of wealth, status, and numbers can occupy a person for an entire lifetime and make them neglect the purpose of their existence and preparation for the Hereafter. The grave is the point at which the false value of worldly competition is exposed, because everything accumulated is left behind. The verse is therefore a reminder to awaken before death and to turn to what lasts: faith, righteous deeds, and accountability before God.

translation: No! You will soon come to know.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Takathur (102:3), is a stern rebuke to those who are distracted by the pursuit of worldly gain and rivalry in wealth, children, and status. The word 'kalla' (No!) rejects their false assumption that accumulating worldly things is the true goal of life. The verse warns that the reality they now ignore will become plain to them. They will understand the consequences of their heedlessness when death arrives, in the grave, and ultimately on the Day of Judgment, when what they were absorbed in proves worthless and they are made to answer for how they spent their lives.

translation: Then again, no! You will soon come to know.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takathur, 102:4) repeats the warning of the preceding verse for emphasis. After rebuking people for being preoccupied with the accumulation of wealth, children and status until they reach their graves, God declares that this distraction is false and misguided, and that they will come to know the truth of their situation. The repetition intensifies the admonition: the first warning points to the realization at death and in the barzakh, while the second points to the greater realization on the Day of Resurrection and Judgment, when the worldly rivalry will be exposed as worthless and each person will face the consequences of their heedlessness.

translation: No! If you only knew with certain knowledge.
interpretation: This verse (Surah At-Takathur, 102:5) follows the rebuke of those distracted by the rivalry of accumulating wealth, children, and status until they reach the grave.
